# AI Agent Monitoring Checklist: What to Watch in Production

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agent-monitoring-checklist/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Monitoring an AI agent in production means watching what it did, what it cost, whether the output was any good and whether anything suspicious happened. This checklist sets out 16 items across six areas, maps each to OpenTelemetry signals where they exist, and cites the NCSC and OWASP guidance on logging and agent risks.

An AI agent monitoring checklist covers what to watch once an agent is live: every run's trace and tool calls, cost and token spend, latency, error and loop rates, sampled quality scores, human approvals and overrides, and security signals such as failed tool calls. The 16 checks below fit on one page. Most can be built from OpenTelemetry's GenAI signals, which were still at Development status on 16 November 2026.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This checklist assumes you already trace your agents. If not, start with [what LLM observability is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/), and for the tools that collect these signals see our ranking of the [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/).

## What should you monitor on an AI agent in production?

Monitor six areas: the trace of each run, cost, performance, output quality, human oversight and security. Uptime alone is not enough, because an agent can return quickly with a success code and still do the wrong thing.

Agents add three risks that a chatbot does not have. They take actions through tools, so a wrong step changes a system of record. They loop, so one confused run can make dozens of model calls. They act under an identity, so a permission mistake has reach. The checklist is built around those three.

## The AI agent monitoring checklist

The table is the full checklist. Each item names the signal to use, with the OpenTelemetry name where the GenAI conventions define one, as read in the repository on 16 November 2026.

| # | Area | What to watch | Signal | Alert or review when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Trace | Every run recorded as one trace with agent, model and tool steps | `invoke\_agent`, inference and `execute\_tool` spans | Any run lacks a trace, or tool steps are missing |
| 2 | Trace | Prompt and output content captured under a written policy | Content capture setting, default `NO\_CONTENT` | Content is captured without a retention rule |
| 3 | Trace | Model and prompt version on every run | `gen\_ai.request.model`, `gen\_ai.response.model`, your prompt version tag | A version changes without a release record |
| 4 | Cost | Tokens and cost per run, per agent and per team | `gen\_ai.client.inference.usage.\*` counters | Cost per completed task rises beyond an agreed band |
| 5 | Cost | Hard limits on spend, rate and run length | Quotas, rate limits, timeouts | A limit is hit, or no limit exists |
| 6 | Performance | End-to-end duration per run | `gen\_ai.invoke\_agent.duration` | The slowest runs grow week on week |
| 7 | Performance | Model and tool calls per run | `gen\_ai.invoke\_agent.inference\_calls`, `.tool\_calls` | A run exceeds its expected call count, a sign of looping |
| 8 | Performance | Errors by type, including provider errors and timeouts | `error.type` on spans | Error rate on any tool or model rises |
| 9 | Quality | Automated scores on a sample of runs | `gen\_ai.evaluation.result` events | A score falls below its release baseline |
| 10 | Quality | Human review of a sample, especially low-scored runs | Annotation queue outcomes | Reviewers and automated scores disagree |
| 11 | Quality | Regression set rerun on every change | Offline eval results | Regression pass rate drops below the near-100% target |
| 12 | Oversight | Approvals, edits and rejections at each approval gate | Approval events joined to the trace | Approval rate rises while edit rate falls, a sign of fatigue |
| 13 | Oversight | Escalations and hand-offs to people | Agent spans and your own events | Escalation rate moves sharply in either direction |
| 14 | Security | Failed and denied tool calls | `execute\_tool` spans with errors | Repeated failures or denials from one session |
| 15 | Security | Actions outside the agent's expected tools or permissions | Tool names and identity on spans | Any tool call not on the agent's allow list |
| 16 | Record | Trace and decision retention matched to your review cycle | Platform retention setting | Retention is shorter than your audit or review period |

## How do you monitor what an AI agent costs?

Track tokens per run and cost per completed task, and set hard limits so a single run cannot spend without bound. Average cost per call hides the problem; agent cost lives in the long tail of runs that loop.

OWASP's entry on Unbounded Consumption, from its 2025 Top 10 for LLM Applications, recommends rate limiting and user quotas, dynamic management of resource allocation, timeouts and throttling for heavy operations, and continuous monitoring of resource use to "detect and respond to unusual patterns". The OpenTelemetry token counters are described in the repository as a "proxy for cost approximation", separated into input, output, cache and reasoning tokens.

Check how your platform bills, too. Datadog's product page, read on 16 November 2026, defines its billing unit as "a single call to an LLM provider" and does not bill tool, workflow, agent, embedding or retrieval spans. Other vendors bill every span or every gigabyte. Our [LLM observability pricing comparison](https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-pricing-compared/) sets out the differences.

## How do you monitor AI agent quality in production?

Score a sample of live runs automatically, send a share to people, and rerun a regression set on every change. Production has no reference answers, so online scoring looks for patterns rather than correctness against a key.

LangChain's LangSmith documentation, read in November 2026, describes online evaluation as targeting "runs and threads from tracing" without reference outputs, focused on quality, safety and anomalies. Langfuse's documentation describes the same practice as scoring "live incoming traces". Anthropic's guidance of 9 January 2026 says regression evals "should have a nearly 100% pass rate", which makes them a clear release gate.

Model graders need watching themselves. Our explainer on [LLM-as-a-judge](https://lowob.com/research/llm-as-a-judge-explained/) covers their biases; the short rule is to sample their scores against human review every month.

> The run that costs most is rarely the one that failed loudly. It is the one that looped quietly for forty steps.

## What security signals should you monitor on AI agents?

Watch failed tool calls, denied permissions and actions outside an agent's expected scope. These are where an injected instruction shows up before it does damage.

The UK NCSC's December 2025 guidance on prompt injection says teams should log "enough information to identify suspicious activity", and that "detecting and responding to failed tool calls or API calls could identify earlier stages of an attack". The trace that helps an engineer debug is the same one a security team needs.

OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications, dated 9 December 2025, names the risks to map alerts against. As listed in TechRepublic's report of 19 December 2025, they include ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse and Exploitation, ASI03 Identity and Privilege Abuse, ASI06 Memory and Context Poisoning and ASI08 Cascading Failures. Items 14 and 15 on the checklist address the second and third directly; item 7 is an early signal for the eighth. Our explainer on [agent identity](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/) covers the permission side.

## How long should you keep AI agent traces?

Keep them at least as long as your review or audit cycle, which is usually far longer than a platform's default. Retention is set by contract and plan, so check it before an incident rather than after.

The spread is wide at list price. LangChain's pricing page, read on 16 November 2026, keeps base traces for 14 days and extended traces for 180 days. Datadog's default for traces and spans is 15 days, with add-ons to 30, 60 or 90. Langfuse's pricing page gives 30 days on its free Hobby plan, 90 days on Core and 3 years on Pro and Enterprise. A regulated firm may also need the [AI audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) to sit outside the observability tool entirely.

## How do you monitor human approval of agent actions?

Join every approval, edit and rejection to the trace of the run it concerns, and watch the edit rate alongside the approval rate. A rising approval rate can mean the agent improved or that reviewers stopped reading.

Our analysis of why [approval rate measures fatigue too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/) sets out the pattern. In **lowob**'s model, the approval sits at an [approval gate](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/), and the record of who approved what, and why, belongs to the business, not to the observability vendor.

## lowob takeaways

- **Trace every run, including tools.** Missing tool steps hide the errors that matter most.
- **Cap cost per run.** Quotas, rate limits and timeouts stop loops before the invoice does.
- **Score a sample and read it.** Automated scores need regular human checks.
- **Alert on failed tool calls.** The NCSC treats them as an early sign of attack.
- **Set retention to the review cycle.** Platform defaults of 14 or 15 days rarely cover it.

## Common questions

### What should you monitor for AI agents in production?

Monitor the trace of every run with its model and tool steps, tokens and cost per run, duration and number of calls, errors by type, sampled quality scores, human approvals and edits, failed or denied tool calls, and trace retention. Set alerts on cost per task, call counts that suggest looping, and actions outside the agent's permitted tools.

### How do you detect an AI agent stuck in a loop?

Track the number of model and tool calls per run and alert when a run exceeds its expected range. OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions define per-run metrics for inference calls and tool calls, as of November 2026. Pair the alert with a hard timeout or step limit, which OWASP recommends for resource-intensive operations.

### How long should AI agent traces be kept?

At least as long as your internal review or regulatory audit cycle. List-price defaults in November 2026 ranged from 14 days for LangSmith base traces and 15 days on Datadog to 3 years on Langfuse Pro. Where traces hold personal data, set retention and access rules before capturing content.

### What security risks should AI agent monitoring cover?

Prompt injection, tool misuse, privilege abuse, memory and context poisoning, and cascading failures, all named in OWASP's December 2025 Top 10 for Agentic Applications. The UK NCSC recommends logging enough to identify suspicious activity and watching failed tool or API calls, which can reveal the early stages of an attack.

# AI Agent Statistics 2026: Adoption, Spend, Reliability and Failure Rates

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agent-statistics-2026/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agents are now common in large companies but rarely run alone. Surveys put agents in production at most large US firms, while McKinsey finds about two in ten respondents scaling agents enterprise-wide. Independent measurements show long tasks completed at 50% success and much shorter ones at 80%, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. Every figure here carries its source, sample and date.

In 2026, AI agents are common in large companies but rarely run alone: 71% of US enterprise leaders in Zapier's September 2026 survey report agents in production, while McKinsey finds only about two in ten respondents scaling agents enterprise-wide. Spending forecasts run into hundreds of billions of dollars, reliability falls sharply on longer tasks, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This page collects the AI agent statistics most often quoted in 2026 and gives each one its source, sample and date. It supports our hub piece, [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/), which sets out the definition used here: a model working in a loop toward a goal, choosing its next step and acting through tools within set limits.

Two warnings before the numbers. First, "agent" and "in production" mean different things in each survey, so adoption figures do not add up across sources. Second, many of the most quoted figures come from vendors and investors with a stake in agent adoption. We label each one.

## What are the headline AI agent statistics for 2026?

The table below is the reference set. Every figure is quoted as published, with the date of publication or fieldwork.

| Statistic | Figure | Source | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Enterprise leaders reporting AI agents in production | 71%, up from 40% in 2025 | Zapier survey of 513 US managers and above at firms with 1,000+ employees (vendor) | Fielded 16 to 21 September 2026 |
| Organisations using or testing AI agents | 88%, up from 72% in 2025 | Zapier (vendor) | September 2026 |
| Leaders saying agents complete more than 60% of assigned tasks without human intervention | 30% | Zapier (vendor) | September 2026 |
| Leaders saying their most mature agent has paid for itself, or expect it to within 12 months | 46% | Zapier (vendor) | September 2026 |

| Claude Opus 4.5, 50% time horizon | About 320 minutes; 95% interval 170 to 729 minutes | METR, Time Horizon 1.1 | 29 January 2026 |
| Time horizon doubling time, models since 2023 | 130.8 days | METR | 29 January 2026 |
| 80% time horizon compared with 50% | Roughly five times shorter | METR, Kwa et al., arXiv 2503.14499 | Version 4, 10 July 2026 |

## How many companies use AI agents in 2026?

Most large US companies say they run at least one agent, but few run agents at scale. Zapier's 71% and KPMG's 62% describe presence; McKinsey's "about two in ten" enterprise-wide figure describes depth.

The gap is size as much as definition. McKinsey found 40% of large organisations scaling agents in at least one function against 22% of smaller ones, and the smaller group did not move year on year. Gartner's 2025 survey of IT application leaders shows how cautious most deployments are: 75% had some form of agent in pilot or production, but only 15% were even considering fully autonomous agents.

Among small firms, the C\_TEC survey found 24% of AI users using agentic AI tools. The Stanford AI Index 2026, drawing on McKinsey's 2025 data, found scaled agent use in single digits for nearly all business functions.

## How much are companies spending on AI agents?

Gartner's forecast is the only figure here that is specific to agent software: $206.5 billion in 2026, up from $86.4 billion in 2025. Menlo Ventures does not give a separate agent figure. Its $176.8 billion covers all enterprise spending on using AI, split into $99.5 billion of infrastructure and $77.3 billion of applications.

Menlo's own numbers need care. Its December 2025 report put 2025 enterprise generative AI spend at $37 billion; its November 2026 report gives the prior year's deployment spend as $33 billion, after reclassifying some vendors, and does not reconcile the two. Quote whichever you use with its date and definition, and do not compare across the two reports as if they measured the same thing.

## How reliable are AI agents in 2026?

Reliability is the weakest number in the set. METR's 50% time horizon for Claude Opus 4.5 was about 320 minutes in January 2026, but the 95% interval runs from 170 to 729 minutes, and METR's earlier study found 80% horizons roughly five times shorter. A task an agent finishes half the time is a draft, not a delegated job.

Business-task benchmarks are lower still. Salesforce AI Research's CRMArena-Pro found leading agents at about 58% success on single-turn tasks and about 35% when the task ran over several turns. The researchers also reported near-zero inherent awareness of confidentiality. Our explainer [What Is an AI Time Horizon?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-time-horizon/) covers the method.

## What share of AI agent projects fail?

No source measures agent project failure directly in 2026. The closest figures are a forecast and a survey of AI projects in general. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs and unclear business value. S&P Global's 451 Research found 42% of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production, with the average organisation scrapping 46% of proofs of concept.

Value evidence is thin. McKinsey found 37% of respondents attributing any EBIT impact to AI in 2026, essentially unchanged from the year before. Our analysis in [Why AI Agent Projects Fail](https://lowob.com/research/why-ai-agent-projects-fail/) maps these figures to causes.

## How should you read AI agent statistics?

Treat each figure as an answer to the question its survey asked, not as a market fact.

| Check | What to look for | Example from this page |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who ran it | Vendor, investor, consultancy, analyst, government or academic | Zapier sells automation; Menlo invests in AI companies |
| Who answered | Size, country and role of respondents | Zapier: US firms with 1,000+ staff; C\_TEC: under 250 staff |
| What "agent" meant | Any AI tool, an assistant with actions, or a goal-seeking loop | KPMG counts "building, deploying or developing" |
| Measured or expected | Observed results or stated expectations | Gartner's 40% cancellation figure is a forecast |
| When | Fieldwork dates, not only publication dates | S&P Global's 42% was fielded in late 2024 |

Our [AI Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/) rates none of its sixty commercial tasks for an agent acting alone, and that is consistent with every reliability figure above.

## lowob takeaways

- **Presence is high, depth is low.** Most large US firms report an agent somewhere; about two in ten scale agents enterprise-wide.
- **Spend figures measure different things.** Gartner forecasts agent software; Menlo estimates all enterprise AI use, and its two reports give different 2025 figures.
- **Plan around the reliable number.** The 80% time horizons are roughly a fifth of the 50% figure, and multi-turn business tasks score lower still.
- **Failure data is mostly forecast.** Gartner's cancellation figure and S&P Global's abandonment rate are the strongest signals, and neither is agent-specific measurement.

## Common questions

### How many companies use AI agents in 2026?

It depends on the survey. Zapier's September 2026 survey of US firms with 1,000 or more employees found 71% with agents in production. KPMG found 62% of US leaders at $1 billion-plus firms building, deploying or developing agents. McKinsey found about two in ten respondents scaling agents across the enterprise, which is the better measure of real depth.

### How much will companies spend on AI agents in 2026?

Gartner forecast AI agent software spending of $206.5 billion in 2026 and $376.3 billion in 2027, up from $86.4 billion in 2025, in a release dated 5 May 2026. Menlo Ventures estimated $176.8 billion of enterprise spending on using AI as of September 2026, but that covers all AI use, not agents alone.

### How reliable are AI agents in 2026?

METR measured Claude Opus 4.5 at about 320 minutes of expert software work at 50% success in January 2026, and its earlier study found 80% horizons roughly five times shorter. On Salesforce AI Research's CRMArena-Pro business benchmark, leading agents reached about 58% on single-turn tasks and about 35% on multi-turn tasks.

### What percentage of AI agent projects fail?

Gartner forecast in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs and unclear business value. S&P Global's 451 Research found 42% of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production. Neither is a measured failure rate for agents specifically, so quote them as a forecast and a general AI figure.

### Are AI agent statistics from vendors reliable?

Use them with labels. Vendor and investor surveys often sample firms already interested in the product and define "agent" broadly. Check who ran the survey, who answered, how "agent" was defined, whether results were measured or expected, and when fieldwork happened. Prefer analyst, government and academic figures when they answer the same question.

# AI Agents for Small Business: What Works Now and What to Skip

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-for-small-business/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Small businesses are adopting AI quickly, and about a quarter of small-business AI users already use agentic tools. The tasks that work are frequent, internal and easy to check: meeting preparation, call summaries, record clean-up and first drafts. Anything that sends to customers, sets prices or changes access should stay with a person. Surveyed small businesses that pay for AI report a median of $250 a month.

For a small business in 2026, AI agents work best as drafting and admin helpers with a person approving the output; 24% of small-business AI users already use agentic tools, according to a US Chamber of Commerce survey. Use them for meeting preparation, call summaries, record clean-up and first drafts. Skip agents that send to customers, set prices or change who can access what.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This guide is for owners of businesses with roughly 2 to 250 staff deciding whether an AI agent is worth trying. It uses the definition in our hub piece, [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/): a model working in a loop toward a goal, choosing its next step and acting through tools within limits. For a small business the limits matter more than the model, because there is rarely a security team to catch a mistake.

## Are small businesses using AI agents yet?

Some are, mostly as assistants rather than as autonomous workers. The US Chamber of Commerce's 2026 survey of 3,732 small businesses found 24% of AI users using agentic AI tools, against 41% using generative AI chatbots.

Other surveys show the same pattern of broad use and shallow automation. In the Ipsos survey for the Chamber Foundation, half of small-business workers used AI at work, 64% said their primary use was personal productivity such as drafting and summarising, and 6% used it to automate workflows with minimal human involvement. Goldman Sachs's survey of 1,256 participants in its 10,000 Small Businesses programme, fielded in January and February 2026, found 76% using AI but 14% with AI fully embedded in core operations.

Government data is lower. The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found under 20% of firms with four or fewer employees using AI in the period to 3 May 2026. The gap reflects who was sampled: programme participants and survey panels on one side, a government sample of all employers on the other. Ramp's October 2026 transaction data, from businesses on its own platform, showed 51.2% of micro-SMB customers and 63.2% of SMB customers paying for AI.

## What can AI agents do for a small business now?

The work that succeeds is frequent, internal and easy to check. The table draws on the **lowob** Agent Task Directory, rated in November 2026, which scores each task for reliability today and the autonomy level it warrants.

| Task | Directory rating | Verdict for a small business |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research a client or prospect before a meeting | High reliability; level 1, draft | Works now |
| Summarise a sales call and extract next steps | High; level 3, act and report | Works now, with the owner reviewing within 48 hours |
| Draft a follow-up email after a meeting | High; level 1, draft | Works now; nothing sends without you |
| Monitor competitors and market news | High; level 3, act and report | Works now, from named sources |
| De-duplicate and clean customer records | High; level 3, act and report | Works now, with reversible changes and a nightly report |
| Turn an interview or voice note into draft posts | High; level 1, draft | Works now |
| Answer routine customer questions | Medium; level 2, act with approval | Only with a person approving |
| Qualify an inbound lead | Medium; level 2, act with approval | Only with a person approving |
| Draft quotes from a price book | Medium; level 1, draft | Only if the price book is current |
| Reply to community or social questions | Medium; level 1, draft | Draft only |
| Send outbound sequences autonomously | Low; level 2 at most | Skip |
| Price a proposal or approve a discount | Low; level 1 and level 0 | Skip |
| Move marketing budget between channels | Low; level 1, draft | Skip |
| Grant or change system access | Low; level 0, answer only | Never delegate |

Our explainer [What AI Agents Can Do: A Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/) lists all sixty tasks with their risks and controls.

## What should a small business skip?

Skip anything that sends to customers unsupervised, commits money or changes access. These are the tasks rated low reliability, and a small business has the least margin to absorb a mistake.

Two security risks drive the advice. An agent that reads inbound email or web forms can be steered by instructions hidden in that content, and OWASP's 2025 guidance on prompt injection states that it is unclear whether foolproof prevention exists. An agent with too many tools or permissions turns a small error into real damage; OWASP calls this excessive agency and recommends the fewest tools and permissions needed, plus a human approval step before high-impact actions. Our piece [Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) explains how to set that gate.

Owners already sense the risk. In the Chamber Foundation survey, 47% of small-business workers cited privacy or security concerns as a barrier to AI use.

## How much do AI agents cost a small business?

Less than most owners expect, if they stay with tools they already have. The US Chamber's 2026 survey found a median monthly AI spend of $250 among small businesses that pay for AI, with 41% using free tools and about half of paying businesses on enterprise tools with flat fees.

Gartner predicted in August 2025 that 40% of enterprise applications will feature task-specific AI agents by 2026, so agent features often arrive inside software you already pay for. Usage-priced agents can cost more as volume grows. Before buying, ask what one run costs and whether you can cap monthly spend. Our guide [How Much Does an AI Agent Cost?](https://lowob.com/research/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost/) breaks down build, buy and running costs.

## How should a small business start with AI agents?

Pick one dull, frequent task, run it at draft level for a month and keep a short log.

1. **Choose one task from the "works now" rows.** Meeting preparation or call summaries are the usual first choice.
2. **Use a tool you already pay for where possible.** The Chamber survey found 64% of small businesses mostly or entirely use externally developed AI tools.
3. **Write down what it can touch.** Which inbox, which records, which folders, and nothing more.
4. **Keep it at draft.** A named person reviews and sends every output.
5. **Check it weekly.** Note errors, time saved and cost; stop or widen the scope on evidence.

Training is the most common gap. In the Chamber Foundation survey, about one in ten small-business workers said they had been offered formal AI training, and 73% of Goldman Sachs respondents said more access to training and implementation resources would benefit them. See [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/) for how to choose the first task.

## lowob takeaways

- **Use agents as drafters first.** The reliable small-business tasks are internal, frequent and checkable.
- **Keep customers, prices and access with a person.** Those tasks are rated low reliability.
- **Start with tools you already own.** Surveyed paying small businesses report a median of $250 a month on AI.
- **Write down what the agent can touch.** It is the cheapest security control a small firm has.

## Common questions

### Are AI agents worth it for a small business?

For narrow, frequent tasks, often yes. Meeting preparation, call summaries, record clean-up and first drafts are rated high reliability in the **lowob** Agent Task Directory and are easy to check. Customer-facing sending, pricing and access changes are rated low and should stay with a person. Start with one task at draft level and judge it on a month of logged results.

### How many small businesses use AI agents?

The US Chamber of Commerce's 2026 survey of 3,732 small businesses, fielded July to August 2026, found 66% using AI and 24% of those users using agentic AI tools. An Ipsos survey for the Chamber Foundation found 6% of small-business workers using AI to automate workflows with minimal human involvement. Census data for the smallest firms is far lower.

### How much do AI agents cost for a small business?

The US Chamber's 2026 survey found a median monthly AI spend of $250 among small businesses that pay for AI, with 41% using free tools. Usage-priced agents can cost more as volume grows, so ask for the cost of one run and whether monthly spend can be capped before you sign.

### What should a small business not use AI agents for?

Avoid agents that send messages to customers unsupervised, price proposals, approve discounts, move budget or change system access. These are rated low reliability. Agents that read inbound email or forms are also exposed to prompt injection, which OWASP says may have no foolproof prevention, so keep them away from actions that send or pay.

# AI Assistant Pricing Compared (2026): Copilot, ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini for Business

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-assistant-pricing-compared-2026/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Business AI assistant seats list at $20 to $21 per user per month on annual billing at Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, with premium seats at $100, while Google includes Gemini in Workspace plans from $7. The seat price is only part of the cost: monthly billing, usage limits, credits and metered agents sit beside it.

For business, Microsoft 365 Copilot Business lists at $21 per user per month on annual billing, ChatGPT Business and Claude Team at $20, and Google includes Gemini in Workspace Business Standard at $14, as checked on vendors' pages on 16 November 2026. Google's price covers the whole suite; the others sit on top of one. The seat is also no longer the whole bill.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Choosing an assistant is mostly about fit, connectors, controls and logging, which our guide [Which AI assistant, which seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/) covers. **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), explains why seat plans are turning into hybrids. This page is the price list, checked on each vendor's own page on 16 November 2026, in US dollars.

## How much do AI assistants cost for business in 2026?

Standard business seats cost $20 to $21 per user per month on annual billing at Microsoft, OpenAI and Anthropic, and premium seats $100. Google bundles Gemini into Workspace suite prices from $7.

| Plan | Annual billing, per user per month | Monthly billing | Seat rules | Metered beside the seat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot Business (add-on) | $21; $18 first-year promotion | $25.20 | Requires an eligible Microsoft 365 Business plan | Copilot Credits for usage-based features; organisation-built custom agents |
| Microsoft 365 Business Standard with Copilot | $23.50 | $28.20 | Up to 300 users | As above |
| Microsoft 365 Business Premium with Copilot | $32.00 | $38.40 | Up to 300 users | As above |
| ChatGPT Business, standard seat | $20 | $25 | At least 2 seats in total | Workspace credits beyond included rate limits |
| ChatGPT Business, premium seat | $100 | $125 | As above | As above |
| Claude Team, standard seat | $20 | $25 | 2 to 150 seats | Usage limits apply |
| Claude Team, premium seat | $100 | $125 | 2 to 150 seats | "5x more usage than standard seats" |
| Claude Enterprise | $20 per seat, plus usage at API rates | Not offered | 20-seat minimum, billed annually | Usage "scales with model and task" |
| Google Workspace Business Starter | $7 | $8.40 | Up to 300 users | Gemini app; Gemini in Workspace apps listed as "Limited" |
| Google Workspace Business Standard | $14 | $16.80 | Up to 300 users | Gemini in Gmail, Docs, Meet and more included |
| Google Workspace Business Plus | $22 | $26.40 | Up to 300 users | As Standard |

Sources: Microsoft 365 Copilot pricing page; OpenAI Help Center, ChatGPT Business; Anthropic Claude pricing page; Google Workspace Help, Business editions. All checked 16 November 2026.

For larger firms, Microsoft's October 2025 announcement of its Copilot Credit pre-purchase plan listed the Microsoft 365 Copilot user licence at $30 per user per month. That figure is a year old, so confirm it on a current quote.

## Which AI assistant is cheapest for a business?

On list price, Gemini, if the firm already runs Google Workspace Business Standard, because there is no separate AI charge. Among add-on assistants, ChatGPT Business and Claude Team standard seats at $20 annual are $1 a month below Copilot Business at $21, or $2 above it during Microsoft's first-year promotion.

The comparison is not like for like. Copilot and Gemini sit inside the suite where email, files and meetings already live. ChatGPT and Claude are bought on top of a suite. The cheapest seat that nobody uses is the most expensive line in the budget; [seat-based pricing for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/) covers how to size seats to a workflow.

## Is Copilot included in Microsoft 365?

Copilot Chat is; the full Microsoft 365 Copilot is not. Microsoft's pricing page, checked 16 November 2026, says "Copilot Chat is a web-grounded AI assistant included at no additional cost with eligible Microsoft 365 plans". Microsoft 365 Copilot Business is an add-on at $21 per user per month annually, available only to existing customers with an eligible Business plan, or bought in a bundle such as Business Standard with Copilot at $23.50.

## Is Gemini included in Google Workspace?

Yes, in Business and Enterprise plans, since January 2025. Google's announcement on 15 January 2025 said customers no longer needed an add-on, and gave the example of a Business Standard customer who had paid $32 per user per month with the Gemini Business add-on now paying $14. On the Starter plan, Google's comparison table, checked 16 November 2026, lists Gemini in Workspace apps as "Limited", with no Gemini in Docs, Sheets or Slides.

## What costs sit outside the seat price?

Usage beyond the seat's limits, and agents.

Microsoft says usage-based features, including Copilot Cowork and Copilot Autopilot, "use Copilot Credits", and that charges apply only when they are used. OpenAI's help centre says Business workspaces can buy credits that "extend usage beyond the included rate limits". Anthropic's footnote says how fast a user reaches a limit "depends on the model you use, how long your chats are, and how large your files are", and its Enterprise plan bills usage at API rates on top of the seat.

OpenAI said on 2 April 2026 that it was cutting the ChatGPT Business annual price from $25 to $20 per seat and adding pay-as-you-go Codex seats billed on token consumption. A 24 June 2026 update said new pay-as-you-go Codex seats were no longer available on Business plans.

## What does a 20-person team pay per year?

Between $3,360 and $5,040 a year for standard seats on list prices, before any metered usage. The arithmetic below uses annual billing for 20 users and the prices in the table above.

| Option | Annual cost for 20 users | What the price covers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gemini in Google Workspace Business Standard | $3,360 | The whole Workspace suite, Gemini included |
| ChatGPT Business, standard seats | $4,800 | The assistant only |
| Claude Team, standard seats | $4,800 | The assistant only |
| Claude Enterprise, 20-seat minimum | $4,800 plus usage at API rates | The assistant; usage billed separately |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot Business add-on | $5,040; $4,320 in the promotional first year | Copilot only, on top of Microsoft 365 licences |
| ChatGPT Business, 5 premium and 15 standard seats | $9,600 | The assistant, with more usage for 5 heavy users |

Monthly billing raises each seat line by 20% to 25%. Buy annual seats only for people with a defined task, and keep pilots monthly until weekly use is known.

## lowob takeaways

- **Standard seats cluster at $20 to $21.** Premium seats cost five times as much at OpenAI and Anthropic.
- **Suite assistants are priced differently.** Gemini is inside the Workspace price; Copilot is an add-on to Microsoft 365.
- **The seat is not the whole bill.** Credits, limits and API-rate usage sit beside it at every vendor.
- **Promotions end.** Microsoft's $18 price applies to the first year only.

## Common questions

### How much does Microsoft Copilot cost for business?

Microsoft's pricing page, checked on 16 November 2026, lists Microsoft 365 Copilot Business at $21 per user per month on annual billing and $25.20 monthly. A promotional $18 applies to the first year for purchases between 1 July and 31 December 2026. It is an add-on for existing Microsoft 365 Business customers, and some usage-based features consume Copilot Credits.

### How much does ChatGPT Business cost per user?

OpenAI's help centre, checked on 16 November 2026, lists ChatGPT Business standard seats at $20 per user per month billed annually or $25 monthly, and premium seats at $100 annually or $125 monthly. A workspace needs at least two seats. Workspaces can buy credits to extend usage beyond the included rate limits.

### How much does Claude Team cost?

Anthropic's pricing page, checked on 16 November 2026, lists Claude Team standard seats at $20 per seat per month on annual billing or $25 monthly, and premium seats at $100 or $125 with five times the usage of standard seats. Teams can have 2 to 150 seats, and usage limits apply. Claude Enterprise charges $20 per seat plus usage at API rates.

### Is Gemini free with Google Workspace?

Gemini is included in Google Workspace Business and Enterprise plans at no extra charge, a change Google announced on 15 January 2025. Google's help centre, updated 10 November 2026, lists Business Standard at $14 per user per month on an annual plan. The Starter plan, at $7, includes the Gemini app but only limited Gemini features inside Workspace apps.

### Which is cheaper, Copilot or ChatGPT for business?

On list prices checked in November 2026, ChatGPT Business standard seats cost $20 per user per month annually, against $21 for Microsoft 365 Copilot Business. During Microsoft's first-year promotion, Copilot is $18. Copilot also requires a Microsoft 365 Business licence, while ChatGPT does not, so compare total cost for the people who will actually use it.

# AI Audit Trail Checklist: What to Log for Every AI Decision

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI audit trail lets a firm rebuild any AI-assisted decision: what the system was asked, what it saw, what it did, who checked it and what happened. This checklist sets out the system-level and decision-level fields to log, the regulatory text behind each, the retention rules that apply and a test that shows whether the trail works.

For every AI decision, log a run ID, the request, the inputs, the retrieved context with versions, the model and prompt versions, each tool call, the output, the reviewer and their action, the final action, the outcome and synchronised timestamps, in tamper-evident storage. Behind those sit system-level records: inventory entry, owner, permissions and change history.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

An audit trail is only as good as the decision you can rebuild from it. Most firms log enough to debug an AI system and too little to explain a decision to a supervisor. This checklist turns the field specification in our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) into a working list, adds the system-level records behind it, and shows which rule each field answers to. The definition sits in [What is an AI audit trail?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/).

The regulatory references below are summaries of public texts for orientation. This checklist is not legal advice; agree the final specification with your compliance function.

## What should an AI audit trail log for every decision?

Fourteen fields, joined by one run ID. The table is the decision-level record; each row names the text that makes a supervisor ask for it.

| # | Field | What to log | Who expects it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Record ID and parent ID | Unique run ID, linked to the case, account or ticket and to any run it supersedes | Joins every other field; without it nothing reconstructs |
| 2 | Request | The instruction as made, the requester, channel and time received | FINRA: track agent actions and decisions |
| 3 | Inputs | Customer and case data passed in, by reference and version, under privacy rules | FCA good practice names consumer prompts; AI Act Art. 12(2) traceability |
| 4 | Retrieved context | Each document or record retrieved, with ID, version, status and date at retrieval | OCC framework: "retrieved sources" |
| 5 | Model and version | Provider, model name and version, deployment or endpoint | FINRA: "which model version was used and when" |
| 6 | Instructions and configuration | Prompt or instruction set version, settings, guardrails and filters applied | FCA names "applied filters"; OCC change logging |
| 7 | Tool calls | Each tool or API called, with parameters, response, permission used and time | FINRA agent risk on scope and authority; OCC "tool calls" |
| 8 | Output | Text, score or recommendation, with any rationale or confidence given | FINRA: prompt and output logs |
| 9 | Reviewer | Name or role, what they were shown, time opened, time spent | FCA warns review can be "box-ticking"; time spent is the evidence |
| 10 | Reviewer action | Approved, edited (with diff), rejected, escalated or overridden, with reason | OCC: override "authority, reasons, patterns" logged; FCA rationale and escalation |
| 11 | Final action | What was sent, executed or filed, by whom and when | SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) for communications sent |
| 12 | Outcome | Complaint, reversal, default, correction or confirmation, with date, written back | SR 26-2 outcomes analysis compares outputs with "real-world outcomes" |
| 13 | Timestamps | Synchronised time for every event above | DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art. 12: clock synchronisation |
| 14 | Retention and integrity | Retention class, legal hold flag, storage type, access log | SEA Rule 17a-4(f); DORA tamper protection; AI Act retention floor |

Fields 1 to 8 usually come from tracing and observability tools. Fields 9 to 12 live in the firm's own workflow, and that is where most trails break. **lowob**'s rule of thumb: rent the wiring, own the record.

## What should be logged before any AI decision is made?

The system-level record: what the AI system is, who owns it, what it may do and how it has changed. Decision logs are hard to interpret without it.

| Field | What to log | Who expects it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory entry | System ID, use case, business function, provider, deployment status | OCC framework inventory; FCA use-case and agent inventories; DORA Art. 8 |
| Owner and approver | Accountable owner, approval authority and approval date | OCC governance component; FCA senior manager accountability |
| Risk tier | Tier and the factors behind it, such as consequence, reversibility and autonomy | OCC illustrative four-tier method; SR 26-2 materiality |
| Permitted use and limits | What the system may and may not do, data it may touch | OCC "defined purpose and permitted use" |
| Permissions | Tools, credentials and actions the agent holds, and their scope | OCC: agent identities and credentials governed "comparable to privileged users" |
| Autonomy level | Answer, draft, act with approval, act and report, or act alone | FINRA human-in-the-loop consideration; OCC human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop |
| Change history | Model, prompt, data, configuration, provider, tool and permission changes, linked to testing | OCC framework; DORA Art. 9(4)(e) change management |
| Testing and validation | Test sets, results, sign-off and date | SR 26-2 validation; NIST AI RMF MEASURE 2.1 |

The change history is the field that links the two tables. When field 5 or 6 in a decision record shows a new version, the change history should show who approved it and what testing preceded it. The OCC framework puts it directly: "Model, prompt, fine-tuning, data, configuration, provider, tool, and permission changes may be logged and linked to testing."

## Which audit trail fields do most firms miss?

Four fields carry most of the risk: retrieved context by version, what the reviewer saw, the final action as distinct from the proposal, and the outcome.

**Retrieved context.** A link to the current version of a policy proves nothing about the version the system saw. Store the ID, version and status at the moment of retrieval. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why records that change in place break reconstruction.

**The reviewer's view.** An approval click without a record of what was on screen, or how long it stayed there, cannot separate a real check from a rubber stamp. The FCA's 19 October 2026 review flagged the risk of human review "being a 'box-ticking' exercise, rather than meaningful oversight." Our essay [A reviewer who does not verify is not a control](https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/) sets out why.

**Final action.** The text a person sent after editing is the record that counts under SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4). Log the diff between proposal and action.

**Outcome.** SR 26-2 describes outcomes analysis as comparing "model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes." Without an outcome field written back to the run ID, no one can say whether the system is improving or drifting.

## How long should AI audit records be kept?

As long as the longest rule that applies to the record type, which is usually years, not months.

| Regime | Retention | Format rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU AI Act Art. 19 and 26(6), high-risk systems | At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise; financial institutions keep logs within financial services documentation | None in the article |
| FINRA Rule 4511(b) | At least six years where no other period applies | Format per SEA Rule 17a-4 |
| SEA Rule 17a-4(a) and (b) | Six years for core records, three for communications | 17a-4(f): time-stamped audit trail or non-rewriteable, non-erasable storage |
| DORA RTS 2024/1774 Art. 12 | Set from business and information security objectives and the ICT risk assessment | Protection "against tampering, deletion, and unauthorised access" |
| OCC framework (examiner resource) | "Periods appropriate to legal, supervisory, audit, customer-remediation, and operational needs" | Not specified |

Personal data cuts the other way. The AI Act retention clauses defer to data protection law, so a trail that stores full customer inputs needs a deletion rule as well as a retention rule. Storing inputs by reference, with the source system holding the data, often resolves the tension.

## How do you test that an AI audit trail works?

Rebuild a real decision from it, against the clock. Pick one AI-assisted decision from about three months ago and try to answer six questions from records alone:

1. What was the system asked, by whom and when?
2. Which data and documents did it see, in which versions?
3. Which model and instruction set produced the output?
4. What did it do, including every tool call?
5. Who reviewed it, what did they see and what did they change?
6. What did the firm finally do, and what happened next?

If any answer needs an interview, an email search or a second team, that field is missing. The OCC framework's documentation component states the goal: records "may support reconstruction of material outputs or actions even when the model cannot produce a rule-based rationale."

Gateway card

### Signs the trail is complete

- One run ID joins trace, approval, final action and outcome
- Retrieved documents are stored by version and status at retrieval
- Reviewer view, time spent, action and reason are logged as events
- Every model, prompt and permission change links to a test record
- Storage is write-once or keeps a full audit trail of changes
- Retention is set to the longest applicable rule, with a deletion rule for personal data
- A three-month-old decision can be rebuilt in minutes, not days

Tools help with parts of this. Our rankings of [LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/) and [AI governance and audit-trail tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/) cover the trace side and the inventory side respectively.

## lowob takeaways

- **Fourteen fields, one ID.** The decision record works only when every field joins on a single run ID.
- **Log the system as well as the decision.** Inventory, permissions and change history explain what a decision log shows.
- **The review half is the weak half.** Reviewer view, time spent, edits and outcome are where most trails are thin.
- **Integrity is a requirement.** SEA Rule 17a-4(f) and DORA both rule out editable logs.
- **Test by reconstruction.** A timed rebuild of an old decision is the only proof the trail works.

## Common questions

### What should an AI audit trail include?

A linked record of each AI-assisted decision: a run ID, the request, inputs, retrieved context with versions, the model and prompt versions, tool calls, the output, the reviewer and their action, the final action, the outcome, synchronised timestamps and retention metadata. Behind it sits a system record with inventory entry, owner, risk tier, permissions and change history.

### Does FINRA require firms to log AI prompts and outputs?

FINRA's 2026 oversight report does not create a new rule, but among its generative AI practices it suggests storing prompt and output logs for accountability and troubleshooting and tracking which model version was used and when. Existing books-and-records rules, Rule 4511 and SEA Rule 17a-4, already require retention of communications and other records an AI tool produces.

### How long should AI decision logs be kept?

Keep them for the longest period that applies to the record type. The EU AI Act sets a six-month floor for high-risk system logs, FINRA Rule 4511 defaults to six years, and SEA Rule 17a-4 sets six years for core records and three for communications. DORA leaves log retention to the firm's risk assessment.

### What is decision traceability in AI?

Decision traceability means a firm can follow an AI-assisted decision from input to action. The OCC's November 2026 examiner framework describes it as covering inputs, outputs, context, retrieved sources, tool calls, approvals, overrides and actions, so that material outputs or actions can be reconstructed even when the model cannot give a rule-based rationale.

### Can AI audit logs be stored in a normal database?

Only if the system meets the applicable format rules. SEA Rule 17a-4(f) requires electronic records to be kept either with a complete, time-stamped audit trail of changes and deletions or in non-rewriteable, non-erasable form. DORA's logging standard requires protection against tampering, deletion and unauthorised access. A table the operating team can edit meets neither.

# AI Credits Explained: How Credit-Based Pricing Works and How to Budget

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-credits-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: AI credits are a prepaid or metered currency that a vendor converts into AI work at its own burn rates. They let one price cover many features, and they move forecasting risk to the buyer. Budget by converting credits into cost per task, and negotiate rollover, true-up and alerts before you commit.

AI credits are a currency a vendor sells in bulk and burns per AI action: Salesforce, for example, sells 100,000 Flex Credits for $500 and charges 20 credits, or $0.10, per agent action, as listed in November 2026. Credits let one price cover many features. They also make the bill harder to read, because the vendor sets the burn rates.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

Credits are one form of usage-based pricing, which **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), compares with seats and outcomes. The general case for metering is in [what usage-based pricing for AI is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/). This page covers the credit mechanics and how to budget for them.

## What are AI credits?

AI credits are units a buyer purchases in advance or pays for as used, which the vendor then deducts at different rates for different AI activities. The credit is an exchange rate between money and work, set by the vendor.

A credit model has three numbers. The purchase price says what a credit costs. The burn rate says how many credits an activity uses. The effective unit price is the first multiplied by the second. Vendors usually publish the first, sometimes the second, and rarely the third.

## How much do AI credits cost?

Published credit prices range from about $0.005 to $0.008 per credit at Salesforce and Microsoft, but burn rates differ, so the per-credit price says little on its own. The table shows what each vendor published on the pages checked on 16 November 2026.

| Vendor and credit | Purchase price | Burn rate | Effective unit price | Rollover and expiry |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce Flex Credits | $500 per 100,000 ($0.005 each) | 20 per action; 30 per voice action | $0.10 per action; $0.15 per voice action | Unused credits do not roll over into later terms |
| Microsoft Copilot Credits (Copilot Studio pack) | $200 per pack of 25,000 per month (about $0.008 each) | "A varying number" by usage; rates not on the pricing page | Not published on the page | Not stated on the pages checked |
| Microsoft Copilot Credits (prepaid plan) | Up to 20% saving for paying up front | As above | Not published on the page | Pay-as-you-go cover when prepaid credits run out |
| OpenAI ChatGPT Business workspace credits | Not stated in the help article | Extend usage beyond included rate limits | Not published in the article | Not stated |

Two contrasts help. Anthropic's Claude Enterprise plan, as listed on 16 November 2026, charges a seat price plus usage "at API rates" instead of credits, so the unit is the token. And Salesforce's per-user add-on, at $125 per user per month, gives unmetered employee use with no credits at all. The same vendor can sell both.

## Why are vendors moving to credits?

Credits let a vendor price many AI features with one currency and change the burn rates without rewriting the price list. Poyar found AI credit models grew 126% year on year in 2025, and that roughly one in two companies above $50 million in annual recurring revenue planned to introduce credits in 2026.

Metronome, a billing vendor that has catalogued more than 50 AI companies, wrote in April 2026 that "nearly every category" in its index features some version of a credit model. It also recorded a move the other way: Windsurf replaced a credit-based system with fixed usage quotas across a tier structure. Credits are popular with sellers and not always kept.

Microsoft describes Copilot Credits as "a common currency for eligible Microsoft services with usage-based billing", per its documentation updated on 3 November 2026. The benefit to the vendor is flexibility. The cost to the buyer is that one currency spread across many services is harder to forecast.

## How do you budget for AI credits?

Convert credits into tasks: tasks per month, multiplied by actions per task, by credits per action and by the credit price. Then add a buffer and test it against a month of real use.

The example is illustrative and uses Salesforce's published rates. A service team expects 2,000 agent conversations a month, each taking four actions.

| Line | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| Actions per month | 2,000 conversations x 4 actions = 8,000 |
| Credits per month | 8,000 x 20 = 160,000 |
| Monthly cost at $500 per 100,000 | $800 |
| Annual prepaid commitment | 1.92 million credits, $9,600 |
| If real use is 30% lower | 576,000 credits unused, $2,880 lost if they do not roll over |
| Same volume at $2 per conversation | $4,000 a month |

The example shows why credits can be cheaper than per-conversation pricing and why they carry forecasting risk. Salesforce's page says Flex Credits and Conversations "will not be supported in the same org", so a buyer cannot hedge by mixing both. Size the first commitment below forecast, and pay for the rest as you go.

Keep the budget honest. Measure actions per task in a pilot rather than accepting a vendor average. Set alerts at 50%, 75% and 90% of the monthly budget; Microsoft's pricing page says administrators manage spending in Cost Management in the Microsoft 365 admin center. And recalculate cost per task each month, since burn rates can change.

## What should you negotiate in a credit contract?

Rollover, true-up, overage rate and notice of burn-rate changes. Salesforce's page sets some useful precedents: "There is no overage penalty", usage beyond the entitlement is billed monthly in arrears at the contracted rate, and its Pre-Commit option includes a "True-up at term end if usage is below commitment".

Ask for the burn rate of every action you expect to use, in the order form, and for notice before any change. [How to negotiate an AI software contract](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-negotiate-an-ai-software-contract/) covers the clauses in order.

## lowob takeaways

- **A credit is an exchange rate the vendor sets.** Ask for purchase price, burn rate and effective unit price.
- **Prepaid credits carry forecasting risk.** Unused Salesforce Flex Credits do not roll over.
- **Commit below forecast.** Pay as you go for the rest until a month of real use is measured.
- **Compare on cost per task.** Credit prices are not comparable across vendors; completed tasks are.

## Common questions

### What are AI credits?

AI credits are a vendor-defined currency bought in advance or paid as used, which the vendor deducts at different rates for different AI activities. Salesforce sells 100,000 Flex Credits for $500 and burns 20 per agent action, so each action costs $0.10, as listed in November 2026. The burn rate, not the credit price, decides what a task costs.

### How much do Microsoft Copilot Credits cost?

Microsoft's Copilot Studio pricing page, checked in November 2026, sells capacity packs of 25,000 Copilot Credits for $200 a month, about $0.008 per credit. A prepaid plan offers savings of up to 20%, and pay-as-you-go needs no up-front commitment. The page does not list how many credits each feature uses.

### Do unused AI credits roll over?

It depends on the contract. Salesforce's pricing page, checked in November 2026, says unused Flex Credits do not roll over into later subscription terms. Zendesk's help centre says unused automated resolutions do not roll over to the next usage period. Negotiate rollover, a smaller commitment, or a true-up before signing a prepaid amount.

### Are AI credits cheaper than per-seat pricing?

Sometimes. Credits are cheaper when usage is low or uneven across users, and dearer when a few heavy users or agents run many actions. Convert both offers into cost per completed task for your own volumes. Salesforce, for example, sells unmetered Agentforce add-ons at $125 per user per month beside its credit option.

For one credit-billed tool, ask the vendor for the burn rate of the three actions you use most, then divide last month's credit spend by tasks completed. If no one can produce the task count, set it up before the next commitment.

# AI Governance Framework Template for Mid-Size Financial Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-governance-framework-template/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI governance framework sets who owns AI risk, what AI the firm runs, how each use is tiered and approved, how people oversee it, how vendors are controlled and what records prove it worked. This template sets out eleven components for a mid-size financial firm, each anchored to NIST's AI RMF, the OCC's November 2026 framework, the FCA's October 2026 review, SR 26-2, DORA and the EU AI Act.

An AI governance framework for a mid-size financial firm is a short written system of named owners, an AI inventory, risk tiers, approval gates, oversight rules, vendor controls, monitoring and records, mapped to the rules that bind the firm. It should fit on a few pages and be provable from records, not from slides.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

Mid-size financial firms sit in an awkward place on AI. They are too regulated to run AI informally and usually too small for a dedicated AI risk function. The answer is a framework short enough to be used, built on the risk, compliance and vendor processes the firm already has. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) explains why the records the framework produces matter most under examination.

This template draws on public supervisory texts and labelled readings. It is not legal advice; adapt it with your compliance function to the rules that apply to you.

## What is an AI governance framework?

It is the written set of roles, rules and records through which a firm decides which AI uses are allowed, who answers for each, and how risk is found and controlled. Our explainer [What is AI governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/) covers the concept; this page is the template.

Three public references shape most frameworks. NIST's AI RMF is voluntary and structured around Govern, Map, Measure and Manage; NIST says it "is being revised as part of the White House AI Action Plan." ISO/IEC 42001 is a certifiable management system standard, covered in our explainer [What is ISO/IEC 42001?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-iso-42001/). For banks, the OCC's November 2026 framework shows what examiners will look for, though the bulletin says it "does not establish supervisory expectations for banks."

## What should an AI governance framework template include?

Eleven components. The table is the template; fill the middle columns for your firm.

| # | Component | What to write down | Typical owner | Evidence | Anchors |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Scope and definitions | What counts as AI, including vendor features and agents; what is out of scope | Chief risk officer | Definition in policy | SR 26-2 model definition; OCC defined purpose |
| 2 | Roles and accountability | Board role, one accountable senior manager, an owner per AI system, second-line review, internal audit | Board and CEO | Responsibilities map | FCA SMF mapping; DORA Art. 5(2)(a); NIST GOVERN 2.1 |
| 3 | Inventory | Every AI system, agent and vendor AI feature, with owner, provider, permissions and status | AI governance lead | Live inventory | NIST GOVERN 1.6; FCA agent inventory; DORA Art. 8 |
| 4 | Risk tiering | Tiers and the factors behind them | Second line | Tier per system with reasoning | OCC illustrative tiers; SR 26-2 materiality |
| 5 | Approval gates | Who approves at intake, before production and after material change | Accountable senior manager | Approval records | OCC "approval authority at meaningful lifecycle gates" |
| 6 | Human oversight and autonomy | Autonomy level per system, review points, override and escalation rules, reviewer competence | System owner | Procedures, training records | OCC human-in-the-loop component; AI Act Art. 26(2); FINRA 2026 report |
| 7 | Third-party AI | Due diligence, contract terms, change notice, data use, exit plans | Procurement and vendor risk | Contracts, register entries | DORA Art. 28 and 30; FCA; NIST GOVERN 6.1 |
| 8 | Testing and monitoring | Pre-deployment tests, ongoing metrics, drift checks, outcomes analysis | System owner, second line | Test reports, monitoring logs | SR 26-2 validation and monitoring; NIST MANAGE 4.1 |
| 9 | Records and audit trail | Decision-level record fields, storage, retention | Compliance | Sample reconstructed decision | FINRA 2026 report; SEA Rule 17a-4(f); AI Act Art. 12, 19, 26 |
| 10 | Incidents and shutdown | What counts as an AI incident, who can stop a system, how fast, who is told | Operations risk | Incident log, shutdown tests | DORA Art. 17 and 19; OCC kill switches; NIST GOVERN 4.3 |
| 11 | Review and reporting | Annual framework review, board reporting, internal audit scope | Accountable senior manager | Review minutes, audit reports | DORA Art. 6(5); SR 26-2 internal audit role |

Two principles keep it small. First, attach components to processes the firm already runs: new product approval, vendor onboarding, change management, incident management. The OCC tells examiners not to require "a separate SI risk appetite." Second, make every component produce a record, so the framework can be shown working rather than described.

## Who should own AI governance in a mid-size firm?

One named senior manager, with a board that receives regular reporting. The FCA's 19 October 2026 review describes good practice as firms that mapped AI responsibilities across senior management functions, with a senior person accountable for overall oversight, and "accountability assigned at the beginning."

Under DORA Article 5(2)(a), the management body bears "the ultimate responsibility for managing the financial entity's ICT risk", which includes AI systems. SR 26-2 describes internal audit's role as evaluating "whether the model risk management practices are rigorous and effective", not duplicating them. Large firms often add an AI board or ethics committee, which the FCA also observed. For a mid-size firm, a standing agenda item at the existing risk committee usually does the same job.

## How should a firm tier its AI uses?

By consequence, not technical sophistication. The OCC's framework scores each use case against seven common factors and maps the result to an illustrative four-tier scale. The factors are decision consequence, reversibility, customer or financial impact, autonomy level, data sensitivity, explainability and provenance. Arnold & Porter's 11 November 2026 reading notes that banks may choose their own number and type of categories.

The OCC gives the two ends of the scale: "a simple internal productivity tool with no customer or financial data exposure sits at Tier 4", whereas "a fully autonomous, customer-facing payment agent sits at Tier 1, regardless of how well it performs in testing."

| OCC tier | OCC description (abridged) | **lowob** autonomy dial | Controls to require (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Critical | Direct action, low or no reversibility, high impact, autonomous or partly autonomous | 3 act and report, or 4 act alone | Independent validation, board-level approval, real-time monitoring, tested shutdown |
| 2 High | Direct action or high-weight decision support, human-on-the-loop, moderate-to-high impact | 2 act with approval, or 3 | Independent validation, senior approval, full decision records |
| 3 Moderate | Decision support with mandatory human-in-the-loop, limited data sensitivity, reversible | 1 draft, or 2 | Owner testing, second-line review, sampled decision records |
| 4 Low | No customer or financial data, no direct action, fully human-controlled | 0 answer, or 1 | Inventory entry and owner; light monitoring |

The dial is **lowob**'s five-step scale for how much a system may do without a person: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. Our explainer [What is human-in-the-loop AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/) covers the oversight models behind it.

## Which rules should the framework map to?

Only the ones that bind the firm, plus one voluntary reference. A mapping column that lists every framework in existence helps no one.

| Firm type | Binding or supervisory texts to map | Voluntary reference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US bank | SR 26-2 for traditional models; OCC framework for generative and agentic AI at national banks | NIST AI RMF |
| US broker-dealer | FINRA Rules 3110, 2210 and 4511; SEA Rule 17a-4; FINRA 2026 report | NIST AI RMF |
| UK bank or insurer | FCA Handbook, including SM&CR; PRA SS1/23 where it applies; FCA October 2026 review | ISO/IEC 42001 or NIST AI RMF |
| EU financial entity | DORA; EU AI Act for high-risk uses from 2 December 2027 | ISO/IEC 42001 |

Our comparison [NIST AI RMF vs ISO/IEC 42001](https://lowob.com/research/nist-ai-rmf-vs-iso-42001/) helps choose the voluntary reference.

## How can a mid-size firm put the framework in place?

In three steps that each produce records. The sequence below is **lowob**'s suggestion, not a regulatory requirement.

1. **Inventory and owners.** List every AI system, agent and vendor AI feature, with a named owner. The FCA's review praised firms that kept "clear inventories of AI use cases and the models they were built on."
2. **Tiers and gates.** Tier each system, then route new uses and material changes through approval at the right level. Our [documentation template](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-document-an-ai-model-for-regulators/) sets out what each tier must record.
3. **Records and a test.** Specify the decision-level record for tier 1 to 3 systems using our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/), then rebuild one real decision from records alone.

Gateway card

### Before the framework goes to the board

- One accountable senior manager named, with responsibilities written down
- An inventory that includes vendor AI features and agents
- A tier for every system, with the reasoning recorded
- Approval gates attached to existing product, change and vendor processes
- A tested way to stop each tier 1 and tier 2 system
- One decision reconstructed end to end from records

## lowob takeaways

- **Extend existing risk management.** The OCC tells examiners not to treat AI as a separate risk category; build on current processes.
- **Name one owner.** The FCA's good practice puts accountability with a senior manager from the design stage.
- **Tier by consequence.** A simple agent that moves money can outrank a sophisticated model that drafts internal notes.
- **Prove it with records.** Each component should leave evidence an examiner can read.

## Common questions

### What should an AI governance framework include?

Eleven components cover most needs: scope and definitions, roles and accountability, an AI inventory, risk tiering, approval gates, human oversight and autonomy rules, third-party AI controls, testing and monitoring, records and audit trail, incident and shutdown procedures, and periodic review and reporting. Each should produce a record so the framework can be shown working in an examination.

### Is there an official AI governance framework for banks?

Not a binding one in the US. SR 26-2 covers traditional models and excludes generative and agentic AI. The OCC's November 2026 framework for generative and agentic AI is a resource for its examiners and sets no supervisory expectations for banks. NIST's AI RMF is voluntary. In the UK and EU, firms rely on existing FCA, PRA and DORA rules.

### How should AI systems be risk-tiered?

By consequence rather than technical sophistication. The OCC's illustrative method scores each use on seven factors, including decision consequence, reversibility, customer or financial impact, autonomy and data sensitivity, then assigns one of four tiers from critical to low. A fully autonomous customer-facing payment agent is critical; an internal drafting tool with no customer data is low.

### Who is accountable for AI risk in a financial firm?

Senior management and the board. The FCA's October 2026 review describes good practice as mapping AI responsibilities to senior management functions with one senior person accountable for oversight. Under DORA, the management body bears ultimate responsibility for ICT risk, including AI systems, and firms stay fully responsible for AI services bought from vendors.

Expect the questions to land on vendors before they land on policy.
