# AI Gross Margin Explained: Why AI Products Earn Less Than SaaS

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-gross-margin-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: AI gross margin is revenue less the direct cost of serving AI features, chiefly inference, compute and human review, divided by revenue. Investor surveys put AI product margins between about 25% and 60%, against 80% to 85% for SaaS licence revenue. The gap comes from a real cost per use, and it is widest on heavy users of flat-priced seats.

AI gross margin is revenue minus the direct cost of delivering AI features, mainly inference, compute and human review, divided by revenue; ICONIQ put the average for AI products at 45% in 2025, against the 80% to 85% SaaS Capital cites for SaaS licence revenue. The gap exists because every AI request has a cost. It is widest where heavy users sit on flat-priced seats.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Margin is where the pricing model is tested. **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), works a support-agent example at $0.99 per resolution that falls from 71.5% to 14% margin when caching lapses and resolution rates drop. This page explains the measure itself, why it sits below SaaS, and what moves it.

## What is AI gross margin?

AI gross margin is the share of AI revenue left after paying the direct, mostly variable costs of serving it. The formula is revenue minus cost of revenue, divided by revenue.

The definition of cost of revenue matters more than the arithmetic. SaaS Capital lists hosting, staff who keep production running, customer support and success staff (excluding account management), third-party software or data in the product, and other direct staff costs needed to deliver the service. Its article does not mention AI costs. Applying its principle that direct, primarily variable delivery costs belong in cost of revenue, AI adds lines that SaaS rarely had.

| Cost line | In classic SaaS | In an AI product |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hosting and compute | Mostly fixed, falls per user with scale | Grows with every request |
| Model inference | None | Per token or per call, from an API or own hardware |
| Tools billed per use | Rare | Search, code execution and runtime, often separate |
| Human review of outputs | None | Staff who check or correct AI work before it ships |
| Support and success | Present | Present, often higher during adoption |
| Third-party data | Sometimes | Often, for retrieval or grounding |

## Why do AI products earn less than SaaS?

Because SaaS has near-zero cost per use and AI does not. A spreadsheet costs its vendor almost nothing extra when a customer opens it twice as often; an assistant answering twice as many questions sends twice as many tokens to a model.

The cost also rises as products mature. ICONIQ's 2026 report says "as products scale, talent's share of cost falls while inference rises", and notes that inference costs rise from beta to general availability. Agents add to it: Anthropic reported in June 2025 that its agents used about 4 times the tokens of chat and multi-agent systems about 15 times.

Usage is also uneven. Poyar estimates, from his own experience rather than his survey, that the top 10% of power users drive more than 70% of token consumption. On a flat seat price, those users set the margin.

## What gross margins do AI companies actually earn?

Investor surveys put AI product margins between about 25% and 60%, against 80% to 85% for SaaS licence revenue. Each figure below is self-reported or estimated by its publisher.

| Group | Gross margin | Source | Date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI products, average | 45% in 2025; 53% projected 2026; 59% projected 2027 | ICONIQ, State of AI, about 300 executives | July 2026 |
| Fastest-growing AI start-ups ("Supernovas") | About 25%, often negative | Bessemer Venture Partners, State of AI | August 2025 |
| Fast-growing AI start-ups ("Shooting Stars") | About 60% | Bessemer Venture Partners, State of AI | August 2025 |
| AI margin targets, median | About 50%; 12% target 80% or more | Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged, 230+ companies | May 2026 |
| SaaS licence revenue | Generally 80% to 85% | SaaS Capital | October 2024 |

Bessemer describes the Supernovas as "often trading distribution for profit in the short term". A low margin can be a growth choice. It cannot be a permanent one.

## How do you calculate gross margin on an AI seat?

Estimate tokens per user per month, price them at the model's list rate, and compare the cost with the seat price for the average user and for a heavy user. The example is illustrative and uses Anthropic's Claude Sonnet 5.5 list prices, checked 16 November 2026: $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output and $0.10 per million cached input.

A seat sells at $25 a month. The average user makes 400 requests a month, each reading 8,000 input tokens and writing 600 output tokens.

| Case | Model cost per month | Margin on a $25 seat, before other costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Average user, no caching | $8.80 | 64.8% |
| Average user, 6,000 of 8,000 input tokens cached | $4.24 | 83.0% |
| Heavy user at 5 times the average, no caching | $44.00 | Negative 76% |
| Heavy user at 5 times the average, with caching | $21.20 | 15.2% |

Two lessons follow. Caching is worth almost 20 points of margin on the average user. And the heavy user decides whether the seat is viable at all. This is why business plans now pair seats with limits: Anthropic's Claude Team page says usage limits apply and sells premium seats with "5x more usage than standard seats", as checked on 16 November 2026.

The example excludes cache-write charges, hosting, support and review. In a real cost of revenue these come on top.

## Should human review count in AI gross margin?

Yes, when the product cannot be delivered without it. SaaS Capital includes "other direct employee costs required to deliver the ongoing service" in cost of revenue. If staff check AI outputs before customers receive them, that time is a delivery cost. Leaving it out flatters the margin and hides the largest line: in the pillar's support example, review cost about five times the model.

## How do you raise AI gross margin?

Lower cost per task and price the variable part of usage. The levers are covered in [what AI inference cost is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/) and [prompt caching](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/). On Anthropic's 16 November 2026 list prices, Claude Haiku 5.5 input costs $0.10 per million tokens against $2 for Sonnet 5.5, and the Batch API halves both input and output prices.

On the price side, move heavy use into a metered or credit component. [AI credits explained](https://lowob.com/research/ai-credits-explained/) covers the mechanics, and [how to price an AI product](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-price-an-ai-product/) sets out where margin fits in the method. Investors ask about the trend: our piece on [raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) covers what they expect to see.

## lowob takeaways

- **AI has a cost per use.** That is the structural reason margins sit below SaaS.
- **Count review in cost of revenue.** It is a delivery cost and often the largest line.
- **Heavy users set the margin.** Model the top decile, not the average.
- **Price the variable part.** Seats with limits, credits or metering protect margin as usage grows.

## Common questions

### What is a typical gross margin for an AI company?

Investor surveys put AI product margins well below SaaS. ICONIQ's July 2026 report found an average of 45% in 2025, projected at 53% for 2026. Bessemer's August 2025 report put its fastest-growing AI start-ups at about 25% and other fast growers at about 60%. SaaS Capital says SaaS licence revenue typically earns 80% to 85%.

### Why are AI gross margins lower than SaaS?

Every AI request has a direct cost in model inference and compute, which classic SaaS largely did not. Costs rise with usage, agents multiply tokens per task, and a small share of heavy users drives most consumption. Many AI products also need people to review outputs, which adds a delivery cost that SaaS products did not carry.

### How do you calculate gross margin for an AI product?

Subtract cost of revenue from revenue and divide by revenue. For AI, cost of revenue should include model inference, compute, per-use tools, third-party data, support and any human review needed to deliver the output. Calculate it per customer segment as well as in total, because heavy users can turn a healthy average into a loss.

### What gross margin should an AI startup target?

Kyle Poyar's May 2026 survey of more than 230 software companies found a median target AI margin of about 50%, with only 12% aiming for 80% or more. A lower margin can be a deliberate growth choice, as Bessemer notes, but the trend should rise as caching, smaller models and pricing changes take effect.

Pull last month's model and review costs by customer and rank customers by cost against revenue. If the top tenth are below your margin floor, price their excess usage before the next renewal cycle.

# AI Pricing Statistics 2026: Models, Price Points and Trends

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-pricing-statistics-2026/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A sourced reference of AI pricing statistics for 2026. Hybrid pricing reached 37% of software companies, consumption pricing 42% and outcome pricing 23% of AI vendors, and AI credits 29%. AI product margins averaged 45% in 2025. Every figure is dated and sourced, and most come from investor or vendor surveys, which we label.

In 2026, 37% of software companies used hybrid pricing (Growth Unhinged, May 2026), consumption pricing reached 42% of AI companies and outcome pricing 23% (ICONIQ, July 2026), and AI product gross margins averaged 45% in 2025. Buyers lean towards metering: 42.9% prefer consumption pricing for GenAI features. Most figures here are surveys run by investors, analysts or vendors.

| Intercom Fin billing unit changed from resolution to outcome | 12 March 2026 | Intercom Help Center | Checked 16 November 2026 |
| Intercom renamed itself Fin | May 2026 | Salesforce press release | 15 June 2026 |

## How reliable are these statistics?

Treat them as directional. Growth Unhinged's survey was supported by Metronome, a billing vendor, and is self-reported. ICONIQ and Bessemer are investors, and their 2026 and 2027 margins are projections. Futurum did not disclose fielding dates in its release. Gartner's figures are forecasts. Vendor prices are list prices and change often; negotiated prices are usually lower. Where sellers and buyers disagree, as on outcome pricing, both can be true: more vendors offer it while fewer buyers say they prefer it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Hybrid is the norm.** Most AI companies combine a fixed fee with usage, credits or outcomes.
- **Buyers want metering for AI.** Preference for outcome pricing on GenAI features is falling.
- **Margins sit below SaaS.** Investor data puts AI products at about 25% to 60%.
- **Date every price.** Units and list prices changed at several large vendors in 2026.

## Common questions

### What percentage of AI companies use usage-based pricing?

ICONIQ's July 2026 survey of about 300 AI executives found consumption-based pricing at 42%, up from 35% six months earlier. Deloitte cited a Maxio survey finding 83% of AI-native SaaS companies offer usage-based pricing. The figures measure different things: ICONIQ counts the model in use, Maxio whether it is offered at all.

### How many software companies use hybrid pricing in 2026?

Kyle Poyar's Growth Unhinged survey of more than 230 software companies, published in May 2026, found 37% use a hybrid pricing model, up from 25% a year earlier. ICONIQ separately found AI companies blend an average of 1.7 pricing models. The survey was supported by Metronome, a billing vendor, and is self-reported.

### What is the average gross margin for AI products?

ICONIQ's July 2026 State of AI report put the average AI product gross margin at 45% in 2025, projected to rise to 53% in 2026 and 59% in 2027. Bessemer's August 2025 report put its fastest-growing AI start-ups at about 25%. SaaS Capital says SaaS licence revenue usually earns 80% to 85%.

### Do buyers prefer outcome-based pricing for AI?

Fewer do than a year ago. The Futurum Group's survey of 830 IT decision makers, released in April 2026, found preference for outcome-based GenAI pricing fell from 30.9% to 26.8%, while preference for consumption pricing rose to 42.9%. Futurum linked the fall to uncertainty about how to define and measure AI outcomes.

### How much do AI assistants cost per user for business?

As checked on vendors' pages on 16 November 2026, Microsoft 365 Copilot Business lists at $21 per user per month on annual billing, ChatGPT Business and Claude Team standard seats at $20, and Google includes Gemini in Workspace Business Standard at $14. Premium seats at OpenAI and Anthropic cost $100 per seat per month on annual billing.

# Business Decision Records vs Architecture Decision Records

Source: https://lowob.com/research/business-decision-records-vs-architecture-decision-records/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An architecture decision record captures one software design choice with its context, decision, status and consequences. A business decision record applies the same discipline to commercial and operating decisions and adds what engineering records usually skip: one named owner, an expected outcome, a falsifier and a check date, so the decision can be graded and its outcome written back.

An architecture decision record (ADR) captures one significant software design choice with its context, decision, status and consequences; a business decision record applies the same format to commercial and operating decisions, and adds one named owner, an expected outcome, a falsifier and a check date. The immutability rule carries over unchanged: an accepted record is superseded, never edited. What changes is the reader, the storage and the need to grade the outcome.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Both formats serve the record layer of the enterprise brain, the part of the loop a company has to write for itself, as argued in [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/). Engineering teams have practised it since 2011; most commercial teams have not.

## What is an architecture decision record?

An ADR is a short document that records one architecturally significant decision, why it was made and what follows from it. Fowler's reference entry, updated 24 March 2026, defines it as "a short document that captures and explains a single decision."

Nygard's November 2011 post set the shape. The context describes "the forces at play" in value-neutral language. The decision is written in full sentences, "We will...". The consequences list everything that follows, and Nygard insisted that "all consequences should be listed here, not just the 'positive' ones." Records are numbered, stored with the code, and kept when reversed: "we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded."

MADR, an open-source template now at version 4.0.0 (17 September 2024), adds decision drivers, considered options and a confirmation section. The UK framework of 4 November 2025 asks for a title, date, status, context, decision, consequences, stakeholders consulted and links to supporting documents.

## What is a business decision record?

A business decision record is the same discipline applied to a commercial or operating decision, such as a discount, a pricing exception, a partner agreement or a hire. Its core fields are the decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date and falsifier.

The [decision record explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) covers the concept and the [decision record template](https://lowob.com/research/decision-record-template/) gives every field. The point of difference is grading. A software architecture choice may take years to prove itself, and its consequences are often qualitative. A renewal discount has a result within a quarter. That makes it possible, and worth the effort, to write down in advance what would prove the decision wrong.

## What is the difference between a business decision record and an ADR?

The structure and the immutability rule are the same; the subject, reader, storage and outcome tracking differ. The table sets out each difference.

| Dimension | Architecture decision record | Business decision record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Subject | One significant software design choice | One recurring commercial or operating decision |
| Origin | Nygard, November 2011 | Adapted from the ADR format |
| Typical author | Engineer or architect | Decision owner: sales, finance, operations or a founder |
| Core sections | Title, context, decision, status, consequences | Decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date, falsifier |
| Statuses | Proposed, accepted, deprecated or superseded | Proposed, accepted, superseded or closed |
| Change rule | Never reopened; superseded by a new record | Same |
| Outcome tracking | Rare; Fowler suggests noting what should prompt re-evaluation | Required: outcome written back on the check date |
| Where it lives | Markdown files in the code repository | CRM object, database table or shared sheet |
| Who reads it | Future developers and AI coding assistants | Sellers, managers, auditors and AI agents |
| Sensitivity | Usually internal technical detail | Often holds client terms; needs permissions |
| Volume | Every architecturally significant decision | The ten or so decision classes that recur and carry money |

## What carries over from ADRs unchanged?

Five conventions transfer directly, and they are the ones most often missing from business records. Each has a reason that holds outside engineering.

- **One decision per record.** Nygard argued that "small, modular documents have at least a chance at being updated." A meeting summary with six decisions in it is not a record of any of them.
- **Sequential numbering.** Numbers are never reused, so a reference to DR-0042 always means the same record.
- **A status.** Proposed, accepted and superseded separate the live answer from history. An AI agent reading a record needs this more than a person does, because it cannot tell from tone which document is current.
- **Supersede, never edit.** Fowler's rule is that an accepted record "should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded." [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why the change and its reason are the most useful information a record holds.
- **Write it for a future reader.** Nygard framed each ADR as a conversation with a future developer. Business records are a conversation with a future seller, owner or auditor. The failure modes he named, "blind acceptance" and "blind reversal", are the same on the commercial side.

AWS's prescriptive guidance, published in March 2022, adds a goal business teams share: records "reduce recurring and time-consuming decision-making efforts." McKinsey's survey of 1,259 respondents (1,228 of them included in the results), published 30 April 2019, found managers spent 37% of their time on decisions and 61% said most of that time was used ineffectively. The figures are self-reported, but they show what re-made decisions cost.

## What has to change for business decisions?

Four things: a gradable outcome, a named owner, storage outside a code repository, and permissions.

**A gradable outcome.** ADRs record consequences; business records must also record a prediction. The falsifier names a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer, so that someone other than the author can say whether the decision worked. [The field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) sets out how to write one.

**A named owner.** An ADR is often the team's decision. A business decision needs one accountable person, because the check date needs someone to turn up.

**Storage people already open.** Fowler notes that repository storage does not suit decisions covering a broader ecosystem, and that git can be hard for non-developers. Commercial records belong beside the CRM or in a structured table with fixed columns, so they can be grouped by decision class, segment and size.

**Permissions.** A discount record may contain a client's name and terms. Precedent can travel as a pattern, such as segment, size and discount band, without exposing another client's details to every reader or agent.

## Can one company use both?

Yes, linked. Engineering decisions often follow business ones: a product team's choice of billing system follows a pricing decision.

Give each record a decision class and link the ADR to the business record that motivated it. When the business decision is superseded, engineers can see which technical choices to re-examine. The [enterprise brain explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/) describes the loop both records feed: store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning.

## lowob takeaways

- **Same rules, different reader.** One decision per record, numbered, with a status, superseded never edited.
- **Business records add a prediction.** Expected outcome, falsifier and check date make them gradable.
- **Store them where owners work.** A CRM object or structured table, not a code repository.
- **Link the two logs.** Technical decisions often follow business ones, and should say so.

## Common questions

### What is an architecture decision record (ADR)?

A short document capturing one significant software architecture decision with its context, the decision, its status and its consequences. Michael Nygard proposed the format in November 2011. Records are numbered, stored with the code and never edited once accepted: a changed decision gets a new record that supersedes the old one, so the history survives.

### Can ADRs be used for business decisions?

The format carries over well, but business decisions need additions. Keep the one-decision rule, numbering, status and supersession. Add one named owner, an expected outcome, a falsifier with a measure, threshold, date and observer, and a check date, then write the outcome back. Store the records where business owners work, not in a code repository.

### What is the difference between a decision record and meeting minutes?

Minutes record what was discussed, in order, often covering several topics. A decision record captures one decision with its reason, owner, status, expected outcome and check date, and links to the minutes as a source. Minutes are not superseded when a decision changes; a decision record is, which is what lets a reader find the current answer.

### Who should own a business decision record?

One named person who is accountable for the decision, usually the person with authority to make it, such as the head of sales for a discount policy. Approvers and people consulted are recorded separately. A single owner matters because someone has to check the falsifier on the check date and write the outcome back.

## Sources and notes

- [Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions](https://www.cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), Cognitect blog, 15 November 2011. Original ADR proposal for software projects.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), updated 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference; notes the idea is worth considering in other contexts.
- [MADR, Markdown Architectural Decision Records](https://adr.github.io/madr), version 4.0.0, 17 September 2024. Open-source template; architecture-focused.
- [GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/architectural-decision-record-framework/architectural-decision-record-framework), DSIT, 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard.
- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance, Using architectural decision records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/welcome.html), March 2022. Vendor guidance.
- [McKinsey, Decision making in the age of urgency](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/decision-making-in-the-age-of-urgency), 30 April 2019. Self-reported online survey fielded February 2018.
- The business decision record fields and the comparison are **lowob**'s adaptation of the ADR format.

# Decision Record Template: Fields, Example and How to Use It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/decision-record-template/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A decision record template is a fixed set of fields for one decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its status, the expected outcome, the check date and the falsifier. This guide gives the full template as a table, a filled composite example and the usage rules borrowed from architecture decision records: never edit an accepted record, supersede it.

A decision record template is a fixed set of fields for writing down one decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its status, the expected outcome, the date to check it and the falsifier that would prove it wrong. The template below has 18 fields, of which 10 are required. Copy it into a spreadsheet or database, fill it at the moment of decision, and never edit an accepted record: supersede it with a new one.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

This template is the record layer of **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, set out in [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/). The brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. Connectors and models can be rented. The record of what the company decided, and why, has to be written by the company, and this is the form to write it in.

## What is a decision record template?

It is a standard form for capturing one decision so that a later reader, human or AI agent, can see what was chosen, why, by whom, whether it is still current and whether it worked. The [decision record explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) covers the concept; this page is the working form.

Software teams have used the pattern since 2011. Nygard's November 2011 post set out five sections and asked that the whole document be "one or two pages long". Fowler's 2026 entry says to keep it "typically a single page". The UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology's framework, published 4 November 2025, requires a title, date, status, context, decision, consequences, stakeholders consulted and links to supporting documents. Business decisions need all of that, plus the fields that let the decision be graded later.

## Which fields does a decision record need?

Ten fields are required on every material decision; the other eight are recommended once the habit holds. Copy the table as it stands.

| # | Field | What to write | Required | Convention it comes from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | ID | A sequential number, such as DR-0042. Never reuse a number | Yes | Nygard 2011: numbers are "sequential and monotonic" |
| 2 | Title | A short noun phrase naming the decision | Recommended | Nygard 2011 |
| 3 | Question | What was being decided, in one line | Recommended | MADR 4.0: context and problem statement |
| 4 | Decision | One sentence, stated first, in the active voice | Yes | Nygard 2011: "We will..." |
| 5 | Reason and evidence | Why, in two or three sentences, with links to the sources | Yes | Fowler 2026: brief rationale and trade-offs |
| 6 | Alternatives considered | Each serious option rejected, and why | Recommended | MADR 4.0: considered options |
| 7 | Owner | One named person accountable for the decision | Yes | **lowob**: accountability needs a name |
| 8 | Approver and consulted | Who signed off; who was asked | Recommended | GOV.UK 2025: stakeholders consulted |
| 9 | Date decided (as-at) | When the organisation took this view | Yes | GOV.UK 2025; Fowler 2021: record time |
| 10 | Effective from (as-of) | When the decision starts to apply, if different | Recommended | Fowler 2021: actual time |
| 11 | Status | Proposed, accepted, superseded or closed | Yes | Nygard 2011; Fowler 2026 |
| 12 | Decision class and tags | Fixed values, such as pricing, segment, size band | Recommended | **lowob**: lets records be grouped |
| 13 | Expected outcome | What should happen if the decision was right | Yes | **lowob**: the record must be gradable |
| 14 | Falsifier | Measure, threshold, date and observer that would prove it wrong | Yes | **lowob**: the field that makes a record a judgment |
| 15 | Check date | When the observer looks; put it in their calendar | Yes | Fowler 2026: changes that should prompt re-evaluation |
| 16 | Supersedes, with reason and trigger | The record this replaces; why; new evidence, correction or reinterpretation | Yes | Nygard 2011 and Fowler 2026: supersede, never edit |
| 17 | Sources | Links to the transcripts, documents and threads relied on | Recommended | **lowob**: keep the sources |
| 18 | Outcome and lesson | What happened, written back on the check date, and one line for next time | Recommended at decision, required at check | **lowob**: outcome write-back |

Field 16 takes "none" when nothing is replaced; a blank looks like a forgotten link.

## What does a filled decision record look like?

The example below shows every field filled for one pricing decision. It is a composite, assembled from patterns common in mid-size B2B firms, not a record from any one company, and the figures are illustrative.

| Field | Composite example entry |
| --- | --- |
| ID | DR-0042 |
| Title | Mid-market renewal discount cap |
| Question | What is the most a seller can discount a mid-market renewal without finance approval? |
| Decision | We will cap mid-market renewal discounts at 10% without finance approval; above 10% needs the finance lead's sign-off |
| Reason and evidence | Discounts above 10% on renewals in the last two quarters did not lift renewal rates against those at 10% or below, and cost margin. Evidence: CRM renewal report, finance margin review |
| Alternatives considered | Keep the 15% cap (rejected: margin cost without retention gain); remove seller discretion entirely (rejected: slows routine renewals) |
| Owner | Head of sales |
| Approver and consulted | Finance lead approved; two account managers and revenue operations consulted |
| Date decided (as-at) | The approval date |
| Effective from (as-of) | First day of the next quarter |
| Status | Accepted |
| Decision class and tags | Pricing; renewal; mid-market; deal size band B |
| Expected outcome | Average renewal discount falls; gross renewal rate in the band holds |
| Falsifier | If gross renewal rate in the mid-market band falls more than 5 points below the prior two-quarter average over the next 30 renewals, the cap was wrong. Observer: revenue operations lead, from the CRM renewal report |
| Check date | After the 30th renewal or at quarter end, whichever comes later |
| Supersedes, with reason and trigger | DR-0017 (15% cap). Reason: margin review. Trigger: new evidence |
| Sources | Links to the renewal report snapshot, the margin review and the approval thread |
| Outcome and lesson | Blank until the check date; then the measured renewal rate, the status decision and one line for the next pricing call |

The falsifier counts renewals rather than weeks, so the check does not arrive before there is enough evidence. The outcome stays blank at decision time.

## How do you write the falsifier?

Name four things: a measure, a threshold, a date or case count, and the person who checks. "If it doesn't work out" has none of them and cannot be graded.

The argument is in [The field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/). The practical rule: ask each decision-maker to write their own falsifier before discussion and then compare. Two people who agree on the choice often write different falsifiers, which shows they are making different bets. Fowler's 2026 entry points the same way from engineering: it suggests recording a confidence level and the changes in context that should prompt re-evaluation.

## How do you use the template day to day?

Fill it at the moment of decision, keep one decision per record, and change records only by superseding them. Six rules keep the habit alive.

1. **One decision, one record.** Nygard scoped each record to one significant decision, noting in 2011 that "small, modular documents have at least a chance at being updated."
2. **Write before discussion closes.** The reason and falsifier written afterwards tend to fit whatever happened.
3. **Never edit an accepted record.** Create a new one, link it with field 16, and mark the old one superseded. Nygard's rule: "If a decision is reversed, we will keep the old one around, but mark it as superseded." [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why the change is the most useful information.
4. **Record the trigger.** New evidence, correction of an error and reinterpretation of the same evidence are different problems. Frequent reinterpretation points at how a view is formed.
5. **Link the sources; do not paste summaries.** A model's summary of a meeting should point to the transcript, not replace it, as argued in [Keep the sources, let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/).
6. **Put the check date in a calendar.** On that date the observer writes the outcome back and sets the status: hold, reverse with a new record, or close.

Nygard named the two failures the rules prevent: "blind acceptance" and "blind reversal" of decisions whose reasons are unknown. AWS's prescriptive guidance, published in March 2022, describes the payoff for engineering teams: a collection of records provides "a hand-over experience and reference documentation."

## Where should decision records live?

In one structured table or database that people and agents can both read, with a fixed set of columns matching the template. A spreadsheet is enough to start.

Engineering teams keep architecture records as numbered Markdown files in the code repository, which Nygard proposed in 2011 and Fowler still describes in 2026. Fowler also notes that repository storage does not suit decisions covering a broader ecosystem, and that git can be hard for non-developers. Business records usually belong next to the systems they govern: a CRM custom object, a database table or a shared sheet with locked columns. Whatever the tool, test one thing before committing: the full record, with its history and links, must export whole if the vendor changes.

Record only the decisions that recur and carry money; [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) lists ten.

## lowob takeaways

- **Ten fields are required.** ID, decision, reason, owner, date, status, expected outcome, falsifier, check date and supersedes.
- **The falsifier makes it gradable.** Measure, threshold, date and observer, written before discussion.
- **Supersede, never edit.** A changed decision is a new record with a reason and a trigger.
- **Write the outcome back.** On the check date, to the same record, with one line for next time.

## Common questions

### What should a decision record template include?

At minimum: an ID, the decision in one sentence, the reason with evidence, one named owner, the date, the status, the expected outcome, a falsifier, a check date and a link to any record it supersedes. Recommended extras are the question, alternatives considered, approvers, tags, sources, and the outcome and lesson written back on the check date.

### What is the difference between a decision record and a decision log?

A decision record captures one decision. A decision log is the ordered collection of records, numbered in sequence. Fowler describes the log as "a valuable historic record" that explains why things turned out as they did. Superseded records stay in the log, linked to their replacements, so the history of each decision survives.

### Can I use an architecture decision record template for business decisions?

Yes, with additions. Nygard's 2011 format of title, context, decision, status and consequences carries over. Business decisions also need one named owner, an expected outcome, a falsifier with a measure, threshold, date and observer, and a check date, because commercial outcomes can be measured within a quarter and should be written back.

### How long should a decision record be?

Short. Nygard asked in 2011 for one or two pages, and Fowler's 2026 entry suggests a single page. For recurring commercial decisions, a single row of a structured table is often enough, provided the reason, falsifier and links to the sources are filled in rather than left for later.

### What happens when a decision changes?

Create a new record, link it to the old one, and set the old record's status to superseded. Record the reason for the change and its trigger: new evidence, correction of an error, or reinterpretation of the same evidence. Never edit the accepted record in place, because the change and its reason are the most useful information.

## Sources and notes

- [Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions](https://www.cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), Cognitect blog, 15 November 2011. The original ADR proposal; written for software projects.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), updated 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference; credits Nygard.
- [MADR, Markdown Architectural Decision Records](https://adr.github.io/madr), version 4.0.0, 17 September 2024. Open-source template; architecture-focused, though the project says it can be used for any decision.
- [GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/architectural-decision-record-framework/architectural-decision-record-framework), DSIT, 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard; mandated only for cross-government decisions.
- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance, Using architectural decision records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/welcome.html), March 2022. Vendor guidance for software teams.
- [Martin Fowler, Bitemporal History](https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/bitemporal-history.html), 7 April 2021. Source for the as-of and as-at distinction.
- The 18-field template, the required set, the falsifier field and the composite example are **lowob**'s working method. The example is a composite and its figures are illustrative.

# DORA and AI: What the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act Means for AI Systems

Source: https://lowob.com/research/dora-and-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: DORA regulates ICT rather than AI as such, but AI systems that EU financial entities run or buy are ICT assets and ICT services, so its rules on ICT risk management, logging, incidents, testing and third parties apply to them. The ESAs' July 2026 statement on frontier AI added no obligations but showed how supervisors read the Act. This explainer maps each DORA duty to an AI system.

DORA, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, reaches AI systems because they are ICT assets and ICT services, so since 17 January 2025 its rules on ICT risk, logging, incidents, testing and third-party contracts have applied to the AI that financial entities run or buy. The ESAs' July 2026 statement on frontier AI added guidance, not new obligations, in Goodwin's reading.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

AI governance in EU finance is usually discussed through the AI Act. For most AI systems a bank or insurer uses, DORA bites first: it already applies, it is not limited to high-risk uses, and its supervisors already examine against it. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) shows how DORA's logging duty sits beside the AI Act, FINRA and FCA expectations.

This page reads the DORA text, its logging standard and 2026 supervisory and law-firm commentary, each labelled. It is not legal advice.

## Does DORA apply to AI systems?

Yes, through its definitions rather than by name. DORA regulates ICT risk, and Article 3 defines ICT services as "digital and data services provided through ICT systems to one or more internal or external users on an ongoing basis." A model hosted by a vendor and called through an API is an ICT service. An agent running on the firm's own infrastructure is an ICT asset.

Practitioners read it the same way. Writing on PayTechLaw on 7 September 2026, Josefine Spengler of Annerton argued that cyber threats amplified by frontier AI "do not constitute a separate new category of risk outside DORA." Goodwin's 6 August 2026 alert reads the ESAs' July statement as showing how regulators expect financial entities to assess frontier AI models used in their ICT services.

## What does DORA require for an AI system?

The same as for any ICT system, applied to the features AI adds: changing models, vendor dependencies and outputs that are hard to trace. The table maps the main articles.

| DORA duty | Article | What it says | What it means for an AI system |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Management responsibility | 5(2)(a) | The management body bears "the ultimate responsibility for managing the financial entity's ICT risk" | AI risk sits with the board, not only with a data science team |
| ICT risk framework | 6(1), 6(5) | "Sound, comprehensive and well-documented", reviewed "at least once a year" | AI systems belong in the documented framework and its annual review |
| Identification and inventory | 8(1), 8(4), 8(6) | Identify and document ICT-supported functions and assets; "maintain relevant inventories" | Every model, agent and AI feature is inventoried with the function it supports |
| Change management | 9(4)(e) | "Documented policies, procedures and controls for ICT change management" | Model, prompt and permission changes are recorded, tested and approved |
| Logging | RTS 2024/1774 Art. 12 | Logging procedures; tamper protection; clock synchronisation; risk-based retention | Agent actions and access events logged in protected storage with reliable timestamps |
| Incident management | 17(1), 17(2) | "Record all ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats" | AI malfunctions that disrupt services are recorded as ICT incidents |
| Major incident reporting | 18(1), 19(1) | Classify incidents by impact; report major ones "to the relevant competent authority" | An AI failure that meets the thresholds is reported like any other |
| Third-party risk | 28(1), 28(3) | Entity stays "fully responsible"; keeps "a register of information" on all ICT contracts | AI vendors and model APIs appear in the register |
| Contract terms | 30(2), 30(3) | Service descriptions, data locations, termination rights; audit rights and exit plans for critical functions | AI contracts carry the same clauses as cloud contracts |

Article 4 applies all of this proportionately, by size, risk profile and the nature and complexity of the entity's services.

## Is an AI model provider an ICT third-party service provider?

Usually yes, when the financial entity uses its service on an ongoing basis. That brings the vendor into the Article 28(3) register "in relation to all contractual arrangements on the use of ICT services", and its contract under Article 30.

For services supporting critical or important functions, Article 30(3) requires "unrestricted rights of access, inspection and audit" for the entity and its supervisor, and "exit strategies, in particular the establishment of a mandatory adequate transition period." Goodwin expects AI providers to face questions on model governance, limitations and failure modes, incident reporting, subcontractors and continuity, resembling cloud outsourcing due diligence.

The largest providers may also be overseen directly. The ESAs published their designation of critical ICT third-party providers on 18 November 2025.

## What did the ESAs say about AI in 2026?

They asked for governance and resilience, not new rules. On 31 July 2026 the EBA, EIOPA and ESMA issued a joint statement calling for a "cross-sectoral, risk-based and consistent supervisory approach" to ICT risks from frontier AI models. The press release describes it as a basis for dialogue between firms and supervisors.

Goodwin reads the statement as encouraging three strategies. Prevention includes up-to-date inventories of IT assets, including AI and machine learning components. Detection includes continuous monitoring. Management includes resilience testing and keeping management accountable. PayTechLaw reports that AI risks are being added to the methodology for overseeing critical providers, with a view to 2027 examinations.

## How does DORA logging fit with AI Act logging?

They stack. Article 12 of Delegated Regulation 2024/1774 requires financial entities to "develop, document, and implement logging procedures, protocols and tools." They must log access, change management, ICT operations and network traffic. Logs must be protected "against tampering, deletion, and unauthorised access", a "failure of logging systems" must be detectable, and clocks must be synchronised to a reliable reference. Retention is set from business and information security objectives and the ICT risk assessment.

The AI Act's Articles 19(2) and 26(6) send high-risk system logs into the documentation kept under financial services law. In our reading, a bank's AI logs should therefore meet DORA's protection and timing rules even where the AI Act's six-month floor is the only explicit period. Our explainer [EU AI Act logging requirements](https://lowob.com/research/eu-ai-act-logging-requirements/) covers the AI Act side.

## Where should a financial firm start?

With the inventory and the register, because every other DORA duty depends on knowing what exists. Three steps cover most of the gap:

1. **Inventory every AI asset and service.** Include features vendors have added to existing software, and the business function each supports.
2. **Put AI changes through change management.** A new model version or system prompt is a change, and Article 9(4)(e) expects it documented, tested and approved.
3. **Review AI contracts against Article 30.** Check audit rights, data locations, incident notice and exit terms, starting with vendors supporting critical or important functions.

Our ranking of [AI governance and audit-trail tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/) covers platforms that hold the inventory side.

## lowob takeaways

- **DORA already covers AI.** AI systems are ICT assets and services, so the Act has applied to them since 17 January 2025.
- **Responsibility does not transfer.** Article 28(1) keeps the financial entity fully responsible when it buys AI from vendors.
- **Logs need integrity, not just content.** The logging standard demands tamper protection, failure detection and synchronised clocks.
- **Start with the inventory.** Article 8 inventories and the Article 28 register decide what the rest of DORA reaches.

## Common questions

### Does DORA apply to artificial intelligence?

Yes. DORA governs ICT risk, ICT assets and ICT services, and AI models, agents and model APIs used by financial entities fall within those definitions on our reading and that of 2026 law-firm commentary. Its rules on risk management, inventories, change management, logging, incidents, testing and third-party contracts have applied to them since 17 January 2025.

### Are AI vendors ICT third-party service providers under DORA?

Usually. A vendor that provides digital and data services through ICT systems on an ongoing basis, such as a hosted model or AI assistant, is an ICT third-party service provider. Its contract belongs in the Article 28(3) register of information and must carry the Article 30 terms, with audit rights and exit strategies where it supports critical or important functions.

### How long must logs be kept under DORA?

DORA's logging standard, Article 12 of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774, sets no fixed period. Financial entities set retention from their business and information security objectives and ICT risk assessment. Logs must be protected against tampering, deletion and unauthorised access, logging failures must be detectable, and system clocks must be synchronised to a documented reliable time source.

### What did the ESAs say about frontier AI and DORA in 2026?

On 31 July 2026 the EBA, EIOPA and ESMA issued a joint statement calling for a cross-sectoral, risk-based and consistent supervisory approach to ICT risks from frontier AI models, and for sound governance and risk management at financial entities. Goodwin reads it as creating no new legal obligations but signalling how supervisors expect AI-related ICT risk to be assessed.

# Enterprise AI Adoption Statistics 2026

Source: https://lowob.com/research/enterprise-ai-adoption-statistics-2026/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most large organisations now use AI somewhere, and fewer than half say it is scaling across the enterprise. Government data shows far lower use across all US businesses, rising sharply with firm size and concentrated in information and finance. Returns lag adoption: McKinsey finds 37% attributing any EBIT impact to AI. Every figure here carries its source, sample and date.

Nearly nine in ten respondents to McKinsey's 2026 survey say their organisations regularly use AI in at least one function, but only 44% say AI is scaling across the enterprise, and the US Census Bureau puts current use at 17% to 20% of US businesses. Adoption rises steeply with company size and is concentrated in information and finance. Measured returns trail far behind use.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This page collects the enterprise AI adoption statistics most cited in 2026, each with its source, sample and date. It is the wider context for our hub piece, [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/): agents are arriving inside companies whose general AI use is broad but often shallow. For agent-specific figures, see [AI Agent Statistics 2026](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agent-statistics-2026/).

The figures disagree because they measure different populations. A survey of large-company executives and a government sample of all US employers will never give the same answer, and neither is wrong.

## What are the key enterprise AI adoption statistics for 2026?

The table below is the reference set, quoted as published.

| US workers who do not use AI much or at all in their job | 65% | Pew Research Center | September 2025 |
| Companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production | 42%, up from 17% | S&P Global, 451 Research, 1,006 respondents | Fielded October to November 2024 |

## What percentage of companies use AI in 2026?

Anywhere from 19.8% to nearly nine in ten, depending on who is asked. The Census Bureau's sample of US employers gives 19.8% as of May 2026; McKinsey's sample of organisations already engaged with AI gives nearly nine in ten.

Ramp's figure sits between the two because it measures something different: a positive transaction for an AI product in a month. Ramp notes that free tools and employees' personal accounts do not show up, so its 56.8% likely understates use among its customers. Menlo's 65% comes from its survey of US enterprise AI decision-makers.

| Source | Population | What counts as adoption |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US Census Bureau BTOS | US employer businesses of all sizes | The business reports using AI |
| McKinsey State of AI | Respondents across 97 countries, 36% at $1bn+ firms | Regular use in at least one business function |
| Ramp AI Index | US businesses on Ramp's platform | A paid AI transaction in the month |
| Menlo Ventures | US enterprise AI decision-makers | Enterprise adoption, as defined by the investor |
| Pew Research Center | US workers | At least some of their own work done with AI |

## Does company size change AI adoption?

Yes, sharply in government data and less so in spending data. The Census Bureau found 37% of firms with 250 or more employees using AI against under 20% of firms with four or fewer.

McKinsey sees the same gradient in depth: 54% of respondents at $1 billion-plus organisations report enterprise-wide scaling, against one-third at smaller ones. Ramp's October 2026 data is the exception, with mid-market (66.7%) and SMB (63.2%) customers ahead of enterprise (59.0%). Ramp's sample is its own customers, so this is not a national picture.

## Which industries use AI the most?

Information and finance lead. As of 3 May 2026 the Census Bureau put AI use at 39.7% in the information sector and 33.9% in finance and insurance, against 19.8% nationally and about 14% in retail trade. Use in the two leading sectors did not change significantly between December 2025 and May 2026.

## How many employees use AI at work?

Fewer than company figures suggest. Pew's September 2025 survey found 21% of US workers doing at least some of their work with AI, while 65% said they do not use AI much or at all in their job.

Among large companies the shift in 2026 was rapid. KPMG's US leaders reported significant workforce adoption at 44% in Q3 2026, up from 10% a year earlier. Zapier's March 2026 survey found 94% of large US organisations using AI in some capacity, alongside 77% calling workforce AI skills an urgent need. Both are self-reports by executives, not usage logs.

## Is enterprise AI adoption producing returns?

For a minority. McKinsey found 37% of respondents attributing any EBIT impact to AI in 2026, essentially unchanged from 2025, and about 6% qualifying as high performers. KPMG's global survey found only 12% consistently assessing AI value against cost.

What separates the high performers is not access to tools. McKinsey reports that nearly three-quarters of them have fundamentally redesigned workflows, against one-quarter of other respondents. Our guide [How to Measure AI ROI](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-measure-ai-roi/) sets out a method for a mid-size firm, and [Which AI Assistant, Which Seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/) covers the first purchase decision.

## lowob takeaways

- **Quote the population with the figure.** 19.8% of US businesses and nearly nine in ten McKinsey respondents are both correct.
- **Size is the strongest predictor.** Census data shows 37% of firms with 250+ employees using AI, against 19.8% nationally.
- **Use is broad, scale is not.** 44% of McKinsey respondents report enterprise-wide scaling, and only 37% attribute any EBIT impact to AI.
- **Workflow redesign marks the leaders.** High performers redesign how work is done, not only which tools are licensed.

## Common questions

### What percentage of companies use AI in 2026?

The US Census Bureau put current AI use at 19.8% of US businesses as of 3 May 2026. McKinsey's August 2026 survey found nearly nine in ten respondents' organisations regularly using AI in at least one function. Ramp found 56.8% of businesses on its platform paying for AI in October 2026. The gap reflects who was sampled, not a contradiction.

### What percentage of large companies use AI?

The Census Bureau found 37% of US firms with 250 or more employees using AI in the period to May 2026. Among McKinsey's respondents, 54% of those at organisations with $1 billion or more in revenue reported enterprise-wide scaling of AI, against one-third at smaller organisations. Menlo Ventures reported enterprise adoption rising from 55% to 65%.

### Which industries have the highest AI adoption?

In US government data, the information sector leads at 39.7% of businesses using AI as of 3 May 2026, followed by finance and insurance at 33.9%. The national rate was 19.8%, and retail trade was about 14%. These figures come from the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey.

### Is AI adoption delivering ROI for companies?

For a minority so far. McKinsey's 2026 survey found 37% of respondents attributing any EBIT impact to AI, essentially unchanged from 2025, and about 6% qualifying as high performers with at least 5% of EBIT from AI. KPMG found only 12% of global leaders consistently assessing AI value against cost in Q3 2026.

# Enterprise Brain vs Knowledge Base: What Is the Difference?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/enterprise-brain-vs-knowledge-base/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A knowledge base stores and retrieves documented answers. An enterprise brain is the whole loop: store, wiring, a record of decisions with reasons and owners, reasoning by models and agents, and outcomes written back. A knowledge base is part of the store and wiring. The difference shows when an AI agent must tell a current decision from a superseded one.

A knowledge base stores and retrieves documented answers to known questions; an enterprise brain is the whole loop of store, wiring, decision record, reasoning and learning, in which a knowledge base is only part of the store and the wiring. A knowledge base tells people and agents what is documented. The brain also records what the company decided, why, who owns it, whether it still stands and whether it worked.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

The two are often sold as one; **lowob**'s position, argued in [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/), is that no single product is the brain. A knowledge base is a valuable component. Calling it the brain hides the part a company has to build for itself.

## What is a knowledge base?

A knowledge base is a curated collection of documented answers, such as how-to articles, policies, product facts and FAQs, organised so people and AI tools can find them. It answers "how do we do this?" and "what is true about this?"

The most developed practice comes from customer service. The Consortium for Service Innovation's Knowledge-Centered Service (KCS) v6 guide organises the work in two loops. The Solve Loop, "the reactive process," has four practices: capture, structure, reuse and improve. The Evolve Loop, "the reflective and continuous improvement process," covers content health, process integration, performance assessment, and leadership and communication. Its core idea is that articles improve through use: "reuse is review."

AI assistants now read knowledge bases directly. Microsoft's guidance on optimising SharePoint content for its Employee Self-Service agents, last updated 3 November 2026, asks for versioning so that "only the latest approved version is visible to end users," and asks teams to archive duplicates so "only one authoritative copy exists." That is the knowledge base model at its best: one current answer per question.

## What is an enterprise brain?

An enterprise brain is the system that lets a company's people and AI agents act on what the company knows, has decided and has learned. It is a loop of five parts, set out in the [enterprise brain explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/): store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning.

The term is also a product name. CMSWire reported on 9 September 2026 that WRITER's Enterprise Brain is "a governed, universal context layer that dynamically captures brand knowledge, decision logic" and live business data, available in early access. That describes the wiring, with some stored guidance. The record of which decision replaced which, and the outcomes written back, remain the company's job.

## What is the difference between an enterprise brain and a knowledge base?

A knowledge base answers what is documented; an enterprise brain also answers what was decided, whether it still stands and whether it worked. The table sets the two side by side.

| Dimension | Knowledge base | Enterprise brain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | An article or answer | A decision record, plus the sources and articles it links to |
| Question it answers | How do we do this? What is true? | What did we decide, why, who owns it, is it current, did it work? |
| How it changes | Articles are edited to stay current | Decisions are superseded; the old record stays, linked to the new |
| History | Version history, rarely read | Supersession chain with date, author, reason and trigger |
| Who writes | Knowledge workers and support staff | Decision owners, at the moment of decision |
| Outcome | Not tracked, beyond article usage | Expected outcome, falsifier and check date; result written back |
| Success measure | Findability, reuse, deflected tickets | Fewer repeated mistakes and re-made decisions |
| Place in the loop | Part of the store and the wiring | All five parts: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning |
| Own or rent | Mostly rented software, owned content | Rent the wiring and models; own the record |

The sharpest line is the change rule: a knowledge base that keeps only the latest approved version is doing its job. A decision record that keeps only the latest version has lost the most useful thing it held: why the company changed its mind. [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) makes the case.

## Where does a knowledge base fit inside the brain?

It sits in the store and the wiring. Articles are part of what the company knows; the search, connectors and permissions that serve them to an assistant are wiring.

| Brain part | What the knowledge base contributes | What it does not supply |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Store | Curated, current articles and policies | Transcripts, deals and the raw sources behind decisions |
| Wiring | Search, metadata, permission-aware retrieval | Shared definitions across systems, unless maintained |
| Record | Links to decisions, if someone adds them | The decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date and falsifier |
| Reasoning | Grounding material for models and agents | Judgment about which precedent applies |
| Learning | Usage signals, such as reuse counts | Outcomes written back against each decision |

## When is a knowledge base enough?

When the questions are stable "how do I" questions and few of them depend on a decision that might change. Product documentation, IT help and HR policy often fit.

Size changes the engineering too. Anthropic noted on 19 September 2024 that if a knowledge base is "smaller than 200,000 tokens (about 500 pages of material)," it can sometimes be placed in the prompt whole, without a retrieval system. The record question remains: a 400-page policy library still needs to say which pricing rule replaced which.

The brain becomes necessary where decisions recur, change and carry money: discounts, pricing exceptions, product claims, partner terms. Those are on the commercial line, which is why **lowob** starts there, as set out in [Why the brain starts at the commercial line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/).

## Why does the difference matter for AI agents?

Because agents fail more often by misreading what they find than by failing to find it. A knowledge base improves finding; a decision record improves reading.

The MemTrace benchmark, posted to arXiv on 15 June 2026, tested 13 memory-system configurations and found that "the dominant bottleneck is evidence use, not retrieval." When an agent finds an old product deck, a meeting summary and a new FAQ, it needs a status field to know which one stands. Gartner's survey of 1,203 data management leaders, fielded in July 2024 and published on 26 February 2025, found 63% of organisations either did not have or were unsure they had the right data management practices for AI. It predicted that through 2026 organisations would abandon 60% of AI projects unsupported by AI-ready data. That is an analyst forecast, not a measured outcome.

## lowob takeaways

- **A knowledge base is a component.** It covers part of the store and the wiring.
- **The brain adds the record.** Decisions with reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date and falsifier.
- **Edit articles; supersede decisions.** The change rule is the clearest difference.
- **Start where decisions recur.** The commercial line shows the difference within a quarter.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an enterprise brain and a knowledge base?

A knowledge base stores documented answers and keeps them current by editing. An enterprise brain is a loop of store, wiring, decision record, reasoning and learning. It records what the company decided, why, who owns it, whether it still stands and what happened, and supersedes rather than edits. A knowledge base is one part of the store and wiring.

### Is an enterprise brain just a knowledge base with AI?

No. Adding an AI assistant to a knowledge base improves how answers are found and phrased, but the assistant still cannot tell which decision is current, who approved it or whether it worked unless those are recorded. The enterprise brain adds decision records and outcomes written back, which no search layer can generate from documents alone.

### Do I need a knowledge base before building an enterprise brain?

You need a usable store, and a knowledge base is often the cleanest part of it. But the brain can start without a large one. Begin with one recurring commercial decision, record each instance with its reason, owner, expected outcome and check date, and link to whatever sources exist. The knowledge base can grow alongside the record.

### What is a knowledge base in AI?

A collection of documents and articles that an AI system retrieves from to ground its answers, usually through search or retrieval-augmented generation. Its quality depends on having one current, authoritative copy of each answer, good structure and metadata, and permissions that match who should see what. It holds what is documented, not why decisions were made.

Pick one policy in your knowledge base that has changed in the last year, such as a discount rule. Check whether anyone can find what it replaced, when and why. If not, write the decision record for the current version this week.

# EU AI Act Logging Requirements: Articles 12, 19 and 26 Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/eu-ai-act-logging-requirements/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Article 12 of the EU AI Act requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically over their lifetime; Articles 19 and 26 require providers and deployers to keep those logs for at least six months, and financial institutions to hold them within their financial services documentation. The Digital Omnibus moved the start date for Annex III systems to 2 December 2027 but left the logging text unchanged.

Under the EU AI Act, Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to record events automatically over their lifetime, and Articles 19 and 26 require providers and deployers to keep those logs for at least six months. Financial institutions keep them within their financial services documentation. For Annex III systems such as credit scoring, the duties apply from 2 December 2027.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

The EU AI Act's logging rules are short, and most of the work they create is design work. The Act says what logs are for and how long to keep them; it leaves most of the content to the provider. This explainer reads the three articles closely and shows what they mean for a bank or insurer. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) sets these duties against FINRA, SEC, FCA and DORA expectations.

This page quotes the Commission's consolidated text and labelled secondary readings. It is not legal advice.

## Which EU AI Act articles cover logging?

Three articles. Article 12 sets the technical capability, Article 19 sets the provider's retention duty and Article 26 sets the deployer's.

| Article | Who it binds | What it requires | Retention | Financial institutions |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 12 Record-keeping | The high-risk system, and so its provider at the design stage | Automatic event logs over the system's lifetime, sufficient for traceability "appropriate to the intended purpose" | Not set here | No special rule |
| 19 Automatically generated logs | Providers | Keep logs generated by their systems "to the extent such logs are under their control" | At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise | Keep logs "as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law" |
| 26(6) Obligations of deployers | Deployers | Keep logs generated by the system, where under their control | At least six months, unless other law provides otherwise | Keep logs within the documentation required by financial services law |
| 26(5) Obligations of deployers | Deployers | Monitor operation against the instructions for use; report risks and serious incidents | Not applicable | Monitoring duty treated as met by complying with financial services governance rules |
| 18 Documentation keeping | Providers | Keep technical, quality and conformity documentation | 10 years after placing on the market | Keep technical documentation within financial services documentation |

## What does Article 12 require?

It requires a capability, not a log format. Article 12(1) says high-risk systems "shall technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system."

Article 12(2) says the logging must ensure "a level of traceability of the functioning" that is "appropriate to the intended purpose of the system." It must record events relevant for:

- "identifying situations that may result in the high-risk AI system presenting a risk" under Article 79(1), "or in a substantial modification";
- "facilitating the post-market monitoring referred to in Article 72"; and
- "monitoring the operation of high-risk AI systems referred to in Article 26(5)."

Article 72 adds context: providers must "actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data" on performance over the system's lifetime, including, where relevant, "interaction with other AI systems."

## What must the logs contain?

For most financial uses, the Act sets no field list. Article 12(3) lists minimum contents only for remote biometric identification systems under Annex III point 1(a): the period of each use, the reference database checked, the input data that matched, and the people who verified the results.

A creditworthiness system under Annex III point 5(b) gets the purposes in Article 12(2) and nothing more specific. The provider has to decide which events show a risk situation, support post-market monitoring and let the deployer monitor operation. In our reading, that usually means each run's inputs, model version, output, the human who acted on it and any override.

Standards may fill the gap later. The only harmonised standard published so far, EN 18286 on 14 October 2026, covers quality management, according to Orrick's 27 October reading; record-keeping and logging is one of ten areas in the Commission's standardisation request. VDE described ISO/IEC 24970, AI system logging, as a draft standard under development in December 2025. Our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/) gives a field list that covers the Article 12 purposes.

## How long must AI Act logs be kept?

At least six months, and often longer. Articles 19(1) and 26(6) both set a period "appropriate to the intended purpose of the high-risk AI system, of at least six months, unless provided otherwise in the applicable Union or national law, in particular in Union law on the protection of personal data."

That clause cuts both ways. Sector rules may require longer retention, and data protection law may require deletion or minimisation. A log that stores full customer inputs needs a retention rule and a deletion rule, agreed with the data protection officer.

## What changes for banks and insurers?

Their logs move into the documentation they already keep. Article 19(2) says providers that are financial institutions "shall maintain the logs automatically generated by their high-risk AI systems as part of the documentation kept under the relevant financial services law." Article 26(6) says the same for deployers.

Two further provisions matter. Under Article 26(5), a financial institution deployer's monitoring duty is treated as fulfilled by complying with its governance arrangements under financial services law. Under Article 72(4), providers that are financial institutions may integrate post-market monitoring for Annex III point 5 systems into their existing arrangements. In practice the AI Act floor of six months sits beneath longer sector periods.

The high-risk uses most likely in finance are Annex III point 5(b), systems "to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score", excluding fraud detection, and point 5(c), risk assessment and pricing for natural persons "in the case of life and health insurance."

## When do the logging duties apply?

From 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026 and entered into force on 27 July 2026, according to White & Case.

The Omnibus moved dates, not logging text. The Commission's AI Act Service Desk marks Omnibus changes as NEW or AMENDED; none appears on Articles 12, 19 or 26 in the consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. By contrast, Article 11 on technical documentation carries an amendment marker, and White & Case notes that the Omnibus extended SME relief such as simplified technical documentation. Our [EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) sets out the full timetable.

## lowob takeaways

- **Article 12 sets purposes, not fields.** Outside remote biometric identification, the provider designs what the log records.
- **Six months is a floor.** Sector rules usually require longer; data protection law may require less personal data.
- **Financial firms fold logs into existing records.** Articles 19(2) and 26(6) route logs into financial services documentation.
- **The dates moved; the text did not.** Annex III duties apply from 2 December 2027 with the logging articles unchanged.

## Common questions

### What does Article 12 of the EU AI Act require?

Article 12 requires high-risk AI systems to technically allow automatic recording of events, or logs, over their lifetime. The logs must give traceability appropriate to the system's purpose and record events relevant to identifying risk situations or substantial modifications, supporting post-market monitoring under Article 72, and letting deployers monitor operation under Article 26(5). Specific minimum fields apply only to remote biometric identification.

### How long must AI logs be kept under the EU AI Act?

Providers under Article 19 and deployers under Article 26(6) must keep logs under their control for a period appropriate to the system's intended purpose, of at least six months, unless other EU or national law provides otherwise, in particular data protection law. Financial institutions keep the logs as part of the documentation required by EU financial services law.

### When do EU AI Act logging requirements apply to credit scoring?

From 2 December 2027. The Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026 and moved Annex III high-risk obligations, which include creditworthiness evaluation and credit scoring of natural persons, to that date. The Commission's consolidated text shows no amendments to the logging duties in Articles 12, 19 and 26.

### Do deployers have to keep AI Act logs?

Yes, for high-risk systems. Article 26(6) requires deployers to keep logs automatically generated by the system, to the extent the logs are under their control, for at least six months unless other law provides otherwise. Deployers must also monitor operation against the provider's instructions and inform the provider and authorities of risks and serious incidents.

## Sources and notes

- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 19](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-19), [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26), [Article 18](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-18), [Article 72](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-72), [Article 11](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-11) and [Annex III](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3), as at 27 July 2026.
