# FINRA and AI in 2026: What Broker-Dealers Must Record and Supervise

Source: https://lowob.com/research/finra-ai-guidance-2026/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: FINRA has no AI-specific rule. Its technology-neutral rules on supervision, communications and books and records apply to AI tools, and its 2026 oversight report added a section on AI agents with seven named risks. This explainer maps the rules to the records a broker-dealer should keep, the retention periods, and the rule changes in progress.

FINRA has no AI-specific rule; it applies its technology-neutral rules, so broker-dealers must supervise AI use under Rule 3110 and keep AI-related books and records under Rule 4511 and SEA Rule 17a-4. Its 2026 oversight report adds that firms using agents should consider how to track agent actions and decisions.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Broker-dealers ask the same question about every AI tool: what does FINRA expect us to keep, and who must check it? The answer comes from rules written long before generative AI, read through FINRA's recent reports and notices. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) compares FINRA with US bank, UK and EU expectations.

This page summarises FINRA and SEC texts and one law-firm summary, each labelled. It is not legal advice.

## What does FINRA say about AI in 2026?

FINRA says its rules "continue to apply when firms use GenAI or similar technologies." The 2026 oversight report's generative AI section, released on 9 December 2025 according to Debevoise & Plimpton, is the main statement of what examiners will look at.

The report defines AI agents as "systems or programs that are capable of autonomously performing and completing tasks on behalf of a user." It lists seven risks: autonomy, scope and authority, auditability and transparency, data sensitivity, domain knowledge, rewards and reinforcement, and the general risks of generative AI such as bias, hallucination and privacy. On auditability it warns that "complicated, multi-step agent reasoning tasks can make outcomes difficult to trace or explain."

The report then lists considerations for firms using agents:

- "how to monitor agent system access and data handling;"
- where to place human-in-the-loop oversight;
- "how to track agent actions and decisions;" and
- how to set guardrails "to limit or restrict agent behaviors, actions or decisions."

These are considerations, not rule text. They show what an examiner is likely to ask.

## Which FINRA and SEC rules apply to AI tools?

Supervision, communications and books-and-records rules apply, because they are technology-neutral. Regulatory Notice 24-09 states that FINRA's rules apply to AI "just as they apply when member firms use any other technology or tool."

| Rule | What it requires | What it means for an AI tool | Retention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FINRA Rule 3110 (Supervision) | "A reasonably designed supervisory system tailored to its business" | Written procedures covering AI use, review points and escalation | Per the records it produces |
| FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications) | Content standards for communications with the public | Apply to AI-drafted communications as to human ones | Per SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) |
| FINRA Rule 4511 (Books and records) | Make and preserve records required by FINRA and Exchange Act rules | Records created by or about AI use fall within it where a rule requires them | At least six years where no other period applies |
| SEA Rule 17a-4(a) | Core records | AI involvement does not change the record class | At least six years, first two easily accessible |
| SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) | Communications "relating to its business as such" | AI-drafted emails, chats and messages sent or received | At least three years |
| SEA Rule 17a-4(f) | Electronic storage standards | Logs and records held in a time-stamped audit-trail system or non-rewriteable storage | Applies for the full period |

## What must broker-dealers record when they use AI?

At a minimum, the records any rule already requires, plus the evidence that supervision worked. The 2026 report's generative AI practices go further, naming prompt and output logs and the model version used.

Three record types matter most:

- **Communications.** An AI-drafted message sent to a customer is a communication like any other. SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) covers originals received and copies sent that relate to the firm's "business as such."
- **Supervisory evidence.** Rule 3110 requires a supervisory system. For AI, the evidence is who reviewed an output, what they saw and what they did. Notice 26-14 would add a duty to keep evidence that supervisory procedures were implemented and provide it on request.
- **Agent activity.** The report's question on tracking agent actions and decisions implies a log of each tool call and decision, joined to the request and the approval.

Some questions remain open. In Regulatory Notice 25-07 of 14 April 2025, FINRA asked "what are members' recordkeeping challenges regarding AI-generated communications", naming chatbot communications and transcripts. It noted that "business as such" is not defined in the rule. Our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/) sets out the fields that cover all three record types.

## How long must AI records be kept?

Usually three or six years, depending on the record type. Rule 4511(b) sets "at least six years" for FINRA records with no specified period. SEA Rule 17a-4(a) sets six years for core records, the first two in an easily accessible place. Rule 17a-4(b) sets three years for communications.

Format matters as much as duration. Under Rule 17a-4(f)(2), an electronic recordkeeping system must either keep a complete, time-stamped audit trail of modifications and deletions, with the identity of the person acting, or keep records "exclusively in a non-rewriteable, non-erasable format." It must also be able to download records and their audit trails in human-readable and usable electronic formats. A prompt log in an editable application table meets neither test.

## How should firms supervise AI agents?

By deciding in advance where a person approves, what the agent may touch, and how its actions are logged. The 2026 report's considerations map onto three controls: access and data-handling monitoring, human-in-the-loop review at defined points, and guardrails that restrict agent actions.

Debevoise & Plimpton's 12 December 2025 summary adds practical steps drawn from the report: formal review and approval processes combining business and technology expertise, documenting generative AI tools across their lifecycle, structured pre-deployment testing and ongoing monitoring. **lowob**'s rule that nothing sends without a person is one way to set the review point; our explainer [What is an approval gate?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) shows where the reviewer's action is captured.

## What is changing in FINRA's rules?

Two proposals bear on AI. Regulatory Notice 26-14, published on 9 July 2026 with comments due by 11 September 2026, proposes replacing Rule 2210's principal pre-use approval of retail communications with risk-based supervisory standards. FINRA says that "applying the principal pre-use approval requirement to AI-generated retail communications can be challenging", and that generative AI tools may form part of a supervisory system "provided they are vetted, tested and monitored."

The notice also states that "members are responsible for their communications, regardless of whether they are generated by a human or AI technology." Notice 25-07, the 2025 request for comment on modernising workplace rules, asked about recordkeeping for AI-generated communications. Neither has produced a final rule change that we could find by mid-November 2026.

## lowob takeaways

- **No AI rule, all the old ones.** Supervision, communications and books-and-records rules apply to AI as to any tool.
- **Track agent actions.** FINRA's 2026 report names auditability as an agent risk and asks how firms track actions and decisions.
- **Keep prompts, outputs and versions.** The report suggests prompt and output logs and a record of which model version was used.
- **Store them properly.** SEA Rule 17a-4(f) requires an audit-trailed or non-rewriteable system for electronic records.

## Common questions

### Does FINRA have rules specifically for AI?

No. FINRA states that its rules are intended to be technologically neutral and continue to apply when firms use generative AI. Supervision under Rule 3110, communications under Rule 2210 and books and records under Rule 4511 all apply. Its 2026 oversight report and Regulatory Notice 24-09 explain how examiners read those rules for AI tools and agents.

### What does FINRA's 2026 report say about AI agents?

The 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report, released on 9 December 2025, defines AI agents as systems that autonomously perform tasks for a user. It lists seven risks, including autonomy, acting beyond authority and difficulty tracing multi-step reasoning, and asks firms to consider how they monitor agent access, place human oversight, track agent actions and decisions, and restrict agent behaviour.

### Do AI-generated communications need to be retained by broker-dealers?

Yes, where they relate to the firm's business. SEA Rule 17a-4(b)(4) requires originals of communications received and copies of communications sent relating to the firm's business as such to be kept for at least three years. FINRA states that firms are responsible for communications whether a human or AI technology generated them.

### How long must broker-dealers keep AI logs?

It depends on what the log is. Records required by FINRA rules with no specified period are kept for at least six years under Rule 4511. Core records under SEA Rule 17a-4(a) are kept six years and communications three years. Electronic records must sit in an audit-trailed or non-rewriteable system under Rule 17a-4(f).

- [FINRA, Regulatory Notice 24-09](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/24-09), 27 June 2024. Primary; technology neutrality, Rules 3110 and 2210.
- [FINRA, Regulatory Notice 26-14](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/26-14), 9 July 2026. Primary; proposal and request for comment, not a final rule.
- [FINRA, Regulatory Notice 25-07](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/notices/25-07), 14 April 2025. Primary; request for comment, including AI-generated communications.

# How Much Does an AI Agent Cost? Build, Buy and Run Costs in 2026

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Published agent prices run from $0.10 per action to $125 per user per month, and from $0.99 per outcome for support agents. A self-built agent's token bill is usually small; human review, retries and engineering time are not. The number to budget on is cost per successful task, including the people who check the work.

An AI agent costs from about $0.10 per action to $125 per user per month to buy, on Salesforce's list prices checked 16 November 2026; running your own can cost tens of dollars a month in tokens, plus far more in human review. The price on the page is rarely the largest cost. Budget on cost per successful task, with review time included.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This page prices one agent. The choice of pricing model (seats, usage or outcomes) is set out in **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), and the token arithmetic in [what AI inference cost is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/). Here the question is narrower: what one agent will cost you a month, bought or built.

## How much does an AI agent cost per month?

For a team handling 2,000 conversations a month, Salesforce's published units put a bought agent at $800 to $4,000 a month, before review time. The table below shows the unit prices that drive that range.

| Product | Billing unit | Published price | Source and date checked |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce Agentforce add-ons (Sales, Service, Field Service, Operations) | Per user per month, unmetered employee use | $125; Industries add-ons $150 | Salesforce pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Salesforce Agentforce Max Edition | Per user per month, with credits | From $550, including 2.75 million Flex Credits per org per year | Salesforce pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Salesforce Flex Credits | Per action | $500 per 100,000 credits; 20 credits per action, 30 per voice action | Salesforce pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Salesforce Conversations | Per conversation | $2 | Salesforce pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Intercom Fin | Per outcome | From $0.99 | Intercom pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Microsoft Copilot Studio | Credit capacity pack | $200 per pack of 25,000 Copilot Credits per month | Microsoft Copilot Studio pricing page, 16 November 2026 |
| Anthropic Claude Managed Agents | Session runtime, plus tokens | $0.08 per session-hour while running | Anthropic API pricing page, 16 November 2026 |

On Salesforce's own rates, 20 credits at $0.005 each is $0.10 per action and 30 credits is $0.15 per voice action. An agent that handles 2,000 support conversations a month would cost $4,000 at $2 a conversation, or $800 under Flex Credits if each conversation takes four actions. Salesforce's page also says Flex Credits and Conversations "will not be supported in the same org", so the unit is a one-way choice per org.

## What does it cost to run an AI agent you build yourself?

The model bill for a self-built agent is usually small; the review bill is not. The example below is illustrative and uses Anthropic's list prices checked on 16 November 2026.

Assume a follow-up drafting agent that runs 500 times a month, takes 8 model steps per run, reads 10,000 input tokens per step (8,000 of them cached instructions and account history) and writes 500 output tokens. A person spends 3 minutes checking each draft at an assumed $40 an hour.

| Line | Claude Sonnet 5.5 | Claude Haiku 5.5 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input, uncached (2,000 tokens a step) | $0.0040 per step at $2 per million | $0.0002 per step at $0.10 per million |
| Input, cached (8,000 tokens a step) | $0.0008 per step at $0.10 per million | $0.00008 per step at $0.01 per million |
| Output (500 tokens a step) | $0.0050 per step at $10 per million | $0.00025 per step at $0.50 per million |
| Model cost per run (8 steps) | $0.078 | $0.004 |
| Model cost per month (500 runs) | $39.20 | $2.12 |
| Review per month (500 runs, 3 minutes, $40 an hour) | $1,000 | $1,000 |
| Cost per successful run, if 80% are usable | $2.60 | $2.51 |

Three things follow. Review costs about 25 times the Sonnet token bill, so cutting review time matters more than switching model. The smaller model is about 18 times cheaper on tokens, but only worth it if it passes the same accuracy test. And the denominator is successful runs: a draft nobody can send still costs money. The example ignores cache-write charges and the 286 to 406 system tokens Anthropic adds when tools are used, both small at this volume.

## What does it cost to build an AI agent?

Build cost is mostly engineering time, and it repeats. Model choice, prompts, tool connections, guardrails, logging and evaluation all need maintenance as models and vendor APIs change. **lowob** does not publish a build figure because it depends on your team's rates and scope. Ask instead how many hours a month the agent will need after launch, and price those hours alongside tokens.

The evidence on build versus buy favours buying or configuring for most mid-size firms; our [build vs buy guide](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) sets out the options. Whichever route you take, Gartner's June 2025 prediction, reported by Reuters, that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of "escalating costs and unclear business value" is a warning to budget the whole cost, not the token line.

## What hidden costs should you budget for?

The costs that surprise buyers are the ones that scale with agent behaviour rather than with headcount.

| Hidden cost | Why it grows | Evidence, with date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Token growth from agent loops | Each step re-reads instructions, tools and history | Anthropic, June 2025: agents about 4 times the tokens of chat, multi-agent systems about 15 times |
| Tool charges | Search and runtime are billed beside tokens | Anthropic lists web search at $10 per 1,000 searches, 16 November 2026 |
| Unused prepaid credits | Commitments sized before usage is known | Salesforce: unused Flex Credits do not roll over, 16 November 2026 |
| Metered custom agents | Agents billed outside the seat | Microsoft lists organisation-built custom agents as metered, 16 November 2026 |
| Human review | Every unchecked error costs more later | **lowob**'s illustrative example above: 96% of monthly cost |
| Failed runs | You pay for attempts, not results | Divide by successful runs, not total runs |

Put a spend cap on each agent before it goes live. An [LLM gateway](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-llm-gateway/) can enforce caps per agent, and [prompt caching](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/) is usually the quickest saving on input tokens.

## How do you estimate an AI agent's cost before you buy?

Multiply runs by steps by tokens or actions per step, add review time, and divide by expected successful runs.

Ask each vendor for the billable event in one sentence, a sample month of usage from a customer of your size, and what happens to the bill if your volume doubles. Run 30 real cases through a trial before you commit to a prepaid amount.

## lowob takeaways

- **The list price is the smallest line.** Review time, retries and engineering hours usually cost more than tokens.
- **Units are not comparable.** Convert actions, credits and conversations into cost per successful task.
- **Model choice changes tokens, not review.** A cheaper model only helps if it passes the same quality bar.
- **Cap every agent.** Set a monthly spend limit before launch, not after the first invoice.

## Common questions

### How much does an AI agent cost per month?

On published November 2026 prices, Salesforce charges $2 per conversation, $0.10 per action under Flex Credits, or $125 per user per month for add-ons, and Intercom charges from $0.99 per outcome. For a team handling a few thousand conversations a month, that means hundreds to a few thousand dollars, before the cost of people reviewing the agent's work.

### How much does it cost to run an AI agent on an API?

Multiply tokens per step by steps per run, runs per month and the provider's per-million price. In **lowob**'s illustrative example, 500 runs a month cost $39.20 on Claude Sonnet 5.5 and $2.12 on Claude Haiku 5.5 at Anthropic's November 2026 list prices. Review time added $1,000, far more than either token bill.

### Is it cheaper to build or buy an AI agent?

For most firms of 20 to 500 people, buying or configuring is cheaper once engineering and maintenance hours are counted. Building gives control of logic and data but adds recurring work as models and APIs change. Compare both on cost per successful task, including review, over twelve months rather than on the first invoice.

### What are the hidden costs of AI agents?

Token growth from multi-step loops, separately billed tools such as web search, prepaid credits that expire unused, metered custom agents outside the seat price, failed runs and, largest of all, human review. Anthropic reported in June 2025 that agents use about 4 times the tokens of chat, so pilot volumes understate production cost.

# How to Build a Company Knowledge Base for AI

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-build-a-company-knowledge-base-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A company knowledge base for AI is a curated, permissioned set of authoritative sources that assistants and agents retrieve from. Build it around one set of recurring questions: gather one current copy of each source, structure and tag it, fix permissions before rollout, link the decision records that explain why policies are what they are, and test it against real questions before widening scope.

To build a company knowledge base for AI, choose one set of recurring questions, gather one authoritative copy of each source, remove duplicates and outdated versions, add owners, dates and metadata, fix permissions before rollout, and test answers against real questions before widening scope. Then link each policy to the decision record that explains it, because an assistant can retrieve a rule but cannot tell why it changed unless someone recorded that.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

A knowledge base is the store and part of the wiring in **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, a loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/) explains why the store is necessary and not sufficient. This guide covers building the store well, and where it has to connect to the record.

## What is a company knowledge base for AI?

It is a curated, permissioned set of authoritative documents that AI assistants and agents retrieve from to ground their answers. Unlike a file share, it has one current copy of each answer, an owner per source and usable metadata.

An [enterprise brain](https://lowob.com/research/enterprise-brain-vs-knowledge-base/) is wider: it also records what was decided, why, by whom and whether it worked.

## How do you build a company knowledge base for AI?

In seven steps, each with a test for when it is done.

| Step | What to do | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Pick the questions | List 20 to 50 real questions one team asks every week | Each question has a named person who can judge a good answer |
| 2. Gather the sources | Find the document that answers each question, and its owner | Every question maps to at least one source with an owner |
| 3. Keep one authoritative copy | Archive duplicates and outdated versions; turn on versioning | A search for each topic returns one current document |
| 4. Structure for retrieval | Summary first, consistent headings, metadata such as product, segment, owner and review date | A reader can tell the topic, owner and date in the first lines |
| 5. Fix permissions first | Review who can see what before connecting an assistant | Restricted material is invisible to unauthorised users in ordinary search |
| 6. Link the decisions | Point each policy to the decision record that set it | Each policy shows what it replaced, when and why |
| 7. Test with real questions | Run the step 1 questions; score answers; fix sources, not prompts | An agreed share of answers is correct, current and cited |

Steps 3 and 5 come before any assistant is connected, because an assistant amplifies whatever disorder the store holds.

## Which questions should a knowledge base answer first?

The ones a team asks every week, whose answers are documented and change occasionally: on the commercial line, pricing rules, approved product claims, discount policy and partner terms.

Starting narrow keeps the test honest: 20 questions with a named judge give a measurable pass rate within days. [Why the brain starts at the commercial line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/) sets out why commercial decisions are the best first scope: they recur weekly and their outcomes show within a quarter.

## How do you prepare documents so AI can use them?

Keep one current copy, put a summary first, use consistent headings and add metadata.

Microsoft's guidance for its Employee Self-Service agents, updated 3 November 2026, is specific. "A concise summary helps large language models (LLMs) quickly understand the main topic, purpose, and intended audience." "Consistent use of header styles (H1, H2, and so on) reduces confusion for both AI and human readers." It calls metadata "a proven best practice for improving both the accuracy and completeness of LLM responses." It recommends versioning so "only the latest approved version is visible," and archiving duplicates so "only one authoritative copy exists."

Retrieval design matters as much as the documents. Anthropic reported on 19 September 2024 that prepending a short explanatory context to each chunk before indexing, which it calls contextual retrieval, cut the top-20-chunk retrieval failure rate by 49% when combined with keyword search, and by 67% with reranking, in its own evaluations. The same post noted that a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, may not need retrieval at all: it can go in the prompt whole.

Anthropic's 29 September 2025 context engineering guidance adds a reason to stay lean: aim for "the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens," because recall degrades as context fills.

## How do you keep permissions intact?

Fix access in source systems first; the assistant inherits it. Microsoft describes Copilot as "grounding responses in the data users already have permission to access."

That design moves the risk: a folder overshared by mistake was once hard to find, and an assistant finds it on request. Microsoft's deployment guidance for Copilot with SharePoint Advanced Management, published 11 November 2026, starts with identifying high-risk sites and files and remediating oversharing before rollout. The [permission-aware retrieval explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/) covers how the access check works, and [The permission problem](https://lowob.com/research/the-permission-problem-when-commercial-context-leaks/) covers commercial material in particular.

## How do you keep the knowledge base current?

Give every source an owner and a review date, and let use drive improvement.

The Consortium for Service Innovation's KCS v6 guide improves knowledge "based on demand and usage with the concept 'reuse is review.'" Its techniques include "Search Early Search Often" and "Flag It or Fix It": whoever finds an article wrong either corrects it or flags it.

Articles can be edited to stay current. Decisions should not be: when a pricing rule changes, the article updates, and a new [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) supersedes the old one, with the reason and the trigger. [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) sets out the rule.

## How do you test a knowledge base for AI?

Run the step 1 questions and score each answer: correct, current and cited. Fix failures in the sources, not in the prompt.

Include questions whose answer changed recently, questions where sources conflict and at least one the knowledge base should decline. The MemTrace benchmark, posted to arXiv on 15 June 2026, found memory systems failed mostly through "evidence use, not retrieval," so a test that only checks whether the right document was found will miss the commonest failure. Gartner's 26 February 2025 release, based on a July 2024 survey of 1,203 data management leaders, treats AI-ready data as an ongoing practice, so test on a schedule, not only at launch.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with real questions.** Between 20 and 50, with a named judge, before any indexing.
- **One authoritative copy.** Versioning on, duplicates archived, owner and review date on every source.
- **Permissions before rollout.** The assistant inherits every sharing mistake.
- **Link policies to decisions.** Edit the article; supersede the decision record.

## Common questions

### How do I build a knowledge base for AI?

Choose 20 to 50 recurring questions from one team, find the source that answers each and its owner, keep one current copy with versioning, add a summary, headings and metadata, fix permissions, and test answers against the questions. Link each policy to the decision record that set it, so the assistant can explain changes as well as state rules.

### What is the best format for documents in an AI knowledge base?

Documents that start with a short summary, use consistent headings, carry metadata such as owner, product and review date, and exist as one authoritative copy. Microsoft's November 2026 guidance for SharePoint recommends exactly these, and advises keeping tables simple. Microsoft also notes its agent cannot read content in list-based accordion web parts, so check that page elements are readable.

### Do I need RAG for a company knowledge base?

Not always. Anthropic noted in September 2024 that a knowledge base under 200,000 tokens, about 500 pages, can sometimes be placed in the prompt whole, with prompt caching to reduce cost. Larger collections need retrieval, and techniques such as adding context to each chunk and reranking results reduced retrieval failures substantially on Anthropic's tests.

### How do you stop an AI assistant from exposing confidential documents?

Fix access in the source systems before connecting it. Assistants such as Microsoft 365 Copilot answer from data the user already has permission to see, so a folder overshared by mistake becomes visible on request. Review high-risk sites and files, remove broad sharing, label sensitive material, and check that restricted content stays invisible to unauthorised users.

### How often should an AI knowledge base be updated?

Continuously for content, and on a schedule for testing. Give every source an owner and a review date, apply expiry policies, and follow the KCS principle that reuse is review: whoever finds an article wrong fixes or flags it. Re-run the test questions monthly, and after any policy change, to catch answers that have gone stale.

# How to Choose an AI Agent Platform: A Buyer's Checklist

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-choose-an-ai-agent-platform/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI agent platform is the software that lets a company build, run and govern agents. Most mid-size firms already own one inside their CRM or productivity suite, so the decision is usually which to switch on, not which to buy. This checklist sets out twelve questions to put to any vendor, the evidence to request, and how to test a platform on your own tasks before signing.

Choose an AI agent platform by testing it on your own tasks against six things: what it decides, which systems it connects to, how it limits permissions, how humans approve actions, what each run costs and whether you can replay a run. Ask for measured success rates on work like yours, repeated over several trials. A platform that cannot show you one complete run is not ready for client-facing work.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This checklist is for an owner, operations lead or revenue leader choosing where their company's agents will run. It applies the definition in our hub piece, [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/): a model working in a loop toward a goal, acting through tools within limits. The platform is the thing that sets those tools and limits.

## What is an AI agent platform?

An AI agent platform is software for building, running and governing agents: it supplies model access, connectors to company systems, the loop that runs the agent, permissions, approval steps and logs.

They come in four forms. Agents built into applications you already pay for, such as a CRM, support desk or productivity suite. Packaged agents from specialist vendors that do one job. General agent builders that let staff configure agents without code. And developer frameworks that engineers build on directly, which we compare in [Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/). For a firm of 20 to 500 people, the first two are the usual starting point.

## What should you check before choosing an AI agent platform?

Put these twelve questions to every vendor in writing. A genuine answer names specifics; a weak one answers in adjectives.

| Area | Question to ask | What good looks like | Evidence to request |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decisions | What does the agent decide for itself? | Names choices: which tool, which record, when to stop | A run log showing those choices |
| Goal and stop | How are a goal and stop condition set? | Step limit, spend cap or defined done state | Configuration screen |
| Connectors | Which of our systems can it read and write, and through what standard? | Native connectors plus an open standard such as MCP | Connector list for your stack |
| Identity | Does each agent run as its own identity? | A registered agent identity, not a person's login or admin key | Admin console view |
| Permissions | Can access be limited per agent and per action? | Least privilege, scoped tools, read-only modes | Permission model documentation |
| Approval | Which actions can require a named person's approval? | Configurable gate per action type, approvals logged | A logged approval record |
| Replay | Can we replay one complete run? | Shows inputs, steps, tool calls, outputs and approver | A live replay of a real run |
| Reliability | What is its success rate on tasks like ours? | A rate on a defined sample, repeated, with the grading method | Evaluation results, not a demo |
| Untrusted input | How does it handle instructions hidden in inbound content? | Separates reading from acting; named injection controls | Security documentation |
| Cost | What does one run cost, and can we cap it? | Per-run cost visible; budgets per agent | Usage report from a pilot |
| Data | Where is our data processed and retained, and is it used for training? | Clear terms, a data processing agreement, regional options | Contract and DPA |
| Exit | Can we take our prompts, logs and records with us? | Export in open formats | Export sample |

### Decisions, goals and connectors

The first question filters out most mislabelled products. If the answer is "nothing", the product is automation, which may be exactly what you need, and should be priced and tested as automation. Gartner estimated in June 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors making agentic claims offered genuine agentic capability; our explainer [What Is Agent Washing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) covers the test.

On connectors, prefer platforms that support open standards. The Linux Foundation announced the Agentic AI Foundation on 9 December 2025 with the Model Context Protocol, contributed by Anthropic, as a founding project, citing more than 10,000 published MCP servers. A connector built to an open standard is less likely to lock you to one vendor.

### Identity, permissions and approval

These three rows carry most of the risk. OWASP's LLM06:2025 entry defines excessive agency as damaging actions taken in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model outputs, and its prevention list includes minimising tools and permissions, requiring user approval for high-impact operations and enforcing authorisation in downstream systems rather than relying on the model. OWASP's prompt injection entry states that it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists. A platform should therefore let you keep agents that read untrusted content away from actions that send or pay.

Buyers are right to be cautious. In Gartner's 2025 survey, 74% of IT application leaders believed AI agents represent a new attack vector, and only 13% strongly agreed they had the right governance structures. KPMG's Q3 2026 survey found 49% of US leaders at $1 billion-plus firms had defined high-risk use cases where agents cannot make autonomous decisions. See [Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) for how to set the gate.

## How do you test an AI agent platform before you sign?

Run it on a fixed sample of your own tasks, several times each, and grade the results against a written standard. A single successful demo tells you little about the hundredth run.

Independent measurements explain why. METR's research found 80% time horizons roughly five times shorter than 50% horizons, and lower performance on messier tasks. Salesforce AI Research's CRMArena-Pro benchmark found leading agents at about 58% on single-turn business tasks and about 35% when the task ran over several turns. A pilot should therefore include multi-step tasks, messy inputs and at least one case designed to fail. Our guide [How to Evaluate an AI Agent](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-evaluate-an-ai-agent/) sets out graders and metrics.

| Pilot step | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Pick one frequent, checkable task | The baseline time and error rate today |
| Run the same tasks repeatedly | Success on every trial, not just the best one |
| Include messy and adversarial inputs | What it did with a hidden instruction or a stale record |
| Keep it at draft level | Every output reviewed by a named person |
| Review cost per run weekly | Tokens or credits consumed, and retries |

## Should you buy an agent platform or build on a framework?

Buy or configure first, unless agents are your product. McKinsey's 2026 survey found 32% of respondents had decided against buying at least one software product because they could build it in-house with agentic coding tools, so building is more practical than it was. It still leaves you owning maintenance, evaluation and security.

Menlo Ventures, an investor in AI companies, reported in November 2026 that model capability, not price, was proving to be the decisive competitive advantage among model providers. For a buyer, that argues for a platform that lets you change the underlying model without rebuilding. Our decision guide [Build vs Buy AI Agents](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) covers the trade-offs.

## What does an AI agent platform cost to run?

Running cost depends on usage more than licence. McKinsey found about 20% of respondents saying AI operating costs, including tokens, had constrained their AI use, and KPMG found 43% of large US firms using usage or token budgets. Ask for per-run cost from the pilot, not a list price. Our pricing guide [How Much Does an AI Agent Cost?](https://lowob.com/research/how-much-does-an-ai-agent-cost/) and the pillar [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) cover the models.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with what you own.** Many firms already have agent features inside their CRM or productivity suite.
- **Ask what it decides.** If the answer is nothing, buy and price it as automation.
- **Insist on replay and approval.** A run you cannot replay is a run you cannot defend.
- **Test repeatedly on your own tasks.** Success on every trial matters more than the best demo.

## Common questions

### How do I choose an AI agent platform?

Test it on your own tasks and ask twelve questions: what it decides, how goals and stops are set, which systems it connects to, whether agents have their own identity, how permissions and approvals work, whether you can replay a run, its measured success rate, how it handles untrusted input, cost per run, data terms and exit options.

### What features should an AI agent platform have?

At minimum: connectors to your systems through an open standard such as MCP, a separate identity for each agent, per-agent permissions, configurable human approval for high-impact actions, complete logs you can replay, cost caps and an evaluation tool for testing on your own tasks. OWASP's 2025 guidance supports the permission and approval requirements.

### Should I build or buy an AI agent?

Most firms of 20 to 500 people should buy or configure an agent on a platform they already use, unless agents are their product. McKinsey's 2026 survey found 32% of respondents had chosen to build at least one product in-house with agentic coding tools, but building leaves you owning maintenance, evaluation and security.

### How do I test an AI agent before buying?

Run it on a fixed sample of your own real tasks, several times each, with a written grading standard. Include multi-step tasks and messy or adversarial inputs, keep outputs at draft level and record cost per run. Benchmarks such as CRMArena-Pro show success falling from about 58% on single-turn tasks to about 35% on multi-turn tasks.

# How to Document an AI Model for Regulators: A Practical Template

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-document-an-ai-model-for-regulators/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Supervisors want AI documentation that someone outside the build team can read, check and audit. This template sets out twelve sections, from purpose and risk tier to monitoring, change history and decision records, and maps each to SR 26-2, the OCC's November 2026 examiner framework, EU AI Act Annex IV and PRA SS1/23. It also covers vendor models, proportionality and retention.

To document an AI model for regulators, keep one current file per AI system covering purpose, owner, risk tier, design and data, vendors, testing, limitations, human oversight, monitoring, change history and links to decision records, written so someone outside the build team can audit it. Scale the depth to the system's consequences.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

Most AI documentation is written for the people who built the system. Supervisors read it to answer a different question: is this use understood, controlled and checked by people with the standing to stop it? This template is built for that reader. It complements the decision-level record in our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/), and our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) explains why the record of what the system did now matters as much as the model file.

The template summarises public supervisory texts for orientation. It is not legal advice, and the final form should be agreed with your compliance and model risk functions.

## What documentation do regulators expect for an AI model?

Documentation that lets an outsider understand the system, check its risk and audit its use. The texts differ in detail but agree on that test.

SR 26-2, the US model risk guidance of 17 April 2026, says "adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management" and can "help maximize the likelihood of continuity of operations." Its predecessor SR 11-7 set the test more sharply: documentation "sufficiently detailed to allow parties unfamiliar with a model to understand how the model operates." The OCC's 4 November 2026 framework, a non-binding resource for examiners reviewing generative and agentic AI, uses the same idea and adds auditability.

For high-risk systems under the EU AI Act, Article 11 requires technical documentation "drawn up before that system is placed on the market or put into service" and "kept up-to date", containing at a minimum the elements in Annex IV. The UK PRA's SS1/23, for banks with internal model approval, applies its five principles to models "regardless of technology." The FCA's 19 October 2026 review lists poor documentation, "with limited audit trails or supporting rationale", as an area for improvement.

## What should an AI model documentation template include?

Twelve sections. The table is the template; each row names the text that asks for it.

| # | Section | What to write | Evidence to attach | Regulatory hook |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Identity and purpose | System name and ID, intended purpose, permitted and prohibited uses, business function | Inventory entry | OCC "defined purpose and permitted use"; Annex IV point 1(a) |
| 2 | Ownership and approval | Accountable owner, approver, approval date, review date | Signed approval | OCC governance and accountability; PRA SS1/23 governance |
| 3 | Risk tier and materiality | Tier, with the factors: consequence, reversibility, customer impact, autonomy, data sensitivity, explainability, provenance | Tiering worksheet | SR 26-2 materiality; OCC illustrative four-tier method |
| 4 | Design and architecture | Model type, provider, version, retrieval sources, tools and integrations, key design choices | Architecture diagram | Annex IV point 2(b) and (c); SR 26-2 conceptual soundness |
| 5 | Data | Training, fine-tuning and retrieval data, provenance, personal data handling | Data inventory and lineage | Annex IV point 2(d); OCC data governance |
| 6 | Third parties | Vendor, base model, hosting, subprocessors, contract terms on changes and data use | Contract extract, vendor documentation | SR 26-2 vendor section; OCC third-party component; Annex IV point 2(a) |
| 7 | Testing and validation | Test sets, metrics, results, who validated and when, open findings | Test reports, validation sign-off | SR 26-2 validation; NIST MEASURE 2.1; Annex IV point 2(g) |
| 8 | Limitations | Known failure modes, populations or tasks where performance is weak, conditions for use | Error analysis | SR 26-2: "a clear understanding of a model's limitations" |
| 9 | Human oversight | Autonomy level, review points, reviewer competence, override and escalation rules | Procedure, training records | OCC human-in-the-loop component; Annex IV point 2(e); AI Act Art. 26(2) |
| 10 | Monitoring | Metrics, thresholds, drift checks, outcome analysis, review frequency | Monitoring dashboard export | SR 26-2 ongoing monitoring and outcomes analysis; Annex IV point 9 |
| 11 | Change history | Every model, prompt, data, configuration, tool and permission change, linked to testing | Change log | OCC change logging; Annex IV point 6; DORA Art. 9(4)(e) |
| 12 | Decision records and retention | Where run-level records live, the ID that joins them, retention class and storage | Sample reconstructed decision | OCC decision traceability; AI Act Art. 19 and 26(6); SEA Rule 17a-4(f) |

Sections 1 to 8 describe the system. Sections 9 to 12 describe how the firm controls and evidences its use. Supervisors increasingly spend their time in the second half.

## How is a regulatory file different from a model card?

A model card describes the model; a regulatory file describes the firm's use of it. Model cards, proposed by Mitchell and colleagues at the FAT\* conference in January 2019, cover model details, intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation and training data, quantitative analyses, ethical considerations, and caveats and recommendations.

That covers much of sections 1, 4, 5, 7 and 8 above. It says nothing about who approved the use, who reviews outputs, how changes are controlled or where decisions are recorded. A vendor's model card is an attachment to section 6, not a substitute for the file. Our explainer [What is a model card?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-model-card/) shows how a buyer should read one.

## How much AI documentation is enough?

Enough for the consequence of the use, and no more. SR 26-2 says "model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality", and more material models warrant "more comprehensive and rigorous oversight."

The OCC framework is explicit about proportion. Documentation "may be proportionate to the use case and may address purpose, ownership, design, data, providers", through to "validation, monitoring, decisions, approvals, incidents, and changes." It adds that documentation "may be scaled to complexity and consequence without creating incentives to select a less suitable" approach. In other words, a team should not pick a weaker tool to avoid paperwork.

A practical scale, using the OCC's illustrative tiers:

| Tier | Example (illustrative) | Sections to complete |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4, low | Internal drafting assistant with no customer or financial data | 1, 2, 3, 6, 11 |
| 3, moderate | Decision support with mandatory human-in-the-loop, reversible outcomes | Add 7, 8, 9 and 10 |
| 2, high | High-weight decision support or human-on-the-loop action | All twelve, with independent validation |
| 1, critical | Autonomous action with high customer or financial impact | All twelve, independent validation, board-level approval |

Under the EU AI Act, SMEs and small mid-caps may use a simplified technical documentation form for Annex IV, which the Commission is to establish under Article 11(1).

## How should vendor AI models be documented?

By recording what the firm understands about the model, how it checks the model in use, and what it changed. Firms rarely see a vendor's training data or weights; supervisors know that.

SR 26-2 calls "developing an understanding of the vendor model" sound practice, along with "ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis to assess whether vendor models" remain fit for purpose. Where vendor models are customised, it expects firms to be "documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments made to customize the model." The OCC framework adds contract points: whether bank data can be used to train the vendor's models, and how the bank learns when "existing vendors may add SI features, functionality or change models." In the OCC's usage, SI, or super intelligence, means the technologies previously called artificial intelligence.

For section 6, attach the vendor's own documentation, the contract clauses on change notice and data use, and the firm's own test results on its data.

## How long must AI model documentation be kept?

It depends on the regime. Under EU AI Act Article 18, providers of high-risk systems keep technical documentation for "a period ending 10 years after the high-risk AI system has been placed on the market or put into service." Providers that are financial institutions keep it "as part of the documentation kept under the relevant Union financial services law."

US guidance sets no fixed period. The OCC framework says records may be retained "for periods appropriate to legal, supervisory, audit, customer-remediation, and operational needs." Keep superseded versions of the file, not only the current one: a supervisor asking about a decision made last year needs the documentation that applied then.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write for the outsider.** The test is whether someone outside the build team can understand, evaluate and audit the system.
- **Document the use, not just the model.** Oversight, monitoring, changes and decision records are where supervisors look.
- **Scale by consequence.** Tier the system first, then complete the sections its tier requires.
- **Keep old versions.** Documentation must answer for past decisions, so supersede rather than overwrite.

## Common questions

### What documentation do regulators require for AI models?

Requirements vary by regime. US bank guidance in SR 26-2 expects adequate documentation supporting model risk management. The EU AI Act requires technical documentation with the Annex IV elements for high-risk systems. The OCC's 2026 examiner framework looks for documentation that lets people other than developers understand, evaluate and audit a system, scaled to its consequences.

### What is in EU AI Act Annex IV technical documentation?

Annex IV lists nine elements: a general description of the system, a detailed description of its elements and development, monitoring and control, performance metrics, the risk management system, lifecycle changes, harmonised standards applied, the EU declaration of conformity, and the post-market monitoring system. It applies to providers of high-risk AI systems, with a simplified form for SMEs and small mid-caps.

### Is a model card enough for regulators?

No. A model card describes a model's intended use, evaluation, training data and limitations. Regulators also ask how the firm uses the model: who approved it, who reviews outputs, how changes are controlled, how performance is monitored and where decision records are kept. Attach a vendor's model card to your file rather than relying on it alone.

### How long should AI model documentation be kept?

Under EU AI Act Article 18, providers of high-risk systems keep technical documentation for 10 years after the system is placed on the market or put into service, and financial institutions keep it within their financial services documentation. US guidance sets no fixed period; the OCC framework points to legal, supervisory, audit, remediation and operational needs.

# How to Evaluate an AI Agent: Tests, Metrics and Graders

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-evaluate-an-ai-agent/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Evaluating an AI agent means testing a multi-step system that acts, not a single answer. The method is a fixed set of real tasks, several trials per task, graders matched to what is being checked, and metrics that capture consistency as well as success. This guide sets out the tests, metrics and graders, with dated guidance from Anthropic, OpenAI, LangChain and Langfuse.

To evaluate an AI agent, run it many times on a fixed set of 20 to 50 real tasks, grade the final outcome and key steps with code, model and human graders, and track both the pass rate and how consistently it passes. Agents fail differently from single model calls: a run can look fluent and still leave the system in the wrong state. Consistency across repeated trials is the number most teams forget to measure.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

This guide covers agents in particular. For the basics of evals see [what AI evals are](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/), and for the tools that run them see our ranking of the [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/).

## What does evaluating an AI agent involve?

It means running the agent on defined tasks, recording everything it did, and scoring the result against agreed success criteria. The unit is the task, attempted several times, not the single prompt.

Anthropic's January 2026 guide gives a usable vocabulary. A task is "a single test with defined inputs and success criteria", and each attempt is a trial. A grader is "logic that scores some aspect of the agent's performance". The transcript, or trace, is the full record of a trial. The outcome is "the final state in the environment at the end of the trial".

## How is evaluating an agent different from evaluating a model?

An agent acts over several steps and changes things, so the right answer is a state, not a sentence. A model eval asks whether a reply is good; an agent eval asks whether the refund was issued, the record updated and the policy followed.

The τ-bench benchmark, published by Yao and colleagues in June 2024, shows the method. A simulated user talks to an agent that has domain tools and policy rules, and the score compares the database at the end of the conversation with the annotated goal state. Its headline finding is the reason to test repeatedly: even state-of-the-art agents succeeded on fewer than half of tasks and were "quite inconsistent", with `pass^8` under 25% in retail.

OpenAI's evaluation guide, read in November 2026, adds two agent checks: correct tool selection and, in multi-agent systems, correct handoffs.

## What should you measure when evaluating an agent?

Measure task success first, then consistency, then the cost of getting there. The table sets out the metrics that matter and how each is usually graded.

| Metric | What it measures | Typical grader | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Task success | Did the final state match the goal? | Code: compare records, files or API state | The only metric the business cares about directly |
| `pass^k` consistency | Did all k trials of the same task succeed? | Code, over repeated runs | Shows whether success is reliable or lucky |
| Tool selection | Did it call the right tool with valid arguments? | Code on the trace | Most agent errors start at a tool step |
| Policy adherence | Did it follow rules, limits and approval steps? | Code for hard rules; model for judgment | A correct outcome reached by breaking policy is a failure |
| Groundedness | Are stated facts present in the sources it used? | Model grader with a rubric | Catches invented facts in drafts and summaries |
| Cost per task | Tokens and calls per completed task | Code on token metrics | Two agents with equal success can differ widely in cost |
| Turns and latency | Steps and time to finish | Code on the trace | Long loops signal confusion before they signal failure |
| Escalation rate | How often it hands to a person | Code on the trace | Too low can mean overconfidence; too high, no value |

Anthropic's guide also separates capability evals, which should start at a low pass rate, from regression evals, which "should have a nearly 100% pass rate". Report them separately.

## How many test cases does an agent eval need?

Start with 20 to 50 tasks taken from real work and real failures, as Anthropic recommended in January 2026. Grow the set each time production shows a new failure.

LangChain's LangSmith documentation, read in November 2026, suggests 5 to 10 curated examples for each critical component, such as retrieval, tool calls and final outputs. The two fit together: component sets catch step faults, and end-to-end tasks catch failures that appear only when steps combine. Include awkward cases on purpose, such as missing records or a tool that times out.

## Which graders should you use for an agent?

Use code wherever the answer can be checked mechanically, a model grader where judgment is needed, and people to calibrate both. Anthropic's guide describes code graders as fast, cheap and reproducible but "brittle to valid variations"; model graders as flexible but non-deterministic and needing calibration; and human graders as the gold standard but slow and expensive.

The same guide advises that "it's often better to grade what the agent produced, not the path it took". Checking for an exact sequence of steps punishes an agent that found a valid alternative route. Grade the path only where the path is the rule, such as an approval that must happen before a payment. Model graders bring their own biases, covered in our explainer on [LLM-as-a-judge](https://lowob.com/research/llm-as-a-judge-explained/).

> An agent that passes once is a demo. An agent that passes eight times in a row on the same task is a candidate for production.

## How do you run agent evals in practice?

Run them offline before each release and online on a sample of production traffic. Both major open tools describe the same split.

Langfuse's documentation, read on 16 November 2026, defines offline evaluation as running the application on a predefined dataset before release, and online evaluation as scoring "live incoming traces". It offers a GitHub Action that fails a build when a score drops below a threshold. LangSmith's documentation draws the same line: offline evaluation targets "examples from datasets", online evaluation targets "runs and threads from tracing" without reference answers.

A workable routine: write success criteria per task with the process owner; run each task at least three times per release and report `pass^k`; gate releases on the regression set; sample production runs for online scoring and human review. Then read transcripts. Anthropic's guide warns that "you won't know if your graders are working well unless you read the transcripts".

In **lowob**'s model, eval results are the evidence for moving an agent along the [autonomy dial](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/), from drafting to acting with approval, for example. Store the results in a record the business owns, not only in the vendor tool.

## lowob takeaways

- **Grade the outcome.** The final state of the system matters more than the wording of the reply.
- **Measure consistency.** Report `pass^k` across repeated trials, not only a single pass rate.
- **Separate capability from regression.** Regression sets should pass at close to 100%.
- **Calibrate graders against people.** Read transcripts before trusting any automated score.

## Common questions

### How do you evaluate an AI agent?

Build a fixed set of real tasks with agreed success criteria, run the agent on each several times, and grade the final outcome with code where possible and model or human graders where judgment is needed. Track task success, consistency across trials, tool selection, policy adherence and cost per task, and rerun the set on every change.

### What is the difference between pass@k and pass^k?

`pass@k` is the chance that at least one of k attempts at a task succeeds, which suits tools where a person picks the best attempt. `pass^k` is the chance that all k attempts succeed, which measures reliability. For an agent that acts without a person choosing, `pass^k` is the more honest number.

### How many test cases do you need to evaluate an AI agent?

Anthropic's January 2026 guidance says 20 to 50 simple tasks drawn from real failures is a good start. LangChain suggests 5 to 10 curated examples per critical component. Start small, include awkward edge cases, and add a task each time production reveals a new failure.

### What metrics should you use to evaluate AI agents?

Track task success against the goal state, consistency across repeated trials, correct tool selection, adherence to policy and approval rules, groundedness of stated facts, cost per completed task, number of turns and escalation rate. Keep capability and regression results separate so a rising capability score cannot hide a slipping regression score.

# How to Negotiate an AI Software Contract: Caps, Credits and Outcome Terms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-negotiate-an-ai-software-contract/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: AI contracts move cost risk into terms that classic software contracts never needed: the billable unit, burn rates, caps, rollover and change notice. Published vendor terms show where the defaults sit. This guide sets out ten clauses with an opening ask, a fallback and a dated precedent for each, and the data to bring to the table.

To negotiate an AI software contract, fix the billable unit and its definition in the order form, cap spend with alerts and a pause option, secure rollover or a true-up on prepaid credits, and get written notice before any metric or price change. Vendors' published terms show the defaults. Most are written for the seller, and most can be moved.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

The terms that matter follow from the pricing model. **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), defines each contract term and why it exists. This page is the buyer's side: what to ask for, what to settle for, and which published precedent to point to.

## What should you negotiate first in an AI contract?

The billable unit and its definition, because every other number depends on it. Put the definition in the order form, not a link to a help page the vendor can edit.

Intercom's 2026 change shows why. Its unit widened from resolutions to outcomes, which now include procedure handoffs to a person and disqualifications. A buyer who budgeted on resolutions pays for more events at the same rate. [Per-resolution vs per-outcome pricing](https://lowob.com/research/per-resolution-vs-per-outcome-pricing/) recounts a month under both definitions. Ask for the old unit to hold until renewal if the vendor changes it. Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

## Which AI contract clauses matter most?

Ten clauses carry most of the cost risk. The table gives an opening ask, a fallback and a published precedent for each, all checked on vendors' pages on 16 November 2026 unless dated otherwise.

| Clause | Opening ask | Fallback | Published precedent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Billable unit | Definition in the order form, fixed for the term | Old unit honoured until renewal | Intercom moved to outcomes on 12 March 2026 |
| Change notice | 90 days' written notice of any unit or rate change | 30 days, with a right to exit | Zendesk gives 30 days' notice before moving accounts to resolution tiers |
| Spend cap | Hard monthly cap per agent and per account | Pause at the limit, with alerts before it | Zendesk lets accounts pause AI features or pay overages as they go |
| Overage rate | Same rate as committed usage | A capped premium over the committed rate | Salesforce: "no overage penalty", billed monthly in arrears at the contracted rate |
| Credit rollover | Full rollover for one term | Partial rollover, or a smaller commitment | Salesforce: unused Flex Credits do not roll over |
| True-up | Under-use credited against renewal | Shortfall payable only at an agreed rate | Salesforce Pre-Commit: "True-up at term end if usage is below commitment" |
| Promotional price | Promotion locked for the whole term | Renewal capped at list price | Microsoft: $18 for the first year only; list $21 |
| Choice of unit | Right to switch billing units mid-term | Switch at renewal without penalty | Salesforce: Flex Credits and Conversations not supported in the same org |
| Data residency | Residency at no uplift | Uplift fixed in the price | Anthropic: 1.1 times token prices for US-only inference |
| Billing evidence | Monthly export of every billable event | Quarterly sample with reasons | Zendesk: a language model verifies each conversation |

## How do you cap AI spend in a contract?

Ask for a hard cap that stops spend, not just an alert. Zendesk's help centre already offers the choice to "automatically pause features" at the limit or "pay for overages as you go". Microsoft's pricing page says administrators manage spending for usage-based Copilot features in Cost Management in the "Microsoft 365 admin center".

Agents need their own caps, because one looping agent can spend a team's budget. Ask whether caps can be set per agent, and route agent calls you build yourself through an [LLM gateway](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-llm-gateway/) that enforces them.

## Can you get unused AI credits to roll over?

Sometimes, but the published defaults say no. Salesforce's page says unused Flex Credits do not roll over into later terms, and Zendesk's says automated resolutions don't roll over to the next usage period.

If rollover is refused, commit lower and pay as you go for the rest. Microsoft's prepaid plan for Copilot Credits offers savings of up to 20% for paying up front, with "automatic pay-as-you-go coverage when prepaid credits run out", per its Copilot Studio page. A smaller commitment with that kind of cover often beats a larger one that expires. Ask what Salesforce's Pre-Commit true-up means in money before signing it. [AI credits explained](https://lowob.com/research/ai-credits-explained/) shows how to size the first commitment.

## How do you negotiate seat prices and renewals?

Trade term length for price, and cap the renewal. Monthly billing costs more: Microsoft lists Copilot Business at $25.20 monthly against $21 annually, and OpenAI lists ChatGPT Business at $25 against $20, as checked on 16 November 2026.

Promotions need a renewal clause. Microsoft's $18 price applies to the first year only, for purchases between 1 July and 31 December 2026. Without a cap, year two renews at list. Microsoft also gives a 7-day window for a prorated refund after a paid subscription begins, so test seat counts quickly. [AI assistant pricing compared](https://lowob.com/research/ai-assistant-pricing-compared-2026/) lists the seat prices side by side.

## What should you bring to the negotiation?

Your own usage data, your cost per task and a credible alternative. Vendors negotiate on their averages; you should negotiate on your numbers.

Bring three months of usage by user or agent, the cost per completed task for each tool, and a quote or published price from a competitor. [Value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/) explains why the buyer's next best alternative sets the ceiling. Kyle Poyar's May 2026 survey found 70% of sellers said AI spend comes out of customers' technology or software budgets, so expect procurement to compare AI lines with other software. Record the outcome of each negotiation with its reason and owner, so the renewal starts from evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **Fix the unit first.** The definition belongs in the order form, with the old unit held until renewal.
- **Cap, do not just alert.** Ask for a pause at the limit and caps per agent.
- **Commit below forecast.** Without rollover, a smaller prepaid amount plus pay-as-you-go is safer.
- **Cap the renewal.** First-year promotions renew at list unless the contract says otherwise.

## Common questions

### What should be in an AI software contract?

A written definition of the billable unit, the rate for each unit, a spend cap or pause option, the overage rate, rollover or true-up terms for prepaid credits, notice before any unit or price change, a renewal cap, data residency terms and the right to export the events behind each charge. Vendors' published defaults favour the seller on most of these.

### Can you negotiate AI credit rollover?

You can ask, but published defaults usually refuse it. Salesforce's pricing page, checked in November 2026, says unused Flex Credits do not roll over into later terms. If rollover is refused, commit below your forecast and pay as you go above it. Microsoft's prepaid Copilot Credit plan, for example, switches to pay-as-you-go when credits run out.

### How do you avoid surprise AI bills?

Negotiate a hard spend cap that pauses usage at a limit, with alerts before it, and set caps per agent as well as per account. Zendesk already lets accounts pause AI features or pay overages as they go. Recalculate cost per completed task each month, because burn rates, units and agent behaviour can all change mid-term.

### Should you sign an annual or monthly AI contract?

Annual is cheaper per seat: Microsoft lists Copilot Business at $21 annually against $25.20 monthly, and OpenAI lists ChatGPT Business at $20 against $25, as checked in November 2026. Monthly suits a pilot whose seat count is not yet proven. Move to annual once weekly use per seat is known, and cap the renewal price.
