# How to Price an AI Product: A Step-by-Step Method

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-price-an-ai-product/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pricing an AI product starts with cost per completed task, because AI has a real marginal cost that SaaS mostly did not. Choose a value metric that tracks how customers get value, set the price between the cost floor and the buyer's next best alternative, check the margin, and run every change as an experiment with a stop rule.

To price an AI product, measure your cost per completed task, choose a value metric that tracks how customers get value, set the price between that cost floor and the buyer's next best alternative, then test it on new customers with a stop rule. Most AI companies now combine a fixed fee with a variable one. The order matters: a price set before the cost is known is a guess.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

The choice between seats, usage and outcomes is covered in **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), with one explainer per model. This page sets out the method around that choice.

## What are the steps to price an AI product?

Seven, each producing a written output that the next step needs.

| Step | Question to answer | Output | Evidence to use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Cost per task | What does one completed task cost us to serve? | A cost figure, including human review | Last month's model, compute and review cost over tasks completed |
| 2. Value metric | What unit grows as the customer gets more value? | One billing unit, defined in a sentence | Customer interviews and usage logs |
| 3. Next best alternative | What would the buyer do without us? | A money value for the alternative | Field interviews, competitor list prices |
| 4. Price band | Where between cost floor and value ceiling do we sit? | A list price and a margin floor | Steps 1 and 3 |
| 5. Packaging | What is fixed, what is variable, what is included? | A one-sentence pricing description | Published hybrids in the market |
| 6. Margin check | Does the price hold for heavy users? | Margin by customer segment | Usage distribution, not the average |
| 7. Test | What would make us reverse the change? | A hypothesis and a stop rule | New-customer cohort results |

## Why start with cost per task?

Because AI has a real cost every time a customer uses it, and that cost varies by customer. Poyar's May 2026 survey found 54% of respondents ranked internal costs and margins as the single most important factor when pricing AI capabilities.

Cost per task is model cost plus compute plus human review, divided by tasks completed. The pillar's worked example shows review costing about five times the model in a healthy month. The token side is explained in [what AI inference cost is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/). If you cannot produce last month's figure, stop here and build the measurement first.

## How do you choose a value metric for an AI product?

Pick the unit that rises when the customer gets more value and that the customer can predict. The three model explainers cover the trade-offs: [seats](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/), [usage](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/) and [outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/).

A quick test: if one customer's heaviest user could cost you more than their seat price, a pure seat metric is risky. Anthropic's Claude Team page, checked 16 November 2026, shows how vendors manage this. It sells standard seats at $20 per seat per month on annual billing and premium seats at $100 with "5x more usage than standard seats", and says usage limits apply to both.

## How do you set the price level?

Set it between your cost floor and the value of the buyer's next best alternative, closer to value where your product is clearly better. [Value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/) explains the method: cost sets the floor, the buyer's alternative sets the ceiling, and the gap is the buyer's reason to sign.

Published prices are reference points, not targets. Intercom lists Fin from $0.99 per outcome and Salesforce lists $2 per Agentforce conversation, as checked on 16 November 2026. Know your own price per equivalent unit. Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

## What gross margin should an AI product target?

Most AI companies target about 50%, well below classic SaaS. Poyar's survey put the median target at about 50% in May 2026. Only 12% aimed for 80% or more, and a similar share targeted 20% or lower. ICONIQ's July 2026 report put average AI product gross margins at 45% in 2025, projected at 53% for 2026.

Set a margin floor per task and check it by segment, not on the average. Poyar estimates from his own experience, not the survey, that the top 10% of power users drive more than 70% of token consumption. [AI gross margin explained](https://lowob.com/research/ai-gross-margin-explained/) covers the calculation.

## Should you charge for AI separately or include it?

Include it when AI is now the expected core of the product; charge separately when it serves a subset of users with a distinct job.

Google included Gemini in Workspace Business and Enterprise plans from January 2025. Its announcement gave the example of a Business Standard customer who had paid $32 per user per month with the Gemini Business add-on now paying $14. Microsoft does both. Its pricing page, checked 16 November 2026, says Copilot Chat is "included at no additional cost" with eligible plans, while Microsoft 365 Copilot Business is an add-on at $21 per user per month on annual billing.

Poyar found 70% of respondents said AI spend comes out of customers' technology or software budgets. A separate AI line competes inside the same budget, so it needs its own case.

## How should you package a hybrid price?

Keep the fixed part for the platform and the variable part for the AI work, and describe the whole price in one sentence. Poyar found 37% of companies used a hybrid model in 2026, up from 25% a year earlier, and 29% let customers choose between pricing models, up from 21%.

| Hybrid shape | When it fits | One-sentence test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seat plus usage allowance | Daily human use with occasional heavy work | "Each seat includes a monthly allowance; extra use is billed at the order-form rate" |
| Platform fee plus credits | Agents whose volume varies by month | "The fee covers the platform; credits pay for agent actions" |
| Platform fee plus outcome fee | Countable results the buyer trusts | "The fee covers the platform; each defined result is billed once" |

If the price needs a calculator to explain, buyers will assume the worst case. [AI credits explained](https://lowob.com/research/ai-credits-explained/) covers how to make a credit model legible.

## How do you test a new AI price?

Run it on new customers first, with a written hypothesis and a stop rule, and keep existing customers on the old price until the result is in. Poyar found three in four software companies changed pricing or packaging in the year to May 2026. Metronome, a billing vendor, noted in April 2026 that Cursor had made four major pricing structure changes in under two years.

Our guide to [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers reading results at low volume. Record each pricing decision with its reason, owner and expected result, so the next change can learn from this one.

## lowob takeaways

- **Cost first.** Know last month's cost per completed task, review included, before choosing a price.
- **Pick a predictable metric.** The unit should grow with value and be forecastable by the buyer.
- **Price to the alternative.** Cost is the floor; the buyer's next best option is the ceiling.
- **Test with a stop rule.** New customers first, existing customers grandfathered until the result is in.

## Common questions

### How do you price an AI product?

Measure cost per completed task, including human review. Choose a value metric that grows with customer value. Set a price between that cost floor and the value of the buyer's next best alternative. Package fixed and variable parts so the price fits in one sentence, check margin by segment, then test the price on new customers with a stop rule.

### What is a good gross margin for an AI product?

Kyle Poyar's May 2026 survey of more than 230 software companies found a median target AI margin of about 50%, with only 12% aiming for 80% or more. ICONIQ's July 2026 report put average AI product gross margins at 45% in 2025, projected at 53% for 2026. Set your own floor per task and check it by customer segment.

### Should AI features be priced separately?

Charge separately when AI serves a subset of users with a distinct job; include it when AI is the expected core. Google included Gemini in Workspace plans in January 2025, while Microsoft sells Microsoft 365 Copilot Business as a $21 add-on and includes Copilot Chat at no extra cost, as listed in November 2026.

### What is hybrid pricing for AI?

A price with a fixed part, such as a platform fee or seats, and a variable part tied to usage, credits or outcomes. Growth Unhinged's May 2026 survey found 37% of software companies used one, up from 25% a year earlier. ICONIQ found AI companies blend an average of 1.7 pricing models.

# Langfuse vs LangSmith: Which LLM Observability Tool to Choose

Source: https://lowob.com/research/langfuse-vs-langsmith/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Langfuse and LangSmith cover the same core jobs: tracing, evaluation, human review and OpenTelemetry ingestion. They differ in licence, how self-hosting is sold, how usage is billed and how long data is kept at list price. This comparison sets out the facts from both vendors' pages as of 16 November 2026 and the situations where each fits.

Langfuse and LangSmith both trace, evaluate and monitor LLM applications; the main structural difference is that Langfuse's core is MIT-licensed and free to self-host, while LangSmith self-hosting is an Enterprise add-on and its paid cloud plan charges $39 per seat a month. Feature coverage is close; the choice turns on hosting, billing shape and your framework.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Both tools appear in our ranking of the [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/), which weights self-hosting heavily for regulated teams. This comparison sets the two side by side so you can weight the differences yourself. Every fact comes from the vendors' own pages, read on 16 November 2026.

## What is the difference between Langfuse and LangSmith?

Both trace, evaluate and review LLM applications and agents. They differ in licence, hosting, billing and ownership, not core features.

Langfuse is open source and has been owned by ClickHouse since an acquisition announced on 16 January 2026. ClickHouse said Langfuse "remains 100% open-source under its existing MIT license for core features". Its repository licence puts `ee/` directories under a separate enterprise licence.

LangSmith is built by LangChain, the company behind the LangChain and LangGraph frameworks. Its client SDK is MIT-licensed; the platform needs a licence key to self-host. LangChain's pricing page also bundles deployment products, such as an Agent Server on Plus.

## How do Langfuse and LangSmith compare?

They match on most features and differ on hosting, billing and retention, as listed by each vendor on 16 November 2026.

|  | Langfuse | LangSmith |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Licence | Core MIT; enterprise features under a separate licence | Platform proprietary; SDK MIT |
| Self-hosting | Free open-source edition; paid Self-Hosted Enterprise and Government editions, custom-priced | Enterprise add-on only, with licence key |
| Self-host stack | PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Redis or Valkey, blob storage; Docker Compose for testing, Kubernetes for production | ClickHouse, PostgreSQL, Redis or Valkey, optional blob storage; Kubernetes with Helm |
| Free cloud tier | Hobby: 50,000 units, 2 users, 30-day data access | Developer: 1 seat, 5,000 base traces |
| Paid cloud plans | Core $29, Pro $199, Enterprise $2,499 a month, each with 100,000 units | Plus $39 per seat a month with 10,000 base traces; Enterprise custom |
| Billing unit | Unit: any trace, observation or score | Seat, plus trace |
| Overage | $8 per 100,000 units, falling to $6 above 50 million | Pay as you go; per-trace rate not stated on the pricing page |
| Users | Unlimited from Core | Every user, including invited users, is a billed seat |
| Retention at list price | 30 days Hobby, 90 days Core, 3 years Pro and Enterprise | 14 days base traces, 180 days extended at an unstated extra fee |
| Evaluation | Datasets, experiments, LLM-as-a-judge, custom scores, user feedback | Datasets, experiments, LLM-as-judge, code, pairwise and human evaluators |
| Human review | Annotation queues: 1 on Hobby, 3 on Core, unlimited on Pro | Annotation queues, single-run and pairwise |
| OpenTelemetry | OTLP at `/api/public/otel`; `gen\_ai.\*` spans become generations | OTLP at `/otel`; maps `gen\_ai.\*`, reads deprecated spellings |
| Framework ties | No framework required; any OpenTelemetry exporter can send traces | Built-in integration with LangChain and LangGraph; any OpenTelemetry client also works |

## Which is cheaper, Langfuse or LangSmith?

It depends on your usage. Langfuse charges by data point, not user; LangSmith charges by user and trace.

Langfuse's unit counts every trace, observation and score, so a deep agent run uses many units. LangSmith's FAQ says a trace "can include many individual steps", so depth does not change the count. But LangSmith bills every user as a $39 seat on Plus, while Langfuse includes unlimited users from its $29 Core plan. A large team with shallow traces will usually pay less on Langfuse at list price; a small team with very deep traces may not.

Two gaps limit exact comparison. LangChain's pricing page did not state its per-trace rate or extended-retention fee on 16 November 2026. Langfuse's self-hosted Enterprise pricing is unpublished and described as "additive to your ClickHouse commercial plan". Our [LLM observability pricing comparison](https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-pricing-compared/) works through examples.

## Can you self-host Langfuse or LangSmith?

Yes, both, but on different terms. Langfuse's open-source edition can be self-hosted free; LangSmith self-hosting requires an Enterprise contract.

Langfuse's documentation lists Docker Compose for testing, a "Single VM without high availability, scaling, or backups", and Kubernetes with Helm for production. Its paid self-hosted edition adds audit logs, SCIM provisioning, project-level access control and data retention management; a Government edition adds FIPS 140-3 modules and air-gapped deployment.

LangSmith's documentation runs it in "your own Kubernetes cluster" with Helm, with Terraform offered for provisioning. Its pricing page also lists a hybrid option on Enterprise, with a SaaS control plane and a self-hosted data plane. Both stacks use ClickHouse for traces and PostgreSQL for operational data.

> The feature lists are close. The contract you need to run it inside your own walls is not.

## Do you need LangChain to use LangSmith?

No. LangChain's OpenTelemetry documentation, read on 16 November 2026, says you can "send traces from any OpenTelemetry-compatible agent" and trace an agent "with a standard OpenTelemetry client".

The integration is deeper for LangChain and LangGraph users, a real advantage if your agents use them. Both map OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes into their own data models, so test an export first; our explainer on the [OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions](https://lowob.com/research/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained/) covers why.

## How do their evaluation features compare?

Both support offline evaluation on datasets and online evaluation of production traces, with model, code and human graders.

LangSmith documents pairwise evaluators that "compare outputs from two application versions", pairwise annotation queues, and Tuned Evaluators in public beta for US Plus and Cloud Enterprise plans. Langfuse documents a GitHub Action that fails a build when an experiment score crosses a threshold. Its documentation says trace-level evaluators stop producing results on Langfuse Cloud after its version 4 cutover on 16 November 2026, so existing users should check their setup.

## Which should you choose?

Neither is better in general. Choose on hosting first, then billing shape, then framework.

**Langfuse tends to fit** teams that must self-host without an enterprise contract, have many users or want long retention at list price. Weigh the roadmap risk after an acquisition, and note that audit logs sit in the paid self-hosted edition.

**LangSmith tends to fit** teams building on LangChain or LangGraph, or wanting LangChain's deployment products or pairwise evaluation. Weigh per-seat cost as the team grows, 14-day base retention and the unstated trace overage rate.

**For either**, export one full agent run in OpenTelemetry format and load it into the other before you sign.

## lowob takeaways

- **Features are close.** Both trace agents, run evals and support human review and OpenTelemetry.
- **Hosting terms differ most.** Langfuse self-hosts free under MIT; LangSmith self-hosting is Enterprise only.
- **Billing shapes differ.** Units and unlimited users against seats and traces favour different teams.
- **Test the exit either way.** Both map OpenTelemetry data into their own models.

## Common questions

### Is Langfuse better than LangSmith?

Neither is better in general. Langfuse's core is MIT-licensed and free to self-host, with unlimited users from $29 a month on its cloud. LangSmith offers deep LangChain and LangGraph integration and pairwise evaluation, at $39 per seat a month, with self-hosting on Enterprise only. Choose on hosting needs, team size and framework.

### Is LangSmith open source?

The LangSmith client SDK is MIT-licensed, but the LangSmith platform is not open source. Self-hosting it requires an Enterprise plan and a licence key, as LangChain's documentation stated on 16 November 2026. Langfuse's core platform is open source under the MIT licence, with some enterprise features under a separate licence.

### How much does LangSmith cost compared with Langfuse?

As listed on 16 November 2026, LangSmith Developer is free for one seat with 5,000 base traces, and Plus is $39 per seat a month with 10,000 base traces, then pay as you go. Langfuse Hobby is free with 50,000 units; Core is $29, Pro $199 and Enterprise $2,499 a month, each with 100,000 units.

### Can I use LangSmith without LangChain?

Yes. LangChain's documentation says LangSmith accepts traces from any OpenTelemetry-compatible agent through its OTLP endpoint, using a standard OpenTelemetry client. LangChain and LangGraph have a built-in integration, which is deeper, but they are not required. Langfuse also accepts OpenTelemetry traces over its own OTLP endpoint.

# LLM-as-a-Judge Explained: When Model Graders Work and When They Fail

Source: https://lowob.com/research/llm-as-a-judge-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: LLM-as-a-judge is the use of a language model to grade AI outputs against a rubric. Research shows strong judges can agree with people about as often as people agree with each other, and also documents position, verbosity, self-preference and leniency biases. This guide sets out when model graders work, when they fail, what they cost and how to check them.

LLM-as-a-judge is the practice of using one language model to score another model's output against a written rubric; strong judges matched human preferences over 80% of the time in a 2023 study, but they show position, length and self-preference biases. Model graders work well for narrow, well-specified checks with constrained answers. They fail when the rubric is vague, the stakes are high or the judge is grading its own work.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Model graders are how most observability tools score traces at scale, so the platforms in our [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/) all offer them. For evals in general, see [what AI evals are](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/).

## What is LLM-as-a-judge?

It is an automated grader built from a prompt. Langfuse's documentation, read on 16 November 2026, defines it as a method where "an LLM is used to assess the quality of outputs produced by another LLM application". The judge receives a rubric, the input, the output and optionally a reference answer, and returns a score with its reasoning.

OpenAI's evaluation guide, read in November 2026, describes two forms: pairwise comparison, where the judge picks the better of two responses, and single-answer grading, where it scores one response in isolation.

## How accurate are LLM judges?

On broad preference tasks, the strongest judges agree with people about as often as people agree with each other. On narrower scoring tasks, agreement varies widely by model and can hide large score gaps.

The founding result comes from Zheng and colleagues, first submitted on 9 June 2023. Using the MT-Bench question set and Chatbot Arena votes, they found GPT-4 as a judge reached "over 80% agreement, the same level of agreement between humans". Their task was choosing between chat answers.

A later study is less reassuring. Thakur and colleagues, first submitted on 18 June 2024, tested 13 judge models on answers from 9 exam-taker models. They found "only the best (and largest) models achieve reasonable alignment with humans", and even those fell well short of agreement between people. Scores could differ from human scores by up to 5 points. Their warning for buyers is direct: "judges with high percent agreement can still assign vastly different scores".

## What biases do LLM judges have?

Four are well documented: position, length, self-preference and leniency. Each has a known mitigation, and none is fixed by choosing a larger model alone.

| Bias | What happens | Evidence | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Position | The judge favours the answer shown first, or second | Wang et al., May 2023: order changes let Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries | Run both orders and combine the results |
| Verbosity | The judge favours longer answers | Zheng et al., 2023; OpenAI's guide, read November 2026 | Control for length; prefer pass or fail criteria |
| Self-preference | The judge scores its own model's outputs higher | Panickssery et al., April 2024 | Use a judge from a different model family |
| Leniency and prompt sensitivity | Scores lean generous and shift with prompt complexity and length | Thakur et al., June 2024 | Fix the rubric, add worked examples, recheck after any prompt edit |

Wang and colleagues proposed fixes for position bias that include averaging across both orders and sending cases where the orders disagree to a person, which targets human review at the cases the judge finds hard.

> A judge is a prompt someone wrote. It earns trust the same way a new reviewer does, by being checked.

## When do model graders work?

They work when the question is narrow, the rubric is specific and the answer is constrained. "Does this brief state a fact that is absent from the CRM record?" is a good judge question. "Is this proposal persuasive?" is not.

OpenAI's guide recommends pairwise comparison or pass or fail grading "for more reliability", and says to scale a judge only once it "consistently agrees with human annotations". Langfuse makes the same point in plainer terms: "A judge is a prompt you wrote, so check that it scores cases the way your reviewers would before you rely on it." Langfuse also advises using a judge model that supports structured output, so scores parse reliably.

A practical calibration routine:

1. **Label 50 to 100 real outputs by hand**, with the process owner agreeing the labels.
2. **Run the judge on the same set** and measure agreement on each label, not only overall.
3. **Read the disagreements** and tighten the rubric, then rerun.
4. **Recheck on a sample each month** and after any change to the judge model or prompt.

## When do LLM judges fail?

They fail on checks that code can do better, on judgments that need context the judge lacks, and wherever nobody checks them. Exact facts such as dates, amounts and record IDs should be checked by code, not by a model.

They also fail in more complex setups. Thakur and colleagues advise "caution when using judges in more complex setups", and Anthropic's agent evaluation guide of 9 January 2026 notes model graders are non-deterministic and need calibration against human graders.

The governance failure is quieter. A judge that is never sampled against people becomes an unverified control, the same problem we describe in [a reviewer who does not verify is not a control](https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/).

## What does an LLM judge cost?

Each judged output is an extra model call, so cost scales with the share of traffic you score. Langfuse's documentation, read on 16 November 2026, puts a typical evaluation at $0.01 to $0.10 per assessment and suggests sampling, targeting specific steps and cheaper judge models to control it.

Some platforms also charge for the scores themselves. Braintrust's pricing page, read on 16 November 2026, includes 50,000 scores on its $249 Pro plan and charges $1.50 per 1,000 after that. As an illustration, scoring every one of 100,000 monthly runs at $0.01 to $0.10 each is $1,000 to $10,000 in judge calls, which is why most teams score a sample. Our [LLM observability pricing comparison](https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-pricing-compared/) sets out the platform side.

## lowob takeaways

- **Judges can match people on narrow tasks.** Agreement over 80% is a 2023 result for chat preferences, not a general guarantee.
- **The biases are known.** Position, verbosity, self-preference and leniency each need a specific counter.
- **Calibrate before you scale.** Measure agreement with human labels and read the disagreements.
- **Use code for facts.** Reserve model graders for judgment, and sample them against people.

## Common questions

### What is LLM-as-a-judge?

LLM-as-a-judge means using a language model to grade another model's output against a written rubric, sometimes with a reference answer. It returns a score, often with reasoning. Observability and evaluation tools use it to score production traces and experiments at a scale human reviewers cannot match, but it needs checking against human labels.

### How accurate is LLM-as-a-judge?

In a 2023 study by Zheng and colleagues, GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, similar to human agreement. A 2024 study of 13 judges found only the best and largest aligned reasonably with humans, with score gaps of up to 5 points. Accuracy depends on the task and rubric.

### What are the biases of LLM judges?

Documented biases include position bias, favouring an answer because of where it appears; verbosity bias, favouring longer answers; self-preference, rating the judge's own model's outputs higher; and leniency. Mitigations include swapping answer order, pass or fail rubrics, a judge from a different model family and regular human sampling.

### How do you validate an LLM judge?

Label a set of real outputs by hand, run the judge on the same set and measure agreement per label. Read every disagreement, tighten the rubric and rerun. OpenAI advises scaling only once the judge consistently agrees with human annotations. Recheck on a sample after any change to the judge model or prompt.

### Should an LLM judge use the same model as the application?

It is safer not to. Panickssery and colleagues found in 2024 that models can recognise their own outputs and tend to score them higher than human raters would. Using a judge from a different model family reduces that self-preference bias, though it does not remove the need for human checks.

## Sources and notes

- [Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685), arXiv, submitted 9 June 2023. Academic study; agreement figures are for chat preference tasks.
- [Thakur et al., Judging the Judges: Evaluating Alignment and Vulnerabilities in LLMs-as-Judges](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.12624v6), arXiv, submitted 18 June 2024, revised August 2025. Academic study.
- [Wang et al., Large Language Models are not Fair Evaluators](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.17926v2), arXiv, submitted 29 May 2023. Academic study of position bias.
- [Panickssery, Bowman and Feng, LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.13076v1), arXiv, submitted 15 April 2024. Academic study of self-preference.
- [OpenAI, Evaluation best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices), accessed 16 November 2026. Model vendor guidance.
- [Langfuse, LLM-as-a-Judge](https://langfuse.com/docs/evaluation/evaluation-methods/llm-as-a-judge), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor documentation; cost range is the vendor's estimate.

## Next move

Take the model grader you rely on most, hand-label 50 of its recent cases and compare. If agreement on any label is below what you would accept from a new reviewer, rewrite the rubric before scoring more traffic.

# LLM Observability Pricing Compared (2026)

Source: https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-pricing-compared/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: LLM observability platforms bill in different units: tracing units, seats and traces, spans and gigabytes, scores, or model-call spans. This comparison sets out list prices, included usage, overage and retention for five platforms as listed on 16 November 2026, prices a small-team workload, and lists the costs that do not appear on pricing pages.

LLM observability tools bill in five different units: Langfuse by tracing unit, LangSmith by seat and trace, Arize by span and gigabyte, Braintrust by gigabyte and score, and Datadog by model call, with first paid plans from $29 to $249 a month in November 2026. The unit matters more than the headline price.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

These are list prices for the five platforms in our ranking of the [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/), read on each vendor's page on 16 November 2026, in US dollars a month. For the general logic of usage pricing, see [seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/).

## How much does LLM observability cost in 2026?

Small workloads often fit a free tier; production workloads cost from a few hundred to several thousand dollars a month at list price.

The spread at volume comes from the billing unit. Per-span billing charges for every step of an agent run; per-model-call billing ignores tool and retrieval steps; per-gigabyte billing charges for prompt and output size; per-seat billing charges for people.

## How do LLM observability pricing models compare?

The table sets out the published terms for each platform as of 16 November 2026. "Not stated" means the pricing page did not publish the figure.

| Platform | Free tier | First paid plan | Billing unit | Included in paid plan | Overage | Retention at list price | Self-hosting |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Langfuse | Hobby: 50,000 units, 2 users | Core $29; Pro $199; Enterprise $2,499 | Unit: a trace, observation or score | 100,000 units; unlimited users | $8 per 100,000 to 1 million, then $7, $6.50 and $6 at volume | 30 days Hobby; 90 days Core; 3 years Pro and Enterprise | Open source free; Enterprise custom |
| LangSmith | Developer: 1 seat, 5,000 base traces | Plus $39 per seat | Seat plus trace | 10,000 base traces | Pay as you go; rate not stated | 14 days base; 180 days extended, fee not stated | Enterprise add-on |
| Arize AX | Free: 25,000 spans, 1 GB | Pro $50 | Span plus GB | 50,000 spans; 10 GB | $0.0008 per span; $3 per GB | 15 days Free; 30 days Pro | Enterprise only |
| Braintrust | Starter: 1 GB, 10,000 scores | Pro $249 | GB processed plus score | 5 GB; 50,000 scores; unlimited users | $3 per GB; $1.50 per 1,000 scores | 14 days Starter; 30 days Pro, extendable at $0.50 per GB a month | Enterprise only |
| Datadog | Free: up to 40,000 LLM spans | Pro $160 | LLM span: one call to a model provider | Up to 100,000 LLM spans | On-demand; rate not stated | 15 days; add-ons to 30, 60 or 90 days | Not offered |

Three details change real bills. Datadog's page says tool, workflow, agent, embedding and retrieval spans are not billed, only model calls. Braintrust's Starter and Pro plans include $10 and $100 of model credits a month. Langfuse's Pro plan needs a Teams add-on at $300 a month for SSO and project-level access control, bringing it to $499.

## What does LLM observability cost for a small team?

Often nothing, or under $120 a month, at list price; the difference is retention and users.

The example is illustrative. A team of three runs an agent 8,000 times a month. Each run produces one trace with 10 spans, of which 3 are model calls, plus one quality score and about 20 KB of data. The per-run assumptions match our pillar's production example.

| Platform and plan | Billed quantity | Monthly list cost | Retention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Langfuse Core | 96,000 units (trace, 10 observations, 1 score per run) | $29 | 90 days |
| LangSmith Plus | 8,000 traces, within 10,000; 3 seats | $117 | 14 days |
| Arize AX Pro | 80,000 spans: 30,000 over at $0.0008 | $74 | 30 days |
| Braintrust Starter | 0.16 GB and 8,000 scores, within free limits | $0 | 14 days |
| Datadog Free | 24,000 LLM spans, within 40,000 | $0 | 15 days |

Langfuse Hobby (50,000 units, 2 users) and LangSmith Developer (1 seat, 5,000 traces) do not fit. The two free options that do keep data for two weeks, which suits debugging but not a review cycle.

> At small volume the price is in the retention column. At large volume it is in the billing unit.

## What does LLM observability cost at production volume?

At 600,000 agent runs a month, published list prices range from about $705 to $4,810, and two vendors need a quote. These figures come from the worked example in our [top 5 ranking](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/), using November 2026 list prices and the same per-run assumptions as above.

In that example, Langfuse Pro came to $705 with 3-year retention, Braintrust Pro to $1,095, and Arize AX Pro to $4,810 before any data charge, which is why a team at that volume would move to Arize's custom Enterprise pricing. LangSmith Plus and Datadog Pro could not be priced, because neither publishes the overage rate needed.

## Which LLM observability costs are not on the pricing page?

Judge-model calls, add-ons, longer retention and self-hosting infrastructure, each of which can exceed the platform fee.

- **Judge model tokens.** Automated scoring runs extra model calls. Langfuse's documentation, read on 16 November 2026, estimates a typical evaluation at $0.01 to $0.10 per assessment. Our explainer on [LLM-as-a-judge](https://lowob.com/research/llm-as-a-judge-explained/) covers why most teams score a sample.
- **Security and access add-ons.** Langfuse's Teams add-on is $300 a month on Pro. LangSmith lists custom SSO and role-based access on Enterprise.
- **Retention.** Datadog bills retention add-ons per 10,000 LLM spans, and LangSmith's extended-retention fee is not stated. Braintrust charges $0.50 per GB a month beyond 30 days on Pro.
- **Self-hosting.** Langfuse's self-hosting documentation lists PostgreSQL, ClickHouse, Redis or Valkey and blob storage; LangSmith's lists a similar stack on Kubernetes. Your infrastructure and staff time replace the licence fee.
- **Exit.** A product that closes can take your history with it, so test an OpenTelemetry export, as our explainer on the [GenAI conventions](https://lowob.com/research/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained/) describes.

## How do you compare LLM observability quotes fairly?

Price your own workload in each vendor's unit, at the retention you need. Measure a week of real runs, convert it to each vendor's unit with published overage, add the retention your review cycle needs and the judge-model cost for the runs you will score, and ask in writing for any rate the page does not state.

## lowob takeaways

- **The unit decides the bill.** Units, seats, spans, gigabytes and model calls give different answers for the same agent.
- **Free tiers buy two weeks.** Retention on the free options that fit a small team was 14 or 15 days.
- **Some rates need a quote.** LangSmith and Datadog did not publish the overage rates needed at volume.
- **Budget beyond the platform.** Judge calls, add-ons and retention can exceed the plan fee.

## Common questions

### How much does LLM observability cost?

As listed on 16 November 2026, paid entry plans range from $29 a month (Langfuse Core) to $249 (Braintrust Pro), with LangSmith at $39 per seat, Arize AX Pro at $50 and Datadog Pro at $160. Free tiers cover small workloads. At 600,000 agent runs a month, published list prices range from about $705 to $4,810.

### What is the cheapest LLM observability tool?

For small workloads, the free tiers of Braintrust and Datadog can cost nothing, with 14- and 15-day retention. Self-hosting Langfuse's open-source edition has no licence fee but needs your own infrastructure. At 600,000 runs a month, Langfuse Pro had the lowest calculable list price in our November 2026 example, at about $705.

### How is LLM observability priced?

By different units. Langfuse bills tracing units, counting each trace, observation and score. LangSmith bills seats plus traces. Arize bills spans plus gigabytes. Braintrust bills gigabytes processed plus scores. Datadog bills LLM spans, meaning calls to a model provider only. Convert your own workload into each unit before comparing.

### Does LLM observability pricing include evaluation costs?

Usually only partly. Platforms may charge for storing scores, as Braintrust does above 50,000 a month on Pro, but the model calls that produce automated scores are billed by your model provider or as credits. Langfuse estimated a typical judge call at $0.01 to $0.10 per assessment in November 2026.

# OpenTelemetry GenAI Semantic Conventions Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions are the open naming standard for traces of model calls, agent runs, tool calls, token use and evaluation scores. They moved to their own repository in June 2026 and every gen_ai attribute is still at Development status. This guide sets out what they define, how vendors use them and what to do while they change.

OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions are an open naming standard for recording model calls, agent runs, tool calls, token counts and evaluation scores as telemetry, so any compatible backend can read the same trace. As of 16 November 2026 every `gen\_ai` attribute is at Development status, and names are still changing. Use them as your exit route from a vendor, but pin the version you instrument against.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

These conventions are the reason trace portability is possible at all, which is why our ranking of the [top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/) weights OpenTelemetry support at 25%. If the wider topic is new, start with [what LLM observability is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/).

## What are the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions?

They are a shared vocabulary for AI telemetry: agreed span, attribute and metric names for generative AI operations. OpenTelemetry publishes them so an agent instrumented once can send the same data to any backend that understands it.

The repository README, read on 16 November 2026, describes its scope as "spans, metrics, and events for GenAI clients, MCP (Model Context Protocol), and provider-specific conventions". Provider pages exist for Anthropic, Azure AI Inference, AWS Bedrock and OpenAI, and there are separate pages for MCP and the Agent2Agent protocol. Shared attributes such as `error.type` and `server.address` still come from the core conventions, and those are the parts marked Stable.

## What do the conventions define?

They define spans, metrics and events for an AI system, each with a fixed name pattern. The table summarises the main ones as they stood in the repository's main branch on 16 November 2026.

| Signal | Name or pattern | What it records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inference span | `{operation} {model}`, for example `chat` plus the model name | One model call; requires `gen\_ai.operation.name` and `gen\_ai.provider.name`; recommends input and output token counts |
| Agent span | `invoke\_agent {agent name}` or `invoke\_workflow` | One agent run, or a workflow whose control flow the application defines |
| Plan span | `plan {agent name}` | The step where an agent decides what to do before doing it |
| Tool span | `execute\_tool {tool name}` | One tool call; MCP tool calls are defined as compatible with it |
| Agent metrics | `gen\_ai.invoke\_agent.duration`, `.inference\_calls`, `.tool\_calls` | How long a run took and how many model and tool calls it made |
| Token metrics | `gen\_ai.client.inference.usage.*` counters and `gen\_ai.client.inference.operation.*` histograms | Tokens spent over time, including cache and reasoning tokens, as a proxy for cost |
| Evaluation event | `gen\_ai.evaluation.result` | A quality score attached to the span it judges, with name, value, label and explanation |

The evaluation event requires `gen\_ai.evaluation.name` and should be parented to the span being evaluated, so a grader's score and the run it scored travel together. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers what those scores should measure.

## Are the GenAI conventions stable?

No. Every GenAI span, metric, event and attribute in the repository was marked Development on 16 November 2026. OpenTelemetry's maturity-level definitions say that at Development, configuration options "might break often" and a component "MAY be removed without prior notice".

Three dated facts set the position. The core repository's changelog for version 1.42.0 lists the move as a breaking change: all `gen\_ai.\*` attributes, metrics, events and spans there "are deprecated in this repository and have moved" to the new one. Dash0's guide, updated 15 September 2026, dates that move to 12 June 2026. The core conventions have since reached version 1.45.0, while the GenAI repository's changelog still shows only an "Unreleased" section.

The changes are real, not theoretical. In version 1.41.0 of the core conventions, token use was a single histogram, `gen\_ai.client.token.usage`, and workflows had their own "Invoke workflow span". In the GenAI repository's main branch on 16 November 2026, tokens are split into separate counters for input, output, cache reads, cache writes and reasoning, and `invoke\_workflow` is an operation name on the internal agent span. Dashboards and cost reports built on the old names would need rework.

## How do the conventions handle prompts and personal data?

Content is off by default. Capturing instructions, prompts, completions, tool arguments, tool results, retrieval queries and memory records requires an explicit opt-in.

The spans document, read on 16 November 2026, says an environment variable for this MUST be named `OTEL\_INSTRUMENTATION\_GENAI\_CAPTURE\_CONTENT`, with four values: `NO\_CONTENT` (the default), `SPAN\_ONLY`, `EVENT\_ONLY` and `SPAN\_AND\_EVENT`. An invalid value should fall back to no content. The conventions also define reference attributes, such as `gen\_ai.input.messages\_ref`, that point to content held in external storage rather than in the trace. Dash0's September 2026 guide describes an earlier example variable name, which shows how quickly these details move.

A sales or service agent's trace can hold client names, prices and email text, so set retention and access rules before switching capture on.

> The standard makes traces portable in principle. Pinning the version is what makes them portable in practice.

## How do observability vendors use the conventions?

Each vendor maps `gen\_ai.\*` spans into its own data model, so support means different things. These were the documented behaviours when we checked in November 2026.

- **Langfuse** accepts OTLP at `/api/public/otel`, and its guide says "OpenTelemetry spans carrying gen\_ai.\* attributes become generations", with model, token and cost fields.
- **LangSmith** accepts OTLP at its API URL plus `/otel`, maps `gen\_ai.usage.input\_tokens` and similar attributes to its own fields, and still reads deprecated spellings such as `gen\_ai.usage.prompt\_tokens`. It also documents sending the same spans to a second backend through an OpenTelemetry Collector.
- **Arize AX** added native ingestion on 11 August 2026, mapping attributes into its OpenInference format while it "also preserves the original gen\_ai.\* attributes on the span".

On exit, what matters is whether the original attributes survive conversion.

## What should a team do while the standard is in Development?

Instrument against the conventions now, and treat the version as a dependency you manage.

1. **Pin the instrumentation library** and record which conventions version or commit it targets.
2. **Keep attribute names in one place** in your code or collector configuration, so a rename is one change.
3. **Set content capture deliberately.** Start at `NO\_CONTENT` in production and enable content per workflow once retention rules exist.
4. **Emit evaluation results as events** on the span they judge, so scores are portable too.
5. **Test the exit.** Send one full agent run to a second backend through a collector and check that tool calls and scores arrive intact.

## lowob takeaways

- **The conventions are the portability layer.** They give model calls, agents, tools and scores shared names.
- **They are not stable.** Every `gen\_ai` item was at Development on 16 November 2026, with no tagged release.
- **Names have already changed.** Token metrics and workflow spans differ between version 1.41.0 and the current repository.
- **Content capture is opt-in.** Set retention and access rules before switching it on.

## Common questions

### What are OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions?

They are OpenTelemetry's standard names for telemetry from generative AI systems: spans for model calls, agent runs, planning and tool calls, metrics for duration and tokens, and an event for evaluation scores. Instrumenting against them means any compatible backend can read the same traces, which reduces lock-in to one observability vendor.

### Are the OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions stable?

No. As of 16 November 2026, every GenAI span, metric, event and attribute is at Development status. The conventions moved to a separate repository in version 1.42.0 on 12 June 2026, and that repository had no tagged release. Pin your instrumentation version and expect attribute names to change.

### Where did the GenAI semantic conventions move to?

In version 1.42.0 of the core semantic conventions, dated 12 June 2026, the GenAI, OpenAI and MCP conventions moved to a dedicated repository, open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai. The core repository marks its old GenAI definitions as deprecated and points instrumentations to the new repository for the schema URL to use.

### Does OpenTelemetry record prompts and responses?

Only if you opt in. The conventions say capturing prompts, completions, tool arguments and results requires explicit configuration, and the environment variable `OTEL\_INSTRUMENTATION\_GENAI\_CAPTURE\_CONTENT` defaults to `NO\_CONTENT`. Content can also be stored externally and referenced from the trace, which helps when traces would otherwise hold personal data.

# Per-Resolution vs Per-Outcome Pricing: What Changed and What to Check

Source: https://lowob.com/research/per-resolution-vs-per-outcome-pricing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Per-resolution pricing charges when an AI agent solves the customer's problem. Per-outcome pricing charges for a wider list of results, including handoffs and lead qualification. In 2026 Intercom moved Fin to outcomes and Zendesk moved to verified resolutions, in opposite directions. Buyers should recount last month's conversations under the new rules before renewal.

Per-resolution pricing charges only when an AI agent solves the customer's issue; per-outcome pricing charges for a wider set of results, which at Intercom since 12 March 2026 includes resolutions, procedure handoffs, qualifications and disqualifications, from $0.99 each. Zendesk moved the other way in May 2026, billing only resolutions its own model verifies. The unit's definition sets the price.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

Outcome-based pricing, explained in [what outcome-based pricing for AI is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/), charges for results rather than seats or volume. **lowob**'s pricing hub, [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/), sets out when it fits. This page covers one detail that now decides the bill: what counts as a result.

## What is the difference between per-resolution and per-outcome pricing?

A resolution is one kind of result: the customer's problem is solved. An outcome, in Intercom's 2026 definition, is any of several results Fin completes, including passing a case to a person through a configured procedure. Per-outcome pricing therefore bills more events than per-resolution pricing, at the same or a higher unit price. Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

|  | Intercom Fin (outcomes) | Zendesk AI agents (resolution tiers) | Sierra (resolutions) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Billable unit | Outcome: resolution, procedure handoff, qualification, disqualification, self-serve routing | Verified resolution | Issue the agent resolves |
| Who decides it counted | Customer confirms, or does not ask for more help | A language model reviews the conversation text | Not published |
| Not billed | Customer asks for a human; procedure failures; spam; abandoned conversations | Assisted escalations; contained resolutions | Escalations to a human |
| Counting window | Not stated in the article | Email 72 hours, messaging 2 hours by default, voice at hang-up | Not published |
| Published price | $0.99; qualification $9.99 | Through sales | Through sales |
| Since | 12 March 2026 | 18 May 2026 | Described in May 2025 |

Sources: Intercom and Zendesk help centres, checked 16 November 2026; Sierra as described in Inference by Sequoia, 8 May 2025.

## What changed at Intercom in March 2026?

Intercom widened the billable unit from resolutions to outcomes on 12 March 2026. Its help article says pricing "will vary by type", and a second Intercom article lists $0.99 for a resolution, procedure handoff, disqualification or self-serve routing, and $9.99 for a qualification.

A resolution still has two forms, both billable. A confirmed resolution is when the customer "explicitly confirms Fin helped". An assumed resolution is when the customer "doesn't ask for more help after Fin's answer". The new categories add events that are not resolutions: a procedure handoff, for example, is when "Fin successfully executes a Procedure that you've configured to end in a handoff to a human or a workflow".

Intercom also lists what is never billed. Escalations from Fin's default behaviour, such as a customer asking for a human or showing frustration, do not count, and neither do procedure failures. Its article states: "You will never be charged for an outcome that didn't happen."

## How does Zendesk count resolutions now?

Zendesk narrowed its unit. Since 18 May 2026, every conversation lands in one of three tiers: an assisted escalation, where "a human agent completed the resolution"; a contained resolution, where the customer did not ask for more help; or a verified resolution, which passes a check "performed by an LLM". Only verified resolutions are paid from the allowance.

Note the contrast. Intercom bills the case where a customer leaves without asking for more help as an assumed resolution. Zendesk's contained resolution, broadly the same event, is not drawn from the allowance unless the model verifies it. Zendesk's older platform, still in place for accounts not yet moved, included 5 to 15 automated resolutions per agent per month by plan, capped at 10,000 a year, with overage billed monthly.

## Which is better for buyers, resolution or outcome pricing?

Neither by default; the better contract is the one whose unit you can audit. A narrow unit costs less per event but depends on the vendor's verifier. A broad unit is easier to count but bills events, such as handoffs, that a buyer may not call success.

Buyers are cautious. Futurum's April 2026 release found preference for outcome-based GenAI pricing fell 4.1 points to 26.8%, which it linked to uncertainty about how to define and measure AI outcomes. Sellers are moving the other way: ICONIQ's July 2026 report found outcome-based pricing rose from 18% to 23% of AI companies in six months.

## How much does a change of unit cost?

Recount last month's conversations under the new definition. The example is illustrative.

| Conversation result (10,000 a month) | Count | Billed per resolution | Billed per outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Resolutions, confirmed or assumed | 5,000 | $4,950 | $4,950 |
| Procedure handoffs to a person | 800 | $0 | $792 |
| Disqualifications | 200 | $0 | $198 |
| Customer asked for a human | 1,500 | $0 | $0 |
| Other, not billed | 2,500 | $0 | $0 |
| Monthly total at $0.99 |  | $4,950 | $5,940 |

The bill rises 20% with no change in what the agent does. The price per actual resolution moves from $0.99 to about $1.19. If you also use Fin for sales qualification, each qualification adds $9.99.

## What should you check before you renew?

Ask for the definition in the order form, not a help-centre link, and recount a month under it. The [top 5 AI customer-service agents by pricing model](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-customer-service-agents-by-pricing-model/) compares vendors on the same questions.

- Which events are billable, in one sentence each, and which are excluded.
- Who decides an event counted: the customer's behaviour or the vendor's model.
- When a conversation is final, and whether a reopened case reverses the charge.
- How much notice you get before the unit changes, and whether the old unit holds until renewal.
- Whether you can export the raw events behind each charge.

[How to negotiate an AI software contract](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-negotiate-an-ai-software-contract/) sets out fallback positions for each.

## lowob takeaways

- **An outcome is not a resolution.** Intercom's unit now includes handoffs and disqualifications.
- **Narrow units need trusted verifiers.** Zendesk bills only what its own model verifies.
- **Recount before renewal.** Apply the new definition to last month's conversations.
- **Put the definition in the contract.** Help pages can change; order forms cannot without notice.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between per-resolution and per-outcome pricing?

Per-resolution pricing charges when an AI agent solves the customer's issue. Per-outcome pricing charges for a wider set of results. At Intercom, since 12 March 2026, an outcome includes resolutions, procedure handoffs to a person or workflow, qualifications and disqualifications, priced from $0.99, so the same conversations can produce a larger bill.

### How much does Intercom Fin cost per outcome?

Intercom's help centre, checked in November 2026, lists $0.99 for a resolution, procedure handoff, disqualification or self-serve routing, and $9.99 for a qualification. Fin is charged at most once per conversation. Customers asking for a human, procedure failures, spam and abandoned conversations are not billed. Check the current list before signing, since it changed in March 2026.

### What is a verified resolution in Zendesk?

A verified resolution is a conversation that a large language model, reviewing the text after it ends, judges to have satisfactorily resolved the customer's request. Since 18 May 2026 only verified resolutions draw on the Zendesk allowance. Assisted escalations and contained resolutions, where the customer simply did not ask for more help, do not.

### Is outcome-based pricing cheaper than per-resolution pricing?

Not necessarily. Outcome pricing usually bills more events, so the total can rise even at the same unit price. In **lowob**'s illustrative recount, adding handoffs and disqualifications raised a $4,950 month to $5,940, 20% more. Compare the price per actual resolution, which in that example rose from $0.99 to about $1.19.

# SR 26-2 vs SR 11-7: What Changed in US Model Risk Guidance

Source: https://lowob.com/research/sr-26-2-vs-sr-11-7/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on 17 April 2026. It raises the relevance threshold to $30 billion in assets, narrows the model definition, drops the annual validation expectation, rewrites effective challenge, gives vendor models their own section and excludes generative and agentic AI. This comparison sets the two side by side and shows which policy clauses to revisit.

SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7 on 17 April 2026, raising the relevance threshold to banks above $30 billion in assets, narrowing what counts as a model, dropping the annual validation expectation and excluding generative and agentic AI from scope. The core lifecycle of inventory, validation, monitoring and governance survives in shorter, principles-based form.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

For 15 years SR 11-7 was the model risk text that US banks, and many firms outside banking, built their programmes around. Its replacement keeps the vocabulary but changes the scope and the tone. This comparison is for model risk, compliance and AI leads who need to decide which parts of an SR 11-7 programme to keep. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) explains why decision records matter more than model files for AI tools.

The comparison draws on the two primary texts and two April 2026 law-firm readings, labelled where used. It is not legal advice.

## What is the difference between SR 26-2 and SR 11-7?

SR 26-2 is shorter, aimed at larger banks, explicit that it is non-binding, and narrower about what a model is. The table sets out the changes clause by clause.

| Topic | SR 11-7 (4 April 2011) | SR 26-2 (17 April 2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Issuers | Federal Reserve and OCC; FDIC adopted it in 2017 | Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC |
| Scope | "All banking organizations supervised by the Federal Reserve", scaled to size and complexity | "Most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 billion in total assets" |
| Model definition | Applies "statistical, economic, financial, or mathematical theories" | "A complex quantitative method"; spreadsheets and deterministic rule-based processes excluded |
| Validation cadence | Each model reviewed "at least annually" (Sullivan & Cromwell reading) | No set cadence; materiality decides depth |
| Validation independence | "Involves a degree of independence from model development and use" | Quality "depends on the rigor and effectiveness of the review rather than on organizational structure" (Orrick reading) |
| Effective challenge | "A combination of incentives, competence, and influence" | Expertise, "sufficient independence to permit objectivity" and standing to effect change (Orrick reading) |
| Board role | Governance "at the highest level by the board of directors and senior management" | "Clear roles and responsibilities with well-defined accountability" (Sullivan & Cromwell reading) |
| Documentation | Detailed enough for "parties unfamiliar with a model to understand how the model operates" | "Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management" |
| Vendor models | Framework "applies equally" to in-house and vendor models | Stand-alone section; principles apply even where banks cannot validate vendor models |
| Status | Non-binding, but framed as "supervisory expectations" | "Does not set forth enforceable standards"; non-compliance alone brings no criticism |
| Generative and agentic AI | Not addressed | "Not within the scope of this guidance" |
| Also superseded | None | SR 21-8, the 2021 BSA/AML model risk statement |

## What stayed the same?

The lifecycle stayed. Orrick's 24 April 2026 reading notes that the three components of validation remain: conceptual soundness, outcomes analysis and ongoing monitoring. Each is treated more briefly.

The inventory remains too. SR 26-2 expects "a comprehensive set of information for models under development or in use", with "sufficient information to understand model risks." SR 11-7's inventory also named models "recently retired", which the SR 26-2 sentence does not mention. Vendor model validation, "either by internal or outside parties", is still described as important.

## Which banks does the change affect most?

Banks between $1 billion and $30 billion in assets see the largest shift. Sullivan & Cromwell's 29 April 2026 memo notes that the FDIC applied a $1 billion threshold when it adopted SR 11-7 in 2017. SR 26-2 moves the main audience to $30 billion.

The OCC's 17 April release adds that the guidance "may also be relevant to smaller institutions with significant model risk exposure." A $10 billion bank with a complex credit model should not read the threshold as permission to stop validating it.

## What changed for validation and effective challenge?

Validation became risk-based rather than calendar-based. Sullivan & Cromwell reads SR 11-7 as requiring review "at least annually"; SR 26-2 instead says "model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality", and immaterial models may be identified and monitored rather than fully validated.

Orrick notes that SR 26-2 omits detailed discussion of items such as VaR backtesting and override analysis. Effective challenge was rewritten around expertise, independence and organisational standing. Sullivan & Cromwell notes that SR 11-7 had suggested tying validator compensation to the quality of validations; that suggestion is gone.

## What happens to generative AI that sat in an SR 11-7 programme?

It leaves model risk scope but stays under supervision. Footnote 3 of SR 26-2 places generative and agentic AI outside the guidance because they are "novel and rapidly evolving", and Orrick reads the guidance as directing banks to broader risk management for them.

For national banks, the OCC issued a non-binding examiner framework for generative and agentic AI on 4 November 2026, OCC Bulletin 2026-54. It uses a four-tier, consequence-based classification and expects records that "support reconstruction of material outputs or actions." Our explainer [What is SR 26-2?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sr-26-2/) covers that framework. Firms that moved chatbots and agents out of the model inventory in April should make sure they landed in another inventory.

## Should banks scrap their SR 11-7 programmes?

No. SR 26-2 removes prescriptive detail, but its footnote keeps supervisory action available for "any violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices", according to Sullivan & Cromwell. The practical task is to re-tier, not to dismantle.

| Policy clause to revisit | SR 11-7-era wording | SR 26-2 position | Suggested action |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model definition | Included mathematical theories, often applied broadly | Complex methods only | Re-classify; move excluded tools to a lighter inventory |
| Validation schedule | Annual review of every model | Materiality-driven | Set cadence by tier and record the reasoning |
| Validation independence | Independence from development and use | Rigour over structure | Keep independence where materiality is high |
| Board duties | Annual policy approval | Clear roles and accountability | Keep board approval for material models; it costs little |
| Generative and agentic AI | Often inside the model inventory | Out of scope | Govern under a separate AI framework with decision-level records |
| Vendor models | Developmental evidence and contingency plans | Understand, monitor, document customisations | Keep exit and contingency planning for material vendors |

Our explainer [What is model risk management for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) sets out the proportionate version of these habits for firms outside banking.

## lowob takeaways

- **Narrower scope, same lifecycle.** SR 26-2 keeps inventory, validation, monitoring and governance but aims at banks above $30 billion.
- **Materiality replaces the calendar.** Validation depth follows purpose and exposure, not an annual cycle.
- **AI moved out, not off the hook.** Generative and agentic AI need a home in another framework and inventory.
- **Re-tier rather than dismantle.** Unsafe practices still draw supervisory action whatever the guidance says.

## Common questions

### What replaced SR 11-7?

SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC. It supersedes SR 11-7 from April 2011 and SR 21-8, the 2021 statement on BSA/AML models. The OCC issued the same guidance as Bulletin 2026-13 and rescinded its 2011 model risk bulletin and Comptroller's Handbook booklet.

### Does SR 26-2 still require annual model validation?

No set cadence appears in SR 26-2. Sullivan & Cromwell reads SR 11-7 as expecting each model to be reviewed at least annually. SR 26-2 instead makes materiality, defined by model purpose and exposure, decide how rigorous oversight should be, and immaterial models with low inherent risk can be identified and monitored rather than fully validated.

### Is SR 11-7 still useful after SR 26-2?

As a reference for practice, yes; as current guidance, no. Its detail on documentation and validation still describes good habits, and many firms outside banking use it as a template. Cite SR 26-2 as the current US guidance, and note that SR 26-2 excludes generative and agentic AI from scope.

### What changed for vendor models under SR 26-2?

Vendor and third-party products now have their own section. Orrick reads it as saying model risk principles still apply when a bank cannot validate a vendor model or get information from its developer. Sound practice includes understanding the model, monitoring outcomes, and documenting, justifying and evaluating any adjustments made to customise it.

Expect the questions to land on vendors before they land on policy.

# What Is a Context Graph?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-context-graph/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A context graph is a connected record of decision traces, such as the rules applied, exceptions granted, approvals given and precedents used, linked to the people, accounts and documents they concern. The term was popularised by Foundation Capital in December 2025 and vendors now define it in different ways. In lowob's model it captures part of the decision record automatically, but not the expected outcome, falsifier or check date.

A context graph is a connected record of decision traces, meaning the rules applied, exceptions granted, approvals given and precedents used, linked to the people, accounts and documents they concern, so an AI agent can see how a company actually decides. The term spread after a December 2025 Foundation Capital essay. Vendors now use it for different things, and most capture what was done and by whom better than whether it worked.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Context graphs try to automate part of the record layer of the enterprise brain, the loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning described in [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/). The buyer's question is which parts of a decision a product captures.

## What is a context graph?

A context graph is a graph of decisions as well as things: each decision trace is linked to the entities, policies and earlier decisions it touched. It answers "how and why was this done?" where a system of record answers "what is the state now?"

Foundation Capital partner Ashu Garg's essay of 26 December 2025, co-written with Jaya Gupta, gives the definition most others cite: "a living record of decision traces stitched across entities and time so precedent becomes searchable." Its example of a trace is "we used X definition, under policy v3.2, with a VP exception, based on precedent Z, and here's what we changed." The essay's sharpest line is about CRMs: "Salesforce knows what happened. It doesn't know why."

## Where did the term come from?

From venture investors, in late 2025. The essay argued that the next generation of enterprise platforms would be "systems of record for decisions, not just objects."

Foundation Capital's follow-up of 30 January 2026, "Context graphs, one month in," called the context graph "institutional memory for how an organization makes decisions" and set out the objections it had received. Critics argued that intent is unobservable, so only actions can be captured; the authors replied that recording the policy applied, the evidence used and the approver is enough to infer reasons from patterns. Others called it "data catalog 3.0." The follow-up also acknowledged that precedent decays when policy or leadership changes. On a Foundation Capital podcast of 16 January 2026, Altimeter's Jamin Ball gave the bear case: context graphs could "become like semantic layers," "great in theory, but never fully realized in practice."

## How do vendors define a context graph?

Differently, and the differences matter more than the shared name.

| Source and date | Type | Definition or description | What it emphasises |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Garg and Gupta, Foundation Capital, 26 December 2025 | Investor essay | "A living record of decision traces stitched across entities and time" | Exceptions, approvals and precedent |
| Glean blog, 5 February 2026 | Vendor | "A model that connects your enterprise entities (people, documents, tickets, systems)" plus traces of actions between them | Aggregated behaviour: "who did what, in which apps, in what order" |
| Arize blog, 8 January 2026 | Vendor | Uses Foundation Capital's framing; treats agent traces as "durable business artifacts" | Agent run logs kept and analysed |
| Neo4j blog, 4 August 2026 | Vendor | "A connected representation of the knowledge, state, history, and decision records" an agent needs | Three memories: enterprise knowledge, conversation, reasoning traces |
| Zep paper, 20 January 2025 | Vendor research | A "temporally-aware knowledge graph engine" for agent memory; not branded a context graph | Facts that change over time, with history kept |

All five come from parties with a product or portfolio interest; none is independently tested. Glean's version, built from views, edits and comments, is a map of how work flows, not a record of who approved which exception. Neo4j's version is closer to a decision record: its example support agent's trace shows it "checked the order record, compared the request against policy" before approving a refund.

## How is a context graph different from a knowledge graph?

A knowledge graph stores entities and their relationships; a context graph adds decisions, actions and their sequence. Glean's February 2026 post puts it in one line: "Traditional data and knowledge systems model things," while a context graph "models behavior."

The two are layered. Glean writes that "activity signals on their own are noisy, you need knowledge graphs underneath." Neo4j treats the knowledge graph as an agent's long-term memory and adds short-term conversation memory and reasoning memory on top. The [knowledge graph explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/) covers the base layer; [Semantic layer vs knowledge graph](https://lowob.com/research/semantic-layer-vs-knowledge-graph/) covers shared definitions.

## How does a context graph relate to a decision record?

A decision trace is a partial decision record, captured automatically. It usually holds the decision, the policy, the approver and the precedent. It rarely holds the expected outcome, the falsifier or the check date.

| Decision record field | Typical context graph trace |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | Captured, as the action taken |
| Reason | Partly: the policy and precedent cited, not the argument |
| Owner and approver | Captured where the approval happened in a connected tool |
| Status | Rarely: traces are events, not current or superseded states |
| Expected outcome | Not captured; it was never written down |
| Falsifier | Not captured; it requires a stated measure, threshold, date and observer |
| Check date | Not captured |
| Supersedes | Sometimes, in temporal designs such as Zep's |
| Outcome written back | Possible where results flow back from the CRM |

The missing fields make a record gradable; [The field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) explains why the falsifier is the one that matters most. Status and supersession matter for agents in particular: a trace from last year's pricing policy is a misleading precedent unless something marks it replaced, which is the decay the Foundation Capital follow-up conceded. [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) sets out the rule, and [Decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) covers how precedents should be selected for an agent.

**lowob**'s rule applies: rent the wiring, own the record. Rent the graph if it captures traces well; own the fields no trace can supply, and check that the record exports whole.

## Does a company need a context graph?

Not as a first step. A mid-size company gains more from recording one recurring decision class well before automating capture.

A context graph earns its cost where decisions are frequent and spread across many tools and people, as in large support, sales and finance operations. For a 50-person firm making a few dozen pricing exceptions a quarter, a structured [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/decision-record-template/) in a shared table captures the same information and adds the fields a graph leaves out.

## lowob takeaways

- **It records decisions, not just things.** Traces of rules, exceptions, approvals and precedents, linked to entities.
- **Definitions vary by vendor.** Check whether a product captures approvals and exceptions or only activity.
- **Traces are partial records.** Expected outcome, falsifier and check date still need a person.
- **Mark what is superseded.** Old precedent misleads an agent unless it is flagged as replaced.

## Common questions

### What is a context graph in AI?

A context graph is a connected record of decision traces, such as the rules applied, exceptions granted, approvals given and precedents used, linked to the people, accounts and documents involved. It lets an AI agent see how an organisation has actually decided similar cases. The term was popularised by a Foundation Capital essay in December 2025 and vendors define it differently.

### What is the difference between a context graph and a knowledge graph?

A knowledge graph stores entities and the relationships between them, such as which contact works at which account. A context graph adds decisions and actions: what was done, under which policy, with whose approval and in what order. Vendors such as Glean and Neo4j build the context graph on top of a knowledge graph rather than in place of one.

### What are decision traces?

Decision traces are records of how a specific case was handled: the policy applied, any exception granted, the precedent relied on, who approved it and what changed. Foundation Capital's December 2025 essay gives the example of a definition used under a named policy version with a VP exception based on an earlier precedent. Traces accumulate into a context graph.

### Is a context graph the same as a decision record?

No. A decision trace captures part of a decision record automatically, usually the action, policy, approver and precedent. A decision record also holds the reason in full, a status, the expected outcome, a falsifier and a check date, which no tool can observe because they exist only when someone writes them down at the moment of decision.
