# What Is Organizational Memory, and How AI Changes It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-organizational-memory/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Organizational memory, as Walsh and Ungson defined it in 1991, is stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions. It lives in people, culture, procedures, structures, workplaces and outside archives, and research led by Linda Argote shows it can decay and resists transfer. AI makes retrieval cheap but adds new risks: answers built on superseded records and summaries that outlive their sources.

Organisational memory is the stored information from a company's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions, held in people, culture, procedures, roles, workplaces and outside archives, as Walsh and Ungson defined it in 1991. Research since shows it decays and resists transfer. AI makes retrieving it cheap, but it does not tell an agent which decision is current or why, so the memory still needs an accountable record.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Organisational memory is the store at the base of **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, a loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/) sets out why memory alone is not enough.

## What is organisational memory?

It is what a company can recall to inform a decision now. Walsh and Ungson's 1991 paper in the *Academy of Management Review* defined it as "stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions."

Argyris and Schön had written in 1978, as Walsh and Ungson quote, that "organizations do not literally remember." Walsh and Ungson accepted that memory is not literal recall, but argued it is real all the same: distributed across people and artefacts, and stored "as a consequence of implementing decisions."

## Where does organisational memory live?

In six places, five inside the firm. The *International Encyclopedia of Organization Studies* (2008) describes this as the traditional framework, five internal archives plus external archives, and later work attributes these "retention bins" to Walsh and Ungson. Linda Argote's 2013 textbook uses the terms "retention bins" and "repositories". The table maps each to a commercial example and to what AI changes.

| Retention bin | What it holds | Commercial example | What AI changes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Individuals | Experience, judgment, who to ask | The account manager who knows why a client was given special terms | Assistants can spread an expert's practice, but cannot recall what was never written |
| Culture | Shared language, stories, norms | "We never discount in the last week of the quarter" | Models absorb the written version of norms, which may lag the lived one |
| Transformations | Procedures that turn inputs into outputs | The approval steps for a pricing exception | Agents can follow written procedures and expose gaps in them |
| Structures | Roles and reporting lines | Who signs off a discount above a threshold | Agent identities and permissions become part of the structure |
| Ecology | The physical and digital workplace | Which channel deals are actually negotiated in | Work moving into chat and calls creates more transcript, not more reason |
| External archives | Records held outside the firm | Clients' copies of contracts, partners' records, filings | Connectors reach some outside sources; most stay unreachable |

The commercial examples and the AI column are **lowob**'s. A seventh bin has arrived since: [agent memory](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/), what an AI system retains between sessions. It records what an agent saw, not what the organisation decided.

## How quickly do organisations forget?

Faster than cumulative experience suggests, on the best-known evidence. How much faster is disputed.

Argote, Beckman and Epple's study of production sites, in *Management Science* in February 1990, reports that "knowledge acquired through production depreciates rapidly" and that cumulative output, the conventional measure of learning, "significantly overstates the persistence of learning." Peter Thompson's 2007 re-analysis of Liberty shipbuilders' wartime records, in the same journal, found rates of forgetting "much smaller than previously reported, and may well be zero." Both concern manufacturing.

Turnover sets the clock for the first bin: the US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on 24 September 2026 that median tenure with the current employer was 4.1 years in January 2026, falling to 3.0 years for workers aged 25 to 34. In Panopto's survey of 1,000 respondents, reported by HR Dive on 18 July 2018, 42% of institutional knowledge was estimated to be unique to the individual: a vendor survey of self-estimates, so treat it as direction.

## Why is organisational knowledge hard to transfer?

Because much of it is embedded in the interaction of people, tasks and tools, which does not move cleanly.

Argote and Ingram, in *Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes* in 2000, argued that "the creation and transfer of knowledge are a basis for competitive advantage in firms." Their framework held that "interactions among people, tasks, and tools are least likely to fit the new context," so knowledge moves more easily inside a firm than between firms. Argote and Fahrenkopf's 2016 review extended it to members, tasks, tools and networks.

On the commercial line, the reason behind a pricing exception lives in a seller's head, a call and a chat thread. When the seller leaves, the procedure survives without its purpose.

## How does AI change organisational memory?

It makes retrieval cheap and spreads expert practice, but cannot supply unrecorded reasons, and adds two risks.

**Spreading practice.** In a study of 5,179 customer support agents, first issued by NBER in April 2023 and published in the *Quarterly Journal of Economics* in 2025, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found an AI assistant raised issues resolved per hour by 14% on average and by 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, with "suggestive evidence that the AI model disseminates the best practices of more able workers."

**Misusing what is found.** The MemTrace benchmark, posted to arXiv on 15 June 2026, tested 13 memory-system configurations and concluded that "the dominant bottleneck is evidence use, not retrieval." When systems failed, the evidence was retrievable ten times more often than it was missing. Finding three versions of a policy is not knowing which one stands; [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) sets out how records mark that.

**Summaries replacing sources.** When a summary is the only surviving copy of a meeting, memory narrows to what one model judged important. [Keep the sources, let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/) covers the evidence and the fix.

## What should a company do about it?

Treat memory as the store and build the record on top.

1. **Record decisions where they are made.** Use a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with the decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome, check date and falsifier.
2. **Capture reasons at handovers.** A handover that lists open decisions and their reasons protects the individuals bin.
3. **Keep sources immutable.** Summaries and agent memory are views over them, not replacements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Memory serves decisions.** Walsh and Ungson defined it by its use in present decisions, not by volume stored.
- **It lives in six places.** No single system holds it, and AI adds a seventh: agent memory.
- **It decays and resists transfer.** The evidence differs on how fast, not on whether maintenance is needed.
- **AI needs the record.** Retrieval is cheap; knowing which decision is current is not.

## Common questions

### What is organisational memory?

Organisational memory is the stored information from an organisation's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions, in Walsh and Ungson's 1991 definition. It is distributed across individuals, culture, procedures, structures, the workplace and external archives, so no single system holds it. In AI terms it is the store an enterprise brain reads before acting.

### What are the retention bins of organisational memory?

The framework associated with Walsh and Ungson's 1991 paper identifies six: individuals, culture, transformations (procedures that turn inputs into outputs), structures (roles), ecology (the physical workplace) and external archives held outside the firm. Linda Argote's textbook on organisational learning uses the terms retention bins and repositories. AI agent memory can be treated as an additional, newer bin.

### How does AI affect organisational memory?

AI makes stored knowledge cheaper to find and can spread expert practice: one study of 5,179 support agents found a 14% average productivity gain. But it cannot recover reasons nobody recorded, and a June 2026 benchmark found memory systems failed mostly by misusing evidence they had found. Decision records marking the current version address that.

### What is the difference between organisational memory and knowledge management?

Organisational memory is what a company retains from its past, wherever it sits, including people's heads and culture. Knowledge management is the deliberate practice of capturing, organising and sharing some of that memory, usually in documents and knowledge bases. Most organisational memory is never formally managed, which is why departures lose it.

### Why do companies lose knowledge when employees leave?

Because much of it is held by individuals and embedded in how they combine people, tasks and tools, which Argote's research shows does not transfer cleanly. Procedures often survive without the reasons behind them. Median US job tenure was 4.1 years in January 2026, so for most teams this loss is routine rather than exceptional.

## In the news

- 24 September 2026 · US Bureau of Labor Statistics[BLS publishes Employee Tenure in 2026](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-09-24-bls-publishes-employee-tenure-in-2026)People move on faster than decisions expire. That is the case for writing down why, not just what.

# What Is SR 26-2? The 2026 US Model Risk Guidance Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sr-26-2/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: SR 26-2 is the Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026. It supersedes SR 11-7 and SR 21-8, is most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets, sets no enforceable standards and places generative and agentic AI outside its scope. This explainer sets out what it covers, what it leaves out and what has happened since.

SR 26-2 is the Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC, replacing SR 11-7 and aimed mainly at banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets. It is principles-based, states that it sets no enforceable standards, and its footnote 3 places generative and agentic AI models outside its scope. Those tools are still supervised, through broader risk management.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

SR 26-2 is the reference text for model risk at large US banks, and the first revision of that guidance in 15 years. It matters well beyond banking because SR 11-7, the letter it replaced, was the template many insurers, lenders and fintechs copied. Our pillar guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) places it alongside FINRA, FCA and EU AI Act expectations.

This page summarises public supervisory texts and named law-firm readings for orientation. It is not legal advice.

## What is SR 26-2?

SR 26-2 is a Federal Reserve supervision letter that transmits interagency model risk guidance. The letter, dated 17 April 2026 and signed by Randall D. Guynn as Director of the Division of Supervision and Regulation, attaches a 12-page document titled Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management.

The OCC's News Release 2026-29 of the same day says the OCC acted "in coordination with" the Federal Reserve Board and the FDIC. The OCC rescinded its own Bulletin 2011-12, Bulletin 2021-19 on BSA/AML models, Bulletin 1997-24 on credit scoring models and the Model Risk Management booklet of the Comptroller's Handbook. Arnold & Porter's November 2026 advisory identifies the OCC's issuance of the guidance as Bulletin 2026-13.

| Item | SR 26-2, as issued on 17 April 2026 |
| --- | --- |
| Full title | Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management |
| Issued by | Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC |
| Supersedes | SR 11-7 (4 April 2011) and SR 21-8 (9 April 2021) |
| Most relevant to | Banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets |
| Status | No enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements |
| Model definition | "A complex quantitative method, system, or approach" applying statistical, economic or financial theories |
| Excluded | Spreadsheet arithmetic, deterministic rule-based processes, generative and agentic AI |
| Structure | Seven sections, 12 pages |
| OCC counterpart | Bulletin 2026-13 |

## Who does SR 26-2 apply to?

It is aimed at banking organisations with more than $30 billion in total assets. The letter says it is "expected to be most relevant" to them, and the OCC adds that it "may also be relevant to smaller institutions with significant model risk exposure."

That is a sharp change. Sullivan & Cromwell's 29 April 2026 memo notes that SR 11-7 itself set no asset threshold, while the FDIC's 2017 adoption of it applied a $1 billion threshold. Banks between those two figures are no longer the main audience, though safety and soundness expectations still apply to their models.

## What counts as a model under SR 26-2?

A model is "a complex quantitative method, system, or approach" that applies statistical, economic or financial theories. The guidance excludes "simple arithmetic calculations, such as those found within spreadsheets", and "deterministic rulebased processes and software where there are no statistical, economic, or financial theories."

Orrick's 24 April 2026 reading points out that the word "mathematical" has gone from the definition. In practice a rules engine that applies fixed thresholds is no longer a model for this purpose, while a statistical credit score still is.

## Does SR 26-2 cover generative AI and AI agents?

No. Footnote 3 states that "Generative AI and agentic AI models are novel and rapidly evolving. As such, they are not within the scope of this guidance." The principles apply to "traditional statistical and quantitative models."

Orrick reads the guidance as directing banks to their broader risk management and governance for these tools. The OCC said on 17 April that the agencies plan "a request for information that addresses model risk management generally and considers, in particular, banks' use of AI, including generative AI and agentic AI and AI-based models." We found no published request by mid-November 2026.

## What does SR 26-2 expect banks to do?

It describes sound practice across the model lifecycle in seven sections: introduction, purpose and scope, overview of model risk, development and use, validation and monitoring, governance and controls, and vendor and third-party products.

| Area | What SR 26-2 says | Evidence a bank keeps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Materiality | "Model purpose, together with model exposure, determines model materiality" | Risk rating per model, with the reasoning |
| Inventory | Should include "sufficient information to understand model risks" | A register of models in use and in development |
| Validation | Evaluates "whether models perform as expected", including reliability | Conceptual soundness review, outcomes analysis |
| Outcomes analysis | "Compares model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes" | Predicted against actual results, over time |
| Monitoring | Whether a model "is performing as expected" | Drift checks and limits, reviewed periodically |
| Effective challenge | Critical analysis "by objective experts" | Named challengers and what they changed |
| Documentation | "Adequate documentation helps to support effective model risk management" | Records that support continuity of operations |
| Vendor models | Validation of vendor products "by internal or outside parties" | Vendor understanding, monitoring, documented customisations |

Effort scales with materiality. Orrick notes that immaterial models with low inherent risk can receive lighter oversight, such as identification and performance monitoring. For customised vendor models, sound practice involves "documenting, justifying, and evaluating adjustments made to customize the model."

Our explainer [What is model risk management for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) explains the discipline behind these components.

## Is SR 26-2 binding?

No. The guidance states that it "does not set forth enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements" and that "non-compliance with this guidance will not result in supervisory criticism against a banking organization." Sullivan & Cromwell notes a footnote preserving supervisory action for violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices.

Our reading: supervisors will judge risk and outcomes, not checklist adherence. A bank still answers for losses caused by a bad model.

## What has happened since April 2026?

On 4 November 2026 the OCC issued Bulletin 2026-54, Super Intelligence: Supervisory Framework. The OCC uses "Super Intelligence" for "the technologies and systems previously encompassed by the term 'Artificial Intelligence'", citing Executive Order 14434.

The framework is a resource for OCC examiners, organised into 16 components across six pillars. The bulletin says it "does not establish supervisory expectations for banks" and that banks are not expected to use it for self-assessment. According to Arnold & Porter's 11 November 2026 reading, the OCC treats the model risk guidance as still applying to non-generative, non-agentic models, while the framework addresses generative and agentic systems. It is an OCC document; the Federal Reserve and FDIC are not named as co-issuers.

The framework's documentation component lists "decision traceability: inputs, outputs, context, retrieved sources, tool calls, approvals, overrides, and actions." That is close to the record our [AI audit trail checklist](https://lowob.com/research/ai-audit-trail-checklist/) sets out.

## lowob takeaways

- **SR 26-2 replaced SR 11-7.** Issued on 17 April 2026 by the Fed, OCC and FDIC, it also superseded the 2021 BSA/AML statement.
- **Scope narrowed twice.** It is aimed at banks above $30 billion and excludes spreadsheets, rule engines and generative and agentic AI.
- **Principles, not rules.** Non-compliance alone does not bring supervisory criticism; unsafe practices still do.
- **AI moved elsewhere.** Since 4 November 2026 a non-binding OCC framework guides examiners reviewing generative and agentic AI at national banks.

## Common questions

### What is SR 26-2?

SR 26-2 is the Federal Reserve letter that issued the Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management on 17 April 2026, jointly with the OCC and FDIC. It replaced SR 11-7 from 2011 and SR 21-8 from 2021, is most relevant to banks above $30 billion in total assets, and sets out principles for model development, validation, monitoring, governance and vendor models.

### Does SR 26-2 apply to generative AI?

No. Footnote 3 of SR 26-2 states that generative and agentic AI models are not within its scope because they are novel and rapidly evolving. Banks govern those tools through broader risk management. For national banks, the OCC issued a separate non-binding examiner framework for generative and agentic AI on 4 November 2026, OCC Bulletin 2026-54.

### Is SR 26-2 legally binding on banks?

No. The guidance says it does not set enforceable standards or prescriptive requirements, and that non-compliance with it will not by itself lead to supervisory criticism. A footnote keeps supervisory action available for violations of law or unsafe or unsound practices, so a weak model risk programme can still draw findings when it causes harm.

### What asset threshold does SR 26-2 use?

SR 26-2 says it is expected to be most relevant to banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets. The OCC adds that it may also be relevant to smaller institutions with significant model risk exposure. SR 11-7 set no threshold itself, though the FDIC applied a $1 billion threshold when it adopted SR 11-7 in 2017.

# Why AI Agent Projects Fail: The Evidence and How to Avoid It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/why-ai-agent-projects-fail/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, and S&P Global found 42% of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production. The causes are consistent across sources: tasks longer than agents can complete reliably, no workflow redesign, value nobody measures, rising running costs, poor data and weak controls. Each has a check a buyer can run before launch.

AI agent projects fail mainly because of escalating costs, unclear business value and agents given long, vague tasks they cannot complete reliably; Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. Poor data and weak controls make each cause worse. Projects that survive start with short, checkable work, redesign the workflow around it and measure the result.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Agent projects fail for reasons that are visible before the contract is signed. This guide sets out the evidence and the checks that catch each cause early. It builds on our hub piece, [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/), and on the limits described in [What AI Agents Still Cannot Do](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-still-cannot-do/).

## How many AI agent projects fail?

No one yet measures agent project failure directly, but the forecasts and adjacent data point to a high rate. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027.

S&P Global's 451 Research found the share of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production rose from 17% to 42% in a year, and the average organisation scrapped 46% of proofs of concept. MIT's Project NANDA, in its July 2025 report "The GenAI Divide", was reported as finding 95% of organisations seeing no business return from generative AI. That report combined a review of more than 300 public initiatives with 52 interviews and 153 survey responses, so treat it as directional.

## Why do AI agent projects fail?

Seven causes recur across the evidence. Most projects that fail show more than one.

| Cause | Evidence | Warning sign | Prevention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Task too long or vague for current reliability | METR: 80% horizons roughly five times shorter than 50% horizons; CRMArena-Pro: about 35% multi-turn success on business tasks (May 2025) | The demo is one impressive end-to-end run | Break the work into short steps a person can check |
| No workflow redesign | McKinsey 2026: nearly three-quarters of high performers redesigned workflows, against one-quarter of others | The agent is added to the old process unchanged | Redraw the process, including who approves what |
| Value never measured | McKinsey 2026: 37% attribute any EBIT impact to AI; KPMG Q3 2026: 12% consistently assess value against cost | No baseline was recorded before launch | Record the before figure and one outcome metric |
| Running costs escalate | Gartner 2025 cites escalating costs; McKinsey 2026: about 20% say AI operating costs, including tokens, constrained use | Usage pricing with no cap or budget owner | Set token or spend budgets per agent |
| Poor data and missing context | Validity 2025: 37% lost revenue to poor CRM data; 76% say less than half of CRM data is accurate and complete | The agent reads records nobody trusts | Clean the records it reads first; mark stale facts |
| Weak controls and excessive agency | OWASP LLM06:2025; KPMG Q3 2026: building controls into agents fell to 30% from 43% two quarters earlier | The agent runs on a person's login or an admin key | Least privilege, approval gates, logs of every action |
| Agent washing | Gartner 2025: only about 130 of thousands of agentic vendors are real | The vendor cannot say what the product decides | Ask what it decides for itself before you buy |

### Tasks too long for current reliability

The most common design error is handing an agent a whole job. METR's original study found that the task length agents complete at 80% success is roughly a fifth of the length they complete at 50%, and that performance is much lower on messier, less structured tasks. On Salesforce AI Research's CRMArena-Pro benchmark, leading agents managed about 58% of single-turn business tasks and about 35% once the task ran over several turns. Commercial work is mostly multi-turn and messy.

### No workflow redesign, no measured value

Projects that bolt an agent onto an unchanged process rarely show a return. McKinsey's distinction between high performers and the rest in 2026 is largely about redesign. Gartner's May 2026 release adds a warning for anyone building the case on headcount: among organisations piloting or deploying autonomous capabilities, about 80% reported workforce reductions, but those reductions did not appear to translate into return on investment.

### Costs, data and controls

Running costs grow with use: each retry, loop and longer context costs tokens. Data quality decides what the agent sees, and an agent reading an inaccurate CRM produces confident, inaccurate work. Controls decide how much damage a wrong step does. OWASP defines excessive agency as damaging actions taken in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs, and names three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy.

## What do successful AI agent projects do differently?

They start small, redesign the work and measure it. Zapier's September 2026 vendor survey found 46% of large-company leaders saying their most mature agent had paid for itself or was expected to within 12 months, and the leaders reporting the most autonomy were those whose agents sat inside broader automated workflows.

Our own view, set out in [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/), is that the first agent should be frequent, checkable, low in risk and doing work people dislike. On the commercial line that usually means meeting preparation, CRM hygiene or follow-up drafts held in a queue. Start at autonomy level 1 (draft) and move to level 2 (act with approval) only on evidence from logged runs.

| Before launch, can you show | If not |
| --- | --- |
| A written goal and stop condition | The task is too vague; narrow it |
| The baseline figure the agent should move | You will not be able to prove value |
| A spend cap and the person who owns it | Costs will surprise you |
| The records it reads, and who keeps them accurate | It will repeat your data problems at speed |
| Its permissions, its identity and its approval gate | A wrong step becomes a wrong action |
| One replayed run: what it saw, what it did and who approved | You cannot debug or defend it |

## lowob takeaways

- **Most failure causes are visible early.** Vague goals, no baseline, uncapped costs and broad permissions can all be spotted before launch.
- **Design around the 80% number.** Agents complete far shorter tasks reliably than the 50% figures suggest.
- **Redesign the work.** The leaders in McKinsey's data changed workflows, not only tools.
- **Headcount cuts are not a return.** Gartner found reductions did not translate into ROI.

## Common questions

### Why do AI agent projects fail?

The main causes are escalating costs, unclear business value, tasks too long or vague for current agent reliability, poor data and weak controls. Gartner cites costs and unclear value in its forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. Most failed projects show several causes at once, often starting with a goal nobody wrote down.

### What percentage of AI agent projects fail?

There is no measured failure rate for agents yet. Gartner forecast in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. S&P Global's 451 Research found 42% of companies abandoning most AI initiatives before production, and the average organisation scrapping 46% of proofs of concept, in a survey fielded in late 2024.

### How do you make an AI agent project succeed?

Start with frequent, checkable, low-risk work, record a baseline before launch and redesign the workflow around the agent. Give it its own identity, the fewest permissions it needs and an approval gate for anything external. McKinsey's 2026 survey found nearly three-quarters of AI high performers had fundamentally redesigned workflows, against one-quarter of others.

### Do AI agents fail because of bad data?

Often. An agent acts on what it reads, so inaccurate records become inaccurate actions. Validity's 2025 report found 76% of CRM users saying less than half of their CRM data is accurate and complete, and 37% losing revenue as a direct consequence of poor data quality. Clean and mark the records an agent will read before it goes live.

- [OWASP, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/). Community security standard.
- [Zapier, AI agents survey](https://zapier.com/blog/ai-agents-survey/), updated 9 November 2026. Vendor survey of 513 US leaders, September 2026.

# What Is an AI Center of Excellence?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-center-of-excellence/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI centre of excellence is an internal team that sets standards for AI use, prioritises requests, runs pilots and spreads skills, so adoption is neither fragmented nor ungoverned. Guidance suggests starting centralised and moving to an advisory role as adoption matures. For a mid-size firm it can be two or three people with a clear mandate.

An AI centre of excellence (CoE) is an internal team that sets the standards for how a company uses AI, decides which requests get built or bought first, runs pilots, and helps other teams build skills. Its purpose is to stop AI adoption from becoming either fragmented or ungoverned. Large firms staff it with data scientists, engineers and governance specialists; a firm of 20 to 500 people can run one with two or three people, provided someone owns it and it has a written mandate.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What an AI centre of excellence means

The term borrows from older centres of excellence for cloud or analytics: a small group concentrates expertise, writes the rules and helps everyone else adopt. Unlike a governance committee, it also does work, running pilots and publishing reusable assets. Unlike a central build team, a CoE done well does not build everything itself.

| An AI CoE is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| The owner of AI standards, intake and the AI inventory | The only team allowed to use AI |
| A source of approved patterns and reusable assets | A queue every request must wait in |
| Accountable to an executive sponsor | A side project of the IT helpdesk |

## What it does

Microsoft's guidance lists eight responsibilities. They map well onto what a mid-size firm needs, with the scale adjusted.

| Responsibility | In a large enterprise | In a firm of 20 to 500 people (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI strategy | Align AI with business goals; responsible AI policy | One page: where AI is used first and why |
| Skills | Learning pathways and hands-on labs | Role-based briefings and a literacy record |
| Pilots | Prioritised proofs of concept | One pilot at a time on the commercial line |
| Standards | Governance, security, bias and transparency reviews | [Acceptable use policy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-acceptable-use-policy/), data rule, approval rules |
| Intake and prioritisation | Structured intake and an AI backlog | A shared list of requests with a monthly decision |
| Reusable assets | Checklists, templates, code libraries | Approved prompts, vendor question set, impact assessment template |
| Measure and report | Adoption, compliance and cycle-time KPIs | Quarterly note to leadership on uses, outcomes and incidents |
| Manage AI services (optional) | Model monitoring and lifecycle management | Usually left to vendors |

The skills row now carries a legal dimension for firms with EU exposure. Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires measures to support staff AI literacy; see [What is AI literacy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/). A CoE is the natural owner of that record.

## How it is organised and how it evolves

Microsoft recommends a named CoE leader, executive sponsorship through a steering group with monthly reviews, and building on existing teams rather than creating a standalone one. Without sponsorship, it says, "the AI CoE can't enforce standards or drive organizational change."

Its guidance on evolution is the most useful part. Centralisation "at the onset accelerates AI adoption", but the CoE should move to an advisory role once governance can be built into platforms and daily operations. The warning signs it lists are approval delays, knowledge bottlenecks, and product teams and the CoE debating priorities instead of delivering value. The aim is to "replace the CoE gatekeeper model that blocks work with an advisory group that sets guardrails."

McKinsey's data points the same way. Risk, compliance and data governance are usually centralised; talent and adoption are more often hybrid, with some resources central and others in functions. Firms with under $500 million in revenue were more likely to centralise talent and adoption fully, which fits a small firm's reality: there are not enough specialists to distribute.

| Stage | Typical model | Sign it is time to move on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting | Centralised: the CoE approves and often delivers | Requests queue for weeks |
| Scaling | Hybrid: standards central, delivery in teams | Teams have their own capable owners |
| Mature | Advisory: CoE sets guardrails and reviews exceptions | Governance runs inside normal approval routes |

## Common mistakes

- **No executive owner.** A CoE without a sponsor publishes standards nobody follows.
- **Building instead of enabling.** If the CoE delivers every use, it becomes the bottleneck it was meant to prevent.
- **Measuring activity.** Counting pilots says little; recording which uses changed an outcome says more.
- **Starting everywhere.** **lowob**'s view is to start on the commercial line, where outcomes are measurable.

## The **lowob** view

In **lowob**'s terms, a CoE's lasting job is to own the record, not the tools: the AI inventory, the autonomy level and approver for each use, the decision log and the outcomes written back each quarter. The wiring can be rented and builds can move to teams. The record is what lets the CoE step back to an advisory role without losing control. Gateway 0 in The Build Order, which names an owner before any tool is bought, is the smallest version of a CoE.

## lowob takeaways

- **Mandate and owner first.** A named leader and an executive sponsor matter more than headcount.
- **Start central, plan to step back.** Guidance recommends moving from control to an advisory role.
- **Own the record.** Inventory, approvals and outcomes are the CoE's durable output.
- **Small is fine.** Two or three people with a written mandate can run one in a mid-size firm.

## Common questions

### What is an AI centre of excellence?

An internal team that sets AI standards, prioritises requests, runs pilots and builds skills, so that AI adoption is neither fragmented nor ungoverned.

### Who should be in an AI centre of excellence?

An executive sponsor, a named leader, business leads who know the use cases, and technical, security and governance expertise, drawn from existing teams where possible.

### Does a small company need an AI CoE?

It needs the functions, not a department: an owner, an inventory, standards, intake and a record of decisions. Two or three people part-time can cover them.

### What is the difference between an AI CoE and an AI governance committee?

A governance committee approves and oversees. A CoE also does work: pilots, reusable assets, skills and support for teams.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft Learn, Establish an AI Center of Excellence](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/cloud-adoption-framework/scenarios/ai/center-of-excellence), last updated 10 April 2026. Vendor guidance from Microsoft's Cloud Adoption Framework; Microsoft sells AI platforms.
- [McKinsey, The state of AI: How organizations are rewiring to capture value](https://www.mckinsey.com/our-insights/the-state-of-ai-how-organizations-are-rewiring-to-capture-value), 12 March 2025. Consultancy survey of 1,491 participants, fielded July 2024; self-reported.
- [Jones Day, OMB directs agencies to accelerate AI adoption and devise governance strategy](https://www.jonesday.com/en/insights/2025/05/omb-directs-agencies-to-accelerate-ai-adoption-and-devise-governance-strategy), May 2025. Law firm summary of OMB memo M-25-21, which binds US federal agencies only.

## Related research

- [What Is AI Governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/)
- [Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/)
- [What Is AI Literacy, and What Does the EU AI Act Require?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/)

## Next move

Write a half-page mandate for your AI CoE this week: its owner, sponsor, the three standards it holds and how requests reach it. Circulate it with the current AI inventory attached.

# What Is Customer Churn?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Customer churn measures how many customers, or how much of their recurring revenue, a firm loses over a period. Logo churn counts customers; gross revenue churn counts lost and downgraded revenue and is the complement of gross revenue retention. Reporting both shows whether losses are concentrated in small or large accounts, and recording the reason for each loss is what lets the next renewal go better.

Customer churn is the loss of customers, or of the recurring revenue they bring, over a set period. Logo churn counts the share of customers lost. Gross revenue churn counts the share of starting recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades, and is 100% minus gross revenue retention. The gap between the two shows whether you are losing many small accounts or a few large ones.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What customer churn means

Churn is the opposite of retention. Of the customers paying at the start of a period, some leave, some pay less and some pay more. Churn measures the losses, and excludes customers won during the period.

There is no single churn number. Andreessen Horowitz's startup metrics guide notes that there are "all kinds of churn", including customer churn, dollar churn and net dollar churn, and that definitions vary between companies. Any churn figure should state its kind and period.

| Term | What it counts | Includes downgrades? | Includes expansion? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Logo churn | Customers lost | No | No |
| Gross revenue churn | Recurring revenue lost | Yes | No |
| Net revenue churn | Revenue lost minus expansion | Yes | Yes |
| Voluntary churn | Customers who chose to cancel | Not applicable | No |
| Involuntary churn | Customers lost to failed payments | Not applicable | No |

## The formulas

**Logo churn rate** = customers lost during the period ÷ customers at the start of the period.

Recurly uses this structure for subscriber churn, and Andreessen Horowitz's monthly version is "lost customers/prior month total".

**Gross revenue churn rate** = recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades during the period ÷ recurring revenue at the start of the period.

Andreessen Horowitz states the monthly form using monthly recurring revenue (MRR). Gross revenue retention (GRR) is 100% minus this figure. SaaS Capital's GRR method caps each continuing customer's later revenue at its earlier level, so upsells and price rises cannot offset losses.

**Net revenue churn rate** = (revenue lost minus expansion revenue) ÷ revenue at the start. It can be negative, which is the same as net revenue retention above 100%. Our explainer on [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) covers that measure, and [NRR vs GRR](https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/) covers which to report.

## A worked example (illustrative)

An illustrative firm starts the year with 200 customers paying £2,000,000 in annual recurring revenue.

| Movement over 12 months | Customers | Annual recurring revenue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Start of year | 200 | £2,000,000 |
| Customers who left | 16 | £80,000 lost |
| Downgrades among those who stayed |  | £40,000 lost |
| Expansion among those who stayed |  | £180,000 gained |
| End of year, same customers | 184 | £2,060,000 |

- **Logo churn:** 16 ÷ 200 = 8%.
- **Gross revenue churn:** (£80,000 + £40,000) ÷ £2,000,000 = 6%, so GRR is 94%.
- **Net revenue churn:** (£120,000 minus £180,000) ÷ £2,000,000 = minus 3%, so NRR is 103%.

Logo churn is higher than revenue churn here, so the firm is losing mainly smaller customers. The reverse pattern, low logo churn and high revenue churn, means a few large accounts are leaving or shrinking, which is usually the more serious problem.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Every pound lost has to be replaced before new business adds growth. Net figures blend upsell with loss, which is why Andreessen Horowitz says "gross churn estimates the actual loss to the business". A firm with healthy expansion can report net retention above 100% while losing many customers. Three measurement errors recur.

**Annualising monthly churn by multiplying.** Recurly notes that "annual churn is not simply 12x monthly churn because of compounding"; 2% a month is about 22% a year, not 24%.

**Counting failed payments as decisions.** Involuntary churn, from failed payments, needs a billing fix. Mixing it with voluntary churn hides both.

**Comparing across segments.** SaaS Capital reports that net retention rises with contract value, so compare with firms of similar contract size.

Firms without subscriptions, such as agencies, can apply the same logic to repeat clients and their fees.

In **lowob**'s model, churn is an outcome to write back. Each lost or shrunk account should carry the customer's stated reason and the account owner's, recorded against the renewal decision that preceded it. [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) sets out the renewal calendar that produces those records. Over time they show which warning signs, from a [customer health score](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/) or elsewhere, preceded real losses.

## lowob takeaways

- **Report logo and revenue churn together.** The gap shows whether small or large accounts are leaving.
- **Use gross, not only net.** Expansion can hide losses that gross churn shows plainly.
- **Separate involuntary churn.** Failed payments need a billing fix, not a retention campaign.
- **Record the reason.** A loss without the customer's reason cannot inform the next renewal.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate customer churn rate?

Divide customers lost during a period by customers at its start, excluding customers won during the period.

### What is the difference between logo churn and revenue churn?

Logo churn counts customers lost. Revenue churn counts recurring revenue lost to cancellations and downgrades, so large losses weigh more.

### What is the difference between gross and net revenue churn?

Gross revenue churn counts only losses. Net revenue churn subtracts expansion revenue from those losses, so it can be negative when expansion exceeds losses.

### Can you convert monthly churn to annual churn by multiplying by 12?

No. Churn compounds: annual churn is one minus monthly retention to the twelfth power, so 2% monthly is about 22% annual.

## Sources and notes

- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/?Ref=adhawk), Jeff Jordan, Anu Hariharan, Frank Chen and Preethi Kasireddy, 21 August 2015. Investor guide; formulas are monthly and written for startups.
- [Recurly, Churn rate benchmarks](https://www.recurly.com/research/churn-rate-benchmarks), data as of July 2026. Billing vendor research on its own network; used here for definitions only, as its industry figures are inconsistent across the page.
- [SaaS Capital, SaaS Retention Benchmarks for Private B2B Companies](https://www.saas-capital.com/research/saas-retention-benchmarks-for-private-b2b-companies/), 18 September 2025. Annual survey of private SaaS firms; self-reported, sample size not stated on the page.

## Related research

- [What Is Net Revenue Retention (NRR)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/)
- [NRR vs GRR: Which Retention Number to Report](https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/)
- [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/)
- [What Is Customer Health Scoring?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/)

## Next move

Pull last year's starting customer list from billing and count who has left. Calculate logo churn and gross revenue churn side by side, then list the five largest losses with the customer's own reason.

# What Is a Buying Committee?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A buying committee, also called a buying group or buying centre, is everyone at a customer who takes part in a purchase decision. Academic work since the 1960s and recent analyst surveys agree it is larger and more conflicted than sellers assume: Forrester found 13 people on average in 2024. For a commercial team the practical step is to record the committee on each opportunity, by role, and to sell to its consensus.

A buying committee is the group of people at a customer organisation who take part in deciding a business-to-business purchase: those who use, evaluate, fund, approve and contract for it. Researchers call it the buying centre; Gartner and Forrester call it the buying group. Recent surveys put it at 5 to 16 people, and conflict within it is common.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a buying committee means

Few B2B purchases are made by one person. A software tool is used by one team, assessed by IT, paid from another budget, reviewed by legal and approved by an executive. Any of them can stop it.

The concept comes from organisational buying research. Frederick Webster and Yoram Wind's 1972 paper in the *Journal of Marketing* modelled industrial buying as "an organizational decision-making process". It set out a concept of roles within the buying centre that later researchers extended. In 1982 Wind and Robertson proposed a sixth, "pin" role to manage interaction inside and outside the group. Wesley Johnston and Thomas Bonoma's 1981 study in the same journal measured real buying centres across 31 firms and 62 purchases, using 241 interviews.

"Buying centre" is the academic term, "buying group" the analysts' and "buying committee" the sellers'. They describe the same thing, though a formal committee is only one form it takes.

## How large it is

| Source | Year | Finding | Sample |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Johnston and Bonoma, *Journal of Marketing* | 1981 | Size grows with purchase importance, complexity and formalisation; services involve fewer people than capital equipment | 31 firms, 62 purchases |
| Gartner, buyer enablement research | Undated | Typical group of six to ten stakeholders | More than 250 B2B customers |
| Forrester, State of Business Buying | 2024 | 13 people on average; 89% of purchases involve two or more departments | Not stated in the release |
| Gartner, sales survey | 2025 | 5 to 16 people across up to four functions | 632 B2B buyers |

Samples and definitions differ, but the direction is consistent: more people than a seller usually meets, from more than one department.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

**Consensus is the hard part.** Gartner's May 2025 release defines unhealthy conflict as members having "conflicting objectives", disagreeing on the best course of action, or being overruled by external decision-makers. It found that content tailored to the group's shared needs improved consensus by 20%, while content focused only on individual relevance reduced it by 59%. Messaging each person separately can pull the group apart, which is the argument of [Positioning for Complex Markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/): give each role a reason to agree to one position.

**Single-threaded deals are fragile.** A deal with one engaged contact depends on that person's influence and tenure. [Revenue intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-intelligence/) tools flag it as a risk.

**Scoring should follow the group.** The case for scoring accounts rather than individual leads is set out in [Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring](https://lowob.com/research/lead-scoring-vs-account-scoring/).

In **lowob**'s model the committee is data in the store, attached to the opportunity as contact roles. Who approved, who objected hardest and who was never reached also feed win-loss reviews and the deal's decision record.

## How to map a buying committee

An illustrative role map for a mid-size services purchase. Role names vary by framework; [MEDDICC](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-meddicc/), for example, names an economic buyer and a champion.

| Role | What they care about | What to record in the CRM | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Economic buyer | Return and risk to the budget | Name, confirmed budget, decision date | Never met by the seller |
| Champion | Solving the problem they own | Name, the case they will make internally | Champion cannot name the approver |
| User lead | Daily workload and fit | Name, requirements raised | No user has seen the solution |
| Technical or IT reviewer | Security, integration, data | Name, review status | Review not started inside the quarter |
| Procurement | Terms, price, supplier risk | Name, process and timeline | Process discovered at the last minute |
| Legal | Liability and contract terms | Name, redline status | Redlines arrive after the close date |

Ask early who else will be involved, and record every answer as a contact role. Build a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/) with a named buyer owner for each step. At each pipeline meeting, check which roles are empty on late-stage deals. Agents can draft role-specific follow-ups, but each goes to the account owner before sending, because a message to the wrong member can undo a champion's work.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume a group.** Most B2B purchases involve people from more than one department.
- **Sell to agreement.** Consensus predicts deal quality better than any one person's enthusiasm.
- **Record roles on the opportunity.** Empty roles on late-stage deals are a forecast risk.
- **Score the account, not the lead.** One contact's activity says little about the committee.

## Common questions

### Who is on a B2B buying committee?

Typically an economic buyer, a champion, users, technical reviewers, procurement and legal. The mix depends on the purchase.

### How many people are on a buying committee?

Forrester's 2024 research found 13 on average. Gartner's 2025 survey found 5 to 16 people across up to four functions.

### What is the difference between a buying committee and a buying centre?

None in substance. Buying centre is the academic term from organisational buying research; buying committee and buying group are the sales and analyst terms.

## Sources and notes

- [Johnston and Bonoma, The Buying Center: Structure and Interaction Patterns](https://vc.uni-bamberg.de/pluginfile.php/2929163/mod_folder/content/0/The%20Buying%20Center%20Structure%20and%20Interaction%20Patterns.pdf), *Journal of Marketing* Vol. 45, No. 3, Summer 1981. Academic study; university-hosted copy; small sample of 31 firms.
- [Webster and Wind, A General Model for Understanding Organizational Buying Behavior](https://scilit.com/publications/83057ca9992eae960e987d45f2af548f), *Journal of Marketing* Vol. 36, No. 2, April 1972. Bibliographic record and abstract only; full text behind a paywall.
- [Kemmerling and Herbst, A Status Quo of Buying Center Analysis](https://impgroup.org/wp-content/uploads/wpallimport/files/papers/8225.pdf), IMP Group conference paper, undated, references to 2013. Academic literature review; source for the Wind and Robertson pin role.
- [Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size for this study not stated.
- [Gartner, Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict"](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), 7 May 2025. Analyst press release; 632 buyers surveyed August to September 2024.
- [Gartner, Buyer Enablement](https://gcom.pdo.aws.gartner.com/en/sales/insights/buyer-enablement), undated. Analyst research summary; survey date not given.

## Next move

Open your five largest deals and count the contacts with a recorded role. Treat any deal with fewer than three roles filled as single-threaded.

# What Is a Small Language Model?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-small-language-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A small language model uses the same design as a large one with far fewer parameters, typically under about 10 billion, so it runs on modest hardware at lower cost. It suits narrow, repeated tasks such as classification, extraction and routing. The practical pattern is a mix: small models for routine steps, a large model where open-ended judgment is needed.

A small language model (SLM) is a language model compact enough to run on ordinary hardware, such as a laptop, a phone or a single server, rather than a large cloud cluster. There is no fixed cut-off; NVIDIA researchers treat most models below about 10 billion parameters as small as of 2025. SLMs are cheaper and faster per request and can run where data must stay. They hold less general knowledge and handle open-ended reasoning less well, so they suit narrow, repeated tasks.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a small language model means

A small language model uses the same Transformer design as a [large language model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-large-language-model/) with far fewer parameters. What counts as small moves as hardware improves.

The NVIDIA Research position paper "Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI" avoids a fixed parameter count. Its working definition is a model that "can fit onto a common consumer electronic device" and respond fast enough to serve one user's agent. As of 2025, the authors would treat "most models below 10bn parameters in size" as SLMs.

Microsoft's Phi-3 report, from April 2024, is a common reference point. For Phi-3-mini, with 3.8 billion parameters, its developers report overall performance that rivals Mixtral 8x7B and GPT-3.5, from a model "small enough to be deployed on a phone". Google's Gemma documentation, accessed November 2026, lists open-weight models from about 2 billion effective parameters, aimed at phones and browsers, up to 31 billion for servers.

Many SLMs are released as [open-weight models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-open-weight-model/), which is why they can run on a firm's own hardware. Others are offered only through a provider's API, usually as its lowest-cost tier.

|  | Small language model | Large language model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical size | Under about 10 billion parameters | Tens to hundreds of billions |
| Where it runs | Laptop, phone, single server, or a provider's cheapest tier | Provider's cloud infrastructure |
| Cost per request | Low | Higher |
| Speed | Fast | Slower |
| General knowledge | Narrower | Broader |
| Best at | Classification, extraction, routing, short drafts | Open-ended reasoning, synthesis, long writing |
| Customisation | Practical to fine-tune for one task | Usually used as supplied |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Most AI calls in a commercial workflow are narrow: tagging an inbound enquiry by segment, pulling renewal dates from contracts, routing a support ticket. These need consistency, speed and a low cost per call, not broad knowledge.

Cost compounds in agents. Each step of an [agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/) is a model call, and many steps are routine. The NVIDIA paper argues that SLMs should be the default in agentic systems, with large models "invoked selectively and sparingly". It cites estimates that serving a 7-billion-parameter model is 10 to 30 times cheaper, in latency, energy and compute, than serving a 70-to-175-billion-parameter one. Those ranges come from cited work and describe serving cost, not list prices; see [AI inference cost](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/).

Gartner's April 2025 prediction points the same way. It expects organisations to implement small, task-specific models with usage at least three times that of general-purpose LLMs by 2027. It pairs the prediction with a condition: tuning depends on company data that has been prepared, quality-checked and versioned.

Location matters for regulated firms. A small model running on the firm's own servers keeps prompts and records inside its perimeter, which can simplify [data residency](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/) questions. It also moves patching, monitoring and capacity planning onto the firm.

The limits are real. Smaller models know less, follow long multi-part instructions less reliably and are weaker on open-ended reasoning. [Fine-tuning](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-fine-tuning/) a small model on one narrow task can close much of the gap for that task, but not for others. Benchmark scores for small models are mostly self-reported by their developers and rarely reflect commercial documents.

In **lowob**'s model of the brain, the reasoning layer is rented and replaceable. Small models make that more true: the model becomes a component chosen per step, while the instructions, test sets and decision record stay with the firm.

## How to decide where a small model fits

| Question | Points to a small model | Points to a large model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Is the task narrow and repeated? | The same task thousands of times | Each request is different |
| Is the output short and structured? | Labels, fields, yes or no | Long synthesis or argument |
| Must data stay on your hardware? | Yes | No constraint |
| Is response time user-facing? | Needs to feel instant | Can wait |
| Can you test it? | 50 or more labelled examples exist | No test set yet |

Run the same labelled set through a small model and your current one, and choose the smallest that meets the accuracy bar. Recheck when either model changes.

## lowob takeaways

- **Small is relative.** Most models under about 10 billion parameters counted as small in 2025, and the line moves.
- **Narrow tasks suit small models.** Classification, extraction and routing rarely need a frontier model.
- **Mix models per step.** Use a large model only where open-ended judgment is required.
- **Test on your own cases.** Benchmarks for small models are mostly self-reported.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an SLM and an LLM?

Mainly size, and therefore cost, speed and breadth. An SLM has far fewer parameters, runs on modest hardware and is cheaper per request, but holds less general knowledge and reasons less well on open-ended tasks.

### How many parameters does a small language model have?

There is no standard. NVIDIA researchers suggest most models under about 10 billion parameters counted as small in 2025; Microsoft's Phi-3-mini, for example, has 3.8 billion.

### Can a small language model run on a laptop or phone?

Many can. Microsoft designed Phi-3-mini to run on a phone, and Google's Gemma line includes models aimed at phones and browsers.

### Are small language models good enough for business use?

For narrow, repeated tasks with clear outputs, often yes, especially after fine-tuning. Test one on your own labelled examples before replacing a larger model.

## Sources and notes

- [Belcak et al. (NVIDIA Research), Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.02153), first posted June 2025. Position paper by researchers at a hardware vendor; cost ranges are drawn from cited work.
- [Microsoft, Phi-3 Technical Report: A Highly Capable Language Model Locally on Your Phone](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.14219), April 2024, revised August 2024. Developer's own benchmark results.
- [Gartner, Gartner Predicts by 2027, Organizations Will Use Small, Task-Specific AI Models Three Times More Than General-Purpose Large Language Models](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-04-09-gartner-predicts-by-2027-organizations-will-use-small-task-specific-ai-models-three-times-more-than-general-purpose-large-language-models), 9 April 2025. Analyst prediction, not measured data.
- [Google, Gemma models overview](https://ai.google.dev/gemma/docs/core), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; the model line-up changes often.

List the AI steps in one commercial workflow and mark each as narrow (label, extract, route) or open-ended. Run 50 labelled examples of one narrow step through a small model and compare cost and accuracy with your current model.

# What Is AI Literacy, and What Does the EU AI Act Require?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI literacy is the skills and understanding people need to use AI systems in an informed way and to recognise their risks. Article 4 of the EU AI Act makes it a duty for providers and deployers. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 kept the duty but changed it from ensuring a sufficient level to taking measures that support it, with no set level guaranteed for any individual.

AI literacy is the skills, knowledge and understanding that let people use AI systems in an informed way and see their opportunities, risks and possible harms. Article 4 of the EU AI Act requires providers and deployers to take measures that support AI literacy among their staff and others using AI on their behalf. Since the Digital Omnibus amendment took effect on 27 July 2026, the duty is one of effort: no specific level has to be guaranteed for any individual.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What AI literacy means

Article 3(56) defines AI literacy as the skills, knowledge and understanding that allow providers, deployers and affected persons to make an informed deployment of AI systems and to gain awareness of their opportunities, risks and possible harm.

In a company, that means role-specific knowledge. A seller using a drafting assistant needs to know it can invent facts and what data must never go into it. An owner of a hiring tool needs far more. Literacy is about limits and judgment, not prompting tips or a general course on neural networks.

## What Article 4 required, and what changed in 2026

The duty has applied since 2 February 2025. The 2026 change is to its strength, not its existence. The consolidated text on the Commission's AI Act Service Desk, as at 27 July 2026, marks all three paragraphs of Article 4 as amended.

| Version | Wording or effect |
| --- | --- |
| Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, original | Providers and deployers "shall take measures to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level of AI literacy" of staff and others acting for them |
| Commission proposal, 19 November 2025 | The Commission and Member States would "encourage" providers and deployers, removing the direct duty on companies (per William Fry's summary) |
| Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force 27 July 2026 | Providers and deployers "shall take measures to support the development of AI literacy"; no specific level must be guaranteed for any individual |

So the proposal to remove the direct duty did not survive. Companies still carry an obligation, but it is judged on the measures taken rather than the level achieved. Bristows describes the result as an obligation "of effort rather than outcome". Amended paragraph 2 commits the Commission and Member States to support providers and deployers, in particular SMEs, including by publishing practical examples. Paragraph 3 asks the AI Board for recommendations.

This is our reading of the published text and guidance. It is not legal advice, and firms with high-risk uses should take their own.

## What the Commission expects

The Commission's AI literacy Q&A, updated on 20 October 2026 to reflect the amendment, is the most practical guidance.

- **Who is covered.** Staff, and other persons operating or using AI on the organisation's behalf, such as contractors and service providers.
- **No certificate.** Organisations can keep an internal record of training and other guidance initiatives instead.
- **No fixed format.** The approach depends on context and the risk of the systems in use. Relying only on a vendor's instructions for use is often ineffective, the Q&A says.
- **Suggested minimum content.** A general understanding of AI in the organisation, the organisation's role as provider or deployer, the risks of the systems in use, and actions tailored to staff knowledge and context, including legal and ethical aspects.
- **Enforcement.** National market surveillance authorities supervise from 2 August 2026 and may impose proportionate penalties.

## A proportionate programme for a commercial team

For a firm of 20 to 500 people, literacy is easiest to organise by role and by autonomy level. The table is illustrative; adjust it to the tools in your inventory.

| Role | What they need to know | Evidence to keep |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Everyone | Approved tools, the data rule, how to report a mistake | Policy briefing, dated |
| Sellers and marketers | Where drafting tools err; disclosure rules for chatbots and synthetic media | Short session per tool |
| Approvers | What to check before approving agent output, and when to reject | Named list, with examples reviewed |
| Agent and tool owners | Autonomy level, limits, logs, kill switch | Owner sign-off on the inventory |
| Owners of high-risk uses | Article 26 oversight duties, the provider's instructions | Training record per person |

The first row is usually an [AI acceptable use policy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-acceptable-use-policy/). The approver row matters most under **lowob**'s rule that nothing sends without a person: an approver who does not know what to check is a signature, not a control.

## The **lowob** view

**lowob** treats literacy as part of the record, not a training event. The useful evidence is a dated line per person and tool: who was briefed, on what, and who approves their output. It sits beside the AI inventory and the decision log, where a regulator or a customer's security review can read it.

## lowob takeaways

- **The duty survived.** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 softened Article 4 to "support" but did not remove it from companies.
- **Effort is judged, not level.** No individual must reach a set standard; the measures must fit the role and risk.
- **Keep a record.** No certificate is needed, but an internal record of who learned what is the natural evidence.
- **Train approvers first.** The people who sign off AI output carry the most risk and need the most specific briefing.

## Common questions

### What does Article 4 of the EU AI Act require?

Since the 2026 amendment, providers and deployers must take measures to support the development of AI literacy among staff and others using AI for them, without guaranteeing a specific level for any individual.

### Was the AI literacy obligation removed by the Digital Omnibus?

No. The Commission proposed shifting it to public authorities, but the final text kept a duty on providers and deployers, reframed as supporting AI literacy.

### Do employees need an AI literacy certificate?

No. The Commission says no certificate is needed; organisations can keep an internal record of training and guidance.

### When is AI literacy enforced?

The duty has applied since 2 February 2025. National market surveillance authorities supervise and enforce it from 2 August 2026.

## In the news

- 20 October 2026 · European Commission[European Commission updates its AI literacy questions and answers](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-20-european-commission-updates-its-ai-literacy-questions-and-a)Official guidance, not law, but it sets the date supervision starts. An acceptable use policy plus training records is the practical answer.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

## Sources and notes

- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 4: AI literacy](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-4), consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text; paragraphs marked as amended by the Digital Omnibus.
- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 3](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-3) and [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26), consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text; definitions and deployer oversight duty.
- [European Commission, AI literacy: questions and answers](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/faqs/ai-literacy-questions-answers), updated 20 October 2026. Official guidance, not legally binding; it describes the amendment as entering into force in mid-July 2026.

- [William Fry, EU Digital Omnibus Proposal: Key AI Proposals](https://www.williamfry.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/EU-Digital-Omnibus-Proposal-Key-AI-Proposals.pdf), December 2025. Law firm briefing on the original proposal, which the final text did not follow on this point.

List every person who approves AI output before it reaches a client, and give each a 30-minute briefing on what to check. Record the date and topic; that is the core of your Article 4 record.
