# What Is a Data Processing Agreement for AI Tools?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-data-processing-agreement-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A data processing agreement is the contract GDPR Article 28 requires when a vendor processes personal data on a company's behalf. For AI tools it decides whether prompts can be used beyond your instructions, which model providers act as sub-processors, and what is deleted at the end. Most vendors publish a standard one.

A data processing agreement (DPA) is the contract that governs how a vendor processes personal data on your behalf. Article 28 of the GDPR, and of the UK GDPR, requires one whenever a processor handles personal data for a controller, with a fixed set of terms. For an AI tool, the DPA shows whether the vendor may use your prompts beyond your instructions, which model providers receive them, and what is deleted at the end.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What a DPA means

When a seller pastes a client email into an AI assistant, or a notetaker records a prospect call, personal data is processed. Usually the company using the tool is the controller and the vendor is the processor, acting on its behalf. Article 28(1) allows only processors that provide "sufficient guarantees" of appropriate measures. The DPA is where those guarantees are written down.

Many AI vendors publish a standard DPA that attaches to their business terms. A personal account on a consumer plan may sit outside it, which is one reason staff using personal accounts is a data protection problem as well as a security one; see [What is shadow AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-shadow-ai/).

| A DPA is | A DPA is not |
| --- | --- |
| A contract required by GDPR Article 28 | A privacy policy aimed at consumers |
| About personal data processed for you | A guarantee that the tool's output is accurate |
| A record of the vendor's sub-processors and transfer terms | A security audit; see [SOC 2 for AI vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/) |
| Binding on the vendor as processor | Proof that your own use of the tool is lawful |

## The Article 28 terms, read for an AI tool

The ICO's guidance lists the compulsory terms. Each has an AI-specific question behind it.

| Article 28(3) term | What to check for an AI tool |
| --- | --- |
| (a) Documented instructions only | Does the vendor use prompts, outputs or files for anything else, such as improving its models? |
| (b) Confidentiality of staff | Can vendor staff review conversations, for safety or support, and under what controls? |
| (c) Security under Article 32 | Encryption, access controls, and the audit reports offered |
| (d) Sub-processors | Which model provider, hosting and logging services receive the data, and in which countries? |
| (e) Help with data subject rights | Can the vendor find and delete one person's data across chats, transcripts and indexes? |
| (f) Help with security, breaches and DPIAs | Breach notice timing; information supplied for an impact assessment |
| (g) Deletion or return at the end | Does deletion cover derived data, such as embeddings, vector indexes and fine-tuned models? |
| (h) Audits and information | Whether you may audit, or must accept a summary of the vendor's reports |

Term (a) carries most of the weight for AI. A processor acting only on your instructions should not use your data for its own purposes. If the commercial terms allow training on customer content, read them with the DPA, and make that a deliberate decision.

## What a vendor DPA looks like in practice

OpenAI's published DPA, updated 1 December 2025, is a useful public reference. OpenAI states it "acts as a Data Processor on the Customer's behalf", processing customer data only to deliver the services. Customers give general authorisation for sub-processors, are notified of changes, and may object within 30 days; an unresolved objection allows either side to terminate the affected service. Transfers from the EEA rely on standard contractual clauses or an adequacy decision, and UK transfers on the clauses as amended by the UK Addendum. Breaches are notified "without undue delay", with no fixed number of hours.

Audit rights are typical of large vendors: information once a year, audits at the customer's expense, or a summary of audit reports instead. A 20-to-500-person firm will rarely negotiate these terms; its real choice is which tools to approve.

### Three AI clauses worth checking beyond Article 28

- **Retention.** How long prompts and outputs are kept, and whether [zero data retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/) is available for the models you use.
- **Upstream terms.** If the tool runs on another firm's model, whether that provider's terms match what the vendor promises you.
- **Location.** Where processing happens, if clients or regulators require it; see [data residency for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/).

This summarises the legal requirements and is not legal advice. Contracts involving special category data or regulated clients need counsel.

## The **lowob** view

A DPA governs the vendor's copy of your data, not the record you keep yourself. **lowob**'s position is to rent the wiring and own the record, so each tool's DPA status goes on the AI inventory: signed, sub-processors checked, training on or off, retention, and reviewer. A buyer's security questionnaire will ask for that line.

## lowob takeaways

- **No DPA, no client data.** If a tool has no DPA for your plan, personal data should not go into it.
- **Read term (a) first.** Use beyond your instructions, including model training, is the AI-specific risk.
- **Follow the sub-processors.** The model provider behind a tool is usually a sub-processor and decides much of the real exposure.
- **Record the review.** Put DPA status, retention and reviewer on the AI inventory, per tool.

## Common questions

### Do I need a data processing agreement with an AI vendor?

Under the GDPR and UK GDPR, yes, whenever the vendor processes personal data on your behalf. Check whether the vendor's standard DPA covers the plan you are on.

### What must a data processing agreement include?

The subject matter, duration, nature and purpose of processing, the data types and data subjects, and terms on instructions, confidentiality, security, sub-processors, data subject rights, assistance, deletion and audits.

### Is an AI model provider a sub-processor?

Often. When a tool sends your data to another company's model, that provider usually acts as a sub-processor and should appear on the vendor's sub-processor list.

### Does a DPA stop an AI vendor training on my data?

Only if its terms say so. Check the DPA's instructions clause together with the vendor's commercial terms on training and retention.

## Sources and notes

- [Springlex, GDPR Article 28: Processor](https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/gdpr/gdpr-regulation/article-28/), reproducing Regulation (EU) 2016/679, OJ L 119, 4 May 2016. Third-party reproduction of the official text.
- [ICO, What needs to be included in the contract?](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/contracts-and-liabilities-between-controllers-and-processors-multi/what-needs-to-be-included-in-the-contract/), accessed November 2026. UK regulator guidance; under review after the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
- [OpenAI, Data Processing Addendum](https://openai.com/policies/data-processing-addendum/), updated 1 December 2025. Vendor contract, shown as an example; terms differ by vendor and plan.

## Related research

- [What Is Zero Data Retention in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/)
- [SOC 2 for AI Vendors: What It Covers and What It Does Not](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/)
- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)

## Next move

For each AI tool that touches client data, find its DPA and sub-processor list this week. Add three columns to your AI inventory: DPA signed, training on or off, and retention period.

# Semantic Layer vs Knowledge Graph

Source: https://lowob.com/research/semantic-layer-vs-knowledge-graph/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A semantic layer defines metrics and business terms once so every tool calculates them the same way. A knowledge graph stores entities and named relationships so a system can follow connections. Both give AI explicit business meaning; they answer different questions, and most commercial teams need the definitions before the graph.

A semantic layer fixes how business terms and numbers are calculated, such as revenue, active client or win rate, so every report and agent gets the same answer. A knowledge graph records how things connect, such as which person signed which contract and which proposal replaced which, so a system can follow those links. The semantic layer answers "how much"; the graph answers "how is this related". Both make business meaning explicit, and most commercial teams need the definitions first.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two terms mean

A [semantic layer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) is a set of agreed business definitions mapped onto the data underneath. dbt Labs' documentation describes MetricFlow as "a SQL query generation tool designed to streamline metric creation across different data dimensions." Its parts are semantic models, which point at tables; entities, which are the join keys; dimensions, which slice results; and metrics, the calculations. Definitions live in YAML, can be committed to version control, and are approved by data and business teams as the "true and only source of information."

A [knowledge graph](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/) stores the facts themselves as a network. The W3C's RDF 1.1 standard, a 2014 Recommendation, makes the triple the basic unit: subject, predicate, object. It also states that identifiers "have global scope", so the same identifier means the same thing wherever it appears. OWL 2, a W3C ontology language, adds "classes, properties, individuals, and data values" with formally defined meaning. A graph can say that a person works at an account, that the account holds a contract, and that the contract superseded an earlier one.

|  | Semantic layer | Knowledge graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main question | How is this number calculated? | How are these things connected? |
| Unit | Metric, dimension, entity | Triple: subject, predicate, object |
| Holds the data? | No; it sits over a warehouse and generates queries | Often yes; the facts are the graph |
| Typical output | A figure, sliced by dimensions | A path, a set of linked records, an explanation |
| Strength | Consistent aggregates across every tool | Multi-step questions across records |
| Standards | Apache Ossie (incubating); vendor formats such as dbt MetricFlow | W3C RDF 1.1 (2014) and OWL 2 (2012) |
| Typical failure | Two metrics with the same name and different logic | Stale or wrong edges that the model follows with confidence |

## Where they overlap, and where they differ

The line is blurrier than it looks. dbt's own documentation says MetricFlow works through YAML files "where a semantic graph links language to data," and calls entities the "edges between semantic models." A semantic layer is a small graph of tables and joins.

The Sequeda, Allemang and Jacob benchmark shows the overlap from the other side. Its knowledge graph was "a contextual layer incorporating an ontology and mappings" over an insurance company's SQL database. The data stayed in the database. What the graph added was explicit meaning: what a policy is, how a claim relates to it. That is the job a semantic layer does, written in graph form. GPT-4 accuracy rose from 16% to 54%. The authors work at data.world, a data-catalogue vendor, so treat it as one domain and one vendor's test. The lesson is that explicit meaning beats raw tables, whichever format holds it.

The real difference is the kind of question each one is built for.

**Semantic layers aggregate.** They are best at "what was net revenue retention in the enterprise segment last quarter", where the answer is a number and the risk is two tools calculating it differently. They rarely store individual facts about individual accounts.

**Knowledge graphs traverse.** They are best at "which open deals depend on a partner whose contract ends this quarter", where the answer is a set of links that no single table holds. Someone has to keep every edge current. Graphs also depend on [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/): if one account appears under three names, the graph has three accounts.

Semantic definitions are moving toward portability. The Apache Ossie proposal describes "a vendor-neutral format for expressing business metrics, dimensions, and their relationships," begun as the Open Semantic Interchange in September 2025 by a coalition including Snowflake, Salesforce and dbt Labs. Graphs already have W3C standards. Definitions in an open format survive a change of tool.

## Which to choose

| If your problem is | Start with | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two dashboards or agents report different revenue | Semantic layer | The fault is in definitions, not connections |
| Agents answer metric questions from raw tables | Semantic layer | Explicit meaning raises accuracy |
| Questions need several hops across records | Knowledge graph | The answer is a path, not a total |
| Decisions need to be traced to accounts, owners and outcomes | A small knowledge graph | Supersession and links are relationships |
| The same customer appears under several names | Entity resolution first | Neither works on duplicated entities |
| No data team and fewer than 100 staff | Five written definitions | Software can follow once terms are agreed |

A short checklist before buying either:

- **Write the definitions first.** Active client, qualified, won and lost, owner and source, each with an owner.
- **List ten real questions.** Mark each as "how much" or "how connected". The split tells you which you need.
- **Name the maintainer.** A graph or a layer with no owner drifts within a quarter.
- **Ask about export.** Prefer tools that support an open format, such as RDF or Ossie.

## The **lowob** view

In **lowob**'s enterprise brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, the semantic layer is part of the wiring. It sits between the store and the models and fixes what words mean. It is a good thing to rent, because the standards are converging and the logic should be portable.

The most useful knowledge graph on the commercial line is narrower: decisions linked to the accounts, owners and outcomes they concern. That is the record stage. Decisions supersede rather than overwrite, and outcomes written back become new edges. That graph is worth owning, because it holds the firm's judgment rather than its arithmetic.

The [vector database vs knowledge graph](https://lowob.com/research/vector-database-vs-knowledge-graph/) comparison covers the retrieval side.

## lowob takeaways

- **Semantic layers fix calculations.** Use one when the problem is inconsistent numbers.
- **Knowledge graphs fix connections.** Use one when answers depend on following links across records.
- **Both supply explicit meaning.** A benchmark found that meaning, not more data, lifted accuracy.
- **Rent the definitions layer; own the decision graph.** The record of judgment is the part to keep.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a semantic layer and a knowledge graph?

A semantic layer defines how business metrics and terms are calculated from underlying data. A knowledge graph stores entities and named relationships, so a system can follow connections between them.

### Is a semantic layer a type of knowledge graph?

They overlap. A semantic layer models tables and joins as a small graph, and a graph with an ontology can act as a semantic layer, but each is built for different questions.

### Do AI agents need a semantic layer or a knowledge graph?

Agents answering metric questions need consistent definitions, which a semantic layer provides. Agents answering relationship questions across records benefit from a graph. Many teams need definitions first.

### What is Apache Ossie?

An Apache Incubator project that grew from the Open Semantic Interchange, launched in September 2025. It is a vendor-neutral YAML format for business metrics, dimensions and their relationships.

## Sources and notes

- [dbt Labs documentation, About MetricFlow](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/about-metricflow), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [W3C, RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax](https://w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/), 25 February 2014, and [W3C, OWL 2 Web Ontology Language Document Overview](https://www.w3.org/TR/owl2-overview/), 11 December 2012. Standards body Recommendations.
- [Apache Incubator, Ossie proposal](https://cwiki.apache.org/confluence/spaces/INCUBATOR/pages/430408796/OssieProposal), last updated 16 June 2026. Project proposal; the specification is at version 0.1 and still changing.

## Related research

# What Is a Quarterly Business Review (QBR)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-quarterly-business-review/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A quarterly business review is a scheduled meeting in which a supplier and a customer review results against the goals they agreed, discuss changes in the customer's business and set goals for the next quarter. Done well, it is the main place where renewal evidence is built. Done badly, it is a usage slide deck. Gartner's research on buyer regret shows why the difference matters.

A quarterly business review (QBR) is a meeting held every three months in which a supplier and a customer review results against the goals they agreed, discuss what has changed in the customer's business and set goals for the next quarter. Its purpose is to keep both sides agreed on the value being delivered, well before a renewal date. A QBR that only presents usage statistics is a report, not a review. The test is whether the customer leaves with decisions and owners.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a quarterly business review means

A QBR is part of account management, not support. It sits between day-to-day contact and the renewal conversation. Gainsight's guide lists five core elements: a review of performance against agreed goals using data, a discussion of the customer's challenges and changes, joint goal-setting for the next quarter, a demonstration of value including return on investment, and next steps with owners and timelines.

The term is used loosely. Three related meetings are often confused.

| Meeting | Who attends (customer side) | Focus | Typical frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| QBR | Managers, team leads and active users | Progress against goals, usage, issues, next quarter's goals | Every three months |
| Executive business review (EBR) | C-suite, vice presidents and directors | Business outcomes and strategic value | Every six months for strategic accounts; yearly for growth accounts (Gainsight) |
| Renewal value review | Sponsor and decision makers | What the term achieved and what the next term should deliver | Once, about 120 days before renewal in **lowob**'s calendar |

For new customers, Gainsight suggests the first EBR after initial value is realised, typically three to six months after implementation. Not every account needs a quarterly meeting; smaller accounts can get a lighter digital review.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buyers often regret what they bought

Gartner's 2023 survey, run from February to March across North America, Western Europe and Asia/Pacific, found 60% of technology buyers involved in renewal or expansion decisions regret nearly every purchase. Gartner attributes most of that regret to dysfunction inside distributed buying teams, not to the supplier or the product. Its recommendations include training customer-facing teams to spot regret signals, such as buyers revisiting decisions or internal conflict, and giving buying teams shared spaces to review objectives and build business cases.

A QBR is the natural place to do both, while there is still time to act.

### Growth is expected from the existing base

Gartner's 2025 survey of chief sales officers found 73% focused on growing revenue from existing customers, and 57% ranked retention and growth among their top three priorities. [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) sets out why: for most mid-size B2B firms the existing base barely grows on its own. QBRs are where the evidence for an expansion is built, in the customer's terms.

> A QBR that shows usage charts is a report. A QBR that ends with agreed goals, owners and dates is a review.

## How to run one

| Section | What to bring | What to leave with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goals from last quarter | The goals agreed at the last review, with results | Each goal marked met, missed or changed, with the reason |
| Customer changes | Questions about strategy, people and budget | Updated sponsor and stakeholder list |
| Value delivered | Outcomes in the customer's measures, not product metrics | An agreed statement of value for the quarter |
| Issues | Open support cases and risks | Owners and dates for each |
| Next quarter | Proposed goals | Two or three goals the customer has agreed |
| Next steps | A draft action list | Actions with owners on both sides |

Three habits separate useful QBRs from routine ones. Send a short pre-read so the meeting is spent on decisions. Let the customer present part of it, so the value statement is theirs. Keep it to an hour, as Gainsight advises.

In **lowob**'s model, the goals agreed at a QBR are decisions with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome. The next QBR is the natural point for [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/): each goal is graded against what happened. Over a year, that record becomes the renewal case, and it feeds the [customer health score](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/) with evidence rather than impressions. An agent can draft the pre-read from CRM, usage and support data at autonomy level 1. A person checks and presents it, and nothing goes to the customer without that review.

## lowob takeaways

- **A QBR is a review, not a report.** It should end with agreed goals, owners and dates.
- **It is an early warning system.** Sponsor changes and internal conflict surface here before renewal.
- **Match the meeting to the account.** QBRs for the top tier, EBRs for executives, lighter reviews for the rest.
- **Grade last quarter's goals.** The written record of goals and results becomes the renewal case.

## Common questions

### What should be included in a quarterly business review?

Results against last quarter's goals, changes in the customer's business, the value delivered in the customer's terms, open issues, and agreed goals and actions for the next quarter.

### What is the difference between a QBR and an EBR?

A QBR reviews progress and usage with managers and users every quarter. An executive business review covers business outcomes with senior leaders, usually every six or twelve months.

### How long should a QBR be?

Gainsight recommends no more than an hour. A pre-read sent in advance keeps the meeting on decisions rather than presentation.

### Do all customers need a QBR?

No. Most firms run them for their largest or most strategic accounts and use lighter, often digital, reviews for smaller ones.

## Sources and notes

- [Gainsight, The Essential Guide to Quarterly Business Reviews (QBRs)](https://www.gainsight.com/essential-guide/quarterly-business-reviews-qbrs/), last modified 22 August 2025. Vendor guide; figures it quotes from third parties are not verified here.
- [Gainsight, How to Run an Executive Business Review That Drives Impact](https://www.gainsight.com/?p=55318), 6 December 2022. Vendor blog; frequencies are recommendations, not benchmarks.
- [Gartner, Gartner Survey Reveals 60% of Technology Buyers Involved in Renewal Decisions Regret Nearly Every Purchase They Make](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-06-14-gartner-survey-reveals-60-percent-of-technology-buyers-involved-in-renewal-decisions-regret-nearly-every-purchase-they-make), 14 June 2023. Analyst survey of 1,503 respondents at firms with $50m+ revenue; technology purchases only.
- [Demand Gen Report, Gartner Survey: 73% of CSOs Prioritizing 2025 Growth from Existing Customers](https://www.demandgenreport.com/?p=49415), 20 May 2025. Trade press report of a Gartner survey of 243 sales leaders.

## Related research

## Next move

Pull the notes from your last three QBRs with your largest account and list every goal agreed in them. If you cannot say which were met, start the next QBR by grading them with the customer.

# What Is Product-Led Growth?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-product-led-growth/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Product-led growth is a go-to-market motion in which people find, try and start paying for a product largely on their own, with sales joining later to expand accounts. Investor benchmarks show it can grow fast but converts only a small share of free users. It fits products that deliver value without a conversation, and breaks when setup, integration or a buying committee stands in the way.

Product-led growth (PLG) is a go-to-market motion in which the product does most of the work of acquiring, converting and expanding customers. People sign up, try it free or cheaply and start paying when it proves useful; sales, if there is a sales team, joins later to grow the account. It suits products that deliver value without a conversation and a buyer who can decide alone. Benchmarks suggest only a small share of free users ever pay, so the economics depend on volume and on what happens after sign-up.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What product-led growth means

In a sales-led motion a seller creates the first experience of the product, usually in a demo. In a product-led motion the product creates it, and an in-product prompt or the pricing page asks for payment.

**lowob**'s comparison of the three main motions, [Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/), sets the conditions. PLG needs value without a conversation, a short time to value and a price low enough for one person to decide. It breaks when setup, integration or approval is required.

PLG comes in several forms. The terms are used loosely, so the table gives the working definitions used here.

| Form | What the user gets | What triggers payment | Fits when | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Freemium | A permanently free tier with limits | Hitting a usage, feature or team limit | Large market, low cost to serve a free user | Free users who never pay but cost money |
| Free trial | Full or near-full product for a fixed period | The trial ending | Value shows inside the trial period | Users who do not activate before it ends |
| Product-led sales | Free or trial use, then a seller contacts active accounts | A sales conversation prompted by usage signals | Larger accounts that need a contract or security review | Sellers chasing usage that is not buying intent |

## How it works

The motion runs as a funnel, and each step has its own measure. Kyle Poyar's summary of OpenView and Pendo's 2023 benchmark, drawn from more than 1,000 products, gives an illustrative freemium funnel: 1,000 unique visitors a day produce about 90 sign-ups, a 9% conversion. Those produce four or five paying customers, about 5% of sign-ups, over 30 to 60 days, with initial spend of $10 to $100 a month.

The arithmetic explains why PLG suits large markets. At those rates, 1,000 visitors a day yield roughly 120 to 150 new paying customers a month. A niche B2B product with 50 visitors a day does not have the volume to run on self-serve alone.

Activation is the step that decides the rest. OpenView's 2022 report found 87% of standout PLG companies identify and track activation, meaning the moment a new user first gets real value. [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) defines it as a first real task within a week of signing up, and argues that a free tier is acquisition spend: report it as a channel with a cost per acquired team, and keep free users out of board numbers.

| Stage | Measure | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visit to sign-up | Sign-up rate | Does the offer make sense before trying it? |
| Sign-up to activation | Share activated within a set period | Does the product show value without help? |
| Activation to paid | Free-to-paid conversion | Is the value worth paying for? |
| Paid to expansion | [Net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) | Does use spread through the account? |
| Free tier cost | Cost per acquired paying team | Is the free tier cheaper than other channels? |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Buyer behaviour supports the motion. Gartner's survey of 646 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2025, found 67% prefer a rep-free experience, up from 61% in its 2024 survey. The same research found 45% had used AI during a recent purchase.

The growth figures need care. OpenView's 2022 finding that product-led companies were twice as likely to double revenue came from a survey of founders who chose to respond, and fast-growing firms may adopt PLG rather than PLG causing fast growth.

PLG also meets a limit in larger deals. Once a purchase needs procurement, security review or several approvers, a [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) takes over and the self-serve path stalls. Most B2B firms that start product-led add a sales team for these accounts.

> The product can win the user. A contract above a certain size still needs a person to win the committee.

In **lowob**'s model, sign-up and usage events are part of the store, and the definition of "activated" belongs in the shared definitions so people and agents read it the same way. An agent can flag accounts whose usage crosses a threshold. The decision to contact one, and the reason, is a recorded decision, and nothing sends to the customer without a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **The product makes the first sale.** Sales joins later, to expand accounts or handle complex purchases.
- **Volume decides viability.** With about 5% of free sign-ups paying, small markets struggle to run on self-serve.
- **Activation is the lead measure.** Define it in writing and track it before free-to-paid conversion.
- **Plan the hand-off.** Record which usage signals trigger a sales contact and whether they predicted a sale.

## Common questions

### What is product-led growth in simple terms?

A way of growing in which customers discover, try and buy the product largely by themselves, and the product's own experience does most of the selling.

### What is the difference between freemium and a free trial?

Freemium offers a permanent free tier with limits; a free trial gives fuller access for a fixed period. Freemium needs a low cost to serve free users; a trial needs value to show before it ends.

### What is a good freemium conversion rate?

OpenView's 2022 benchmark found 5% of freemium sign-ups converted to paid. Rates vary widely by product and price, so track your own trend.

### Can product-led growth work without a sales team?

For small, simple purchases, yes. Once deals need procurement or several approvers, most B2B firms add sellers to work the active accounts.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Product-Led Growth: A Forrester Overview](https://www.forrester.com/report/product-led-growth-a-Forrester-overview/RES171827), updated 6 August 2025. Analyst summary page; full report behind paywall.
- [OpenView, Third Annual Product Benchmarks Report (press release)](https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/openviews-third-annual-product-benchmarks-report-reveals-plg-companies-2x-more-likely-to-grow-quickly-301562090.html), 7 June 2022. Investor research; self-selected sample of product-led founders, growth findings are correlation.
- [Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged: Your guide to SaaS product metrics](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/your-guide-to-saas-product-metrics), 19 July 2023. Investor commentary on OpenView and Pendo's 2023 benchmark; the funnel is an illustrative average.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), 9 March 2026. Analyst survey of 646 buyers; stated preference, not observed behaviour.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 61% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Buying Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience), 25 June 2025. Analyst survey of 632 buyers in 2024; used for the year-on-year comparison.

- [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)

## Next move

Write down, in one sentence, what counts as an activated user for your product, then pull last quarter's sign-ups and count how many met it within a week. If nobody can agree the sentence, that is the first decision to make.

# Building the Commercial System at 20, 50 and 200 People

Source: https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Thirty parts describe a full commercial system. No firm should build all of it at once. This capstone maps each part to three sizes, using lowob's scale ladder: at 20 people the job is to write the founder's system down, at 50 to make words mean the same thing across teams, and at 200 to let reasoning travel without its author. For each size it sets out what to own, what to rent and what to leave until the next rung.

The commercial system is the same set of decisions at every size: who to sell to, how to reach them, what to charge, what to forecast and how to learn from the result. What changes is the problem it has to solve. At around 20 people, the system lives in the founders' heads and the job is to write it down. At around 50, the same words start to mean different things in different teams, and the job is shared definitions with owners. At around 200, managers make most decisions, and the job is reasoning that travels without its author. Build for the next size, not two sizes up.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Thirty parts ago we set out to describe the commercial system as a whole, from positioning to pricing experiments. Read as a list, it looks like a 500-person firm's operating manual.

No firm should build it all at once. A 20-person firm with a revenue operations team, a partner programme and a quarterly business review for every account is not mature. It is spending scarce attention on problems it does not yet have, and missing the one it does.

## The rule: build for the next size

**lowob**'s [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/) describes the problems a company meets as it grows: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at about ten, meaning at about fifty, delegation at about two hundred, and governance at about a thousand. The rungs are approximate. A regulated fintech may meet governance at 80 people; a research-heavy firm may stay at the meaning problem for years. The diagnosis is by problem, not headcount.

Its central rule is the one this capstone applies: build the layer the next stage will break, not the one the stage after that. [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) adds the second rule: rent the context layer as it matures, and own the record of how you decide.

Each part of the commercial system has a minimum version and a full version. The question at each size is which one, and the honest answer is usually smaller than the plan.

There is outside evidence that the pressures grow with size. The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found AI use rising over the six months to May 2026 among firms with 20 or more employees, reaching 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more, while use among firms under 20 did not change significantly. Bessemer Venture Partners' analysis of cloud companies found general and administrative spending falling from about 70% of revenue at $1 million to $10 million of annual recurring revenue to about 20% beyond $50 million, while sales and marketing stayed at around half of revenue or more. The commercial system is the part of the firm that stays expensive as it grows, which is why it repays being built at the right size. Bain's research on what it calls the founder's mentality adds the organisational side. Its Founder's Mentality score fell from 72.3 out of 100 among companies with revenues of $500 million or less to 56.1 among those of $5 billion or more. In the same work, 85% of executives surveyed said internal obstacles, not external ones, kept their companies from growing profitably. Those are much larger firms than this series addresses, but the direction is the same: growth breaks the way decisions are made before it breaks the market.

## At around 20 people: write the founder's system down

At 20 people the commercial system usually works, because the founder runs it. The founder knows which customers fit, what the last discount was and why the big deal stalled. The problem the scale ladder names for this stage is the first stranger: people join who were not there for the history, and they cannot ask the founder everything. Our piece [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/) covers it in detail.

The job is therefore to write down a small number of things, in a form a newcomer can use.

**A one-page ICP** (Part 3, and [*How to write an ICP*](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)). Which customers to pursue and which to decline, with reasons.

**One pipeline with written stage definitions** ([*What are pipeline stage definitions?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)). Five or six stages, each with an exit criterion a stranger could apply.

**A weekly commercial meeting** (Part 6). Thirty minutes on pipeline, decisions due and last week's outcomes.

**A loss reason that includes no decision** ([*What is a closed-lost reason?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/)). One field, filled honestly.

**A founders' ledger of commercial calls.** Pricing exceptions, pursue-or-pass choices and big discounts, each with a reason. [*Two people: the founders' ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) describes the habit.

**A simple discount rule.** A standard limit and one person who approves anything beyond it (Part 21).

What to leave: a revenue operations team, a formal partner programme, a key account programme and any tool that needs an administrator. The distribution parts (14 to 19) describe choices a 20-person firm should make once, deliberately, rather than build programmes around.

## At around 50 people: make the words mean the same thing

At 50 people there are teams, and each team has started to use the commercial vocabulary in its own way. Marketing's qualified lead is not sales' qualified opportunity. "Committed" means one thing in the forecast call and another in the board pack. Our piece [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/) describes the pattern.

The job at this size is shared meaning, with owners.

**Definitions with owners.** Stage definitions, forecast categories, the ICP and the main KPIs (Part 7), each with a named owner and a change log.

**Decision rights.** Who can approve a discount, a non-standard term, a partner deal or a change to a forecast category. Written down, so nobody negotiates authority deal by deal.

**One home for the record.** Commercial decisions recorded in one place with the same fields: decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back ([*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

**A monthly rhythm** on top of the weekly one: pipeline quality, forecast against outcome, and the decisions due for a check.

**A first capacity model** (Part 26). The Bridge Group's 2026 study put average AE ramp at 6.2 months; at 50 people, a hiring plan that ignores ramp will miss the year.

**A handover pack template** (Part 27) and **a few win-loss interviews a month** (Part 25), run by someone outside the deal team.

What to leave: a full deal desk, a dedicated revenue operations function, a formal partner tiering scheme and an ontology of commercial concepts. The glossary with owners is enough.

## At around 200 people: let reasoning travel without its author

At 200 people, managers make most commercial decisions, and the founder no longer sees them. The problem the scale ladder names is delegation: the reasons behind decisions must reach people who were not in the room. Our piece [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/) sets out what breaks.

The job is to turn the habits of the 50-person firm into routines that do not depend on particular people.

**Decision classes and templates.** The ten or so commercial decisions that recur, each with a template that asks for the same fields.

**A deal desk** for pricing exceptions, non-standard terms and complex quotes, with approval records the handover can link to.

**A revenue operations function.** Gartner predicted in 2021 that by 2025, 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a revenue operations model, to break down silos between sales, marketing and customer success. Forrester's 2024 definition stresses that revenue operations should not become another silo, and can sit within sales or marketing. At 200 people it is usually a small team that owns definitions, data and the planning cycle ([*What is revenue operations?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/)).

**A standing win-loss programme**, a **top-twenty account routine** (Part 28), a **quarterly planning cycle** with capacity built from your own ramp and attainment history, and **pricing experiments** run with a decision rule (Part 29).

**First calibration.** Forecasts and expected outcomes recorded with a probability and checked against results ([*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/)).

What to leave: a platform team, a single enterprise-wide data model, and the governance apparatus of a 1,000-person firm, unless regulation brings it forward.

> The commercial system is the same set of decisions at every size. What changes is who makes them, and whether the reasons survive.

## The full map

The table maps each part of the series to the three sizes. "Minimum" means the smallest version that does the job; "full" means the version described in the part itself.

| Part of the system | Around 20 people | Around 50 people | Around 200 people |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning and segments (Parts 2, 3, 5) | One-page ICP and positioning | ICP with an owner; one market map | Segment plans with evidence; market map used in account selection |
| Pricing architecture (Part 4) | One price list, one discount limit | Packages and decision rights | Pricing experiments with a decision rule (Part 29) |
| Operating rhythm (Part 6) | Weekly meeting | Weekly plus monthly | Weekly, monthly and quarterly |
| KPIs (Part 7) | Five numbers the founder trusts | Defined KPIs with owners | Board-grade KPIs with a definition log |
| Demand and content (Parts 8 to 13) | Founder-led, a few channels | First team-led programme with a cost per opportunity | Full demand economics and brand measures |
| Distribution (Parts 14 to 19) | One deliberate partner or channel choice | First partner programme with rules of engagement | Channel design and conflict rules |
| Qualification and proposals (Parts 20, 22) | A short qualification checklist | One framework, one proposal template | Proposal standards and review |
| Discount governance (Part 21) | One limit, one approver | Decision rights by size | Deal desk with recorded exceptions |
| Forecasting and capacity (Parts 23, 26) | Founder's forecast with a written reason | Forecast categories and a first capacity model | Calibrated forecast; capacity from own history |
| Renewals and handover (Parts 24, 27) | Founder or seller handles both | Handover pack template; renewal dates tracked | Joint handover on large deals; renewal and expansion plays |
| Win-loss and account planning (Parts 25, 28) | Loss reason with no decision | A few interviews a month; plans for the top eight to ten | Standing programme; monthly top-twenty review |

## Own, rent, not yet

The second rule, rent context and own judgment, gives each size a short list. It is consistent with the size guide in [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/), applied to the commercial line.

| Size | Rent | Own | Not yet |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Around 20 | A CRM used as it comes; an assistant; transcription | ICP, stage definitions, founders' ledger of commercial calls | Revenue operations team, wiki, integrations beyond the CRM |
| Around 50 | Meeting and writing tools that export; enrichment | Glossary with owners, decision rights, one home for the record | Ontology, deal desk software, partner portal |
| Around 200 | Workflow tools that can hold a precedent; forecasting and conversation tools | Decision classes, templates, handover packs, first calibration | Platform team, single enterprise data model |

Before renting anything that touches decisions, apply the export test from that piece: can the tool export every decision record with its history, will the records survive a change of vendor, and does the firm control retention? If not, keep the record elsewhere and let the tool read from it.

## How to tell you have moved up a size

Headcount is a rough guide. These symptoms are better ones.

| Symptom | What it means | What to build next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New sellers ask the founder the same questions | The first-stranger problem has arrived | Written ICP, stage definitions, ledger |
| Marketing and sales disagree about lead counts | Meaning has diverged | Definitions with owners |
| Discounts are negotiated internally deal by deal | Decision rights are missing | Written approval limits |
| The forecast misses in the same direction each quarter | Capacity and forecast are not reconciled | Capacity model; calibration |
| A senior seller leaves and an account wobbles | Reasoning lives in one person | Account plans and handover packs |
| Managers make calls the leadership cannot reconstruct | Delegation has arrived | Decision classes and templates |

The scale ladder suggests revisiting the diagnosis each time headcount roughly doubles. For the commercial system, the annual plan is the natural moment.

Illustrative example: a 60-person firm resisting the 200-person build

Decision
:   Defer a dedicated revenue operations team and deal desk software for a year; instead, give the head of sales operations ownership of definitions and write decision rights for discounts.

Reason and owner
:   The symptoms present were divergent definitions and negotiated discounts, both 50-person problems. Delegation symptoms were not yet visible. Owned by the chief executive, agreed with the revenue lead.

What changed
:   A glossary with owners, a discount approval table and one home for commercial decisions. The diagnosis is revisited at the next annual plan.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Build for the next size.** The commercial system should solve the problem you are about to meet, not one two rungs away.
- **At 20, write it down.** ICP, stage definitions, a weekly rhythm and a ledger of commercial calls.
- **At 50, agree the words.** Definitions with owners, decision rights and one home for the record.
- **At 200, let reasoning travel.** Decision classes, a deal desk, revenue operations and calibration.

Gateway card

### Before your next annual commercial plan

- The firm's current size problem named: first stranger, meaning or delegation
- The symptoms table checked against the last two quarters
- The map row for each part of the system reviewed, with the current version noted
- One thing to build for the next size, and one thing deliberately deferred
- Every tool touching decisions checked against the export test
- The plan recorded with its reasons, owner and check date

## Common questions

### When does a company need a revenue operations team?

In our experience, usually around 200 people, when managers make most commercial decisions and definitions, data and planning need a single owner. Before that, a head of sales operations or a revenue lead owning definitions is often enough.

### What sales processes does a 20-person company need?

A one-page ideal customer profile, one pipeline with written stage definitions, a weekly commercial meeting, a loss reason that includes no decision, a simple discount rule and a written record of major commercial calls.

### How should a sales team change between 50 and 200 employees?

It moves from shared definitions to delegated decisions: decision classes and templates, a deal desk for exceptions, a standing win-loss programme, a top-account review and capacity plans built from the firm's own history.

### What is the biggest mistake when scaling a commercial team?

Building the system of the wrong size: too much too early, which wastes time and produces structures that are wrong by the time they matter, or too little too late, which loses the reasons behind past decisions.

# How to Raise for an Emerging Tech Company: The Complete Guide

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-raise-for-an-emerging-tech-company/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Venture totals hit records in 2026, but the money is concentrated: rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42%. This guide brings together lowob's nine fundraising pieces: what each stage is buying, why evidence beats narrative, how to run the round like a sales process, how to diagnose a stall, and what changes for AI, regulated, long-cycle and media companies.

Raising for an emerging tech company in 2026 means raising in a market with record totals and narrow access. US venture deal value reached $515.8 billion through September, but rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of first-half dollars, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion year on year. The companies that raise normal-sized rounds do four things: they raise against evidence, not narrative; they run the round like a sales process; they read pass reasons when it stalls; and they adjust for what their category changes, whether that is inference cost, a licence, a long sales cycle or a platform-dependent audience.

*This guide is operating and commercial guidance, not investment, legal or regulatory advice. **lowob** advises on narrative and readiness; it doesn't arrange, value or negotiate rounds, act as a placement agent or take a percentage of anything raised.*

## The market in late 2026: record totals, narrow access

Start with the numbers, because they explain why most of the advice in this guide is about proof.

The Q3 2026 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor recorded $515.8 billion of US venture deal value through September, about 44% above the full-year record set in 2021. AI companies took 82.7% of it. Globally, Crunchbase counted a record $510 billion in the first half, of which OpenAI and Anthropic together took $217 billion, or 43%. Foley & Lardner's summary of Crunchbase's third-quarter data shows $159 billion invested in the quarter, with roughly a third going to 27 companies that raised rounds of $1 billion or more.

Underneath the totals, access is narrow. PitchBook's second-quarter report found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the US in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024. Carta, which sees rounds raised by companies on its platform, recorded seed capital falling from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and Series B capital falling from $13.5 billion to $10.4 billion.

The supply of funds is concentrating too. Through September, funds of $500 million or more took 78.1% of US venture fundraising while making up 6.0% of funds closed, and only 81 first-time funds closed, on pace for a decade low. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that emerging managers who raised in 2021 or 2022 had likely used most of their dry powder.

Not every signal is negative. PitchBook expects a record number of US first financings in 2026. Carta's down-round rate fell to 11.4% in the first quarter, the lowest in nearly four years. Hardware capital on Carta's platform rose from $8.6 billion to $14.3 billion year on year. Capital is available. It is going to companies that have already removed some risk.

## What each stage is buying

Every round buys a specific proof. Knowing which one your round is buying sets the evidence, the investor list and the size.

| Stage | Median post-money on Carta, Q1 2026 | What the round is buying | Evidence investors weight most |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-seed | Not reported in the Q1 report | A founder and a sharp problem | Founder-market fit, 5 to 10 named people who would use it |
| Seed | $21.6 million | Proof that someone uses it | Design partners with usage, early retention, a few paying users |
| Series A | $63 million | Proof that it repeats | Repeatable acquisition, recurring revenue, a channel that scales |
| Series B | $177 million | Proof that it scales efficiently | Retention, margin and payback at a larger base |

Two facts follow from Carta's data. First, the price roughly triples between seed and Series A, so a Series A investor is paying for proof that seed-stage evidence repeated. Second, Carta's median gap is two years from seed to Series A and 2.1 years from Series A to Series B. A round has to fund the company until the next proof exists, plus the time to raise again.

Valuations are also splitting by category. PitchBook data reported in August 2026 shows AI companies posting a median valuation step-up of 2.2x in 2026 against 1.6x for non-AI companies, and companies that last raised in 2021 trading at a median 59.1% discount on secondary markets. A company still carrying a 2021 price is raising against that price as well as against its evidence.

## Evidence before narrative

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) is the core argument of this guide. Investors price risk. Narrative asks them to imagine the risk away; evidence removes some of it. Even a small amount of real evidence changes which investors take the call, how fast they move and what they ask for.

Evidence is what a non-founder has done with the product. Keep it in one dated evidence log with five lines: usage, quotes, commitments, community work done by people you did not pay, and losses with reasons. The log is the source for the deck, the data room and customer case studies. Because the median gap to the next round is two years, write each entry so that someone who was not there can understand it.

Three kinds of activity look like evidence and are not:

- **Paid-for activity.** Points programmes, airdrops and incentive campaigns produce numbers that look like adoption until the incentive stops.
- **Demos.** A demo proves a model can do something once. Investors want to see a customer let it do the job every day.
- **Free usage.** Free-tier activity is acquisition cost, not demand.

Put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3, before the market slide, and let the market slide answer the question it raises: how many more buyers look like this one? DocSend's pitch deck index recorded investors spending an average of about two and a half minutes per deck in 2023 and 2024. Evidence that sits on slide 11 may not be read.

When there is no evidence yet, the honest move is to raise less, from investors who back founders at the idea stage, or to spend four to six weeks getting first evidence. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

> Capital is available in 2026. It is going to companies that have already removed some risk.

## Running the round like a sales process

[Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) treats investors as accounts. The steps are the ones a good sales team follows.

1. **Build a fit-first list.** A fund fits if it has invested at your stage and in your category in the last 12 months, and has room in its current fund. Aim for 40 to 60 named funds with a written reason for each, in two tiers. Check the year each fund closed: a fund raised in 2021 may be reserving what it has left for its existing portfolio.
2. **Research the partner, not the firm.** Find the person who invests in your area and name one specific reason you are relevant to them.
3. **Get in warm.** The best route is a founder in their portfolio who knows your product. Send the introducer a forwardable three-line email: who you are, what you've proven, why this investor.
4. **Compress the window.** Run first meetings within two to three weeks. Overlapping interest creates urgency; a raise that drips out over four months signals that nobody wants it.
5. **Track a pipeline.** Researched, intro requested, first meeting, deep dive, term sheet, passed. Log every pass reason in the investor's words.
6. **Have the data room ready before meeting one.** Deck, one-page memo, model, cap table and token allocation, evidence log, audits or security reviews, and two or three reference customers.

Separate investor types before writing a word. Crypto-native funds, generalists with a crypto practice and ecosystem funds want different stories, and ecosystem money often wants deployment on its chain. AI infrastructure funds and AI application funds price on different logic. Tier 1 funds come second, after a week of practice in Tier 2 meetings.

## When the round stalls

[The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) sets out the diagnosis. A stalled round is a process fault or an evidence gap, and the pass reasons tell you which. The five usual faults are: pass reasons never logged, a window that dripped, Tier 1 pitched first, diligence that waited on the founder, and a real evidence gap.

Read every pass in the investor's own words and count the matches. If three match, that is the gap: fix it in weeks and relaunch, or pause the round, tell the live funds why and name a return date. If nothing repeats, the fault is process: put every live conversation in a two-week window, tell each fund the date, finish the data room and answer every homework request within 48 hours.

Two moves rarely help. Widening the list to hundreds of names produces more passes, not more offers. Cutting the price does not supply missing evidence, and with down rounds at 11.4% of rounds on Carta in the first quarter, a cut is now the exception and reads as distress. The exception to the exception is a company still priced at a 2021 valuation, where the pass reasons usually name the price.

## AI companies: priced like software, plus two costs

[Raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) starts from a split. Model companies are priced on capability, compute and research talent. Application companies are priced like software companies, on retention, margin, distribution and replaceability, with two extra costs: inference, which hits gross margin, and platform risk, because the provider can ship your feature.

The label no longer differentiates. Carta found 60.7% of capital raised on its platform in the first quarter of 2026 went to AI companies, and 83% of SaaS capital went to those building with AI. Investors ask five questions early: gross margin after inference, what happens when the provider ships your feature, switching cost between models, data rights in customer contracts, and how much usage is paid.

Switching has become a live question. Menlo Ventures' November 2026 enterprise survey, which is investor research, found Anthropic's share of enterprise API spend rose from 40% to 55% in a year while Google's fell from 21% to 9%. A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could. Lead with the customer and the workflow; the model and eval results go in the appendix. Credits are a cost reduction with an expiry date, never revenue.

## Regulated categories: trust and durability

[Raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) argues that fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Four things change the raise.

**The licence is an asset.** A granted licence shows a regulator said yes and sets the time a competitor needs to catch up. Davis Wright Tremaine's August 2026 review traced one de novo US national bank from application in December 2025 to conditional OCC approval in May 2026, and recorded conditional OCC approvals for fintechs including Mercury and Upstart and final approval for Circle's national trust bank in July 2026. In the UK, the FCA reported that new firm and payment services authorisations both missed their service targets in April to June 2026. Show the path with dates, budget and a named owner.

**The unit is the funded account.** Build acquisition cost, revenue and payback per funded account, and state the sign-up-to-funded ratio.

**Compliance and losses get their own model lines**, with trends and the control changes that moved them.

**The partner bank question gets one slide.** After the 2024 bankruptcy of Synapse, the FDIC proposed recordkeeping and reconciliation rules for fintech custodial accounts, and banks already apply the 2023 interagency third-party risk guidance to their fintech partners. Investors will ask who the partner is, what they control, what is concentrated, who holds the ledger and what the exit plan is.

For crypto companies the regulatory path is still moving. PitchBook's second-quarter report noted the US CLARITY Act had cleared the Senate Banking Committee but still lacked a floor vote, and the OCC granted conditional national trust charters to several digital-asset firms in December 2025. Treat any charter or registration the business depends on the same way: dated, budgeted and owned.

## Long cycles: milestones, not time

[Raising for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/) covers robotics, compute, energy and other companies whose pilots take a year and procurement another. The round is sized to the next milestone that makes the company worth more, and each round retires one named risk: technical de-risking in a real deployment, a paying pilot, or regulatory clearance.

The capital stack is layered, and each layer carries a different risk. Non-dilutive money funds what investors will not yet, but it is slow: US SBIR and STTR authority lapsed for six months before reauthorisation to 2031 on 13 April 2026, according to the Congressional Research Service. Project finance funds proven units only. Mayer Brown's guide to the US Office of Energy Dominance Financing notes a preferred technology readiness level of 8 and that research, pilot and demonstration projects will be denied. Runway must cover the full sales cycle plus about six months to raise again.

[Revenue models for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/revenue-models-for-long-cycles/) is the companion piece. Choose the model by who carries the capital and the service tail; measure gross margin per unit including service from the first deployment; price pilots as projects with a conversion price; write production contracts with terms a lender can read. Report converted pilots and contracted annual value, never letters of intent.

## Media: repeat revenue, not reach

[What investors fund in media now](https://lowob.com/research/what-investors-fund-in-media-now/) applies the evidence argument to audiences. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% in a year. Its Digital News Report 2026 found about 17% of people across 20 countries pay for online news. Investors fund owned audiences that pay, proprietary data, licensing with signed terms, events with margins and software on the audience, and they read renewal before growth.

## Which article for which situation

| Your situation | The question to answer first | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Preparing a first or second round | What has a non-founder done with the product? | [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) |
| Building the investor list and timeline | Which funds fit, and do they have capital left? | [Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) |
| Meetings keep happening, nothing closes | Do the pass reasons match? | [The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) |
| Raising for an AI application company | What is gross margin after inference, and can you switch models? | [Raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) |
| Raising for a fintech or licensed business | What is the licence path, and what happens if the partner bank leaves? | [Raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) |
| Hardware, energy or deep tech with long pilots | Which milestone does this round fund, and how long is the cycle? | [Raising for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/) |
| Pricing pilots and production contracts | Who carries the capital and the service tail? | [Revenue models for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/revenue-models-for-long-cycles/) |
| Raising for a media or audience business | What share of revenue repeats and survives a platform change? | [What investors fund in media now](https://lowob.com/research/what-investors-fund-in-media-now/) |
| Unsure where fundraising sits in the wider plan | Which step of the system are you skipping? | [Raise, Rally, Revenue: the whole series on one page](https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/) |

## Fundraising is one part of one system

The [Raise, Rally, Revenue series](https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/) puts fundraising at steps three and four of a ten-step order: name the buyer, write one truth, collect evidence, raise against it, give the community a job, recruit the first hundred, make first customers design partners, distribute, measure, hand over. Most fundraising problems are problems earlier in that order. A round that stalls on "want to see traction" is a design-partner problem. A deck that lands with investors but not customers is a product-truth problem.

The order matters more than any tactic. Every failure in the series came from doing a right thing at the wrong time.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the market as concentrated, not closed.** Capital goes to companies that have already removed some risk.
- **Know what your round is buying.** Each stage buys a different proof, and the next round is about two years away.
- **Raise against evidence.** Keep a dated log, strip out paid-for activity and put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3.
- **Run a pipeline, not a drip.** Fit-first list, warm routes, a two- to three-week window and every pass logged.
- **Adjust for the category, keep the process.** Inference, licences, long cycles and audiences change the proof, not the method.

Gateway card

### Before you send the first investor email

- A dated evidence log, with paid-for activity separated from organic activity
- The proof this round buys, and the milestone the next round needs, written down
- 40 to 60 named funds with recent deals at your stage and capital in the current fund
- A forwardable three-line introduction email
- First meetings planned inside a two- to three-week window
- A pipeline tracker with a column for pass reasons in the investor's words
- A complete data room, including the category-specific shelf: inference margins, licences and partner agreements, or deployment data

## Common questions

### How do you raise money for an emerging tech startup in 2026?

Raise against evidence a non-founder has created, run the round like a sales process with a fit-first list and a two- to three-week window, log every pass reason, and adjust the proof for your category. Capital is concentrated, so proof matters more than in earlier cycles.

### How long does it take to go from seed to Series A?

Carta's data puts the median gap at two years in early 2026, and 2.1 years from Series A to Series B. Plan runway for the evidence the next round needs plus about six months to raise.

### What do investors look for in AI, crypto and fintech startups?

For AI applications, retention and gross margin net of inference. For crypto, usage that survives without incentives and audits with names and dates. For fintech, licences, economics per funded account and a partner bank plan.

### Is venture funding concentrated in AI in 2026?

Yes. AI took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026, and rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of first-half US dollars, per PitchBook-NVCA.

## Next move

Write one sentence that names the proof your next round is buying, then list the three strongest entries in your evidence log that support it. If you cannot fill the list, spend the next four to six weeks on evidence before you contact an investor.
