# Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring

Source: https://lowob.com/research/lead-scoring-vs-account-scoring/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Lead scoring ranks individual people by fit and engagement so sales can work the best leads first. Account scoring ranks companies, combining firmographic fit with the activity of everyone engaged from that company. B2B purchases involve groups, so most firms need both, with the account score deciding priority and the lead score deciding who to contact.

Lead scoring ranks individual people by how well they fit your ideal customer and how engaged they are. Account scoring ranks companies, combining how well the company fits with the engagement of everyone you know there. Lead scores answer "who should we call?"; account scores answer "which companies should we work on?". Because B2B purchases are made by groups, most firms should let the account score set priority and the lead score pick the person.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What the two terms mean

**Lead scoring** assigns points to a person for fit, such as role, seniority and company size, and for engagement, such as visits, form fills and meetings. Our explainer on [lead scoring](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-scoring/) covers rules-based and predictive versions and how to test them.

**Account scoring** moves the unit from the person to the company. Fit is scored on firmographics: industry, size, region, technology used, and match to your [ICP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/). Engagement is scored on the combined activity of every known contact at the account, sometimes with third-party intent added. Salesforce's Account Engagement product shows the predictive form: Einstein Key Accounts Identification gives each account a tier from A to D, where A indicates the highest likelihood of an opportunity being created within the next six months.

| Dimension | Lead scoring | Account scoring |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | One person | One company and its known contacts |
| Answers | Who to contact next | Which companies to work on |
| Fit inputs | Role, seniority, company attributes | Industry, size, region, technology, ICP match |
| Engagement inputs | That person's actions | Everyone's actions, rolled up, plus intent |
| Typical owner | Marketing operations | RevOps, with sales and marketing |
| Conversion event | Lead becomes qualified or an opportunity | Opportunity created on the account |
| Main failure | Ranks one busy researcher above a real buying group | Hides who is engaged inside the account |

## Why the unit matters

Forrester principal analyst Simon Daniels gives the clearest example. One person downloading three assets usually scores well. Three people from the same account each taking one action is worth more, because it signals a buying group forming. A lead score ranks those the wrong way round. Forrester research cited in his November 2023 post found 46% of B2B buyers decided in groups of two or three and 28% in groups of four to nine. Its 2024 study put the average at 13 people. The figures come from different studies and definitions, but the direction is the same.

Account scoring is not free of choices. The most consequential one is how contact engagement rolls up. HubSpot's company scores offer four aggregation settings: sum, average, minimum and maximum. They rank accounts differently.

An illustrative comparison of two accounts, each scored on contact engagement:

| Account | Contacts and engagement points | Sum | Average | Maximum |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account A | Three contacts at 20 points each | 60 | 20 | 20 |
| Account B | One contact at 50 points | 50 | 50 | 50 |

Sum ranks Account A first, which matches Forrester's buying-group argument. Average and maximum rank Account B first, which repeats the lead-scoring bias at company level. Sum has its own weakness: large companies with many loosely engaged contacts can outscore smaller, more focused ones. Some firms cap points per contact or count only contacts in relevant roles.

The second choice is data volume. Predictive account models need history. Salesforce recommends at least 200 accounts with won opportunities and 200 with lost ones from the last two years for Key Accounts Identification, and at least six months of engagement data and 20 prospects linked to opportunities for its person-level Behavior Scoring. Many firms of 20 to 500 people will start with rules.

## Which to use, and how to combine them

| Situation | What fits |
| --- | --- |
| High-volume, low-price sales to individuals or very small firms | Lead scoring alone |
| Several people per deal and named target accounts | Account scoring for priority, lead scoring for contact choice |
| Fewer than about 200 won and 200 lost accounts in two years | Rules-based account scoring |
| Account-based marketing programme | Account scoring, tied to the [ABM](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/) tiers |
| Sellers complain that high-scoring leads are students or competitors | Add account fit as a gate before lead engagement counts |

A working combination for most B2B firms:

1. **Score account fit first.** Only accounts that match the ICP enter the engaged queue.
2. **Roll up engagement by sum, with caps.** Limit points per contact, and count contacts in buying roles more heavily.
3. **Count engaged people.** Track the number of distinct contacts active in the last 30 days as its own field.
4. **Use lead scores inside the account.** Once an account is prioritised, the lead score suggests who to contact first.
5. **Test against opportunities.** Compare opportunity creation for the top and bottom thirds of account scores each quarter.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, a score is a piece of context. It is computed from the store, often in a warehouse, and synced to where sellers work. It is not a decision. An agent can calculate account scores, draft the account brief and suggest the first contact. A person decides to commit sales time to the account.

That decision, the reason and the expected outcome belong in the record, alongside the score at the time. The learning step then checks whether prioritised accounts produced opportunities and writes the result back, which is how the weights improve. Without that write-back, scoring rules set in a workshop stay unchanged for years. Our piece on [the commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) treats account prioritisation as one of them.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the unit deliberately.** Lead scores pick people; account scores pick companies.
- **The roll-up rule decides the ranking.** Sum favours buying groups; average and maximum favour single enthusiasts.
- **Predictive needs history.** Below a few hundred won and lost accounts, start with rules.
- **Record the prioritisation.** The score is context; the decision to pursue is yours to record and test.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between lead scoring and account scoring?

Lead scoring ranks individual people by fit and engagement. Account scoring ranks companies, combining firmographic fit with the engagement of all known contacts at that company.

### Should B2B companies replace lead scoring with account scoring?

Usually they should combine them. The account score decides which companies get attention; the lead score decides which person inside a prioritised account to contact first.

### How do you calculate an account score?

Score company fit against your ICP, then add engagement from each known contact, rolled up by a chosen rule such as sum with a cap per contact. Some firms add third-party intent.

### How much data do you need for predictive account scoring?

It varies by tool. Salesforce recommends at least 200 accounts with won and 200 with lost opportunities from the last two years for Einstein Key Accounts Identification.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Saying Goodbye To MQLs: A Parting That Is All Sweet And No Sorrow](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/saying-goodbye-to-mqls-sweet-and-no-sorrow), 21 November 2023. Analyst blog; some conversion figures are from Forrester clients.
- [Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Press release on Forrester's own survey; sample size not stated on the page.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Build lead scores](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/scoring/build-lead-scores), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; available score types depend on subscription.
- [Salesforce, Account Engagement Einstein Implementation Guide](https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/244/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/pardot_einstein_implementation_guide.pdf). Vendor documentation for one release; thresholds may change.
- The comparison table, roll-up example and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

# SOC 2 vs ISO 27001 for AI Vendors

Source: https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-vs-iso-27001/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: SOC 2 is an attestation report in which a CPA firm tests a service organisation's controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. ISO/IEC 27001 is an international standard for an information security management system, certified by an accredited body. Neither currently tests model behaviour, so buyers of AI tools need both kinds of evidence plus questions of their own.

SOC 2 is an attestation: a CPA firm examines a service organisation's description of its system and tests its controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria, then issues a restricted report. ISO/IEC 27001 is a certification: an accredited certification body confirms that the organisation runs an information security management system (ISMS) that meets the standard's requirements. SOC 2 shows how specific controls performed; ISO/IEC 27001 shows that a management system exists and keeps improving. Neither currently tests whether an AI model is accurate or well governed.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What the two terms mean

**SOC 2** comes from the American Institute of CPAs. A licensed CPA firm examines the vendor's own description of its system and tests the controls behind it. The AICPA's guide for practitioners notes that customers and business partners typically need information about a service organisation's controls and often request a SOC 2 report. The output is an opinion, the system description and the tests performed with results. Our explainer on [SOC 2 for AI vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/) covers Type 1 and Type 2 reports and the AI gaps in detail.

**ISO/IEC 27001** is published jointly by ISO and the IEC. It sets requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving an ISMS, for organisations of any size and sector. The organisation defines a scope, assesses its information security risks and selects controls, using Annex A as a reference list. An accredited certification body then audits it. ISO's own guidance asks firms to cite the full edition, "certified to ISO/IEC 27001:2022", rather than "ISO 27001". The ISO Survey 2022 counted over 70,000 certificates across about 150 countries.

| Dimension | SOC 2 | ISO/IEC 27001 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Type of assurance | Attestation report by a CPA firm | Certification by an accredited certification body |
| Criteria owner | AICPA Trust Services Criteria | ISO and IEC |
| What is assessed | Controls for a described system, against chosen categories | A management system for a defined scope |
| Control set | Vendor designs its own controls to meet the criteria | Risk-based selection, with 93 Annex A reference controls |
| Output | Detailed report, usually shared under NDA | Certificate stating the scope; audit report stays private |
| Evidence of operation | Type 2 tests controls over a period | Annual surveillance audits within a three-year cycle |
| AI coverage today | None specific; AI points of focus proposed for 2027 | None specific; ISO/IEC 42001 is the AI counterpart |

## What each proves, and what neither proves

The two answer different questions. A SOC 2 Type 2 report says that named controls, such as access reviews or change approvals, operated effectively over a stated period, and it lists any exceptions. It is detailed and specific to one system. ISO/IEC 27001 says the organisation has a working process for finding and treating security risks, with management review and internal audit. It is broader and less detailed about any single control.

The AICPA has published a mapping between the Trust Services Criteria and ISO 27001, posted in May 2018 and available to members. Overlap is substantial, which is why many vendors hold both. Overlap is not equivalence: a certificate does not show test results, and a SOC 2 report does not show a management system.

For AI vendors, the same gaps appear in both:

- **Scope can exclude the AI.** A SOC 2 system description or an ISMS scope statement may not cover a newly launched AI feature.
- **Model providers sit outside.** Third-party model providers are often carved out of SOC 2 reports and treated as suppliers within an ISMS.
- **Model behaviour is untested.** Accuracy, drift and bias are outside both frameworks as written.

The AICPA's exposure draft of 28 October 2026 proposes points of focus on AI governance, model monitoring, prompt manipulation, data poisoning and training data management. If approved, they would apply to engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027. For AI management itself, [ISO/IEC 42001](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-iso-42001/) is the certifiable standard.

## Which to ask for

| Situation | What to ask the vendor for |
| --- | --- |
| US enterprise buyers, or a procurement team that names SOC 2 | SOC 2 Type 2, period ending within 12 months |
| International buyers, or tenders that name ISO | ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certificate and its scope statement |
| Vendor holds client confidential data | Either, plus confidentiality in SOC 2 scope |
| AI outputs drive decisions or customer messages | SOC 2 with processing integrity, plus evaluation evidence |
| Vendor claims AI governance maturity | ISO/IEC 42001, or a written answer on drift and evaluation |
| New vendor with neither | A dated plan, and a bridge of your own controls in the meantime |

A short checklist when reading either document:

1. **Check the date and edition.** A 27001 certificate should name the 2022 edition; a SOC 2 period should be recent.
2. **Read the scope.** Confirm that the product and AI features you are buying are inside it.
3. **Find the model providers.** Ask which are carved out and how the vendor monitors them.
4. **Ask for the Statement of Applicability.** For 27001, it shows which Annex A controls were included or excluded, and why.
5. **Record what you accepted.** Note the evidence, the gaps and the review date.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, an AI vendor usually supplies part of the wiring or the reasoning. SOC 2 and ISO/IEC 27001 are evidence that the vendor protects what passes through it. They say nothing about whether your firm should let the tool draft, act with approval or act alone.

That judgment is yours, and it belongs in your own record: which AI uses are approved, at what autonomy level, on what evidence, with what review date. As we argue in [Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/), that chain of decisions is what scrutiny turns to. Rent the wiring, accept the vendor's certificates as hygiene, and own the decision record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Attestation versus certification.** SOC 2 tests named controls; ISO/IEC 27001 certifies a management system.
- **Overlap is not equivalence.** Many vendors need both, depending on who buys from them.
- **Read the scope first.** AI features and model providers are the most common exclusions.
- **Neither tests the model.** Ask separately about evaluation, drift and ISO/IEC 42001.

## Common questions

### Is SOC 2 or ISO 27001 better?

Neither is better in general. SOC 2 gives detailed test results for specific controls; ISO/IEC 27001 certifies an information security management system. Buyer location and contract terms usually decide which is required.

### Does ISO 27001 certification replace a SOC 2 report?

Not for buyers who ask for SOC 2. The control areas overlap, but a certificate does not include the test results and exceptions that a SOC 2 report shows.

### How long is an ISO 27001 certificate valid?

Typically three years, with annual surveillance audits and a recertification audit at the end of the cycle. Certificates to the 2013 edition ceased to be valid after 31 October 2025.

### Does SOC 2 or ISO 27001 cover AI risks?

Not specifically today. The AICPA has proposed AI points of focus for 2027, and ISO/IEC 42001 covers AI management systems separately.

## In the news

- 28 October 2026 · AICPA and CIMA[AICPA proposes updated SOC 2 trust services criteria](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-28-aicpa-proposes-updated-soc-2-trust-services-criteria)An exposure draft, so the criteria can still change. AI vendors in security review should know it is coming.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

Product page for the paid practitioner guide; description only.
- [AICPA, AICPA proposes update of SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/news/article/aicpa-proposes-update-of-soc-2-r-trust-services-criteria-to-enhance-the-relevance-usability-and-value-of-cpas-reports), 28 October 2026. Exposure draft announcement; criteria not yet final.

Certification body guide and national accreditation body notice; cycle details vary by certifier.

# What Is an Open-Weight Model?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-open-weight-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An open-weight model publishes its trained parameters so anyone permitted by the licence can run and modify it. That is not the same as open source AI, which the Open Source Initiative's 2024 definition says also requires training code and data information. For a business, open weights trade per-token fees and provider control for hosting, safety and licence work.

An open-weight model is an AI model whose trained parameters, called weights, are published so that anyone permitted by the licence can download, run and modify it on their own hardware. Open weights are not the same as open source. The Open Source Initiative's definition also requires the training code and detailed information about the training data, and many open-weight licences add conditions on use. For a business, open weights mean control over where the model runs, in exchange for running it.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What an open-weight model means

A trained model is, at bottom, a large file of numbers, its parameters or weights. A closed model keeps them on the provider's servers, and customers send requests through an API. An open-weight model publishes the file. Anyone the licence allows can run it on a laptop, a private server or a cloud account they control.

The NTIA, the US Commerce Department agency directed to review the question, described open-weight models as letting developers build on and adapt previous work, widening access for small companies and researchers.

"Open" is used loosely, so it helps to separate four levels.

| Level | What is published | Example of terms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Closed, API only | Nothing; access through the provider | Provider's terms of service |
| Open weights, restricted licence | Weights, usually inference code | Custom licence with use or scale limits, such as Llama 2's 700 million user clause |
| Open weights, permissive licence | Weights under a standard licence | gpt-oss under Apache 2.0 |
| Open source AI, OSI definition | Weights, full training and inference code, detailed training-data information | OSI-approved terms for every component |

The OSI definition grants four freedoms: to use the system "for any purpose and without having to ask for permission", to study it, to modify it and to share it. To exercise them, it requires the preferred form for making modifications. That means data information detailed enough for a skilled person to build a substantially equivalent system, the complete code used to train and run it, and the parameters. Most open-weight releases publish the parameters and stop there. A licence with a user cap or a field-of-use restriction also fails the "any purpose" test.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

**Where data goes.** Running a model on your own infrastructure means prompts, CRM records and contracts need not leave it. For firms with strict [data residency](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/) or client confidentiality terms, that can settle a procurement question an API cannot.

**What you can change.** Weights can be [fine-tuned](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-fine-tuning/) on the firm's own examples, and a version can be frozen. A closed model can be changed or retired on the provider's schedule; a downloaded one changes only when you change it.

**What it costs.** There are no per-token fees to the developer, but there is hosting. OpenAI states gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU and gpt-oss-20b in about 16 GB of memory. That hardware, engineering time and patching now sit with the buyer, and at low or uneven volume an API is often cheaper; see [AI inference cost](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/).

**Who carries safety work.** A provider's API applies its own filtering and abuse monitoring. With open weights, the controls are whatever you add. OpenAI said that before releasing gpt-oss it fine-tuned a version on specialised biology and cybersecurity data to test misuse, and that version did not reach high capability levels. Few firms will run tests like that, so their own [guardrails](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-guardrails/) and [evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) carry more weight.

**What the licence says.** Read it as a contract. The Llama 2 licence, for example, incorporates Meta's acceptable use policy, requires a separate licence above 700 million monthly active users, and bars using outputs to improve other large language models. Later Llama versions have their own licences.

In **lowob**'s terms, an open-weight model is still rented reasoning, even when the firm hosts it. The weights can be swapped next year. The record of what was decided, and why, is the asset that stays.

## How to evaluate an open-weight model

| Question | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| Licence | Standard (Apache 2.0, MIT) or custom; user or revenue caps; acceptable use policy; limits on use of outputs |
| Openness | Weights only, or code and training-data information too |
| Hardware | GPU memory needed at the precision you will run |
| Hosting route | Your own servers, your own cloud account, or a managed host serving the same weights |
| Safety | What the developer tested; what filtering and monitoring you must add |
| Fit | Accuracy on your own test set against your current API model |

## lowob takeaways

- **Open weights are downloadable parameters.** You run the model, and the prompts stay with you.
- **Open weights are not open source.** The OSI definition also requires code and training-data information.
- **Read the licence.** User caps and use restrictions vary by model and version.
- **Control comes with work.** Hosting, safety and evaluation become your job.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between open-weight and open-source AI?

Open-weight means the trained parameters are published. Open source AI, under the OSI's 2024 definition, also requires the full training and inference code and detailed training-data information, all under OSI-approved terms, with freedom to use the system for any purpose.

### Is Llama open source?

Not by the OSI's test. The Llama 2 licence publishes the weights but requires a separate licence above 700 million monthly active users and binds users to an acceptable use policy, so it does not grant use for any purpose.

### Are open-weight models safe for business data?

They can keep data inside your own infrastructure, which helps confidentiality. They also leave filtering, monitoring and patching to you, so safety depends on how you deploy them.

### Are open-weight models cheaper than API models?

Not always. You avoid per-token fees but pay for hardware and staff. At steady high volume, self-hosting can cost less; at low or uneven volume an API is usually cheaper.

## Sources and notes

- [Open Source Initiative, The Open Source AI Definition 1.0](https://opensource.org/ai), October 2024. Standards body definition; voluntary, and developers' use of the word "open" is not bound by it.
- [Meta, Llama 2 Community License Agreement](https://ai.meta.com/llama/license/), July 2023. Vendor licence; later Llama versions carry their own terms.
- [OpenAI, Introducing gpt-oss](https://openai.com/index/introducing-gpt-oss/), 5 August 2025. Vendor announcement; hardware and safety claims are OpenAI's own.
- [NTIA, NTIA Supports Open Models to Promote AI Innovation](https://www.ntia.gov/press-release/2024/ntia-supports-open-models-promote-ai-innovation), 30 July 2024. US government report summary; policy may have changed since.

## Related research

- [What Is a Small Language Model?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-small-language-model/)
- [What Is Data Residency for AI Tools?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/)
- [What Is Fine-Tuning, and When Is It Worth It?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-fine-tuning/)
- [Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/)

## Next move

For any open-weight model on your shortlist, have someone read the licence in full and note any user or revenue caps, limits on outputs and the acceptable use policy. Then price one month of hosting against your current API bill.

# LTV:CAC vs CAC Payback: Which Unit Economics Metric to Trust

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ltv-cac-vs-cac-payback/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: LTV:CAC divides an estimate of a customer's lifetime gross profit by the cost of acquiring them. CAC payback counts the months of gross profit needed to recover that cost. LTV:CAC depends heavily on a churn assumption that young firms cannot yet observe, so payback is usually the safer metric for budget decisions, with LTV:CAC used once retention history exists.

LTV:CAC is the ratio of a customer's estimated lifetime value, usually lifetime gross profit, to the cost of acquiring that customer. CAC payback is the number of months of gross profit it takes to recover the acquisition cost. Both start from the same inputs. The difference is that LTV:CAC needs a forecast of how long customers stay, while payback does not. For most firms of 20 to 500 people, payback is the number to trust for budget decisions, and LTV:CAC is a check once several years of retention data exist.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What the two terms mean

Both metrics start with customer acquisition cost (CAC): sales and marketing spend in a period divided by new customers won. Our explainer on [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) covers what belongs in CAC and how to keep it honest.

The formulas, using monthly figures:

- **Monthly gross profit per customer** = monthly revenue per customer × gross margin
- **CAC payback (months)** = CAC ÷ monthly gross profit per customer
- **Simple LTV** = monthly gross profit per customer ÷ monthly churn rate
- **LTV:CAC** = LTV ÷ CAC

Dividing by the churn rate assumes an average customer lifetime of one divided by churn. Skok notes this simple formula only holds where customers pay roughly the same amount and no expansion is expected. Andreessen Horowitz goes further: lifetime value should be net profit, not revenue or gross margin, and a revenue-based LTV "suggests a higher upper limit" on acquisition spend than the business can afford.

| Dimension | LTV:CAC | CAC payback |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Ratio, such as 3x | Months |
| Question | Is a customer worth more than they cost? | How long is cash at risk? |
| Needs a churn forecast | Yes, and it dominates the result | No |
| Captures expansion | Only with a more complex formula | No |
| Captures churn after payback | Yes | No |
| Common guideline | 3x or more | Under 12 months for SMB; longer for enterprise |
| Main weakness | False precision from assumed lifetimes | Ignores everything after the payback month |

## A worked example

An illustrative firm with these inputs:

| Input | Value |
| --- | --- |
| CAC | £15,000 |
| Monthly revenue per new customer | £1,500 |
| Gross margin | 75% |
| Monthly gross profit per customer | £1,125 |
| Monthly churn | 1.5% |

**CAC payback** = 15,000 ÷ 1,125 = 13.3 months.

**Simple LTV** = 1,125 ÷ 0.015 = £75,000, implying an average lifetime of about 67 months.

**LTV:CAC** = 75,000 ÷ 15,000 = 5.0x.

Now change only the churn assumption:

| Monthly churn | Implied lifetime | LTV | LTV:CAC | CAC payback |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1.0% | 100 months | £112,500 | 7.5x | 13.3 months |
| 1.5% | about 67 months | £75,000 | 5.0x | 13.3 months |
| 3.0% | about 33 months | £37,500 | 2.5x | 13.3 months |

The ratio moves from comfortably above Bessemer's 3x threshold to below it on a two-point change in a number that a young firm has rarely measured for long. Payback does not move.

Payback has its own blind spot. The 13.3 months assumes each customer stays until repaid. Across a cohort losing 1.5% a month, cumulative gross profit per starting customer passes £15,000 only in month 15. That is closer to what the cash flow will show.

Andreessen Horowitz suggests a conservative alternative for firms with limited history: measure 12-month and 24-month LTV from observed data instead of projecting a lifetime. On the same cohort, 24-month gross profit per starting customer is about £22,800, or roughly 1.5x CAC. That is less flattering than 5.0x and much harder to dispute.

## Which to trust

Jason Cohen, writing on his blog A Smart Bear in 2013, argued that LTV "overcomplicates and misleads" because its inputs can shift by large amounts within a year, and recommended payback alongside its separate inputs. Bessemer reaches a similar place more gently, using payback as its primary efficiency metric and LTV:CAC as a guideline.

| Situation | Metric to lead with |
| --- | --- |
| Setting next quarter's channel budget | CAC payback, by channel and segment |
| Cash is tight or funding is uncertain | CAC payback, with a cohort view that counts churn |
| Fewer than about two years of retention data | Payback, plus observed 12- and 24-month LTV |
| Comparing segments with several years of history | LTV:CAC, with churn measured per segment |
| NRR well above 100% | Payback; the simple LTV formula breaks when customers expand |
| Advisory or project firms with one-off clients | Payback within the engagement; LTV only if clients repeat |

Whichever you report, state the assumptions beside the number: what CAC includes, which margin, which churn rate and over what period. A ratio without its churn assumption is not comparable across firms or even across quarters.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, both metrics are forecasts used to make funding decisions. The decision to fund a channel, hire sellers or enter a segment rests on an assumed payback and an assumed churn rate. Those assumptions are the expected outcome, and they belong in the record with the owner and the date.

The learning step closes the loop. Two or three quarters later, write back the payback and churn actually observed for that cohort. Our explainer on [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers how. Over time the firm builds its own evidence on which channels repay and how long customers stay, which is more useful than any published benchmark.

## lowob takeaways

- **Same inputs, different exposure.** LTV:CAC depends on a churn forecast; payback does not.
- **Small churn changes swing the ratio.** In the example, moving from 1% to 3% monthly churn moves LTV:CAC from 7.5x to 2.5x.
- **Use payback for budgets.** It is harder to flatter and closer to cash.
- **Record the assumptions.** Funding decisions should carry the payback and churn expected, then the result.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between LTV:CAC and CAC payback?

LTV:CAC compares estimated lifetime gross profit from a customer with what it cost to win them. CAC payback counts how many months of gross profit it takes to recover that cost.

### What is a good LTV to CAC ratio?

A common guideline is 3x or more, used by Bessemer and by David Skok. It is only meaningful if the churn rate behind the LTV has been measured, not assumed.

### Is CAC payback better than LTV:CAC?

For budget decisions, usually. Payback does not depend on forecasting customer lifetime, so it is harder to inflate. LTV:CAC is useful once several years of retention data exist.

### How do you calculate LTV for SaaS?

The simple version is monthly revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin, divided by monthly churn. It assumes no expansion, so firms with high expansion need a cohort-based method.

## Sources and notes

- [Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million](https://www.bvp.com/assets/uploads/2021/09/scaling-to-100-million-by-mary-d-onofrio.pdf), 2021. Investor research; benchmarks reflect a high-growth cloud sample.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), accessed November 2026. Investor guidance on LTV and CAC definitions.
- [David Skok, For Entrepreneurs, SaaS Metrics 2.0: Detailed Definitions](https://forentrepreneurs.com/saas-metrics-2-definitions-2/), July 2014, updated December 2020. Venture investor's guidelines; the author notes the payback rule dates from 2011.
- [Jason Cohen, A Smart Bear, Why I don't like the LTV metric (LifeTime Value)](https://longform.asmartbear.com/ltv/), October 2013, updated 2025. Personal blog essay; opinion, not research.
- The worked example is illustrative. The choice table and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Next move

Recalculate your LTV:CAC at your measured churn rate and at double that rate, and put both beside CAC payback in the next board pack. If the ratio falls below 3x at double churn, lead with payback.

# What Is an Approval Gate for AI Agents?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: An approval gate is the point where an AI agent stops and waits for a person before an action takes effect. OWASP recommends it for high-impact actions, and the main agent frameworks now build it in. The design questions are which actions to gate, who approves, what the approver sees and how the decision is logged.

An approval gate is a checkpoint where an AI agent pauses before a chosen action, such as sending an email or updating a price, until a named person approves, edits or rejects it. The decision and the evidence behind it are logged. In The Build Order it is Gateway 1: nothing an agent produces leaves the company until a person has approved it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an approval gate means

An agent works in a loop: it reasons, calls a tool, observes the result and continues. An approval gate interrupts that loop at a defined tool call. The agent proposes the action and its arguments. A person sees the proposal and decides. Only then does the action run.

The idea is not new. A deal desk does the same for discounts, and a publishing workflow does it for articles. What is new is that agent frameworks now provide the mechanism directly.

OpenAI's Agents SDK documents a `needs\_approval` setting on tools. When a call needs approval, "execution pauses", and the pending items appear as interruptions. The application then calls approve or reject and resumes the run. Pending state can be stored "in a database or queue", so an approval can wait hours without the agent holding a session open.

LangChain's middleware takes the same approach, with three outcomes. Approve runs the tool "with the original arguments as proposed by the agent". Edit lets the reviewer "modify the tool arguments before execution". Reject skips the call and returns feedback to the agent. The documentation states that "human-in-the-loop requires checkpointing to handle interrupts".

| A gate is | A gate is not |
| --- | --- |
| A pause before a named action | A review of the agent's reasoning after the fact |
| Three outcomes: approve, edit, reject | A single "OK" button |
| A logged decision with an approver | A chat message saying "looks fine" |
| Placed by action type and risk | Applied to every step, which breeds rubber-stamping |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The security case comes first. OWASP lists excessive agency sixth in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications. Its mitigations include requiring approval for high-impact actions and "complete mediation": authorisation should sit in the downstream system "rather than relying on an LLM to decide if an action is allowed". In plain terms, the gate must be enforced by software, not requested in a prompt.

The regulatory case follows. Article 14 of the EU AI Act requires that overseers of high-risk systems can "disregard, override or reverse the output". Most commercial uses are not high-risk under the Act, but the ability to override is a sensible baseline for any agent that acts.

The commercial case is simpler. A wrong email to a prospect, or a quote at the wrong price, costs more than the time to approve it. Products now expose the choice. HubSpot's prospecting agent offers "Review emails: you'll review and approve each message before it goes out" or "Send without review". Someone in the firm decides which, and that decision should itself be recorded.

One technical caution from OpenAI's documentation: "Approval permits a tool call to execute; it does not guarantee exactly-once execution." Tools with side effects, such as sending email, need safeguards against running twice.

## Where to place gates

Gate by action type, not by agent. The autonomy level on **lowob**'s dial (0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone) is set per task.

| Action | Reversible? | Suggested level | Gate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Summarise an account for a seller | Yes | 0 or 1 | None; output stays internal |
| Draft a follow-up email | Yes, until sent | 2 | Approve, edit or reject before sending |
| Update CRM stage or close date | Yes, with history | 2, then 3 on evidence | Approve until error rate is known |
| Send a quote or price | Hard to reverse | 2 | Approver from the discount matrix |
| Post publicly or contact a new prospect list | No | 2 | Named owner; batch approval with spot-checks |

Three design rules keep the gate useful. Show the approver the sources the agent used, so checking does not mean redoing the work. Make rejecting as quick as approving. Track edit and return rates per task, since an approval rate alone rises with fatigue as well as quality.

## lowob takeaways

- **Enforce the gate in software.** A prompt that asks the agent to wait is not a control.
- **Offer three outcomes.** Approve, edit and reject, each logged with the approver.
- **Gate by action, not by agent.** External, irreversible and priced actions come first.
- **Record the setting itself.** Choosing "send without review" is a decision with an owner.

## Common questions

### What is an approval gate in AI?

A checkpoint where an AI agent pauses before a specified action until a person approves, edits or rejects it, with the decision logged.

### How do you add human approval to an AI agent?

Most agent frameworks let you mark specific tools as needing approval. The run pauses at that tool call, stores its state, and resumes once a person decides.

### Which AI agent actions need human approval?

Actions that leave the company, are hard to reverse or carry a price: client emails, quotes, public posts and changes to contracts or payments.

### Does an approval gate slow agents down?

It adds review time to gated actions only. Internal drafts and summaries usually need no gate, so most agent work runs without one.

## Sources and notes

- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/), 2025. Community security standard.
- [OpenAI Agents SDK (Python), Human-in-the-loop](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/human_in_the_loop), undated. Vendor developer documentation.
- [LangChain, Human-in-the-loop](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langchain/human-in-the-loop/index.html), undated. Vendor developer documentation for an open-source framework.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Use the prospecting agent](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/prospecting/use-the-prospecting-agent?cid=482), undated. Vendor product documentation.
- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 14: Human oversight](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14). Official text; applies to high-risk systems only.

## Related research

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [What Is an AI Autonomy Level?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/)

## Next move

List every action your AI tools can take that reaches a client or changes a price. For each, write down whether a person approves it first, and whether that approval is logged.

# RevOps vs Sales Ops: What Changed and Why It Matters

Source: https://lowob.com/research/revops-vs-sales-ops/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Sales operations gives the sales team its processes, tools, analytics and plans. Revenue operations extends that work across marketing, sales and customer success, with one set of definitions, data and systems. The change matters more now because AI assistants and agents read across all three functions and inherit every inconsistency between them.

Sales operations (sales ops) is the function that gives a sales team its processes, tools, data and plans: territories, quotas, compensation, CRM administration and the forecast. Revenue operations (RevOps) runs the same kind of work across the whole revenue line, so marketing, sales and customer success share one set of definitions, one data model and one set of systems. The change is one of scope and ownership. It matters more now because AI tools read across all three functions and inherit every disagreement between them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What the two terms mean

**Sales operations** grew up to make a sales team efficient. Gartner's description covers designing and managing the team that supports the revenue process, improving sales analytics and data quality, raising data literacy among sellers and managers, and designing compensation plans and quotas. In practice a sales ops lead owns the CRM configuration, territory design, pipeline reporting and the forecast cadence. The customer is the sales leader.

**Revenue operations** takes the same disciplines and applies them to every function that touches revenue. Gartner frames it as one operating model organised into strategy, process, workflow, data, analysis and technology across go-to-market teams. Forrester's definition is "a highly configured, iterative commercial execution strategy designed to maximize customer value and company performance." Our explainer on [revenue operations](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/) covers the function in more depth. Here the question is what differs from sales ops.

| Dimension | Sales ops | RevOps |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | The sales team | Marketing, sales and customer success, sometimes partners |
| Main customer | Head of sales | Chief revenue officer or chief executive |
| Owns definitions of | Opportunity stages, forecast categories | The whole customer lifecycle, from lead to renewal |
| Systems owned | CRM and sales tools | The go-to-market stack and the data flowing between tools |
| Typical metrics | Pipeline coverage, win rate, quota attainment | The same, plus conversion across functions, retention and net revenue retention |
| Planning | Territories, quotas, compensation | Capacity and targets across all revenue teams |
| Typical failure | Optimises sales while marketing and success use other numbers | Becomes a reporting team without authority to change process |

## What changed, and why

The shift was a response to handoffs. Gartner's 2021 announcement argued that separate departments passing customers between each other, each with its own tools and methods, slow revenue growth. Its answer was to align sales, marketing and customer success technology, data and KPIs so the revenue process can be managed as one system.

Three changes follow from that.

**One set of definitions.** A marketing-qualified lead, a sales-accepted opportunity and a renewal at risk are defined once, in writing, and every system uses them. Without that, marketing reports leads that sales does not recognise, and customer success forecasts renewals on criteria nobody else sees. Clear [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) are the usual starting point.

**One data model.** Accounts, contacts and deals link across the marketing tool, the CRM and the customer success platform. Recurring revenue made this more pressing: in a subscription business, much of the revenue arrives after the sale, in renewals and expansion that sales ops never owned.

**One owner for the stack.** Tools are bought and configured against the whole process, not team by team.

Forrester's point about structure, made about Asia Pacific organisations, is worth noting for smaller firms. RevOps does not always mean a new department. In some firms a separate team takes on the work; in others, existing sales and marketing operations teams expand their remit.

## Why it matters more with AI

AI assistants and agents make the difference between the two models visible. An assistant preparing a renewal brief reads marketing engagement, the sales history and support tickets. If those three systems define "active customer" differently, the brief is confidently wrong. An agent that updates CRM fields after calls needs to know which definitions and fields it may touch, and who owns them.

Under a pure sales ops model, nobody owns the seams between functions. Under RevOps, someone does. That is why we treat RevOps as the natural owner of the work described in [AI Agents in Commercial Operations](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-commercial-operations/): hygiene, routing, forecast preparation and the records agents depend on.

## Which model fits

A renamed team with the same remit is still sales ops. The test is scope and authority, not title.

| Signal in your firm | Model that fits |
| --- | --- |
| Sales is the only go-to-market motion and marketing is small | Sales ops, with clear definitions shared with marketing |
| Leadership disputes lead or pipeline numbers every month | RevOps, starting with shared definitions |
| A large share of revenue comes from renewals and expansion | RevOps, so customer success data is part of the model |
| Each team buys and configures its own tools | RevOps, with one owner for the stack |
| AI assistants or agents read across more than one function | RevOps, or at least one named owner of cross-system definitions |
| Under about 50 people, one ops generalist | Either label; give that person the remit across all functions |

A short checklist for a firm moving from sales ops to RevOps:

- **Write the lifecycle definitions first.** Lead to renewal, on one page, signed off by each function head.
- **Give the role authority over process.** A RevOps team that can only report will not fix handoffs.
- **Map every system to the facts it owns.** One home per fact, as in [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/).
- **Decide who records commercial decisions.** Discounts, exceptions and priority calls need an owner and a reason.

## The **lowob** view

The enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. Sales ops maintains one part of the store, the CRM, for one team. RevOps is the function best placed to own the definitions across the whole store and the wiring that connects marketing, sales and customer success systems.

It is also the natural keeper of the record and the learning stage. A record of [commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/), each with a reason, owner, status and expected outcome, needs a function that spans the revenue line. So does writing outcomes back: whether the discount won the deal, whether the at-risk renewal held. Those results are what make the next forecast and the next agent draft better.

Rent the tools. Have RevOps own the definitions, the decision record and the write-back, because those are what any AI the firm adopts will depend on.

## lowob takeaways

- **The difference is scope.** Sales ops serves sales; RevOps serves the whole revenue line.
- **Handoffs drove the change.** Separate tools and numbers between functions slow revenue.
- **AI raises the stakes.** Assistants and agents read across functions and inherit their inconsistencies.
- **Authority beats the title.** RevOps needs the remit to change process, not only to report on it.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between RevOps and sales ops?

Sales ops supports the sales team with processes, tools, data and plans. RevOps does that work across marketing, sales and customer success, with shared definitions, data and systems.

### Does RevOps replace sales operations?

Often it absorbs it. Sales operations work such as territories, quotas and the forecast continues inside a wider RevOps remit, sometimes run by the same people.

### When should a company move from sales ops to RevOps?

When functions dispute each other's numbers, when renewals and expansion are a large share of revenue, or when tools and AI systems need to read across teams.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, Sales Operations: Strategies that Boost Performance](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/insights/sales-operations), accessed November 2026. Analyst firm overview page; marketing for paid research.
- [Gartner, Revenue Operations (RevOps): Best Practices to Grow Your Business](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/defining-revenue-operations), accessed November 2026. Analyst firm overview page; definition only, no data.
- [Gartner, Gartner Predicts 75% of the Highest Growth Companies Will Deploy a RevOps Model](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2021-05-17-gartner-predicts-75--of-the-highest-growth-companies-), 17 May 2021. A prediction, not a measured outcome.
- [Forrester, Why Revenue Operations (RevOps) Should Be On Your Radar](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/why-revenue-operations-revops-should-be-on-your-radar), 20 August 2024. Analyst blog with an Asia Pacific focus.
- The comparison table, fit signals and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is Revenue Operations (RevOps)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/)
- [AI Agents in Commercial Operations: The RevOps Tasks Worth Handing Over](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-commercial-operations/)
- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)

- [What Is Data Enrichment?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-enrichment/)

## Next move

Ask your heads of marketing, sales and customer success to each write their definition of an active customer and a qualified opportunity. If the answers differ, that is the first RevOps job, whatever the team is called.

# Pricing Experiments in B2B

Source: https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Price is the strongest profit lever most firms have and the one they test least. A 1992 Harvard Business Review analysis of 2,463 companies found a 1% price improvement lifted operating profit by 11.1%, more than any other lever. B2B firms rarely have the volume or the anonymity for consumer-style A/B tests, so this piece sets out the experiments that do work: cohort changes, packaging tests, discount guardrails and stated-preference research, with the record each one needs and the competition-law line not to cross.

A pricing experiment is a deliberate, recorded change to price, packaging or discount rules, made for a defined group of customers or deals, with a measure and a date to judge it. B2B firms seldom have the volume or the anonymity to run consumer-style A/B tests on list price, but they can test price for new cohorts, test packaging, test discount guardrails and run structured buyer research. The payoff is large: Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis of 2,463 companies found a 1% price improvement lifted operating profit by 11.1%. The discipline is the same as any test: decide in advance what result would change the decision.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most mid-size B2B firms change their prices rarely and test them almost never. A price list is set during a planning cycle, discounts fill the gap between the list and what buyers will pay, and nobody can say afterwards whether the list was right.

The reluctance is understandable. B2B buyers talk to each other, contracts run for years, and a single large deal can swamp a quarter's results. But the alternative to testing is not stability. It is a price set by the accumulated discounts of individual sellers, which is a test nobody designed and nobody reads.

## Why price deserves the effort

The case rests on arithmetic that has held for three decades.

Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello's 1992 *Harvard Business Review* article, "Managing Price, Gaining Profit", used the average economics of 2,463 companies in the Compustat database. A 1% improvement in price raised operating profit by 11.1%. The same improvement in variable cost raised it by 7.8%, in volume by 3.3% and in fixed cost by 2.3%.

McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 10-K filings from 140 listed distribution companies reached a similar conclusion in one sector: a 1% price increase was associated with a more than 22% boost in EBITDA margin.

| Lever, 1% improvement | Effect on operating profit (Marn and Rosiello, 1992) |
| --- | --- |
| Price | 11.1% |
| Variable cost | 7.8% |
| Volume | 3.3% |
| Fixed cost | 2.3% |

These are averages across very different firms, and the exact multiplier depends on margin. The ranking is what matters. For most firms, a small, durable improvement in realised price is worth more than a large effort on volume.

## Where the money actually leaks

Marn and Rosiello's second contribution was the pocket price waterfall: the sequence of discounts, rebates, payment terms and allowances between list price and what the firm actually keeps. They found the same product selling across a wide band of pocket prices, 35% from highest to lowest in one of their examples.

McKinsey's 2026 distribution research describes the same pattern in modern form. One building materials distributor's sales teams had been overriding system prices in more than half of transactions. After changes to pricing tools and rules, it cut manual overrides by 80% and expanded margins by more than 200 basis points.

Most mid-size firms can draw their own waterfall from data they already hold: list price from the price book, invoice price from billing, and the deductions in between from contracts and credit notes. The first version is usually rough, but even a rough waterfall shows which deductions are largest and which are granted most inconsistently.

That points to where a mid-size firm should start. The first experiments are rarely about list price. They are about the discount rules, approval thresholds and packaging decisions that determine how far realised price falls below it. Part 21 of this series covered discount governance; this piece is about testing whether those rules are right.

> The alternative to testing price is not stability. It is a price set by every seller's last discount.

## Experiments that work at B2B volumes

Consumer firms can show two prices to two random groups and count conversions. Most B2B firms cannot: volumes are too low, buyers compare notes, and showing two customers different prices for the same thing creates a fairness problem that outlasts the test. The methods below are designed around those constraints.

| Method | What it tests | Fits when | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New-cohort price change | A new list price or rate for new customers only, from a set date | Steady flow of new deals; existing contracts protected | Comparison with earlier cohorts is confounded by market changes |
| Packaging test | A new tier, bundle or add-on, offered alongside the current one | Several offers already exist; buyers choose | Cannibalising the current offer |
| Discount guardrail test | A tighter discount limit or approval threshold for one segment, team or region | Discounting is frequent and recorded | Sellers route deals around the rule |
| Staggered renewal increase | A price change applied at renewal in waves | Renewal base is large enough to stagger | Churn in the first wave is read too early |
| Stated-preference research | Willingness to pay from structured interviews or surveys, such as Van Westendorp or Gabor-Granger questions, or conjoint analysis | Before a launch or major change | What buyers say differs from what they pay |

Four rules make any of these readable.

**Decide the decision first.** Write down what result would lead you to keep, extend or reverse the change, before the test starts. In [*Tests that close questions*](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/) we argued that a test without a pre-stated decision rule rarely ends; it gets reinterpreted.

**Pick a comparison.** A hold-out segment, an earlier cohort, or a matched set of deals from the same quarter. A B2B test seldom needs statistical perfection, but it does need a reasonable answer to "compared with what?". The answer matters more than it looks: Gordon, Zettelmeyer and colleagues compared common observational measurement methods with 15 randomised advertising experiments at Facebook and found the observational methods generally overestimated the effect, though sometimes they underestimated it. A before-and-after reading of a price change carries the same risk.

**Do not read the result early.** Fix the check date and hold to it. Johari, Pekelis and Walsh showed that repeatedly checking a test and stopping at the first favourable reading can raise the false positive rate fivefold, even at 10,000 observations. Price tests run on far fewer, so an early reading is even less reliable.

**Measure realised price, not only win rate.** A test that raises win rate while lowering average realised price may have found a discount, not a better price. Track win rate, average discount, realised price and, where the cycle allows, early retention.

## Reading the evidence you already have

Many firms already hold the data for a first experiment. They have simply not read it as one.

Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, built from 4.2 million opportunities, found that offering a discount early in the cycle was associated with a 39% drop in win rates. That is a vendor correlation, not a controlled result: deals that need early discounts may be weaker deals. It is a hypothesis, and a cheap one to test. Hold the discount back until a defined stage in one segment for a quarter, and compare win rate and realised price with a segment that kept the old rule.

Everstage's 2026 survey of 195 North American revenue leaders found 47% took three or more days to approve a pricing exception. Approval delay is itself a pricing variable. A faster route for exceptions within a band, and a slower one outside it, can be tested like any other rule.

Pricing models are also moving. Metronome's 2026 review of more than 50 AI and software pricing models found hybrid pricing, mixing subscriptions with usage, credits or overages, to be the norm, and noted one company that made four major pricing structure changes in under two years. For firms considering usage or outcome pricing, [*Seats, usage or outcomes*](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) sets out the trade-offs; packaging tests are how to try them without betting the base.

## The legal and fairness line

Testing your own prices is ordinary commercial practice. Two lines need care.

**Competitors' data.** In November 2025 the US Department of Justice announced a proposed settlement with RealPage, a pricing-software provider, over allegations that pooling competitors' non-public, competitively sensitive data to generate pricing recommendations violated Section 1 of the Sherman Act. Paul, Weiss's analysis of the settlement draws practical lessons: risk is highest where current or forward-looking non-public competitor data feeds recommendations, auto-accept features should be opt-in, and the user should keep the decision. A firm's own data and its own tests are treated differently. The rule for a pricing experiment is simple: its inputs are your own prices, costs and outcomes, and public information.

**Price discrimination.** Charging different customers different prices is lawful in most B2B contexts, but not all. In the US, the Robinson-Patman Act restricts some forms of price discrimination between competing purchasers of goods, which matters for firms selling through resellers or distributors. The FTC's guidance sets out the tests: the Act applies to commodities, not services, to goods of like grade and quality sold to at least two purchasers around the same time, and only where competition may be injured. Its two main defences are a price difference justified by cost and a concession made in good faith to meet a competitor's price. Take advice before testing different prices on customers who compete with each other.

Fairness is a commercial constraint as well as a legal one. Buyers compare notes, and a customer who learns they paid more for the same thing during a test is a renewal risk. Tests on new cohorts, packaging and internal rules avoid most of that exposure.

## The record every experiment needs

A pricing experiment is a commercial decision with an unusually clear outcome, and it belongs in the record with the same fields as any other: the change, the reason, the owner, the group affected, the expected result and decision rule, the check date, and the outcome written back.

The record matters more for pricing than for most decisions because pricing knowledge decays fast. Two years after a test, the people who ran it may have gone, and the next team will rerun it. A recorded test, superseded rather than overwritten when the price changes again, is how a firm builds its own evidence on what buyers will pay.

Illustrative example: testing a discount guardrail

Decision
:   For one quarter, require approval for any discount offered before the proposal stage in the mid-market segment; leave the enterprise segment on the existing rule.

Reason and owner
:   Recorded deals showed early discounts were common in mid-market and win rates were no higher where they were given. Owned by the revenue lead, with finance agreeing the decision rule in advance: keep the change if win rate falls by less than three points and average realised price rises.

What changed
:   Win rate, average discount and realised price are compared across the two segments at quarter end, and the result is written to the record.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price is the strongest lever.** A 1% improvement in realised price beats a 1% gain in volume by a wide margin.
- **Start with leakage.** Discount rules, overrides and packaging usually matter more than list price.
- **Design for B2B constraints.** New cohorts, packaging, guardrails and staggered renewals avoid the fairness problem of random price tests.
- **Stay on your own data.** Never feed competitors' non-public prices into a pricing decision.

Gateway card

### Before you run a pricing experiment

- The change, the group affected and the comparison group written down
- A decision rule agreed with finance before the test starts
- Realised price and discount tracked, not only win rate
- Existing contracts and competing resellers checked for legal or fairness exposure
- Inputs limited to your own data and public information
- A check date and an outcome field in the record

## Common questions

### Can you A/B test prices in B2B?

Rarely in the consumer sense, because volumes are low and buyers compare notes. B2B firms usually test with new-customer cohorts, packaging options, discount rules or staggered renewal changes instead.

### How much does a 1% price increase affect profit?

In Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis of 2,463 companies, a 1% price improvement raised operating profit by 11.1% on average, against 3.3% for a 1% gain in volume. The effect depends on a firm's margin.

### What is a pocket price waterfall?

The sequence of discounts, rebates, payment terms and allowances between list price and the revenue a firm actually keeps from a transaction. Marn and Rosiello introduced it to show where realised price leaks.

### Is it legal to charge B2B customers different prices?

Generally yes, but some rules apply, such as the US Robinson-Patman Act for competing purchasers of goods, and competition law forbids using competitors' non-public pricing data. Take legal advice for your market.

# MCP vs API Integrations: What Changes and What Does Not

Source: https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-api-integrations/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A traditional API integration is a fixed path a developer codes against one system. The Model Context Protocol lets an AI application discover a system's tools at run time and lets the model decide when to call them. The API usually still sits underneath, so permissions, data quality and approvals matter as much as before.

An API integration is code that a developer writes against one system's interface, following a path fixed in advance. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard that lets an AI application connect to many systems the same way, discover what tools each one offers, and let the model decide when to call them. MCP changes who chooses the call and how connections are packaged. It does not replace the API underneath, and it does not remove the need for permissions, clean data or a person approving actions.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two terms mean

An API (application programming interface) is the door a system offers to other software. A CRM exposes endpoints to read a contact, create a deal or update a stage. Most modern web APIs are documented in the OpenAPI format, which the OpenAPI Initiative describes as letting people and machines understand a service without reading its source code. An API integration is the code that uses those endpoints: a sync job, a webhook handler or a workflow step. A developer chose every call when they wrote it.

MCP adds a layer designed for AI applications. In the specification's architecture, a host application, such as an AI assistant, runs one client per connection, and each client talks to an MCP server. The server exposes tools, resources and prompt templates through JSON-RPC messages. The client asks the server for its tool list, each tool described with a name and a JSON Schema for its inputs. The model reads that list and decides which tool to call, with what arguments, as the task unfolds. Our explainer on [the Model Context Protocol](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/) covers its history and governance.

In practice, an MCP server for a CRM is usually a thin wrapper around the CRM's existing API, which still does the work.

| Dimension | Direct API integration | MCP integration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built for | Developer code | AI applications and agents |
| Who decides when to call | The developer, in advance | The model, at run time, within what the host allows |
| How capabilities are found | A developer reads the documentation | The client requests a tool list from the server |
| Interface | HTTP endpoints, often described in OpenAPI | JSON-RPC tools with JSON Schema inputs |
| One connection serves | One integration | Any MCP-compatible host |
| Predictability | Same path every run | Path varies with the task |
| Main risk | A bug in a known path | A wrong or manipulated call with real permissions |

## What changes

**The cost of connecting.** Anthropic's case for MCP was that every new data source needed its own custom implementation. With MCP, a system publishes one server and any compatible host can use it.

**Who chooses the call.** In an API integration the path is written down. With MCP the model chooses, which is the point and the risk. The specification calls tools model-controlled, and recommends that applications show which tools are exposed, signal when one is invoked, and ask the user to confirm operations.

**Where trust sits.** The specification tells clients to treat tool descriptions and annotations from untrusted servers as untrusted. A poisoned tool description can steer a model, which is a form of [prompt injection](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/). The 2025-11-25 architecture also states that servers "should not be able to read the whole conversation", with the host enforcing boundaries between them.

## What does not change

**The API's permissions.** An MCP server can do only what its credentials allow. If the service account can delete records, so can the model. The authorisation rules, based on OAuth 2.1 for HTTP connections, forbid passing a client's token through to downstream APIs, but they do not decide which scopes you grant. That remains your call.

**Data quality.** MCP gives a model faster access to the same fields. If stage definitions are loose or owner fields are stale, the model reads loose, stale data more quickly.

**Rate limits and cost.** The specification requires servers to rate-limit tool invocations. A model that calls a tool repeatedly still consumes the underlying API quota.

**Accountability.** The protocol says clients should log tool usage for audit purposes. It does not say who owns the outcome. That is a management decision.

## Which to choose

Both will run side by side. The test is whether the steps are fixed or chosen at run time.

| Job | Better fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nightly sync from CRM to the data warehouse | Direct API | Fixed path, high volume, needs to be identical each run |
| Create a CRM record from a web form | Direct API or workflow tool | Known trigger and known fields |
| Assistant that prepares a call brief from CRM, email and tickets | MCP, read-only tools | The model picks which sources to read |
| Agent that drafts follow-ups and logs activity | MCP, with write tools behind approval | Model-chosen steps that touch customer records |
| Updating prices or contract terms | Neither without a person | High blast radius |

Before switching on any MCP server, check five things:

- **Who publishes it?** Prefer the system vendor's official server over an unreviewed community one.
- **Which tools does it expose?** Start with read-only tools and add write tools one at a time.
- **What credentials does it run with?** Grant the narrowest scopes the job needs.
- **Does the host ask before acting?** Confirmation prompts should be on for anything that writes or sends.
- **Where do the logs go?** Every tool call should land somewhere a person can review.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, MCP is wiring. It is a good standard to rent, because the alternative is maintaining custom connectors for every assistant you try. It does not turn a CRM into a brain, and it is not the record.

The part to own is what happens around each call: which tools an agent may use, at which point on the autonomy dial, and a record of what it read, proposed and was approved to do. Read tools can start at level 0 or 1, answer or draft. Write tools start at level 2, act with approval. The specification's own advice, a human able to deny tool invocations, matches our rule that [nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/). The learning stage then uses those logs to decide which tools have earned a notch more autonomy.

## lowob takeaways

- **MCP standardises the plug, not the system.** The API, its permissions and its data stay the same.
- **The model chooses the call.** That flexibility is useful and is also the main new risk.
- **Use direct APIs for fixed paths.** Syncs and form handlers do not need a model deciding.
- **Gate the write tools.** Start read-only, add write access behind approval, and log every call.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between MCP and an API?

An API is the interface a system exposes. MCP is a standard way for AI applications to discover and call tools, which are usually built on top of those APIs.

### Does MCP replace APIs?

No. Most MCP servers wrap an existing API. MCP changes how an AI application finds and calls a system, not how the system itself works.

### When should I use a direct API integration instead of MCP?

When the steps are fixed and should run identically every time, such as a nightly data sync or a form-to-CRM handler.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Introducing the Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol), 25 November 2024. Vendor announcement by MCP's original developer.
- [Model Context Protocol specification, Tools (revision 2026-07-28)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools), accessed November 2026. Protocol specification; recommendations marked SHOULD are not mandatory.
- [Model Context Protocol specification, Authorization (revision 2025-11-25)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/basic/authorization), accessed November 2026. Protocol specification; later revisions may change details.
- [Model Context Protocol specification, Architecture (revision 2025-11-25)](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2025-11-25/architecture), accessed November 2026. Protocol specification; describes design principles, not how any product implements them.
- [OpenAPI Initiative, OpenAPI Specification v3.1](https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.1), accessed November 2026. Standards document; version 3.2 has since been published.
- The decision table, checklist and autonomy levels are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [MCP vs A2A: How the Two Agent Protocols Fit Together](https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-a2a/)

## Next move

List every MCP server or AI connector your team has switched on, and for each one write down its credentials, its write tools and where its logs go. Turn off any write tool that has no named owner.
