# What Is a System Prompt?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-prompt/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-26 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A system prompt sets an AI model's role, rules and output format before a user types anything. Model makers give it more authority than user messages, which makes it the right place for job instructions. OWASP warns it is neither secret nor a security control, so permissions and limits must live elsewhere.

A system prompt is the standing set of instructions that a developer or operator gives an AI model before any user message. It defines the model's role, the task, the rules it should follow and the format of its answers. Model providers give it more authority than what users type. It is the right place to describe a job, and the wrong place to enforce security: OWASP advises that it should not be treated as secret or used as a control.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a system prompt means

A conversation with a language model is a list of messages. The system prompt is the first, written by whoever built the application rather than by the person using it. In Anthropic's API it is a separate `system` parameter. Other providers call it a system or developer message.

Its content is the job description: who the model is acting as, what it is for, what it should and should not do, and how its answers should look. Anthropic's prompting guidance puts the purpose plainly: "Setting a role in the system prompt focuses Claude's behavior and tone for your use case." It suggests thinking of the model as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows".

| Belongs in a system prompt | Belongs elsewhere |
| --- | --- |
| Role and task: "You draft follow-up emails for account managers" | Permissions: which records and tools the agent may use |
| Tone, format and length rules | Credentials, API keys, connection strings |
| Reasons behind rules, so the model can generalise | Discount limits and approval thresholds that must hold |
| Pointers to where context will appear | The context itself, which should be retrieved fresh |
| A few worked examples | Customer data that changes daily |

## How it works

### Authority

Model makers rank instructions by source. OpenAI's Model Spec, its public description of intended model behaviour, sets out a chain of command: root rules, then system, developer, user and guideline levels. It states that when developer and user messages are both present, "the developer messages have greater authority." Tool outputs, quoted text and file contents sit at the bottom with no authority by default, and instructions inside them "MUST be treated as information rather than instructions to follow."

That hierarchy is why system prompts work. It is also why they are a target. An attacker who cannot change the system prompt tries to make content look like it carries the same authority, which is the mechanism of prompt injection.

### Writing one well

Anthropic's guidance favours being explicit, explaining why a rule exists and giving examples. Its own illustration: a bare "NEVER use ellipses" works less well than explaining that responses will be read aloud by text-to-speech software that cannot pronounce them. It recommends three to five varied examples, marked off from the instructions.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### It is where the job is defined

A drafting agent's quality depends heavily on its system prompt: who the audience is, what a good follow-up contains, what never to promise. That makes the system prompt a commercial document, not a technical one. Revenue leaders should read it and sign it off.

### It is not a lock

OWASP's LLM07:2025, system prompt leakage, is blunt: the system prompt "should not be considered a secret, nor should it be used as a security control." Its examples include prompts that reveal internal transaction limits, which help an attacker work around them. The mitigations are to keep sensitive data out of the prompt, enforce controls outside the model and run agents with least privilege.

For a commercial agent, a line such as "never offer more than 10% discount" is guidance, not enforcement. The enforceable version is a deal desk rule that flags any draft above the limit, and an approval step before it is sent.

> The system prompt describes the job. Permissions, limits and approvals hold the line.

## How to manage system prompts

| Practice | What it involves |
| --- | --- |
| Owner | One named person approves changes, usually the business owner of the agent |
| Version control | Every change dated and kept, with the reason |
| Re-test on change | Run the agent's eval set before a new version goes live |
| Leakage check | Assume users can extract it; nothing in it should embarrass or expose the firm |
| Separation | Retrieved documents and inbound content clearly marked as data, not instructions |
| Review cycle | Read it quarterly against current pricing, products and policies |

Prompts drift silently. A product line changes, a policy is updated, and the system prompt keeps describing last year's firm. Logging every change, as with any other commercial decision, keeps the instruction set and the business aligned.

## lowob takeaways

- **It defines the job.** Role, task, rules, format and examples belong in the system prompt.
- **It outranks users.** Model makers give developer instructions more authority than user messages.
- **It is not secret.** Assume it can be extracted and keep credentials and limits out.
- **Enforce elsewhere.** Permissions, caps and approvals belong in systems the model cannot talk its way past.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a system prompt and a user prompt?

The system prompt is written by the developer or operator and sets standing instructions for every conversation. A user prompt is what the person using the application types in a given turn.

### Can users see the system prompt?

Usually not directly, but it can often be extracted by asking cleverly. OWASP advises treating it as public and keeping sensitive information out of it.

### How long should a system prompt be?

As long as the job needs. A single sentence of role changes behaviour; a production agent typically needs task, rules with reasons, format and a few examples.

### Can a system prompt stop prompt injection?

No. It can reduce some attacks, but OWASP advises enforcing controls outside the model, through least-privilege permissions, independent checks and human approval.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices). Vendor documentation for its own models; principles broadly transfer.
- [OpenAI, Model Spec](https://model-spec.openai.com/2025-10-27), version of 27 October 2025. Vendor's statement of intended model behaviour, not a guarantee of it.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm072025-system-prompt-leakage/), 2025. Community standard; mitigations are recommendations.

## Related research

- [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/)
- [What Is Context Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/)
- [What Are AI Guardrails?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-guardrails/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)

## Next move

Ask for the system prompt of every AI tool your team built or configured. Highlight any number, limit or credential in it, and move each one into a rule the model cannot override.

# What Is a Reasoning Model?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-reasoning-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Reasoning models spend extra computation on intermediate steps before answering, a method made mainstream by OpenAI's o1 in September 2024 and DeepSeek-R1 in January 2025. They are stronger on multi-step problems but slower and costlier, and research shows their visible reasoning often omits what actually drove the answer, so it cannot replace a recorded reason.

A reasoning model is a large language model trained to work through a problem in a series of intermediate steps before giving its answer, spending extra computation at the moment of the request. OpenAI's o1, released in September 2024, and DeepSeek-R1, in January 2025, made the approach mainstream, and other major providers, including Anthropic, now offer a reasoning or "thinking" setting. Reasoning models are stronger on multi-step problems, slower and more expensive, and their visible reasoning is not a reliable account of why they answered as they did.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a reasoning model means

A standard model produces its answer directly, one token after another. A reasoning model first produces a long run of intermediate tokens, often called a chain of thought, in which it breaks the problem down, tries approaches and checks its work. Only then does it write the answer.

OpenAI described o1 as trained with "a large-scale reinforcement learning algorithm" that "teaches the model how to think productively using its chain of thought". It reported that performance improved with more training and with more time spent thinking at the moment of use. That second lever, often called test-time compute, is what buyers now pay for.

DeepSeek's R1 paper reported that pure reinforcement learning produced behaviours such as self-reflection, verification and changing strategy mid-problem. It also showed that reasoning patterns from large models could be used to improve smaller ones, which is part of why reasoning settings spread quickly across providers.

|  | Standard model | Reasoning model |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How it answers | Directly | After hidden or summarised intermediate steps |
| Speed | Faster | Slower |
| Cost | Pay for visible output | Also pay for reasoning tokens |
| Strong at | Drafting, summarising, lookups, classification | Maths, code, planning, multi-step checks |
| Main control | Prompt and context | Prompt, context and an effort setting |
| What you see | The answer | The answer, plus a summary of the reasoning on some products |

## How it works in practice

Providers expose reasoning as a dial. OpenAI's API has a `reasoning.effort` setting; the documentation calls medium the "default configuration for most workloads" and advises treating effort "as a tuning knob, not the primary way to recover quality". Anthropic's API has moved from a fixed thinking budget, with a minimum of 1,024 tokens, to adaptive thinking, where the model decides whether and how much to think and the developer sets an effort level. At low effort it may skip thinking on easy inputs.

Cost is easy to miss. OpenAI's documentation states that reasoning tokens are not visible through the API but "still occupy space in the model's context window and are billed as output tokens". It recommends reserving at least 25,000 tokens for reasoning and output when experimenting. If a response hits its token cap, the buyer may pay for reasoning and receive no answer.

In an agent, reasoning can happen between tool calls. Anthropic's documentation describes interleaved thinking, where the model reasons about each tool result before choosing its next step. That is useful in a long [agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/), where a wrong turn early compounds.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Reasoning helps where a task has several steps that must agree: checking a proposal against pricing rules and past concessions, reconciling a forecast against stage definitions, or planning which records an agent should read first. It adds little to finding a contact, tagging a lead or tidying a note, where a fast setting is cheaper and just as accurate.

The larger issue is explanation. It is tempting to read a model's reasoning summary as the reason for a recommendation. Anthropic's alignment researchers tested this by planting hints in prompts and checking whether models admitted using them. Averaged across hint types, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned the hint 25% of the time and DeepSeek-R1 39% of the time. When models exploited planted shortcuts, they disclosed it less than 2% of the time in most scenarios, and often wrote a plausible rationale instead.

So the reasoning trace is diagnostic material, not a record. In **lowob**'s model the reason for a commercial decision is written by the person who owns it, in the [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/). Rent the models; own the instructions, the precedents and the reasons.

## How to choose a setting

1. Take 30 real tasks from one workflow, with known good answers.
2. Run them at the lowest and highest effort settings your provider offers.
3. Score accuracy, cost per task and time per task.
4. Choose the lowest setting that meets your accuracy bar, and recheck when the model changes.

## lowob takeaways

- **Reasoning models think before answering.** They spend extra computation on intermediate steps.
- **Better on hard, multi-step work.** Little gain on lookups and simple drafting.
- **Hidden tokens cost money.** Reasoning is billed as output even when you cannot see it.
- **The trace is not the reason.** Record decisions and reasons separately, with a named owner.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a reasoning model and a regular LLM?

A regular model answers directly. A reasoning model is trained to produce intermediate steps first, which improves performance on multi-step problems at the cost of speed and tokens.

### Are reasoning models more accurate?

On maths, coding and multi-step tasks, usually yes; OpenAI's o1 rose from 12% to 74% on one maths exam against GPT-4o. On simple tasks the gain is small and the extra cost is not.

### Can I trust a reasoning model's chain of thought?

Not as a full explanation. Anthropic found models often omit what actually influenced their answer, so treat the reasoning as a debugging aid and record decision reasons separately.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Learning to reason with LLMs](https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/), 12 September 2024. Vendor-reported benchmark results.
- [DeepSeek-AI, DeepSeek-R1: Incentivizing Reasoning Capability in LLMs via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948), January 2025; published in *Nature* 645, 2025. Developer's own paper, peer reviewed.
- [OpenAI, Reasoning models guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/reasoning), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; model names and settings change often.
- [Anthropic, Extended thinking documentation](https://platform.claude.com/docs/build-with-claude/extended-thinking), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Reasoning models don't always say what they think](https://www.anthropic.com/research/reasoning-models-dont-say-think), 3 April 2025. Vendor research on its own and a competitor's model; controlled experiments, not production use.

## Related research

## Next move

Pick one recurring commercial check, such as reviewing proposals against your discount rules, and run ten past examples at a low and a high reasoning setting. Compare the cost per correct answer before you choose a default.

# Build vs Buy AI Agents: A Decision Guide for Mid-Size Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Enterprise buyers have shifted toward buying AI: one investor survey found 76% of use cases were purchased in 2025. For a firm of 20 to 500 people the real choice is between buying a packaged agent, configuring one on a platform it already uses, and building on a framework. lowob's rule is to rent the wiring and own the record.

Buying an AI agent means paying a vendor for a packaged product that does a defined job. Building one means assembling models, tools and orchestration code yourself. For most firms of 20 to 500 people the answer is to buy or configure the agent, and to own the part no vendor can supply: the record of what was decided, by whom, and what happened next.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What the options really are

"Build or buy" hides three choices. A mid-size firm rarely writes its own model, so building means building the agent around someone else's model.

**Buy** a packaged agent from a specialist vendor: an AI SDR, a support agent, a meeting-notes agent. The vendor owns the logic, the prompts and the integrations.

**Configure** an agent inside a platform you already pay for: your CRM, your productivity suite or your support desk. You set goals, tools and limits; the platform runs it.

**Build** on a model API and an agent framework, with your own code for tools, memory and guardrails. You own everything, including the maintenance.

|  | Buy | Configure | Build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time to first use | Fastest | Fast, if the platform fits | Slowest |
| Upfront cost | Low; subscription | Low to medium; platform add-on | High; engineering time |
| Running cost | Per seat, usage or outcome | Platform pricing, often usage | Model tokens, hosting, staff |
| Fit to your process | Vendor's process | Platform's limits | Exactly yours |
| Who maintains it | Vendor | Vendor and your admin | You |
| Data and record ownership | Contract-dependent | Usually inside your platform | Yours |
| Main risk | Vendor lock-in, agent washing | Platform ceiling | Cost overrun, key-person risk |

## What the evidence says

The market has moved toward buying. Menlo Ventures, an investor in AI companies, found the purchased share of enterprise AI use cases rose from 53% to 76% between 2024 and 2025. MIT NANDA's *The GenAI Divide* reached a similar conclusion from 150 leader interviews, a survey of 350 employees and a review of 300 public deployments: partnerships and vendor tools succeeded more often than internal builds.

Buying is not safe by default. Gartner's estimate that only about 130 agentic AI vendors are real means many products sold as agents are chatbots or fixed workflows; see [What is agent washing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/). Its cancellation forecast applies to bought and built projects alike. Analyst Anushree Verma described most current projects as "early stage experiments or proofs of concept."

Building has a narrow case at this size. It is justified when the process is a genuine differentiator, when no vendor reaches the systems involved, or when regulators require control a vendor cannot document. Even then, OpenAI's guide to building agents recommends human oversight for high-risk actions and limits on retries, which a builder must engineer and maintain.

## Decision checklist

Answer each question for one specific job, not for "AI agents" in general.

| Question | If yes, lean toward |
| --- | --- |
| Does a vendor already do this exact job for firms like yours? | Buy |
| Does a platform you already pay for offer an agent that reaches the right systems? | Configure |
| Is the process how you win against competitors? | Build, or configure deeply |
| Do you have an engineer who can own it for two years, not just ship it? | Build is possible |
| Would losing the vendor lose your decision history? | Fix the contract, or do not buy |
| Can you export runs, approvals and outcomes in a usable format? | Required for any option |
| Is the job client-facing or hard to check? | Start at draft level whichever you choose |

## The **lowob** view

**lowob**'s rule is rent the wiring, own the record. In the brain loop (store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning), a bought agent supplies reasoning and usually some wiring. Those are improving fast and are cheaper to rent than to build. The record is different. It holds each decision with its reason, owner, status and expected outcome, and the learning step writes the result back. It is specific to your firm, accumulates value over years, and is what you lose if a vendor holds it.

So the buying test is less about features and more about exit. Before signing, confirm three things. You can export every run, approval and outcome. The agent's credentials are scoped to named systems. Outcomes can be written back to a record you control. The size-by-size version of this argument is in [Buy context, own judgment](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/).

Whatever the choice, set the autonomy dial separately from the purchase: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. A bought agent that can send email should still start at draft, with a person approving.

## lowob takeaways

- **There are three options, not two.** Buy a packaged agent, configure one on your platform, or build on a framework.
- **Most mid-size firms should buy or configure.** Survey evidence favours vendor and partner routes over internal builds.
- **Own the record whichever you choose.** Decisions, approvals and outcomes must be exportable and yours.
- **Autonomy is a separate decision.** Start every agent at draft level until the record shows it can go further.

## Common questions

### Should a small or mid-size company build or buy AI agents?

Usually buy or configure. Build only where the process is a true differentiator, no vendor reaches the systems involved, and an engineer can maintain it for years.

### What is the success rate of building AI in-house versus buying?

MIT NANDA reported in 2025 that vendor and partnership tools succeeded about 67% of the time, and internal builds about one-third as often. It is one study with its own definition of success.

### What should I check before buying an AI agent?

Which systems it can write to, which actions need approval, whether you can export runs and outcomes, and whether the vendor's demo shows real decision-making rather than a fixed workflow.

## Sources and notes

- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The state of generative AI in the enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-AI-in-the-enterprise/), 9 December 2025. Survey by an AI investor; 495 US respondents, self-reported.
- [Fortune via Yahoo Finance, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing](https://finance.yahoo.com/news/mit-report-95-generative-ai-105412686.html), 18 August 2025. News report of MIT NANDA research; success definitions are the authors' own.
- [Reuters via The Star, Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027, Gartner says](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says), 25 June 2025. News report of an analyst prediction, not a measured outcome.
- [OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents](https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf), 2025. Vendor guide; guardrail and human-oversight patterns for builders.
- "Rent the wiring, own the record" and the autonomy dial are **lowob**'s framework.

## Related research

- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)
- [Workflow Automation vs AI Agents: Which Do You Need?](https://lowob.com/research/workflow-automation-vs-ai-agents/)
- [Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production, by State Model and Cloud](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)
- [AI Agent vs Chatbot: The Difference That Matters to a Buyer](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agent-vs-chatbot/)

## Next move

Pick the one agent you are closest to buying and ask the vendor for a sample export of a week's runs, approvals and outcomes. If they cannot produce one, treat that as the deciding answer.

# NRR vs GRR: Which Retention Number to Report

Source: https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Net revenue retention shows what a customer cohort pays now against a year ago, including expansion. Gross revenue retention shows what was kept after churn and downgrades, before expansion, and is capped at 100%. Two firms with the same NRR can have very different businesses, so boards and investors should see both, and the gap between them.

Net revenue retention (NRR) is what a group of existing customers pays you now, divided by what the same customers paid a year ago, including expansion. Gross revenue retention (GRR) uses the same cohort but excludes expansion, so it shows only what you kept after churn and downgrades, and it cannot exceed 100%. NRR tells you whether the base grows on its own; GRR tells you how much of it leaks. Report both, because the same NRR can hide very different levels of churn.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What the two terms mean

Both are cohort measures. You fix the customers who were paying at the start date, usually 12 months ago, and follow only their recurring revenue. Revenue from customers won during the year is excluded from both. Our explainer on [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) covers NRR's definition and common errors; here the question is how the two numbers relate.

The formulas:

- **NRR** = (starting revenue + expansion - contraction - churn) ÷ starting revenue
- **GRR** = (starting revenue - contraction - churn) ÷ starting revenue
- **Expansion rate** = expansion ÷ starting revenue = NRR - GRR

Expansion covers upsells, cross-sells and price increases. Contraction covers downgrades and lost seats. Churn covers customers who left. SaaS Capital adds that churn is one minus gross retention.

| Dimension | NRR | GRR |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Includes expansion | Yes | No |
| Range | 0% to well above 100% | 0% to 100% |
| Main question | Does the base grow without new customers? | How much of the base do we keep? |
| Moved most by | Upsell, cross-sell, pricing | Product fit, service, onboarding |
| Natural owner | Account management and pricing | Customer success and delivery |
| Weakness | A few large expansions can mask broad losses | Says nothing about growth potential |

## A worked example

Two illustrative firms, each starting the year with £2,000,000 of recurring revenue from existing customers:

| Movement over 12 months | Firm A | Firm B |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting revenue | £2,000,000 | £2,000,000 |
| Expansion | +£500,000 | +£200,000 |
| Contraction | -£100,000 | -£40,000 |
| Churn | -£300,000 | -£60,000 |
| Ending revenue from the same customers | £2,100,000 | £2,100,000 |
| **NRR** | **105%** | **105%** |
| **GRR** | **80%** | **95%** |
| Expansion rate (NRR - GRR) | 25 points | 10 points |

Firm A: (2,000,000 + 500,000 - 100,000 - 300,000) ÷ 2,000,000 = 2,100,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 105%. GRR is (2,000,000 - 400,000) ÷ 2,000,000 = 80%.

Firm B: (2,000,000 + 200,000 - 40,000 - 60,000) ÷ 2,000,000 = 105%. GRR is (2,000,000 - 100,000) ÷ 2,000,000 = 95%.

The headline NRR is identical. Firm A loses a fifth of its starting revenue each year and buys it back through expansion. If expansion slows, its NRR falls quickly. Firm B keeps 95% and grows modestly on top. An acquirer, a lender or a board would value these businesses differently, and only GRR shows why.

## What the benchmarks say

Benchmarks depend on sample, contract size and definitions, so compare like with like.

- **Private SaaS overall.** The KeyBanc and Sapphire survey, published October 2024, reported net retention of about 101% and gross retention of about 90%, which it described as relatively consistent.
- **By contract size.** SaaS Capital's 2025 survey found median NRR of 102% for companies with annual contracts of $25,000 to $50,000, with a top quartile of 111% and a bottom quartile of 97%. It reports that higher NRR correlates with higher contract values, and that companies with the very highest contract values have the highest GRR.
- **Growth link.** In the same survey, companies with NRR of 110% or more grew faster than the 24% median for firms above $1 million of ARR; those below 100% grew more slowly.
- **High-growth cloud.** Bessemer's 2021 report showed average NRR of 140% at $1 million to $10 million of ARR, falling to 120% at larger scale, with gross retention at 85% to 90%. Its sample skews to fast-growing companies.

## Which number to report

| Audience or purpose | Lead with | Show beside it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Board pack | Both, side by side | Expansion rate and logo retention |
| Fundraising or debt diligence | Both, by cohort and segment | Top ten expansions and losses |
| Customer success targets | GRR | Contraction and churn reasons |
| Account management targets | NRR | Expansion by product and by price |
| Pricing decisions | NRR with price rises split out | GRR, to check rises did not drive churn |
| Firm with few, large clients | GRR by client | Concentration of revenue |

Three rules keep the numbers honest. Build the cohort from billing data, not CRM close dates. Split price increases out of expansion, because a one-off price rise may not repeat. Report the gap: if NRR minus GRR is more than about 15 points, list the accounts that produced the expansion and ask whether it will recur.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, retention is a learning signal. It tells you whether earlier commercial decisions worked: which segments were chosen, how onboarding was run, which renewals were discounted, which upsells were pushed.

The numbers alone do not say which decisions mattered. Each renewal, contraction, loss and expansion should carry a reason and an owner in the record, written back when the outcome is known. Then GRR can be explained by cause, not just reported. Firm A's problem in the example above is invisible in NRR and obvious once losses carry reasons. Our playbook on [renewals and expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) sets out how to run that calendar.

## lowob takeaways

- **Same cohort, different question.** NRR measures growth from the base; GRR measures what leaks.
- **The gap is expansion.** NRR minus GRR shows how much growth depends on upsell and price.
- **Report both together.** Identical NRR figures can describe very different businesses.
- **Give every loss a reason.** GRR becomes useful when each movement is recorded with its cause.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between NRR and GRR?

NRR includes expansion such as upsells, cross-sells and price rises, so it can exceed 100%. GRR excludes expansion and counts only revenue kept after churn and downgrades, so it cannot exceed 100%.

### How do you calculate gross revenue retention?

Take starting recurring revenue from a customer cohort, subtract revenue lost to churn and downgrades over the period, and divide by the starting revenue. Ignore expansion and new customers.

### What is a good GRR?

The 2024 KeyBanc and Sapphire survey put private SaaS gross retention at about 90%. Bessemer found 85% to 90% typical, with successful SMB-focused firms at 70% to 80%.

### Should a company report NRR or GRR to its board?

Both. NRR shows whether the base grows; GRR shows how much is lost. The gap between them shows how much growth depends on expansion.

## Sources and notes

- [SaaS Capital, SaaS Retention Benchmarks for Private B2B Companies](https://www.saas-capital.com/research/saas-retention-benchmarks-for-private-b2b-companies/), 18 September 2025. Lender's annual survey; total sample size not stated on the page.
- [Sapphire Ventures, KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures Private SaaS Company Survey](https://sapphireventures.com/press/keybanc-capital-markets-and-sapphire-ventures-private-saas-company-survey-reveals-a-continued-focus-on-operational-efficiency-and-profitability/), October 2024. Investor press release on a survey of 100+ private SaaS companies.
- [Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million](https://www.bvp.com/assets/uploads/2021/09/scaling-to-100-million-by-mary-d-onofrio.pdf), 2021. Investor research; sample skews to high-growth cloud companies.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), accessed November 2026. Investor guidance; defines churn on a monthly basis.
- The worked example is illustrative. The reporting table and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is Net Revenue Retention (NRR)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/)
- [What Is Customer Churn?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/)
- [Commercial KPIs a Board Will Trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/)

## Next move

Calculate last year's NRR and GRR from billing data for the same cohort, then subtract one from the other. If the gap is wider than 15 points, list the ten accounts that produced most of the expansion and note whether each will repeat.

# Five Invariants, From Two People to Ten Thousand

Source: https://lowob.com/research/five-invariants-from-two-people-to-ten-thousand/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Almost everything about an enterprise brain changes with size, but five things do not: decisions recorded with a reason and falsifier, sources kept, views superseded rather than overwritten, outcomes written back, and an organisation-owned record. Each has an established precedent outside AI. They cost almost nothing at two people and are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand.

Almost everything about an enterprise brain changes with size: the tools, the owners, the governance, the automation, whether it can learn. Five things do not. Decisions are recorded with a reason and a falsifier; sources are kept and summaries treated as views; views are superseded, never overwritten; outcomes are written back; and the organisation owns the record. Get those right at two people and they carry you to ten thousand. Get them wrong at ten thousand and no platform will save you.

This is the closing piece of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The series has described six rungs: a founders' document, a ledger strangers can read, a glossary, decision classes, a governed trace, a federated learning layer. Each rung is different. Underneath them is a short list of properties that are the same at every size. They are what make the record a record of judgment rather than a pile of content. The previous piece, [*Ten thousand people*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/), argued a large firm should set these centrally.

## The five invariants

**1. Decisions are recorded with a reason and a falsifier.** What was decided, why, and what would prove it wrong by when. At two people it is a line in a document. At ten thousand it is a required field in every workflow. Same idea. Our piece [*The field that makes a record a judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) explains why the falsifier is the one field that cannot be skipped.

**2. Sources are kept, and summaries are views.** The evidence behind a decision survives the summary of it, with a timestamp and an origin. A generated summary is a lossy compression made by one model on one day, as [*Keep the sources; let the summary regenerate*](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/) argues.

**3. Views are superseded, never overwritten.** When the organisation changes its mind, the old view remains, linked to the new one with a reason and a date.

**4. Outcomes are written back.** Someone checks the falsifier on its date and records what actually happened. Without this, nothing learns, at any size. Our explainer [*What is outcome write-back?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers the mechanics.

**5. The organisation owns the record.** It can be exported, with history, and survives the replacement of any tool, vendor or person, including the people who built it.

> The invariants cost almost nothing at two people. They are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand.

## Why these five, and the precedents behind them

None of the five is new. Each is a discipline another field adopted the hard way.

Software teams adopted decision records with reasons. Michael Nygard's 2011 format for architecture decision records asks for context, decision, status and consequences, "not just the positive ones". It also keeps reversed decisions, marked as superseded, because a newcomer who finds an unexplained decision can only blindly accept or blindly change it.

Finance adopted superseding for figures. Martin Fowler's 2021 account of bitemporal history separates actual history from record history: what was true, and what the organisation knew when. His payroll example, a backdated raise confirmed after the payroll had run, shows why overwriting the old value destroys the ability to explain past actions.

Forecasting adopted outcome write-back. The Good Judgment Project's results, summarised by Mellers, Tetlock and colleagues, depend on recorded probabilities scored against what happened: teams beat individuals, and the best aggregation beat the simple mean by as much as 60%. None of that is measurable without the outcome.

Law has started to require ownership. The EU Data Act, applicable since 12 September 2025, gives customers of data processing services the right to switch providers, with a transition period of at most 30 days after notice and, from 12 January 2027, no switching charges at all. The right is only as useful as the record's format: data held in a tool's private structure, without history, ports badly.

| Invariant | Precedent outside AI | What it prevents |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reason and falsifier | Architecture decision records | Blind acceptance or blind reversal of past decisions |
| Sources kept, summaries as views | Audit evidence behind financial statements | A summary becoming the only surviving copy |
| Superseded, never overwritten | Bitemporal history in finance and payroll | Losing what the organisation believed and when |
| Outcomes written back | Scored forecasting | Claims of learning with nothing to learn from |
| Organisation owns the record | Data portability and switching rights | Losing the record with the vendor |

## What scales on top

Volume, which makes learning possible. Automation, which makes capture cheap. Governance, which makes the record defensible. Federation, which lets many records coexist. Each matters more as the organisation grows. None of them substitutes for the invariants, and all of them amplify whatever the invariants are, good or bad.

| Rung | What scales on top | What the invariants look like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two people | A weekly habit | A line per decision in one shared document |
| Ten people | An assistant over the record | Entries strangers can read, superseded not edited |
| Fifty people | A glossary and decision rights | Definitions with effective dates and owners |
| Two hundred people | Decision classes and precedent | Required fields, first calibration |
| One thousand people | Trace and evidenced review | Every AI-assisted decision reconstructable |
| Ten thousand people | Federation and a learning layer | Central invariants, one export format |

## One question per rung

If you remember nothing else from this series, ask the question for your size.

**Two:** would we both describe last month's big decision the same way?

**Ten:** can a new hire find out why we do this without asking a founder?

**Fifty:** do our teams mean the same thing by our ten most important words?

**Two hundred:** does a new manager see the three closest prior decisions before making one?

**One thousand:** could we reconstruct an AI-assisted decision from three months ago, end to end?

**Ten thousand:** do we know, by decision class, whether our judgment is getting better?

## Back to the thesis

This series began with a claim: the enterprise brain that compounds is not the one that remembers most, but the one that can show what it decided, why, what would have proved it wrong, and when it changed its mind. The five invariants are that claim, made operational. They cost almost nothing at two people. They are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand, because the history they protect cannot be recreated once it is lost. That asymmetry is the best argument there is for starting small, and starting now. [*Whoever holds the record holds the company*](https://lowob.com/research/whoever-holds-the-record-holds-the-company/) makes the commercial case for owning it.

**In practice:** score your organisation against the five invariants today: present, partial or absent. Fix the first absent one before buying or building anything else. Ask your rung's question at the next leadership meeting, and write down the answer.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations that lack one or more invariants at small scale and add them later at large scale, at low cost and without losing the history they skipped.

## lowob takeaways

- **Record the reason and the falsifier.** What was decided, why, and what would prove it wrong by when.
- **Keep the sources.** Summaries are views that can be regenerated; evidence cannot.
- **Supersede, never overwrite.** Link the old view to the new one with a reason and a date.
- **Write outcomes back.** Check every falsifier on its date and record what happened.
- **Own the record.** Exportable with history, and independent of any tool, vendor or person.

## Common questions

### What are the core principles of a company decision record?

Decisions are recorded with a reason and a falsifier, sources are kept, views are superseded rather than overwritten, outcomes are written back, and the organisation owns the record in an exportable form.

### When should a company start keeping a decision log?

Now, and small. The five invariants cost almost nothing at two people and are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand, because skipped history cannot be recovered.

### Can automation or governance make up for a weak decision record?

No. Volume, automation, governance and federation matter more as an organisation grows, but none substitutes for the invariants and all amplify whatever the invariants are, good or bad.

### What does supersede, never overwrite mean?

When a decision or definition changes, the old version stays in the record, marked as superseded and linked to its replacement with a reason and a date, so past actions can still be explained.

- [Mellers, Tetlock, Baker, Friedman and Zeckhauser, Improving the accuracy of geopolitical risk assessments](https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/improving_the_accuracy_of_geopolitical_risk_assessments.pdf), University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019. Book chapter on forecasting tournaments, not business decisions.

# The 5 Enterprise Context Platforms, Ranked for Regulated Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-5-enterprise-context-platforms-ranked-for-regulated-firms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Every vendor now calls this layer an enterprise brain; what they sell is a context layer that connects documents, data and permissions to agents. For a regulated firm the deciding questions are whether permissions follow the user, whether you can reconstruct what an agent saw and did, and whether you can leave. Glean ranks first, then Microsoft Work IQ, Google Gemini Enterprise, Writer and Dust.

Every vendor now calls this layer an "enterprise brain". What they actually sell is memory, meaning and governance: a context layer that connects a firm's documents, data and permissions to its AI agents. For a regulated firm the deciding questions are whether permissions follow the user, whether you can reconstruct what an agent saw and did, and whether you can leave with your context intact. Glean ranks first on evidence of real use across vendors, followed by Microsoft Work IQ, Google Gemini Enterprise, Writer's Enterprise Brain and Dust.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Our explainer on [what an enterprise brain is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/) sets out **lowob**'s view: the brain is a loop, not a product, and no single tool is the brain. The context layer is the wiring in that loop. **lowob**'s advice is to rent the wiring and own the record, which makes exit, not features, the first test of any vendor here. Our flagship piece [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/) makes the full argument.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Governance and permissions | 30% | Over-permissioning, not the model, is the largest real exposure in deployed copilots. |
| Evidence of real use | 25% | Weekly use and revenue, not seats sold or agents registered. |
| Auditability | 25% | Supervisors now expect the full chain of automated activity to be reconstructable. |
| Portability | 20% | Whether your context and decision history survive a change of vendor. |

The permissions criterion carries the most weight because of how these products work. Microsoft's own documentation states that Copilot "only surfaces organizational data to which individual users have at least view permissions", and tells customers to use the permission models in services such as SharePoint to make sure the right people have the right access. That is the correct design, and it means the agent is exactly as safe as the permissions underneath it. A folder shared too widely five years ago becomes an answer today. Our explainer on [permission-aware retrieval](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/) covers what to check.

## The list

**1. Glean**

**Best for:** firms running more than one productivity suite, or that want a context layer independent of their suite vendor.

**Why it ranks first:** the strongest evidence of real use among independents. Glean announced $300 million in annual recurring revenue on 28 May 2026, 15 months after reaching $100 million. It says more than 85% of customers use it across five or more departments and that it holds a 45% ratio of weekly daily active to weekly monthly active users. Its site lists more than 275 connectors, and its platform now centres on a model hub and an MCP gateway, so it sits across vendors rather than inside one. Its developer documentation is specific on permissions: a document "is only returned to a user who is allowed to see it", checked at query time against allowed users and groups that should mirror the source system.

**Watch out for:** its claim that its context beats raw MCP tool access comes from its own benchmark, in which Glean says it was preferred about 2.5 times as often as off-the-shelf MCP tools, which used about 30% more tokens. A reported $7.2 billion valuation was not confirmed from a primary source.

**Pricing:** through sales; no public list price.

**What would change its rank:** the suite vendors' native layers matching it on cross-system coverage at no extra cost.

**2. Microsoft Work IQ (with Agent 365)**

**Best for:** firms standardised on Microsoft 365.

**Why it ranks here:** Microsoft announced the Work IQ API on 2 June 2026 with general availability on 16 June. It ships a REST API, A2A for agent-to-agent work and a redesigned remote MCP server that consolidates hundreds of operations into ten generic tools. Microsoft says "every request runs in the context of a specific user", with a policy engine enforcing finer rules on each request. API access does not require a Copilot licence; custom and third-party agents are billed on consumption. Agent 365 is the most developed agent registry on the market.

**Watch out for:** usage depth and inherited permissions. Microsoft has said there are 40 million agents deployed in its ecosystem, against about 30 million Copilot seats sold, according to an August 2026 report; neither figure measures weekly use, and the agent count was not defined. Because Work IQ runs as the user, it inherits every over-shared SharePoint permission that user holds. Audit the permissions before you connect agents, not after.

**Pricing:** consumption-based for custom and third-party agents; Microsoft says "Work IQ cost is variable based on what you are using".

**What would change its rank:** independent evidence of weekly use rising.

**3. Google Gemini Enterprise (the October 2026 Gemini agent)**

**Best for:** firms on Google Workspace, or those wanting the most complete memory design.

**Why it ranks here:** the 8 October launch maps most closely to how memory research describes the problem. The Gemini agent uses four memory types: session, semantic, procedural and episodic. A Knowledge Catalog maps business terms to metrics from connected data, so every agent uses "net margin" the same way. An Agent Gateway acts as what Google calls "an AI network firewall", and persistent coworker agents get their own Workspace identity, email, calendar and storage, so their actions are not logged as a human user's. Google says nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 use Gemini Enterprise.

**Watch out for:** it is weeks old. Futurum's analyst noted that "Google gave few general availability dates", and no independent production evaluation exists yet. The Fortune 100 figure is Google's own.

**Pricing:** not disclosed for most announcements. Google said it does not plan a per-seat licence for coworker agents in Workspace.

**What would change its rank:** published pricing and the first independent production reviews.

**4. Writer (Enterprise Brain)**

**Best for:** marketing, brand and content-heavy teams that want governed AI from a single vendor.

**Why it ranks here:** the first mainstream product sold under the "Enterprise Brain" name, unveiled on 9 September 2026 as "a governed, universal context layer" capturing brand knowledge, decision logic and live business data across teams and agents. A team-level Agent Memory layer, which captures decisions and preferences across sessions, launched alongside it and is generally available.

**Watch out for:** maturity. Enterprise Brain itself is in early access for selected customers, and we found no recent independent revenue or usage figure.

**Pricing:** not published.

**What would change its rank:** customer evidence outside content and marketing workflows.

**5. Dust**

**Best for:** mid-sized firms wanting shared, multiplayer agents quickly.

**Why it ranks here:** Dust has built its position on shared agents that teams create and use together, and reports high engagement among mid-sized customers. It suits firms that want agents in use within weeks rather than a platform programme.

**Watch out for:** fewer of the governance and audit features a large regulated firm will need. Dust's usage and funding figures are self-reported, and we could not re-verify them this month, so treat this placement as provisional.

**Pricing:** check directly; we could not open its pricing page this month.

**What would change its rank:** a large regulated reference customer, or verified usage figures.

## Side by side

|  | Glean | Microsoft Work IQ | Google Gemini Enterprise | Writer | Dust |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Position | Independent, cross-suite | Inside Microsoft 365 | Inside Google Workspace and Cloud | Single-vendor governed AI | Mid-market shared agents |
| Permissions | Checked at query time against source ACLs | Every request runs as a named user | Agent Gateway; coworker agents with own identity | Governed layer, details not public | Not verified this month |
| Agent protocols | MCP gateway | MCP and A2A | Gateway for agents | Not verified | Not verified |
| Evidence of use | $300m ARR; 45% weekly active ratio | 40m agents deployed, undefined | "Nearly 90%" of Fortune 100, Google's figure | Early access | Self-reported |
| Availability | Generally available | Generally available since 16 June 2026 | Few dates given | Early access; Agent Memory GA | Generally available |
| Public pricing, November 2026 | No | Consumption, variable | Not disclosed | No | Not verified |

> An agent that runs as the user is exactly as safe as the permissions that user already has. Most firms have never audited them.

## Left out, and why

**Palantir.** Its ontology is the oldest working version of this layer, but it is a platform-plus-engineers engagement, not a product you choose from a list.

**Amazon Quick.** AWS's current product in this layer, which enforces document-level access controls in real time, according to an October 2026 AWS post. We did not find enough evidence of use to rank it.

**Memory-only vendors.** They store what an agent learns; they do not govern access to a firm's documents. See our list of [the five agent memory layers worth testing](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-agent-memory-layers-worth-testing-and-how-to-test-them/).

## Three questions to ask any vendor

1. **Show us an agent's full trace for one task:** what it retrieved, under whose permissions, and what a human changed. Our explainer on [AI audit trails](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) lists the fields that trace should hold, and our piece on [what regulators want](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) explains why the chain matters more than the model.
2. **Export our definitions, decisions and history in a documented format**, and show it reading back without your product.
3. **What share of your customers' users were active last week?** Seats sold and agents registered are not the same number.

## lowob takeaways

- **Glean ranks first on evidence of use.** $300 million in recurring revenue and a cross-vendor position, with permissions checked at query time.
- **Work IQ is permission-aware by design.** That makes your existing SharePoint permissions the real control.
- **Google has the best design and the least evidence.** Four memory types and a policy gateway, few dates and no pricing.
- **Rent the wiring, own the record.** Test the export before the demo.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for an enterprise context platform

- Permissions are checked per request, as the user, against the source system
- Over-shared folders are found and fixed before agents are connected
- One agent task can be traced end to end: retrieval, permissions, human edits
- Definitions, decisions and history export in a documented format and read back elsewhere
- The vendor states last week's active-user share, not seats sold
- Pricing is modelled at ten times today's agent volume

## Common questions

### What is the best enterprise context platform for a regulated firm?

This list ranks Glean first for evidence of real use across vendors, followed by Microsoft Work IQ with Agent 365, Google Gemini Enterprise, Writer's Enterprise Brain and Dust. Firms standardised on one suite should test that suite's native layer first.

### What should regulated firms look for in an enterprise AI context layer?

Whether permissions follow the user on every request, whether you can reconstruct what an agent retrieved and did, and whether you can leave with your definitions, decisions and history in a documented format.

### Does Microsoft Copilot respect SharePoint permissions?

Yes. Microsoft states that Copilot only surfaces data a user has at least view permission to. That means any content shared too widely in SharePoint is available to that user's Copilot and agents, so permissions need auditing first.

### Why was Palantir left off the enterprise context platform list?

Its ontology is the oldest working version of this layer, but it is a platform-plus-engineers engagement, not a product you choose from a list.

# The Build Order for Industrial Distribution

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-industrial-distribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: In industrial distribution the commercial line is quoting, the store is the ERP and the context layer is the price book and the specification library. Quotes are graded in days, so the record pays back faster than in any other sector. The walls are competitors' non-public prices, supplier cost and rebate terms in customer-facing drafts, and export-controlled technical data.

In industrial distribution the commercial line is quoting. Inside sales teams decide all day which requests to quote, what discount to give against the price book and what lead time to promise, and each quote is won or lost within days. That makes distribution the fastest-learning sector in this series. The store is the ERP rather than a CRM, and the context layer is mostly the price book and the specification library. The walls are specific: competitors' non-public prices must never feed the quoting logic, supplier cost and rebate terms must never surface in a customer-facing draft, and export-controlled technical data must stay behind its own access controls.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Distribution rarely appears in discussions of enterprise brains. It should. Few businesses make as many similar commercial decisions as a distributor, and few see the outcome as quickly. A request for quote arrives, someone prices it against the book, applies a discount, promises a lead time, and within days the customer orders or does not. That loop is what the rest of this series spends its time trying to create.

Part 10 followed a composite parts distributor through the build. This edition generalises it for distributors of 50 to 500 people selling electrical, mechanical, MRO, fluid power or building products, and runs the full sequence (Gateway 0, tooling, context, record, reasoning and Gateways 1 to 3) with the evidence that applies to the sector.

## Where the commercial line sits

A distributor's commercial line is not a pipeline in the CRM sense. It is the quote desk. Field sales staff open accounts and hold relationships, but most commercial decisions are made by inside sales: whether to quote, at what price, with what substitution if the specified item is unavailable, and with what delivery promise.

The economics make those decisions unusually valuable. McKinsey's July 2026 analysis of pricing in distribution, based on the 10-K filings of 140 public distributors, found that a 1% price increase can lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%. The same piece reports that in one distributor, sales teams overrode system prices in more than half of transactions, and it sets out good practice as 80% to 90% of transactional prices generated automatically, with people concentrating on the exceptions. The exceptions are the decisions worth recording.

Buyers are moving too. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 B2B buyers found 61% prefer a buying experience without a sales rep. In distribution that preference is served by e-commerce for catalogue items. It leaves the quote desk with the work that cannot be self-served: large orders, project pricing, substitutions and specified items. Those are exactly the decisions where a record of reasons pays back.

| Industry lens | Industrial distribution |
| --- | --- |
| Where the commercial line sits | Quoting: which requests to quote, discount against the price book, lead time promised |
| The store | The ERP's customer, item and order tables; often a light CRM for field sales |
| What joins the context layer | Price book and customer tiers, specification sheets, stock and lead times, quote history |
| Outcome lag | Days for most quotes; a project cycle for large bids |
| Who defends the decision | Sales director on margin, branch or regional managers |
| The sector's walls | Competitors' non-public prices; supplier cost and rebate terms; export-controlled technical data |
| Regulatory pressure | Competition law on pricing information; export controls on technical data |

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in distribution | The main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | An owner with authority over pricing, the suite of record, and the ERP named as the commercial store | Treating the build as an IT project when it is a pricing project |
| Tooling | Assistant seats for inside sales and pricing analysts | A chat assistant with no access to the price book or stock |
| Context | Price book, customer tiers, stock and lead times, specification library, quote history | Product codes and "in stock" defined differently by each branch |
| Record | Every quote with the discount reason, the approver and the outcome | Free-text reasons nobody can analyse |
| Reasoning | A first agent that drafts quotes from the request, the book and the customer's history into a queue | Drafts that quote a price or lead time nobody checked |
| Gateway 1 | A person approves every quote before it reaches a customer | Approval by habit at the end of a busy day |
| Gateway 2 | Margin at stake on every quote, outcome written back within days | Numbers that contradict what the sales team believes |
| Gateway 3 | The record extends to purchasing, inventory and finance | Purchasing decisions made on quote data without the reasons |

**Gateway 0 is a pricing decision.** In most sectors the owner sits in operations or revenue. In distribution the owner needs authority over the price book, because within a quarter the record will raise questions only a pricing owner can answer. Part 3 sets out the three decisions; the third, the CRM, usually becomes "the ERP, plus whatever field sales actually update".

**Context is mostly definitions.** The context layer in distribution is less about connecting email and more about agreeing what words mean. A product code that maps to three supplier part numbers, a customer tier that differs by branch, and "in stock" meaning on the shelf in one warehouse and on order in another will all make a quoting agent wrong in ways that look right. McKinsey's distribution research describes a building materials distributor that used generative AI to clean and enrich more than a million catalogue items, processing them six times faster, with manual price overrides falling 80% and margins rising more than 200 basis points. That is consultancy-reported and a single case, but it shows where the work sits: the data before the agent.

> Distribution learns fastest because a quote is graded within days. The first numbers the record produces are usually the uncomfortable ones.

## The walls: what never feeds the quote

Distribution has three walls rather than one.

**Competitors' non-public prices.** The US Department of Justice announced a proposed settlement with RealPage on 25 November 2025 over algorithmic pricing in rental housing. Under its terms, as summarised by Paul, Weiss, RealPage may not use one user's non-public, competitively sensitive information as an input when generating pricing recommendations for another. Such data may train pricing models only once it is at least 12 months old, and price data and localised data are largely barred from training even then. An "auto accept" feature must be switched on manually by the user rather than by default. The case is about rental housing, but its logic travels. A distributor should not connect non-public competitor pricing to its quoting logic, and should ask any pricing software vendor whether its models pool non-public data across competing distributors.

**Supplier cost and rebate terms.** A quoting agent needs cost to check margin. It must never let cost, rebate levels or supplier programme terms appear in a customer-facing draft. Many supplier agreements treat those terms as confidential. The rule is that cost informs the margin check inside the queue, and the draft the customer sees contains price, lead time and specification only.

**Export-controlled technical data.** Specification libraries often hold drawings and data sheets. Most are public. Some are not. The US Bureau of Industry and Security defines a deemed export as the release of controlled technology or source code to a foreign person in the United States. A context layer that lets any employee retrieve any document through an assistant can turn a controlled drawing into a release. Controlled items need their own classification and access control, and they should stay out of the general context layer until both exist.

| What the quoting agent can see | What it must never see or show |
| --- | --- |
| Price book, customer tier, quote history for that customer | Competitors' non-public prices, or vendor models trained on pooled competitor data |
| Cost, to check margin inside the review queue | Cost, rebates or supplier terms in any customer-facing draft |
| Public specification sheets and substitution tables | Export-controlled drawings and technical data without classification and access control |
| Stock and lead times by warehouse | Another customer's pricing or project details |

## The record and the first agent

The record in distribution is the quote itself with two fields added: the reason for any discount beyond the standard tier, and the outcome. Part 9 describes the decisions worth recording; the quote is close to the ideal case. Reasons should be a short pick list (competitive situation, project pricing, volume commitment, retention risk, error correction) with free text only as a supplement, because a reason nobody can count is a reason nobody can learn from. *What is a closed-lost reason?* covers the same discipline for pipelines.

The first agent drafts quotes. It reads the request, matches items against the specification library, prices them from the book and the customer's tier, checks stock and lead time, and places the draft in a queue with any discount flagged for a reason. A person checks and sends. McKinsey's distribution blog describes a water technologies company whose generative AI assistant for requests for quote produced $1.8m in quotes for 45,000 customers within four weeks of deployment. That is a consultancy case study rather than a measured comparison, but it shows the shape of a first agent that works: narrow, measurable and attached to an existing process. Part 7 explains why the first agent should be this boring.

The store will need work before the agent can rely on it. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers, as reported by MarTech, found 62% said poor CRM data had probably or definitely cost their organisation revenue. In distribution the same problem appears in the ERP's item master, and it costs margin rather than pipeline.

Composite example: a fluid power distributor records discount reasons

Decision
:   Require a reason from a five-item pick list for every discount beyond the standard tier, and record the outcome of every quote within ten working days.

Reason and owner
:   The sales director could not say which discounts were winning business. Owned by the sales director, with the pricing analyst maintaining the pick list.

What changed
:   After two quarters the record showed that "competitive situation" discounts in two product families won no more often than standard-priced quotes. Discretion in those families was reviewed; the rule is revisited each quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a distributor of around 180 people across six branches, built from patterns across engagements.

## The gateways in distribution

**Gateway 1: nothing sends without a person.** A quote is a commercial commitment: a price and a lead time a customer can hold the distributor to. Every quote the agent drafts goes to a named person before it leaves. The risk is volume. Inside sales staff clearing a queue at the end of a day approve by habit, and *Approval rate measures fatigue too* describes the signs. Sampling approved quotes each week for a second check is a cheap control.

**Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision.** Distribution reaches this gateway faster than any other sector because the outcome arrives in days and margin is already calculated on every line. The difficulty is not measurement. It is that the numbers can contradict what the team believes, as the composite above shows. That is the brain doing its job. It is also the point at which the build becomes a pricing conversation, which is why Gateway 0 named a pricing owner.

**Gateway 3: commercial is ready to share its brain.** Purchasing and inventory want to know which items were quoted and lost on availability; finance wants margin by reason. Both are legitimate. The record should travel with its reasons attached, so purchasing does not overstock an item that was lost on price, not stock.

## lowob takeaways

- **Quoting is the commercial line.** It is where decisions are most frequent, most similar and graded fastest.
- **Agree definitions before the agent.** Product codes, customer tiers and "in stock" decide whether a draft quote is right.
- **Hold three walls.** No non-public competitor prices, no cost or rebate terms in customer drafts, no export-controlled data without access control.
- **Expect uncomfortable numbers.** Fast outcomes mean the record challenges pricing habits within a quarter or two.

Gateway card

### Before a distributor switches on a quoting agent

- A named owner with authority over the price book
- Product codes, customer tiers and stock status defined once across branches
- A five- to seven-item pick list for discount reasons, required on every exception
- Written confirmation that no non-public competitor pricing feeds the quoting logic or the vendor's models
- Export-controlled technical data classified and excluded from the general context layer
- A named approver for every drafted quote

## Common questions

### How are distributors using AI for quoting?

The most dependable pattern is an agent that drafts quotes from the request, the price book, the customer's tier and history, and current stock, then places them in a queue for a person to check and send. Discounts beyond the standard tier carry a recorded reason.

### Is AI pricing software legal for distributors?

Pricing software is lawful in general, but competition authorities are scrutinising tools that use competitors' non-public data. The DOJ's November 2025 settlement with RealPage bars using one user's non-public data to price for another and limits training to data at least 12 months old.

### What data should an industrial distributor clean before using AI?

The item master, customer tiers, price book and stock status, with product codes and "in stock" defined once across branches. A quoting agent working from inconsistent definitions produces drafts that look right and are wrong.

### Do export controls apply to AI assistants that read specification sheets?

They can. The US Bureau of Industry and Security treats the release of controlled technology to a foreign person in the US as a deemed export, so controlled drawings and data need classification and access control before any assistant can retrieve them.

## Sources and notes
