# The Handover From Sales to Delivery

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Forrester found that 81% of B2B buyers are dissatisfied with the provider they chose, and win-loss interviews suggest some won customers are already at risk on signature. Much of that risk is created at the handover, when the deal team's knowledge of promises, stakeholders and concessions fails to reach delivery. This piece sets out a handover pack, a timing rule and a measure that tells you whether it is working.

The handover from sales to delivery is the point where a won deal becomes work, and where most of what the deal team learned is lost. A good handover passes on more than the contract: the promises made, the buying group and its politics, the concessions and why they were granted, the risks raised, and what success means to the buyer. Forrester's 2024 research found 81% of B2B buyers dissatisfied with the provider they chose. The handover cannot fix a bad sale, but it is the cheapest place to stop a good sale turning into a disappointed customer.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

In most firms of 20 to 500 people, the person who wins the work is not the person who does it. That is true in software, where an account executive hands to an onboarding team, and in services, where a partner who sold the engagement passes it to a project lead. Even where the seller stays involved, a new group of people starts making decisions about the client.

The handover is the moment knowledge has to cross that line. In [*Handovers are where reasoning pours out*](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) we argued that the facts usually survive a handover while the reasons behind them do not. The commercial version of that problem is sharp, because the reasons often carry money: a discount granted against a promise, a timeline agreed to beat a rival, a scope line dropped to get under a budget.

## What goes wrong, and how often

The evidence on what buyers experience after signing is thin but consistent.

Forrester's *State of Business Buying, 2024* found that 81% of buyers were dissatisfied with the provider they chose at the end of the purchase process, and that 86% of purchases stalled at some point. It put the average buying group at 13 people, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Delivery teams inherit all of those people, most of whom they have never met. Forrester's analyst Barbara Winters, writing on the same research, added that the dissatisfaction ran to 91% among Gen Z and Millennial buyers, and that buyers were not satisfied with the technology, domain and industry expertise providers demonstrated. Expertise is exactly what a delivery team shows first, and it shows less of it when it starts without the deal team's context.

A Showpad interview with Clozd's co-founder, published in August 2026, reported that about 10% of closed-won customers were already at risk when interviewed after the decision, often because of implementation problems or doubts about the solution. It is a vendor figure without a published sample, so we treat it as indicative. It describes a customer who signed while unconvinced, and a delivery team that may not know.

Gartner's 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found that buyers with high decision confidence were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal. Decision confidence is built during the sale and either reinforced or eroded in the first weeks of delivery. The handover decides which.

| Failure at handover | What delivery experiences | Typical cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Promise not passed on | Client cites a commitment nobody in delivery recognises | Unplanned scope, or a credibility loss in week one |
| Concession without its reason | Delivery treats a discounted line as standard | Margin given away twice |
| Stakeholder map missing | The sceptic in the buying group is not engaged | Late objections, slower sign-off |
| Success criteria vague | Delivery measures outputs; client expected outcomes | Dispute at the first review |
| Known risk not flagged | Risk surfaces as a surprise | Rework, escalation, early churn |

## The cost shows up in delivery and renewal

For services firms the cost of a weak handover appears first in utilisation. SPI Research's 2026 benchmark, published with Deltek, put average billable utilisation at 66.4%, the lowest in nearly two decades, against 75% for high performers. SPI's report page adds that top firms achieved 82% on-time delivery in the prior year, which sets a delivery standard a handover either supports or undermines. Not all of the utilisation gap is handovers. But hours spent rediscovering what the client was promised are hours nobody can bill, and they cluster at the start of an engagement.

For recurring-revenue firms the cost appears at renewal. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks put median net revenue retention at 102% for companies with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000. A customer whose first 90 days were a series of surprises is less likely to be one who expands. Part 24 of this series covered renewals and expansion; the handover is where the renewal conversation starts.

The Bridge Group's 2026 study adds a structural point. It found 38% of account executives now own renewal and expansion, nearly double the 2024 share. Where the seller will come back to the account, a poor handover is a cost the seller pays later.

> The facts survive the handover. The reasons do not, and in commercial work the reasons carry the money.

## What a handover pack should hold

A handover pack is short. Its value comes from containing the things that are in nobody's system yet. Most of them are reasons.

| Section | What it records | Who writes it | Why delivery needs it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What we sold | Scope, exclusions, and the reason for each exclusion | Deal lead | Prevents excluded work drifting back in |
| What we promised | Every commitment made in meetings or emails, verbatim where possible | Deal lead | These are the client's expectations, whatever the contract says |
| What success means | The buyer's own measure, in their words | Deal lead, confirmed with the buyer | Lets delivery report against the right outcome |
| The buying group | Who decided, who influenced, who was sceptical and why | Deal lead | Delivery needs to win the sceptic, not only the sponsor |
| Concessions | Every discount or term beyond standard, with the reason and the approver | Deal desk or revenue lead | Stops delivery treating a concession as a precedent |
| Risks | Known doubts, competing priorities, dependencies on the client | Deal lead and delivery lead together | Turns surprises into managed risks |
| Open questions | What nobody knows yet | Both | Gives the kickoff an agenda |

Two of these sections connect to other parts of the commercial system. Concessions come from discount governance: if each exception was recorded with its reason and approver, the handover can link to that record rather than reconstruct it. Promises and success criteria come from the proposal, which is one reason Part 22 treated proposal standards as part of the commercial system: a proposal that states outcomes in the buyer's own words gives the handover something to copy rather than reconstruct.

[*The context layer, followed through one account*](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/) showed how an account's history ends up scattered across inboxes, recordings, proposal versions and memory. The handover pack is the commercial team's deliberate answer: one document, written once, that delivery can trust.

## Timing: before signature, not after

Most handovers happen after the contract is signed. By then the deal team's attention has moved to the next opportunity, and the incentive to write anything down has passed.

Three timing rules work better.

**Introduce delivery before the final proposal.** On deals above a set value, a delivery lead should meet the buyer before the proposal is final. That tests whether what is being sold can be delivered, and it lets the buyer meet the person they will work with. It also addresses the implementation doubts that win-loss interviews find late in the cycle.

**Write the pack before signature.** Make a draft handover pack a condition of moving a deal to its final stage. The seller still has the context and still has a reason to cooperate.

**Hold a joint kickoff.** The first client meeting after signature should include the deal lead, the delivery lead and the buyer's sponsor. The deal lead's job in that meeting is to restate the promises and the success measure in front of everyone.

| Deal size | Delivery involvement before signature | Pack | Kickoff |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small, standard scope | None | Template, completed by the seller | Delivery-led |
| Mid-size or custom scope | Review of the draft proposal | Full pack, reviewed by delivery | Joint |
| Large or strategic | Meeting with the buyer before the final proposal | Full pack, signed off by both leads | Joint, with the buyer's sponsor |

## Measuring whether the handover works

A completed form is not a measure. The measure is what delivery finds that the pack did not tell it.

Ask the delivery lead to log every material surprise in the first 30 days: a promise not in the pack, a stakeholder not mapped, a risk not flagged, a concession not explained. Count them per engagement and review the count monthly with the revenue lead. A falling count means the pack is working. A count that stays high in one segment or for one seller is a coaching conversation.

Keep the definition of a material surprise narrow: something that changed scope, cost, timeline or a key relationship, and that someone on the deal team knew before signature. Minor gaps in detail do not count. A narrow definition keeps the log honest and stops it turning into a complaints list about sales.

Two lagging measures confirm the trend: time to first value, defined as the buyer defines it in the pack, and early churn or early escalation. Both arrive later and are noisier, which is why the surprise count is the one to watch weekly.

The surprise log is also a decision record. Each recurring surprise is a reason to change the pack, the proposal standard or the qualification questions, and the change should be recorded with an owner and a check date, as in [*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/).

Illustrative example: the concession that crossed the line

Decision
:   Add a concessions section to the handover pack, linked to the discount approval record, and make it a condition of the final deal stage.

Reason and owner
:   Delivery logged the same surprise on three engagements in a quarter: a reduced day rate agreed in exchange for a case study, which delivery did not know to request. Owned by the revenue lead, agreed with the head of delivery.

What changed
:   Concessions now arrive with their reason and their condition. Surprises per engagement are reviewed monthly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consulting firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pass on reasons, not only facts.** Why a discount, exclusion or timeline was agreed matters more than the fact that it was.
- **Write the pack before signature.** After signature, the context and the incentive both leave.
- **Introduce delivery early on large deals.** It tests deliverability and builds the buyer's confidence.
- **Count surprises.** Material surprises in the first 30 days are the honest measure of a handover.

Gateway card

### Before the next deal crosses to delivery

- A one-page handover pack template with the seven sections above
- A draft pack required before the final deal stage
- Concessions linked to their approval record, with the reason
- The buyer's success measure written in their words
- A joint kickoff for mid-size and larger deals
- A 30-day surprise log reviewed monthly by revenue and delivery leads

## Common questions

### What should be included in a sales-to-delivery handover?

The scope and its exclusions, every promise made, the buyer's own success measure, the buying group and its sceptics, any concessions with their reasons, known risks and open questions.

### When should the sales handover to delivery happen?

Before signature for anything beyond a standard deal. Delivery should review the draft proposal on mid-size deals and meet the buyer before the final proposal on large ones, with the handover pack written while the seller still holds the context.

### How do you measure handover quality?

Count the material surprises delivery logs in the first 30 days: promises, stakeholders, risks or concessions that the handover did not mention. Time to first value and early escalation confirm the trend later.

### Why do customers become dissatisfied after buying?

Forrester's 2024 research found 81% of B2B buyers dissatisfied with the provider they chose. A common cause is a gap between what the buyer understood they were promised and what delivery was told.

# Top 5 AI Governance and Audit-Trail Tools

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI governance platforms became a real category in 2026, when Gartner published its first Magic Quadrant for them in June. For banks and insurers, the platforms differ most on whether they map explicitly to model-risk guidance; most map to the EU AI Act and NIST and leave bank supervision implicit. This ranking verifies each vendor's analyst standing, features and prices as listed in November 2026.

AI governance platforms became a real category in 2026: Gartner published its first Magic Quadrant for them on 16 June, assessing 13 vendors. For banks and insurers they differ most on one point. Some map explicitly to model-risk guidance such as SR 26-2; most map to the EU AI Act and the NIST framework and leave bank supervision implicit. We rank IBM watsonx.governance first, ServiceNow AI Control Tower second, then Credo AI, ValidMind and ModelOp.

This list is for heads of AI risk, model risk and compliance at banks and insurers who need an inventory of every AI system, a risk process around it, and evidence an examiner will accept. **Skip it if** you need runtime tracing of agent behaviour; that is covered in [Top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/).

## Why the category matters to banks now

Three supervisory developments in 2026 turned governance tooling from a nice-to-have into evidence.

First, US bank model-risk guidance narrowed. SR 26-2, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC, replaced SR 11-7 and states in footnote 3 that generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance." Banks must still govern those tools, through their broader risk management, and the agencies have said they plan a request for information on AI use. A platform that only implements the old model-risk workflow will cover traditional models and leave the newest, fastest-growing AI estate on spreadsheets. Our explainer [What is model risk management for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) sets out what changed.

Second, the FCA described what good looks like. Its 19 October 2026 review of AI in financial services names as good practice firms that "registered agents in a central inventory", kept "clear records of third-party arrangements and AI use case inventories", and held "auditable records of decisions, including rationale, challenge, and escalation." It also states that "firms can outsource AI services, but remain responsible for them." Those are inventory, vendor and evidence requirements in all but name.

Third, the EU AI Act fixed the logging duty for high-risk systems, including credit scoring of individuals, from 2 December 2027. Our guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) maps those duties regime by regime.

A governance platform holds the inventory, the risk assessment, the approvals and the evidence pack. It does not, on its own, hold the decision-level trace of what an agent did on a given day. That is why this list and the observability list are separate, and why the best stack usually needs both.

> A governance tool nobody opens is a filing cabinet. A governance tool that cannot see your vendor's agents is a filing cabinet with the wrong files.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Coverage of agents and vendor AI | 30% | The inventory has to include agents and third-party models, not just models you built. The FCA names both. |
| Mapping to the rules that bind you | 25% | EU AI Act, NIST AI RMF, ISO/IEC 42001, and for US banks the model-risk guidance (SR 26-2). |
| Analyst and customer evidence | 25% | Independent placement and named regulated customers. |
| Fit with existing systems | 20% | A governance tool nobody opens is a filing cabinet. |

We checked each vendor fact on the vendor's own page, an analyst's own publication or named trade press, in November 2026. Vendor claims are labelled as such. Prices are as listed in November 2026.

## The list

**1. IBM watsonx.governance**

**Best for:** large institutions that want the most recognised name and an on-premises option.

**Why it ranks first:** it is the only vendor here named a Leader in both Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant for AI Governance Platforms and The Forrester Wave: AI Governance Solutions, Q3 2025, according to IBM's own pages. Its pricing page lists AI asset detection, use case onboarding, risk assessment, compliance applicability assessment, model inventory and documentation, evaluation and monitoring. It is sold as SaaS on IBM Cloud and AWS, and as software priced by virtual processor core.

**Watch out for:** pricing has four entry points with different units, and the pricing page does not mention agents. IBM Promontory's April 2026 paper on SR 26-2 is advisory material, not a product mapping.

**Pricing (as listed in November 2026):** Risk and Compliance Basic from $3,500 a month on IBM Cloud; Risk and Compliance Advanced from $6,450 a month as enterprise software; watsonx.governance on AWS from $42,000, with the period not stated. All prices are indicative and exclude taxes.

**What would change its rank:** clearer agent coverage from a challenger with equal analyst standing.

**2. ServiceNow AI Control Tower**

**Best for:** firms already running ServiceNow.

**Why it ranks here:** a Gartner Leader, and the broadest stated agent coverage. ServiceNow's May 2026 release says the product discovers AI assets across AWS, Google Cloud, Azure, SAP, Oracle and Workday, assesses risk across agents, models, data sets and prompts, adds an AI Gateway with real-time controls for MCP transactions, and can detect an agent that "goes off script" and "shut it down in real time." ServiceNow's Amit Zavery said more than 500 customers were live in the first six months.

**Watch out for:** the 500-customer figure is the company's own, relayed by SiliconANGLE. The same October 2026 analysis, based on 15 customer interviews, found 14 described runtime enforcement as external, custom, human-mediated or unproven at scale, and 7 of the 8 who compared costs reported overruns. The May enhancements were due for general availability in August 2026. Best value comes only on the ServiceNow platform.

**Pricing:** through sales. ServiceNow moved to Foundation, Advanced and Prime AI tiers in spring 2026, paired with usage meters.

**What would change its rank:** explicit mapping to bank model-risk guidance, or independent evidence that runtime enforcement works across non-ServiceNow agents.

**3. Credo AI**

**Best for:** firms that want a specialist governance vendor rather than a platform add-on.

**Why it ranks here:** a Leader in the Forrester Wave for AI Governance Solutions, Q3 2025, which assessed 10 vendors, and a Visionary in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant. Credo AI's own page lists use case, model and vendor registries, a policy pack and control library, "policy-to-code governance", dynamic risk scoring and audit trails and reporting. Its Mastercard case study describes an AI registry covering internal and third-party tools, risk-based intake, an audit trail of reviewer approvals and a vendor portal for third-party evidence.

**Watch out for:** its AI Agent Registry and Agent Governor are labelled research previews on its own page, so agent coverage is earlier than the registry suggests. Bank model-risk alignment is not explicit on its site.

**Pricing:** through sales.

**What would change its rank:** an explicit SR 26-2 mapping, and agent features out of preview.

**4. ValidMind**

**Best for:** US and Canadian banks whose first concern is model risk management.

**Why it ranks here:** the most explicit fit with bank supervision. Its documentation, dated 30 October 2026, maps SR 26-2's model definition, inventory, tiering and materiality, ongoing monitoring, validation, documentation and audit trails to product features. Its February 2025 partnership with Experian named SR 11-7, Canada's E-23, the UK's SS1/23 and the EU AI Act, and covered documentation, validation and bias testing for credit and fraud models.

**Watch out for:** small and early, with an $8.1 million seed round led by Point72 Ventures in March 2024 and no later round verified here. It is not among the 13 vendors in Gartner's Magic Quadrant. Its SR 26-2 page notes that generative and agentic AI are out of SR 26-2's scope, and we did not verify agent-specific depth.

**Pricing:** through sales.

**What would change its rank:** evidence of agent governance at a large bank.

**5. ModelOp**

**Best for:** firms that need one system of record across classic models, generative AI, agents and vendor AI.

**Why it ranks here:** a Visionary in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant that describes itself as a system of record for AI assets across machine learning, generative and agentic systems. Its financial services page cites SR 11-7 and pre-packaged EU AI Act templates, and names Fidelity Investments and RBC Capital Markets. Its customer story for Prudential Financial reports a risk-rating process cut from two weeks to one day.

**Watch out for:** the performance claims are its own, its financial services page does not reference SR 26-2, and NIST AI RMF and ISO/IEC 42001 appear there as links rather than described mappings.

**Pricing:** not published.

**What would change its rank:** an updated mapping to SR 26-2.

## Left out, and why

**Truyo.** A Leader in Gartner's 2026 Magic Quadrant. We have not yet assessed it against our criteria; its placement means it belongs on any shortlist.

## Buyer checklist

Ask every vendor on your shortlist to show, not describe, each item. The [AI audit trail explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) lists the evidence fields behind several of them.

| Check | What a good answer looks like | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rules mapping | A document mapping features to the rules that bind you, including SR 26-2 for a US bank and SS1/23 for a UK bank with model approval | Mapping is the difference between a tool and evidence |
| Generative and agentic scope | A clear statement of how out-of-scope AI under SR 26-2 is governed in the same inventory | That is where the gap now sits |
| Vendor agents | A demonstration of a bought-in agent entering the inventory, and who is notified when it changes | The FCA says outsourced AI remains your responsibility |
| Evidence pack | An export for one AI system as an examiner would see it: owner, risk tier, approvals, validation, monitoring | Examiners ask for packs, not dashboards |
| Decision trace link | How a record in the platform links to the run-level trace in your observability tool | The inventory says what exists; the trace says what it did |
| Runtime control | A live test of stopping an agent outside the vendor's own platform | US supervisors are asking how banks would shut agents down |
| Retention and export | Retention settings, immutability and a full export in an open format | Records outlive contracts |
| Price | A written quote at your expected number of use cases and users | Published entry prices rarely match a bank's scale |

Gateway card

### Before you sign

- A rules mapping you can hand to your model risk function
- A vendor agent demonstrated entering the inventory
- An examiner-style evidence pack exported for one live system
- A tested link from the inventory record to the decision trace
- An exit plan: full export, retention and immutability terms in the contract

## lowob takeaways

- **IBM ranks first on standing.** A Leader in both the 2026 Gartner Magic Quadrant and Forrester's Q3 2025 Wave, with published prices and on-premises software.
- **ServiceNow's agent claims need testing.** Broad stated coverage, but a customer study found runtime enforcement largely unproven.
- **ValidMind fits bank supervision most explicitly.** It publishes an SR 26-2 mapping, but it is small and outside the Magic Quadrant.
- **Check agent features are generally available.** Credo AI's agent registry is a research preview.
- **Ask for the evidence pack.** It is what an examiner will see.

# What AI Agents Still Cannot Do, and How to Tell Before You Buy

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-still-cannot-do/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Across sixty commercial tasks in the lowob directory, none is rated for an agent acting alone and six are rated low reliability. Five failure patterns explain the limits: long horizons, changed facts, prompt injection, excessive agency and judgement calls with no graded precedent. Benchmarks confirm fast progress on well-specified tasks and much weaker reliability on messy, repeated work. A seven-question buyer test separates genuine agents from rebadged automation.

AI agents can now complete multi-hour software tasks half the time, and they still cannot be trusted alone with most commercial work. Across the sixty tasks in the **lowob** directory, none is rated for level 4 (act alone), and six are rated low reliability: pricing, discounts, autonomous outbound, budget moves, shared definitions and access changes. Five failure patterns explain why: long horizons, changed facts, prompt injection, excessive agency, and judgement calls with no graded precedent. Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. A buyer who asks seven plain questions before signing can avoid being one of them.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

The previous five parts of this series walked the [**lowob** Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/) one function at a time: sales, marketing, commercial operations, partners and customer success. This part looks across all sixty tasks at once and asks where the ceiling is, why it is there, and how a buyer can tell a genuine agent from a relabelled chatbot before the contract is signed.

## The shape of the limit across sixty tasks

The ratings describe a clear boundary. Agents are rated highly on internal, frequent, checkable work, and held back wherever work reaches a client, commits money or changes who can see what.

| Measure across 60 tasks | Count | What it says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rated level 4 (act alone) | 0 | No commercial task in the directory warrants approval-free action with no report |
| Rated level 3 (act and report) | 21 | Agents act within fixed bounds and report, mostly on internal records |
| Rated level 2 (act with approval) | 7 | A named person approves each action |
| Rated level 1 (draft) | 29 | The largest group: the agent prepares, a person decides |
| Rated level 0 (answer) | 3 | The agent informs a decision it must never make |
| High reliability | 24 | Research, summaries, monitoring, record hygiene, internal drafts |
| Medium reliability | 30 | Useful with review; quality varies with data and definitions |
| Low reliability | 6 | The agent's output should not be relied on without full human work |

### The six low-reliability tasks

| Function | Task | Autonomy | Main risk | Failure pattern behind it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sales | Price a proposal | 1 Draft | Margin loss; inconsistent pricing | Judgement with no graded precedent |
| Sales | Approve a discount | 0 Answer | Commits money without accountability | Judgement with no graded precedent |
| Sales | Send outbound sequences autonomously | 2 Act with approval | Reputational and deliverability damage | Excessive agency; long horizon |
| Marketing | Reallocate campaign budget | 1 Draft | Spend moved on weak evidence | Judgement with no graded precedent |
| Commercial operations | Maintain shared definitions | 0 Answer | Definitions drift silently | Changed facts |
| Commercial operations | Grant or change system access | 0 Answer | Excessive agency; data exposure | Excessive agency; prompt injection |

Three of the six are commercial judgement calls on money. Two are about control of the system itself. One, autonomous outbound, is the most requested first agent in commercial teams and the one we most often advise against, for the reasons set out in [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/).

## Five failure patterns

Every low rating and most medium ratings trace back to one of five patterns. None is a simple bug. Each is a property of how current agents work, and each has a control.

| Pattern | What happens | Evidence | Tasks most exposed | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Long horizons | Success falls as tasks lengthen and steps compound | METR time horizons; TheAgentCompany | Autonomous outbound; end-to-end case resolution; forecasting | Break work into short, checkable steps |
| Changed facts | The agent weighs an outdated fact as current | MEMTRACK; directory risks marked "stale" | Account research; shared definitions; QBR decks | Mark records current or superseded |
| Prompt injection | Instructions hidden in inbound content steer the agent | OWASP LLM01:2025 | Marketplace leads; community replies; inbound email | Read-only agents for untrusted input |
| Excessive agency | Too many tools or permissions turn an error into damage | OWASP LLM06:2025 | Access changes; outbound sending; budget moves | Least privilege; approval for high-impact actions |
| No graded precedent | The agent has no record of similar past calls and how they turned out | **lowob** directory; Gartner on maturity | Pricing; discounts; budget; account prioritisation | Record decisions and write outcomes back |

### Long horizons

The longer a task runs, the more steps can go wrong, and errors compound. Carnegie Mellon's TheAgentCompany benchmark simulates a small software company with internal chat, code hosting, file storage and project tools. In its September 2025 version, the best agent completed about 30% of 175 tasks autonomously, rising to 39.3% with partial credit. Administrative, finance and data science tasks scored lowest, as did tasks requiring conversation with simulated colleagues. Those are the categories closest to commercial work.

### Changed facts

Commercial facts change: a price book is revised, a contact leaves, a definition of "qualified" is tightened. Patronus AI's MEMTRACK benchmark tested agents on timelines of interleaved, noisy and sometimes conflicting messages across Slack, Linear and Git. The best model reached about 60% correctness. The failure is rarely that the agent cannot find the information. It finds both the old and the new, and weighs them badly. Our view, set out in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/), is that the fix sits in the record: each fact marked current or superseded, so the agent does not have to guess.

### Prompt injection

An agent reads instructions wherever they appear. OWASP's LLM01:2025 entry distinguishes direct injection, from a user's own prompt, and indirect injection, from external content such as a web page or file. It states that it is unclear whether fool-proof prevention exists, given the stochastic nature of the models. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" gives buyers a practical test: an agent that combines access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally can be made to leak data. Every agent that reads inbound email, partner portal submissions or community posts is exposed. See [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/).

### Excessive agency

OWASP's LLM06:2025 defines excessive agency as a system taking damaging actions in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated outputs. It names three root causes: excessive functionality, excessive permissions and excessive autonomy. Its mitigations are architectural: grant the minimum tools and permissions, enforce authorisation in downstream systems rather than trusting the model, and require human approval for high-impact actions. This is why "grant or change system access" sits at level 0 in the directory and is never delegated.

### Judgement calls with no graded precedent

Pricing an unusual deal, approving a discount, moving budget between channels and choosing which accounts to prioritise are low-volume calls whose outcomes arrive months later. The agent has nothing to learn from unless the company recorded similar past decisions with their reasons and what happened next. Most companies have not. Gartner's analyst Anushree Verma made a related point when explaining the cancellation forecast: current models lack the maturity to pursue complex goals autonomously. A record with graded outcomes does not make the model wiser. It gives the person approving the call better evidence.

> An agent that has never seen how your last ten discounts turned out is not making a judgement. It is making a guess with good grammar.

## What benchmarks and time horizons show

The most cited independent measure is METR's task-completion time horizon: the length of task, measured in expert human time, that an agent completes at a given success rate.

| Measure | Figure | Status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Claude Opus 4.5, 50% time horizon (Time Horizon 1.1, January 2026) | About 320 minutes; 95% interval 170 to 729 minutes | Published by METR |
| Task suite | 228 tasks, of which 31 take humans eight hours or more; only 5 of those 31 have measured human baselines | Published by METR |
| Doubling time since 2023 | About 131 days under the updated suite | Published by METR |
| 80% horizon versus 50% horizon | Roughly five times shorter | METR's original study (arXiv 2503.14499) |
| Later 2026 model figures | Higher estimates have circulated | Secondary coverage only; not used here |
| TheAgentCompany, best agent | About 30% of 175 workplace tasks completed | Academic benchmark, September 2025 |
| τ-bench, consistency over eight attempts | Below 25% in retail for the leading agent tested | Academic benchmark, June 2024; authors at a service AI vendor |

Three readings matter for a buyer. First, the 50% figure describes a coin toss, not a delegated job. METR's original study put 80% horizons at roughly a fifth of the 50% figure, and that is closer to the reliability a commercial process needs. Second, the tasks are software, machine learning and cybersecurity tasks with checkable answers. METR's own study found lower performance on messier, less structured tasks, which is what most commercial work is. Third, consistency is its own problem. τ-bench introduced pass^k, the chance that an agent succeeds on all of k repeated trials of the same task. An agent that succeeds once may fail the next three times on an identical request. A business process runs the same task hundreds of times.

The trend is real and fast. That is why the directory is re-rated quarterly. But the gap between benchmark progress and commercial reliability closes more slowly than headlines suggest. Our explainer [What Is an AI Time Horizon?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-time-horizon/) covers the method in more depth.

## Why so many projects will be cancelled

Gartner's June 2025 forecast was that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. In a January 2025 Gartner poll of 3,412 webinar attendees, 19% reported significant investment in agentic AI and 42% conservative investment. Gartner also named "agent washing": vendors relabelling assistants, robotic process automation and chatbots as agentic without substantial agentic capability. It estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of agentic vendors were genuine, and noted that many use cases positioned as agentic do not need agentic implementations at all.

The three cancellation causes map onto the five failure patterns. Cost escalates when long-horizon tasks loop and retry. Value stays unclear when nobody records the decision and writes back the outcome. Risk controls fail when excessive agency meets untrusted content.

## A buyer test for agent washing

Ask a vendor these seven questions. Write down the answers. A genuine agent product will answer most of them specifically. A washed one will answer in adjectives.

| Question | A genuine answer | A washing answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What does it decide for itself? | Names the choices: which tool, which record, when to stop | "It uses AI to automate your workflow" |
| What is the stop condition? | A defined goal, step limit or spend cap | No answer, or "it runs until done" |
| What can it touch, and with whose identity? | Lists tools and permissions; runs as its own registered identity | Uses a person's login or an admin key |
| Which actions need approval? | A configurable gate per action type, with logs of who approved | "You can review outputs" |
| Can I replay one run? | Shows what it read, what it did and who approved it | Shows a summary or a dashboard only |
| What is its success rate on tasks like mine, measured how? | A rate on a defined sample, ideally repeated, with the grading method | A single demo or a customer logo |
| How does it handle untrusted inbound content? | Separates reading from acting; names its injection controls | "Our model is trained to ignore attacks" |

If the answer to the first question is "nothing", the product is automation. That is not a criticism: automation is often the right tool. It should be bought, tested and priced as automation, and our explainer [What Is Agent Washing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) sets out how.

Illustrative example: running the buyer test on two proposals

Decision
:   Accept a meeting-preparation agent at level 1 and decline an "autonomous revenue agent" pending answers to four of the seven questions.

Reason and owner
:   The first vendor named its tools, stop condition and approval gate and replayed a run. The second could not say what its product decided for itself, ran on a shared admin key and offered a demo in place of a measured success rate. Owned by the chief operating officer.

What changed
:   The second proposal was reclassified as workflow automation and re-scoped against automation pricing; the first went into a four-week pilot with a weekly spot-check.

Illustrative: a composite of a 150-person professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **No commercial task warrants level 4 today.** Across sixty tasks, the ceiling is act and report on internal work.
- **Plan around the reliable number.** A 50% time horizon is a draft; the 80% horizon is roughly a fifth as long.
- **Most limits are structural.** Long horizons, changed facts, injection, excessive agency and missing precedent each need a control, not a better model.
- **Ask what it decides for itself.** If the answer is nothing, buy it as automation.

Gateway card

### Before you buy an agent

- The vendor has named what the product decides, its stop condition and its tools
- It runs as its own identity with least-privilege permissions
- High-impact actions pass an approval gate that logs who approved
- You have replayed one complete run
- A success rate measured on tasks like yours, over repeated trials
- Untrusted inbound content cannot trigger external actions

## Common questions

### What can't AI agents do yet?

They cannot reliably act alone on commercial work that reaches clients, commits money or changes access. Across sixty rated tasks, none warrants full autonomy, and pricing, discounts, budget moves, autonomous outbound, shared definitions and access changes are rated low reliability.

### Why do AI agents fail on long tasks?

Errors compound across steps. METR's research found agents complete far shorter tasks at 80% success than at 50%, and benchmarks such as TheAgentCompany show the best agents completing about 30% of realistic workplace tasks.

### What is agent washing?

Gartner's term for vendors relabelling chatbots, assistants or automation as agentic without real agentic capability. Gartner estimated only about 130 of thousands of agentic vendors were genuine.

### Why will so many agentic AI projects be cancelled?

Gartner expects over 40% to be cancelled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. Choosing client-facing, long-horizon tasks first makes all three more likely.

# AI Agent vs Chatbot: The Difference That Matters to a Buyer

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agent-vs-chatbot/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A chatbot answers questions in a conversation; an AI agent pursues a goal and takes actions through tools. OpenAI's own guide says simple chatbots are not agents. For a buyer the difference is what the system can change, who is liable when it is wrong, and what evidence it leaves behind.

A chatbot is a conversational interface that answers a person's questions, from a script or a language model. An AI agent is given a goal and works toward it, choosing its next step and acting through tools such as a CRM, a billing system or email. For a buyer, the useful question is what the system is allowed to change, because that sets the risk, the controls and the price.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the two terms mean

A chatbot holds a conversation. Older ones follow decision trees; newer ones put a language model behind the window, often with retrieval over help articles. Either way the output is a reply.

An agent holds a goal. OpenAI defines agents as "systems that independently accomplish tasks on your behalf": a model manages the workflow and makes decisions, and it has tools that reach external systems. The same guide places simple chatbots, single-turn model calls and sentiment classifiers outside the definition.

The line is not the interface. Many agents are reached through a chat window. The line is whether the system can change something outside the conversation: issue a refund, update a record, send an email.

|  | Chatbot | AI agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts from | A message | A goal, from a person or a trigger |
| Output | A reply | A completed task, or a task handed back |
| Touches other systems | Reads, if at all | Reads and writes through tools |
| Who decides the next step | The person in the chat | The agent, within set limits |
| Autonomy dial | 0 answer | 1 draft up to 4 act alone |
| Typical failure | A confident wrong answer | A wrong action taken with real permissions |
| Evidence needed | Conversation transcript | Trace of each decision, tool call and approval |

## Why the difference matters to a buyer

**Liability does not move to the software.** In *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024 BCCRT 149), the airline's chatbot wrongly told a customer he could claim a bereavement fare after travel. The tribunal found negligent misrepresentation. It wrote that Air Canada "is responsible for all the information on its website", whether it "comes from a static page or a chatbot." The award was about CA$812. The principle matters more than the sum: a firm answerable for a chatbot's words is answerable for an agent's actions.

**Regulated firms have duties a chatbot can break.** The CFPB's June 2023 issue spotlight found that all ten of the largest US commercial banks use chatbots. It warned they can give inaccurate information, miss when a consumer is invoking federal rights, and trap customers in loops with no route to a person. An agent that can act on an account carries the same duties.

**The controls differ in kind.** A chatbot needs content controls: scope limits, grounding in approved sources, a handoff to a human. An agent needs those plus action controls. OpenAI recommends rating each tool's risk and names two triggers for human intervention: exceeding failure thresholds, and high-risk actions such as cancelling orders or authorising large refunds.

**The price follows the capability.** Chatbots are usually priced per seat or per conversation. Agents are increasingly priced per resolution, which only works if someone defines a resolution and checks it.

## How to test a vendor's claim

Vendors use "agent" loosely; the pattern is covered in [What is agent washing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/). Five questions settle most claims in one demo.

| Question to ask | Chatbot answer | Agent answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which systems can it write to, with whose credentials? | None | A named list, with scoped service accounts |
| Does the path change for a different case? | No, same flow every time | Yes, steps vary with the input |
| What happens when a step fails? | Hands off to a person | Retries within a limit, then hands off |
| Which actions need approval first? | Not applicable | A named list, set by you |
| What record does each run leave? | Transcript | Decisions, tool calls, approvals and outcome |

## The **lowob** view

**lowob** treats both as parts of one loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. A chatbot sits on the reasoning step and draws on the store through retrieval; it rarely writes anything back. An agent touches every step. It reads through the wiring and acts. It should then leave a record of what it decided, on what evidence, who approved it and what was expected. The outcome flows back so the next run learns.

So the buying decision is about permissions, not labels. A system that only answers can start at dial level 0, with a clear handoff to a person. Anything that writes to a customer record, a price or an outbound message starts at level 1 or 2, with a person approving before it sends. Move up one notch at a time, on evidence from the record.

## lowob takeaways

- **The test is what it can change.** A system that only replies is a chatbot, whatever the label says.
- **Liability stays with the firm.** A tribunal has already held a company responsible for its chatbot's answers.
- **Agents need action controls.** Scoped credentials, approval lists and failure limits, on top of content controls.
- **Buy the record with the agent.** Each run should leave decisions, tool calls, approvals and the outcome.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a chatbot and an AI agent?

A chatbot replies to messages in a conversation. An AI agent is given a goal and works toward it, choosing steps and acting in other systems through tools, within set limits.

### Is a company liable for what its chatbot says?

In Moffatt v. Air Canada (2024), a Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for its chatbot's inaccurate answer. Rules vary by jurisdiction, but buyers should assume the liability stays with them.

### Should a customer service team replace its chatbot with an AI agent?

Only for tasks where actions can be scoped, checked and approved. Keep the answering layer, add actions one at a time, and keep a person approving refunds, credits and anything irreversible.

US regulator report, since archived; the 37% figure is an estimate for 2022.

# The 10 AI Regulatory Dates to Watch Through 2027

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-10-ai-regulatory-dates-to-watch-through-2027/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The AI-specific rules keep slipping, but the record-keeping, supervision and resilience rules that already apply do not. Refreshed in November 2026, this list covers the ten dates that change what a financial firm in the US, UK or EU must do or show, and what happened to the ones that have passed. Every date points to the same need: a record you can reconstruct.

The AI-specific rules keep slipping. The record-keeping, supervision and resilience rules that already apply do not. Most of what binds a bank's AI in 2027 is old law, newly read to cover agents. This list, refreshed on 16 November 2026, sets out the ten dates that change what a financial firm in the US, UK or EU must do or show, and what happened to the dates that have passed since it was first published.

This list is for heads of AI, risk and compliance at financial firms operating in the US, UK or EU. Skip it if your AI use is limited to drafting internal documents with no customer impact.

## How we chose

We kept dates that change what a financial firm must do or show, in the order they arrive, and left out consultations with no deadline attached. Every date is from a regulator, a court record, a law firm's reading of the text or a named press report, cited below. Where a date is not fixed, we say so rather than guess.

## What happened since October

Four items from the first version of this list, or close to it, have now passed.

**4 November 2026: OCC examiner framework for generative and agentic AI.** The OCC issued Bulletin 2026-54, a supervisory framework that tells its examiners how to evaluate banks' use of generative and agentic AI, which the OCC calls "super intelligence". It covers the ground SR 26-2 left out, but it is examiner guidance only and does not establish supervisory expectations for banks. The interagency request for information is still pending.

**End of October 2026: ECB AI cyber-threat plans.** According to Reuters, the ECB gave euro zone lenders until the end of October to produce plans to counter AI-enabled cyber threats, including better back-up and recovery. Banks were also asked to map how AI is used across their businesses and third-party providers, and to make sure they could switch systems off and restart them in a controlled way. Reuters reported on 13 October that some firms still had significant gaps. The ECB has not published a read-out of the submissions. DORA, which has applied since 17 January 2025, remains the legal frame for that work.

**19 October 2026: the FCA's AI good practice review.** The FCA published *AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement*. It sets no new rules, but it names the records it expects: prompts, outputs, model versions, applied filters and escalation decisions, and auditable decisions with rationale and challenge. It also flags firms whose AI decisions were "poorly documented with limited audit trails".

**14 October 2026: the first harmonised standard.** The Commission published EN 18286, a quality management system standard, under the AI Act. Following it gives providers a presumption of conformity for the requirements it covers. It does not yet cover logging, which remains in the standardisation pipeline.

## The list

| # | When | What happens | Who it affects | What to do now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 2 December 2026 | Two new EU AI Act prohibitions apply: systems that generate child sexual abuse material or non-consensual intimate imagery. Machine-readable marking of synthetic output under Article 50(2) also applies to generative systems already on the market | Any firm offering generative AI in the EU | Confirm your vendors mark synthetic output and that your own builds do too |
| 2 | December 2026 (expected) | FINRA's 2027 oversight report, if it follows the 2026 report's release on 9 December 2025 | US broker-dealers | Re-read the 2026 report's agent section and check you can track agent actions and decisions |
| 3 | 1 January 2027 | Colorado's Automated Decision-Making Technology in Consequential Decisions Act takes effect, replacing the 2024 Colorado AI Act: notice before use, an explanation within 30 days of an adverse outcome, and meaningful human review on request | Developers and deployers using automated decisions in lending, insurance, employment and other covered areas for Colorado consumers | Identify which automated decisions reach Colorado consumers; deployers keep compliance records for three years after each use |
| 4 | Q1 2027 | The FCA publishes its evaluation of the second AI Live Testing cohort: Aereve, Barclays, Coadjute, Experian, GoCardless, Lloyds Banking Group (Scottish Widows), Palindrome and UBS. Testing ends by the end of 2026 | UK firms | Read it for the supervisor's view of production AI in banking, payments and credit data |
| 5 | Not yet dated | The US banking agencies' request for information on model risk and "banks' use of AI, including generative AI and agentic AI", promised in April when SR 26-2 left both out of scope. Not in the Federal Register as of 24 October 2026 | US banks | Prepare your answer now: how you validate retrieval, guardrails and agent actions, and how you would stop an agent |
| 6 | Not yet dated | A ruling on OpenAI's and Microsoft's summary judgment motions in the news publishers' copyright cases, including *New York Times v. OpenAI*. The publishers filed their opposition in October 2026; no ruling date has been set | Anyone training or fine-tuning on third-party content | Inventory the provenance of every corpus your models touch |
| 7 | Not yet dated | The first lawsuit brought in the name of the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, created under the executive order of 11 December 2025. The DOJ intervened on 24 April 2026 in xAI's challenge to the 2024 Colorado AI Act, which Colorado then repealed and replaced | Firms planning around state AI laws | Avoid building compliance around any single state regime until this settles |
| 8 | 2 August 2027 | General-purpose AI models placed on the EU market before 2 August 2025 must comply; each member state must have at least one operational AI regulatory sandbox | Model providers directly; firms that fine-tune or rebrand models | Ask your model vendors for their compliance position and documentation |
| 9 | 2 December 2027 | EU AI Act high-risk obligations for Annex III systems apply, including creditworthiness and credit scoring of individuals, life and health insurance pricing, and recruitment | Lenders, insurers and employers using AI in the EU | Start conformity and logging work now; deployers must keep logs for at least six months |
| 10 | 2 August 2028 | High-risk obligations for AI built into products regulated under Annex I apply | Product makers, rarely financial firms | Note it; little action for most financial firms |

Three items deserve a closer reading.

**Colorado is the US date with teeth.** The original Colorado AI Act was due to take effect on 30 June 2026. The replacement law signed on 14 May 2026 narrows the focus to automated decision-making in consequential decisions, keeps enforcement with the state Attorney General under consumer protection law, and has no private right of action. Its three-year record duty for deployers is a reconstruction requirement in all but name.

**The US bank RFI is late, but the questions are not.** SR 26-2 placed generative and agentic AI outside its scope in April. Reuters reported on 13 October that the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC were nonetheless asking banks whether agent decisions can be tracked and audited, who approves agent actions, and how a bank would shut autonomous systems down. Firms that wait for the RFI to define expectations will meet them first in an examination.

**The EU high-risk date moved; the logging duty did not change.** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026, moved Annex III obligations to 2 December 2027. Articles 12, 19 and 26, which require automatic logs and their retention, carry no amendment markers in the Commission's consolidated text. Our guide [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) maps those duties against US and UK rules.

> Every date on this list asks the same question in a different accent: show us what the system saw, what it did and who checked.

## What already applies, and is easy to forget

**EU transparency duties.** Most Article 50 duties for chatbots and deepfakes have applied since 2 August 2026. The delay that grabbed headlines covered high-risk systems, not these. Our explainer [The EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) covers the disclosure duties.

**US supervision and records.** FINRA's rules are technologically neutral, and its 2026 report lists tracking agent actions and decisions and keeping prompt and output logs among firms' considerations. FINRA Rule 4511 and SEA Rule 17a-4 set retention of three to six years.

**UK accountability.** The FCA says it does not plan AI-specific rules. Its October review places AI inside the Consumer Duty, senior manager accountability, operational resilience and outsourcing rules that already apply.

## Left out, and why

**SEC predictive data analytics rule.** The SEC formally withdrew the proposal on 12 June 2025, with 13 other proposals.

**ISO/IEC 42001 certification.** Voluntary, and it does not give presumption of conformity under the AI Act. Our comparison [NIST AI RMF vs ISO/IEC 42001](https://lowob.com/research/nist-ai-rmf-vs-iso-42001/) explains where it helps.

## The one thing to build regardless

Every date above points to the same artefact: a record you can reconstruct, showing what an AI system saw, what it produced, who checked it, and what was done. Colorado asks deployers to keep it for three years. The AI Act asks for logs. FINRA asks how firms track agent actions. US bank supervisors ask whether agent decisions can be audited. Build that record once and most of this calendar becomes paperwork rather than a project. Our explainer [What is an AI audit trail?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) sets out the fields.

## lowob takeaways

- **2 December 2026 is the next EU date.** New prohibitions and machine-readable marking of synthetic output.
- **Colorado applies from 1 January 2027.** Notice, adverse-outcome explanation, human review and three-year records.
- **Annex III high-risk applies from 2 December 2027.** Credit scoring and life and health insurance pricing are in scope.
- **Build the reconstructable record.** It answers every date on the list.

## Common questions

### When do EU AI Act high-risk rules apply to credit scoring?

After the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, high-risk obligations for Annex III systems, including creditworthiness and credit scoring of individuals, apply from 2 December 2027.

### When does Colorado's AI law take effect?

Colorado repealed its 2024 AI Act and replaced it with a law on automated decision-making in consequential decisions, signed on 14 May 2026. It takes effect on 1 January 2027.

### What changes in the EU AI Act on 2 December 2026?

Bans on AI systems that generate child sexual abuse material or non-consensual intimate imagery apply, and generative systems already on the market must mark synthetic output in a machine-readable format.

### Have US bank regulators issued AI guidance for generative and agentic AI?

Not yet. SR 26-2 excludes generative and agentic AI, and the promised request for information had not been published by late October 2026, though supervisors are asking banks about agent audit trails and shutdown.

# The Transitions That Break the Brain

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-transitions-that-break-the-brain/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Organisations rarely lose their reasoning gradually; they lose it at transitions such as the first hire, an acquisition, a founder's departure or a platform migration. Each is predictable and has a specific defence, and the defence is always cheaper before the transition than after it. Regulation and standard practice already describe several of the defences.

Organisations rarely lose their reasoning gradually. They lose it at transitions: the first hire, the first manager layer, an acquisition, a regulator's first visit, a founder's departure, a reorganisation, a platform migration. Each is predictable, and each has a specific defence. The failure is almost always the same: the transition is planned in terms of people, money and systems, and the reasoning is assumed to follow on its own. It does not.

*Figure: The Build Order: three decisions, four layers on the commercial line, then three gateways before the brain spreads.*

The rungs of company growth describe steady states. Our [scale ladder](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/) sets them out, from two people to ten thousand. The damage happens in between. Each transition changes who decides, who remembers, or where records live, and each tends to happen under time pressure, when nobody is thinking about the record.

## Why transitions, not drift

Software teams learned this first. AWS's guidance on architecture decision records describes the collection as providing "a hand-over experience and reference documentation", so that "current and future stakeholders" can see both the decision and the thought process behind it. The record exists because people change. The [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) explainer shows how the same format applies to commercial decisions.

The decisions most exposed at transitions are also the least practised. McKinsey's 2019 survey of 1,228 managers distinguished frequent "delegated" decisions from "big bets", the infrequent, high-stakes decisions such as acquisitions, and found respondents least familiar with big bets. Only 30% were familiar with all three decision types studied. A company does few acquisitions, has one founder's departure and migrates its core platform rarely. Nobody gets good at these by repetition, which is why the defence has to be planned.

> The transition is planned in terms of people, money and systems. The reasoning is assumed to follow on its own. It does not.

## Seven transitions

| Transition | What breaks | Defence | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The first hire | The assumption that everyone was there | Make the ledger readable by strangers | Before they arrive |
| The first manager layer | Founders as the default decision-makers | Write decision rights and the first decision classes | The month managers are appointed |
| An acquisition | Definitions, decision histories and leaders, all at once | Handover packs, mapped glossaries, the acquired graveyard kept | Before close |
| First regulator or major customer audit | Informal decision-making in any process now in scope | Traces and evidenced review for in-scope classes | Before the request |
| A founder's or long-tenured leader's departure | The largest single store of unwritten reasoning | Extraction interviews, graveyard and relationships first | Months ahead |
| A reorganisation | Ownership of records | Reassign record ownership in the reorganisation plan | With headcount and budgets |
| A platform migration | History and links | Test the export; reconstruct sample decisions | Before signing and after cutover |

**The first hire.** Breaks: the assumption that everyone was there. Defence: make the ledger readable by strangers before they arrive, not after. [Ten people: the first stranger](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/) covers what "readable" means.

**The first manager layer.** Breaks: founders as the default decision-makers. Defence: write decision rights and the first decision classes the month managers are appointed.

**An acquisition.** Breaks: everything at once. Two organisations with different definitions, different decision histories, and leaders who may leave within a year. Defence: treat integration as the largest handover the company will ever do. Run handover packs for every acquired leader who owns decisions. Map the acquired glossary to yours rather than overwriting it, and open a conflicts list for definitions that diverge. Keep the acquired company's decision history intact and searchable, marked with its origin. Its [graveyard](https://lowob.com/research/the-graveyard/) is especially valuable: it records what the acquired team already tried in markets you are about to enter.

**The first regulator or major customer audit.** Breaks: informal decision-making in any process that is now in scope. Defence: identify in-scope decision classes early, and introduce traces and evidenced review there first, before the request arrives. The bar is documented. The Federal Reserve's SR 26-2, issued in April 2026 to replace SR 11-7, says adequate documentation supports "the tracking of recommendations, responses, and exceptions" and expects an inventory with "sufficient information to understand model risks". It excludes generative and agentic AI from scope, but it shows what a supervisor expects to be able to reconstruct. In the EU, the AI Act requires deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months once those obligations apply, from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems under the 2026 amendments. Our explainer on [the AI audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) covers the detail.

**A founder's or long-tenured leader's departure.** Breaks: the largest single store of unwritten reasoning in the company. Defence: start the extraction interviews months, not weeks, before. Prioritise the graveyard and relationships, which are least likely to exist anywhere else. [From founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) covers the commercial version of the same handover.

**A reorganisation.** Breaks: ownership of records. Decision classes move between teams, and the old owner's records become orphaned. Defence: reassign record ownership explicitly as part of the reorganisation plan, alongside headcount and budgets.

**A platform migration.** Breaks: history and links. Records move, but supersession links, sources and outcomes often do not. Defence: test the export before signing the new contract, and verify after migration that a sample of decisions can still be fully reconstructed. EU law now helps at the edges. Since 12 September 2025, the Data Act's switching rules have required providers of data processing services, SaaS included, to complete porting within a 30-day transition and to treat input and output data "including metadata" as exportable. That covers the data. Whether a supersession chain or an outcome link survives in usable form is a test only the buyer can run.

## What a reconstruction test checks

| Check | Pass |
| --- | --- |
| The decision and its reason | Readable without the old system |
| Owner and date | Present and correct |
| Supersession links | Old and new records still linked |
| Sources | Linked source snapshots still open |
| Outcome | Written-back outcome still attached |

Run it on ten decisions chosen at random, not the ten best documented. A migration that passes on the showcase records and fails on ordinary ones has failed.

## The common pattern

Every one of these is known in advance. The defence is always cheaper before the transition than after it. The failure is almost always the same: the transition is planned in terms of people, money and systems, and the reasoning is assumed to follow on its own. It does not. [Handovers are where reasoning pours out](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) covers the person-to-person version of the problem.

## In practice

Add "what happens to the decision record" to the checklist for every acquisition, reorganisation, leadership change and platform migration. For acquisitions, run handover packs for every acquired leader and keep the acquired graveyard. For reorganisations, reassign record ownership in the same document that reassigns teams.

For migrations, run a reconstruction test before and after.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations that take no specific action on records during these transitions showing no measurable loss of decision quality or institutional memory afterwards.

## lowob takeaways

- **Reasoning is lost at transitions.** Seven of them are predictable.
- **Plan the record with the people.** Ownership moves in the same document as headcount.
- **Keep the acquired history.** Mapped, not overwritten, with its graveyard intact.
- **Test reconstruction.** Ten random decisions, before signing and after cutover.

## Common questions

### When do companies lose institutional knowledge?

Mostly at transitions: the first hire, the first manager layer, an acquisition, a first regulator or customer audit, a leader's departure, a reorganisation, and a platform migration.

### How do you preserve decision history during an acquisition?

Run handover packs for every acquired leader who owns decisions, map the acquired glossary to yours rather than overwriting it, and keep the acquired company's decision history intact, searchable and marked with its origin.

### How do you avoid losing records in a software migration?

Test the export before signing the new contract, and after migrating verify that a random sample of decisions can still be fully reconstructed, including supersession links, sources and outcomes. In the EU, the Data Act requires providers to port data and metadata within 30 days.

### How should a company prepare for a founder leaving?

Start extraction interviews months ahead, and prioritise the decisions that failed and the relationships, which are least likely to be written down anywhere else.

## Sources and notes

- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance, Using architectural decision records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/welcome.html), March 2022. Vendor guidance for software teams.
- [McKinsey, Decision making in the age of urgency](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/decision-making-in-the-age-of-urgency), April 2019. Self-reported survey of 1,228 managers.
- [Federal Reserve, SR 26-2 attachment: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602a1.pdf), 17 April 2026. US bank supervisory guidance; excludes generative and agentic AI.
- [EU AI Act Service Desk, Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26), consolidated text as of 27 July 2026. Official Commission resource; high-risk systems only.
- [Cooley, New switching rules will become applicable in EU](https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2025/2025-09-08-paas-iaas-or-saas-be-aware-new-switching-rules-will-become-applicable-in-eu), September 2025. Law-firm summary of the EU Data Act; not legal advice.
- The seven transitions, defences and reconstruction test are **lowob**'s framework.
