# Top 5 AI Customer-Service Agents, by Pricing Model

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-customer-service-agents-by-pricing-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Customer service is the one place outcome pricing has taken hold, because a resolved ticket can be counted, so the definition of "resolved" is the most important line in the contract. The ranking is Fin, Zendesk AI agents, Sierra, Salesforce Agentforce and Decagon, with prices as listed in November 2026.

Customer service is the one place outcome pricing has taken hold, because a resolved ticket can be counted. That makes the definition of "resolved" the most important line in the contract. Fin and Zendesk now publish exactly what counts as a billable event; Salesforce publishes three pricing models for Agentforce; Sierra and Decagon still ask you to call sales. Fin ranks first for a published $0.99 price and the largest customer base, followed by Zendesk, Sierra, Agentforce and Decagon.

Outcome-based pricing means paying per counted result rather than per seat or per call. Our explainer on [outcome-based pricing for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/) sets out how it works, and **lowob**'s piece [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) argues when each model fits. Customer service is where the model works best because the unit is visible: a conversation either ended with the customer's problem solved or it did not. Zendesk's 2024 announcement put it simply: customers "will only incur costs for issues that are resolved autonomously by AI". Sierra's co-founder Bret Taylor described the idea in 2025 as "let's pay for a job well done". The hard part is the word "resolved".

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pricing transparency | 30% | A published unit price is the only way to model cost before a sales call. |
| What counts as billable | 25% | "Resolution", "outcome" and "conversation" mean different things and cost different amounts. |
| Evidence of scale | 25% | Customers, revenue and resolution rates, ideally beyond the vendor's own claims. |
| Fit with an existing stack | 20% | Switching help desks to get an agent is rarely worth it. |

## The list

**1. Fin (formerly Intercom; Salesforce agreed to buy it in June 2026)**

**Best for:** teams that want a published price and the largest customer base.

**Why it ranks first:** $0.99 per outcome on a public price list, charged at most once per conversation even if Fin takes several actions. A resolution counts when the customer confirms the answer helped or leaves without asking for more, and "only when Fin provides an actual answer"; a greeting alone does not count. Salesforce agreed on 15 June 2026 to buy Fin for about $3.6 billion, citing more than 30,000 customer companies and examples of AI agents resolving on average 76% of support volume end to end.

**Watch out for:** "outcome" is now broader than "resolution". A procedure handoff to a human or workflow, a disqualified prospect and a self-serve routing each cost $0.99, and a qualified prospect costs $9.99. Model your volume on the new definition, not last year's. Voice and high-volume pricing go through sales. The acquisition also raises roadmap questions for firms that do not run Salesforce; the June release did not say whether Fin stays available on other help desks.

**Pricing:** $0.99 per resolution, procedure handoff, disqualification or self-serve routing; $9.99 per qualification, for chat and email (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** product or pricing changes as it is folded into Salesforce.

**2. Zendesk AI agents**

**Best for:** teams already on Zendesk.

**Why it ranks here:** the clearest rule on what is billable. Under resolution tiers introduced on 18 May 2026, every conversation lands in one of three buckets. An assisted escalation, where a human finished the job, is not counted. A contained resolution, where the customer did not ask for more help, is not counted either. Only a verified resolution is billed, and verification is "performed by an LLM that evaluates the text of the conversation". A conversation ends 72 hours after the first email, two hours after the first message by default, or when a call ends.

**Watch out for:** the verification is still Zendesk's own model marking Zendesk's own work. Ask how often a verified resolution is reopened. Zendesk's help article describes the tiers but not the price; third-party teardowns put it at about $1.50 per automated resolution on a committed annual plan and about $2.00 pay-as-you-go, falling with volume, with a small included allowance per agent.

**Pricing:** about $1.50 committed and $2.00 pay-as-you-go per verified resolution, per third-party reporting in July 2026; confirm on your quote.

**What would change its rank:** a published rate card on Zendesk's own pages, or disclosed resolution rates.

**3. Sierra**

**Best for:** large consumer brands wanting a fully managed agent.

**Why it ranks here:** priced on outcomes, with customers billed when the agent resolves a case and nothing when a human has to take over, and the strongest growth story in the category. Sierra told TechCrunch it reached $100 million in annual recurring revenue in late November 2025 and $150 million in early February 2026, and claims more than 40% of the Fortune 50 as customers. On 4 May 2026 it announced a $950 million round led by Tiger Global and GV at a valuation above $15 billion.

**Watch out for:** no published rates, so every price is negotiated, and every growth figure above is the company's own.

**Pricing:** outcome-based, through sales.

**What would change its rank:** a published rate card.

**4. Salesforce Agentforce**

**Best for:** Salesforce shops that want agents across sales and service, not service alone.

**Why it ranks here:** the broadest product, and all its pricing models are published. Customer-facing agents can be bought at $2 per conversation, or on Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 credits, where a standard action costs 20 credits (about $0.10) and a voice action 30. Per-user add-ons for sales, service and field service are $125 a month with unmetered employee use, and Max Edition starts at $550 per user a month with 2.75 million Flex Credits a year included.

**Watch out for:** complexity. Flex Credits and per-conversation pricing cannot be used in the same org, switching means replacing every conversation SKU, and unused Flex Credits do not roll over. Salesforce notes the prices are for information and may change. With Fin also now under Salesforce, expect the two product lines to converge.

**Pricing:** $2 per conversation; Flex Credits $500 per 100,000; add-ons from $125 per user a month (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** a simpler buying model.

**5. Decagon**

**Best for:** enterprises that want a challenger with room to negotiate.

**Why it ranks here:** a $250 million Series D at a $4.5 billion valuation announced on 27 January 2026, which Decagon says tripled its valuation in under six months. It says it added more than 100 enterprise customers in its last fiscal year and names Avis Budget Group, Deutsche Telekom, Block, Affirm and Chime among them.

**Watch out for:** no published rates and no disclosed revenue. Reports have described a choice of per-conversation or a higher per-resolution price on annual contracts, but Decagon's own announcement does not mention pricing, and we could not confirm it.

**Pricing:** through sales.

**What would change its rank:** published pricing and independent resolution data.

## Side by side

|  | Fin | Zendesk AI agents | Sierra | Salesforce Agentforce | Decagon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Billing unit | Outcome, at most one per conversation | Verified resolution | Resolved case | Conversation, Flex Credit action or user | Not published |
| Who decides it counted | Customer confirmation or no further request | LLM verification by Zendesk | Not published | Metered by Salesforce | Not published |
| Published price, November 2026 | $0.99; qualification $9.99 | Tiers published; price via third parties | No | $2; $500 per 100,000 credits; $125 a user | No |
| Not billed | Greetings without an answer | Escalations and contained resolutions | Human takeovers | Depends on model chosen | Not published |
| Scale disclosed | 30,000+ companies | Not disclosed for AI | $150m ARR (Feb 2026); 40%+ of Fortune 50 | Not verified this month | 100+ new enterprise customers |
| Best fit | Any help desk; Salesforce owner | Zendesk shops | Large consumer brands | Salesforce shops | Negotiating enterprises |

> In an outcome contract, the definition of the outcome is the price. Read it before you read the rate.

## Left out, and why

**ServiceNow.** Strong for internal service desks, which is a different category; this list is about customer-facing agents, and we could not confirm a list price for its AI on its own pages this month.

## Three questions for any vendor

1. **Exactly what event triggers a charge, and who verifies it?** Fin bills on customer behaviour; Zendesk on its own model's verdict. Both are reasonable; neither is neutral.
2. **Show us last quarter's resolution rate for a customer like us, measured by the customer, not the vendor.** Ask for the reopen rate on billed resolutions alongside it.
3. **What happens to the price if our volume doubles, or halves?** Committed tiers, minimums and non-rolling credits all change the answer. Our explainer on [usage-based pricing for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/) covers how to model it.

Whatever you buy, keep a person on anything that commits the firm: refunds above a threshold, contract changes, anything legal. Our piece [Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out where that line usually sits.

## lowob takeaways

- **Fin ranks first on transparency.** $0.99 per outcome, published, but "outcome" now covers handoffs, disqualifications and routings.
- **Zendesk has the clearest billing rule.** Only LLM-verified resolutions are billed, since 18 May 2026.
- **Sierra has the growth and no rate card.** Outcome pricing, negotiated every time.
- **Agentforce publishes everything and simplifies nothing.** Three models, and two cannot be mixed.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for an AI customer-service agent

- The contract defines the billable event in one sentence
- You know who verifies that the event happened, and can audit a sample
- Escalations, greetings and reopened tickets are explicitly not billed
- The reopen rate on billed resolutions is reported monthly
- The price at double and half your current volume is written into the quote
- A person approves refunds, credits and contract changes above a set threshold

## Common questions

### How much do AI customer-service agents cost?

As listed in November 2026, Fin is $0.99 per outcome, Agentforce is $2 per conversation, Flex Credits at $500 per 100,000 or add-ons from $125 per user a month; Zendesk is reported at about $1.50 to $2.00 per verified resolution. Sierra and Decagon price through sales.

### What is outcome-based pricing for AI support agents?

You pay per counted result, such as a resolved conversation, rather than per seat. That makes the contract's definition of "resolved" or "outcome", and who verifies it, the most important terms.

### What counts as a resolution in Zendesk AI agents?

Since 18 May 2026, only a verified resolution is billed: the AI agent resolved the request, the customer did not ask for more help, and a language model reviewing the conversation confirmed it. Escalations and unverified containments are not billed.

### What should I ask an AI customer-service vendor before buying?

Exactly what event triggers a charge and who verifies it, last quarter's resolution and reopen rates for a similar customer measured by the customer, and what happens to the price if volume doubles or halves.

# What Is a Mutual Action Plan?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A mutual action plan is a document both buyer and seller can see, listing the steps to a decision and go-live, each with a date and an owner. It exists because buying groups are large and revisit decisions: Gartner found 95% go back at least once. A plan only helps when the buyer has agreed it, dates are real and each change is recorded.

A mutual action plan (MAP) is a shared document, agreed by buyer and seller, that lists the steps to a purchase decision and the start of work, each with a date and a named owner. It turns a close date the seller hopes for into a sequence the buyer has accepted. A plan the buyer never confirmed is a forecast assumption, not a mutual plan.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a mutual action plan means

Deals often slip on steps nobody listed: a security review, a legal redline, a budget sign-off in another department. A MAP lists those steps in advance, in the buyer's order, each assigned to a person on one side or the other.

Outreach account executive Ryan Jander, in a 2021 company blog post, calls it "a shared document that helps a buyer and seller collaborate on a shared buying process". His contents list includes a value summary, go-live dates, milestones, deadlines, an owner and outcomes. Aviso's product documentation calls it "a collaborative workspace designed to align buyers and sellers on key milestones", with buyer and seller roles and a due date on each action item.

| A mutual action plan is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| Agreed with the buyer and visible to them | An internal close plan the buyer never sees |
| A list of buyer and seller steps, each with an owner | A list of the seller's tasks only |
| Dated backwards from the buyer's go-live or decision date | Dated forwards from the seller's quarter end |
| Updated as steps move, with changes kept | Rewritten so it always looks on track |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Buying decisions are not linear. Gartner's buyer enablement research describes a typical buying group of six to ten stakeholders and six "buying jobs": problem identification, solution exploration, requirements building, supplier selection, validation and consensus creation. Gartner also found that 95% of buying groups go back to revisit decisions at least once as new information emerges. A plan must be able to record those loops.

Consensus is where deals stall. In a May 2025 release, Gartner reported that 74% of buyer teams in a survey of 632 B2B buyers showed "unhealthy conflict". Groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. A MAP does not create consensus, but it shows which members of the [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) have taken part and which steps wait on them.

It also tests the forecast. A deal in Commit needs evidence, as set out in [What Is a Forecast Category?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-forecast-category/). Buyer procurement and legal steps dated inside the quarter are that evidence; blank steps are a warning.

In **lowob**'s model, the MAP is a shared record of commitments, and each change is a small decision. When the buyer moves the security review back two weeks, the plan should show the old date, the new date and the reason. Some tools sync the plan into the CRM; Trumpet's help pages say its MAP on the HubSpot deal record "stays in sync". The reasons for changes still need recording. [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) applies to dates as much as to prices.

## How to build one

An illustrative MAP for a services engagement, dated backwards from the buyer's start date:

| Step | Owner | Side | Due | Evidence it is done |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Confirm problem and success measures | Head of operations | Buyer | Week 1 | Written success measures |
| Scoping workshop | Account lead | Seller | Week 2 | Agreed scope note |
| Proposal and pricing | Account lead | Seller | Week 3 | Proposal sent |
| Security and data review | IT lead | Buyer | Week 5 | Questionnaire returned |
| Commercial and legal terms | Procurement and counsel | Buyer | Week 6 | Redlines closed |
| Budget approval | Finance director | Buyer | Week 7 | Purchase order raised |
| Signature and kick-off date | Economic buyer | Buyer | Week 8 | Signed contract |

Write it with the buyer, not for them, working back from their decision date. Put buyer steps first, since sellers cannot control them. Review it at every meeting and record each date change with its reason.

Agents can draft the first version from past deals of the same type. Under **lowob**'s Gateway 1, the draft goes to the account lead before the client sees it, because a MAP sent in error commits the firm to dates the client never agreed.

## lowob takeaways

- **Mutual means the buyer agreed.** A plan the buyer has not confirmed is an assumption.
- **List buyer steps first.** Security, legal and budget approvals are where deals slip.
- **Keep the changes.** Every moved date is a small decision with a reason.

## Common questions

### What should a mutual action plan include?

The steps to a decision and go-live, each with an owner, a due date and evidence of completion, plus agreed success measures.

### What is the difference between a mutual action plan and a close plan?

A close plan is usually the seller's internal plan to win a deal. A mutual action plan is shared with and agreed by the buyer.

### When should you introduce a mutual action plan?

Once the buyer has confirmed a problem and a decision date, usually after discovery and before the proposal.

### Do mutual action plans shorten sales cycles?

Vendors say so, but the vendor material reviewed here gives no figures. The clearer benefit is earlier sight of buyer-side steps.

## Sources and notes

- [Outreach, How we're using mutual action plans to transform enterprise sales](https://www.outreach.ai/resources/blog/how-were-using-mutual-action-plans-to-transform-enterprise-sales), Ryan Jander, 26 October 2021, updated 2026. Vendor blog; no outcome figures given.
- [Aviso documentation, Mutual Action Plan](https://dochelp.aviso.com/mutual-action-plan), undated. Vendor product documentation, cited as a category example.
- [Trumpet Help Center, View and update mutual action plans in HubSpot](https://intercom.help/trumpet/en/articles/13638431-view-and-update-mutual-action-plans-in-hubspot), undated. Vendor product documentation, cited for CRM sync only.
- [Gartner, Buyer Enablement](https://gcom.pdo.aws.gartner.com/en/sales/insights/buyer-enablement), undated. Analyst research summary; survey of more than 250 B2B customers, no date given.
- [Gartner, Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict"](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), 7 May 2025. Analyst press release; 632 buyers surveyed August to September 2024.

# What Is an Agent Framework?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-framework/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An agent framework handles the plumbing of an AI agent: calling the model, running tools, keeping state between steps, pausing for a person and tracing what happened. LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Google's Agent Development Kit are the main options. Choose on state, approvals and tracing, and keep instructions and records outside the framework.

An agent framework is software that runs agent loops for you. It calls the model, executes the tools the model asks for, keeps state between steps, pauses for a person's approval and records what happened. LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Google's Agent Development Kit are the best-known options. Choose one on how it handles state, approvals and tracing rather than on demos, and keep your instructions, tests and decision record outside it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an agent framework means

Without a framework, a team writes the [agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/) by hand: send the prompt, parse any tool call, run the tool, append the result, handle errors, retry, enforce a turn limit, save state, and log every step. A framework packages that work. Our glossary's definition is short: software that runs agent loops, manages state and pauses for approval.

It helps to place a framework among the other layers an agent depends on.

| Layer | What it does | Examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Reads context and decides the next step | Claude, GPT, Gemini |
| Protocol | Standard way to reach tools or other agents | MCP for tools, A2A for agent-to-agent |
| Framework | Runs the loop, state, approvals, tracing | LangGraph, OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework, Google ADK, Claude Agent SDK |
| Hosting | Runs agents at scale | Azure AI Foundry, Google Cloud Run, a team's own servers |
| Record | What was decided, why, by whom, and with what result | Yours to keep |

A framework is not a model and not an agent. It is the harness one or more agents run in.

## What frameworks provide

The main options converge on a similar feature list, with different emphasis.

**State and durable execution.** LangGraph lists durable execution as a core capability, so agents "persist through failures and can run for extended periods". For commercial work this matters when a run must wait days for an approval and then resume where it stopped.

**Human in the loop.** LangGraph lets people inspect and modify agent state mid-run. The OpenAI Agents SDK lists built-in mechanisms for involving humans during runs. This is where autonomy levels are enforced in code.

**Guardrails.** OpenAI's SDK treats input and output validation as a primitive. A guardrail can block a draft that quotes a price outside policy before anyone sees it.

**Tracing.** OpenAI's SDK has built-in tracing; Microsoft says it contributed to OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard, so agent traces can flow into existing monitoring tools.

**Multi-agent patterns.** Microsoft's 1.0 release supports sequential, concurrent, handoff and group-chat orchestration. Google's ADK supports fixed "workflow agents" alongside model-led routing. Many commercial tasks need none of these at first.

**Open standards.** Microsoft names MCP, A2A and OpenAPI support. Standard tool interfaces are what keep a framework replaceable.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Most mid-size firms do not need to choose a framework first. An assistant with connectors covers answering and drafting, levels 0 and 1 on **lowob**'s dial. A framework becomes necessary when a firm builds its own agent that acts on systems: updating CRM records, routing approvals, or running overnight jobs at level 3.

The framework is wiring for the reasoning layer. Rent it. What should not live inside it are the things that carry a firm's judgment: the instructions, the precedents, the evaluation cases and the decision record. If those sit in plain files and databases you control, moving from one framework to another is an engineering task, not a loss of history. We compare five production options in [Top 5 agent frameworks for production](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/).

## What to check before choosing

| Question | Why it matters | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can a run pause for approval and resume days later? | Commercial approvals are slow | Checkpointed state that survives restarts |
| Can it stop before a named action? | Enforces the autonomy level | Per-tool approval or blocking hooks |
| Is every step traced and exportable? | Audit and debugging | Standard trace format, exportable logs |
| Does it support several model providers? | Avoids lock-in to one model | Documented support for more than one |
| Are tools connected through MCP or OpenAPI? | Keeps tools reusable | Standard interfaces, not custom glue |
| Is there a long-term support commitment? | Frameworks are young and change | Stable release with stated support |

## lowob takeaways

- **A framework runs the loop.** It handles state, tools, approvals and tracing.
- **Most firms need one later than they think.** Assistants with connectors cover answering and drafting.
- **Choose on state and approvals.** Demos show the happy path; pauses and resumes show the product.
- **Keep judgment outside it.** Instructions, precedents, tests and records stay yours.

## Common questions

### What are AI agent frameworks?

Software libraries that handle the repeated work of running an AI agent: calling the model, executing tools, keeping state, pausing for approval and logging each step. Examples include LangGraph, the OpenAI Agents SDK, Microsoft Agent Framework and Google ADK.

### Do I need an agent framework to use AI agents?

Not to start. Assistants with connectors cover answering and drafting. A framework matters when you build your own agent that acts on systems or runs unattended.

### What replaced AutoGen?

Microsoft Agent Framework, announced in October 2025 and released as 1.0 in April 2026, is the successor for new work. AutoGen now receives bug fixes and security patches only.

# LLM Observability vs Application Monitoring

Source: https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-vs-apm/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Application performance monitoring tracks latency, traffic, errors and saturation. LLM observability adds what those signals miss: prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, token cost and output quality. OpenTelemetry now defines conventions for both, so most firms should extend one telemetry pipeline rather than run two stacks.

Application performance monitoring (APM) tells you whether a service is available, fast and free of errors. LLM observability tells you what a model or agent was given, what it did, what it cost and whether the result was any good. A model call can return in under a second with a success code and still be wrong, so APM alone cannot see the failures that matter most in AI systems.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What each one measures

APM grew up around web services. Its core question is whether requests are served well. Google's *Site Reliability Engineering* book puts it simply: "If you can only measure four metrics of your user-facing system, focus on these four." Latency is the time to serve a request. Traffic is demand on the system. Errors are failed requests. Saturation is how full the service is. Traces show where time goes across services.

LLM observability starts from the same plumbing and adds a different question: was the output right, and why did the system produce it? That needs data APM tools were not built to hold. It needs the prompt and system instructions, the documents retrieved, each tool call and its result, token counts, model version, and a quality score attached afterwards.

|  | Application monitoring (APM) | LLM observability |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core question | Is the service up and fast? | Was the answer or action right, and at what cost? |
| Unit of analysis | Request, endpoint, host | Prompt, model call, agent run, tool call |
| Main signals | Latency, traffic, errors, saturation | Tokens, cost, retrieved context, tool calls, quality scores |
| Definition of failure | Error code, timeout, resource limit | Wrong, ungrounded or unsafe output, often with a success code |
| Who reads it | Engineering and SRE | Engineering, plus the owners of the business process |
| Typical content stored | Metadata and logs | Metadata, plus prompts and outputs if opted in |
| Standard | OpenTelemetry traces, metrics, logs | OpenTelemetry GenAI conventions, at Development stability |

## Where the two overlap

The good news for a mid-size firm is that the plumbing is converging. OpenTelemetry, the open standard for traces, metrics and logs, now defines generative AI conventions. They cover inference spans named after the operation and model, an `invoke\_agent` span for an agent run, and an `execute\_tool` span for each tool call. Standard attributes include input and output token counts. Two metrics, token usage and operation duration, sit alongside ordinary service metrics, and token usage can be priced to give cost per run.

Two cautions apply. First, the GenAI conventions are at Development stability and moved to their own repository in June 2026, so pin the instrumentation version you use. Second, content is opt-in. The conventions keep prompts and outputs out of span attributes and in a separate event, because that content often holds personal data. Many teams capture full content in testing and metadata only in production, or redact before data leaves their systems.

## What APM cannot see

A support agent that answers a refund question from an out-of-date policy will show normal latency and no errors. So will a sales assistant that drafts an email quoting the wrong price. Neither is a service failure; both are judgment failures. Catching them takes evaluation on top of telemetry: sampled human review, rule checks and model-graded scoring. Zheng and colleagues found GPT-4 as a judge agreed with human preferences over 80% of the time, about the rate humans agree with each other. They also documented position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so model graders need human spot checks.

## Which to choose

Most firms already run some APM. The decision is how far to extend it.

| Situation | What to use |
| --- | --- |
| One model call inside an existing app, internal users only | Existing APM with GenAI spans and token metrics |
| Customer-facing answers, or retrieval over company documents | Add an LLM observability or evaluation tool with content capture and scoring |
| Agents that call tools or write to systems | LLM observability with full agent traces, plus a decision record |
| Regulated outputs: advice, pricing, credit, claims | All of the above, with retention rules and named reviewers |

For the tools themselves, see the [Top 5 LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/).

## The **lowob** view

**lowob** places observability across two steps of the brain loop (store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning). Traces describe the reasoning step: what the model saw and did. They are not the record. A trace says an agent drafted a discount at 15%. The record says who approved it, why, and what outcome was expected. The learning step joins the two when the deal closes or does not.

Keep traces for engineers and short retention. Keep the record for the business and long retention. Write outcomes back to the record so quality scores reflect real results, not only a grader's opinion.

## lowob takeaways

- **APM sees service health.** Latency, traffic, errors and saturation, but not whether an answer was right.
- **LLM observability sees the run.** Prompts, context, tool calls, tokens and quality scores.
- **Extend one pipeline.** OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions let both share the same plumbing.
- **Traces are not the record.** Decisions, approvals and outcomes belong in a record the business owns.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between LLM observability and APM?

APM tracks whether a service is available and fast through latency, traffic, errors and saturation. LLM observability tracks what a model was given and did, its token cost, and the quality of its output.

### Can Datadog or another APM tool monitor LLMs?

Some APM tools now offer LLM features, and OpenTelemetry's GenAI spans give them a common format. Check whether a tool captures prompts, retrieved context and tool calls, and whether it supports quality scoring.

### Do I need to log prompts and responses?

For quality review, usually yes, at least on a sample. OpenTelemetry makes content capture opt-in because it often holds personal data, so set redaction and retention rules first.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, Site Reliability Engineering, chapter 6: Monitoring distributed systems](https://sre.google/sre-book/monitoring-distributed-systems/), Rob Ewaschuk. Primary practitioner text; predates LLM workloads.
- [Dash0, OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions explained](https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained), updated 15 September 2026. Vendor explainer of the specification; conventions may change.
- [OpenTelemetry, Semantic conventions for generative AI repository](https://github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai), accessed November 2026. Primary specification source; no tagged release at time of writing.
- [Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685), arXiv, June 2023. Academic study; agreement figures are for chat preference tasks, not business outputs.

## Related research

- [What Is LLM Observability?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/)
- [What Is an AI Audit Trail?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/)
- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [Top 5 LLM Observability and Evaluation Platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/)

## Next move

Pick the one AI feature your customers see and check whether you can pull a single run's prompt, retrieved context, output and cost today. If you cannot, add GenAI spans to your existing telemetry before buying anything new.

# Top 5 AI Notetakers for Decision Capture

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-notetakers-for-decision-capture/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Every notetaker now transcribes well; the difference is whether it helps you capture what was decided and why, whether you own and can export the record, and whether everyone knew they were recorded. Granola ranks first, then Fireflies.ai, Fathom, Circleback and Google Meet with Gemini notes, with prices as listed in November 2026.

Every notetaker now transcribes well. The difference is what happens next: whether it helps you pull out what was decided and why, whether you own and can export the record, and whether everyone on the call knew they were being recorded. Granola ranks first because it drafts notes you correct, deletes audio after transcription and exposes notes through MCP on every plan. Fireflies.ai, Fathom, Circleback and Google Meet with Gemini notes follow.

A notetaker is the capture end of what our explainer on [conversation intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversation-intelligence/) describes: software that records, transcribes and summarises calls. For decision capture the summary is not the point. What matters is getting three things out of the call and into a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) the same day: what was decided, why, and what would change your mind. **lowob**'s piece on [the reason nobody types](https://lowob.com/research/the-reason-nobody-types/) explains why the reason is the field that goes missing.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision and action extraction | 30% | A transcript is evidence; a decision record is what you use next month. |
| Ownership and export | 25% | Your meeting history should not be trapped in a vendor. |
| Consent and security | 25% | Recording without clear consent is now a legal risk, not just a manners question. |
| Price for a small team | 20% | Most useful features sit behind the first paid tier. |

Consent carries a quarter of the weight for a legal reason. Several US states, including California, require the consent of every party to record a confidential conversation. California's section 632 applies to anyone who records "without the consent of all parties to a confidential communication", with fines of up to $2,500 per violation for a first offence. A notetaker that joins a call without everyone knowing is a liability for the person who invited it, whatever the vendor's terms say. This is not legal advice; check the rules where your participants are.

## The list

**1. Granola**

**Best for:** founders who want notes they edit, without a bot joining the call.

**Why it ranks first:** it runs on your laptop or phone and uses the device's audio, then drafts notes from what you jotted during the meeting. In Granola's words, "Your notes stay in black. AI additions appear in gray." That draft-and-correct pattern keeps capture fast and keeps a person responsible for what the record says, which is the property a decision record needs. Granola says "audio is deleted after transcription on every plan", reports SOC 2 Type II certification since July 2025, and offers an MCP server on every plan, so notes can feed other tools and agents. A third-party tracker records a $125 million Series C at a $1.5 billion valuation in March 2026.

**Watch out for:** because no bot joins, the other people on the call get no visible notice. Granola's own guidance is simply to tell your team you are transcribing. You have to say it, every time. On the free tier, MCP covers only the last 30 days of notes and there is no API.

**Pricing:** Basic free with 30 days of history; Business $14 per user a month; Enterprise $35, adding SSO, SCIM, HIPAA-compliant workspaces and an audit API (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** a built-in consent notice for other attendees.

**2. Fireflies.ai**

**Best for:** teams that want summaries and action items pushed into a CRM.

**Why it ranks here:** broad integrations, annual independent SOC 2 Type II audits, and a clear statement that "Fireflies does not use your meeting data to train AI models", with its AI vendors contractually barred from doing so. Admins can manage retention, and Enterprise adds organisation-wide retention rules and a HIPAA option with private storage.

**Watch out for:** the free tier's shared pool of AI credits covers only a handful of summaries, and the meeting bot is visible, which is good for consent and sometimes awkward with external guests.

**Pricing:** Free; Pro $10 per user a month billed annually ($18 monthly); Business $19 ($29 monthly); Enterprise $39 billed annually (third-party summary of Fireflies' pricing, July 2026; we could not open Fireflies' own pricing page this month).

**What would change its rank:** stronger decision extraction, not just action items.

**3. Fathom**

**Best for:** teams that want the most useful free tier.

**Why it ranks here:** generous free use, with a choice of bot or bot-free capture on the free plan. Bot-free recording is marked beta and was reported to be Mac-only in 2026.

**Watch out for:** AI action items start on Premium, CRM field sync and deal views need Business, and SSO moved to Enterprise in July 2026. We could not verify Fathom's security certification against a report this month.

**Pricing:** Free; Premium $16 a month billed annually ($20 monthly); Team $15 per seat annually, two-seat minimum; Business $25 annually; Enterprise by quote (per a third-party tracker's snapshot of Fathom's pricing page, July 2026, checked October 2026).

**What would change its rank:** a SOC 2 report we can review.

**4. Circleback**

**Best for:** technical teams that want to wire meeting outputs into their own systems.

**Why it ranks here:** API, MCP and command-line access are included from the free plan, with automations into Notion, HubSpot, Salesforce, Attio and webhooks on Pro, and a bot-free desktop app as an option. Business adds custom data retention, which matters if your policy says how long recordings may be kept.

**Watch out for:** a small team behind it, and its pricing page does not state a security certification; check its security site before you connect it to client calls.

**Pricing:** Free with 30 days of history; Pro $15 per user; Business $25 with custom retention; Enterprise $35 with SSO, SCIM and HIPAA (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** evidence of scale.

**5. Google Meet with Gemini notes**

**Best for:** teams that live in Google Workspace.

**Why it ranks here:** "Take notes for me" is included in Business Standard and Business Plus, and the notes land in Google Docs that you already own and can export, with no extra vendor or data processor.

**Watch out for:** it works on Meet calls only, and not on Business Starter.

**Pricing:** included in Business Standard at $14 per user a month on an annual plan ($16.80 flexible) and Business Plus at $22 ($26.40 flexible), as listed in November 2026.

**What would change its rank:** support for calls on other platforms.

## Side by side

|  | Granola | Fireflies.ai | Fathom | Circleback | Google Meet with Gemini |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capture | Device audio, no bot | Meeting bot | Bot, or bot-free beta | Bot, or bot-free desktop app | Inside Meet |
| How notes are made | You jot, AI enhances, you edit | AI summary and action items | AI summary; action items on Premium | AI notes and custom insights | AI notes in Docs |
| Export and agent access | MCP on all plans; API on Business | CRM integrations | Integrations; CRM sync on Business | API, MCP and CLI from free | Google Docs |
| Training on your data | Audio deleted after transcription | Stated: no | Not verified | Not verified | Workspace terms |
| Security stated | SOC 2 Type II | SOC 2 Type II, audited annually | Not verified | Not stated on pricing page | Workspace controls |
| Entry paid price, November 2026 | $14 per user a month | $10 annual | $16 annual | $15 | Business Standard, $14 annual |

> The notetaker will catch the decision only if someone says it out loud. Say the decision, the reason and what would change your mind before the call ends.

## Left out, and why

**Otter.ai.** Large and capable, but a proposed class action filed in the US District Court for the Northern District of California in August 2025 alleges that its notetaker can join meetings without the consent of any participant when calendars are linked, and that recordings are used to train its AI without permission. Otter's privacy policy says it gets explicit permission for training and de-identifies audio first. Wait for the case to resolve before recommending it for decision records.

**Read.ai.** Its meeting "engagement scoring" can put attendees off, and enterprise security features sit on its top tier.

**tl;dv.** We could not confirm current prices on its own site.

**Zoom AI Companion and Teams Copilot recap.** Good if you are already on those platforms, but tied to one meeting tool.

## How to use any of them for decisions

1. **Say at the start of the call that it is being recorded, and why.** With a bot-free tool, this is the only notice anyone gets.
2. **Before the call ends, say the decision and the reason out loud.** Add who owns it and what would make you revisit it. The notetaker will catch it.
3. **Copy the decision, reason and "what would change our mind" into your decision record the same day.** Our list of [tools for a founders' decision ledger](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-tools-for-a-founders-decision-ledger/) covers where to keep it, and our piece on [the founders' ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) covers the habit.
4. **Set a retention period for recordings** that matches your policy, and delete the audio once the record exists.

## lowob takeaways

- **Granola ranks first for draft-and-correct notes.** Audio deleted after transcription, MCP on every plan, but no notice to other attendees.
- **Consent is a legal question.** All-party consent states such as California make an unannounced recording the host's problem.
- **Ownership means export.** Prefer tools with an API, MCP or notes in documents you already hold.
- **The record beats the transcript.** Say the decision and reason aloud, then write them down that day.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for a decision-capture notetaker

- Every attendee is told the call is recorded, and why, by the tool or by you
- The vendor states in writing whether it trains on your meetings
- Notes export through an API, MCP or documents you already own
- Recordings have a retention period you can set
- A security report you can read, not only a badge
- The first paid tier includes the features you will actually use

## Common questions

### What is the best AI notetaker for capturing decisions?

This list ranks Granola first for bot-free, draft-and-correct notes that you edit, followed by Fireflies.ai, Fathom, Circleback and Google Meet with Gemini notes.

### Is it legal to use an AI notetaker without telling people?

Not everywhere. California and several other US states require the consent of all parties to record a confidential conversation, and California's fines run up to $2,500 per violation for a first offence. Tell everyone on the call. This is not legal advice.

### How much do AI notetakers cost?

As listed in November 2026, Granola Business is $14 per user a month, Circleback Pro $15, Fathom Premium $16 billed annually, Fireflies Pro $10 billed annually, and Gemini notes come with Google Workspace Business Standard at $14.

### How do I use an AI notetaker to record decisions?

Announce the recording and why at the start, state the decision and reason aloud before the call ends, and copy the decision, reason and what would change your mind into a decision record the same day.

# Top 5 Tools for a Founders' Decision Ledger

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-tools-for-a-founders-decision-ledger/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: None of these tools is truly append-only; every one lets someone edit an old entry. The ranking is Notion, Slite, Airtable, Obsidian and Tana, judged on version history, open export, ease of the weekly habit, and AI drafting and price as listed in November 2026. A shared document with a weekly review beats a perfect database nobody opens.

None of these tools is truly append-only. Every one lets someone edit an old entry. What matters is how long the tool keeps history, whether you can get everything out in an open format, and whether it is easy enough that the weekly habit survives. Notion ranks first for flexibility and AI drafting, followed by Slite, Airtable, Obsidian and Tana. A shared document and a 30-minute weekly review beat a perfect database nobody opens.

A decision ledger is the simplest form of what our explainer on [decision records](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) describes: one entry per decision, with the reason, the owner, the alternatives rejected and the outcome you expect. The idea is older than any of these tools. Michael Nygard named the architecture decision record in 2011, and Martin Fowler's summary states the rule that matters most here: a record "should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded". **lowob**'s piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) argues the same for commercial decisions. No tool on this list enforces that rule, so the ranking is about how well each one lets you see what an entry said on the day it was written.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Version history | 30% | You need to see what an entry said when the decision was made, not after someone tidied it. |
| Open export | 25% | The record should outlive the tool. |
| Ease of the weekly habit | 25% | The ledger only works if people write in it within the hour. |
| AI drafting and price | 20% | Drafting entries from calls and memos makes capture cheap. |

## The list

**1. Notion**

**Best for:** teams that want a database of decisions with views by owner, date and status, plus AI drafting.

**Why it ranks first:** flexible enough to hold a proper decision record (decision, reason, what would prove it wrong, review date, outcome) and easy enough that people use it. A database of decisions can be filtered by owner and sorted by review date, which turns the weekly review into a single view. Custom agents can draft entries from meeting notes and memos.

**Watch out for:** page history is 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus, 90 on Business and unlimited only on Enterprise. On the cheaper plans, an entry edited three months after the decision can lose its original wording for good. Agents run on paid credits, at $10 per 1,000 credits after a free trial.

**Pricing:** Free; Plus $10 per member a month billed annually ($12 monthly); Business $20 ($24 monthly); Enterprise custom (as listed in October and November 2026, per a third-party snapshot of Notion's pricing page).

**What would change its rank:** longer history on cheaper tiers, or a locking feature for past entries.

**2. Slite**

**Best for:** teams that want a clear record of who and what changed an entry.

**Why it ranks here:** its June 2026 update made the activity log record where every edit came from, whether the app, the API, MCP or Slite's own agent, with three months of history backfilled. That matters more as agents start writing into the ledger: you can tell a person's edit from a machine's. MCP access is now included on all plans, including Basic, so an agent can read and draft entries.

**Watch out for:** a smaller vendor, less flexible than a database, and we could not confirm version history limits or security certification by tier on Slite's pages this month.

**Pricing:** Basic $10 per user a month billed annually ($12 monthly); Pro $20 ($25 monthly); Enterprise custom (as listed in November 2026, per a pricing tracker's snapshot of Slite's page). There is no free tier, only a 14-day trial.

**What would change its rank:** structured fields for falsifiers and review dates.

**3. Airtable**

**Best for:** teams that want a strict, structured ledger with required fields and linked records.

**Why it ranks here:** the most rigorous structure: every decision is a row, with required fields, links to evidence and views for review dates. Revision and snapshot history run for a year on Team and Business, which covers a full cycle of quarterly reviews. Read-only collaborators are not billed, so the whole company can read the ledger while only the people who write in it pay.

**Watch out for:** expensive for what a small team needs, and a year of history is not forever. Export the base before the year runs out on decisions you expect to revisit.

**Pricing:** Free with two weeks of history; Team $20 per collaborator a month billed annually ($24 monthly); Business $45 ($54 monthly); Enterprise Scale through sales (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** history longer than a year on the Team plan.

**4. Obsidian**

**Best for:** founders who want plain files they own outright.

**Why it ranks here:** the best answer on ownership: every decision is a Markdown file on your machine, readable by anything, for as long as the file exists. The app is "free without limits". Paid Sync adds version history across devices. Because files are plain text, you can also put the folder under version control, which gives you a permanent history of every change.

**Watch out for:** weak team permissions and no built-in AI, so it suits two founders better than twenty people. Obsidian's pricing page does not state how long Sync keeps version history; check before you rely on it.

**Pricing:** app free; commercial licence $50 per user a year; Sync $4 per user a month billed annually ($5 monthly) (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** better team sharing.

**5. Tana**

**Best for:** founders who think in outlines and want an AI meeting agent feeding the ledger.

**Why it ranks here:** an outliner with structure and a botless meeting companion for Zoom, Teams and Google Meet on every plan, so decisions can flow from calls into structured records. Tana lists SOC 2 Type 2 on all tiers.

**Watch out for:** a steep learning curve for new team members, which works against the weekly habit.

**Pricing:** Free; Pro $15 per member a month billed yearly; Business custom (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** an easier start for new team members.

## Side by side

|  | Notion | Slite | Airtable | Obsidian | Tana |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shape of the ledger | Database with views | Documents | Strict table with required fields | Markdown files | Structured outline |
| History on entry paid plan | 30 days (Plus) | Edit-source log; limits not verified | 1 year (Team) | Sync history; length not stated | Not verified |
| History on free plan | 7 days | No free plan | 2 weeks | Local files only | Not verified |
| Open export | Not verified this month | API and MCP | Not verified this month | Plain files you hold | Not verified |
| AI drafting | Custom agents on credits | Slite agent; MCP | Not ranked on AI | None built in | Botless meeting agent |
| Entry paid price, November 2026 | $10 a member a month, annual | $10 a user a month, annual | $20 a collaborator a month, annual | $50 a user a year licence | $15 a member a month, annual |

> The tool cannot stop someone editing an old entry. Only the rule can: never edit, always supersede.

## Left out, and why

**Google Docs.** The simplest option and often the right one for two founders. Not ranked because it has no structure, but a single shared document with a weekly review is a perfectly good ledger.

**Coda.** We could not confirm its current plans and direction on its own pages this month.

**Linear, Confluence and Attio.** An issue tracker, a heavyweight wiki and a CRM: each can hold decisions, none is built for it.

## A template that works in any of them

| Field | What goes in it |
| --- | --- |
| Date and decision | One line |
| Why | One or two sentences |
| Rejected | The alternatives you did not choose |
| What would prove it wrong | The signal, and the date to check it |
| Who disagreed | Their name and what they predicted |
| Outcome | Filled in on the check date |
| Supersedes | A link to the entry this one replaces, if any |

Never edit an old entry. Add a new one that supersedes it, and link the two. The field list follows the architecture decision record format, which Fowler describes as the decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences, adapted for commercial decisions. Our piece on [the field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) explains why "what would prove it wrong" is the one to protect, and our piece on [the founders' ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) covers how the habit starts with two people.

## lowob takeaways

- **Notion ranks first for flexibility.** But its page history is 7 to 90 days below Enterprise, so the supersede rule matters most there.
- **Airtable keeps a year.** One year of revision history on Team and Business, and readers are free.
- **Obsidian wins on ownership.** Plain Markdown files on your machine, readable by anything.
- **The rule beats the tool.** Never edit an old entry; supersede it and link the two.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for a decision ledger tool

- You know how long the plan you will actually buy keeps history
- An entry can be exported in an open format and read without the tool
- Writing an entry takes less than five minutes
- Each entry has a reason, an owner, a falsifier and a review date
- Superseding entries link to the ones they replace
- A weekly 30-minute review is in the calendar before the tool is bought

## Common questions

### What is the best tool for keeping a startup decision log?

This list ranks Notion first for flexibility and AI drafting, followed by Slite, Airtable, Obsidian and Tana. The habit matters more than the tool, and a shared document with a weekly review is a perfectly good ledger for two founders.

### How long does Notion keep page history?

As listed in October 2026, 7 days on Free, 30 on Plus, 90 on Business and unlimited only on Enterprise, so an edited entry can lose its original wording on cheaper plans.

### What should a decision log entry include?

The date and decision in one line, why, what was rejected, what would prove it wrong and when to check, who disagreed and what they predicted, and the outcome on the check date, plus a link to any entry it supersedes.

### Should you edit old entries in a decision log?

No. The architecture decision record practice is that an accepted record is never changed but superseded by a new one that links back, so the log shows what was believed at the time.

# What Is Revenue Intelligence?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-intelligence/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Revenue intelligence software captures sales activity from email, calendars and calls, joins it to CRM data and uses it to score deals, flag risk and support forecasts. In December 2025 Gartner folded the category into a wider market it calls revenue action orchestration. The evaluation questions are what activity it captures, whether its scores can be checked against outcomes, and what it is allowed to do without a person.

Revenue intelligence is software that captures what sellers and buyers actually do, such as emails, meetings and calls, joins it to CRM data and uses it to score deals, flag risks and support the forecast. It tests whether a deal is as healthy as the seller says. Gartner now files it within a wider market, revenue action orchestration, which adds AI assistants and agents that act on the signals.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What revenue intelligence means

A CRM records what sellers type in. Revenue intelligence adds what happened: emails, meetings, attendees and, through [conversation intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversation-intelligence/), what was said on calls. It compares that activity with the CRM's stage, amount and close date. A deal in negotiation with no buyer reply for three weeks is a risk the CRM alone does not show.

Salesforce's Trailhead material shows the typical parts: Revenue Insights dashboards, Pipeline Inspection, which "gives sellers a consolidated view of opportunities and pipeline metrics", and Salesforce Forecasting. Underneath sit Einstein Activity Capture, which syncs email and calendar data, deal health predictions and Opportunity Scoring from 1 to 99.

Gong's deal boards "integrate with your CRM while adding AI insights", show a timeline of calls and emails, and let users update CRM fields from the board.

| Component | What it does | Typical inputs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Activity capture | Logs emails, meetings and calls against accounts and deals | Email, calendar, dialler, video platforms |
| Deal scoring | Rates each deal's health or likelihood to close | Activity, CRM fields, past outcomes |
| Risk warnings | Flags patterns such as silence or one engaged contact | Activity and stage history |
| Pipeline inspection | Shows changes in amount, stage and close date over time | CRM history snapshots |
| Forecasting | Rolls deals into a forecast, with AI predictions beside seller calls | Forecast categories, scores, history |

## Where the category sits now

Gartner has redrawn the category lines. Its Magic Quadrant for revenue action orchestration, dated 15 December 2025, was the first for that market. Gartner's market page describes it as "a category of technology vendors that use AI to improve sales productivity" and says it "serves as the primary system of seller action and a single source of truth for sales interactions".

Gartner lists seven mandatory features: deal scoring and pipeline analytics, sales skills coaching, an AI sales assistant, data interoperability including Model Context Protocol support, advanced activity intelligence, AI-guided actions that can dispatch agents, and programmable action orchestration with governance controls. A vendor press release describes the category as uniting sales engagement, revenue intelligence and sales force automation; that is the vendors' summary. For a buyer, a "revenue intelligence" shortlist now spans products that only observe and products that also act.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The main use is deal and forecast review. A manager can see whether the buyer has replied, who attended meetings and how the close date has moved. How to combine these signals with seller calls is set out in [Forecasting That Holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/).

In **lowob**'s model, revenue intelligence spans the wiring and the reasoning layer: it reads the store and produces signals. Three cautions follow. A deal score is a prediction, so score it against what closed, like any forecast call. Acting on a signal moves up the autonomy dial. A warning is level 0 and a drafted follow-up level 1; an agent emailing the buyer waits, under Gateway 1, for a person to approve. And a score drop says a deal weakened, not what the team decided to do; that decision belongs in the decision record.

## How to evaluate it

| Criterion | Question to ask |
| --- | --- |
| Capture coverage | Which email, calendar, call and meeting sources does it read, and for which users? |
| Data handling | Where are captured emails and recordings stored, and who sees them? |
| Score transparency | Can a manager see which signals moved a deal's score? |
| Back-testing | Can past scores be compared with what actually closed? |
| CRM write-back | Do updates land in the CRM with the person who confirmed them? |
| Action controls | Which actions can agents take, at what autonomy level, with what approval? |
| Interoperability | Can other assistants read its data, for example through MCP? |

Start with one meeting: the weekly pipeline review for late-stage deals. Run it from the tool for a quarter and compare its risk flags with the deals that slipped.

## lowob takeaways

- **It shows what happened, not what was typed.** Activity data tests the seller's view of each deal.
- **Score the scores.** A deal score is a prediction and should be checked against outcomes.
- **Watch the line from flag to action.** Agents that act on signals move up the autonomy dial and need approval.
- **Reasons still need a record.** A falling score is a fact; the response to it is a decision.

## Common questions

### What is revenue intelligence software?

Software that captures emails, meetings and calls, links them to CRM deals, and uses them to score deals, flag risk and support the forecast.

### What is the difference between revenue intelligence and conversation intelligence?

Conversation intelligence analyses what is said on calls. Revenue intelligence uses that as one input, with email, calendar and CRM data.

### What is revenue action orchestration?

Gartner's name for a market, first assessed in December 2025, combining deal analytics, activity intelligence, coaching and AI-guided actions that can dispatch agents.

### Does revenue intelligence replace the CRM?

No. It reads from and writes back to the CRM, which remains the system of record for accounts and opportunities.

- [Gartner Peer Insights, Revenue Action Orchestration market](https://www.gartner.com/reviews/market/revenue-action-orchestration), undated. Gartner's market definition and mandatory features; the full Magic Quadrant is behind a paywall.
- [Business Wire, Clari Recognized as a Leader and Salesloft a Visionary in the First 2025 Gartner Magic Quadrant for Revenue Action Orchestration](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251216171118/en/Clari-Recognized-as-a-Leader-and-Salesloft-a-Visionary-in-the-First-2025-Gartner-Magic-Quadrant-for-Revenue-Action-Orchestration), 16 December 2025. Vendor press release; used only for the report date and the vendors' description of the category.

- [Gong Help Center, Understanding Gong deals](https://help.gong.io/docs/understanding-gong-deals), undated. Vendor product documentation, cited as a category example.

Take last quarter's slipped deals and check how many had no buyer reply in the final three weeks. If most did, activity data would have flagged them; that is the case for a trial.

# Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build

Source: https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At every company size, rent the context layer as it matures and own the record of how you decide. Most enterprises now buy rather than build their AI, which makes the decision record, and the right to take it with you, the part to control. What 'own' means grows from a document and a habit at two people to a governed service at ten thousand.

At every size, the same rule holds: rent the context layer as it matures, and own the record of how you decide. Models, connectors, search, assistants and agent registries are products you can rent and replace. Approvals, reasoning, decision history and the ability to change vendors are what the company must control. Most firms now buy rather than build their AI, so the practical question is less "build or buy" than what to keep portable, and that answer grows with headcount.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

AI tools make company information easier to find. But before buying an enterprise brain, decide what the company needs to retain control of: approvals, reasoning, history and the ability to change vendors.

The buy-versus-build question isn't settled for every business. Some teams rent models and search systems; others have specific reasons to build. The more useful starting point is deciding what information and decision history the company needs to control. Our [build vs buy guide for AI agents](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) covers the agent layer in detail.

## Most firms are already renting

The market has largely answered the narrow question. Menlo Ventures' survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers, fielded in November 2025, found 76% of AI use cases were purchased rather than built internally, against 53% a year earlier. Enterprise spend on generative AI reached an estimated $37 billion in 2025, split roughly evenly between applications and infrastructure.

Buying does not guarantee results. McKinsey's 2025 global survey found 88% of organisations using AI in at least one function but only 39% attributing any enterprise-level EBIT impact to it, most of them less than 5%. The high performers were more likely to have redesigned workflows and to have defined processes for when model outputs need human validation. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027. Rented tools are replaced often. That is exactly why the record of decisions should not live only inside them.

The question changes as the organisation grows. Buying everything can leave decision history locked into vendor tools; building every system internally can create complexity before anyone knows what is needed.

## What changes as the company grows

| Size | Buy or rent | Own | Don't build yet |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Two | A model, transcription, a shared document | The founders' ledger and the weekly review | Knowledge base, taxonomy, integrations |
| Ten | An assistant that can read your documents | The ledger, readable by strangers; first definitions | A wiki organised by topic |
| Fifty | Meeting and writing tools that export | Glossary with owners; decision rights; one home for records | An ontology |
| Two hundred | Workflow tools that can carry a precedent slot | Decision classes, templates, handover packs, first calibration | A platform team |
| One thousand | Enterprise search, agent registry, identity and permissions | Trace specification; function-owned records; evidenced review | A single enterprise ontology |
| Ten thousand | Most of the context layer, at scale and under contract | Central invariants, export format, calibration, the learning layer | Anything that forces divisions into one model |

These rows are **lowob**'s illustrations, not universal rules. Each rung has its own piece: [the founders' ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/), [the first stranger](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/), [when words start to mean different things](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/), [reasoning that travels without its author](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/), [when governance arrives](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/) and [the case for federation](https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/). For the commercial side of the same progression, see [Building the commercial system at 20, 50 and 200 people](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/).

The column worth reading twice is "Don't build yet". A precedent slot, described in [A loop with good context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/), is worth carrying at two hundred people because there are enough comparable decisions to fill it. At ten people, the same effort is better spent making the ledger readable by someone who was not in the room.

> Rented tools are replaced often. That is exactly why the record of decisions should not live only inside them.

## Three tests before buying anything that touches decisions

| Test | Question | Pass looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Export | Can the tool export every decision record, including its history, in a documented format? | A published schema and a sample export your team can read without the vendor |
| Replaceability | Will those records remain usable if the vendor is replaced? | Records stored as data with links, not as model state or prompts |
| Control | Does the company control retention and deletion for individual records? | Record-level retention settings and a deletion log |

If any answer is no, either negotiate it into the contract or keep the record elsewhere and let the tool read from it.

Regulation sets a floor in the EU. Since 12 September 2025, the Data Act has required providers of data processing services, SaaS included, to support switching within a 30-day transition and to port exportable data "including metadata", with switching charges eliminated from 12 January 2027. It does not cover everything a decision record holds, and it does not apply outside its scope, so the three tests still matter. [Whoever holds the record holds the company](https://lowob.com/research/whoever-holds-the-record-holds-the-company/) sets out the contract clauses.

For governance, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, released in January 2023 and intended for voluntary use, organises the work into four functions: Govern, Map, Measure and Manage. Its Generative AI Profile followed in July 2024. Neither prescribes the size-based rows above; they are a way to decide how much of that governance a company needs at each stage.

## The cost of getting it wrong in each direction

Over-building early costs time, money and, more subtly, accuracy: structures designed before the organisation knows what it needs encode guesses that later have to be unwound. An ontology built at fifty people fixes definitions the company has not yet argued about. Our piece on [what we would cut from the build order](https://lowob.com/research/what-we-would-cut-from-the-build-order/) lists the common cases.

Under-owning late costs more. An organisation that let its decision history accumulate inside several vendors' products discovers, at the first migration or audit, that its judgment is spread across systems it cannot query together and may not be able to export.

| Error | When it happens | What it costs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Over-building | Two to fifty people | Time, money, and definitions fixed before they were understood |
| Under-owning | Two hundred people and up | Decision history trapped across vendors; failed reconstruction at migration or audit |

## In practice

Start with the company-size guide above and check whether you are building something before you need it. Apply the three questions to tools that write important decisions, then review export and retention provisions with procurement, legal and security before the next contract renewal.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations that rent their entire judgment record inside vendor products, never owning it, and suffer no loss of capability or bargaining power through migrations, audits and renewals.

## lowob takeaways

- **Rent the tools, own the record.** Rent useful tools where they solve a real task; keep important decision records portable.
- **Use the size table as a starting point.** It is an illustration, not a universal architecture rule.
- **Run the three tests.** Export, replaceability and record-level retention, before committing.
- **Watch both errors.** Over-building early and under-owning late.

## Common questions

### Should a company build or buy its AI tools?

Mostly buy: 76% of enterprise AI use cases were purchased in 2025 in Menlo Ventures' survey. Rent models, connectors and search, but own the record of decisions, with reasons, history and outcomes, in a form you can take with you.

### What should a small company build for AI first?

At two to ten people, a decision ledger and a weekly review, with a model, transcription and a shared document rented. Knowledge bases, taxonomies and integrations can wait.

### How do I check whether an AI tool will lock in my decision history?

Ask whether it exports every decision record with history in a documented format, whether the records stay usable if the vendor is replaced, and whether you control retention record by record. If not, negotiate or keep the record elsewhere.

### When does a company need an enterprise ontology?

Rarely as a single model. Up to fifty people it fixes definitions too early; at a thousand or more, a single enterprise ontology usually forces divisions into one model. Owned glossaries and an export format travel better.

## Sources and notes

- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/), 9 December 2025. Investor research; survey of 495 US enterprise decision-makers.
- [McKinsey, The state of AI in 2025](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/artificial-intelligence/the-state-of-ai-2025), 5 November 2025. Self-reported survey of 1,993 respondents.
- [w.media, Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects could face the axe by end of 2027: Gartner](https://w.media/over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-could-face-the-axe-by-end-of-2027-gartner/), June 2025. Analyst forecast reported secondhand.
- [Cooley, New switching rules will become applicable in EU](https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2025/2025-09-08-paas-iaas-or-saas-be-aware-new-switching-rules-will-become-applicable-in-eu), September 2025. Law-firm summary of the EU Data Act; not legal advice.
- [NIST, AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework). Voluntary US framework; the company-size examples here are **lowob** illustrations, not NIST recommendations.
- The size table, three tests and cost comparison are **lowob**'s framework.
