# The Financial Data Providers Your Agents Can Call Today

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-financial-data-providers-your-agents-can-call-today/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: In about twelve months every major financial data provider adopted the same agent connection protocol, MCP, so agents can call licensed data from inside Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and the cloud marketplaces. FactSet ranks first because it is the only one that quantifies AI's share of growth; the others differ on disclosure, entitlements and how clearly they price.

In about twelve months every major financial data provider adopted the same agent connection protocol, MCP. Agents can now call licensed data from inside Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini and the cloud marketplaces. The providers differ on how much they disclose about real use, how tightly they enforce entitlements and how clearly they price. FactSet ranks first because it is the only one that has put a number on AI's share of its growth; S&P Global, LSEG, Moody's and Bloomberg follow.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

The Model Context Protocol is the shared standard that lets an agent discover and call a tool or data source without custom integration code for each one. Our explainer on [what MCP is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/) covers the mechanics, and our comparison of [MCP and API integrations](https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-api-integrations/) explains what changes and what does not. For a financial firm the change is commercial: the data you already license can now reach your agents through the same assistant your analysts use, and the provider has to check, every time, whether that agent is allowed to see it.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disclosed adoption | 35% | Client counts and usage growth, stated publicly, are the best available sign the integration works. |
| Breadth of AI surfaces | 25% | Whether your agents can reach the data from the tools your firm already uses. |
| Entitlements and audit | 20% | Every call should be checked against your licence and logged. |
| Pricing clarity | 20% | Consumption pricing is still being invented; clearer is better for budgeting. |

Most of the adoption figures below come from earnings calls and press releases. They are statements to investors and customers, not audited usage, and each provider counts differently: "engaged", "using or trialling" and "customers using" are not the same measure.

## The list

**1. FactSet**

**Best for:** buy-side and banking teams that want the provider with the most evidence behind its AI products.

**Why it ranks first:** it is the only peer that quantifies AI's share of growth. On its fiscal third-quarter call on 1 July 2026, its chief executive said "over 10% of the ASV growth came directly from AI SKUs", up from close to zero a year earlier. More than 450 clients were "actively engaged under contracts and trials" on its MCP service, more than 20% of its top 100 clients were using MCP on a paid basis, and call volume in the quarter was 13 times the previous quarter's. Clients can reach the data through all the major model platforms, including Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft.

**Watch out for:** its adjusted operating margin was 34%, down about 300 basis points year on year. The finance chief put that down to targeted investments, marketing and performance-related pay, plus a foreign-exchange hedging loss. Expect investment of that size to show up in pricing.

**Pricing:** most renewals in the quarter were enterprise agreements or multi-year terms, with FactSet seeking minimum commitments; management said consumption pricing for AI is growing but still modest relative to total subscription value.

**What would change its rank:** a peer disclosing comparable revenue attribution.

**2. S&P Global (Kensho)**

**Best for:** teams that use Capital IQ and want it inside their own agents.

**Why it ranks here:** on its second-quarter call on 28 July 2026, S&P Global said customers using its Kensho LLM-ready APIs and MCP-connected solutions "exceeded 500", up more than 70% on the quarter, with API call volume more than five times first-quarter levels.

**Watch out for:** S&P has not said what share of revenue these products bring in, and its reported adoption counts customers "using", which is a looser measure than paid contracts.

**Pricing:** not disclosed in the materials we reviewed.

**What would change its rank:** revenue attribution like FactSet's.

**3. LSEG**

**Best for:** teams already on Workspace who want its data through Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot or Gemini.

**Why it ranks here:** the broadest set of AI surfaces on this list. LSEG's MCP page names Claude, ChatGPT, Microsoft 365 Copilot, Gemini, Amazon Quick and Databricks, as well as its own Workspace and direct connections from clients' applications. Existing licensed credentials govern access, with no separate sign-up. At its half-year results in July 2026 it said it had engaged more than 200 customers on MCP since launching late in 2025, that tool calls rose nearly fivefold from May to June, and that MCP came up in about a third of its AI-related commercial discussions.

**Watch out for:** its finance chief said MCP revenue "would not materially affect 2026 results". Availability on partner platforms is, in LSEG's words, "subject to licensing and phased rollout".

**Pricing:** LSEG says it is already billing some customers under its pricing framework but does not publish it; ask your account team.

**What would change its rank:** published client numbers for paid use.

**4. Moody's**

**Best for:** credit, lending and compliance teams that want workflows, not just data.

**Why it ranks here:** it ships whole agent workflows rather than raw data. Its April 2026 partnership with Anthropic brought credit memo generation, peer comparison, scorecard assessment, entity profiling, ownership mapping, adverse media and sanctions screening into Claude through a purpose-built MCP application, over an estate of 600 million entities and 2 billion ownership links. A credit memo workflow is listed on AWS Marketplace. By its July 2026 call it reported more than 100 MCP and Smart API connections used or trialled by customers.

**Watch out for:** it has not disclosed AI revenue or a paying-client count. "Connections used or trialled" is the weakest adoption measure on this list.

**Pricing:** not published.

**What would change its rank:** a published commercial model and client count.

**5. Bloomberg**

**Best for:** large institutions that want their own agents to reach licensed Bloomberg data.

**Why it ranks here:** the most careful entitlement design. Its Enterprise MCP, launched for Data License Plus clients by October 2026, gives clients' agents access to more than 100 million securities and more than 50,000 fields, with field metadata and plain-language search instead of Bloomberg mnemonics. "Requests are checked against a client's entitlements before any data is returned", and tool-level limits cap how many securities and fields a single call can pull. It also ships reusable skills for tasks such as outlier detection and sanctions screening.

**Watch out for:** no adoption or pricing disclosed. Bloomberg hosts the service itself rather than listing in the major model catalogues, so your agents connect to it rather than finding it in an assistant's directory.

**Pricing:** offered under existing data licences; clients license the content domains they need.

**What would change its rank:** any disclosed usage.

> The question is not whether a provider supports MCP. They all do. It is whether every agent call is checked against your licence and written down.

## Left out, and why

**Fitch.** No AI platform of its own disclosed; it supplies content into a third-party platform instead.

**Morningstar.** An assistant inside its own adviser workflow, not yet a service other agents can call.

## Three questions for any provider

1. **Is every agent call checked against our licence, and can we see the log?** Bloomberg describes a per-request check; ask the others for the same in writing. Our explainer on [AI audit trails](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) lists what the log should hold.
2. **Does the licence forbid using the data to train models?** None of the pages we reviewed answered this. Get it in writing.
3. **How will pricing work at ten times today's call volume?** Agents use far more data than people: FactSet's call volume rose 13-fold in one quarter. Our explainer on [usage-based pricing for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/) covers how to model it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Every major provider now speaks MCP.** The differences are disclosure, entitlements and price.
- **FactSet has the strongest evidence.** Over 10% of subscription value growth from AI products and 450+ clients engaged.
- **LSEG reaches the most assistants.** Six named AI platforms, with existing credentials governing access.
- **Bloomberg has the clearest entitlement check and no disclosed use.** Ask for logs and training terms from all of them.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for agent access to licensed data

- Every agent call is checked against the firm's licence before data is returned
- Each call is logged with the agent, the user, the data and the time
- The contract states, in writing, whether the data may be used to train models
- Pricing is modelled at ten times today's call volume
- The provider names the AI platforms it supports and the rollout dates for yours
- Adoption claims are stated as paid clients, not "engaged" or "trialling"

## Common questions

### Which financial data providers support MCP for AI agents?

FactSet, S&P Global (Kensho), LSEG, Moody's and Bloomberg lead this list. Dun & Bradstreet, MSCI and Verisk also offer agent connections through ChatGPT or Claude.

### Which financial data provider has the strongest AI adoption?

FactSet, on disclosed evidence. In July 2026 it said more than 10% of its subscription value growth came from AI products, more than 450 clients were engaged on MCP, and call volume rose 13-fold in a quarter.

### Does Bloomberg have an MCP server?

Yes. Bloomberg's Enterprise MCP gives Data License Plus clients' agents access to more than 100 million securities and 50,000 fields, checking every request against entitlements. Bloomberg has disclosed no adoption or pricing.

### What should I ask a data provider before connecting agents to it?

Whether every agent call is checked against your licence with a log you can see, whether the licence forbids using the data to train models, and how pricing works at ten times today's call volume.

# Top 5 LLM Observability and Evaluation Platforms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-20 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The top five LLM observability and evaluation platforms, ranked for regulated teams, are Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize, Braintrust and Datadog. The deciding questions are whether you can self-host, whether it supports OpenTelemetry so you are not locked in, and whether human review is logged alongside traces. This guide compares them side by side, prices them at production volume and sets out where the OpenTelemetry standard stands.

The top five LLM observability and evaluation platforms for regulated teams are Langfuse, LangSmith, Arize, Braintrust and Datadog, in that order. For a regulated firm the deciding questions are whether you can host it yourself, whether it speaks the OpenTelemetry standard so you are not locked in, and whether human review is logged alongside the traces. The category consolidated hard in 2026: Humanloop is gone, Helicone is in maintenance mode and Galileo is now part of Cisco. Skip this list if you only need basic logs for a prototype.

This list is for teams that need to trace what their agents did, evaluate quality and show a supervisor the record. If the terms are new, start with [what LLM observability is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/) and [how it differs from application monitoring](https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-vs-apm/). The reason regulated firms care is the record itself: an [AI audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) has to show what the system saw, what it did and who approved it.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-hosting and data control | 30% | Many regulated firms cannot send prompts and outputs to a third-party cloud. |
| Open standards | 25% | OpenTelemetry support means your traces outlive your vendor. |
| Agent tracing and human review | 25% | The trace a supervisor needs includes tool calls and who approved what. |
| Price at production volume | 20% | Free tiers are small; real usage is where the bills differ. |

Every vendor fact and price below was checked on the vendor's own pages in November 2026. Prices are monthly list prices in US dollars. The ranks are unchanged from our October edition; where a fact has changed, we say so.

## The list

### 1. Langfuse

**Best for:** regulated teams that must self-host.

**Why it ranks first:** the core product is open source under the MIT licence and free to self-host "without any limitations", using Docker Compose or Kubernetes. Cloud plans run in US, EU or Japan regions. It accepts OpenTelemetry traces over HTTP at `/api/public/otel`, and spans carrying `gen\_ai.\*` attributes become generations with model, token and cost fields. ClickHouse acquired Langfuse on 16 January 2026 and said it "remains 100% open-source under its existing MIT license for core features" and that for self-hosted deployments "nothing changes". Fintechs Ramp and Trade Republic appear among the testimonials on its enterprise page.

**Watch out for:** roadmap risk after the acquisition. SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certify Langfuse Cloud, not your self-hosted copy. Audit logs, project-level access control and data retention management are paid Self-Hosted Enterprise features. Air-gapped deployment is listed under a separate Government edition, and Langfuse's enterprise FAQ says full air-gapped documentation is still in development.

**Pricing (November 2026):** Hobby free with 50,000 units; Core $29, Pro $199 and Enterprise $2,499 a month, each with 100,000 units. Overage is graduated per 100,000 units: $8 up to 1 million, $7 to 10 million, $6.50 to 50 million and $6 above. A unit is any tracing data point: a trace, an observation or a score. Self-hosted Enterprise is custom-priced.

**What would change its rank:** any move away from the open-source core.

### 2. LangSmith

**Best for:** teams building on LangChain or LangGraph.

**Why it ranks here:** deep integration with LangChain's frameworks, an OTLP endpoint at `/otel` that maps `gen\_ai.\*` attributes to LangSmith fields, and annotation queues for human feedback. Its documentation also shows how to send the same OpenTelemetry traces to other backends through a collector, which is the portability test in practice.

**Watch out for:** self-hosted and hybrid deployment are listed only on Enterprise. Base traces are kept for 14 days; extended traces are kept for 180 days at an extra fee that the pricing page does not state. LangChain's pricing page lists cloud data location as US or EU (November 2026). The pull towards the LangChain ecosystem is real.

**Pricing (November 2026):** Developer free for one seat with 5,000 base traces; Plus $39 per seat a month with 10,000 base traces, then pay as you go; Enterprise custom, invoiced annually.

**What would change its rank:** self-hosting below the Enterprise tier.

### 3. Arize (Phoenix and AX)

**Best for:** teams that want a free tool to start and an enterprise product to grow into.

**Why it ranks here:** Phoenix is free to self-host, and from version 15.10.0 (May 2026) converts OpenTelemetry GenAI attributes to Arize's OpenInference format on arrival, including tool calls. On 11 August 2026 Arize AX added native ingestion of `gen\_ai.\*` spans, keeping the original attributes on each span.

**Watch out for:** the Pro tier covers 50,000 spans a month with 30-day retention, so production use means Enterprise pricing. Self-hosting AX is Enterprise only. Human-review logging was the least documented of the five in the pages we checked.

**Pricing (November 2026):** AX Free with 25,000 spans and 15-day retention; Pro $50 a month; Enterprise custom. Listed overage is $0.0008 per span and $3 per GB.

**What would change its rank:** clearer human-review features.

### 4. Braintrust

**Best for:** teams whose main problem is evaluation, not monitoring.

**Why it ranks here:** built around experiments, scoring and human review, with unlimited users, playgrounds and experiments on every plan, configurable human-review scores, OTLP ingestion at `api.braintrust.dev/otel/v1/traces` and SOC 2 Type II.

**Watch out for:** no open-source edition is listed, on-premises deployment is an Enterprise option, and a HIPAA business associate agreement is Enterprise only. We found no named regulated financial customers on the pages we checked. In October we cited a reported funding round and named customers; we could not reconfirm them on a primary source for this edition and have removed them.

**Pricing (November 2026):** Starter free; Pro $249 a month with 5 GB of processed data ($3 per GB after) and 50,000 scores ($1.50 per 1,000 after); Enterprise custom. Pro retention is 30 days, extendable to 180 days at $0.50 per GB a month.

**What would change its rank:** a regulated reference customer.

### 5. Datadog LLM Observability

**Best for:** firms already running Datadog for everything else.

**Why it ranks here:** tracing across "prompts, retrieval steps, tool calls, and agent decisions", evaluations, annotations and human review, and OpenTelemetry ingestion, inside the monitoring tool many operations teams already use. Datadog now markets the product as Agent Observability.

**Watch out for:** SaaS only; the local tracing option is for development, not a self-hosted backend. Default retention is 15 days, with paid add-ons to 30, 60 or 90.

**Pricing (November 2026):** Free up to 40,000 LLM spans; Pro $160 a month for up to 100,000 LLM spans, where an LLM span is one call to a model provider. On-demand use above that is billed at a rate the page does not state. In October we could not confirm pricing at all; it is now published, which narrows but does not remove this watch-out.

**What would change its rank:** a self-hosted option, or a published overage rate.

## Side by side

|  | Langfuse | LangSmith | Arize | Braintrust | Datadog |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Self-hosting | Yes, free (MIT core); paid Enterprise adds audit logs and retention controls | Enterprise only (self-hosted, hybrid, BYOC) | Phoenix free; AX on Enterprise | Enterprise only | No |
| OpenTelemetry | OTLP over HTTP; maps `gen\_ai.\*` | OTLP; maps `gen\_ai.\*`; documents fan-out export | Native `gen\_ai.\*` in AX (Aug 2026) and Phoenix (May 2026) | OTLP endpoint; GenAI mapping not named on page | Accepts OpenTelemetry |
| Agent and tool tracing | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Human-review logging | Scores on traces and observations | Annotation queues | Least documented | Human-review scores | Annotations and human review |
| Retention at list price | 30 days (Hobby) to 3 years (Pro, Enterprise) | 14 days base, 180 days extended | 15 to 30 days; configurable on Enterprise | 14 to 30 days; up to 180 paid | 15 days; add-ons to 90 |
| Pricing model | Platform fee plus graduated per-unit | Per seat plus per trace | Tier plus per span and per GB | Platform fee plus per GB and per score | Tier per LLM span |

> A trace that expires after 14 days is a debugging aid. A supervisor's record has to outlast the review cycle.

## Where the OpenTelemetry GenAI standard stands

The case for OpenTelemetry is that your traces outlive your vendor. The status of the standard tempers that case without undoing it.

Every `gen\_ai.\*` span, metric and attribute is at Development status, the earliest of OpenTelemetry's maturity levels, which run through Alpha, Beta and Release Candidate to Stable. Dash0's guide, updated in September 2026, notes that only three attributes on a GenAI span are stable, all inherited from the core conventions, and that GenAI attributes can be renamed between releases. On 12 June 2026, in version 1.42.0, the GenAI conventions moved out of the core repository into a separate `semantic-conventions-genai` repository, which covers spans, metrics and events for GenAI clients, MCP and provider-specific conventions. That repository has no tagged release and lists its schema URL as "TODO".

The conventions already define agent operations such as `invoke\_agent` and `execute\_tool`, and an agent calling a tool over MCP emits the same `execute\_tool` shape as a direct call. Vendors are converging on them in different ways. Arize maps them into its own OpenInference schema and keeps the originals; LangSmith maps them and flags some as deprecated; Langfuse turns them into generations.

| What the status means | Practical step |
| --- | --- |
| Attribute names can change without a deprecation window | Pin the instrumentation library version and record which schema it targets |
| Vendors map `gen\_ai.\*` into their own schemas | Ask whether the original attributes are kept on export |
| No stable release yet | Treat OTLP export as the exit route, and test it before you need it |
| Agent and MCP spans are defined but not stable | Check that tool calls and agent steps survive a round trip to a second backend |

Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers what the scores attached to these traces should measure.

## What it costs at volume: a worked example

The example is illustrative. A team runs an agent 20,000 times a day, or 600,000 runs in a 30-day month. Each run produces one trace with 10 spans, of which 3 are model calls, plus one quality score. Each run carries about 20 KB of prompt and output data. The calculation uses each vendor's mid-tier plan at November 2026 list prices.

| Vendor and plan | Billed quantity | Calculation | Monthly list cost | Retention |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Langfuse Pro | 7.2 million units (trace, 10 observations and a score per run) | $199 + 9 × $8 (to 1 million) + 62 × $7 (to 7.2 million) | $705 | 3 years |
| Braintrust Pro | 12 GB processed; 600,000 scores | $249 + 7 GB × $3 + 550 × $1.50 | $1,095 | 30 days |
| Arize AX Pro | 6 million spans | $50 + 5.95 million × $0.0008, before any GB charge | $4,810 | 30 days |
| LangSmith Plus | 600,000 traces, plus seats at $39 | Per-trace rate not stated on the pricing page | Ask for a quote | 14 days |
| Datadog Pro | 1.8 million LLM spans | $160 covers 100,000; on-demand rate not stated | Ask for a quote | 15 days |

Three things follow. The cheapest list price here also comes with the longest retention, which supports Langfuse's rank. The billing unit drives the answer as much as the rate: Braintrust charges by data and scores, so the same workload with 100 KB per run would add about $144 in data, while scoring every run is the largest line. And at this volume Arize Pro is no longer the right plan; the figure shows why a team would move to Enterprise pricing. Self-hosting Langfuse or Phoenix replaces the licence fee with your own infrastructure and staff cost, which this table does not price.

## Gone, folded in, or left out

**Humanloop.** Its changelog announced "Humanloop joins Anthropic" and the platform was sunset on 8 September 2025, after which its data became permanently inaccessible.

**Helicone.** Acquired by Mintlify, announced 3 March 2026. Helicone says its services "will remain live for the foreseeable future in maintenance mode", with security fixes and new models still shipping, and Mintlify is helping customers migrate.

**Galileo.** Cisco has completed its acquisition, and Splunk now sells it as "Galileo, now Splunk Agent Observability".

**W&B Weave.** Now part of CoreWeave, a GPU cloud; its roadmap may follow that business.

**PromptLayer.** Strong on prompt management, narrower on full observability.

Analysts are catching up. Gartner published its first *Market Guide for AI Evaluation and Observability Platforms* on 2 February 2026, and, as quoted by Comet, predicted that 60% of software engineering teams will adopt such platforms by 2028, up from 18% in 2025. The Humanloop case is the strongest argument for the export test below: a vendor that closes can take three years of records with it.

## Buyer's checklist

Three questions for any vendor. Can we run it entirely inside our own environment, and what features do we lose? If we leave, can we export every trace in OpenTelemetry format? Show us one agent run with its tool calls and the human approval, on one screen.

The checklist below turns those questions into a test you can run in a two-week trial. Our pieces on [governance and audit trail tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/) and on [reviewer minutes per useful decision](https://lowob.com/research/reviewer-minutes-per-useful-decision/) cover what happens to the record after it leaves the observability layer.

## lowob takeaways

- **Langfuse ranks first for regulated teams that must self-host.** Check which controls, such as audit logs, sit in the paid self-hosted edition.
- **Self-hosting is an Enterprise line item everywhere else.** Datadog does not offer it.
- **OpenTelemetry is the exit route, not yet a guarantee.** The GenAI conventions are at Development status; pin versions and test export.
- **Price the workload, not the plan.** Units, spans, traces and gigabytes give very different bills for the same agent.
- **Retention is a compliance question.** Fourteen days suits debugging; a supervisor needs the review cycle covered.

Gateway card

### Before you sign an observability contract

- A self-hosted or in-region deployment option, with the list of features it lacks
- An OTLP export of a full agent run, re-imported into a second backend, with tool calls intact
- One agent run showing tool calls and the human approval on one screen
- Retention at your plan level that covers your review and audit cycle
- A monthly cost calculated on your own runs, spans and data volume, including overage
- A written answer on data residency, certifications for the deployment you will use, and what happens to your data if the product is sold or closed

## Common questions

### What is the best LLM observability platform for regulated companies?

Langfuse ranks first because its core is open source and free to self-host, it accepts OpenTelemetry traces and records agent and tool steps. Check that audit logs and retention controls are in the paid self-hosted edition.

### How much does Langfuse cost?

Hobby is free; Core is $29, Pro $199 and Enterprise $2,499 a month, each with 100,000 units, then $8 per 100,000 units falling to $6 at volume, as listed in November 2026. Self-hosting the open-source core is free.

### Is the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic convention stable?

No. As of November 2026 the GenAI conventions are at Development status and moved to a separate repository in June 2026 with no tagged release. Pin your instrumentation version and test export.

### What happened to Humanloop and Helicone?

Humanloop joined Anthropic and its platform was sunset on 8 September 2025. Helicone was acquired by Mintlify, announced 3 March 2026, and runs in maintenance mode.

# What Is an AI Autonomy Level?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI autonomy level is a design setting for how much an agent may do without a person, chosen per task and separate from model capability. lowob uses a five-step dial from answer to act alone. Usage data shows autonomy drifts upward as people get used to an agent, so the level should be set and changed on evidence.

An AI autonomy level is a setting that states how much an AI system may do without a person: answer a question, draft work, act once approved, act and report afterwards, or act alone. It is a design decision made for each task, separate from how capable the model is. **lowob** uses a five-step dial from 0 to 4. Most commercial value today sits at levels 1 to 3, and anything that reaches a client stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an autonomy level means

The idea comes from driving. SAE International's J3016 standard, last revised in 2021, defines six levels of driving automation, from 0 to 5, by who performs the driving task and whether a human must respond when asked. **lowob**'s dial asks the same of work: what the agent may do before a person is involved.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

| Level | What the agent does | What the person does | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0. Answer | Responds to a question | Decides and acts | "What did we quote this client last year?" |
| 1. Draft | Prepares work in a queue | Reviews, edits and sends | A renewal email waiting for the account owner |
| 2. Act with approval | Acts once a named person approves | Approves each action | Moves deal stages after a manager signs off |
| 3. Act and report | Acts within fixed bounds, then reports | Reads the report, can reverse | Tags lead sources overnight and sends a summary |
| 4. Act alone | Acts with no review inside hard limits | Monitors and can switch off | Rare in commercial work today |

The level belongs to a task, not to an agent. One agent can answer pricing questions at level 0 and update CRM fields at level 3.

## How it compares with other scales

Other frameworks map onto the dial only roughly. The Knight Institute paper, by Kevin Feng, David McDonald and Amy Zhang, defines five levels by the user's role, from operator to observer, where the only control left is an emergency off-switch. It also proposes "autonomy certificates" stating the maximum level an agent may operate at. AWS's matrix, built for security teams, pairs each scope with the controls it needs.

| **lowob** dial | Nearest AWS scope | What AWS says the scope means |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 Answer, 1 Draft | Scope 1: No agency | Read-only; recommends but cannot change systems without a person acting |
| 2 Act with approval | Scope 2: Prescribed agency | Proposes and prepares changes; a person approves each one before it runs |
| 3 Act and report | Scope 3: Supervised agency | Acts within set limits without per-action approval; needs monitoring and shutoff |
| 4 Act alone | Scope 4: Full agency | Self-initiating, continuous, minimal oversight; needs the most advanced controls |

The mapping is **lowob**'s reading of the AWS definitions, not an AWS equivalence.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Autonomy drifts unless someone sets it. Anthropic's study of millions of interactions found new Claude Code users (under 50 sessions) used full auto-approve in roughly 20% of sessions, rising to over 40% for experienced users. Experienced users also interrupted more often, in about 9% of turns against 5% for new users. Oversight shifted from approving each step to watching and stepping in. That is a move from level 2 to level 3, made by habit rather than by decision.

The same study shows where commercial risk concentrates. Across nearly a million API tool calls, only 0.8% of actions appeared irreversible, and Anthropic's example of one was sending an email to a customer. Software engineering accounted for nearly half of tool calls; sales, finance and customer service each took a few percentage points. Commercial agent use is early, and its riskiest actions are the ones that leave the building. That is why **lowob** holds client-facing work at level 2 or below: nothing sends without a person.

## How to set and change a level

1. **List tasks, not agents.** Record each task's level, owner and what the agent may touch. Our [agent task directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/) rates sixty commercial tasks this way.
2. **Start low.** Most first agents belong at level 1.
3. **Promote on evidence.** Set a review date and a test, such as four weeks of logs with edits to drafts below an agreed rate. Approval rate alone is weak, because reviewers tire.
4. **Demote on incident.** One wrong client-facing action resets the task to level 1.
5. **Keep a switch.** From level 3 up, someone must be able to stop the agent at once.

## lowob takeaways

- **Autonomy is a dial, not a switch.** Five levels, set per task.
- **Capability does not set the level.** A strong model can still run at level 1.
- **Habit raises autonomy quietly.** Usage data shows auto-approval doubling with experience.
- **Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below.** Promote only on logged evidence.

## Common questions

### What are the levels of autonomy for AI agents?

Scales differ. **lowob** uses five: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. Academic and vendor scales use four to six levels, counting the user's role or the controls required.

### What autonomy level should an AI sales agent have?

For anything a client will see, level 2 or below: the agent drafts or prepares, and a named person approves before it sends. Internal housekeeping such as CRM tagging can reach level 3 with a nightly report.

### Is autonomy the same as capability?

No. Capability is what an agent can do; autonomy is what it is allowed to do without a person. A highly capable agent can be required to ask before every action.

## Sources and notes

- [Feng, McDonald and Zhang, Levels of Autonomy for AI Agents](https://knightcolumbia.org/content/levels-of-autonomy-for-ai-agents-1), Knight First Amendment Institute, 28 July 2025. Academic working paper; the certificate idea is a proposal, not a standard.
- [AWS, Agentic AI Security Scoping Matrix](https://aws.amazon.com/ai/security/agentic-ai-scoping-matrix/), undated web page, accessed November 2026. Vendor framework.
- [Anthropic, Measuring AI agent autonomy in practice](https://www.anthropic.com/research/measuring-agent-autonomy), 18 February 2026. Vendor research on its own products; human-involvement figures are stated as upper bounds.
- [ANSI blog, SAE levels of driving automation, J3016-2021](https://blog.ansi.org/sae-levels-driving-automation-j-3016-2021/). Secondary summary of a paid standard.
- The five-level dial and the promotion rules are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [What Is an Approval Gate for AI Agents?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/)

## Next move

Take every AI tool your commercial team uses and write one line per task: the autonomy level it runs at today, and who decided that. Any task without a named decider is your first review.

# Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide

Source: https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Most company communities are audiences with a chat room, recruited for a payout and measured by headcount. This guide brings together lowob's research on community into one sequence: name what you have, give it a job, recruit the first hundred by hand, design the spaces and roles, treat incentives as acquisition costs, and measure contribution and retention after the money stops.

A community that lasts is a group of people doing a job together, with a reason to return that does not depend on being paid. Most company communities fail one of three tests: they are audiences rather than groups whose members create value for each other, they were recruited with incentives that selected for people who leave, or they are measured by member count, which says little about either. This guide sets out the sequence **lowob** recommends, from naming what you have to measuring who is still there after the incentives stop, and points to the article that covers each stage in depth.

## Why most communities do not last

Three findings explain most failures, and they come from different kinds of evidence.

**Participation is unequal by nature.** Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: in most online communities about 90% of people read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 observational study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research tested this in four digital health networks with 63,990 members. The top 1% wrote 74.7% of posts, the next 9% wrote 24.0% and the other 90% wrote 1.3%. Adding members mostly adds readers. A community lasts if its small active core lasts.

**Newcomers leave fast unless someone responds.** Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got none. On English Wikipedia, Halfaker and colleagues found active editor numbers stopped growing in early 2007 and then declined, driven by falling retention of good-faith newcomers whose first edits were increasingly reverted. Groups that ignore or reject first contributions stop renewing themselves.

**Incentives select for people who leave.** In a study of nine major airdrops, Messias, Yaish and Livshits found up to 66% of tokens were sold soon after claiming in some cases, and concluded airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own". Two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed 93% of recipients had sold all their UNI and about 98% had never voted in governance.

The field still counts heads. CMX's 2025 survey of 589 community professionals found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%, and only 24% could confidently put a financial value on their community.

## The guide in one table

| Stage or problem | The question it answers | Read |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Naming what you have | Is this an audience, a user base, a network or a community? | [Audience vs community](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-audience/) |
| Choosing the job | What work does the community do that the company would otherwise pay for? | [Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) |
| Recruiting the first hundred | Who do we ask, what do we ask, and how do 30 names become 100? | [The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) |
| Running the first hundred | What counts as caring, which ritual, which roles, when to grow? | [Find your first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/) |
| Designing the spaces | Which channels, rules and platforms does the job need? | [Discord is not a community strategy](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/) |
| Staffing | Who runs it, and is that a social media job? | [Community management vs social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) |
| Using incentives | What do airdrops, points, ambassadors and referrals teach members? | [Airdrops can buy attention](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) |
| Surviving a token distribution | How do we keep users after the airdrop? | [Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) |
| Paying creators | How do we know whether a KOL campaign produced users? | [KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) |
| Media and paid membership | How does a newsletter audience become a membership? | [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/) |
| Turning around a silent group | What do we do with 40,000 members who do nothing? | ["40,000 members and nobody does anything"](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/) |

## Stage 1: Name what you have

An audience receives. A customer transacts. A user engages with a product. A network participant, such as a developer, liquidity provider or node operator, makes a shared system more useful. A community member participates in a group whose value is partly created by other members. One person can be all of these, but the strategies differ.

The quickest test is the peer-value test: remove the company for a week and see whether members still help each other, share knowledge and organise. If activity stops, the company has an audience or a support channel. That is not a failure. The mistake is designing for one group while measuring another.

The test can also be run on data. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found members replied to each other 28% of the time outside GitHub, against 13% for staff. Where staff answer everything, the community is a help desk.

Some companies should stop here: products that need onboarding and support more than peer relationships should invest in those. Our piece on [audience vs community](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-audience/) sets out the four groups, the "members return because" sentence and when not to build a community at all.

## Stage 2: Give it a job

A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for. **lowob**'s framework names five jobs:

| Job | What members do | Contribution measure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Test | Use early builds, report bugs, give feedback | Bugs found, release sign-offs |
| Teach | Answer questions, write guides, onboard newcomers | Share of questions answered by members |
| Refer | Bring customers, partners or hires | Referred sign-ups and their conversion |
| Build | Integrate, extend, ship on top of you | Integrations and plugins in use |
| Govern | Make decisions with real consequences | Participation by people who are not whales or the team |

Pick one or two. A community asked to do all five does none of them well.

Governance needs particular care in crypto. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap found only about 5% of tokens were cast on a typical proposal and the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote. Counting the largest wallets measures concentration, not community.

The job also protects against platform risk. On 15 January 2026, X revoked API access for apps that paid users to post, and The Block reported the KAITO token fell 14.5% that day. [Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) covers the design choices that follow from each job: channel, rituals, recognition and ownership of the record.

> Silence is the correct response to no job. A community with nothing to do will do nothing, however many people are in it.

## Stage 3: Recruit and run the first hundred

The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Paul Graham's essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" makes the general point for start-ups: "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually."

**lowob** splits this stage across two pieces.

**[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) covers recruitment.** List 30 names: potential customers, respected builders, operators and sharp critics. Ask each for judgment on a real decision rather than attention. Give those who say yes a job with an end date. Close the loop in public, so they can see what changed because of them. Ask each for the next name. Because participation is unequal, the aim is to get the people who will do most of the work into the first hundred.

**[Find your first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/) covers operation.** Define an active member by behaviour (answering a question, testing the product, creating a resource, returning over several weeks) rather than by joining. Write a narrow member thesis. Start with one recurring ritual, such as a weekly teardown or an integration clinic, and make sure every newcomer's first question gets answered, which is what the Kraut findings point to. Give members consequential roles, run a weekly member-health review and invite the next cohort only when the first is getting consistent value. Growth through density beats growth through size: Common Room found engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, highest in smaller communities.

Kraut and Resnick's *Building Successful Online Communities* (MIT Press) turns the research behind this stage into design claims on contribution and commitment.

For media businesses, the first hundred are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in a sponsor deck. [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/) applies the same recruitment by name to paid membership, where the market is tight: the Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found 17% of people across 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news.

## Stage 4: Design the spaces and staff them

Opening a Discord or Telegram is one of the fastest ways for a project to feel operational. The interface resembles a community before the relationships exist. [Discord is not a community strategy. Neither is Telegram.](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/) argues for starting with the jobs members need the environment to do, then building a small architecture: a start-here space with rules and security warnings, read-only announcements, structured help, one or two discussion spaces, a contribute space and events.

Platform metrics help if read correctly. Discord's Server Insights tracks visitors, communicators who post, and the share of new members who return after a week, and suggests about 30% communicators as a healthy goal. These measure presence, not whether the job is getting done.

Staffing follows from the same logic. [Community management vs social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) sets out why they are different jobs. Social media management is editorial: the company's voice on its accounts. Community management is hosting: members' voices in the company's spaces. Combining them by default means one gets neglected, and which one depends on the person's temperament rather than the company's needs. The resourcing gap is real: CMX found 17% of organisations had no one working full time on community, the highest share it had recorded.

## Stage 5: Use incentives as acquisition costs

Incentives can overcome a cold start, distribute ownership and reward early users. They also redefine what participation means. If a project rewards transaction count, participants maximise transactions; if it rewards posting, they maximise posts. [Airdrops can buy attention. They cannot buy belief.](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) sets out the questions to answer before launching any incentive: the behaviour being rewarded, the durable value it creates, how it can be farmed and what happens when the reward ends.

The evidence on airdrops is consistent. Beyond the Messias and Dune findings above, Keyrock, a crypto market maker, reviewed 62 airdrops in 2024 and found only eight trading above their launch price after 90 days, with larger distributions holding up better than small ones.

[Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) turns this into a plan. Treat the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected sell-through. Weight allocation to repeated usage over time. Build sybil filters before the snapshot, publish the rules and keep an appeals channel a human reads. Give holders a job: test, curate, govern or refer.

Paid creators are the same problem in a different channel. [KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) argues for defining the action before buying placements and judging spend by cost per activated, retained user rather than reach. For the wider cost logic, see [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/).

## Stage 6: Measure contribution and retention

Member count is the easiest number to inflate and one of the weakest indicators of health. Replace it with measures that match the job and show whether people stay.

| Measure | What it shows | Where it fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaningful first contributions by newcomers | Whether people move past reading | Every community |
| Time to a useful response | Whether newcomers are being answered | Every community; critical in the first hundred |
| Share of questions answered by members | Peer value exists | Teach job |
| Distinct contributors per month | Breadth of the active core | Every community |
| Contribution to the chosen job | Bugs, referrals, integrations, guides | Test, refer, build, teach |
| Governance participation excluding the largest holders and team | Real distribution of decisions | Govern job |
| Retained usage 30 days after incentives stop | The community that remains | Any incentive programme |
| Member retention and paid revenue from referring members | Whether peer value funds the business | Media memberships |

The single most important line is the retained-usage figure. Define the action that means someone is using the product, not visiting it. Run incentives for a set period, stop, and count how many keep doing it. Write the decision you will make on the result before you start; [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how. Keep that record (a member list, a contribution log and a way to reach people) on systems you own, so a platform policy change cannot take it.

## When it has gone wrong

A large, silent group was usually recruited for a payout, lives on a rented platform and shares only an interest in price or launch news. Some silence is normal, but a large group with no active core has a design problem. ["40,000 members and nobody does anything"](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/) sets out the turnaround: pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people from the channel history who asked real questions or helped others, ask them for judgment on a real decision, close the loop in public, switch incentives off for a month and count who stays. Do not buy more members or announce a token to wake the group up.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the group.** Run the peer-value test before calling anything a community.
- **Assign one or two jobs.** Test, teach, refer, build or govern, each with its own contribution measure.
- **Recruit the first hundred by hand.** Ask for judgment, close the loop and answer every first contribution.
- **Design small and host it.** A few spaces with clear jobs, run by a host rather than a publisher.
- **Cost the incentives.** Airdrops, points and paid creators are acquisition spend with an expected loss rate.
- **Count who stays.** Retained contribution after incentives stop is the community.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a community

- You can complete "members return because they can \_\_\_ with people they could not easily \_\_\_ elsewhere"
- One or two named jobs, each with a contribution measure
- A named first hundred, recruited by hand, with a record of each person's first contribution
- One recurring ritual and a host responsible for answering newcomers
- Every incentive costed, with a date it stops and a retained-usage count planned
- Member records held on systems you own

## Common questions

### How do you build an online community that lasts?

Decide whether you need a community at all, give it one or two jobs, recruit the first hundred members by hand, run one recurring ritual, treat incentives as acquisition costs and measure who keeps contributing after the incentives stop.

### What is the 90-9-1 rule?

Jakob Nielsen's observation that about 90% of community members only read, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most content. A 2014 study of four health networks found the top 1% wrote about 75% of posts.

### Do airdrops build community?

Rarely on their own. Studies of major airdrops find most recipients sell quickly; two years after Uniswap's, 93% of recipients had sold all their tokens. Airdrops can attract users, but a job and a reason to return are what keep them.

### What metrics should a community team report?

Contribution to the community's job, newcomers' first contributions, time to a useful response, distinct contributors and retained usage after incentives stop. Member count alone says little about health or value.

# Sales Capacity and Quota Setting

Source: https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Most quota plans start from the board's number and divide it by headcount. Benchmarks suggest that leaves fewer than half of sellers at quota, while ramp times lengthen. This piece sets out a capacity model built from ramp, attainment and hiring dates, the gap it usually exposes, and how to record the quota decision so next year's plan can learn from this one.

Sales capacity is the revenue a team can realistically produce in a period, given who is in seat, how long new hires take to ramp and what share of quota sellers usually attain. Quota setting should start from that number and then reconcile it with the target, not the other way round. The Bridge Group's 2026 study of 158 B2B companies found 48% of account executives at quota, down from 51% in 2024, with average ramp time at 6.2 months, the longest in the study's history. A plan that ignores those two figures is a wish with a spreadsheet attached.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every annual plan contains a moment where a revenue target meets a sales team. In most firms of 20 to 500 people, that meeting is a division: the target divided by the number of sellers, adjusted a little for seniority and territory. The result is called a quota.

The division has the advantage of always balancing. Its disadvantage is that it encodes no evidence about what the team can carry. The quota becomes a statement of what the firm needs, and attainment becomes a measure of how far the need exceeded the capacity.

## What the benchmarks say about attainment

The evidence on attainment is consistent across sources, and it is not encouraging.

The Bridge Group's 2026 study of AE models and metrics, drawn from 158 B2B companies surveyed in the first half of 2026, found 48% of reps at quota, down from 51% in 2024. The median AE quota was $960,000 against median on-target earnings of $200,000, a quota-to-OTE ratio of 4.6, up from 4.2 in 2024. The firm's 2024 edition noted that median quota had grown at about 2% a year since 2012 while on-target earnings grew at more than 5%.

Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, built from 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, report that an average of 69% of reps were falling short in 2024, and that only 15% of sales teams had more than half their reps reach 80% of quota. They also found that average quota targets had been cut by 19%, and that 79% of reps would have missed at unchanged quotas.

KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures' 2024 private SaaS survey, of more than 100 companies, found quotas rose more than 10% in 2023 while expected attainment rose from about 70% to about 75%.

| Source | Sample | Attainment finding | What it implies for planning |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bridge Group, 2026 | 158 B2B companies | 48% of AEs at quota, down from 51% | Plan on fewer than half the team hitting target |
| Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 | 4.2m opportunities, 530 companies | 69% of reps falling short on average | Quota cuts were needed mid-year in many teams |
| KeyBanc and Sapphire, 2024 | 100+ private SaaS firms | Quotas up 10%+; expected attainment about 75% | Firms raised targets and expectations together |

These are vendor and investor datasets weighted towards software, and definitions of attainment differ. They agree on the direction: a quota that most of the team misses is the norm, not the exception.

The ratios point the same way. When median quota rises faster than the evidence of what sellers close, attainment falls, and the difference is usually absorbed in one of three places: mid-year quota cuts, missed forecasts or seller turnover. Each of those costs more than an honest plan would have. A services firm faces the same arithmetic with billable targets in place of quota.

> If most of the team misses quota, the quota was a forecast error before it was a performance problem.

## Building capacity from the bottom

A capacity model answers one question: if the plan goes as expected, how much will the team sell? It needs four inputs per seller.

**Productive quota.** What a fully ramped seller in this role and segment has historically sold, not what they were asked to sell. Use the median of the last four quarters for ramped sellers, not the top performer.

**Ramp curve.** How many months a new hire takes to reach productive quota, and what share they deliver along the way. The Bridge Group's 6.2-month average is a reasonable default where the firm has no history of its own.

**Start date.** A seller hired in month seven of a twelve-month year cannot contribute a full year, and in most cases contributes little before the year ends.

**Attrition.** Some sellers will leave. Gartner's 2022 survey of 908 B2B sellers found 89% reporting burnout and 54% actively looking for another job. A plan that assumes everyone stays all year overstates capacity.

The table shows the effect of start date on first-year contribution, assuming, for illustration only, a six-month linear ramp.

| Start month | Months in seat this year | Approximate full-quota equivalent this year |
| --- | --- | --- |
| January | 12 | About 75% |
| April | 9 | About 50% |
| July | 6 | About 25% |
| October | 3 | Under 10% |

Under these assumptions, a team of eight ramped sellers plus four hires spread through the year does not have twelve sellers' worth of capacity. It has roughly nine and a half, before attrition. That gap between headcount and capacity is the number most plans never write down. Apply an attrition assumption on top, and add back a ramp period for every replacement hire, and the figure usually falls further.

[*What is pipeline coverage?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-pipeline-coverage/) makes the parallel point for pipeline: the right ratio comes from your own win rate, not a rule of thumb. Capacity works the same way. Use your own ramp and attainment history once you have four quarters of it.

## Reconciling capacity with the target

The capacity model usually produces a number below the target. That is the useful moment, because the gap now has a size and the leadership team can choose how to close it.

There are five honest ways to close it. Each has a cost that belongs in the plan.

| Lever | What it does | What it costs | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hire earlier | Adds ramped months this year | Cash and management time now | Hire dates the plan depends on |
| Raise productivity | Lifts productive quota per seller | Enablement, tools or support roles | The specific change and its expected effect |
| Shift the mix | Moves effort to higher-yield segments or channels | Coverage elsewhere | Which accounts lose attention |
| Over-assign quota | Sum of quotas exceeds the target, as a buffer | Lower expected attainment and morale | The buffer size and why |
| Lower the target | Aligns the plan with capacity | A harder board conversation | The evidence presented |

Productivity is the lever most often assumed and least often evidenced. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently. A plan that counts on higher productive quota should name the change that removes work from sellers, and its expected effect, rather than assume the same people will simply sell more.

The dishonest way is to leave the gap unstated and distribute it across quotas. Gartner's 2022 survey found 67% of sellers saying their leadership was overly optimistic and disconnected from seller reality. A gap hidden in quotas is one reason that perception forms.

## Setting the individual number

Once the team number reconciles, individual quotas can be set. Three principles hold up across the evidence.

**Set quotas from territory potential, not from last year plus a percentage.** A territory with more accounts in the ideal customer profile can carry more. [*How to write an ICP*](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) covers how to define that profile so it can be counted.

**Design for the middle of the team.** Steenburgh and Ahearne's research, published in *Harvard Business Review* in 2012, found that sales forces divide into laggards, core performers and stars, and respond differently to plan design. Tiered targets motivated core performers; quarterly bonuses kept laggards on track, and moving them to annual bonuses was associated with a revenue drop of about 10%; caps on commission led stars to stop selling once they hit target.

**Change quotas mid-year only by a rule.** Ebsta and Pavilion's finding that average quotas were cut by 19% shows how common mid-year resets are. If resets happen, the rule for when and how should be written before the year starts, so a reset is a planned response rather than a negotiation.

The Bridge Group's 2026 study also found that 38% of AEs now own renewal and expansion, nearly double the 2024 share. Where that is true, quota must state how renewal and new business are weighted, or sellers will choose the easier number.

## Recording the plan so next year can learn

The capacity plan is a commercial decision in the sense of [*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/): it is made once a year, defended to a board, and graded within twelve months. It is also one of the least often recorded with its reasoning.

The record needs six lines: the target, the capacity estimate with its assumptions, the gap, the levers chosen to close it, the owner, and the check date. At the year's end, write back the outcome: actual ramp, actual attainment, actual attrition. Over two or three cycles, the firm builds its own benchmarks, and the plan stops depending on borrowed ones.

This is also where forecasting and capacity meet. Part 23 of this series covered forecasting; a forecast that keeps missing in the same direction is often a capacity plan that was never reconciled.

Illustrative example: closing the gap in the open

Decision
:   Set the new-business target at the capacity estimate plus an 8% over-assignment buffer, and move two hires from the third quarter to the first.

Reason and owner
:   The bottom-up model, using the firm's own six-month ramp and last year's median attainment, came in below the board's first target. Agreed by the chief executive and the revenue lead; owned by the revenue lead.

What changed
:   The board saw the gap, the levers and the buffer. Actual ramp and attainment are written back at year end.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Model capacity before quota.** Ramp, start date, attainment and attrition decide what the team can carry.
- **State the gap.** The difference between capacity and target is a decision, not a rounding error.
- **Design for the core performers.** Tiered targets and regular bonuses matter more than the headline number.
- **Write the plan down with its assumptions.** Next year's plan should learn from this year's outcome.

Gateway card

### Before you publish quotas

- Productive quota per role taken from the median of ramped sellers
- A ramp curve from your own history, or a stated default
- Start dates for every planned hire
- An attrition assumption
- The gap between capacity and target written down, with the levers chosen
- A written rule for any mid-year quota change

## Common questions

### What percentage of salespeople hit quota?

Fewer than half in recent benchmarks. The Bridge Group's 2026 study of 158 B2B companies found 48% of account executives at quota, and Ebsta and Pavilion report an average of 69% of reps falling short in 2024.

### How long does it take a new account executive to ramp?

The Bridge Group's 2026 study puts the average at 6.2 months, the longest in the study's history. Firms should use their own ramp history once they have it.

### How do you calculate sales capacity?

For each seller, multiply productive quota by the share of the year they will be in seat and ramped, adjust for expected attainment and attrition, and sum across the team.

### Should quotas be set top-down or bottom-up?

Both. Build capacity bottom-up from ramp, attainment and territory potential, compare it with the top-down target, and record how the gap was closed.

# Ten Thousand People: Density, and the Case for Federation

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At ten thousand people, an enterprise has enough volume across decision classes for a learning layer to earn its keep. A single unified enterprise brain tends to stall; the workable design is federated: central invariants and one export format, records and local definitions kept by functions, and a map between them. Data architecture reached the same design under the name data mesh.

At ten thousand people, there is finally enough volume in enough decision classes for a learning layer to earn its keep. The challenge is no longer whether to record judgment, but how one organisation runs many records without forcing them into one. The tempting answer is a single enterprise brain with one ontology. The workable design is federated: invariants set centrally, records kept locally by the functions, and a map between local and enterprise definitions. Map, do not unify.

This is the sixth rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*One thousand people: governance arrives*](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/), made decisions defensible. At ten thousand, there are enough defensible decisions to learn from.

## Why density changes the problem

A large enterprise makes thousands of comparable decisions a week in dozens of classes: credit approvals, alerts, claims, renewals, procurement, hiring, pricing. Outcomes arrive on a known schedule. Experts handle the exceptions. Someone will have to defend the calls. This is the zone where judgment systems genuinely learn, and where the measurement discipline in the rest of this series pays off.

Firms of this size are rare. The SBA Office of Advocacy counts 21,041 US businesses with 500 or more employees against about 6.4 million smaller employer firms, and those at 10,000 are a small subset of that group. They are also where external obligations stack highest: the EU's amended due diligence directive applies only above 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5 billion of turnover.

Below this scale, as our piece [*Below the volume floor*](https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/) argues, no model will learn a firm's judgment from a few hundred dissimilar decisions a year. Above it, the volume exists, and the question is whether the records are consistent enough to learn from.

## What becomes possible

**Calibration at scale.** Enough outcomes per class to see, within a quarter or two, where judgment is overconfident and who reads which situations well. The forecasting research shows how much value sits in recorded probabilities. Mellers, Tetlock and colleagues, summarising the Good Judgment Project, report that teams beat individuals and that the best aggregation of forecasts beat the simple mean by as much as 60%. Our piece [*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) sets out the method.

**Staggered rollouts as standard.** Every change to a decision workflow deployed in waves, so each wave is the control for the next.

**Seeded errors and second looks** across every review queue, with catch rates reported like any other control.

**Precedent across divisions.** A credit officer in one region seeing how a comparable case was handled in another, with outcome.

**Noise measured, not assumed.** In the insurer noise audit reported by Insurance Thought Leadership, executives expected a 10% spread between underwriters' quotes on the same case and found a typical spread of 55%. At ten thousand people the same audit can be run continuously, class by class, because comparable cases arrive every day.

| Capability | Minimum volume needed | What it reports |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calibration by class | Hundreds of outcomes per class per quarter | Where stated confidence and results diverge |
| Staggered rollout | Enough decisions per wave to compare | Whether a workflow change helped |
| Seeded errors | A steady review queue | Reviewer catch rates |
| Cross-division precedent | Shared template and outcome fields | Comparable cases elsewhere, with results |
| Continuous noise audit | Comparable cases arriving daily | Spread between deciders on similar cases |

## The federation problem

The tempting response is one enterprise brain: a single ontology, a single definition of every term, a single store. These programmes tend to stall. Divisions have legitimately different meanings for some terms, different regulators, different data, and different speeds. Forcing them into one model takes years and produces a compromise nobody uses.

That is **lowob**'s observation from practice rather than a measured failure rate, and we know of no reliable study of how often such programmes fail. The supporting evidence is that data architecture reached the same conclusion independently. Zhamak Dehghani's 2020 statement of data mesh, published on martinfowler.com, rests on four principles: domain-oriented ownership, data as a product, a self-serve platform, and federated computational governance. In her account, domains keep autonomy over local decisions, such as their own data models, while a federation sets the global rules needed for interoperability, such as how a customer who spans several domains is identified.

> Map, do not unify. Local definitions are mapped to the enterprise terms rather than replaced by them.

## The federated design

**Set centrally:** the invariants. Every record has a decision, reason, falsifier, sources and outcome. Supersede, never overwrite. One trace specification. One export format. A short enterprise glossary for the terms that cross divisions: revenue, customer, exposure.

**Kept locally:** the records themselves, owned by the functions. Local definitions where they genuinely differ, mapped to the enterprise terms rather than replaced by them. Local decision classes and templates.

**Bridged:** a map between local and enterprise definitions, and a conflicts process for when they diverge.

| Layer | What sits there | Who owns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Central | Five invariants, trace specification, export format, enterprise glossary | Enterprise standards group with function representatives |
| Local | Records, local definitions, decision classes, templates | Each business function |
| Bridge | Definition map, conflicts process | Joint, with a named owner per mapped term |

Our comparison [*Semantic layer vs knowledge graph*](https://lowob.com/research/semantic-layer-vs-knowledge-graph/) covers the tools that typically hold the bridge, and [*What is a knowledge graph?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/) explains where a graph helps with the mapping.

## The data provider's two brains

One nuance applies to firms whose product is itself data and analytics. They run two brains: the internal one that records how the firm decides, and the external one they sell, the context layer their clients' agents consume. The two can reinforce each other. A provider that helps clients keep a structured, exportable record of how they used its data is selling the start of a judgment layer, not just cargo. That may be the most interesting product opportunity at this scale.

**In practice:** publish the central invariants and the export format, and leave records with the functions. Map local definitions to a short enterprise glossary instead of replacing them. Make staggered rollout and seeded errors standard for every decision workflow change. Report calibration for the five highest-volume decision classes quarterly, with outcomes written back as described in [*What is outcome write-back?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/).

**What would prove this wrong:** large enterprises that deploy a single unified ontology across all divisions on schedule, with high adoption, outperforming federated designs. The closing piece, [*Five invariants, from two people to ten thousand*](https://lowob.com/research/five-invariants-from-two-people-to-ten-thousand/), sets out what the central layer must hold.

## lowob takeaways

- **Use the volume.** Calibration, staggered rollouts, seeded errors and cross-division precedent all become practical.
- **Set only the invariants centrally.** Decision, reason, falsifier, sources and outcome; supersede, never overwrite; one export format.
- **Leave records with functions.** Local definitions and templates stay local.
- **Map, do not unify.** A definition map and a conflicts process beat a single ontology.
- **If you sell data, sell the record too.** Clients' agents need context; clients need a record of how they used it.

## Common questions

### Should a large enterprise build one unified knowledge graph or ontology?

Usually not. Single-ontology programmes tend to stall and produce a compromise nobody uses. A federated design, with central invariants and local records mapped to a short enterprise glossary, is more workable.

### What should be standardised centrally in an enterprise decision record system?

The invariants: every record has a decision, reason, falsifier, sources and outcome; records are superseded, never overwritten; one trace specification, one export format and a short glossary for cross-division terms.

### What is federated governance in data mesh?

A model in which domain teams own their data and local decisions, while a federation of domain and platform owners sets global standards, such as shared identifiers, so data can be combined across domains.

### Why do decision-learning systems work better in large companies?

Large enterprises make thousands of comparable decisions a week with outcomes on a known schedule, giving enough volume per class to see where judgment is overconfident.

- [Mellers, Tetlock, Baker, Friedman and Zeckhauser, Improving the accuracy of geopolitical risk assessments](https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/improving_the_accuracy_of_geopolitical_risk_assessments.pdf), University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019. Book chapter on forecasting tournaments.
- [Paul Carroll, Our Big Problem With 'Noise'](https://www.insurancethoughtleadership.com/our-big-problem-with-noise/), Insurance Thought Leadership, 18 May 2021. Secondary account of one insurer's noise audit.
- [DLA Piper, EU Omnibus I Directive amending CSRD and CSDDD will enter into force on 18 March 2026](https://www.dlapiper.com/insights/blogs/environment-health-safety-and-product-compliance/2026/eu-omnibus-i-directive-amending-csrd-and-csddd-will-enter-into-force-on-18-march-2026), March 2026. List the terms your divisions define differently, starting with customer and revenue. For each, keep the local definitions and write one enterprise definition with a map to them, rather than forcing a single meaning.
