# The 5 Agent Memory Layers Worth Testing, and How to Test Them

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-5-agent-memory-layers-worth-testing-and-how-to-test-them/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: No memory layer has yet shown, under independent test, that it makes agents better at long tasks, and the hardest case, a fact that has changed, is where every system tested so far is weakest. Zep, Mem0, Letta, Cognee and Supermemory are worth testing, ranked mainly on how they handle change over time. Run your own two-week test rather than trust vendor scores.

No memory layer has yet shown, under independent test, that it makes agents better at long tasks. The best independent benchmark we found tested how well memory systems handle a fact that has changed, and every method scored poorly when the answer needed more than one step of reasoning. Vendor scores in the 90s are real results on the vendors' own harnesses, not independent reproductions. So this is a list of what is worth testing, with a protocol for testing it, not a list of what works. Zep ranks first because its graph records when a fact stopped being true instead of overwriting it.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Agent memory is what lets an agent carry facts, preferences and past decisions from one session to the next. Our explainer on [what agent memory is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/) covers the four types and their limits. The practical question for a buyer is narrower: when a fact changes, does the memory layer know which version is current, and can it tell you where each version came from? That is the failure **lowob** argues matters most, and the one our piece on [superseding rather than overwriting](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) makes the case for.

## What the independent evidence says

Most published memory scores come from the vendors. Zep's own paper, posted in January 2025, reports 94.8% on the Deep Memory Retrieval benchmark against 93.4% for MemGPT, and accuracy gains of up to 18.5% on LongMemEval. Those are genuine results, run by the vendor on public benchmarks, and they have not been independently reproduced.

The most useful independent test we found is MemoryAgentBench, published by Yuanzhe Hu, Yu Wang and Julian McAuley at UC San Diego in July 2025. It includes a "FactConsolidation" task that feeds a system facts, then contradicts some of them, then asks questions. The results are sobering:

| System tested | Single-step questions on changed facts | Multi-step questions on changed facts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mem0 | 18% | 2% |
| MemGPT (Letta's research ancestor) | 28% | 3% |
| GPT-4o with the full history in context | 60% | No higher than 7% |
| Best of all methods tested |  | About 7% |

The authors conclude that conflict resolution "remains a major challenge for memory mechanisms". They attribute part of Mem0's weakness to its design: it extracts facts from inputs, which "inherently discards a substantial portion of the original content". A reasoning model did much better on a small version of the task, then fell sharply as the history grew. Zep was discussed in the paper but not tested, and Letta's current product has moved on from MemGPT. The benchmark is a year old. It is still the clearest evidence that the hardest question in agent memory, how did this change, is unsolved.

> A memory layer that cannot tell you a fact has been superseded will answer confidently from the old one.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Handles change over time | 35% | The weakest category in every benchmark is "how did this change?" Memory that cannot mark a fact as superseded will blend old and new. |
| Independent evidence | 25% | Has anyone outside the vendor reproduced the claims, with a published harness? |
| Provenance and ownership | 20% | Can you see where a memory came from, export it and self-host? |
| Adoption and backing | 20% | Funding, integrations, and whether it will still exist in two years. |

## The list

**1. Zep (Graphiti)**

**Best for:** agents whose facts change, such as accounts, positions or policies.

**Why it ranks first:** it is built on a bi-temporal knowledge graph. Each edge carries two timelines: when the system recorded the fact and when it expired, and when the fact became true and stopped being true in the world. When a new episode contradicts an existing fact, Graphiti sets the old edge's expiry rather than deleting it, and rewrites its text to say the fact held until the change. If information arrives out of order, it compares the real-world dates and expires the earlier fact. That is the right structure for the hardest failure in agent memory, and it is what a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) needs too.

**Watch out for:** its headline scores are its own and have not been reproduced. Graphs also cost more to keep fresh than to build: every ingested episode is billed, while retrieval is not.

**Pricing:** Free with 10,000 credits a month; Flex $125 a month for 50,000 credits; Flex Plus $375 a month for 200,000 credits; Enterprise custom (as listed in November 2026). An episode costs one credit per 350 bytes; retrieval and storage are unmetered. Zep states SOC 2 Type II certification and offers deployment in your own cloud through sales.

**What would change its rank:** an independent benchmark in which the temporal graph does no better than flat memory.

**2. Mem0**

**Best for:** teams that want the most widely adopted option and an AWS integration.

**Why it ranks here:** the most traction in the category. TechCrunch reported in October 2025 that Mem0 had raised $24 million across a seed and a Series A led by Basis Set Ventures, that API calls rose from 35 million in the first quarter of 2025 to 186 million in the third, and that its Python package had passed 13 million downloads. The same report carries Mem0's claim to be the exclusive memory provider for AWS's agent SDK. Its open-source edition is Apache 2.0 licensed and self-hostable, which scores well on ownership.

**Watch out for:** the widest gap between vendor and independent results on this list. Mem0's extraction design is the one MemoryAgentBench blamed for information loss, and it scored 2% on multi-step questions about changed facts. Pricing has also moved: a third-party tracker's 9 November 2026 snapshot of Mem0's pricing page shows the Starter and Pro tiers no longer sold to new accounts.

**Pricing:** Free tier with limited adds and retrievals; paid use on custom, sales-led pricing; open source free (per a third-party tracker's snapshot of Mem0's page, as listed in November 2026; we could not open Mem0's page directly).

**What would change its rank:** a published, reproducible harness that closes the gap with its own claims.

**3. Letta**

**Best for:** teams that want agent state they can inspect and control, from the research group behind MemGPT.

**Why it ranks here:** the operating-system-style "paging" design it descends from is one of the founding ideas in agent memory, and the lineage is academic: Letta is the company behind the MemGPT open-source project, spun out of UC Berkeley. Agent state is a first-class, inspectable object rather than a hidden store.

**Watch out for:** smaller and earlier. TechCrunch reported a $10 million seed led by Felicis at a $70 million post-money valuation in September 2024. The MemGPT design scored 3% on multi-step changed-fact questions in MemoryAgentBench, though Letta's product has developed since.

**Pricing:** Free for up to three stateful agents; Pro $20 a month including $20 of model credits and up to 20 agents; Enterprise custom with role-based access and SSO (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** a new funding round, or an independent benchmark of the current product either way.

**4. Cognee**

**Best for:** teams already committed to a graph approach and willing to work with an early vendor.

**Why it ranks here:** a memory engine that combines graph and vector storage, with an open-source core of more than 12,000 GitHub stars. It raised a $7.5 million seed led by Pebblebed on 19 February 2026 and says it is live at more than 70 companies, with pipeline runs growing from about 2,000 to more than one million during 2025.

**Watch out for:** very early; every figure above is self-reported, and Cognee was among the systems that, like every method tested, scored poorly on MemoryAgentBench's multi-step changed-fact questions. We could not open its pricing page this month.

**Pricing:** open-source core free; check the cloud price directly.

**What would change its rank:** production references in regulated firms.

**5. Supermemory**

**Best for:** small teams and prototypes.

**Why it ranks here:** a lightweight memory API that builds a knowledge graph from files, documents, chats and email, backed by a $2.6 million seed reported in October 2025, with named early customers.

**Watch out for:** the smallest backing on the list, no independent results, and the self-hosted binary is free but not open source.

**Pricing:** Free; Pro $19 a month; Max $100; Scale $399, which adds SOC 2, a HIPAA agreement and a self-hosted option; Enterprise custom (as listed in November 2026).

**What would change its rank:** independent benchmark results or a larger round.

## Side by side

|  | Zep | Mem0 | Letta | Cognee | Supermemory |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Memory structure | Bi-temporal knowledge graph | Extracted facts, vector plus graph | Inspectable agent state, paging design | Graph plus vector | Knowledge graph over ingested content |
| Handles changed facts | Expires old edge, keeps history | 2% multi-step in independent test | MemGPT ancestor scored 3% | Weak on multi-step in independent test | No independent evidence |
| Open source | Graphiti library | Yes, Apache 2.0 | MemGPT lineage | Core, yes | No |
| Self-host or own cloud | Own cloud via sales | Yes, open-source edition | Not stated on pricing page | Yes, core | Scale tier and above |
| Compliance stated | SOC 2 Type II | Not verified this month | SSO on Enterprise | Not verified | SOC 2, HIPAA on Scale |
| Entry paid price, November 2026 | $125 a month | Custom | $20 a month | Not verified | $19 a month |

## Left out, and why

**The platform-native options.** Google's Gemini agent, announced on 8 October 2026, ships four memory types: session, semantic, procedural and episodic. Microsoft's Work IQ, generally available since 16 June 2026, is a governed context layer that runs every request as a specific user. If you are already on one of those platforms, test its native memory before adding another vendor. They are bundled rather than standalone, so they are not ranked here; our [ranking of enterprise context platforms](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-enterprise-context-platforms-ranked-for-regulated-firms/) covers them.

**A plain database with good discipline.** For many teams the right answer is records with a status, validity dates and supersession links in a database you already run. It is not a product, so it is not ranked, but it is often what wins.

## How to test any of them in two weeks

1. **Build 50 questions from your own history:** 20 lookups, 20 "how did this change?" questions, and 10 that assume something you have since reversed.
2. **Run your agent with no memory layer, then with each candidate, on the same model.** Include a run with the full history in the context window as a ceiling; in MemoryAgentBench, that beat every memory system on single-step questions.
3. **Score correctness, and separately score how often it corrects the false premise.** Our piece on [false premises](https://lowob.com/research/the-false-premise-is-the-expensive-failure/) explains why that second score matters more.
4. **Ask each vendor for its benchmark harness, not just its score.** A vendor that will not share one has told you something.

Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to keep a test set like this honest over time.

## lowob takeaways

- **No independent gain yet.** The best independent test found every memory method weak on multi-step questions about changed facts.
- **Zep ranks first on structure.** Its graph records when a fact stopped being true instead of overwriting it.
- **Mem0 leads on adoption, not evidence.** It has the most usage and the widest gap between its own and independent results.
- **Test on your own history.** Fifty questions, with and without each layer, on the same model, including a full-context ceiling.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for an agent memory layer

- A changed fact is marked as superseded, with dates, and the old version stays readable
- Every memory shows where it came from
- Memories export in a documented format, or the store can be self-hosted
- The vendor shares its benchmark harness, not only its score
- Your own 50-question test beats a no-memory run on the same model
- Pricing is modelled on ingestion volume, not only retrieval

## Common questions

### Do AI agent memory layers like Mem0 and Zep actually improve performance?

Not yet under independent test. Vendor scores in the 90s come from the vendors' own runs. In MemoryAgentBench, an independent 2025 benchmark, every memory method scored poorly on multi-step questions about facts that had changed, and Mem0 scored 2%.

### Which agent memory layer is best for facts that change over time?

Zep, through its Graphiti library, because its bi-temporal knowledge graph records when each fact was true and expires a contradicted fact rather than overwriting it.

### How much does an agent memory layer cost?

As listed in November 2026, Zep starts at $125 a month for 50,000 credits, Letta Pro is $20 a month, Supermemory Pro is $19 a month, and Mem0's paid tiers are now custom. Most offer a free tier and bill on ingestion more than on retrieval.

### How do I test an agent memory layer?

Build 50 questions from your own history: 20 lookups, 20 "how did this change?" and 10 with a reversed premise. Run with no memory, with each candidate and with full history in context, on the same model, and ask vendors for their benchmark harness.

# Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production, by State Model and Cloud

Source: https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Framework choice in 2026 is mostly a cloud and vendor decision, because the serious options now share the same tool protocol. For a regulated team the differences are whether a run can pause for a human, resume after a crash and run on more than one model. LangGraph ranks first, followed by Microsoft Agent Framework, the Claude Agent SDK, Google's ADK and the OpenAI Agents SDK.

Framework choice in 2026 is mostly a cloud and vendor decision, not a technical one. The serious options all connect to tools through the same protocol, MCP, so what separates them for a regulated team is narrower: whether a run can pause at a named step for a person, resume after a crash without losing state, and run on more than one model. On those tests LangGraph ranks first, followed by Microsoft Agent Framework, the Claude Agent SDK, Google's Agent Development Kit and the OpenAI Agents SDK.

*Figure: Five plug points: identity and limits, context in, precedent in, the gate, and the outcome written back.*

A framework is the code that runs an agent's loop: it calls the model, executes the tools the model chooses, keeps state between steps and decides when to stop. Our explainer on [what an agent framework is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-framework/) covers the category. This list is narrower. It ranks five frameworks on what a supervisor, an auditor or an incident review will ask of a production agent, and it leaves the prototyping questions aside.

## How we ranked

| Criterion | Weight | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| State and checkpointing | 30% | An agent that cannot resume after a failure, or pause at a named step for approval, cannot be supervised. |
| Human-approval gates | 25% | Supervisors now expect a review step that leaves evidence of who approved what. |
| Model and cloud neutrality | 25% | Locking orchestration to one model vendor is the hardest dependency to unwind later. |
| Cost transparency | 20% | Multi-agent patterns multiply model calls quietly. |

Tool connection is not on the list because it no longer separates the field. The Model Context Protocol is the shared standard for connecting agents to tools and data, covered in our explainer on [what MCP is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/). Microsoft restated MCP support in its 1.0 release, and Anthropic lists MCP as a built-in SDK capability. Agent-to-agent traffic has its own standard, A2A, which shipped its first stable specification in March 2026 and became a hosted project of the Agentic AI Foundation on 17 August 2026, with more than 150 supporting organisations. Our comparison of [MCP and A2A](https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-a2a/) explains how the two fit together.

## The list

**1. LangGraph**

**Best for:** teams that need durable, inspectable workflows across models.

**Why it ranks first:** it models an agent as a graph of steps with a checkpointer underneath. LangChain's documentation describes checkpointers as persisting "a thread's graph state as checkpoints", and lists the jobs that depend on them: resuming after an interruption, recovering from a failure, human-in-the-loop workflows and time travel through past states. Pausing is explicit. Calling `interrupt()` inside a node suspends execution, saves the state and waits as long as needed; the run resumes when the same thread ID is invoked with a resume value. That maps directly onto what a supervisor will ask for: show me the step, show me the state, show me who released it.

**Watch out for:** more design work up front than role-based frameworks. The documentation also notes a detail that matters for side effects: on resume, the paused node restarts from its beginning, so any code before the `interrupt()` call runs again. Anything consequential before an interrupt needs to be idempotent. The commercial tracing and hosting product, LangSmith, is a separate purchase decision.

**Pricing:** the framework is open source. LangSmith's Developer plan is free for one seat and 5,000 base traces a month; Plus is $39 per seat per month with 10,000 base traces and one small serverless agent server included; Enterprise is custom, with self-hosted and hybrid options (as listed in November 2026). Hosted agent servers are metered in LangSmith units of $1.00, charged on compute and memory time.

**What would change its rank:** another framework matching its checkpointing with less engineering.

**2. Microsoft Agent Framework**

**Best for:** firms standardised on Azure and Microsoft 365.

**Why it ranks here:** version 1.0 reached general availability on 3 April 2026 with "stable APIs, and a commitment to long-term support", unifying Semantic Kernel and AutoGen. Its workflow checkpoints capture the state of every executor, pending messages, pending requests and responses, and shared state, and are written at the end of each superstep. A checkpoint can be restored into the same run or rehydrated into a new workflow instance, and Cosmos DB storage is the documented production option. It is also more model-neutral than its parentage suggests: the 1.0 release lists first-party connectors for Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini and Ollama.

**Watch out for:** the cost of conversational multi-agent patterns. A group chat of four agents running five rounds is at least 20 model calls before any tool is used. At 1.0, Microsoft said A2A 1.0 support was "coming soon". Its own documentation also warns that checkpoint storage is a trust boundary: never load a checkpoint from a source that could have been tampered with.

**Pricing:** no framework fee is listed; you pay for the models and the Azure services you run it on.

**What would change its rank:** evidence of production use outside the Microsoft stack.

**3. Claude Agent SDK**

**Best for:** teams building on Claude that want the deepest support for the shared tool protocol.

**Why it ranks here:** the SDK gives developers the same tools, agent loop and context management that power Claude Code, in Python and TypeScript. MCP, permissions that decide which tools run automatically and which need approval, lifecycle hooks, subagents and resumable sessions are all built in rather than added through adapters. Anthropic's feature table shows the SDK running on every route it supports: Anthropic's own API, Amazon Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform and Microsoft Foundry. That makes it more cloud-portable than it first appears.

**Watch out for:** it runs Claude models only, so it fails the model-neutrality test by design. Some features differ by provider; web search, for example, is not available through Amazon Bedrock. Use is governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service.

**Pricing:** you pay for Claude model usage on whichever provider you choose.

**What would change its rank:** support for other model providers.

**4. Google Agent Development Kit (ADK)**

**Best for:** teams on Google Cloud that need agents to talk to other agents.

**Why it ranks here:** native support for A2A. ADK can expose an agent as an A2A server, and its `RemoteA2aAgent` client lets a local agent call a remote one as if it were a tool. Google's documentation is specific about when to use it: A2A for a separate service, an agent maintained by another team or one written in another language, and local sub-agents for internal code organisation or anything that needs shared memory. ADK is open source and available in Python, TypeScript, Go and Java.

**Watch out for:** the documented production routes are Google's own: Runtime, Cloud Run and Google Kubernetes Engine. If your firm does not run on Google Cloud, budget for the deployment work yourself.

**Pricing:** the framework is open source; you pay for models and Google Cloud hosting.

**What would change its rank:** easier, documented deployment outside Google Cloud.

**5. OpenAI Agents SDK**

**Best for:** simple, handoff-based agents on OpenAI models.

**Why it ranks here:** a clean handoff model that is quick to learn and widely documented. Its human-in-the-loop support is better than its reputation: a tool can be marked `needs\_approval`, the run pauses with a list of pending interruptions, and the run state can be serialised to a database and resumed later, even in another process. Sessions keep conversation history across runs, with backends from SQLite and Redis to SQLAlchemy, MongoDB and Dapr.

**Watch out for:** pausing for approval is built in; checkpointing every step of a long workflow and recovering mid-run after a crash are largely yours to build. OpenAI's own guidance says approval "doesn't guarantee exactly-once execution", and tells developers to use idempotency keys for consequential actions and to reconcile outcomes before retrying after a crash.

**Pricing:** the SDK is free to use; you pay for model calls.

**What would change its rank:** native durable state at the step level.

## Side by side

|  | LangGraph | Microsoft Agent Framework | Claude Agent SDK | Google ADK | OpenAI Agents SDK |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| State model | Graph state saved by a checkpointer per thread | Workflow checkpoint at the end of each superstep | Sessions that can resume or fork | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | Sessions for history; serialisable run state |
| Resume after a crash | Yes, from the last checkpoint | Yes, same run or rehydrated instance | Session resume | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | Approval pauses only; mid-run recovery is yours |
| Human approval | `interrupt()` at any node | Pending requests captured in checkpoints | Permission rules per tool | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | `needs\_approval` per tool |
| Models | Any | Seven first-party connectors, including Claude and Gemini | Claude only | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | OpenAI first; third-party adapters listed |
| Clouds | Any; LangSmith for hosting | Azure first; Cosmos DB for production checkpoints | Anthropic, AWS, Google Cloud, Microsoft Foundry | Google Cloud routes documented | Any |
| A2A | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | "Coming soon" at 1.0 | Not covered in the pages we reviewed | Native | Not covered in the pages we reviewed |
| Paid layer, as listed in November 2026 | LangSmith Plus $39 per seat per month | None listed | Model usage | Model and hosting | Model usage |

"Not covered in the pages we reviewed" means what it says. It is not a claim that the feature is missing, only that we could not confirm it on the vendor's own pages this month.

> The question for a regulated team is not which framework is cleverest. It is which one can show you the step, the state and the person who released it.

## Left out, and why

**CrewAI.** Role-based and quick to prototype with. Conversational role patterns tend to add model calls, and we did not find documentation that would place it above the five on checkpointing or logged approval. It is a reasonable choice for a demo and a harder one to defend in front of a supervisor.

**Writing your own.** Large firms with unusual workflows sometimes build a custom orchestrator that runs workflows defined in configuration. It is defensible at that scale, where the firm already runs a platform team. At most firms it is a maintenance bill, and it rebuilds checkpointing and approval logging that the frameworks above already ship. Our [build versus buy guide](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) sets out the test.

## How to test any of them before you choose

Run three tests on a workflow you actually intend to ship, not on the vendor's sample.

1. **Kill the process halfway through a run.** Restart it. Does it resume from the last completed step, and can you open the saved state and read it? Check whether any tool call before the failure runs twice.
2. **Put a named step behind a person.** Make the agent wait before it sends, pays or changes a record. Confirm the approval is logged with who approved, when and what they saw. Our explainer on [approval gates](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) lists what that log should hold.
3. **Swap the model.** Change providers and count the lines of code that change. If the answer is "the whole agent", you have chosen a model vendor, not a framework.

Add a fourth test if cost matters, which it does: run the same task in a single-agent and a multi-agent pattern and compare the number of model calls. The difference is usually larger than the team expects. An observability tool makes this visible; our [ranking of LLM observability platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/) covers the options.

## lowob takeaways

- **Rank on state, not features.** LangGraph leads because a checkpointer saves state at every step and `interrupt()` can pause any node for a person.
- **Microsoft is more neutral than it looks.** Agent Framework 1.0 ships connectors for seven model providers, including Claude and Gemini.
- **The Claude Agent SDK trades model choice for depth.** Claude only, but on four clouds, with MCP and approval permissions built in.
- **Approval is not durability.** The OpenAI SDK pauses for approval well; crash recovery mid-run is still your job.

Gateway card

### Buyer's checklist for an agent framework

- A run killed halfway resumes from the last step, and the saved state is readable
- Code before a pause or a crash does not repeat a consequential action
- At least one named step waits for a person, with who, when and what they saw logged
- Swapping the model changes configuration, not the agent
- Checkpoint storage is access-controlled and treated as a trust boundary
- Model calls per task are measured in both single-agent and multi-agent patterns

## Common questions

### What is the best AI agent framework for production in a regulated industry?

LangGraph ranks first on this list, because its checkpointer saves state at every step, so runs can recover from failures and pause for human approval at any node. Microsoft Agent Framework is the stronger fit for firms standardised on Azure.

### Does the OpenAI Agents SDK support human-in-the-loop and state persistence?

Partly. Tools can require approval, a paused run's state can be saved to a database and resumed later, and sessions keep conversation history. Checkpointing every step of a long workflow and recovering mid-run after a crash are largely yours to build.

### Can the Claude Agent SDK use models other than Claude?

No. It runs Claude models only, but it can reach them through Anthropic's API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Microsoft Foundry, so it is portable across clouds even though it is tied to one model family.

### How do I test an agent framework before choosing it?

Kill the process mid-run and check it resumes with readable state, make a named step wait for a logged human approval, and count how much code changes when you swap the model.

# Human-in-the-Loop vs Human-on-the-Loop

Source: https://lowob.com/research/human-in-the-loop-vs-human-on-the-loop/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Human-in-the-loop means a person approves each AI output before it takes effect; human-on-the-loop means the system acts while a person monitors and can intervene. The terms come from defence and EU ethics guidance, and the EU AI Act asks for oversight in proportion to risk and autonomy. The right choice is per task, set by reversibility and who is affected.

Human-in-the-loop means a person approves each AI output before it takes effect. Human-on-the-loop means the system acts on its own while a person monitors, reviews afterwards and can intervene or stop it. In the loop is safer and slower; on the loop is faster and depends on the monitoring being real. The choice should be made task by task, based on whether the action can be undone and who it reaches.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the two terms mean

Our explainer on [human-in-the-loop AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/) covers the in-the-loop pattern and what regulators expect of it. This page compares it with the on-the-loop alternative.

The vocabulary comes from two places. In defence, the US Department of Defense's Directive 3000.09, updated in January 2023, distinguishes a semi-autonomous weapon system, which engages only targets "selected by an operator", from an autonomous one that, once activated, selects and engages targets "without further intervention by an operator." Within the autonomous class it names operator-supervised systems, designed so that operators can override them. That is the original in-the-loop and on-the-loop split: a person chooses each action, or a person watches and can halt.

In civilian AI policy, the European Commission's High-Level Expert Group on AI set out three models in its Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI, presented on 8 April 2019. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) is the "capability for human intervention in every decision cycle of the system." Human-on-the-loop (HOTL) is intervention during the design cycle and "monitoring the system's operation." Human-in-command (HIC) is the capability to oversee the system's overall activity and "decide when and how to use the system in any particular situation."

The guidelines also state the trade-off plainly: the less oversight a human can exercise, "the more extensive testing and stricter governance is required."

|  | Human-in-the-loop | Human-on-the-loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When the person acts | Before each output takes effect | During or after; the system does not wait |
| What the person does | Approves, edits or rejects each item | Monitors, samples, reviews exceptions, can stop |
| Speed | Limited by reviewer capacity | Limited by the system |
| Main failure | Rubber-stamping under volume | Nobody notices a drift until damage accumulates |
| Suits | Client-facing, irreversible or regulated actions | Internal, reversible, high-volume actions |
| Evidence it works | Edit and return rates, seeded-error catch rate | Exception reports read, time to halt, errors found in sampling |
| **lowob** autonomy dial | Level 1 draft, level 2 act with approval | Level 3 act and report |

Human-in-command sits above both. It is the person or group who decides whether a system is used at all, for which tasks, and who holds the [kill switch](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-kill-switch/).

## What regulators expect from each

**The EU AI Act does not mandate one model.** Article 14 requires high-risk systems to allow effective oversight, and says measures shall be "commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use." The overseer must be able to understand the system's limits, stay aware of over-reliance on its output, "disregard, override or reverse" an output, and interrupt it through a "stop" button or similar. Those requirements fit either model, but on-the-loop designs must make the stop path genuinely available.

**UK data protection pushes significant decisions in the loop.** Article 22 of the UK GDPR restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects. The ICO's guidance says that, for human review to be meaningful, involvement "should come after the automated decision has taken place and it must relate to the actual outcome." A person who only supplies input data is not meaningfully involved. Monitoring a dashboard of completed decisions is unlikely to meet that test for a decision about an individual.

**Each model fails differently.** In the loop, the risk is automation bias: approvals become reflex as volume rises, which is why the AI Act names over-reliance explicitly. On the loop, the risk is silence: the system acts correctly for weeks, monitoring lapses, and an error repeats a thousand times before anyone reads a report.

## Which to choose

Put each task through four tests. If any answer points left, keep the task in the loop.

| Test | In the loop | On the loop |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can the action be undone cheaply? | No: a sent email, a signed quote, a payment | Yes: a CRM field, a tag, an internal note |
| Does it reach a client or the public? | Yes | No |
| Does it affect an individual's rights or money? | Yes, and the ICO test applies | No |
| Is there a track record on this task? | Not yet | Weeks of logged runs with low edit rates |

Commercial examples, all illustrative:

- **In the loop:** follow-up emails to prospects, proposal text, discount approvals, contract changes, anything posted publicly.
- **On the loop:** updating deal stages from meeting notes, filling missing CRM fields, tagging inbound leads, deduplicating contacts, with a daily change report and a named reviewer.
- **Not yet automated:** pricing decisions and anything where the reason matters more than the speed.

Moving a task from in the loop to on the loop should be a recorded decision with evidence, not drift. A rising approval rate is weak evidence, because it also rises with reviewer fatigue. Seeded errors, sampled audits and edit rates are stronger.

## The **lowob** view

**lowob**'s [autonomy dial](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/) maps directly onto the two terms: levels 1 and 2 are in the loop, level 3 is on the loop, and level 4 is out of it. Our rule for the commercial line is that nothing sends without a person, so anything client-facing stays at level 1 or 2.

In the enterprise brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, both models only work if the record is kept. In the loop, the record holds who approved what, when and on which evidence. On the loop, it holds every action taken, so the monitor has something to read and the learning stage has outcomes to write back. An on-the-loop agent without that log is an out-of-the-loop agent with a dashboard.

## lowob takeaways

- **In the loop means approval first.** Use it for anything client-facing, irreversible or affecting an individual.
- **On the loop means monitoring after.** Use it for internal, reversible, high-volume work with a track record.
- **Name the person in command.** Someone decides where each system is used and holds the stop button.
- **Move tasks on evidence.** Seeded errors and audits, not approval rates, justify moving a task along the dial.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop?

Human-in-the-loop means a person approves each AI output before it takes effect. Human-on-the-loop means the system acts and a person monitors, reviews afterwards and can intervene or stop it.

### What is human-in-command in AI?

A term from the EU's 2019 Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI for the capability to oversee an AI system's overall activity and decide when and how it is used in any situation.

### Does the EU AI Act require human-in-the-loop?

No single model is mandated. Article 14 requires oversight proportionate to risk, autonomy and context, including the ability to override outputs and stop the system.

### When is human-on-the-loop acceptable?

For actions that are internal, cheap to reverse and have a logged track record, with a named reviewer reading exception reports and able to halt the system.

## Sources and notes

- [European Commission High-Level Expert Group on AI, Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI: Requirements of Trustworthy AI](https://ec.europa.eu/futurium/en/ai-alliance-consultation/guidelines/1.html), text hosted on the Commission's Futurium platform; publication date confirmed by the [Commission's library page](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/ethics-guidelines-trustworthy-ai), 8 April 2019. Non-binding expert guidance.
- [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight](https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/ai-act/ai-act-regulation/article-14/), Official Journal text via SpringLex, 12 July 2024. Applies to high-risk systems only.
- [UK Information Commissioner's Office, What is the impact of Article 22 of the UK GDPR on fairness?](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/how-do-we-ensure-fairness-in-ai/what-is-the-impact-of-article-22-of-the-uk-gdpr-on-fairness), regulator guidance. Applies to decisions about individuals under UK law.
- [DefenseScoop, Pentagon updates guidance for development, fielding and employment of autonomous weapon systems](https://defensescoop.com/2023/01/25/pentagon-updates-guidance-for-development-fielding-and-employment-of-autonomous-weapon-systems/), 25 January 2023. Trade press report of DoD Directive 3000.09; definitions as quoted there.

List every AI task your team runs and mark it in the loop or on the loop. For each on-the-loop task, name the person who reads its change report and check when they last did.

# NIST AI RMF vs ISO/IEC 42001

Source: https://lowob.com/research/nist-ai-rmf-vs-iso-42001/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is voluntary US guidance organised around govern, map, measure and manage. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard for an AI management system that a third party can certify. They overlap heavily, NIST publishes a crosswalk, and neither on its own gives presumption of conformity under the EU AI Act.

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is free, voluntary guidance from the US National Institute of Standards and Technology on identifying and managing AI risk. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard that sets requirements for an AI management system, which an accredited auditor can certify. In practice, firms use the NIST framework as a vocabulary and checklist, and ISO/IEC 42001 when a customer or regulator wants proof.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What each one is

Each has its own explainer, linked below; this piece compares them.

The AI RMF is a framework. It describes outcomes to aim for under four functions: govern, map, measure and manage. It does not say how much is enough, and nobody audits against it. Its value is a shared language for AI risk that buyers, auditors and other frameworks refer to.

ISO/IEC 42001 is a management system standard, built on the same clause structure as ISO 27001 and ISO 9001. It requires a defined scope, an AI policy, assigned roles, risk and impact assessment, chosen controls, internal audit, management review and continual improvement. A certificate says that system exists and runs. It does not say any AI output is correct.

|  | NIST AI RMF | ISO/IEC 42001 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Publisher | US National Institute of Standards and Technology | ISO and IEC, international |
| Type | Voluntary framework of outcomes | Requirements for a management system |
| Certifiable | No | Yes, by an accredited certification body |
| Cost to obtain | Free | Paid standard, plus audit fees if certifying |
| Structure | Four functions: govern, map, measure, manage | Clauses 4 to 10, plus reference controls in annexes |
| What it produces | A risk vocabulary and profiles | Documented policy, assessments, records and audit evidence |
| Status in 2026 | 1.0, under revision | 2023 edition |
| EU AI Act standing | None formal | Not sufficient alone for presumption of conformity |

## Where they overlap and differ

The overlap is large. The crosswalk on NIST's AI Resource Center pairs, for example, GOVERN 2.3 on executive responsibility with ISO clause 5 on leadership and clause 9.3 on management review. MAP 1.1 on intended purpose maps to ISO's AI system impact assessment. MEASURE 2.4 on monitoring in production maps to clause 9.1 on monitoring and measurement.

The differences are about obligation and evidence. NIST describes what good looks like; ISO requires you to show it to an external auditor. ISO also forces the dull parts: document control, competence records, corrective actions. NIST says more about the AI risks themselves.

## How regulation changes the choice

Neither framework is a legal requirement in itself. For firms selling into the EU, the AI Act's high-risk obligations now apply to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027, after Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 amended the timetable. The route to presumption of conformity is harmonised European standards. The first, EN 18286 for quality management systems, was published by the Commission on 14 October 2026. Orrick notes it uses the same management system structure as ISO/IEC 42001 and is designed to sit on top of it, but that 42001 alone does not confer the presumption.

US banks have a separate line. SR 26-2, issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026, replaced SR 11-7 as model risk guidance. Neither NIST nor ISO substitutes for it; see [What is model risk management?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/).

## Which to choose

| Situation | Start with |
| --- | --- |
| First AI policy, no customer pressure yet | NIST AI RMF, free, as the structure for an inventory and risk register |
| Enterprise buyers asking for AI governance evidence in security reviews | ISO/IEC 42001 gap assessment, then certification if deals depend on it |
| Already certified to ISO 27001 | ISO/IEC 42001, reusing the same management system |
| Building or selling high-risk AI into the EU | ISO/IEC 42001 as the base, with EN 18286 layered on |
| US-regulated bank or lender | SR 26-2 first, with NIST as the AI risk vocabulary |
| Mostly using vendor tools, low exposure | NIST functions as a checklist; no certification |

## The **lowob** view

**lowob**'s view is that both frameworks are asking for the same thing in different tones: a record. In the brain loop (store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning), the frameworks live on the record and learning steps. NIST's map function is an inventory of each AI use and its context. ISO's documented information, management review and continual improvement are a decision record with outcomes written back. Regulators want the chain from decision to result, an argument made in [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/).

So build one record and map it to both. Keep a register of each AI use with owner, purpose, data, autonomy level and approver. Log each material decision with its reason, status and expected outcome, and review the outcomes quarterly. That serves a NIST self-assessment today and an ISO audit later, without a second set of paperwork.

## lowob takeaways

- **NIST is guidance; ISO is evidence.** One gives the vocabulary, the other a certificate a buyer can check.
- **They map closely.** NIST's crosswalk pairs AI RMF subcategories with ISO clauses.
- **Neither is EU compliance alone.** Harmonised standards such as EN 18286 carry the presumption of conformity.
- **Both need a record.** An AI register and a decision log serve either framework.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001?

The NIST AI RMF is free, voluntary US guidance on managing AI risk. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard for an AI management system that can be certified by an accredited auditor.

### Can you be certified to the NIST AI RMF?

No. NIST publishes it for voluntary use, and there is no certification scheme. Firms that need a certificate use ISO/IEC 42001.

### Does ISO 42001 make you compliant with the EU AI Act?

Not on its own. It does not give presumption of conformity; harmonised standards such as EN 18286 do. It is a sound base for the management system the Act expects.

## Sources and notes

- [NIST, AI Risk Management Framework](https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework), page updated 13 August 2026. Primary source; release date and revision status.
- [IEC Webstore, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Artificial intelligence management system](https://webstore.iec.ch/publication/90574), 18 December 2023. Standard abstract; full text is paid.
- [NIST AI Resource Center, NIST AI RMF to ISO/IEC 42001 crosswalk](https://airc.nist.gov/docs/NIST_AI_RMF_to_ISO_IEC_42001_Crosswalk.pdf), undated. Maps to the draft (FDIS) text of the standard; clause numbers may differ slightly from the final edition.
- [Orrick, First harmonised technical standard published under the EU AI Act](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/10/First-Harmonised-Technical-Standard-Published-Under-the-EU-AI-Act), 27 October 2026. Law firm analysis of EN 18286.
- [Steptoe via Mondaq, EU AI Act amendments enter into force](https://webiis08.mondaq.com/technology/1824674/eu-ai-act-amendments-enter-into-force), 30 July 2026. Law firm summary of Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 and the revised dates.
- [Federal Reserve, SR 26-2: Revised guidance on model risk management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr2602.htm), 17 April 2026. Primary supervisory letter; applies to US banking organisations.

# Agentic AI vs Generative AI: What Changes When the Model Can Act

Source: https://lowob.com/research/agentic-ai-vs-generative-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Generative AI produces text, images or code in response to a prompt; agentic AI wraps the same models in a loop that plans steps and calls tools that change other systems. The model is often identical. What changes is who acts, which controls apply, and what evidence each run must leave behind.

Generative AI is a model that produces content, such as text, images or code, in response to a prompt, and hands it to a person. Agentic AI uses the same kind of model inside a loop that plans steps, calls tools and acts in other systems to reach a goal. The model is often identical; the permissions are not. Once a model can act, the question becomes what it may change and who approves it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the two terms mean

Generative AI is a capability. NIST's Generative AI Profile, a companion to its AI Risk Management Framework, takes its definition from US Executive Order 14110: the class of models that emulate the structure and characteristics of input data in order to generate derived synthetic content. In practice that means a [large language model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-large-language-model/) writing a draft for a person to read and use.

Agentic AI is a way of using that capability. Our explainer on [agentic AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agentic-ai/) covers the definition. In Anthropic's December 2024 guidance, the basic unit is a model "enhanced with augmentations such as retrieval, tools, and memory." In an agent, the model "dynamically" directs its own process and tool use. OpenAI's guide adds the test that matters most to a buyer. A system is an agent when the model manages the workflow and has tools that reach external systems. A chatbot that only replies does not qualify.

So the terms are not rivals. Almost every agent has a generative model inside it; the difference is the loop around it and tools that write as well as read.

|  | Generative AI | Agentic AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts from | A prompt | A goal, from a person or a trigger |
| Produces | Content: text, images, code | A completed task, or a task handed back |
| Who acts on the output | A person | The agent, within set limits |
| Touches other systems | Rarely; reads at most | Reads and writes through tools |
| Typical failure | A wrong or invented statement | A wrong action taken with real permissions |
| Main risk register | NIST AI 600-1 risks, such as confabulation | OWASP excessive agency, on top of the generative risks |
| Evidence needed | The prompt and the output | A trace of each step, tool call, approval and outcome |

## What changes when the model can act

**The failure moves from words to actions.** NIST lists confabulation, its term for confidently stated false content, among twelve generative AI risks. With generative AI, a confabulated figure sits in a draft until someone reads it. With an agent, the same figure can be written into a CRM, a quote or an email. OWASP's entry on excessive agency defines the problem as a vulnerability that "enables damaging actions to be performed" in response to flawed model output, whatever caused the flaw.

**Errors compound.** Anthropic warns that the autonomous nature of agents means "higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors." A wrong early step becomes the input to every later one. Anthropic recommends sandboxed testing and stopping conditions, such as a maximum number of iterations.

**The controls change in kind.** Generative AI needs content controls, such as approved sources and review before use. Agents need action controls as well. OWASP's mitigations are concrete: limit the tools an agent can call to the minimum necessary, limit each tool's permissions, and "require a human to approve high-impact actions before they are taken." OpenAI's guide names two triggers for human intervention: exceeding failure thresholds, and high-risk actions such as cancelling orders or authorising large refunds.

**Cost and speed change.** One prompt is one model call; an agent may make dozens. Anthropic notes that agentic systems "often trade latency and cost for better task performance."

**Adoption lags the talk.** McKinsey's self-reported survey, fielded in May and June 2026, found about two in ten respondents scaling agents across their organisation. Most firms are still at the generative stage.

## Which to choose

The choice is per task. Start with generative AI, and add agentic steps where a task repeats, its steps vary and its actions can be checked. The [workflow automation vs AI agents](https://lowob.com/research/workflow-automation-vs-ai-agents/) comparison covers the third option: fixed steps with a model inside.

| Task | Start with | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Draft a proposal section from approved material | Generative AI | A person reads every word before it leaves |
| Keep CRM fields current after each meeting | Agent at dial level 2 or 3 | Repetitive, internal and reversible |
| Research an account across several sources and assemble a brief | Agent at dial level 1 | Steps vary by account; output is still a draft |
| Send follow-up emails to prospects | Generative AI drafting, a person sending | Client-facing; nothing sends without a person |
| Approve discounts or change prices | Neither acting alone | A judgment with an owner, recorded with its reason |

Four questions settle most cases:

- **Does the task change anything outside the conversation?** If not, it is a generative task, whatever the product is called.
- **Do the steps vary from case to case?** If they are fixed, a workflow is cheaper and easier to test than an agent.
- **Is each action reversible?** Irreversible actions stay behind an [approval gate](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/).
- **Will each run leave a trace?** If not, keep a person approving every action.

## The **lowob** view

**lowob**'s enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. Generative AI sits in reasoning. It drafts from what the wiring hands it and writes nothing back, so the record depends on the person who uses the draft.

An agent reaches every stage. It reads through the wiring, reasons, and acts. That makes the record compulsory rather than optional. Each consequential step should leave what was decided, on what evidence, by whom it was approved, and what outcome was expected.

So the move from generative to agentic is a move along the [autonomy dial](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/), one task at a time. Level 0 answers and level 1 drafts; both are generative uses. Levels 2 and 3 are agentic, with approval or reporting. Level 4, acting alone, should be rare on the commercial line. Rent the models and the agent frameworks. Own the record of what they did.

## lowob takeaways

- **Same model, different permissions.** Agentic AI is generative AI given a loop and tools that write.
- **Risk moves from words to actions.** A confabulated fact in a draft becomes a wrong record once an agent can act.
- **Agents need action controls.** Minimum tools, minimum permissions and approval before high-impact steps.
- **Make the record part of the build.** An agent without a trace of its decisions cannot be audited or improved.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between generative AI and agentic AI?

Generative AI produces content in response to a prompt for a person to use. Agentic AI uses generative models inside a loop that plans steps and calls tools to act in other systems toward a goal.

### Is agentic AI a type of generative AI?

Most agentic systems are built on generative models, so they depend on generative AI. What makes them agentic is the loop, the tools and the authority to act.

### Is agentic AI riskier than generative AI?

It carries the same content risks plus action risks. OWASP calls the main one excessive agency: too many tools, too many permissions or too little oversight.

### Should a company start with generative AI or agentic AI?

Usually generative AI, with a person using every output. Add agentic steps for internal, reversible tasks first.

## Sources and notes

- [NIST, Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. US standards body; voluntary guidance, and its definition quotes US Executive Order 14110.
- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), 19 December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance; the page notes its tooling details have since changed.
- [OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents](https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf), 2025. Vendor guide; definitions and guardrail patterns.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/), 2025. Community security standard.
- [McKinsey, The state of AI in 2026: On the road to ROI](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/quantumblack/our-insights/the-state-of-ai), 25 August 2026. Self-reported online survey of 1,719 respondents.
- The decision table, four questions and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

# What Is a Model Card?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-model-card/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A model card is a short document published with an AI model that sets out what it is for, how it was evaluated, where it performs poorly and what it was trained on. The format comes from a 2019 paper by Mitchell and colleagues and is now standard on model hubs. It describes the model, not the use a buyer puts it to.

A model card is a short document that accompanies an AI model and reports what it is intended for, how it was evaluated, how it performs across different groups and conditions, what data it was trained on, and its known limits. The idea was proposed by Margaret Mitchell and colleagues in 2019 and is now the default format on model hubs. For a business buyer it is the first thing to read about a model, and the last word on nothing: it describes the model, not your use of it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a model card means

The original paper made a simple argument. Trained models were being released with no standard account of where they worked and where they failed. A short card, published with the model, would report performance broken down by the groups and conditions that matter, and say plainly which uses it was not meant for. The examples in the paper were a smiling-face detector and a toxic-comment classifier, but the authors said the format applies to any trained model.

The nine sections the paper proposed are still the core.

| Section (Mitchell et al., 2019) | What it records |
| --- | --- |
| Model details | Developer, version, type, training approach, licence, contact |
| Intended use | Primary uses and users, and uses out of scope |
| Factors | Groups, instruments and conditions that may affect performance |
| Metrics | Performance measures, decision thresholds, how uncertainty is handled |
| Evaluation data | Datasets used for the reported results, and why |
| Training data | What the model learned from, at least its distribution across factors |
| Quantitative analyses | Results by single factor and by combinations of factors |
| Ethical considerations | Sensitive data, high-stakes uses, known harms and mitigations |
| Caveats and recommendations | Remaining concerns, gaps in evaluation, suggested further tests |

## How model cards are used now

Model hubs made the format routine. Hugging Face's annotated template splits intended use into direct, downstream and out-of-scope use, and gives a section to bias, risks and limitations, which it defines carefully: a bias is "a stereotype or disproportionate performance (skew) for some subpopulations", a limitation "a likely failure mode". It also asks for hardware, hours and estimated carbon emitted.

Regulation has picked up the same idea. Article 53(1)(b) and Annex XII of the EU AI Act require providers of general-purpose AI models to give downstream providers information including the tasks the model is intended for, applicable acceptable use policies, release date, architecture and parameter count, input and output modalities, licence, and information on training, testing and validation data. That is a model card in all but name, and it is owed to firms that build products on the model.

Some model providers also publish longer "system cards" for their largest models, which usually add safety testing to performance. They are written by the developer too, and deserve the same reading.

## How a buyer should read one

A 20-to-500-person firm rarely chooses a model directly. It chooses a tool that uses one. The model card still matters, because the tool inherits the model's limits.

| Look for | Why it matters | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Out-of-scope uses | Your use may be listed as unsuitable | Your use case appears on the list |
| Evaluation data | Results on unlike data say little about yours | Only public benchmarks, none near your domain |
| Disaggregated results | Averages hide weak groups or languages | One headline number |
| Training data cut-off and sources | Affects freshness and copyright exposure | No information at all |
| Version and date | Cards describe one version | Card older than the model you are calling |
| Licence | Governs commercial use, especially for [open-weight models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-open-weight-model/) | Licence differs from the vendor's claim |

Two limits apply to every card. It is written by the developer, so it is a disclosure, not an audit. And it says nothing about your prompts, your data or your process. Testing that is your job; see [What are AI evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/).

US banks have a separate documentation regime. SR 26-2, issued by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC on 17 April 2026, replaced SR 11-7 as model risk guidance; see [What is model risk management?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) for its scope.

## The **lowob** view

A model card describes the model. A firm also needs a record of each use: which tool, which model and version, what it is allowed to do, at what autonomy level, who approves its output and what outcome is expected. **lowob** keeps that as a line in the AI inventory, linked to the vendor's card. When the card changes because the model changed, the use line is where the firm decides whether its own approval still holds.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the out-of-scope section first.** It is the quickest way to rule a model out.
- **Distrust single numbers.** Useful cards report results by group and condition.
- **It is a disclosure, not an audit.** The developer wrote it; test your own use.
- **Track the version.** A card describes one model version, and vendors change models.

## Common questions

### What is a model card in machine learning?

A short document published with a trained model that reports its intended use, evaluation, performance across groups and conditions, training data and known limitations.

### Who created model cards?

Margaret Mitchell and colleagues, in the paper "Model Cards for Model Reporting", presented at the FAT\* conference in January 2019.

### What is the difference between a model card and a system card?

A model card describes one model. System cards, published by some large providers, usually also cover the surrounding system and safety testing. Both are written by the developer.

### Does the EU AI Act require model cards?

Not by that name. Annex XII requires general-purpose AI model providers to give downstream providers similar information, including intended tasks, licence and training data.

## Sources and notes

- [Mitchell et al., Model Cards for Model Reporting, arXiv:1810.03993](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.03993v2), revised 14 January 2019. Peer-reviewed conference paper, FAT\* 2019; the origin of the format.
- [Hugging Face, Annotated model card template](https://huggingface.co/docs/hub/en/model-card-annotated), accessed November 2026. Platform documentation from a model hub vendor.
- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Annex XII](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-12), accessed November 2026. Primary legal text on information owed to downstream providers.
- [OWASP CycloneDX, Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM](https://cyclonedx.org/guides/OWASP_CycloneDX-Authoritative-Guide-to-AI-ML-BOM-en.pdf), First Edition Revision 1, 10 June 2026. Open standard guidance; covers model cards inside an ML-BOM.
- [Federal Reserve, SR 26-2: Revised guidance on model risk management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr2602.htm), 17 April 2026. Primary supervisory letter; applies to US banking organisations.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Bill of Materials?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-bill-of-materials/)
- [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/)
- [What Is an Open-Weight Model?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-open-weight-model/)
- [The Model Is Not the Product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/)
- [What Is an AI Center of Excellence?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-center-of-excellence/)

For your two most-used AI tools, ask the vendor which model and version each feature calls, and find that model's card. Note any out-of-scope use that matches yours on your AI inventory.
