# Running a Win-Loss Programme

Source: https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Most firms have tried win-loss once. Few run it as a programme, and the evidence suggests seller-recorded loss reasons rarely match what buyers say. This piece sets out the design choices that keep a programme alive past its first report: a sampling rule, a neutral interviewer, a fixed coding frame, and a route from each theme to a named owner and a recorded decision.

A win-loss programme is a standing process that asks buyers why they chose as they did, codes the answers against a fixed frame, and routes each recurring theme to someone who must decide what to change. The one-off study is common; the programme is rare. Gartner analyst Todd Berkowitz has argued that no more than a third of sales organisations run win-loss with rigour, and win-loss vendor Clozd reports that buyer and seller loss reasons align only 15% of the time. The fix is less about better interviews than about what happens after them: a sampling rule, a neutral interviewer, and a decision record for every finding.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most firms with more than a handful of sellers have run a win-loss exercise at some point. Someone interviews a dozen buyers, writes a deck, presents it to the leadership team, and the deck is filed. A year later the same losses are being explained in the same way.

The definition is settled and we will not repeat it here: [*What is win-loss analysis?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers what it is and how a first round works. This piece is about the harder part, which is keeping it running long enough to change decisions.

## Why most programmes stop after one round

The one-off study fails for structural reasons rather than for lack of effort. Three are common.

**It has no sampling rule.** The first round interviews whoever will talk, which usually means friendly wins and a few dramatic losses. Nobody can say whether the findings describe the pipeline or the anecdotes.

**It reports once.** A single annual readout arrives months after the deals it describes, when the people involved have moved on. Clozd's own guidance is to deliver findings in small, regular doses rather than a year-end report, and to run collection continuously rather than in bursts.

**It routes to nobody.** The deck names themes ("pricing", "implementation concerns") but not owners. A theme with no owner is an observation, and observations do not get funded.

Gartner research summarised in trade press reports that organisations running rigorous, ongoing programmes see up to a 50% improvement in win rates; Clozd quotes the Gartner analyst Todd Berkowitz giving the same figure alongside a 15% to 30% increase in revenue. The baseline and method behind that figure are not published, so we treat it as direction. The direction matters: the benefit is attributed to the ongoing programme, not the study. Clozd's 2025 State of Win-Loss report, sponsored with The Alliance and drawing on more than 1,000 professionals, points the same way: 85% of ongoing, cross-functional programmes reported positive return on investment, against 55% of project-based ones, and 39% of companies said they ran an ongoing programme. Clozd sells win-loss services, so read both figures as vendor-reported.

## What the evidence says about the reasons you already have

Every CRM holds a loss reason of some kind. The case for a programme rests on how often that field is wrong.

Clozd's figure of 15% alignment is the most quoted. A Showpad interview with Clozd's co-founder, published in August 2026, adds three more vendor-reported findings: about 85% of CRM loss reasons do not match what buyers say drove the decision; about 77% of the factors that influenced a decision never came up in sales conversations, based on comparing interviews with call recordings; and about 10% of closed-won customers were already at risk when interviewed, often because of implementation doubts.

The no-decision finding is the one most firms are not set up to capture. Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's analysis of about 2.5 million recorded conversations, summarised by Challenger in 2024, found that 40% to 60% of lost deals ended with the buyer doing nothing. Their explanation is fear of making a mistake rather than preference for a rival. A CRM reason list that offers "lost to competitor" and "price" but not "no decision" will misclassify half the losses before anyone interviews anyone.

| Evidence source | What it gives you | Main weakness | Cost per deal |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CRM loss reason | Coverage of every deal | Recorded by the seller, often under time pressure | Near zero |
| Call recordings and transcripts | What was said, verbatim | Misses what the buyer never raised with you | Low once recorded |
| Post-decision survey | Scale and comparable scores | Low response; shallow answers | Low |
| Buyer interview | The buyer's actual reasoning, including internal politics | Slow; needs a skilled, neutral interviewer | Highest |

Forrester's 2025 best-practice report on win-loss treats surveys, interviews and call transcripts as complementary sources, and that is the right frame. The CRM field is the census. Interviews are the audit of the census. The design question is how to make the audit regular enough that the census improves.

> A theme with no owner is an observation, and observations do not get funded.

## Designing the programme

Five design choices decide whether a programme survives. Each has a sensible default that changes with size.

**The sampling rule.** Decide in advance which deals are eligible: by size, by segment and by outcome. Include no-decisions explicitly. Academic work on interview saturation points lower for a homogeneous group: Guest, Bunce and Johnson found the main themes in 60 interviews were present by about 12, and Hennink and colleagues found code saturation at nine interviews but that 16 to 24 were needed to understand the issues in depth. Clozd reports that thematic saturation tends to arrive at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, which sets the ambition for a mid-size firm: one or two segments done properly beats six done thinly.

**The interviewer.** Buyers are more candid with someone who did not sell to them. Clozd's position, unsurprisingly for a third-party provider, is that sellers rarely get honest answers about their own losses. A smaller firm can use a senior person from outside the deal team, such as an operations lead or a partner from another practice. The rule is that the interviewer has no stake in the deal.

**Timing.** Interview within weeks of the decision, while the buyer still remembers the internal discussion. Enrol each eligible deal as it closes rather than batching at quarter end.

**The coding frame.** Fix a short list of themes before the first interview and code every answer against it. Add themes deliberately, with a date, rather than letting each analyst invent categories. Without a fixed frame, nobody can compare this quarter with last.

**The readout cadence.** Monthly to the revenue leader, quarterly to the leadership team. The monthly note is short: what came up, which themes are rising, which decisions are due for a check.

| Design choice | Around 20 to 50 people | Around 200 people |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sample | Every lost deal above a value threshold, plus every no-decision | Rule by segment, with quotas per outcome |
| Interviewer | Senior person outside the deal team | Dedicated analyst or third party |
| Volume | Two to four interviews a month | Enough to reach saturation per segment each half-year |
| Coding frame | Eight to ten themes on one page | Versioned frame owned by revenue operations |
| Readout | Monthly note to the founder or revenue lead | Monthly note plus quarterly review with product and finance |
| Where findings live | The decision record, one line per theme | The decision record, linked to the deals that raised it |

## From finding to decision

The step most programmes skip is the one that matters: turning a coded theme into a decision someone owns.

Each recurring theme should produce one entry in the commercial decision record, using the same fields we set out in [*The commercial decisions worth recording*](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/): the decision, the reason, the owner, the status, the expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back.

| Recurring theme | Natural owner | Typical decision | What to check, and when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buyers could not tell us apart from a rival | Marketing lead | Rewrite the positioning for one segment | Win rate against that rival, two quarters on |
| Deals stalled after the proposal | Revenue lead | Add a risk-reduction step to the proposal standard | No-decision rate in that segment |
| Implementation worries late in the cycle | Delivery lead | Introduce delivery staff before the final proposal | Late-stage slippage and early churn |
| Price objections in one size band | Finance and revenue | Test a package change in that band | Discount depth and win rate in the band |
| Seller misread the buying group | Sales managers | Change qualification questions | Stage conversion, next quarter |

Two habits keep this honest. First, the record keeps the theme's evidence: how many interviews raised it, in which segment. Second, when a decision is revisited, it is superseded rather than edited, so the firm can later see what it believed and when, which is the argument of [*Supersede, never overwrite*](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

## Feeding the census back

The programme should also improve the CRM field it audits. Once a quarter, compare the coded interview reason with the seller's recorded reason for the same deals. Where they disagree, ask whether the reason list is wrong or the recording habit is.

HubSpot's default deal properties, for example, include a separate closed-lost reason field with customisable options. Most CRMs offer an equivalent. The interview programme is how you decide what those options should be. [*What is a closed-lost reason?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) covers how to design a list people will fill in honestly. The minimum change is to add "no decision" as a reason in its own right, and to require a note when it is chosen.

Over time the gap between the census and the audit should narrow. If it does not, the problem is incentive rather than design. Sellers who expect a loss reason to be used against them will choose the least damaging option, and [*The reason nobody types*](https://lowob.com/research/the-reason-nobody-types/) explains why that pattern is predictable.

## Where the programme sits in the commercial system

Win-loss is the point where the commercial system checks its own work. Qualification decides which deals to pursue. Discount governance decides what to concede. Proposals decide how to frame the offer. Forecasting decides what to expect. Win-loss is the only routine that asks the buyer which of those calls were right.

For the build order, that makes it the outcome half of the record. A qualification decision written down in March becomes evidence when a buyer explains in June why the deal went nowhere. Without the programme, the record holds decisions and outcomes but not causes, and a system trained on it can learn only correlation.

Illustrative example: one theme, one decision

Decision
:   Bring a delivery lead into every proposal meeting above a set deal value for two quarters.

Reason and owner
:   Six of the last nineteen interviewed losses in the mid-market segment named implementation risk as the deciding factor, and most were recorded in the CRM as price. Owned by the head of delivery, agreed with the revenue lead.

What changed
:   The proposal standard gained a delivery section; the no-decision rate in the segment is checked at the end of the second quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Run a programme, not a study.** The benefit comes from ongoing collection and regular readouts, not one deck.
- **Sample by rule.** Decide eligible deals in advance and include no-decisions explicitly.
- **Keep the interviewer neutral.** Someone with no stake in the deal hears the real reason.
- **Route every theme to an owner.** Each recurring finding becomes a recorded decision with a check date.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a programme

- A written sampling rule, including no-decision deals
- An interviewer with no stake in the deals interviewed
- A fixed coding frame of eight to ten themes
- A monthly readout with a named recipient
- Every recurring theme linked to one decision, one owner and one check date
- "No decision" added to the CRM's loss reason list

## Common questions

### How many win-loss interviews do you need?

Enough to reach saturation in the segment you care about. Win-loss vendor Clozd reports that new themes tend to stop appearing at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, so a mid-size firm should focus on one or two segments rather than spreading interviews thinly.

### Should salespeople conduct win-loss interviews?

Generally not for their own deals. Buyers are more candid with someone who had no stake in the outcome, such as a senior colleague outside the deal team or a third party.

### How soon after a deal closes should you interview the buyer?

Within weeks, while the buyer still remembers the internal discussion. Enrolling each eligible deal as it closes works better than batching at the end of a quarter.

### What is the difference between win-loss analysis and a win-loss programme?

Analysis is the study of why deals were won or lost. A programme is the standing process around it: a sampling rule, regular interviews, a fixed coding frame, and a route from each finding to a decision someone owns.

## Sources and notes

Peer-reviewed; health research interviews, not buyer interviews, and it also summarises Guest, Bunce and Johnson (Field Methods, 2006).

Secondary summary; no date, sample or baseline given.

# One Thousand People: Governance Arrives

Source: https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At around a thousand people, auditors, regulators, security teams and large customers start asking how decisions were made, and "we discussed it" stops being an answer. The record's job becomes governance: a trace specification, an evidenced review gate, registered agents and agreed retention. Each decision record should be owned by the business function whose decisions it records.

At around a thousand people, auditors, regulators, security teams and large customers start asking how decisions were made, and "we discussed it" stops being an answer. The enterprise brain's job becomes governance. Four things have to exist: a trace specification for each AI-assisted decision class, a review gate that leaves evidence, registered agents with owners and scoped permissions, and retention rules agreed with counsel. The risk becomes a platform that nobody in the business owns.

This is the fifth rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/), was about delegation inside the firm. At a thousand, people outside the firm, and functions inside it whose job is oversight, start asking to see the reasoning.

## Who starts asking

Somewhere in this range, often earlier for regulated firms, the organisation acquires functions whose job is to ask questions about other functions' decisions. Risk. Compliance. Internal audit. Information security. Procurement teams at large customers who send hundred-question security reviews. Each wants to know who decided, on what basis, and who checked.

Regulation arrives at explicit size thresholds. The EU's Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, narrowed the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive to EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450 million of turnover. Its due-diligence counterpart now starts at 5,000 employees. Neither is an AI rule, but both bring the audit habit with them: documented processes, assurance, and a record of who approved what.

At the same time, AI use has spread. Agents act on behalf of employees: drafting, routing, approving small things, triggering workflows. Our piece [*Regulators want the chain, not the model*](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) sets out what supervisors ask for when they examine AI-assisted decisions.

| Who asks | What they want to see | Typical trigger |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Internal audit | Who decided, on what evidence, and who reviewed | Annual audit plan |
| Risk and compliance | Controls on AI-assisted decisions, and evidence they ran | New deployment or regulatory change |
| Large customers | How their data is used, and by which agents | Security questionnaire in procurement |
| Regulators | Reconstruction of a specific decision, end to end | Examination or complaint |
| Sustainability assurance | Documented processes behind reported figures | CSRD scope at 1,000 employees |

## What the rules now say about AI

The regulatory picture changed in 2026, and the change cuts both ways.

In US banking, SR 26-2, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, the OCC and the FDIC, superseded SR 11-7 and is expected to be most relevant to banks with more than $30 billion of assets. Its footnote 3 states that generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance", and that a bank's own risk management and governance practices should determine the controls for them. US bank supervisors have not issued agent-specific logging rules. That leaves the design of those controls to the firm, and a firm that cannot show how an agent-assisted decision was made will still have to explain it.

In the EU, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force from 27 July 2026, moved the AI Act's Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and Annex I to 2 August 2028. It softened the Article 4 AI literacy obligation to a duty to support literacy. On 14 October 2026 the Commission published EN 18286, the first harmonised standard under the Act, covering the quality management system in Article 17. Orrick notes that it is designed to sit on top of ISO/IEC 42001 and that conformity with it gives a presumption of conformity for the requirements it covers. Our explainer [*The EU AI Act for commercial teams*](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) covers which uses are high-risk.

> The absence of an agent-specific rule is not the absence of an expectation. Someone will still ask how the decision was made.

## What has to exist now

**A trace specification.** For every AI-assisted decision class: inputs, evidence with its standing, model and prompt versions, output, every human action with timing, final action, and outcome. Written with compliance, before the next production deployment. Our explainer [*What is an AI audit trail?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) covers the fields.

**An evidenced review gate.** Review that leaves proof: sources opened, time on item, class of edit, blind second looks on a sample. [*A reviewer who does not verify is not a control*](https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/) explains why approval alone proves little.

**Agent identity and permissions.** Every agent registered, with an owner, a scope, and permissions that follow the user it acts for. This is the area where the large software vendors are competing hardest, and for most organisations it is a buy, not a build. Microsoft's Entra Agent ID, for example, documents agent identities created from blueprints, named owners and sponsors, inheritable permissions, conditional access policies for agents and lifecycle governance, with Agent 365 as a control plane built on it. Our explainer [*What is agent identity?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/) compares the approaches.

**Retention and deletion, agreed with counsel.** What is kept, for how long, who can see it, and how deletion leaves a tombstone rather than a hole.

## Who owns the record

This is the stage where a platform team typically forms around AI. That is useful and also dangerous. A platform team that owns the judgment record will manage it as infrastructure: uptime, schemas, cost. The record will be technically sound and commercially empty.

The better arrangement: each decision record is owned by the function whose decisions it records. Credit owns credit decisions. Sales owns deal decisions. The platform team owns the standards, the trace, the tooling and the export, and serves the functions. Risk and compliance oversee. Banking's model risk practice, covered in [*What is model risk management?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/), separates ownership from oversight in a similar way.

## Buy the context layer, own the judgment record

At this size, connectors, enterprise search, assistants and agent registries are mature products. Build them only for real differentiation. What you should not rent is the record of how you decide: the decision classes, the falsifiers, the outcomes, the precedents. Own that, in a format you can export, whatever tools sit on top. [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) sets out the rule across every size.

**In practice:** write the trace specification with compliance for each AI-assisted decision class. Register every agent with an owner, scope and inherited permissions. Assign each decision record to its business function, and give the platform team standards and tooling. Run a reconstruction drill: rebuild a three-month-old decision end to end, and time it.

**What would prove this wrong:** thousand-person organisations passing audits, examinations and customer security reviews of AI-assisted decisions without traces or evidenced review. The next rung, [*Ten thousand people: density, and the case for federation*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/), is where those traces become numerous enough to learn from.

## lowob takeaways

- **Expect outsiders to ask.** Auditors, regulators and large customers want the chain of a decision, not a description of the model.
- **Do not wait for an agent rule.** SR 26-2 leaves agentic AI to firms' own governance, which means the firm must design it.
- **Write the trace before deploying.** Inputs, evidence, versions, human actions, final action and outcome.
- **Buy agent identity.** Register every agent with an owner, scope and permissions that follow its user.
- **Keep the record with the business.** Functions own their decisions; the platform owns standards and export.

## Common questions

### What AI governance does a company need at 1,000 employees?

A trace specification for each AI-assisted decision class, an evidenced review gate, registered agents with owners, scopes and inherited permissions, and retention and deletion rules agreed with counsel.

### Does SR 26-2 cover generative or agentic AI?

No. SR 26-2, issued in April 2026, states in a footnote that generative and agentic AI models are outside its scope, and that a bank's own risk management and governance should determine the controls for them.

### Who should own AI decision records in a large company?

The function whose decisions the record holds, such as credit owning credit decisions. The platform team owns standards, trace, tooling and export, and risk and compliance oversee.

### How can a company test whether its AI decisions are auditable?

Run a reconstruction drill: pick a three-month-old AI-assisted decision, rebuild it end to end from the record, and time how long it takes.

# The Build Order for Retail, DTC and Luxury

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-retail-dtc-and-luxury/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: In retail, DTC and luxury the order holds, but client consent governs what can be connected. GDPR's absolute right to object to direct marketing, California's new CCPA regulations and twenty US state privacy laws set the outer limit; what clients told an adviser in confidence sets a tighter one. The first record is who was invited or offered what, and the first agent prompts advisers rather than writing to clients.

The Build Order holds in retail, DTC and luxury, but client consent governs what can be connected. The commercial line runs through clienteling: advisers, their client books and the decisions about who to invite, what to offer and when. The law sets the outer limit on that context. GDPR gives people an absolute right to object to direct marketing, including profiling; California's updated CCPA regulations took effect on 1 January 2026; and twenty US states have comprehensive privacy laws in effect this year. What clients told an adviser in confidence sets a tighter limit still. The first agent prompts the adviser. It never writes to the client.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

Retail is the sector where the gap between what a company could connect and what it should connect is widest. A DTC brand can join web sessions, email engagement, order history and loyalty data into one profile in an afternoon. A luxury house can, in principle, ingest years of adviser notes and messaging threads. The capability is not the constraint. Consent is, and so is the client's sense that a relationship with a person has not become a relationship with a database.

This edition runs the full sequence (Gateway 0, tooling, context, record, reasoning and Gateways 1 to 3) for brands of 20 to 500 people: DTC labels, specialist retailers and luxury houses with boutiques and a wholesale arm. Part 10 tested the sequence on a composite jeweller. This piece generalises it to the sector and sets out the consent rules as they stand in 2026.

## Where the commercial line sits

In retail the commercial line depends on the price point. For a mass DTC brand it runs through campaigns, segments and offers, decided weekly by a growth team. For a luxury house it runs through people: client advisers who know a few hundred clients each, and the decisions about who sees a new piece first.

The luxury economics explain why those decisions matter. Bain and Altagamma's 2025 study put the personal luxury goods market at about €358bn, largely flat for the year, with the customer base falling to about 340 million from 400 million in 2022. Bain expects growth of 3% to 5% in 2026 and warned that persistent price increases have left some customers feeling "betrayed". With fewer clients, each relationship carries more of the revenue, and each decision about a client carries more risk.

Clients are already using AI themselves. McKinsey's May 2026 research on luxury in the agentic age reported that 85% of luxury consumers in its sample use a general-purpose AI assistant for shopping decisions, while only 29% prefer to use AI shopping tools in stores. McKinsey treats those figures as directional because the luxury sample was small. Its conclusion is the useful part: human judgment should stay at the point of purchase commitment, and AI should give advisers context rather than replace them.

| Industry lens | Retail, DTC and luxury |
| --- | --- |
| Where the commercial line sits | DTC: campaigns, segments and offers. Luxury: clienteling, previews, allocation of scarce pieces |
| The store | Commerce platform, clienteling app or CRM, point of sale, email and SMS platform |
| What makes it harder | Adviser knowledge lives in personal notes and messaging apps |
| Outcome lag | Days for a DTC campaign; a season for clienteling |
| Who defends the decision | Head of retail or clienteling, growth lead, store directors |
| The sector's wall | What clients told an adviser in confidence, and data without a lawful basis for marketing |
| Regulatory pressure | GDPR and UK GDPR, CCPA as amended, twenty US state privacy laws |

## Consent decides what connects

Most sectors in this series have a regulator or a professional rule that draws the wall. In retail the wall is drawn by the client's consent, and the rules differ by market. A brand selling in Europe and the US needs to design for the strictest of them.

**Europe and the UK.** The UK Information Commissioner's Office describes the right to object to direct marketing as effectively absolute: if someone objects, the business must stop, and there are no grounds on which it can refuse. The right covers profiling for direct marketing too, and the ICO's own example is using location data to infer what products someone might want. A clienteling agent that scores clients for a preview is profiling for direct marketing. A client who has objected must drop out of it entirely. The ICO recommends keeping a suppression list rather than deleting the record, so the objection survives the next data import.

**California.** The California Privacy Protection Agency's updated regulations took effect on 1 January 2026. They cover risk assessments, cybersecurity audits and automated decisionmaking technology. Risk assessment obligations began on 1 January 2026, with attestations due by 1 April 2028. Businesses using automated decisionmaking technology for significant decisions must comply from 1 January 2027. A brand should check with counsel whether any clienteling or offer logic falls within that definition before the agent is built, not after.

**Other US states.** MultiState counted twenty states with comprehensive privacy laws in effect in 2026, three of which (Indiana, Kentucky and Rhode Island) took effect on 1 January. These laws give consumers rights to opt out of targeted advertising, sale of their data and certain profiling, and generally require opt-in consent to process sensitive data. Rhode Island's law carries penalties of up to $10,000 per violation with no cure period.

| Consent question | What it means for the wiring |
| --- | --- |
| Has the client objected to direct marketing? | Excluded from every prompt and segment, kept on a suppression list |
| Did the client opt in to adviser contact? | Only then can adviser outreach history join the context layer |
| Is any field sensitive data (health, for example sizes linked to a medical need)? | Opt-in required under most US state laws; leave out by default |
| Was the data collected for service, not marketing? | Alterations and repairs history stays in service unless the notice covers marketing |
| Does the logic make a significant decision about a person? | Check against California's ADMT rules, applicable from 1 January 2027 |

> In retail, the context layer is only as wide as the client's consent. The record of who was invited and why is what the brand owns.

## The wall: the adviser's private knowledge

The law sets the outer limit. The sector's wall sits inside it.

Luxury advisers hold knowledge no system was given: a client's anniversary, who a gift was for, a partner's name, a preference mentioned once at a fitting. Much of it lives in personal phones and messaging apps. Taylor Wessing's employment analysis of digital clienteling notes that advisers contacting clients by text and WhatsApp gives them direct access to client details, that employers must ensure that data is protected and that clients know how it will be used, and that customers may follow an adviser who leaves. It also notes that non-solicitation terms are easier to enforce where communication happens on work devices.

That creates a tension the build has to resolve deliberately. The brand has a legitimate interest in moving client relationships onto its own systems, so they survive an adviser's departure. It has no licence to ingest everything an adviser knows. The rule we use:

- **Connect** order history, preview attendance, stated preferences the client recorded through the brand, and outreach logged on brand channels.
- **Move, then connect** adviser contact onto a brand-owned messaging channel with a clear notice, rather than scraping personal threads.
- **Never connect** private confidences, notes about third parties such as gift recipients, and anything the client shared with a person rather than the brand.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in retail and luxury | The main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | An owner in clienteling or growth, the suite of record, and one client record used in boutiques and online | Advisers keeping their real client book outside the system |
| Tooling | Assistant seats for clienteling leads and the growth team, not every store associate | Seats issued before the client record is trusted |
| Context | Order history, preview attendance, consented preferences, brand-channel outreach | Ingesting personal messaging threads and adviser notes wholesale |
| Record | Preview invitations, allocation of scarce pieces and offer decisions, each with reason and owner | Recording the invitation but not why that client was chosen |
| Reasoning | A first agent that prompts advisers: an anniversary near, a requested piece in stock | Agent-written messages going straight to clients |
| Gateway 1 | Nothing reaches a client that an adviser did not write | Approval becoming a click on a draft the adviser never read |
| Gateway 2 | Sales within 90 days of each invitation or offer written back to the decision | Crediting the agent for purchases the adviser would have made anyway |
| Gateway 3 | The record extends to merchandising and wholesale allocation | Client-level data flowing into wholesale or dealer conversations |

**The record.** The first record is the decision to invite or offer: who was invited to a preview, who was offered a scarce piece, who received a private appointment, and why. These decisions recur every season, resemble each other and are graded within one: the client bought, or did not. In DTC the equivalent is the offer decision, which segment received which discount and whether it changed behaviour, and the lag is days rather than a season. Part 9 covers which decisions to record and *The field that makes a record a judgment* covers the reason field, which is where most retail records are thinnest.

**The first agent.** For luxury it prompts the adviser and sits at level 0 or 1 on the autonomy dial: it answers questions and drafts notes for the adviser's own use. It does not draft messages to clients. For a DTC growth team the first agent can sit one step higher, drafting segment briefs and offer rationales for a person to approve, because the outcome lag is short and the relationship is with the brand rather than an adviser.

Composite example: a luxury house moves the client book in-house

Decision
:   Move adviser outreach onto a brand-owned messaging channel over one season, and connect only that channel, order history and recorded preferences to the clienteling context layer.

Reason and owner
:   Two senior advisers had left with client relationships held on personal phones, and the brand could not show clients had agreed to their adviser notes being used for marketing. Owned by the head of clienteling, with the data protection lead.

What changed
:   Preview invitations are now recorded with a reason, and objection status is checked before any prompt. Advisers keep their own private notes outside the system, by agreement.

Illustrative: a composite of a luxury house of around 200 people with boutiques and a wholesale arm, built from patterns across engagements.

## The gateways in retail

**Gateway 1, in reverse.** In most sectors the gate guards against a bad message. In luxury it also guards against a good relationship starting to feel automated. That is why the rule is stricter than "nothing sends without a person": nothing reaches a client that the adviser did not write. A brand that lets advisers approve agent drafts with one click will see approval rates rise and relationships thin. *Approval rate measures fatigue too* explains how to tell the difference.

**Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision.** Each invitation or offer carries the value at stake and the outcome within a set window, such as 90 days. The hard part is attribution. Many top clients would have bought anyway, so the honest comparison is against similar clients who were not invited. *Attribution vs incrementality* sets out the method.

**Gateway 3: commercial is ready to share its brain.** Merchandising wants to know which pieces were requested and not available; wholesale wants allocation signals. Both are legitimate uses of aggregate data. Neither needs a named client. Before the record extends, decisions and outcomes should be shareable as aggregates, with client identity staying in clienteling.

## lowob takeaways

- **Consent sets the width of the context layer.** Design for the strictest market you sell into, and keep objections on a suppression list.
- **Record who was invited and why.** Preview, allocation and offer decisions are frequent, similar and graded within a season.
- **Move the client book before connecting it.** Bring adviser contact onto brand channels with a notice; do not scrape personal threads.
- **Keep the first agent low on the dial.** It prompts advisers. Nothing reaches a client that an adviser did not write.

Gateway card

### Before a retail or luxury brand connects its client data

- Objection and opt-in status available as fields and checked before any prompt or segment
- Sensitive data identified and excluded by default
- Adviser outreach moving to a brand-owned channel with a clear notice
- Preview, allocation and offer decisions recorded with reason, owner and value at stake
- A written rule that no agent drafts messages to clients

## Common questions

### How can luxury brands use AI for clienteling without losing the personal touch?

Use agents that prompt client advisers, for example about an anniversary or a requested piece now in stock, and keep the decision and the message with the adviser. Nothing should reach a client that the adviser did not write.

### Does GDPR allow AI profiling for marketing?

Profiling for direct marketing needs a lawful basis and a clear notice, and people have an absolute right to object to it. The UK ICO's guidance says that once someone objects, the business must stop using their data for direct marketing, including profiling.

### Which US state privacy laws took effect in 2026?

Indiana, Kentucky and Rhode Island's comprehensive privacy laws took effect on 1 January 2026, and California's updated CCPA regulations took effect the same day. MultiState counts twenty states with comprehensive privacy laws in effect in 2026.

### Can a retailer use sales associates' WhatsApp chats in its CRM?

Not by default. Clients shared those details with a person, often on a personal device. The safer route is to move adviser contact to a brand-owned channel with a clear notice, and to connect only that channel.

# The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Every 'enterprise brain' product on the market is the same three things: memory, meaning and governance. That is a real context layer, but not a brain, because nobody has shipped the fourth layer, judgment: how the organisation decides. The brain that compounds is a record of decisions that can be audited and revised.

An enterprise brain is an accountable record that people and AI agents read before they act and write to afterwards, not a mind that thinks for the company. Products sold under the name supply memory, meaning and governance well. They do not supply the fourth requirement, judgment: a dated record of what the company decided, why, who approved it, what it replaced and whether it worked. Agent memory research agrees: agents usually fail after the evidence is found, when they must work out which version is current.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Imagine asking your company's AI assistant why the sales team stopped promising a particular feature. It finds an old product deck, a meeting summary and a new FAQ. All three sound plausible. Only one reflects the current decision.

That is the promise, and the limitation, of an **enterprise brain**: a shared place where AI agents can find company context. But finding information is not the same as knowing **which decision is current, who approved it, and why an earlier answer no longer applies**. This piece sets out what the brain is, why a mind is the wrong metaphor, what the market sells and how to build toward it.

## What an enterprise brain can do, and what it still needs

Companies store useful knowledge in contracts, slide decks, meeting notes, customer records and conversations. Different teams often see different parts of it. When someone leaves, or a project changes direction, the reasoning behind a decision is easily lost.

In September 2026, WRITER introduced Enterprise Brain, which it describes as a shared context layer for marketing, sales and other AI agents, bringing together brand knowledge, decision logic and live business data, with a team-level agent memory layer. Other vendors describe related approaches as workplace intelligence or company knowledge layers. These are useful products, not just a catchy metaphor; our ranking of [enterprise context platforms](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-enterprise-context-platforms-ranked-for-regulated-firms/) covers how to choose.

Most enterprise brain systems are trying to connect three things: **memory**, what the company has said and done; **meaning**, shared definitions so the same financial or commercial term is not interpreted differently by each team; and **governance**, rules about who can see, change and approve information. The harder fourth requirement is **judgment**: a reliable record of why a decision was made, what evidence mattered and when that decision was superseded. Vendors are adding decision records, but the existence of a record does not guarantee it will be interpreted correctly later.

**lowob** uses two vocabularies for one system. This article and *The first two-fifths* describe what the brain must hold; The Build Order describes the layers in the order a firm builds them.

| This article | The first two-fifths | Build Order layer | What it covers |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| (assumed) | Knowledge | Store | Documents, data and records where they already sit |
| Memory | Memory | Store, read over time | What happened, across sessions, people and versions |
| Meaning | Meaning | Wiring (context layer) | Shared definitions every agent and report uses |
| Governance | Governance | Wiring, plus the approval gate | Permissions, identities, approvals and audit |
| Judgment | Judgment | Record, plus learning | Decisions with reason, owner, status, expected outcome, and outcomes written back |
| Not listed | Not listed | Reasoning | Models and agents, which are rented and read from everything above |

Neither component list names reasoning, because the model is the part every firm already rents; the [Build Order explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/) counts it as a layer. Both vocabularies agree that the record of judgment is the part no vendor can supply.

This is where an enterprise brain becomes more than a searchable archive. If a decision changes, the system needs to connect the old version to the new one, and show which instruction people should follow today. Otherwise, the same confident AI answer can be wrong for months.

## Why a mind is the wrong metaphor

"Brain" invites the idea of a mind that understands the company and decides. That picture leads buyers to spend on a bigger model or more autonomy, when the gap is elsewhere. Three older bodies of work describe it better.

**Organisational memory research.** Walsh and Ungson's 1991 paper in the *Academy of Management Review*, widely treated as the field's seminal work, defined organisational memory as "stored information from an organization's history that can be brought to bear on present decisions". Their framework holds that this memory is spread across individuals, culture, procedures and formal systems, roles and structures, and sources outside the firm. The definition is about decisions, not documents. The failure it predicts is familiar: the person who held the reason leaves, and the procedure survives without its purpose.

**Case-based reasoning.** Aamodt and Plaza's 1994 survey set out the standard cycle: retrieve similar past cases, reuse their solution, revise it by checking whether it worked, and retain the checked solution as a new case. The learning happens in revise and retain, which depend on knowing the outcome. Most enterprise AI products in 2026 do the first two steps well and leave the last two to the customer.

**Decision records in engineering.** Michael Nygard proposed architecture decision records in 2011. Martin Fowler's account sets out the rules: a short record of the decision, context, alternatives and consequences; a status of proposed, accepted or superseded; no editing after acceptance. A changed decision gets a new record linked to the one it replaces. That rule, argued in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/), lets a reader tell the current answer from the history.

| A mind (the metaphor) | A record (what works) |
| --- | --- |
| Holds beliefs and updates them silently | Holds dated entries and supersedes them visibly |
| Answers from what it absorbed | Answers from cited records a person can open |
| Improves by becoming more capable | Improves when outcomes are written back to decisions |
| Fails by sounding sure and being wrong | Fails by being incomplete, which can be seen and fixed |

> A mind that is wrong sounds the same as a mind that is right. A record that is wrong can be found, dated and superseded.

The model still matters: it reads the record, compares cases and drafts the next decision. But it is rented and replaceable. The record makes its reasoning specific to one company and survives a change of vendor.

## What the market sells under the name

The table summarises each vendor's own positioning; none of it has been independently tested.

| Product (vendor description) | Date | Memory | Meaning | Governance | Judgment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| WRITER Enterprise Brain | 9 Sep 2026, early access | Team-level Agent Memory | Brand and messaging standards | Described as governed | Claims to capture "decision logic" |
| Glean | $300m ARR, 28 May 2026 | Activity graph | Enterprise Graph and Enterprise Context | Not the headline claim | Not claimed |
| Google Gemini agent (Gemini Enterprise) | 8 Oct 2026 | Four memory types, including execution history | Business term definitions via Knowledge Catalog (preview) | Agent Gateway; agents with their own accounts | Not claimed |
| Microsoft Agent 365 with Work IQ | Agent 365 count given 29 Jul 2026 | Work IQ grounding | Not the main claim | Nearly 40 million agents registered in two months | Not claimed |

Three patterns stand out. Governance has the most money behind it. Microsoft's chief executive told investors on 29 July 2026 that "just 2 months in, Agent 365 now has nearly 40 million agents registered across tens of thousands of companies", describing a control plane for agent identity and security. Meaning is arriving through catalogues of business definitions. And the only vendor that names judgment treats it as content to capture. SiliconANGLE's launch report describes WRITER's layer as holding "hard-won judgments that shape how work gets done". That is stored guidance, not a record of which decision replaced which, with a check date and an outcome.

The adoption evidence shows why the gap matters. MIT Project NANDA's *The GenAI Divide* (July 2025), drawing on more than 300 public initiatives, 52 interviews and 153 survey responses, found a learning gap: "Most GenAI systems do not retain feedback, adapt to context, or improve over time." Its headline 95% no-return figure rests on a small sample, so treat it as direction. McKinsey's 2025 survey of 1,993 respondents is more conservative: 88% use AI in at least one function, but only 39% report any EBIT impact, most of them under 5%. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing cost, unclear value and weak risk controls.

None of this argues against context layers, only for naming them accurately.

## The missing layer: why the company decided

Consider a fictional fintech company preparing a new campaign. The growth team wants to describe the product as offering instant withdrawals. Compliance rejects that language because some transfers can take longer. Three weeks later, product changes the withdrawal flow, and the wording is reviewed again.

An enterprise brain could retrieve all three conversations and still write the wrong thing if it treated the original draft as current. What would help is a brief, dated record: **the approved claim, the reason behind it, who signed off, what evidence was reviewed, and which older claim it replaced**.

Illustrative example: one claim, recorded

Decision
:   Do not promise instant withdrawals in public marketing.

Reason and owner
:   Some transfers take longer. Compliance approved the new wording on a named date.

What changed
:   When the withdrawal process changes, check the actual product behaviour, record a fresh approval and mark the older guidance as superseded.

This is an illustrative workflow, not a client case or a claim about any vendor's system.

The record should link to the evidence rather than replace it. A summary written by an AI model should not become the only source anyone can inspect; [Keep the sources, let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/) covers why.

The fields are few; the guide to [what a decision record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) has the full version.

| Field | What it holds | Why the brain needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Question | What was being decided | Lets a later reader find comparable cases |
| Decision and status | What was chosen; proposed, current or superseded | Separates the live answer from the history |
| Reason and evidence | Why, with links to sources | Makes the decision checkable |
| Alternatives | What was rejected and why | Stops the same option being re-proposed blind |
| Owner and approver | Who is accountable; who signed off | Governance with a name attached |
| Expected outcome and check date | What should happen if the call was right, and when to look | Turns a log into something that can learn |
| Supersedes | The record this one replaces | Lets assistants flag outdated answers |
| Outcome | What happened, written back | The input to the next similar decision |

## Why the distinction matters in practice

A 2026 research paper, MemTrace, studied long-term memory systems for AI agents, testing 13 configurations across four designs. Its central finding was that mistakes were often caused by failing to *use* retrievable evidence, not because the evidence could not be found: "the dominant bottleneck is evidence use, not retrieval." When those systems failed, the relevant evidence was available roughly ten times more often than it was absent. Systems that handled a fact's current and earlier states could still fail to track how it changed, and systems that declined to answer when evidence was absent did not necessarily correct a false premise. This is a research benchmark, not a direct test of enterprise products, but its failure modes are the fintech example in miniature.

Other benchmarks agree. LongMemEval (2024), which tests abilities including knowledge updates, found commercial assistants losing about 30% accuracy over sustained interactions. Patronus AI's MEMTRACK, built from simulated work across Slack, Linear and Git, found the best model at about 60%, and adding the Mem0 or Zep memory layers gave no significant improvement. More storage fixes none of this. A record that marks which entry is current removes the guess.

There is also evidence that AI can be valuable when it helps employees use experience that would otherwise stay with a few people. In a study of 5,179 customer-support workers, Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond found that access to an AI assistant increased issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, with larger gains among less experienced workers. Those results come from support work, not a test of a company-wide decision-memory system.

The point is not that an enterprise brain cannot remember or help people decide. A convincing answer is not enough: a reliable system should also show what the answer was based on and whether that evidence is current. [Retrieval is not the bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/) made this argument before the benchmarks caught up; the guide to [decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) covers putting comparable past decisions in front of an agent.

## How to make an enterprise brain useful

A useful enterprise brain does not have to begin with an expensive platform. The build order is the same at 30 people and 3,000.

1. **Start with one recurring problem.** Outdated product claims, inconsistent customer promises, unclear partnership approvals or sales materials that drift from the latest terms. The [commercial line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/) is the best first place: decisions recur weekly and outcomes show within a quarter.
2. **Clean the store you have.** [Your CRM is memory, not a brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/) sets out the eight fields worth keeping current.
3. **Rent the wiring.** Connectors, permission-aware retrieval and shared definitions are good products. Restrict confidential material to authorised people and tools from the start.
4. **Own the record.** For each important decision, keep the question it answered, the evidence, alternatives considered, who approved it, when it should be revisited and what it supersedes. Keep a link to the underlying source documents.
5. **Write outcomes back.** On the revisit date, record what later results taught the team. This is the step that makes the system improve rather than accumulate.

Then test the system with realistic questions, not with a demo.

| Test | What a pass looks like |
| --- | --- |
| A new salesperson looks for the latest approved explanation | They find it, with the reason and the approver, in one step |
| An assistant meets an outdated answer | It identifies it and explains why it changed |
| Two sources conflict | It flags the disagreement instead of choosing a confident-sounding answer |
| A decision's check date passes | Someone is prompted to record the outcome |
| The vendor changes | The record exports whole, with history and links |

The best measure is fewer mistakes and less repeated work, not the number of documents the AI has indexed. A system that can say "this was the old decision, here is the newer one and why it changed" is more useful than one that remembers everything without distinguishing between versions.

What would prove this wrong: a horizontal product that measurably improved decisions across unrelated decision classes without per-client outcome plumbing, with independent evidence. We had seen none by November 2026.

## lowob takeaways

- **Memory, meaning and governance are essential.** An enterprise brain needs company information, shared definitions and clear access rules. But people also need to know which decisions are current.
- **Record the reasoning behind important decisions.** Keep the evidence, approval, date and older version with the decision itself.
- **Make correction part of the system.** An assistant should be able to flag conflicting or outdated information, not repeat it confidently.
- **Test usefulness with real work.** Fewer incorrect claims and faster, safer handovers matter more than the size of a document archive.

## Common questions

### What is an enterprise brain?

It is the system that lets a company's people and AI agents act on what the company knows, has decided and has learned: a loop with an accountable decision record at its centre, not a product or a model that thinks for the company.

### Is an enterprise brain the same as enterprise search or a knowledge base?

No. Search and knowledge bases find documents. A brain also records which decision is current, who approved it, why, what it replaced and what happened next, so an assistant can tell a live answer from a superseded one.

### What is the difference between agent memory and a decision record?

Agent memory stores what an agent saw or did, to carry context between tasks. A decision record stores what the organisation decided, with reason, owner, status, expected outcome and the record it supersedes.

### How do you build an enterprise brain?

Start with one recurring decision, clean the store it depends on, rent the connectors and permissions, and record each decision with its evidence, approver, check date and what it replaces. Write the outcome back on the check date, then extend.

# What Is Structured Output in AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-structured-output/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Structured output constrains an AI model's response to a schema the developer supplies, so it parses and contains the required fields. OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all enforce schemas during generation. The guarantee covers shape, not truth: values still need checking before anything acts on them.

Structured output is a model feature that makes an AI response follow a fixed format, usually a JSON schema the developer supplies, so software can read it without guessing. The main providers now enforce the schema during generation, so the output parses and contains the required fields. It does not make the values correct. Structured output is how AI can write into a CRM, a queue or an approval step safely, provided the values are checked before anything acts on them.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What structured output means

A language model writes text. Software needs fields. Without help, the gap is closed by asking the model for JSON and hoping. Anthropic's documentation lists what goes wrong: invalid JSON syntax, missing required fields, inconsistent data types and schema violations that need retries.

Providers have moved through several stages.

| Approach | What it guarantees | Remaining risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asking in the prompt | Nothing | Malformed or incomplete output |
| JSON mode | Valid JSON is more likely, but not a particular schema | Wrong or missing fields |
| Structured output | The response matches the supplied schema, in most cases | Wrong values, refusals, truncation |
| Strict tool use | Tool names and arguments match the tool's schema | Well-formed but wrong arguments |

OpenAI introduced Structured Outputs in its API on 6 August 2024. It converts the schema into a grammar and, after each token, masks every next token that would break it. On its complex schema eval, the company reported 100% with the feature, against 93% for the same model without it and under 40% for an older model. Anthropic describes its version as "constrained sampling with compiled grammar artifacts", in two parts: JSON outputs for the response and strict tool use for function arguments. Google's Gemini API takes a schema alongside the request in the same way.

Structured output is a close relative of [function calling](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-function-calling/). A tool call is itself a structured request, and strict modes apply the same guarantee to its arguments.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Every time AI writes into a system, a format is involved. An enquiry classified by segment, size and urgency. Renewal terms pulled from a contract into named fields. A meeting summary turned into next steps with an owner and a date. A draft placed in an [approval queue](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) with the account ID attached. If the format breaks, the integration breaks, or writes to the wrong field.

Structured output solves the format problem. It does not solve the truth problem. OpenAI's announcement says it "doesn't prevent all kinds of model mistakes". Google's documentation tells developers to "always validate values in your application", because output can match the schema and still be wrong. A renewal date that parses is not necessarily the renewal date in the contract; see [AI hallucination](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/).

The guarantee also has edges. Anthropic and OpenAI both note that a refusal, or a response that hits the maximum token limit, may not match the schema. Each provider supports only part of JSON Schema. Google strips constraints such as minLength and maxLength during decoding rather than enforcing them. Anthropic caps strict tools at 20 per request and rejects schemas too complex to compile. The first request with a new schema is slower while the grammar is built; Anthropic caches compiled grammars for 24 hours from last use.

One finding argues for care in design. Tam and colleagues' 2024 study "Let Me Speak Freely?" found that requiring formats such as JSON significantly reduced models' reasoning performance, and that stricter constraints generally caused larger drops. For a judgment step, such as assessing deal risk, a common pattern is to let the model reason in free text first and fill the structured fields last. Another is to place a reasoning field ahead of the answer fields in the schema.

In **lowob**'s model of the brain, structured output is how the [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) gets filled consistently: decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome and check date. A schema with an enumerated status and a required reason cannot be saved half-empty. A person still checks that the reason is true, because nothing sends without a person.

## How to use it well

| Practice | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Use enums for fixed lists such as stages, segments and loss reasons | Keeps values aligned with your [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/); Anthropic notes enum values can differ in capitalisation, so compare without case |
| Make the reason field required | Blank reasons are the most common gap in commercial records |
| Validate values in code after parsing | Schema compliance is not accuracy |
| Handle refusal and token-limit stops explicitly | Both can break the schema |
| Keep schemas flat and short | Complex schemas compile slowly or are rejected |
| Keep personal data out of schema definitions | Anthropic caches schemas for up to 24 hours |

## lowob takeaways

- **Structured output fixes the format.** The response parses and has the required fields.
- **It does not fix the facts.** Validate values before anything acts on them.
- **The guarantee has edges.** Refusals, truncation and unsupported schema features need handling.
- **Let the model reason before it formats.** Strict formats can reduce reasoning quality.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between JSON mode and structured outputs?

JSON mode makes valid JSON more likely but does not enforce a particular schema. Structured outputs constrain generation so the response matches the schema you supply.

### Does structured output stop AI hallucinations?

No. It guarantees shape, not content. A field can be well-formed and wrong, so values still need checking against the source.

### Which AI providers support structured output?

OpenAI, Anthropic and Google all offer schema-enforced output in their APIs, each supporting a subset of JSON Schema. Check each provider's list of unsupported features before designing a schema.

### How is structured output related to function calling?

A function call is a structured request for an action. Strict modes apply the same schema guarantee to tool arguments that structured output applies to the response.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Introducing Structured Outputs in the API](https://openai.com/index/introducing-structured-outputs-in-the-api/), 6 August 2024. Vendor announcement; eval results are OpenAI's own.
- [Anthropic, Structured outputs](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/structured-outputs), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Google, Gemini API structured outputs](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/structured-output.md.txt), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; supported schema features change by model.
- [Tam et al., Let Me Speak Freely? A Study on the Impact of Format Restrictions on Performance of Large Language Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02442), August 2024, revised October 2024. Academic study; tested models and constraint methods predate current schema enforcement.

- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)

## Next move

Pick one AI output your team copies into the CRM by hand and write its fields as a schema, with enums for every fixed list and a required reason field. Run 20 past examples through it and count how many parse and how many are correct.

# Two Hundred People: Reasoning That Travels Without Its Author

Source: https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At a few hundred people, founders make a small fraction of decisions, managers inherit precedents from people they never met, and turnover is constant. The decision record's job becomes delegation: formal decision classes, a precedent slot, standard handover packs and a first calibration, without sliding into compliance theatre.

At a few hundred people, founders make a small fraction of the decisions. Managers make most of them, many managers have never met the people whose decisions they inherit, and turnover becomes constant. The enterprise brain's job becomes delegation: letting good reasoning travel. Four things do that: formal decision classes, a precedent slot before each decision, a standard handover pack, and a first calibration in one high-volume class. The trap is compliance theatre.

This is the fourth rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/), dealt with shared meaning. At two hundred, the problem is delegation.

## What delegation breaks

Growth introduces a middle layer. Decisions that a founder once made in a minute, with full context, are now made by a team lead with partial context, often following a precedent set by someone who has since left. The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

Turnover makes this routine rather than occasional. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported median tenure with the current employer of 4.1 years in January 2026, and 3.9 years in the private sector. In a firm of two hundred, people change roles or leave most months, and every move takes reasons with it. Our piece [*Handovers are where reasoning pours out*](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) describes the mechanism.

The result is inconsistency that nobody sees until someone measures it. Daniel Kahneman and colleagues described the method in *Harvard Business Review* in October 2016 as a noise audit: several professionals in the same role assess the same cases, and the spread of their answers measures the noise. In one audit at an insurer, as reported by Insurance Thought Leadership, executives expected about a 10% difference between the high and low quotes their 48 underwriters set on the same case. The typical difference was 55%.

This is also the first stage at which some decision classes become frequent enough to learn from. Sales deals, support escalations, hiring decisions and discount approvals each run into the hundreds a year.

> The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

## Decision classes, formally

Define the recurring classes properly now. For each: the owner, the template, the needs list (what a good decision in this class requires), and the falsifier convention. A discount approval should look the same wherever in the company it is made, and be comparable with every other discount approval.

| Element | What it specifies | Example: discount approval |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | Who is accountable for the class and its template | Head of revenue operations |
| Template | The fields every decision in the class records | Deal size, discount, reason, approver, expected effect |
| Needs list | What a good decision must have considered | Margin floor, competitor price evidence, renewal terms |
| Falsifier convention | How "this was wrong" is defined, and when it is checked | Customer churns or downgrades within 12 months |
| Precedent rule | Which prior decisions count as comparable | Same segment, deal size within 30%, last 18 months |

Kahneman's prescription for noise points the same way: where a formula is not feasible, give people procedures that structure their judgment so similar cases are treated alike. A shared template and needs list is that procedure. Our piece on [the deal desk](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/) shows how one commercial class is usually run at this size.

## Precedent for managers

The single most valuable feature at this stage is the precedent slot: before a manager decides, the three most comparable prior decisions in that class, with outcomes. It gives a new team lead the benefit of the decisions their predecessors made, without needing the predecessors.

Precedent only works if decisions in the class were recorded the same way, which is why the classes come first. With a consistent template, finding the three closest prior cases is a straightforward retrieval task. Our explainer [*What is decision precedent in AI?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) covers how assistants can surface it, and why the outcome field matters more than the summary.

## Handovers become routine

With regular departures and internal moves, handovers happen most months. Make the five-part handover pack standard for any role that owns decisions.

| Part | What it contains |
| --- | --- |
| Decisions | The open and recent decisions the role owns, with reasons and falsifier dates |
| Open threads | Commitments in progress, with the next action and its date |
| Relationships | The people inside and outside the firm who matter, and the state of each |
| Graveyard | What was tried and abandoned, and why, so it is not retried blindly |
| Question log | What the outgoing person was asked most, and the answers |

It is the cheapest protection against losing reasoning when people move. On the commercial line, the same idea applies to deals moving from sales to delivery, covered in [*The handover from sales to delivery*](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/).

## The first calibration

Pick the highest-volume class with outcomes that arrive within two quarters, often sales deals or renewals, and add a probability to each decision. After a year you will know, for the first time, whether the organisation's judgment in that class is well calibrated, and whose calls are reliable.

The forecasting research supports the effort. Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues, summarising the Good Judgment Project, report that training in probabilistic reasoning helps, that teams forecast significantly better than individuals working alone, and that well-designed aggregation of forecasts beat the simple average by as much as 60%. None of that is possible without a recorded probability and a recorded outcome. Our piece [*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) sets out the method.

## The trap: compliance theatre

The trap at two hundred is compliance theatre. Templates get longer, fields multiply, and people fill them to satisfy the process rather than to record their thinking. Hold the line on the three-field floor: decision, reason, what would change your mind. Draft the rest. Measure capture time and keep it under a minute.

**In practice:** define the ten most common decision classes with owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention. Add a precedent slot to the workflow for each class. Make the handover pack mandatory for any role that owns decisions. Start calibration in one high-volume class with short outcome lag. Audit capture time quarterly, and cut any field that is not used.

**What would prove this wrong:** two-hundred-person organisations without structured decision classes or precedent showing no more inconsistency in similar decisions, and no slower manager ramp-up, than those with them. A noise audit in one class is the cheapest way to find out. The next rung, [*One thousand people: governance arrives*](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/), is where outsiders start asking to see the record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume inconsistency until measured.** Run a small noise audit in one class before arguing about it.
- **Formalise the classes.** Owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention for the ten most common.
- **Show precedent before the decision.** Three comparable prior cases, with outcomes.
- **Standardise handovers.** Decisions, open threads, relationships, graveyard and question log.
- **Guard the floor.** Three required fields, everything else drafted, capture under a minute.

## Common questions

### How do growing companies keep decisions consistent as managers change?

Define recurring decision classes formally and add a precedent slot that shows the three most comparable prior decisions, with outcomes, before a manager decides.

### What should a handover pack include?

Five parts: decisions, open threads, relationships, graveyard and question log. It should be standard for any role that owns decisions.

### What is a noise audit?

A test in which several people in the same role assess the same cases independently. The spread of their answers measures inconsistency, which is usually much larger than leaders expect.

### How do you stop decision templates becoming bureaucratic?

Hold a three-field floor: decision, reason and what would change your mind. Draft the rest, keep capture under a minute, and cut fields nobody uses.

Publisher's abstract page; authors include consultants.
- [Paul Carroll, Our Big Problem With 'Noise'](https://www.insurancethoughtleadership.com/our-big-problem-with-noise/), Insurance Thought Leadership, 18 May 2021. Secondary account of the underwriter audit; one firm.
- [US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Employee Tenure in 2026](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/archives/tenure_09242026.htm), 24 September 2026. US wage and salary workers.
- [Mellers, Tetlock, Baker, Friedman and Zeckhauser, Improving the accuracy of geopolitical risk assessments](https://scholar.harvard.edu/sites/scholar.harvard.edu/files/rzeckhauser/files/improving_the_accuracy_of_geopolitical_risk_assessments.pdf), in The Future of Risk Management, University of Pennsylvania Press, 2019. Book chapter on forecasting tournaments, not business decisions.
- [Project Wizards, Brooks's law (glossary)](https://www.projectwizards.net/en/project-management-glossary/brooks-law). Vendor glossary summarising Brooks's 1975 book.
- The decision class and handover tables are **lowob**'s framework.
