# What Is an LLM Gateway?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-llm-gateway/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An LLM gateway is a proxy that every AI request passes through on its way to a model provider. It gives a firm one place to issue keys, cap spend, route between models and keep logs. It is wiring, so rent it; the value appears once more than one app or provider is in use.

An LLM gateway is a proxy that sits between a company's applications and the AI model providers they call. Every request passes through it, so the gateway can check who is calling, enforce budgets and rate limits, route to a different model if one fails, filter sensitive data and log each call. It turns many separate API keys and bills into one control point.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an LLM gateway means

Without a gateway, each application or agent holds its own API key for each model provider. Spend appears on several invoices, logs live in several places, and switching models means changing code in several systems. A gateway puts one layer in the middle.

LiteLLM's documentation describes its gateway as "one OpenAI-compatible endpoint for 100+ LLM providers, MCP tools, and A2A agents". Cloudflare's AI Gateway offers a hosted equivalent. Both sit in the request path, which is what makes their controls enforceable rather than advisory.

| An LLM gateway is | An LLM gateway is not |
| --- | --- |
| A proxy every model call passes through | A model, or a replacement for one |
| The place to issue, limit and revoke keys | An evaluation tool that scores answers |
| A source of call-level logs and cost data | A full trace of an agent's reasoning |
| Rented wiring | Something a mid-size firm should build |

## How it works

### Identity and spend

LiteLLM lets an administrator give "each user, team, and project a virtual key". Each key carries its own allowed models, budget and rate limit, and the gateway records the cost of every request by key, team and tag. Cloudflare offers spend limits, in beta at the time of writing, that track cumulative dollar spend by model, provider or user, and custom costs so negotiated rates show correctly.

For agents this matters more than for people. If each agent has its own key, its spend, volume and errors can be seen separately, and its access can be cut without affecting anything else. That is the practical form of agent identity.

### Routing and resilience

Both products route requests between models. LiteLLM describes load balancing, fallbacks and retries that "move traffic between deployments when a provider has a problem". Cloudflare offers routing that changes models without changing application code, fallbacks when a model is unavailable and caching that serves identical requests from its cache.

### Filtering and logs

Gateways increasingly add guardrails. LiteLLM applies content filters and personal data masking to requests and responses; Cloudflare lists guardrails and data loss prevention, both in beta. Logs flow to observability tools: LiteLLM names Langfuse, Datadog, OpenTelemetry and Prometheus.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Runaway cost is a listed risk

OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications includes unbounded consumption (LLM10). It covers denial of wallet, where an attacker exploits pay-per-use pricing to run up unsustainable costs. The first mitigation OWASP lists is rate limiting and user quotas. An agent stuck in a loop has the same effect without an attacker. Usage-based pricing makes caps a commercial control, not only a technical one.

### One switch for every agent

**lowob**'s governance model requires a named person able to stop every agent at once. A gateway is the natural place for that switch: revoke or suspend the keys, and every model call stops, whichever tool made it.

> If every model call passes through one place, that place is where you set the budget, keep the log and pull the plug.

## How to evaluate one

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Can each agent and team have its own key? | Separate spend, limits and revocation |
| Are budgets hard caps or alerts? | Alerts do not stop a loop at 3am |
| Which providers and models are supported? | Avoid a second gateway later |
| Where do logs go, and for how long? | Retention must match your data policy |
| Is it hosted or self-hosted? | Hosted is faster; self-hosted keeps traffic in your network |
| Does it support your data residency needs? | Requests and logs may cross borders |

Rent, do not build. Open-source and hosted gateways already cover the common needs. The work for the firm is policy: which keys exist, who owns each, what each may spend and who can revoke them.

## lowob takeaways

- **One path for every call.** A gateway makes keys, limits and logs enforceable in one place.
- **Key per agent.** Separate keys give each agent its own budget, log and off switch.
- **Caps beat alerts.** Unbounded consumption is a listed risk; hard limits contain it.
- **It records, it does not judge.** Pair the gateway with evals and observability for quality.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an LLM gateway and an API gateway?

An API gateway manages traffic to any web service. An LLM gateway is specialised for model calls, adding token-based cost tracking, model routing, fallbacks and AI-specific filtering.

### Do small companies need an LLM gateway?

Not for one tool used through its own interface. It becomes useful once several apps or agents call models directly, or more than one provider is in use.

### Can an LLM gateway prevent prompt injection?

Not on its own. It can filter some inputs and log every call, but containment depends on limiting what agents can reach and requiring approval for outbound actions.

### Is LiteLLM an LLM gateway?

Yes. LiteLLM's proxy server is an open-source, self-hosted gateway offering one endpoint for many providers, with virtual keys, budgets, fallbacks and logging.

## Sources and notes

- [LiteLLM Docs, LiteLLM AI Gateway](https://docs.litellm.ai/docs/simple_proxy/). Open-source project documentation; feature list changes with releases.
- [Cloudflare Docs, AI Gateway features](https://developers.cloudflare.com/ai-gateway/features/). Vendor documentation; several features marked beta.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm102025-unbounded-consumption/), 2025. Community standard; mitigations are recommendations.

## Related research

- [What Is LLM Observability?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/)
- [What Is Agent Identity and an Agent Registry?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/)
- [What Is an AI Kill Switch?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-kill-switch/)
- [What Is Usage-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/)

Count the API keys for AI providers your firm holds and who holds each. If any agent shares a key with a person or another agent, give it its own key this week.

# What Is Decision Precedent in AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Decision precedent means placing comparable past decisions, each with its reason, owner and outcome, in a model's context when it helps with a new decision. The idea draws on case-based reasoning and on evidence that well-chosen examples improve model output. In lowob's model it lives in a precedent slot of three to five records, including at least one that went badly, drawn from the decision record.

Decision precedent in AI means giving a model comparable past decisions, each with its reason, owner and outcome, as context when it helps with a new decision. The model's recommendation then reflects how the company has actually decided before and what happened as a result, not only general rules. In **lowob**'s model this lives in a precedent slot: a reserved part of the agent's context holding three to five comparable past decisions, including at least one that went badly. Precedent comes from the decision record. Without recorded reasons and outcomes, there is nothing useful to retrieve.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What decision precedent means

Commercial decisions are rarely made from rules alone. A seller asking for a 15% discount on a renewal will be told the policy, and then someone will ask what was done last time a similar client asked. That second question is precedent.

An AI system can be given the same material. Precedent differs from the other things a model is usually given.

| Context type | What it holds | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rule | A standing policy | "Discounts above 10% need finance approval" |
| Precedent | A specific past decision with reason, owner and outcome | "Approved 15% on a three-year renewal; reason: competing quote; owner: revenue lead; outcome: renewed, margin held" (illustrative) |
| Memory | What an agent recalls from earlier sessions | "This user prefers short briefs" |
| Example | A sample of the format wanted | A model meeting brief |

The idea has a long history. Aamodt and Plaza's 1994 paper in *AI Communications* framed case-based reasoning as a cycle of case retrieval, reuse, solution testing and learning. Language models made it cheap: instead of hand-built case libraries, past decisions can be retrieved and placed in context as text.

The evidence that selection matters is also older than agents. Liu and colleagues showed GPT-3's results depended heavily on which examples it was shown, and that retrieving examples semantically similar to each new input outperformed random selection. For a commercial decision, "similar" should mean the same decision class, segment and size, not just similar wording.

## How the precedent slot works

**lowob**'s precedent slot is a fixed part of an agent's context, filled before it reasons about a decision. Each entry carries the fields of a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/).

| Field | Why the model needs it |
| --- | --- |
| What was decided | The comparison point |
| Reason | So the model can judge whether the same reason applies now |
| Owner | So a person can be asked, and accountability is visible |
| Status | Superseded decisions are excluded or marked as replaced |
| Expected outcome | What the owner thought would happen |
| Actual outcome | What did happen, written back later |

The slot holds three to five entries, including at least one that went badly. Fewer gives the model too little to compare; more adds noise. Anthropic's guidance on context makes the same trade-off in general terms: find the "smallest possible set of high-signal tokens", because recall degrades as context grows. The bad outcome is there because a model shown only successes will recommend repeating them.

The model is asked to say which precedent it relied on and why the current case is like or unlike it. A person decides. The new decision is recorded, and when its outcome arrives it is [written back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/). That record becomes a future precedent. This is the brain's loop in miniature: record, reasoning, learning.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Most firms already make decisions by precedent; they keep it in people's heads. The investor Ashu Garg's essay on context graphs put the gap well: "Salesforce knows what happened. It doesn't know why." An opportunity record shows the final price, not that a vice-president approved the deviation on a call, or which earlier deal it was meant to match.

An AI system cannot retrieve reasons nobody recorded. That is why **lowob** starts the record on the commercial line, with [the decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/), before asking agents to reason over it.

## Common mistakes

- **Successes only.** The slot then teaches repetition, not judgment.
- **Superseded precedents.** A decision made under an old pricing policy should be marked as replaced, never silently reused. See [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).
- **Client detail travelling.** Precedent can be passed as a pattern, such as segment, size and discount, without another client's name or terms.
- **No outcome field.** Without outcomes, precedent is just history.

## lowob takeaways

- **Precedent is past decisions as context.** Each with reason, owner and outcome.
- **Three to five, one bad.** A small, mixed set beats a large or flattering one.
- **Similarity should be structural.** Match on decision class, segment and size, not wording.
- **No record, no precedent.** Reasons and outcomes must be written down first.

## Common questions

### What is a precedent slot in an AI agent?

A reserved part of the agent's context holding three to five comparable past decisions, each with its reason, owner and outcome, including at least one that went badly. The term is **lowob**'s.

### How is decision precedent different from few-shot prompting?

Few-shot examples show a model the format or behaviour wanted. Precedents are real past decisions with reasons and outcomes, chosen because they resemble the decision at hand.

### Where does an AI agent get precedents from?

From a decision record: a structured log of what was decided, why, by whom, its status, and its expected and actual outcomes.

## Sources and notes

- [Aamodt and Plaza, Case-Based Reasoning: Foundational Issues, Methodological Variations, and System Approaches](https://www.doi.org/10.3233/AIC-1994-7104), *AI Communications* 7(1), 1994. Academic paper; predates language models.
- [Liu et al., What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3?](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.06804), January 2021. Academic preprint; benchmark tasks, not business decisions.
- [Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
- [Ashu Garg, AI's trillion-dollar opportunity: Context graphs](https://ashugarg.substack.com/p/ais-trillion-dollar-opportunity-context), 26 December 2025. Investor essay; argument, not evidence.
- The precedent slot, its size and the one-bad-outcome rule are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [A Loop With Good Context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/)
- [What Is a Decision Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/)
- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)

## Next move

Pick one recurring decision, such as discount exceptions, and write up the last five with reason, owner and outcome. If you cannot fill the reason and outcome fields, you have found what to record first.

# CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse: Which Holds What

Source: https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A CRM is the working system for relationships and deals. A customer data platform builds unified customer profiles and shares them with other tools. A data warehouse holds current and historical data from every system for analysis. All three are storage, and none of them records why a commercial decision was made.

A CRM (customer relationship management system) is where a commercial team works: contacts, accounts, interactions and the deal pipeline, mostly entered by people. A customer data platform (CDP) collects customer data from many sources, links it into one profile per customer and shares those profiles with other tools, mainly for marketing. A data warehouse holds current and historical data from all of these systems for analysis and reporting. Most firms of 20 to 500 people need a CRM, many need a warehouse, and fewer need a CDP.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What the three terms mean

A **CRM** is an operational system. Sellers, account managers and customer success staff use it every day to log calls, move deals through stages and see who owns an account. Salesforce's own description lists contact details, "all previous interactions with your company" and visibility into "every opportunity or lead". Most of its data is typed in by people or captured from their email and calendars.

A **CDP** is a marketing data system. The CDP Institute's definition has three parts. It is packaged software rather than a custom build. It creates a persistent, unified database, linking records that belong to the same customer and tracking behaviour over time. And it is accessible to other systems, which use the profiles for analysis and to manage interactions. The Institute's RealCDP certification requires a product to accept data from any source, capture full detail, retain it, build unified profiles, share data with any destination, respond within one second and govern customer data.

A **data warehouse** is an analytical system. Google Cloud's definition describes it as an enterprise system for analysis and reporting of structured and semi-structured data from many sources, naming customer relationship management among them. It keeps history, and it runs separately from operational systems so that heavy queries do not slow them down.

| Dimension | CRM | CDP | Data warehouse |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Main job | Run relationships and deals | Unify customer profiles and send them to tools | Analyse and report across systems |
| Main users | Sellers, account managers, sales managers | Marketing and growth teams | Analysts, finance, RevOps |
| Typical data | Accounts, contacts, activities, opportunities | Web and app events, email engagement, identities | Copies of every system's data, with history |
| How data arrives | People entering it, email and calendar capture | Event streams and connectors | Scheduled loads and streams |
| Unit of record | Account, contact, deal | Person or customer profile | Table, row, time period |
| Speed | Interactive | Near real time | Batch, increasingly near real time |
| Who owns definitions | Sales operations or RevOps | Marketing operations | Data team or RevOps |

## Which holds what

The useful question is where each kind of data should live. One home per fact avoids three systems reporting three revenue numbers.

| Data | Home | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account owner, contacts, deal stage and amount | CRM | The working truth for the pipeline |
| Meeting notes and call activity | CRM | Or a notetaker that writes into the CRM |
| Website visits and product usage events | CDP, or the warehouse | Too many events for a CRM |
| One identity per customer across channels | CDP, or the warehouse with [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/) | The CDP's core job |
| Pipeline snapshots and historical stage changes | Warehouse | CRMs show the current state better than history |
| Board metrics such as net revenue retention | Warehouse, with a [semantic layer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) | One definition, used everywhere |
| Scores to show sellers inside the CRM | Warehouse, synced back by [reverse ETL](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-reverse-etl/) | Compute in one place, display where people work |
| Why a discount was approved, by whom, expecting what | A decision record | None of the three holds this by default |

The last row is the gap. Illustratively, a CRM records that a deal closed at a 15% discount. It rarely records who approved it, why, and what outcome they expected. A warehouse can show the discount trend across a year but not the reasoning behind any single one.

## Which to choose

For most business-to-business firms in this size range, the sequence is CRM first, warehouse when history across systems matters, and a CDP only when behavioural data and real-time personalisation become central.

| Situation | What you need |
| --- | --- |
| Under about 100 people, one CRM and a marketing tool | CRM, with clean stage definitions |
| Reporting needs data from three or more systems, or history the CRM cannot show | Add a warehouse |
| Leadership disputes basic numbers each month | A warehouse with a semantic layer, before any new tool |
| High-volume web or product events driving campaigns across many channels | Consider a CDP |
| A warehouse already holds clean customer data | Consider a warehouse-native approach before a separate CDP |

The CDP Institute's own checklist now assesses composable and warehouse-native architectures, while not making them core requirements. These are designs in which CDP functions run on top of the warehouse instead of on a separate copy of the data.

Questions to ask before buying any of the three:

- **Which facts will this system own?** If the answer overlaps another system, decide which one wins.
- **Who maintains the definitions?** A field nobody owns decays.
- **How does data flow back to where people work?** Analysis that never reaches the CRM changes little.
- **Where will AI agents read from?** Agents need one current answer per question, with permissions.

## The **lowob** view

In the brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, all three systems are the store. They hold facts and events. As we argue in [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/), a well-run CRM remembers what happened. It does not hold judgment.

The wiring, often a context layer or a set of connectors, lets assistants and agents read across the three with each user's permissions. The record is the missing piece: commercial decisions with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome. The warehouse then earns a second role in the learning stage, because it is where you measure whether the expected outcome happened. That result is written back to the decision, closing the loop.

Rent the CRM, the warehouse and, if needed, the CDP. Own the definitions and the decision record, because those are what make the data mean the same thing to every person and every agent.

## lowob takeaways

- **CRM for work, warehouse for history, CDP for profiles.** Each has a different main user and speed.
- **One home per fact.** Decide which system owns each number before adding tools.
- **A CDP is optional for most B2B firms.** A warehouse often covers the same need at this size.
- **None of them holds the reason.** Decisions need their own record, linked to all three.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a CRM and a CDP?

A CRM is where people manage relationships and deals, mostly with data they enter. A CDP collects behavioural and identity data from many sources, unifies it into customer profiles and shares them with other tools.

### Is a data warehouse the same as a CDP?

No. A warehouse stores data from all systems for analysis. A CDP is packaged software that builds unified customer profiles and sends them to marketing and other tools, often in real time.

### Does a small B2B company need a CDP?

Usually not at first. A clean CRM and, once reporting spans several systems, a data warehouse cover most needs. A CDP matters more with high-volume behavioural data.

## Sources and notes

- [Salesforce, What is CRM?](https://salesforce.com/crm/what-is-crm/), accessed November 2026. Vendor explainer from a CRM provider.
- [CDP Institute, RealCDP Customer Data Platform Certification Program](https://www.cdpinstitute.org/resources/realcdp-customer-data-platform-certification-program), accessed November 2026. Industry body; certification is a capability checklist, not a performance test.
- [Gilbane, Customer Data Platform Definition from the Customer Data Platform Institute](https://gilbane.com/?p=57062), page last modified October 2020. Reproduces the CDP Institute's definition; secondary source.
- [Google Cloud, What is a data warehouse?](https://cloud.google.com/learn/what-is-a-data-warehouse?lang=en), accessed November 2026. Vendor explainer from a warehouse provider.
- The data placement table, sequence and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

# What Is a Multi-Agent System?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-multi-agent-system/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A multi-agent system divides work among several AI agents with their own instructions, tools and context. Anthropic reported a 90.2% gain on research tasks from a lead agent with parallel subagents, at about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Research on 1,600 traces found 14 distinct failure modes, so most commercial teams should start with one agent and split only parallel work.

A multi-agent system is a setup in which several AI agents, each with its own instructions, tools and context, work on parts of a task and pass results between them, usually under a lead agent that plans the work and combines the answers. It helps when work splits into independent parts that can run in parallel, such as broad research. It uses far more tokens than a single agent and fails in new ways when agents need to share context. Most commercial teams should start with one agent.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a multi-agent system means

A single agent runs one [agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/) with one context window. A multi-agent system runs several, and adds a way for them to divide work and exchange results. The common patterns are few.

| Pattern | How it works | Good fit | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Orchestrator and workers | A lead agent plans, starts subagents, then merges their findings | Broad research with independent threads | Lead misjudges how to split the work |
| Handoff | One agent passes the whole task to a specialist | Triage, then a specialist reply | Context lost at the handover |
| Sequential pipeline | Each agent does one stage, then passes it on | Fixed stages, such as research then draft then check | Errors carried forward |
| Group chat | Several agents discuss and a manager decides | Exploring options | Cost, and agreement mistaken for accuracy |
| Cross-vendor | Agents from different vendors exchange tasks | Work spanning two companies' systems | Trust, identity and logging across boundaries |

Microsoft Agent Framework 1.0 ships sequential, concurrent, handoff and group-chat orchestration. Cross-vendor exchange is what the [Agent2Agent protocol](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-agent2agent-protocol/) standardises.

## The evidence for and against

The strongest published case for multiple agents comes from Anthropic. Its research feature uses a lead agent on Claude Opus 4 with subagents on Claude Sonnet 4 that search in parallel. On Anthropic's internal research evaluation it beat single-agent Opus 4 by 90.2%. The explanation was largely spend: on the BrowseComp benchmark, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in performance. Multi-agent runs used about 15 times the tokens of a chat. Anthropic also named poor fits: tasks where agents must share the same context, tasks with many dependencies between agents, and most coding.

Cognition's essay "Don't Build Multi-Agents", by Walden Yan, made the opposite case for tightly coupled work. Its example: split "build a Flappy Bird clone" between two subagents, and one builds a background resembling Super Mario Bros while the other builds a bird that does not match. Each made reasonable choices the other never saw. Its principles were to share full context and full traces, and to recognise that every action embeds decisions.

The academic evidence points the same way. Cemri and colleagues analysed more than 1,600 annotated traces from seven popular frameworks, with high agreement between annotators, and sorted the failures into system design issues, inter-agent misalignment and task verification. Those are failures of setup, coordination and checking, which a better model alone does not fix.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The split that works is research-shaped. An illustrative case: profiling 40 target accounts before a planning session, where each account can be researched independently and the lead agent assembles a table. Errors in one profile do not corrupt another, and a person can check each row.

The split that fails is judgment-shaped. A proposal where pricing, scope and terms must agree is the Flappy Bird problem: a pricing agent and a scope agent will make choices that conflict. One agent with the full context, and a person approving, is safer.

Accountability matters too. Each agent should be its own registered identity with its own permissions, as set out in [What Is Agent Identity?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/). Where several agents contribute, a single person still owns what leaves the building.

## How to decide

1. **Are the parts independent?** If each part can be done without seeing the others, parallel agents can help.
2. **Can the merged result be checked?** If a person cannot verify the combined output quickly, do not split.
3. **Is the cost acceptable?** Budget for roughly 15 times chat-level token use, on Anthropic's figures.
4. **Who owns the output?** Name one person before the system runs.

## lowob takeaways

- **Several agents, one task.** A lead agent splits work, subagents run in parallel, results are merged.
- **Good for breadth.** Independent research threads gain the most.
- **Bad for tightly coupled work.** Agents that cannot see each other's choices produce conflicts.
- **Cost and failure modes multiply.** Start with one agent and split only what is parallel.

## Common questions

### What is an example of a multi-agent system?

Anthropic's research feature: a lead agent plans a query, starts several subagents that search in parallel, and combines their findings into one answer.

### Are multi-agent systems better than single agents?

For broad, parallel research, published results suggest yes, at much higher token cost. For tasks where every step depends on earlier choices, single agents are usually more reliable.

### Why do multi-agent systems fail?

Research on more than 1,600 traces found 14 failure modes in three groups: poor system design, misalignment between agents, and weak verification of the final result.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), 13 June 2025. Vendor engineering post; results are on Anthropic's internal evaluation.
- [Walden Yan, Don't Build Multi-Agents](https://cognition.com/blog/dont-build-multi-agents), Cognition, 12 June 2025. Vendor essay; argument, not measurement.
- [Cemri et al., Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657v3), March 2025, revised October 2025. Academic preprint.
- [Visual Studio Magazine, Microsoft ships production-ready Agent Framework 1.0](https://visualstudiomagazine.com/articles/2026/04/06/microsoft-ships-production-ready-agent-framework-1-0-for-net-and-python.aspx), 6 April 2026. Trade press reporting a vendor release.

## Next move

If a vendor proposes a multi-agent design, ask which parts of the task run independently and what the token cost is per run against a single agent. If neither answer is clear, pilot a single agent first.

# Fifty People: When Words Start to Mean Different Things

Source: https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At around fifty people, teams form and vocabularies drift, and AI tools amplify the confusion. The decision record's job becomes meaning: a short glossary with owners, written decision rights, a conflicts list, and one company-owned place where records live, which every new AI tool must write to.

At around fifty people, teams form and vocabularies drift. Sales, product and finance use the same words for different things, and AI tools amplify the confusion. The enterprise brain's job becomes meaning: shared definitions, clear decision rights, and one place where records live. Large organisations eventually build semantic layers and ontologies for this. A fifty-person company does not need either. It needs the lightweight version.

This is the third rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/), was about newcomers who cannot see why anything is done. At fifty, the newcomers have formed teams, and the teams have started to speak different dialects.

## Why words drift at fifty

With a few teams, each develops its own habits and its own language. "Customer" means a signed contract to finance, an active account to customer success, and anyone in a trial to marketing. "Churn" is measured three ways. Nobody notices until two dashboards disagree in a board meeting.

The structure explains why it happens here. Brooks's n(n-1)/2 gives 1,225 possible channels at fifty people, far more than anyone can maintain, so communication starts to run through teams. Research on social group sizes by Zhou, Sornette, Hill and Dunbar found that human groups cluster in layers that grow by a ratio close to three, so closeness breaks in steps rather than smoothly. Inside a team, words stay aligned through daily contact. Between teams, nothing keeps them aligned unless someone writes the definition down.

> Tools are replaceable. A fragmented record is very hard to reassemble.

## A glossary with owners

Keep a short list of the terms that matter commercially, perhaps 20 to 30. Each has one definition, one owner, the date it was last changed, and a link to the decision that set it. When a definition changes, the old one is superseded with a reason, not edited away.

| Field | Example: "active customer" | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Term | Active customer | The word as people use it |
| Definition | A paying account with at least one login in the last 30 days | One meaning, testable against data |
| Owner | Head of customer success | Someone decides when it changes |
| Effective from | The date the definition took effect | Lets numbers be compared across quarters |
| Supersedes | The previous definition, with the reason for the change | Old reports stay interpretable |
| Linked decision | The ledger entry that set it | The reason survives the definition |

That last point matters for AI. Agents and assistants that read a glossary need to know which definition is current, and analysts comparing numbers across quarters need to know when a definition changed. Finance has long handled the same problem for figures. Martin Fowler's 2021 description of bitemporal history uses a payroll example: a raise backdated by a letter that arrived after the payroll run means the firm must track both what the salary was and what it believed at each run. A glossary with effective dates and superseded entries applies that discipline to words. Our piece [*Supersede, never overwrite*](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) makes the general case.

The glossary is the lightweight version of what larger firms build as a semantic layer, described in our explainer [*What is a semantic layer?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/). At fifty people, a shared document with owners does the job.

## Decision rights

The second thing that breaks at fifty is knowing who decides what. Write it down for the recurring decision classes: discount approvals, hiring, roadmap priorities, vendor choices, exceptions to policy. One line each: who decides, who must be consulted, who is informed.

It sounds bureaucratic. It removes more friction than almost anything else at this size. Paul Rogers and Marcia Blenko of Bain, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2006, reported that a survey of more than 350 global organisations found only about 15% practised effective decision making, and traced much of the problem to unclear roles. Their RAPID framework names five: recommend, agree, perform, input and decide, with a single person holding the "D". A fifty-person firm does not need the full framework. It needs the one line per class that says who holds the D.

| Decision class | Decides | Consulted | Informed |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discount above the standard limit | Head of sales | Finance | Account owner |
| New hire within budget | Hiring manager | Team lead, one peer | Leadership |
| Roadmap priority change | Head of product | Sales, customer success | All staff |
| New vendor or AI tool | Operations lead | Security owner, budget holder | Users |
| Exception to policy | Policy owner | Legal, if relevant | Requester |

The rows are illustrative; the shape is the point. Our piece on [discount governance](https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/) works through the first row in detail.

## The first conflicts

With several teams writing records, contradictions appear. Sales records that a customer was promised a feature; product records that it was deprioritised. Start a simple conflicts list, with an owner for each and a date by which it is resolved. It will be short. It will also be the most read part of the record.

Each resolved conflict becomes a ledger entry: what the two records said, which stands, and why.

## The tool sprawl problem

Fifty people is when every team adopts its own AI tools: a meeting assistant here, a writing tool there, a research agent somewhere else. Each keeps its own memory. The organisation's reasoning fragments across half a dozen products, none of which talk to each other and none of which the company controls.

The evidence says this happens whether or not leadership chooses tools. Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, a survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries, found 78% of AI users were bringing their own AI tools to work. Our explainer [*What is shadow AI?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-shadow-ai/) covers the risks that follow.

Decide now where records live: one place, owned by the company, that every tool writes to or can be exported into. Tools are replaceable. A fragmented record is very hard to reassemble. The same test appears in [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/): before renting any tool that touches decisions, check that it can export every record with its history.

**In practice:** write a glossary of the 20 to 30 terms that matter, each with an owner and a date. Supersede definitions instead of editing them. Write one-line decision rights for the ten most common decision classes. Choose one company-owned home for decision records, and require new AI tools to write to it or export to it.

## What would prove this wrong

This would be wrong if fifty-person companies with no shared glossary or decision rights reported no more definitional disputes or slower decisions than those with them. If that holds, the effort belongs at the next rung, [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/), where managers make most decisions.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write 20 to 30 definitions.** Each with one meaning, an owner, an effective date and a linked decision.
- **Supersede, do not edit.** Old definitions stay, so old numbers stay interpretable by people and agents.
- **Name who holds the D.** One line per recurring decision class: decides, consulted, informed.
- **Keep a conflicts list.** Short, owned, dated, and read more than anything else.
- **Pick one home for records.** Every new AI tool writes to it or exports into it.

## Common questions

### What breaks when a startup grows to about fifty people?

Teams develop their own vocabularies, so words like customer and churn mean different things, and nobody is sure who decides what. AI tools adopted team by team fragment the record further.

### Does a fifty-person company need a semantic layer or ontology?

No. It needs the lightweight version: a short glossary of key terms with owners and effective dates, and written decision rights. Tooling can follow at a later stage.

### How do you write decision rights for a growing company?

List the recurring decision classes, such as discounts, hiring, roadmap and vendors, and write one line for each: who decides, who must be consulted and who is informed. Keep a single decider per class.

### How do you stop AI tools fragmenting a company's knowledge?

Decide on one place, owned by the company, where records live, and require every tool to write to it or export into it, with history.

## Sources and notes

- [Paul Rogers and Marcia Blenko, Who Has the D? How Clear Decision Roles Enhance Organizational Performance](https://www.bain.com/fr/insights/who-has-the-d/), Bain & Company, first published in Harvard Business Review, 2006. Consultancy research; survey of more than 350 large organisations.
- [Microsoft and LinkedIn, 2024 Work Trend Index](https://news.microsoft.com/source/2024/05/08/microsoft-and-linkedin-release-the-2024-work-trend-index-on-the-state-of-ai-at-work/), 8 May 2024. Vendor survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries; not broken down by firm size.
- [Zhou, Sornette, Hill and Dunbar, Discrete hierarchical organization of social group sizes](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0403299), 2004 preprint, published by the Royal Society in 2005. Social network data, not workplaces.
- [Martin Fowler, Bitemporal History](https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/bitemporal-history.html), 7 April 2021. Practitioner essay on data modelling.
- [Project Wizards, Brooks's law (glossary)](https://www.projectwizards.net/en/project-management-glossary/brooks-law). Vendor glossary summarising Brooks's 1975 book.
- The glossary fields and decision rights tables are **lowob**'s illustrations.

## Related research

- [The Scale Ladder](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/)

## Next move

Put the ten words your teams argue about most in one shared document this week, each with one definition, one owner and today's date. Then list every AI tool in use and check which can export to it.

# Renewals and Expansion

Source: https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Benchmarks put median net revenue retention for private B2B software firms at around 100%, which means the existing base is barely growing on its own. Renewals are often treated as paperwork and expansion as opportunism. A firm that runs renewals on a fixed calendar, chooses expansion motions by signal and records each renewal decision with its reason learns which accounts will grow before the contract date arrives.

Renewals and expansion are how a firm grows revenue from customers it already has. For most mid-size B2B firms the existing base is barely growing on its own: a KeyBanc and Sapphire Ventures survey of more than 100 private SaaS companies put median net revenue retention at about 101% and gross retention at about 90%. The firms that do better treat renewal as a process with a calendar, not a contract date. They decide each renewal months ahead, choose the expansion motion that fits the account's signals and record the reason for every renewal decision, so the next cohort can be predicted rather than hoped for.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

New logos get the attention. Existing customers get the revenue. For a firm selling recurring services or software, the renewal date is the point at which most of next year's revenue is already decided, and expansion is the cheapest growth it can buy. Yet in many mid-size firms renewal is handled by whoever owns the contract, 30 days before it expires, and expansion happens when a customer asks.

The explainers on [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) and [customer health scoring](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/) cover the metrics. This piece covers the operating practice: the calendar, the choice of expansion motion and the record that connects them.

## Most bases barely grow on their own

The benchmarks are sobering. The KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures survey of private SaaS companies, published in October 2024 and covering more than 100 firms with a median annual recurring revenue of about $26m, reported median net revenue retention of about 101% and gross retention of about 90%. In plain terms, the typical firm lost about a tenth of its starting revenue each year to churn and downgrades, and won back only slightly more through expansion.

SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks for private B2B companies found that the median net retention for firms with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000 was 102%, with a top quartile of 111% and a bottom quartile of 97%. Firms with net retention of at least 110% grew faster than the 24% median growth rate in its sample; those below 100% grew more slowly. Growth Unhinged's 2025 benchmark of more than 800 mostly US software firms found that companies combining high net retention with low customer acquisition payback averaged 71% growth, against 10% for those with the opposite profile.

The case for retention goes beyond software. Frederick Reichheld's work at Bain, set in financial services, argued that a 5% increase in customer retention could produce more than a 25% increase in profit, because long-standing customers cost less to serve, buy more over time and refer others. The figure is old and sector-specific, but the mechanism applies to most recurring B2B relationships.

## Why renewals are lost late

Most renewals are not lost in the renewal conversation. They are lost months earlier, and the firm finds out at the end.

Size is a poor guide to who will grow. Gartner's 2021 survey of 69 chief sales officers found that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed quota on key accounts, and that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of large spend were 51% less likely to increase that spend over time. Key-account managers reporting high cross-functional collaboration saw about three times the spend from their key customers. The accounts that grow are the ones the whole firm works with, not simply the largest.

Experience is a reason to leave. McKinsey's 2024 research on B2B buyers found that more than half said they were likely to switch suppliers if they did not have a smooth experience across channels. Among those likely to switch, 54% cited poor digital experiences and 51% cited not being connected to the right person for help. Both show up in support tickets and account conversations long before the renewal date.

Regulation is also shortening the notice a supplier gets. The EU Data Act's switching rules for data processing services, which include SaaS, IaaS and PaaS, have applied since 12 September 2025. According to Cooley's summary, customers can switch with a maximum notice period of two months, porting must normally be completed within 30 days, and switching and data egress charges must be removed from 12 January 2027. Providers outside the EU are covered if they serve EU customers. For a supplier with EU customers, a long notice clause is no longer a dependable early warning.

## Run renewals on a calendar

The fix is to make renewal a process that starts well before the contract date, with fixed checkpoints and an owner at each.

| Days before renewal | Step | Owner | Output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 180 | Account review: usage, outcomes against the original case, health score, open issues | Account owner | A renewal risk rating and a draft expansion hypothesis |
| 120 | Value review with the customer: what was achieved, what is next | Account owner with delivery lead | Agreed outcomes for the next term, named sponsor confirmed |
| 90 | Renewal decision recorded internally: renew as is, renew with change, expand or prepare for loss | Revenue leader | A decision record with reason and expected outcome |
| 60 | Commercial proposal sent, including any price change and expansion option | Account owner and deal desk | A proposal that follows the firm's proposal standard |
| 30 | Signature, or escalation if not on track | Account owner, executive sponsor if needed | Signed renewal or an escalation decision |
| After | Outcome written back, including reasons for churn or downgrade | Revenue operations | Updated record and health score inputs |

The 90-day decision is the step most firms lack. It forces the firm to state what it expects to happen and why, which is the only way to know later whether its view of the account was right. Contracts with shorter notice periods, including those now covered by the Data Act, simply move the calendar earlier.

The value review at 120 days matters because renewals are decided on outcomes, not activity. The customer should be able to say what the last term achieved in their terms. If the account owner cannot, the renewal is at risk regardless of the health score.

> A renewal is decided long before the contract date. The firm just finds out on the contract date.

## Choose the expansion motion by signal

Expansion is not one motion. Each form needs a different signal and carries a different risk, and choosing the wrong one can put the renewal itself at risk.

| Expansion motion | Signal that it fits | Main risk | Who leads |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price increase at renewal | Outcomes delivered and documented; price below current list | Triggers a competitive review | Account owner with finance |
| More seats, usage or volume | Usage near the contracted limit; new teams asking for access | Low engagement among existing users | Account owner |
| Cross-sell of another service or product | A recorded problem the second offer solves | Stretching delivery before the first service is stable | Account owner with a specialist |
| New division or region of the same customer | A sponsor willing to introduce the firm internally | Starting a new sale without the new buyer's case for change | Account owner as a new opportunity |

The signal column is what a health score should feed. Gainsight's documentation describes scorecards built from weighted measures, such as usage, support and relationship, grouped and combined into one score, with weights that can be redistributed when a measure is missing. A score is only useful for expansion if it has been checked against which past accounts actually grew. Gartner's recommendation for key accounts was similar: monitor relationship health systematically and re-tier accounts on performance, not size.

Expansion into a new division is the motion most often mishandled. It is a new sale to a new buying group, and it needs its own qualification and case for change (Parts 20 and 22). Treating it as an add-on to the existing contract skips both.

Price increases deserve their own decision. A price rise at renewal is a discount decision in reverse, and the same governance applies (Part 21): a reason, an owner, an expected outcome and a review once the renewal closes.

## Record every renewal decision

Each renewal is a commercial decision that is frequent, similar to past cases, graded within a contract term and defended by a revenue leader. That makes it a good fit for the decision record described in [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/). The record should hold the 90-day decision, its reason, the expected outcome (renewal value, expansion, or loss), the owner and, once known, the result.

Churned and downgraded accounts need the buyer's reason as well as the account owner's. The same mismatch that affects new-business win-loss applies here, so the explainer on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) is a useful guide for exit interviews.

After a year of records, the firm can answer questions that most cannot: which risk ratings at 180 days were right, which expansion hypotheses came true, and which health-score measures actually predicted the outcome.

Illustrative example: moving the renewal decision earlier

Decision
:   Record a renew, change, expand or loss decision for every account 90 days before renewal, with a value review at 120 days.

Reason and owner
:   Two lost renewals in a quarter had both shown declining usage and an unanswered sponsor change months earlier, but neither had been reviewed until 30 days out. Agreed by the revenue leader; owned by the head of account management.

What changed
:   Accounts rated at risk at 90 days now get an executive sponsor call and a delivery review. The firm will compare its 90-day ratings with actual outcomes after four quarters and adjust the health score weights accordingly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software and services firm with EU customers, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The base rarely grows by itself.** Median net retention near 100% means expansion has to be managed, not waited for.
- **Decide renewals at 90 days.** A recorded decision with a reason is what lets the firm learn which accounts it read correctly.
- **Pick the expansion motion by signal.** Price, volume, cross-sell and new divisions each need different evidence and owners.
- **Size is not a growth signal.** Accounts chosen for their spend alone were less likely to grow in Gartner's research.

Gateway card

### Before the next renewal cohort

- Every renewal in the next two quarters listed with its date and notice period
- A 180-day review and 120-day value review booked for each
- A 90-day renewal decision recorded with reason, owner and expected outcome
- An expansion hypothesis per account, tied to a named signal
- Notice periods checked against the EU Data Act for any EU cloud or SaaS customer
- Churn and downgrade reasons collected from the customer, not only the account owner

## Common questions

### What is a good net revenue retention rate for B2B software?

Benchmarks for private SaaS firms put the median at around 100 to 102%. SaaS Capital found firms at 110% or more grew faster than its sample median, while those below 100% grew more slowly.

### When should the renewal process start?

Many firms start around 180 days before the renewal date, with a customer value review at about 120 days and an internal renewal decision at 90 days. Shorter notice periods move the calendar earlier.

### What is the difference between upselling and cross-selling at renewal?

Upselling increases what the customer buys of the same product or service, such as seats, usage or tier. Cross-selling adds a different product or service that solves another recorded problem.

### How does the EU Data Act affect SaaS renewals?

Since 12 September 2025, customers of data processing services, including SaaS, can switch providers with a maximum notice period of two months, and switching charges must be removed from 12 January 2027, according to legal summaries of the Act.

# MCP vs A2A: How the Two Agent Protocols Fit Together

Source: https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-a2a/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The Model Context Protocol standardises how an AI application reaches tools and data; the Agent2Agent protocol standardises how one agent delegates a task to another. They sit at different layers and are designed to be used together. Both now sit under the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation, and neither keeps the record of what was decided.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is a standard for connecting an AI application to tools and data, such as a CRM search or a document store. The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) is a standard for one agent to hand a task to another agent, often from a different vendor, and follow its progress. MCP is how an agent uses a tool; A2A is how an agent delegates work. Most multi-agent systems will use both, and neither keeps the record of who decided what.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the two protocols do

Our explainers on the [Model Context Protocol](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/) and the [Agent2Agent protocol](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-agent2agent-protocol/) cover each in full.

**MCP connects a model to capabilities.** The current specification, dated 28 July 2026, describes three roles that exchange JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. Hosts are the AI applications, clients are the connectors inside them, and servers are services that provide context and capabilities. Servers offer resources (data), prompts (templates) and tools ("functions for the AI model to execute"). The model reads a tool's description and decides when to call it: [function calling](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-function-calling/), standardised across vendors.

**A2A connects an agent to another agent.** Google's April 2025 launch post describes a client agent that formulates a task and a remote agent that acts on it. Agents advertise what they can do in an Agent Card in JSON. A task has a lifecycle and its output is an "artifact". Agents collaborate without sharing memory, tools or context, so the remote agent stays opaque: the caller sees the task and the result, not the internals.

|  | MCP | A2A |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connects | An AI application to tools and data | One agent to another agent |
| The other side is | A server exposing defined functions | An agent that plans its own work |
| What the caller sees | Tool names, inputs and outputs | An Agent Card, task status and artifacts |
| Unit of work | A tool call, usually short | A task, which may run for hours |
| Discovery | The client lists a server's tools | The client reads an Agent Card |
| Waiting on a person | Elicitation: a server asks the user for input | Task states such as input required and auth required |
| Transport | JSON-RPC 2.0 | JSON-RPC, gRPC or HTTP with JSON bindings |
| Origin and governance | Anthropic, November 2024; Agentic AI Foundation since December 2025 | Google, April 2025; Agentic AI Foundation since August 2026 |
| Main risk | Tool poisoning, over-broad credentials | Delegation that blurs accountability |

## How they fit together

The two work at different layers of one system. A worked example, illustrative only: an internal renewal agent prepares a proposal. It uses MCP to read the account from the CRM and the contract from the document store. It then uses A2A to ask a finance platform's agent for a payment-risk view, and that agent uses its own MCP servers to reach the billing data. The renewal agent receives an artifact, never the billing system.

The Agentic AI Foundation's builder's guide to A2A 1.0 notes that one server can do both, and an A2A agent may call MCP servers to do its work.

The boundary is blurring. MCP now has an optional Tasks extension for "asynchronous execution of long-running operations", which overlaps with what A2A tasks do. The useful test for a buyer is what sits on the other side. If it is a function with predictable behaviour, it is a tool, and MCP fits. If it is a system that plans its own steps and may ask for more input, it is an agent, and A2A fits.

Governance has converged. Anthropic donated MCP to the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation co-founded with Block and OpenAI, in December 2025. At that point Anthropic reported more than 10,000 active public MCP servers. The foundation's blog reports that A2A moved into it on 17 August 2026, after version 1.0 froze in March. Both protocols are now vendor-neutral, which lowers lock-in risk.

## Which to ask about, and when

Most firms of 20 to 500 people will meet both inside products rather than build on them, so the questions are for procurement.

| Situation | Protocol that matters | Question to ask the vendor |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Your assistant needs to read your CRM or drive | MCP | Is there an official server, scoped to read-only? |
| An assistant should create tasks or notes | MCP | Which tools write, and does the host ask for consent before each call? |
| A vendor's agent will take work from your agents | A2A | Does it publish an Agent Card, and what authentication does it require? |
| Your agent will delegate to a vendor's agent | A2A | Under whose permissions does the delegated task run? |
| A task crosses several agents | Both | Is every tool call and every delegated task logged with its result? |
| Anything reaches a client | Both | Can the final step return a draft for a person to approve? |

The MCP specification is direct about where responsibility sits. It says hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool, that tool descriptions "should be considered untrusted" unless they come from a trusted server, and that MCP "cannot enforce these security principles at the protocol level." With A2A, tracing an error across two vendors' agents means joining two sets of logs. Ask for [agent identity](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/) and an [audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) on both sides before connecting them.

## The **lowob** view

In **lowob**'s enterprise brain loop of store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning, both protocols are wiring. MCP wires reasoning to the store. A2A wires one reasoning unit to another. Both are open and neutrally governed: rent them.

Neither protocol carries the record. An A2A artifact says what a remote agent produced, not why a discount was approved or who owned the decision. An MCP tool call says what was written, not what outcome was expected. That record lives outside the agents, in a store the firm owns, so the learning stage can compare expectation with result.

Start with MCP, read-only, on one system. Add A2A only when there is a real task to hand to another vendor's agent. See [MCP vs API integrations](https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-api-integrations/) for what MCP changes beneath the agent.

## lowob takeaways

- **MCP is for tools; A2A is for agents.** One reaches functions and data; the other hands off whole tasks.
- **They are designed to stack.** A delegated agent often uses MCP to do the work it was given.
- **Both are now neutral infrastructure.** The Agentic AI Foundation hosts both, which reduces lock-in.
- **Neither keeps the record.** Log every tool call and delegated task, and keep decisions in a store you own.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between MCP and A2A?

MCP standardises how an AI application connects to tools and data. A2A standardises how one agent delegates a task to another agent and receives status updates and results.

### Are MCP and A2A competitors?

No. Google launched A2A as a complement to MCP, and both are now hosted by the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. Many systems use both.

### Do I need A2A if I already use MCP?

Only if your agents must hand whole tasks to agents on other platforms. To connect one assistant to your systems, MCP is enough.

### Who governs MCP and A2A?

Both are projects of the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation. MCP joined in December 2025 and A2A in August 2026.

## Sources and notes

- [Google for Developers, Announcing the Agent2Agent Protocol (A2A)](https://developers.googleblog.com/en/a2a-a-new-era-of-agent-interoperability/), 9 April 2025. Vendor launch post; describes the protocol at launch, before version 1.0.
- [Agentic AI Foundation, A2A v1.0: a builder's guide, part 1](https://aaif.io/blog/a2a-v1-0-a-builder-s-guide-part-1-discovery-tasks-and-clients), 27 August 2026. Foundation blog by an individual contributor; source of the governance move and task states.
- [Anthropic, Donating the Model Context Protocol and establishing the Agentic AI Foundation](https://anthropic.com/news/donating-the-model-context-protocol-and-establishing-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation), 9 December 2025. Vendor announcement; usage figures are self-reported.

For each AI product your team uses, note whether it supports MCP, A2A or neither, and which systems it can write to. Any product that can write but cannot show a log of its calls goes to the top of the review list.

# Intent Data vs First-Party Data

Source: https://lowob.com/research/intent-data-vs-first-party-data/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Intent data, as usually sold, is a third-party feed inferring which companies are researching a topic across publisher networks. First-party data is information a firm collects directly from its own customers and prospects, with consent. Intent sees research before buyers arrive; first-party data is more accurate, owned and specific to people. Most B2B firms should organise their first-party data before adding a feed.

Intent data, in the sense most vendors sell it, is a third-party feed that infers which companies are researching a topic, based on content consumed across publisher networks. First-party data is information a firm collects directly from its own customers and prospects: CRM records, website and product behaviour, email engagement, support tickets and billing. Intent sees research before a buyer reaches you, at company level and with uncertainty. First-party data sees less of the market but is owned, more accurate and often tied to named people. For most B2B firms, first-party data is the cheaper and more reliable place to start.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two terms mean

The terms overlap, so it helps to be precise. **First-party data** is everything you collect directly. Some of it signals intent, such as a pricing page visit or a trial sign-up, which is why practitioners talk about first-party intent. **Intent data** as a product category means third-party intent: research behaviour captured on sites you have no relationship with, resolved to companies by a provider and sold as a feed. Our explainer on [intent data](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-intent-data/) covers how those feeds are collected, resolved and scored.

| Dimension | Third-party intent data | First-party data |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where it comes from | Publisher networks and co-ops | Your site, product, CRM, email, support, billing |
| What it sees | Research on topics, before buyers find you | Behaviour of buyers already aware of you |
| Unit | Usually the company | Often a named person, linked to an account |
| Accuracy | Inferred through identity resolution | Observed directly, subject to your data quality |
| Ownership | Licensed; ends when the contract ends | Owned, if collected lawfully |
| Lawful basis | The provider's, plus your own for use | Yours, set at collection |
| Typical cost | Annual subscription | Mostly the cost of capture and clean-up |
| Main failure | Noise mistaken for demand | Data scattered across tools and never joined |

## How they differ in practice

**Coverage against accuracy.** Third-party intent's advantage is reach: it can flag accounts that have never visited your site. The cost is inference. Signals are resolved from IP addresses, logins and identity graphs, and are usually reported as a change against a baseline. First-party data covers fewer accounts, but you know what happened, when and often who did it.

**Who, not just which.** Forrester's survey found the top execution challenge for intent users was identifying the right decision-makers inside accounts showing intent, and noted that few providers deliver signals from known contacts. First-party data often supplies exactly that: the three people from one account who attended a webinar and opened a proposal.

**Decay.** Forrester calls intent "among the most time-sensitive data types available" and says stored signals need a decay model. The same applies to first-party engagement, but you control the timestamps and the rules.

**Compliance.** Forrester's advice is direct: firms need their own lawful basis for storing and using prospect data, whatever the vendor's position. With first-party data, the basis is set when you collect it, and you can document it.

**Cookies did not settle the question.** For years the case for first-party data rested partly on Chrome ending third-party cookies. Google's April 2025 decision to keep its current approach removed that deadline. The argument for first-party data now rests on accuracy and ownership instead.

**Most firms underuse what they have.** In BCG research conducted with Google and published in 2021, only about 30% of companies were creating a single customer view across channels. The sample was 23 companies and seven agencies, mostly consumer-facing, so treat it as directional for B2B.

## Which to use first

| Situation | Where to start |
| --- | --- |
| Website, product and CRM data are not linked to accounts | First-party: join them before buying a feed |
| Most pipeline comes from inbound or existing customers | First-party, scored at account level |
| Outbound to accounts that have never engaged | Third-party intent, tested against a control group |
| New category with no clear topic taxonomy | First-party; intent topics may not describe you |
| Already using several intent providers | Audit overlap and test each against first-party outcomes |
| Account teams cannot tell who is engaged inside target accounts | First-party contact engagement, rolled up to the account |

A practical sequence for a firm of 20 to 500 people:

1. **List your first-party sources.** Site analytics, forms, product events, email, meetings, support and billing, each with its owner.
2. **Link them to accounts.** Match people to companies with [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/), in the CRM or a warehouse.
3. **Define a few strong signals.** Pricing page visits, a second stakeholder engaging, a trial reaching a usage threshold.
4. **Add third-party intent for reach.** Use it for accounts with no first-party history, and test it before scaling spend.
5. **Compare against outcomes.** Each quarter, check which signals preceded opportunities, and drop the ones that did not.

## The **lowob** view

The enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. First-party data is the store, and it is yours. Third-party intent is rented context, one more input to the wiring that tells a person or an agent where to look. Neither is a decision.

The decision to prioritise an account, the reason and the owner belong in the record. The learning step closes the loop: write back whether accounts flagged by each signal turned into opportunities, so next quarter's spend follows evidence. That write-back is itself first-party data, and over time it becomes the most valuable signal a firm holds. In outbound, a signal earns its place when it gives a seller a real reason to get in touch; see [Cold Outreach Works Better With a Real Reason to Talk](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Intent offers reach; first-party offers truth.** One flags unknown accounts, the other shows what known buyers did.
- **Join your own data first.** Most firms already hold stronger signals than they use.
- **Own the lawful basis.** Vendor compliance does not cover your use of prospect data.
- **Write back what converted.** The record of which signals worked is first-party data you cannot buy.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between intent data and first-party data?

Intent data, as usually sold, is inferred from research on third-party sites and resolved to companies. First-party data is collected directly from your own customers and prospects through your site, product, CRM and email.

### Is first-party data better than intent data?

It is more accurate and owned, but it only sees buyers already aware of you. Third-party intent adds reach. Most B2B firms get more from organising first-party data first.

### Is first-party intent data the same as first-party data?

It is a subset. First-party intent is the part of your own data that signals buying interest, such as pricing page visits, trial activity or several people from one account engaging.

### Did Google remove third-party cookies from Chrome?

No. In April 2025 Google said it would keep its current approach to third-party cookie choice in Chrome and would not introduce a new standalone prompt.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Intent Data Expectations Vs. Reality: What's Working, And Where Are The Gaps?](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/intent-data-expectations-vs-reality-whats-working-and-where-are-the-gaps), 26 October 2023. Analyst blog summarising its Q1 2023 survey; sample size not stated in the post.
- [Forrester, The 10 Biggest Intent Data Mistakes For B2B Marketing And Sales](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-10-biggest-intent-data-mistakes-for-b2b-marketing-and-sales), 17 February 2023. Analyst opinion, not survey data.
- [Google Privacy Sandbox, Next steps for Privacy Sandbox and tracking protections in Chrome](https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-next-steps), 22 April 2025. Primary announcement from the browser vendor.
- [BCG, The Value of First-Party Data](https://www.bcg.com/en-ca/publications/2021/the-value-of-first-party-data), March 2021. Research conducted with Google, which sells advertising; small, consumer-leaning sample.
- The comparison table, sequence and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is Intent Data, and How Reliable Is It?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-intent-data/)

- [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse: Which Holds What](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/)
- [Lead Scoring vs Account Scoring](https://lowob.com/research/lead-scoring-vs-account-scoring/)
- [What Is a Press Release, and When Is It Worth It?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-press-release/)

## Next move

List every first-party source that records buyer behaviour and mark whether it links to an account in your CRM. Fix the largest unlinked source before renewing or buying any intent feed.
