# What Is a Customer Data Platform?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-customer-data-platform/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A customer data platform is packaged software that collects customer data from many sources, links it into one persistent profile per customer and makes those profiles available to other systems. The CDP Institute tracked 213 active vendors in July 2026, and Gartner reports that marketers use only about half of the capabilities they buy. For a B2B firm the key questions are account-level support, the warehouse it already has, and who will own the profiles.

A customer data platform (CDP) is packaged software that collects customer data from many sources, links it into one persistent profile per customer and shares those profiles with other systems, mostly for marketing. It differs from a CRM, which people work in, and a data warehouse, which holds history for analysis. Many B2B firms of 20 to 500 people can meet the need with a warehouse; a CDP earns its place when high-volume behavioural data must reach many channels quickly.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a customer data platform means

The same customer appears in web analytics, an email platform, a product database and a CRM, each with a different identifier. A CDP collects these records, decides which belong to the same person or account, and keeps one profile that grows over time. Other tools read it to target campaigns or personalise pages.

The CDP Institute, the category's industry association, says a CDP "ingests data from any source, captures full detail, builds unified and persistent customer profiles", with the data made available in real time to other systems. Gartner's definition, from senior principal analyst Rachel Smith, is narrower: "software applications that support marketing and customer experience use cases by unifying a company's customer data".

The Institute's RealCDP checklist turns the definition into seven tests.

| RealCDP capability | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Ingest any source | Accepts data from web, app, CRM, billing, files and other systems |
| Capture full detail | Keeps individual events, not only summaries |
| Persist the data | Retains history rather than passing data through |
| Unified profiles | Links records that belong to the same customer |
| Open access | Shares profiles with any other system |
| Real-time response | Answers requests fast enough for live interactions |
| Govern customer data | Applies consent, privacy and access controls |

Which data belongs in a CDP, a CRM or a warehouse is covered in [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/).

## How it works

The core job is identity resolution, a form of [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/). Twilio Segment's documentation describes an identity graph that "merges the complete history of each customer into a single profile", using cookie IDs, device IDs, email addresses and custom IDs. Salesforce's Data 360 uses match rules to group records and reconciliation rules to choose field values. The result is a [golden record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-golden-record/) per customer. Marketers then build audiences from those profiles and send them to advertising, email or personalisation tools.

The market is crowded. The CDP Institute counted 213 active vendors in July 2026 and $13.5 billion of cumulative disclosed financing. Gartner's critical capabilities cover data collection, profile unification, integrations, segmentation, experimentation, and data science and privacy.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The case for a CDP is one profile, updated as customers act, available to every tool. The case against is underuse. Smith reports marketers used only 53% of CDP capabilities on average in 2024, and that a 2025 Gartner survey of business buyers found an average of five groups funding a CDP purchase. A purchase with five funders and no single owner is hard to run.

B2B firms need more than individual identity. Purchases are made by a group at one account, so account-level profiles matter; Segment's group calls are one example of vendor support.

In **lowob**'s model the CDP is the store. It answers "who is this customer and what have they done", not why a price was offered or a campaign chosen; those reasons belong in the decision record. Its profiles can feed the wiring that agents read from, provided permissions follow the data.

## How to evaluate a CDP

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Do we already have a warehouse with clean customer data? | A warehouse-native approach may avoid a second copy of the data |
| Does it model accounts and buying groups, not only individuals? | B2B decisions are made by groups at one account |
| Which identity rules does it use, and can we see them? | Hidden matching rules produce merges nobody can explain |
| Who will own the profiles and the definitions? | Gartner's five-funder finding suggests ownership is often unclear |
| How are consent and deletion handled across destinations? | Governance is a RealCDP test, and some products are audited against it |

Start with a use case, not a platform: the decision the profiles will improve, such as which accounts receive a renewal campaign. Then check that the data is not already in the CRM or warehouse.

## lowob takeaways

- **A CDP unifies identity.** Its core job is one persistent profile per customer, shared with other tools.
- **Check the warehouse first.** Many B2B firms can meet the need with data they already hold.
- **Name one owner.** Underused capability and many funders point to unclear ownership.
- **It is store, not judgment.** Profiles say who and what; decision records say why.

## Common questions

### What does a customer data platform do?

It collects customer data from many sources, links records that belong to the same customer into one persistent profile, and shares those profiles with marketing and other tools.

### What is the difference between a CDP and a CRM?

A CRM is where people manage relationships and deals with data they mostly enter. A CDP gathers behavioural and identity data automatically and shares unified profiles.

### Do B2B companies need a CDP?

Some do, mainly those with high volumes of web or product data feeding many channels. Others can meet the need with a warehouse and their CRM.

## Sources and notes

- [CDP Institute, Learning Center and CDP basics](https://www.cdpinstitute.org/?p=1133), page undated, figures dated July 2026. Industry association page; vendor counts and financing totals are its own tracking.
- [Rachel Smith, Gartner: What to look for in a customer data platform](https://computerweekly.com/feature/Gartner-What-to-look-for-in-a-customer-data-platform), Computer Weekly, undated. Analyst article excerpted from Gartner research; survey samples not given.
- [Twilio Segment, Identity Resolution overview](https://www.twilio.com/docs/segment/unify/identity-resolution), undated. Vendor product documentation, cited as a category example.
- [Salesforce Trailhead, Unify Your Data (Data 360)](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/projects/explore-data-cloud-core-functionality/unify-your-data), undated. Vendor training project, cited as a category example.

## Related research

- [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse: Which Holds What](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/)
- [What Is a Golden Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-golden-record/)
- [Intent Data vs First-Party Data](https://lowob.com/research/intent-data-vs-first-party-data/)
- [What Is Reverse ETL?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-reverse-etl/)
- [What Is Prompt Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-engineering/)

## Next move

List every system holding customer identifiers and the ID each uses. If your warehouse already joins three or more, test a warehouse-native approach before shortlisting a CDP.

# What Is Value-Based Pricing?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Value-based pricing sets a price from the value an offer creates for a defined buyer, measured against that buyer's next best alternative. Pricing research treats it as the strongest approach and finds it the least used. The difficulty is less the arithmetic than measuring value, segmenting by it and holding the price once sellers start to negotiate.

Value-based pricing sets a price from the value an offer creates for a specific buyer, measured against that buyer's next best alternative, rather than from the seller's cost or a competitor's list price. Pricing researchers generally rank it as the strongest of the three main approaches, and the evidence says it is the least used. The arithmetic is simple. The hard parts are measuring value with real customer data and holding the price once a negotiation starts.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What value-based pricing means

Most firms set price in one of three ways. Hinterhuber's review, published in the *Journal of Business Strategy*, averaged nearly two dozen studies of pricing practice across the US, Europe and Asia.

| Approach | Starting point | Share of firms in Hinterhuber's review | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost-based | Cost plus a target margin | 37% | Ignores what the buyer would pay |
| Competition-based | Competitors' prices | 44% | Ignores how the offer differs |
| Customer value-based | Value to the buyer against the next best alternative | 17% | Needs customer data that is hard to collect |

Value-based pricing does not mean charging the full value. Cost sets the floor. The buyer's estimate of value sets the ceiling. The price sits between them, and the share of value left with the buyer is their reason to choose you. For a services firm the next best alternative may be an internal team, a competitor or doing nothing.

## How it works

The method has four steps: name the alternative, list the differences, put a money value on each, and choose where in the band to price. Hinterhuber and Liozu's article in *MIT Sloan Management Review* gives a worked case from a European supermarket chain pricing a private-label yogurt.

| Step | Figure in the published case |
| --- | --- |
| Cost of goods | €1.29 |
| Original price | €1.99 |
| Next best alternative: branded yogurt | €2.99 |
| Value of added health benefit | about +€0.30 |
| Penalty for no brand name | about −€0.50 |
| Estimated perceived value | about €2.80 |
| Recommended price, after testing price sensitivity and competitor reaction | €2.49 |

The authors report that sales beat volume targets at the higher price and profits were nearly six times the plan. It is one consumer case, reported by its authors. In business markets the differences are usually money the buyer saves or earns.

In B2B, the value estimate should come from customers, not from the seller's slide. Anderson and Narus proposed customer value models built mainly through field value assessments, either for one customer or for a segment. Expert interviews, buyer workshops and conjoint analysis are the usual tools, and [Pricing Experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to test a price once it is set.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Value-based pricing sets the list price within a [pricing architecture](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/). It fails most often after the price is set.

Hinterhuber's workshops with executives at nine companies identified six obstacles. Two sit in the commercial team: segmenting customers by need, and sales force management, where unnecessary discounts cause "value leakage". The remedies he describes are clear discount authority, pay, training and monitoring. That is the subject of [Discount Governance](https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/).

Realisation is the wider problem. Simon-Kucher's 2025 Global Pricing Study, covering 28 countries and 39 industries, found firms keep less than half of the price increases they announce. A value-based list price that sellers discount back to the competitor's level is competition-based pricing with extra work.

Value-based pricing also shapes the value metric. If value appears per completed task, a seat price undercharges; [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) covers that choice.

> Cost sets the floor and value sets the ceiling. The gap between price and value is the buyer's reason to sign.

## How to start

| Test | Question to answer | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Alternative | What would this buyer do if you did not exist? | "There is no alternative" |
| Differences | Which two or three differences matter most to the buyer, in money? | A feature list with no figures |
| Evidence | Where did each value figure come from? | Only internal estimates |
| Segment | Does value differ enough by segment to justify different offers? | One price for every buyer |
| Realisation | What did you actually collect on the last ten deals? | Nobody knows |
| Record | Who owns the value estimate, and when is it checked? | It lives in one person's head |

In **lowob**'s model a price is a commercial decision like any other. It belongs in the record with its reason, the value estimate behind it, its owner, the expected result and a check date. An agent can draft the value case from call notes and CRM history at autonomy level 1. The price itself stays with a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start from the alternative.** Value is always measured against what the buyer would otherwise do.
- **Use customer evidence.** Value figures from field interviews hold up in negotiation; internal estimates do not.
- **Protect realisation.** A value-based list price only matters if discount rules hold it.
- **Record the estimate.** The reason behind a price is what lets the next price improve.

## Common questions

### What is value-based pricing in simple terms?

Setting a price from what the offer is worth to the buyer, compared with their next best option, rather than from your costs or competitors' prices.

### What is the difference between value-based and cost-plus pricing?

Cost-plus adds a margin to cost and ignores what buyers would pay. Value-based starts from the buyer's value and uses cost only as a floor.

### Why do so few companies use value-based pricing?

Research by Hinterhuber points to the difficulty of measuring and communicating value, segmenting customers by need, controlling discounts and winning senior support.

### Can services firms use value-based pricing?

Yes, where the outcome can be described in the client's terms, such as cost avoided or revenue protected. It usually pairs with a fixed or hybrid fee rather than an hourly rate.

## Sources and notes

- [Management and Accounting Web, summary of Hinterhuber, "Customer value-based pricing strategies: why companies resist", Journal of Business Strategy 29(4)](https://maaw.info/ArticleSummaries/ArtSumHinterhuber2008.htm), 2008. Academic summary of a review of 1983 to 2006 studies; shares are averages across differing surveys.
- [Hinterhuber and Liozu, Setting Prices Based on Customer Value, MIT Sloan Management Review](https://sloanreview.mit.edu/article/setting-prices-based-on-customer-value), 2012. Excerpt from an academic article; the yogurt case is a single example reported by the authors.
- [Management and Accounting Web, summary of Hinterhuber and Liozu (2012)](https://maaw.info/ArticleSummaries/ArtSumHinterhuberLiozu2012.htm). Academic summary; interview study of 15 US industrial firms, small sample.
- [Kellogg School of Management, Anderson and Narus, Business Marketing: Understand What Customers Value](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/research/detail/1998/business-marketing-understand-what-customers-value), Harvard Business Review, 1998. Abstract page only; older work on method, not measured outcomes.
- [Simon-Kucher, The State of Pricing 2025: Global Pricing Study](https://www.simon-kucher.com/en/insights/global-pricing-study), 2025. Consultancy survey of 2,200+ leaders; realisation figure is self-reported.

# Forecasting That Holds

Source: https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Surveys find that fewer than half of sales leaders trust their forecasts and that most miss by more than 10% a quarter. The cause is rarely the method. It is that stage probabilities are borrowed, close dates slip without consequence and nobody scores past calls. A forecast holds when each call is recorded with its basis, compared with what happened, and used to correct the next one.

A forecast holds when the firm can say, before the period ends, how far off its last ten forecasts were and why. Most cannot. Gartner found that only 45% of sales leaders and sellers had high confidence in their organisation's forecast accuracy, and a Forrester Consulting study found that 55% of revenue teams missed their quarterly forecast by more than 10% on average. The method is rarely the main problem. Stage probabilities are borrowed from software defaults, close dates slip without consequence and past calls are overwritten instead of scored. The fix is to record each forecast call with its basis, compare it with the outcome and use the error to correct the next call.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every revenue team forecasts. Few check their forecasts. The number is set in week one, adjusted in week six, explained in week thirteen and then replaced by next quarter's number. The error is felt, but it is not measured, so the same bias repeats.

The explainer on [sales forecasting](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-forecasting/) covers what a forecast is and the main methods. This piece covers why forecasts miss in practice, which method fails in which way, and the record that turns a forecast from a negotiation into a measurement.

## How far off forecasts usually are

The best public evidence points the same way. Gartner's 2020 research on sales operations found that fewer than half of sales leaders and sellers, 45%, had high confidence in their organisation's forecast accuracy. Only 47% believed their organisation had high-quality data, and 13% said their data quality was poor. Gartner warned that low confidence pushes leaders towards decisions based on intuition rather than evidence, including approving discounts they would normally reject.

The size of the miss is larger than most boards assume. A 2021 Forrester Consulting study commissioned by Clari surveyed 327 US software-industry revenue operations decision-makers. Of the 303 who measured forecast accuracy, only 18% said their quarterly forecast was within 5% of actual revenue. More than half, 55%, said they missed their quarterly forecast by more than 10% on average, and more firms were off by 20% or more than were within 5%. The study was vendor-commissioned and self-reported, so it may understate the problem among firms that do not measure at all.

Better tooling has not closed the gap on its own. A Gartner survey of 303 sales leaders, reported in 2024, found 84% said sales analytics had affected performance less than expected, with poor data quality cited by 44% as a top barrier. The same research found analytics led by the chief sales officer were 2.3 times more likely to achieve higher forecast accuracy, which suggests ownership matters as much as software.

## Why forecasts miss

Four causes account for most of the error, and none is solved by a better model.

Borrowed probabilities. Most CRMs ship with stage probabilities that are placeholders. HubSpot's default deal pipeline, for example, assigns 20% to "appointment scheduled", 40% to "qualified to buy", 60% to "presentation scheduled", 80% to "decision maker bought-in" and 90% to "contract sent". Those numbers describe no real firm. A firm that never replaces them with its own historical conversion rates is forecasting on someone else's history.

Slipping close dates. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmark, a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, found that 44% of deals were pushed back at the peak, and that slipped deals saw win rates fall by 67%, with the steepest falls for deals delayed more than eight weeks. A close date that moves without a recorded reason is a forecast error in waiting.

Weak stage definitions. If "proposal" means a document has been sent in one team and a price agreed in another, the stage-weighted number mixes two different things. The explainer on [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) covers how to write exit criteria that make stages comparable. Part 20 covered how qualification fields can feed them.

Overwritten calls. Most forecasting tools let managers adjust the number. Salesforce's forecasting documentation notes that an adjustment changes the forecast amount while leaving the underlying opportunity data unchanged. That is useful, but if the original call and the reason for the adjustment are not kept, nobody can later tell whether the adjustment improved the forecast or worsened it.

## Three numbers, side by side

The practical answer is not one better forecast. It is three, recorded together, so their differences can be seen and scored.

| Forecast | What it uses | Typical failure | When it is most reliable |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stage-weighted | Open pipeline value multiplied by the firm's own historical conversion rate per stage | Wrong when stage definitions drift or when probabilities are software defaults | Large volumes of similar deals with stable stages |
| Seller commit | Each seller's call on which deals will close this period | Optimism early in the quarter, sandbagging near quota thresholds | Few large deals where the seller knows the buyer well |
| Manager call | The manager's judgment across the team, adjusting for known seller bias | Reflects the manager's own pressure from above | When the manager has a scored record of past calls |

Salesforce's forecast categories (Pipeline, Best Case, Commit, Closed, with an optional Most Likely) are a common way to collect the seller view. The categories only help if their meaning is written down. "Commit" should mean something specific, such as the economic buyer has confirmed and the paper process has started, rather than "I feel good about it".

When the three numbers agree, the forecast is probably sound. When they diverge, the gap is information. A stage-weighted number well below the seller commit usually means deals are sitting in late stages that do not deserve them. A manager call well above both usually means pressure from the next level up.

> A forecast that is never scored cannot improve. It can only be explained.

## The forecast record

The step most firms skip is keeping the calls. Each week, or at least at fixed points in the period, the firm should record its forecast as a decision with a basis, an owner and a date, and keep it once the period closes. Earlier calls are superseded, never overwritten, which is the principle set out in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

| Field | Example | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Date of call | Week 4 of the quarter | Lets error be measured by how far ahead the call was made |
| Forecast type | Manager call | Separates the three numbers |
| Amount | The figure called | The thing to be scored |
| Basis | Two large deals moved to Commit after procurement started | Shows what the call relied on |
| Owner | Regional sales manager | Makes calibration personal and fair |
| Adjustment and reason | Raised by 8% on a verbal from one buyer | Shows whether adjustments help |
| Outcome (written back) | Actual revenue at period end | Turns the call into evidence |

With a few periods of records, error can be scored simply. For each call, take the difference between forecast and actual as a share of actual. Track it by forecast type, by owner and by how many weeks ahead the call was made. Over time this shows which number to trust at which point in the quarter, and which sellers are consistently high or low. The piece on [calibration as the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) makes the wider case.

Slips need their own field. A close date that moves should carry a reason code and a count of how many times it has moved. Given the Ebsta finding on slipped deals, a deal on its third slip should come out of the commit number automatically.

Data quality is the foundation under all of it. Gartner's recommendations were plain: set data standards that follow from why the firm has a CRM, inspect data quality in regular manager and seller conversations, and show sellers how good data helps them. The explainer on [CRM data hygiene](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/) covers the practical steps.

Illustrative example: scoring the manager call

Decision
:   Record all three forecasts each fortnight, keep them after the quarter closes, and report error by forecast type.

Reason and owner
:   The board had seen three quarters of misses above 10%, each explained differently. Agreed by the chief revenue officer; owned by revenue operations.

What changed
:   After two quarters, the stage-weighted number had the lowest error early in the quarter and the manager call had the lowest error in the last month. The firm now reports the stage-weighted number to the board until week eight, then the manager call, and will review the rule after two more quarters.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Replace default probabilities.** Use the firm's own stage conversion history, or the stage-weighted number means nothing.
- **Keep three numbers.** Stage-weighted, seller commit and manager call, recorded side by side; their gaps are information.
- **Never overwrite a call.** Supersede it, keep the reason, and score every call against the outcome.
- **Treat slips as data.** A close date that moves needs a reason, and repeated slips should leave the commit.

Gateway card

### Before you present the next forecast to the board

- Stage probabilities replaced with the firm's own conversion history
- Written definitions for each forecast category, especially Commit
- Stage-weighted, seller and manager forecasts recorded together each week or fortnight
- Adjustments kept with their reasons, not overwritten
- Close-date changes logged with a reason code and a slip count
- Error from the last four periods calculated by forecast type and owner

## Common questions

### How accurate should a sales forecast be?

There is no universal standard, but in a Forrester Consulting survey only 18% of revenue teams forecast quarterly revenue within 5% of actual, and 55% missed by more than 10%. A firm should measure its own error and aim to reduce it period by period.

### Why are sales forecasts usually wrong?

Common causes are default stage probabilities, close dates that slip without consequence, inconsistent stage definitions, poor CRM data and the absence of any record comparing past forecasts with outcomes.

### What is the difference between a commit forecast and a weighted pipeline forecast?

A weighted pipeline forecast multiplies open deal values by stage probabilities. A commit forecast is the seller's or manager's judgment of which specific deals will close in the period.

### How do you measure forecast accuracy?

Record each forecast call with its date and owner, then compare it with actual revenue at period end. Express the difference as a share of actual and track it by forecast type, owner and how far ahead the call was made.

# Ten People: The First Stranger

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Somewhere between the third and tenth hire, a company gains people who were not there when anything was decided. The decision record's job becomes answering 'why do we do it this way?' without a founder in the room. A topic wiki is the trap; a time-ordered ledger readable by strangers, with a few 'why we do it' pages and first definitions, is the defence.

Somewhere between the third and the tenth hire, the company gains people who were not there when anything was decided. The enterprise brain's job becomes answering "why do we do it this way?" without a founder in the room. The founders' ledger stays, rewritten so strangers can read it, with three additions: short "why we do it this way" pages, a handful of first definitions with owners, and onboarding through the record. The trap is a topic wiki.

This is the second rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/). The previous rung, [*Two people: the founders' ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/), dealt with false shared memory. At ten people the problem is the first stranger.

The first employees join a company whose habits, choices and quirks all have reasons, and almost none of the reasons are written down. They ask. The founders answer. That works for a while, and then it becomes the founders' main job without anyone noticing.

## The founders become the memory

The arithmetic changes quickly. Brooks's formula for communication paths, n(n-1)/2, gives one channel at two people and 45 at ten. Most of those channels carry questions about history toward the same one or two people. J. Richard Hackman, the Harvard team researcher, warned in 2009 that the links a team must manage grow "at an accelerating, almost exponential rate", and gave "no double digits" as his rule for team size.

The cost of searching for context is well measured in larger firms. McKinsey Global Institute estimated in 2012 that interaction workers spend nearly 20% of their time looking for internal information or tracking down colleagues who can help with specific tasks, and that a searchable record of knowledge could cut that search time by as much as 35%. At ten people, "tracking down a colleague" usually means interrupting a founder.

The symptom is easy to spot. Count how many questions in a week end with a founder answering them. If that number grows with every hire, the founders have become the organisation's memory, and memory does not scale by working longer hours.

> If the questions founders answer each week grow with every hire, the founders have become the company's memory.

## What changes

The founders' ledger stays, but it must now be readable by people who were not there. That means writing entries so a stranger can follow them: context in the first line, no private shorthand, links to the evidence.

Michael Nygard's 2011 case for architecture decision records describes exactly what happens without this. A newcomer who finds a past decision without its reasoning has two options: blindly accept it, which is harmful when the context has changed, or blindly change it, which can break something nobody wrote down.

Three additions earn their place.

**"Why we do it this way" pages.** Short explanations of the five to ten practices new people question most: pricing, how leads are qualified, why a particular tool, why a market was deprioritised. Each links to the ledger entries behind it.

**First definitions.** The handful of terms that already cause confusion. What counts as a qualified lead. What "launched" means. When a customer is "active". Write them down once, with an owner. This is the seed of the glossary the next rung needs.

**Onboarding through the record.** Every new hire spends part of their first week reading the ledger. It is the fastest way to absorb how the company thinks, and their questions reveal which entries are unclear.

| Addition | What it contains | Owner | Done when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Readable ledger | Every entry rewritten with context in the first line | Founders | A new hire can follow the last 20 entries unaided |
| "Why we do it" pages | Five to ten practices, each linked to its ledger entries | The founder who made the call | New hires stop asking about those practices |
| First definitions | Five to ten terms that already cause confusion | One named person per term | Two people give the same answer to "what counts as active?" |
| Record-based onboarding | Reading the ledger in week one, questions logged | Hiring manager | Each new hire's questions produce at least one clarified entry |

## AI at this stage

This is the first point where an assistant over the record is clearly worth it. A new hire asks "why did we stop selling to agencies?" and gets the ledger entry, the date and the reason. The question no longer interrupts a founder. If the record cannot answer, the question is logged, and the founder writes the missing entry once instead of answering it five times.

The mechanism is ordinary retrieval, covered in our explainer [*What is retrieval-augmented generation?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/). Two conditions make it work at this size. The assistant must answer from the ledger and cite the entry, not from a model's general knowledge. And the unanswered-question log must be reviewed weekly, in the same 30 minutes as the ledger review, or the gaps never close.

## The trap

The trap at ten people is a wiki. Someone sets up a large knowledge base, populates it enthusiastically for two weeks, and then it decays. Wikis organised by topic go stale because nobody owns keeping them current. A decision record organised by time does not go stale in the same way, because old entries are meant to be old; they are superseded, not updated.

|  | Topic wiki | Time-ordered decision record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organised by | Subject | Date of decision |
| What "out of date" means | A page that is silently wrong | An entry that has been superseded, with a link to its successor |
| Who maintains it | Nobody in particular | Whoever made the decision |
| What a newcomer learns | What someone once wrote about a topic | What was decided, why, and what replaced it |
| Failure mode | Decays within weeks of launch | Gaps where decisions were not written down, visible in the question log |

Our piece [*Supersede, never overwrite*](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why keeping the old view, linked to the new one, is safer than editing it away. The first hire is one of [*the transitions that break the brain*](https://lowob.com/research/the-transitions-that-break-the-brain/), and our explainer [*What is a system of record?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/) shows where the ledger fits.

**In practice:** count questions answered by founders each week, and aim for that number to fall as headcount rises. Rewrite ledger entries so someone who was not there can follow them. Write "why we do it this way" pages for the five most-questioned practices, and make reading the ledger part of every new hire's first week.

## What would prove this wrong

Ten-person companies where founders answer every contextual question without strain or slowdown. Then the record is premature at this size, and the effort belongs at the next rung, [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/), where teams form and vocabularies drift.

## lowob takeaways

- **Measure founder load.** If the questions founders answer each week grow with every hire, the founders have become the memory.
- **Write for strangers.** Context in the first line, no private shorthand, links to evidence.
- **Add three things only.** "Why we do it" pages, first definitions with owners, onboarding through the record.
- **Let the assistant log its gaps.** An unanswered question becomes one written entry, not five interruptions.
- **Avoid the wiki.** Topic pages decay; time-ordered records are superseded, not updated.

## Common questions

### How do startups stop founders being the bottleneck for every question?

Make the founders' decision ledger readable by people who were not there, write "why we do it this way" pages for the most-questioned practices, write down first definitions with an owner, and onboard new hires through the record.

### Should a 10-person startup set up a wiki?

Usually not. Topic wikis decay because nobody owns keeping them current. A decision record organised by time does not go stale the same way, because old entries are superseded with a link to the new one.

### When is an AI assistant over company knowledge worth it?

From about ten people, when it answers from the decision record, cites the entry, and logs questions it cannot answer so a founder writes the missing entry once.

### What should new hires read in their first week at a startup?

The decision ledger and the "why we do it this way" pages. They are the fastest way to absorb how the company thinks, and a new hire's questions show which entries are unclear.

## Sources and notes

- [McKinsey Global Institute, The social economy](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/the-social-economy), July 2012. Consultancy estimate across large firms; predates generative AI.
- [Diane Coutu, Why Teams Don't Work (interview with J. Richard Hackman)](https://bu.edu/sph/files/2019/01/Why-Teams-Don%E2%80%99t-Work.pdf), Harvard Business Review, May 2009. Interview, hosted copy; about teams, not companies.
- [Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), 15 November 2011. Practitioner essay on software teams.
- [Project Wizards, Brooks's law (glossary)](https://www.projectwizards.net/en/project-management-glossary/brooks-law). Vendor glossary summarising Brooks's 1975 book.
- The additions table and the wiki comparison are **lowob**'s framework.

## Next move

For one week, tally every question a founder answers about why something is done. Turn the three most frequent into "why we do it this way" pages linked to their ledger entries.

# AI Agents in Customer Success and Account Management

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-customer-success-and-account-management/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Customer success is where agents meet existing revenue, so a wrong answer costs a relationship as well as a deal. Of nine tasks in the lowob directory, five are rated high reliability, all internal briefs, summaries and scheduling. Answering and resolving customer cases can work with an approved knowledge base and sampling, but the company stays liable for what the agent says. Start with ticket summaries, renewal briefs and review decks.

Customer success is the function where AI agents touch revenue a company already has. That makes the internal tasks very attractive and the customer-facing ones expensive to get wrong. Of the nine customer success and account management tasks in the **lowob** directory, five are rated high reliability: renewal briefs, ticket summaries, adviser reminders, scheduling and review decks, all of them prepared for a person. Answering and resolving customer questions can run with an approved knowledge base, an escalation path and sampling, but a tribunal has already held a company liable for its chatbot's wrong answer. Start inside the account team, and earn the customer-facing tasks with measured evidence.

*Figure: The wiring turns nine places into one brief. It cannot retrieve a decision nobody wrote down; that is the record's job.*

Customer success sits between the sale and the renewal. Its records are richer than most: usage data, support tickets, delivery records, invoices, meeting notes. Its decisions are slower and more consequential: whether an account is at risk, what to propose at renewal, when to bring in a senior person. Agents are good at the first part and should be kept on a short lead in the second.

## Where customer work stands

The forecasts point in two directions at once. In March 2025 Gartner predicted that by 2029 agentic AI would autonomously resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention, with a 30% reduction in operational costs. Three months later it predicted that by 2027, 50% of organisations that expected to significantly reduce their customer service workforce would abandon those plans. That second forecast drew on a March 2025 poll of 163 service leaders, 95% of whom planned to keep human agents.

Customers lean the same way. A Gartner survey of 5,728 customers, run in December 2023, found 64% would prefer companies did not use AI for customer service, and 53% would consider switching to a competitor if they learned a company was going to. The top concern was that it would become harder to reach a person.

Read together: routine resolution is coming, and the relationship stays human. For an account management team at a mid-size firm, the useful split is between work done for the account owner and work done in front of the customer.

## The nine tasks, rated

Every customer success and account management task in the [**lowob** Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/), with the brain layer each depends on most: store, context, record, reasoning or learning.

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control | Brain plug point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prepare a renewal brief from usage and delivery data | 1 Draft | High | Missing a known issue | Account owner review | Store |
| Flag at-risk accounts | 3 Act and report | Medium | False alarms or missed churn | Health score calibrated against outcomes | Learning |
| Draft a renewal or expansion proposal | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong pricing or terms | Proposal approver | Record |
| Summarise support tickets for an account | 3 Act and report | High | Misread sentiment | Linked to source tickets | Store |
| Answer routine customer questions | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Wrong answer stated as fact | Approved knowledge base; escalation path | Context |
| Resolve support cases end to end | 3 Act and report | Medium | Incorrect resolution | Outcome-priced tools allow measurement; sampling | Reasoning |
| Remind advisers of client moments (clienteling) | 3 Act and report | High | Relationship feels automated | Adviser writes every client message | Context |
| Schedule quarterly business reviews | 3 Act and report | High | Clashes and missed stakeholders | Calendar rules | Context |
| Draft a quarterly business review deck | 1 Draft | High | Stale or cherry-picked metrics | Figures pulled from live sources and checked | Store |

Two things stand out. First, the high-reliability tasks cluster on the store: they depend on the agent seeing complete, current account data. If usage, tickets and delivery sit in three systems with no shared account identifier, those tasks drop to medium in practice. Second, the five level 3 tasks are not all equal. Ticket summaries, adviser reminders, scheduling and at-risk flags are internal. Resolving cases end to end is customer-facing, and its level 3 rating depends entirely on sampling.

> The account owner can delegate the preparation. The relationship stays with the person whose name is on the email.

## Five tasks that decide whether it works

### Answer routine customer questions

The directory rates this level 2: the agent answers from an approved knowledge base, with an escalation path for anything outside it, and a person approves answers in categories that carry commercial or contractual weight. The legal reason is Moffatt v Air Canada, decided by the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal in February 2024. The airline's website chatbot told a passenger he could claim a bereavement fare within 90 days of ticketing; the airline's own policy page said otherwise. Air Canada argued the chatbot was responsible for its own statements. The tribunal rejected that, found negligent misrepresentation and held that the company was responsible for all information on its website, static or generated. The award was about CA$650 plus interest and fees. The amount was small. The principle applies to every business: the agent's answer is your answer.

### Resolve support cases end to end

The appeal is real. Outcome-priced tools have made the economics visible: Intercom's Fin, for example, charges US$0.99 per outcome, and counts a resolution when no further help is requested after its last answer. That pricing makes measurement easier, which is why the directory cites it in the control. It does not make the outcome correct. A customer who stops replying may be satisfied, or may have given up. The control is sampling: each week, pull a random set of closed cases and have a person grade them as correct, partial or wrong. The academic evidence supports the caution. Sierra's τ-bench, which tests agents on simulated retail and airline service tasks, found that leading function-calling agents succeeded on fewer than half of tasks, and that consistency across eight repeated attempts fell below 25% in retail. A single good run is not a reliable process. Our ranking of [AI customer service agents by pricing model](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-customer-service-agents-by-pricing-model/) covers how the commercial terms differ. Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about US$3.6 billion.

### Flag at-risk accounts

Rated level 3 at medium reliability. The agent reads usage, tickets, payment status and meeting cadence, and flags accounts against a health score. The control, calibration against outcomes, is a learning-layer job. Every quarter, compare the accounts flagged with the accounts that actually churned or shrank, and the accounts that churned without a flag. If the score is not calibrated, the agent will produce confident lists that the team learns to ignore. We set out the method in [Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/).

### Draft a renewal or expansion proposal

Medium reliability because the drafting is easy and the commercial content is not. Renewal proposals carry price changes, discount history, contract terms and promises made by people who may have left. The agent drafts from the price book and the account's decision history; a named proposal approver signs off before anything reaches the customer. The record matters most here. If the last renewal's discount and its reason were recorded, the agent can show them. If not, it guesses from the invoice, and the approver inherits the guess.

### Remind advisers of client moments

Clienteling, the practice of prompting a relationship manager about a client's anniversary, a contract milestone or a product they asked about, rates high reliability at level 3. The agent acts by sending the reminder to the adviser, never to the client. The control is unusual and important: the adviser writes every client message. In relationship businesses such as private banking, wealth management and luxury retail, the value of the message is that a person wrote it. An agent that drafts the message removes the point.

## Where each task plugs into the brain

| Brain layer | What it must hold for customer work | Tasks that depend on it | What breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Store | Usage, tickets, delivery records and invoices joined on one account identifier | Renewal briefs; ticket summaries; review decks | Briefs miss the known issue because it sits in another system |
| Context | Approved knowledge base, calendar rules, client preferences and consent | Routine answers; scheduling; clienteling | Answers drawn from outdated pages; wrong stakeholders invited |
| Record | Past renewal decisions with price, discount, reason and approver | Renewal and expansion proposals | Last year's discount repeated with no reason attached |
| Reasoning | Agent identity, escalation rules, scope of actions in the help desk | End-to-end case resolution | Agent closes cases it should have escalated |
| Learning | Health-score flags compared with actual churn; sampled case grades | At-risk flags; case resolution | Scores drift and nobody notices |

The store row is the precondition for most of the table. In [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) we described how account data fragments after the first sale. An agent will not fix that fragmentation, but it will expose it quickly: every renewal brief that misses a known issue points to a join that does not exist.

## Start here: three tasks in order

| Order | Task | Level | Why it goes here | What to measure for four weeks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Summarise support tickets for an account | 3 Act and report | Internal, frequent, every summary links back to its tickets | Account owner time to prepare; summaries that misread sentiment on spot-check |
| 2 | Prepare a renewal brief from usage and delivery data | 1 Draft | Tests whether the store is joined; uses step 1's summaries | Known issues the brief missed; owner edit time |
| 3 | Draft a quarterly business review deck | 1 Draft | Builds on steps 1 and 2; forces figures to come from live sources | Figures corrected on review; time to prepare a review |

Each step uses the output of the one before it, and none reaches a customer without the account owner. After four weeks, the measures tell you whether the store is good enough for at-risk flagging. Customer-facing answers come next, at level 2, with a knowledge base the support lead has approved and a weekly sample of answers graded by a person. End-to-end resolution comes last, once sampling shows a stable correct rate over several months.

Illustrative example: putting account preparation before customer answers

Decision
:   Postpone a customer-facing answer agent and deploy ticket summaries and renewal briefs for the account team first.

Reason and owner
:   The first renewal briefs missed open delivery issues because tickets and delivery records used different account names; a customer-facing agent would have answered from the same gaps. Owned by the head of customer success.

What changed
:   The account identifier was fixed across three systems within the first month, missed issues on spot-check fell, and the answer agent was scoped at level 2 with an approved knowledge base for the following quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software company with a dedicated account management team, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Prepare for the account owner before you speak to the customer.** The five high-reliability tasks are all internal.
- **Your agent's answer is your answer.** Approved knowledge base, escalation path, and a person on anything contractual.
- **Count resolutions, then grade them.** A vendor's resolution count is a start; a weekly sample tells you if they were right.
- **Calibrate the health score.** At-risk flags that are never checked against churn become noise.

Gateway card

### Before a customer success agent goes live

- Usage, tickets and delivery joined on one account identifier
- An approved knowledge base with a named owner and review date
- An escalation path the agent cannot override
- A weekly random sample of answers and resolutions graded by a person
- Every client message in relationship accounts written by the adviser

## Common questions

### Can AI agents do customer success work?

Much of the preparation, yes: renewal briefs, ticket summaries, review decks, scheduling and reminders. The relationship decisions and anything contractual stay with the account owner.

### Is a company liable for what its AI chatbot tells customers?

In Moffatt v Air Canada (2024), a Canadian tribunal held the airline liable for its chatbot's wrong answer and rejected the argument that the chatbot was responsible for its own statements. Treat agent answers as company statements.

### Can AI predict customer churn?

An agent can flag at-risk accounts from usage, tickets and payment data, but the flags are only as good as the health score behind them. Check the score against actual churn every quarter.

### How do you measure an AI support agent?

Count resolutions, then grade a weekly random sample as correct, partial or wrong. A resolution counted because the customer stopped replying is not proof the answer was right.

# The Build Order for B2B SaaS

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-b2b-saas/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: B2B SaaS looks like the easiest sector for an enterprise brain because it already holds a CRM, billing data and product telemetry. The order holds, but product usage data joins the context layer early, renewal and expansion decisions are the first worth recording, and the data customers store inside the product must never reach the commercial build.

The Build Order holds in B2B SaaS, with one change: product usage data joins the context layer early, because in a recurring-revenue business the strongest commercial signal is what customers do inside the product. The first decisions worth recording are renewals, expansion offers and the discounts attached to both, since retention drives growth more than new logos for most private SaaS firms. The sector's wall is the content customers store inside the product. Usage metadata can inform a renewal brief. A customer's own records, tickets and documents cannot, because the vendor holds them as a processor on the customer's instructions.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Most sectors in this series start the build with a store that needs work and a context layer that has to be assembled from scattered systems. B2B SaaS companies start further along. Their CRM is usually current enough to forecast from, billing sits in a subscription platform, product analytics record every login and feature used, and support tickets live in a help desk with an API. That is a head start. It is also a trap, because a firm with this much context is tempted to connect all of it at once and call the result a brain.

This edition runs the full sequence (Gateway 0, tooling, context, record, reasoning and Gateways 1 to 3) for a SaaS company of 50 to 500 people. It covers where the commercial line really sits, what the context layer should and should not connect, and where the build tends to stall.

## Where the commercial line sits in SaaS

In a services firm the commercial line is mostly new business. In SaaS, a large share of revenue is decided after the first contract is signed. Renewal, expansion and contraction decisions recur every month across the customer base, and each one has a number attached.

The retention data shows why this matters. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks for private B2B SaaS put median net revenue retention at 102% for companies with $25,000 to $50,000 annual contract values, ranging from 97% in the lowest quartile to 111% in the top. The same research finds that higher retention correlates with higher contract values. The 2025 SaaS Benchmarks Report from Growth Unhinged and High Alpha, drawn from more than 800 private companies, found that firms combining high retention with a short CAC payback grew at 71% a year, against 10% for those with low retention and long payback.

The buyer side is shifting too. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 61% prefer to buy without a sales rep, 73% avoid suppliers that send irrelevant outreach, and 69% see inconsistencies between what a vendor's website says and what its sellers tell them. For a SaaS company, that is an argument against using the first agent to generate more outbound. It is an argument for using it to make each customer conversation better prepared.

| Industry lens | B2B SaaS |
| --- | --- |
| Where the commercial line sits | New business, but more so renewals, expansion and the discounts attached to both |
| The store | CRM, subscription billing, product analytics, help desk |
| What joins the context layer early | Product usage: seats active, features adopted, usage against plan limits |
| Outcome lag | Weeks for expansion offers; one contract term for renewals |
| Who defends the decision | Head of customer success, revenue leader, finance on discounts |
| The sector's wall | Content customers store inside the product, held as a processor |
| Regulatory pressure | No sector regulator, but data processing agreements and, in the EU, the Data Act's switching rules |

## The build order, stage by stage

The sequence is the one set out in Part 1. What changes in SaaS is the content of each stage and the risk that comes with it.

| Stage | What it means in SaaS | The main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | An owner in revenue operations, the suite of record, and one CRM that customer success also updates | Customer success running its own tool, so renewal context never reaches the CRM |
| Tooling | Assistant seats for account executives, customer success managers and renewal owners | Seats for the whole company before the commercial team uses them |
| Context | CRM, email, calendar and call notes, plus product usage aggregates and billing status | Piping raw product data into the assistant instead of agreed usage measures |
| Record | Renewal decisions, expansion offers and discounts, each with reason, owner and expected outcome | Recording only the discount, not why it was given |
| Reasoning | A first agent that drafts renewal and account review briefs into a queue | An agent that emails customers when a usage threshold trips |
| Gateway 1 | A named person approves every message the agent drafts | Confusing approved lifecycle templates with agent-written outreach |
| Gateway 2 | Annual recurring revenue at stake on every recorded decision, with outcomes written back | Measuring briefs produced rather than revenue retained |
| Gateway 3 | The record extends to product and finance: pricing, packaging, roadmap commitments | Sales promises in the record treated as roadmap decisions |

Two stages deserve a closer look.

**Gateway 0 is where SaaS builds most often fail quietly.** Many SaaS firms split the customer record between a CRM owned by sales and a customer success platform owned by another team. Renewal risk, health scores and save plays then live in a system the commercial build never sees. Part 3 sets out the three decisions; in SaaS the CRM decision usually means agreeing which system holds the renewal record of truth.

**Context is where the sector differs most.** Product usage is the signal other sectors lack. A drop in active seats, a feature that never got adopted, or a customer running against its plan limit tells an account team more than any email thread. The discipline is to bring it in as agreed measures, defined once, rather than as raw event streams. A context layer that exposes every click invites the assistant to make up its own definition of "healthy". Part 5 follows one account through the context layer; the SaaS version simply adds a usage panel to it.

> In SaaS the richest context is what customers do inside the product. The most dangerous is what they keep there.

## The wall: telemetry, yes; customer content, no

Every sector in this series has context that must never be connected. In SaaS it sits inside the product itself.

A SaaS vendor holds two kinds of data about each customer. The first is data about the customer's use of the service: logins, seat counts, features used, storage consumed, support volume. The vendor generates it and generally decides how to use it, within its contract and privacy notice. The second is the content the customer puts into the product: its records, documents, tickets and often personal data about its own clients and staff. For most SaaS vendors that content is processed on the customer's behalf.

The UK Information Commissioner's Office is clear about what that means. A processing contract must require the processor to handle personal data only on the controller's documented instructions. If a processor goes beyond those instructions and decides for itself the purpose and means of processing, it is treated as a controller for that processing and takes on a controller's liability. An account team that reads a customer's stored data to spot an upsell is, in this framing, using that data for the vendor's own purposes.

The practical rule for the build:

- **Connect usage aggregates.** Active seats, feature adoption and usage against plan, defined once and refreshed on a schedule.
- **Connect support metadata, not support content.** Ticket counts, categories and resolution times are context. Ticket bodies often contain the customer's own data and should be summarised into fields by the support team, or left out.
- **Never connect tenant content.** The commercial assistant should have no path to what customers store in the product, whatever the technical permissions allow.

Regulation in the EU raises the stakes on the renewal record. The EU Data Act's switching rules have applied since 12 September 2025 and cover SaaS, including productivity suites and CRM platforms. Customers can give a maximum of two months' notice, providers must support moving exportable data within a 30-day transition period, and switching and egress charges must be eliminated from 12 January 2027. The cost of leaving is falling. A record of why customers renewed, contracted or left becomes more valuable as that cost falls, because the firm can no longer rely on friction to hold the base.

## The record and the first agent

The first record in SaaS is the renewal and expansion decision, and the discount attached to it. Each entry carries the same fields as anywhere else in this series: the decision, the reason, the owner, the status, the expected outcome and the date to check. In SaaS the expected outcome has a natural unit: annual recurring revenue retained or added.

These decisions pass the test in *Where judgment arrives first*. They are frequent across a customer base, similar from one account to the next, graded at the next renewal or within weeks for an expansion offer, and defended by a revenue leader and, on discounts, by finance. Part 9 lists the commercial decisions worth recording in general; in SaaS the three to start with are:

1. **Renewal terms**, including any price hold or multi-year discount, with the reason.
2. **Expansion offers**: which accounts were offered more seats or a higher tier, and why now.
3. **Save decisions**: what was offered to an account at risk, and whether it stayed.

The first agent drafts a renewal brief 90 days before each contract ends. It reads the CRM, the billing status, the usage measures and the record of past decisions on the account, and places the brief in a queue for the customer success manager. It does not email the customer. That is deliberately unglamorous, and Part 7 explains why.

The store will need work first. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers, as reported by MarTech, found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for the AI tools they use or plan to use, and 62% said poor CRM data had probably or definitely cost their organisation revenue. The same survey found 45% already use agentic AI that can act without human review. In SaaS that combination is the one to avoid: an agent acting on usage thresholds and a CRM nobody fully trusts.

Composite example: a vertical SaaS company walls off the product

Decision
:   Connect product usage aggregates and support metadata to the commercial context layer; exclude ticket bodies and all customer-stored content.

Reason and owner
:   The firm processes its customers' client records under data processing agreements, and the head of revenue operations could not show that commercial use fell within the customer's instructions. Owned by the head of revenue operations, signed off by the data protection lead.

What changed
:   Renewal briefs now show seat trends, feature adoption and ticket volume. Customer success managers report fewer surprises at renewal, and the discount field became mandatory on every renewal record.

Illustrative: a composite of a vertical SaaS company of around 120 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## The gateways in SaaS

**Gateway 1: nothing sends without a person.** SaaS companies already send a great deal of automated email: onboarding sequences, usage nudges, renewal reminders. Those are templates a person approved once. An agent-written message is different, because its content changes every time. The rule we use is simple. A template approved by a named owner can run on a trigger. Anything an agent composes for a specific account goes to a named approver before it leaves. Part 8 covers the gate, and *Approval rate measures fatigue too* covers what happens when a renewal team approves hundreds of drafts a week.

**Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision.** SaaS has the easiest version of this gateway, because every renewal and expansion already carries a contract value. The discipline is writing the outcome back to the decision that caused it. A price hold granted to keep an account should show, a year later, whether the account renewed at the expected value. Over a few quarters the record shows which save offers work and which only defer churn.

**Gateway 3: commercial is ready to share its brain.** In SaaS the next functions are usually product and finance. Product wants to know which missing features lost deals; finance wants to know which discounts held. The risk is that a commitment a seller made in a renewal call enters the record looking like a roadmap decision. Before the record extends to product, decisions need a status that separates "promised to a customer" from "agreed by product".

## lowob takeaways

- **Bring usage in early, as agreed measures.** Product usage is the strongest commercial signal in SaaS, and raw event streams invite the assistant to define health on its own.
- **Start with renewals and expansion.** Retention drives growth for most private SaaS firms, and these decisions carry their own contract value.
- **Wall off what customers store in the product.** The vendor processes it on the customer's instructions; commercial use breaks that line.
- **Separate templates from agent drafts.** Approved lifecycle templates can run on triggers; agent-written messages go through a person.

Gateway card

### Before a SaaS team switches on its first agent

- One system named as the renewal record of truth, used by sales and customer success
- Five to ten usage measures defined once and agreed with product
- A written rule that no customer-stored content reaches the commercial context layer
- Renewal, expansion and save decisions recorded with reason, owner and ARR at stake
- A named approver for every agent-drafted message

## Common questions

### How should a B2B SaaS company use AI agents in customer success?

Start with an agent that drafts renewal and account review briefs from the CRM, billing status, usage measures and past decisions, placed in a queue for the customer success manager. Keep it away from sending messages until approval and outcome tracking are in place.

### Can a SaaS company use customer product data for sales?

Usage metadata such as seat counts and feature adoption is generally the vendor's own operational data, within its contracts and privacy notice. Content customers store in the product is usually processed on their instructions, and using it for the vendor's own sales purposes risks breaching the data processing agreement.

### What is a good net revenue retention rate for B2B SaaS?

SaaS Capital's 2025 data for private B2B SaaS puts the median at 102% for companies with $25,000 to $50,000 annual contract values, ranging from 97% in the bottom quartile to 111% in the top. Retention tends to rise with contract value.

### Does the EU Data Act apply to SaaS companies?

Yes. Its switching rules have applied since 12 September 2025 and cover SaaS, including CRM platforms and productivity suites. Customers can switch on a maximum of two months' notice, and switching charges must be eliminated from 12 January 2027.

# Raise, Rally, Revenue: The Whole Series on One Page

Source: https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-07 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Fundraising, community and customers are one system, not three projects, and it runs in a fixed order: name the buyer, write one truth, collect evidence, raise against it, give the community a job, make first customers design partners, distribute, measure, then hand over. 2026 funding and buyer data make the order matter more: capital is concentrated, buyers fund from new budgets, and platforms send less traffic.

Fundraising, community and customers are one system, not three projects, and it runs in a fixed order: name the buyer, write one truth, collect evidence, raise against it, give the community a job, make first customers design partners, distribute, measure, then hand over. Every failure in the series came from doing a right thing at the wrong time. The 2026 data makes the order harder to skip: venture capital is concentrated in a few very large rounds, enterprise buyers are funding new tools from new budgets, and platforms are sending publishers and brands less traffic than they did.

## One system, forty parts

Most early teams run three projects: a deck for investors, a Discord for the community, a list for customers. Three stories, three calendars, three people who don't talk. The round stalls because investors ask about customers. The community goes quiet because it has nothing to do. The customers don't convert because the story they heard was written for someone else.

It is one system. [The commercial system](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) sets out the same idea for established firms; this series applies it to a company that is still raising. This is the order it runs in.

| # | Step | The rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | One system | Name the buyer, not the market. One calendar, one owner. |
| 2 | One truth | One product truth; one belief per audience; a claims register for what you can prove. |
| 3 | Evidence | Raise against what a non-founder has done with the product, not the narrative. |
| 4 | The round | A researched list, warm routes, a three-week window, a pipeline with pass reasons. |
| 5 | The job | A community earns its keep by doing work you'd otherwise pay for. Measure the job. |
| 6 | The hundred | Recruit the first hundred by name. Ask for judgment, give them a job, close the loop. |
| 7 | Design partners | The first ten customers: a success test, a named owner, a price after the pilot. |
| 8 | Distribution | Partners, referrals, creators, owned media, answer engines. Paid last. |
| 9 | Measure | Activation, retention, revenue, efficiency, source. Never reach. |
| 10 | Handover | Accounts, records, runbooks and reasons in the company's name. It runs when you stop. |

## Why the order matters more in 2026

Three pieces of 2026 evidence each support one link in the chain.

**Evidence before the raise.** The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor recorded $515.8 billion of US deal value through September, with AI taking 82.7%. But megadeals took 87.5% of first-half value, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% from 43.8% in 2024. Carta's platform data shows seed capital falling from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026. A company raising a normal round competes for a smaller pool, and evidence is what separates it. The full method is in [How to raise for an emerging tech company](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-raise-for-an-emerging-tech-company/).

**Design partners before the channel.** Menlo Ventures' November 2026 survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers found new budgets funded 55% of incremental AI spend, against 22% from existing software budgets. When the budget line is new, the first customers decide what it is called, who owns it and what it is measured against. That is a design partner's job, not a channel's.

**Owned distribution before paid.** The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% between November 2024 and November 2025, and Facebook referrals fell 43% over about three years. Publishers are not startups, but the direction applies to anyone who rented attention. Distribution that depends on one platform's terms is a risk to price, not a plan.

> Every failure in these forty parts came from doing a right thing at the wrong time.

## What changes by market

Each vertical changes four things and leaves the rest alone.

|  | Who buys | What proof counts | Which channels are open | What to measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **AI** | The team that owns the workflow, then the budget holder | Output quality on the buyer's own data; a security pack that passed review | Marketplaces, developer communities, answer engines | Retained paid teams, gross margin, cost per task |
| **Crypto** | Users with funds at stake, then integrators, allocators and holders | Retained usage without incentives; named, dated audits; a token with a job | Issuers, integrations, curators, ecosystems | Protocol revenue, retained deposits, incentive cost per sticky dollar |
| **Fintech** | The person trusting you with money, and the compliance owner behind them | Licences, the custodian, loss ratios, funded accounts that stay | Partners who hold the customer, practitioners, comparison sites | Funded accounts, cost per funded account, 90-day retention |
| **Media** | Readers first, then sponsors, licensees and data buyers | Owned audience, paid conversion, renewal, sponsor results | Owned lists, membership, being the cited source, events | Paid conversion, churn, revenue per subscriber, platform independence |
| **Emerging tech** | The cost owner, reached through integrators, OEMs and consortia | Field deployments that passed a success test; risk retired | Integrators, OEMs, platform programmes, standards bodies | Converted pilots, contracted annual value, margin including service |

The measures column is where most teams drift. Our guide to [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) covers how to choose a short set and keep their definitions fixed.

## The order matters more than any tactic

Product truth before the pitch. Evidence before the raise. Design partners before the channel. Direct before partners. Pilots before contracts. Measurement before reporting.

| Out of order | What happens | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pitch before product truth | Investors, users and buyers hear three different companies | Write one truth and a claims register first |
| Raise before evidence | Passes cluster around "too early" | Get one design partner using it weekly |
| Channel before design partners | Spend reaches buyers the product does not yet fit | Ten named customers with a success test |
| Paid before owned | Acquisition stops when the budget stops | Owned lists, partners and referrals first |
| Reporting before measurement | Reach in the board pack, nothing behind it | Define five measures and their sources |

Where are you? Ten questions, scored 0 to 5. Under 30 and you are probably spending on step eight with steps two and three unanswered. [Take the self-score in Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/). For the wider strategy behind the order, see [What is a go-to-market strategy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Run one system, not three projects.** One calendar and one owner for investors, community and customers.
- **Evidence before the raise.** In a concentrated market, proof is what gets a normal-sized round done.
- **Design partners before the channel.** When the budget line is new, the first customers define it.
- **Owned distribution before paid.** Platform traffic is falling; rented attention is a risk to price.

## Common questions

### Should fundraising, community and customer acquisition be run separately?

No. Run them as one system with one calendar and one owner, because investors ask about customers, communities need a job, and customers need a story written for them.

### What order should an early-stage company do go-to-market in?

Product truth before the pitch, evidence before the raise, design partners before the channel, direct before partners, pilots before contracts, and measurement before reporting.

### What should a crypto company measure instead of reach?

Protocol revenue, retained deposits and incentive cost per sticky dollar, which together show whether usage survives when incentives stop.

### What should an AI startup measure for investors?

Retained paid teams, gross margin net of inference and cost per task. Free usage and reach are acquisition cost, not evidence.
