# Two People: The Founders' Ledger

Source: https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At two people, the enterprise brain is a single append-only decision document and a 30-minute weekly review. Its job is to stop two honest founders remembering the same decision differently, a problem with good evidence behind it, and it is worth more than any tool at this stage.

At two people, the enterprise brain is a single document and a weekly habit. Its job is to stop two honest people remembering the same decision differently, and it is worth more than any tool you could buy at this stage. One append-only ledger, one line per material decision with its reason, what was rejected, what would prove it wrong and where the founders disagreed, reviewed for 30 minutes a week.

This is the first rung of [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/), the series on how a company's decision record should change as it grows. At two people, the problem the record must solve is false shared memory.

Two founders make dozens of significant decisions in the first year, mostly in conversation: on a walk, on a call, at 11pm in a message thread. Both remember them. They remember them differently.

## Why two honest founders remember differently

This is not a trust problem. Memory is reconstructive. Each founder retains the version that fits their own view of why it was decided, and over months the versions drift.

The research on joint work explains the mechanism. In Ross and Sicoly's classic 1979 study, married couples each estimated their own share of household tasks, including making important decisions. Added together, the estimates exceeded 100%, so at least one partner had to be wrong. Caruso, Epley and Bazerman, reviewing that work in 2006, attribute the pattern mainly to accessibility: people notice and recall their own contributions more easily than other people's. In their own study of academic co-authors, the self-assessed shares of authors who did not first consider their colleagues' contributions summed to an average of 140%.

Two founders are in exactly that position, with higher stakes. The drift surfaces at the worst moments: in a disagreement about direction, in front of an investor, when a co-founder relationship is already under strain.

The cost of that strain is large. CNN, reporting Harvard Business School professor Noam Wasserman's research on 10,000 founders, gave the figure that 65% of high-potential startups fail because of conflict among co-founders. The same reporting noted that teams of friends and family failed most often, because they avoided difficult conversations to protect feelings. A written record cannot prevent conflict, but it removes one common fuel for it: two sincere and incompatible accounts of the same decision.

> Recording a disagreement calmly at the time defuses it later. Two memories of the same argument rarely do.

## The ledger

One document, append-only, that both founders can see. Each material decision gets a short entry.

| Field | What goes in it | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Date and decision | One line, written as a commitment | Fixes what was decided before memory edits it |
| Why | A sentence or two | The reason is what drifts first |
| What was rejected | The options not taken | Stops the same debate restarting from zero |
| What would prove it wrong, and when to check | A falsifier with a date | Turns a decision into a judgment that can be checked |
| Where the founders disagreed | Who held which view, and what was agreed | Defuses the argument before it becomes a grievance |
| Link to the evidence | The call note, email or numbers | Keeps the source alive behind the summary |

The disagreement line is the one most founders skip and most need. "We disagreed on the price; A wanted higher; we went with B's view and agreed to review after twenty deals" is a far better artefact than two memories of the same argument. It also corrects for the bias above: writing down the other founder's view at the time is, in effect, the "consider the other person's contribution" step that reduced overclaiming in Caruso's study, from 140% to about 123% on average.

The falsifier line matters for a different reason. A decision with no stated test cannot be learned from, at any size. Our piece [*The field that makes a record a judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) sets out why this one field separates judgment from a press release. Our explainer [*What is a decision record?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) covers the basic structure.

Append-only means entries are never edited away. When the founders change their minds, they write a new entry that names the old one and says why. Software teams reached the same convention independently: Michael Nygard's 2011 format for architecture decision records keeps a reversed decision and marks it as superseded, because it still matters that the choice was once made.

## The habit

Thirty minutes once a week. Read last week's entries. Add any that were missed. Check any falsifier whose date has passed. That is the entire system.

AI makes it cheaper. Record and transcribe the founders' calls, with everyone's consent, and have a model draft candidate ledger entries from them. The founders correct and accept. Capture drops from a chore to a few minutes of editing. Our ranking of [AI notetakers for decision capture](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-notetakers-for-decision-capture/) compares tools on what matters here, extracting what was decided and why, and our explainer on [conversation intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversation-intelligence/) covers the wider category.

A model's draft is a proposal, not the record: the founders accept or correct each entry. Keep the transcript linked as the source. For tool choices, our [*Top 5 tools for a founders' decision ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-tools-for-a-founders-decision-ledger/) notes that none of the common options is truly append-only, so the discipline has to come from the habit.

## Uses you will discover

**Investor updates write themselves.** The ledger is a record of what was decided and why, which is most of what a good update contains.

**Due diligence becomes easier.** A buyer or a lead investor asking why the company pivoted can be shown the entry, written at the time.

**The first hire gets context.** When the third person joins, the ledger is their best onboarding document, by far. That is the problem of the next rung, covered in [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/).

## What not to build

No knowledge base. No taxonomy. No tagging scheme. No integrations beyond transcription. At two people, every hour spent on infrastructure is an hour not spent on customers, and the structure will be wrong by the time it matters anyway.

The arithmetic supports the restraint. Two people have exactly one communication channel between them; Brooks's n(n-1)/2 formula does not start to bite until the team grows. The problem at this size is not finding information or coordinating many people. It is agreeing on one version of a handful of decisions. A document and a habit solve that, and anything larger solves a problem from a higher rung.

**In practice:** start one shared, append-only decision document today. Record disagreements explicitly, with who held which view. Hold a 30-minute weekly review, and check falsifiers on their dates. Use transcription and AI drafting to keep capture under five minutes a week.

## What would prove this wrong

Founding teams with no written decision record experiencing no more disputes about past decisions, and no slower onboarding of early hires, than those with one. The overclaiming research suggests that is unlikely, but it has not been tested on founding teams directly.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume your memories differ.** Founders remember decisions differently because memory favours their own view, not because of a trust problem.
- **Write the disagreement down.** Recording who held which view, at the time, defuses the argument later.
- **Add a falsifier.** What would prove the decision wrong, and when to check.
- **Keep the habit small.** One document, 30 minutes a week, AI drafting with human acceptance.
- **Build nothing else yet.** No knowledge base, taxonomy, tagging scheme or integrations beyond transcription.

## Common questions

### How should co-founders keep track of decisions?

Keep one shared, append-only document with an entry per material decision: date, decision, why, what was rejected, what would prove it wrong and when, and where the founders disagreed. Review it for 30 minutes a week.

### Why do co-founders remember decisions differently?

Memory is reconstructive and favours each person's own contribution. Studies of couples and co-authors find that individual estimates of their share of joint work routinely sum to more than 100%.

### Can AI help founders keep a decision log?

Yes. Record and transcribe calls with everyone's consent and have a model draft candidate entries, which the founders correct and accept. Keep the transcript linked as the source.

### What is the best tool for a startup decision log?

A shared document both founders can edit and export is enough. The discipline of never overwriting old entries matters more than the tool, since most common tools let anyone edit history.

## Sources and notes

- [Caruso, Epley and Bazerman, The costs and benefits of undoing egocentric responsibility assessments in groups](https://anderson-review.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/Caruso-et_al_Undoing_Egocentrism_JPSP2006.pdf), Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 2006. Summarises Ross and Sicoly (1979); studies of couples and academics, not founders.
- [CNN Money, Fighting co-founders doom startups](https://money.cnn.com/2014/02/24/smallbusiness/startups-entrepreneur-cofounder), 24 February 2014. Secondary reporting of Noam Wasserman's research; methods not described in the article.
- [Michael Nygard, Documenting Architecture Decisions](https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions), 15 November 2011. Practitioner essay on software teams.
- [Project Wizards, Brooks's law (glossary)](https://www.projectwizards.net/en/project-management-glossary/brooks-law). Vendor glossary summarising Brooks's 1975 book; the formula counts possible channels.
- The ledger fields table is **lowob**'s framework.

- [Ten People: The First Stranger](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/)

## Next move

Open one shared document today and write entries for the last three material decisions, including where you disagreed. Put a 30-minute weekly review in both calendars.

# Vector Database vs Knowledge Graph

Source: https://lowob.com/research/vector-database-vs-knowledge-graph/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A vector database finds passages that resemble a question; a knowledge graph follows explicit, typed relationships between things. The two are converging, with graph databases adding vector indexes and Postgres adding vectors. For a commercial team, the vector index is a rebuildable convenience and the relationships in the record are the asset worth owning.

A vector database stores text as embeddings, lists of numbers that capture meaning, and finds the items closest to a question. A knowledge graph stores facts as entities and the named relationships between them, such as "account A is owned by person B". Vectors are good at "find me things like this". Graphs are good at "show me how these things connect, and prove it". Many AI systems use both, and the products are converging.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two terms mean

A [vector database](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-vector-database/) holds embeddings. Each document chunk, email or call note is turned into a long list of numbers, and items with similar meaning end up close together. A question is embedded the same way, and the database returns the nearest items. Most systems use an index such as HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world) to make this fast. The open-source pgvector extension, now at version 0.8.7, adds the same capability to Postgres with HNSW and IVFFlat indexes and cosine, inner product and Euclidean distance.

A [knowledge graph](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/) holds things and the links between them. In the W3C's RDF 1.1 standard, a graph is "a set of RDF triples", each one a subject, a predicate and an object. Property graph databases use nodes and relationships with attributes. Either way, the relationship is stored explicitly: "contract X renews on date Y", "deal Z was approved by person W". A query follows those links rather than measuring resemblance.

| Dimension | Vector database | Knowledge graph |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stores | Embeddings of text, images or records | Entities and typed relationships |
| Question it answers well | "Find passages like this one" | "How are these connected, and through what?" |
| How a query works | Nearest neighbours by similarity score | Traversal along named links |
| Exactness | Approximate by design | Exact, if the data is right |
| Effort to build | Low: chunk, embed, index | Higher: define entity types, resolve duplicates, maintain links |
| How it explains a result | A similarity score | A path you can read |
| Typical weakness | Multi-step and whole-corpus questions | Nuance in unstructured text, and gaps in coverage |
| Examples | pgvector, dedicated vector databases, vector indexes in search engines | RDF triple stores, property graph databases |
| Place in the brain loop | Wiring: a retrieval index | Store and record: the structure of what is known |

## Where each one breaks

Vector search struggles when the answer is not in any single passage. The GraphRAG paper by Edge and colleagues at Microsoft names the problem directly: questions that need an understanding of a whole corpus are summarisation tasks, not retrieval tasks. Their method uses a language model to extract an entity graph from the text, then summarises clusters of related entities. On two datasets of about 1 million and 1.7 million tokens, it produced more comprehensive and diverse answers to whole-corpus questions than a vector baseline.

Vectors also blur exact facts. Two contracts with different renewal dates may embed almost identically. A seller asking "which accounts share a parent company with our largest client" needs a relationship, not a resemblance.

Graphs break in a different place. Someone has to decide what the entities are and keep them clean. If the same company appears under three names, the graph has three companies, which is why [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/) matters more for graphs than for vectors.

The benchmark by Sequeda, Allemang and Jacob shows what structure buys. GPT-4 answered questions over an enterprise SQL database with 16% accuracy when asked directly, and 54% when the same data was exposed as a knowledge graph. It is one benchmark on the authors' own test set, so treat the size of the gain as directional.

## The products are converging

The choice is less binary than vendor marketing suggests. Neo4j, a graph database, now offers vector indexes built on Apache Lucene's HNSW implementation, with cosine similarity as the default for text embeddings. Postgres, a relational database, gains vector search through pgvector. A common pattern is to find candidate passages by vector similarity, then use the graph to expand, filter or verify them. GraphRAG runs the other way, using a model to build the graph from text.

## Which to choose

| If your main question is | Start with | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Find the policy, case study or past answer that matches this" | Vector index | Fast to stand up from existing documents |
| "Who owns this account, and who approved its last discount?" | Graph or relational record | An exact fact with a named owner |
| "What themes run through two years of lost-deal notes?" | Graph-based summarisation, or a long-context model | Whole-corpus question |
| "Which contacts link these two accounts?" | Graph | Multi-hop relationship |
| "Brief me before this call" | Both | Vectors find the notes; the graph supplies the structure |

A short checklist before buying either:

- **Write down ten real questions.** Mark each one "resemblance" or "relationship".
- **Check what you already run.** Postgres or an existing graph database may cover both needs.
- **Count your entity types.** Accounts, contacts, deals and decisions are a small, valuable graph. Modelling everything is not.
- **Ask who maintains the links.** A graph nobody updates is worse than none.

## The **lowob** view

The enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. A vector index belongs to the wiring. It is derived from documents and can be regenerated whenever the embedding model changes, so it is a sensible thing to rent. We make the same point in [Keep the Sources, Let the Summary Regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/).

The record is different. A decision record links a decision to an account, an owner, a reason, an expected outcome and the earlier decision it replaced. That is graph-shaped data, whether it sits in a graph database or in well-linked relational tables. It cannot be regenerated, because the reasons were written once by the people who made the call. Own it, keep it structured, and [supersede rather than overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/). The learning stage then writes outcomes back onto the same links, which is what lets the next brief show what happened last time.

## lowob takeaways

- **Vectors find resemblance.** Use them to locate passages that match a question.
- **Graphs hold relationships.** Use them where the answer is an exact, traceable connection.
- **You may already have both.** Graph databases add vector indexes and Postgres adds vectors.
- **Own the links; rent the index.** The relationships in the record are the asset; the index can be rebuilt.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a vector database and a knowledge graph?

A vector database finds items by similarity of meaning using embeddings. A knowledge graph stores entities and named relationships, and answers by following those links.

### Is a knowledge graph better than a vector database for RAG?

For questions about exact relationships or whole-corpus themes, graphs often do better. For finding relevant passages in documents, vector search is faster to build. Many systems combine both.

### What is GraphRAG?

A Microsoft Research method that uses a language model to build a knowledge graph from documents, summarises clusters of related entities, and answers questions that need a view of the whole corpus.

## Sources and notes

- [pgvector on PGXN](https://pgxn.org/dist/vector), version 0.8.7, October 2026. Open-source project documentation.
- [Neo4j, Cypher Manual: Vector indexes](https://www.neo4j.com/docs/cypher-manual/25/indexes/semantic-indexes/vector-indexes/), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [W3C, RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/), 25 February 2014. Standards body Recommendation.
- [Edge et al., From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130), arXiv, April 2024, revised February 2025. Microsoft-authored preprint; results on the authors' own datasets.
- [Sequeda, Allemang and Jacob, A Benchmark to Understand the Role of Knowledge Graphs on LLM Accuracy for Question Answering on Enterprise SQL Databases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07509), arXiv, November 2023. Single benchmark on the authors' own test set.
- The decision table, checklist and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Next move

Write down ten questions your sellers ask before a call and mark each one "resemblance" or "relationship". If most are relationships, fix how accounts, owners and decisions link in your record before you buy a vector database.

# RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which One Your Use Case Needs

Source: https://lowob.com/research/rag-vs-fine-tuning/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Retrieval-augmented generation changes what a model reads when it answers; fine-tuning changes how the model behaves. OpenAI's own guidance treats them as two separate levers, and published comparisons find retrieval better at adding knowledge. For a commercial team, facts belong in the store and the record, not in model weights.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives a model relevant passages from your own documents at the moment it answers. Fine-tuning further trains the model on your examples so that it behaves differently every time. RAG is the tool for knowledge: facts, prices, policies and anything that changes. Fine-tuning is the tool for behaviour: format, tone and consistency on a narrow, repeated task. Most commercial use cases need RAG first, and many never need fine-tuning at all.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two terms mean

RAG is a retrieval step placed in front of the model. A question arrives, a search system finds the most relevant passages in an approved set of documents, and those passages go into the prompt alongside the question. The model answers from what it was handed and can point to the source. Our explainer on [retrieval-augmented generation](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/) covers the mechanics.

Fine-tuning is further training. You give the model hundreds or thousands of example inputs with the outputs you want, and the training run adjusts its weights. OpenAI's documentation lists supervised fine-tuning, which learns from examples of correct responses, and direct preference optimisation, which learns from pairs of better and worse responses. The result is a new model version that behaves differently without being told to in every prompt.

The cleanest statement of the difference comes from OpenAI's guide to optimising accuracy. It says you optimise context when the model lacks knowledge, because it is out of date or the information is proprietary. You optimise the model when results are inconsistent, the formatting is wrong, or the tone and reasoning drift. The guide also notes that the two "stack" rather than compete.

| Dimension | RAG | Fine-tuning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What it changes | What the model reads at answer time | How the model behaves, through its weights |
| Best for | Facts, policies, prices, account history | Format, tone, a narrow task done the same way each time |
| Keeping it current | Re-index the changed document | Run a new training job |
| Showing its source | Can cite the passage it used | Cannot point to where a learned fact came from |
| Access control | Retrieval can filter by the user's permissions | What the model learned is available to every user of that model |
| Typical failure | Retrieves the wrong or a stale passage | States an outdated fact with full confidence |
| Place in the brain loop | Wiring | Reasoning |

## What the evidence says

The research points in one direction on knowledge. Ovadia, Brief, Mishaeli and Elisha compared unsupervised fine-tuning with RAG on knowledge-intensive tasks across several subjects. Fine-tuning gave some improvement, but RAG "consistently outperforms it, both for existing knowledge encountered during training and entirely new knowledge."

The agriculture study by Balaguer and colleagues is the strongest case for using both. Testing Llama 2 13B, GPT-3.5 and GPT-4, they reported that fine-tuning raised accuracy by over 6 percentage points and RAG added about 5 more. Farming is a domain with stable knowledge and a large, curated question set. Few commercial teams have either.

Vendor guidance adds the practical case for fine-tuning: more consistent formatting, shorter prompts that save tokens at scale, and the option to train "a smaller, cheaper, faster model" for one task. OpenAI's model optimisation page now also says its fine-tuning platform is closed to new users, with existing fine-tuned models available until their base models are retired. The technique remains available elsewhere, such as on open-weight models, but the change shows where one large provider sees value.

## Which to choose

If the answer depends on facts in your documents or systems, use retrieval. If only the shape of the output is wrong, try better prompts and examples first, then consider fine-tuning.

| Use case | Start with | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answer questions from the policy library or product documentation | RAG | Knowledge that changes, and answers need a citation |
| Brief a seller before a call from CRM, email and tickets | RAG with [permission-aware retrieval](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/) | Different users may see different records |
| Draft proposals in the house structure | Prompt and template | A good template usually fixes format without training |
| Classify thousands of inbound emails into a fixed taxonomy | Fine-tune a smaller model, if prompting is too slow or costly | Narrow, stable, high volume |
| Answer with current prices, discounts or terms | RAG from the system of record | Never put a price list in model weights |
| Match the firm's written tone across all outputs | Prompt with examples; fine-tune only if inconsistency persists | Behaviour, not knowledge |

A short checklist before anyone commissions a fine-tuning project:

- **Is the gap knowledge or behaviour?** If the model gives wrong facts, fine-tuning is the wrong tool.
- **Has prompting been tried properly?** OpenAI notes that prompt engineering "may be all you need".
- **Is there a labelled set of good examples?** Without hundreds of them, there is nothing to train on.
- **Will the facts change within a year?** If so, they belong in retrieval, where an update is a re-index.
- **Is there an evaluation set?** Both approaches need one, and the [long context vs RAG](https://lowob.com/research/long-context-vs-rag/) choice depends on it too.

## The **lowob** view

The enterprise brain is a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. RAG sits in the wiring. It connects the reasoning layer to the store at the moment of the question, and it can respect who is asking. Fine-tuning changes the reasoning layer itself. Both are legitimate, but neither is where a firm's knowledge should live.

Commercial facts change weekly: who owns an account, what was agreed, which discount was approved and why. Those belong in the store and in the decision record, with an owner and a date, where they can be superseded rather than overwritten. A fine-tuned model holds a frozen snapshot that nobody can audit line by line. The learning stage writes outcomes back to the record, so the next retrieval improves without retraining.

Rent the model and the retrieval tooling. Own the documents, the record and the evaluation set. As we argue in [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/), the harder problem is usually what the record contains, not how the model reads it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Knowledge goes to retrieval.** Facts that change belong in documents and records the model reads at answer time.
- **Behaviour goes to prompts first.** Fine-tune only when a narrow task stays inconsistent after good prompting.
- **The evidence favours RAG for facts.** Published comparisons find fine-tuning a weak way to add new knowledge.
- **Neither is the record.** Decisions, owners and outcomes need a home that both approaches can read.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

RAG retrieves relevant passages from your documents and gives them to the model when it answers. Fine-tuning retrains the model on examples so it behaves differently without being told each time.

### Is RAG better than fine-tuning?

For adding knowledge, published studies find RAG more effective. For consistent format, tone or a narrow repeated task, fine-tuning can help, and the two can be combined.

### Can you use RAG and fine-tuning together?

Yes. OpenAI describes the two as stacking, and a 2024 agriculture study found accuracy gains from each that added up.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Optimizing LLM accuracy](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/optimizing-llm-accuracy), accessed November 2026. Vendor guidance; source of the two-axis framing.
- [OpenAI, Model optimization](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/model-optimization), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; platform availability is subject to change and the page gives no fixed dates.
- [Ovadia, Brief, Mishaeli and Elisha, Fine-Tuning or Retrieval? Comparing Knowledge Injection in LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.05934), arXiv, December 2023, revised January 2024. Academic preprint; tests unsupervised fine-tuning only.
- [Balaguer et al., RAG vs Fine-tuning: Pipelines, Tradeoffs, and a Case Study on Agriculture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08406), arXiv, January 2024. Preprint; results are for one domain and the authors' own evaluation method.
- The decision table, checklist and brain-loop placement are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

## Next move

Take the AI use case your team most wants and write one line for it: is the model missing knowledge or getting the behaviour wrong? If it is knowledge, list the documents and records it should read, and who owns each one.

# The Scale Ladder

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: There is no single right enterprise brain; the right one depends on the organisation's stage. Each size, from two people to ten thousand, has a different problem for the decision record to solve: false shared memory, the first stranger, meaning, delegation, governance and density. This hub sets out the whole ladder, what to build at each rung, the risk at each, and the five invariants that hold at every size.

There is no single right enterprise brain. There is a right one for two people, a different one for fifty, and a very different one for 10,000. What changes as an organisation grows is not whether it needs a record of its judgment, but which problem that record has to solve: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at ten, meaning at fifty, delegation at two hundred, governance at a thousand and density at ten thousand. The mistake at every size is building the brain of the wrong stage. The rule is to build for the next rung, not two rungs up.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Most writing about enterprise brains assumes a large, regulated organisation with platform teams, data stewards and a compliance function. Most organisations are not that, and the ones that are did not start that way. Every 10,000-person firm was once two people in a room, deciding things and remembering why, until one day they did not.

The SBA Office of Advocacy's 2026 profile, built on 2022 Census data, counts about 6.4 million small employer firms and 21,041 large businesses with 500 or more employees. Small businesses employ 45.9% of private-sector workers. Advice written for a 10,000-person firm does real harm when applied at fifty.

This piece is the hub of an eight-part series, with a page for each rung and a closing piece on the five invariants. Our companion piece [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) covers which layers to rent and which to own at each size, and [*Building the commercial system at every size*](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/) applies the same ladder to sales, marketing and pricing.

## Why one design cannot fit every size

The first reason is arithmetic. Fred Brooks observed in *The Mythical Man-Month* (1975) that adding people to a late software project makes it later, partly because communication paths grow as n(n-1)/2. The formula describes possible channels, not actual conversations, but it shows why informal memory stops working.

| Headcount | Possible pairwise channels | What that means for memory |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 1 | Two memories of every decision, and no third party to settle disputes |
| 10 | 45 | Founders can still answer every question, but it becomes their main job |
| 50 | 1,225 | Teams form, and each develops its own vocabulary |
| 200 | 19,900 | Most decisions are made by people the founders never talk to |
| 1,000 | 499,500 | Functions exist whose job is to question other functions' decisions |
| 10,000 | 49,995,000 | Enough repeated decisions to learn from, and too many records to unify |

The organisational research points the same way. J. Richard Hackman, interviewed in *Harvard Business Review* in 2009, said the number of links a team must manage rises "at an accelerating, almost exponential rate" as it grows, and gave his rule of thumb for team size as "no double digits". An organisation is not a team, but it is made of them, and the links between teams grow the same way.

Research on social group sizes suggests the breaks come in steps rather than smoothly. Zhou, Sornette, Hill and Dunbar's analysis, published by the Royal Society in 2005, found human group sizes cluster in a hierarchy with a scaling ratio close to three. That pattern, not any single number, is why a ladder with distinct rungs is a better model than a smooth curve.

The second reason is that scrutiny and tooling change with size too. The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found AI use rising among firms with 20 or more employees in the six months to May 2026, reaching 32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees and 37% of those with 250 or more. Fewer than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using it. Regulation bites at size thresholds as well, as the governance rung below shows.

## Six rungs, six problems

**Two people: false shared memory.** Two founders remember the same decision differently, and neither is lying. Memory favours the version that fits each person's own view. Ross and Sicoly's classic 1979 study, as summarised by Caruso, Epley and Bazerman in 2006, found that when spouses each estimated their own share of household tasks, including important decisions, the estimates summed to more than 100%. The record's job is to be the one version both founders wrote at the time. See [*Two people: the founders' ledger*](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/).

**Ten people: the first stranger.** New hires do not share the founders' history, and every "why do we..." question routes to a founder. McKinsey Global Institute estimated in 2012 that interaction workers spend nearly 20% of their time looking for internal information or tracking down colleagues who can help. At ten people, the colleague is usually a founder. See [*Ten people: the first stranger*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-people-the-first-stranger/).

**Fifty people: meaning.** Teams form, and the same words start to mean different things in different rooms. "Customer" means a signed contract to finance and anyone in a trial to marketing. At the same time, each team adopts its own AI tools: Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index found 78% of AI users were bringing their own tools to work. Each tool keeps its own memory. See [*Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*](https://lowob.com/research/fifty-people-when-words-start-to-mean-different-things/).

**Two hundred people: delegation.** Founders no longer make most decisions; managers do, and the reasoning has to travel without them. Inconsistency becomes measurable. In a noise audit described by Daniel Kahneman and colleagues, executives at an insurer expected about a 10% difference between underwriters' quotes on the same case; the typical difference was 55%. See [*Two hundred people: reasoning that travels without its author*](https://lowob.com/research/two-hundred-people-reasoning-that-travels-without-its-author/).

**One thousand people: governance.** Auditors, regulators, risk functions and security teams arrive, and "we decided it in a meeting" stops being an acceptable record. In the EU, the Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470, in force from 18 March 2026, sets the scope of the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive at more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450 million of turnover. See [*One thousand people: governance arrives*](https://lowob.com/research/one-thousand-people-governance-arrives/).

**Ten thousand people: density.** There is finally enough volume in enough decision classes for a system to learn, and the challenge is federation: one organisation, many records. The same Omnibus I Directive puts the due diligence directive's scope at more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5 billion of turnover. See [*Ten thousand people: density, and the case for federation*](https://lowob.com/research/ten-thousand-people-density-and-the-case-for-federation/).

> What changes as an organisation grows is not whether it needs a judgment record. It is which problem the record has to solve.

## The ladder in one table

The table summarises each rung. The headcounts are approximate; the problems are the diagnosis.

| Rung | Approximate headcount | What breaks | What the record must do | What to build | The risk at this rung |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founders | 2 | Shared memory: two honest versions of each decision | Be the single version both wrote at the time | One append-only ledger, a 30-minute weekly review, transcription with consent | Building a knowledge base instead of the habit |
| First stranger | About 10 | Context: newcomers cannot see why anything is done | Answer "why do we do it this way?" without a founder | A ledger strangers can read, "why we do it" pages, first definitions, onboarding through the record | A topic wiki that decays within weeks |
| Meaning | About 50 | Vocabulary: teams define the same words differently | Hold one current definition of each term, and one home for records | A glossary of 20 to 30 terms with owners, written decision rights, a conflicts list | Every team's AI tool keeping its own memory |
| Delegation | About 200 | Precedent: managers inherit decisions from people who have left | Let reasoning travel without its author | Formal decision classes, a precedent slot, handover packs, first calibration | Compliance theatre: long templates filled to satisfy a process |
| Governance | About 1,000 | Defensibility: outsiders ask how decisions were made | Let any AI-assisted decision be reconstructed end to end | A trace specification, an evidenced review gate, agent registration, retention rules | A platform team owning a record that is technically sound and commercially empty |
| Density | About 10,000 | Unity: one model of everything stalls | Let many records learn, and map between them | Central invariants and export format, local records, a definitions map | A single enterprise ontology that takes years and is used by nobody |

Each rung has a characteristic failure, and each is a good idea at the wrong size. The ten-person wiki is a large firm's tool used too early. The single enterprise ontology is a small firm's instinct, one definition of everything, applied at a size it cannot survive.

## Five things that change with size

**Decision volume per class.** Low and heterogeneous when small; high and repetitive when large. Two founders make a few dozen significant decisions in their first year, nearly all different. A large lender or insurer can make thousands of comparable calls a week. Only the second can be learned from, which is why our piece [*Below the volume floor*](https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/) argues against expecting a small firm's record to train anything.

**Distance between decider and consequence.** Zero at two people; several layers at 10,000. The further a decision travels, the more its reason must be written down.

**Turnover of context.** Rare at first; constant later, through hiring, rotation and departures. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported median tenure with the current employer of 4.1 years in January 2026, and 3.9 years in the private sector. In a firm of several hundred, many of the people who set a precedent will have gone before it is questioned.

**External scrutiny.** Investors at first; then customers, auditors and regulators. The thresholds are explicit. In US banking, SR 26-2, issued on 17 April 2026 by the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC, replaced SR 11-7 and is expected to be most relevant to banks with more than $30 billion of assets. In the EU, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 moved the AI Act's Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

**Who maintains the record.** Founders; then everyone; then a function; then a platform. Each change of maintainer is a moment when the record can lose its purpose.

| Variable | 2 people | 50 people | 1,000 people | 10,000 people |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Decision volume per class | A handful, all different | Dozens, some recurring | Hundreds, classed | Thousands, comparable |
| Decider to consequence | Same person | One team away | Several layers | Divisions apart |
| Context turnover | Rare | Each new hire | Monthly | Constant |
| External scrutiny | Investors | Investors, early customers | Auditors, regulators, large customers | All of these, in several jurisdictions |
| Record maintained by | Founders | Everyone, with owners for terms | Business functions, with platform standards | Functions locally, invariants centrally |

## Build for the next rung, not two rungs up

The practical rule is to build the layer the next stage will break, not the one the stage after that. A ten-person company that builds a governed ontology is spending money on a problem it does not have, and the ontology will be wrong by the time it matters. A 1,000-person company still running decisions through a founders' document is about to discover the problem it skipped.

The two errors are not symmetrical. Over-building early costs time and money, and the structure goes stale before it is needed. Under-building late costs more, because the reasons behind past decisions cannot be recovered once their authors have left. Michael Nygard's 2011 case for architecture decision records describes the result: a newcomer facing an unexplained decision can only blindly accept it or blindly change it. Neither is safe.

The rungs are approximate, and the evidence on group size supports reading them loosely. Lindenfors, Wartel and Lind's 2021 re-analysis of the data behind "Dunbar's number" found estimates of maximum human group size so uncertain that the 95% interval for their main model ran from about 4 to 292. A fixed cognitive limit on group size, they concluded, cannot be derived in this way. Headcount is a proxy for the problem, not the problem itself.

A regulated fintech may hit the governance rung at 80 people, when a bank partner or regulator asks how a credit decision was made. A research lab may stay at the meaning rung for years. A firm that grows by acquisition can meet federation at 2,000 people, because it has inherited several records at once. Read the problem, not the headcount.

| Symptom | Rung it signals | First thing to build |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The founders describe last month's big decision differently | Founders | An append-only ledger |
| Founders answer more questions each week as hiring continues | First stranger | Ledger entries a stranger can read |
| Two dashboards disagree in a board meeting | Meaning | A glossary with owners |
| Similar cases get different answers from different managers | Delegation | Decision classes and a precedent slot |
| A customer security review asks who approved an AI action | Governance | A trace specification |
| A central data model has been "nearly finished" for two years | Density | Central invariants and a definitions map |

**In practice:** identify the current rung by its problem. Name the problem of the next rung, and build only what solves that. Revisit the diagnosis every time headcount roughly doubles, or when an event such as an acquisition, a regulator or a large customer changes the problem without changing the headcount.

## The five invariants underneath

Almost everything about the record changes with size: the tools, the owners, the governance, the automation, whether it can learn. Five things do not. They are what make the record a record of judgment rather than a pile of content, and our closing piece, [*Five invariants, from two people to ten thousand*](https://lowob.com/research/five-invariants-from-two-people-to-ten-thousand/), sets them out in full.

| Invariant | At two people | At ten thousand people |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decisions carry a reason and a falsifier | A line in a shared document | A required field in every decision workflow |
| Sources are kept; summaries are views | A link to the call note or email | Evidence stored with timestamp and origin |
| Views are superseded, never overwritten | A new entry that names the old one | Version history enforced by the platform |
| Outcomes are written back | A weekly check of falsifier dates | Calibration reports by decision class |
| The organisation owns the record | A document both founders can export | An export format every tool must support |

The invariants cost almost nothing at two people and are the hardest thing to retrofit at ten thousand. Each rung adds volume, automation, governance or federation on top of them. None of these substitutes for the invariants, and all of them amplify whatever the invariants are, good or bad. Our explainer [*What is a decision record?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) covers the basic fields.

## What would prove this wrong

The ladder is a claim about sequencing, and it can be tested. It would be wrong if organisations that build the full large-scale stack early gained from it at every stage, without excess cost or rework. Then the ladder is a false economy, and firms should build the 10,000-person brain at fifty.

It would also be weakened if the problems did not arrive in roughly this order. If most firms met governance before meaning, the ladder would need reordering. Regulated sectors are the clearest exception we know of.

## lowob takeaways

- **Diagnose by problem, not headcount.** Memory, strangers, meaning, delegation, governance and density arrive roughly in that order, at sizes that vary by sector.
- **Build for the next rung.** Solve the problem you are about to meet, not one two rungs away.
- **Expect each rung's characteristic failure.** The wiki at ten, tool sprawl at fifty, compliance theatre at two hundred, platform ownership at a thousand, the single ontology at ten thousand.
- **Hold the five invariants from day one.** They are cheap at two people and nearly impossible to retrofit at scale.
- **Revisit at each doubling.** Or sooner, when an acquisition, regulator or large customer changes the problem.

## Common questions

### How should a company's knowledge system change as it grows?

The record has to solve a different problem at each stage: false shared memory at two people, the first stranger at about ten, meaning at fifty, delegation at two hundred, governance at a thousand, then density and federation at ten thousand. Build only for the next stage.

### What breaks first when a startup grows?

Shared memory, then context. Two founders remember decisions differently, and from the first hires onward every "why do we do this?" question routes to a founder unless the reasons are written down.

### Should a small startup build a knowledge graph or ontology?

No. A ten-person company that builds one is spending on a problem it does not have, and the structure will be wrong by the time it matters. A shared, append-only decision ledger does more at that size.

### Is Dunbar's number a reliable guide to when a company needs more structure?

Only loosely. Group sizes appear to cluster in steps, but a 2021 re-analysis found the evidence too uncertain to support a fixed limit near 150. Diagnose by symptoms, such as conflicting definitions or inconsistent decisions, not by a headcount threshold.

# What Is Shadow AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-shadow-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Shadow AI is the use of AI tools at work without the organisation's approval or oversight. Surveys suggest it is the norm rather than the exception, and IBM-sponsored research links it to costlier breaches. Bans rarely work; an approved alternative, a short policy and an inventory do.

Shadow AI is the use of AI tools at work without the organisation's knowledge, approval or oversight: a personal chatbot account used for client emails, a free notetaker joining sales calls, a browser extension reading the CRM. It is usually well-meant. The risk is that company and client data flows to services nobody has assessed, and that decisions get made with tools nobody can audit.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What shadow AI means

The term follows "shadow IT", the long-standing problem of staff adopting software without IT's involvement. Shadow AI is the same pattern applied to AI: tools adopted by individuals or teams, outside procurement and security review.

It differs from shadow IT in one respect that matters. Most AI tools work by receiving content. Using one means sending it text, files, call audio or screen contents. A spreadsheet app used without approval stores data; an AI assistant used without approval processes it, and the provider's terms decide what happens next.

| Form of shadow AI | Typical commercial example | Main exposure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Personal chatbot accounts | Pasting a client's RFP into a free assistant | Client confidential data leaves the firm |
| Meeting notetakers | A bot joins a prospect call from a rep's own account | Recording without consent; transcripts stored externally |
| Browser extensions | An AI writing aid with access to every page, including the CRM | Broad read access to systems |
| AI features in approved tools | A new AI option switched on in an existing app | Terms change without review |
| Unregistered agents | A rep connects an agent to their inbox | Actions taken in the firm's name, unlogged |

## Why it happens and what it costs

### It is the norm

Microsoft and LinkedIn's 2024 Work Trend Index, a survey of 31,000 people in 31 countries, found 75% of knowledge workers used AI at work and 78% of AI users brought their own tools. The same report found 60% of leaders worried their company lacked a plan and vision for AI. When the firm has no approved option, staff find their own.

Gartner's survey of 302 cybersecurity leaders, run between March and May 2025, found 69% suspected or had evidence of employees using prohibited public generative AI. Gartner predicts that by 2030 more than 40% of enterprises will experience security or compliance incidents linked to unauthorised shadow AI.

### Breaches cost more

IBM's Cost of a Data Breach 2025, researched by the Ponemon Institute across 600 breached organisations, found one in five reported a breach due to shadow AI. Organisations with high levels of shadow AI saw breach costs an average of $670,000 higher than those with low or none. Among breached organisations, 63% had no AI governance policy or were still writing one.

### Commercial teams are exposed

Sales and account teams handle exactly the data that should not leave: client lists, pricing, proposals, call recordings. They are also under time pressure and quick to adopt tools that save it. A drafting assistant on a personal account is the commonest form of shadow AI in commercial work.

> Shadow AI is a signal that people need a tool. The fix is a better approved option, not a louder ban.

## How to bring it into the open

Gartner's recommendations are to set enterprise-wide policies for AI tool use, audit regularly for shadow AI activity, and add generative AI risk to SaaS assessments. NIST's generative AI profile adds the inventory: enumerate the organisation's AI systems (action GV-1.6-001). For a mid-size firm, that becomes five steps.

| Step | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Ask, without penalty | Survey staff on which AI tools they use and for what; amnesty gets honest answers |
| Provide the approved option | Choose an enterprise assistant with data protections and make it easy to get |
| Publish a one-page policy | Approved tools, data that must never be entered, what needs review |
| Keep an inventory | Every AI tool and agent, its owner, its data access and its terms |
| Check quarterly | Review expense claims, browser extensions, OAuth grants and meeting bots |

The sequence matters. A policy without an approved tool drives use further underground. An approved tool without a policy leaves people guessing what they can paste into it. Gateway 0 in The Build Order, which settles the owner, the suite and the CRM before any AI tool is bought, exists partly for this reason.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume it exists.** Surveys show most AI users bring their own tools.
- **It costs real money.** IBM's 2025 study puts the added breach cost of high shadow AI use at $670,000 on average.
- **Offer before you forbid.** An approved assistant reduces shadow use more than a ban.
- **Inventory everything.** Tools, agents, owners, data access and terms, reviewed quarterly.

## Common questions

### What is an example of shadow AI?

A salesperson pasting a client's proposal into a personal chatbot account, or a free AI notetaker joining client calls from an individual's account, without the company's approval.

### What is the difference between shadow AI and shadow IT?

Shadow IT is any technology used without IT approval. Shadow AI is the AI subset, with added risk because AI tools receive and process the content users send them.

### Should companies ban generative AI tools?

Bans tend to push use out of sight. Most guidance favours providing an approved tool, a clear policy on data use and regular audits.

### How do you detect shadow AI?

Ask staff directly under an amnesty, then check expense claims, browser extensions, third-party app permissions on email and calendar, and bots joining meetings.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft and LinkedIn, 2024 Work Trend Index on the state of AI at work](https://blogs.microsoft.com/blog/2024/05/08/microsoft-and-linkedin-release-the-2024-work-trend-index-on-the-state-of-ai-at-work/), 8 May 2024. Vendor-run survey; Microsoft sells AI workplace tools.
- [IBM, Cost of a Data Breach Report 2025 press release](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2025-07-30-ibm-report-13-of-organizations-reported-breaches-of-ai-models-or-applications,-97-of-which-reported-lacking-proper-ai-access-controls), 30 July 2025. Research by Ponemon Institute, sponsored by IBM, a security vendor.
- [Gartner, Gartner Identifies Critical GenAI Blind Spots That CIOs Must Urgently Address](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-11-19-gartner-identifies-critical-genai-blind-spots-that-cios-must-urgently-address0), 19 November 2025. Analyst survey of 302 security leaders; the 2030 figure is a prediction.
- [NIST, AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. Voluntary US government guidance.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Acceptable Use Policy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-acceptable-use-policy/)
- [Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/)
- [Which AI Assistant, Which Seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/)
- [What Is AI Governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/)

## Next move

Send your commercial team a two-question survey this week: which AI tools do you use for work, and for what tasks? Promise no penalty, and use the answers to start your inventory.

# Long Context Windows vs RAG

Source: https://lowob.com/research/long-context-vs-rag/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A long context window lets a model read whole documents at once; retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) fetches only the passages a question needs. Research finds long context often scores higher when well resourced, while RAG costs far less, and both degrade in known ways. For a commercial team the deciding factors are corpus size, permissions and how often the content changes.

Long context means putting whole documents directly into the model's prompt and letting it read everything. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means searching a store first and giving the model only the passages that look relevant. Long context is simpler and often more accurate on a bounded set of documents. RAG is cheaper, scales to large and changing collections, and is the natural place to enforce who may see what.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What the two approaches mean

A context window is the amount of text a model can take in one request; **lowob**'s explainer on [context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/) covers how teams decide what goes into it. With long context, the application loads the source material straight in: a full contract, a year of account emails, a product manual. The model reads all of it for each question.

RAG adds a retrieval step. Documents are split into passages, indexed, usually as embeddings in a vector store, and searched at question time. The model sees only the top results. Quality then depends on two things: whether retrieval found the right passages, and whether the model used them.

|  | Long context | RAG |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What the model sees | Everything loaded, every time | The passages retrieval selects |
| Setup effort | Low: load and ask | Higher: chunking, indexing, search tuning |
| Cost per question | High, scales with document size | Low, scales with passages returned |
| Corpus size | Bounded by the window | Effectively unbounded |
| Fresh content | Reload each time | Re-index changed documents |
| Typical failure | Misses facts buried in the middle | Retrieves the wrong passage, or none |
| Permissions | All-or-nothing per request | Can filter by user before the model sees anything |
| Traceability | Hard to say which part was used | Each answer can cite retrieved passages |

## What the research says

The best direct comparison is Li and colleagues' *Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs?*, accepted to the EMNLP 2024 industry track. Their finding has two halves. With enough resources, long-context models outperformed RAG on average. RAG's much lower cost remained its distinct advantage. Their hybrid, Self-Route, lets the model decide per query whether retrieved passages are enough, and falls back to long context only when they are not.

Advertised window size overstates usable size. RULER, a 2024 benchmark, found that almost all 17 models tested scored near-perfectly on the basic needle-in-a-haystack test. Yet almost all showed large drops on harder tasks as inputs grew, and only half stayed satisfactory at 32,000 tokens. Liu and colleagues' *Lost in the Middle* showed the position effect: performance was highest when the relevant fact sat at the start or end of the input. Both studies tested 2023 and 2024 models, so the lesson is to measure current models on your own documents rather than trust a headline window.

Cost has moved too. Anthropic's documentation prices a five-minute cache write at 1.25 times the base input rate and a cache read at 0.1 times or less. For a document asked about repeatedly in a short period, such as one contract under negotiation, caching makes long context much cheaper than the list price suggests. It does not help a question that spans thousands of documents.

## Which to choose

| Situation | Better fit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One contract, RFP or call transcript, many questions | Long context, with caching | Bounded, and the whole document matters |
| Comparing a few long documents side by side | Long context | Cross-references are lost when text is chunked |
| Thousands of help articles, policies or past proposals | RAG | Too large for any window, and changes often |
| Users with different access rights | RAG with permission filters | Long context cannot hide part of a prompt from the reader |
| Answers that must cite a source | RAG | Retrieved passages give a natural citation |
| Mixed workload, uncertain which applies | Route per query | The Self-Route pattern: try retrieval, fall back to long context |

## The **lowob** view

**lowob**'s view is that retrieval is rarely the bottleneck, an argument made at length in [Retrieval is not the bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/). In the brain loop, long context and RAG are both choices about the wiring: how material in the store reaches the reasoning step. Neither fixes a store that holds the wrong material, and neither replaces the record.

Two rules follow. First, permissions belong in the wiring, before the model. If a sales rep should not see a client's credit file, it must not enter the prompt. A long window makes that easier to get wrong. Second, the most valuable context is often a past decision with its reason: why a discount was approved, or why a deal was lost. That lives in the record and comes back through retrieval. A bigger window does not supply reasons nobody wrote down.

## lowob takeaways

- **Long context suits bounded documents.** One contract or transcript, read whole, often with caching.
- **RAG suits large, changing, permissioned collections.** It is cheaper and can cite its sources.
- **Measure the usable window.** Benchmarks show performance falls well before the advertised limit.
- **Neither fixes the record.** Reasons for past decisions have to be written down before any model can use them.

## Common questions

### Do long context windows make RAG obsolete?

No. Research finds long context can score higher on bounded tasks, but RAG costs far less, scales to large collections and allows permission filtering. Many teams use both.

### When should I use long context instead of RAG?

When the material is a handful of documents that fit comfortably in the window, the whole text matters, and the same users may see all of it.

### Is long context more accurate than RAG?

Often, on average, when well resourced, according to a 2024 EMNLP study. Accuracy still drops with length and when key facts sit in the middle of the input.

## Sources and notes

- [Li et al., Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.16833), arXiv, July 2024, revised October 2024. Peer-reviewed industry paper (EMNLP 2024); tested models are now superseded.
- [Hsieh et al., RULER: What's the Real Context Size of Your Long-Context Language Models?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.06654v2), arXiv, April 2024. Academic benchmark; results for 2024 models.
- [Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172v3), arXiv, July 2023, revised November 2023. Academic preprint; tested models are now superseded.
- [Anthropic, Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; multipliers vary by model and change over time.

## Related research

- [What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/)
- [What Is a Context Window?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-context-window/)
- [RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which One Your Use Case Needs](https://lowob.com/research/rag-vs-fine-tuning/)
- [What Is Permission-Aware Retrieval?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/)
- [Gateway 3: When Commercial Is Ready to Share Its Brain](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-three-when-commercial-is-ready-to-share-its-brain/)
- [Vector Database vs Knowledge Graph](https://lowob.com/research/vector-database-vs-knowledge-graph/)

## Next move

Take the AI use case your team relies on most and write down its corpus size, how often it changes and who may see it. If it is small, static and shared, try long context with caching; if not, keep retrieval and check its permission filters.

# Proposal Standards That Win and Teach

Source: https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Buyers now evaluate suppliers with fewer seller interactions, in groups of a dozen or more, so a proposal has to make the case without its author in the room. A proposal standard sets what every proposal must prove and who signs it off. Tagged with its outcome and the buyer's reasons, each proposal also becomes evidence the firm can learn from.

A proposal standard is a short, written rule set that says what every proposal must prove, which sections it must contain, who reviews it and what gets recorded once the buyer decides. It matters because the proposal is now read mostly by people the seller never meets. Forrester's 2024 survey found an average of 13 people involved in a B2B purchase, and Gartner's 2026 survey found two-thirds of buyers preferred a rep-free experience. A proposal that wins makes the case for change, the case for this supplier and the case for acting now, in that order, for readers who were not in the room. A proposal that teaches is tagged with its outcome and the buyer's reasons, so the next one starts from evidence.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most firms have a proposal template. Fewer have a proposal standard. The template fixes the fonts and the order of sections. The standard fixes what each section must prove, what evidence counts and who has to agree before the document leaves the building.

The difference shows up after the decision. A firm with templates has a folder of past proposals and a vague sense of which ones won. A firm with a standard has a record: each proposal tagged with its outcome, the buyer's stated reasons and the decision behind its pricing. This piece covers both halves: the standard that helps a proposal win, and the record that lets each one teach.

## Who actually reads the proposal

The seller writes for the person they met. The proposal is read by everyone else. Forrester's *State of Business Buying 2024*, a survey of more than 16,000 buyers, found an average of 13 people inside the buying organisation involved in a decision, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Finance, procurement, IT and the eventual users each read for something different, and most of them will form their view from the document.

Buyers also do more of their evaluation alone. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Its 2025 survey of 632 buyers found that buyers turned to sellers mainly for tasks needing contextual judgment, such as whether a product fits their needs, and that 69% had found mismatches between what a supplier's website said and what its sellers told them. A proposal that contradicts the website, or that cannot be summarised accurately by a buyer's AI assistant, loses ground before anyone reads it closely.

The third fact is indecision. Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's research on about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found that 40 to 60% of lost deals were lost to indecision, and that calls with high buyer indecision were won about 6% of the time. Forrester reported that 86% of purchases stall. Many proposals are written as if the buyer's only choice is between suppliers. More often the choice is between acting and waiting.

## What a proposal must prove

A useful standard defines a proposal by what it must prove, not by what it must contain. Three cases, in order, cover most B2B decisions.

The case for change: why the buyer should act at all, stated in the buyer's terms and numbers. This is where the metrics and pain gathered in qualification belong (Part 20 compared the frameworks that collect them). Without it, the proposal is a quote.

The case for this supplier: why this firm, against the named alternatives, including doing nothing. Evidence here should be specific and checkable: comparable work, named methods, references the buyer can call. The piece on [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/) covers the standard for this kind of evidence.

The case for acting now: what it costs to wait, what the first step is and how risk is limited. This is the section that answers indecision. A smaller first phase, a clear exit point or a guarantee on a defined outcome all reduce the buyer's fear of getting it wrong.

| Section | What it must prove | Evidence that counts | Who signs it off |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Summary (one page) | The whole case, readable without the rest | The buyer's own figures and stated objectives | Account owner |
| The buyer's situation | That the firm understood the problem | Quotes or figures from discovery, confirmed with the buyer | Account owner |
| Proposed approach | That the approach fits this buyer, not buyers in general | Method, phases, named team, comparable work | Delivery lead |
| Evidence | That the firm has done this before | Case studies, references, outcomes with dates | Account owner |
| Commercials | That price and terms are clear and defensible | Price, assumptions, what is excluded, approved discount if any | Finance or deal desk |
| Risk and first step | That acting now is safer than waiting | Phase one scope, exit points, decision date | Account owner and delivery lead |

The summary deserves its own rule. It should stand alone, because it is the page most readers will see and the page an AI assistant will most often be asked to condense. If it cannot be read by the CFO in two minutes and understood, the rest of the document will not rescue it.

> The proposal is read by people the seller never met. Write it for them, not for the meeting.

## Review gates

A standard needs a small number of review points with named owners. Too many and the proposal arrives late; too few and pricing or delivery promises slip through.

| Gate | Question it answers | Owner | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qualification | Should we write this at all? | Sales manager | Before drafting starts |
| Solution | Can we deliver what we are about to promise? | Delivery lead | Before the approach section is final |
| Commercials | Is the price inside policy, and is any exception approved and recorded? | Finance or deal desk | Before pricing is shared |
| Final read | Does the summary stand alone, and does it match what the buyer has seen elsewhere? | Someone outside the deal | Before sending |

The qualification gate saves the most time. Responding to every request for proposal is a common way to lose money in a services firm. A recorded pursue-or-pass decision, with reason and owner, is one of the ten classes in [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/), and it is the cheapest proposal decision to get right.

The commercials gate connects the proposal to discount governance (Part 21). Any discount in the proposal should already carry its reason, its trade and its approver. The final read is the gate firms skip. It needs someone who was not in the meetings, because their confusion is the closest proxy for that of the readers the seller never met.

Forrester's analysts have reported that sellers have access to about 1,400 sales assets on average, and that pricing and implementation options carry more weight late in the buying process. A standard should therefore name the few approved sources for each section, rather than leaving sellers to search a library.

## How each proposal teaches

The second half of the standard happens after the buyer decides. Every proposal should be tagged with four things: the outcome (won, lost, no decision), the buyer's stated reasons, the price offered against the price realised, and the date of the decision.

The buyer's reasons are the hard part, and the seller's own account is not enough. Clozd, a win-loss research vendor, reports that buyer and seller explanations of lost deals align only about 15% of the time in its interview data. The explainer on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers how to get the buyer's view, and [What is a closed-lost reason?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) covers how to code it.

Once tagged, the proposal library becomes evidence. After two quarters a firm can compare won and lost proposals on things it controls: whether the summary used the buyer's figures, whether a phased first step was offered, how far the price moved from the first draft. Those comparisons are the material for revising the standard. They are also what makes a proposal library useful to an AI assistant later: a model drafting from tagged, outcome-linked proposals is drawing on what worked, not just on what was written.

Illustrative example: adding a first-step section

Decision
:   Make a priced, time-limited first phase a required section in every proposal above a set value.

Reason and owner
:   Two quarters of tagged proposals showed most large losses ending in no decision, and buyer interviews cited the risk of a full commitment. Agreed by the head of sales and the delivery lead; owned by the proposal manager.

What changed
:   Every large proposal now offers a first phase with an exit point. The firm will compare no-decision rates for the following two quarters before deciding whether to extend the rule to smaller proposals.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consulting and implementation firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write for the readers you never meet.** A dozen people may read the proposal; most will not have been in the meeting.
- **Prove three cases in order.** Change, this supplier, and acting now; the third answers indecision.
- **Gate before writing, not only before sending.** The pursue-or-pass decision saves more time than any edit.
- **Tag every proposal with its outcome and the buyer's reasons.** That is what turns a folder of documents into evidence.

Gateway card

### Before you adopt a proposal standard

- A rule that the one-page summary must stand alone
- The six standard sections and what each must prove
- Four review gates with named owners and timing
- A recorded pursue-or-pass decision before drafting starts
- Approved sources named for evidence and commercials
- An outcome tag on every proposal: result, buyer's reasons, price offered and realised, decision date

## Common questions

### What should a B2B sales proposal include?

A standalone summary, the buyer's situation, the proposed approach, evidence of comparable work, clear commercials with assumptions and exclusions, and a low-risk first step with a decision date.

### Why do B2B proposals lose to no decision?

Research on millions of sales conversations found 40 to 60% of lost deals were lost to buyer indecision. Proposals that do not reduce the risk of acting, for example through a phased first step or clear exit points, are more exposed to it.

### Who should review a proposal before it is sent?

Typically a sales manager at qualification, a delivery lead on the approach, finance or the deal desk on pricing, and someone outside the deal for a final read of the summary.

### How can a company learn from its past proposals?

Tag each proposal with its outcome, the buyer's stated reasons from a win-loss interview, the price offered and realised, and the decision date, then compare won and lost proposals each quarter.

Survey of 632 B2B buyers, August to September 2024.
