# Built to Be Kept Without Us

Source: https://lowob.com/research/built-to-be-kept-without-us/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The honest test of a judgment system, and of anyone who installs one, is whether it keeps working after they leave. That requires client ownership, full export, documented routines and a handover pack. Regulators in the EU and UK now treat switching barriers as a market problem, but no law makes a record readable without its builders. A record nobody maintains depreciates, so the handover should include a small maintenance rhythm.

The honest test of any judgment system, and of anyone who installs one, is whether it keeps working after they leave. A system whose operators cannot be removed without the record degrading has the same flaw it was built to fix. Regulators now treat switching barriers as a market failure: the EU Data Act bans cloud switching charges from January 2027, and the UK's competition authority found egress fees and interoperability barriers limit customer choice. Those rules help you leave a vendor. They do not make a record readable without the people who built it, which is the harder test.

Most enterprise software, and most advisory work, is built to be needed. The vendor holds the data, the model and the definitions. The consultant holds the context. Leaving is expensive by design, and that expense is part of the business model.

A judgment record argues for the opposite. Its whole value is that reasoning survives the people who produced it. That has to include the people who built the system. If the record only makes sense while a particular vendor, team or advisor is present to interpret it, it is not institutional memory. It is a dependency with good documentation.

## Lock-in is now a regulatory concern

Switching costs used to be treated as a commercial matter between buyer and supplier. That has changed in two large markets.

In the EU, the Data Act's switching rules have applied since 12 September 2025 to infrastructure, platform and software-as-a-service providers serving EU customers. Contracts must let a customer start switching on no more than two months' notice, the switch must normally be completed within 30 days, the contract must specify which data and digital assets can be exported, and providers must support the customer's exit strategy. Switching charges have been limited to cost since January 2024 and are prohibited outright from 12 January 2027.

In the UK, the Competition and Markets Authority's 2025 cloud market investigation found that data egress fees and interoperability barriers limit customer choice by making switching and multi-cloud use harder. In March 2026 it announced a package of further actions, including a strategic market status investigation into Microsoft's business software ecosystem.

These rules address one kind of lock-in: the cost of moving data. A judgment record has a second kind. The data can be exported in full and still be useless if nobody can read the reasoning, run the routines or tell which views are current. That is the lock-in an installer controls, and no regulation removes it.

## What "kept without us" requires

**Ownership.** The organisation owns the records, the sources and the accounts. Not a licence to view them; ownership.

**Portability.** Everything can be exported, with history, supersession links and outcomes, in a documented format that can be read without the original tools.

**Operability.** The routines that keep the record alive (capture, conflict adjudication, the falsifier sweep) are documented and can be run by the organisation's own people.

**A handover at the end.** Every engagement closes with a handover pack of the builder's own reasoning: what was recommended, what was rejected and why, what to watch, and the graveyard of approaches tried and dropped during the engagement.

| Requirement | What it means | How to test it | Failure it prevents |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ownership | Records, sources and accounts held by the organisation | Check whose name each account and storage location is in | Access withdrawn at cancellation |
| Portability | Full export with history, supersession links and outcomes | Export everything and open it without the original tools | Data that moves but cannot be read |
| Operability | Routines documented for the organisation's own people | Someone else runs a week of routines from the documents alone | Only the builder can keep it alive |
| Handover pack | The builder's reasoning, including rejected options | Ask a new hire to explain a past decision from the pack | The next team repeats dropped approaches |

The portability test has a precedent in software. Michael Nygard's 2011 proposal for architecture decision records kept each decision as a short text file in the project's own repository, with its context, status and consequences. Superseded records stay, marked with what replaced them, and numbers are never reused. Plain files in the client's own store are about as portable as a record can be. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) applies the same rule to judgment records, and our explainer on [what a decision record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) sets out the fields.

## The honest caveat: a static record depreciates

Ownership is necessary and not sufficient. A judgment record that nobody maintains loses value. Precedents age. Conditions change. Views that were current become superseded in the world but not in the record, and an unmaintained record starts to mislead rather than inform.

So say it plainly, in the same breath as handing it over: you own this, and it depreciates unless someone keeps it current. Then give the organisation what it needs to do that itself: a maintenance rhythm small enough to survive, with a weekly decision review, a quarterly falsifier sweep and an annual read of what keeps going wrong.

| Rhythm | What happens | What it catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weekly decision review | New decisions captured; open ones checked for owner and status | Decisions made but never recorded |
| Quarterly falsifier sweep | Each live view checked against what would have proved it wrong | Views the world has superseded |
| Annual read | Patterns across the year's outcomes and dropped approaches | The mistakes the organisation keeps repeating |

The cost of skipping it is measurable in other settings. Panopto's 2018 survey of 1,000 workers estimated that 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role, and that knowledge workers lost 5.3 hours a week waiting for or recreating information. A record that is not maintained drifts back toward that state, one stale entry at a time. Where AI agents draw on the record as [decision precedent](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/), a stale entry is worse than a missing one, because it is retrieved and trusted.

> Handing over the memory gives up one reason to be rehired. That is deliberate.

## The standard we hold ourselves to

At **lowob** the client owns the records, the sources and the accounts, and can export everything with its history at any time. Every engagement ends with a handover pack of our own reasoning. Cancellation never holds a client's memory hostage. And when we hand the record over, we say clearly that it is a depreciating asset without maintenance, and show how to maintain it.

Handing over the memory gives up one reason to be rehired. That is deliberate.

## The bet

Organisations rehire the people and products that left them better off, not the ones they could not get rid of. In a market where every vendor can reach the same data through the same protocol with the same models, trust earned that way may be the most durable advantage left.

The enterprise brain worth having is the one that can show what it decided, why, what would have proved it wrong, and when it changed its mind, and that still can, after everyone who built it has gone. Our explainer on [what an enterprise brain is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/) sets out the loop the record sits inside.

**In practice**

Test whether your judgment record survives the removal of its builders: export it, and have someone else run a week of routines from the documentation alone. Put ownership, export and exit terms in every contract that touches decision records. End every engagement with a handover pack of the builder's own reasoning. Tell clients, in writing, what maintenance the record needs to keep its value.

**What would prove this wrong:**

Evidence that clients consistently prefer, and get better outcomes from, judgment systems operated entirely by vendors, with no ownership or portability, over several years.

## lowob takeaways

- **Own it outright.** The organisation should own the records, sources and accounts, not hold a licence to view them.
- **Test the exit early.** Export the record and have someone else run a week of routines from the documentation alone.
- **Hand over the reasoning.** Every engagement should end with a pack of the builder's own reasoning, including rejected approaches.
- **Budget for maintenance.** A record without a weekly, quarterly and annual rhythm depreciates and starts to mislead.

## Common questions

### How do I avoid vendor lock-in with a decision record or knowledge system?

Put ownership, export and exit terms in every contract that touches decision records, and make sure everything exports with its history in a documented format that can be read without the original tools.

### Does the EU Data Act stop SaaS lock-in?

It helps. Since September 2025 providers serving EU customers must support switching on no more than two months' notice, usually within 30 days, and switching charges are banned from 12 January 2027. It moves the data; it does not make the reasoning readable.

### What should a consultant hand over at the end of an engagement?

A handover pack of their own reasoning: what was recommended, what was rejected and why, what to watch, and the approaches tried and dropped.

### Does a judgment record keep its value once it is handed over?

No. An unmaintained record depreciates and starts to mislead. It needs a maintenance rhythm such as a weekly decision review, a quarterly falsifier sweep and an annual review.

Law firm summary of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854; not legal advice for any specific contract.
- [UK Competition and Markets Authority, CMA announces package of actions on business software and cloud services](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/cma-announces-package-of-actions-on-business-software-and-cloud-services), 31 March 2026. Regulator press release; UK market, focused on large cloud providers.

Test a record by exporting it and having someone else run a week of routines from the documentation alone. Note every point where they had to ask the builder, and write those answers into the documentation.

# What Is a Golden Record?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-golden-record/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A golden record is the best current version of one entity, such as an account, built from several matching source records. Entity resolution decides which records belong together; survivorship rules then decide which value wins for each field. For a commercial team it is the account that agents and reports should read, provided the source records and the lineage behind it are kept.

A golden record is the single, trusted version of one real-world entity, such as a customer, account or product, assembled from matching records held in several systems. Entity resolution decides which records belong together; survivorship rules decide which value wins for each field. A good golden record keeps its source records, so every value can be traced.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a golden record means

Most firms hold the same account in several places. The CRM has the trading name and the owner; billing has the registered name and invoice address; support has a web domain. Each is partly right. A golden record combines the best of each into one version every system and report can agree on.

The term comes from master data management (MDM), the discipline of keeping core business entities consistent across systems. TechTarget's definition, by Jack Vaughan and Craig Stedman, describes well-managed master data as "a single version of the truth". Informatica calls the result a master record; Salesforce calls the customer version a unified profile. A golden record is not a copy of whichever system loaded last, and not a merge that deletes the losing records.

## How it works

### Step one: match

First the system decides which records describe the same entity. That is [entity resolution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-entity-resolution/). Poor matching merges a subsidiary into its parent, or splits one client across two accounts.

### Step two: survivorship

Survivorship then decides which value wins for each field. Informatica's Trailhead module for its cloud MDM product sets out the options. Administrators "rank source systems by their reliability", for a whole entity, a group of fields or one field. Values carry a trust score, and decay lowers trust as a value ages. A maximum rule keeps the most trusted value; a minimum rule keeps the least, which Informatica suggests for fields such as risk ratings.

Salesforce's Data 360, formerly Data Cloud, uses match rules to group records and reconciliation rules to choose field values. Its Trailhead project says data "can be reconciled based on frequency of a value, recency, or based on the object it came from".

| Survivorship rule | How it picks a value | Good for | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Source priority | The highest-ranked system wins | Legal name from billing, owner from CRM | A trusted source with a blank field |
| Recency | The most recently updated value wins | Phone numbers, job titles | A bulk import that touches every record |
| Frequency | The value most sources agree on wins | Industry, country | Three stale copies outvoting one correct one |
| Highest trust score | The value with the best computed trust wins | Mixed sources of varying quality | Scores nobody can explain |
| Steward override | A named person sets the value | Disputed or high-value accounts | Overrides that are never reviewed |

### Step three: keep the lineage

The source records are kept. Informatica stores each system's data "in source records" and keeps manual edits separately, so the origin of each value stays visible. Salesforce keeps unified link objects that "act as a bridge between your source data and your unified profile data". Both designs make the golden record traceable and reversible.

TechTarget also describes four MDM styles, from a lightweight registry that indexes master data for analysis to a transaction style that moves all updates to a central hub. In **lowob**'s view, most firms of 20 to 500 people need nothing heavier than a registry or consolidation hub.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

A golden account record ends a common argument about which address, owner or contract value is right. It matters more once agents arrive. An agent reading three conflicting records picks one, often silently. An agent reading the golden record gets one answer and can show where each field came from.

It is also where the [system of record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/) question is settled field by field: billing may own the legal name while the CRM owns the account owner.

Two limits follow from **lowob**'s model. A golden record is part of the store: it says what is true now, not why a discount was approved. Those reasons belong in a decision record linked to the golden account ID. And it should follow [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/): changed values are kept as history, not erased.

## How to start

Begin with accounts, which are fewer than contacts and carry the contracts. List the ten fields that matter most, such as legal name, domain, owner and contract end date. For each, name the winning system, the rule and the person who resolves disputes. Then count the accounts where sources disagree on any of those fields. That number is the size of the job.

## lowob takeaways

- **Match first, then choose.** Survivorship is only as good as the entity resolution beneath it.
- **Write a rule per field.** Different fields deserve different winners, and the choice should be explicit.
- **Keep the sources.** A golden record without lineage cannot be checked or reversed.
- **State is not reasoning.** Link decisions to the golden ID; do not expect the record to hold them.

## Common questions

### What is a golden record in master data management?

The single trusted version of an entity, such as a customer or product, built from matching records in several systems.

### What are survivorship rules?

Rules that decide which source value survives into the golden record, for example by ranking sources, preferring recent values or keeping the value with the highest trust score.

### Does a small company need MDM software for a golden record?

Often not. Clear field ownership in the CRM, a warehouse and written survivorship rules are enough for most firms with a few thousand accounts.

## Sources and notes

- [TechTarget, What is master data management (MDM)?](https://www.techtarget.com/searchDataManagement/definition/master-data-management), Jack Vaughan and Craig Stedman, published 5 July 2024. Reference definition; describes the four MDM styles.
- [Salesforce Trailhead, Get Started with Source Records and Survivorship (Informatica Cloud MDM)](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/de/content/learn/modules/match-merge-and-survivorship/get-started-with-source-records-and-survivorship), undated. Vendor training material for Informatica's product; option names are Informatica's.
- [Informatica, Establish the best version of the truth](https://onlinehelp.informatica.com/IICS/prod/mde/en/cg-c360-bvt-records/Establish_the_best_version_of_the_truth.html), undated. Vendor product documentation.
- [Salesforce Trailhead, Unify Your Data (Data 360)](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/projects/explore-data-cloud-core-functionality/unify-your-data), undated. Vendor training project; describes match and reconciliation rules in Salesforce's product only.

Pick your twenty largest accounts and compare legal name, domain and billing address across the CRM and billing system. Write down, for each field, which system should win.

# What Is an AI Acceptable Use Policy?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-acceptable-use-policy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI acceptable use policy sets the rules for how staff use AI at work: approved tools, data that must never be entered, uses that need review and who to ask. NIST's generative AI profile recommends one, and the EU AI Act's literacy duty makes training on it an expectation. One page that people read beats twenty they do not.

An AI acceptable use policy is a short document that tells staff which AI tools they may use at work, what data they may and may not put into them, which uses need review or approval, and who to ask when unsure. It is the practical front end of AI governance. For a firm of 20 to 500 people, a one-page policy with a clear data rule and a named owner does more than a long one nobody reads.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What an AI acceptable use policy means

Acceptable use policies are familiar from IT: rules for email, devices and internet use. An AI version applies the same idea to tools that receive and process whatever staff give them. It answers the questions people actually have: can I use this, can I paste this into it, and do I need to tell anyone?

It is narrower than an AI governance programme. Governance covers inventories, risk assessment, vendor review and accountability. The acceptable use policy is the part every employee reads.

| An AI acceptable use policy is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| Rules for how staff use AI tools at work | The full AI governance programme |
| Short enough to read in five minutes | A legal document only counsel understands |
| Specific about data classes and approved tools | A general statement of ethical principles |
| Owned, dated and reviewed | A file written once and forgotten |

## Why it matters

### Frameworks expect one

NIST's *Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile* (AI 600-1, July 2024) includes the policy among its suggested governance actions. Action GV-1.4-002 calls for transparent acceptable use policies that address illegal use of generative AI. GV-3.2-003 calls for policies covering interfaces, modalities and human-AI configurations. GV-6.1-010 asks that they be updated to cover both proprietary and open-source tools.

### The EU expects training on it

Article 4 of the EU AI Act sets an AI literacy duty for providers and deployers of AI systems. According to Covington's summary of the European Commission's May 2025 Q&A, it requires organisations to train anyone directly dealing with AI systems. The obligation has applied since 2 February 2025. Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 softened it in July 2026 to a duty to take measures to support AI literacy, with no specific level required of any individual. The Commission's updated Q&A says national authorities supervise it from 2 August 2026 and no certificate is required. See [What Is AI Literacy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/) for the amended text. There is no prescribed curriculum, but relying only on instructions for use may not be enough. A clear policy, with a record of who has been briefed on it, is a reasonable foundation.

### Most firms have nothing written

IBM's 2025 Cost of a Data Breach study, researched by the Ponemon Institute, found 63% of breached organisations had no AI governance policy or were still developing one. Gartner, reporting a survey of cybersecurity leaders in November 2025, put defining clear enterprise-wide policies for AI tool usage first among its recommendations against shadow AI.

> The policy people read is the one that tells them, in a sentence, what they must never paste.

## What to put in it

Eight sections cover most firms. Each should fit in a few lines.

| Section | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| Purpose and owner | Why the policy exists; the named person who maintains it |
| Approved tools | The list, how to request access, how to request a new tool |
| Data rules | What may never be entered; what may be entered only into approved tools |
| Uses needing review | Client-facing output, pricing, legal or HR content, anything sent externally |
| Prohibited uses | Illegal uses, impersonation, recording without consent, decisions about people without review |
| Agents and automation | No agent may send, pay or delete without a named person approving |
| Disclosure | When to tell clients or colleagues that AI was used |
| Incidents and review | How to report a mistake or leak; date of next review |

### A simple data rule

The data section carries most of the risk. A three-tier rule is easy to remember.

| Tier | Examples | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Never | Passwords, payment card data, health data, data under a client NDA forbidding it | Not into any AI tool |
| Approved tools only | Client names, pricing, proposals, CRM exports, call recordings | Only into tools on the approved list |
| Open | Public information, generic drafting with no client detail | Any tool, with judgment |

### Tie it to autonomy

For agents, the policy should say what level of autonomy is allowed without further approval. **lowob**'s default is that nothing sends without a person: an agent may answer or draft, and may act with approval, but outbound messages, payments and deletions need a named approver. Writing that into the policy makes it a rule rather than a habit.

## lowob takeaways

- **One page.** A short policy that staff read beats a long one they skip.
- **Lead with data.** Say exactly what must never be entered into any AI tool.
- **List the approved tools.** A policy without an approved option drives use out of sight.
- **Own and date it.** Name the owner, record who was briefed and review it at least twice a year.

## Common questions

### What should an AI acceptable use policy include?

The policy's owner, approved tools, data that must never be entered, uses that need review, prohibited uses, rules for agents, disclosure expectations and how to report incidents.

### Do small businesses need an AI policy?

Any firm whose staff use AI tools with client or company data benefits from one. Without it, people make their own rules, and shadow AI follows.

### Is an AI acceptable use policy required by law?

Not as such in most places. The EU AI Act requires AI literacy among relevant staff, and a written policy with briefing records is a common way to support that.

### How often should an AI policy be updated?

At least twice a year, and whenever a new tool is approved, a major model changes or an incident occurs.

## In the news

- 20 October 2026 · European Commission[European Commission updates its AI literacy questions and answers](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-20-european-commission-updates-its-ai-literacy-questions-and-a)Official guidance, not law, but it sets the date supervision starts. An acceptable use policy plus training records is the practical answer.

Write the three-tier data rule for your firm this week and send it to the commercial team, with the list of approved tools. Record who received it; that is the start of your literacy record.

# Handovers Are Where Reasoning Pours Out

Source: https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Organisations leak reasons constantly, but at handovers the reasoning behind live decisions leaves all at once, on a known date. That makes the handover the cheapest and most obvious place to start a judgment record. A five-part handover pack, started four weeks before departure, captures what a standard document dump loses.

Reasons leak from organisations all the time. At handovers they pour out, all at once, on a date everyone knows in advance. The standard handover transfers files, logins and a status list, which is what was already written down, and loses the reasoning, which was not. A five-part pack started four weeks before departure keeps it: extracted decisions, open threads, relationships, a graveyard of abandoned approaches, and a question log for the first 90 days. For an organisation with no judgment record, it is the cheapest place to start one.

A programme lead rotates. A committee's season ends and a new panel starts cold. The first commercial hire inherits a CRM and a folder of half-finished documents. An agency's work comes in-house. An advisor's engagement closes. Each time, the reasons behind dozens of live decisions leave with the person, usually within a two-week notice period spent mostly on other things.

The standard handover makes this worse, not better. It is a document dump: the files, the logins, a status list. It transfers what is already written down and loses what is not, which is the part that mattered.

## Why reasoning does not transfer on its own

Three bodies of evidence explain why the reasoning is the part that goes missing.

**Unshared information stays unshared.** Garold Stasser and William Titus's 1985 experiments found that when members of a group held different information, discussion centred on what they already shared, and information only one member held was rarely raised. A handover meeting is a small group with exactly that structure. The outgoing person talks about what both people can see on screen. What only they know stays in their head unless something forces it out.

**The why lives outside the systems.** Ashu Garg's 2025 essay on context graphs observes that systems of record hold the what but not the why: approvals happen on calls and in direct messages, and "the org chart creates a role to carry the context that software doesn't capture." When that role changes hands, the context goes with the person.

**Records exist for exactly this moment.** Martin Fowler describes the architecture decision record as a short document capturing one decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences, so that people joining months or years later can understand "why the system is constructed in the way that it is". The UK government's 2025 framework for the same practice adds status, stakeholders consulted and links to evidence. A handover is when the person joining is about to arrive.

| What a standard handover transfers | What it loses | Where the loss shows up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Files and folders | Why the important ones say what they say | The new person re-litigates settled questions |
| Logins and system access | Which data in those systems is unreliable | Decisions made on fields everyone else ignores |
| A status list | What would change each item, and by when | Deadlines missed because nobody knew they existed |
| Contact names | What was promised, and what each person is sensitive about | A relationship damaged in the first month |
| Nothing | What was tried and abandoned | A failed approach tried again |

## The five parts of a handover pack

**1. Decisions, extracted.** The outgoing person's ten to twenty most significant recent calls, each with the situation, the choice, what was rejected, why, and what happened. Done as a structured interview, not a form, because nobody writes these down unprompted. Sixty to ninety minutes is usually enough. One question reliably produces the most valuable answer: "What would you tell your replacement not to do?" Each answer becomes an entry in a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/).

**2. Open threads.** Every decision in flight, with its current state, the next move, the date it matters by, and what would change it.

**3. Relationships.** Who matters and why. What was promised to them, and by whom. What they are sensitive about. This is the part that exists only in the outgoing person's head, and it is the part whose loss is noticed last and costs most.

**4. The graveyard.** What was tried and abandoned, why, and what would make it worth trying again. The incoming person's first instinct will often be to try one of these. The graveyard tells them whether that is a good idea. We cover the format in [The graveyard](https://lowob.com/research/the-graveyard/).

**5. A question log for the first 90 days.** The incoming person asks the record before asking around. Every question the record cannot answer is logged, which shows exactly what the handover missed, and is filled while the outgoing person can still be reached.

> A document dump transfers what is already written down. The reasoning is the part that was not.

## Timing

| When | What happens | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Four weeks before departure | Schedule the extraction interview; start the open-threads list | Incoming person or their manager |
| Three weeks before | Extraction interview, 60 to 90 minutes; draft decisions and graveyard | Interviewer, with the outgoing person |
| Two weeks before | Relationship walkthrough; introductions made in person where possible | Outgoing person |
| Departure | Pack signed off; question log opened | Incoming person |
| Day 30 | Agreed follow-up with the outgoing person to answer the accumulated log | Incoming person |
| Day 90 | Review unanswered questions; file the pack as part of the record | Manager |

Start four weeks out, not in the last week. The extraction interview should happen while the person is still engaged with the work, not mentally gone. The 30-day follow-up needs agreeing before departure, while goodwill is highest.

## Why it is the best place to start

Handovers are timed. You know they are coming. They have an obvious owner, the incoming person, who is highly motivated to get the reasoning. And they produce immediate, visible value: the new person makes fewer avoidable mistakes in their first quarter.

For an organisation with no judgment record at all, the handover is the easiest point at which to begin one. Each handover seeds a decision record, a graveyard and a relationship map for that role. After a few, the organisation has the start of a record without ever having launched a programme. The same logic applies to the commercial handover between teams, covered in [The handover from sales to delivery](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/), and to the organisational transitions in [The transitions that break the brain](https://lowob.com/research/the-transitions-that-break-the-brain/).

## How to tell if it worked

| Measure | How to read it |
| --- | --- |
| Time to first independent decision | Days until the incoming person makes a material call without checking with anyone |
| Share of "why did we..." questions answered by the record | Rising means the pack is doing its job |
| Repeat failures | Abandoned approaches tried again without new evidence; this should be zero |
| Questions still unanswered at day 90 | The specific gaps to fix in the next handover template |

## What would prove this wrong

Incoming people with a five-part pack ramping no faster, and repeating no fewer abandoned approaches, than those with a conventional handover. The research cited here explains why reasoning is lost; it does not measure this pack directly, so the first few handovers should be compared against the last few conventional ones.

## lowob takeaways

- **The dump keeps the files and loses the why.** Reasoning only transfers if something forces it out.
- **Interview, do not ask for a form.** Sixty to ninety minutes, and ask what the replacement should not do.
- **Start four weeks out.** And agree the 30-day follow-up before the person leaves.
- **Keep every pack.** Together they become the first version of the organisation's judgment record.

## Common questions

### What should a good handover document include?

Five parts: the outgoing person's ten to twenty most significant recent decisions with reasons, every open thread, key relationships and what was promised, a graveyard of what was tried and abandoned, and a question log for the first 90 days.

### When should a handover start?

Four weeks before departure, not in the last week, while the person is still engaged with the work. Agree a 30-day follow-up with the outgoing person to answer questions logged since.

### What is the best question to ask someone leaving a role?

"What would you tell your replacement not to do?" It reliably produces the most valuable answer in the extraction interview, because it surfaces the failures and sensitivities nobody writes down.

### How do you know if a handover worked?

Track time to first independent decision for the incoming person, the share of "why did we" questions answered by the record, repeat failures, and questions still unanswered at day 90.

## Sources and notes

Laboratory experiment; group decisions, not handovers specifically.

# The Agency You Hired Spent $50K. What Did You Actually Get?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-agency-spent-50k-and-i-have-nothing-to-point-at/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: When an agency has spent the budget and nothing connects to a customer, the money usually went out before measurement, ownership or an agreed result existed. Separate fees, media and production; get the accounts and data into the company's name; agree what counts as a result; then decide whether the current agency can improve. None of this makes the agency dishonest; it makes the setup wrong.

A company can spend $50,000 on marketing, receive every promised campaign and report, and still be unable to say whether the work attracted a single valuable customer. That is not necessarily evidence that the agency is dishonest or ineffective. It usually means the money went out before anyone agreed what success would look like, who owned the accounts, or how results would be measured. Buyers are noticing: 39% of marketing leaders in Gartner's 2025 survey planned to cut agency budgets. Separate what the money bought, get the accounts and data back, agree what counts as a result, and only then decide whether to change agencies.

A company can spend $50,000 on marketing, receive every promised campaign and report, and still be unable to say whether the work attracted a single valuable customer.

That's not necessarily evidence that the agency is dishonest or ineffective. It may mean the company and the agency never agreed on what success would look like. We should separate the work completed from what actually changed for the business.

## First, what the $50K actually paid for

Imagine a small crypto exchange hiring an agency for three months. The agency launches advertisements, coordinates creator posts and delivers a monthly report. As an **illustrative example**, suppose $18,000 paid the agency, $24,000 was spent on advertising platforms and $8,000 paid for design and creator fees. These amounts are hypothetical, not a documented **lowob** client result.

| Line | Illustrative amount | What it bought | The question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agency fees | $18,000 | Strategy, management and reporting | Did the agency deliver the work it billed for? |
| Paid advertising | $24,000 | Ad placements on platforms | Did the advertising reach appropriate people? |
| Production | $8,000 | Design, videos and creator fees | Did the creative explain the product? |

Each expense deserves a different question. Most importantly, what was the work supposed to accomplish?

The media line deserves a closer look than most reports give it. When the ANA traced log-level programmatic data from 21 large advertisers in 2023, it found only 36 cents of each dollar spent through demand-side platforms effectively reached the consumer; the ANA points to supply-chain transaction costs and low-quality inventory, such as made-for-advertising sites, as the main leaks. A small company buying mostly on self-serve social platforms will lose less in the chain, but the lesson holds: "spent on ads" and "seen by the right people" are different numbers. Ask which campaigns actually ran, what was paused or rejected, and where the placements appeared.

## What counts as a result

A report showing 500,000 impressions tells you ads appeared on screens about that many times. It does not mean 500,000 distinct people saw them or that anyone became a customer. Platforms count reach, the number of unique people shown an ad, separately from impressions, which include repeat views by the same person. A report showing website visitors is a little more useful, but it still doesn't tell you what happened after they arrived.

For a DeFi lending protocol, a meaningful result might be someone making a first deposit and remaining active after a month. For a fintech app, it could be a verified customer making a transaction. For a business selling payments infrastructure, it might be a conversation with a company that has the budget and authority to buy.

That doesn't make awareness unimportant. If you hired an agency to help potential customers understand a new category, reasonable evidence may include relevant reach, message recall, or qualified inquiries. The key is to decide on the goal together *before* the campaign starts.

| Job the agency was hired for | Evidence that fits the job | Evidence that does not prove it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awareness in a new category | Relevant reach, recall, branded search, qualified inquiries | Raw impressions or total views |
| Creator or community programme | Quality and number of useful posts, creators worth keeping | Follower counts of the creators |
| Acquisition | Funded accounts, first transactions, active users after 30 days | Clicks and cost per click alone |
| B2B pipeline | Qualified conversations with buyers who have budget and authority | Form fills and downloads |

The evidence should match the job. Supplier case studies often report a falling cost per click without saying how many customers the clicks produced; a lower price for a visit is a real gain, but it is not the same as a customer. Our piece [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) sets out the measures that show something happened, and [what lead source attribution is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) covers how to record where customers came from, and where that record misleads.

> The most valuable thing in an agency's report isn't a large number. It's an explanation of what happened, what remains uncertain and what the company should change next.

## This week: get the accounts and the data back

Before any decision about the agency, make sure the company owns what the money built. Ad accounts, analytics, tag managers, pixels, creative files and reporting dashboards should sit in the company's name, with the agency given access. Meta's business tools are built this way: an owning business grants a partner agency access to specific tasks, such as advertising or analysis, and can remove the agency from the asset. An agency cannot pass on access to assets it only holds as an agency. If the agency owns the ad account, it owns the history.

The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey found data ownership was one of the reasons large advertisers bring work in-house: they want to own, control and protect their first-party data. A small company does not need an in-house agency to get the same protection. It needs the accounts opened in its own name and a contract that says so. The ANA's 2023 media buying contract template goes further, with audit rights, a schedule of transaction data to obtain from vendors, and a requirement for the advertiser's prior consent before an agency uses AI applications in delivering services. Our piece [Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) lists the accounts, records and routines to own.

Then instrument what matters: the one action that counts as a result, tracked in the company's own systems, from the source of the visit to the outcome. Without that, the next $50,000 will produce the same argument.

## Four questions to ask before changing agencies

**What did we agree to buy?** Compare the actual contract and campaign brief with the delivered work. Was it content, awareness, new users, or qualified sales inquiries?

**Where did the budget go?** Separate the agency's fees, media spend and outside costs. Ask which campaigns actually ran and what was paused or rejected.

**What can we measure?** Pick a meaningful action for the business. Show the direct evidence, and explain anything the data cannot establish.

**Can the current agency improve?** Clearer goals, better reporting or account access might solve the problem. A new agency won't fix an unclear assignment by itself.

Gartner's survey covered mostly larger companies, not early-stage startups, but the 39% planning cuts reflects an expectation that applies at every size: clients want to understand what they are getting for the money. Switching has costs of its own, in time, lost history and a new learning curve, so make the first three questions settle the fourth.

Paid advertising does not always have to come last. A fixed fee is not automatically better than every other contract model. The fair test is whether the arrangement is transparent, suitable for the work, and helps both sides make better spending decisions. Our guide to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) covers what each fee model rewards, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to set a budget against cost per qualified outcome.

The most valuable thing in an agency's report isn't a large number. It's an explanation of what happened, what remains uncertain and what the company should change next.

## lowob takeaways

- **An agency can deliver what it promised without helping the business grow.** Compare the work completed with the business goal, not just the number of posts or ads.
- **Know what the money bought.** Separate what the agency charged from the money spent on ads, production and creators.
- **Ask what people did after seeing the marketing.** A click is not automatically a funded account, an active wallet, or a qualified customer.
- **Keep access to your accounts and data.** An agency can run campaigns without controlling the only copy of your reports, accounts and creative files.

## Common questions

### What should I do if my marketing agency is not getting results?

First separate what the money bought: fees, media and production. Then get every account into the company's name, agree in writing what counts as a result, and instrument it. Only then decide whether the current agency can improve with a clearer brief.

### Who should own the ad accounts, the agency or the client?

The client. Ad, analytics and creative accounts should be opened in the company's name, with the agency granted access. Platforms such as Meta support this: the owning business grants and removes partner access.

### What is the difference between impressions and reach?

Impressions count how many times an ad was displayed, including repeat views. Reach counts unique people shown the ad. Neither tells you whether anyone became a customer.

### How do I measure whether an agency is worth the money?

Agree before the campaign which action counts as a result for the job the agency was hired to do, such as a first deposit, a qualified conversation or relevant reach for awareness, and track it in your own systems.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, 2025 CMO Spend Survey](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-12-gartner-2025-cmo-spend-survey-reveals-marketing-budgets-have-flatlined-at-seven-percent-of-overall-company-revenue), 12 May 2025. Analyst survey of 402 marketing leaders; mostly larger companies, not early-stage startups.
- [ANA, Programmatic Media Supply Chain Transparency Study](https://ana.net/programmatic), December 2023, with quarterly benchmark updates. Log-level data from 21 large advertisers; programmatic buying through DSPs, not self-serve social.
- [ANA, In-house agencies no longer a trend: they're here to stay](https://ana.net/content/show/id/79185), 2 May 2023. Survey of 162 ANA members; large US advertisers.
- [ANA, Updated media buying contract template](https://ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2023-06-updated-media-buying-contract), 6 June 2023. Trade-association template summary; the template itself is a members' resource.
- [Meta for Developers, Business-to-business asset management](https://developers.facebook.com/docs/business-management-apis/business-asset-management/guides/business-to-business). Platform developer documentation describing owner and agency access; endpoint access restricted since 2021.
- [Mailchimp, Reach vs impressions](https://mailchimp.com/resources/reach-vs-impressions/). Vendor glossary; used only for the standard definitions.
- The spend split is a hypothetical illustration, not a client result. The evidence table is **lowob**'s framework.

This week, list every ad, analytics and creative account the agency uses and check whose name each is in. Move any that are not yours, then write one sentence defining the result the next month of spend should produce.

# What Is a Forecast Category?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-forecast-category/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A forecast category records a seller's judgment of whether a deal will close in the current period. Salesforce, HubSpot and Microsoft Dynamics all ship similar categories and all let them default from deal stage. The category is only useful when it is defined in writing, can differ from stage, and is checked against what actually closed.

A forecast category is a label a seller puts on a deal to say how likely it is to close in the current period, typically Pipeline, Best Case or Commit. It is separate from the deal's stage, which says where the deal is in the sales process. The category is useful only when each label has a written definition and can differ from what the stage implies.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a forecast category means

Every deal in a CRM carries two different pieces of information. The stage describes progress through the firm's sales process, such as discovery, proposal or negotiation. The forecast category describes a judgment: whether the deal will close in this period.

The two often agree, but not always. A deal can sit in the negotiation stage while the buyer's budget is frozen. That deal belongs in an advanced stage and a low category. Keeping the two fields apart is what lets the forecast carry information the stage does not.

The three most common CRMs use similar labels.

| Product | Default categories | How the category is set |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Salesforce | Pipeline, Best Case, Most Likely (optional), Commit, Closed | Default mapping from opportunity stage; admins can change it |
| HubSpot | Not forecasted, Pipeline, Best case, Most likely, Commit, Closed won | Deal property; can be automated from deal stage or set by hand |
| Microsoft Dynamics 365 | Pipeline, Best case, Committed, Omitted, Won, Lost | Set on the opportunity; Won and Lost set automatically on close |

Microsoft's documentation gives the clearest written definitions. Pipeline is an "early-stage or stalled deal, low confidence". Best case is a deal that "is progressing" where there is "no commitment yet". Committed means the "customer has made a verbal or contractual commitment" and the seller is "mainly waiting on paperwork or final approvals". Omitted excludes a deal "from all forecast totals", for example when it is on hold.

## How it works in a forecast

Categories roll up into totals. Salesforce's Trailhead material describes cumulative rollups: the Commit forecast covers Commit and Closed deals, and the Best Case forecast adds Best Case and Most Likely deals to those. A manager therefore sees a floor (Commit), a stretch (Best Case) and the open pipeline behind them.

Managers can also adjust. Salesforce lets admins choose whether "sales managers can apply their judgment about a deal included in the forecast". An adjustment changes the forecast value without changing the underlying opportunity.

The main design risk is automation. HubSpot offers an "Automate forecast categories" switch, after which "existing and new deals will be categorized into one of the forecast categories based on their deal stage". Salesforce provides a default stage mapping. Both save effort. Both turn the category into a copy of the stage unless sellers can override it. If every deal in negotiation is automatically Commit, the category adds nothing.

The method question, how to combine stage-weighted numbers, seller calls and manager calls, and how to score forecast error, is covered in [Forecasting That Holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/). This explainer covers only the category itself.

## How to write definitions that hold

Write one line of evidence for each category. Sellers then argue about facts rather than feelings. An illustrative set:

| Category | Evidence required | Who can set it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pipeline | Qualified opportunity with a close date in the period | Seller |
| Best Case | Proposal delivered; buyer has a decision date in the period | Seller |
| Commit | Economic buyer has confirmed; paper process has started | Seller, reviewed by manager |
| Omitted | On hold or outside the period, with a reason | Seller or manager |

Three rules keep the labels honest. Let the stage set a default, but require a reason when a seller moves a deal into or out of Commit. Freeze the category view at fixed points in the quarter, so changes are visible. At period end, compare each category with what closed. If Commit deals close at a much lower rate than the definition implies, the definition or its use needs fixing.

In **lowob**'s model, moving a deal into Commit is a recorded decision. It has an owner, a reason, a status and an expected outcome: this amount, by this date. The outcome is written back when the period closes, which is how a sales team learns whose Commit can be trusted.

## lowob takeaways

- **Stage and category are different fields.** Stage is progress; category is a judgment about this period.
- **Write the evidence for each label.** Commit should mean something specific, not confidence.
- **Watch the automation.** Stage-driven categories save time but can erase the seller's view.
- **Score the categories.** Compare Commit with what closed, every period.

## Common questions

### What are forecast categories in sales?

Labels such as Pipeline, Best Case and Commit that record a seller's judgment of whether a deal will close in the current period.

### What is the difference between forecast category and deal stage?

Stage shows where a deal is in the sales process. Forecast category shows how likely it is to close this period. A late-stage deal can still be low confidence.

### What does Commit mean in a sales forecast?

A deal the seller expects to close in the period. Microsoft defines it as one where the customer has made a verbal or contractual commitment.

### What does Omitted mean in a forecast?

A deal excluded from all forecast totals, for example because it is on hold or belongs to a later period.

## Sources and notes

- [Salesforce Trailhead, Configure Sales Forecasting in Salesforce](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/sales-forecasting/configure-sales-forecasting-in-salesforce), undated. Vendor training documentation on categories, rollups and adjustments.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Set up the forecast tool](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/forecast/set-up-the-forecast-tool?data=data), undated. Vendor product documentation.
- [Microsoft Learn, Capture forecast category for opportunity](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-ca/dynamics365/sales/capture-forecast-category-opportunity), undated. Vendor product documentation; source of the category definitions quoted.

## Related research

- [Forecasting That Holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/)
- [What Is Sales Forecasting, and Why Is It Usually Wrong?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-forecasting/)
- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [What Is a Sales Engagement Platform?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-engagement-platform/)

## Next move

Pull every deal currently in Commit and ask each seller for one sentence of evidence. Any deal without a confirmed buyer and a started paper process is a candidate to move back to Best Case.

# What Is a Sales Engagement Platform?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-engagement-platform/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A sales engagement platform coordinates a seller's outreach across email, phone and social channels as scheduled sequences, and records activity back to the CRM. Outreach, HubSpot and Salesforce document the core features. Sending limits, mailbox provider rules and CRM sync decide whether a platform helps, and AI features now add drafting that should sit behind an approval gate.

A sales engagement platform is software that runs a seller's outreach as sequences: planned series of emails, calls, social touches and tasks, sent or prompted on a schedule from one console. It logs every activity back to the CRM. It differs from marketing automation, which sends to lists, and from an AI SDR, which also decides what to write and send.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a sales engagement platform means

A seller working a list of prospects has to remember who to email, who to call and when to follow up. A sales engagement platform turns that into a schedule. The seller enrols a prospect in a sequence, and the platform sends automatic steps and creates tasks for manual ones.

Outreach's documentation lists the usual step types. An automatic email sends "to Prospects at each step's set interval". A manual email creates a task so the seller can personalise the message before sending. A call step creates a call task that completes when the call is logged. Generic tasks cover anything outside the tool, and LinkedIn tasks cover connection requests and messages. A sequence schedule "determines what days the Sequence sends emails or sets due dates for tasks".

The category is easiest to see beside its neighbours.

| Tool | Main job | Who writes the message | Typical unit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CRM | System of record for accounts and deals | Not applicable | Record |
| Marketing automation | Campaigns to lists and segments | Marketer, once for many | Campaign |
| Sales engagement platform | One-to-one outreach in sequences | Seller, from templates | Sequence step |
| AI SDR | Research, write and send with some autonomy | The agent, with or without approval | Lead or meeting |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The platform's value is consistency. Follow-ups happen on schedule, sellers see a daily task list, and managers can compare which sequences and steps produce replies. Activity lands in the CRM without manual logging.

The risks come from volume. A platform makes it easy to send more email than the domain can sustain. Limits exist at two levels. HubSpot's documentation sets a sequence limit per user of "up to 500 emails per day" on a Sales or Service Professional seat and "up to 1,000 emails per day" on Enterprise. It also warns that "each email provider has its own rate limits", which HubSpot cannot override.

Mailbox providers set the second level. Google's sender guidelines apply extra rules to senders of more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail accounts, including SPF, DKIM and DMARC authentication. Spam rates should stay below 0.10% and never reach 0.30%. Marketing messages must support one-click unsubscribe. The usual mechanism is RFC 8058, an IETF proposed standard from January 2017. It lets a mail client unsubscribe a user with a single HTTPS request, signalled by a List-Unsubscribe-Post header.

AI features are now standard in the category: drafted emails, suggested next steps, reply classification. Each sits somewhere on **lowob**'s autonomy dial. A drafted email that a seller edits and sends is level 1. An automatic step that an AI writes and sends unseen is level 3 or 4, and it belongs behind an approval gate until the error rate is known.

## How to choose one

| Criterion | Question to ask |
| --- | --- |
| CRM sync | Do activities, replies and outcomes write back to the CRM as the system of record, in both directions? |
| Sending controls | Can admins set daily limits per user and per domain? |
| Deliverability | Does it support authentication checks, one-click unsubscribe and bounce handling? |
| Opt-out handling | Is an unsubscribe in one sequence honoured across every sequence and tool? |
| Manual steps | Can sellers personalise before sending, rather than only automate? |
| AI features | Which AI actions send without review, and can each be set to draft only? |
| Reporting | Can you see reply and meeting rates by sequence and by step? |
| Pricing basis | Is it per seat, and are AI features or credits charged separately? |

A firm with a few sellers may find the CRM's built-in sequences enough. A dedicated platform earns its cost when several sellers run many sequences and managers need step-level reporting.

## lowob takeaways

- **It schedules one-to-one outreach.** Sequences of emails, calls and tasks, not campaigns to lists.
- **Volume is the main risk.** Per-user caps and mailbox provider rules both apply.
- **The CRM stays the record.** The platform should write activity and outcomes back.
- **Gate the AI steps.** Drafts are low risk; unseen automatic sends need approval first.

## Common questions

### What does a sales engagement platform do?

It runs sellers' outreach as scheduled sequences of emails, calls, social touches and tasks, and logs the activity to the CRM.

### What is the difference between a sales engagement platform and a CRM?

The CRM is the system of record for accounts and deals. A sales engagement platform is the tool sellers use to carry out outreach, writing its activity back to the CRM.

### What is the difference between sales engagement and marketing automation?

Marketing automation sends campaigns to lists. Sales engagement runs one-to-one outreach by individual sellers, mixing automatic and manual steps.

### Is a sales engagement platform the same as an AI SDR?

No. A sales engagement platform runs sequences that people design. An AI SDR also researches prospects and writes and sends messages itself.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner Peer Insights, Sales Engagement Applications](https://www.gartner.com/reviews/market/sales-engagement-applications), accessed November 2026. Review-site market definition; full analyst research is behind a login.
- [Outreach Support, Outreach Sequence Overview](https://support.outreach.io/hc/en-us/articles/360045065834), undated. Vendor product documentation.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Sales email send limits](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/connected-email/sales-email-send-limits?rd=1), undated. Vendor product documentation; limits vary by seat.
- [Google Workspace Admin Help, Email sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/a/answer/81126?hl=en-GB), undated. Mailbox provider requirements.
- [IETF, RFC 8058: Signaling One-Click Functionality for List Email Headers](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8058), January 2017. Internet standards document.

- [What Is an AI SDR?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-sdr/)

- [Cold Outreach Works Better With a Real Reason to Talk](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/)

## Next move

Export last month's sequences with sends, replies and unsubscribes per step. Retire any step that produces unsubscribes but no replies, and check that each unsubscribe reached the CRM.

# What Is an AI Bill of Materials?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-bill-of-materials/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-10-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI bill of materials, or AI-BOM, is a structured inventory of the components of an AI system: models, datasets, software dependencies and infrastructure, with versions and provenance. In May 2026 CISA and G7 partners published voluntary minimum elements in seven clusters. For most firms it is something to ask vendors for, not to build.

An AI bill of materials (AI-BOM) is a structured, usually machine-readable list of what an AI system is made of: the models and their lineage, the datasets used to train and test them, the software libraries and services they depend on, and the infrastructure they run on. It extends the software bill of materials (SBOM) that security teams already use. In May 2026, CISA and G7 partners published voluntary minimum elements for one. For most firms of 20 to 500 people it is something to request from vendors, not something to produce.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What an AI bill of materials means

An SBOM lists the software components inside a product, so that when a vulnerability is found in a library, a firm can tell quickly whether it is affected. An AI system has extra components that an SBOM does not capture well. The model has a lineage: a base model, fine-tunes, adapters. It was trained on datasets with their own provenance, licences and sensitivity. Its behaviour depends on infrastructure and on settings that change between versions.

The AI-BOM records those parts. The OWASP AIBOM project puts the aim as providing "transparency into how AI models are built, trained, and deployed".

| Document | What it covers | Who writes it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SBOM | Software components, versions, licences, dependencies | The software supplier |
| AI-BOM | SBOM content plus models, datasets, infrastructure, security and performance properties | The AI system supplier |
| [Model card](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-model-card/) | One model's intended use, evaluation, limits and training data, in prose | The model developer |
| AI inventory | Every AI use in your firm, with owner, purpose, data and autonomy level | You |

## What the 2026 guidance asks for

The CISA and G7 document is the first government-backed baseline. Morgan Lewis's summary sets out the seven clusters.

| Cluster | Examples of what it records |
| --- | --- |
| Metadata | Author of the BOM, version, format, signature, timestamp |
| System-level properties | The AI system as a whole and how its parts fit |
| Models | Model identity, lineage and training properties |
| Datasets | Provenance and sensitivity of training and test data |
| Infrastructure | Compute and hosting the system depends on |
| Security properties | Controls against adversarial attack and prompt injection |
| Key performance indicators | Measures of how the system performs |

Some fields carry over from ordinary SBOMs: component identifiers, cryptographic hashes, licence information and dependency relationships. CISA's announcement stresses that the elements reflect G7 expert consensus and will expand over time.

The guidance creates no legal duty. It is relevant to firms selling into governments and critical infrastructure, where SBOM requests are more established, and it gives every buyer a checklist for vendor questions. The EU AI Act's documentation duties for providers, such as Annex XII information for downstream providers, ask for overlapping facts in prose.

### Formats

Two open formats dominate. OWASP CycloneDX added machine-learning BOM support in version 1.5; a model is declared as a component of type "machine-learning-model" and datasets as data components, and model card data can sit inside the BOM. SPDX 3.0, the other main format, has AI and Dataset profiles for the same purpose. A buyer does not need to read either format directly, but should ask that one is used, so the file can be loaded into existing tools.

## How a buyer should use one

Morgan Lewis suggests several uses for buyers. Three fit a mid-size firm well.

| Use | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Procurement | Ask AI vendors which models, third-party components and datasets their product relies on, and for limits on performance |
| Contract | For higher-risk uses, require updated AI-BOM information when models, datasets or components change |
| Incident response | When a model, dataset or library is reported compromised, check which tools are affected |

The second use matters most. AI products change their models more often than ordinary software changes libraries, and a model swap can alter behaviour without any visible release. A clause asking for notice of model changes is easier to obtain than a full AI-BOM, and covers much of the same risk. See [What is model drift?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-drift/) for why that matters.

## The **lowob** view

An AI-BOM answers what is inside a vendor's system. It does not answer what the firm has allowed that system to do. **lowob**'s position is that the second question is the one a firm must own. Keep the vendor's AI-BOM, or its answers to the questions above, attached to the tool's line in your AI inventory, next to its owner, autonomy level and approver. When a model changes, the BOM tells you something moved; the inventory tells you who decides whether the approval still stands.

## lowob takeaways

- **It extends the SBOM.** An AI-BOM adds models, datasets, infrastructure and performance to the software list.
- **There is now a baseline.** CISA and G7 partners published seven clusters of voluntary minimum elements in May 2026.
- **Ask, do not build.** Most mid-size firms need vendor answers, not their own AI-BOM.
- **Get notice of model changes.** It is the clause that covers the most risk for the least negotiation.

## Common questions

### What is an AI bill of materials?

A structured list of an AI system's components, including models and their lineage, datasets, software dependencies and infrastructure, with versions and provenance.

### What is the difference between an SBOM and an AI-BOM?

An SBOM lists software components. An AI-BOM adds AI-specific parts: models, training and test datasets, infrastructure, security properties and performance measures.

### Is an AI bill of materials required by law?

Not in general. The May 2026 CISA and G7 minimum elements are voluntary, though customers in government and critical infrastructure may require one by contract.

### What format is used for an AI-BOM?

Usually OWASP CycloneDX, which supports machine-learning BOMs from version 1.5, or SPDX.

## Sources and notes

- [CISA, CISA and G7 partners release joint guidance on the minimum elements of a software bill of materials for AI](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/USDHSCISA/bulletins/416bd74), 12 May 2026. US government announcement; the guidance is voluntary.
- [Morgan Lewis, US CISA, G7 partners in Europe and Asia release minimum elements for AI software bills of materials](https://www.morganlewis.com/ru/pubs/2026/06/us-cisa-g7-partners-in-europe-and-asia-release-minimum-elements-for-ai-software-bills-of-materials), June 2026. Law firm summary of the seven clusters; not legal advice.
- [OWASP, AI Bill of Materials (AIBOM) project](https://owasp.org/www-project-aibom), accessed November 2026. Open community project; tooling still in development.
- [OWASP CycloneDX, Authoritative Guide to AI/ML-BOM](https://cyclonedx.org/guides/OWASP_CycloneDX-Authoritative-Guide-to-AI-ML-BOM-en.pdf), First Edition Revision 1, 10 June 2026. Open standard guidance for one of the two main formats.
- [Bennet et al., Implementing AI Bill of Materials (AI BOM) with SPDX 3.0, arXiv:2504.16743](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.16743), October 2024. arXiv preprint; describes the SPDX 3.0 AI and Dataset profiles.

## Related research

- [What Is a Model Card?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-model-card/)
- [SOC 2 for AI Vendors: What It Covers and What It Does Not](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/)
- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)
- [What Is AI Governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/)
- [NIST AI RMF vs ISO/IEC 42001](https://lowob.com/research/nist-ai-rmf-vs-iso-42001/)

## Next move

Send your three most important AI vendors one question this week: which models and versions does your product call, and will you notify us before changing them? Record the answers on your AI inventory.
