# The Build Order for Crypto and Digital Assets

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Crypto and digital-asset firms run The Build Order as written, but Gateway 1 is stricter than anywhere else, because public posts can be marketing communications under MiCA and financial promotions in the UK. The commercial line is distribution: integrations, listings, grants, incentives and creator campaigns. The wall is signing keys, treasury wallets and non-public token information.

Crypto and digital-asset companies can run The Build Order as written. The commercial line is distribution: which integrations to pursue, which grants to fund, which creators to pay and how much to spend on incentives. Two things are different. First, Gateway 1 is stricter than in any other sector, because a post on X, Telegram or Discord can be a marketing communication under the EU's MiCA regulation or a financial promotion under UK law, and MiCA's transitional period for unauthorised providers ended on 1 July 2026. Second, the wall is physical as well as informational: signing keys, treasury wallets and deployment credentials must never be reachable by any agent. Chainalysis counted more than $3.4bn stolen from crypto services and users in 2025, with attacks on private key infrastructure and signing processes behind the largest losses.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This is the fourth industry edition of The Build Order. In *The RFP nobody can answer yet* we said the order holds for crypto and digital assets, and that public statements make Gateway 1 strict. This piece explains why, sets out the sector's build order, and names the context that should never be connected to any AI system.

Crypto firms adopt tools early. Many already run community bots, AI-written threads and automated monitoring of on-chain activity. That makes it tempting to start at the far end of the build, with an agent that posts. The evidence in this sector argues for starting at the other end.

## Where the commercial line sits

For most crypto companies, the commercial line is distribution rather than a sales pipeline. A protocol grows when wallets, exchanges, fintechs and developers integrate it. An exchange grows through listings, market makers and partner channels. An infrastructure provider grows through API customers and ecosystem programmes. Our piece *Issuers, integrations and curators* describes the channel structure.

| Lens | What it looks like in crypto and digital assets |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Integrations and partnerships, listings, grants, incentive and points programmes, creator and KOL campaigns |
| Store | Often a spreadsheet, Telegram groups and Notion; sometimes a CRM; on-chain data alongside |
| Outcome lag | Days for on-chain activity; 30 to 90 days for retained users and integrations that stay live |
| Who defends the decision | Head of growth or business development, the foundation's grants committee, finance |
| Main rules | MiCA in the EU; the UK financial promotions regime; US securities law, with market structure legislation unresolved |
| The wall | Signing keys, treasury and deployer wallets, and non-public information on listings, token releases or treasury moves |
| Gateway that bites | Gateway 1: public statements |

The decisions pass the test from *Where judgment arrives first*. A growth team decides weekly which integration partners to prioritise, which grant applications to fund, which creators to pay and how to set incentive rates. The decisions resemble each other and have an owner who must defend the spend.

The outcome lag is the sector's distinctive feature. On-chain data is public and fast: deposits, transactions, active addresses and volume arrive within days. That means the record can pay back sooner than in almost any other sector. It also means the obvious outcome measure is easy to inflate. Incentive programmes attract capital that leaves when rewards end, and campaign metrics can be bought. Our pieces *Community that survives the airdrop* and *Web3 KOL campaign measurement* cover how to choose outcomes that survive; the short version is to grade on retained users and integrations still live at 90 days, not on the first week.

## What the evidence says

**Security.** Chainalysis reported more than $3.4bn stolen in 2025, including $1.5bn from the February compromise of the Bybit exchange. It attributed at least $2.02bn to North Korean actors. Sophisticated attacks on private key infrastructure and signing processes drove the largest losses at centralised services. Personal wallets were compromised in 158,000 incidents affecting at least 80,000 victims. For an AI build, the lesson is direct: anything that can reach a signing process is part of the attack surface, and an agent with tool access is one more path to it. Our explainer *What is prompt injection?* explains why a model that reads untrusted text, such as Discord messages, cannot be trusted with privileged tools.

**EU marketing rules.** MiCA's Article 7 requires marketing communications for crypto-assets to be clearly identifiable as such, fair, clear and not misleading, and consistent with the white paper where one is required. They must state that a white paper has been published and carry a prescribed statement that the communication has not been reviewed or approved by any competent authority. ESMA's public statement of 23 June 2026 said that, from 1 July 2026, providers without MiCA authorisation must stop onboarding new EU clients and stop marketing and solicitation. Serving EU clients from outside the EU is permitted only on the client's own exclusive initiative.

**UK promotions.** Since 8 October 2023 every firm marketing crypto-assets to UK consumers, including overseas firms, must use one of four permitted routes, apply prescribed risk warnings and a 24-hour cooling-off period, and keep promotions fair, clear and not misleading. The FCA describes the regime as technology-neutral and applying to social media. A promotion outside the permitted routes is a criminal offence under section 21 of FSMA, carrying up to two years' imprisonment, an unlimited fine or both.

**US position.** The SEC's 2022 settlement with Kim Kardashian, who was paid $250,000 to promote a token on Instagram without disclosing the payment and agreed to pay $1.26m, remains the reference case on undisclosed paid promotion. Federal market structure law is unresolved. Orrick reported that the CLARITY Act passed the House in July 2025, then failed a Senate cloture vote 49 to 50 on 15 September 2026. The SEC proposed its own Regulation Crypto Assets in August 2026, and the SEC and CFTC issued a joint interpretation setting out a crypto-asset taxonomy in March 2026. The GENIUS Act of 2025 covers payment stablecoins.

Taken together, a crypto firm's public statements are regulated in every major market, its keys are the most targeted assets in the sector, and the rules are still moving. That is the setting for the build.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in crypto and digital assets | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | Owner, suite and a real CRM replacing the spreadsheet; a security lead as data-access approver | Telegram stays the system of record |
| Tooling | Seats for business development, growth and partnerships; capture of partner chats into the CRM where terms allow | Personal accounts and bots with broad permissions |
| Context | CRM, partner and grant pipelines, approved public materials, on-chain analytics read-only | A connector with any path to signing or deployment |
| Record | Integration priorities, grants, incentive rates and creator deals, each with expected 90-day outcome | Grading on first-week volume |
| Reasoning | A first agent that prepares partner briefs and triages grant applications into a queue | An agent that reads community channels and holds tools |
| Gateway 1 | Nothing public posts without a named person; anything on price, yield, listings or rewards gets compliance review | Community bots that reply on their own |
| Gateway 2 | Value at stake on each grant, incentive or creator deal; retained outcome written back | Mercenary capital counted as growth |
| Gateway 3 | Extension to treasury reporting and operations, read-only, under security sign-off | Read access becoming write access |

**Gateway 0.** The three standing decisions apply, with a sector twist on the third. Many crypto teams have no CRM; relationships live in Telegram groups and one person's head. Choosing a CRM people will keep current is the most important Gateway 0 decision here, and the build should budget for moving partner history into it. The data-access approver is the security lead, not the head of growth. Part 3, *Gateway 0*, sets out the rest.

**Tooling.** Seats for the business development, growth and partnerships teams. Community bots are tooling too, and should be inventoried: what each can read, what it can post, and under whose account.

**Context.** Connect the CRM, the integration and grant pipelines, the library of approved public materials (white paper, documentation, approved announcements) and read-only on-chain analytics. Read-only means a data provider or indexer, never a node or wallet connection that can sign.

**Record.** The first decision classes are integration priorities and grants. Each record holds the reason, the owner, the value at stake and the expected outcome at 90 days: for an integration, live and carrying activity; for a grant, the milestone delivered. Incentive rates and creator deals follow, with the same 90-day check. Part 9 lists the fields.

**Reasoning.** The first agent prepares business development staff for partner calls and triages grant applications against the programme's criteria, with a person deciding. It does not read public community channels while holding any tool beyond drafting. Part 7, *The first AI agent should be boring*, makes the general case.

## Gateway 1: why public statements make it strict

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

The autonomy dial runs from 0 (answer) to 4 (act alone). In most sectors a first agent sits at 1, drafting. In crypto, anything that faces the public should stay at 1 for longer than elsewhere, and some categories should never move past it.

Three features of the sector make Gateway 1 strict:

- **Every channel is a promotion channel.** A post in a project's Telegram, a reply on X or an announcement in Discord may be a marketing communication under MiCA or a financial promotion in the UK. Under MiCA it must be consistent with the white paper. An agent that improvises a description of token utility or rewards can breach that in a sentence.
- **Statements move prices.** A drafted post that hints at a listing, a token release or a partnership before it is public can move a market. Information of that kind is treated as inside information under MiCA's market abuse rules.
- **Paid promotion must be disclosed.** The SEC's Kardashian settlement and the FCA's guidance to influencers both turn on undisclosed or unauthorised promotion. An agent drafting creator briefs must include the disclosure terms every time.

The rules for this sector are tighter than "nothing sends without a person". Nothing posts publicly without a named person. Anything that mentions price, yield, rewards, listings or token releases passes compliance review as well. Community support agents may answer from approved documentation only, and hand off anything about funds, rewards or eligibility to a person. Part 8, *Nothing sends without a person*, explains how to log approvals.

> In crypto, every public sentence is potentially a regulated communication, and every tool an agent holds is potentially a path to the keys.

## The wall: keys and non-public information

Two categories must never be connected to any AI system, at any gateway.

**Keys and the processes that use them.** Private keys, seed phrases, multisig signing, treasury and deployer wallets, and admin credentials for contracts and exchanges. No agent should hold credentials that can sign, deploy, move funds or change contract parameters, and no agent that reads untrusted input should share an environment with one that can. Chainalysis's account of 2025 losses is the reason.

**Non-public information.** Listing negotiations, vesting and token release schedules not yet published, treasury moves, market maker terms and security incidents under investigation. These stay with named people. The decision record can note that a listing decision was made and by whom, but its details stay out of the commercial context until they are public.

The wall is recorded: every connector has an entry naming what it reads, who approved it, and confirming it has no path to signing or deployment.

## Gateways 2 and 3

**Gateway 2.** Most crypto commercial decisions spend money directly: grant amounts, incentive budgets, creator fees. Put the figure on each record and write back the retained outcome at 90 days. The first uncomfortable finding is usually that a large share of incentive spend bought activity that left when rewards ended. Our piece *Protocol revenue, fees, real yield and what to report* explains which numbers to trust.

**Gateway 3.** The record extends to treasury reporting and operations, read-only and under the security lead's sign-off. Read access to treasury balances for reporting is reasonable. Any path from that access to a signing process is not.

Illustrative example: an infrastructure provider records its grants and locks down its bots

Decision
:   Record every integration priority and ecosystem grant with an expected 90-day outcome, and restrict the community bot to approved documentation with no tools.

Reason and owner
:   The team was paying grants and incentives on first-week activity and could not say which integrations were still live a quarter later. Its community bot could post announcements under the project's account. Owned by the head of business development, with the security lead as data-access approver.

What changed
:   The first agent prepares partner briefs and triages grant applications into a queue. Public posts need a named approver, and any mention of rewards, listings or token releases also goes to compliance. After one quarter, the 90-day checks showed fewer than half of funded integrations still carrying activity, and the grants committee moved to milestone-based payments.

Illustrative: a composite of a crypto infrastructure company of around 90 people selling APIs to exchanges and fintechs, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with distribution decisions.** Integrations, grants, incentives and creator deals are frequent, costly and quickly graded.
- **Grade at 90 days, not seven.** On-chain outcomes are fast, but first-week numbers are the easiest to inflate.
- **Make Gateway 1 stricter than elsewhere.** Nothing posts without a named person; price, yield, rewards, listings and token releases get compliance review.
- **Keep keys out of reach.** No agent holds signing, deployment or treasury credentials, at any gateway.
- **Treat non-public token information as walled.** Listings, token releases and treasury moves stay with named people.

Gateway card

### Before a crypto company connects its first agent

- A CRM chosen and partner history moved out of Telegram and spreadsheets
- A security lead named as data-access approver, separate from the build owner
- An inventory of bots and agents: what each reads, posts and holds
- Written confirmation that no connector has a path to signing, deployment or treasury movement
- Integration and grant decisions recorded with a value and a 90-day expected outcome
- A public-statement rule: named approver for every post, compliance review for price, yield, rewards, listings and token releases

## Common questions

### Can crypto companies use AI to write social media posts?

They can use AI to draft them, but a named person should approve every public post. In the EU, posts can be marketing communications under MiCA and must be fair, clear, not misleading and consistent with the white paper; in the UK, crypto promotions must use a permitted route and carry risk warnings.

### Should an AI agent have access to a crypto wallet?

Not to any wallet or credential that can sign, deploy or move funds. Chainalysis attributed the largest 2025 losses to attacks on private key infrastructure and signing processes, and an agent with tool access adds another path to them. Read-only analytics through a data provider is a safer alternative.

### What changed for crypto firms in the EU on 1 July 2026?

MiCA's transitional period ended. ESMA said providers without authorisation must stop onboarding EU clients and stop marketing and solicitation, with serving EU clients from outside the EU allowed only at the client's own initiative.

### How should Web3 teams measure the results of incentive programmes and grants?

Record the spend and the expected outcome when each decision is made, then grade at 90 days on retained users, integrations still live and milestones delivered, rather than on first-week volume or deposits.

- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 7, marketing communications](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-7-marketing-communications). Regulation text; Articles 29 and 53 set parallel rules for other token types.

List every bot and agent that can post under your project's name, and every credential each one holds. If any list contains a key that can sign, remove it this week, before any new tool is added.

# What Is Ecosystem-Led Growth?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ecosystem-led growth is a go-to-market approach that uses a company's partners, and the customers it shares with them, as a main source of pipeline, deal support and retention. The term comes largely from account-mapping vendors, and most of its headline numbers are vendor data. Analyst research confirms the underlying point: many B2B purchases already run through partners.

Ecosystem-led growth (ELG) is a go-to-market approach in which a company uses its partners, and the customers it shares with them, to find, win and keep business. It differs from partner-led growth in one main way: the partner does not have to resell anything. The partner's customer overlap, relationships and product integrations help the company's own sellers. The term was popularised by account-mapping vendors, so its most quoted figures are vendor data and should be read that way.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What ecosystem-led growth means

A company's ecosystem is the set of other firms that sell to, integrate with or advise the same customers. ELG treats that set as a source of commercial signal. Before calling an account, a seller checks which partners already work there.

The core technique is account mapping: two companies compare customer and prospect lists to find where they overlap. Crossbeam lists it as its flagship capability, described as finding account overlaps with partners. The overlap then drives three plays: a warm introduction to a prospect, a joint approach to a shared prospect, and support for an existing customer who uses both products.

|  | Partner-led growth | Ecosystem-led growth | Co-selling with a platform |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who sells | The partner sells or refers | Your sellers, helped by partners | Both sales teams on a shared deal |
| What the partner contributes | Distribution and often delivery | Introductions, account insight, integration proof | Access to the platform's customers and contracts |
| Main data | Partner-sourced pipeline | Account overlap and partner touches | Co-sell registrations and marketplace transactions |
| Main risk | Partners do nothing after signing | Activity without measured effect | Platform rules change; your deal is small to them |
| Where **lowob** covers it | [Partner Channel Design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) | This page | [Co-Selling With Platforms](https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/) |

[Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/) argues that a company should choose one primary motion. ELG fits that view. It is usually a support layer on a sales-led or product-led motion, not a fourth motion of its own.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buyers already buy through partners

Forrester's 2023 data snapshot called partner purchasing an "undeniable indication" of the role partners play. Its 2025 survey of partner ecosystem and channel marketing leaders found 67% planned for indirect revenue to grow above or significantly above the previous year. Two-thirds expected the same of partner-influenced revenue. For a mid-size firm, the question is less whether partners touch its deals than whether it knows which ones.

### The numbers need careful reading

Crossbeam's November 2024 analysis of its own network found an average win-rate lift of 11.7% when partners were involved. The lift was 37.1% for companies with more than 50 connected partners and 9.4% for those with one to five. One group, enterprise companies with five to ten partners, saw win rates fall by 1%. The article does not say whether lift is relative or in percentage points, and it describes correlation. Companies that invest in partners may simply be better run.

Crossbeam's ELG page also quotes larger figures, such as deals 53% more likely to close, without a stated sample or date. Treat those as marketing claims.

> Partners touching a deal is an observation. Partners changing the outcome is a finding, and only your own record can show it.

## How to start

A mid-size firm does not need a large partner programme to test ELG. It needs a few partners with real customer overlap and a way to record what happens.

| Step | What to do | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Choose partners | Pick three whose customers match your ideal customer profile | Why each partner was chosen |
| Agree the data | Write down which fields each side shares and for what use | The signed data terms |
| Map accounts | Find shared customers and shared open prospects | Overlap count by segment |
| Run one play | Ask for introductions on ten shared prospects | Each request, its owner and its expected outcome |
| Compare | After a quarter, compare win rate and cycle length with similar deals without a partner touch | The outcome, written back to each deal |

The comparison is the step most programmes skip. Without it, partner influence becomes a field sellers fill in after the deal closes.

In **lowob**'s model the mapping tool is wiring: rent it. The record of which introduction was asked for, by whom, with what expected result, is yours to own. An agent can scan overlap and draft introduction requests at autonomy level 2. A person approves each one, because the partner relationship is the asset at risk.

## lowob takeaways

- **ELG uses overlap, not resale.** Partners help your sellers find and win accounts they already know.
- **It supports a primary motion.** Treat it as a layer on sales-led or product-led growth.
- **Most figures are vendor data.** Read win-rate lifts as correlation until your own record says otherwise.
- **Record every partner touch.** The outcome against each introduction is what proves the effect.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between ecosystem-led growth and partner-led growth?

In partner-led growth the partner sells, refers or delivers. In ecosystem-led growth the company's own team uses partners' customer overlap and relationships to support its deals.

### What is account mapping?

Comparing customer and prospect lists with a partner to find shared accounts, usually through a tool that limits what each side can see.

### Who coined ecosystem-led growth?

The term has been promoted mainly by Crossbeam, an account-mapping vendor, and by a book of the same name by Bob Moore featured on its site.

### Does ecosystem-led growth work for small companies?

It can, with a few well-matched partners. Crossbeam's own data showed smaller lifts for companies with few connected partners, so measure before scaling.

## Sources and notes

## Next move

Ask your three closest partners for a list of shared customers, under written data terms, and count the overlap with your open pipeline. If the overlap is under a handful of deals, ELG is not yet your lever; if it is larger, run one introduction play for a quarter and record the outcomes.

# Below the Volume Floor

Source: https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: At around 150 material decisions a year, all different, no model will learn a company's judgment, and pooling across companies does not rescue it. What works is the company's own prior reasoning, recorded properly, plus public base rates, read and argued with by a person. Forecasting research supports starting from the reference class.

At 150 decisions a year, all different, no model will learn your judgment, and pooling across companies does not rescue it. The arithmetic is unforgiving: split 150 decisions across ten classes and a calibration curve needs years per class to stabilise. What still works is narrower and still valuable: your own prior reasoning, recorded properly, plus public base rates, read and argued with by a person. Forecasting research supports starting from the base rate.

The enterprise designs that work rest on volume. Enough similar cases that exceptions recur and patterns form. A large financial institution can run tens of thousands of comparable credit or compliance decisions a year through the same workflow. At that density, rare variations cluster, and a system can learn from the experts who handle them.

A founder-led company, or a small specialist team inside a large one, has the opposite profile.

## Different physics

| Property | Large enterprise workflow | Founder-led company |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Material decisions a year | Tens of thousands in one class | About 150 across many classes |
| Similarity | High; same product, same form, same criteria | Low; a pricing exception, a partnership, a first sales hire |
| Cost of one wrong call | Small, absorbed by the portfolio | Can be the company, or the year |
| Time to outcome | Weeks to months | Often eighteen months or more |
| Noise in the outcome | Low; the outcome is mostly the decision's | High; confounded by everything else that happened |

Perhaps 150 material commercial decisions a year. A pricing exception. A partnership choice. The sequence of a launch. Whether to hire a first salesperson. They share almost nothing with each other. Each one is expensive.

And the outcomes are slow and noisy. A partnership is graded in eighteen months, and the grade is confounded by everything else that happened in those eighteen months.

That combination (low volume, high heterogeneity, slow and noisy outcomes) defeats pattern learning. It is not a matter of waiting longer.

## Why waiting longer does not fix it

Run the numbers. Split 150 decisions a year across ten decision classes and each class gets about 15 cases a year. In [Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) we suggest a few dozen outcomes per probability band before a calibration curve is stable, and forty to fifty outcomes before plotting one at all. At 15 cases a year, the first plot arrives in year three. If the outcome takes eighteen months to read, add another year and a half. By then the company, the market and the people making the decisions have changed.

Pattern learning has the same problem in a sharper form. A model that learns from examples needs repeated, comparable cases with clean labels. Our explainers on [fine-tuning](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-fine-tuning/) and [decision precedent](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) cover why a handful of heterogeneous examples is enough to retrieve but not enough to train on.

> Fifteen companies times 150 decisions is 2,250 records. It is not 2,250 samples.

## Why pooling does not fix it

The obvious response is to pool: fifteen companies times 150 decisions is 2,250 records. It is not 2,250 samples. Within any segment comparable enough to learn from (same stage, same model, same market, same kind of decision), the effective sample may be in single digits.

Pooling also raises problems that matter more than statistics. Did each client consent to their decisions informing someone else's? Who owns a pattern derived from several clients? What happens when it helps a competitor? And in narrow markets, a pattern assembled from three accounts can be recognisable without a single name attached. De-identification is not anonymity when the market has twenty players.

## What does work at this scale

**Your own prior reasoning.** The single most transferable thing at low volume is the company's own reasoning on its nearest comparable decision. That needs one organisation, no consent architecture, and a record kept with discipline: evidence, alternatives, a falsifier, the outcome. Martin Fowler's description of the architecture decision record is a good template: one decision, its context, the alternatives considered and the consequences, with the record superseded rather than edited when the decision changes. Our piece [Two people: the founder's ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) shows the smallest working version.

**Public base rates.** Where a decision has a public reference class, use it. Forecasting research has long found that starting from the outside view, how similar efforts usually turn out, beats starting from the specifics of your own plan. In the Good Judgment Project, Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues found that training forecasters to use reference classes, along with simple heuristics such as averaging estimates, improved both calibration and resolution. Some domains have rich public outcome data. Credit is the clearest: S&P Global publishes default rates by rating back to 1981, including a five-year cumulative default rate of 0.34% for AAA-rated corporates. Launches, listings, funding rounds and programme results have thinner but usable equivalents. Base rates are a weaker claim than patterns, and a more honest one.

**AI as drafter and checker, not learner.** At this scale the model's job is to draft the entry from a call or a memo, propose the alternatives nobody named, suggest a falsifier, flag contradictions with earlier entries, and surface the nearest prior case before the next meeting. A person reads it and argues with it. This is close to what Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein call decision hygiene: sequencing information so judgment is not formed too early, and breaking a complex judgment into parts.

| Job | What the model does | What the person does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capture | Drafts the record from a call, memo or thread | Corrects it in under five minutes |
| Challenge | Proposes alternatives and a falsifier | Accepts, rejects or sharpens them |
| Consistency | Flags contradictions with earlier entries | Decides which one still holds |
| Recall | Surfaces the nearest prior case and a base rate | Reads it aloud before deciding |

## A rhythm that fits

A 30-minute weekly decision review for anything material. A quarterly sweep of every falsifier whose date has passed. An annual read of the whole record by the leadership team, asking one question: what did we keep getting wrong?

That is not a scaled-down enterprise brain. It is the one layer of one that works at any size, because it does not depend on a model learning from repetition. Our guide to [building the commercial system at every size](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/) places it in the wider sequence.

## What would prove this wrong

Pooled cross-company models producing demonstrably better decisions for low-volume, heterogeneous classes than a company's own disciplined record plus public base rates, under independent evaluation.

## lowob takeaways

- **Volume is the precondition for learning.** At 15 cases a class a year, waiting does not help.
- **Pooling adds records, not samples.** And it brings consent, ownership and recognisability problems.
- **Start from the base rate.** Forecasting research shows reference classes improve judgment.
- **Use AI to draft and challenge.** A person reads the nearest prior case and argues with it.

## Common questions

### Can AI learn a small company's decision-making judgment?

Not at around 150 material decisions a year that share little with each other. Low volume, high heterogeneity and slow, noisy outcomes defeat pattern learning, and waiting longer does not fix it.

### Does pooling decision data across companies help train a model?

Rarely. Within any segment comparable enough to learn from, the effective sample may be in single digits, and pooling raises consent, ownership and recognisability problems in narrow markets.

### What should a small team use instead of a learned decision model?

Its own prior reasoning on the nearest comparable decision, recorded with evidence, alternatives, a falsifier and the outcome, plus public base rates for the decision's reference class.

### What is reference class forecasting?

Starting an estimate from how similar efforts usually turn out, the outside view, before adjusting for the specifics of your own case. Forecasting tournaments found training in it improved accuracy.

## Sources and notes

- [Mellers et al., Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/0956797614524255/), *Psychological Science*, 2014. Peer-reviewed; geopolitical questions, not company decisions.
- [S&P Global, Ratings track record: standing the test of time](https://investorfactbook.spglobal.com/sp-global-ratings/ratings-track-record-standing-the-test-of-time/), citing the corporate default study of 27 March 2025. Rating agency's own investor material; an example of a public base rate.
- [strategy+business, How noisy is your company?](https://www.strategy-business.com/article/How-noisy-is-your-company?gko=5a57c), Theodore Kinni, 19 May 2021. Article on Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein's decision hygiene.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference from software architecture.
- The volume arithmetic, comparison and job tables are **lowob**'s analysis; the 150-decision figure is **lowob**'s working estimate, not a survey result.

## Related research

- [Two People: The Founders' Ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/)
- [What Is Decision Precedent in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/)
- [Building the Commercial System at 20, 50 and 200 People](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/)
- [Top 5 Tools for a Founders' Decision Ledger](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-tools-for-a-founders-decision-ledger/)

## Next move

Write down your last five material decisions with the evidence, the alternatives and what would prove each wrong. For each, find one public base rate. Read the nearest one aloud before your next decision of the same kind.

# Discount Governance

Source: https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A 1% change in realised price moves operating profit far more than a 1% change in volume, which makes discounting one of the most consequential decisions a sales team makes every week. Most firms govern it with an approval chain and little else. Good discount governance sets bands, attaches a trade to every concession, rules fast and records the reason, so the pattern of exceptions can be reviewed.

Discount governance is the set of rules that decides who may offer what discount, in exchange for what, and how the decision is recorded. It matters because price changes have outsized effects on profit: the classic Harvard Business Review analysis found that a 1% improvement in realised price lifted operating profit by 11.1% for an average large firm, against 3.3% for a 1% rise in volume. Most firms govern discounts with an approval chain and nothing else, which slows deals without teaching anyone anything. A working system sets discount bands, attaches a trade to every concession, rules within a stated time and records the reason, so that the pattern of exceptions can be reviewed and the bands improved.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Discounting is one of the most frequent commercial decisions a firm makes, and one of the least examined. A seller asks for 15% to close by quarter end. A manager approves it because the forecast needs the deal. Nobody records why, and nobody checks a year later whether the customer renewed at the discounted price or the list price.

Part 4 of this series covered pricing architecture: how list prices, packages and terms are set. This piece covers what happens after: how a firm decides, deal by deal, how far to move from the price it set. The explainer on [deal desks](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/) covers the team that often runs this process; this piece covers the rules it runs.

## Why small discounts matter more than they look

The arithmetic is old and still decisive. In "Managing Price, Gaining Profit", published in Harvard Business Review in 1992, Michael Marn and Robert Rosiello used the average economics of 2,463 companies in the Compustat database to compare profit levers. A 1% improvement in price, with volume held steady, lifted operating profit by 11.1%. A 1% cut in variable cost lifted it by 7.8%, and a 1% rise in volume by 3.3%. The same arithmetic runs in reverse: a 1% average discount gives up about 11% of operating profit.

The effect is stronger where margins are thin. McKinsey's July 2026 analysis of 10-K filings from 140 public distributors found that a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%.

Marn and Rosiello also showed why firms underestimate the leak. They traced the "pocket price waterfall", the fall from list price to invoice price to the revenue actually kept once payment terms, volume rebates, promotional allowances and freight were taken off. In their examples the drop from invoice price to pocket price ranged from 16.7% in consumer packaged goods to 28.9% in lighting products. For a single product at similar volumes, the range of pocket prices customers actually paid ran from 35% in one case to 500% in another. Most of that variation was not a decision anyone had made. It was the sum of exceptions granted one at a time.

Services and software firms have fewer off-invoice items, but they have their own: free implementation days, extended payment terms, uncapped usage, multi-year price locks and early renewal credits. Each is a discount that does not appear in the discount field.

## What goes wrong in practice

Three failures recur, and each shows up in the evidence.

The first is speed. Everstage's 2026 survey of 195 VP-level revenue leaders in North America, a vendor-run and self-reported study, found that 47% of teams took three days or more to approve a pricing exception, and 40% still built quotes and configured pricing by hand. A slow approval chain does not stop discounting. It teaches sellers to ask for more than they need, so the approved number lands where they wanted.

The second is timing. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmark of 4.2 million opportunities reported that offering discounts early in the sales process was associated with a 39% lower win rate. The figure is from a vendor dataset and is a correlation, but it fits what buyers say: an early discount tells the buyer that the first price was a starting point, and invites a second round.

The third is that overrides become the norm. McKinsey's 2026 distribution work describes a building materials distributor whose sellers overrode system-generated prices in more than half of all transactions. Overrides fell by 80% once the firm fixed its product data. The lesson is that frequent overrides are often a signal that the price list is wrong, not that sellers are undisciplined.

There is also a forecasting link. Gartner's 2020 research on forecast confidence warned that inaccurate forecasts lead leaders to approve discounts they would normally reject. Discounts granted to rescue a quarter are the ones least likely to be reviewed.

## The rules: bands, rights and trades

A discount policy that works fits on one page. It sets bands, says who can approve each band, sets a turnaround time and lists the trades a seller should ask for in return.

| Discount band (off list or standard price) | Who approves | Turnaround | What must be recorded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Within standard band (for example up to 5%) | Seller | Immediate | Reason code |
| Above standard, below senior threshold | Sales manager | Same working day | Reason, the trade obtained, competing offer if any |
| Above senior threshold | Deal desk or revenue leader with finance | Two working days | Reason, trade, margin after discount, renewal price |
| Non-price concessions (free services, extended terms, price locks) | Same as the cash-equivalent band | As above | Cash-equivalent value, reason, trade |
| Below the floor | Named executive only | Two working days | Full case, expected outcome, review date |

The band thresholds are the firm's own decision and should be set from its margin structure, not copied. The point of the table is that each level has an owner, a clock and a record. The last row matters: a floor that anyone can breach with enough pressure is not a floor.

The second rule is give-get. Every concession above the standard band should buy something the firm values. Common trades are a longer term, upfront payment, a larger initial commitment, a case study or reference, a faster signature, or reduced scope. A discount with no trade attached is a price cut.

| Concession requested | Trade worth asking for | Why it is a fair exchange |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Higher discount on year one | Multi-year term at stepped prices | Lower year-one price is recovered over the term |
| Extended payment terms | Price at or near list | Terms cost the firm working capital, not margin |
| Free implementation days | Named reference or case study rights | Lowers the firm's future selling cost |
| Price lock on renewal | Larger committed volume | Locks in revenue as well as price |
| Discount for end-of-quarter signature | Signature date written into the approval | Makes the trade testable after the fact |

The third rule is speed. The turnaround times above are as important as the approval levels. A same-day answer removes the incentive to pad the request. McKinsey's distribution research recommends an override-rate threshold, enforced with execution data, alongside price floors and clear escalation paths for strategic accounts. That is the same idea: measure how often the rules are broken, and treat a rising rate as a signal to examine the rules.

> A discount with nothing traded for it is a price cut, and it should be approved as one.

## Learn from every exception

The approval chain decides each deal. The record decides whether the policy improves. Every exception above the standard band is a commercial decision with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome, which is the shape set out in [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/). Discount approvals were one of the decisions that piece singled out, because they recur weekly and their outcome is known within a sales cycle.

The field that matters most is the expected outcome. "Approved 18% to beat a competing quote" is a reason. "Approved 18% to beat a competing quote; expect renewal at list in year two" is a prediction, and it can be checked. The piece on [the field that makes a record a judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/) makes the case in general.

A quarterly review then asks four questions of the exception log. Which reason codes appear most often, and do they point to a list price that is wrong for a segment? Which sellers or managers approve most often, and are their deals renewing? Did the trades recorded actually happen: did the case study get written, did the multi-year customer stay? And what is the spread of realised prices for similar deals, the modern version of Marn and Rosiello's pocket price band?

If the same exception is granted for the same reason ten times in a quarter, it is no longer an exception. Change the band or the price, and record that decision too.

Illustrative example: a discount band that was wrong

Decision
:   Raise the standard discount band for one segment from 5% to 10%, and remove manager approval for that range.

Reason and owner
:   A quarter's exception log showed most deals in the segment approved at 8 to 10% against the same competitor, with no difference in renewal rates. Agreed by the revenue leader and finance; owned by the deal desk.

What changed
:   Approval volume fell and turnaround for the remaining exceptions shortened. The firm set a review for two quarters later to check realised price and renewal rates in the segment.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software and services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price moves profit more than volume.** A 1% average discount can cost around a tenth of operating profit, which justifies a written policy.
- **Speed is part of control.** Slow approvals teach sellers to pad requests; same-day answers remove the reason to.
- **Trade for every concession.** If nothing is given in return, approve it as a price cut.
- **Read the exception log quarterly.** Repeated exceptions mean the band or the price is wrong.

Gateway card

### Before you publish a discount policy

- Discount bands set from the firm's own margin structure
- An approver and a turnaround time named for each band
- A floor that only one named executive can breach
- Non-price concessions converted to a cash-equivalent value
- A give-get list sellers can use in negotiation
- Reason, trade and expected outcome captured on every exception
- A quarterly review of the exception log booked with finance

## Common questions

### What is discount governance in sales?

Discount governance is the set of rules that decides who can approve which discounts, how fast, in exchange for what, and how each decision is recorded and reviewed.

### How much does a discount affect profit?

In Marn and Rosiello's analysis of 2,463 companies, a 1% change in realised price changed operating profit by about 11%, so even small average discounts have a large effect on profit.

### Who should approve sales discounts?

Most firms let sellers approve within a small standard band, sales managers approve the next band, and a deal desk or revenue leader with finance approve larger discounts, with a single executive for anything below the floor.

### What is a give-get in sales negotiation?

A give-get is a rule that every concession, such as a discount or free services, is exchanged for something of value to the seller, such as a longer term, upfront payment or a reference.

# Reviewer Minutes per Useful Decision

Source: https://lowob.com/research/reviewer-minutes-per-useful-decision/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The number that decides whether an AI judgment system pays for itself is human review time per decision that actually helped, not token cost. Productivity research predicts that metric will rise before it falls. Put the crossover date in writing at the start, and treat a miss as a decision to redesign, narrow or reprice.

Token costs get the attention. The number that decides whether a judgment system pays for itself is human review time per decision that actually helped. Expect it to rise before it falls: economists call the pattern a productivity J-curve, and it is where most programmes lose their sponsor. Measure the baseline, predict the peak, put the crossover date in writing, and treat a miss as a decision.

## Tokens are the visible cost

AI cost conversations focus on inference. That is understandable: token bills are new, visible and growing. Stanford's 2025 AI Index found that the cost of querying a model performing at GPT-3.5 level fell about 280-fold between November 2022 and October 2024. Prices for equivalent performance collapsed.

Spend did not. Menlo Ventures' bottom-up estimate put enterprise generative AI spend at $37 billion in 2025, against $11.5 billion in 2024, with $12.5 billion of it on foundation model APIs. In 2026 some listed software companies began reporting the bill. In August, Trend Micro cut its full-year operating income forecast from ¥56.4 billion to ¥44.4 billion, about 21%, after cloud-related expenses "including AI token costs tied to model usage" rose beyond its projections. Our explainer on [AI inference cost](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/) covers why falling unit prices and rising bills are consistent.

Those numbers matter. For a judgment system they are not the biggest cost.

## The human cost dominates

Every record needs a reviewer. Every conflict needs an adjudicator. Every falsifier needs someone to check it on the date. Every seeded error needs someone to catch it. In most deployments the hours of skilled people spent on review and adjudication cost far more than the tokens.

The arithmetic is simple enough to do on a napkin. The figures below are illustrative assumptions, not benchmarks; substitute your own.

| Cost line per decision brief | Illustrative assumption | Illustrative cost |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model tokens | 50,000 input and 5,000 output tokens at mid-tier list prices | Well under $1 |
| Reviewer time | 12 minutes of a senior person costed at $120 an hour | $24 |
| Adjudication of a conflict | 1 in 5 briefs, 20 minutes each, same rate | $8 on average |
| Falsifier check and error sampling | 5 minutes per decision, spread over the year | $10 |

On assumptions like these, people cost more than forty times what the model does. A 50% cut in token prices barely moves the total. A 50% cut in review time changes the business case.

If review time does not fall as the record grows, the system is a service with software attached, and it should be priced and staffed as one.

> If review time does not fall as the record grows, the system is a service with software attached.

## The metric

**Reviewer minutes per useful decision** = total human time spent on review, adjudication and falsifier checks, divided by the number of decisions where the decision-maker judged, at the time, that the system's preparation helped.

Three properties make it the right headline.

It includes all the human cost, not just the approval click.

It counts only useful decisions, so a system producing volume nobody values scores badly.

It cannot be gamed by fatigue. Tired reviewers approve faster, but they do not judge more decisions useful; if anything, fewer. In [Approval rate measures fatigue too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/) we set out why speed-based measures mislead.

The "did it help?" question has to be asked at the moment of decision, not in a survey later. People misjudge their own productivity with AI by wide margins: in METR's 2025 trial, experienced developers were measured 19% slower with AI tools and still believed they had been 20% faster. A judgment captured in the moment is noisy but honest. A retrospective one measures belief.

## Expect a J-curve

Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson describe a "productivity J-curve" for general-purpose technologies such as AI. Getting value requires heavy investment in complementary intangibles: new processes, new skills, new ways of working. That investment is real but poorly measured, so measured productivity looks worse in the early years and better once the intangibles pay off.

A gated judgment system goes through the same curve in miniature. In its early weeks it adds review. Precedent does not yet exist, the schema is being tuned, reviewers are learning the tool. The metric will rise before it falls. That is normal, and it is also where most programmes lose their sponsor, because nobody said it would happen.

So say it, in writing, at the start.

| Step | When | What is written down |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | Before launch | Minutes per decision without the system, by decision class |
| Predicted peak | Business case | Expected peak in minutes per useful decision and the week it occurs |
| Crossover date | Business case | Date by which the metric must fall below the baseline |
| Review | On the crossover date | Crossed, or a decision: redesign, narrow scope, or reprice as a service |

If the crossover is missed, treat the miss as a decision point, not a reason to wait another quarter. Our [Gateway 2](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-two-a-dollar-figure-on-every-commercial-decision/) piece covers how to put a dollar figure on each decision class so the redesign-or-reprice choice is made on numbers.

## What this means for margins

In our own modelling of an operator-run desk, the economics only work once review time per client falls to under half of what the first month requires. Above that, margins are thin. Below it, they are healthy. The ratio will differ for every organisation. The existence of a threshold will not. For the wider method of measuring returns, see [how to measure AI ROI](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-measure-ai-roi/).

## What would prove this wrong

Judgment systems in which review time per useful decision stays flat or rises indefinitely while the organisation still captures clear net value. Then the metric is measuring the wrong thing, perhaps because the value lies in better decisions rather than cheaper ones. If that happens, the remedy is to add an outcome measure beside the time measure, not to stop counting minutes.

## lowob takeaways

- **Count people, not just tokens.** Review, adjudication and checks usually cost far more than inference.
- **Divide by useful decisions.** Volume nobody values should make the metric worse, not better.
- **Ask "did it help?" in the moment.** Retrospective judgments of AI productivity are unreliable.
- **Write the J-curve down.** Baseline, peak and crossover date go in the business case, and the review happens on that date.

## Common questions

### What is the biggest cost of running an AI decision-support system?

Usually human review. The hours skilled people spend on review, adjudication and falsifier checks typically cost far more than the tokens, especially as token prices for equivalent performance keep falling.

### How do you measure the ROI of human review in AI systems?

Use reviewer minutes per useful decision: total human time on review, adjudication and falsifier checks, divided by decisions where the decision-maker judged at the time that the system's preparation helped. Compare it with a pre-launch baseline.

### Why does review time go up after launching an AI system?

Precedent does not yet exist, the schema is being tuned and reviewers are learning the tool. Economists describe the same early dip for new technologies as a productivity J-curve. Predict the peak and set a crossover date.

### What should happen if review time does not fall?

Treat the miss as a decision point: change the design, narrow the scope, or reprice the work as a service. If review time never falls as the record grows, the system is a service with software attached.

Trade press summary of Stanford HAI's 2025 AI Index.

# What Is an Agent Loop?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The agent loop is the repeated cycle of reason, act and observe that turns a language model into an agent. The pattern was set out in the ReAct paper and is now built into every major agent SDK. Because the loop is standard, the useful controls sit at its edges: what enters context, which tools it may call, where it pauses for a person and when it stops.

An agent loop is the repeated cycle in which an AI model reads the current state, decides on a next step, calls a tool, observes the result and goes round again until it finishes or a limit stops it. It is what separates an agent from a single model call. The loop itself is now standard in every major agent toolkit. What differs between agents is the context that goes in and the limits placed around it.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an agent loop means

A model on its own answers once. An agent keeps going. Each pass through the loop has the same shape, and each step has its own failure mode.

| Step | What happens | Where it goes wrong | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read | The model receives instructions, history and retrieved material | Stale or missing context | Current records, scoped retrieval, precedents |
| Decide | It chooses to answer or to call a tool | Misread goal, wrong tool | Clear tool descriptions, few tools |
| Act | The application runs the tool call | Over-broad action | Permissions, draft-only tools, blocking hooks |
| Observe | The result is added to context | Hostile or misleading tool output | Treat tool output as data, not instructions |
| Stop | The model gives a final answer, or a limit is hit | Runs long, costs too much | Turn and budget caps, a defined finish |

The pattern has a short history. ReAct, from researchers at Princeton and Google Research, had models write a reasoning step, take an action such as a Wikipedia lookup, read the result and continue. Grounding each step in retrieved facts reduced the hallucination and error propagation seen when models reasoned without acting.

## How it works in today's toolkits

Anthropic's documentation for its Claude Agent SDK walks through a four-turn example. Asked to fix failing tests, the agent runs the tests, reads two files, edits one and reruns the tests, then replies in text with no tool call. That text-only reply ends the loop. The SDK offers a maximum number of turns and a maximum spend in dollars; both default to no limit, and the documentation recommends a budget as "a good default for production agents".

OpenAI's Agents SDK describes the same cycle with one addition: a handoff, where control passes to a different agent. If the run exceeds its `max\_turns` setting, the SDK raises a `MaxTurnsExceeded` error.

Two details matter for business use. First, context accumulates. Every tool result stays in the conversation, and when the window fills, Anthropic's SDK summarises older history. Its documentation warns that instructions from early in a session may not survive, so standing rules belong in a file reloaded on every request. Second, both SDKs let code intervene between deciding and acting. Anthropic's "hooks" can block a tool call before it runs, and its permission modes range from asking before each tool to running without approval.

An illustrative commercial loop: a meeting-prep agent searches the CRM for the account, reads the last email thread, opens the current proposal, drafts a brief and stops. Four or five turns, all read-only except one draft. Nothing in that loop needs to send.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Because the loop is a commodity, buying decisions should not rest on it. As we argued in [A loop with good context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/), two agents running the same loop on the same model differ in what they are given to read and what they are allowed to do. Anthropic's own guidance makes the same point in engineering terms: agents need "ground truth" from the environment at each step, and it is "common to include stopping conditions (such as a maximum number of iterations) to maintain control".

It also means the loop is the wrong tool when the steps are known. If a process always runs the same five steps in the same order, a fixed workflow is cheaper, faster and easier to test. Use a loop when the next step depends on what the last one found.

## Common mistakes

- **No cap.** A loop with no turn or budget limit can run for a long time on an open-ended request.
- **Judging only the final answer.** Review the trace: which tools were called, in what order, with what inputs.
- **Too many tools.** Each tool definition takes context and adds a wrong choice the model can make.
- **Letting the loop send.** Keep outbound actions as drafts. The loop's last step should hand work to a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **The loop is standard.** Reason, act, observe and repeat is built into every major SDK.
- **The edges are where control lives.** Context in, tools allowed, approvals and stop rules.
- **Set a cap from day one.** Some defaults allow unlimited turns and spend.
- **Use a workflow when the steps are fixed.** A loop earns its cost only when the next step is uncertain.

## Common questions

### What is the agentic loop in AI?

The cycle in which a model decides what to do next, calls a tool, reads the result and repeats until it finishes or reaches a limit. It is the defining feature of an AI agent.

### What is the ReAct pattern?

A method, published in 2022 and presented at ICLR 2023, in which a model alternates written reasoning steps with actions such as searches, using each result to decide the next step.

### How does an AI agent know when to stop?

It stops when the model returns a final answer with no further tool calls, or when a limit set by the developer, such as a maximum number of turns or a spending cap, is reached.

## Sources and notes

- [Yao et al., ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2210.03629), ICLR 2023. Academic paper; benchmark tasks, not business workflows.
- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), 19 December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance; the page notes some tooling has since changed.
- [Anthropic, How the agent loop works (Claude Agent SDK)](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/agent-loop), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; options change between versions.
- [OpenAI, Running agents (Agents SDK)](https://openai.github.io/openai-agents-python/running_agents), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.

## Related research

- [A Loop With Good Context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/)
- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [What Is Function Calling (Tool Use) in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-function-calling/)
- [What Is an Agent Framework?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-framework/)

## Next move

Pick one agent your team already uses and read a full trace of a single run, step by step. Note every tool it called and whether any limit would have stopped it if it had kept going.

# What Is Sales Velocity?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-velocity/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Sales velocity turns four pipeline measures into one figure: revenue produced per day. Its value is diagnostic, because it shows which of the four levers is moving and by how much. This explainer gives the formula and a worked example, explains why recent benchmark data shows all four levers under pressure, and sets out how a mid-size team can use it without gaming it.

Sales velocity is the revenue a sales pipeline produces per day. It multiplies the number of qualified opportunities by average deal size and win rate, then divides by the average sales cycle in days. The single number matters less than its four inputs: velocity shows which lever is moving, and lets a team test whether a change in one is worth a loss in another.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What sales velocity means

The formula, as set out in Pipedrive's guide:

**Sales velocity = (number of opportunities × average deal size × win rate) ÷ sales cycle length in days**

Each input has a precise meaning. Opportunities are qualified deals entering the pipeline in the period, not raw leads. Average deal size is total won value divided by the number of deals won. Win rate is the share of opportunities won. Cycle length is the average time from first contact to close.

Pipedrive's example uses 20 deals, a $5,000 average, a 40% win rate and a 60-day cycle. That gives $40,000 of expected won value divided by 60 days, or about $667 a day.

This is a different measure from selling time. [What Is Selling Time?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/) covers how much of a seller's week goes to customers. Velocity measures what the pipeline produces, whoever is working it.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Velocity is useful because the four levers trade against each other. Moving upmarket raises deal size but usually lengthens the cycle and lowers win rate. Tighter qualification cuts the number of opportunities but should raise win rate. Velocity shows the net effect.

The sensitivity is easy to see on Pipedrive's baseline:

| Change (others held constant) | New velocity per day | Change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Baseline | $667 | none |
| Opportunities +10% (22) | $733 | +10% |
| Deal size +10% ($5,500) | $733 | +10% |
| Win rate +10% (44%) | $733 | +10% |
| Cycle −10% (54 days) | $741 | +11% |
| Cycle +25% (75 days) | $533 | −20% |

Recent data shows several levers moving at once. Ebsta and Pavilion's analysis of 4.2 million opportunities found win rates fell 18% and average deal values fell 21% in 2023 against 2022, while sales cycles grew 38% against 2021 before shortening towards the end of 2023. On the formula, falls of that size compound.

Buyer behaviour explains part of the cycle effect. Forrester's 2024 survey of more than 16,000 business buyers found 13 people on average involved in a buying decision, 89% of purchases involving two or more departments, and 86% of purchases stalling during the process. Gartner's 2026 survey of 646 buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. More stakeholders and more self-directed research tend to stretch the time from first contact to close.

## How to use it without gaming it

Velocity is easy to inflate. Count unqualified leads as opportunities and it rises. Drop stalled deals from the win-rate denominator and it rises again. The safeguards are mostly about definitions.

| Input | Common distortion | Safeguard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Opportunities | Counting leads or meetings | Count only deals past a written qualification stage |
| Deal size | Using list price or one large outlier | Use median won value as a cross-check |
| Win rate | Excluding no-decision losses | Include closed-lost and no-decision in the denominator |
| Cycle length | Starting the clock at opportunity creation | Start at first meaningful contact, and state the rule |

A practical routine for a 20 to 500 person firm:

1. **Calculate it by segment.** New business and expansion, or mid-market and enterprise, usually have very different velocities.
2. **Track it monthly, on a trailing 12-month window.** Short windows swing on single deals.
3. **Change one lever at a time.** If the team tightens qualification, expect opportunities to fall and win rate to rise, and judge the change on the net.
4. **Write down the reason.** When velocity moves, record which lever moved and why. That note is more useful next year than the figure itself.

In **lowob**'s model, velocity is a reading of the commercial record. An assistant can calculate it in seconds, but it cannot fix stage definitions, missing loss reasons or rolling close dates. Those belong to whoever owns the record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Four levers, one number.** Velocity combines volume, deal size, win rate and cycle time.
- **Cycle length bites hardest.** Shortening the cycle helps slightly more than an equal gain elsewhere, and lengthening it hurts more.
- **Definitions decide the figure.** Loose qualification or excluded losses make velocity look better than it is.
- **Use it to compare trade-offs.** Its main value is showing the net effect of changing one lever.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate sales velocity?

Multiply the number of qualified opportunities by average deal size and win rate, then divide by the average sales cycle in days. The result is revenue per day.

### What is a good sales velocity?

There is no universal benchmark because it depends on deal size and segment. Compare your own figure over time and between segments.

### How can I increase sales velocity?

Raise opportunity volume, deal size or win rate, or shorten the cycle. Tighter qualification often lifts win rate and shortens cycles at the cost of fewer opportunities.

### What is the difference between sales velocity and pipeline coverage?

Coverage compares pipeline value with a target at a point in time. Velocity measures how fast pipeline converts into won revenue.

## Sources and notes

- [Pipedrive, What Is Sales Velocity and How Do You Boost It?](https://pipedrive.com/en/blog/sales-velocity), September 2026. Vendor guide; source of the formula and worked example.
- [Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks](https://www.ebsta.com/ebsta-pavilion-b2b-sales-benchmarks-2024/), 2024. Vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies.
- [Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), December 2024. Analyst press release; source of the 89% and 86% figures.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying: Companies Still Struggle To Meet Buyer Expectations](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/state-of-business-buying-2024/), December 2024, by Barbara Winters. Analyst blog; survey of more than 16,000 global business buyers.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025.

- [What Is Selling Time, and Why Do Sellers Spend So Little of It Selling?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/)
- [What Is a Closed-Lost Reason, and Why Does It Matter for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/)

## Next move

Calculate sales velocity for new business over the last 12 months, then again with no-decision losses included in the win rate. If the two figures differ by more than a fifth, your qualification stage needs a written exit rule.

# What Are AI Evals?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-27 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Evals are structured tests that measure an AI system's output against agreed criteria, using a set of real examples and a scoring method. Vendor guidance from OpenAI and Anthropic puts evals before prompt tuning or fine-tuning and warns against judging quality by feel. A small, task-specific eval set is the cheapest control a commercial team can build.

AI evals, short for evaluations, are structured tests that measure whether an AI system does a specific task well. Each eval pairs a set of realistic inputs with a way of scoring the outputs, by exact match, by a person or by another model. Evals turn "it seems to work" into a number you can track across prompt changes, model upgrades and vendors. They are the basis for deciding how much autonomy an AI tool gets.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What AI evals mean

A traditional software test checks that a function returns the right value. AI outputs vary from run to run and are often prose, so a single pass or fail rarely captures quality. An eval runs many examples and reports a score.

There are two broad kinds. Public benchmarks compare models on shared datasets, such as general knowledge or coding tests. Custom evals measure your own application on your own tasks. OpenAI's evaluation guide focuses on the second kind, and so should a commercial team. A model's benchmark rank says little about how well it drafts your renewal emails.

The UK AI Security Institute's Inspect framework shows the standard structure. A dataset holds samples, each with an input and a target answer or grading guidance. A solver produces the output, from a single model call to a full agent using tools over many turns. A scorer grades the output by text comparison, model grading or a custom scheme.

| An eval is | An eval is not |
| --- | --- |
| A fixed set of real examples with agreed scoring | A demo on a few hand-picked prompts |
| Repeated on every prompt, model or vendor change | A one-off acceptance test |
| Specific to one task and its failure modes | A general measure of model intelligence |
| A source of evidence for autonomy decisions | A guarantee of behaviour on unseen inputs |

## How evals work, and why they matter for a commercial team

Anthropic's documentation starts with success criteria. Good criteria are specific and measurable. Its example of a weak one is "the model should classify sentiments well". Its strong version names a held-out test set of 10,000 posts, an F1 score of at least 0.85 and a 5% improvement on the current baseline. Criteria commonly cover task fidelity, consistency, tone, privacy, latency and price.

OpenAI's guide sets out five stages: set an objective, collect a dataset, define metrics, run and compare, then evaluate continuously. It recommends logging during development so real cases can be mined for the eval set, and running evals on every change.

Grading is where most of the effort goes.

| Method | Strengths | Weaknesses | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Code-based | Fast, reliable, cheap at scale | Misses nuance | Did the lead get the right segment label? |
| Model-based | Fast, flexible, handles judgment | Must be validated; position and length bias | Does the brief cite only facts in the CRM record? |
| Human | Highest quality, most flexible | Slow and expensive | Would you send this proposal section? |

Anthropic advises choosing the fastest reliable method and notes that more questions with slightly noisier automated grading usually beat fewer hand-graded ones. Model graders need a detailed rubric and a constrained output, such as pass or fail. OpenAI adds that they tend to favour the first answer shown and longer answers, so they should be checked against human judgments before use.

For a revenue or operations team, evals do two jobs. They show whether a tool is good enough to adopt at all. They also show when it is good enough to move up **lowob**'s autonomy dial, from draft to act with approval, for example. Approval rate alone is a weak signal, because reviewers tire and approve more over time. An eval set gives a stable baseline that does not drift with reviewer fatigue.

## How to build a first eval

An illustrative example: a mid-size services firm wants an assistant to draft pre-meeting account briefs.

1. **Pick one task and define success.** "The brief states the correct open opportunity, the last contact date and the next step, with no facts absent from the CRM."
2. **Collect 30 to 50 real cases.** Use past meetings, including awkward ones: empty records, conflicting notes, a recent change of contact.
3. **Write the expected answer or rubric** for each case. Have the person who owns the process agree it.
4. **Choose scoring.** Code checks for the date and opportunity name; a model grader with a pass-or-fail rubric for invented facts; a human spot-check of 10%.
5. **Run and record a baseline.** Rerun on every prompt change, model upgrade or vendor switch.

Keep the eval set in your own records, not inside a vendor tool. It is the asset that lets you switch models without starting over.

## lowob takeaways

- **Evals replace impressions with scores.** A fixed set of real cases makes quality measurable.
- **Build custom, not benchmark.** Your tasks and failure modes are what matter.
- **Validate model graders.** Check them against people before trusting them at scale.
- **Own the eval set.** It is what lets you change model or vendor safely.

## Common questions

### What are evals in AI?

Evals are structured tests that run an AI system on a set of example inputs and score the outputs against agreed criteria, so quality can be measured and compared over time.

### What is the difference between an AI benchmark and an eval?

A benchmark is a public, shared test used to compare models. An eval in practice usually means a custom test built on your own tasks and data.

### What is LLM-as-a-judge?

It means using one language model to grade another's output against a rubric. It scales well, but OpenAI notes biases toward answer order and length, so validate it against human grading.

### How many examples does an AI eval need?

Enough to cover the real variety of inputs, including edge cases. Many teams start with 30 to 50 cases and grow the set as new failures appear in production.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Evaluation best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/evaluation-best-practices), accessed November 2026. Vendor guidance.
- [Anthropic, Define success criteria and build evaluations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/test-and-evaluate/develop-tests), accessed November 2026. Vendor guidance; the sentiment example is Anthropic's own.
- [UK AI Security Institute, Inspect](https://inspect.aisi.org.uk), accessed November 2026. Government-backed open-source framework.
- The account brief example and the link to autonomy levels are **lowob**'s illustration and working method.

## Related research

- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [Top 5 LLM Observability and Evaluation Platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/)

## Next move

Choose the one AI task your team relies on most and write down 30 past cases with the output you would have accepted. Score your current setup against them and keep the result as a baseline.
