# AI Agents in Partners and Distribution: What Works and What Leaks

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-partners-and-distribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-26 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Partner work runs across two companies' records, which is why agents leak value here faster than anywhere else on the commercial line. Of nine partner and distribution tasks in the lowob directory, five are rated high reliability, all internal drafting or monitoring. The tasks that touch credit, conflict and terms need written rules first. Start with marketplace monitoring, enablement packs and quarterly review preparation.

Partner and distribution work is a good place for AI agents to draft and monitor, and a poor place for them to decide. Of the nine partner tasks in the **lowob** directory, five are rated high reliability, and every one of those is internal drafting or monitoring. The tasks that settle who gets credit, which partner owns a deal, or what terms are on offer depend on rules that most partner programmes have never written down. An agent cannot apply a rule that does not exist. Start with marketplace monitoring, enablement packs and quarterly review preparation, and write the rules of engagement before you automate attribution or conflict.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

Partner programmes are growing in both size and weight. Forrester's July 2025 analysis of its Partner Ecosystem Marketing Survey found 67% of respondents expected indirect revenue, meaning revenue transacted by partners, to grow above or significantly above the prior year. Canalys forecast in August 2024 that software sold through hyperscaler cloud marketplaces would rise from US$16 billion in 2023 to US$85 billion by 2028, with more than half flowing through the channel by 2027.

That growth arrives with a measurement problem. Forrester's September 2025 note on partner attribution argued that attribution is broken in most B2B organisations, because legacy models count sourced revenue and miss the influence of alliances, integrators and technical partners. Agents are being offered as the fix. In most programmes they will make the problem faster rather than smaller, unless the rules come first.

## Why partner work leaks

A sales agent works inside one company's CRM. A partner agent works across a boundary. The partner holds half the relationship, half the pipeline view and, often, the customer's trust. The agent sees your records and the partner's submissions, which arrive as forms, emails, portal entries and marketplace notifications.

Three things leak across that boundary.

**Credit.** When two partners touch the same account, or a partner and a direct seller both claim a deal, the answer depends on rules of engagement. Where those rules are verbal, the agent will apply whatever pattern it finds in past records, which usually means the pattern of whoever complained loudest last quarter.

**Terms.** Partner economics are specific. On AWS Marketplace, for example, a channel partner private offer starts with a selling authorisation in which the software vendor sets the wholesale cost as a discount from list, and the channel partner then sets the buyer's price by marking it up. An agent drafting partner outreach that invents or rounds those terms creates a commitment nobody approved.

**Context.** Partner managers carry the relationship in their heads: who is frustrated, which co-sell promise slipped, what the partner's own leadership cares about this year. None of it is in the CRM. An agent preparing a quarterly review from records alone produces something accurate and slightly wrong.

> An agent cannot apply a rule of engagement that exists only in the partner manager's memory.

## The nine tasks, rated

The table walks every partner and distribution task in the [**lowob** Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/), with the brain layer each one depends on most. The layers are the five parts of the loop we use across this library: store (where the data sits), context (the wiring that brings it to the agent), record (decisions with reason, owner and status), reasoning (the model and agent) and learning (outcomes written back).

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control | Brain plug point |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research and rank potential partners | 1 Draft | Medium | Partners chosen on surface signals | Human selection; record the reasoning | Record |
| Draft partner outreach | 1 Draft | High | Overpromising terms | Approved terms only | Context |
| Track referrals and attribute partner-sourced deals | 3 Act and report | Medium | Disputes over credit | Agreed attribution rules | Record |
| Prepare partner quarterly reviews | 1 Draft | High | Missing context from the relationship | Partner manager edits | Store |
| Monitor marketplace listings and reviews | 3 Act and report | High | Missed negative signal | Weekly human read | Context |
| Respond to marketplace leads | 1 Draft | Medium | Slow or wrong first response | Queue with response-time alert | Reasoning |
| Draft co-marketing content | 1 Draft | High | Partner brand or claims breach | Both parties approve | Context |
| Detect channel conflict on a deal | 3 Act and report | Medium | Two partners claim the same deal | Rules of engagement written down | Record |
| Prepare partner onboarding and enablement packs | 1 Draft | High | Inconsistent messaging across partners | Approved enablement kit as the only source | Store |

The pattern is clean. The five high-reliability tasks are drafts or monitoring, built from material the company already controls: approved terms, an enablement kit, marketplace pages, partner performance data. The four medium tasks share a dependency on something outside the agent's reach: a selection judgement, a credit rule, a conflict rule, or a fast response to a stranger. Three of the four map to the record layer, which is the layer partner programmes most often lack.

## Five tasks that decide whether it works

Not every row carries the same weight. These five decide whether an agent makes the partner programme more trusted or less.

### Track referrals and attribute partner-sourced deals

This is the task partner leaders most want automated, and the one most likely to start an argument. The agent can match referral submissions to opportunities, timestamp them and apply a rule. It cannot invent the rule. Forrester's four-step path for fixing attribution (discover the strategy, define partner types, assign values to each type, align metrics) is a human design exercise. Run it first, write the result down as the attribution rules, and let the agent apply them at level 3 with a weekly report of every attribution it made and why. When a partner disputes a call, the dispute and its resolution go into the record, so the next run sees the precedent.

### Detect channel conflict on a deal

Conflict detection is a matching problem with a policy on top. Matching two registrations against the same account is well within an agent's reach. Deciding which partner wins is policy, and the agent should only flag. The control in the directory is plain: rules of engagement written down. In practice that means a one-page document covering registration windows, what counts as an approved registration, how ties are broken and who arbitrates. Without it, the agent's flags are noise and its silences are dangerous. Our explainer on [deal registration](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-deal-registration/) covers the mechanics.

### Respond to marketplace leads

Marketplace leads arrive from buyers who are often comparing several listings at once, so speed matters. That pressure tempts teams to let an agent reply directly. Keep it at level 1: the agent drafts the first response within minutes, places it in a queue, and an alert fires if nobody has approved it within the agreed response time. Two reasons. A wrong first answer on price or availability is public to that buyer and hard to retract. And the inbound message is untrusted content. Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta" names the dangerous combination: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. An auto-replying marketplace agent with CRM access holds all three.

### Draft partner outreach

Rated high reliability because the drafting is easy. The risk is the content of the offer. The control, approved terms only, means the agent reads terms from a maintained source (margin tiers, marketplace discount structures, co-sell commitments) and never generates them. If a partner asks for something outside the approved set, the draft says so and routes the request to the partner manager. That routing is where the record gains a new decision.

### Monitor marketplace listings and reviews

A good level 3 task: frequent, internal and checkable. The agent watches your listings, competitors' listings and reviews, and reports changes weekly. The main risk is a missed negative signal, which the weekly human read covers. One boundary matters. The agent monitors and summarises reviews; it does not write them or solicit them on its own. The US Federal Trade Commission's final rule on consumer reviews, announced in August 2024, bans fake and AI-generated reviews, insider reviews without clear disclosure, and conditioning compensation on positive sentiment, and lets the FTC seek civil penalties against knowing violators.

## Where each task plugs into the brain

Partner tasks lean harder on the record than any other function in the directory, because partner disputes are decided by precedent. This table shows what each layer must hold before the tasks that depend on it can run.

| Brain layer | What it must hold for partner work | Tasks that depend on it | What breaks without it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Store | Partner performance data, registrations, enablement kit, marketplace listings | Quarterly reviews; enablement packs | Reviews built from partial data |
| Context | Approved terms, brand and claims rules for both parties, marketplace feeds | Outreach; co-marketing; listing monitoring | Terms invented; partner brand misused |
| Record | Attribution rules, rules of engagement, past disputes and their resolutions, partner selection reasons | Attribution; conflict detection; partner ranking | The agent applies last quarter's argument as policy |
| Reasoning | Agent identity, tool scope, response-time alerts, separation of read and write permissions | Marketplace leads; all level 3 tasks | Untrusted inbound content drives actions |
| Learning | Which partners recruited on which reasons went on to produce revenue; which disputes recurred | Partner ranking; attribution rules | The same selection mistakes repeat |

The learning row is the one almost nobody builds. When an agent ranks potential partners, the ranking is a draft and the selection is a decision. Record the reasons at selection, and twelve months later write back what the partner produced. That is how the next ranking stops relying on surface signals such as logo size or social following. Our piece on [integrators, OEMs and channel partners](https://lowob.com/research/integrators-oems-and-channel-partners/) covers which partner types tend to produce revenue and which produce activity.

## Start here: three tasks in order

Choose first tasks that are frequent, checkable, low in blast radius and disliked, the four tests from [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/). In partner work, three pass cleanly.

| Order | Task | Level | Why it goes here | What to measure for four weeks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Monitor marketplace listings and reviews | 3 Act and report | Internal, weekly, no partner or buyer contact | Changes caught; negative signals found by the agent versus by people |
| 2 | Prepare partner onboarding and enablement packs | 1 Draft | Forces you to name one approved kit, which every later task needs | Time to onboard a partner; messaging inconsistencies found on review |
| 3 | Prepare partner quarterly reviews | 1 Draft | Builds the store and exposes what the records miss | Partner manager edit time; facts added from memory that belong in the record |

The third task does double duty. Every fact a partner manager adds by hand to the agent's draft is a fact that should have been in the store or the record. Log those additions for a month and you have the specification for your partner data.

Attribution and conflict detection come after these, and only once the rules are written and signed by the head of partnerships and the head of sales. Marketplace lead response comes when you have an approval queue with an alert and a clear separation between the agent that reads inbound messages and any system that can send.

Illustrative example: writing the rules before automating attribution

Decision
:   Defer an agent that would auto-attribute partner-sourced deals; first write attribution rules and rules of engagement, then run the agent at level 3 with a weekly report.

Reason and owner
:   Two partners had claimed the same three deals in one quarter and there was no written tie-break rule; an agent would have applied whichever pattern dominated past records. Owned by the head of partnerships, with sales leadership co-signing the rules.

What changed
:   The agent's first month of attributions produced two disputes instead of a recurring dozen, and both resolutions were recorded as precedent for the next run.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size software vendor selling through resellers and a cloud marketplace, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Draft and monitor first.** The five high-reliability partner tasks are all internal drafting or monitoring.
- **Write the rules before you automate them.** Attribution and conflict agents apply policy; they cannot create it.
- **Treat partner and marketplace inputs as untrusted.** Keep the agent that reads them away from anything that sends.
- **Record selection reasons and write back results.** That is how partner ranking improves beyond surface signals.

Gateway card

### Before a partner agent goes live

- Approved terms and enablement kit named as the only sources the agent may draw from
- Attribution rules and rules of engagement written and signed
- Inbound partner and marketplace content handled by an agent with read-only access
- Every client- or partner-facing draft routed to a named partner manager
- A weekly report of every attribution, conflict flag and listing change

## Common questions

### Can AI agents manage a partner programme?

Not end to end. Agents reliably draft outreach, enablement packs, co-marketing and quarterly reviews, and they monitor marketplace listings well. Partner selection, credit disputes and terms stay with people.

### Can an AI agent handle partner attribution?

It can apply attribution rules at scale and report every decision, but only once those rules are written and agreed. Without written rules it repeats whatever pattern is in past records.

### Should an AI agent reply to marketplace leads automatically?

Not yet. Have it draft a first response within minutes and queue it for approval with a response-time alert. Automatic replies combine untrusted inbound content with external communication, which is a known security risk.

### How do AI agents detect channel conflict?

By matching deal registrations from different partners against the same account and flagging overlaps. The agent flags; a person applies the rules of engagement and decides.

# What Is a Computer-Use Agent?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-computer-use-agent/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-26 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A computer-use agent reads screenshots and decides where to click and what to type, so it can work in software with no API. Benchmarks show it well below human success rates, and anything on screen can try to instruct it. Providers advise an isolated machine, minimal access and a person confirming every consequential action.

A computer-use agent is an AI agent that operates software the way a person does: it looks at screenshots and decides where to click, what to type and when to scroll. It can work in applications that have no API or connector. It is also slower, less reliable and more exposed to manipulation than an agent working through APIs. Providers advise running it on an isolated machine with minimal access, and asking a person to confirm anything with real-world consequences.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a computer-use agent means

Most agents act through [function calls](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-function-calling/): structured requests to an API, a database or an [MCP](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/) server. A computer-use agent acts through the screen. Microsoft's documentation describes the loop in three stages. Perception captures a screenshot. Reasoning judges the current state against the goal. Action clicks, types or scrolls. The loop repeats until the task is done or needs a person.

Anthropic's documentation is explicit that the model never touches the machine. The application receives the model's requests, translates them into actions in its own computing environment, captures screenshots and returns them. The available actions include taking a screenshot, zooming, clicking, dragging, scrolling, typing and pressing keys.

|  | API-based agent | Computer-use agent | RPA robot |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How it acts | Structured calls to APIs and tools | Clicks and keystrokes chosen from screenshots | Scripted clicks and keystrokes |
| Needs an API | Yes | No | No |
| When a screen changes | Not affected | Often copes, by reading the new screen | Usually breaks |
| Speed | Fast | Slow | Fast |
| Predictability | High | Low to medium | High |
| Main risk | Excessive permissions | Instructions hidden on screen; wrong clicks | Silent failure after a layout change |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The appeal is reach. Many commercial teams still depend on systems with no usable API, such as a partner portal or an old quoting tool. Microsoft describes computer use as "especially useful in scenarios where APIs aren't available". Unlike [robotic process automation](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-robotic-process-automation/), it can cope with a button that has moved.

The evidence on reliability is sobering. OSWorld tested agents on 369 tasks in real operating systems and applications. At publication in April 2024, humans completed 72.36% and the best model 12.24%. Most failures came from locating elements on screen and from operational knowledge. OpenAI's Computer-Using Agent, announced in January 2025, reached 38.1% on OSWorld and 58.1% on the browser benchmark WebArena, against human scores of 72.4% and 78.2%. Scores have risen since, but public benchmarks rarely match a firm's own screens.

Providers' own limitations lists agree. Anthropic warns that the model "might make mistakes or hallucinate when outputting specific coordinates", that reliability may be lower in niche applications, and that it may be too slow compared with a person. Microsoft notes its tool can struggle with dropdowns, date pickers and custom widgets, and "might repeat actions or get stuck". In OpenAI's own examples, one text-editing task succeeded 4 times in 10.

It is also costly in tokens. Anthropic's pricing page, accessed 16 November 2026, lists about 4,520 tokens of overhead for its computer-use toolset definition, before any screenshots are added.

Security is the larger issue. A computer-use agent reads everything on screen, including text placed there by others. Anthropic's documentation states that instructions on webpages or in images "might override your instructions". It now scans screenshots with classifiers for [prompt injection](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/), but says its other precautions remain important. Microsoft warns that pauses for clarification "might not trigger in every situation where a person would want a pause", and that they should not be relied on as a fail-safe.

This is why **lowob** places computer use low on the [autonomy dial](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/). Reading a portal and drafting what it found is level 0 or 1. Submitting an order, a form or a message has consequences, so it sits at level 2 at most, with a named person approving each one. OpenAI's agent asked for confirmation before submitting orders or sending email and declined banking transactions. Anthropic advises confirmation before financial transactions or agreeing to terms of service.

## How to pilot one safely

| Control | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Isolated machine | A dedicated virtual machine or container, never a person's own laptop |
| Least-privilege account | Its own login, read-only where possible; see [agent identity](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/) |
| No credentials in reach | Anthropic advises against giving the model login details |
| Domain allowlist | Only the sites the task needs |
| Approval before submit | A person confirms every form, order or message at an [approval gate](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) |
| Logs and screenshots kept | Every action reviewable after the run |
| API first | If an API or connector exists, use it instead |

Start with a read-only task, such as collecting order status from a partner portal into a draft summary.

## lowob takeaways

- **It works through the screen.** Screenshots in, clicks and keystrokes out.
- **Reach comes at a price.** Slower and less reliable than API-based agents.
- **The screen can carry instructions.** Treat on-screen content as untrusted.
- **Isolate it and gate its actions.** A separate machine, minimal access and a person approving every submission.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a computer-use agent and RPA?

RPA follows a recorded script and breaks when a screen changes. A computer-use agent decides each step from a screenshot, so it adapts to changes but is slower and less predictable.

### How accurate are computer-use agents?

Below human level on public benchmarks. OSWorld's original paper reported 12.24% for the best model against over 72% for humans, and OpenAI reported 38.1% for its agent in January 2025. Test on your own tasks.

### Is it safe to let an AI agent use my computer?

Not directly. Providers advise a dedicated virtual machine with minimal privileges, no stored credentials, a domain allowlist and human confirmation for consequential actions.

### When should I use computer use instead of an API?

Only when no API or connector exists and the task cannot wait for one. Where an API exists, it is faster, uses fewer tokens and is easier to control.

## Sources and notes

- [Xie et al., OSWorld: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents for Open-Ended Tasks in Real Computer Environments](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.07972), April 2024. Academic benchmark; scores reflect models available at publication.
- [OpenAI, Computer-Using Agent](https://openai.com/index/computer-using-agent/), 23 January 2025. Vendor-reported benchmark results.
- [Anthropic, Computer use tool](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/computer-use-tool), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; the feature is labelled beta.
- [Microsoft, FAQ for computer use in Copilot Studio](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-copilot-studio/faqs-computer-use), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Pricing (Claude API documentation)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor list prices and token overheads; change often.

## Related research

- [What Is Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in the Age of Agents?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-robotic-process-automation/)
- [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/)
- [What Is an AI Autonomy Level?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is a Multi-Agent System?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-multi-agent-system/)

## Next move

List the systems your commercial team uses that have no API or connector. For the one used most, run a computer-use agent read-only on a separate virtual machine for a week, and compare its summaries with a person's.

# Qualification Frameworks Compared

Source: https://lowob.com/research/qualification-frameworks-compared/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Qualification frameworks are lists of questions a seller must answer before a deal is worth forecasting. They differ in what they test: the buyer's capacity to buy, the buying process or the urgency of the problem. Benchmark data suggests the framework matters less than whether it is used consistently and tied to stage rules. The choice should follow the shape of the deal.

A sales qualification framework is a fixed set of questions a seller must answer, with evidence from the buyer, before a deal is treated as real. The common ones test different things. BANT checks whether the buyer can buy now. CHAMP starts from the buyer's problem. MEDDICC maps how the buying organisation will decide. SPICED tests whether the problem is urgent enough to act on. Benchmark data suggests that teams which apply any framework consistently outperform those which do not, and that the framework matters less than whether its answers decide stage movement. Pick the one that matches the deal you sell, then make every letter a field.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most sales teams have a qualification framework in name. Fewer have one in practice. The letters appear in onboarding slides and in the pipeline review, but the CRM holds a stage, an amount and a close date, and the qualification is in the seller's head.

The choice of framework is usually made by whoever joined from a firm that used one. This piece compares the main frameworks by what they actually test, sets out what the evidence says about using them, and gives a way to choose. The explainers on [MEDDICC](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-meddicc/) and [BANT](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-bant/) cover each framework's elements in detail; this piece does not repeat them.

## The problem qualification has to solve

Qualification exists because selling time is scarce and most opportunities do not close. Two features of current B2B buying make it harder than it was.

The first is the size of the buying group. Forrester's *State of Business Buying 2024*, a survey of more than 16,000 business buyers, found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, with 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments and 86% stalling at some point. Forrester also reported that 81% of buyers were dissatisfied with the provider they chose. A framework that asks only whether "the decision maker" is engaged is asking about one person in thirteen.

The second is that buyers do much of their evaluation without a seller present. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Qualification signals that once came from conversation now have to be inferred from fewer, later meetings.

Forrester has argued for some time that the unit of qualification should be the buying group, not the lead. Its analysts report that fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, and that clients who delivered three or more buying group members to sales saw a 50% increase in meeting-to-closed-won conversion.

## What each framework tests

The frameworks are not competing answers to one question. Each was built for a different kind of deal, and each tests a different risk.

| Framework | Elements | What it tests | Fits best | Main gap |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| BANT | Budget, Authority, Need, Timeline | Whether this buyer can buy now | Transactional and mid-market deals with one or two decision makers | Assumes a known budget and a single authority; weak on buying groups |
| CHAMP | Challenges, Authority, Money, Prioritisation | Whether the problem is real and ranked, before money is discussed | Solution sales where budget is created after the problem is agreed | Light on how the buyer will decide |
| MEDDICC and MEDDPICC | Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, (Paper process), Identify or implicate pain, Champion, Competition | How the buying organisation will decide and sign | Complex enterprise deals with several functions and procurement | Slower to complete; can become a form-filling exercise |
| SPICED | Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical event, Decision | Whether the problem is urgent enough to act on now | Recurring-revenue sales where the case for change is the hard part | Less explicit about procurement and competition |

MEDDIC was developed at PTC in 1996, according to the training firm that now teaches it, and later gained Competition and Paper Process to become MEDDPICC. Its own definition of Paper Process, the steps from decision to signature, describes it as where many deals are lost, usually in legal and procurement. That is the clearest sign of the framework's purpose: it was built to make a forecast survive contact with a buyer's contracting process.

SPICED, associated with the consultancy Winning by Design, puts the critical event, the date by which the buyer must act, at the centre. BANT's Timeline element asks a similar question, but SPICED asks why the date exists, which is the better test of whether it will hold.

## What the evidence says about using them

Independent evidence comparing frameworks head to head is thin. The most detailed public data comes from Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmark, a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities and more than a million hours of recorded conversations across 530 companies. Its figures are relative multipliers without published baselines, so treat them as direction rather than measurement.

| Finding (Ebsta and Pavilion, 2023 data) | Figure reported |
| --- | --- |
| Top performers following a qualification methodology effectively | 588% more likely than others |
| Top performers with the economic buyer engaged before the solution was presented | 489% more likely |
| Meetings and contacts to reach above 80% completion, SPICED | 4.7 meetings, 3.4 contacts |
| Meetings and contacts to reach above 80% completion, MEDDPICC | 5.6 meetings, 5.2 contacts |
| Win likelihood for deals completing the framework by the solution stage | SPICED 307% more likely, MEDDPICC 324% more likely |
| Effect of spending 50% longer than average in qualification | 120% more likely to slip |

Two readings follow. First, the gap between the two frameworks' win effects is small next to the gap between completing one and not completing either. Consistency matters more than the choice. Second, MEDDPICC asks for more contacts because it maps more of the buying group. That is its cost and its point: if the deal really involves 13 people, a framework that completes after three contacts has probably missed some.

The evidence also shows what no framework covers well. Dixon and McKenna's research on about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found that 40 to 60% of lost deals were lost to indecision, with about half of all losses ending in no decision. Calls with high buyer indecision were won about 6% of the time. A buyer can pass every letter of MEDDICC and still fail to decide. Pain, critical events and champions are proxies for decisiveness; none measures it.

> The framework matters less than the rule that a deal cannot move stage until its answers are written down.

## How to choose

The choice should follow the shape of the deals, not the background of the sales leader. Three questions settle most cases.

How many people sign? If one or two people decide and buy within a quarter, BANT or CHAMP is enough, and MEDDPICC will slow sellers down for little gain. If several functions and procurement are involved, a framework that maps the decision process and paper process earns its extra meetings.

Where are deals lost? Look at the last two quarters of closed-lost reasons (see [What is a closed-lost reason?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/)). If deals die in procurement, Paper Process matters. If they die in no decision, the critical event and the size of the impact matter more. If they die on price, the economic buyer and metrics were probably never established.

What can the team sustain? A seven-element framework that sellers complete halfway is worse than a four-element one they complete fully. Ebsta's completion figures suggest that the bigger framework needs about one more meeting and two more contacts per deal.

Some firms run two: a light framework for smaller deals and a full one above a deal-size threshold. That works if the threshold is written down and the CRM enforces which fields apply.

## Make every letter a field

A framework changes outcomes only when it governs stage movement. The practical build has four parts, and each one is a small change to the CRM rather than a training programme.

Each element becomes a field with a short evidence note, not a tick box. "Economic buyer: identified" says little; "Economic buyer: CFO, met 12 March, confirmed budget owner" can be checked.

Stage exit criteria name the elements that must be complete before a deal moves. The explainer on [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) covers how to write them. A deal in the proposal stage with no decision criteria recorded is a forecast risk, and the CRM should show it.

Disqualification is recorded as a decision. When a seller drops an opportunity, the reason, owner and date go on the record. That turns qualification from a filter into data: after a quarter, the firm can see which elements most often fail and in which segments. This is the decision-record discipline from [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) applied to the earliest decision in the funnel.

Completion is reviewed against outcomes. Once a quarter, compare framework completion on won deals with completion on lost ones. If they look the same, the framework is being filled in after the fact.

Illustrative example: changing frameworks by deal size

Decision
:   Replace a single BANT checklist with BANT below a set deal size and MEDDPICC above it.

Reason and owner
:   Closed-lost review showed most large deals dying in procurement and no decision, neither of which BANT tests. Agreed by the revenue leader; owned by revenue operations.

What changed
:   Paper process and critical event became required fields for large deals before the proposal stage. The firm agreed to review win rates by band after two quarters before deciding whether to keep the split.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size software firm selling to mid-market and enterprise buyers, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose by deal shape.** BANT and CHAMP suit small buying groups; MEDDPICC suits deals that pass through procurement; SPICED suits deals where urgency is the hard part.
- **Consistency beats selection.** The benchmark gap between using a framework and not using one is far larger than the gap between frameworks.
- **No framework tests indecision.** Track no-decision losses separately and treat critical events and impact as the nearest proxies.
- **Fields, not slides.** Each element needs an evidence note and a role in stage exit criteria.

Gateway card

### Before you adopt or change a qualification framework

- Last two quarters of closed-lost reasons grouped by where deals died
- Typical number of people involved in your buyers' decisions, by segment
- One framework chosen per deal band, with the band threshold written down
- Each element added as a CRM field with an evidence note
- Stage exit criteria updated to name required elements
- A quarterly review comparing framework completion on won and lost deals

## Common questions

### What is the difference between BANT and MEDDICC?

BANT checks whether a buyer has the budget, authority, need and timeline to buy now. MEDDICC maps how the buying organisation will decide, including its metrics, economic buyer, criteria, process, pain, champion and competitors, and suits complex deals with several decision makers.

### Which sales qualification framework is best?

None is best for every deal. Lighter frameworks such as BANT suit small buying groups and short cycles, while MEDDPICC suits enterprise deals that pass through procurement. Applying one consistently matters more than which one you choose.

### What does SPICED stand for in sales?

SPICED stands for Situation, Pain, Impact, Critical event and Decision. It focuses on whether the buyer's problem is urgent enough to act on by a specific date.

### How do you make a sales team actually use a qualification framework?

Turn each element into a CRM field with an evidence note, make named elements a condition for moving a deal to the next stage, and review framework completion on won and lost deals each quarter.

## Sources and notes

Take the last ten deals your team lost and mark, for each, which framework element was missing or wrong at the time. The element that appears most often is the one your current framework, or your use of it, is not testing.

# The Humans Carrying Context Are the Price Signal

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-humans-carrying-context-are-the-price-signal/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Enterprises are paying forward-deployed engineers to carry the context their software cannot hold, and that spending is the clearest market price for a missing organisational record. Spend data shows the context layer underfunded relative to models. The fix is not removing the people but making their context a client-owned deliverable.

Enterprises are paying expensive people to carry the context their software cannot hold. Forward-deployed engineers, embedded consultants and integration teams spend most of their time on how a particular client's world works, not on models. That spending is the clearest market price for the missing layer, and the clearest specification of what it should contain. The practical move is not to remove the people but to make sure their context does not leave with them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## Read the role as a price

In our reading of the market, the forward-deployed engineer has become a standard part of how many AI vendors and integrators deliver. An engineer sits with the client, learns how the work is actually done, and makes the product function inside it. The role is expensive, and organisations keep paying for it.

Read that as a price. Organisations are paying, at high rates, for people whose job is to understand how a particular client's world works. Ashu Garg's December 2025 essay on context graphs makes the general point about every such role: "The org chart creates a role to carry the context that software doesn't capture." His examples are the support lead whose cross-system synthesis happens in their head, and the vice-president's approval given on a call or in a direct message. Neither reaches a system of record. "Salesforce knows what happened. It doesn't know why."

## What these people actually carry

Watch what a forward-deployed engineer spends their time on, and very little of it is model work. It is context. That list is a specification: it is what a durable organisational record would hold, if one existed. The engineer is, functionally, a walking judgment layer.

| What the engineer carries | Where it should live | Example entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| How the data is actually shaped, as opposed to how the documentation says it is | Data quirks register | "Region field blank for accounts migrated before 2023; use billing country" |
| Which definitions differ between teams, and which is authoritative | Shared definitions | "Active customer: finance uses paid in 90 days; success uses logged in in 30" |
| Which exceptions matter and which are noise | Exceptions log | "Discounts above cap allowed for multi-year renewals, approved by the CFO" |
| What was tried before, and why it did not stick | Graveyard | "Automated renewal emails, stopped after complaints from top accounts" |
| Who decides what, and who must be consulted | Decision rights | "Pricing exceptions: head of sales decides, finance consulted" |
| Decisions made during the engagement, with reasons | Decision records | Status, reason, owner, date, what would change it |

Martin Fowler's description of an architecture decision record is a useful model for the last row. It captures the decision, its context, the alternatives and the consequences, so that people joining later can understand "why the system is constructed in the way that it is". Our explainers on [decision precedent](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) and [systems of record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/) cover the rest.

> The engineer is, functionally, a walking judgment layer. The question is whether anything is left when they walk.

## The spend split says the same

Menlo Ventures' bottom-up estimate of 2025 enterprise generative AI spend put $12.5 billion on foundation model APIs, and $1.5 billion on the infrastructure that "manages the storage, retrieval, and orchestration of data that connects LLMs to enterprise systems". Another $4.0 billion went on model training infrastructure. The estimate excludes chips, cloud inference and AI features built into existing software, and it reflects one investor's model of a US survey of 495 decision-makers, so the precise ratio should not be leaned on.

The direction is the point. The layer that holds context is funded at roughly an eighth of the models it feeds, and labour is filling the gap. Our walkthrough of [the context layer through one account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/) shows what that layer does when it is built.

## Why this context is so hard to keep

Economists have a name for this kind of asset. Erik Brynjolfsson, Daniel Rock and Chad Syverson argue that general-purpose technologies such as AI require large investments in complementary intangibles, including new processes, business models and worker skills, and that official statistics capture these poorly even when they create valuable firm assets. Context held by a deployment team is exactly such an intangible. It is built at real cost, it makes the technology work, and it appears on no balance sheet.

It is also fragile in a specific way. Group research going back to Stasser and Titus in 1985 shows that information held by only one member of a group is the least likely to be raised and recorded. Knowledge that lives in one engineer's head does not spread by being in the building.

And it cannot simply be poured into a model. Anthropic's engineering guidance treats context as "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns" and advises finding "the smallest set of high-signal tokens" for each task. A transcript of everything the engineer ever said is not context. A structured record of definitions, exceptions and decisions is.

## Convert context into a deliverable

**If you buy forward-deployed work,** make the context record a contractual deliverable: a documented set of definitions, exceptions, data quirks, decisions and their reasons, owned by you and maintained throughout the engagement, not written in the final week. Measure the engagement partly by what it leaves behind. Our [build vs buy guide](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) covers the wider contract questions.

**If you sell it,** measure how much faster your second deployment in a similar client is than your first, and why. If the answer is "because the same engineer remembered", the knowledge is still in a head, not a product. The risk is familiar from every services-heavy software model: high revenue, low margins, and growth limited by hiring.

| Measure | Buyer or seller | What a good result looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Context record delivered and current | Buyer | Updated monthly, owned by a named client employee |
| Time to productive use for a new engineer on the same account | Buyer | Falls with each rotation |
| Second-deployment speed in a familiar segment | Seller | Faster, and explained by the record, not by the person |
| Share of client questions answered from the record | Both | Rising across the engagement |

## What would prove this wrong

Forward-deployed demand falling sharply as products mature, without any durable context record being built. Then the labour was transitional integration, not a missing layer.

## lowob takeaways

- **The role is a price signal.** Paying people to carry context is paying for a layer that does not exist yet.
- **Their work is a specification.** Data quirks, definitions, exceptions, history and decision rights are what the record needs.
- **The context layer is underfunded.** One 2025 estimate put it at about an eighth of model API spend.
- **Own the record.** Make it a named, client-owned deliverable, and treat context in one head as an operational risk.

## Common questions

### What does a forward-deployed engineer actually do?

Works inside the client to make a product function there. Most of the time goes on context: how the client's data is really shaped, which definitions differ between teams, which exceptions matter, what was tried before, and who decides what.

### Why are companies paying for forward-deployed engineers?

Because their software cannot hold the organisation's context, so people carry it instead. That spend is effectively the price of a missing organisational record.

### How do I keep knowledge when a consultant or deployment engineer leaves?

Make a client-owned context record a contractual deliverable, structured as definitions, exceptions, data quirks, decisions with reasons and open questions, and maintained throughout the engagement.

### How can vendors tell whether deployment knowledge is in the product or in people?

Measure how much faster the second deployment in a similar client is than the first. If it is faster because the same engineer remembered, the knowledge is still in a head.

## Sources and notes

- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/), 9 December 2025. Investor research; US survey of 495 decision-makers and a bottom-up market model; excludes chips and cloud inference.
- [Ashu Garg, AI's trillion-dollar opportunity: Context graphs](https://ashugarg.substack.com/p/ais-trillion-dollar-opportunity-context), 26 December 2025. Investor essay; argument, not evidence, and the investor backs companies in this space.
- [Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson, The Productivity J-Curve](https://www.nber.org/papers/w25148), NBER Working Paper 25148, 2018, revised 2020. Economy-wide analysis, not a study of deployment teams.
- [Stasser and Titus, Pooling of unshared information in group decision making](https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/stasser_titus_unsharedinfogroupdisc_jpsp1985.pdf), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, 1985. Laboratory experiment with student groups.
- [Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference.
- The context and measures tables are **lowob**'s framework; example entries are illustrative.

## Related research

- [What Is Context Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/)
- [What Is Decision Precedent in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/)
- [Build vs Buy AI Agents: A Decision Guide for Mid-Size Firms](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/)
- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)

## Next move

If you have an integrator or deployment team on site, ask them this week for a one-page list of the data quirks and exceptions they have learned. If they cannot produce it, that is the deliverable to add to the contract.

# "We Shipped Everything and the Number Went Down"

Source: https://lowob.com/research/we-shipped-everything-and-the-number-went-down/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: If the product is proven and the core number still fell, the problem has moved to distribution. Most shipped features are rarely used and most ideas do not move the metric, so more releases are not the fix. Stop building for sixty days, name one lead story you can prove, work one channel, usually partners who already have your buyer, and report the number with and without incentives.

The product is proven and the number still fell, so the problem has moved to distribution; stop building, name one story, and work one channel. Shipping more is rarely the fix. Pendo's analysis of 615 software products found 80% of features were rarely or never used, and at Microsoft only about a third of tested ideas improved the metric they targeted. Supply went up. Demand did not follow, because nobody was working demand.

## What it usually means

The call comes after a big month of releases. The team moved fast. The core number (deposits, weekly active teams or paid seats) went down anyway.

Three things are usually true at once.

First, the product objection is dead. The thing works. It has worked for real users, repeatedly, across versions. Nobody who churned said it was broken.

Second, there is no lead story. The team has been telling three stories to three audiences. Each one is plausible. Together they cancel out. A buyer who hears three reasons to care hears none.

Third, shipping was the comfortable work. A release is visible, finite and hard to criticise. Distribution is slow, repetitive and easy to criticise. Given the choice, most teams build.

An onchain protocol launches a dozen new markets in a month and deposits fall. An AI product adds an integration every week while weekly active teams stay flat. The pattern is the same. Supply went up. Demand did not follow, because nobody was working demand.

This is a good month, even if it does not feel like one. It removes an explanation. The team can no longer say the product is not ready.

## Why more releases do not move the number

The evidence on shipped features is consistent. Pendo, a product analytics vendor, aggregated three months of usage across 615 customer products in its 2019 Feature Adoption Report. About 12% of features generated 80% of daily usage, and 80% of features were rarely or never used. The sample is Pendo's own customers and the definition of a feature is a tagged part of an interface, so the exact figure is soft. The shape is not: most of what a team ships is not what users come for.

Controlled experiments say the same about ideas in general. Kohavi and Thomke reported in *Harvard Business Review* in 2017 that about a third of Microsoft's experiments improved their target metric, a third were neutral and a third made it worse. At Google and Bing the positive share was 10% to 20%. Those teams measure each change. A team that ships twelve unmeasured changes in a month has no way to know which of them hurt, and some probably did.

| Signal | What it suggests |
| --- | --- |
| Churned users say the product works | The product objection is dead |
| Three audiences hear three stories | No lead story; messages cancel out |
| Releases up, core number flat or down | Supply added without demand work |
| New markets or integrations with no named partner behind them | Releases went out into no channel |
| Number moves only when incentives run | The market will take it, not pay for it |

## Where it traces to

This traces to [Part 1](https://lowob.com/research/you-dont-have-three-problems/) and [Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/).

[Part 1](https://lowob.com/research/you-dont-have-three-problems/) asked for one system, not three problems. One named buyer, one calendar, one owner. A team running three stories has skipped this. The shipping cadence filled the gap where the buyer definition should have been.

[Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) covered distribution when platforms are closed. The channel sort (open, restricted, closed) was meant to be done before the roadmap was set. If it was never done, releases went out into no channel at all.

In crypto this also traces to Parts 19 and 20. New markets without [issuers, integrations and curators](https://lowob.com/research/issuers-integrations-and-curators/) lined up are supply with no demand. Protocol revenue does not follow from more venues. It follows from the venues that already have the depositor.

In AI it traces to [Part 13](https://lowob.com/research/developers-marketplaces-and-the-answer-engines/). A shallow integration is not distribution. The partner who already has the team is.

## The first move this week

Stop building for sixty days. Fixes and security work continue. New features do not. Put it in writing so the team knows it is a decision, not a mood.

Name one lead story. Not the best one, the one you can prove. Write it in a sentence a partner could repeat without you in the room.

Pick one channel band and work it exclusively. For most teams at this point it is partners who already have your buyer. They have the trust and the list. You have the product that works. The scale of that route is large: Canalys, an industry analyst, forecast that partners would deliver 70% of the $5.44 trillion spent on IT worldwide in 2025. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the partner's role and economics before recruiting, and [ecosystem-led growth](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/) covers using partner customer overlap to pick the twenty. Make a list of twenty, contact all of them, and run it like [Part 4](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) said to run a round.

> The market did not change in the month you shipped twelve things. Your attention did.

## Report the number two ways

Report the core number two ways from this week on.

| Line | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| With incentives and free tier | What the market will take when paid to take it |
| Without incentives and free tier | What the market will pay for |

If the second line is flat while the first moves, you have been buying the number. Now everyone can see it.

The split matters because incentive effects are often temporary and hard to read without a comparison. Gauntlet, a risk-modelling firm, analysed Uniswap's liquidity-mining programme for the protocol's governance forum in June 2023, comparing incentivised pools with control pools. Results were mixed: some pools settled at a higher level after rewards stopped, one large spike in deposits disappeared, and two pools showed no statistically significant lift. Without the control pools and the post-programme read, the lasting effect could not have been separated from the paid one. The same logic applies to a free tier in a [product-led motion](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-product-led-growth/): free usage shows reach, paid conversion shows demand.

## What not to do

Do not ship one more feature. The next one will not be the one.

Do not announce more partnerships. A logo on a slide is not a partner working your buyer.

Do not blame the market. The market did not change in the month you shipped twelve things. Your attention did.

## How you know it worked

Two signs. The core number without incentives moves up, even slightly, within the sixty days. And at least one partner is bringing buyers without being chased each week.

Illustrative example: sixty days without a release

Decision
:   Freeze new features for sixty days, lead with one story about settlement speed, and work twenty payment partners who already served the target merchants.

Reason and owner
:   Eleven releases in a quarter had coincided with a fall in paying accounts, and churned users cited price and fit, not defects. Owned by the CEO, with the head of partnerships running the list.

What changed
:   Three partners began referring merchants without prompting by week seven. Paying accounts without incentives rose slightly while the incentivised total was flat, which showed the earlier growth had been bought.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage fintech infrastructure company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the falling number as a distribution signal.** If the product works and the number fell, building more will not fix it.
- **Most shipped features go unused.** Supply without a lead story and a channel adds cost, not demand.
- **Freeze, name, work.** Sixty days without new features, one provable story, one channel band and a list of twenty.
- **Split the number.** With and without incentives, every week, so nobody mistakes bought growth for demand.

Gateway card

### Before the next release ships

- A written sixty-day build freeze, with the exceptions named
- One lead story in one sentence, and one channel band with a list of twenty
- The core number reported with and without incentives, every week
- A named partner who will carry the release to buyers

## Common questions

### Why did our metrics drop after a big product release?

Usually because the product works but there is no single lead story and nobody was working demand. Supply went up and demand did not follow. Most features also go unused, so more of them rarely moves the core number.

### What should a startup do when shipping more features doesn't grow usage?

Stop building new features for sixty days, name one lead story you can prove, and work one channel band, often partners who already have your buyer, starting with a list of twenty.

### How can I tell if incentives are inflating my growth numbers?

Report the core number with and without incentives and free tier. If the second line is flat while the first moves, you have been buying the number.

### What percentage of software features are actually used?

In Pendo's 2019 vendor analysis of 615 products, about 80% of features were rarely or never used, and roughly 12% of features generated 80% of daily usage.

## Sources and notes

- [Pendo, The 2019 Feature Adoption Report](https://www.pendo.io/resources/the-2019-feature-adoption-report/), 2019. Vendor analysis of 615 of its own customers' products over three months; "feature" is Pendo's tagging unit.
- [Kohavi and Thomke, The surprising power of online experiments](https://web-docs.stern.nyu.edu/executive/The%20Surprising%20Power%20of%20Online%20Experiments.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, September to October 2017. Large technology firms; hosted copy.
- [Canalys, IT spending forecasts 2025](https://canalys.com/insights/it-spending-forecasts-2025), November 2024. Analyst forecast of partner-delivered share; covers IT broadly, not crypto or early-stage AI.
- [Gauntlet, Uniswap liquidity mining analysis](https://gov.uniswap.org/t/uniswap-liquidity-mining-analysis/21416), 6 June 2023. Paid risk consultant to the protocol; five pools, post-programme data one week after rewards ended.

# What Is Lead Scoring?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-scoring/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Lead scoring assigns points to leads for fit and engagement so sales can prioritise. Modern CRMs offer rules-based and predictive versions, but Forrester argues that scoring individuals misses how B2B buying groups actually decide. This explainer covers how lead scores are built, what predictive scoring needs, and how to check whether a score works.

Lead scoring is a method of ranking leads by how likely they are to become customers, so sales and marketing work the best ones first. Most scores combine fit, meaning how closely the person and company match your ideal customer, with engagement, meaning what they have done recently. Scores work as a queue-ordering tool, provided they are checked against conversions and extended from single people to the buying group.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What lead scoring means

A lead is a person who has shown interest. Most firms get more leads than sellers can follow up properly, so they need a rule for who goes first. Lead scoring is that rule, expressed as points.

There are two dimensions. Fit asks whether this is the kind of buyer you win: industry, company size, region, role, seniority. Engagement asks whether they are active now: pages visited, emails opened, webinars attended, meetings booked. HubSpot's lead scoring tool shows the standard design. Fit scores use property rules, engagement scores use event rules, and combined scores use both. Thresholds turn the numbers into labels: A to C for fit and 1 to 3 for engagement, so a contact labelled C1 is highly engaged but a poor fit.

| Approach | How it works | Needs | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rules-based | Points assigned by people for attributes and actions | An agreed ICP and a few months of data | Points reflect opinion, not evidence |
| Predictive | Model trained on which past leads converted | Volume: Einstein needs 1,000 leads and 120 conversions | Opaque; learns past biases |
| Account or buying-group | Scores the company and its active people together | Contacts linked to accounts and opportunities | Harder to set up in lead-centric CRMs |

## How it works

### Rules-based scoring

Marketing and sales agree a set of rules: for example, 20 points for a target industry, 15 for a director-level title, 10 for a pricing page visit, minus 20 for a personal email domain. HubSpot allows a cap on each group of rules and on repeated events, so that one person downloading ten papers cannot outscore a better-fit buyer. It also supports decay, which reduces a score by a set percentage as events age.

### Predictive scoring

Predictive tools train a model on your conversion history. Salesforce's implementation guide states that Einstein Lead Scoring requires at least 1,000 leads created in the last 200 days, of which at least 120 were converted to an account and contact. Each segment must meet that threshold. Below it, Einstein uses a global model trained on anonymised data from many customers, then switches to your own model once there is enough data and it performs better. A firm with a modest lead volume may not meet that threshold in every segment.

## Where lead scoring misleads

Forrester principal analyst Simon Daniels set out the core objection in November 2023. Lead scoring rates one person's activity and misses the rest of the buying group. Forrester's research found 46% of B2B buyers decided in groups of two to three and 28% in groups of four to nine. Daniels' example: three people from one account each taking one action is more valuable than one person downloading three assets, but a lead score ranks the opposite way. Forrester also reports that fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals.

Other common failures:

- **Fit points are opinions.** Weights set in a workshop are rarely checked against which leads actually closed.
- **Engagement rewards researchers.** Students, competitors and job seekers can be highly engaged.
- **Thresholds become targets.** If marketing is measured on leads over a score, the score drifts upward.
- **No feedback loop.** Sellers reject leads but the reason is not recorded, so the model never learns.

## How to check whether a score works

1. **Pull 12 months of leads.** Include the score each had at handover and whether it became an opportunity and a customer.
2. **Bucket by score.** Compare conversion rates for the top, middle and bottom thirds. If the top third does not convert clearly better, the weights are wrong.
3. **Check fit and engagement separately.** Often fit predicts well and engagement adds little, or the reverse.
4. **Add an account view.** Count active contacts per account and test whether accounts with several engaged people convert better than single high scorers.
5. **Record rejections.** Require a reason when sales rejects a lead, and review the reasons monthly.

In **lowob**'s terms, a lead score is context, not a decision. The decision to contact, and the reason, belongs to a person and goes in the record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Separate fit from engagement.** They answer different questions and fail in different ways.
- **Check scores against conversions.** Points that do not predict outcomes are just opinions.
- **Score the buying group.** One person's activity rarely reflects how a B2B decision is made.
- **Use decay and caps.** Old or repeated activity should not outrank a better-fit buyer.

## Common questions

### What is lead scoring?

It is a method of ranking leads by likelihood to become customers, usually by assigning points for fit with your ideal customer and for recent engagement.

### What is the difference between fit and engagement scoring?

Fit scoring rates who the lead is, such as industry, size and role. Engagement scoring rates what they have done, such as visits, form fills and meetings.

### How much data do you need for predictive lead scoring?

It depends on the tool. Salesforce's Einstein Lead Scoring needs at least 1,000 leads created and 120 converted in the last 200 days for a model based on your own data.

### Is lead scoring still relevant for B2B?

As a queue-ordering tool, yes. Forrester argues it should be extended to buying groups and opportunities, because B2B decisions are usually made by several people.

## Sources and notes

- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Build lead scores](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/scoring/build-lead-scores). Vendor product documentation; features depend on subscription.
- [Salesforce, Sales Cloud Einstein Implementation Guide](https://resources.docs.salesforce.com/242/latest/en-us/sfdc/pdf/sales_einstein_implementation_guide.pdf). Vendor documentation; thresholds may change between releases.
- [Forrester, Saying Goodbye To MQLs: A Parting That Is All Sweet And No Sorrow](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/saying-goodbye-to-mqls-sweet-and-no-sorrow), November 2023. Analyst blog; some conversion figures are client-reported.

## Related research

- [What Is Lead Source Attribution?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/)
- [How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)
- [What Is Account-Based Marketing? A Small-Team Version](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Export last year's leads with their handover score and outcome. Compare conversion for the top and bottom thirds, and if the gap is small, rewrite the fit rules first.

# The EU AI Act for Commercial Teams: What Applies and When

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-23 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most commercial teams are deployers under the EU AI Act, not providers, and most of their uses are not high-risk. What reaches them first are the prohibitions, AI literacy and the Article 50 transparency duties for chatbots, deepfakes and published text. After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027.

For a sales, marketing or customer team, the EU AI Act mostly applies through four routes: a short list of banned practices; a duty to support AI literacy; transparency rules for chatbots, deepfakes and AI-written public-interest text; and stricter rules if a tool falls into a high-risk category such as recruitment or credit scoring. Most commercial teams are deployers of other firms' tools, not providers. After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Provider or deployer: which one is your team?

The Act assigns duties by role. A provider develops an AI system or places it on the market under its own name. A deployer uses a system under its own authority in a professional setting. A marketing team using a copywriting tool, a sales team using a CRM assistant and a service team using a vendor's chatbot are deployers.

The line moves when a team builds. A company that wires a model API into its own branded website assistant may be the provider of that assistant, and takes on the provider duties that come with it.

## What applies to commercial teams, and when

| Date | What applies | Commercial relevance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 February 2025 | Prohibited practices (Article 5) and AI literacy (Article 4) | Bans include manipulative techniques causing significant harm and emotion inference in the workplace |
| 2 August 2025 | General-purpose AI model rules and penalties | Mainly falls on model providers, not on their business customers |
| 27 July 2026 | Digital Omnibus amendments in force | Literacy duty softened to "support"; high-risk dates moved |
| 2 August 2026 | Article 50 transparency duties | Chatbot disclosure, deepfake labels, AI-generated public-interest text |
| 2 December 2026 | New Omnibus prohibitions; end of Article 50(2) grace period | Generative tools must mark synthetic output in machine-readable form |
| 2 December 2027 | Annex III high-risk obligations | Recruitment, credit scoring, life and health insurance pricing |
| 2 August 2028 | Annex I high-risk obligations | AI embedded in regulated products such as machinery |

**Transparency.** Article 50(1) requires providers of systems that interact directly with people to tell those people they are dealing with an AI, unless that is obvious. A website sales assistant or a voice agent qualifies. Article 50(2) requires providers of generative systems to mark output as artificially generated in a machine-readable format. Article 50(4) puts two duties on deployers: disclose deepfake images, audio and video, and disclose AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. The text duty does not apply where a person has reviewed the content and someone holds editorial responsibility for it.

**Prohibited practices.** Two are worth checking: manipulative or deceptive techniques that materially distort behaviour and cause significant harm, and inferring emotions in the workplace, which can catch call-coaching tools that score sellers' emotional state.

**High-risk uses.** Annex III lists eight areas. The ones a commercial function is most likely to touch are recruitment and worker management, creditworthiness of individuals, and risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Scoring business accounts for sales priority is not on the list. A deployer of a high-risk system must follow the provider's instructions, assign human oversight to competent people, keep logs for at least six months, inform workers before workplace use, and tell individuals when the system is used in decisions about them.

**Standards.** On 14 October 2026 the Commission published EN 18286, a quality management system standard prepared by CEN and CENELEC, as the first harmonised standard under the Act. Providers of high-risk systems that follow it gain a presumption of conformity for the requirements it covers, including the Article 17 quality management system. Its use is voluntary, and it is aimed at providers, so commercial teams acting as deployers will mostly meet it through their vendors.

> The Act asks most commercial teams for an inventory, a disclosure and a person who reviewed the output. Few need more before December 2027.

## A practical checklist

| Step | Question | Output |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory | Which tools use AI, including features inside existing software? | List with owner and vendor |
| Role | For each, are we provider or deployer? | Role column, with built tools flagged |
| Transparency | Does it talk to customers, or generate images, audio, video or published text? | Disclosure wording and placement |
| Risk class | Does it touch hiring, consumer credit or life or health insurance? | High-risk flag and 2027 plan |
| Literacy | Have the people using it been trained on its limits? | Training record |
| Oversight | Who reviews output before it reaches a customer? | Named approver per use |

The last line is the **lowob** rule that nothing sends without a person. It is not required for every use, but it supports the editorial-responsibility exception for published text and the oversight duty for high-risk systems.

## lowob takeaways

- **Settle the role first.** Using a vendor tool makes you a deployer; building your own assistant may make you a provider.
- **Transparency is the near-term duty.** Article 50 applies from 2 August 2026 to chatbots, deepfakes and public-interest text.
- **High-risk is narrow for commercial teams.** Hiring, consumer credit and insurance pricing are the main triggers, from December 2027.
- **Review creates the exemption.** Human editorial control takes published text out of the disclosure duty.

## Common questions

### Does the EU AI Act apply to marketing teams?

Yes, mainly through AI literacy, the prohibitions and Article 50 transparency duties, such as labelling deepfakes. Most marketing uses are not high-risk.

### Do AI chatbots have to disclose that they are AI under the EU AI Act?

Yes. From 2 August 2026, providers must design systems that interact with people so those people are told they are dealing with an AI, unless it is obvious.

### When do the EU AI Act high-risk rules apply?

After the Digital Omnibus, Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027 and Annex I product-embedded obligations from 2 August 2028.

### Is AI lead scoring high-risk under the EU AI Act?

Scoring business accounts is not listed in Annex III. Credit scoring of individuals, recruitment and life or health insurance pricing are.

## Sources and notes

- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 50: Transparency obligations](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-50), consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text.
- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Annex III](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/annex-3), [Article 26](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-26), [Article 4](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-4) and [Article 99](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-99), consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text.
- [Future of Privacy Forum, The AI Act implementation timeline: what changes under the AI Omnibus?](https://fpf.org/blog/the-ai-act-implementation-timeline-what-changes-under-the-ai-omnibus), July 2026. Policy analysis of the revised dates.
- [Orrick, EU AI Act update: Digital Omnibus finalizes 8 compliance changes](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/05/EUs-Digital-Omnibus-on-AI-7-Key-Changes-You-Need-to-Know), updated 29 July 2026. Law firm summary, including the Article 50(2) grace period.
- [Orrick, First harmonised technical standard published under the EU AI Act](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/10/First-Harmonised-Technical-Standard-Published-Under-the-EU-AI-Act), 27 October 2026. Law firm analysis of EN 18286 and Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274; not legal advice.

## Next move

Pick every AI tool that talks to customers or produces images, audio or video for campaigns. Check this week that each has a visible AI disclosure and a named person who reviews output before release.
