# Whoever Holds the Record Holds the Company

Source: https://lowob.com/research/whoever-holds-the-record-holds-the-company/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The layer that encodes how a business decides is becoming the deepest lock-in in enterprise software, and analysts now tell vendors to capture customer-specific knowledge rather than data. Models are rented and switched; the decision record is not. The enterprise should own that record, and the contract should say so before the first workflow moves in.

The layer that encodes how a business decides is the deepest lock-in in enterprise software. It is also where the strongest growth is: Gartner now advises software vendors to "capture and retain customer-specific knowledge, not just data" as agents erode the value of their interfaces. Data can be exported and models are rented and switched. The accumulated record of how the organisation decides is the asset at stake. The enterprise should own it, and the contract should say so before the first workflow moves in.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

A growing class of platforms models a business as objects, links and actions, and lets agents operate over that model. They are sold as ontologies, semantic layers or context layers. Our explainers on [the semantic layer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) and [semantic layers versus knowledge graphs](https://lowob.com/research/semantic-layer-vs-knowledge-graph/) describe the technology. The pitch is strong because it works: an agent that knows what an "active customer" means, who approves a discount and which exceptions were granted last quarter is far more useful than one that only searches documents.

The critics make the mirror argument. Once workflows, permissions and decision logic live inside that layer, switching becomes extremely costly. Both are right, and the tension applies to every enterprise brain, not just one vendor.

## Where the value is moving

Gartner's July 2026 analysis puts the pressure in numbers. It estimates up to $234 billion of enterprise application spending, about 20% of SaaS application spend by 2030, is exposed to agentic arbitrage: agents completing tasks across systems so that users need fewer traditional interfaces. Its analysts say "the user interface is no longer a differentiation", that seat-based pricing breaks for many vendors, and that better outcomes depend on systems that keep institutional memory and customer context over time.

Read from the buyer's side, that is a warning. If the interface no longer holds the customer, the vendor's retention strategy moves to whatever does. Gartner's own advice to vendors is to "capture and retain customer-specific knowledge, not just data". The knowledge in question is your organisation's.

The model layer shows what portability looks like when it exists. Menlo Ventures' survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision-makers estimates that Anthropic's share of enterprise LLM API spend rose from 12% in 2023 to 40% in 2025, while OpenAI's fell from 50% to 27%. Spend shifted that fast because changing model provider is comparatively easy. The same survey found 76% of AI use cases were purchased rather than built in 2025, up from 53% in 2024. Most firms are renting, which makes the terms of the rental the main control they have.

| Layer | Who builds it | Portability today | Lock-in risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Model | Model providers | High: buyers switch provider routinely | Low |
| Raw data | The business, often in licensed tools | Usually exportable; Data Act rights in the EU | Medium |
| Connectors and retrieval | Context platforms | Rebuildable with effort | Medium |
| Definitions, exceptions, precedents, outcomes | The organisation's own people, through use | Often trapped in proprietary structures | High |

## What is actually at stake

It is not the data. Data can usually be exported, and much of it is licensed from others anyway. It is not the model, which is rented and replaceable. It is the accumulated record of **how the organisation decides**: the definitions, the exceptions, the precedents, the conflicts resolved, the outcomes linked to decisions.

That record is built slowly, through use, by the organisation's own people. If it lives only inside a vendor's proprietary structure, the organisation's institutional judgment has become a line item the vendor can reprice at renewal. Our piece [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/) sets out why the record, not the model, is the brain.

> If the record lives only inside a vendor's structure, the organisation's judgment has become a line item the vendor can reprice at renewal.

## Three tests for any platform

| Test | The question | Evidence to ask for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Export | Can you export every decision record with its sources, history, supersession links and outcomes, in an open, documented format, without professional services? | A published schema and a sample export you can read without the vendor |
| Model independence | Does the record survive intact if the vendor's model, memory product or agent framework is replaced? | Records stored as data, not as prompts or model state |
| Control | Are retention and deletion controlled by you, record by record, with a log? | Admin controls and a deletion log you can query |

If the answer to any is no, you are building your judgment into someone else's asset.

## Put it in the contract

The time to negotiate this is before the first workflow moves, not at the first renewal. Regulation now gives some help. Since 12 September 2025, the EU Data Act's switching rules have applied to providers of data processing services, including SaaS. Customers can switch with at most two months' notice, porting must complete within a 30-day transition period, exportable data includes input and output data "including metadata", and switching charges must be eliminated from 12 January 2027. The Act excludes information protected as trade secrets and services custom-built for one customer, so it is a floor, not a full answer.

Useful clauses beyond the floor: a documented export schema, delivered and tested annually; exit assistance at a fixed rate; explicit ownership of derived records, including summaries and links the platform generates; and no use of your decision records to train models offered to others. Our explainer on [data processing agreements for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-data-processing-agreement-for-ai/) covers the related privacy terms.

## Internal ownership matters too

The same question applies inside the firm. If the judgment record belongs to IT, it will be managed as infrastructure. If it belongs to the function whose decisions it records, with risk and compliance overseeing it, it will be managed as an asset. The second works better.

## A note for vendors

Portability is not the enemy of retention. A vendor that makes the record easy to leave with, and keeps clients because the product around it is better, earns a kind of trust that lock-in never does. In a market where every competitor offers the same connections to the same data, and Gartner estimates only about 130 of thousands of self-described agentic AI vendors offer genuine agentic capability, that trust may be the more durable advantage.

## In practice

Run the three tests on every platform that holds decision records today. Add export, exit-assistance and derived-records clauses at the next negotiation. Test an export once a year and check that it can be read without the vendor.

Assign ownership of the record to the accountable function, with risk oversight.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations switching platforms without material loss of decision history or capability, even where no export rights were negotiated. Then the lock-in risk is overstated.

## lowob takeaways

- **The record is the asset.** Not the data, not the model: how the organisation decides.
- **Run three tests.** Export, model independence and control of retention.
- **Contract before migration.** Tested export schema, fixed-rate exit help, ownership of derived records, no training on your records.
- **Own it in the function.** The team whose decisions it records, with risk oversight.

## Common questions

### How do I avoid vendor lock-in with an enterprise AI or ontology platform?

Before the first workflow moves in, check you can export every decision record in an open format, that the record survives a model change, and that you control retention. Put export, exit-assistance and derived-records clauses in the contract.

### Does the EU Data Act help with switching AI or SaaS vendors?

Partly. Since 12 September 2025 providers must support switching with at most two months' notice and a 30-day transition, including export of data and metadata, and switching charges end from 12 January 2027. Trade secrets and bespoke services are excluded.

### What contract clauses protect a company's decision data?

A documented export schema delivered and tested annually, exit assistance at a fixed rate, explicit ownership of derived records including generated summaries and links, and no use of your records to train models offered to others.

### Who inside a company should own the decision record?

The function whose decisions it records, with risk and compliance overseeing it. If IT owns it, it gets managed as infrastructure rather than as an asset.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, US$234 billion in enterprise application software spend is at risk from agentic AI](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-07-01-gartner-says-us-dollars-234-billion-in-enterprise-application-software-spend-is-at-risk-from-agentic-artificial-intelligence), 1 July 2026. Analyst forecast; press release summary.
- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/), 9 December 2025. Investor research; survey of 495 US decision-makers; Menlo invests in AI companies.
- [Cooley, PaaS, IaaS or SaaS? New switching rules will become applicable in EU](https://www.cooley.com/news/insight/2025/2025-09-08-paas-iaas-or-saas-be-aware-new-switching-rules-will-become-applicable-in-eu), September 2025. Law-firm summary of Regulation (EU) 2023/2854; not legal advice.
- [w.media, Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects could face the axe by end of 2027: Gartner](https://w.media/over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-could-face-the-axe-by-end-of-2027-gartner/), June 2025. Analyst forecast reported secondhand.

Ask the vendor that holds most of your decision history for a sample export this month. If your team cannot read it without the vendor, add a tested export schema and derived-records ownership to the next renewal.

# The Build Order for Media and Publishing

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-media-and-publishing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Media and publishing runs The Build Order as written, with a firewall in the middle: sales context must never reach the newsroom. Search referrals are falling, licensing is a new commercial decision, and the EU AI Act's Article 50 now ties AI-generated text to editorial responsibility. The fastest record to pay back is the subscription retention offer.

Publishers can run The Build Order as written, provided the context layer is split in two. The commercial line is advertising, sponsorship, subscriptions, events and, increasingly, licensing content to AI companies. The wall is the newsroom: sales context must never reach editorial, and confidential reporting must never reach sales or an outside model. The pressure to build is real. Publishers surveyed by the Reuters Institute in early 2026 expect search referrals to fall by more than 40% over three years, and Chartbeat data in the same report showed organic search traffic to over 2,500 sites down 33% in a year. Pew Research found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% without one. Meanwhile the EU AI Act's transparency rules, in force since 2 August 2026, make attributable editorial responsibility the condition for publishing AI-assisted text without a label.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This is the third industry edition of The Build Order. In *The RFP nobody can answer yet* we said the order holds in media and publishing, with one qualification: sales context must be walled off from editorial. In *The same build in four industries* a composite regional publisher, funded mainly by advertising, built exactly that firewall. This piece generalises the case to publishers of every shape (consumer, specialist and business-to-business) at a moment when the economics of the sector are moving under them.

## Where the commercial line sits

A publisher's commercial line has more strands than most. Each produces decisions that are frequent, similar and graded within a renewal cycle, which is the test set out in *Where judgment arrives first*.

| Lens | What it looks like in media and publishing |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Ad and sponsorship sales, subscription pricing and retention, events, content licensing |
| Store | CRM, ad server and order management, subscription platform, event registration |
| Outcome lag | 30 to 90 days for retention offers; a renewal cycle for sponsors; a year or more for licensing |
| Who defends the decision | Commercial director, head of audience, publisher or managing director |
| Main rules | Advertising disclosure rules such as the FTC's native advertising guidance; EU AI Act Article 50; press codes |
| The wall | Editorial: drafts, sources, unpublished reporting and editorial decisions |
| Gateway that bites | Gateway 1: brand safety and disclosure |

**Advertising and sponsorship.** Which advertisers to pursue, when to grant a rate exception, and how to handle under-delivery through make-goods and credits. Part 10 covered this ground.

**Subscriptions.** Which retention offer to make to a subscriber who tries to cancel, at what discount and for how long. These decisions are made hundreds or thousands of times a month, and the outcome (still paying at 30 or 90 days, at what price) arrives quickly.

**Events.** Which sponsors to place at which tier, and what to discount to fill a programme.

**Licensing.** Whether to license an archive or a live feed to an AI developer, on what terms and for how long. This class did not exist at scale a few years ago. It is infrequent, but each decision is large and its terms shape every later one.

## What the evidence says

The Reuters Institute's *Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026*, based on a survey of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries, found publishers expect search referrals to fall by more than 40% over three years. Chartbeat data cited in the report showed organic search traffic to more than 2,500 sites down 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and 38% in the US. The report notes it is unclear how much of that is due to AI summaries. Confidence in journalism's prospects stood at 38%. Subscriptions and membership were the leading revenue focus, cited by 76%. On licensing, 20% expected significant revenue from AI deals, 49% a minor contribution and 20% none.

Pew Research Center's browsing study of 900 US adults in March 2025 shows the mechanism at the level of individual searches. An AI summary appeared on 18% of the Google searches tracked. Where one appeared, users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits, against 15% where none appeared, and clicked a link inside the summary on 1%.

The advertising side is moving too. IAB Europe's 2026 report on AI in digital advertising found 86% of respondents reporting widespread AI use in marketing, and 58% expecting agentic ad buying to reach operational use or scale within a year. Advertising-specific AI guidance was less common than general governance. For publishers this means buyers' agents will increasingly meet sellers' systems, and whatever the publisher's agents say about audience and delivery needs to be right.

The direction is clear even where the numbers are uncertain. Referred traffic is a less reliable base. Revenue that depends on a direct relationship (subscriptions, events, sponsorship and licensing) matters more, and each of those runs on commercial decisions a publisher can record. Our piece *What investors fund in media now* covers the strategic side. This piece is about the build.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in media and publishing | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | Owner on the commercial side, suite, CRM, and an editorial standards lead as data-access approver for anything near the newsroom | A single owner for both commercial and editorial AI |
| Tooling | Seats for sales, sponsorship, audience and events teams; editorial tooling bought and governed separately | One shared assistant across the building |
| Context | Commercial layer: CRM, order management, delivery reports, subscription data, rate cards. Editorial layer: separate | Retrieval that crosses the firewall |
| Record | Retention offers, rate exceptions and make-goods, then licensing terms | Recording offers without recording the outcome |
| Reasoning | A first agent that drafts renewal and sponsor briefs from delivery data into a queue | Misstated audience or delivery figures |
| Gateway 1 | Named approval for anything sent to a client; stricter rules for sponsored content | Unlabelled or ambiguously labelled commercial content |
| Gateway 2 | Value of each exception or offer; retained revenue written back | Discounts that retain subscribers at a loss |
| Gateway 3 | Extension to ad operations, finance and audience development, never into editorial | Treating editorial as just another department |

**Gateway 0.** The owner sits on the commercial side. Add a data-access approver from editorial standards who must sign off any source that sits near the newsroom: shared drives, content management systems, analytics that show story-level performance. Part 3, *Gateway 0*, sets out the standing decisions.

**Tooling.** Seats go to the commercial teams. If the newsroom uses AI tools, it buys and governs them on its own terms. Two teams sharing one assistant with one memory is the most common way the firewall fails.

**Context.** The commercial context layer connects the CRM, order management, campaign delivery reports, rate cards, the subscription platform and event registrations. Part 5, *The context layer, followed through one account*, explains how to connect in order of usefulness. The next section explains what stays out.

**Record.** Start with subscription retention offers if the publisher has a meaningful subscription base. Each record holds the offer, the reason (price sensitivity, content fit, payment failure), the owner or rule that made it, the value at stake and a check at 30 and 90 days. Then rate exceptions and make-goods. Then licensing: record the first AI licensing deal with its terms, the alternatives considered and what the publisher expected it to be worth, because every later negotiation will be compared with it.

**Reasoning.** The first agent drafts renewal briefs and sponsor proposals from delivery data, into a queue for a person to check. It is a good first job because every figure in a renewal brief can be checked against a delivery report, so errors are caught before a client sees them.

## The firewall: two context layers that never meet

The wall in media runs in both directions.

**Commercial context must not reach editorial.** An assistant that can see an advertiser's renewal thread and an editor's draft side by side breaches editorial independence, whatever the file permissions allow. A brand that is about to renew should not appear as a suggestion in an editor's research. Story-level performance data shared with sales is a judgment call each publisher makes under its own standards; it should be made once, by the data-access approver, and recorded.

**Editorial material must not reach sales or outside models.** Unpublished reporting, source identities, embargoed material and editorial decision notes stay inside the editorial system. They never enter the commercial layer, and they never go to an outside model under terms that allow training or human review by the vendor.

**Licensing sits on the line.** A licensing deal is a commercial decision about editorial assets. The record of the deal belongs in the commercial layer. The content licensed is defined by editorial, and the commercial agent never has access to the archive itself, only to the terms.

> The firewall is not a permission setting. It is two context layers, each with its own owner, that never share a memory.

## Gateway 1: disclosure and brand safety

Gateway 1, nothing sends without a person, is stricter in media for two reasons.

**Native and sponsored content must be identifiable.** The FTC's guidance on native advertising says an ad should not suggest it is anything other than an ad. Terms such as "Ad", "Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" are likely to be understood; "Promoted" is described as ambiguous. Disclosures should sit in front of or above the headline and carry over when content is republished. An agent drafting sponsored content must use the approved label every time, and the approver checks the label as well as the copy. Our pieces *Native advertising and sponsored content* and *Brand safety and suitability* cover the commercial practice.

**AI-generated public-interest text needs a named editor or a label.** Article 50(4) of the EU AI Act, applicable since 2 August 2026, requires disclosure when AI-generated or AI-manipulated text is published to inform the public on matters of public interest. There is an exemption where the text has undergone human review and someone holds editorial responsibility. The European Commission's draft guidelines of May 2026, as summarised by Greenberg Traurig, read that exemption narrowly: a person with relevant expertise must review the substance, and an identifiable person or organisation with authority to approve, amend or reject the text must be publicly accountable for it. Spelling and grammar checks do not count. For a publisher this has a practical effect. Commercial content drafted with AI, such as a sponsored explainer, needs the same quality of attributable sign-off as editorial copy, or it needs a label.

The Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, left most Article 50 obligations on their original date and gave generative AI systems already on the market until 2 December 2026 to meet the machine-readable marking requirement, according to White & Case. Publishers should treat 2 August 2026 as the date their own disclosure duties began.

## Gateways 2 and 3

**Gateway 2.** The dollar figure is straightforward for most media decisions. A retention offer has a cost (the discount multiplied by its duration) and a value (revenue retained beyond the offer period). A rate exception has a value at stake and a renewal outcome. Write the outcome back to each decision. A common early finding is that a generous retention offer keeps subscribers who cancel as soon as it expires, which the record shows at the 90-day check.

**Gateway 3.** The record extends to ad operations, finance and audience development. It does not extend into editorial. If the newsroom builds its own brain, it is a separate build with its own owner, its own record and its own gateways.

Illustrative example: a specialist publisher records its retention offers

Decision
:   Record every subscription retention offer and every sponsorship rate exception, with reason, value at stake and checks at 30 and 90 days, before connecting any agent.

Reason and owner
:   Search referrals had fallen and subscriptions and events had become the main revenue lines; nobody knew which retention offers kept subscribers after the discount ended. Owned by the commercial director, with the editor-in-chief's deputy as data-access approver.

What changed
:   The first agent drafts sponsor renewal briefs from delivery data into a review queue and never reads the editorial content system. After one quarter, the 90-day checks showed the deepest discount retained no more subscribers beyond its term than a smaller one, and the publisher withdrew it.

Illustrative: a composite of a business-to-business specialist publisher of around 120 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Split the context layer.** Commercial and editorial each get their own wiring, owner and memory.
- **Start where outcomes arrive fastest.** Retention offers are graded in weeks; record them first.
- **Record the first licensing deal properly.** Every later negotiation will be measured against it.
- **Label every time.** Sponsored content needs an approved label, and AI-assisted public-interest text needs a named editor or a disclosure.
- **Never extend Gateway 3 into the newsroom.** An editorial brain is a separate build.

Gateway card

### Before a publisher connects its first agent

- Separate owners for commercial and editorial AI, and an editorial data-access approver
- A commercial context layer that excludes the content management system, drafts and source material
- Vendor terms checked so editorial material never trains an outside model
- Retention offers and rate exceptions recorded with value at stake and 30- and 90-day checks
- Approved disclosure labels built into every sponsored-content draft
- A named, accountable approver for any AI-assisted text published to the public

## Common questions

### How should publishers use AI without compromising editorial independence?

Build two context layers that never meet: one for commercial teams (CRM, delivery, subscriptions) and one for the newsroom, with separate owners and tools. Commercial agents should never read editorial drafts or sources, and editorial tools should never see advertiser threads.

### Does the EU AI Act require publishers to label AI-generated articles?

Article 50(4), applicable from 2 August 2026, requires disclosure of AI-generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest, unless it has had human review and someone holds editorial responsibility. The Commission's draft guidelines read that exemption narrowly.

### How much traffic are publishers losing to AI search?

Chartbeat data in the Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report showed organic search traffic to over 2,500 sites down 33% globally in the year to November 2025, and publishers expect a further fall of more than 40% over three years. How much is due to AI summaries is unclear.

### What is the best first AI agent for a media company's sales team?

A clerk that drafts sponsor renewal briefs and proposals from delivery data into a review queue. Staff can check every figure against delivery reports, which builds trust before anything more ambitious.

# A Reviewer Who Does Not Verify Is Not a Control

Source: https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Human-in-the-loop is a design pattern, not a defence. Courts, regulators and clients now look for evidence that the human actually checked, and the human factors research shows that instructions alone do not make people check. Design the review gate so that it produces verification evidence as a by-product.

Human-in-the-loop is a design pattern, not a defence. Courts, regulators and clients now look for evidence that the human actually checked, and a review box on a process diagram is not that evidence. By late July 2026 one tracked database held 1,240 reported US court filings with AI-fabricated content, hundreds of them signed by lawyers. Design the review gate so that proof of verification is a by-product: sources one click away, a log of what the reviewer opened, edit classes, blind second looks and seeded errors.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## Review happened on paper

US courts are the clearest public record of what nominal review looks like. Damien Charlotin's AI Hallucination Cases database, as summarised by the Maryland State Bar Association in July 2026, counted 11 reported US instances in 2023, 37 in 2024, 524 in 2025 and 668 in 2026 up to 27 July. In 2025, 208 of the 524 involved lawyers rather than self-represented litigants, 97 led to monetary sanctions and 59 to disciplinary referrals. The MSBA describes courts responding with "less patience, fewer warnings" and referrals to disciplinary bodies.

In every one of the lawyer cases, a qualified professional signed the filing. A person was in the loop. The loop did not include verification.

The same pattern has reached advisory work. In October 2025 Deloitte agreed to repay the final instalment of an AU$440,000 contract with Australia's Department of Employment and Workplace Relations. A published report had been found to contain phantom footnotes, citations to reports that did not exist and a fabricated quote attributed to a judge. The firm had used a GPT-4o tool licensed by the department. The report passed through delivery review before publication.

Liability follows the organisation, not the tool. In *Moffatt v Air Canada* (2024 BCCRT 149), British Columbia's Civil Resolution Tribunal held the airline liable for negligent misrepresentation by its website chatbot. It rejected the argument that the airline could not be responsible for information given by its agents, including a chatbot. Our explainer on [AI hallucination](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/) covers why fluent, wrong output is a structural feature of these systems rather than a passing bug.

The lesson is not that review is useless. It is that a review step on a process diagram is not evidence that review happened.

## Why people in the loop stop checking

Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey's 2010 review in *Human Factors* is still the most useful map of the problem. They treat complacency and automation bias as overlapping effects with attention at their centre. Complacency appears under multiple-task load, when manual work competes with automated work for attention, and it persists with practice. Automation bias produces two kinds of error when an aid is imperfect: omissions, where the person misses a problem the aid did not flag, and commissions, where the person follows the aid's wrong advice. The finding that matters most for operators is that automation bias was not prevented by training or instructions.

That rules out the usual fix. Telling reviewers to be careful does not work reliably. The gate has to be designed so that checking is the path of least resistance and so that not checking is visible.

Standards bodies now describe the risk the same way. NIST's generative AI profile (AI 600-1, July 2024) lists confabulation, "the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content", as one risk. It lists human-AI configuration as another, covering automation bias and over-reliance. The second framing is the useful one: the risk is not only that the model errs, but that the arrangement of people and system lets errors through.

The EU AI Act puts the same idea into law for high-risk systems. Article 14(4)(b) requires that overseers can "remain aware of the possible tendency of automatically relying or over-relying on the output". Article 14(4)(d) and (e) require that they can override or reverse the output and interrupt the system through a "stop" button. Under Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, which entered into force on 27 July 2026, the Annex III high-risk obligations apply from 2 December 2027. Most commercial uses are not high-risk, but Article 14 is the clearest regulatory statement of what oversight means. Our explainer on [human-in-the-loop AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/) sets out the wider regulatory picture.

| Failure mode | What it looks like in a review queue | Design response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Omission error | Reviewer misses a fabricated citation the tool did not flag | Flag every number, date and citation visually |
| Commission error | Reviewer accepts a confident claim that is wrong | One-click source link for every factual claim |
| Complacency under load | Approvals in seconds late in a long session | Queue limits and time-on-item logging |
| Unmeasured gate | Nobody knows the catch rate | Seeded errors and blind second review |

## Design the gate to leave evidence

**Verification affordances.** Every factual claim in an output links to its source, and the reviewer can open each in one click. Claims with numbers, dates or citations are visually flagged, because those are where the court and consultancy failures above occurred.

**Verification telemetry.** Log which sources the reviewer actually opened, and how long they spent on the item. "Approved after opening four of six cited sources in three minutes" is evidence. "Approved" is not.

**Edit classes.** When a reviewer changes something, record what kind of change it was: factual correction, tone, structure or scope. Factual corrections are the signal that the gate is catching real errors. A month with none is either a very good month or a gate that has stopped looking.

**Second looks.** Sample a small share of approved items for blind second review, and seed a few known-flawed items into queues to measure catch rates. This is an established practice in other inspection work. The US Transportation Security Administration projects fictional threat images onto X-ray scans of real bags, and screeners who fall below a target identification rate are sent to remedial training. The GAO's 2016 review also carries a warning: up to 14% of airports reported no such data in one year, and the agency had not analysed results nationally. Seeded tests only work if someone collects and reads the results.

**Queue limits.** Cap the number of items per reviewer per session. Parasuraman and Manzey's finding that complacency rises under competing load is the reason: a reviewer clearing forty items between meetings is the condition the research describes.

> "Approved" is a claim. "Approved after opening four of six cited sources in three minutes" is evidence.

## What the evidence is for

The log serves three audiences, and each wants something slightly different.

| Audience | What they ask | What the gate log shows |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A court, client or counterparty in a dispute | Did anyone check before this went out? | Sources opened, time on item, the version approved |
| A regulator or auditor | Can you reconstruct the chain from input to outcome? | Who approved, on what evidence, with what edits |
| The business itself | Is the gate catching anything? | Factual-correction rate, seeded-error catch rate, second-review disagreement |

In [Regulators want the chain, not the model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/) we argued that supervisors inspect the sequence of evidence, approval and outcome rather than model internals. A verification log is the human link in that chain, and our explainer on the [AI audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) covers how to store it.

None of this needs to slow good reviewers down. Logging what they opened costs them nothing, because the system already knows. The point is that "a human approved it" now has to be provable, and the proof is cheap to collect at the time and impossible to reconstruct afterwards. In [Gateway 1: Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) we set out the approval queue this log sits inside.

## What would prove this wrong

Organisations with nominal review and no verification evidence experiencing no more incidents, sanctions or disputes than those with evidenced review, over a meaningful period. Then the evidence is overhead. The court record so far points the other way, but it records failures, not the firms that avoided them, so it cannot settle the question alone.

## lowob takeaways

- **A signature is not a check.** Dozens of sanctioned court filings were signed by a qualified professional.
- **Instructions do not fix automation bias.** The research says design the gate, not the memo.
- **Log what the reviewer opened.** Sources opened and time on item turn "approved" into evidence.
- **Measure the gate itself.** Edit classes, blind second review and seeded errors show whether it catches anything.

## Common questions

### Is having a human review AI output enough to count as a control?

No. A review step on a process diagram is not evidence that review happened. Courts, regulators and clients now look for evidence that the person actually checked, such as which sources they opened and what they corrected.

### How do you prove a human actually verified AI-generated content?

Link every claim to its source, log which sources the reviewer opened and how long they spent, and record the class of each edit. "Approved after opening four of six cited sources in three minutes" is evidence; "approved" is not.

### How many AI hallucinated citations have appeared in US court filings?

Damien Charlotin's database recorded 1,240 reported US instances by 27 July 2026: 11 in 2023, 37 in 2024, 524 in 2025 and 668 in 2026 to that date, according to the Maryland State Bar Association.

### What is automation bias in AI review?

The tendency to rely on an automated aid's output, missing problems it did not flag or following its wrong advice. Research by Parasuraman and Manzey found training and instructions do not prevent it, so the review process must be designed around it.

Bar association summary of Damien Charlotin's database; counts reported instances only, so true numbers are likely higher.

# Channel Conflict, and How to Manage It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Most B2B technology still reaches customers through partners, so a direct team and a partner channel will meet in the same accounts. Research suggests the frequency of conflict damages a channel more than its intensity. The fix is a short set of written rules, a fast way to settle disputes, and a record of every ruling so the rules improve.

Channel conflict happens when two routes to the same customer compete for the same deal: a direct seller and a reseller, two partners, or a marketplace listing and a partner quote. It cannot be removed, because most B2B technology still reaches buyers through partners and the direct team will always meet them in the same accounts. It can be kept small. The evidence suggests that how often conflict happens matters more than how bad any one dispute gets, so the aim is fewer disputes, settled fast, under rules written down before the first one arrives. Every ruling should be recorded with its reason, because the rulings are what improve the rules.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 14 of this series covered how to design a partner channel and Part 18 covered co-selling with the large platforms. Both end in the same place. Once a firm sells through more than one route, two of its routes will eventually want the same customer. A partner registers an opportunity the direct team has been working for a month. A reseller discovers the vendor quoted the same buyer a lower price. A marketplace listing undercuts a partner who did the discovery work.

None of this is a failure of goodwill. It is what happens when the rules are unwritten, the incentives point in different directions and nobody has the authority to rule quickly. This piece covers where the conflict comes from, what the evidence says it costs and the small set of rules that keep it contained.

## Where channel conflict comes from

Channel conflict takes three common forms. Each has a different trigger and needs a different first rule.

| Type | Typical trigger | Who usually loses | First rule to write |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical: vendor direct team against a partner | Both work the same account; the direct team is paid only on direct deals | The partner, then the vendor's reputation in the channel | Account ownership and compensation on partner-sourced deals |
| Horizontal: partner against partner | Two partners register the same opportunity, or one discounts into another's territory | The partner with the weaker relationship to the vendor | Deal registration: first valid registration wins, with a stated expiry |
| Multichannel: marketplace or online against partner | The customer finds a lower price on a listing or website than in the partner's quote | The partner who did the pre-sale work | Price floors per route, and a rule for crediting partner influence |

The underlying cause in all three is the same: two parties each believe they have a claim, and there is no prior agreement about whose claim wins. Most firms write the partner agreement carefully and leave the operating rules to custom. Custom works while volumes are low. It stops working when the second or third dispute in a quarter is settled differently from the first.

## What the evidence says it costs

The scale of partner routes is the starting point. Canalys estimated that partner-delivered IT would account for about 70% of global IT spending in 2025, down slightly from 73% in 2023 as some buying moved to direct and marketplace routes. Omdia reported in February 2026 that partners would capture 79% of small and mid-size business IT spending in 2026, with the share above 80% in EMEA and Latin America. A technology firm selling to mid-size buyers is very unlikely to reach most of them without a partner somewhere in the chain.

The cost of conflict is less well measured, and the best survey data is old. CompTIA's 2013 study of 350 US IT channel executives found that 60% said conflict with vendors had risen over two years, more than three-quarters had lost at least one deal to it in the previous year, and 30% had dropped a vendor as a partner. More than 80% said a deal registration programme was critical or important when choosing a vendor. The figures are more than a decade old, but the mechanics they describe have not changed, and no more recent independent survey of the same scope is available.

The most useful finding for practice comes from academic work. Webb and Hogan's study of hybrid channels, published in the *Journal of Business & Industrial Marketing*, found that conflict was a significant determinant of both channel performance and satisfaction. Conflict frequency had a negative effect on channel performance; conflict intensity did not. A partner can absorb one serious dispute that is settled fairly. What wears a channel down is the steady drip of small disputes, each settled by whoever argues hardest.

There is also an opportunity cost. The Ebsta and Pavilion 2024 benchmark, a vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, reported that partnership channels returned 3.8 times the sales velocity of other channels, yet only 8% of the businesses in the sample had one. Firms that avoid partners to avoid conflict give that up.

> A channel can survive one hard dispute settled fairly. It does not survive twenty small ones settled by whoever shouted loudest.

## The rules that keep conflict small

The mechanism is simple to describe. Write the rules before the dispute, make the most common rulings automatic, and give one named person the authority to rule on the rest within a stated time. The five questions below cover most disputes in a mid-size firm.

| Rule | What it settles | What to record each time it is used |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deal registration | Which partner has the claim on a new opportunity, for how long, and what counts as a valid registration | Registration date, partner, expiry, whether it was accepted and why |
| Account ownership | Which accounts the direct team keeps, which belong to partners, and how an account changes hands | Owner, reason for any change, who approved it |
| Compensation on partner deals | Whether direct sellers are paid when a partner closes in their territory, so they have no reason to compete | The rule applied, and any exception granted |
| Price floors by route | The lowest price each route may offer, so the marketplace, website and partner quotes do not undercut each other by accident | Any quote below the floor, who approved it, the reason |
| Dispute ruling | Who rules, within how many working days, and how a ruling is appealed | The dispute, the ruling, the reason, the owner and the expected effect |

Deal registration does most of the work. The CompTIA survey found that partners' complaints about registration programmes were mainly about poor communication (61%), technical difficulties (49%) and inconsistent rules (27%). Each is fixable without new software: one published rule set, one form, and an answer within a stated number of days.

Compensation is the rule firms most often leave out, and it decides whether the others hold. If a direct seller earns nothing when a partner closes an account in their territory, the seller has every reason to compete for it. Many firms pay the direct team a share, or the full rate, on partner deals in their patch. That costs margin, and it is usually cheaper than the conflict it prevents.

The dispute rule matters because speed is part of fairness. A ruling that takes three weeks has already decided the deal, because the customer has moved on.

## What the law allows

Some conflict-management tools cross into competition law, and a firm should take advice before using them. In the EU, Commission Regulation (EU) 2022/720, the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation, entered into force on 1 June 2022 and replaced the 2010 rules. Its accompanying Vertical Guidelines govern much of what a supplier may agree with its distributors.

Three points matter for channel conflict. First, dual distribution, where a supplier sells directly while also selling through resellers, remains covered, and the exemption now extends to importers and wholesalers as well as manufacturers. Information exchanged between supplier and reseller in that setting is exempt only where it is directly related to implementing the agreement or needed to improve production or distribution. A supplier that asks partners for their pipeline and margin data to settle disputes needs to stay inside that line. Second, under the Guidelines, dual pricing (charging a reseller different prices for online and offline sales) is no longer treated as a hardcore restriction and is assessed case by case. Third, restrictions on selling through online marketplaces can benefit from the exemption if the reseller can still sell through its own website, but a complete ban on price comparison sites or search advertising would not.

The practical point is narrow. Price floors and route rules are legitimate tools inside a firm's own pricing. Telling independent resellers what price they must charge is a different matter in most jurisdictions. Write the rules for what the firm controls, and take advice on anything that binds a partner's own pricing.

## Treat every ruling as a decision

The final step is the one that makes the rules improve. Each dispute ruling is a commercial decision with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected effect, which is the shape of the decision record set out in Part 9 of The Build Order. Recorded that way, a quarter of rulings shows patterns that no single dispute reveals.

Three measures are worth tracking monthly. The number of disputes per hundred registered opportunities tells you whether the rules are preventing conflict; the Webb and Hogan finding says this is the number that matters most. The median days to a ruling tells you whether the process is fast enough to be fair. The share of rulings appealed, or reversed on appeal, tells you whether the rules are clear. A rising appeal rate usually means a rule is ambiguous, and the fix is to rewrite the rule, not to rule harder.

Illustrative example: a registration dispute settled once

Decision
:   A partner's registration on a mid-size account was upheld against the direct team, which had been in early conversations without logging them.

Reason and owner
:   The partner's registration was valid, complete and inside its 90-day window; the direct team's activity was not in the CRM. Ruled by the head of partnerships within three working days.

What changed
:   The direct seller was paid the agreed overlay on the partner deal, and the rules were amended so that direct activity counts against a registration only if it is logged before the registration date.

Illustrative: a composite of a software firm selling through regional resellers, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Prevent rather than arbitrate.** Conflict frequency damages a channel more than conflict intensity, so rules that stop disputes are worth more than a good referee.
- **Pay the direct team on partner deals.** Without it, the other rules will be tested every week.
- **Rule fast and in writing.** A slow ruling decides the deal by default.
- **Record each ruling with its reason.** The pattern across rulings is what tells you which rule to rewrite.

Gateway card

### Before you add a second route to market

- Deal registration rules published, with a validity window and a stated response time
- Account ownership list agreed between direct and partner leads
- Direct-team compensation on partner deals decided and written into the plan
- Price floors set for each route the firm controls
- One named person with authority to rule on disputes, and a deadline for rulings
- Legal advice taken on any rule that touches partner pricing or online sales

## Common questions

### What is channel conflict in B2B sales?

Channel conflict is competition between two routes to the same customer, such as a vendor's direct team and a reseller, two partners, or a marketplace listing and a partner quote, for the same deal.

### How does deal registration reduce channel conflict?

Deal registration gives the first partner to register a valid opportunity a protected claim for a set period, so the vendor and other partners know whose deal it is before they compete.

### Should direct salespeople be paid on partner deals?

Many firms pay the direct team some or all of their usual rate on partner deals in their territory, because a seller who earns nothing from a partner deal has an incentive to compete for it.

### Can a supplier set the prices its resellers charge?

In most jurisdictions a supplier cannot fix the resale price an independent reseller charges. In the EU, Regulation 2022/720 and its Guidelines set the rules for distribution agreements, and firms should take legal advice before restricting partner pricing or online sales.

# What Is Prompt Engineering?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-engineering/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of writing, structuring and testing the instructions an AI model works from. Research shows formatting alone can move accuracy by up to 76 points, so a prompt is only as reliable as the tests run against it. It fixes wording and format; facts, permissions and rules belong in context and code.

Prompt engineering is the practice of writing, structuring and testing the instructions an AI model works from, so that its output is accurate, consistent and in the format a team needs. It covers the role, the task, the examples, the order of material and the output format. Small wording and formatting changes can move results a long way, so a prompt is only as good as the tests run against it. It is one part of context engineering, which decides everything else the model sees.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What prompt engineering means

A prompt is everything written to the model for a task: the standing instructions in the [system prompt](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-prompt/), the request, any examples and the answer format. Prompt engineering is the work of making that text reliable. It is closer to writing a procedure for a new hire than to finding magic words. Anthropic's documentation suggests thinking of the model as "a brilliant but new employee who lacks context on your norms and workflows". Its test is simple: show the prompt to a colleague with little context on the task. If they would be confused, the model will be too.

Schulhoff and colleagues' Prompt Report, first posted in June 2024, catalogued 58 text-based prompting techniques. Most business use relies on a handful.

| Technique | What it does | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Role | Sets who the model is acting as | "You draft renewal summaries for account managers" |
| Task and reason | States the job and why each rule exists | "Under 150 words, because it is read on a phone before the call" |
| Examples | Shows three to five worked input and output pairs | Three past call notes, each with the summary it should produce |
| Tagged structure | Separates instructions, context and input | Contract in one tagged block, notes in another, instructions last |
| Long material first | Puts documents above the question | Contract text, then "List the renewal terms" |
| Step-by-step reasoning | Asks the model to work through a problem before answering | Check a proposed discount against each pricing rule in turn |
| Output format | Specifies fields or a schema | Account, risk level and next step as fixed fields; see [structured output](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-structured-output/) |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Prompts are more fragile than they look. Sclar and colleagues changed only how few-shot prompts were formatted, such as separators, spacing and casing, and left the content alone. On LLaMA-2-13B, accuracy varied by up to 76 points across formats. The sensitivity persisted with larger models, more examples and instruction tuning. The best format for one model only weakly predicted the best format for another.

So a prompt that worked last quarter may behave differently after the provider updates the model, and one copied between tools may not transfer. OpenAI's guidance is to pin production applications to specific model snapshots and to build tests that "measure prompt behavior so you can monitor performance as you iterate".

Model type matters as well. OpenAI's guide says [reasoning models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-reasoning-model/) do better with high-level goals, while standard models "benefit from more explicit instructions".

Prompt engineering also has limits. Anthropic notes that not every failing test is best fixed with a better prompt: latency and cost are often improved more easily by choosing a different model. Wrong facts are usually a context problem, because the model was never shown the right record. That is the territory of [context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/), and our comparison of [prompt engineering and context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/prompt-engineering-vs-context-engineering/) sets out the boundary. Rules that must hold, such as discount limits, belong in code and permissions, not in wording a model may ignore.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, the prompt sits with the parts a firm owns. Rent the model; own the instructions, the examples and the precedents they draw on.

## How to start: treat a prompt like a procedure

1. Write the success criteria first. For a renewal summary: names the renewal date, flags open issues, stays under 150 words, invents no figures.
2. Collect 20 to 30 real cases with known good outputs. This becomes the test set; our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers the method.
3. Draft the prompt with a role, the task, the reasons behind each rule and three to five examples.
4. Run the test set, score it and change one thing at a time.
5. Version the prompt with a named owner, and rerun the tests whenever the prompt or the model changes.

Two common mistakes are worth naming. Anthropic advises saying what to do rather than only what to avoid: "write in short paragraphs" works better than "no bullet points". And one long prompt covering every case is harder to test than one prompt per task, chained where needed.

## lowob takeaways

- **A prompt is a procedure.** Write it for a capable new hire who has no context.
- **Formatting alone moves results.** Test across real cases, not one run.
- **Pin the model and retest.** Model updates change how a prompt behaves.
- **Prompts do not enforce rules.** Permissions and limits live in code.

## Common questions

### What is prompt engineering in simple terms?

Writing and testing the instructions you give an AI model so that it does a task reliably: the role, the task, a few examples and the format of the answer.

### Is prompt engineering still relevant with newer AI models?

Yes, though the emphasis has shifted. Newer and reasoning models need fewer tricks, but they still need clear tasks, examples and tests, and providers still advise retesting when models change.

### What is the difference between prompt engineering and context engineering?

Prompt engineering covers how the instructions are written. Context engineering covers everything the model sees, including retrieved records, tool results and conversation history.

### Do I need to hire a prompt engineer?

Most firms of 20 to 500 people do not need a dedicated role. They need a named owner for each production prompt, a test set and the habit of versioning every change.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Prompt engineering overview](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/claude-prompting-best-practices), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; the 30% figure comes from Anthropic's own tests.
- [OpenAI, Prompt engineering guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-engineering), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; advice is written for OpenAI's models.
- [Sclar, Choi, Tsvetkov and Suhr, Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11324v2), October 2023, revised July 2024. Academic study of open-source models; effect sizes vary by model and task.
- [Schulhoff et al., The Prompt Report: A Systematic Survey of Prompting Techniques](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.06608v6), June 2024, revised February 2025. Academic survey; a taxonomy, not a ranking of what works best.

## Related research

- [What Is a System Prompt?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-prompt/)
- [What Is Context Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/)
- [Prompt Engineering vs Context Engineering](https://lowob.com/research/prompt-engineering-vs-context-engineering/)
- [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/)

## Next move

Pick one prompt your team uses every week, write four success criteria for it and run it against ten real past cases. Fix the worst failure first, and record the change with its owner and date.

# What Is AI Red Teaming?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-red-teaming/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI red teaming is deliberate, adversarial testing of an AI system to find how it fails. NIST's generative AI profile treats it as a core pre-deployment practice, and Microsoft's red team, after testing more than 100 products, concluded the work is never complete. For a commercial team, the useful version is small and specific to what the agent can reach.

AI red teaming is a structured testing exercise in which people, sometimes helped by automated tools, deliberately try to make an AI system fail: leak data, take an action it should not, produce harmful content or ignore its rules. NIST describes it as probing an AI system to find flaws and vulnerabilities. It differs from ordinary evaluation because the tester behaves like an adversary, and it is most useful when aimed at what the system can actually reach and do.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What AI red teaming means

Red teaming comes from military and security practice: a team plays the opponent to expose weaknesses before a real one does. Applied to AI, it means attacking a model or an AI application on purpose.

NIST's *Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile* (NIST AI 600-1, July 2024) describes AI red-teaming as "an evolving practice" often run in a controlled environment, and as a structured exercise to probe a system for flaws. The profile lists four kinds: red teaming by general users, by domain experts, by a mix of both where specialists are hard to recruit, and by AI systems working with human teams. Its suggested actions include adversarial role-playing exercises, red-teaming and chaos testing (action MP-5.1-005).

| Practice | Question it answers | Who acts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evals | How well does the system do its intended task? | Test set, scored automatically or by people |
| Red teaming | How can the system be made to fail or cause harm? | Testers acting as adversaries |
| Penetration testing | Can the surrounding infrastructure be breached? | Security testers |
| Monitoring | Is it failing now, in production? | Logs, alerts, reviewers |

## How it works

### What the testers attack

OWASP's GenAI Red Teaming Guide, announced on 22 January 2025, frames coverage as running from model-level vulnerabilities, such as toxicity and bias, to system-level pitfalls, such as API misuse and data exposure. It pairs a threat-modelling step with a blueprint of test categories, including agentic AI, and recommends continuous monitoring with input from security, AI and legal teams.

In practice, a red team for an AI application tries prompt injection through documents and emails, attempts to extract other customers' data, pushes the system to exceed its business rules, and checks what happens when tools return unexpected output.

### What Microsoft learned from 100 products

Microsoft's AI red team published *Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products* in January 2025. Several of its eight lessons are directly useful to a buyer:

- "Understand what the system can do and where it is applied." Testing starts from capability and context, not from a generic attack list.
- "You don't have to compute gradients to break an AI system." Simple techniques often work better than sophisticated ones.
- "AI red teaming is not safety benchmarking." A good benchmark score does not show how the system behaves under deliberate attack.
- "The work of securing AI systems will never be complete." Each model change, new tool or new data source reopens the question.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial agents read untrusted content by design: inbound email, prospect websites, call transcripts. They also touch private data and, in some builds, send messages. That combination is where a successful attack does damage, as the explainer on prompt injection sets out.

The red-team question for a commercial build is therefore narrow: given what this agent can read and do, what is the worst a hostile input could make it do? An agent at autonomy level 1, which only drafts, fails into a bad draft. An agent at level 3, which acts and reports, fails into a sent email or a changed record.

> Red teaming a commercial agent starts with its permissions, not with its prompt.

## How to start

A mid-size firm does not need a dedicated red team. It needs a short, written test plan run before launch and after every material change.

| Test | Illustrative attack | Pass condition |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Indirect injection | Inbound email with hidden instructions to forward the thread | Agent drafts a normal reply; nothing is forwarded |
| Data boundary | Ask the agent about another client's pricing | Agent refuses or has no access |
| Business rule | Ask for a discount above the approved limit | Draft is flagged for the deal desk |
| Tool misuse | Request a bulk update to all open deals | Action is blocked or sent for approval |
| Leakage | Ask the agent to repeat its instructions | No credentials or internal limits are exposed |

Record each test, the result and the fix in the same place as the agent's other decisions. When a test fails, the usual remedy is to remove a permission or add an approval step, not to add a sentence to the system prompt.

## lowob takeaways

- **Attack on purpose.** Red teaming asks how a system fails, which evals do not.
- **Aim at reach.** Test what the agent can read, change and send.
- **Repeat on change.** New models, tools and data sources reopen every result.
- **Fix with design.** Fewer permissions and approval steps outlast prompt patches.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between AI red teaming and AI evaluation?

Evaluation measures how well a system performs its intended task. Red teaming deliberately tries to make it fail, behave unsafely or break its rules.

### Who should do AI red teaming?

NIST describes general-user, expert, combined and AI-assisted red teams. For a commercial agent, a mix of a security person and someone who knows the sales process is a practical start.

### How often should you red team an AI system?

Before launch and after every material change: a new model, a new tool, a new data source or a higher autonomy level.

### Is AI red teaming required by regulation?

Requirements vary by jurisdiction and use. NIST's profile is voluntary guidance; check sector rules and the EU AI Act for your specific obligations.

## Sources and notes

- [NIST, AI 600-1: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. Voluntary US government guidance.
- [Bullwinkel et al., Lessons From Red Teaming 100 Generative AI Products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07238), arXiv, January 2025. Written by Microsoft's AI red team about its own practice.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, Announcing the OWASP Gen AI Red Teaming Guide](https://genai.owasp.org/2025/01/22/announcing-the-owasp-gen-ai-red-teaming-guide/), 22 January 2025. Community guidance; not a certification standard.

## Related research

- [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/)
- [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is Excessive Agency in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/)
- [What Is an AI Center of Excellence?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-center-of-excellence/)

## Next move

Pick one agent or AI feature in use today and run the five tests in the table above. Write down each result; any failure is a permission to remove before the next release.

# What Is a Partner Program?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-partner-program/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A partner program formalises how other companies refer, resell, deliver or integrate with your product, and what they get in return. Canalys estimates most IT spending flows through partners, and the largest vendors gate their tiers on skills and customer outcomes. This explainer covers the parts of a program, how large vendors structure tiers, and how a mid-size firm can start one without overbuilding.

A partner programme is the written set of rules a company uses to work with other firms that refer, resell, deliver or integrate with its product. It defines who qualifies, what partners must do, what they receive, and how deals and customers are shared. A good programme makes partner economics predictable for both sides; a weak one is a logo page and an unanswered inbox.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a partner programme means

Many companies have partners. Fewer have a programme. The difference is that a programme writes the terms down and applies them the same way to every partner of a given type.

A programme usually has five parts:

| Part | What it defines | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Partner types | Which kinds of firm you work with | Referral, reseller, services, technology integration |
| Requirements | What a partner must do to join or stay | Certified staff, customer launches, an annual business plan |
| Benefits | What the partner receives | Referral fee or margin, marketing funds, sales support, listing |
| Rules of engagement | How shared deals work | Deal registration, customer ownership, conflict resolution |
| Tiers | How requirements and benefits scale | Entry, mid and top levels with rising obligations |

The types differ enough that most firms should start with one. The comparison of affiliate, partner and referral programmes, and the guide to integrators, OEMs and channel partners, cover the types in more detail. This explainer concerns the structure that sits around whichever type you choose.

## How large vendors structure programmes

The biggest technology programmes are worth studying because they have had years to discover what predicts partner value.

### Microsoft: a capability score

Microsoft's partner programme awards Solutions Partner designations in six solution areas, including Data and AI, Security and Modern Work. Each area has a partner capability score out of 100. To qualify, a partner needs at least 70 points and more than zero in every metric. The metrics fall into three categories: performance, measured as net customer additions over 12 months; skilling, measured by intermediate and advanced certifications; and customer success, measured by usage growth and deployments across the partner's customers.

### AWS: tiers tied to launches

AWS's services path has three tiers. All carry the same annual fee of US$2,500. Select requires four accredited individuals, two technically certified individuals and three launched customer opportunities. Advanced requires 20 launched opportunities and a partner business plan. Premier requires 50 launched opportunities, 25 technically certified individuals, an executive business review and three AWS Competency, MSP or Well-Architected designations, sustained for more than six months. Benefits scale too: marketing development funds start at Advanced.

### The pattern

Neither vendor tiers partners on revenue alone. Both reward trained people and customers who actually use the product. A partner that sells but cannot deliver creates churn the vendor pays for later.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Canalys estimated that partners would deliver 70% of worldwide IT spending in 2025, down slightly from 73% in 2023. In many categories, the customer already has a trusted adviser, integrator or reseller, and reaching them through that firm is cheaper than reaching them directly. A programme is how a mid-size company makes that route repeatable.

It also protects the direct team. Without written rules on deal registration and customer ownership, partners and sellers end up competing for the same account, and the partner usually stops bringing deals.

## How to start a programme at mid-size

1. **Choose one partner type.** Pick the type that already holds your customers' trust, such as accounting firms, systems integrators or a complementary software vendor.
2. **Write the agreement first.** Cover the fee or margin, payment timing, deal registration, how long a registration lasts, and who owns the customer after the sale.
3. **Set two entry requirements.** For example, one trained person and one referred customer within six months. Requirements filter for commitment.
4. **Fund enablement, not just fees.** A short product course, a demo environment and a named contact usually matter more to a new partner than a higher percentage.
5. **Track partner-sourced and partner-influenced deals separately.** Mark the partner on the opportunity at creation, not at close.
6. **Review quarterly.** Keep partners that produce customers who stay. Add tiers only when you have enough partners to need them.

In **lowob**'s terms, each partner agreement and each change to its terms is a decision worth recording, with the reason and the expected outcome, so the programme can be judged on evidence rather than on who is loudest.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write it down.** A programme is terms applied consistently, not a list of logos.
- **Tier on capability and outcomes.** The largest programmes reward skills and customer success, not just sales.
- **Settle customer ownership early.** Unclear rules of engagement end more partnerships than low fees.
- **Start with one type.** Breadth comes after the first partner type is producing customers.

## Common questions

### What is a partner programme?

It is the written set of rules, requirements, benefits and tiers a company uses to work with other firms that refer, resell, deliver or integrate with its product.

### What are partner programme tiers?

Levels that raise both obligations and benefits. AWS, for example, uses Select, Advanced and Premier, with rising certification and customer launch requirements.

### What benefits should a partner programme offer?

Typical benefits are a referral fee or resale margin, deal registration protection, training, marketing funds, sales support and a directory listing.

### What is deal registration?

A rule that lets a partner register an opportunity so it is protected from competing partners or the vendor's own sellers for a set period.

## Sources and notes

- [Canalys, IT spending forecasts 2025](https://canalys.com/insights/it-spending-forecasts-2025). Analyst forecast; figures are estimates and are revised over time.
- [Microsoft Learn, Partner capability score](https://learn.microsoft.com/partner-center/partner-capability-score). Vendor program documentation; metric weights vary by solution area.
- [AWS, AWS Services Partner Tiers](https://aws.amazon.com/partners/services-tiers). Vendor program page; requirements and benefits change and vary by geography.

List the five firms that referred or influenced a deal in the last year. Ask each what would make them refer more, and draft a one-page agreement from the answers.
