# "40,000 Members and Nobody Does Anything"

Source: https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A large, silent community was usually recruited for a payout and never given a job. Pick one job, recruit thirty people by name, ask them for judgment on a real decision, close the loop in public, and count who stays when incentives stop.

A large, silent community was recruited for a payout and never given a job. Pick one job, recruit thirty people by name, ask for judgment, close the loop, and count who stays when the incentives stop. Some silence is normal: most people in any online group read without posting. But a group of 40,000 where nobody acts has a design problem, not a participation problem.

This is the turnaround chapter of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## How much silence is normal

Not all silence is failure. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: about 90% of people in an online community read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 study of four digital health networks with 63,990 members found fewer than a quarter had ever posted, and the top 1% wrote 74.7% of posts. Discord's Server Insights guidance suggests about 30% of members posting as a healthy goal for a server.

On those patterns, a 40,000-member group should have hundreds of regular contributors and a few thousand occasional ones. If it has almost none, the group is not merely skewed. Something stopped people acting, or nothing ever asked them to.

| Signal | Normal inequality | A group with no job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share who have ever posted | A minority, often a quarter or less | A tiny fraction, mostly asking about dates |
| What the active core does | Answers, builds, tests, argues | Little beyond reacting to announcements |
| Activity between announcements | Steady | Near zero |
| New member retention after a week | Tracked and improving | Not tracked, or falling |
| Who answers questions | Members, often | Staff, or nobody |

## What it usually means

The number is not the problem. The number is the symptom. When forty thousand people are present and nobody acts, three things are usually true at once.

**They were recruited for a payout.** An airdrop, a points programme, a giveaway, a quest. The incentive did its job and brought people in. It also selected for people who wanted the incentive. When it ended, their reason for being there ended with it. They did not leave. They just stopped. The on-chain record is consistent with this: a study of nine major airdrops by Messias, Yaish and Livshits found a large share of tokens were sold soon after claiming, up to 66% in some cases, and concluded airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own". Two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed about 98% of recipients had never voted in governance.

**They live on a rented platform.** The record of who they are, what they said and what they did sits in a server or group you do not control. You can broadcast to them. You cannot really reach them, and you cannot take them with you.

**The only shared interest is price or launch news.** There is no problem being solved together, no product being tested, no decision being made. So the channel fills with questions about dates and goes quiet in between.

A community is a group of people doing a job together. This group was never given one.

## Where it traces to

[Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) set out five jobs: test, teach, refer, build, govern. If none of those was ever assigned, the community has nothing to do. Silence is the correct response to no job.

[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) said the first hundred are recruited by name, asked for judgment, given a job and shown what happened to their input. The forty thousand skipped the first hundred. The foundation was never laid.

[Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) explains, for crypto teams, why a token or points programme produced a list rather than a group, and what to do about it.

There is also a newcomer problem. Kraut and colleagues' study of online groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day, and those whose first post got no reply were far less likely to stay. In a large server where questions go unanswered, the people who might have become the active core left early.

> Silence is the correct response to no job.

## The first move this week

**Pick one job.** Not five. One. The right one is whatever your product most needs this quarter. Early product means testing. Complex product means teaching. Working product means referring.

**Hand-recruit thirty people by name.** Go through the channel history and find the people who asked a real question, filed a bug or helped someone else. Message each one directly. Tell them what the job is and why you picked them.

**Ask them for judgment on a real decision.** Not a poll. Not a sentiment check. A choice you have not made, where their answer changes what you do: pricing, a feature cut, a launch order. Then make the decision.

**Close the loop in public.** Tell the wider channel what the thirty said, what you decided and why. This is the moment a list starts becoming a community. People see that input leads somewhere.

**Switch incentives off for a month.** No points, no quests, no rewards for activity. Count who is still present at the end. That number is your real community. Build from it. Treat the month as a test with a decision written in advance; our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set one up so the result means something.

**Move the record to channels you own.** An email list, a members' directory, a database of who did what. The rented platform can stay as the venue. The record leaves.

## What not to do

**Do not buy more members.** Adding people to a group with no job adds silence.

**Do not run another quest campaign.** It will produce a spike in activity and then exactly the same quiet, with a larger list.

**Do not announce a token to wake it up.** A token is an incentive. You have just learned what incentives recruit. It also creates a promise you will have to keep in public, under worse conditions. Our piece on [airdrops and points](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) sets out what any incentive teaches a community to value.

## How you know it worked

Two signs. First, the thirty are still active thirty days after the incentives stopped, and at least half of them have done the job without being asked twice. Second, one decision you made this month can be traced to their judgment, and the channel knows it.

Illustrative example: from 40,000 to 30

Decision
:   A DeFi protocol with a large, quiet Discord paused its points programme for a month and invited 30 members, chosen from the channel history, to judge the order of two planned features.

Reason and owner
:   The server had grown after a points campaign, but almost every question was about token dates. The head of growth owned the change.

What changed
:   Twenty-two of the thirty took part. The team shipped in the order they chose and explained why in the announcements channel. A month later, most of the thirty were still answering newcomers' questions, and the team started its member record from them.

Illustrative: a composite of patterns across crypto communities, not a single project.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read silence correctly.** Most members of any group lurk; a group with no active core has a design problem.
- **Assign one job.** Testing, teaching or referring, matched to what the product needs this quarter.
- **Start from thirty.** Hand-recruit people who asked real questions, filed bugs or helped others.
- **Stop paying for activity.** Do not buy members, run another quest or announce a token to wake the group up.

## Common questions

### Why is my large crypto community so inactive?

Usually because members were recruited for a payout, live on a rented platform and share only an interest in price or launch news. They were never given a job to do together.

### What percentage of community members are normally active?

Usually a minority. The 90-9-1 pattern suggests about 10% contribute at all, and Discord suggests about 30% posting as a healthy server goal. Near zero means something more than normal inequality.

### How do I revive a dead Discord or Telegram community?

Pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people by name, ask them for judgment on a real decision, then report back publicly what they said and what you decided.

### Will launching a token re-engage a quiet community?

No. A token is an incentive, and incentives recruit people who leave when they stop. It also creates a public promise you will have to keep under worse conditions.

## Sources and notes

- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; health networks, not crypto communities.
- [Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights](https://discord.com/community/understanding-server-insights), undated. Platform documentation; the 30% goal is guidance, not research.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops; exchange flows used as a proxy for selling.
- [Dune, The Uniswap Airdrop: Lessons for the Industry](https://community.dune.com/blog/uni-airdrop-analysis), late 2022. Community analysis on Dune's analytics platform; one airdrop.
- [Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities](https://www.dhi.ac.uk/san/waysofbeing/data/communication-zangana-kraut-2008.pdf), manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups.
- The diagnostic table and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

## Next move

Pick one job, hand-recruit thirty people by name, ask them for judgment on a real decision, then report back publicly what they said and what you decided.

# Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model

Source: https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Financial supervisors in the US, UK and EU are not asking to inspect your model; they want you to reconstruct what it did, step by step, and who checked. This guide maps what each regime expects to be reconstructable and for how long, and sets out a field-by-field specification for an AI decision record. That record is also what a judgment system needs to learn, so build it once as the product's spine.

Financial supervisors are not asking to inspect your model. They are asking you to reconstruct what it did, step by step, and who checked. FINRA's 2026 oversight report asks firms to track agent actions and decisions; the FCA's October 2026 review praises firms that kept records of prompts, outputs, model versions and escalation decisions; US bank supervisors have been asking whether banks can audit what their agents decide; and the EU AI Act requires high-risk systems to log events automatically. That trace is the same object a judgment system needs in order to learn. Build it once, as the spine of the product.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

Most firms still prepare for an AI examination by assembling model documentation: cards, validation reports, vendor attestations. That material matters, but it answers a question supervisors are asking less often. The questions now arriving are about a particular decision on a particular day: what the system saw, what it did, who approved it and what happened next. A firm that cannot answer those from its records will rebuild the answer under examination, from logs that were never designed for it.

This guide sets out what each major financial regime expects a firm to be able to reconstruct, how long the evidence must be kept, and a field-level specification for the record. Our explainer [What is an AI audit trail?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) covers the basic definition; this piece is the regulatory detail behind it.

## What supervisors are asking for

**FINRA.** The 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report, released on 9 December 2025, added a section on AI agents, defined as "systems or programs that are capable of autonomously performing and completing tasks on behalf of a user." It lists seven risks. Three bear directly on records: agents "acting autonomously without human validation and approval"; agents that "may act beyond the user's actual or intended scope and authority"; and the warning that "complicated, multi-step agent reasoning tasks can make outcomes difficult to trace or explain, complicating auditability." Two more explain why output sampling is not enough: general-purpose agents "may lack the necessary domain knowledge", and "misaligned or poorly designed reward functions" could lead an agent to optimise decisions in ways that harm investors, firms or markets.

The report's supervisory considerations follow from that list: how to track agent actions and decisions, where to place human-in-the-loop oversight, and how to set guardrails on agent behaviour. Its general generative AI section suggests "storing prompt and output logs for accountability and troubleshooting" and "tracking which model version was used and when." FINRA states that its rules are technologically neutral and apply "just as they apply when firms use any other technology or tool."

The sharpest reading of the report came from a law firm, not the regulator. Snell & Wilmer argued in December 2025 that "once an AI system can take action, rather than merely generate content", a firm's obligations shift; that agent behaviour should be "subject to the same controls applicable to any associated person performing a comparable function"; that a system can reach "a superficially compliant result through noncompliant intermediate conduct"; and that "the firm must be able to reconstruct the full chain of activity" because "outputs alone are insufficient." These are the firm's interpretation, labelled as such, but they follow closely from FINRA's own list of risks.

**US bank supervisors.** Reuters reported on 13 October 2026 that the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC were sending written and verbal questions to large, mid-size and smaller banks about advanced AI. According to the six people Reuters cited, the questions covered how agent actions are monitored and approved, whether agent decisions can be tracked and audited, what stops an agent exceeding its authority, and how a bank would shut autonomous systems down. The agencies were gathering information, not prescribing practice, and declined to comment.

**The FCA.** On 19 October 2026 the FCA published *AI in financial services: good practice and areas for improvement*. It states that its examples "do not create new requirements", but they show what supervisors have seen and liked. Good practice included firms that "kept records of consumer prompts, outputs, model versions, applied filters and escalation decisions", firms with "auditable records of decisions, including rationale, challenge, and escalation", and smaller firms that recorded whether staff approved, overrode or escalated an output, which "created an audit trail showing how oversight operated in practice." Areas for improvement included decisions on AI tools that were "poorly documented with limited audit trails or supporting rationale."

> A supervisory trace and a learning record are the same object seen from two sides.

The pattern across three supervisors is consistent. None asked to see model weights. All asked, in different words, for the chain from input to action to approval to outcome.

## The AI-specific rules are late. The record-keeping rules are not.

Purpose-built AI rules for financial firms are still forming, and some are moving backwards in scope.

**US model risk.** On 17 April 2026 the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC issued SR 26-2, *Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management*, superseding SR 11-7 (2011) and the 2021 BSA/AML model risk statement. It is "most relevant to" banking organisations with over $30 billion in total assets, states that it is not enforceable, and in footnote 3 says generative and agentic AI models "are not within the scope of this guidance" because they are "novel and rapidly evolving." Orrick's reading is that banks should rely on their broader risk management and governance for those tools. The OCC said the agencies plan a request for information on model risk management that considers "banks' use of AI, including generative AI and agentic AI." As of 24 October 2026 none had appeared in the Federal Register. On 4 November 2026 the OCC filled part of the gap for its own examiners: Bulletin 2026-54 sets out a supervisory framework for generative and agentic AI, which the OCC calls "super intelligence". It is examiner guidance only and says it does not establish supervisory expectations for banks, but it tells examiners to look at use-case inventories, risk tiers and a tested way to shut systems down. Our explainer [What is model risk management for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) compares SR 11-7 and SR 26-2 in detail.

For vendor models that remain in scope, SR 26-2 says sound practice includes understanding the model's "conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance", and "ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis" to check that vendor models remain fit for purpose. That is guidance, not a rule, but it describes evidence a bank can only produce if it records how a vendor model was used and what resulted.

**EU AI Act.** Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, entered into force on 27 July 2026. It moved Chapter III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems and 2 August 2028 for Annex I systems. The deferral covers high-risk duties only; most Article 50 transparency duties for chatbots and synthetic content applied from 2 August 2026, with machine-readable marking for generative systems already on the market due from 2 December 2026. The Commission's consolidated text shows no amendment markers on Articles 12, 19 or 26, so the logging duties are unchanged; only their start date moved. The [EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) sets out the full timetable.

**Resilience and records.** Meanwhile the older obligations apply now. DORA has applied since 17 January 2025. FINRA Rule 4511 and SEA Rule 17a-4 predate generative AI by decades. In July 2026, according to Reuters, the ECB asked euro zone banks for plans to counter AI-enabled cyber threats by the end of October, and to map AI use across their businesses and third parties so they could switch systems off and restart them in a controlled way. The FCA's October review folded AI into operational resilience, model failure planning and third-party dependency.

The result is that the AI-specific instruments tell you less than the general ones. Supervision, books-and-records and resilience rules already apply, and supervisors are reading them to cover agents.

## Regime by regime: what must be reconstructable

The table maps each regime to the evidence it implies and the retention it sets. Where a regime sets no period of its own, the period comes from the firm's other record-keeping obligations, and that is noted.

| Regime | What must be reconstructable | Retention | Source |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| US banks: SR 26-2 (Fed, OCC, FDIC) | For in-scope models: an inventory with "sufficient information to understand model risks"; vendor model design, data and performance; monitoring and outcome analysis. Generative and agentic AI out of scope, governed through broader risk management | None set; follows the bank's record policies | SR 26-2 and attachment, 17 April 2026 |
| US banks: supervisory questions | Whether agent decisions can be tracked and audited, who approves agent actions, and how systems are shut down | None set | Reuters, 13 October 2026 (press report of non-public inquiries) |
| US broker-dealers: FINRA | Agent actions and decisions; prompts and outputs; model version used and when; supervision under Rule 3110 | At least six years where no other period applies (Rule 4511(b)); format per SEA Rule 17a-4 | FINRA 2026 report; Rule 4511 |
| US broker-dealers: SEC | Business communications, including AI-drafted ones sent or received | Three years for communications under 17a-4(b)(4), six years for core records under 17a-4(a), first two years easily accessible; electronic systems need a time-stamped audit trail or non-rewriteable storage | 17 CFR 240.17a-4 |
| UK: FCA | Prompts, outputs, model versions, filters and escalation decisions; decision rationale, challenge and escalation; agent inventory with owners and controls | Existing Handbook rules; for in-scope recorded communications, five years, or seven if the FCA asks (SYSC 10A) | FCA good practice review, 19 October 2026; Global Relay summary of SYSC 10A |
| UK: PRA SS1/23 | Model identification and classification, governance, development and use, independent validation, mitigants, for models used in business decisions "regardless of technology", including vendor and machine learning models | None set | PRA SS1/23, version effective 23 April 2026 |
| EU AI Act: providers (Art. 12, 19) | Automatic event logs over the system's lifetime, sufficient to identify risk situations, support post-market monitoring and monitor operation | At least six months; financial institutions keep logs within their financial services documentation | AI Act Service Desk, consolidated text at 27 July 2026 |
| EU AI Act: deployers (Art. 26) | Operation monitored against the instructions for use; human oversight assigned to competent people; logs under the deployer's control | At least six months; financial institutions keep logs within their financial services documentation | As above; applies to Annex III systems from 2 December 2027 |
| EU: DORA | ICT-related incidents and significant cyber threats; root causes; logs of access, change management, ICT operations and network traffic | Set by the firm from its ICT risk assessment; logs protected against tampering, deletion and unauthorised access; clocks synchronised | Regulation (EU) 2022/2554 Art. 17; Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1774 Art. 12 |

Four points in the table are easy to miss.

**The EU minimum is a floor, not the answer.** Six months is the AI Act's minimum. A financial institution keeps the same logs "as part of the documentation kept pursuant to the relevant Union financial service law", which in practice points to the longer periods in sector rules. A credit decision made with a high-risk system in 2028 may need its log long after six months have passed.

**High-risk scope is narrow but includes core lending.** Annex III point 5(b) covers systems "to evaluate the creditworthiness of natural persons or establish their credit score", excluding fraud detection; point 5(c) covers risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance. Business account scoring and most internal drafting tools fall outside. For those, the logging duty comes from FINRA, the SEC, the FCA and DORA rather than the AI Act.

**Format matters as much as content.** SEA Rule 17a-4(f) allows electronic records only if the system keeps a complete, time-stamped audit trail of modifications and deletions, with the identity of the person acting, or stores records in non-rewriteable, non-erasable form. DORA's logging standard requires protection against "tampering, deletion, and unauthorised access." A trace held in a mutable application table, editable by the team that runs the agent, meets neither.

**Guidance labels are not the boundary of scrutiny.** SR 26-2 excludes generative AI from scope; US supervisors were asking about agent audit trails six months later. The FCA sets no new rules; its review still describes the records it expects good firms to hold.

## What the trace must contain

A usable trace for an AI-assisted decision records, with timestamps and actors, the request, the evidence, the system, the output, every human action, the final action and the outcome. The table turns that into fields. Each field names the regulatory reason for keeping it, so that compliance can sign off the specification line by line.

| Field | What to store | Why a supervisor needs it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Record ID and parent ID | A unique ID per run, linked to the case, account or ticket and to any earlier run it supersedes | Joins the trace, the approval and the outcome; without it nothing reconstructs |
| Request | The instruction as made, the requester, channel and time received | Shows what the system was asked to do and by whom |
| Inputs | Customer and case data passed to the system, by reference and version, with personal data handled under the firm's privacy rules | Lets a reviewer replay the situation; FCA good practice names consumer prompts |
| Retrieved context | Each document or record retrieved, with its ID, version, status, date and source at the moment of retrieval | Proves which evidence the answer rested on, even after the source changes |
| Model and version | Provider, model name and version, deployment or endpoint | FINRA suggests tracking "which model version was used and when"; FCA names model versions |
| Instructions and configuration | Prompt or instruction set version, system settings, guardrails and filters applied | Explains behaviour that a model version alone cannot; FCA names applied filters |
| Tool calls | Each tool or API called, with parameters, response, permission used and time | FINRA's "track agent actions"; shows whether the agent stayed within its authority |
| Output | The text, score or recommendation produced, with any confidence or rationale the system gave | The thing a reviewer approved or rejected |
| Reviewer | Name or role, what they were shown, time opened, time spent | FCA warns that review can become "box-ticking"; time spent is the evidence it did not |
| Reviewer action | Approved, edited (with the diff), rejected, escalated, with reason | Rationale, challenge and escalation are what the FCA called auditable records |
| Final action | What was actually sent, executed or filed, by whom, and when | Separates what the system proposed from what the firm did |
| Outcome | Complaint, reversal, default, correction or confirmation, written back when it arrives, with date | Outcome analysis under SR 26-2; the learning signal for the firm |
| Timestamps | Synchronised time for every event above | DORA requires clock synchronisation; sequence is the chain |
| Retention and integrity | Retention class, legal hold flag, write-once or audit-trailed storage, access log | SEA Rule 17a-4(f) format; DORA tamper protection; AI Act retention floor |

Two fields cause most of the trouble in practice. The first is retrieved context. Storing a link to the current version of a policy is not enough; the trace needs the version the agent saw, with its status at that moment. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why records that change in place break reconstruction. The second is the reviewer. An approval click with no record of what was shown, or how long it took, cannot distinguish a real check from a rubber stamp, and our piece [A reviewer who does not verify is not a control](https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/) argues that distinction is the one that matters.

That list is also, almost exactly, what a judgment system needs to learn: the situation, the evidence, the recommendation, the human correction, the decision and the result. Our [approval gate explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) shows where the reviewer fields are captured in the workflow.

## Spine, not afterthought

Teams that treat tracing as an engineering nicety will rebuild it under examination, at speed, from logs that were never designed to answer a supervisor's questions. Observability tools capture the first half of the table well: inputs, model calls, tool calls and latency. Our list of [LLM observability and evaluation platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/) covers them. They rarely capture the second half: who reviewed, what they changed, what the firm finally did and what happened afterwards. That half lives in the firm's own workflow and belongs in a record the firm owns.

Teams that design the trace as the product's spine get two things at once: supervision that is close to free, and a learning loop with complete data.

One caution: a trace is a record, so it inherits record-keeping obligations. Agree retention, immutability and access with compliance before the first production decision, not after the first request. That includes personal data. The AI Act's retention clause defers to data protection law, so a trace that stores full customer inputs needs a lawful basis and a deletion rule as well as a retention rule.

Illustrative example: the three-month reconstruction drill

Decision
:   A mid-size wealth manager's compliance lead picked one AI-drafted client email from three months earlier and timed how long it took to rebuild the chain.

What changed
:   The firm added a run ID to every draft, stored retrieved documents by version, logged reviewer edits as diffs, and moved the approval into the workflow. The same drill now takes minutes.

Illustrative: a composite built from patterns across regulated firms, not a single client.

**In practice**

Write the trace specification first, with compliance, and build the workflow around it. Make every human action in the review gate a logged event with duration. Store the evidence standing at the moment of retrieval, not just a link to the current version. Put the trace in storage that meets the strictest format rule that applies to you.

Test reconstruction: pick a decision from three months ago and time how long it takes to rebuild the full chain.

## What would prove this wrong

The argument fails if examinations of agentic systems accept model documentation and output sampling without asking for step-level reconstruction. Then the trace is good practice rather than an obligation.

The evidence so far points the other way. FINRA names auditability as a distinct agent risk. US bank supervisors, by Reuters' account, have asked directly whether agent decisions can be tracked and audited. The FCA's review describes audit trails as the evidence of how oversight "operated in practice." Two developments would change the picture: a US request for information that settles on documentation-led expectations for generative AI, or EU harmonised standards for logging that set a lighter bar than sector rules. Neither had appeared by mid-November 2026. The Commission's standardisation request includes record-keeping and logging, but the only harmonised standard published so far, EN 18286 in October 2026, covers quality management.

Gateway card

### Before the first production decision

- A trace specification agreed with compliance, field by field
- One run ID that joins trace, approval, final action and outcome
- Retrieved evidence stored by version and status at retrieval
- Reviewer identity, view, time spent and action logged as events
- Retention set to the longest rule that applies, not the AI Act floor
- Storage that is write-once or keeps a full audit trail of changes
- A timed reconstruction test on a three-month-old decision

## lowob takeaways

- **Supervisors want the chain.** FINRA, US bank supervisors and the FCA all ask for reconstruction of actions, approvals and outcomes, not model internals.
- **Old rules carry the weight.** Rule 4511, SEA Rule 17a-4, DORA and FCA record-keeping already apply to AI-assisted work.
- **Six months is a floor.** The AI Act's retention minimum sits under sector rules that run three to six years or more.
- **Specify the review fields.** Reviewer view, time spent, edits and reasons are where most traces are thin.
- **Build it once.** The supervisory trace and the learning record are the same object.

## Common questions

### What do financial regulators expect from an AI audit trail?

The ability to reconstruct what an AI system did and who checked it. FINRA asks firms to consider how to track agent actions and decisions, the FCA cites records of prompts, outputs, model versions and escalation decisions as good practice, and US bank supervisors have asked whether agent decisions can be audited.

### How long must AI decision records be kept in financial services?

It depends on the regime. The EU AI Act sets a six-month minimum for high-risk system logs, FINRA Rule 4511 defaults to six years, SEA Rule 17a-4 sets three or six years by record type, and DORA leaves log retention to the firm's risk assessment.

### Does SR 26-2 apply to generative AI and AI agents?

No. Footnote 3 of SR 26-2 places generative and agentic AI models outside its scope. Banks govern them through broader risk management, and the agencies have said they plan a request for information on AI use.

### What should an AI decision audit record contain?

A run ID, the request, inputs, retrieved context with versions, model and version, instruction set, tool calls, output, reviewer and their action, the final action, the outcome, synchronised timestamps and retention metadata.

# What Is Customer Health Scoring?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A customer health score summarises how likely an account is to renew or grow, using weighted measures such as product usage, support history and sentiment. Most scores are built from intuition and never checked against outcomes. This explainer covers how health scores are structured, what inputs to use, and how to test whether a score actually predicts churn.

Customer health scoring is the practice of combining several signals about an account, such as product usage, support activity, relationship strength and payment history, into a single score that indicates renewal risk or growth potential. It lets a small team decide which accounts need attention first. A score is only useful if it has been checked against what actually happened to past customers.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What customer health scoring means

A customer success or account team cannot give every customer the same attention. A health score is a triage tool: one number or colour per account, updated regularly, that tells the team where to look.

Scores are usually built as weighted composites. Gainsight's documentation shows the common structure. Individual measures, such as login frequency or open support tickets, each produce a score. Measures sit in groups, such as "adoption" or "relationship". Each measure is weighted within its group, each group is weighted in the overall score, and neither set of weights can exceed 100%. When a measure has no data, its weight is redistributed across the others in proportion.

| Input category | Example measures | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Usage or adoption | Active users, feature breadth, consumption against contract | High usage can coexist with an unhappy buyer |
| Support | Ticket volume, severity, time to resolve | Some tickets signal engagement, not risk |
| Relationship | Executive sponsor in place, meeting cadence, champion changes | Often subjective; needs a written definition |
| Sentiment | Survey scores, CSM assessment | Low response rates; recency bias |
| Commercial | Payment status, contraction, open expansion | Lags behind the underlying cause |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Retention compounds

The economic case predates the software. Reichheld, writing for Bain in 2001, argued that small increases in retention translate into large profit gains, and gave the example that in financial services a 5% increase in customer retention produced more than a 25% increase in profit. The figure is sector-specific and two decades old, so treat it as an illustration of the mechanism rather than a benchmark for your business.

### Renewals are decided early

By the time a customer sends notice, the decision has usually been made. A health score exists to surface the earlier signals: a champion leaving, usage falling after a reorganisation, a run of severe tickets. The value is the lead time it gives a person to act.

### It focuses scarce time

Gartner's guidance on key accounts makes the same point from the growth side: monitor account health continuously and re-tier accounts based on performance, so resources are not spent on underperformers. A health score is how that monitoring becomes routine rather than anecdotal.

## How to build and test a first score

### Start small

Gainsight's guidance, from a 2019 post by Ryan Toben, is to include only measures that are meaningful, actionable and consistently applicable, to start without waiting for perfect data, and to keep the number of variables small. Five to seven measures across three or four groups is enough for a first version.

### Use what you have

Usage data is helpful but not essential. One example Gainsight describes is an on-premise business with no usage data that combined a CSM score and a partner score with finance metrics, support cases, product requests and software version. Another used credit drawdown as a stand-in for usage.

### Back-test before trusting it

This is the step most teams skip.

1. **List last year's outcomes.** Every account that churned, contracted, renewed flat or expanded.
2. **Reconstruct the score.** Calculate what your proposed score would have shown for each account 90 days before its renewal date.
3. **Compare.** If churned accounts were mostly red and expanded accounts mostly green, the score has signal. If the colours are mixed, change the measures or weights.
4. **Set thresholds from the data.** Choose the red and amber cut-offs where churn rates actually change, not at round numbers.
5. **Re-test each year.** Products, customers and teams change. A score that predicted churn two years ago may not now.

### Attach an action to each colour

A red score should trigger a defined play with an owner and a deadline. In **lowob**'s terms, each intervention is a decision in the record, with a reason and an expected outcome, and the renewal result is written back so next year's back-test has better evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat the score as triage.** Its job is to tell a person where to look first.
- **Keep it small.** A handful of clean, explainable measures beats a long list of noisy ones.
- **Back-test it.** A score that would not have flagged last year's churn will not flag next year's.
- **Tie colours to actions.** A red account without an owner and a play is just a report.

## Common questions

### What is a customer health score?

It is a single score or colour per account, built from weighted signals such as usage, support history, relationship strength and payment status, that indicates renewal risk or growth potential.

### What metrics go into a customer health score?

Common inputs are product usage or consumption, support ticket patterns, executive sponsor and champion status, survey sentiment and commercial signals such as payment history or contraction.

### Can you build a health score without product usage data?

Yes. Gainsight documents scores built from consumption, support cases, finance metrics and CSM judgment where usage data was unavailable.

### How do you know if a health score works?

Back-test it. Calculate what the score would have shown for past accounts before renewal and check whether churned accounts scored lower than renewed ones.

## Sources and notes

- [Bain & Company, Prescription for cutting costs](https://www.media.bain.com/Images/BB_Prescription_cutting_costs.pdf), Frederick Reichheld, 2001. Consultancy brief; retention figure is specific to financial services.
- [Gainsight, Measure Weights in Scorecards](https://support.gainsight.com/Gainsight_NXT/05Scorecards/02Admin_Guides/Measure_Weights_in_Scorecards). Vendor product documentation.
- [Gainsight, 3 Ways to Structure Your Customer Health Score (No Usage Data Required)](https://www.gainsight.com/blog/3-ways-to-structure-your-customer-health-score-no-usage-data-required/), March 2019. Vendor blog describing customer examples.
- [Gartner, Gartner Survey Shows 95% of Chief Sales Officers Expect Higher Growth From Key Accounts](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/gartner-survey-shows-95--of-chief-sales-officers-expect-higher-g), October 2021. Analyst press release; recommendation on monitoring account health.

## Related research

- [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [What Is Revenue Operations (RevOps)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/)

## Next move

List the accounts that churned or contracted in the last 12 months. For each, write down what your current health score said 90 days before, and count how many it flagged.

# What Is Prompt Caching?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Prompt caching stores the processed form of a prompt's fixed opening, such as instructions, tools or a policy document, so later requests that start the same way skip that work. Cache hits are billed at a fraction of the input price and answers start sooner; output is unchanged. The saving depends on prompt order and on keeping the fixed part identical.

Prompt caching is a provider feature that stores the processed form of the fixed start of a prompt, such as instructions, tool definitions or a long document, so later requests that begin the same way skip that work. Cached input is billed at a fraction of the normal rate and the response starts sooner. The answer itself is unchanged. It only works if the repeated part comes first and stays identical, so prompt design decides whether a team gets the saving.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What prompt caching means

Before a model writes anything, it processes every input token. A request that opens with 20,000 tokens of policy repeats that work, and that charge, on every call.

Prompt caching keeps the result of that processing for a short period. Research came first: Gim and colleagues' 2023 paper "Prompt Cache" stored precomputed attention states for frequently reused text segments on the inference server. They reported time-to-first-token improvements of about 8 times on GPUs and 60 times on CPUs, with output accuracy preserved.

Providers now offer caching as a billing feature, and the mechanics differ.

|  | Anthropic | OpenAI | Google Gemini API |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| How it is turned on | A cache breakpoint on a block, or one top-level setting for automatic caching | On by default for supported models | Implicit caching on by default for Gemini 2.5 and newer |
| Minimum prompt size | 512 to 4,096 tokens, by model | 1,024 tokens on recent models | 2,048 to 4,096 tokens, by model |
| How long it lasts | 5 minutes, refreshed on each use; 1-hour option | Typically 5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to an hour; extended retention up to 24 hours | Not stated for implicit caching |
| Price of a hit | 0.1 times input on most models, lower on some | Discounted up to 95% | Savings passed on automatically |
| What must match | Everything up to the breakpoint | The entire rendered prefix | Google advises common content first, with similar requests sent close together |

Anthropic's documentation states that caching "has no effect on output token generation": the response is the same as it would be without the cache.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Most commercial AI work has a large fixed part and a small variable part. A proposal checker carries the same pricing rules and discount policy on every call; only the proposal changes. An account assistant carries the same [system prompt](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-prompt/) and tool definitions; only the question changes. An agent re-sends its instructions and tools at every step of its loop. The fixed part is where caching pays.

A worked example, illustrative, using Anthropic's list prices for Claude Sonnet 5.5 on 16 November 2026: $2 per million input tokens, $2.50 for a five-minute cache write and $0.10 for a cache read. A 20,000-token policy prefix is sent 100 times in a session, with no gap longer than five minutes. Uncached, that prefix costs $4.00. Cached, one write costs $0.05 and 99 reads cost about $0.20, so about $0.25 in total, or roughly 94% less. Output and the variable part are billed as normal. See [AI inference cost](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/) for the other levers.

Speed improves too: Anthropic says caching generally improves time-to-first-token for long documents, and OpenAI that it reduces input processing time before the response starts.

Caching also rewards a discipline **lowob** recommends anyway: stable, versioned instructions. A system prompt edited ad hoc during the day, or a timestamp placed at the top of every prompt, breaks the cache on every call. Anthropic's documentation states that "changes at each level invalidate that level and all subsequent levels". Editing a tool definition, for example, invalidates the tools, system and message caches together.

On privacy, Anthropic says caches "are isolated between organizations", and on its own API also by workspace. OpenAI says caches "are not shared across organizations". Cached content is still held for the cache lifetime, so firms with [zero data retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/) terms should confirm how caching is treated under them.

Prompt caching is different from response caching, which some [LLM gateways](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-llm-gateway/) offer. A response cache returns a stored answer to an identical request without calling the model. A prompt cache still calls the model.

## How to design for caching

| Do | Avoid |
| --- | --- |
| Put fixed material first: tools, system prompt, policies, reference documents | Dates, user names or request IDs at the top of the prompt |
| Put the variable question or record last | Reordering tool definitions between calls |
| Version system prompts and change them deliberately | Small edits to live instructions during the day |
| Check the usage fields: cache\_read\_input\_tokens at Anthropic, cached\_tokens at OpenAI | Assuming caching worked because it is switched on |
| Send related calls close together | Spacing calls so the cache expires between them |

## lowob takeaways

- **Caching reuses the fixed start of a prompt.** Input gets cheaper and faster; the answer is unchanged.
- **Order decides the saving.** Fixed material first, variable material last.
- **Any change to the prefix breaks it.** Version instructions and tools.
- **Verify in the usage fields.** Track cache hits per task.

## Common questions

### Does prompt caching change the AI model's answer?

No. Anthropic's documentation states the response is identical to what you would get without caching. Only the cost and speed of processing the input change.

### How long does a prompt cache last?

Minutes, typically. Anthropic's default is five minutes, refreshed on each use, with a one-hour option. OpenAI's caches typically last 5 to 10 minutes of inactivity, up to an hour, with extended retention of up to 24 hours.

### Is prompt caching the same as caching AI responses?

No. Response caching returns a stored answer without calling the model. Prompt caching still calls the model and generates a new answer; it only reuses the processing of the prompt's opening.

### Can other customers see my cached prompts?

Anthropic and OpenAI both state that caches are isolated between organisations, even when prompts are identical.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Pricing (Claude API documentation)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor list prices; change often.
- [OpenAI, Prompt caching guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; retention periods are typical, not guaranteed.
- [Google, Gemini API context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/interactions/caching.md.txt), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; this page covers implicit caching only.
- [Gim et al., Prompt Cache: Modular Attention Reuse for Low-Latency Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.04934), November 2023, revised April 2024. Academic preprint; latency gains measured on the authors' own setup.

## Related research

## Next move

Take your highest-volume AI task and move every fixed element (instructions, tools and policy text) to the start of the prompt, with anything dated or user-specific at the end. Then check the cache-read field on the next hundred calls.

# What Is Seat-Based Pricing for AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Seat-based pricing charges per named user per month, as most AI assistants do. It is predictable, but seats now come with usage limits and metered extras, and agents weaken the link between users and value. Gartner and Deloitte both expect hybrid pricing to spread. Buyers should size seats to a workflow, read the usage terms and track weekly use per seat.

Seat-based pricing charges a fixed fee for each named user of an AI tool, usually per month and often with an annual commitment. It is the standard model for AI assistants because it is easy to budget. Its weakness is that a seat measures access, not work: seats go unused, and an agent that works for many people does not fit the per-user model well.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What seat-based pricing means

A seat is a licence for one named person. The buyer pays the same amount whether that person uses the tool every hour or never opens it. Most business AI assistants are sold this way, often with a cheaper rate for annual commitment.

Two vendor pages show the pattern. Prices below were checked on the vendors' own pages in November 2026 and change often.

| Plan | Annual billing | Monthly billing | Notes on the vendor page |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot Business (add-on) | $21.00 per user per month; $18.00 promotional for the first year | $25.20 per user per month | Promotion runs 1 July to 31 December 2026; some features listed as "Metered" |
| Claude Team, standard seat | $20 per seat per month | $25 per seat per month | Teams of 2 to 150; usage limits apply |
| Claude Team, premium seat | $100 per seat per month | $125 per seat per month | "5x more usage than standard seats" |

The table shows two things that a headline seat price hides. Monthly billing costs 20% to 25% more per seat than the standard annual price on these plans. And a seat is no longer a flat entitlement. Anthropic's page says usage limits apply and that how fast a user reaches one "depends on the model you use, how long your chats are, and how large your files are". Microsoft's page lists some capabilities as metered. In practice many seat plans are already hybrids.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The first issue is waste. A seat bought for someone with no defined task is a recurring cost with no return. Our analysis of AI assistants found that seats bought ahead of a workflow drift into low weekly use. The fix is to buy for the people in one commercial workflow and expand where use and results both move.

The second issue is structural. An agent does work on behalf of many people. If one agent drafts follow-ups for a whole sales team, charging per user undercharges for the work, and vendors know it. Gartner's July 2026 release put the point plainly: agentic AI "breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth for many enterprise software vendors". It estimated up to $234 billion of enterprise application spend exposed through 2030.

Deloitte's 2026 technology predictions draw the conclusion for buyers. It says "subscriptions and seat-based licensing" could give way to hybrids, and expects that mixes of licences with "usage-, value-, or outcome-based pricing become standard". It cites Gartner's projection that by 2030 at least 40% of enterprise SaaS spend will shift towards usage-, agent- or outcome-based pricing.

For the buyer this means the seat price is the start of the cost, not the whole of it. Credits, metered agents and premium tiers sit beside it.

## How to buy seats well

| Check | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Name the workflow each seat serves | A seat without a task is the main source of waste |
| Compare annual and monthly billing | Annual is cheaper but locks in seats before use is proven |
| Read the usage limits and overage terms | Heavy users can hit limits or trigger metered charges |
| Separate assistant seats from agent costs | Agents are often priced by usage or credits, not seats |
| Track weekly active users per seat | The ratio shows whether to expand, hold or cut |
| Check promotional end dates | First-year discounts renew at list price |

Seats suit tools a person uses daily, where that person's time is the value. Usage or outcome pricing suits agents whose value scales with volume. Many firms will run both: seats for the assistant, metered pricing for the agents.

## lowob takeaways

- **A seat buys access, not work.** Value depends on whether the person has a task for it.
- **Seat plans are already hybrids.** Usage limits, credits and metered features sit beside the fee.
- **Agents strain the model.** One agent can serve many users, so vendors are moving to usage and outcomes.
- **Buy for a workflow.** Expand seat by seat on measured weekly use.

## Common questions

### What is seat-based pricing?

A pricing model that charges a fixed fee for each named user of a software tool, usually per month, regardless of how much each user uses it.

### Is seat-based or usage-based pricing better for AI?

Seats suit assistants a person uses daily. Usage suits agents whose work scales with volume. Many contracts now combine the two.

### Why are AI vendors moving away from per-seat pricing?

Agents can do work for many people, so user counts no longer track the value delivered. Gartner says this breaks the link between user growth and revenue growth.

### How many AI seats should a company buy?

Enough for the people in the first defined workflow. Expand as weekly use and the workflow's own results improve.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft, Microsoft 365 Copilot plans and pricing](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-copilot/pricing), accessed November 2026. Vendor pricing page; US prices, promotional terms time-limited.
- [Anthropic, Claude pricing](https://claude.com/pricing), accessed November 2026. Vendor pricing page; usage limits described, not quantified.
- [Gartner, $234 billion in enterprise application software spend is at risk from agentic AI](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-07-01-gartner-says-us-dollars-234-billion-in-enterprise-application-software-spend-is-at-risk-from-agentic-artificial-intelligence), 1 July 2026. Analyst press release; projection, not measured spend.
- [Deloitte Insights, TMT Predictions 2026: SaaS and AI agents](https://www.deloitte.com/us/en/insights/industry/technology/technology-media-and-telecom-predictions/2026/saas-ai-agents.html), 2026. Consultancy predictions; the 40% figure is Gartner's, cited by Deloitte.

## Next move

Export your AI tool's seat list and its weekly active users for the last month. Any seat unused for four weeks is a candidate to cut or to reassign to someone in a defined workflow.

# Co-Selling With Platforms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Co-selling means working joint opportunities with a platform's own sales team. Most mid-size vendors join the programmes, share a few deals and hear nothing back. The reason is incentive: platform sellers prioritise partners that grow the platform's consumption and customer outcomes. We explain how the AWS and Microsoft mechanics work, what co-selling costs in time and data, a four-stage path from listed to joint planning, and how to measure whether it pays.

Co-selling is a structured arrangement in which a vendor and a platform's sales team work the same customer opportunity: the vendor shares deals with the platform, the platform's account team supports them, and, once the vendor has earned it, the platform refers opportunities back. The large cloud programmes, including AWS's ACE programme and Microsoft's partner programme, provide the mechanics. Whether they produce anything depends on one question: does your product grow the platform's own number? Platform sellers are measured on their platform's revenue, consumption and customer outcomes, and they spend time on partners that move those. A vendor that cannot show how it does will share pipeline and receive little back.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

The usual experience runs like this. A vendor joins a cloud partner programme, lists on the marketplace, and shares a handful of opportunities through the partner portal. Months pass. The platform's account managers do not call. The partner manager concludes co-selling does not work.

It can work, but the arrangement has a logic that many vendors miss. Part 14 of this series covers partner channels where the vendor recruits partners to sell its product. Co-selling reverses the direction: the vendor is the partner, and the platform decides whether to spend its sellers' time on it. Part 16 covers marketplace listings, the transaction route that co-selling often depends on.

## What platform sellers want

A platform's account manager has a target, a set of accounts and too many partners asking for attention. The partners who get time are those who help the account manager hit the target. The design of the partner programmes makes that explicit.

| Programme feature | What it rewards | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AWS services tiers: Select, Advanced, Premier | Certified people, and launched customer opportunities with minimum monthly revenue (3 opportunities at Select, 20 at Advanced, 50 at Premier) | AWS Services Partner Tiers |
| AWS ACE programme | Sharing and updating opportunities; discounts for originating new customer opportunities; eligibility to receive AWS referrals | AWS ACE programme page |
| Microsoft partner capability score | Net customer adds, certifications, customers' usage growth and deployments; 70 of 100 points to qualify for a designation | Microsoft Learn |
| Microsoft Partner Admin Link | Automatic attribution of influenced and Azure-consumed revenue to the partner's access in the customer's environment | Microsoft Learn |
| Microsoft Azure IP co-sell eligible status | At least $100,000 of Azure consumed revenue over a trailing 12 months, or $100,000 of cumulative marketplace billed revenue; a transactable offer primarily platformed on Azure | Microsoft Learn |
| Google Cloud Partner Network tiers and competencies | Tiers (Select, Premier, Diamond) based on joint customer outcomes; competencies measured on certifications and contributions to validated closed/won opportunities | Google Cloud |

Every row measures customer outcomes on the platform: launched workloads, usage growth, deployments, consumed or marketplace-billed revenue, closed opportunities. None measures the vendor's revenue outside the platform. A vendor whose product increases the customer's cloud consumption, or speeds up a migration, or brings a new workload onto the platform, has something to offer the account manager. A vendor whose product runs anywhere and consumes little has a weaker case, however good the product.

The scale explains why platforms invest in this. Canalys forecast that 70% of customer spending on technology, IT services and telecom services would go through partners in 2025. Platforms rely on partners to reach and serve customers, and their programmes are built to direct partner effort toward the platform's growth.

## How the mechanics work

The programmes differ in detail but share a structure: register, share pipeline, attribute influence, and transact.

| Step | On AWS | On Microsoft | What the vendor should do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Join | Join the partner network at no cost and accept the ACE terms in Partner Central | Join the AI Cloud Partner Program; reach co-sell-ready status with a published marketplace offer, a complete business profile, a sales contact per co-sell geography, a one-pager and a pitch deck | Choose one platform first, based on where most of your customers run |
| Share pipeline | Submit opportunities to the ACE Pipeline Manager and keep them updated through the opportunity's life | Co-sell opportunities in Partner Center, shared with Microsoft sales teams or other partners, or logged as private deals for Microsoft's reporting | Share only qualified opportunities, with accurate stage and value |
| Attribute influence | Launched opportunities count toward tier requirements | Partner Admin Link and Digital Partner of Record link the partner to customer subscriptions | Set up attribution with every customer, or the influence will not be credited |
| Transact | Marketplace private offers; some purchases count toward customer spend commitments | Microsoft Marketplace; sales of Azure IP co-sell eligible offers count toward customers' Azure consumption commitments (MACC) | Route suitable deals through the marketplace (Part 16) |
| Receive | Become ACE-eligible to receive AWS referrals | Microsoft sales teams can identify and share opportunities with co-sell partners | Respond fast; a slow reply to a platform referral is rarely forgiven |

Two details are easy to miss. On Microsoft, Digital Partner of Record can be set only by the customer, one partner per subscription, while Partner Admin Link requires the partner's user or service principal to have access in the customer's environment. If the vendor does not set these up, its influence on the customer's consumption may never be credited. On AWS, funding programmes such as marketing development funds are available only from the Advanced tier, and partner opportunity acceleration funding for proofs of concept from Select, so tier progress affects what support a vendor can request.

Google Cloud is changing its structure. It announced the Google Cloud Partner Network in December 2025 for rollout in the first quarter of 2026, applying to ISVs and services partners alike. Tiers are based on customer outcomes, and engagements are applied automatically toward a partner's tier and competency progress. Its announcement says the programme rewards successful co-sell efforts but does not set out the co-sell mechanics.

These descriptions come from each platform's own documentation and change regularly. Check the current terms before building a plan around any benefit.

## What co-selling costs

Co-selling looks free because joining is free. The real costs are people, time, data and dependence.

**Certified people.** AWS's services tiers require accredited and certified individuals, from four accredited individuals and four certifications at Select to twenty accredited individuals and thirty-five certifications at Premier. Microsoft's capability score includes skilling metrics. For a 50- to 500-person firm, certifying staff is a real cost in time.

**A partner manager's time.** Opportunities must be kept updated through their life. A pipeline shared once and left stale signals a partner not worth the account manager's time.

**Pipeline data.** Sharing an opportunity means telling the platform the customer, the deal size and the stage. Check what your customer contracts allow, agree internally what is shared and what is not, and record the rule. Some customers will not want a platform told about a purchase before it is signed.

**Dependence.** A vendor whose pipeline comes mainly from one platform's referrals has moved its single-channel risk rather than removed it. Our piece *Single-channel dependency* covers the warning signs.

> Platform sellers are paid on the platform's number. Show how you grow it, or expect silence.

## Four stages, in order

Most vendors move through co-selling in four stages. Each needs the one before it, and trying to skip ahead is the most common reason the arrangement stalls.

| Stage | What happens | Evidence the vendor needs | Signal to move on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Listed | Marketplace listing live; partner programme joined | A product that runs on the platform and a clear description of the workload it brings | First deals transacted through the marketplace |
| 2. Sharing | Vendor shares qualified opportunities and keeps them updated | Accurate pipeline; attribution set up with customers | Platform account managers start responding on shared deals |
| 3. Receiving | Platform sellers refer opportunities to the vendor | Launched customers, tier requirements met, a short case for how the product grows consumption | Referrals arrive without being chased |
| 4. Joint planning | Vendor and platform agree target accounts and plans together | A record of co-sold wins and their effect on platform consumption | Named contacts on both sides and a shared account list |

The evidence at stage 3 is a single page an account manager can use: which workloads the product brings to the platform, what consumption a typical customer adds, and two or three customers willing to be named. That page is often what changes the relationship.

## Measuring whether co-selling pays

Four numbers, tracked quarterly, tell a vendor whether the arrangement earns its cost.

| Measure | Question |
| --- | --- |
| Co-sold win rate against non-co-sold | Do deals with platform involvement win more often? |
| Cycle time, co-sold against not | Does platform involvement shorten the deal? |
| Platform-referred pipeline | Is the platform sending deals, or only receiving them? |
| Stakeholders added per co-sold deal | Did the platform's account team open doors the vendor could not? |

The last is worth tracking because breadth of contact predicts outcomes. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found won deals had about nine engaged contacts at the solution stage against about two in lost deals. A platform account team that knows the customer's architecture and budget holders can add contacts a vendor would take months to reach. The Ebsta figure is correlational; it does not prove the platform caused the win.

Co-selling decisions, such as which platform to commit to, which certifications to fund and what pipeline data to share, belong in the decision record The Build Order describes (*The commercial decisions worth recording*). The data-sharing rule in particular is a decision someone will later need to defend, and our piece *Nothing sends without a person* applies: no opportunity should be shared with a platform automatically without a named person approving what goes.

Illustrative example: an observability vendor moves from sharing to receiving

Decision
:   Commit to one cloud platform for co-selling, fund the certifications for its next tier, and write a one-page case for platform account managers.

Reason and owner
:   A year of sharing opportunities had produced no referrals; most customers ran on that platform and the product typically increased their monitored workloads. Owned by the head of partnerships, with sales leadership agreeing the data-sharing rule.

What changed
:   Attribution was set up with every live customer, shared opportunities were updated weekly, and co-sold win rate and cycle time were reported quarterly beside non-co-sold deals.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size observability software vendor, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Show how you grow the platform's number.** Platform programmes reward customer consumption and outcomes, not your revenue.
- **Set up attribution with every customer.** On Microsoft, influence that is not linked may never be credited.
- **Count the real costs.** Certified staff, a partner manager's time, pipeline data and the risk of dependence.
- **Move through the stages in order.** Listed, sharing, receiving, joint planning; evidence at each one earns the next.

Gateway card

### Before you commit to co-selling with a platform

- One platform chosen, based on where most customers run
- A one-page case for how your product grows the platform's consumption
- Attribution set up with live customers
- A written rule on what pipeline data is shared, approved by a named person
- Co-sold win rate, cycle time and referred pipeline tracked quarterly

## Common questions

### What is co-selling with AWS?

Working joint customer opportunities with AWS sellers through the APN Customer Engagements (ACE) programme. Partners share and update opportunities in Partner Central and, once eligible, can receive referrals from AWS.

### How do you get referrals from Microsoft or AWS sellers?

Show that your product increases customer consumption on the platform, meet the programme's tier or designation requirements, keep shared opportunities accurate, and set up partner attribution with your customers.

### Is co-selling with cloud providers worth it for a small software company?

It can be if most customers run on one platform and the product adds workloads there. If customers are spread across clouds and the product consumes little, the return is usually weaker.

### What is Partner Admin Link?

A Microsoft mechanism that links a partner's ID to its user or service principal in a customer's Azure environment, so Microsoft can attribute influenced and consumed revenue to that partner.

Write the one-page case for a platform account manager this week: the workload your product brings to the platform, the consumption a typical customer adds, and two customers who will vouch for it. If you cannot write it, co-selling is not yet your next move.
