# The Build Order for Financial Services and Fintech

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-financial-services-and-fintech/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Financial services is where The Build Order bends. Supervisors expect firms to reconstruct what an AI system did and who approved it, and the April 2026 US model risk guidance leaves generative and agentic AI to firms' own governance. So the decision record and audit trail come before the first agent. The commercial line still comes first; credit, KYC and suspicious activity data sit behind a wall.

Financial services is one of two sectors where The Build Order bends. The commercial line is still the right place to start, but the decision record and the audit trail come before the first agent rather than after it. The reason is supervisory. FINRA's 2026 oversight report covers AI agents for the first time and asks firms how they will track agent actions and decisions. The US banking agencies' April 2026 model risk guidance, SR 26-2, explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope, which leaves firms to govern those tools through their own risk frameworks. The EU AI Act's high-risk obligations, including credit scoring, now apply from 2 December 2027 after the Digital Omnibus. In each case the question a supervisor asks is the same: show us what happened, who approved it and why. A firm that builds the record first can answer it.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This is the second industry edition of The Build Order. In *The RFP nobody can answer yet* we said the sequence bends in two of eight sectors, and financial services is one of them: a supervisor may ask the firm to reconstruct any automated decision. In *The same build in four industries* a composite mid-market lender moved its record of pricing exceptions ahead of the first agent for that reason. This piece sets out the general case for banks, brokers, payments firms and fintech lenders, using the supervisory sources that apply in late 2026.

The bend is narrow. The commercial line still comes first, the wiring is still rented, and the first agent is still boring. What moves is the record: it becomes part of the foundation rather than the third layer.

## Where the commercial line sits

Fintech and financial services firms grow through a small set of repeated commercial decisions. Which partner or referral channel to prioritise. Which pricing exception to approve for a merchant, borrower or institutional client. Which campaign to run, and to whom. Which accounts to expand or let lapse. Each is frequent and similar enough to learn from, and each has an owner who must defend it, often to a compliance function as well as a budget holder.

| Lens | What it looks like in financial services and fintech |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Partner and referral prioritisation, pricing exceptions, campaigns, account expansion |
| Store | CRM, partner portal, pricing approvals, marketing automation |
| Outcome lag | Months: a loan funds, an account is funded, a merchant processes volume |
| Who defends the decision | Commercial head, finance, compliance, and in the end the supervisor |
| Main regulators | FINRA and the SEC for broker-dealers; US banking agencies; the PRA and FCA in the UK; EU national authorities under the AI Act |
| The wall | Credit files, KYC and AML data, transaction data, suspicious activity reports |
| Gateway that bites | Gateway 1: every client-facing word already passes compliance review |

The difference from other sectors is not the shape of the decisions. It is that someone outside the firm may ask to see them. A pricing exception that went wrong in a software company is a lesson. In a regulated lender it may be a fair-lending question. A campaign message drafted by an agent is a marketing asset in most firms; at a broker-dealer it is a communication with the public, subject to supervision and retention.

## What the supervisors say in 2026

The supervisory picture changed during 2026, and several older references in vendor material are now out of date.

**FINRA.** The 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report, published in December 2025, has a standalone generative AI section that covers AI agents for the first time. It defines agents as "systems or programs that are capable of autonomously performing and completing tasks on behalf of a user". The risks it names include agents acting without human validation and approval, acting beyond the user's actual or intended authority, and multi-step reasoning that makes outcomes hard to trace. Among the considerations it lists: where to have human-in-the-loop oversight, how to track agent actions and decisions, and guardrails on agent behaviour. Its monitoring guidance points to storing prompt and output logs and tracking which model version was used and when. It notes that generative AI can implicate rules on supervision, communications, recordkeeping and fair dealing.

**US banking agencies.** On 17 April 2026 the OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC jointly issued revised model risk management guidance (SR 26-2 at the Fed), rescinding SR 11-7, OCC Bulletin 2011-12 and the FDIC's 2017 adoption of them. The new guidance is shorter and principles-based, narrows the definition of a model, and is described as most relevant to organisations with more than $30bn in assets. A footnote excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope and directs banks to their broader risk management and governance practices instead. The agencies said they plan a request for information on AI use.

That exclusion matters more than it first appears. There is no longer a model risk framework that a bank can point to for an assistant or an agent. The bank's own governance record has to carry the weight.

**PRA.** In the UK, Supervisory Statement SS1/23 sets five model risk principles: model identification and risk classification, governance, development and use, independent validation, and risk mitigants. It took effect in May 2024 and the current version took effect on 23 April 2026. It is written for banks with internal model approval and covers models used to inform business decisions, with a sub-principle on risks from AI techniques. Its first principle, an inventory of models and their uses, is in practice a record.

**EU AI Act.** The Digital Omnibus on AI, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, entered into force on 27 July 2026. It moved high-risk obligations for Annex III systems, which include credit scoring of individuals, to 2 December 2027. Most transparency obligations under Article 50 applied from 2 August 2026. Most commercial agents (meeting preparation, partner briefs, draft emails) are not high-risk systems. A creditworthiness model is, and the commercial build must stay on the right side of that line.

**Adoption.** The Bank of England and FCA's 2024 survey of 118 firms found 75% already using AI, with a further 10% planning to within three years. A third of use cases were third-party implementations, 46% of firms reported only a partial understanding of the AI they use, and 55% of use cases involved some automated decision-making, with 2% fully autonomous.

| Source | Date | What it asks for | What it means for the build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FINRA 2026 oversight report | December 2025 | Human-in-the-loop decisions, tracking agent actions, prompt and output logs, model versions | Log every agent draft and approval before the agent goes live |
| SR 26-2 (OCC, Fed, FDIC) | 17 April 2026 | Principles-based model risk; generative and agentic AI out of scope | The firm's own record is the control for assistants and agents |
| PRA SS1/23 | Effective May 2024; current version April 2026 | Model inventory, governance, validation, mitigants | Keep an inventory of AI tools and the decisions they inform |
| EU AI Act after the Digital Omnibus | In force 27 July 2026 | Annex III high-risk duties from 2 December 2027 | Keep commercial agents out of credit decisions |

> When the guidance leaves agents to your own governance, your own record is the only evidence you have.

## Why the record moves first

In most sectors the record is the third layer: tooling and wiring first, then decisions worth keeping, then an agent. In financial services the record is built alongside the tooling, and two things are logged before any agent is connected.

**The commercial decisions themselves.** Pricing exceptions, partner approvals and campaign approvals, each with the request, the reason, the approver, the value at stake, the expected outcome and a check date. Part 9, *The ten commercial decisions worth recording*, lists the fields. In financial services add one more: the policy or limit the decision relied on, so a reviewer can see whether it sat inside delegated authority.

**The AI audit trail.** For every AI-assisted output: the prompt or instruction, the sources it drew on, the output, the model and version, the person who approved or rejected it, and what was finally sent. This is close to what FINRA's monitoring guidance describes, and it answers the auditability risk the report names. Our explainer *What is an AI audit trail?* covers the mechanics, and *Supersede, never overwrite* explains why records are corrected by adding new entries rather than editing old ones.

The reason for doing this first is practical rather than theoretical. A trail added after the first agent goes live has a gap at exactly the period a supervisor is most likely to ask about: the pilot. And an agent that has been running without logs cannot easily be given them retrospectively, because nobody recorded what it was asked.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in financial services and fintech | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | Owner, suite and CRM, plus a data-access approver from compliance who decides what crosses the wall | The build owner also approves data access |
| Tooling | Seats for partnership, sales and marketing staff; retention of AI interactions configured before use | Assistant use outside retained, supervised channels |
| Record (moved up) | Pricing exceptions and partner approvals, plus the AI audit trail, live before any agent | Logs added after the pilot, leaving a gap |
| Context | CRM, partner portal, pricing approvals, approved marketing library; credit and KYC systems excluded | A connector that reaches account or credit data |
| Reasoning | A first agent that prepares staff for partner and client meetings and drafts into a compliance queue | An agent drifting into eligibility or pricing advice |
| Gateway 1 | Every external communication approved by a named person and retained, inside existing review | Review queues fill once drafting is cheap |
| Gateway 2 | Value at stake on each exception; outcome written back at funding or first volume | Long outcome lag hides the result |
| Gateway 3 | Extension to operations and finance, with compliance sign-off on each new source | Reaching risk models by the back door |

**Gateway 0.** Part 3 described the fourth decision regulated firms add: who signs off on data access. In financial services this person sits in compliance or risk and is not the build owner. They decide which systems the context layer may read and keep a register of those decisions.

**Tooling.** Seats go to the people on the commercial line: partnership managers, relationship staff, marketing. Before anyone uses them for client work, confirm that interactions are retained in a way that meets the firm's recordkeeping obligations. This is a configuration task, and it is much harder to fix after six months of unlogged use.

**Context.** Connect the CRM, the partner portal, pricing approvals and the library of approved marketing material. Everything else waits.

**Reasoning.** The first agent prepares partnership and relationship managers for meetings, from the CRM and the decision record. It drafts follow-ups into the compliance review queue. It does not quote rates, assess eligibility or suggest products to an individual customer.

**Gateways 1 to 3.** Gateway 1 already exists in most regulated firms, because client communications pass compliance review. The friction is volume, which is why *Approval rate measures fatigue too* matters here. Gateway 2 needs patience: outcomes arrive at funding, first transaction volume or account activity, often months later, so choose a leading indicator such as funded accounts within 90 days and say so in the record. Gateway 3 extends the record to operations and finance one source at a time, each with the data-access approver's sign-off.

## The wall

Four kinds of data must never reach the commercial context layer:

- **Credit files and underwriting data.** A commercial agent that can see a customer's credit file can, in effect, take part in a credit decision. That pulls it towards the Annex III category in the EU and fair-lending scrutiny in the US.
- **KYC and AML records.** Identity documents and risk ratings exist for financial crime controls, not for prospecting.
- **Suspicious activity reports and investigations.** These carry legal confidentiality duties in the US and UK. A system that could surface one in a sales brief is a serious control failure.
- **Customer account and transaction data.** Useful for product teams under their own governance; not inputs to a commercial assistant without a specific, approved purpose.

The wall is enforced in the wiring by the data-access approver, and it is recorded: every connector has an entry saying what it reads, who approved it and when.

Illustrative example: a digital brokerage logs before it drafts

Decision
:   Build the record of partner fee exceptions and the AI audit trail before connecting any agent, and keep account, KYC and suitability data out of the context layer.

Reason and owner
:   The firm is FINRA-registered and grows through adviser and employer partnerships; every partner communication is already reviewed and retained. Owned by the head of partnerships, with the chief compliance officer as data-access approver.

What changed
:   The first agent prepares partnership managers for meetings from the CRM and the exception record, and drafts follow-ups into the compliance queue with prompt, sources, model version and approver logged. The leading indicator for each exception is funded accounts within 90 days.

Illustrative: a composite of a digital brokerage and wealth platform of around 250 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Record before you automate.** Where a supervisor will ask why, the record and audit trail come before the first agent.
- **Read the 2026 sources, not the 2011 ones.** SR 11-7 is rescinded; SR 26-2 leaves agents to your own governance.
- **Log the AI, not just the decision.** Prompt, sources, output, model version, approver and what was sent.
- **Wall off credit, KYC, SAR and account data.** The commercial build has no reason to read them.
- **Pick a leading indicator.** Outcome lags run to months, so name the proxy and record it.

Gateway card

### Before a financial services firm connects its first agent

- A data-access approver in compliance or risk, separate from the build owner
- AI interactions retained in line with recordkeeping obligations
- Pricing and partner exceptions recorded with reason, approver, limit relied on and value at stake
- An audit trail of prompt, sources, output, model version and approver, already live
- Credit, KYC, suspicious activity and account systems excluded from the context layer, in writing
- A leading indicator chosen for each decision class with a long outcome lag

## Common questions

### Has SR 11-7 been replaced?

Yes. On 17 April 2026 the OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC issued revised model risk management guidance (SR 26-2 at the Fed) and rescinded SR 11-7. The new guidance excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope and directs banks to their broader risk management practices.

### What does FINRA expect from firms using AI agents?

FINRA's 2026 oversight report asks firms to consider where to keep humans in the loop, how to track agent actions and decisions, and what guardrails to set, and suggests storing prompt and output logs and the model version used.

### When do EU AI Act high-risk rules apply to credit scoring?

After the Digital Omnibus, Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, high-risk obligations for Annex III systems, which include credit scoring of individuals, apply from 2 December 2027.

### Should fintech companies build an AI audit trail before deploying agents?

Yes. A trail added after the pilot leaves a gap in exactly the period a supervisor is likely to ask about, and agents that ran without logs cannot be given them retrospectively.

## Sources and notes

- [FINRA, 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report: GenAI](https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/guidance/reports/2026-finra-annual-regulatory-oversight-report/gen-ai), December 2025. Regulator report; FINRA presents agent oversight points as considerations, not new rules.
- [Federal Reserve, SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602.htm), 17 April 2026. Joint guidance with the OCC and FDIC; principles-based and not itself a rule.

# What Is an AI Impact Assessment?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-impact-assessment/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI impact assessment is a documented review of how an AI system could help or harm the people and groups it affects, carried out before deployment and repeated when the system or its use changes. ISO/IEC 42005, published in May 2025, gives guidance. The EU AI Act requires a fundamental rights impact assessment from some deployers of high-risk systems, and the GDPR requires a DPIA for high-risk processing.

An AI impact assessment is a documented review of how an AI system could affect the people and groups it touches: who is affected, what could go wrong for them, what benefits are expected and what controls apply. It is done before deployment and repeated when the system, its data or its use changes. ISO/IEC 42005 gives guidance on how to do one; the EU AI Act and the GDPR make specific versions mandatory in specific cases.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What an AI impact assessment means

A risk assessment asks what could go wrong for the organisation. An impact assessment asks what could go wrong, and right, for the people on the receiving end, including groups who are not users at all. ISO/IEC 42005 draws this distinction explicitly in an annex that separates general AI risk management under ISO/IEC 23894 from impact assessment.

According to CMS's summary, 42005 covers the system description, intended and unintended uses, affected stakeholders including vulnerable groups, and positive and negative impacts, each with magnitude and likelihood. Its annexes include a harms and benefits taxonomy and an example template.

| An AI impact assessment is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| About effects on people and groups | Only a risk register for the company |
| Specific to one system in one context | A general statement of AI principles |
| Linked to controls and an owner | A document filed and forgotten |

## Which assessment applies when

Four reference points overlap. Most mid-size firms will need a DPIA long before a FRIA.

| Assessment | Source | Status | Who must do it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AI system impact assessment | ISO/IEC 42005:2025 | Voluntary guidance | Anyone; expected inside an ISO/IEC 42001 system |
| Fundamental rights impact assessment | EU AI Act, Article 27 | Mandatory where it applies | Public bodies, private providers of public services, deployers of Annex III credit-scoring and life and health insurance systems |
| Data protection impact assessment | GDPR and UK GDPR, Article 35 | Mandatory for high-risk processing | Controllers whose processing is likely to result in high risk |
| Map function | NIST AI RMF | Voluntary framework | Anyone using it as structure |

### The FRIA under the EU AI Act

Article 27 sets out what the FRIA must describe: the deployer's processes in which the system is used, the period and frequency of use, the categories of people likely to be affected, the specific risks of harm to them, how human oversight is implemented, and the measures if risks materialise, including complaint mechanisms. It applies to first use, may rely on earlier assessments in similar cases, and must be updated when an element changes. Results go to the market surveillance authority. The FRIA attaches to Annex III high-risk systems, whose obligations now apply from 2 December 2027 after Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.

For a commercial team, the trigger is narrow. Scoring business accounts is not in Annex III; scoring individuals' creditworthiness and pricing life or health insurance are. See [The EU AI Act for Commercial Teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/).

### The DPIA

Most firms meet the DPIA first. The ICO's list of high-risk processing includes "the novel application of existing technologies (including AI)", which requires a DPIA when combined with one other criterion, such as profiling. An AI notetaker on client calls, or a model scoring individual leads, can reach that bar.

## How to run one proportionately

For a firm of 20 to 500 people, one page per AI use is usually enough. The structure below combines 42005's elements with Article 27's list.

| Section | Questions to answer |
| --- | --- |
| System and purpose | What does it do, for which process, and how often? |
| Affected people | Who is touched directly and indirectly, and are any vulnerable? |
| Impacts | What benefit is expected; what harm is plausible, how likely and how serious? |
| Oversight | Autonomy level; who approves output; who can stop it |
| Controls | Data rules, testing, logging, complaint route |
| Triggers to reassess | New data, new users, new model, new law, a complaint |
| Owner and date | Named owner; next review date |

The reassessment triggers do the most work. 42005 lists changes in intended use, users, environment and law, and a vendor's model update can change behaviour with no change on your side. Pair the assessment with [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) so a model change prompts a test as well as a review.

This is general guidance, not legal advice. Deployers in credit, insurance or public services should take advice on Article 27.

## The **lowob** view

An impact assessment is a decision record with a forecast in it: what the firm expects to happen, to whom, and who owns the outcome. **lowob**'s loop adds the step most assessments skip, writing back what did happen. When a complaint or a quarterly review shows a different outcome, update the assessment against the original, so the next one starts from evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **People, not just the firm.** An impact assessment looks at effects on those the system touches.
- **The DPIA comes first.** For most mid-size firms the GDPR's DPIA is the assessment actually required.
- **The FRIA is narrow.** It reaches public services, consumer credit and life or health insurance, from 2 December 2027.
- **Reassess on change.** A vendor model update is a trigger, as is a new use or a complaint.

## Common questions

### What is an AI impact assessment?

A documented review of how an AI system could affect people and groups, covering benefits, harms, likelihood, oversight and controls, done before use and repeated on change.

### What is ISO/IEC 42005?

An international standard, published in May 2025, that gives guidance on conducting AI system impact assessments. It is guidance and is not certified on its own.

### Who needs a fundamental rights impact assessment under the EU AI Act?

Public bodies, private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk systems for individual credit scoring or life and health insurance pricing.

### Is a DPIA the same as an AI impact assessment?

No. A DPIA covers risks from processing personal data. An AI impact assessment is wider, though a FRIA may reuse relevant parts of a DPIA.

## Sources and notes

- [ISO, ISO/IEC 42005:2025 AI system impact assessment](https://www.iso.org/standard/42005), May 2025. Standard listing; full text is paid.
- [CMS, ISO/IEC 42005:2025: a new blueprint for legal and commercial leaders](https://cms.law/en/gbr/legal-updates/iso-iec-42005-2025-a-new-blueprint-for-legal-and-commercial-leaders-navigating-ai-risk-and-governance), 3 September 2025. Law firm summary of the standard's structure and annexes.
- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 27: Fundamental rights impact assessment](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-27), consolidated text as at 27 July 2026. Primary legal text; paragraphs 4 and 5 amended by the Digital Omnibus.
- [ICO, Examples of processing likely to result in high risk](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/accountability-and-governance/data-protection-impact-assessments-dpias/examples-of-processing-likely-to-result-in-high-risk), accessed November 2026. UK regulator guidance on when a DPIA is required.

## Related research

- [What Is ISO/IEC 42001?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-iso-42001/)
- [The EU AI Act for Commercial Teams: What Applies and When](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/)
- [What Is a Decision Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/)
- [What Is a Data Processing Agreement for AI Tools?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-data-processing-agreement-for-ai/)
- [What Is AI Literacy, and What Does the EU AI Act Require?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-literacy/)

## Next move

Pick the one AI tool that touches the most individuals' data, such as a call recorder or lead scorer, and write a one-page impact assessment using the seven sections above. Set its review date and owner.

# What Is AI Inference Cost?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-16 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Inference cost is the running cost of using an AI model, billed per million input and output tokens plus caching, tool and regional charges. Unit prices for a given level of performance have fallen between 9 and 900 times a year, but agents and reasoning multiply tokens per task. The measure that matters is cost per successful task.

AI inference cost is what it costs to run a trained model each time it is used: to read a request and produce an answer. For API users it appears as a price per million input and output tokens, plus charges for caching, tools, processing tier and regional processing. For self-hosted models it is hardware, energy and staff. Unit prices have fallen fast, but agents, reasoning and long context raise the tokens used per task, so total spend often rises.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What AI inference cost means

Training builds a model; inference uses it, on every draft and every agent step.

For most firms the bill arrives through an API priced per million [tokens](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-token-in-ai/), with separate rates for input, the text the model reads, and output, the text it writes. On Anthropic's pricing page, accessed 16 November 2026, Claude Sonnet 5.5 is listed at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output. Claude Haiku 5.5 is listed at $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens.

The per-token rate is only one line of the bill.

| Cost component | What drives it | From provider pages, accessed 16 November 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input tokens | Instructions, documents, history, tool definitions | Charged on every call, including each re-read |
| Output tokens | Length of the answer | Five times input on Anthropic's main models |
| Reasoning tokens | Thinking before answering | Billed as output; see [reasoning models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-reasoning-model/) |
| Cached input | A repeated prompt prefix | Anthropic cache reads at 0.1 times input on most models; OpenAI lists a separate cached-input rate |
| Tool overhead | Tool definitions and server tools | Anthropic adds 286 to 406 system tokens when tools are used on its 5.5 models; web search $10 per 1,000 searches |
| Processing tier | Batch, standard or faster service | Anthropic Batch API 50% off; OpenAI's tables price Batch below Standard and Fast above it |
| Regional processing | Data residency | Anthropic 1.1 times for US-only inference; OpenAI 10% uplift on regional endpoints for newer models |

For self-hosted [open-weight models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-open-weight-model/), per-token fees give way to hardware, energy and engineering time.

## Why unit prices fall while bills rise

Stanford's AI Index reports that querying a model at GPT-3.5's level, 64.8% on the MMLU benchmark, cost $20 per million tokens in November 2022 and $0.07 by October 2024, a more than 280-fold fall. Epoch AI, tracking six benchmarks over three years, found declines of 9 to 900 times a year depending on task and performance level. It cautioned that "it's less clear" the fastest recent drops "will persist".

Meanwhile usage per task is rising, for three reasons.

**Agents re-read context.** Each step in an [agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/) sends the instructions, tool definitions and history again. Anthropic's engineering team reported in June 2025 that agents typically used about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems about 15 times. On its browsing evaluation, token usage alone explained 80% of the variance in performance. More spend often bought better results, so cost has to be judged against value.

**Reasoning is billed as output.** Reasoning settings can spend thousands of hidden tokens before an answer appears, at the more expensive rate.

**Context grows.** Account histories pasted into every call raise input cost at every step; [context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/) is partly a cost discipline.

A worked example, illustrative, on Anthropic's 16 November 2026 list prices. A nightly CRM hygiene job checks 2,000 records, reading 3,000 tokens and writing 200 for each. That is 6 million input and 400,000 output tokens a night. On Haiku 5.5 it costs about $0.80, or $0.40 through the Batch API. On Sonnet 5.5 it costs about $16, or $8 batched. The larger model is twenty times dearer for the same job, so model choice outweighs every other lever, provided the smaller one passes your accuracy test.

In **lowob**'s model, inference is the rented part of the brain. The owned part is the measure: cost per successful task, set beside what the task is worth.

## How to control inference cost

| Lever | When to use it | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smaller model for routine steps | Classification, extraction, routing | Test accuracy first; see [small language models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-small-language-model/) |
| [Prompt caching](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/) | The same long instructions or documents on many calls | Any change to the prefix breaks the cache |
| Batch processing | Overnight or non-urgent jobs | Results are not immediate |
| Trimmed context | Every call | Dropping a record the task needed |
| Short, [structured outputs](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-structured-output/) | Fields instead of prose | Output is the expensive token |
| Spend and step caps | Every agent | Set per agent, ideally through an [LLM gateway](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-llm-gateway/) |
| Lower reasoning effort | Lookups and simple drafts | Quality on hard steps |

Log tokens per task for two weeks, then divide cost by tasks that met the quality bar, not by attempts. An agent that costs $0.50 a run and succeeds half the time costs $1 per useful result.

## lowob takeaways

- **Inference is the running cost.** Every call is billed, re-reads included.
- **Unit prices fall; usage rises.** Agents and reasoning multiply tokens per task.
- **Model choice is the largest lever.** The same job can cost twenty times more on a larger model.
- **Measure cost per successful task.** Compare it with the value of the task.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between AI training cost and inference cost?

Training cost is the one-off expense of building a model, carried by its developer. Inference cost is the recurring cost of running it on each request.

### Why is my AI bill going up if token prices are falling?

Usage per task is rising. Agents re-read their context at every step, reasoning settings bill hidden thinking as output, and more work is automated.

### How do I estimate inference cost for an AI agent?

Multiply tokens read and written per step by the number of steps and by the provider's per-million prices. Then divide by the share of runs that succeed.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Pricing (Claude API documentation)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor list prices; change often.
- [OpenAI, API pricing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/pricing), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor list prices; tier names changed during 2026.
- [Stanford HAI, AI Index 2025: State of AI in 10 Charts](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-index-2025-state-of-ai-in-10-charts), April 2025. Independent academic index; based on list prices.
- [Epoch AI, LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks](https://epoch.ai/data-insights/ai-inference-price-trends), 12 March 2025. Independent research; list prices across six benchmarks.
- [Anthropic, How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system), 13 June 2025. Vendor engineering report on its own system.

## Related research

- [What Is a Token in AI, and Why Does It Drive Cost?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-token-in-ai/)
- [What Is Usage-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/)
- [What Is Prompt Caching?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/)
- [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)
- [How to Measure AI ROI in a Commercial Team](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-measure-ai-roi/)

## Next move

Pick the AI task your team runs most often and price it on your current model and on the provider's cheapest. Run 30 real cases through both, and divide each total cost by the number of acceptable results.

# Where Judgment Arrives First

Source: https://lowob.com/research/where-judgment-arrives-first/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI judgment layers will work first where decisions are frequent, similar and graded quickly, and where someone will later have to defend them. Research on expertise points the same way: judgment can be learned only in environments regular enough to learn from, with feedback. Map decision classes on volume and outcome lag before choosing where to build; elsewhere, judgment is a practice before it is a product.

Judgment layers will work first where decisions are frequent, similar and graded quickly, and where someone will later have to defend them. Research on expertise says the same thing about people: skilled judgment is learnable only where the environment is regular and feedback arrives. Map your decision classes on volume and outcome lag before choosing where to build. Everywhere else, judgment is a practice before it is a product.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

Look at where AI is shaping decisions in 2026, rather than drafting documents about them. Screening and compliance alerts. Fraud and financial-crime investigation. Early-warning signals on loan books. Credit memo preparation. Support resolutions. Code review. Vendors in each of these areas publish striking figures about alerts avoided and hours saved. Those are vendor-reported and should be treated as such. But the pattern in where they appear is consistent, and independent evidence supports it.

## What the independent evidence shows

The Bank of England's 2024 survey of 118 UK financial firms is one of the few regulator-run views of where AI is actually used. It found 75% of firms already using AI, with a further 10% planning to within three years. Among the most common uses were optimisation of internal processes (41%), cybersecurity (37%) and fraud detection (33%). More telling for this argument: 55% of all AI use cases had some degree of automated decision-making, but only 2% were fully autonomous. Most decision use sits in the middle, where a system prepares or proposes and a person decides the hard cases.

Customer support is the other clear example. Gartner predicted in March 2025 that by 2029 agentic AI will resolve 80% of common customer service issues without human intervention. That is a forecast, not a result, but it is a forecast about exactly the conditions described below: high volume, similar cases and quick confirmation of whether the issue was resolved.

The firms with the most decision use are also the ones that must defend decisions. US bank supervisors' revised model risk guidance, SR 26-2, issued in April 2026 to replace SR 11-7, describes outcomes analysis as comparing "model outputs to corresponding real-world outcomes" and requires "effective challenge" by objective experts. It explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope, but the discipline it describes (record the call, compare with the outcome, let someone challenge it) is the same loop a judgment layer needs. Our explainer on [model risk management for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/) covers the regulatory side.

## Four conditions

Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein, who began from opposite views of expert intuition, agreed in a 2009 paper that whether to trust an intuitive judgment depends on "the predictability of the environment in which the judgment is made" and on the judge's opportunity to learn its regularities. In a 2010 interview Klein added feedback as the second condition, and Kahneman said he would be "less trusting of intuition" where problems are unique. A machine learning from an organisation's decisions faces the same constraints.

**Volume of similar decisions.** Enough cases of the same kind that exceptions recur. At tens of thousands of comparable cases a year, rare variations cluster and patterns surface in weeks.

**Expert judgment at the exceptions.** The rulebook handles most cases, and a skilled person decides the rest. That person's decisions are what the system learns from.

**Outcomes that arrive soon enough.** A false positive is known in days, a credit outcome in months. Both are short enough to close the loop.

**Someone who must defend the decision.** A regulator, a budget holder, an investment committee. This is what makes the record worth paying for, not just possible.

| Decision class | Volume of similar cases | Outcome lag | Defender | Where it sits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Screening or fraud alerts | Very high | Days | Regulator | Build the learning layer now |
| Support resolutions | Very high | Hours to days | Budget holder | Build now |
| Loan early warnings, credit memos | High | Months | Credit committee, supervisor | Build with leading indicators |
| Renewal discounts | Medium | One quarter | Revenue leader | Record and review; learning is possible |
| Partnerships, market entries | Low | Years | Board | Practice, not product |

The rows are illustrative; the volumes and lags in your firm will differ.

> Below the floor, the value is not that the system gets smarter. It is that the organisation's own reasoning survives and is argued with before the next call.

## Map before you build

Take your organisation's decision classes and place each on two axes: annual volume of comparable decisions, and time until the outcome is known. Mark the ones where someone must later defend the call.

High volume and short lag, with a defender: that is where a learning system can be built and evidenced now.

High volume and long lag: possible, with care, using leading indicators as interim outcomes. Choose those indicators deliberately, because a system will learn to optimise whatever proxy you give it. A collections model rewarded for promises to pay, rather than payments, will learn to collect promises (an illustrative case).

Low volume and long lag: strategic decisions, partnerships, market entries. Patterns will not form. McKinsey's 2019 survey of 1,228 managers found respondents least familiar with "big bets", the infrequent, high-stakes decisions such as acquisitions, and only 30% familiar with all three decision types it studied. What works here is a disciplined record that a person reads, with AI drafting, checking and surfacing precedent rather than learning.

For most mid-size companies the first qualifying class is on the commercial line, where decisions recur weekly and outcomes arrive within a quarter. [Why the brain starts at the commercial line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/) makes that case, and [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) lists the candidates.

## Below the floor is a different object

The mistake is to treat the low-volume case as a smaller version of the same product and to promise it the same learning. It is a different object, with different value: not that the system gets smarter, but that the organisation's own reasoning survives and is argued with before the next call. [Below the volume floor](https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/) sets out what that practice looks like.

## In practice

List your top twenty decision classes and estimate annual volume and outcome lag for each. Mark the classes where someone must later defend the decision. Build the learning layer only in the high-volume, short-lag, defended quadrant, and set the autonomy level there one notch at a time on evidence.

For the rest, deploy the record and the review discipline, and say clearly that it is a practice.

**What would prove this wrong:** a judgment system showing measurable learning in low-volume, long-lag, heterogeneous decision classes, under independent evaluation. Then the volume floor is lower than it looks.

## lowob takeaways

- **Judgment arrives where decisions repeat.** Volume, exceptions, quick outcomes and a defender.
- **Most decision AI is semi-autonomous.** Only 2% of UK financial-services use cases were fully autonomous in 2024.
- **Choose proxies with care.** A system learns whatever interim outcome you reward.
- **Below the floor, keep a record, not a model.** AI drafts and surfaces precedent; a person decides.

## Common questions

### Where is AI most useful for business decision-making?

Where decisions are frequent, similar and graded quickly, and someone must later defend them, such as screening and fraud alerts, support resolutions, loan early-warning signals and credit memo preparation.

### Can AI learn from strategic decisions like partnerships or market entries?

Patterns will not form in low-volume, long-lag decisions. What works there is a disciplined record that a person reads, with AI drafting, checking and surfacing precedent rather than learning.

### How should a company decide where to build an AI judgment system?

List your top twenty decision classes, estimate annual volume and outcome lag for each, and mark where someone must defend the decision. Build the learning layer only in the high-volume, short-lag, defended quadrant.

### What is the risk of using leading indicators to train AI on long-lag decisions?

A system will learn to optimise whatever proxy you give it, so choose the leading indicators deliberately and check them against the real outcome when it arrives.

## Sources and notes

- [Kahneman and Klein, Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19739881/), *American Psychologist* 64(6), 2009. Academic review about human experts, applied here by analogy.
- [McKinsey Quarterly, Strategic decisions: When can you trust your gut?](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/our-insights/strategic-decisions-when-can-you-trust-your-gut), March 2010. Interview; opinion, not new data.

US bank supervisory guidance; excludes generative and agentic AI.

# AI Agents in Commercial Operations: The RevOps Tasks Worth Handing Over

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-commercial-operations/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Commercial operations has the highest share of tasks an agent can run and report on, and the two tasks that must never be delegated. This guide walks the twelve operations rows of the lowob Agent Task Directory, maps each to the layer of the brain it builds or maintains, sets a starting autonomy level, and names the first three tasks to hand over.

Commercial operations is where agents can do the most on their own and where two tasks must never leave a person. Seven of the twelve operations tasks in the **lowob** Agent Task Directory are rated level 3, act and report: record clean-up, enrichment, the pipeline pack, delivery reconciliation, outcome write-back, commission calculation and agent monitoring. Three stay as drafts, and two, maintaining shared definitions and granting system access, stay with a named person. Operations is also the function that builds the brain the other agents depend on, so start with the monitoring that keeps every other agent honest.

*Figure: Five plug points: identity and limits, context in, precedent in, the gate, and the outcome written back.*

Revenue operations owns the systems the rest of the commercial line runs on: the CRM, the price book, the definitions, the reports and, increasingly, the agents. That makes it different from sales or marketing. A sales agent uses the brain. An operations agent maintains it. Its mistakes are less visible to clients and more damaging to everything downstream, because a wrong merge or a drifted definition quietly corrupts every report and every other agent that reads the store.

The data starts in poor shape. Validity's State of CRM Data Management 2025, a survey of 602 CRM users and administrators, found 76% say less than half their CRM data is accurate and complete, 37% report losing revenue directly to data quality, and 45% say their CRM data is not ready for AI. The ratings below are **lowob**'s working framework from the [Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/), reviewed quarterly. Without the listed control, drop the task one level.

## The twelve operations tasks, rated

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| De-duplicate and clean CRM records | 3 Act and report | High | Wrong merge of distinct accounts | Merge rules; reversible changes; nightly report |
| Enrich records with third-party data | 3 Act and report | Medium | Inaccurate or non-consented data | Approved sources; privacy rules |
| Draft quotes from a price book | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong price becomes a binding offer | Quote reviewer; price book marked current |
| Check contract terms against standard | 1 Draft | Medium | Missed non-standard clause | Legal owner reviews flagged items |
| Prepare the weekly pipeline review pack | 3 Act and report | High | Misleading summary | Links to underlying records |
| Reconcile delivery against what was sold | 3 Act and report | High | Under-delivery missed | Exceptions routed to account owner |
| Record decisions with reasons | 1 Draft | Medium | Reasons invented after the fact | Captured at the moment of approval |
| Write outcomes back to decisions | 3 Act and report | Medium | Wrong outcome linked | Owner confirms at check date |
| Maintain shared definitions | 0 Answer | Low | Definitions drift silently | Named owner per definition |
| Grant or change system access | 0 Answer | Low | Excessive agency; data exposure | Never delegated to an agent |
| Run the commission calculation | 3 Act and report | Medium | Disputes and trust loss | Finance review before payout |
| Monitor agent activity and cost | 3 Act and report | High | Runaway spend or loops | Spend caps; kill switch |

Level 3 here means the agent acts within written rules and reports what it did, with a person reading the report. It does not mean unsupervised. Zapier's 2026 survey of 513 US managers found only 30% of leaders say agents handle a majority of tasks without human help, and operations is where that minority is most defensible.

## Where each task plugs into the brain

The brain is a loop: the **store** of records, the **context** layer of definitions and permissions, the **record** of decisions with reason, owner, status and expected outcome, **reasoning** by models and agents, and **learning** when outcomes are written back. Operations tasks are unusual in that several of them are the loop. Recording decisions and writing outcomes back are the record and learning layers in working form.

| Task | Main layer | Start at | Move up when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| De-duplicate and clean records | Store | 2, then 3 | Merge rules tested; pre-merge state kept |
| Third-party enrichment | Store | 2, then 3 | Approved source list and privacy check |
| Quotes from a price book | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Contract terms check | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Weekly pipeline pack | Context | 2, then 3 | Two cycles with every figure linked |
| Delivery reconciliation | Store | 2, then 3 | Exception routing tested with owners |
| Decision records | Record | 1 | Stays at 1; owner confirms each entry |
| Outcome write-back | Learning | 1, then 3 | Check dates on every decision |
| Shared definitions | Context | 0 | Never |
| System access | Context | 0 | Never |
| Commission calculation | Record | 1, then 3 | A quarter of shadow runs that match payroll |
| Agent activity and cost monitoring | Reasoning | 3 | From day one |

Read the "start at" column as a rule of thumb. Tasks that change the store start one level below the directory rating until the change can be undone. Tasks that only read and report can start at the directory level once their links to source records work.

## The five tasks that decide the programme

### De-duplication and enrichment

Record hygiene is the most valuable operations task and the easiest to get badly wrong. Two companies with similar names, or a parent and its subsidiary, merge into one account, and their histories become inseparable. HubSpot's documentation is plain: "It's not possible to unmerge records", and the primary record's property values take precedence in a merge. Where the CRM cannot reverse a merge, the agent must make it reversible: stage proposed merges, keep a snapshot of both records, and apply only merges that pass written rules, with a nightly report of every change. Enrichment carries a second risk. Third-party data may be inaccurate or collected without the consent your use requires, so the agent draws only from an approved source list. See [What Is CRM Data Hygiene?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/) for the rules to write first.

### Quotes and contract checks

Both are drafts. A quote is an offer, and a stated price can bind the firm: in *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024) the tribunal held the company responsible for what its chatbot told a customer. The control is a reviewer for every quote and a price book marked current, with superseded prices kept but flagged. Contract review is where models are improving fastest. A 2024 study, "Better Call GPT", reported that advanced models matched or exceeded junior lawyers and outsourced reviewers on identifying legal issues, at a fraction of the time and cost. It is one study on a defined contract set. The directory keeps the task at level 1 because the costly error is the missed non-standard clause, and a legal owner reviews every flagged item.

### Decision records and outcome write-back

These two tasks are the record and learning layers. An agent can draft a decision record when a discount, a stage change or a budget move is approved: the decision, the reason, the owner and the expected outcome. The risk is reasons invented after the fact. Validity's survey reported that 37% of staff regularly fabricate data to tell leaders what they want to hear, which is why the reason must be captured at the moment of approval, not reconstructed at quarter end. Write-back is level 3: at each decision's check date, the agent links the outcome and the owner confirms it. Without check dates, there is nothing to write back. [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) lists where to start and [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers the mechanics.

### Commission calculation

Commission is rule-based and checkable, which suits an agent, and it is the fastest way to lose a sales team's trust when wrong. Run the agent's calculation in shadow alongside the current method for a full quarter, reconcile every difference, and keep finance review before any payout. NIST's Generative AI Profile warns of automation bias, "excessive deference to automated systems". A reviewer who has seen a quarter of matching runs is most at risk of approving the wrong one, so sample the payouts rather than reading only the totals.

### Access, definitions and agent monitoring

Granting access and maintaining definitions are level 0. OWASP's 2025 guidance on excessive agency names excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy as its root causes. It recommends that agents act in the user's own context with minimal privileges, and that authorisation is enforced by downstream systems, not by the model's judgment. An agent that can change its own permissions has no meaningful limits. Definitions drift the same way: a "qualified opportunity" changes meaning one edit at a time. Each definition has a named owner, and the agent may only answer questions about it.

Monitoring is the opposite: level 3 from day one. Anthropic's guidance on building agents notes that autonomy brings "higher costs, and the potential for compounding errors", and recommends stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations. In operations terms that means a spend cap per agent, a loop limit, a log of every tool call and a [kill switch](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-kill-switch/) a named person can use without asking.

> A sales agent uses the brain. An operations agent maintains it, so its mistakes travel further.

## Start here: the first three tasks

1. **Monitor agent activity and cost.** Level 3, before any other agent goes live. Daily report of runs, tool calls, spend against cap and any loop stopped. Control: a named owner of the kill switch.
2. **De-duplicate and clean CRM records.** Level 2 for four weeks: the agent proposes merges and fixes, an operations analyst approves them in batches. Move to level 3 once the merge rules hold and the pre-merge snapshot is tested. Baseline: duplicate count from the clean-up described in [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/).
3. **Prepare the weekly pipeline review pack.** Level 2 for two cycles, then level 3. Every figure links to the underlying records so a reviewer can check any number in one click. Baseline: hours spent building the pack.

Decision records and outcome write-back follow, once the pack is trusted. Commission runs in shadow from the second quarter.

Illustrative example: sequencing a RevOps agent rollout

Decision
:   Deploy agent monitoring and staged de-duplication first; defer an enrichment agent until an approved source list exists; refuse a vendor request for the agent to manage user permissions.

Reason and owner
:   The CRM could not reverse merges, so every merge is staged with a snapshot; enrichment sources had no consent review; access changes are never delegated. Owned by the head of revenue operations.

What changed
:   Duplicate counts fall over six weeks with no wrong merge reaching a seller; the pipeline pack moves to level 3 after two clean cycles.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## How to move an operations task up the dial

The tests are those in [Part 1](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/): four weeks with the control in place, a clean weekly sample, and a recorded reason for the decision touched. Operations adds one: the change is reversible, or staged so that it can be. Any task that writes to the store without a way back stays at level 2, whatever its accuracy.

## lowob takeaways

- **Make every change reversible first.** Where the CRM cannot undo, the agent must stage and snapshot.
- **Capture reasons at the moment of approval.** Reasons reconstructed later are guesses.
- **Never delegate access or definitions.** These set the limits every other agent works within.
- **Monitor agents before you deploy them.** Spend caps, loop limits and a kill switch come first.

Gateway card

### Before an operations agent goes live

- Task found in the directory and set at or below its level
- Agent monitoring live, with spend caps and a named kill-switch owner
- Merge rules written; pre-merge snapshots kept and restorable
- Approved source list for any enrichment
- Every report figure linked to its source record
- No agent holds permission to change access or definitions

## Common questions

### What can AI agents do in revenue operations?

They can clean and de-duplicate CRM records, enrich them from approved sources, build the weekly pipeline pack, reconcile delivery against what was sold, write outcomes back to decisions, calculate commission for finance review and monitor other agents.

### Can an AI agent merge duplicate CRM records automatically?

Yes, under written merge rules with a nightly report. Some CRMs cannot reverse a merge, so the agent should stage merges and keep a snapshot of both records first.

### Should an AI agent calculate sales commission?

It can, after a quarter of shadow runs that match the current method. Finance should review before every payout and sample individual payments, not only totals.

### What should an AI agent never do in operations?

Grant or change system access, or change shared definitions. Both set the limits other agents work within.

# The Graveyard

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-graveyard/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The most valuable thing an organisation knows is what it tried and abandoned, and why, and it is the first thing lost when people move. Research on organisational forgetting and on lessons-learned systems shows both the loss and why most archives go unread. A judgment system should make the graveyard first-class, distinguish what was disproven from what was merely under-tried, and surface the closest record when a new proposal is made.

The most valuable thing an organisation knows is what it tried and abandoned, and why. It is also the first thing lost when people move. A judgment system should make the graveyard first-class, and distinguish what was disproven from what was merely under-tried. The research supports both halves: knowledge built through work depreciates quickly, and NASA's own inspector general found that only 57% of project managers surveyed used the agency's lessons-learned system at all.

Every function has a graveyard. The channel that did not work. The pricing model withdrawn after a quarter. The partnership that looked perfect and was quietly ended. The analytics vendor dropped after the pilot. The reasons live in the heads of whoever was there.

When those people move on, a new owner arrives with fresh eyes and, very often, revives one of the abandoned ideas. Sometimes because a vendor pitched it, sometimes because a board member suggested it, sometimes because it simply looks obvious. Occasionally conditions have changed and it works. Often it fails again, for the same reason, at full cost, and nobody connects the two failures.

## How the graveyard gets lost

Three findings explain why the reasons disappear.

**Knowledge depreciates.** Argote, Beckman and Epple studied learning across multiple industrial organisations in a 1990 *Management Science* paper. They found that knowledge acquired through production depreciates rapidly, and that cumulative experience overstates how much an organisation still knows. What a team learned three years ago is not what it knows today.

**Knowledge sits with individuals.** Panopto, a video platform vendor, surveyed 1,000 workers in 2018 and reported that 42% of the institutional knowledge in a role was unique to the person in it. The figure is self-reported and vendor-run, so read it as direction. It matches the experience of anyone who has inherited a function: the shared drive holds the decks, not the reasons.

**Failures go unreported.** Amy Edmondson, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2011, asked executives how many of the failures in their organisations were truly blameworthy. They answered 2% to 5%. Asked how many were treated as blameworthy, they said 70% to 90%. Her conclusion was that many failures are never reported and their lessons are lost. An organisation that punishes failure will not write down why things died.

## Not every death is the same

The most useful thing a graveyard record can do is say why something died, because the reasons have very different implications for revival.

**Disproven**: tried properly, with resources, and it did not work. Revive only with new evidence that the conditions have changed.

**Under-tried**: abandoned for lack of time, budget or attention, before it was really tested. These may be good ideas that were never given a fair chance.

**Overtaken**: worked, but was replaced by something better or made redundant by events.

**Political**: stopped because of who sponsored it or who opposed it, not because of its merits.

Many ideas that organisations believe were disproven were actually under-tried. That distinction alone can save a promising idea from permanent burial, and save the organisation from repeating a genuine failure. Edmondson's work gives one reason the confusion is common: her spectrum of failure runs from deliberate deviation at one end to thoughtful experimentation at the other, and she warns that pilots are too often run under optimal conditions rather than representative ones. A pilot that was under-resourced, or run in the wrong conditions, did not disprove anything.

| Classification | Test for it | What revival requires |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Disproven | Ran for its planned period, with its planned resources, against a written threshold | New evidence that a named condition has changed |
| Under-tried | Stopped early, under-funded, or without an owner | The missing resource or owner, stated in advance |
| Overtaken | Worked, then replaced or made redundant | The replacement failing, or the event reversing |
| Political | Stopped by sponsorship or opposition, not results | A sponsor and a fair test |

> Many ideas that organisations believe were disproven were actually under-tried.

## The record

For each abandoned approach: what was tried, for how long, with what resources; what happened; why it was stopped, classified as above; and **what would make it worth trying again**. That last field turns a tombstone into a reopenable option with a stated condition.

| Field | Example entry (illustrative) |
| --- | --- |
| What was tried | Partner referral programme for mid-market accounts |
| Duration and resources | Two quarters, one part-time owner, no budget for partner enablement |
| What happened | Four referrals, one closed |
| Why stopped | Under-tried: owner reassigned in month four |
| Revival condition | A dedicated owner and an enablement budget agreed before relaunch |
| Recorded by, and when | Head of sales, at the quarterly review |

The format is a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with one extra field. The revival condition is what the record of a lost deal is to sales: our explainer on [closed-lost reasons](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) makes the case that the reason field is the one AI systems most need and CRMs most often leave blank. When conditions change, add a new entry that supersedes the old one rather than editing it; [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) covers why.

## Surfacing it at the right moment

A graveyard nobody consults is just storage. NASA learned this at some cost. Its Office of Inspector General reviewed the agency's Lessons Learned Information System in March 2012. Of 28 project managers surveyed, 16, or 57%, said they had used the system, and 12, or 43%, had contributed to it. Managers called it outdated, hard to use and short of information relevant to their projects. The agency was spending about three quarters of a million dollars a year on it, and the inspector general questioned whether that was a prudent investment.

The lesson is not that recording fails. It is that an archive which waits to be searched will not be searched. Match new proposals against graveyard records on the situation, not the wording, and surface the match when the proposal is made: "A similar approach was tried in 2025 and stopped after two quarters; classified as under-tried; revival condition: dedicated owner." That one message is often worth more than the rest of the system combined. Supplying comparable past decisions to a model at the moment of a new one is what [decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) describes, and the graveyard is its most valuable source.

The moment of greatest risk is a change of owner. Our piece on [handovers](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) covers why reasoning leaks when people move, and the graveyard should be part of every handover pack.

## What to count

**Repeat failures**: an abandoned approach tried again without new evidence, and failing for the same reason. It should be zero.

**Successful revivals**: graveyard items reopened because their revival condition was met, that then worked. These prove the graveyard is not just a list of reasons to say no.

## In practice

Backfill the graveyard for one function: the ten most significant abandoned initiatives of the last three years. Classify each as disproven, under-tried, overtaken or political, with a revival condition. Match new proposals against it automatically and surface the closest record.

Report repeat failures and successful revivals once a year.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations with a maintained graveyard showing no fewer repeat failures, and no more successful revivals, than those without. Then the past is less informative than this piece assumes. We know of no controlled study of graveyard records specifically; the evidence above is on forgetting and on archives, not on this format.

## lowob takeaways

- **Classify every death.** Disproven, under-tried, overtaken or political, because each has different implications for revival.
- **Write the revival condition.** It turns a tombstone into a reopenable option.
- **Push, do not wait.** Surface the closest record when a proposal is made, as NASA's unread archive shows.
- **Count two things.** Repeat failures, which should be zero, and successful revivals.

## Common questions

### How do companies avoid repeating failed initiatives?

Keep a graveyard record of each abandoned approach: what was tried, for how long and with what resources, what happened, why it stopped and what would make it worth trying again. Match new proposals against it and surface the closest record when the proposal is made.

### What is the difference between a disproven idea and an under-tried one?

A disproven idea was tried properly, with resources, and did not work; revive it only with new evidence that conditions changed. An under-tried idea was abandoned for lack of time, budget or attention before it was really tested.

### Why do lessons-learned databases go unused?

They wait to be searched. NASA's inspector general found only 57% of project managers surveyed used the agency's system, citing outdated content and poor relevance. Records need to be pushed at the moment of a related proposal.

### How do you start capturing institutional knowledge about abandoned projects?

Backfill the graveyard for one function with the ten most significant abandoned initiatives of the last three years, classify each, and give each a revival condition.

- [Edmondson, Strategies for learning from failure](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/53761774e4b0e8c9b2acd2a4/t/629fcc85185ef04c9d2549bc/1654639749195/Strategies+for+Learning+from+Failure.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, April 2011. Practitioner essay; the blameworthiness figures are executive estimates, hosted copy.

## Next move

# What Is Model Drift?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-drift/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Model drift is the gradual or sudden change in how an AI system performs after it goes live. Classic drift comes from the world changing under a trained model. With hosted language models there is a second cause: the provider changes or retires the model. Both are caught the same way, by re-running fixed tests on a schedule.

Model drift is the change in an AI system's behaviour or accuracy over time after it has been deployed. It has two broad causes. The world can change, so the data a model sees no longer resembles what it was built on. Or the model itself changes, because a provider updates or retires the version you call. Drift is caught by re-running the same tests on a schedule and comparing the results.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What model drift means

In classic machine learning, drift describes a gap opening between the data a model was trained on and the data it now sees. **Data drift** is a change in the inputs: a lead scoring model trained when most buyers came from one industry now sees a different mix. **Concept drift** is a change in what the inputs mean: the signals that used to predict a purchase stop predicting it.

Hosted large language models add a third kind. The model behind an API name can change. Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia and James Zou compared the March and June 2023 versions of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 across seven task types. On identifying prime versus composite numbers, GPT-4's accuracy dropped from 84% to 51%. The authors found that both models' behaviour changed substantially over that short period, and argued for continuous monitoring of LLM services.

| Type of drift | What changes | Commercial example (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data drift | The inputs | A new segment brings inbound leads unlike past ones |
| Concept drift | What inputs mean | A pricing change alters which signals predict a win |
| Provider change | The model behind the API | An updated model writes longer, more hedged drafts |
| Context drift | Prompts, documents, definitions | Someone edits the playbook the agent retrieves |
| Retirement | The model stops working | Calls to a retired model version fail |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Quiet changes in output

An agent that drafts follow-up emails can start producing drafts that are longer, more formal or less accurate without anyone touching the build. Approvers notice, but often read it as a bad week rather than a change. Approval rates fall slowly and nobody links the fall to a model update. That pattern is why **lowob** treats approval rate as an imperfect signal: it measures reviewer fatigue as well as quality.

### Governance expects it

NIST's generative AI profile (AI 600-1, July 2024) names "GAI system changes over time (e.g., fine-tuning, drift, decay)" among the things organisations should plan for (action GV-6.2-007). It also recommends policies for continuous monitoring of third-party generative AI systems in deployment (GV-6.2-004). For most mid-size firms every model is third-party, so this applies to all of them.

### Retirement is scheduled drift

Providers publish lifecycles. Anthropic's documentation describes four states: active, legacy, deprecated and retired, where requests to retired models fail. It commits to at least 60 days' notice before retiring a publicly released model. For example, its documentation lists `claude-3-7-sonnet-20250219` as retired on 19 February 2026. Every build that names a model version needs an owner who reads those notices.

> A build that nobody changed can still behave differently next month. The test set is how you find out.

## How to detect and manage it

| Control | What it involves | Catches |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pin versions | Call a dated model snapshot, not a floating alias | Silent provider changes |
| Fixed eval set | 30 to 50 real tasks with expected outcomes, re-run monthly | All five types |
| Change log | Record every prompt, document and model change with a date | Context drift |
| Outcome tracking | Approval, edit and win rates per agent, by week | Gradual degradation |
| Deprecation owner | One person tracks provider lifecycle pages | Retirement |
| Re-test on upgrade | Run the eval set before switching versions | Regressions on upgrade |

The eval set matters most. It turns "the drafts feel worse" into a number you can compare. Keep it small, drawn from real tasks, and stable for at least a quarter so comparisons hold.

For predictive models in the CRM, such as lead or health scores, the same logic applies with a different test: compare the score's predictions with outcomes written back each quarter. If high-scoring leads stop converting at a higher rate than low-scoring ones, the model has drifted and needs retraining or retiring.

## lowob takeaways

- **Two sources.** The world changes, and so does the model behind the API.
- **Pin and test.** A dated model version plus a fixed eval set catches most drift.
- **Log your own changes.** Prompts and documents drift too, and leave no trace unless recorded.
- **Own the lifecycle.** Someone must read provider deprecation notices before calls start failing.

## Common questions

### What causes model drift?

Changes in the data the model sees, changes in what that data means, provider updates to the model, edits to prompts or retrieved content, and model retirement.

### What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?

Data drift is a change in the inputs, such as a new mix of customers. Concept drift is a change in the relationship between inputs and outcomes, such as signals that no longer predict a purchase.

### Do large language models drift?

Their weights do not change on their own, but providers update and retire models. A 2023 study measured large changes in GPT-4's behaviour between March and June versions.

### How do you monitor for model drift?

Re-run a fixed set of real test cases on a schedule, track approval and outcome rates per agent, and log every change to models, prompts and source documents.

## Sources and notes

- [Chen, Zaharia and Zou, How Is ChatGPT's Behavior Changing over Time?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09009v2), arXiv, July 2023. Academic study of 2023 model versions; specific figures will not hold for current models.
- [NIST, AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. Voluntary US government guidance.
- [Anthropic, Model deprecations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations). Vendor documentation; other providers set different notice periods.

## Related research

- [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/)
- [What Is LLM Observability?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)

Check which model version each of your AI tools or agents calls, and whether it is pinned. Write down the provider's retirement date for each, and the name of the person who will act on it.
