# What Is Zero Data Retention in AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Zero data retention is an arrangement under which an AI provider keeps no prompts or outputs at rest once a response is returned. It is approved per customer, covers only eligible endpoints, and keeps exceptions for flagged content and legal holds. In 2026 providers began limiting it for their most capable models, so buyers should check retention per model and per feature.

Zero data retention (ZDR) is an arrangement under which an AI provider does not store a customer's prompts or the model's outputs once the response has been returned. It is not a default setting: providers approve it per customer, it covers only some endpoints and features, and it keeps exceptions for content flagged by safety systems and for legal requirements. Since mid-2026 some providers have also required retention for their most capable models, so ZDR must now be checked model by model.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What zero data retention means

Every call to a hosted model sends data to the provider. Without special terms, some of it is kept for a period: in logs used to detect abuse, in stored conversation state, and in files or indexes a feature needs to work. ZDR removes the first two for eligible calls, so nothing is held at rest once the answer is sent.

| ZDR means | ZDR does not mean |
| --- | --- |
| No prompts or outputs stored at rest after the response | That data never leaves your network |
| Content excluded from routine abuse logs | That every feature or endpoint is covered |
| A contractual arrangement approved per customer or organisation | A setting any user can switch on |
| Data is not available for later review or training | That flagged content or legal holds are exempt |

ZDR is also distinct from a no-training commitment. Most business API terms already exclude customer data from training. ZDR goes further by removing the stored copy.

## What is usually excluded

The exclusions are where most of the practical detail sits. Any feature that must remember something between calls cannot work under strict ZDR.

| Category | OpenAI API | Anthropic Claude API |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Core model calls | Eligible, with stored state forced off | Messages API eligible |
| Stored threads and assistants | Not eligible; kept until deleted | Message threads not eligible |
| File storage | Not eligible; kept until deleted or expired | Files API not eligible |
| Batch jobs | Not eligible | Not eligible; 29-day retention |
| Code execution containers | Not listed | Not eligible; up to 30 days |
| Flagged content | CSAM-flagged images retained for review | Flagged sessions may be retained up to 2 years |
| Chat apps for staff | Separate terms | ZDR does not cover consumer plans or Team and Enterprise interfaces, except Claude Code on Enterprise |

Short-lived caches are often allowed. OpenAI keeps prompt caching data for up to 24 hours; Anthropic lists prompt caching as eligible and caches structured-output schemas, not content, for up to 24 hours.

## What changed in 2026

ZDR rests on a trade-off. Abuse that is spread across many requests is hard to detect if no request is kept. In 2026 providers began to address that trade-off differently.

Anthropic designated a set of covered models, starting with Claude Fable 5 and Claude Mythos 5 on 9 June 2026, that retain prompts and completions for at least 30 days. Its stated reason is that "some forms of misuse only become detectable across many requests". Eligible customers can get a limited-time ZDR option for the Fable models for internal business applications. OpenAI took a different route, previewing Private Safety Processing, which analyses interaction patterns on customer-controlled infrastructure or in storage encrypted with customer-held keys and returns only a narrow signal about flagged activity.

For buyers, the consequence is that ZDR is no longer an account-level fact. It needs checking for each model and feature a tool uses.

## What to ask a vendor

Many commercial AI tools are built on a model provider's API. The vendor's ZDR position depends on its own agreement upstream.

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Do you have ZDR with your model provider, in writing? | Your vendor's terms cannot exceed its supplier's |
| Which models and features does it cover? | Covered models, batch jobs and file stores may be excluded |
| What do you store yourselves? | The vendor's own logs and databases sit outside the provider's ZDR |
| What happens to flagged content? | Safety exceptions can mean retention for up to 2 years |
| How would a legal hold be handled? | Retention can be required by law regardless of contract |

The third question is often the decisive one. A sales tool may call a model under ZDR and still store every draft in its own database, which is usually the point. **lowob**'s view is that the commercial record should be kept deliberately, by you, in a system you control. ZDR governs the model provider's copy; it does not replace a decision about what your own record holds.

## lowob takeaways

- **ZDR is approved, not assumed.** Providers grant it per customer and organisation.
- **Check features, not only accounts.** Files, threads, batches and code execution are commonly excluded.
- **Check models too.** Since June 2026 some frontier models require 30-day retention.
- **Ask what the vendor stores.** The tool's own database often holds more than the model provider ever does.

## Common questions

### What is zero data retention in AI?

An arrangement under which an AI provider does not store a customer's prompts or outputs at rest after returning a response.

### Does OpenAI offer zero data retention?

Yes, for approved API customers on eligible endpoints. Features that store state, such as assistants, files and vector stores, are not eligible.

### Does zero data retention mean no data is ever kept?

No. Providers can still retain content flagged by safety systems or required by law, and short-lived caches may apply.

### Is zero data retention the same as not training on my data?

No. Most business terms already exclude customer data from training. ZDR additionally removes the stored copy of prompts and outputs.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Data controls in the OpenAI platform](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; retention periods and ZDR eligibility.
- [Anthropic, API and data retention](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/api-and-data-retention), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; ZDR scope and exclusions.
- [Anthropic, Covered models](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15425695-covered-models), accessed November 2026. Vendor policy; retention requirements and designation dates.
- [Channel Insider, OpenAI challenges Anthropic's data retention approach with a privacy-focused alternative](https://www.channelinsider.com/ai/news-openai-anthropic-data-retention-private-safety-processing/), 20 August 2026. Trade press on Private Safety Processing; feature was in preview.

## Related research

- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)
- [Which AI Assistant, Which Seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/)
- [Whoever Holds the Record Holds the Company](https://lowob.com/research/whoever-holds-the-record-holds-the-company/)
- [The RFP Nobody Can Answer Yet](https://lowob.com/research/the-rfp-nobody-can-answer-yet/)

## Next move

Send each AI vendor that handles client data one question this week: which model provider do you call, under what retention terms, and what do you store yourselves? Record the answers on your AI inventory.

# Events That Pay Back

Source: https://lowob.com/research/events-that-pay-back/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Events are among the largest lines in a B2B marketing budget and among the hardest to defend, because most are judged after the fact on badge scans. In-person contact still matters to business buyers, especially with new suppliers. We set out a five-number business case to write before booking, the event types and the job each does, and a measurement method that compares met and unmet target accounts over two quarters.

An event pays back when the meetings it produces lead to pipeline that would not otherwise have existed, at a cost the firm would accept from any other channel. Most B2B event spend cannot show that, because the case for it is written after the event, from badge scans and impressions. In-person contact still matters: McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found 41% prefer in-person channels when dealing with new suppliers. The fix is a short business case written before booking, meetings set before arrival, a follow-up rule, and a comparison of target accounts met against those not met over two quarters.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Event budgets survive on anecdote. Someone remembers the deal that started at a dinner, and the booth is renewed for another year. Someone else remembers the conference that produced nothing, and the next one is cut. Neither memory is a measure.

This piece is about deciding which events to attend, sponsor or host, and how to tell afterwards whether they worked. It builds on two earlier **lowob** pieces. *Sponsorships, events, newsletters and podcasts* argues that a sponsorship buys access to an audience someone else built, and that a logo without access is a poor purchase. Our event calendars, *The 10 crypto events worth the trip* and *Top 10 applied AI events*, cover where to go in two sectors. Here the subject is the business case and the measurement.

## What in-person still does in B2B buying

The case for events rests on what face-to-face contact does that remote and digital channels do less well.

| Finding | Source | What it means for events |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 41% prefer in-person channels with new suppliers; 40% for first-time purchases | McKinsey B2B Pulse, September 2024, nearly 4,000 decision makers | Events matter most for new relationships, less for existing customers |
| Buyers use an average of 10 interaction channels, up from 5 in 2016; interactions split roughly into thirds across in-person, remote and self-serve | McKinsey, 2024 | An event is one channel among many and must hand off to the others |
| In-person sales account for 17% of revenue, down 5 points | McKinsey, 2024 | The in-person moment is rarer, so each one carries more weight |
| 13 people involved in the average purchase; 86% of purchases stall | Forrester, State of Business Buying 2024 | Events can reach stakeholders a seller has not met and restart stalled deals |
| Won deals had about 9 engaged contacts at the solution stage, lost deals about 2 | Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 benchmarks, 4.2 million opportunities | Breadth of contact predicts wins; events are one of the few ways to add it fast |

These are surveys and vendor benchmark data, and the Ebsta figure is a correlation, not proof that more contacts cause wins. Together they suggest where events earn their cost: meeting new buyers in person, and widening contact within accounts already in play.

They also suggest where events do not. Most attendees at any conference are not buying this quarter. The B2B Institute's 95:5 rule, developed with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, holds that only a small share of business buyers are in market at any time; John Dawes's 2021 report estimated something like 5% in a quarter. An event judged only on pipeline sourced within the quarter will look poor, and an event judged only on reach will look good regardless. Neither is honest. Payback can be measured, though it takes care: Gopalakrishna, Lilien, Williams and Sequeira's 1995 *Journal of Marketing* study of one firm at one trade show found positive economic returns on incremental sales and profits, and concluded that under carefully controlled conditions trade show returns can be measured and quantified. It is a single case, so treat it as proof of method, not a benchmark.

## The business case, written before booking

The single most useful discipline is to write five numbers before committing to an event. If they cannot be written, the event is a brand purchase and should be judged as one (Part 13 of this series covers brand measurement).

| Number | Question | Example entry |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Target accounts attending | How many accounts on our target list will be there? | 25, from the organiser's attendee list or past years |
| Meetings set in advance | How many will we book before we arrive? | 12 meetings, at least half with stakeholders we have not met |
| Full cost per meeting | Total cost, including travel and staff time, divided by meetings held | Compared with the cost of a meeting from outbound or paid channels |
| Expected pipeline at two quarters | What pipeline do we expect from met accounts, beyond what they would have produced anyway? | A figure the revenue leader will sign |
| Follow-up rule | Who follows up each meeting, and by when? | Named owner, within three working days |

The academic evidence supports booking ahead. Dekimpe, Gopalakrishna, Lilien and colleagues, studying trade shows in the US and UK for the *Journal of Marketing* in 1997, found pre-show promotion was a significant predictor in both countries of how much of a firm's target audience visited its stand. Their measure was stand attraction, not sales, but it is the step meetings depend on.

The attendee list is the hinge. Our sponsorship piece recommends asking for it before signing; for attended events, past speaker lists, sponsor lists and the organiser's audience data are a reasonable proxy. If fewer than a handful of target accounts will attend, the meeting target cannot be met, and the event fails the case before it starts.

Staff time belongs in the cost. A team of four spending three days at a conference, plus travel, often costs more than the sponsorship. Leaving it out flatters every event.

## Five event types, five jobs

Events are not one channel. Each type does a different job and should be measured against it.

| Event type | Main job | Primary measure | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Attending a large industry conference | Meetings with target accounts and partners | Meetings held with target accounts | Going without meetings booked |
| Sponsoring a conference | Access: speaking slots, hosted sessions, attendee data | Qualified conversations per unit of spend | Buying a logo tier with no access |
| Hosting a small roundtable or dinner | Depth with a few senior buyers | Target accounts attending; stakeholders added per account | Inviting customers only, which feels good and adds little pipeline |
| Customer event | Retention and expansion | Renewal and expansion rate of attending accounts against non-attending | Judging it on new pipeline |
| Partner event | Enabling partners to sell | Partner-sourced pipeline in the following two quarters | Treating partners as an audience rather than a channel (Parts 14 and 15) |

Small hosted events are often the best-value format for a 50- to 500-person firm. Twelve senior buyers at a well-chosen dinner can produce more stakeholder contact than a booth at a large show, at a fraction of the cost. They are also easier to measure, because every attendee is known.

> If you cannot write the meeting target before you book, you are buying a brand event. Judge it as one.

## Measuring payback without fooling yourself

Badge scans, booth traffic and social impressions measure activity. They do not measure payback. Three methods do better.

**A two-quarter window.** Most B2B cycles are long. 6sense's 2025 survey put the average buying cycle at about ten months. Judge an event on pipeline created and progressed among met accounts over the following two quarters, not within the same month.

**A matched comparison.** Take the target accounts the team met at the event, and a similar set of target accounts it did not meet, by size, segment and stage. Compare pipeline created, stage progression and stakeholders engaged over the two quarters. The difference is a reasonable estimate of what the event added. It is not a controlled experiment, because the accounts that agreed to meet may already have been warmer, but it is far better than counting every met account's pipeline as event-sourced. Our piece *Attribution vs incrementality* explains the distinction.

**Stakeholder breadth.** Count how many new contacts were engaged per target account. Given the Ebsta finding on contact breadth in won deals, an event that adds two or three senior stakeholders to five live opportunities may be worth more than one that adds twenty unknown leads.

| Counts toward payback | Does not count |
| --- | --- |
| Pipeline created in met target accounts, above the matched comparison | Every met account's pipeline, regardless of what it would have produced |
| New stakeholders engaged in live opportunities | Badge scans with no meeting |
| Stalled deals that progressed after an event meeting | Booth visits and social impressions |
| Partner-sourced pipeline after a partner event | Leads from people outside the target market |

## Events in the record

Every event is a decision with a cost, an owner and an expected outcome, which makes it a natural entry in the decision record The Build Order describes (*The commercial decisions worth recording*). The five-number case is the record. The check date is two quarters after the event. When the check comes, the record shows whether the meeting target was hit, whether follow-up happened inside the rule, and whether met accounts outperformed the comparison.

After a year, that record answers the question every events budget faces: which events to repeat. Part 6 of this series puts the review in the quarterly commercial rhythm. Over time the firm builds its own evidence of which formats and which conferences pay back for its market, which is worth more than any industry benchmark.

Illustrative example: a fintech infrastructure firm resets its events budget

Decision
:   Cut from six conference sponsorships to two, with access packages, and add four hosted dinners for target accounts.

Reason and owner
:   A review of the past year found most booth leads were outside the target market and follow-up had happened in under half of meetings. Owned by the head of marketing, agreed with the revenue leader.

What changed
:   Each event now has a five-number case written before booking, a named follow-up owner per meeting, and a two-quarter check comparing met and unmet target accounts.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size fintech infrastructure firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the case before booking.** Target accounts, meetings set, cost per meeting, expected pipeline and a follow-up rule.
- **Match the measure to the event type.** Conferences, sponsorships, dinners, customer events and partner events do different jobs.
- **Count staff time.** It is often the largest cost and the one most often left out.
- **Compare met and unmet accounts.** Over two quarters, that difference is a fair estimate of what the event added.

Gateway card

### Before you book the next event

- Target accounts likely to attend counted from a real list
- Meetings booked in advance, with a target number
- Full cost per meeting, including staff time and travel
- A follow-up owner and deadline for every meeting
- A two-quarter check date and a matched comparison set

## Common questions

### How do you measure the ROI of a B2B event?

Compare pipeline created and progressed among target accounts met at the event with a similar set of target accounts not met, over the following two quarters, and divide by the full cost including staff time.

### Are in-person events still worth it in B2B?

Often, for new relationships. McKinsey's 2024 survey found 41% of B2B decision makers prefer in-person channels with new suppliers. They are less useful for buyers you already know well.

### How many meetings should you book before a trade show?

Enough to justify the full cost at a cost per meeting you would accept from other channels. If you cannot book a meaningful number with target accounts in advance, reconsider attending.

### What is the best type of B2B event for a small company?

Small hosted events such as roundtables and dinners for target accounts often give the best value, because every attendee is known and stakeholder contact is deep.

## Sources and notes

- [McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/five-fundamental-truths-how-b2b-winners-keep-growing), 12 September 2024. B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers; self-reported preferences.

# What Is a System of Record?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A system of record is the authoritative source for one type of business data. The idea dates from enterprise IT, where Gartner and Geoffrey Moore set it against faster-moving systems of engagement and innovation. For a commercial team the practical work is naming one system and one owner per data type, then deciding which of those systems AI agents may read and write.

A system of record is the one system a business treats as authoritative for a given type of data, such as the CRM for accounts and opportunities or the finance system for invoices. When two systems disagree, the system of record wins. It stores what is true now. It rarely stores why a decision was made, and that is the gap AI agents expose.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a system of record means

The term describes a role, not a product category. TechTarget's definition is an information storage and retrieval system that holds valuable data about an organisational system or process. Its key condition is that, "to ensure data integrity and validity, there must be only one SOR for a given piece of information."

Most firms already have several systems of record without having named them. Trouble starts when a second copy of the same data is treated as equally true.

| Data type | Typical system of record | Common rival copy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts and contacts | CRM | Marketing automation, personal spreadsheets |
| Opportunities and pipeline | CRM | Forecast spreadsheet |
| Invoices and booked revenue | Finance or ERP system | CRM "closed won" amount |
| Signed contract terms | Contract repository or e-signature tool | Email attachments |
| Prices and discount rules | Price book in the CRM or quoting tool | Old proposal documents |
| People and roles | HR system | Directory, org chart slides |

The idea has a long history in enterprise IT. In 2011, Geoffrey Moore's white paper for AIIM described systems of record as the "tools, repositories, and systems upon which organizations have built their business processes". The newer systems of engagement, such as collaboration tools, "overlay and complement" them. Gartner's pace-layered model, set out by Yvonne Genovese in 2012, adds a reason for caution: because systems of record are "regulated or foundational to running an organization, changes will be carefully controlled".

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The first cost of an unnamed system of record is argument. A board pack shows one revenue figure from the CRM and another from finance, and the meeting is spent reconciling rather than deciding. Naming which system wins, and who owns it, ends most of these disputes.

The second cost arrives with AI. An agent preparing a renewal brief reads from several systems. If nobody has named the authoritative source for contract value, the agent uses whichever copy it reaches first. The output looks confident and may be wrong. The same applies to writing: an agent that updates a field should update it in the system of record, through its own identity and permissions, not in a side copy.

The third point is about what a system of record does not hold. It stores the current value of a field. It rarely stores the reasoning behind a change. Standard Salesforce field history tracking covers 20 fields per object, with 18 months visible in the interface and up to 24 months through the API. Field Audit Trail raises the limit to 200 fields per object and longer retention. Even then, the history shows that a discount changed from 10% to 25%. It does not show who argued for it, why, or what renewal price was expected.

In **lowob**'s model that is a separate layer. The CRM is memory, not a brain. The system of record holds state; a decision record holds the reason, owner, status and expected outcome. Agents need both.

## How to map yours in a week

1. **List the disputed data.** Write down the ten data types the commercial team argues about most, such as pipeline value, contract end dates and discount levels.
2. **Name one system and one owner for each.** The owner decides definitions and fixes errors. Everyone else reads.
3. **Mark every other copy.** Each rival copy is either synced from the system of record or retired. A spreadsheet that people edit by hand is a rival, not a copy.
4. **Set agent rules.** For each system of record, decide whether agents may read it, draft changes to it, or write to it, and at which autonomy level. Most firms start at level 1 (draft) for writes.
5. **Add the missing record.** Decide where the reasons for commercial decisions will live, since no system of record holds them by default.

## lowob takeaways

- **One type of data, one authoritative system.** Two equally trusted copies of the same number are the root of most reporting disputes.
- **Name an owner, not just a tool.** A system of record without an owner drifts.
- **Agents should read from and write to the system of record.** Side copies give agents confident wrong answers.
- **State is not reasoning.** Field history shows what changed; a decision record shows why.

## Common questions

### What is an example of a system of record?

A CRM is the usual system of record for accounts, contacts and opportunities. A finance or ERP system is the usual system of record for invoices and booked revenue.

### What is the difference between a system of record and a system of engagement?

A system of record is the authoritative store for a type of data. A system of engagement, such as a collaboration or messaging tool, sits on top of it to help people work with that data.

### Can a company have more than one system of record?

Yes. Most have several, one for each type of data. The rule is one authoritative system per data type, not one system for everything.

### Is a data warehouse a system of record?

Usually not. A warehouse holds copies drawn from systems of record for analysis. It becomes authoritative only for data created there, such as derived metrics.

## Sources and notes

- [TechTarget, What is a system of record (SOR)?](https://www.techtarget.com/whatis/definition/system-of-record-SOR), last updated November 2022. Reference definition; no named author.
- [AIIM, New Geoffrey Moore white paper on the future of enterprise IT](https://info.aiim.org/aiim-blog/newaiimo/2011/01/19/new-geoffrey-moore-white-paper-on-future-of-enterprise-it), 19 January 2011. Industry association summary of Moore's paper on systems of record and engagement.

Ask finance and sales for last quarter's revenue figure separately. If the numbers differ, write down which system each came from, and name the one that wins and the person who owns it.

# Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too

Source: https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: "Accepted without edit" rises when an AI system improves, but also when reviewers tire, trust fluent output, see only easy cases, or accept blander work. Clinical alert research and automation-bias studies show why. Report approval rate only beside an independently measured error rate and a seeded-error catch rate.

"Accepted without edit" rises when an AI system improves. It also rises when reviewers get tired, trust fluent text, stop seeing hard cases, or ask for less. Read alone, the number cannot tell these apart, and the people producing it cannot either: experienced developers in a 2025 randomised trial were 19% slower with AI and believed they were 20% faster. A few cheap measures can separate improvement from fatigue. Report approval rate beside them or not at all.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

It is the most popular metric in human-in-the-loop AI: the share of outputs approved without changes. It goes up over time, it is easy to compute, and it looks like learning. Sponsors like it. In our approval gate design, [Gateway 1](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/), it is one of the numbers the queue produces automatically, which is exactly why it gets reported first.

## Four forces that raise it without quality

| Force | Mechanism | What it looks like in the queue |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fatigue | Vigilance is finite and declines within a session | By the fortieth item of the afternoon, approval is a click |
| Automation bias | Fluent output is trusted whether or not it is correct | Fewer edits as the model's prose improves, with no change in factual accuracy |
| Selection | Routing sends the system only easy cases | Approval rises while usefulness stays flat |
| Narrowing ambition | Outputs drift toward safer, blander content because that is what passes | Less to correct, and less of value |

**Fatigue.** The best-documented analogue comes from clinical decision support. Heleen van der Sijs and colleagues reviewed 17 studies of drug safety alerts in computerised prescribing systems and found clinicians overrode them in roughly 49% to 96% of cases. The authors are careful: many overrides were justified. But they name the conditions that make people stop reading, including low specificity, unclear information and unnecessary disruption to work. An approval queue full of routine, mostly correct drafts creates the same conditions. The reviewer learns that the right answer is usually "yes", and the click becomes a habit.

**Automation bias.** Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey's 2010 review describes how people relying on an imperfect aid make omission errors, missing problems it did not flag, and commission errors, following its wrong advice. It also found the bias was not prevented by training or instructions. As language models become more fluent, there is more surface for this bias to act on. Fluency is not accuracy, but it feels like it.

**Selection.** If routing logic sends the system only cases it handles well, its approval rate rises while its contribution stays the same. This is common when a team scopes a pilot to "start with the easy ones" and then never widens it.

**Narrowing ambition.** Outputs drift toward what gets approved without edits. A draft that names no risk, commits to no number and makes no recommendation is hard to fault. There is less to correct, and less of value.

## The perception problem

Asking reviewers whether they are still paying attention does not work, because people misjudge their own performance with AI. METR's randomised trial in early 2025 followed 16 experienced open-source developers across 246 real tasks in codebases they knew well. Before starting, they predicted AI tools would make them 24% faster. Measured completion time rose by 19%. Afterwards, they estimated AI had made them 20% faster.

If experienced professionals misjudge their own speed by that margin, reviewers will misjudge their own vigilance. Self-report cannot rescue this metric. Only independent measurement can.

> A rising approval rate with flat or falling error detection is a warning, not a win.

## Four measures that can

| Measure | How | What it tells you | Cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Independent error sampling | A second reviewer assesses 3 to 5% of approved outputs blind | The critical-error rate behind the approval rate | A few reviewer hours a month |
| Seeded errors | Insert a handful of outputs with known, material flaws each month | Whether the gate catches what it should | Writing the flawed items |
| Time on item | Plot the distribution of review times by task | Approvals in seconds on complex items are not reviews | Free if the queue logs it |
| Ambition drift | Compare month-one and month-six outputs on similar cases | Whether outputs say less over time | An hour a quarter |

**Independent error sampling.** Take a random few percent of approved outputs and have a second reviewer assess them without seeing the first decision. The critical-error rate in that sample is the number that matters. Read approval rate only beside it.

**Seeded errors.** Insert a small number of outputs with known, material flaws into the review queue and measure how many reviewers catch. Inspection functions have used planted test items for years. The US Transportation Security Administration projects fictional threat images onto X-ray scans of real bags to test screeners, with monthly reviews and remedial training below a target rate. The GAO's 2016 audit found the data incomplete at some airports, which is the practical lesson: a seeded test is only a measure if someone reads the results. It is the most direct test of whether the gate works.

**Time on item.** Look at the distribution of review time, not the average. A long tail of three-second approvals on complex items is fatigue made visible.

**Ambition drift.** Periodically compare outputs from month one and month six on similar cases for specificity: numbers, named risks, concrete recommendations. If later outputs say less, approval rates are rising for the wrong reason. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to keep a fixed comparison set for this.

## Reading the two numbers together

| Approval rate | Independent error rate | Seeded-error catch rate | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Rising | Falling | Stable or rising | The system is improving and the gate still works |
| Rising | Flat or rising | Falling | Fatigue or automation bias; the gate is weakening |
| Rising | Falling | Falling | Easier cases or blander output; check selection and ambition drift |
| Falling | Flat | Stable | Reviewers are engaged; look at edit classes for the cause |

The second row is the one that matters most and the one approval rate alone will never show. It is also the row that should block any move along the autonomy dial. Our comparison of [human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop](https://lowob.com/research/human-in-the-loop-vs-human-on-the-loop/) explains why a task should only move from approval to monitoring on evidence of a low independent error rate, never on approval rate.

## What would prove this wrong

Approval rates that track independently sampled error rates closely across systems, reviewers and time. Then approval rate is a sufficient proxy and the extra measures are overhead. The alert-override and automation-bias literature gives good reason to expect they will diverge, but it comes from clinical and laboratory settings, so each organisation should test the relationship on its own queue before relying on either assumption.

## lowob takeaways

- **Four forces push approval up.** Fatigue, automation bias, easy-case selection and narrowing ambition all look like improvement.
- **Do not ask reviewers to self-assess.** People misjudge their own performance with AI by wide margins.
- **Sample and seed.** Blind re-review of 3 to 5% of approvals and a monthly seeded-error test.
- **Report in pairs.** Never put approval rate on a dashboard without the error rate beside it.

## Common questions

### Is approval rate a good metric for human-in-the-loop AI?

Not on its own. It rises when the system improves but also when reviewers tire, trust fluent output, see only easy cases, or accept blander output. Report it beside an independently sampled error rate.

### How do I check whether AI output reviewers are actually catching errors?

Insert a small number of outputs with known, material flaws into the review queue each month and measure how many reviewers catch. It is the most direct test of whether the gate works.

### How much of approved AI output should be re-reviewed?

Blind re-review of 3 to 5% of approved outputs by a second reviewer is enough for most queues. Report the critical-error rate from that sample beside the approval rate.

### What is alert fatigue and does it apply to AI review?

Alert fatigue is the habit of dismissing frequent prompts without reading them; clinicians override drug safety alerts in roughly 49% to 96% of cases. An approval queue of mostly correct drafts creates similar conditions.

## Sources and notes

- [van der Sijs, Aarts, Vulto and Berg, Overriding of drug safety alerts in computerized physician order entry](https://repub.eur.nl/pub/60465), *Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association* 13(2), 2006. Peer-reviewed review of 17 studies; clinical setting, and many overrides were judged appropriate.
- [Parasuraman and Manzey, Complacency and Bias in Human Use of Automation: An Attentional Integration](https://trid.trb.org/View/1085175), *Human Factors* 52(3), June 2010. Peer-reviewed review; predates generative AI.
- [The Register, AI coding tools make developers slower but they think they're faster, study finds](https://www.theregister.com/2025/07/11/ai_code_tools_slow_down/), 11 July 2025. Trade press report of METR's randomised trial; 16 developers, one task type, early-2025 tools.
- [US GAO, GAO-16-704: TSA should ensure testing data are complete and fully used](https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-16-704.pdf), September 2016. Government audit of airport screening tests; used here for the seeded-test method, not as AI evidence.
- The four-force, measures and reading tables are **lowob**'s framework.

## Related research

- [A Reviewer Who Does Not Verify Is Not a Control](https://lowob.com/research/a-reviewer-who-does-not-verify-is-not-a-control/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is an Approval Gate for AI Agents?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/)
- [Human-in-the-Loop vs Human-on-the-Loop](https://lowob.com/research/human-in-the-loop-vs-human-on-the-loop/)

## Next move

Before the next dashboard review, pull fifty approved items at random and have a second person assess them blind. Put the critical-error rate beside the approval rate and see whether they tell the same story.

# "The Round Has Stalled"

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-11 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A stalled round is either a process fault or an evidence gap, and the pass reasons tell you which. Read every pass, fix the gap or pause cleanly, then compress the remaining live conversations into a two-week window. In a 2026 market where capital is concentrating in fewer companies, a stall is common and usually diagnosable.

A stalled round is a process fault or an evidence gap, and the pass reasons tell you which. Read them, fix the gap or pause, then compress what is left into two weeks. Stalls are more common in 2026 than the headline numbers suggest: deals under $100 million took only 12.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of the year, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42%, so many companies are competing for a smaller pool.

*This is operating guidance, not investment, legal or financial advice.*

## What it usually means

A stalled round looks like one thing from the inside. Meetings keep happening and nothing closes. From the outside, it is usually one of five faults.

| Fault | What it looks like | Where it traces to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pass reasons never logged | Three firms said no for the same reason in different words; the founder heard three opinions | Pipeline tracking |
| The window dripped | Outreach went out as introductions arrived, over months; no fund had to decide while another was deciding | Window compression |
| Tier 1 went first | The best-fit funds saw the weakest deck, as practice, and passed | List tiering |
| Diligence waited on the founder | Half-built data room; each homework request took a week | Data room readiness |
| The gap is real | No organic evidence yet; no process fixes that | Evidence |

The first four are process. The fifth is evidence. The honest answer to the fifth is to go and get the evidence, then come back.

## Why stalls are common in 2026

The headline numbers are records. Crunchbase data summarised by Foley & Lardner shows $159 billion invested globally in the third quarter of 2026, up 53% year on year, with roughly a third going to 27 companies raising rounds of $1 billion or more. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the US in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024.

For a company raising a normal-sized round, the pool is smaller than it looks. Carta's first-half data shows seed capital on its platform falling from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion, and Series B from $13.5 billion to $10.4 billion. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that companies struggling to keep growing quickly faced difficulty raising follow-on rounds. A stall in this market is not proof the company is weak. It is proof that the bar for a normal round moved, and that the process has to work harder to clear it.

## Where it traces to

This traces to [Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/), with [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) behind it.

The sales-process piece said forty to sixty named funds, warm routes, a three-week window, a pipeline with pass reasons logged. Every process fault above is a step that was skipped or done out of order. The round is not unlucky. It is unmanaged.

The evidence piece said raise on what customers have done. When pass reasons cluster around "too early" or "want to see traction", the round has not stalled. It has arrived at the evidence gap. A good process cannot close a round the evidence has not earned.

> The round is not unlucky. It is unmanaged.

## The first move this week

Read every pass. Not the summary you wrote at the time, the actual words. Email, call notes, whatever exists. Put each reason on one line in a sheet. Treat each as a [closed-lost reason](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/) in a sales pipeline: recorded in the buyer's words, then given a category you can count.

| Pass reason, in their words | Count | Fixable this month? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Want to see more customer evidence" | 3 | Only by selling |
| "Not our stage" | 2 | List fault, remove |
| "Team gap in go-to-market" | 1 | Possibly |

If three reasons match, that is the gap. Decide in one sitting whether it can be fixed in weeks or needs months. If weeks, fix it and relaunch. If months, pause the round, tell the live funds why, and name the date you will return. Investors respect a clean pause more than a slow fade.

If no reason repeats, the fault is process. Compress. Take every live conversation and put it inside a two-week window. Tell each fund the date. Overlap creates the urgency the drip never did.

Finish the data room before the window opens. Then hold a rule: every homework answer goes back within 48 hours. Diligence should never wait on you.

The same discipline runs a [win-loss programme](https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/) in sales: the value is in the pattern across losses, which only appears once each loss is written down the same way.

## What not to do

Do not widen the list to 400 names. More of the wrong funds produces more passes, not more offers. The list was sized for a reason.

Do not drop the price in a panic. If the gap is evidence, a lower price does not supply it. If the gap is process, the price was never the issue. The market data points the same way: Carta recorded down rounds at 11.4% of rounds in the first quarter of 2026, the lowest in nearly four years and half the 22.2% of early 2024, and PitchBook data put flat and down rounds at 13.1% of US deals in the first half. A cut price is now the exception, and it signals distress more loudly than it did in 2023.

The exception is a company still carrying a 2021 valuation. PitchBook data reported in August 2026 showed companies that last raised in 2021 trading at a median 59.1% discount on secondary markets. For those companies the price may genuinely be the gap, and the pass reasons will usually say so.

Do not keep "ongoing" conversations alive for months. Ask each one for a decision date. A fund that will not give one has passed and is being polite.

## How you know it worked

Two signs. Every live fund has a stated decision date inside the next fourteen days. And the pass reason that clustered has stopped appearing in new conversations, because you fixed it or stopped pitching the funds who care about it.

If the round pauses instead, the clock matters. Carta's median gap between seed and Series A is two years. A pause of three months to get evidence is affordable inside that; a slow fade of six months is not.

## lowob takeaways

- **Diagnose before you act.** Four of the five usual faults are process; one is evidence.
- **Read every pass in the investor's own words.** Three matching reasons are the gap.
- **Pause cleanly or compress.** A named return date, or a two-week window with stated decision dates.
- **Do not widen the list or cut the price in a panic.** Neither fixes an evidence gap.

## Common questions

### What should I do when my fundraising round stalls?

Log every pass reason in the investor's own words. If reasons cluster, fix the gap or pause with a named return date; if not, compress live conversations into a two-week window with stated decision dates.

### Should I lower my valuation if my round has stalled?

Usually not. If the gap is evidence, a lower price does not supply it. If the gap is process, the price was never the issue. The exception is a company still priced at a 2021 valuation, where pass reasons often name the price directly.

### How do I create urgency with investors?

Put every live conversation inside one two-week window and tell each fund the date. Overlap creates urgency that a drip of meetings never does.

### Why is it hard to raise a normal-sized round in 2026?

Capital is concentrated. Deals under $100 million took 12.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of 2026, down from 43.8% in 2024, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by 42% year on year.

## In the news

- 13 October 2026 · Foley & Lardner[Q3 2026 venture data: billion-dollar rounds mask a narrowing market](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-13-q3-2026-venture-data-billion-dollar-rounds-mask-a-narrowing)Headline totals are carried by a few very large rounds. Most companies are raising in a tighter market than the totals suggest.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

Law firm summary of Crunchbase and PitchBook-NVCA data; global totals.
- [PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, Q2 2026](https://pitchbook.brightspotcdn.com/0d/6f/a177ca2443a1a687153e0346a4f5/q2-2026-pitchbook-nvca-venture-monitor.pdf), data as of 30 June 2026. US only; recent quarters are revised upward.

- [The Next Web, Megadeals took 87.5% of US venture dollars](https://thenextweb.com/news/pitchbook-q2-2026-megadeals-87-percent-us-venture-vintage-discount), 12 August 2026. News report on PitchBook and Forge secondary data; flat and down round share and vintage discounts.

Read every pass. Not the summary you wrote at the time, the actual words. Put each reason on one line in a sheet, count the matches, and decide in one sitting whether to fix, pause or compress.

# What Is an AI Kill Switch?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-kill-switch/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: An AI kill switch is a control that lets a named person halt one AI agent or all of them quickly. The EU AI Act asks for a stop button on high-risk systems and NIST's AI RMF asks for assigned responsibility to deactivate systems. In practice it is several layers, from pausing one agent to revoking its credentials, and it only counts if it has been tested.

An AI kill switch is a control that lets a named person stop an AI agent, or every agent, immediately. It is rarely one button. It is a set of layers: pause the agent, revoke its credentials, cut its tools and cap its spending. A kill switch that has never been tested is an assumption, not a control.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What an AI kill switch means

The term suggests a single red button. In a working firm it means knowing, quickly, who can stop the agents, how they do it, and what happens to work already in progress.

The glossary definition in this library is short: a control that lets a named person stop every agent immediately. The word "named" matters. A button that nobody is sure they may press does not stop anything.

Stopping can happen at different depths. Each layer stops something different.

| Layer | What it stops | Example mechanism | What it does not stop |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pause the agent | New runs of one agent | Deactivate in the agent platform | Runs already queued elsewhere; other agents |
| Revoke the identity | The agent signing in to anything | Disable its account or agent identity | Tokens already issued, unless revoked too |
| Cut the tools | Specific actions, such as sending email | Remove the connector or API key | Reading data through other routes |
| Cap the rate and spend | Volume of damage | Rate limits, daily send limits, budget caps | A single harmful action |
| Stop everything | All agent activity | A documented runbook covering all of the above | Nothing, if the runbook is complete |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Regulation sets the expectation. Article 14(4)(e) of the EU AI Act requires that people overseeing a high-risk system can "intervene in the operation of the high-risk AI system or interrupt the system through a 'stop' button or a similar procedure". Most commercial agents are not high-risk under the Act. The principle is still the one auditors and enterprise buyers ask about.

NIST's framework puts the weight on people. MANAGE 2.4 asks that "responsibilities are assigned and understood" for deactivating systems whose "performance or outcomes" are "inconsistent with intended use". A button with no owner fails that test.

Vendors now provide the mechanisms, with caveats that matter. Microsoft's Entra Agent ID documentation describes disabling an agent identity to "prevent an agent identity from receiving tokens and authenticating". The same page warns that disabling "might have broader consequences" and that "existing agents running in your organization might begin to fail". It does not say how quickly the change takes effect. Salesforce's CLI reference says deactivating an agent "makes it unavailable to your users". Neither page describes what happens to a task halfway through.

That gap is why rate limits matter. OWASP's guidance on excessive agency recommends rate limiting "to reduce the number of undesirable actions that can take place within a given time period". An agent that can send 20 emails an hour does less harm in the minutes before someone notices than one that can send 2,000.

## How to set one up and prove it works

1. **Name the owner and a deputy.** One person can stop every agent, and a second person covers absence. Publish both names.
2. **Write the runbook.** For each agent, list where to pause it, which identity and keys to revoke, and which connectors to cut.
3. **Set caps before launch.** Daily send limits, rate limits and spend caps, so that a fault is bounded even before anyone acts.
4. **Decide what happens to in-flight work.** Queued emails, half-written CRM updates and pending approvals each need a rule: cancel, hold or finish.
5. **Run a drill.** Stop a test agent on a schedule, time how long it takes, and record what kept running. Repeat quarterly.

An agent register helps. If each agent is listed with its identity, tools, autonomy level and owner, the runbook can be written from the register rather than from memory.

## lowob takeaways

- **A kill switch is layers, not a button.** Pause, revoke, cut tools and cap volume.
- **Name the person.** NIST asks for assigned responsibility, not just a mechanism.
- **Caps limit damage before anyone notices.** Set rate and spend limits at launch.
- **Test it.** Time a drill and record what kept running.

## Common questions

### What is an AI kill switch?

A control that lets a named person stop one AI agent or all of them quickly, by pausing the agent, revoking its access and cutting its tools.

### Does the EU AI Act require a kill switch?

For high-risk AI systems, Article 14 requires that human overseers can interrupt the system through a stop button or similar procedure that brings it to a halt in a safe state.

### How do you stop an AI agent immediately?

Deactivate it in the platform that runs it, disable its identity and API keys, and remove its connectors. A written runbook makes this fast.

### Who should own the AI kill switch?

One named person with authority to stop every agent, usually in operations or security, plus a named deputy.

## Sources and notes

- [European Commission AI Act Service Desk, Article 14: Human oversight](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-14). Official text; obligations apply to high-risk systems.
- [Ankura, Implementing the NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage](https://ankura.com/insights/implementing-the-nist-artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-manage). Consultancy summary quoting the MANAGE subcategories of NIST AI 100-1.
- [Microsoft Learn, Disable agent identities in your tenant](https://learn.microsoft.com/entra/agent-id/disable-agent-identities), May 2026. Vendor documentation; timing of effect not stated.
- [Salesforce CLI Command Reference, agent deactivate](https://developer.salesforce.com/docs/platform/salesforce-cli-reference/guide/cli_reference_agent_deactivate.html), undated. Vendor developer documentation.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/), 2025. Community security standard.

## Related research

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is Agent Identity and an Agent Registry?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/)

## Next move

Pick one agent in use today and ask its owner to stop it while you time them. Write down how long it took, which steps they had to look up, and what kept running afterwards.

# Dissent Is the Data You Are Throwing Away

Source: https://lowob.com/research/dissent-is-the-data-you-are-throwing-away/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When a committee decides, the minority view is smoothed out of the record, and group research shows discussion tends to bury information only some members hold. Capture independent views before discussion in one attributed line with a probability, review them against outcomes, and protect dissenters.

When a committee decides, the minority view is smoothed out of the record. Over time, recorded dissent is often the most predictive signal an organisation has, and it costs one line to keep. Four decades of group research explain why it disappears: discussion favours what everyone already knows, members follow the most senior voice, and role-played objections carry less weight than real ones. Capture views before discussion, attribute them, attach a probability, and check them against outcomes.

Decision records usually store the result of a discussion: approved, with conditions. Minutes record consensus because that is what minutes are for. The analyst who argued against it, and the specific risk they named, disappears into the memory of the people who were in the room.

That is a loss twice over.

First, the dissent is frequently where the real falsifier lives. The person who disagreed was usually pointing at the risk that, if anything, would later materialise. When it does, the organisation discovers it was warned only if someone remembers.

Second, dissent histories are the clearest view you will ever get of who reads a class of situation well. Agreement tells you little about individual judgment. Disagreement that turns out right tells you a lot.

## Why groups lose the minority view

The mechanism is well studied. Garold Stasser and William Titus gave members of small groups different information about candidates, arranged so that the best candidate only became visible if members pooled what they privately knew. Their 1985 paper in the *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* found groups discussed the information they already shared, usually chose the candidate a plurality favoured at the start, and that discussion "tended to perpetuate, not to correct" the distorted picture. Unshared information that argued against the winner was rarely raised. This design became known as the hidden profile, and it describes most committees: the member with the inconvenient fact is the one least likely to be heard.

Seniority makes it worse. In *Wiser*, Cass Sunstein and Reid Hastie describe groups acting as herds behind their "most senior, most talkative, most authoritative members", and members self-censoring information only they possess. Their advice to leaders is to consider "remaining silent, holding their cards close to their chest" to lower the reputational cost of speaking up.

Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass Sunstein reach the same conclusion from a different direction. Their "decision hygiene" practices include sequencing information so judges do not leap to conclusions, and "aggregating multiple, independent judgments". Independence is the operative word. Once the room has heard the most senior view, the judgments being aggregated are no longer independent.

| What happens in the room | Research finding | What it does to the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discussion centres on shared facts | Stasser and Titus, 1985 | The fact only the dissenter held never reaches the minutes |
| Members follow the senior voice | Sunstein and Hastie, 2015 | Views captured after discussion are already diluted |
| Independent judgments converge | Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein, 2021 | The aggregate looks like agreement, not evidence |
| Dissent feels risky | Edmondson, 1999 | People stop recording it, or stop holding it |

## How to capture it well

**Independent views first.** Ask each participant to record their view and probability before discussion. Once the most senior person has spoken, views converge, and the dissent you capture afterwards is already diluted.

**One line, attributed, with a probability.** "Against. Customer concentration risk understated; 35% this account is lost within a year." That is enough. The probability makes it scoreable later, using the same method as in [Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/).

**Genuine, not assigned.** A designated devil's advocate produces weaker signal than real disagreement, because everyone knows it is a role. Charlan Nemeth, whose research on dissent spans decades, puts it directly: "devil's advocates don't make you think about the alternative decision." Real conviction is what makes the majority reconsider. Sunstein and Hastie do recommend devil's advocates and red teams as tools for testing a plan, and they have a place. The point is to record assigned challenges separately from genuine dissent, so the two are never mixed when hit rates are calculated.

> Agreement tells you little about individual judgment. Disagreement that turns out right tells you a lot.

## How to use it

At the falsifier check date, review the dissent alongside the outcome. Was the minority right? About the thing they named, or something else?

| Field | Example | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Position | Against | Separating dissent from conditional support |
| Reason | Customer concentration risk understated | Checking whether the named risk occurred |
| Probability | 35% the account is lost within a year | Scoring the dissent against the outcome |
| Type | Genuine or assigned | Keeping devil's advocacy out of hit rates |
| Owner | The person who held the view | Building each person's record by decision class |
| Check date | The decision's falsifier date | Triggering the review |

Over several cycles, track each person's dissent hit rate by decision class. After a while you can weight a dissent from someone with a strong record in that class differently from one without. That is the closest thing to institutional wisdom a system can hold: not a rule, but a memory of whose doubts deserve attention. These fields sit naturally in a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/), and they are the same discipline a [win-loss programme](https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/) applies to deals: compare what people believed with what happened.

## Protecting dissenters

A visible record of who predicted what can feel like exposure, and in some cultures it will suppress candour rather than encourage it. Amy Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company defined team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking", and found it associated with learning behaviour, which in turn related to performance. A dissent record that punishes the people who disagree will destroy the very behaviour it is trying to capture.

So decide deliberately who can see dissent: the panel, the function head, or only the review gate. Do not use dissent records in performance evaluation in the first year. Show people their own hit rate privately before anyone else sees it. The aim is to make disagreement safer, not riskier.

## What would prove this wrong

If recorded dissent proves no more predictive of bad outcomes than majority views over a meaningful number of decisions, then dissent is noise, and the record is clutter. The group research shows why minority information gets lost; it does not prove that the minority is usually right, which is why the record needs outcomes, not just positions.

## lowob takeaways

- **Collect views before discussion.** Independence disappears once the senior person speaks.
- **One attributed line with a probability.** Enough to score later, short enough to keep.
- **Separate genuine from assigned.** Devil's advocacy has uses but does not belong in hit rates.
- **Protect the dissenter.** Limited visibility, private feedback, and no performance use in year one.

## Common questions

### Why should committees record dissenting views?

The dissenter is often pointing at the risk that later materialises, and dissent histories show who reads a class of situation well. Research on group discussion shows minority information is otherwise rarely surfaced or kept.

### How do I capture dissent in decision meetings?

Ask each participant to record their view and a probability before discussion, then keep dissent as one attributed line with a probability, separate from assigned challenges, and review it at the decision's check date.

### Does a devil's advocate count as dissent?

Not for scoring. Charlan Nemeth's research finds role-played objections stimulate less reconsideration than genuine dissent. Record assigned challenges separately.

### What is a hidden profile in group decision making?

An experimental setup in which the best option only becomes clear if members pool information they hold privately. Stasser and Titus found groups mostly discussed shared information and missed it.

## Sources and notes

- [Stasser and Titus, Pooling of unshared information in group decision making](https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/stasser_titus_unsharedinfogroupdisc_jpsp1985.pdf), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 48(6), 1985. Peer-reviewed laboratory experiment with student groups.
- [Inside Story, Groups are dumber than you think (but we can make them smarter)](https://insidestory.org.au/groups-are-dumber-than-you-think-but-we-can-make-them-smarter), Paul 't Hart, 14 May 2015. Review of Sunstein and Hastie's *Wiser*; secondary account of the book.
- [strategy+business, How noisy is your company?](https://www.strategy-business.com/article/How-noisy-is-your-company?gko=5a57c), Theodore Kinni, 19 May 2021. Interview-based article on Kahneman, Sibony and Sunstein's *Noise*.
- [Behavioral Scientist, Stop playing devil's advocate, and other advice for better decision making](https://behavioralscientist.org/stop-playing-devils-advocate-and-other-advice-for-better-decision-making/), 10 July 2018. Interview with Charlan Nemeth; summarises her research rather than presenting new data.
- [Edmondson, Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams](https://dash.harvard.edu/entities/publication/13a7b031-0fdd-45ec-a7e0-2b80e2bc679f), *Administrative Science Quarterly* 44(2), 1999. Peer-reviewed field study of 51 teams in one company.
- The dissent record fields are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is a Decision Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/)
- [Running a Win-Loss Programme](https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/)
- [Calibration Is the Honest Learning Signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/)
- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [The Build Order for Retail, DTC and Luxury](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-retail-dtc-and-luxury/)

## Next move

At the next committee decision, ask every member to write their view and a probability on paper before anyone speaks. Keep any dissent as one attributed line in the record, and diary the date you will check it.

# What Is Data Residency for AI Tools?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Data residency for AI tools covers two separate questions: where data is stored at rest and where model inference runs. Vendors now offer both, but differently: OpenAI lists ten residency regions, while Anthropic's API offers US-only inference at a 10% premium. GDPR does not require residency, so the right setting depends on contracts, sector rules and what buyers ask.

Data residency for AI tools is the ability to control the geographic location where your prompts, files, conversation history and outputs are stored, and where the model processes them. For AI the second part matters as much as the first: a vendor can store data in Europe and still run inference in another region. Residency is usually a contract or security requirement rather than a legal one, so the right choice depends on what customers, sector rules and your own data map require.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What data residency means for AI

A traditional SaaS application stores records in a database in a chosen region. An AI tool handles data in more places, and each can sit in a different country.

| Where data goes | Example | Residency question |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Storage at rest | Saved conversations, uploaded files, custom assistants | Which region holds the stored copy? |
| Inference | The model call that processes a prompt | Which region's servers run the model? |
| Logs and safety review | Abuse monitoring logs, flagged content | Where are logs held, and for how long? |
| Support access | Engineers investigating a ticket | From which countries can staff see data? |
| Subprocessors | Cloud hosts, search tools, connectors | Do third parties process data elsewhere? |

Residency is not the same as zero data retention, which is about whether data is stored at all. A vendor can offer one without the other. It is also not the same as sovereignty: storing data in a region controls where it sits, not by itself which governments can compel a provider to produce it.

## What vendors offer in 2026

Offerings differ in what they localise and who can use them.

| Provider | What is offered | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu | Conversations, files, custom GPTs and image outputs stored at rest in the selected region | New workspaces; announcement covers storage, not inference location |
| OpenAI API | Region-specific projects with in-region request handling | For enterprise customers approved for advanced data controls |
| Anthropic Claude API | Inference geo "us" or "global"; workspace geo for storage | Only "us" storage available; US inference at 1.1 times standard price |
| Microsoft cloud services | EU Data Boundary for customer data, pseudonymised personal data and support data | Core services in EU and EFTA; limited global security transfers |

Two points are easy to miss. First, residency usually applies to new workspaces or projects, so an existing account may need migrating. Second, features differ: on Anthropic's API, for example, older models do not support the inference geography setting and return an error if it is set.

## Is data residency legally required?

For most commercial data, no. The GDPR regulates transfers of personal data outside the EEA rather than requiring storage inside it. Transfers to US providers certified under the EU-US Data Privacy Framework rely on an adequacy decision that the General Court upheld in September 2025 in Latombe v Commission. That decision is under appeal, which is one reason some European buyers ask for EU residency as a fallback.

Residency requirements more often come from three other places: customer contracts and security questionnaires, sector rules in areas such as financial services, health and the public sector, and internal policy for sensitive categories of data.

## What to ask an AI vendor

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Is residency for storage, inference, or both? | Many offers cover one only |
| Which products, models and features are included? | Tools, connectors and older models may fall outside |
| Where are abuse monitoring and safety logs held? | Logs are a copy of your data |
| Can it apply to our existing workspace? | Some vendors require a new workspace or project |
| What is the price difference? | Regional inference can cost more per token |
| Which subprocessors handle data outside the region? | Contractual commitments should list them |

Before asking any of these, map which AI uses touch personal or client-confidential data. **lowob**'s Gateway 0 places that question before tool choice. A sales assistant drafting outreach from public information has different needs from a service agent reading support tickets with account details. Residency settings belong on the inventory line for each use, alongside the owner and the autonomy level.

## lowob takeaways

- **Ask about inference, not only storage.** For AI the model call is a separate location from the database.
- **Residency is not retention.** Where data is kept and whether it is kept are different controls.
- **GDPR regulates transfers, not location.** Residency demands usually come from contracts and sector rules.
- **Check the fine print.** New workspaces, supported models and price premiums vary by vendor.

## Common questions

### What is data residency in AI?

Control over the geographic region where an AI tool stores prompts, files and outputs, and where the model processes them.

### Does GDPR require data to be stored in the EU?

No. GDPR regulates transfers of personal data outside the EEA, for example through adequacy decisions or standard contractual clauses, rather than requiring EU storage.

### Does ChatGPT Enterprise offer EU data residency?

Yes. OpenAI offers residency in Europe and nine other regions for new ChatGPT Enterprise and Edu workspaces, storing content at rest in the chosen region.

### What is the difference between data residency and zero data retention?

Residency controls where data is stored and processed. Zero data retention means the provider does not store prompts and outputs after responding.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Expanding data residency access to business customers worldwide](https://openai.com/index/expanding-data-residency-access-to-business-customers-worldwide), 25 November 2025. Vendor announcement; regions and scope.
- [Anthropic, Data residency (Claude Platform docs)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; inference and workspace geography, pricing.
- [Microsoft, Microsoft completes landmark EU Data Boundary](https://blogs.microsoft.com/on-the-issues/2025/02/26/microsoft-completes-landmark-eu-data-boundary-offering-enhanced-data-residency-and-transparency/), 26 February 2025. Vendor announcement.
- [Wilson Sonsini, EU court upholds the validity of the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework](https://www.wsgr.com/en/insights/eu-court-upholds-the-validity-of-the-eu-us-data-privacy-framework.html), September 2025, and [WilmerHale, European Court of Justice to review challenge to EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework](https://www.wilmerhale.com/en/insights/blogs/wilmerhale-privacy-and-cybersecurity-law/20251201-european-court-of-justice-to-review-challenge-to-eu-us-data-privacy-framework), 1 December 2025. Law firm analyses of the judgment and appeal.

## Related research

- [Which AI Assistant, Which Seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/)
- [Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/)
- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)
- [The RFP Nobody Can Answer Yet](https://lowob.com/research/the-rfp-nobody-can-answer-yet/)
- [What Is an AI Impact Assessment?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-impact-assessment/)

## Next move

For each AI tool your teams use, find out this week whether storage and inference each run in a known region, and record both on the inventory. Flag any tool that handles client data with neither answer.
