# The Build Order for Professional Services Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-professional-services-firms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Professional services firms run The Build Order almost unchanged, with one addition: confidentiality and conflict walls arrive with the context layer, not after it. The commercial line is the pitch, the fee quote and the go or no-go decision. Utilisation pressure makes Gateway 0 the hardest gate, and fee realisation gives Gateway 2 its dollar figure.

Law, accounting and consulting firms can run The Build Order almost as written. The commercial line is real and well defined: which work to pitch for, what fee to quote, and which write-offs to accept. What changes is the wiring. The same partners who win the work also deliver it, so their inboxes hold both pitch context and client confidences, and the conflict walls a regulator already expects must be built into the context layer on day one. The evidence says firms are using AI faster than they can measure it. Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey of more than 1,500 professionals found 40% say their organisation uses generative AI, while only 18% say it tracks return on investment. Billable utilisation fell to 66.4% in 2025 in SPI Research's benchmark, which makes the protected time Gateway 0 requires unusually expensive to give.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

This is the first of four industry editions of The Build Order. Each runs the full sequence (Gateway 0, tooling, context, record, reasoning and Gateways 1 to 3) for one sector, using that sector's regulators, surveys and failure modes. In *The RFP nobody can answer yet* we said the order holds in professional services, with one qualification: confidentiality and conflict walls arrive with the context layer. This piece explains what that means in practice.

Professional services is the sector the series was first drawn from, so it is a useful baseline. Pitches are discrete, the CRM maps reasonably well to how the business runs, and the decisions worth recording are easy to name. The difficulty is not finding the commercial line. It is keeping the commercial line from absorbing everything else a partner knows.

## Where the commercial line sits

In a law firm, an accounting practice or a consultancy, revenue arrives through a small number of repeated decisions. A partner decides whether to pursue a tender or a referral. Someone sets a fee estimate, fixed or hourly, and decides how far to discount it. After the work, someone decides how much of the recorded time to write off. Around those sit panel reviews, cross-selling choices and the conflict check that decides whether the firm can act at all.

| Lens | What it looks like in professional services |
| --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Pursue-or-pass on pitches, fee estimates, discounts and write-offs |
| Store | Practice management system, CRM (often thin), proposal library, partner inboxes |
| Outcome lag | Weeks for a pitch result; one billing cycle for realisation |
| Who defends the decision | Practice heads, the managing partner, finance |
| Main regulator or code | Bar and law society rules, the SRA in England and Wales, accounting ethics codes |
| The wall | Client confidences and conflicts: one client's matter must never inform another's pitch |
| Gateway that bites | Gateway 0: protected time and a CRM partners will keep current |

Those decisions pass the test we set out in *Where judgment arrives first*. They are frequent (a mid-size firm makes several pursue-or-pass calls a week), similar to past cases, graded quickly and defended by someone who owns a budget or a practice. They also produce a clean outcome field. A pitch is won or lost. A fee is realised or written down.

The weak spot is the store. Many firms keep their most valuable relationship data in partner inboxes and the practice management system rather than in a CRM. The CRM, where it exists, records contacts and marketing lists but not the reasoning behind a pitch decision. That is the first thing the build has to fix.

## What the evidence says

The sector's own survey data describes firms that have adopted AI faster than they have learned to govern or measure it.

Thomson Reuters' 2026 AI in Professional Services Report surveyed more than 1,500 professionals across legal, tax, accounting, risk, fraud and government. Of those surveyed, 40% said their organisation uses generative AI, up from 22% a year earlier. Only 18% said their organisation tracks return on investment, and 40% did not know whether it was measured at all. Agentic AI was reported in use by 15%, with another 53% planning or considering it. Two-thirds of corporate respondents want their outside firms to use AI, but fewer than 20% require it. Clients are signalling interest, not setting terms, which leaves firms to decide what to build first.

The economics add pressure. SPI Research's Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, published with Deltek, put billable utilisation at 66.4% in 2025, which it describes as a near two-decade low, down from 73.2% in 2021. EBITDA averaged 9.9% against a benchmark expectation of 15%. Firms are under pressure to find hours, and the temptation is to buy assistant seats for everyone and hope the hours appear. Part 6, *Which AI assistant, which seats*, makes the case for buying seats only for the people in the first workflow.

The regulators have been specific about responsibility. The American Bar Association's Formal Opinion 512, issued in July 2024, applies the duties of competence, communication, fees, confidentiality and supervision to generative AI. It says informed client consent may be required before client information goes into a self-learning tool, and that fees must reflect time actually worked. In England and Wales, the Divisional Court's June 2025 judgment in *Ayinde* and *Al-Haroun* found that 18 of 45 authorities cited in one case did not exist. The court said managing partners and heads of chambers must take practical and effective measures to make sure everyone providing legal services understands their duties when using AI.

Taken together: clients want AI used, regulators hold leadership accountable for how it is used, and most firms cannot yet say what it returns. A build that starts with recorded commercial decisions answers all three.

## The build order, stage by stage

| Stage | What it means in professional services | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0 | A named owner with protected hours, the suite of record, a CRM partners will update, and a data-access approver (usually the general counsel or risk partner) | The owner is a fee earner whose protected hours are the first to go |
| Tooling | Assistant seats for business development staff and the partners who pitch most, plus capture of email and meetings into the CRM | Firm-wide seats with no first job |
| Context | Proposals, credentials, CRM and pitch email connected, with information barriers mirrored from the conflicts system | Partner inboxes connect pitch context and client confidences in one place |
| Record | Pursue-or-pass decisions and fee estimates, each with reason, owner, expected fee and check date | Recording only the wins |
| Reasoning | A first agent that assembles pitch preparation packs from approved credentials and the record | The agent quotes a confidential matter as a credential |
| Gateway 1 | Nothing reaches a client or prospect without a named partner's approval, logged | Approval becomes a signature on a draft nobody checked |
| Gateway 2 | Expected fee recorded at pitch; realised fee written back at final bill | Realisation is held in finance and never joined to the pitch |
| Gateway 3 | The record extends to staffing, delivery and finance, with walls intact | Delivery files flood the commercial context |

**Gateway 0.** The three standing decisions apply: an owner, the suite (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) and the CRM. Professional services firms should add the fourth decision that regulated firms need: a data-access approver who is not the build owner. In a law firm that is usually the general counsel or risk partner. The harder problem is time. If utilisation is the firm's main performance measure, the owner's four protected hours a week will be the first casualty of a busy month. Set the protected time as a non-billable target with a code of its own, so its loss is visible. Part 3, *Gateway 0*, covers the rest.

**Tooling.** Buy seats for the people who pitch and the business development team that supports them. Set up automatic capture of email and meetings into the CRM for those people only, so the store fills without partners typing. A CRM that depends on partner data entry will not survive the first quarter.

**Context.** This is where the sector's qualification bites, and the next section covers it in detail. Connect the proposal library, the credentials database, the CRM and pitch correspondence. Do not connect matter files or engagement workpapers.

**Record.** The first decision class is pursue-or-pass, recorded with the reason, the owner, the expected fee and a date to check. The second is the fee estimate, with any discount beyond standard and its reason. Part 9, *The ten commercial decisions worth recording*, lists the fields. Record losses as carefully as wins: a firm that records only wins will learn that every pitch was a good idea.

**Reasoning.** The first agent should be the pitch preparation clerk: it reads the request for proposal, the client's history in the CRM, approved credentials and similar past pitch decisions, then drafts a preparation pack for the partner. It does not draft the proposal itself in the first month.

## The wall: confidences and conflicts

Every sector has context that must never be connected. In professional services it is the confidential information of one client, used for the benefit of another.

The rule is old. The SRA's guidance on conflicts explains that where a firm holds confidential information for one client that is material to another, it may act only if effective safeguards are in place. Those safeguards include separate fee earners and an established, structural separation within the firm, so that the information cannot pass between the lawyers acting for each client. Where the information cannot be protected, the firm must not act. Accounting and consulting firms work under comparable ethics codes and client contracts.

An assistant connected to a partner's whole inbox breaks that structure invisibly. A query for "our experience in logistics restructuring" may surface a live engagement for a competitor of the prospect, including figures the prospect would pay to see. The permissions on the files may technically allow it, because the partner can read both. The ethics rules do not.

Four rules keep the wall in the wiring rather than in a policy document:

- **Mirror the conflicts system.** Information barriers recorded in the conflicts or intake system become access rules in the context layer. If two teams are walled, their documents never appear in each other's retrieval.
- **Connect credentials, not matters.** Pitch agents read from an approved credentials library, written to be shareable, rather than from matter files.
- **Keep the record clean.** A pursue-or-pass record holds the reason in commercial terms ("sector fit, fee below our floor"), never client facts from another engagement.
- **Follow the vendor terms.** The Law Society's guidance on generative AI, updated in September 2025, advises firms not to put confidential data into free online tools, to check whether a tool trains on firm inputs, and to document inputs and outputs where a tool keeps no history.

> A partner can read both files. That does not mean an agent working for the partner should read them together.

## Where firms get stuck, and what to do about it

In our experience, professional services builds stall in three places, and each has a sector-specific fix.

**Gateway 0: the owner's time.** Covered above. The fix is a non-billable code and a named deputy, so the build survives a busy quarter.

**Gateway 1: approval as signature.** Partners already sign everything that goes to a client, so "nothing sends without a person" feels like an existing rule. The risk is the opposite of the one most sectors face. The approval exists, but it is a signature on a draft the partner did not read closely. *Ayinde* is the cautionary case: the citations were submitted under a professional's name. For AI-assisted pitch material, the approver confirms three things before anything leaves: every credential is approved for external use, every fee figure matches the estimate in the record, and no client is named without permission. Our piece *Approval rate measures fatigue too* explains why a near-100% approval rate should prompt a check rather than reassurance.

**Gateway 2: the dollar figure.** Professional services firms have an unusually good one: realisation. Record the expected fee when the pursue-or-pass decision is made. When the final bill goes out, write back the fee billed and collected. The gap between the two, by pitch type and discount level, is the first number the brain produces that a managing partner will act on. It often shows that some discounts that won work also lost money on it.

**Gateway 3: extending to delivery.** Only when the commercial record is trusted should the build extend to staffing and delivery. Even then, the walls stay. A staffing agent that sees engagement data must respect the same barriers as the pitch agent, and in a firm with active conflicts that may mean separate context layers for separate teams.

Illustrative example: an accounting and advisory firm records its pitch decisions

Decision
:   Record every pursue-or-pass decision on tenders above a set fee threshold, with the reason, the owner, the expected fee and a check date at final bill.

Reason and owner
:   Partners believed fixed-fee tenders in one sector were profitable; nobody had compared quoted fees with realised fees. Owned by the head of business development, with the risk partner as data-access approver.

What changed
:   The first pitch preparation agent reads only the approved credentials library and the record, never engagement files. After two quarters, realisation data showed one tender category consistently realising well below estimate, and the firm raised its floor fee for that category.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size accounting and advisory firm of around 140 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The order holds, with walls built in early.** Confidentiality and conflict barriers belong in the context layer from day one.
- **Start at the pitch.** Pursue-or-pass decisions and fee estimates are frequent, gradable and defended by a practice head.
- **Protect the owner's time explicitly.** In a utilisation-driven firm, unprotected build time disappears first.
- **Use realisation as the dollar figure.** Expected fee at pitch, realised fee at final bill, joined in one record.
- **Treat partner sign-off as a control, not a ritual.** Approval means checking credentials, figures and names.

Gateway card

### Before a professional services firm connects its first agent

- A named owner with a non-billable code for protected hours, and a deputy
- A data-access approver who is not the build owner
- Information barriers from the conflicts system mirrored in the context layer
- An approved credentials library the agent reads instead of matter files
- Pursue-or-pass decisions recorded with expected fee and a check date
- A three-point approval check for anything sent to a client or prospect

## Common questions

### How should a law firm start using AI agents?

On the commercial line, with a record of pursue-or-pass decisions and fee estimates, and a first agent that prepares pitch packs from approved credentials. Information barriers from the conflicts system should be built into the context layer before any agent is connected.

### Can AI tools see confidential client information across matters?

They can if they are connected to partner inboxes or document systems without barriers. Permissions that let a partner read two files do not make it acceptable for an agent to combine them. Mirror the firm's conflict walls in the AI tools' access rules.

### Do lawyers need client consent to use generative AI?

ABA Formal Opinion 512 says informed consent may be required before client information is entered into a self-learning tool, depending on the risks. Firms should check engagement terms and regulator guidance in each jurisdiction where they practise.

### How do professional services firms measure AI ROI?

Join the expected fee recorded at the pitch decision to the fee realised at final bill. Realisation by pitch type and discount level is a money figure a managing partner will act on, unlike hours-saved estimates.

# Calibration Is the Honest Learning Signal

Source: https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A system cannot claim to learn by grading its own outputs. It can by comparing human predictions, made with a probability before the decision, against outcomes it did not produce. Rating agencies have published this kind of scorecard for decades, and forecasting research shows calibration can be trained. Enterprises can extend it to renewals, approvals and pricing for one number per decision.

A system cannot claim to learn by grading its own outputs. It can by comparing human predictions with outcomes it did not produce. Someone records a probability before a decision; the world produces a result; the gap is information nobody can game afterwards. Rating agencies have published this kind of scorecard for decades, and the largest forecasting experiments show calibration can be trained. Almost no other business function does it at all, and it costs one number per decision.

## Why most learning claims are circular

Most claims that a system "learns" are circular. It finds a pattern, applies it, and then scores itself on how often later cases matched the pattern. Of course they did: the pattern was applied to them. Approval rates, acceptance rates and pattern hit rates all share this flaw to some degree. In [Approval rate measures fatigue too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/) we set out the other forces that push such numbers up.

The honest learning signal is external. Someone makes a prediction with a probability. The world produces an outcome the system did not cause. The gap between the two is information nobody can game after the fact. This is also what [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) is for: without the outcome recorded against the decision, there is nothing to compare.

## The model already exists

Credit rating is calibration at institutional scale. S&P Global Ratings publishes annual default and transition studies showing how often issuers at each rating actually defaulted over different horizons. Its corporate study covers 1981 to 2024. Across that period, AAA-rated corporates had a five-year cumulative default rate of 0.34%, fewer than four defaults per 1,000 ratings, and S&P states that "lower-rated issuers and securities have generally exhibited higher default rates."

That is a public scorecard for judgment. If the ratings mean anything, default rates should rise steadily as ratings fall, and the pattern should hold over time. When it does not, the market notices.

Weather forecasting got there first. Glenn Brier introduced his score in the *Monthly Weather Review* in 1950 to verify forecasts expressed as probabilities. "70% chance of rain" became something that could be checked.

The insight for an enterprise is to extend that discipline from the core product to every decision class where outcomes arrive: renewals, approvals, early-warning flags, hiring, partnerships, pricing. Most functions have no equivalent of a default study, so they cannot tell whether their judgment is improving. Our playbook on [forecasting that holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/) applies the same logic to the sales forecast.

## How it works, in plain terms

When a decision is made, the decision-maker records a probability for the outcome they expect. "Renews at or above current value: 70%." "Ships within six months: 60%." When the outcome arrives, it is recorded against the prediction.

Over enough cases, two things become visible.

**Calibration**: of everything predicted at 70%, did roughly 70% happen? If only half did, the judgment is overconfident at that level.

**Discrimination** (forecasting researchers also call it resolution): did the things predicted at 90% happen much more often than those predicted at 50%? A person who says 60% about everything can be perfectly calibrated and useless.

The Brier score combines both. For yes-or-no outcomes it is the mean squared difference between each probability and what happened, coded 1 or 0. It runs from 0 (perfect) to 1, and lower is better. A forecaster who always says 50% scores 0.25. The table below shows three illustrative forecasters on the same ten renewals, six of which renew.

| Forecaster | What they said | What happened | Brier score | Reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The hedger | 60% on all ten | 6 of 10 renewed | 0.240 | Calibrated, no discrimination |
| The discriminator | 90% on six, 20% on four | 5 of the six and 1 of the four renewed | 0.162 | Calibrated and informative |
| The optimist | 95% on all ten | 6 of 10 renewed | 0.363 | Overconfident |

*Illustrative arithmetic, **lowob**'s example.* The discriminator wins even though one of their confident calls was wrong, because their probabilities carried information. The score rewards honest, informative probabilities over hedging, and punishes confidence that the outcomes do not support.

> A person who says 60% about everything can be perfectly calibrated and useless.

## The signal can be trained

The strongest evidence that calibration feedback is worth collecting comes from the Good Judgment Project, run by Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues in a US government forecasting tournament. In their 2014 paper in *Psychological Science*, three interventions improved accuracy over two years. Training in probability reasoning reduced biases, taught forecasters to use reference classes and gave them simple heuristics such as averaging estimates. Teaming let forecasters share information and argue about reasons. Tracking placed the top 2% of first-year performers into elite teams. All three improved both calibration and resolution.

Two cautions apply. The tournament asked geopolitical questions with clear resolution dates, which most business decisions lack. And the gains came from training plus feedback, not from showing people a chart. The practical reading is that a calibration record is necessary but not sufficient: it gives people something to learn from, and a short training session on base rates gives them a way to learn.

## What it needs

| Requirement | Why | Practical threshold |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Volume within a comparable class | Calibration is invisible on a handful of cases | A few dozen outcomes per probability band before the picture is stable |
| Prediction captured before the outcome | Collected afterwards, a probability measures memory and self-image, not judgment | Field locked once the decision is recorded |
| The person who made the call | Team or averaged probabilities hide whose judgment is improving | One named forecaster per decision |
| A safe introduction | Early league tables teach people to predict 50% about everything | Private feedback for the first cycles |

Volume is why calibration works first where decisions are frequent and similar, such as renewals, discount approvals and early-warning flags. Where decisions are rare and all different, a calibration curve may take years to stabilise; our piece [Below the volume floor](https://lowob.com/research/below-the-volume-floor/) covers what works instead.

Within a few cycles, the organisation can see where its judgment is overconfident, which categories it systematically misreads, and whose calls in which areas tend to be right. That is the closest thing to measurable institutional learning available today. Adding the probability is one field in the [decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/).

## What would prove this wrong

Calibration feedback producing no improvement in decision-makers' later calibration or discrimination over several cycles. Then the signal is honest but not useful. The forecasting evidence suggests improvement is possible with training, but it has not been shown at scale for commercial decisions, so the first cycles should be treated as a test of this claim.

## lowob takeaways

- **Grade against the world, not the system.** Only outcomes the system did not produce are an honest signal.
- **One probability per decision.** Recorded before the meeting, by the person making the call.
- **Score with a proper rule.** The Brier score rewards informative probabilities over hedging.
- **Start private.** Show people their own curve first; league tables come later, if ever.

## Common questions

### How can you tell if an organisation's judgment is improving?

Record a probability for the expected outcome when each decision is made, then compare predictions with outcomes over enough cases to measure calibration and discrimination, scored with a rule such as the Brier score.

### What is the difference between calibration and discrimination?

Calibration means outcomes predicted at a given probability happen about that often. Discrimination means high-probability predictions come true much more often than low ones; someone who says 60% about everything can be calibrated but useless.

### What is a Brier score?

The mean squared difference between probability forecasts and outcomes coded 1 or 0. It runs from 0 to 1, lower is better, and always saying 50% scores 0.25. Glenn Brier introduced it for weather forecasts in 1950.

### How many outcomes do you need before calibration data is useful?

A few dozen outcomes per probability band within a comparable decision class. In practice, plot predicted against actual after forty to fifty outcomes and treat early curves as directional.

## Sources and notes

- [S&P Global, Ratings track record: standing the test of time](https://investorfactbook.spglobal.com/sp-global-ratings/ratings-track-record-standing-the-test-of-time/), citing S&P Global Ratings' corporate default study of 27 March 2025. Rating agency's own investor material; covers 1981 to 2024.
- [Mellers et al., Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/0956797614524255/), *Psychological Science*, 2014. Peer-reviewed; geopolitical questions with clear resolution, not business decisions.
- [University of Virginia Library, A Brief on Brier Scores](https://library.virginia.edu/data/articles/a-brief-on-brier-scores), Jacob Goldstein-Greenwood, 15 February 2021. University statistics explainer; cites Brier's 1950 *Monthly Weather Review* paper.
- The three-forecaster table is **lowob**'s illustrative arithmetic; the requirements table is **lowob**'s working method.

## Next move

Pick one decision class with outcomes inside two quarters (renewals are the usual choice) and add a locked probability field to the record this week. Plot predicted against actual once forty outcomes are in.

# What Is Reverse ETL?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-reverse-etl/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Reverse ETL moves data out of the warehouse and into operational tools such as the CRM, so scores and usage figures appear where sellers and agents work. The category is consolidating into wider data movement platforms. The main risk is not technical: it is a sync overwriting fields that people own.

Reverse ETL is the process of copying modelled data from a data warehouse back into the operational tools a team uses, such as the CRM, the marketing platform or the support desk. It runs in the opposite direction to ordinary ETL, which loads data into the warehouse. For a commercial team it is how product usage, health scores and finance figures reach the account record where sellers, and now agents, actually read.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What reverse ETL means

ETL stands for extract, transform, load. In the usual direction, data is extracted from operational systems, transformed and loaded into a warehouse for analysis. In the ELT variant, raw data is loaded first and transformed inside the warehouse. DataCamp's 2024 guide defines reverse ETL as the process of extracting data from a data warehouse, reshaping it for operational systems and loading it into them.

The point is location. Analysts may hold a churn score or usage summary in the warehouse, but sellers do not work there. Reverse ETL puts those values on the account record.

| Pattern | Direction | Where the logic lives | Typical output |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ETL | Apps to warehouse | Before loading | Reporting tables |
| ELT | Apps to warehouse | Inside the warehouse | Modelled tables |
| Reverse ETL | Warehouse to apps | Inside the warehouse | Fields in the CRM, audiences, support context |
| Native integration | App to app | Inside each vendor | Point-to-point copies |

## How it works

Hightouch's documentation describes the parts in plain terms. A **source** is the system where data resides, such as Snowflake, BigQuery or PostgreSQL. A **model** defines what data to query, and every model needs a unique primary key so the tool can track changes between runs. A **destination** is the system where data is consumed. A **sync** sets how data appears in the destination and when: the sync mode (insert, update, upsert or archive), the mapping of columns to fields, and a schedule that can run on an interval, on a cron expression or when a tool such as dbt Cloud or Airflow triggers it.

The market is consolidating. On 1 May 2025 Fivetran, which moves data into warehouses, announced an agreement to acquire Census, describing it as the leader in reverse ETL and data activation. The direction of travel is one vendor for data moving both ways.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### It puts the evidence on the record

A seller preparing a renewal call wants the customer's usage trend, open support tickets and payment status on one screen. Without a sync, that means three logins or a request to the data team. DataCamp lists syncing customer insights to the CRM and campaign metrics to marketing tools as the core use cases.

### Agents read what the sync writes

In **lowob**'s model, the CRM is the store and the context layer is the wiring that lets AI read it. Reverse ETL is part of that wiring. An agent drafting a renewal note will read the health score field whether or not anyone checked how it was calculated. A wrong model in the warehouse becomes a wrong sentence in front of a client.

> A sync that writes into the CRM is a decision about what every person and agent will believe about an account.

## How to run it safely

Most problems come from unclear authority, not from the tooling. Before any sync goes live, settle who owns each field.

| Check | Question to answer | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Field authority | Is this field owned by the warehouse or by a person? | A sync must never overwrite judgment fields such as next step or loss reason |
| Primary key | What uniquely matches a warehouse row to a CRM record? | Weak keys create duplicates or write to the wrong account |
| Sync mode | Insert, update, upsert or archive? | Upsert on a weak key is the common source of duplicate accounts |
| Definition | Is the metric defined once, with an owner? | Two definitions of "active" produce two truths |
| Schedule | How fresh does the value need to be? | Hourly syncs burn API limits for values that change monthly |
| Change log | Can you see what the sync changed, and when? | Needed to trace an agent's output back to its input |

Three practical rules follow. First, write computed values into dedicated, read-only fields, labelled as system-maintained, rather than into fields people edit. Second, sync definitions that already exist in a semantic layer, so the CRM and the board report agree. Third, do not delete history: when a value changes, keep the previous one, in line with **lowob**'s rule to supersede, never overwrite.

Reverse ETL is wiring, so rent it. The real decision is which fields deserve a sync at all. Start with two or three a seller would use on a call this week.

## lowob takeaways

- **It is plumbing in reverse.** Warehouse data goes back into the tools where people work.
- **Authority comes first.** Decide which fields the warehouse owns before you schedule anything.
- **Agents raise the stakes.** Whatever a sync writes, an agent will treat as fact.
- **Start small.** Two or three fields a seller will use beat fifty nobody reads.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between ETL and reverse ETL?

ETL moves data from operational systems into a warehouse for analysis. Reverse ETL moves modelled data from the warehouse back into operational tools such as the CRM.

### Is reverse ETL the same as a customer data platform?

No. A CDP stores and unifies customer data itself. Reverse ETL uses the warehouse as the store and only moves data out of it, although vendors in both categories now overlap.

### What data should a sales team sync with reverse ETL?

Values that change a conversation: product usage trend, health score, open support tickets, billing status and lifetime value. Each should have one written definition.

### What are the risks of reverse ETL?

Overwriting fields people maintain, creating duplicates through weak matching keys, and exhausting CRM API limits with schedules more frequent than the data requires.

## Sources and notes

- [DataCamp, What is Reverse ETL? A Helpful Guide](https://www.datacamp.com/blog/reverse-etl), 20 September 2024. Educational overview; tool lists change quickly.
- [Hightouch Docs, Core concepts](https://docs.hightouch.com/getting-started/concepts). Vendor documentation; other tools use similar terms.
- [Fivetran, Fivetran Signs Agreement to Acquire Census](https://www.fivetran.com/press/fivetran-signs-agreement-to-acquire-census-delivering-the-first-end-to-end-data-movement-platform-for-the-ai-era), 1 May 2025. Vendor press release; market leadership claims are the vendor's own.

## Related research

- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)
- [What Is a Semantic Layer (Shared Definitions for AI)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [CRM vs CDP vs Data Warehouse: Which Holds What](https://lowob.com/research/crm-vs-cdp-vs-data-warehouse/)

## Next move

List every CRM field that is written by an integration or sync. For each, mark whether a person also edits it; any field with two writers needs a single owner this week.

# Marketplace Listings for B2B Sellers

Source: https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-07 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: B2B sellers treat cloud marketplace listings as a discovery channel and are disappointed. Their real value is procurement: the purchase lands on a bill the buyer already pays, through terms its legal team may already accept, and some purchases count toward committed cloud spend. We explain public listings, private offers and reseller offers, the costs sellers overlook, and how to decide whether a listing is worth the work.

A cloud marketplace listing lets a buyer purchase your software or services through a platform such as AWS Marketplace, Microsoft's marketplace or Google Cloud's, with the charge landing on the bill they already pay the platform. For most B2B sellers its value is procurement, not discovery. A deal that would take months to pass vendor onboarding can close as a line item on an existing cloud bill, under terms the buyer's legal team may already accept, and some marketplace purchases count toward the buyer's committed spend with the platform. The work is in private offers, finance operations and sales compensation, not in the listing page.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Most B2B sellers list on a cloud marketplace for the wrong reason. They expect buyers to browse the catalogue, find the product and buy it. A few do. In the deals we see, most enterprise buyers arrive at the marketplace having already chosen the vendor through the usual process, and use it to buy.

Our earlier piece *Developers, marketplaces and the answer engines* covers marketplace listings as discovery for AI products: writing the listing as a sales page and building integrations deep enough to rank. This piece covers the other half: marketplaces as a procurement and contracting route for B2B sellers whose deals are negotiated, and the operating work that route requires.

## Why buyers buy through a marketplace

The reasons are financial and administrative, which is why they matter to the buyer's procurement and finance teams more than to the person who chose the product.

**One bill, no new vendor.** AWS describes channel partner purchases as appearing as a line item on the customer's AWS bill, with no separate purchase order needed. Microsoft's buyer documentation says customers receive a single consolidated monthly invoice covering Azure charges and marketplace purchases, itemised as separate line items. For a buyer, that can mean skipping supplier onboarding, a new set of payment terms and a new security questionnaire on the commercial side. The product still needs to pass the buyer's technical and security review.

**Committed spend.** Large cloud customers often commit to a level of spend with the platform. AWS states that some marketplace purchases count toward customer spend commitments. Microsoft says purchases of eligible marketplace offers count toward a customer's Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment (MACC), and eligible solutions carry a badge saying so. Google Cloud states that 100% of spend on Marketplace services, other than listed exclusions such as professional services and services not running on Google Cloud, may count toward commitment obligations. Where that applies, buying your product through the marketplace draws down money the buyer has already committed, which changes the budget conversation. Eligibility rules differ by platform and product, and should be checked for each deal.

**Consolidated billing.** AWS's buyer guide notes that a private offer accepted from an organisation's management account can be shared with member accounts, and that marketplace subscriptions appear in the monthly bill with a line item per kind of usage.

**Buyers prefer less friction.** Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% prefer a rep-free experience. A marketplace does not remove the seller, but it removes much of the paperwork that sits between agreement and signature.

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's November 2025 report *Easy to Find* frames this as physical availability: being present where buying happens. For a firm selling to buyers who already run on a major cloud, the marketplace is one of those places.

## Public listings, private offers and reseller offers

A marketplace offers three ways to sell, and most negotiated B2B deals use the second or third.

| Route | What it is | Who sets the price and terms | Best for | Main watch-out |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Public listing | A published product page with public pricing | Seller, publicly | Self-serve or low-touch products; credibility for enterprise buyers who check the catalogue | Public price becomes a reference point in negotiation |
| Private offer | Custom pricing and terms extended to named buyer accounts | Seller, per deal | Negotiated enterprise deals | Every offer has an expiry date and needs managing like a quote |
| Reseller (channel partner) private offer | A partner, authorised by the seller, extends the offer at its own price | Partner, from an authorised wholesale price | Deals where a reseller or integrator owns the relationship | Margin and pricing authority must be agreed in advance |

AWS's documentation sets out the mechanics of private offers. The seller creates a pricing plan for each offer, adds legal terms and sales documents, and extends it to specific buyer accounts, up to 25 per offer. A custom licence agreement can carry up to five documents, upfront payments can be split into an instalment plan, and a buyer can accept only before the offer's expiry date. A buyer can hold only one subscription to a product at a time, public or private. For SaaS contracts, sellers can offer upgrades and renewals on accepted agreements.

For reseller deals, AWS's Channel Partner Private Offers let a software vendor authorise a consulting partner to receive wholesale pricing. The partner can then set the customer price and duration, replace the standard licence with an existing agreement, and add its own services. AWS cites a Forrester study, commissioned by AWS and based on 14 partner interviews, reporting 234% return on investment for partners that build a marketplace practice. That is vendor-commissioned research on a small sample; treat it as an indication of interest, not a benchmark.

The other two platforms have equivalents. Microsoft's multiparty private offers let a software company send a private offer to a channel partner. The partner sets a customer adjustment percentage on the partner price and extends the offer to the customer, and Microsoft invoices the customer and pays both parties. Microsoft's documentation notes that multiparty private offers do not support the sale of professional services. On Google Cloud, a vendor turns on reselling for its published products and creates private offer plans with a fixed reseller discount, so resellers can create their own private offers. Google's drawdown rules exclude services bought through resellers where the vendor has not opted into the resale programme.

> A marketplace listing rarely finds the buyer. It shortens the distance between the buyer saying yes and the money arriving.

## What a listing costs the seller

The listing itself is the smallest cost. Four others decide whether the route pays.

| Cost | What it involves | How to handle it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform fee | Each marketplace deducts a fee from disbursements; AWS deducts it in the offer currency, and Microsoft charges a 3% standard store service fee on transact offers | Check the current rate for your product type and deal size; build it into the deal desk's margin model |
| Finance operations | Disbursements, tax handling, refunds and reconciliation through the platform rather than your own invoicing | Assign an owner in finance before the first private offer, not after the first payment |
| Pricing discipline | A public price sets an anchor; private offers multiply the number of live quotes | Route private offers through the same approval rules as any other discount (Part 21) |
| Sales compensation | Sellers paid less on marketplace deals will avoid them | Pay the same on marketplace and direct deals, net of the fee only if the firm decides to |

Sales compensation is the cost most often missed. If a seller's commission is lower because a deal ran through the marketplace, the seller will steer buyers away from it, even when the marketplace would close the deal sooner. The decision to absorb the fee or share it with the seller should be made once, recorded, and reviewed after a few quarters of data.

Private offers also add a quoting problem. Each offer is a live price with an expiry date. A firm running a dozen at once needs the same discipline it applies to proposals: who approved the price, what it was compared against, and what happened. Those are entries for the decision record The Build Order describes (*The commercial decisions worth recording*), and Part 4 of this series covers the pricing architecture they sit inside.

## When a listing is worth the work

A marketplace route is not right for every B2B seller. The test is whether your buyers already buy through it.

| Your buyer looks like | Marketplace priority | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mid-market or enterprise, already a large customer of one cloud | High | Procurement and committed-spend benefits apply directly |
| Enterprise with a strict supplier onboarding process | High | The marketplace may replace much of the commercial onboarding |
| Buys through an integrator or reseller already active on the marketplace | Medium to high | Reseller offers keep the partner in the deal |
| Small businesses buying by card | Low | Your own checkout is simpler and cheaper |
| Regulated buyer whose procurement rules exclude marketplace purchases | Low | Check before building; some public bodies and banks have their own routes |
| Spread across several clouds with no dominant one | Medium | List on the platform most of your largest deals run on first |

A practical start is to ask the last ten enterprise buyers which cloud they run on, whether they hold a spend commitment, and whether their procurement team has bought through a marketplace before. If most answer yes on the same platform, list there first and run the next suitable deal as a private offer. If few do, the listing can wait.

Listing on a marketplace also opens the platform's co-selling programmes, which are a separate decision with their own costs. Part 18 of this series covers co-selling with platforms. Part 14 covers the partner design that reseller offers depend on.

Illustrative example: an analytics vendor runs its first private offer

Decision
:   List on the marketplace of the cloud most enterprise customers use, and offer the next three enterprise renewals as private offers.

Reason and owner
:   Two renewals had stalled for weeks in supplier onboarding, and both buyers held committed spend with the platform. Owned by the revenue leader, with finance owning disbursement and reconciliation.

What changed
:   Sales compensation was set to match direct deals, private offer prices went through the standard discount approval, and each offer's outcome and time to signature were recorded against comparable direct renewals.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size analytics software vendor, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat the marketplace as procurement, not discovery.** Its value is a faster route from agreement to payment.
- **Most negotiated deals run as private offers.** Manage each like a quote, with approval, expiry and a recorded outcome.
- **Keep partners in the deal.** Reseller offers let an integrator sell your product through the marketplace at an authorised price.
- **Fix compensation before the first deal.** Sellers paid less on marketplace deals will avoid them.

Gateway card

### Before you list on a cloud marketplace

- The last ten enterprise buyers asked which cloud they use and whether they hold committed spend
- The platform's current fee for your product type checked
- A finance owner named for disbursements, tax and refunds
- Private offers routed through standard discount approval
- Sales compensation on marketplace deals decided and recorded

## Common questions

### What is a private offer on a cloud marketplace?

A custom price and set of terms that a seller extends to named buyer accounts through the marketplace. On AWS a private offer can go to up to 25 accounts, carry custom licence terms and use an instalment plan.

### Do marketplace purchases count toward cloud spend commitments?

Some do. AWS states that some marketplace purchases count toward customer spend commitments, Microsoft counts eligible offers toward a MACC, and Google Cloud counts most Marketplace spend, with listed exclusions. Eligibility depends on the platform, the product and the buyer's agreement, so check each deal.

### Is a cloud marketplace listing worth it for a B2B software company?

Usually, if your enterprise buyers already run mainly on one cloud and use its marketplace. It is rarely worth it for small-business buyers who pay by card.

### Can resellers sell through a cloud marketplace?

Yes. On AWS, Channel Partner Private Offers let a vendor authorise a reseller to receive wholesale pricing and extend its own offer to the customer through the marketplace.

# The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A decision record without a stated falsifier is a press release. The one field that turns it into judgment is "what would prove this wrong, by when": a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer. It turns a decision into a prediction that can be graded, and it reveals at the moment of decision whether the people agreeing actually agree.

A decision record without a stated falsifier is a press release. The one field that turns it into judgment is "what would prove this wrong, by when". A good falsifier names a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer, which turns a decision into a prediction that someone other than the author can grade. It is also the field that reveals, at the moment of decision, whether the people agreeing actually agree.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

A rationale is an argument, and arguments do not expire. Most decision templates ask for context, options, the choice and the rationale. Every one of those can be written persuasively after the fact, and none of them can be checked. The [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) explainer calls the remedy the expected outcome; this piece is about writing it well.

A falsifier does what a rationale cannot. "If renewal rates in this segment fall below 85% within two quarters, this pricing change was wrong." It names a measure, a threshold and a date, and someone other than the author can observe it. It turns a decision into a prediction, and predictions can be graded.

## Why predictions beat rationales

The strongest evidence that explicit, graded predictions improve judgment comes from forecasting research. In the geopolitical forecasting tournament reported by Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues in *Psychological Science* in 2014, forecasters made explicit probability judgments that were scored against what happened. Three interventions improved both calibration and resolution: training in probabilistic reasoning, teaming so forecasters could share the reasoning behind their beliefs, and tracking the best performers into elite teams.

None of that is possible with a rationale. A business decision is not a geopolitical forecast, and most firms will never score themselves the way a tournament does. The transferable lesson is narrower: judgment improves when a claim is stated in a form that the world can contradict, and when someone checks.

Daniel Kahneman and Gary Klein reached a related conclusion from opposite directions. In their 2009 paper on intuitive expertise they argued that judging whether to trust an expert's intuition depends on how predictable the environment is and whether the expert has had the chance to learn its regularities. In a 2010 interview with *McKinsey Quarterly*, Klein added feedback as the second condition. A falsifier is how an organisation manufactures feedback for decisions that would otherwise never get any.

## Anatomy of a good falsifier

Four parts, all required:

| Part | What it is | Weak version | Why the weak version fails |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Measure | A quantity or an observable event, not a feeling | "If it doesn't work out" | No measure |
| Threshold | The level at which you would say the decision was wrong | "If adoption is disappointing" | No threshold |
| Date | When you will look | "If we don't see results" | No date |
| Observer | Who checks, and from what source | Left blank | Nobody looks |

Weak falsifiers are not falsifiers. They are permission to decide later what the decision meant.

Some examples across decision classes:

| Decision class | Falsifier |
| --- | --- |
| Credit | "If the leverage ratio exceeds 5.5x at the next two reporting dates, the approval assumptions failed." |
| Pricing | "If win rate in the mid-market band drops more than 8 points over the next 40 opportunities, the new price is wrong." |
| Partnership | "If the partner has not sourced three qualified introductions by end of Q2, the channel thesis is wrong." |
| Hiring | "If the new team lead has not run the weekly review independently by month four, the internal promotion was the wrong call." |

Notice that the pricing example counts opportunities rather than weeks. Where volume is low, a count-based date stops the check arriving before there is enough evidence to read. Our piece on [campaign tests that reach a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) applies the same logic to marketing experiments.

## The falsifier as an alignment test

Writing a falsifier does work at the moment of decision. It forces each person to state what they are actually betting on. Two people who agreed on the choice often write different falsifiers, because they agreed on what to do but not on why. One supports the price change because it will lift margin; the other because it will screen out bad-fit customers. Those are different bets with different failure signals.

That disagreement is worth more than the agreement. Surfacing it before the decision is cheaper than discovering it in the post-mortem. Klein's premortem works on the same principle: the team imagines the project has already failed and lists why. Klein cites 1989 research by Deborah Mitchell, Jay Russo and Nancy Pennington finding that this kind of prospective hindsight "increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%". Kahneman called the premortem "a low-cost, high-payoff kind of thing". A falsifier is a premortem reduced to one line and attached to the record.

The order matters. Ask each decision-maker to write their own falsifier before discussion, then compare. Written after discussion, falsifiers converge on whoever spoke first. Our piece [Dissent is the data you are throwing away](https://lowob.com/research/dissent-is-the-data-you-are-throwing-away/) makes the wider case for recording the disagreement.

> Two people who agree on a choice often write different falsifiers. They agreed on what to do, not on why.

## What happens when one triggers

Record it as triggered. Then make one of three explicit choices: reverse the decision, hold it with a new and recorded reason, or accept the loss and close the record. What must never happen is a quiet edit of the threshold. Moving the goalposts is sometimes legitimate, but it is a new decision, and it should be recorded as a supersession with its own reason, as set out in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

The outcome itself goes back to the same record. Our explainer on [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers the mechanics.

## Calibrating the falsifiers themselves

Track the share of decisions whose falsifiers trigger. If it is close to zero, the falsifiers are too safe and are measuring nothing. If it is very high, either the decisions are too bold or the thresholds too tight. Somewhere in between, you are learning. There is no published benchmark for the right share in business decisions; the useful signal is the trend in your own record and whether people can explain it. [Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) covers how to read that trend.

| Report monthly | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Share of material decisions with a valid falsifier | Whether the habit is holding |
| Share checked on or before the date | Whether observers are doing their part |
| Share triggered | Whether thresholds are honest |
| Share triggered and quietly edited | Whether goalposts are moving |

## In practice

Make measure, threshold, date and observer required on every material decision. Ask each decision-maker to write their own falsifier before discussion, then compare. Put the check date in the observer's calendar, not just the record.

Report the share with valid falsifiers, the share reviewed on time, and the share triggered.

**What would prove this wrong:** decisions recorded with falsifiers showing no better follow-through, learning or later outcomes than decisions recorded without them. Then the field is ritual.

## lowob takeaways

- **Four parts, all required.** Measure, threshold, date and observer.
- **Write them before discussion.** Different falsifiers reveal different bets.
- **Never move the threshold quietly.** A changed threshold is a new decision with its own record.
- **Watch the trigger rate.** Near zero means the falsifiers are too safe.

## Common questions

### What is a falsifier in a decision record?

A statement of what would prove the decision wrong, by when. It names a measure, a threshold, a date and an observer, which turns a decision into a prediction that can be graded.

### How do I write a good falsifier for a business decision?

Include a measure that is a quantity or observable event, a threshold at which the decision is wrong, a date or case count when you will look, and who checks from what source. For example: if renewal rates in this segment fall below 85% within two quarters, this pricing change was wrong.

### What is the difference between a falsifier and a premortem?

A premortem asks a team to imagine a decision has failed and list why. A falsifier states, in one line attached to the record, the observable result that would show it failed, so it can be checked later.

### What should happen when a decision's falsifier is triggered?

Record it as triggered, then explicitly reverse the decision, hold it with a new recorded reason, or accept the loss and close the record. Changing the threshold is a new decision and should be recorded as a supersession.

## Sources and notes

- [Mellers et al., Psychological Strategies for Winning a Geopolitical Forecasting Tournament](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/0956797614524255/), *Psychological Science*, 2014. Academic study; geopolitical questions, not business decisions.
- [Gary Klein, Performing a Project Premortem](https://wiki.duraspace.org/download/attachments/104563925/ProjectPremortem.pdf?api=v2), *Harvard Business Review*, September 2007. Practitioner article; the 30% figure is from 1989 research it cites. Copy hosted by a third party.
- [Kahneman and Klein, Conditions for intuitive expertise: a failure to disagree](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19739881/), *American Psychologist* 64(6), 2009. Academic review; abstract only.
- [McKinsey Quarterly, Strategic decisions: When can you trust your gut?](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/strategy-and-corporate-finance/our-insights/strategic-decisions-when-can-you-trust-your-gut), 1 March 2010. Interview with Kahneman and Klein; opinion, not new data.
- The four-part falsifier, the alignment test and the trigger-rate report are **lowob**'s working method.

## Next move

At your next material decision, ask each person to write their own falsifier before discussion, with a measure, threshold, date and observer. Compare them before you decide, and put the check date in the observer's calendar.

# "The Story Isn't Landing"

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-story-isnt-landing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When a pitch story isn't landing, the deck is usually aimed at the wrong audience, built on a category word instead of a buyer, or hiding its evidence too late. Fix those three structural faults before touching anything else. Seed decks now get less than two minutes of reading on average, so the evidence has to come first.

When the story isn't landing, the deck is usually aimed at the wrong audience, built on a category word instead of a buyer, or hiding its evidence too late. Fix those three before touching anything else. The reading conditions make the third fault the most expensive: DocSend's platform data showed average seed-deck viewing time falling below two minutes in 2023, while time on traction slides rose. Three afternoon fixes, done in order, usually change the questions investors ask within two meetings.

## What it usually means

Founders hear "the story isn't landing" as a narrative problem. It rarely is. It is almost always one of three structural faults.

The first is audience. The deck was written for customers and is being shown to investors, or the reverse. Customers need to know what changes for them on Monday. Investors need to know why this becomes a large business and why you are the team to build it. One deck cannot carry both jobs. When it tries, each reader gets half of what they came for. Investors are explicit about their half. In a survey of almost 900 venture capitalists, Gompers, Gornall, Kaplan and Strebulaev found 95% of firms named the team as an important factor and 47% named it the most important; 83% named the business model.

The second is the product truth. Read the one-liner on slide 1. If it says "a platform for X" or "the leading Y for Z", there is a category word where a buyer should be. Categories are for analysts. Investors fund a named buyer with a named problem and a reason to pay now, because that is what lets them judge the business model they say they weigh. April Dunford, whose positioning method is widely used in B2B software, describes a market category as a starting point that sets assumptions about a product. In her words, it "doesn't replace your messaging or your sales pitch". A one-liner that is only a category has not started the pitch.

The third is evidence placement. The best non-founder proof, a paying customer, a renewal, a partner that shipped, sits on slide 9. By then the reader has sat through market size, trend slides and a vision statement. Attention is gone before the proof arrives.

| Fault | Symptom in meetings | Test | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong audience | Investors ask about the business; the deck talks about features | Count slides that would matter to a customer but not an investor | A separate investor deck built on one investor belief |
| Category word, no buyer | "Help me understand what this is" | Can a partner repeat the one-liner without notes? | Rewrite as "we help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]" |
| Evidence too late | Questions about traction the deck already answers | Which slide holds the best non-founder proof? | Move it to slide 2 |

## Why the order of slides matters more now

The reader has less time and more choice. DocSend, which tracks how decks are viewed on its sharing platform, reported that average seed-deck viewing time fell below two minutes in 2023 for the first time. Time on traction slides rose 33% at seed and 25% at pre-seed; at seed, "why now" had the third-longest viewing time. These are vendor platform data, not a census of investors, but they describe a reader who skims and stops at the evidence.

The capital is also more concentrated. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor, as reported by SiliconANGLE, found that rounds under $100 million drew 12.5% of US venture deal value in the first half of 2026, down from 43.8% in 2024. Fewer dollars are chasing ordinary rounds, so a deck that makes the reader work to find the proof loses to one that does not.

## Where it traces to

This traces to two earlier pieces: [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) and [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/).

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) said one product truth, one belief per audience, and a claims register. If the deck does not land, check whether the truth has a buyer in it and whether a belief was ever written for the investor. Most decks skip that step and hope the product sells itself.

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) said raise against evidence, not narrative. The evidence log exists so you can lead with the strongest organic proof. If the log is thin, or full of incentivised signals, the deck will feel like narrative no matter how well it is written. That is a different problem, and no rewrite fixes it: the answer is to go and produce better evidence before the next meeting.

> Design makes a clear story cleaner. It cannot find a buyer that is not there.

## The first move this week

Three moves, in order. Each takes an afternoon.

| Move | What changes | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence to slide 2 | Best non-founder proof follows the title | Reader believes before they are asked to imagine |
| Rewrite the truth | Remove the category word, insert the buyer and the problem | Investor can repeat it to a partner without notes |
| One investor belief | A single sentence they must accept to invest | Every slide either proves it or gets cut |

Start with the evidence. Pull the log from [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/). Pick the one item a sceptic would find hardest to dismiss. Put it on slide 2, with a number and a date if you have them, and nothing else on the slide.

Then the truth. Write it as "we help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]". Resist the urge to sound bigger. Specific reads as credible. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the buyer and the alternative behind that sentence.

Then the belief. Write it down, then walk the deck and mark each slide as proof, context or filler. Cut the filler. Move the context behind the proof.

Send the revised deck to the next two meetings only. Compare the questions you get with the questions you were getting before.

## What not to do

Do not add market slides. The investor already knows the market exists or they would not have taken the meeting. If a sizing slide is needed, build it bottom-up from the named buyer, as set out in [What are TAM, SAM and SOM?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-tam-sam-som/), rather than adding another top-down total.

Do not hire a deck designer. Design makes a clear story cleaner. It cannot find a buyer that is not there.

Do not change the valuation. A price cut on a story that is not landing tells the investor you are not sure either. Fix the story, then talk about terms. If meetings are happening but nothing is moving, [The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) covers the process side.

## How you know it worked

Two signs. First, the questions in meetings shift from "help me understand what this is" to "how do you get more of these customers". Second, at least one investor repeats your truth back to you in their own words, correctly, without looking at the deck.

Illustrative example: moving one slide

Decision
:   Move a named customer's renewal, with its date and contract value band, from slide 9 to slide 2, and cut two market-trend slides.

Reason and owner
:   Meeting notes from five investor calls showed the first ten minutes spent explaining the category, and two investors asking for traction the deck already contained. Owned by the CEO.

What changed
:   In the next two meetings the opening questions were about how the company found that customer and whether the pattern repeated.

Illustrative: a composite of a seed-stage B2B software company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Split the decks.** One deck cannot serve both customers and investors; each reader gets half of what they came for.
- **Put proof on slide 2.** The best non-founder evidence, with a number and a date, before any market slide.
- **Replace the category word with a buyer.** "We help [buyer] do [thing] so that [outcome]" reads as credible.
- **Do not reach for cosmetic fixes.** Market slides, a designer or a lower valuation will not fix a structural fault.

Gateway card

### Before the next investor meeting

- Best non-founder evidence is on slide 2, with a date
- The product truth names a buyer and a problem, with no category word
- One investor belief is written down, and every remaining slide proves it
- Each slide is marked proof, context or filler, and the filler is gone

## Common questions

### Why isn't my pitch deck landing with investors?

Usually one of three structural faults: the deck is written for the wrong audience, the one-liner uses a category word instead of a named buyer and problem, or the best evidence sits too late in the deck.

### Where should traction go in a pitch deck?

On slide 2, right after the title: the one non-founder proof a sceptic would find hardest to dismiss, with a number and a date if you have them, and nothing else on the slide.

### How long do investors spend reading a pitch deck?

Not long. DocSend's platform data showed average seed-deck viewing time fell below two minutes in 2023, with more of that time going to traction slides. Lead with the evidence.

### How do I know my revised pitch is working?

Meeting questions shift from "help me understand what this is" to "how do you get more of these customers", and at least one investor repeats your truth back correctly without looking at the deck.

## Sources and notes

# What Is Intent Data, and How Reliable Is It?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-intent-data/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Intent data records research behaviour, such as content consumption on publisher networks or visits to your own site, and infers which companies may be in market. Forrester finds most users report benefits but fall short of expectations, especially in sales. This explainer covers the types of intent data, how third-party signals are built, and how to test a provider before trusting it.

Intent data is behavioural evidence that an organisation is researching a topic, used to infer that it may be preparing to buy. It comes from your own channels, from partner sites and from third-party publisher networks. It is a useful timing signal at account level and a weak one at person level, so it should prioritise attention, not replace qualification.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What intent data means

Intent data is a record of research behaviour attributed to an organisation.

There are three common sources. First-party intent comes from your own properties: website visits, content downloads, pricing page views, product usage and email engagement. Second-party intent is another company's first-party data shared with you, typically a review site or marketplace reporting which accounts viewed your category. Third-party intent is aggregated from networks of publishers you have no relationship with, then resolved to companies and sold as a feed.

| Type | Where it comes from | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First-party | Your site, product, emails | You control it and know the context | Only sees buyers already aware of you |
| Second-party | Review sites, marketplaces, partners | Close to a buying decision | Narrow coverage, one source's audience |
| Third-party | Publisher co-ops and networks | Sees research before buyers find you | Inferred, account-level, hard to audit |

## How third-party intent is built

The mechanics explain most of the reliability questions, so they are worth understanding.

### Collection

Bombora, a third-party intent provider, collects through a data co-op of publishers, most specialising in B2B content. In a 2021 post it said the co-op captures "over 1 billion visits worth of data per day", uses consented data, mainly first-party cookies, and does not use bidstream data. Topics are assigned by analysing the content and metadata of the pages consumed.

### Identity resolution

Each visit then has to be attributed to a company. Bombora describes matching consented IP addresses, publisher logins with business email, partner identity graphs and behavioural modelling. Bombora itself acknowledged that the shift to remote work from spring 2020 made identity resolution harder across the industry, because home connections do not map to employers.

### Scoring

Most feeds report a change against a baseline rather than an absolute count. Documentation for Bombora's Company Surge score, published by data platform Ocean.io, describes a score from 60 to 100, where 60 or above signals a significant increase, calculated by comparing the past week's topic consumption with the prior 12 weeks, with new data added weekly. A relative score means a small company with little baseline activity can surge on a handful of visits, while a large company's genuine project can be diluted across thousands of employees.

## How reliable it is

Forrester's survey, summarised by principal analyst Brett Kahnke in October 2023, gives a balanced picture. Adoption is high and most users report gains, most often higher outbound response rates and better prospecting. But expectations outran results, particularly for sales and overall revenue growth. Only half used intent data for pipeline acceleration and fewer than a third for any customer-focused use. Many lacked reporting that tied intent to revenue.

The practical limits follow from the mechanics:

- **Account, not person.** Most third-party intent tells you a company is researching, not who. Forrester names this as the top execution challenge.
- **Research, not buying.** A surge can come from a competitor, a consultant or a student.
- **Topic taxonomy.** You choose from the provider's topic list. If your category is new, the topics may not describe it.
- **Overlap.** Using three providers that draw on similar publishers can triple-count the same signal.

## How to test a provider before trusting it

Run a test that compares accounts with and without the signal, rather than asking whether surging accounts ever converted.

1. **Fix the population.** Take accounts that already match your ICP, so intent is tested on top of fit.
2. **Split by signal.** Record which accounts surged on your chosen topics during a fixed window, and which did not.
3. **Treat them the same.** Give both groups the same outreach, or none, for 60 to 90 days.
4. **Compare outcomes.** Meetings booked, opportunities created and stage progression. If the surging group does not convert measurably better, the signal is not earning its cost for you.
5. **Record the decision.** Write down which topics you kept, why, and the review date. Signals and topics drift.

In **lowob**'s terms, intent data belongs in the context layer: rented wiring that helps a person decide where to look. The decision to contact an account, and the reason, belongs in your own record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Use intent for timing, not qualification.** It suggests when to look, not whether an account is a fit.
- **Expect account-level signals.** Plan how you will find the right people before you buy the feed.
- **Test against a control group.** Conversion of surging accounts alone proves nothing.
- **Watch for overlap.** More providers can mean the same signal counted several times.

## Common questions

### What is intent data in B2B marketing?

It is behavioural evidence, such as content consumption or site visits, that an organisation is researching a topic, used to infer which accounts may be in market.

### What is the difference between first-party and third-party intent data?

First-party intent comes from your own website, product and emails. Third-party intent is aggregated from publisher networks you do not own and resolved to companies by a provider.

### How accurate is intent data?

Accuracy varies by provider and by company size. Forrester finds most users see benefits but fewer than expected, so test it against a control group of your own accounts.

### Can intent data identify individual buyers?

Usually not. Most third-party intent is resolved to the company level, and Forrester reports that finding the right decision-makers is the top challenge for users.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Intent Data Expectations Vs. Reality: What's Working, And Where Are The Gaps?](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/intent-data-expectations-vs-reality-whats-working-and-where-are-the-gaps), October 2023. Analyst blog summarising Forrester's Q1 2023 Global B2B Intent Data Survey; sample size not stated in the post.
- [Bombora, Company Surge intent data still works despite challenges like remote work and the cookieless future](https://bombora.com/blog/bomboras-company-surge-intent-data-still-works-despite-challenges-like-remote-work-and-the-cookieless-future/), October 2021. Vendor's own account of its collection and identity methods.
- [Ocean.io, Intent and Surge Score explained](https://support.ocean.io/en/articles/7039013-intent-and-surge-score-explained). Third-party product documentation describing Bombora's score scale and baseline; not Bombora's own documentation.

Pull the accounts that surged on your intent topics last quarter and the ICP accounts that did not. Compare how many in each group became opportunities, and decide whether the feed is earning its cost.
