# What Is a Context Window?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-context-window/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A context window is the working memory of a language model: everything it can read and write in a single request, measured in tokens. Windows have grown to a million tokens on current models, but research shows accuracy falls as inputs get longer and when key facts sit in the middle. What goes into the window matters more than its size.

A context window is all the text a language model can consider in a single request, including the response it is writing. It works as the model's working memory, separate from what it learned in training, and it is measured in tokens. Current frontier models offer windows of up to a million tokens. Research shows that accuracy falls as inputs grow, so choosing what goes in matters more than how much fits.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a context window means

A language model has two kinds of knowledge. The first is what it absorbed in training, fixed at a cut-off date. The second is what it is given in the current request. Anthropic's documentation calls the second a "working memory" and defines the context window as everything the model can reference while generating, including its own reply.

The window is measured in tokens. Using OpenAI's English rule of thumb of about 75 words per 100 tokens, a 200,000-token window holds roughly 150,000 words and a million tokens roughly 750,000. These are approximations; each provider's tokeniser counts differently.

When a request is too large, it fails or stops. Anthropic's API returns a "prompt is too long" error if the input alone exceeds the limit. On newer models, if generation reaches the limit mid-reply, the output stops with a specific stop reason.

| The context window is | The context window is not |
| --- | --- |
| The model's working memory for one request | Long-term memory across sessions |
| Shared between input and output | Reserved space for your documents only |
| A hard technical limit in tokens | A measure of how much the model will use well |
| Reset for each new request unless history is resent | A record of what was decided |

## How it works, and why it matters for a commercial team

Everything in a request competes for the same space. Anthropic's documentation lists the system prompt, every message, tool results, images, documents and tool definitions as input. The model's output, including any extended thinking, counts too. Cached prompt prefixes still occupy the window; caching changes the price, not the space used.

For an agent this fills up quickly. A sales assistant preparing for a renewal might carry instructions, ten tool definitions, three CRM records, the last email thread and a contract. After several tool calls the window holds everything returned so far. The window resets on the next request, so anything not resent is gone.

Size is not the same as attention. Anthropic's own documentation states that "as token count grows, accuracy and recall degrade", a pattern it calls context rot. Independent research supports this. Liu and colleagues' 2023 paper "Lost in the Middle" tested multi-document question answering and found accuracy was highest when the relevant passage was at the start or end of the input. It dropped when the passage sat in the middle, even for models built for long contexts. Chroma's July 2025 report tested 18 models, including GPT-4.1, Claude 4 and Gemini 2.5, and found models do not use their context uniformly.

The commercial implication is that a bigger window does not remove the need to choose. Pasting a full account history into a million-token window is possible. It is slower, costs more per request and can bury the one fact that matters. In **lowob**'s model, deciding what reaches the model is the job of the wiring stage, the context layer, not the model.

## How to fill a context window well

| Practice | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- |
| Retrieve, do not dump | Send the five relevant records, not the whole CRM export |
| Put key material at the edges | Instructions and the decisive facts at the start or end |
| Count before you send | Use the provider's token counter to estimate size |
| Compact long conversations | Summarise earlier turns, keeping decisions and open questions |
| Keep tool results short | Return the fields needed, not full records |
| Store the decision outside | Write outcomes to a record; the window forgets them |

A common mistake is treating the window as memory. A conversation that ran yesterday is not in today's window unless something resends it. Another is choosing a model for its window size alone. A model with a smaller window and well-chosen inputs will often beat a larger one fed everything. Test both on your own documents before deciding.

## lowob takeaways

- **It is working memory.** The window holds one request's inputs and output, then resets.
- **Everything counts.** Tool definitions, results and hidden reasoning use the same space.
- **Longer inputs degrade.** Accuracy and recall fall as the window fills; position matters.
- **Choose what goes in.** Retrieval and a context layer beat a bigger window.

## Common questions

### What is a context window in AI?

It is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider in one request. It includes the prompt, attached material, conversation history and the model's reply.

### How big is a 1-million-token context window?

Roughly 750,000 English words, using OpenAI's rule of thumb of about 75 words per 100 tokens. The exact figure depends on the tokeniser and the language.

### Does a bigger context window mean better answers?

Not necessarily. Studies show accuracy falls as inputs grow and when relevant facts sit in the middle. Well-chosen inputs usually matter more than size.

### Is the context window the same as AI memory?

No. The window is cleared after each request. Memory across sessions needs a separate store that resends relevant information into the window.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Understanding the context window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; window sizes change with new models.
- [Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172v3), July 2023, revised November 2023. Academic preprint; tested models now superseded.
- [Chroma, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot), July 2025. Technical report by a vector database vendor.
- [OpenAI, What are tokens and how to count them](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/4936856-what-are-tokens-and-how-to-count-them), accessed November 2026. Vendor help article; word ratios are approximate.

## Related research

- [What Is Context Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/)
- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)
- [What Is Agent Memory?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/)
- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)
- [The People Who Vouch for You](https://lowob.com/research/the-people-who-vouch-for-you/)

## Next move

Take one AI prompt your team reuses and count its tokens with your provider's counter. Remove anything the model does not need and compare the answers side by side.

# Discord Is Not a Community Strategy. Neither Is Telegram.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Opening a Discord or Telegram makes a Web3 project feel operational before the relationships and operating system exist. Start from the jobs members need done, build the smallest set of spaces that serves them, treat moderation and security messaging as product design, and move durable knowledge out of chat. Choose the platform after the behaviour.

A Discord server or Telegram group is infrastructure, not a strategy. Start from the jobs members need done, decide which need real-time chat and which need durable documentation, and build the smallest set of spaces that serves them. In crypto, safety is part of the design: the FBI recorded $11.4 billion in crypto-related fraud losses in 2025, and a chat full of impersonators is where much of it starts. Choose the platform after the behaviour.

Opening a Discord or Telegram is one of the fastest ways for a Web3 project to feel operational. There are channels, roles, moderators, bots, announcements and a visible member count. The interface resembles a community before the relationships and operating system exist.

The result is often a familiar pattern: dozens of empty channels, repeated support questions, speculative price conversation, scam attempts, overwhelmed moderators, and a small number of genuine contributors buried beneath noise. Our piece [40,000 members and nobody does anything](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/) describes where that ends. This playbook is part of our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## Begin with jobs, not channels

List the jobs members need the environment to perform, then decide where each belongs. Real-time chat is good at some of them and bad at most.

| Member job | Best home | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Receive authoritative announcements | Read-only channel, mirrored to email and the website | Needs one canonical source that cannot be spoofed in replies |
| Get product or wallet support | Structured help channel or ticket | Sensitive details should not sit in public chat |
| Learn how the protocol works | Searchable documentation and FAQ | Durable answers should not scroll away |
| Meet collaborators | Discussion space, events, smaller groups | Needs real-time conversation and repeat contact |
| Give structured feedback | Forum or form with an owner | Needs to be counted and answered |
| Contribute code, research, governance or content | Briefs, working groups, a governance forum | Needs a durable record and recognition |
| Discuss the market | One clearly labelled channel | Keeps speculation away from official guidance |

An FAQ belongs in searchable documentation. A sensitive support issue belongs in a ticket. A product workshop may belong on a call. A governance proposal needs a durable forum. A critical announcement needs a canonical home, even if it is distributed through chat.

## Design the minimum viable architecture

For an early project, a small number of clearly differentiated spaces usually works better than a sprawling structure:

- **Start here:** orientation, rules, security warnings, official links and how to get help.
- **Announcements:** read-only updates with clear source authority.
- **Help:** structured questions with searchable answers and escalation rules.
- **Discussion:** one or two spaces tied to the project's main member interests.
- **Contribute:** specific opportunities, briefs, working groups and recognition.
- **Events:** schedule, preparation, notes and follow-up.

Create additional channels only when repeated behaviour justifies them. Empty segmentation makes the community look less active and raises navigation cost.

Both platforms now have native tools for this. Discord's Community Onboarding lets members answer questions that assign them roles and channels; Discord requires at least seven default channels, at least five of which everyone can view and post in, so the minimum architecture above fits the tool. Telegram added Topics in November 2022, which turn a large group into separate threads with their own media and notification settings, and admins control who can create them. Telegram's own FAQ draws the line between its two formats: groups, up to 200,000 members, are for collaboration; channels, with unlimited subscribers, are "a tool for broadcasting messages to large audiences". Use a channel for announcements and a group with Topics for conversation, rather than one group doing both.

## Build a visible member journey

A new member should immediately understand where they are, whether it is official and safe, what is valuable here, what to do first, who can help and how to contribute.

The first meaningful action should be more useful than posting an introduction nobody reads. Ask members to select a relevant path, attend a recurring session, answer a focused question or use a starter resource. Discord's onboarding questions can route a developer, a user and a liquidity provider to different starting channels on day one. Our guide to the [first 100 community members](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/) covers who those first members should be.

## Treat moderation and security as product design

Moderation is not merely deleting spam. It defines the behaviour the environment rewards.

Publish rules that address scams, impersonation, harassment, price discussion, unsolicited promotion, direct-message safety, disclosure and enforcement. Give moderators documented escalation paths. Discord's guidance recommends letting automation handle routine issues around the clock while recognising that "not every violation will have a simple solution", and keeping enforcement "as fair and consistent as possible". Its AutoMod tool supports custom keyword rules of up to 1,000 terms, a spam content filter, a cap on mentions per message and alerts to a private moderator channel. Use those for repeatable protection and keep humans responsible for context.

In Web3, security communication should be repetitive by design. The stakes are measurable. The FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report recorded $11.366 billion in crypto-related losses across 181,565 complaints, with crypto investment fraud alone at $7.2 billion. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with personal wallet compromises accounting for 20% of value stolen. Not all of that starts in a community chat, but impersonated admins, fake support DMs and spoofed links are a common entry point.

So state, in the start-here space and in every announcement that matters: where official announcements appear, that team members will never initiate direct messages, how wallet links are verified and how incidents are reported. Telegram's own FAQ models the tone: it says it has no other support accounts on social platforms, and that anyone elsewhere claiming to be Telegram is not.

> In a crypto community, the security message is not a one-time rule. It is the most repeated sentence the project publishes.

## Prevent knowledge from disappearing into chat

Real-time conversation creates information and then rapidly buries it. Every week, extract recurring questions, unresolved product confusion, valuable member answers, feature requests, emerging risks or rumours, decisions from working sessions and resources worth preserving.

Move durable knowledge into documentation, an FAQ, a forum or the project's public playbooks, and link back to the canonical answer. Discord's own guidance suggests a read-only FAQ channel members are pointed to before they ask. This reduces repeated work and turns community activity into organisational knowledge. The same principle runs through our playbook on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/): a durable answer needs an owner and a review date, or it drifts from the product.

## Measure whether the environment creates value

Useful measures include time to first useful response, percentage of questions resolved, repeat participation by cohort, member-to-member help, unique contributors, movement into product use or contribution, safety incidents and response time, and recurring questions eliminated through better documentation.

Message volume can indicate engagement or confusion. Context determines which. A spike in the help channel after a release is a product signal, not a community win.

## Choose the platform after the behaviour

Telegram may suit fast-moving announcements and lightweight conversation. Discord may better support structured roles, onboarding, topic areas, events and moderation. Forums and documentation are better for durable knowledge. Email reaches people who will not monitor another chat. Smaller private groups may produce more trust than one public server.

The right answer is often a simple system across several surfaces, each with a defined job. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) makes the same point for the commercial side: write down which system holds which record before adding tools.

## lowob takeaways

- **Jobs before channels.** List what members need done, then give each job a home.
- **Small and differentiated.** About six spaces for an early project; add channels only when behaviour demands them.
- **Security is repetitive by design.** State where announcements live, that the team never DMs first, and how to report incidents.
- **Extract weekly.** Move durable answers out of chat into documentation and link back.

## Common questions

### Should a crypto project use Discord or Telegram?

Decide after listing member jobs. Telegram channels suit broadcast announcements and groups with Topics suit lightweight conversation; Discord suits structured roles, onboarding, events and moderation. Many projects use both, with documentation and email for durable information.

### How many channels should a new Discord server have?

Start small: orientation, announcements, help, one or two discussion spaces, contribution and events. Discord's Community Onboarding needs at least seven default channels, so build to that and add more only when repeated behaviour justifies them.

### How do you protect a crypto community from scams?

Publish rules on impersonation and direct messages, state that the team never initiates DMs, verify official links in one canonical place, use automated filters for spam and links, and give moderators a documented escalation path for incidents.

### How do you measure a Discord community?

Time to first useful response, share of questions resolved, repeat participation by cohort, member-to-member help, unique contributors, safety incidents and recurring questions removed by better documentation. Message volume alone can mean engagement or confusion.

## Sources and notes

- [Discord, Community Onboarding FAQ](https://support.discord.com/hc/en-us/articles/11074987197975). Platform documentation; feature requirements may change.
- [Discord, AutoMod FAQ](https://support.discord.com/hc/articles/4421269296535). Platform documentation; some filters are English-only.
- [Discord, Tools for automating server management](https://discord.com/community/automating-moderation-community-support). Platform guidance.
- [Telegram, Topics in groups](https://telegram.org/blog/topics-in-groups-collectible-usernames), 5 November 2022. Platform announcement.
- [Telegram, FAQ](https://telegram.org/faq). Platform documentation on groups, channels and impersonation.
- [The Block, FBI says crypto-related fraud losses hit record $11.4 billion in 2025](https://www.theblock.co/post/397134/fbi-says-crypto-related-fraud-losses-hit-record-11-4-billion-in-2025-with-seniors-bearing-the-brunt), 12 April 2026. News report of the FBI IC3 2025 report; complaint data are self-reported by victims.
- [Chainalysis, 2025 crypto theft reaches $3.4 billion](https://www.chainalysis.com/blog/crypto-hacking-stolen-funds-2026/), 18 December 2025. Vendor research from a blockchain analytics company; covers January to early December 2025.
- The member-jobs table and minimum architecture are **lowob**'s framework.

- ["40,000 Members and Nobody Does Anything"](https://lowob.com/research/40-000-members-and-nobody-does-anything/)

## Next move

List the jobs your members need done this week and give each one a home. Archive any channel that has had no meaningful activity in 30 days, and pin a three-line security notice at the top of the start-here space.

# What Is Data Enrichment?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-enrichment/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Data enrichment fills gaps in contact and company records using external providers, so routing, scoring and segmentation have something to work with. It is now built into major CRMs and offered as multi-provider waterfalls. This explainer covers how enrichment works, how it differs from data hygiene, the privacy rules that apply, and how to set it up so it improves records rather than overwriting them.

Data enrichment is the process of adding missing or more current details to CRM records from outside sources. Typical additions are company size, industry, location and technology for accounts, and job title, seniority and contact details for people. It makes records usable for routing, scoring and segmentation, but it can also overwrite good data with bad, so the setup matters as much as the provider.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What data enrichment means

Most CRM records start thin. A form gives a name and an email address. A rep logs a company name from memory. Enrichment takes a key the record already has, usually a work email for a person or a domain for a company, and looks up further attributes from a provider's database.

HubSpot's documentation shows the typical inputs: first name, last name and work email for contacts, and company domain for companies. Enrichment can run on a single record, in bulk, on import or automatically on new records, and HubSpot's continuous enrichment refreshes previously enriched records monthly when new data is available.

It is different from CRM data hygiene, though the two are often bought together.

|  | Data enrichment | CRM data hygiene |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purpose | Add missing or newer attributes | Keep existing records correct |
| Source | External providers | Internal rules, checks and people |
| Typical work | Append industry, size, title, phone | Deduplicate, standardise, archive |
| Main risk | Overwriting good data with wrong data | Decay between clean-ups |
| Cadence | On create, then periodic refresh | Continuous, with monthly review |

## How it works

### Single provider

The simplest setup uses one provider, often the one built into the CRM. HubSpot's standard enrichment, for example, does not consume its paid credits, while its AI-generated smart properties do. Single-provider enrichment is easy to govern but limited to whatever that one provider's database holds.

### Waterfall

Waterfall enrichment chains providers. Each record is sent to the first provider; if no confident result comes back, it moves to the second, and so on. Clay, which sells this approach, describes it as "a fallback chain, not a single lookup" and reports coverage rising from 40% with the first provider to 63% with a second and 80% with its full waterfall. These are vendor figures, and coverage is not the same as accuracy: a filled field can still be wrong.

### Agent-assisted research

A newer pattern uses AI agents to read a company's website, filings or job posts and write a summary or classification into a field. It fills attributes no database holds, such as "sells to regulated industries". It also produces plausible errors, so these fields should be marked as inferred and checked before they drive routing.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Routing, lead scoring, territory design and account selection all depend on fields such as industry and employee count. If those fields are blank, the rules fail silently: leads go to a default queue and scores undercount fit. Gartner's estimate that poor data quality costs the average organisation $12.9 million a year is a broad figure across all data, not CRM alone, but it indicates the scale analysts attach to the problem.

Enrichment also carries legal obligations. The UK Information Commissioner's Office calls this practice "data matching or appending" and says that if people have not agreed to you having the details, it is "likely to be unfair in most cases" to obtain them for direct marketing. Where you collect personal data indirectly, the ICO says you must provide privacy information within a reasonable period and at the latest within a month, and it warns that "it is not enough to simply accept a third party's assurances" about compliance. The ICO notes this guidance is under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025. Company-level firmographics carry far less risk than personal contact data.

## How to set it up

1. **Decide which fields matter.** List the five to ten fields that drive routing, scoring and reporting. Enrich those, not everything a provider offers.
2. **Protect what people entered.** Keep the default of not overwriting existing values. Allow overwrite only for fields where the provider is more reliable than your team, such as employee count.
3. **Record the source and date.** Each enriched value should carry where it came from and when. Without that, nobody can tell a stale value from a fresh one.
4. **Separate company and personal data.** Treat appended phone numbers and personal emails as a privacy decision, with a lawful basis written down.
5. **Sample before scaling.** Enrich 100 records, check 20 by hand, and measure the error rate before switching on automatic enrichment.

In **lowob**'s terms, enrichment is wiring you rent. The record of who decided which fields to trust, and why, is yours.

## lowob takeaways

- **Enrich the fields you use.** Coverage of unused fields is cost without value.
- **Never overwrite by default.** A human-entered value is usually better than an appended one.
- **Track source and date.** An enriched field without provenance cannot be trusted later.
- **Treat contact data as a privacy decision.** Regulators expect due diligence, not vendor assurances.

## Common questions

### What is data enrichment in a CRM?

It is the process of adding missing or more current details to contact and company records, such as industry, size or job title, using external data providers.

### What is the difference between data enrichment and data cleansing?

Enrichment adds new attributes from outside sources. Cleansing, or hygiene, corrects, standardises and deduplicates the data you already hold.

### What is waterfall enrichment?

It queries several data providers in sequence, moving each record to the next provider only if the previous one returned no confident result, to increase coverage.

### Is data enrichment legal under GDPR?

It can be, with a lawful basis and transparency. The UK ICO says buying and appending contact details for marketing without agreement is likely to be unfair in most cases.

## Sources and notes

- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Get started with data enrichment](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/records/get-started-with-data-enrichment). Vendor product documentation; features and plan requirements change.
- [Clay, Waterfall enrichment guide](https://clay.com/guides/waterfall-enrichment). Vendor guide; coverage figures are self-reported.
- [Information Commissioner's Office, Collect information and generate leads](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/direct-marketing-guidance/collect-information-and-generate-leads). UK regulator guidance; under review following the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025.
- [TechTarget, 4 data quality challenges that hinder data operations](https://www.techtarget.com/news/4-data-quality-challenges-that-hinder-data-operations/843537/), October 2022. Trade press citing a Gartner estimate; methodology not given.

Export 100 recently enriched records and check 20 against the company's website or LinkedIn. Count the wrong values by field, and switch off overwrite for any field with more than a couple of errors.

# What Is Function Calling (Tool Use) in AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-function-calling/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Function calling is the mechanism by which a language model asks for an action: it returns a structured request naming a function and its arguments, and the application decides whether to run it. OpenAI introduced it to its API in June 2023, and Anthropic and other providers now offer it too. It is the point where permissions, validation and approvals belong.

Function calling, also called tool use, is the mechanism that lets a language model ask for an action. The application tells the model which functions exist and what each one does. The model replies with a structured request naming a function and its arguments, the application runs it, and the result goes back to the model. The model never runs anything itself. Function calling is the building block under agents, connectors and MCP, and it is where permissions and approvals belong.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What function calling means

Before function calling, getting a model to trigger software meant asking for text and parsing it, which broke whenever the wording changed. Function calling makes the request structured. Each function is described with a name, a plain-language description and a schema for its inputs.

Take an illustrative commercial example. A team defines a tool called `find\_open\_deals` that takes an account name. A seller asks: "What is still open with this client?" The round trip runs like this:

1. The application sends the question and the tool definition to the model.
2. The model replies with a tool call: `find\_open\_deals`, account name filled in.
3. The application checks the request, queries the CRM and returns the result.
4. The model writes its answer from that result.

In Anthropic's API the model's reply carries a `tool\_use` stop reason, and the application returns a `tool\_result` that references the call. OpenAI's API follows the same pattern with different field names.

| Term | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| Tool or function definition | Name, description and input schema the model reads |
| Tool call | The model's structured request to run one function with given arguments |
| Tool result | What the application sends back after running it |
| Tool choice | Whether the model may decide (auto), must call a tool, or may not call one |
| Parallel calls | Several tool calls in one reply, run together |
| Client tool | Runs in your application, under your permissions |
| Server tool | Runs on the model provider's infrastructure, such as web search |
| Strict mode | Forces calls to match the schema exactly |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Every action an agent takes passes through a function call, which makes it the natural checkpoint. The model proposes; the application disposes. Three design choices follow.

**Design tools at the autonomy level you want.** If an agent should never send email, do not give it a `send\_email` tool. Give it `create\_draft`. A tool that does not exist cannot be misused. This is how **lowob**'s rule that nothing sends without a person is enforced in practice.

**Validate arguments in code, not in the prompt.** If discounts above 10% need finance approval, the function that applies a discount should check the figure and refuse or route it. A prompt instruction can be ignored or overridden; a check in code cannot.

**Treat tool output as data.** OpenAI's 2023 warning still stands: text returned by a tool, such as an inbound email or a web page, can contain instructions. Our explainers on [prompt injection](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/) and [excessive agency](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/) cover the attacks and the controls.

Function calling also explains how MCP fits. The [Model Context Protocol](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/) standardises how tools are described and served across applications. Function calling is how the model then asks to use them.

## Common mistakes

- **Vague descriptions.** Anthropic's documentation notes the model "determines when to call a tool based on the user's request and the tool's description". "Gets data" is not a description.
- **Too many tools.** Each definition takes context, and every extra tool is another wrong choice available.
- **Tools that do too much.** A single `update\_crm` tool with free-form fields is harder to check than `set\_deal\_stage` with fixed values.
- **Trusting benchmark scores for long tasks.** BFCL's results suggest single calls are largely solved; multi-step sequences with state are not. Test your own sequences.

## lowob takeaways

- **The model asks; your software acts.** Function calling returns a structured request, never an executed action.
- **The tool list is a permission list.** Leave out actions the agent should not take.
- **Put rules in code.** Validate arguments where the function runs.
- **Tool output can carry instructions.** Treat it as untrusted data.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between function calling and tool use?

They are the same mechanism. OpenAI mostly says function calling; Anthropic mostly says tool use. Both mean the model returns a structured request for your application to run.

### Does the AI model execute the function itself?

No, for functions you define. The model only proposes the call; your application decides whether to run it. Some providers also offer server tools, such as web search, that they run on their own infrastructure.

### How is function calling related to MCP?

MCP is a standard for describing and serving tools so any compatible application can use them. Function calling is the model-side mechanism that requests those tools.

### Is function calling safe for sending emails or updating records?

Only with controls. Expose draft actions rather than send actions, validate arguments in code and require a person's approval for anything client-facing.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Function calling and other API updates](https://openai.com/index/function-calling-and-other-api-updates), 13 June 2023. Vendor announcement.
- [Anthropic, Tool use with Claude](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/overview), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Patil et al., The Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL): From Tool Use to Agentic Evaluation of Large Language Models](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v267/patil25a.html), ICML 2025. Academic benchmark; tasks are general, not commercial.
- The draft-not-send tool design is **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [MCP vs API Integrations: What Changes and What Does Not](https://lowob.com/research/mcp-vs-api-integrations/)
- [What Is an Agent Loop?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/)
- [What Is Excessive Agency in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)

## Next move

List every tool your current assistant or agent can call. Strike out any that send, delete or pay, and replace each with a draft or request version that a person completes.

# The Modular GTM Team: Specialist Depth Without a Full-Service Agency

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI and Web3 companies often need specialist depth for short periods without carrying every specialist on payroll. A modular GTM team keeps a small senior core accountable for the commercial problem and brings in focused support when the bottleneck changes. Large advertisers already work this way, keeping most work in-house and buying agencies for capacity and specialist skill. The model works only if one team stays accountable for the outcome.

AI and Web3 companies often need strong specialists for specific periods, without needing every specialist on payroll. A modular GTM team keeps a small group accountable for the strategy and brings in focused support when the work requires it. The pattern is not new at the top of the market: in the ANA's 2023 survey, large advertisers' in-house teams handled an average of 61% of company work, and the work that went outside went mainly for capacity or specialist skills. What makes the model work is not the roster. It is one team that stays accountable for the outcome.

*AI and Web3 companies often need specialist depth without needing a large permanent team. That gap is becoming an operating model of its own.*

## Why the usual staffing options fall short

The traditional agency model is built around handing a broad problem to one outside team and expecting an integrated answer.

The freelancer model works the other way. Bring in specialists as needed and manage the system internally.

A lot of AI and Web3 companies fit awkwardly into both.

The mix of work can be unusually broad. A company may need technical positioning, founder content, ecosystem marketing, business development, partnerships, paid distribution, creative, community, events, research, automation, and regional expertise, all sometimes within the same quarter. At the same time, there may not be enough steady volume in any one area to justify building a full in-house function.

So the first problem is often organisational, not tactical.

A large full-service agency can give a company breadth, but breadth alone does not guarantee that the people doing the work are close enough to the commercial problem. The familiar failure mode is that senior people sell the engagement, execution gets split across teams, and the client ends up reconnecting strategy, media, creative, and sales themselves.

A collection of freelancers can produce the opposite problem. The specialists may be excellent, but the company becomes the project manager and integration layer. Someone still has to brief everyone, resolve conflicting recommendations, maintain context, set priorities, manage dependencies, and make the final call. Context is the expensive part. Panopto's 2018 survey of 1,000 workers estimated that 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role. Spread that across six freelancers with no shared record and most of the reasoning lives in other people's heads.

|  | Full-service agency | Freelancer roster | Modular GTM team |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who owns the commercial problem | The agency, at a distance | The company, by default | A named senior core |
| Who integrates the work | Split across agency teams | The client | The core |
| Strength | Breadth, scale, procurement fit | Specialist quality, low overhead | Specialist depth with one strategy |
| Typical failure | Senior people sell, juniors deliver | Company becomes project manager | Becomes a roster if ownership slips |
| Best fit | Stable needs across many channels, large budget | One defined function with repeatable volume | Market and message still being worked out |

## The senior core keeps the commercial context

The modular GTM model is a practical middle ground.

A small senior core stays close to the business and owns the commercial problem: who the customer is, what the product needs to communicate, what the immediate objective is, which channels matter, how success will be measured, and what should happen next.

Specialists then plug in where there is a real need. That might mean programmatic media, creative, PR, development, automation, data, creator programmes, ecosystem research, events, regional execution, or a very specific technical skill.

The model only works if accountability stays clear.

Without someone owning the whole picture, a modular team is just a nicer name for a freelancer roster.

In practice that ownership needs artefacts, not just a person. The core keeps the shared brief, the definitions of what counts as a result, the record of decisions and the handoffs between specialists. Our piece on [the commercial system](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) sets out the shared definitions and records that let several contributors work to one plan.

> Without someone owning the whole picture, a modular team is just a nicer name for a freelancer roster.

## Bring in specialist capacity when the problem changes

That ownership matters especially in markets where the bottleneck changes quickly. One month the issue is positioning. The next is distribution. Then the company needs strategic partners, a launch, a stronger content engine, or a more qualified pipeline. Building a fixed team around every temporary need gets expensive fast.

A modular structure lets the execution layer change without forcing the company to reinvent the commercial strategy every time a new specialist gets involved.

| Quarter's bottleneck | What the core keeps | Specialist brought in | Leaves when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning | Customer, message, measure | Technical writer or researcher | The message is tested and written down |
| Distribution | Channel plan and budget | Programmatic or creator specialist | The channel reads, or is ruled out |
| Partnerships | Target list and terms | Ecosystem or BD specialist | Agreements are signed and owned in-house |
| Launch | Timeline and success test | PR, events, regional execution | The launch report is written |

The table is illustrative, but the logic is the one large advertisers describe. The ANA's 2023 survey of 162 members found 65% had moved established work from outside agencies to in-house over the previous three years, while 92% still used external agencies. The reasons for going outside were capacity, when the in-house team was too busy, and specialised capabilities the company lacked. The difference for a smaller company is that its core is a few senior people rather than a department.

## When this model actually fits

This is by no means an argument that full-service agencies are obsolete. They are not. Large agencies make sense when a company needs scale, standardised execution, geographic reach, procurement compatibility, or substantial production capacity.

The more useful question is which operating model matches the actual bottleneck.

If the need is one well-defined function with repeatable volume, hire or retain a specialist. If the company has stable needs across many channels and enough budget to support a large integrated account team, a traditional agency may be the right answer. But when the market, message, and commercial motion are still being worked out, a senior-led modular team can be more efficient and easier to adapt.

The labour market is moving the same way. Lightcast, a labour-market analytics firm, found at least 34,000 US workers had "fractional" in their job title in 2025, up 265% from 2019, and that 97% of US fractional postings in 2026 came from small and medium-sized companies. Part-time senior leaders are one common way a smaller company fills its core. Our guide to [agencies, consultancies, advisors and fractional executives](https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/) sets out what each sells.

## AI raises the value of the core

AI is pushing this further. Research, first drafts, workflow automation, analysis, prototyping, and creative iteration are all becoming faster and cheaper. That does not remove the need for specialists. It means a smaller senior team can coordinate more work, while context and judgment become even more important.

Buyers report the same shift. Gartner's 2025 survey of 402 marketing leaders found 22% said generative AI had reduced their reliance on external agencies for creativity and strategy, and 39% planned to cut agency budgets. Cheaper production moves the scarce resource from output to direction.

Media works much the same way. A company may not need a permanent in-house expert for every buying platform, publisher relationship, creator network, region, or campaign type. It does need access to the right operator when the opportunity is real, with one strategy connecting the work.

That is the value of the modular model: specialist depth without carrying the organisational weight all the time. Our capstone on [building the commercial system at 20, 50 and 200 people](https://lowob.com/research/building-the-commercial-system-at-every-size/) shows how the core changes as the company grows.

Keep the commercial thinking close to the business. Bring in specialists when the problem calls for them. Keep one team accountable for the outcome.

For AI and Web3 companies still figuring out exactly how they win, that flexibility can matter more than having every capability permanently on the org chart.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the owner.** Keep the commercial problem and outcomes with a named senior core.
- **Buy specialists for gaps.** Bring them in for a defined bottleneck rather than duplicating a full-time organisation.
- **Keep the artefacts central.** Shared briefs, definitions, decisions and handoffs stop a modular team becoming a roster.
- **Change the layer, not the strategy.** Specialists rotate as the bottleneck moves; the plan stays with the core.

## Common questions

### What is a modular GTM team?

A go-to-market model in which a small senior core owns the commercial problem, including the customer, message, objective and measure, and brings in specialists for defined gaps such as media, PR, creative or partnerships.

### Is a modular team better than a full-service agency?

It depends on the bottleneck. Full-service agencies suit stable needs across many channels with a large budget. A modular team suits companies whose market, message and commercial motion are still being worked out.

### How is a modular team different from hiring freelancers?

With a freelancer roster the company is the integrator. In a modular team a senior core owns the brief, the priorities, the handoffs and the final call, so specialists work to one strategy.

### Do large companies use specialists instead of one agency?

Many combine in-house teams with outside specialists. The ANA's 2023 survey found 82% of members had an in-house agency and 92% still used external agencies, mainly for capacity and specialist skills.

## Sources and notes

## Next move

List the decisions and outcomes that matter this quarter, and write one name beside each. Where no name fits, that is the gap the senior core must fill before you bring in another specialist.

# What Are TAM, SAM and SOM?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-tam-sam-som/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: TAM, SAM and SOM describe a market at three levels: everything that could be bought, the part a firm can serve, and the share it can realistically win. The numbers are only as good as the market definition behind them, as a public 2014 dispute over Uber's valuation showed. This explainer defines the three terms, compares top-down and bottom-up methods, and sets out how a 20 to 500 person firm can build a SOM its sales team recognises.

TAM, SAM and SOM are three nested estimates of market size. TAM (total addressable market) is total annual demand for a category, SAM (serviceable available market) is the part a firm can reach with its current product and channels, and SOM (serviceable obtainable market) is the share it can realistically win in a set period. For planning, the smallest number matters most, and it should be built from countable accounts rather than from an industry report.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What TAM, SAM and SOM mean

The three terms answer three different questions. Wing Venture Capital defines TAM as "the total possible market for your company's product or service", SAM as the TAM "within reach, usually in geographic or cultural terms", and SOM as "the portion of the SAM you can realistically capture". Naming varies: HubSpot's guide calls the middle tier the serviceable addressable market. The logic is the same.

| Term | Question it answers | Typical inputs | Main use |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TAM | How big is the whole category? | Industry reports, census or registry data | Investor narrative, long-range ambition |
| SAM | How much can we serve today? | TAM filtered by geography, segment, product fit, channel | Territory design, ICP scope |
| SOM | How much can we win, and by when? | Account counts, win rates, sales capacity | Targets, hiring plans, budget |

A SOM should be traceable to named segments, a price the firm has actually achieved, and a team that exists or is funded.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Market sizing is a commercial decision presented as a number. The clearest public example is Uber in 2014. Damodaran started from what he called "a total market for taxi and limo services of $100 billion", assumed Uber would take 10%, which he described as "at the optimistic end of the spectrum", and reached a base-case value of $5.895 billion. Investors had recently valued the company at about $17 billion.

Gurley's reply, "How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber's Potential Market Size", took aim at the assumption about the total available market. If a new service expands its category, today's spend in that category may be the wrong TAM. Neither side's arithmetic was the issue. The disagreement was about which market to measure.

The same choice shows up inside smaller firms. SAM sets territories and the edge of the ideal customer profile. SOM sets quota, hiring and marketing budget, so an inflated SOM inflates every plan built on it.

In **lowob**'s model, the sizing assumption is a decision worth recording, with a reason, an owner and an expected outcome. That lets the firm check it against actual win rates and deal sizes a year later, rather than quietly re-basing the number.

## Top-down or bottom-up: how to build one

Both methods have a place. HubSpot's guide describes top-down as quick but reliant on assumptions, and bottom-up as more defensible but more time-intensive. Wing adds that top-down figures can look impressive but be unrealistic.

A bottom-up SOM for a 20 to 500 person firm can be built in five steps:

1. **Define the buyer.** Write the ideal customer profile: sector, size band, geography and the trigger that creates need.
2. **Count the accounts.** Use a named source, such as a company registry or an enrichment database, and record the date.
3. **Apply your own price.** Use the median annual contract value from closed deals, not list price.
4. **Cut to SAM.** Remove accounts you cannot serve: unsupported languages, regulated markets you are not licensed for, or segments your product does not fit.
5. **Set SOM from capacity.** Multiply sellers by realistic opportunities per seller, then by your historical win rate. If that figure is far below the share you hoped for, the plan needs more capacity or a narrower target.

An illustrative check: a mid-size advisory firm counts 4,000 accounts in its SAM at a median contract of £30,000, a SAM of £120 million. Its five sellers can each run 40 qualified opportunities a year at a 25% win rate, which is 50 wins, or about £1.5 million. That is the SOM, about 1.25% of SAM, whatever the board deck says.

| Mistake | Why it misleads | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| TAM taken from a headline industry report | Category boundaries rarely match your product | Rebuild from countable accounts |
| List price used for value | Discounts and smaller first deals cut real value | Use median closed-won contract value |
| SOM as a flat percentage of TAM | Not linked to any team or channel | Derive from capacity and win rate |
| No date or source on inputs | Cannot be checked or refreshed | Record source, date and owner |

## lowob takeaways

- **Three numbers, three uses.** TAM tells a story, SAM shapes territory, and SOM sets targets.
- **The definition drives the number.** Choosing which market to measure matters more than the multiplication.
- **Build SOM from the bottom.** Accounts, real prices and real capacity produce a figure the sales team will accept.
- **Record the assumption.** A sizing decision with an owner and expected outcome can be tested against results.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between TAM, SAM and SOM?

TAM is total demand for a category, SAM is the part your product and channels can serve, and SOM is the share you can realistically win in a set period.

### How do you calculate SOM?

Count the accounts in your serviceable market, apply your median contract value, then limit the result by sales capacity and historical win rate.

### Should I use top-down or bottom-up market sizing?

Use top-down for a quick sense of scale and bottom-up for planning, because each bottom-up input can be checked.

### What is a good SOM as a percentage of SAM?

There is no standard percentage. A credible SOM is one that matches the deals your team can run and win, whatever share of SAM that turns out to be.

## Sources and notes

- [Wing Venture Capital, Understanding TAM (and SAM and SOM)](https://docs.wing.vc/docs/product/understanding-tam-and-sam-and-som), undated. Venture firm guidance; source of the definitions quoted.
- [HubSpot, TAM, SAM and SOM: What Do They Mean and How Do You Calculate Them?](https://blog.hubspot.com/marketing/tam-sam-som?ld=SDINBlogDirect), updated February 2026. Vendor guide; useful on top-down versus bottom-up trade-offs.
- [Aswath Damodaran, A Disruptive Cab Ride to Riches: The Uber Payoff](https://aswathdamodaran.substack.com/p/a-disruptive-cab-ride-to-riches-the-14-06-09), June 2014. Academic's own valuation; a worked top-down example, not a forecast to rely on.
- [Bill Gurley, Above the Crowd, posts tagged TAM](https://abovethecrowd.com/tag/tam/), July 2014. Investor's rebuttal; the full post is "How to Miss By a Mile: An Alternative Look at Uber's Potential Market Size".

# Keep the Sources; Let the Summary Regenerate

Source: https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A generated summary must never be the only surviving copy of a decision, because every summary is a lossy compression made by one model on one day. Research finds model summaries drop qualifiers and add unsupported content. Keep immutable source snapshots, treat each summary as a regenerable, versioned view over them, and handle deletion with tombstones.

A generated summary must never be the only surviving copy of a decision. Every summary is a lossy compression made by one model on one day, and research shows what gets lost: a 2025 study found model summaries of scientific papers were nearly five times more likely than expert summaries to turn hedged findings into broad generalisations. Provenance is the asset. The summary is a view. Keep immutable sources, version every summary with the model and prompt that made it, and regenerate when models improve.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

The tempting design stores what is useful. Each interaction becomes a clean summary, tagged and embedded. The raw notes, transcripts and documents are discarded, or left in some other system with a different retention policy. Within a year the summaries are all that remain, and nobody decided that on purpose. Our review of [AI notetakers for decision capture](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-notetakers-for-decision-capture/) shows how easily this happens by default.

## Why that is dangerous

Every summary is a compression made with a particular model, prompt and set of assumptions. It keeps what that model judged important and drops the rest. Often what it dropped is a hedge, a caveat, a minority view, or the exact wording of a commitment. Those are precisely the things a later dispute turns on.

The evidence on what gets dropped is specific. Uwe Peters and Benjamin Chin-Yee had 10 large language models produce 4,900 summaries of scientific abstracts and articles, in tests run in early 2024 and March 2025, for a paper forthcoming in *Royal Society Open Science* at the time of the draft. Model summaries were "nearly five times more likely to contain broad generalizations" than expert summaries of the same articles. Some models overgeneralised in 26% to 73% of cases, while Claude models did not differ significantly from the originals. Newer models tended to do worse than older ones, and prompting for accuracy roughly doubled the odds of a generalised conclusion.

The older problem is content that was never there. Maynez and colleagues reported at ACL 2020 that human annotators found "substantial amounts of hallucinated content in all model generated summaries" they evaluated. Models have improved since, but the failure has not disappeared: Stanford researchers found retrieval-backed legal research tools still gave incorrect information in more than 17% of queries in 2024. Our explainer on [AI hallucination](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/) covers the causes.

| What a summary tends to lose | Why a later review needs it |
| --- | --- |
| Hedges and qualifiers | "Likely in this segment" becomes "works" |
| Minority views and dissent | The objection that turned out right disappears |
| Exact wording of a commitment | Disputes turn on what was actually promised |
| Who said what | Accountability and a person to ask |
| What was left undecided | Open questions read as settled |

> When a decision is challenged, the organisation should not be left defending what a model once wrote about what happened.

## Summaries of summaries drift further

Summaries are often summarised again: a meeting summary feeds a weekly digest, which feeds a quarterly review. Each step compresses the last. A related effect is documented in model training. Shumailov and colleagues showed in *Nature* in 2024 that models trained on model-generated data lose the rare, low-probability parts of the original distribution and produce a narrower range of output, which they called model collapse. A chain of summaries is not model training, but the mechanism rhymes: each pass keeps the typical and drops the unusual, and the unusual is often what mattered.

When a decision is challenged eighteen months later, by a regulator, an auditor, a counterparty or a new owner, there is nothing to go back to. And models change. The summary written in 2026 reflects a 2026 model's sense of salience. In 2028 you will have a better one and nothing for it to read.

## The rule

Keep immutable source snapshots. Each carries a retrieval timestamp, its origin, and who verified it if anyone did. Treat every summary as a regenerable view over those sources, versioned with the model and prompt that produced it.

| Object | Mutable | Stored with it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Source snapshot (transcript, email, document) | No | Timestamp, origin, verifier, retention basis |
| Summary | Replaced, never edited | Model, prompt version, date, links to sources |
| Decision record | Superseded, never edited | Links to the sources and summaries it relied on |
| Tombstone | No | What was deleted, when, why, under which obligation, dependants |

Then three things become easy. When the model improves, regenerate the summaries. When a decision is challenged, open the sources. When two summaries disagree, check whether they came from different sources or different models. The same principle, that a changed view is a new record rather than an edit, is set out in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

## The one hard case: deletion

Immutability collides with obligations to delete: privacy requests, retention limits, the end of a client relationship. Under Article 17 of the GDPR, a controller must erase personal data "without undue delay" where one of the listed grounds applies, though the duty does not apply where processing is needed for a legal obligation or "for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims". Those exceptions are for lawyers to apply, case by case, not for a system to assume.

Handle this explicitly rather than quietly. Deleting a source should leave a tombstone: what was deleted, when, why, under which obligation, and which summaries and decisions depended on it. Those dependent records are then marked as resting on removed evidence. That is honest, auditable, and much better than a summary that silently outlives its source. Our explainer on [zero data retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/) covers the vendor side of retention.

## The economics

Storage is cheap. Reconstructing why a decision was made a year and a half ago, from people who have moved on and a summary nobody trusts, is not. Even for heavy document estates, keeping sources is almost always the cheaper side of that trade. Where regulation applies, keeping records is not optional anyway: the EU AI Act requires deployers of high-risk systems to keep automatically generated logs for at least six months once those obligations apply.

## In practice

Store raw sources immutably with timestamp, origin and verifier. Version every summary with the model and prompt that produced it, and link it to its sources. Regenerate summaries when you change models, and compare old and new for drift, paying particular attention to dropped qualifiers.

Design deletion as tombstones that flag dependent records, working with legal and compliance.

**What would prove this wrong:** evidence that summary-only stores resolve later disputes and reviews as reliably as source-backed ones. If compression loses nothing that matters, keeping sources is overhead.

## lowob takeaways

- **Summaries drop hedges.** Model summaries were nearly five times more likely than expert ones to overgeneralise.
- **Keep sources immutable.** Timestamp, origin and verifier on every snapshot.
- **Version every summary.** Model, prompt and links to sources, regenerated when models change.
- **Delete with a tombstone.** Flag every summary and decision that rested on the removed source.

## Common questions

### Should I keep raw meeting transcripts if I have AI summaries?

Yes, where the law allows. A summary keeps what one model judged important and drops the rest, often the caveat or exact wording a later dispute depends on. Keep immutable sources and treat summaries as regenerable views.

### Do AI summaries leave out important details?

Often. A 2025 study of 4,900 summaries from 10 models found they were nearly five times more likely than expert summaries to turn qualified findings into broad generalisations, and asking for accuracy made it worse.

### How do you reconcile keeping sources with data deletion obligations?

Deleting a source should leave a tombstone recording what was deleted, when, why and under which obligation, and mark dependent summaries and decisions as resting on removed evidence.

### What should be stored alongside an AI-generated summary?

The model and prompt version that produced it, the date, and links to the source snapshots it was made from.

## Sources and notes

- [Peters and Chin-Yee, Generalization Bias in Large Language Model Summarization of Scientific Research](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2504.00025), 2025. Academic paper (penultimate draft for *Royal Society Open Science*); scientific texts, not business records.
- [Maynez et al., On Faithfulness and Factuality in Abstractive Summarization](https://aclanthology.org/2020.acl-main.173), ACL 2020. Academic paper; models tested predate current LLMs.
- [Shumailov et al., AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data](https://ideas.repec.org/a/nat/nature/v631y2024i8022d10.1038_s41586-024-07566-y.html), *Nature* 631, July 2024. Academic paper on model training; applied here by analogy.
- [Stanford HAI, AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 (or More) Benchmarking Queries](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-trial-legal-models-hallucinate-1-out-6-or-more-benchmarking-queries), May 2024. Academic study of commercial legal tools; products have changed since.
- [UK legislation.gov.uk, GDPR Article 17: Right to erasure](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2016/679/article/17/adopted/data.htm), text as adopted 2016. Official text; national implementation and later amendments apply.

# What Is an AI Connector?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-connector/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI connector is an integration that lets an assistant or agent read from, or act in, one business system such as a CRM, inbox or drive. Synced connectors copy content and permissions into an index; live connectors, increasingly built on MCP, fetch at query time. Connectors are wiring to rent, and the permissions they inherit are the main thing to check.

An AI connector is an integration that makes one business system, such as email, a CRM or a shared drive, readable or writable by an AI assistant or agent. Some connectors copy content into an index ahead of time; others fetch it live when someone asks, increasingly through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). A good connector carries the source system's permissions with it, which makes those permissions the first thing to check. Connectors are wiring: rent them rather than build them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What an AI connector means

An assistant on its own knows only what is typed into it. A connector gives it a route into a system the company already runs. Our glossary's definition: an integration that makes one system (email, CRM, drive) readable or writable by an assistant or agent.

There are two main designs; Microsoft and Glean both document the two.

|  | Synced (indexed) connector | Live (federated) connector |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Where data sits | Copied into the AI vendor's index | Stays in the source system |
| Freshness | As of the last sync | Current at the moment of the query |
| Permissions | Copied with each item, as of the last sync | Checked by the source, usually through the user's own sign-in |
| Strong at | Fast search across large volumes of documents | Current records and taking actions |
| Weak at | Lag on changes, including permission changes | Speed, and depends on the source's API limits |
| Typical build | Vendor crawler or indexing API | MCP server or direct API call |

Microsoft's documentation describes the synced kind precisely. Each item ingested "includes content, metadata (like title and URL), and an access control list (ACL) that enforces permissions". Connectors periodically check for changes, and admins set the sync frequency. Federated connectors keep data in the source and fetch it "in real time when users query Copilot or Search".

Connectors can also be read-only or able to write. A connector that can create a CRM task or draft an email is an action surface, and its tools should be set to an autonomy level like any agent. A connector that can send should usually be configured not to.

## How permissions carry over

The promise of every enterprise connector is the same: a user sees through the assistant only what they could already open. Microsoft states that search and Copilot "only show items to users who have access in the source system". Glean states that results "only show a user what they're already allowed to see in the source application".

Two details decide whether that promise holds. First, the connector must know who people are. Glean's native connectors collect identities, roles, groups and access control information alongside content. If group memberships are missing or stale, permissions are wrong. Second, the credential matters. Anthropic's documentation notes that a custom connector using a shared credential can reach whatever that credential can access, regardless of who is asking. A connector set up with an administrator's token gives every user an administrator's view.

This is why [permission-aware retrieval](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/) is only as good as the permissions beneath it.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Connectors are what turn a general assistant into a commercial one. A meeting brief that draws on the CRM, the last email thread and the current proposal needs three connectors and no custom code. In **lowob**'s model they sit in the wiring stage, between the store and reasoning. The principle is to rent the wiring and own the record. Vendors maintain connectors for their own systems, and switching assistants should not mean rebuilding them.

Anthropic's documentation also notes that enabling a connector for an organisation "doesn't automatically grant anyone access": each person authenticates. That is the right default. It means access follows people, and leavers lose it when their accounts close.

## What to check before connecting

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Does it use each person's own sign-in, or a shared credential? | Shared credentials flatten permissions |
| How often does it sync content and permissions? | A revoked share stays visible until the next sync |
| Which objects and fields does it read? | Pricing and notes fields are often the sensitive ones |
| Can it write, and can each write tool require approval? | Writes are actions at an autonomy level |
| Are its calls logged, and can you export the logs? | Audit and incident review |
| What happens when someone leaves? | Access should end with their account |

## lowob takeaways

- **A connector is a route into one system.** It gives an assistant read or write access.
- **Synced and live designs trade freshness for speed.** Know which one you have.
- **Permissions are inherited, good and bad.** Check credentials and sync lag.
- **Rent connectors, own the record.** Wiring is replaceable; decisions are not.

## Common questions

### What are connectors in AI tools?

Integrations that let an AI assistant or agent read from, and sometimes act in, a business system such as a CRM, email or file store, so its answers can draw on company data.

### What is the difference between a connector and MCP?

A connector is the general idea of linking an AI tool to one system. MCP is an open standard many connectors are now built on, so one server can serve any compatible assistant.

### Do AI connectors respect file permissions?

Enterprise connectors are designed to show users only what they can already open in the source system. That depends on correct identity data, current syncs and per-user credentials.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft Learn, Microsoft 365 Copilot connectors gallery overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365/copilot/connectors/prebuilt-connectors-overview), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; connector count is vendor-stated.
- [Microsoft Learn, Copilot connectors overview](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoftsearch/connectors-overview), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Use the connectors directory to extend Claude's capabilities](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/11724452-use-the-connectors-directory-to-extend-claude-s-capabilities), accessed November 2026. Vendor help article; plan features change.

For each connector your assistant already uses, find out whether it runs on each person's sign-in or on one shared account. Any shared account connected to commercial systems goes to the top of this week's list.
