# What We Would Cut From the Build Order

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-we-would-cut-from-the-build-order/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: After thirteen parts, a retrospective. The evidence on AI project failure points more often to over-building than under-building: RAND's interviews name chasing technology over the problem as a leading cause, and Anthropic's own guidance is to find the simplest solution that works. For firms under about 50 people, several steps in The Build Order shrink to a habit or disappear. Four do not: a named owner, one recorded decision class, nothing sends without a person, and a handover that keeps the reasoning.

The Build Order was written for firms of 20 to 500 people, and at the small end parts of it are too heavy. A 25-person firm does not need a formal Gateway 0, a purchased context layer, a decision-record system, a value at stake on every decision class or a Gateway 3. It needs a named owner, one decision class recorded in a shared table with outcomes, a rule that nothing sends without a person, and a handover habit that keeps the reasoning when someone leaves. The wider evidence supports cutting. RAND's study of failed AI projects names chasing the latest technology over the user's problem as one of the most frequent pathways to failure, and Anthropic's guidance on agents recommends the simplest solution possible, adding complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes. What should not be cut is the part that is cheapest: writing down why.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

A series that argues for a sequence owes its readers a view of where the sequence is wrong. Thirteen parts have added steps: three decisions before any tool, a context layer, a record with six fields, a first agent, three gateways and a permission review. Each was argued on evidence. Taken together, for a firm of 25 people with one person running sales, they describe more process than the firm can carry.

This piece goes back through the order and marks what we would cut, by size, and what we would keep regardless. It also sets out what the evidence says about over-engineering, because the most common failure we see is not a firm that built too little. It is a firm that bought for the stage after next.

## What the evidence says about over-engineering

The failure literature on AI projects is consistent on one point: complexity added before the problem is understood is a leading cause of waste.

| Source | Finding | What it implies for the order |
| --- | --- | --- |
| RAND, 2024 | Five root causes from 65 practitioner interviews, including focusing on the latest technology rather than real problems for users; "chasing the latest and greatest advances in AI for their own sake is one of the most frequent pathways to failure" | Start from a decision, not a tool |
| Anthropic, 2024 | Find the simplest solution possible and increase complexity only when needed; frameworks can obscure prompts and responses | Workflows before agents; no framework until one is needed |
| Gartner, 2025 | Over 40% of agentic projects cancelled by 2027 on cost and unclear value; about 130 genuine agentic vendors among thousands | Most "agent" purchases are not what they claim |
| MIT NANDA, 2025 | Generic tools such as ChatGPT outperformed bespoke enterprise tools in the study, even on the same underlying models | Rent the general assistant before building a custom one |
| McKinsey, 2025 | Redesigning individual workflows was among the strongest contributors to impact; high performers nearly three times as likely to have done it | Change the work, not the stack |

RAND's report also cites estimates that more than 80% of AI projects fail, about twice the rate of other IT projects. That figure is an estimate the authors quote rather than measure, and RAND notes its interviewees were mostly engineers, who may be quicker to blame leadership. The direction is still clear, and it matches the Gartner and MIT findings from different angles: the expensive mistake is building or buying ahead of a defined problem.

There is a counterweight. The US Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey found 19.8% of US businesses using AI in any business function as of May 2026, with use under 20% among firms of four or fewer employees, 32% at 100 to 249, and 37% at 250 or more. For small firms the larger risk may be not starting at all. A lighter order is meant to make starting easier, not to argue for waiting.

## Part by part: what we would cut

The table marks each step for three size bands. "Keep" means as written; "shrink" means a lighter version; "cut" means skip until the firm reaches the next band. These are judgments, not measurements.

| Step in the order | 20 to 50 people | 50 to 200 people | 200 to 500 people |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gateway 0: owner, suite, CRM | Shrink: name the owner; suite and CRM are usually already settled | Keep | Keep |
| Assistant seats on the commercial line | Keep, for the people who sell | Keep | Keep |
| A purchased context layer | Cut: use the suite's native assistant and connectors | Shrink: native connectors plus the CRM | Keep |
| Permission review before connection | Shrink: one hour on the shared drive's broadest shares | Keep | Keep |
| Decision record with six fields | Shrink: one shared table, one decision class | Keep, two or three classes | Keep |
| First agent | Shrink: a prompt template or saved workflow, not an agent | Keep | Keep |
| Gateway 1: nothing sends without a person | Keep | Keep | Keep |
| Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision | Shrink: on one class, compared against expectation | Keep | Keep |
| Gateway 3: extend to other functions | Cut: sales and delivery are usually the same people | Shrink: delivery handover only | Keep |
| Governance platform, agent framework, memory layer | Cut | Cut | Shrink: only where an obligation requires it |

Five cuts deserve a sentence each.

**A formal Gateway 0.** In a firm of 25 the suite and the CRM were chosen years ago. The one decision that still matters is who owns the build and how many hours a week they have for it.

**A purchased context layer.** Native connectors in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, plus the CRM's own assistant, cover most of what a small commercial team needs. The rule in [*Buy context, own judgment*](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) still applies: rent the wiring, and at this size the suite is the rental.

**A record system.** A shared table with the six fields is enough below about 50 people, provided it can be exported. The fields matter; the software does not.

**A first agent.** For a small team, a saved prompt that prepares meeting briefs from the CRM and the inbox does the job [Part 7](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/) assigned to the first agent. Anthropic's distinction is useful here: a workflow follows a predefined path, an agent directs its own. Most small-firm needs are workflows.

**Value at stake on every class.** [Part 11](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-two-a-dollar-figure-on-every-commercial-decision/) noted that below about ten decisions a month in a class, comparison groups are too thin. A small firm should put a dollar figure on its one recorded class and compare outcomes against what was expected at the time.

> Cut the software before you cut the habit. The fields of a decision record cost nothing; the system that holds them can wait.

## What we would never cut

Four steps stay at every size because they are cheap and their absence is expensive.

1. **A named owner with protected time.** Without one, the build is a purchase, not a change in how the firm works.
2. **One decision class recorded with reasons and outcomes.** This is the only part of the brain a firm cannot rent and cannot recover later.
3. **Nothing sends without a person.** At small sizes one bad message reaches a larger share of the client base.
4. **No agent with private data, untrusted content and an outbound channel at once.** [Part 12](https://lowob.com/research/the-permission-problem-when-commercial-context-leaks/)'s structural control costs nothing to apply and does not depend on firm size.

## Where the order is underbuilt: handovers

The retrospective found one place where the sequence asks for too little. Small firms lose more reasoning per departure than large ones, because each person carries a larger share of what the firm knows. A ten-person firm losing its head of sales loses most of its commercial memory in a single notice period.

The series has treated handovers as a later concern, something for the transitions a growing firm meets. For a small firm it is the first record. In [*Handovers are where reasoning pours out*](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) we set out a five-part handover pack: recent decisions extracted in a structured interview, open threads, relationships, the graveyard of abandoned approaches, and a 90-day question log. A handover is scheduled, has a motivated owner in the incoming person, and produces visible value. For a firm under 50 people, a handover pack for every commercial role may do more for the brain than any tool in the order.

## What would change our mind

The cuts above are judgments, and they can be tested.

| If we saw this | We would conclude |
| --- | --- |
| Small firms that skip the record and still stop repeating the same commercial mistakes | The record is less necessary at small sizes than we argue |
| Small firms that buy a full context layer early and get measurable value without rework | The cut was too aggressive |
| Firms that pass Gateway 2 without an owner with protected time | Ownership matters less than the series claims |
| Native suite assistants failing on basic commercial preparation for small teams | Renting the suite is not enough, and a purchased layer belongs earlier |

We have not seen the first three. The fourth is plausible, and it is the cut we hold most loosely.

Illustrative example: the light build order

Decision
:   Run a shortened build for a 30-person firm: owner named, native assistant seats for the four people who sell, a shared table recording pursue-or-pass decisions, a rule that nothing reaches a client unapproved, and a handover pack for the departing head of business development.

Reason and owner
:   The full order would have taken a quarter before anything changed. Owned by the managing director, with two protected hours a week.

What changed
:   Within a quarter the table showed which pitches the firm should stop pursuing, and the handover pack captured the reasons behind three live client relationships before the departure.

Illustrative: a composite of a small professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The evidence favours cutting.** Most AI waste comes from building ahead of a defined problem.
- **Below about 50 people, most steps shrink.** The context layer becomes the suite, the record becomes a table, and Gateway 3 waits.
- **Four steps stay at every size.** Owner, one recorded class, nothing sends without a person, no lethal trifecta.
- **Handovers are the small firm's first record.** Each departure carries a larger share of what the firm knows.

Gateway card

### Before you build more than you need

- Firm size band identified, and the table above applied to it
- A named owner with protected hours
- One decision class recorded with reasons and outcomes
- Nothing reaches a client without a person
- No agent combining private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel
- A handover pack scheduled for the next commercial departure
- No platform, framework or memory layer bought without a named obligation or problem

## Common questions

### Do small businesses need an enterprise AI strategy?

Not in the enterprise sense. A firm under about 50 people needs a named owner, assistant seats for the people who sell, one decision type recorded with reasons and outcomes, and a rule that nothing reaches a client without a person.

### Why do AI projects fail?

RAND's 2024 study identified five root causes, including leaders misunderstanding the problem, insufficient data, and focusing on the latest technology rather than the user's problem. Gartner has forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027 on cost and unclear value.

### Should a small company build AI agents or use off-the-shelf tools?

Start with the general assistant in the suite you already use and saved workflows. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and add complexity only when it demonstrably improves outcomes.

### What is the most important AI step for a small firm?

Recording why the firm makes its most frequent commercial decision, and what happened afterwards. It is the one part of the build that cannot be bought later.

## Sources and notes

- [RAND, The Root Causes of Failure for Artificial Intelligence Projects and How They Can Succeed](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2680-1.html), August 2024. 65 practitioner interviews; mostly engineers; the 80% figure is a quoted estimate.
- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents), December 2024. Guidance from a model provider.
- Gartner forecast and agent-washing estimate, June 2025, as reported by [Reuters via The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says). Analyst estimates.
- MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide, as reported by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/08/18/generative_ai_zero_return_95_percent), August 2025. Small interview and survey sample.
- [McKinsey, The state of AI in 2025](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/artificial-intelligence/the-state-of-ai-2025). 1,993 participants; correlation, not causation.
- [US Census Bureau, Large firms with at least 20 employees biggest AI users](https://census.gov/library/stories/2026/05/ai-use-businesses.html), May 2026. Business Trends and Outlook Survey; question wording changed in November 2025.
- The size bands, cuts and falsifiers are **lowob**'s judgments, drawn from patterns across engagements, not a measured study.

# The False Premise Is the Expensive Failure

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-false-premise-is-the-expensive-failure/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI systems have become good at saying 'I don't know' but remain bad at saying 'that's not right any more'. In the 2026 MemTrace benchmark, a widely used memory layer abstained correctly 99.3% of the time but resolved premises that contradicted its memory only 14.6% of the time. The fix is a premise check against the record, tested on your own superseded views.

AI systems have become good at saying "I don't know". They remain bad at saying "that's not right any more". In one 2026 benchmark, a widely used memory layer declined to answer 99.3% of questions about facts it had never seen, but resolved only 14.6% of prompts whose premise contradicted what it remembered. The second failure is the one that costs money. The fix is a premise check against the record, run on questions tied to live decisions and tested on your own reversed views.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## Two numbers from the same system

Xianxuan Long, Jiliang Tang and colleagues built MemTrace in 2026 to probe what headline accuracy scores on memory benchmarks miss. Two of their measures, read together, describe the problem precisely. Boundary abstention tests whether a system declines to answer questions about facts never mentioned in its history. Conflict probes test whether it corrects a prompt whose premise contradicts what it remembers.

Mem0, a widely used memory layer, scored 99.3% on boundary abstention and 14.6% on conflict probes. The paper reports the same shape for the other systems in that comparison: abstention of 97.4% and 94.0%, conflict scores of 20.1% and 35.1%. In the authors' words, they "rarely resolve conflict probes".

The industry has largely solved the failure everyone worried about in 2023: confidently answering when nothing supports the answer. It has barely touched a subtler one. When a question smuggles in an assumption that the record contradicts, the system answers the question as asked.

A second 2026 benchmark, MemSyco-Bench, found the same pattern from a different angle. Memory systems "do not reliably mitigate memory-induced sycophancy", and for three of them 61 to 62% of errors happened after the relevant memory had been retrieved. The record was found. It was not allowed to overrule the question. This is the practical meaning of [Retrieval is not the bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/).

| Failure | What the system does | Benchmark behaviour | Business cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unsupported answer | Answers with nothing behind it | Largely fixed: high abstention rates | Visible; usually caught |
| False-premise acceptance | Answers a question built on an outdated or wrong assumption | Low conflict-resolution rates | Invisible; every fact may be correct |

## What this looks like inside a firm

An analyst asks: "Given that the client's loan condition was waived last year, what should we watch this quarter?" If the waiver was reversed in July, the record knows. But the question presupposes the waiver, and the system will usually produce a fluent, well-sourced answer about monitoring a waived condition.

A relationship manager asks: "Since procurement approved the budget, what's the fastest path to signature?" The budget approval was a forecast, never confirmed. The answer is a confident plan built on nothing.

These are not hallucinations in the usual sense. Every fact in the answer may be correct. The error is in what the answer accepted without checking. Our explainer on [AI hallucination](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/) covers the more familiar failure.

False premises are not rare. Xinyan Velocity Yu and colleagues' CREPE study at ACL 2023 found about 25% of questions on online information-seeking forums contained a false presupposition. In a 2026 annotation of 100 real chatbot questions, Shenran Wang, Vered Shwartz and Hila Gonen found about 13%. Inside a firm, where questions refer to deals and decisions that change status weekly, the share on live matters is unlikely to be lower.

## Why people do not catch it either

Questions from senior people carry premises that junior people rarely challenge. A system that would push back on a false premise is, among other things, a way to correct a senior colleague without the politics. That is a real organisational benefit, and it only exists if the system is built to do it. Benchmarks show the default behaviour is the opposite: the memory systems tested deferred to the question.

> The industry taught systems to say "I don't know". It has not yet taught them to say "that's not right any more".

## The premise check

The fix is a step before answering, and it is cheap to build.

Extract the presuppositions in the question. Models are good at this when asked directly: "What does this question assume to be true?"

Check each presupposition against current records, using status and validity dates. This works best when records are superseded rather than overwritten, as argued in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/), because the system can then see both the old view and the date it changed.

If any presupposition is contradicted or superseded, say so first, with the record and date, before answering anything.

Then answer the question that should have been asked, or ask whether the user still wants the original.

The evidence adds one important limit. Wang, Shwartz and Gonen found that methods scoring better on false-premise questions tended to score worse on true ones, because "weak fact checking modules" also rejected true presuppositions they could not verify. Weighted to a realistic mix of questions, answering directly beat aggressive premise detection. So the check should be narrow:

| What the record shows about the premise | Action |
| --- | --- |
| Contradicted or superseded, with a date | Say so first, cite the record, then answer the corrected question |
| Confirmed and current | Answer as asked |
| Not in the record | Answer as asked; note the premise was not verified |
| Recorded as a forecast, not a fact | Flag the status ("forecast, unconfirmed") before answering |

Challenge only what the record contradicts. Do not challenge what the record merely lacks. The check costs one extra call and a few hundred tokens per question. On questions that touch live decisions, that is an easy trade.

## Test for it explicitly

Most evaluation sets test whether a system finds the right answer. Add a set that tests whether it refuses a wrong question. Your own superseded records are the ideal source: take twenty views the organisation once held and later reversed, and write questions that assume the old view. Score how often the system pushes back. Expect a low number at first.

Add twenty questions with true premises as a control, so that a check that challenges everything is caught as quickly as one that challenges nothing. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to keep both sets fixed across releases, and [What is agent memory?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/) covers where superseded views should be stored.

## What would prove this wrong

Systems without a premise check correcting false premises at rates close to their abstention rates on independent tests. Then the gap has closed on its own and the extra step is redundant. The 2026 benchmarks show it has not closed yet.

## lowob takeaways

- **Abstention is not correction.** High "I don't know" rates say nothing about outdated assumptions.
- **Retrieval is not enough.** Most memory errors in one benchmark happened after the right memory was found.
- **Check only against the record.** Challenge what it contradicts, not what it lacks, or ordinary answers get worse.
- **Test with your own reversals.** Twenty superseded views, twenty true controls, every release.

## Common questions

### What is a false-premise error in AI?

When a question assumes something the record contradicts and the system answers the question as asked. Every fact in the answer may be correct; the error is in the assumption it accepted without checking.

### How can I stop an AI assistant from answering questions based on outdated assumptions?

Add a premise check before answering: extract what the question assumes, check each assumption against current records with status and dates, and flag any that are contradicted or superseded before answering.

### How do I test whether my AI system catches false premises?

Take twenty views your organisation once held and later reversed, write questions that assume the old view, and score how often the system pushes back. Add twenty true-premise questions to catch over-correction.

### Do AI memory systems correct false premises?

Rarely, on current evidence. In the 2026 MemTrace benchmark, Mem0 abstained correctly on 99.3% of unanswerable questions but scored 14.6% on prompts whose premise contradicted its memory.

## Sources and notes

- [Long et al., MemTrace: Probing What Final Accuracy Misses in Long-Term Memory](https://arxiv.org/html/2606.17328v1), arXiv preprint, 2026. Academic benchmark, not peer-reviewed; synthetic conversation histories, not enterprise records.
- [Xiang et al., MemSyco-Bench: Benchmarking Sycophancy in Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.01071), arXiv preprint, 2026. Academic benchmark, not peer-reviewed.
- [Yu, Min, Zettlemoyer and Hajishirzi, CREPE: Open-Domain Question Answering with False Presuppositions](https://virtual2023.aclweb.org/paper_P2678.html), ACL 2023. Peer-reviewed; forum questions, not business queries.
- [Wang, Shwartz and Gonen, Weak Presupposition Verification Degrades General QA Performance](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.06539), arXiv preprint, 2026. Academic study; the 13% estimate comes from 100 annotated questions.
- The failure table and premise-check rules are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is Agent Memory?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/)
- [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)
- [Ask for the Gap, Not the Summary](https://lowob.com/research/ask-for-the-gap-not-the-summary/)

## Next move

List twenty positions your organisation held last year and has since reversed. Turn each into a question that assumes the old view, run them through your assistant, and count how many it corrects.

# What Is MEDDICC?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-meddicc/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: MEDDICC is a checklist for qualifying complex B2B deals, built around the evidence a seller needs before a forecast can be trusted. It began at PTC in the 1990s and has since gained letters for competition and the paper process. This explainer sets out what each element means, why it suits buying groups of a dozen or more people, and how to turn it into CRM fields rather than a training slide.

MEDDICC is a sales qualification framework for complex B2B deals. The letters stand for Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion and Competition. Each element is a question the seller must answer with evidence from the buyer, not with an opinion. It works best when each letter becomes a field in the CRM and a condition for moving a deal to the next stage.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What MEDDICC means

MEDDICC exists to answer one question: is this a real deal, and will it close when the forecast says? Each letter names a piece of evidence. The definitions below follow those published by MEDDICC, the training firm that maintains the framework.

| Element | What the seller must establish | Evidence that it is true |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Metrics | The quantified value the buyer expects | A number the buyer stated, such as hours saved or cost avoided |
| Economic buyer | The person with overall authority for the decision | A meeting or written confirmation from that person |
| Decision criteria | The requirements the buyer will use to judge options | A written list or RFP requirements |
| Decision process | The steps the buyer will take to decide | Named steps, owners and dates |
| Identify pain | The business problem driving the purchase, and its cost | The buyer's description of consequences if nothing changes |
| Champion | An insider with power, influence and credibility who sells for you | Actions taken, such as arranging a meeting or sharing internal plans |
| Competition | Anything competing for the same resources, including doing nothing | Named alternatives, internal builds or a no-decision risk |

MEDDICC's own site defines competition broadly, as "anything that competes for the same resources as your solution". That includes an internal project and the option of doing nothing, which often matter more than a rival vendor.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The original problem MEDDICC addressed is still the main one: forecasts built on seller optimism. MEDDICC's published history says the framework was born at PTC in 1996, and credits it with part of PTC's growth to $1 billion in sales within a decade. That claim comes from the framework's own promoters and has not been independently tested.

What has changed is the shape of buying. Forrester found 13 people involved in the average decision and 86% of purchases stalled at some point. With that many stakeholders, the questions about economic buyer, decision process and champion are not formalities. A deal with a keen user and no economic buyer is a conversation, not an opportunity.

Buyers also arrive later. Gartner's 2026 survey found 67% of B2B buyers preferred a rep-free experience, and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. By the time a seller is involved, decision criteria may already be set. MEDDICC helps a seller find out quickly whether they are shaping the criteria or responding to someone else's.

In **lowob**'s terms, MEDDICC fields are context. An assistant drafting a deal summary, or an agent flagging risk, can only reason about what has been recorded. A blank economic buyer field is a signal in itself.

## How to put it into practice

A common failure is a training course and a slide with no change to the CRM. A working version needs three things.

1. **Make each letter a field.** Use short structured fields where possible: economic buyer as a contact link, decision process as dated steps, competition as a picklist with free text.
2. **Tie fields to stages.** Write exit criteria so that a deal cannot move to proposal without, for example, metrics and a confirmed economic buyer. [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) covers how to write them.
3. **Inspect in deal reviews.** Managers ask for the evidence behind each field, not a score out of seven.

| Deal size and complexity | Suggested depth |
| --- | --- |
| Small, single buyer, short cycle | A lighter screen such as BANT may be enough |
| Mid-market, a few stakeholders | Metrics, economic buyer, pain and champion as required fields |
| Enterprise, buying group, procurement | Full MEDDICC, plus paper process (MEDDPICC) |

For a comparison with the older, lighter framework, see [What Is BANT, and Is It Still Useful?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-bant/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Evidence, not opinion.** Each element needs something the buyer said or did.
- **Fields beat slides.** MEDDICC changes forecasts only when it lives in the CRM and the stage rules.
- **Competition includes doing nothing.** No-decision is often the strongest alternative in the deal.
- **Match depth to deal size.** Full MEDDICC is overhead on a small, single-buyer sale.

## Common questions

### What does MEDDICC stand for?

Metrics, Economic buyer, Decision criteria, Decision process, Identify pain, Champion and Competition.

### What is the difference between MEDDIC, MEDDICC and MEDDPICC?

MEDDIC is the original six elements. MEDDICC adds Competition. MEDDPICC also adds Paper process, the steps from decision to signed contract.

### Who created MEDDIC?

It was developed at PTC in 1996. MEDDICC's published history credits Dick Dunkel, working with John McMahon and Jack Napoli.

### Is MEDDICC better than BANT?

For complex deals with buying groups, MEDDICC asks for more of the evidence that predicts a close. For small, fast sales, BANT is often sufficient.

## Sources and notes

- [MEDDICC, Who Created MEDDIC?](https://meddicc.com/resources/who-created-meddic), November 2026. Published by the framework's training firm; origin story and growth claims are not independently verified.
- [MEDDICC, MEDDPICC](https://www.meddicc.com/meddpicc), undated. Training firm's definitions of each element.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying: Companies Still Struggle To Meet Buyer Expectations](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/state-of-business-buying-2024/), December 2024. Analyst survey of more than 16,000 business buyers.
- [Forrester, To Master B2B Buying Mayhem, Providers Must Prioritize Buyers' Needs](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), December 2024. Press release; source of the 89% and 86% figures.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers.

## Related research

- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)
- [What Is BANT, and Is It Still Useful?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-bant/)
- [What Is Win-Loss Analysis?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/)
- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)

## Next move

Pick your five largest open deals and fill in the seven MEDDICC fields for each from what is actually recorded. Any blank economic buyer or champion is a forecast risk to raise this week.

# AI Agents in Marketing: What They Can Do Now, Task by Task

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-marketing-what-they-can-do-now/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A task-by-task guide to AI agents in marketing, built on the thirteen marketing rows of the lowob Agent Task Directory. Agents draft well and monitor well; they should not publish, move budget or speak for the company alone. The guide maps each task to the layer of the brain it depends on, sets a starting autonomy level, and names the first three tasks to hand over.

Marketing ties with sales, partners and customer success for the most tasks rated High reliability in the **lowob** Agent Task Directory, and few of them should run alone. Agents monitor competitors, draft campaign variants, write content briefs and assemble monthly reports well. The limits come from where marketing output goes: to the public, to regulators and to the budget. Of thirteen tasks, three can act and report, three can act with approval and seven stay as drafts, including publishing and budget moves. Start with monitoring, interview-to-draft content and the monthly report.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Marketing teams adopted generative tools earlier than most functions, and the pressure to go further is real. Gartner's 2025 CMO Spend Survey of 402 marketing leaders found budgets flat at 7.7% of company revenue, with 59% saying they lack the funds to deliver their strategy and 22% saying generative AI has reduced their reliance on external agencies. That pressure pushes teams toward agents that publish and optimise on their own. The ratings below explain why the drafting tasks should be automated first and the publishing tasks last.

The ratings are **lowob**'s working framework for 20- to 500-person teams, from the [Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/), reviewed quarterly. They assume the listed control is in place. Without it, drop the task one level.

## The thirteen marketing tasks, rated

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monitor competitors and market news | 3 Act and report | High | Missing a material change | Named sources; weekly human read |
| Turn an interview into draft posts | 1 Draft | High | Claims the company cannot support | Claims checked by a subject owner |
| Publish social posts | 1 Draft | Medium | Public error; regulatory breach in finance or crypto | Nothing publishes without a person |
| Draft campaign variants for testing | 1 Draft | High | Off-brand or unapproved claims | Brand and claims rules in context |
| Reallocate campaign budget | 1 Draft | Low | Spend moved on weak evidence | Budget holder approves; record expected outcome |
| Build audience segments from CRM data | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Consent or privacy breach | Consent fields respected; privacy review |
| Write SEO and answer-engine content briefs | 1 Draft | High | Thin or duplicative content | Editorial owner; check existing pages first |
| Draft long-form research | 1 Draft | Medium | Invented sources or statistics | Every figure opened and cited by a person |
| Score leads | 3 Act and report | Medium | Scores that encode old bias | Quarterly calibration against outcomes |
| Produce a monthly marketing report | 3 Act and report | High | Activity reported as impact | Report against agreed outcome measures |
| Personalise website content | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Wrong message to the wrong audience | Approved variants only |
| Reply to community questions | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong or market-moving statements | Named communications owner approves |
| Translate and localise approved content | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Mistranslated claims in regulated markets | Native reviewer for regulated content |

The split between reliability and autonomy is the main lesson of this table. Drafting campaign variants is High reliability and still level 1, because a variant goes in front of the public once approved. Lead scoring is Medium reliability and level 3, because a score is internal, reversible and can be calibrated against closed deals. Autonomy follows the consequence of an error, not the quality of the average output.

## Where each task plugs into the brain

The brain is a loop: the **store** (CRM, analytics, ad platforms, content library), the **context** layer that applies definitions, brand rules and consent, the **record** of decisions with reason, owner and expected outcome, **reasoning** by models and agents, and **learning** when outcomes return. Marketing tasks lean harder on context than sales tasks, because brand rules, claims rules and consent all live there.

| Task | Main layer | Start at | Move up when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Competitor and market monitoring | Context | 3 | Named source list agreed first |
| Interview to draft posts | Reasoning | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Publish social posts | Record | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Campaign variants | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Budget reallocation | Record | 0, then 1 | Expected outcomes recorded for a quarter |
| Audience segments | Context | 1, then 2 | Consent fields complete and tested |
| SEO and answer-engine briefs | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Long-form research drafts | Reasoning | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Lead scoring | Learning | 2, then 3 | One quarter of calibration against outcomes |
| Monthly marketing report | Learning | 2, then 3 | Outcome measures agreed with finance |
| Website personalisation | Context | 1, then 2 | Variant library approved |
| Community replies | Record | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Translation and localisation | Context | 1, then 2 | Glossary of approved claims per market |

Seven of thirteen tasks stay at level 1 for the foreseeable future. That is not a verdict on the technology. It reflects that the output is public, and that public statements carry legal weight regardless of who drafted them.

## The five tasks that decide the programme

### Publishing and community replies

These two are rated level 1 for the same reason: they are the company speaking. Regulators treat AI-drafted statements like any other. In September 2024 the FTC announced Operation AI Comply, five actions including one against a writing tool used to generate fake consumer reviews, with the chair stating there is "no AI exemption from the laws on the books". The FTC's 2024 rule on fake reviews and testimonials covers reviews attributed to people who do not exist, which includes AI-generated ones, and allows civil penalties against knowing violators.

In finance and crypto the stakes rise. The FCA's FG24/1 guidance on social media promotions says the rules are technology neutral, that firms remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made, and that an unapproved promotion by an unauthorised person may be a criminal offence under section 21 of FSMA. It notes that memes are common in cryptoasset promotion and can fall within the regime. A community agent that answers a token question in a public channel is making a statement the firm owns. The *Moffatt v. Air Canada* tribunal reached the same conclusion about a chatbot in 2024. The control is a named communications owner who approves every public reply. [Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out the gate.

### Long-form research and content briefs

Agents are good at structuring a brief, checking what the site already says and drafting a first pass. They also confabulate. NIST's Generative AI Profile (AI 600-1, July 2024) defines confabulation as "the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content". In research content this shows up as invented statistics and plausible but wrong citations. The control is non-negotiable: a person opens every source and checks every figure before publication.

Search engines do not penalise AI drafting as such. Google's guidance on AI-generated content says its focus is "on the quality of content, rather than how content is produced", while using automation primarily to manipulate rankings breaches its spam policies. The real risk with briefs is duplication: a site that publishes ten near-identical answers to one question. That is why the control is to check existing pages first. See our [LLM optimisation checklist](https://lowob.com/research/llm-optimization-checklist/) for the editorial test.

### Audience segments from CRM data

Segmentation is level 2 because the failure is a privacy breach, not a bad open rate. The UK ICO's guidance on electronic mail marketing says organisations normally must have consent before sending unsolicited marketing email to individual subscribers. It applies the same rule to sole traders and ordinary partnerships, and states there is no third-party list that is compliant with the soft opt-in. Corporate subscribers can be emailed without consent, but the identity rules still apply. An agent building segments must read consent fields as hard filters, and a privacy reviewer approves any segment that crosses jurisdictions or data sources. This is the context layer's permission job, done before the reasoning starts.

### Budget reallocation

Moving spend is rated level 1 and Low reliability. Platform dashboards report attributed conversions that may not reflect incremental effect, and an agent that optimises toward the dashboard can move money confidently in the wrong direction. Our piece on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the measurement problem. The control is a budget holder who approves each move and records the expected outcome: the metric, the size of the change and the date to check. Without that entry, the learning layer has nothing to grade.

### Lead scoring

Scoring is one of the few level 3 tasks in marketing. It is internal and reversible, and it can be tested against what actually closed. The risk is that a model trained on last year's wins encodes last year's market. The control is quarterly calibration: compare score bands with conversion and revenue, and retrain or reweight when a band drifts. Run the new score alongside the old one for a quarter before it routes leads.

> In marketing, autonomy follows where the output goes, not how good the draft is.

## Start here: the first three tasks

The best first marketing tasks are internal, frequent and quick to check.

1. **Monitor competitors and market news.** Level 3 from the start, with a named source list and a weekly digest a person reads. Baseline: how often the team learned of a material change late. Control: the source list is reviewed monthly.
2. **Turn founder and customer interviews into draft posts.** Level 1. The agent drafts from the transcript; a subject owner checks every claim; a person publishes. Baseline: drafts produced per interview and time to first draft. See the [founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) for the workflow.
3. **Produce the monthly marketing report.** Level 2 for the first two cycles, then level 3. The agent pulls the figures and drafts the commentary; the marketing lead checks it against agreed outcome measures, not activity counts. Baseline: hours spent assembling the report.

Campaign variants and content briefs are the natural next pair. Segments, personalisation and translation follow once consent fields and approved libraries are in place. Publishing, community replies and budget moves stay with a person.

Illustrative example: re-scoping a marketing agent request

Decision
:   Replace a proposed agent that would post to social channels and adjust paid budgets with three internal tasks: competitor monitoring, interview-to-draft posts and the monthly report.

Reason and owner
:   The firm markets a regulated financial product, so every public post needs approval, and the paid dashboards had no incrementality test. Owned by the marketing lead, with compliance approving the posting workflow.

What changed
:   Draft volume rises with no unapproved post published; budget moves are logged with expected outcomes, and the first quarter's entries are graded at the next planning cycle.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size fintech marketing team, built from patterns across engagements.

## How to move a marketing task up the dial

Use the same three tests as in [Part 1](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/). The control has run for four weeks or more. A weekly random sample shows errors that are few and internal. The decision touched is recorded with a reason and an expected outcome. For marketing add a fourth: the task's output has not reached the public without a person's approval. If any public error occurs, drop the task one level until the cause is fixed and recorded.

## lowob takeaways

- **Automate the draft, not the publish.** Seven of thirteen tasks stay at level 1 because their output is public.
- **Put brand, claims and consent rules in context.** Most marketing failures start at the context layer.
- **Open every figure.** Confabulation is a known property of the models, not an edge case.
- **Record the expected outcome of every budget move.** Otherwise the learning layer has nothing to grade.

Gateway card

### Before a marketing agent goes live

- Task found in the directory and set at or below its level
- Brand and claims rules loaded into the agent's context
- Consent fields used as hard filters for any segment
- Named owner for every public channel; no publish permission for the agent
- A person opens every source in research content
- Budget moves logged with metric, expected change and check date

## Common questions

### What marketing tasks can AI agents automate today?

Competitor monitoring, lead scoring with quarterly calibration and the monthly report can run and report. Campaign variants, content briefs and interview-based drafts are reliable but should stay as drafts for a person to approve.

### Can an AI agent post to social media for a business?

Technically yes, but it should not post without a person's approval. Regulators hold the company responsible for what it publishes, and finance and crypto promotions carry specific rules.

### Does Google penalise AI-written content?

Google says it rewards quality regardless of how content is produced, but using automation mainly to manipulate rankings breaches its spam policies. Thin or duplicative pages are the practical risk.

### Should an AI agent manage the marketing budget?

It can propose moves with the evidence. A budget holder should approve each one and record the expected outcome, because dashboards often overstate the effect of the channel being optimised.

# How to Run a Marketing RFP Without Wasting a Quarter

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-run-a-marketing-rfp/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-01 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most marketing RFPs select for the best proposal writer, not the best partner, and they are expensive: an ANA and 4A's study put the cost of a typical US agency review at about $1 million across client and agencies. A good RFP describes the real situation and outcome, asks for approach and evidence rather than free work, and weights category experience and fee incentives over polish. Better still: a short brief, a few conversations and a paid first engagement.

A long agency RFP often rewards polished proposals rather than the team most likely to solve the problem, and it costs more than most buyers realise. The ANA and 4A's estimated in 2023 that a typical US agency review with three finalists costs about $1 million across the client and the agencies, and the European agency association found the average agency spends about €43,800 on each new-business pitch. A good RFP describes the real situation and outcome, asks for approach and evidence rather than free work, and weights category experience and incentives over polish. For most companies below enterprise scale, a short brief, a few conversations and a paid first engagement find the partner faster.

A request for proposals (RFP) is a formal process for selecting a vendor: the company describes what it needs, several candidates respond with proposals, and the company chooses. For marketing partners it is common at larger companies and increasingly at smaller ones that want to appear disciplined.

Most marketing RFPs select for the firm best at writing proposals. That is a different skill from the one being bought.

## What a pitch actually costs

The cost is usually invisible to the buyer, because most of it sits on the agencies' side. The ANA and 4A's interviewed more than 300 US marketers and agency executives in March 2023. They estimated a client spends about $374,000 to $409,000 running a review, a non-incumbent agency about $204,000 to compete, and an incumbent defending the account about $406,000. With three finalists, the total reached about $1 million without an incumbent and $1.2 million with one. Those figures come from large US advertisers, but the structure applies at every size.

In Europe, the European Association of Communications Agencies surveyed 412 agencies in 2025. The average agency spent about €651,000 a year on pitching, with teams of five to eight people each contributing over 44 hours per pitch. Only four in ten winning creative ideas were implemented by the client. To cover its annual pitching cost at a 10% EBITDA margin, an agency would need at least €7 million in won business.

That cost does not vanish. It is recovered in fees, from you or from other clients. A process that demands more unpaid work than the decision needs makes every candidate more expensive.

## What an RFP should contain

**The situation.** What the company does, for whom, where it is commercially, and what has been tried. Include the uncomfortable parts: the rejected ad accounts, the channel that stopped working, the budget that was cut. Candidates who know the real situation propose real things.

**The outcome sought.** Stated as a business result over a time frame, not as a list of services. "Reduce cost per funded account by a third within two quarters" invites strategy. "Provide paid social management" invites a rate card.

**The constraints.** Budget range, timeline, category restrictions, compliance requirements, internal resources, and what the company will not do.

**What is asked of respondents.** Specific, limited, and answerable in a few pages: how they would approach the outcome, who would do the work, relevant experience in this category, how they are paid, and what they would need from the company.

**How the decision will be made.** Criteria, weights, timeline, and who decides.

The industry bodies say the same about briefing. The ANA and 4A's guidelines warn that a review without a thorough brief risks "garbage in, garbage out", and recommend a brief at every phase with detail increasing as the field narrows. The WFA and Agency Mania Solutions study of 69 multinationals, reported in September and October 2026, found advertisers scored a good brief at 5.6 out of 6 as a driver of agency performance, well above financial incentives at 3.9. The brief is the cheapest performance lever the buyer has.

| Section | What it must say | What weak responses reveal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situation | Real position, including what failed | Generic plans that ignore the failures |
| Outcome | A business result and a time frame | Service lists and rate cards |
| Constraints | Budget range, restrictions, compliance, resources | Plans that need a budget you do not have |
| Ask | Approach, team, category evidence, fees, dependencies | Long credentials, little on your problem |
| Decision | Criteria, weights, timeline, decider | Lobbying the wrong person |

## What to leave out

Requests for free strategy. An RFP that asks candidates to produce a full plan, a media plan, or a creative concept is asking for unpaid work, and the firms that comply are recovering the cost from other clients or will recover it from you. The good ones increasingly decline. Ask for approach and evidence, not for the deliverable. EACA's own recommendation is that agency selection should start with credentials and case studies before any speculative strategic or creative work, and the UK's IPA asks clients to screen "the right number of agencies, at clearly defined stages" without asking them to incur excessive costs.

Long questionnaires about company history, insurance, and diversity policies before shortlisting. Collect those from the finalists.

## How to evaluate responses

Weight relevant category experience heavily, particularly for restricted categories, where a firm that has never had an account rejected will learn on your budget. Read the fee structure for the incentive it creates; our guide to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) sets out what each model rewards. Look for what the response declines to do; a firm that says "we would not recommend X for you" has thought about you. Discount polish. Check references by asking what went wrong and how the firm handled it. And meet the people who would actually do the work, not the people who sold it.

The ANA and 4A's cost study draws a further lesson: consider whether a review is needed at all. Its recommendations start with weighing alternatives to a review and investing in the existing relationship, because the disruption and delay are costs too. If the current partner has never had a clear brief, write one before replacing them.

> Never award a significant engagement on the strength of a document. Award a small one, and let the work make the case for the next.

## A shorter process that works better

For most companies below enterprise scale, a full RFP is more process than the decision needs. The alternative: a two-page brief covering situation, outcome, constraints, and budget range, sent to three to five candidates identified by reference and by evidence of category experience. A forty-five-minute conversation with each. A short written approach from the two or three that were credible, no free deliverables. Then a paid, scoped first engagement, a diagnostic with a defined end and a written output, with the preferred candidate, priced so that walking away is easy.

|  | Full RFP | Shorter process |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duration | About a quarter | About three weeks |
| Candidates | Long list, then finalists | Three to five by reference and category evidence |
| What candidates produce | Long proposals, often speculative work | A conversation and a short written approach |
| What the buyer learns | Who writes the best document | How the firm works on your actual problem |
| Final step | Award the full scope | A paid, scoped first engagement |

That process takes three weeks rather than a quarter, produces evidence rather than proposals, and selects for the firm that does the work rather than the firm that describes it. Our explainer on [what a distribution diagnostic is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-distribution-diagnostic/) sets out what that first engagement should contain, and our piece on [proposal standards](https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/) covers what a good written response looks like from the seller's side.

## The one rule

**Never award a significant engagement on the strength of a document. Award a small one, and let the work make the case for the next.**

## lowob takeaways

- **Describe the business problem.** Situation, outcome and constraints, not only a service list.
- **Do not ask for free work.** Ask for approach, evidence and the actual team.
- **Brief well.** Advertisers rate a good brief far above incentives as a driver of agency performance.
- **Use a paid first engagement.** Let a small piece of real work decide the large one.

## Common questions

### What should a marketing agency RFP include?

The real situation, including what has failed; the outcome sought as a business result over a time frame; constraints such as budget range and category restrictions; a short, specific ask of respondents; and how the decision will be made.

### How much does an agency pitch cost?

An ANA and 4A's study in 2023 estimated about $1 million in total for a typical US review with three finalists, split between client and agencies. EACA found European agencies spend about €43,800 on an average new-business pitch.

### Should agencies be paid for pitch work?

If you ask for strategy, plans or creative concepts, you are asking for real work. Either pay for it or ask instead for approach and evidence, then pay for a scoped first engagement with the preferred firm.

### How long should an agency selection process take?

For most companies below enterprise scale, about three weeks: a two-page brief, conversations with three to five candidates, short written approaches from two or three, and a paid first engagement.

Ask any agency what the fee is tied to before you sign.

# Referral Partners Without Leakage

Source: https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A B2B referral programme loses value at six points: paying for deals already in the pipeline, introductions that go cold, fees paid late or disputed, referrals diverted elsewhere, contact data passed without a lawful basis, and payments the buyer never knew about. We set out a referral record and a set of terms that close each leak, and borrow two attribution rules from the largest cloud partner programmes.

A referral partner is a firm or person who introduces a buyer and steps back: an adviser, a consultant, an accountant, a complementary vendor or a customer. Referral programmes in B2B rarely fail for lack of introductions. They fail because value leaks between the introduction and the payment, in both directions. The vendor pays for deals it already had, the partner sees its introductions go cold or its fees arrive late, and both carry regulatory risk if contact data or payments are handled loosely. Six leaks account for most of the loss, and each is closed by a rule written before the first referral, not after the first dispute.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Referral partners are the cheapest route to a warm buyer most B2B firms have. They are also the route most often run on goodwill and a spreadsheet. A founder agrees a fee over coffee, a partner sends three introductions, one closes six months later, and nobody remembers who promised what.

Our piece *Affiliate program: asset or coupon leak?* covers the consumer version of this problem: paying publishers for sales that would have happened anyway. The B2B referral problem is different. The volumes are smaller, each referral is worth more, the partner usually advises the buyer, and the relationship between vendor and partner matters more than the commission rate. Part 14 of this series covers where referral sits among partner roles. This piece covers how to run it without loss.

## Why referral partners are worth protecting

Referral partners reach buyers before vendors can. 6sense's 2025 survey of more than 4,000 buyers found that 94% of buying groups had ranked preferred vendors before first contact, and that the preferred vendor won about 80% of deals. Forrester's 2024 *State of Business Buying* found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase and advised providers to build influencer programmes so buyers trust the vendors their wider network respects. Gartner's March 2026 survey found 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience.

These are vendor and analyst surveys of self-reported behaviour. Read together, they describe a buyer who forms a shortlist from people they already trust, often without speaking to a seller. A trusted adviser who names you at that stage is worth more than most outbound activity. That is the asset the leaks erode.

## The six leaks

| Leak | What happens | Who loses | Early sign | Rule that closes it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Duplicate claim | A partner refers an account already in your pipeline or customer base | Vendor pays for revenue it had | Referred accounts with open opportunities or past contact | Check every referral against the CRM at registration; existing open opportunities are excluded |
| Cold introduction | A referral is accepted but nobody follows up for days | Both; the partner's credibility with its client suffers | Long gap between registration and first meeting | Service level for first contact, and status visible to the partner |
| Late or disputed fee | Fees depend on memory, are paid late or are argued over | Partner, then vendor when referrals stop | Partners asking for statements; referral volume falling | Fee schedule tied to cash received, with a monthly statement |
| Diverted referral | The partner sends the next buyer to a rival that pays faster or responds better | Vendor | Fewer referrals from a partner whose clients still buy in the category | Faster follow-up and outcome feedback, not only a higher fee |
| Data without a basis | The partner passes a contact's details without telling them, or without a lawful basis | Vendor carries the compliance risk | Referred contacts surprised to hear from you | Introductions made by the partner, or evidence of what the contact agreed to |
| Undisclosed payment | The buyer does not know its adviser is paid for the introduction | Both; reputational and legal exposure | Partners reluctant to mention the fee to clients | Written disclosure terms in the agreement |

The first four are commercial. The last two are regulatory, and they matter more in B2B than many firms assume.

**Data.** The UK Information Commissioner's Office guidance on buying or receiving leads says the receiving organisation is responsible for compliance with data protection law and PECR, and that "it is not enough to simply accept a third party's assurances." It asks firms to check where the data came from and whether the individual named them when they consented. For a referral programme, the clean route is a warm introduction: the partner emails the buyer and the vendor together, and the buyer replies. The vendor then holds the contact's own message as its starting record.

**Disclosure.** The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance on native advertising restates the principle in its Endorsement Guides: a third-party endorsement may be deceptive if there is an undisclosed material connection, and the FTC has acted against operators of affiliate networks as well as advertisers. The Guides themselves, as revised in July 2023, say that where a connection between endorser and seller might materially affect the weight or credibility of the endorsement and is not reasonably expected by the audience, it must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, and that material connections can include a business relationship. A paid referral from an adviser is such a connection. Many professions also have their own rules on referral payments. In the UK, section 7 of the Bribery Act 2010 makes a commercial organisation guilty of an offence if a person associated with it bribes another person. Section 8 defines an associated person as one who performs services for or on its behalf, and the defence is to have adequate procedures in place. A written referral agreement with disclosure terms is part of those procedures. The safe default is to require partners to tell their clients they are paid, and to say so in the agreement.

## The referral record

Most referral disputes are disputes about facts: who introduced whom, when, and what was already in progress. A referral record settles them in advance. It belongs in the CRM, not in a partner spreadsheet, because the duplicate check and the outcome both live there.

| Field | Why it exists |
| --- | --- |
| Partner and named contact at the partner | Who to credit and who to update |
| Referred organisation and contact | What is being claimed |
| Registration date and time | Settles "who was first" |
| Duplicate check result | Existing customer, open opportunity, or clear |
| Accepted or declined, with reason | A declined referral with a reason is still useful feedback |
| Protection window end date | How long the partner's claim lasts without a deal |
| Stage and outcome | Shared with the partner on a schedule |
| Fee due, fee paid, date paid | The statement the partner sees |
| Closed-lost reason, if lost | Tells the partner what kind of referral to send next |

The largest platforms solve the same problem at scale with explicit attribution rules. AWS asks partners to register and update opportunities in its ACE Pipeline Manager and rewards partners for originating new opportunities. Microsoft's Digital Partner of Record lets only the customer designate the servicing partner on a subscription, one partner at a time, while Partner Admin Link attributes revenue automatically from the partner's access to the customer's environment. Two lessons transfer to a 50- to 500-person firm. Attribution follows a rule both sides know in advance. And where it is cheap, the customer confirms who introduced them.

> Most referral disputes are disputes about facts. Record the facts at registration and the dispute rarely happens.

## Terms that keep partners referring

Higher fees are the instinctive response when referrals slow. They rarely fix the cause. Partners stop referring when their introductions are handled badly, when they cannot see what happened, or when payment is unreliable. The terms below address those causes first.

| Term | Recommended default | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Registration | Written, before or at the introduction, checked against the CRM within two working days | Removes duplicate claims early |
| Protection window | A fixed period, set to roughly your median sales cycle | Long enough to be fair, short enough to lapse if nothing happens |
| Fee basis | A share of revenue actually received, for a defined period | Pays for outcomes, not signatures |
| Payment timing | Within a fixed number of days of the customer's payment, on a monthly statement | Reliability matters more than rate |
| Clawback | Fee reversed if the customer is refunded within a defined period | Aligns the partner with good-fit referrals |
| Disclosure | Partner tells its client the fee exists | Removes the regulatory leak |
| Feedback | Monthly status and closed-lost reasons shared | Improves the next referral |

The fee rate itself depends on deal size, margin and how much work the partner does after the introduction, and is a pricing decision, not a programme default. Part 21 of this series covers discount and fee governance more generally. Whatever the rate, record it, and record any exception with a reason and an owner. Fee exceptions are among the commercial decisions The Build Order recommends recording first (*The commercial decisions worth recording*).

## Running the programme monthly

A referral programme with a dozen active partners needs about an hour a month of review, not a dedicated team. The review answers four questions from the referral record: how many referrals were registered and from whom; how many were duplicates; how long first contact took; and which fees are due and paid. Referral volume by partner over six months is the early warning for a diverted partner.

Our piece *The people who vouch for you* describes how a practitioner network can work as a trust system in fintech. The same logic holds here: a referral partner is lending you its reputation with a client. The programme's job is to make that loan safe to repeat.

Illustrative example: a security software firm closes its referral leaks

Decision
:   Move partner referrals from a shared spreadsheet into the CRM with registration, a duplicate check and a protection window, and pay fees monthly against cash received.

Reason and owner
:   Two partners had claimed the same account, one referral had waited eleven days for a reply, and a third partner had stopped referring after a fee arrived four months late. Owned by the head of partnerships.

What changed
:   Duplicate claims were caught at registration, first contact moved inside two working days, and partners received a monthly statement with status and closed-lost reasons. Fee exceptions were recorded with an owner.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size security software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Register before you credit.** A timestamp and a duplicate check against the CRM settle most disputes before they start.
- **Speed and visibility keep partners.** A referral that goes cold costs the partner credibility with its client.
- **Pay against cash, on schedule.** Reliable fees matter more than generous ones.
- **Close the regulatory leaks.** Prefer warm introductions to passed contact lists, and require partners to disclose that they are paid.

Gateway card

### Before you accept the next referral

- A referral record in the CRM with registration time and duplicate check
- A protection window set to your median sales cycle
- A first-contact service level the partner can see
- Fees tied to cash received, on a monthly statement
- Disclosure and data terms written into the partner agreement

## Common questions

### How do you run a B2B referral partner programme?

Register every referral in the CRM with a timestamp and duplicate check, follow up within a set time, share status and outcomes with the partner, and pay fees on a fixed schedule against revenue actually received.

### How long should a referral protection period be?

Roughly as long as your median sales cycle. Long enough that a partner is credited for a slow deal, short enough that a claim lapses if nothing is happening.

### Do referral fees need to be disclosed?

In many cases, yes. The FTC's Endorsement Guides require that a material connection the audience would not expect be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, and many professions have their own rules on referral payments. Requiring partners to disclose is the safe default.

### Can a referral partner share a prospect's contact details?

Only with care. UK ICO guidance says the receiving firm remains responsible for compliance and should check where the data came from. A warm introduction, where the prospect replies directly, is the cleaner route.

- [6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report, via Business Wire](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20251112018032/en/), 12 November 2025. Vendor research; survey of 4,000+ buyers; self-reported.
- [Forrester, The State of Business Buying 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024/), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; full report is paywalled.
- [Gartner, sales survey on rep-free buying](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), 9 March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers.
- [ICO, Direct marketing guidance: collect information and generate leads](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/direct-marketing-and-privacy-and-electronic-communications/direct-marketing-guidance/collect-information-and-generate-leads). UK regulator guidance; applies to UK data protection and PECR, not other regimes.
- [FTC, Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses](https://ftc.gov/tips-advice/business-center/guidance/native-advertising-guide-businesses), December 2015. US regulator guidance; cited for its statement of the Endorsement Guides principle on material connections.
- [eCFR, 16 CFR Part 255: Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255), as revised 26 July 2023 (88 FR 48102). Primary US regulatory text; guides, not binding rules, and written for advertising.
- [legislation.gov.uk, Bribery Act 2010, sections 7 to 9](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/ukpga/2010/23/crossheading/failure-of-commercial-organisations-to-prevent-bribery). Primary UK legislation; whether a given referral fee is a bribe depends on the facts, so take legal advice.
- [AWS, APN Customer Engagements (ACE) Program](https://aws.amazon.com/partners/programs/ace/). Vendor programme page.
- [Microsoft Learn, Link a partner ID to your accounts (PAL and DPOR)](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/partner-center/membership/link-partner-id-for-azure-performance-pal-dpor). Vendor documentation; describes Azure attribution only.
- The six leaks, the record fields and the default terms are **lowob**'s framework, not findings from these sources. Take legal advice on disclosure and data rules in your markets.

Pull every referral from the past year and check three things: how many were already in your CRM, how long first contact took, and how long fees took to pay. The worst of the three is your first leak to close.
