# A Distribution Plan for a Product the Platforms Restrict: One Fintech Company, Ninety Days.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/restricted-category-distribution-worked-example/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-09-01 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A composite consumer fintech with two rejected ad accounts and an unspent budget works through the method over ninety days: a band map built from the platforms' own policies, a one-week test of three open channels with written thresholds, one channel built properly, and the rest added in proportion. No channel ends above half of funded accounts, and nothing depended on getting past a review.

This is the restricted-category method applied to one composite company: a consumer fintech app with a yield-bearing account through a partner bank, two ad accounts rejected and a budget sitting unspent. Over ninety days it maps the bands from the platforms' own policies, spends $14,000 testing three open channels against written thresholds, builds the one that read, and adds the rest in proportion. At day ninety no channel carries more than half of funded accounts, finance can reconcile the cost per funded account, and nothing required getting past a review.

Abstract frameworks are easy to nod at. This is what the method looks like on one company.

Illustrative example: the company

Illustrative: a composite built from patterns across engagements. No figure below is a client result.

## Weeks one and two: the map and the sounding

The first job is to write down where the company cannot be seen, from each platform's own published policy, with the date it was read.

| Channel | What the policy requires | Band at week one |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meta | Financial ads to US audiences run in a special ad category: fixed age range, no gender targeting, minimum location radius, no lookalike audiences. Documentation the company can supply, with no defined review timeline | Restricted, paperwork filed |
| Google Ads | Financial services verification in the locations that require it, with licences and registration numbers; physical address and fees disclosed on the page | Restricted, paperwork filed |
| TikTok | Local licensing, disclosures and 18+ targeting; in the company's main market the product sits in a category needing pre-approval it cannot yet obtain | Closed for now |
| Programmatic exchanges | Carry the category against the company's own audience definitions | Open |
| Affiliate networks | At least one network carries the category | Open |
| Creators | Carry it with disclosure and compliant claims | Open |
| Owned email and content | No platform approval | Open |

So: two channels in the restricted band with paperwork filed and nothing forecast, one closed for now, and four open.

The second job is a one-week measurement across three of the open channels, each with a written question.

| Channel | Written question | Threshold set in advance |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Affiliate | Can comparison and personal-finance publishers produce funded accounts below $100 each on a bounty model, with the company's own tracking confirming the funding event? | Cost per funded account under $100 |
| Creators | Can mid-tier personal-finance creators, on a cost-per-funded-account basis and with pre-approved claims, produce at least forty funded accounts in a week? | 40 funded accounts |
| Programmatic | Against an audience the company defines, with a real-CPM standard and a rejection rule, can display and short video produce installs that fund at a rate comparable to organic? | Funding rate close to organic |

$14,000 across the three. Tracking in the company's own analytics. A decision written in advance for each. [Campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) explains why the decision is written before the test, and why small B2B and fintech volumes should be read as direction rather than proof.

## Week two's result

Affiliate read. Eleven publishers recruited by hand, sixty-three funded accounts confirmed, a cost per funded account of $71, no coupon partners admitted. For context, WordStream's 2026 search benchmarks put the average Google Ads cost per lead in finance and insurance at $74.44. A lead is not a funded account, so the comparison flatters search rather than affiliate; the affiliate figure is for the outcome that matters.

Creators read partially: strong cost per account from three of the eight, nothing from the rest. Programmatic did not read: installs were cheap, funding was poor, and the rejection rate on the initial buy was near zero, which explained the cheap installs.

The decision, per the written thresholds: build the affiliate programme now, expand the three creators into a structured programme, and hold programmatic until a proper desk with inventory standards can be stood up.

> None of it required getting past a review. All of it required knowing where the answer was already yes.

## Weeks three to eight: build the thing that read

The affiliate programme gets terms: a bounty on funded accounts above a minimum balance, a thirty-day cookie, a validation period long enough to catch reversals, no brand bidding, no scraped codes, coupon partners tiered at a lower rate and capped. It is placed on one network that carries the category, with a direct platform for the hand-recruited publishers. Forty partners are recruited in six weeks, each with creative, an FAQ and a compliance-approved claims sheet. [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) and our piece on [affiliate programmes that do not pay for coupon leaks](https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-program-asset-or-coupon-leak/) cover each term.

The creator programme gets a brief, disclosure language, per-creator tracking and cost-per-funded-account terms. The three that converted recruit the next tier. The disclosure language follows the US Federal Trade Commission's 2023 Endorsement Guides, which added a definition of "clear and conspicuous" and warned that a platform's built-in disclosure tool might not be adequate. The guides also set out the potential liability of advertisers as well as endorsers, which is why the claims sheet is the company's, not the creator's.

Owned channels get the neglected fix: every partner and creator link lands on a page that asks for an email, and the list gets a fortnightly message compliance has reviewed.

## Weeks nine to thirteen: add the desk

With affiliate and creators producing, programmatic is revisited under proper terms: a flat fee per account, an inclusion list, a verification standard, a rejection rule that discards inventory failing it, and a real-CPM report. The buy is optimised to funded accounts, not installs. It reads, at a higher cost per outcome than affiliate, and is kept at a size that does not crowd the channel that works. Our piece on [programmatic numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) covers the standard.

The Meta approval arrives in week eleven. It is added as a fourth channel, capped, and its outcomes compared with the others on incrementality rather than on its own attribution. The special ad category limits matter here: without lookalikes or detailed demographic targeting, Meta behaves less like a precision tool and more like broad reach, which is another reason to judge it against a holdout. [Attribution vs incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the method.

## What the numbers had to show

| Measure at day ninety | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Share of funded accounts by channel | Affiliate about half; creators about a quarter; programmatic and Meta the rest |
| Largest channel share | No channel above half |
| Largest partner share | No partner above a third of affiliate outcomes |
| Cost per funded account | A real figure finance can reconcile, by channel |
| Owned audience | An email list that did not exist in week one |
| Band map | A written record of which channels are closed and why |

At no point did the company attempt to disguise its category or open a replacement account. Google's circumventing systems policy suspends accounts for that on detection, without warning and permanently. The plan would have been worth less than the risk.

A restricted-category distribution plan is a map, a week of cheap measurement, one channel built properly, and the rest added in proportion. The approvals are a bonus, never the foundation.

## lowob takeaways

- **Map from the platforms' own pages.** Record the band, the requirement and the date for every channel.
- **Write the threshold before the test.** Each open channel answers one question with a number set in advance.
- **Build the channel that read, with terms.** Bounties on funded accounts, validation periods and coupon caps.
- **Add late approvals capped.** Judge them on incrementality against the channels already working.
- **End with no channel above half.** The map, the list and a reconciled cost per funded account are the assets.

## Common questions

### How do you build a distribution plan for a fintech the ad platforms restrict?

Map every channel as open, restricted or closed from the platforms' own policies, test two or three open channels for a week against written thresholds, build the one that reads properly, and file restricted applications with nothing forecast against them.

### What is a good cost per funded account for a fintech affiliate programme?

It depends on account value and retention. Set the threshold from your own unit economics before testing; in this composite it was under $100, and the programme read at $71.

### How should affiliate terms for a fintech be structured?

Pay a bounty on funded accounts above a minimum balance, with a validation period that catches reversals, no brand bidding, no scraped codes, and coupon partners tiered lower and capped.

### What changes when a Meta financial ad approval finally arrives?

Add it as a capped channel and compare it with the others on incrementality. For US audiences it runs in a special ad category without lookalikes, so judge it against a holdout rather than its own attribution.

Write the three test questions for your own open channels this week, each with a threshold set from your unit economics, and agree with finance which event counts as a funded account before any money is spent.

# AI Is Making Execution Cheap. Judgment Is Becoming the Marketing Moat.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/judgment-is-the-moat/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-31 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI has made marketing output fast and cheap, and most B2B teams now use it to create content under pressure to produce more. Volume is no longer a differentiator. The advantage moves to judgment: choosing the problem, checking the claims, keeping an accountable person on consequential decisions, and measuring what changed rather than what shipped.

A team can now produce a month's worth of posts, landing-page drafts and campaign ideas in an afternoon. If nobody has decided who the work is for or what it needs to accomplish, faster production does not solve much. In the Content Marketing Institute's 2026 survey, 88% of B2B marketers said their organisation uses AI content tools and 65% faced more pressure to produce content faster. When everyone can produce, knowing what is worth publishing, and checking whether it worked, is the advantage.

This is a useful distinction for companies buying AI marketing tools or hiring people to use them. Producing the material is getting easier. Knowing *what is worth publishing* remains difficult. Our task-by-task review of [AI agents in marketing](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-marketing-what-they-can-do-now/) covers what the tools can do; this piece is about what they cannot decide.

## More output isn't the same as better marketing

AI can turn a founder interview into a blog post, a newsletter, a series of social updates and a set of sales messages. It can summarise competitors, suggest headlines and help a small team do work that previously required several specialists. Those are real advantages.

But they only help when the underlying idea is worth communicating. The Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs surveyed 861 B2B marketers between June and August 2026. 88% said their organisation uses AI-powered content creation tools, and 60% of those had expanded their use in the past year. 65% said they faced more pressure to produce content faster. The most cited AI content problems were ensuring accuracy and maintaining quality control, each at 54%, and maintaining brand voice at 52%. This is a self-reported survey, not proof that more content made those businesses more successful.

The wider evidence on AI value points the same way. McKinsey's 2025 global survey found 88% of organisations using AI in at least one function, but only 39% attributing any enterprise-level EBIT impact to it, mostly under 5%. The minority that reported significant value were nearly three times as likely to have redesigned workflows, and more likely to have defined when model outputs need human validation. Adoption is common. Results follow from how the work is organised.

When so many teams can produce the same kinds of material, the number of articles or social posts published is a poor measure of whether the marketing is doing its job. Our piece [AI made average marketing cheaper](https://lowob.com/research/ai-made-average-marketing-cheaper/) makes the same point about quality.

> A team that knows when not to publish has an advantage over one that treats every draft as an asset.

## What judgment looks like in an actual project

Imagine a DeFi app whose website attracts visitors but whose wallet-connection numbers barely move. An AI assistant can suggest dozens of campaigns about the product's yield, its security and the size of the market. It cannot settle the basic question on its own: **are people confused by the message, or is the product itself difficult to use?**

The first useful move is to look at the experience. Where do visitors leave? Can they tell what happens after connecting a wallet? Do the people the company hopes to reach actually trust the product? If the problem is an unclear deposit process, commissioning more promotional content is unlikely to fix it.

This example is hypothetical, but the distinction is practical. Choosing the next piece of content depends on knowing what is stopping customers, not just on having a tool capable of writing it.

Good marketing judgment is often a sequence of ordinary decisions: choose one audience, understand what it needs to believe, test whether your claims are supportable, and decide which work deserves time or money. The final output comes after that thinking, not instead of it. [Content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) turns that sequence into a one-page brief.

## Give AI a clear job, and keep people responsible for the decisions

AI is most useful when a team can tell whether its work is right. Those tasks are easier to review because the underlying information is available.

| Task | Can the team check it? | Who decides |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Organise interview notes or call transcripts | Yes, against the source | AI prepares, a person reviews |
| Compare drafts with approved product facts | Yes, against the fact sheet | AI flags, a person corrects |
| Summarise objections from sales calls | Yes, against the calls | AI drafts, a person confirms |
| Prepare variants of a message already chosen for testing | Yes, against the brief | AI drafts, a person approves |
| Make claims about safety, reliability or performance | Only with specialist knowledge | A named expert, before publication |
| Choose the audience, the budget or the position | Not by the model | An accountable person |

It is less sensible to let a polished draft quietly become the company's position. A model can produce convincing claims about a protocol's safety, an AI product's reliability or a fintech service's advantages without knowing whether the company can substantiate them. Even specialist tools built on retrieval get this wrong: Stanford researchers found leading legal research products gave incorrect information in more than 17% of benchmark queries in 2024. Someone with the relevant knowledge still needs to check the claims before they are published.

The stakes have risen because buyers increasingly read without a seller present. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Its analyst noted that sellers "can't rely on static collateral to carry influence in those moments". A wrong claim in published content now travels further, and gets summarised by someone else's model.

**Use AI to prepare.** Gather notes, organise information, explore possible explanations and make first drafts that people can inspect.

**Use evidence to choose.** Look at customer questions, product use, sales objections and campaign results before deciding what deserves attention.

**Keep someone accountable.** Name the person who approves the claim, the audience, the budget and the final published work.

## Measure whether the decision helped

Suppose the DeFi app decides to replace five generic awareness posts with one explanation of the deposit process. The useful measure isn't that the article was delivered quickly. It's whether people who read it understand the product better and complete the next step more often. The team should also check whether any improvement was caused by a product change or a different audience, not assume the article deserves all the credit. [Campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set that test up.

| Business | Activity measure (weak) | Outcome measure (stronger) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumer DeFi app (illustrative) | Posts published | Readers who complete a deposit |
| Infrastructure sold to businesses | Articles shipped | Fewer confused sales calls; more conversations with the right buyers |
| Developer product | Docs pages added | Successful integrations |

The measures should follow the commercial problem.

More AI-assisted work can be good. More unnecessary work is still unnecessary. A team that knows when *not* to publish has an advantage over one that treats every draft as an asset.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with the problem, not the prompt.** Know whom you're trying to help and what is currently stopping them.
- **Let AI speed up work you can evaluate.** Research summaries and drafts are useful when someone can verify the result.
- **Keep consequential decisions with an accountable person.** Product claims, audience priorities and budget choices need real context and ownership.
- **Judge the work by what changed.** Published assets are evidence of activity; customer understanding and valuable actions tell you more about effectiveness.

## Common questions

### How many marketers use AI to create content?

Most. In the Content Marketing Institute's 2026 survey of 861 B2B marketers, 88% said their organisation uses AI-powered content creation tools, and 65% reported more pressure to produce content faster.

### What marketing work should AI do, and what should people do?

Give AI work the team can check: organising notes, comparing drafts with approved facts, summarising objections and preparing variants. Keep claims, audience choice, budget and final approval with a named person.

### Does publishing more AI content improve marketing results?

Not by itself. Surveys show volume rising, but not that the extra content improved results. Measure outcomes such as completed next steps or fewer confused sales calls instead of output.

### Who should approve AI-generated marketing claims?

Someone with the relevant product, legal or technical knowledge, named in advance. A model can write convincing claims the company cannot substantiate.

Read it for where budgets are moving, not for what works.

# Revenue Models for Long Cycles

Source: https://lowob.com/research/revenue-models-for-long-cycles/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-31 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pick an emerging tech revenue model by who carries the capital and the service tail, price pilots and production differently, and report only what would survive due diligence. Gross margin per unit including measured service cost decides whether any model works, and contracted cash flows decide whether the units can be financed with debt instead of equity.

Pick the revenue model by who carries the capital and the service tail, price pilots and production differently, and report only what would survive due diligence. The revenue model also decides how the company is financed. US federal energy lenders, for example, prefer technology at readiness level 8, deny pilot and demonstration projects and look for contracted cash flows, so the contract terms you write today decide whether your fiftieth unit is funded by debt or by more dilution.

## Five models, one question

Every emerging tech revenue model answers the same question: who carries the capital and who carries the risk of the thing not working. Match the model to the answer your buyer and your balance sheet can live with.

**Hardware plus service** is the default. The buyer pays for the unit upfront and a recurring fee for software, monitoring, maintenance and updates. Capital sits with the buyer. Your margin is visible on day one. The weakness is that the upfront price triggers capex approval, which is often the slowest door in the building.

**Hardware-as-a-service** moves the unit onto your balance sheet and charges a monthly or annual fee. The buyer's capex problem disappears. Yours appears. This model works only with financing behind it: equipment finance, a leasing partner or a project finance vehicle. Without that, every unit you deploy consumes equity, and the runway maths in [Raising for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/) breaks.

**Outcome or usage pricing** charges per inspection, per kWh delivered, per verification, per task completed. It aligns you with the buyer completely. It also requires two things most early companies lack: a measurement the buyer trusts and enough deployment history to price the risk. Use it only when both exist, and expect to start with a floor fee. Our explainer on [outcome-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/) covers the same trade-off in software.

**Licensing and royalties** suit IP-heavy companies with an OEM route, as [Integrators, OEMs and channel partners](https://lowob.com/research/integrators-oems-and-channel-partners/) described. Low margin per unit, no service tail, wide reach. Pair a licence fee with a per-unit royalty and a minimum commitment.

**Network or token models** apply to DePIN and only if the test in [Token or no token](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) is passed: the token must do a job the network cannot do without it. If it fails that test, it is a financing mechanism dressed as a revenue model and will be priced as one.

| Model | Who carries capital | Service tail risk | Needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hardware plus service | Buyer | You, priced in | Clear unit economics |
| Hardware-as-a-service | You | You | Financing partner |
| Outcome or usage | You | You | Trusted measurement |
| Licence and royalty | OEM | OEM | Protected IP, minimums |
| Network or token | Network | Operators | The token test passed |

## Gross margin and the service tail

The number that decides whether any of this works is gross margin per unit including the service tail. Not hardware margin. Not software margin. The blended number after field service, spares, remote monitoring, firmware support and the hours a customer success engineer spends on site.

Most emerging tech companies know their bill of materials and guess their service cost. Measure it from the first deployment. Log every site visit, every spare, every support hour against the unit it served. After ten units you will have a real number. It will be worse than the model. That is fine. Price the next contracts on it, using [value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/) where the buyer's saving is measurable.

> Before a deployment passes its success test, the unit is research. After, it is a financeable asset.

## Project finance or equity

[Raising for long cycles](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/) covered the capital stack. The revenue model decides which layer pays for what.

Equity pays for things that reduce technical and commercial risk: engineering, the first deployments, the playbook. Project finance or asset finance pays for things that are already de-risked: the fiftieth unit of a design that has run for a year at three sites. Using equity to fund fleet deployment is the most common and most expensive mistake in this vertical. Using debt before the design is stable is the second.

Lenders state the line plainly. Mayer Brown's August 2026 guide to the US Office of Energy Dominance Financing, formerly the Loan Programs Office, says projects must use technically viable and commercially ready technology, with a preferred technology readiness level of 8, and that research, pilot or demonstration projects will be denied. It advises applicants to consider long-term offtake agreements or other contracted cash flows, notes that sponsors must contribute significant equity, and says loans cannot exceed 80% of eligible project costs, with debt typically covering 40% to 60% and direct loans typically $500 million or more. Most startups will never borrow at that scale, but private equipment lenders ask the same questions at smaller sizes.

Public grant programmes draw a similar line earlier. The EU's EIC Accelerator offers grants from technology readiness level 6 to 8 and reserves its equity for market entry at level 9. In the US, the SBIR Strategic Breakthrough awards created in April 2026, worth up to $30 million, go only to companies with a prior Phase II award and must be matched dollar for dollar by new private capital or other funds. Investors are funding the category: Carta's platform data shows hardware capital rising from $8.6 billion to $14.3 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026. But each source funds a specific stage of proof.

| Stage of proof | What funds it well | What the revenue contract must show |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lab to first field unit | Grants, seed equity | Nothing yet; a defined success test |
| Paid pilot | Equity, pilot fees | Fixed fee, scope, success test, conversion price |
| First production contracts | Equity, strategic capital | Term, minimums, service level |
| Fleet deployment | Equipment, asset or project finance | Contracted cash flows a lender can underwrite |

The line between equity and debt is the same success test from [First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet](https://lowob.com/research/first-customers-in-a-market-that-doesnt-exist-yet/). Once a deployment has passed it, the unit is a financeable asset. Before that, it is research.

## Pilots as projects, production as contracts

Price a pilot as a project. Fixed scope, fixed fee, fixed duration, a defined success test and a stated conversion price if it passes. The fee should cover your cost. A free pilot teaches the buyer that your product is worth nothing and teaches you nothing about their procurement.

Price production as a contract with a term. A minimum number of units or sites, a minimum duration, a service level, a renewal clause and an exit cost. The term is what makes contracted annual value a real number and what makes the business financeable, because it is the contracted cash flow a lender reads.

Never let a pilot drift into production on pilot terms. Set the conversion date in the pilot agreement. Our guide to [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to test a conversion price without discounting the first contracts away.

## What to report, and what to stop

[Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) said report what happened, not who saw it. For emerging tech, the equivalent is to stop reporting intent.

| Report | Stop reporting |
| --- | --- |
| Paid pilots converted to contracts, as a count and a rate | Letters of intent |
| Contracted annual value, with term | Pipeline value |
| Gross margin per unit including service | Hardware margin alone |
| Deployment lead time from signature to commissioning | Units "ordered" with no deposit or delivery date |
| Performance against the success test, per site | Demo results |
| Risk retired this quarter, in plain words | Category size |

Each item in the right-hand column is a story about the future. Investors have heard the story. Customers never see it. Neither will pay for it. The left-hand column is what a board can trust, as our guide to [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) sets out.

## Closing the series

This piece closes the emerging tech section of Raise, Rally, Revenue. The spine applies everywhere: one system, one product truth, evidence before the raise, a round run like a sales process, community with a job, design partners, distribution built because the platforms are closed, measurement instead of reach, and a company that runs without you. Each vertical changes who buys, what proof counts, which channels are open and what to measure. [The whole series on one page](https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/) sets out the order and the vertical table, and [How to raise for an emerging tech company](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-raise-for-an-emerging-tech-company/) brings the fundraising parts together.

The order matters more than any tactic. Every failure we have seen in this series came from doing a right thing at the wrong time.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the model by who carries capital and the service tail.** Then check your balance sheet can carry your part.
- **Measure service cost from unit one.** Gross margin including service is the number that decides.
- **Write contracts a lender can read.** Terms, minimums and contracted cash flows turn units into financeable assets.
- **Report what happened.** Converted pilots and contracted annual value, never intent.

## Common questions

### How should a hardware startup price a pilot?

As a project with fixed scope, fee and duration, a defined success test and a stated conversion price. The fee should cover cost, and the conversion date should be set in the pilot agreement.

### When does hardware-as-a-service make sense?

Only with financing behind it, such as equipment finance, a leasing partner or a project finance vehicle, and only for a design that has passed its success test. Without that, every deployed unit consumes equity.

### Should deep tech companies use equity or project finance for deployments?

Equity should fund what reduces technical and commercial risk. Project or asset finance should fund units of a proven design with contracted cash flows; US federal energy lenders, for example, deny pilot and demonstration projects.

### What should emerging tech companies report to their board?

Converted pilots as a count and rate, contracted annual value with term, gross margin per unit including service, deployment lead time, performance against the success test and risk retired. Not letters of intent or pipeline value.

Law firm guide; US federal energy and critical minerals lending only.

Pull every site visit, spare and support hour logged against your deployed units and calculate gross margin per unit including service. Then reread your open pilot agreements and add a conversion date to any that lack one.

# Supersede, Never Overwrite

Source: https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-31 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A memory that edits itself in place cannot explain itself, because the change is the information. Judgment records should keep two dates (when a view was true and when it was held) and replace old views by linked supersession rather than editing them. Databases, architecture decision records and at least one agent-memory design already work this way.

Finance already knows how to store what was true and when it was known. Apply the same discipline to beliefs. A memory that edits itself in place cannot explain itself, and the change is the information. Judgment records should carry two dates (when a view was valid and when the organisation held it), and a changed view should be a new record linked to the old one by an explicit supersession, with a date, an author, a reason and a trigger.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

Most knowledge stores are updated like documents: open, edit, save. The previous version may survive in a history panel nobody reads. For a judgment system this is fatal, because when an organisation changes its mind, the change itself, and the reason for it, is the most valuable thing to record. Our explainer on [the decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) sets out the fields; this piece is about what happens when one of them changes.

## Two clocks, not one

Data teams have long distinguished between two times. Martin Fowler's account of bitemporal history calls them **actual time**, when something was true in the world, and **record time**, when we learned it and what we believed at each point. Risk and regulatory teams often call them as-of and as-at. A restated figure has an as-of date in the past and an as-at date today.

Fowler's worked example is a salary. Payroll runs on 25 February at the old rate. On 15 March, HR reports a raise effective 15 February. On 5 April, HR corrects the amount. The record of what was believed on 25 February must stay as it was, because a payment was made on that belief, while the actual history is revised twice. Records are appended, not overwritten.

The database world standardised this. SQL:2011 introduced application-time periods, which track "the history of the thing out there", and system-versioned tables, which track when the database changed. A 2019 survey of implementations found IBM DB2 and MariaDB supporting bitemporal tables that combine both, and every major database surveyed supporting at least one kind of period.

| Clock | Question it answers | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| As-of (actual or valid time) | When was this view true? | "Account at risk from 1 March" |
| As-at (record or transaction time) | When did the organisation hold this view? | "Recorded on 20 March, replaced on 2 June" |

Judgment records need the same two clocks. When was this assessment valid? And when did the organisation hold it? Without both, you cannot answer the question every review eventually asks: what did we believe at the time we decided?

## What a supersession records

When a new view replaces an old one, the old record is not edited. A new record is created, linked to the old one by an explicit supersedes relation. Software teams already do this with architecture decision records. Fowler's reference entry, updated in March 2026, says an accepted record "should never be reopened or changed - instead it should be superseded", so that the log shows what was decided and how long each decision governed the work.

Agent memory can do it automatically. Zep's published design keeps two timelines for every fact: the order of events and the order of ingestion. When new information contradicts an existing fact, the system sets the old fact's end date to the new fact's start date rather than deleting it, preserving what its authors call "historical records of relationship evolution over time". This is a vendor's description of its own product, but it shows the pattern is buildable.

The link should carry four things:

| Field | What to write | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Date | When the view changed | Fixes the as-at boundary |
| Author | Who made the change | Accountability and a person to ask |
| Reason | One sentence | The most useful line in the record |
| Trigger | New evidence, correction of an error, or reinterpretation of the same evidence | Separates learning from wavering |

That last field is underrated. An organisation that frequently changes its mind on the same evidence has a different problem from one that changes its mind because new facts arrived. Fowler's salary example contains both: the raise was new information, the corrected amount was an error.

> When an organisation changes its mind, the change, and the reason for it, is the most valuable thing to record.

## What it buys

**Hindsight-free review.** Baruch Fischhoff's 1975 experiments found that people told an outcome judged it as more inevitable than people who were not told, which he called "creeping determinism". A past decision reviewed against today's knowledge will look either obvious or reckless. Judged against what was knowable at the time, it is fairer to the people who made it and more useful for learning. Our piece on [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers how outcomes return to the record.

**Regulatory answers.** "What did you believe when you approved this, and on what basis?" becomes a query rather than a forensic exercise. Under the EU AI Act, once the high-risk rules apply (from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems, as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744), deployers of high-risk systems must keep automatically generated logs for at least six months; a supersession history gives those logs a business meaning. Our explainer on [the AI audit trail](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/) covers the wider requirement.

**Reversal patterns.** Over time you can see which kinds of belief the organisation revises most often, and how long each view typically survives. A view that is reversed every six months is telling you something about how it is formed.

**Replay.** You can rerun a decision with the record as it stood, to test whether a new model or process would have done better on the same information.

**Cleaner retrieval.** Memory benchmarks find systems weakest on questions about how a fact changed. Explicit supersession links let a system return a timeline instead of guessing one, as argued in [Retrieval is not the bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/).

## The cost

Storage and a little discipline. Records grow by a fraction of their size each time a view changes. Retrieval needs to default to current records and expose history on request. Both are trivial next to an organisation that cannot say why it changed its mind.

The one real design choice is deletion. Where a record must be erased for legal reasons, the supersession chain should keep a tombstone saying something was removed, when and why, as set out in [Keep the sources; let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/).

## In practice

Add as-of and as-at dates to every judgment record. Replace edit-in-place with supersession: new record, explicit link, date, author, reason, trigger. Default retrieval to current records, with history one click away.

Once a quarter, list the most frequently reversed views and ask why. Split them by trigger: a high share of reinterpretations of the same evidence is the signal to look at how those views are formed.

**What would prove this wrong:** organisations with edit-in-place memory doing as well on hindsight-free review, regulatory reconstruction and learning from reversals as those with full supersession history. Then the history is not earning its keep.

## lowob takeaways

- **Keep two clocks.** As-of for when a view was true, as-at for when it was held.
- **Supersede, never overwrite.** New record, explicit link, date, author, reason.
- **Record the trigger.** New evidence, correction and reinterpretation are different problems.
- **Default to current.** History one click away, not in the way.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between as-of and as-at dates?

As-of is when something was true in the world. As-at is when the organisation knew or recorded it. Database designers call these actual (or valid) time and record (or transaction) time.

### Why should a knowledge base never overwrite old entries?

When an organisation changes its mind, the change and its reason are the most valuable thing to record. Edit-in-place makes it impossible to say what was believed at the time of a decision.

### What should a supersession record contain?

The date of the change, who made it, the reason in a sentence, and the trigger: new evidence, correction of an error, or reinterpretation of the same evidence.

### How do AI agent memories handle facts that change?

Better designs mark the old fact invalid from a date and link it to the new one, rather than deleting it. Zep's temporal knowledge graph, for example, keeps both event time and ingestion time for every fact.

## Sources and notes

- [Martin Fowler, Bitemporal History](https://www.martinfowler.com/articles/bitemporal-history.html), 7 April 2021. Practitioner reference; the salary example is his.
- [Paul A. Jungwirth, Survey of SQL:2011 Temporal Features](https://illuminatedcomputing.com/posts/2019/08/sql2011-survey/), September 2019. Independent practitioner survey; database support may have changed since.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), 24 March 2026. Practitioner reference; credits Nygard's 2011 original.
- [Rasmussen et al., Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory](https://arxiv.org/html/2501.13956), January 2025. Vendor research paper describing its own product.
- [Fischhoff, Hindsight is not equal to foresight (PSNet summary)](https://psnet.ahrq.gov/issue/hindsight-foresight-effect-outcome-knowledge-judgment-under-uncertainty), *Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance* 1(3), 1975. Laboratory experiments; summary page from AHRQ.

- The four supersession fields and the quarterly reversal review are **lowob**'s working method.

Add as-of and as-at dates to your decision records this week, and change the edit button to "supersede". The first time someone changes a view, ask them for the trigger.

# What Is a Large Language Model (LLM)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-large-language-model/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-31 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A large language model is a neural network trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token. Most use the Transformer architecture published in 2017. Costs have fallen sharply, with GPT-3.5-level performance dropping more than 280-fold in price in about two years, which makes the model the cheapest and most replaceable part of any AI system.

A large language model (LLM) is a neural network trained on very large amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it write, summarise, classify and answer questions in plain language. Most current LLMs use the Transformer architecture, first published in 2017. An LLM is the reasoning engine inside assistants and agents, not the whole product. It knows what it was trained on and what you put in front of it, nothing more.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What a large language model means

An LLM is a statistical model of language. During training it reads a very large body of text and adjusts billions of internal numbers, called parameters, so that it gets better at predicting the next piece of text. "Large" refers to both the training data and the parameter count.

The design that made this practical is the Transformer. The 2017 paper that introduced it proposed an architecture "based solely on attention mechanisms", dropping the recurrent designs that came before. Attention lets the model weigh every part of the input against every other part, which suits long passages of text.

The commercial turning point came with scale. OpenAI's GPT-3 paper in May 2020 showed that a 175-billion-parameter model could perform new tasks from a few examples written into the prompt, with no retraining. It handled translation, question answering and three-digit arithmetic this way. That finding is why instructions and examples in a prompt matter so much today.

| An LLM is | An LLM is not |
| --- | --- |
| A model that predicts likely text from its input | A database that looks facts up |
| The reasoning component inside an assistant or agent | The assistant, agent or product itself |
| Fixed at its training date unless given new context | Aware of your CRM, inbox or files by default |
| Probabilistic, so outputs vary from run to run | A guarantee that an answer is true |

## How it works, and why it matters for a commercial team

Text goes in and is split into tokens. The model calculates the probability of each possible next token, picks one, adds it to the text and repeats. A paragraph of output is a few hundred of these steps. Pricing follows the same unit: providers charge per million tokens read and written.

Three practical consequences follow. First, an LLM does not check sources unless it is connected to them, through retrieval or a protocol such as MCP. Second, it can produce fluent text that is wrong; NIST's July 2024 generative AI profile calls this confabulation. Third, the same prompt can give different answers, so quality has to be measured over many runs, not judged from one.

For a revenue or operations team, the useful tasks are bounded ones: summarising a call, drafting an account brief, classifying inbound enquiries, or producing a first-pass answer to a questionnaire for a person to check. The model does the language work. The data, the permissions and the decision stay with the business.

Cost is moving in the buyer's favour. Stanford's 2025 AI Index reports that querying a model at GPT-3.5's level (64.8% on the MMLU benchmark) fell from $20 to $0.07 per million tokens in about 18 months, a more than 280-fold drop. Depending on the task, it found inference prices falling between 9 and 900 times a year.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, the LLM sits in the reasoning stage of the loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning, learning. It is the part most likely to be swapped as prices fall and models improve. That is the argument for renting the model and owning the record of what was decided and why.

## How to choose and use one

Most commercial teams will not train a model. The choice is which hosted model to use, through which product, for which task.

| Criterion | What to check | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Task fit | Run 20 to 50 real examples from your own work | Public benchmarks rarely match your documents |
| Context window | How much text fits in one request | Limits how much account history it can read at once |
| Price | Input and output price per million tokens | Output usually costs several times more than input |
| Data terms | Whether your inputs are retained or used for training | Determines what you can safely send |
| Access route | Chat seat, API or a tool that embeds a model | Affects logging, permissions and cost control |

The common mistakes are predictable. Teams treat the model as a source of facts rather than a reader of facts supplied to it. They pick a model from a leaderboard rather than from their own test set. They let it send client-facing text without review. Each is fixed by design rather than by a better model: supply the data, write a small evaluation, and keep a person between the draft and the send.

## lowob takeaways

- **An LLM predicts text.** It is fluent by design and accurate only when given the right context.
- **The model is the replaceable part.** Prices fell more than 280-fold in two years; plan to switch.
- **Test on your own work.** Twenty real examples tell you more than a public benchmark.
- **Keep a person before the send.** Fluent and wrong is the default failure, not the exception.

## Common questions

### What is a large language model in simple terms?

It is an AI system trained on a very large amount of text to predict the next word or word fragment. That one skill lets it draft, summarise, translate and answer questions.

### How is an LLM different from ChatGPT or Claude?

ChatGPT and Claude are products. Each runs one or more LLMs and adds an interface, memory, tools, safety controls and account management around them.

### Do large language models know my company's data?

Not by default. A model knows its training data up to a cut-off date. It sees your data only when it is supplied in the prompt, through retrieval or through connected tools.

### Why do LLMs make things up?

They generate likely text, not verified text. NIST calls this confabulation. Grounding answers in supplied sources and reviewing outputs reduces the risk but does not remove it.

## Sources and notes

- [Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), June 2017. Original Transformer paper; academic preprint.
- [Brown et al., Language Models are Few-Shot Learners](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165), May 2020. OpenAI's GPT-3 paper; authors' own results.
- [Stanford HAI, AI Index 2025: State of AI in 10 Charts](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-index-2025-state-of-ai-in-10-charts), April 2025. Independent academic index; prices are list prices at a fixed benchmark level.
- [NIST, AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. US standards body guidance.
- [OpenAI, What are tokens and how to count them](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/4936856-what-are-tokens-and-how-to-count-them), accessed November 2026. Vendor help article; ratios are approximate and for English.

- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)

## Next move

Pick one recurring writing task, such as call summaries, and collect 20 past examples with the outputs you would have accepted. Run them through the model your team already pays for and score the results.

# Workflow Automation vs AI Agents: Which Do You Need?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/workflow-automation-vs-ai-agents/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Workflow automation follows a path designed in advance; an AI agent decides its next step at run time. Anthropic and OpenAI both advise starting with the simplest option, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by 2027. Most commercial processes need a workflow with a model step inside it, and an agent only where judgment or unstructured input dominates.

Workflow automation runs a fixed sequence of steps that a person designed in advance; an AI agent is given a goal and decides its own steps and tool calls as it works. Workflows are predictable, cheap per run and easy to audit. Agents handle judgment, exceptions and unstructured inputs, at higher cost and with less predictable behaviour. Most commercial processes need a workflow with one or two model steps inside it, not an agent.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the two terms mean

Workflow automation is a trigger, a set of conditions and a list of actions. A new form submission arrives, the system checks territory and company size, creates a CRM record and assigns an owner. Tools in this category include Zapier, Make, n8n, Microsoft Power Automate and the workflow builders inside most CRMs. The path is written down before the first run.

A model can sit inside a workflow without turning it into an agent. A step that classifies an email, extracts fields from call notes or drafts a reply still sits on a fixed path. Anthropic's December 2024 guide calls these LLM workflows and describes patterns such as prompt chaining and routing.

An agent works in a loop. It reads the goal, chooses an action, calls a tool, reads the result and decides what to do next, until it judges the task complete. Nobody knows the exact path in advance, which is the source of both its flexibility and its risk. Automation vendors draw the same line: UiPath's documentation describes its robots as "deterministic, rule-based" and its agents as "probabilistic, adaptive".

| Dimension | Workflow automation | AI agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who decides the next step | The designer, in advance | The model, at run time |
| Typical inputs | Structured fields, known formats | Emails, documents, transcripts, mixed sources |
| Same input, same output | Yes | Not guaranteed |
| Cost per run | Low and fixed | Higher, varies with the steps taken |
| How to audit | Read the flow definition and event log | Step-level traces of each decision and tool call |
| Typical failure | Stops visibly on an unexpected input | Proceeds confidently down a wrong path |

## How to decide for a commercial process

The first test is whether the rules can be written down. If a sales operations lead can describe the routing logic on one page, a workflow will run it more reliably and more cheaply than an agent. OpenAI's guide makes the same point: if a use case does not clearly need judgment, unwieldy rules or unstructured data, a deterministic solution may be enough.

The second test is how much the input varies. Call notes and inbound emails are unstructured, but the destination is often fixed: a workflow with a model step.

The third test is whether the steps themselves change from case to case. Preparing for a renewal call can mean reading the CRM, the last three support tickets, recent email threads and a usage report, in a different order for each account. That is where an agent earns its cost.

| Commercial task | Recommended approach | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Route inbound leads by territory and size | Workflow | Rules are known and stable |
| Enrich a new contact from a data provider | Workflow | Fixed API calls in a fixed order |
| Turn call notes into CRM fields | Workflow with a model step | Unstructured input, fixed destination |
| Draft a renewal brief from CRM, email and tickets | Agent at autonomy level 1 (draft) | Sources and steps vary by account |
| Draft answers to a buyer's security questionnaire | Agent at level 1, with human approval | Judgment across many documents |

## Common mistakes

**Buying an agent for a rules problem.** Gartner describes "agent washing": AI assistants and chatbots without meaningful agentic capability rebranded as agents. If the vendor's demo follows the same path every time, the product is a workflow and should be priced and governed like one.

**Letting autonomy follow capability.** **lowob** treats autonomy as a dial: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. An agent that can send email does not need to. On the commercial line, nothing sends without a person, whether the sender is a workflow or an agent.

**Skipping the record.** A workflow's behaviour is documented in its definition. An agent's is not, so each run needs a trace of what it read, what it decided and why.

**Ignoring cost per run.** Agents call models several times per task, so a high-volume process can cost far more as an agent than as a workflow with one model step.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with the rules test.** If the logic fits on one page, build a workflow.
- **Put models inside workflows first.** Classification, extraction and drafting rarely need an agent.
- **Reserve agents for variable paths.** Use them where the steps change by case, not only the inputs.
- **Set the autonomy level separately.** Capability to act is not permission to act.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between workflow automation and an AI agent?

Workflow automation follows a sequence of steps designed in advance. An AI agent is given a goal and decides its own steps and tool calls at run time.

### Is a Zapier flow with ChatGPT in it an AI agent?

Usually not. If the steps are fixed and the model only classifies, extracts or drafts within one step, it is a workflow with a model step.

### When should a company use an AI agent instead of automation?

When the task needs judgment, the rules have become too complex to maintain, or the steps vary with unstructured inputs from case to case.

### Are AI agents more expensive than workflow automation?

Generally yes per run, because an agent calls a model several times and its path varies. Anthropic notes agents trade latency and cost for task performance.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), 19 December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance; definitions of workflows and agents.
- [OpenAI, A practical guide to building agents](https://cdn.openai.com/business-guides-and-resources/a-practical-guide-to-building-agents.pdf), 2025. Vendor guide; criteria for when to build an agent.
- [Reuters via The Star, Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027, Gartner says](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says), 25 June 2025. News report of a Gartner analyst prediction, not a measured outcome.
- [UiPath, About agents](https://docs.uipath.com/agents/automation-cloud/latest/user-guide/about-agents), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation contrasting deterministic robots with probabilistic agents.

## Next move

List the ten most repetitive tasks in your sales and customer teams and mark each one "rules" or "judgment". Build the rules tasks as workflows first, and pilot an agent only on one judgment task, at the draft level.

# What Is Account Planning?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-planning/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Account planning sets out, for one important customer, what they are trying to achieve, where you can help, and who will do what by when. Gartner research suggests most key account programmes underperform, and that plans which are kept current do measurably better. This explainer covers what an account plan contains, why plans fail, and how a mid-size firm can write one that stays alive.

Account planning is the practice of writing, and then keeping current, a plan for growing a specific existing customer. A good plan starts from the customer's goals rather than your product list, names the people on both sides, sets objectives with measures, and assigns actions to owners. Its value comes from being used in decisions every month, not from being completed once a year.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What account planning means

Account planning applies to customers you already have, usually the 10 to 50 that matter most to revenue. For each one, the team writes down what the customer is trying to achieve, how their organisation makes decisions, where the relationship is strong or thin, and which opportunities are worth pursuing.

It is related to account-based marketing but not the same thing. Account-based marketing coordinates marketing and sales effort against a list of target accounts, often before they are customers. Account planning is the operating plan for growing one relationship, owned by the account lead and reviewed with the people who serve that customer.

CRM vendors now treat the plan as a record type. Salesforce's Account Plans feature, for example, holds an account vision, a SWOT analysis, a customer landscape of priorities and success metrics, and a competitive landscape, and Salesforce describes the plan as "a living document".

| An account plan is | An account plan is not |
| --- | --- |
| Built around the customer's stated goals | A list of products you want to sell them |
| A map of named people and their influence | An org chart copied from LinkedIn |
| Objectives with owners, measures and dates | A forecast with a narrative attached |
| Reviewed and changed monthly or quarterly | A template filled in once for an annual review |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Most key account programmes underperform

Gartner's 2021 survey of 69 chief sales officers found near-universal ambition for key accounts and widespread shortfall. 95% expected key accounts to grow faster than other accounts, 58% of sales organisations missed quota on them, and 46% had rebuilt the programme at least twice in seven years. Repeated rebuilds suggest the problem is the method rather than the people.

### Selection is the first mistake

The same research found that customers promoted to key account status mainly because they already spend a lot were 51% less likely to increase spend. Gartner's recommendation is to set enterprise-wide criteria for growth potential, such as access to senior executives, understanding of the customer's long-term goals and willingness to partner, and to re-tier accounts as performance changes.

### Internal coordination is the second

Gartner reports that 66% of key account managers say internal coordination limits their ability to plan for growth, and that managers reporting high cross-functional collaboration see on average three times the spend from key customers. A plan written by the account lead alone tends to promise things that delivery, product or finance have not agreed to.

### Current plans outperform stale ones

The strongest Gartner finding concerns use, not format. Organisations that update account plans frequently and use them to guide customer decisions are three times more likely to build customer decision confidence. Gartner separately associates high decision confidence with customers being ten times more likely to make a high-quality, low-regret purchase. These are analyst figures without a published sample on the summary page, so treat them as direction rather than benchmark.

## How to write a first plan

A mid-size firm can draft a usable plan for one account in two working sessions.

1. **Pick the account on potential, not size.** Score your top 20 customers on growth potential and relationship access. Plan for the top three or four first.
2. **Write the customer's goals in their words.** Use what they have said in reviews, board materials or public filings. If nobody on your side can state the customer's top three priorities, that is your first finding.
3. **Map the people.** List the decision-makers, influencers and users, your relationship owner for each, and how strong that relationship is.
4. **Set two to four objectives.** Each needs a measure, an owner and a date. "Expand into the second business unit by Q3, owner: account lead" is an objective. "Grow the account" is not.
5. **Agree it across functions.** Review the plan with delivery, product and finance before it goes to the customer, so promises are deliverable.
6. **Review it on a fixed cadence.** Each review updates status and records what changed and why.

In **lowob**'s terms, each objective is a decision in the record: what was decided, the reason, the owner, the status and the expected outcome. When the outcome arrives, it is written back against the objective, so next year's plan starts from evidence rather than memory.

## lowob takeaways

- **Plan around the customer's goals.** A product list is a sales target, not an account plan.
- **Select on potential.** Gartner's research suggests high current spend is a poor predictor of growth.
- **Write it across functions.** Coordination, not effort, is where most plans break.
- **Keep it current.** A plan used monthly in decisions is worth more than a thorough one filed annually.

## Common questions

### What is account planning in sales?

It is the practice of writing and maintaining a plan for growing one existing customer, covering their goals, key people, opportunities, objectives and the actions each owner will take.

### What is the difference between account planning and account-based marketing?

Account-based marketing coordinates marketing and sales effort against a set of target accounts. Account planning is the operating plan for one relationship, usually an existing customer.

### What should a key account plan include?

The customer's goals, a map of people and relationship strength, a SWOT or similar assessment, competitive position, and two to four objectives with measures, owners and dates.

### How often should account plans be updated?

Monthly for the most important accounts and at least quarterly for the rest. Gartner associates frequently updated plans with stronger customer outcomes.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, Gartner Survey Shows 95% of Chief Sales Officers Expect Higher Growth From Key Accounts](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/gartner-survey-shows-95--of-chief-sales-officers-expect-higher-g), October 2021. Survey of 69 CSOs, August to September 2021; small sample.
- [Gartner, Account Management Strategies Every CSO Should Know](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/account-growth). Analyst summary page; survey dates and samples not stated.
- [CRM Magazine, Here's Why 58 Percent of B2B Sales Organizations Miss Quota on Key Accounts](https://www.destinationcrm.com/Articles/CRM-News/CRM-Featured-Articles/Heres-Why-58-Percent-of-B2B-Sales-Organizations-Miss-Quota-on-Key-Accounts-150646.aspx), December 2021. Trade press coverage of the Gartner research.
- [Salesforce Trailhead, Explore and Create Account Plans](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/account-based-selling/explore-and-create-account-plans). Vendor training module describing one CRM's account plan structure.

## Related research

- [What Is Account-Based Marketing? A Small-Team Version](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)

- [How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)

## Next move

Ask the owner of your largest account to write the customer's top three priorities in the customer's own words. If they cannot, book a meeting with the customer to ask, and start the plan from the answer.
