# Partner Channel Design

Source: https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Most partner programmes are written after the first partners sign, which is why so many partners do nothing. We set out five design decisions to make first: the role partners play in the sale, the partner types that fit it, the economics each needs, what tiers should reward, and the rules of engagement. We draw on how the largest cloud programmes tier partners and on where partner-delivered spend actually sits.

Partner channel design is the set of decisions a firm makes before recruiting partners: what job partners do in the sale, which partner types fit that job, how each is paid, what earns a higher tier, and who owns the customer when two parties touch the same deal. The stakes are large in technology markets: Canalys estimated that 70% of worldwide IT spending in 2025 flowed through partners. Most mid-size programmes skip the design and start with a partner agreement and a logo page. The result is a long list of signed partners and a short list of partner-sourced revenue.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

The usual sequence in a 50- to 500-person firm runs backwards. A few partners appear, often through a founder's network. A partner agreement is drafted from a template. A partner page goes up. Only when partners fail to produce pipeline does anyone ask what they were meant to do.

Our earlier piece *Integrators, OEMs and channel partners* covers the partner's side of this: what a partner must believe before it will carry a product, and the stages from recruited to scaling. This piece covers the vendor's side: the five design decisions that should precede recruitment, and how the largest programmes make them.

## Where partners sit in the buying process

The case for partners rests on where buyers already are.

| Finding | Source | Implication for channel design |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 70% of IT spending flowed through partners in 2025, down from 71% in 2024 and 73% in 2023 | Canalys, IT spending forecast 2025 | Partners remain the main route, but direct and marketplace routes are gaining share |
| On average 13 people are involved in a business purchase; 89% of purchases span two or more departments | Forrester, State of Business Buying 2024 | Partners often hold relationships with stakeholders the vendor never meets |
| 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience | Gartner, March 2026 | Buyers lean on advisers and platforms they already trust |
| B2B marketers use an average of 3.7 sales channels | Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, November 2025 | Channel choices are rarely deliberate; most firms inherit their mix |

The Canalys figures are analyst estimates and are revised over time. The trend matters more than the level. A small decline in partner share each year means partners are not disappearing, but the roles they play are shifting, with more weight on implementing, managing and advising, and with some transactions moving to cloud marketplaces (Part 16 of this series).

The Ehrenberg-Bass report *Easy to Find* offers a useful check. If a channel carries 30% of category revenue, a brand should expect roughly 30% of its own revenue there. A firm with almost no partner revenue in a category where most buying runs through integrators has a presence gap, not a product gap.

## Decision one: the role partners play in the sale

The first design decision is the partner's job. Five roles cover most technology programmes, and each implies a different contract.

| Role | What the partner does | Who holds the customer contract | Typical payment | What the vendor must supply | First measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Refer | Introduces a buyer and steps back | Vendor | One-off or time-limited fee on paid revenue | Fast follow-up and visible status | Referred deals reaching paid |
| Influence | Shapes the shortlist or specification, often as adviser | Vendor | Usually none directly; access, co-marketing, certification | Evidence partners can repeat to clients | Deals where the partner was named by the buyer |
| Resell | Buys and resells, owning billing | Partner | Margin between wholesale and resale price | Pricing sheet, deal registration, quoting tools | Partner-sold revenue and renewal rate |
| Deliver | Implements, integrates or manages the product | Usually vendor, with partner services contract | Services revenue the partner bills itself | Training, certification, a support path | Time to go-live; customer retention |
| Embed | Builds the product into its own offering | Partner | Royalty or per-unit fee | Technical integration and roadmap visibility | Units shipped; attach rate |

Most mid-size firms need two of these, not five. A software firm selling to regulated mid-market buyers might pair deliver partners, who implement, with influence partners, the consultants who write the buyer's requirements. Choosing roles first prevents the common mistake of signing resellers in a market where buyers want to contract directly. Our explainer *Affiliate vs partner vs referral* covers where referral schemes and affiliate programmes fit alongside these roles, and Part 15 covers referral partners in detail.

## Decision two: economics that cover the partner's cost of sale

A partner programme is a margin structure before it is a relationship. The test is simple: does the partner make enough from your product to justify the time it takes to sell, implement and support?

Partners count their own costs: the seller's time, presales engineering, certification, the risk of a failed implementation. A reseller margin that looks generous against the vendor's list price may be thin against those costs, especially on a first deal. That is why programmes often reward origination more than fulfilment (AWS's ACE programme, for example, offers discounts to partners for originating new customer opportunities), and why services revenue often matters more to a deliver partner than any fee from the vendor.

An illustrative check, labelled as such: if a deliver partner needs about ten days of consultant time to implement your product and its services rate covers that, the product earns its place. If implementation takes thirty days and customers will only pay for ten, no fee you offer will keep that partner selling. The fix is in the product and the playbook, not the margin.

## Decision three: what tiers should reward

Tiers exist to decide who gets scarce vendor resources: leads, funding, technical support and executive time. The largest cloud programmes show what a tier can reward when it is designed around customer outcomes.

| Programme | Tier structure | What qualifies a partner | What the higher tier opens up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| AWS Partner Network, services path | Select, Advanced, Premier | Accredited and certified individuals, and launched customer opportunities: 3 at Select (combined monthly revenue of at least $1,500), 20 at Advanced, 50 at Premier | Marketing development funds from Advanced; Premier requires a partner business plan and executive review, and adds early access to sponsorship packages |
| Microsoft AI Cloud Partner Program, Solutions Partner designations | Designation per solution area | A partner capability score of at least 70 of 100 points, with every metric above zero, across performance, skilling and customer success | Designation benefits; separate enterprise and SMB tracks with different thresholds |
| Google Cloud Partner Network, announced December 2025 for rollout in early 2026 | Select, Premier and a new Diamond tier, for all partner types | Joint customer outcomes for tiers; competencies measured on certifications and sales credentials, and on contributions to validated closed/won opportunities | Higher designations; engagements applied automatically toward tier and competency progress |

Two design choices stand out. All three programmes count certified people, which measures whether the partner can deliver. And all three count customer outcomes: launched opportunities at AWS, net customer adds, usage growth and deployments at Microsoft, validated closed/won opportunities at Google Cloud. None tiers on revenue alone.

A mid-size vendor does not need three tiers. Two are usually enough: a registered tier with access to training and deal registration, and a committed tier with joint planning, named support and any marketing funds. The qualifying criteria should be things the vendor can verify from its own records, such as certified staff, customers live and renewed, and partner-sourced pipeline, rather than self-reported revenue.

## Decision four: rules of engagement

Rules of engagement decide what happens when the vendor's sellers and a partner touch the same account. They need to be written before the first joint deal, because the first dispute will set the precedent otherwise.

The minimum set covers four things. **Deal registration:** how a partner claims an opportunity, what evidence is required, and how long the claim lasts. **Account ownership:** which accounts the direct team keeps, and whether partners may work them. **Pricing authority:** who may discount, and how far. **Hand-offs:** what happens to a partner-registered deal the partner cannot progress.

Competition law sets limits on some of these choices. In the EU, Regulation 2022/720, the Vertical Block Exemption Regulation, has applied since 1 June 2022 and runs to 31 May 2034. It decides which restrictions a supplier may place on its distributors and resellers without falling foul of EU competition rules. The Commission's accompanying Guidelines on vertical restraints describe the safe harbour as applying where neither party's market share exceeds 30%. They confirm that resale price maintenance is a hardcore restriction. They also give separate guidance on information exchange where a supplier sells directly in competition with its distributors, which is the position of any vendor running a direct team alongside resellers. Programmes that set partner pricing, allocate territories or run a direct team alongside resellers should have counsel review the rules once, early. Part 19 of this series covers channel conflict in practice.

## Decision five: what gets recorded

Every partner programme generates decisions that later need defending: why a partner was moved up a tier, why a margin changed, why a registered deal was given to the direct team. These belong in the decision record The Build Order describes, with a reason, an owner and an expected outcome (*The commercial decisions worth recording*).

The single measure that matters most is the one our earlier piece recommends: partner-sourced pipeline that reaches a paid outcome, reported monthly beside the direct equivalent. A programme that cannot report it does not yet know whether it works. Our explainer *What is a distribution diagnostic?* describes how to test a partner route before committing a team to it.

> Design the partner's job, pay and rules before you sign the first partner. Otherwise the first partner designs them for you.

Illustrative example: a data platform redesigns its partner channel

Decision
:   Replace a single reseller tier with two roles: deliver partners for implementation and influence partners for advisory firms that write requirements.

Reason and owner
:   Eighteen signed resellers had produced two deals in a year; buyers in the segment preferred to contract directly. Owned by the head of partnerships, agreed with the revenue leader.

What changed
:   Deliver partners were tiered on certified staff and customers live; influence partners received certification and evidence packs, not fees. Partner-sourced pipeline was reported monthly beside direct pipeline.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size data platform, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the partner's role first.** Refer, influence, resell, deliver and embed each need a different contract and payment.
- **Pay for the partner's cost of sale.** If implementation costs more than customers will pay, no margin fixes it.
- **Tier on what you can verify.** Certified people and customers live are better criteria than self-reported revenue.
- **Write the rules before the first joint deal.** Registration, ownership, pricing authority and hand-offs set every later precedent.

Gateway card

### Before you recruit the next partner

- One or two partner roles chosen and written down
- The partner's cost of sale estimated for a first deal
- Two tiers defined with criteria you can verify from your own records
- Deal registration, account ownership and pricing authority written
- Partner-sourced pipeline to paid reported monthly beside direct

## Common questions

### How do you design a partner programme?

Decide the role partners play in the sale, the partner types that fit it, how each is paid, what earns a higher tier and the rules on shared accounts, then recruit partners who fit that design.

### What are the main types of channel partners?

In technology markets, partners usually refer, influence, resell, deliver (implement or manage) or embed the product. Each role implies a different contract, payment and support model.

### How many tiers should a partner programme have?

A mid-size vendor usually needs two: a registered tier with training and deal registration, and a committed tier with joint planning and named support. More tiers add administration without changing behaviour.

### What share of IT spending goes through partners?

Canalys estimated about 70% of worldwide IT spending in 2025 flowed through partners, down from 73% in 2023.

- [AWS, AWS Services Partner Tiers](https://aws.amazon.com/partners/services-tiers). Vendor programme page; requirements and benefits vary by geography and change.
- [AWS, APN Customer Engagements (ACE) Program](https://aws.amazon.com/partners/programs/ace/). Vendor programme page; incentive amounts are not published.

# Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck

Source: https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Independent benchmarks find that AI memory systems usually retrieve the right evidence and then fail to use it, especially when facts have changed. Better search will not fix that. Giving every piece of evidence a standing, with status, validity dates, provenance and supersession links, and answering change questions with a timeline, will.

The right evidence is usually there. Memory systems fail at weighing and applying it, especially when it has changed. A June 2026 benchmark found that when memory systems failed, the relevant evidence was retrievable about ten times more often than it was missing, and that questions about how a fact changed were the weakest category. Better search will not fix that. Giving every piece of evidence a standing, with status, validity dates, provenance and links to what it replaced, will.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

Most memory roadmaps assume the hard problem is finding the right fact. So the investment goes into better embeddings, a knowledge graph, re-ranking, a bigger context window. The independent evidence of the last two years points somewhere else. Our explainer on [agent memory](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/) covers the main designs; this piece is about why they fail.

## What the benchmarks actually found

MemTrace, a benchmark released on arXiv on 15 June 2026 by Xianxuan Long and colleagues, probed 835 knowledge points, each a single typed fact about a user, across 13 memory-system configurations in four paradigms. Its central finding is in the abstract: when systems fail, "the evidence was retrievable 10× more often than it was missing". In a 300-probe replay, the gap attributable to reaching the evidence was 7.0%; the gap attributable to using it was 73.3%. The authors treat the ratio as directional, because it depends on the single retriever they used.

The weakest category was trajectory questions: how did this change, and when. The best systems answered about half of those correctly on fresh data. Mem-T scored 47.2% fresh and fell to 19.8% once its store had filled up; HippoRAG-v2 fell from 33.0% to 13.4%. Performance got worse as memory grew, which is the opposite of what a brain should do.

This is consistent with earlier work. LongMemEval, first published in October 2024 and revised in March 2025, tested five memory abilities including temporal reasoning and knowledge updates. Its authors report that long-context models showed a 30 to 60% performance drop on the larger version of the benchmark, and that "simplistic memory designs perform poorly on temporal reasoning questions".

| Study | What it tested | Finding that matters here |
| --- | --- | --- |
| MemTrace (June 2026) | 835 facts, 13 memory configurations | Evidence retrievable 10 times more often than missing when systems failed |
| MemTrace, trajectory questions | How a fact changed over time | Best systems about half right fresh, about one in five once memory filled |
| LongMemEval (2024, revised 2025) | 500 questions over long chat histories | 30 to 60% drop for long-context models; temporal reasoning weak |
| Stanford RegLab legal tools (May 2024) | Retrieval-backed legal research products | Wrong answers in more than 17% of queries, despite retrieval |

The legal study is a useful outside check because the products were built on retrieval. Stanford researchers found Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI gave incorrect information more than 17% of the time and Westlaw's AI-Assisted Research more than 34%. Part of the cause, they wrote, was retrieved sources that did not apply to the question's jurisdiction or time period. The system found documents. It could not tell which ones still governed.

## What it looks like in practice

The system retrieves both the March view and the June view of the same account. It blends them into one confident paragraph, or it picks whichever is written more fluently. Nothing in the store says which one superseded which, who asserted each, or whether either was verified. The model is asked to adjudicate with no basis for doing so.

> The system found the documents. It could not tell which ones still governed.

## Give evidence a standing

The fix is structural, and it is mostly about metadata the model can reason over.

| Field | Values | What it lets the model do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status | Current, superseded, disputed, unverified | Prefer what still governs |
| Validity dates | When the claim became true, when it stopped | Answer "as of when" questions |
| Provenance | Who asserted it, from what source, whether anyone checked | Weigh a verified primary source above a summary |
| Supersession link | Pointer to the claim it replaced, with a reason | Explain the change instead of blending |

Retrieval then returns evidence with its standing, and the instructions tell the model how to use standing. Verified beats unverified. Current beats superseded. Primary source beats summary. When two current claims conflict, say so rather than choose.

At least one memory vendor builds this in. Zep's published architecture records, for each fact, when it was true and when it was ingested, and when new information contradicts an existing fact it marks the old one invalid from the new one's start date rather than deleting it. That is a vendor's own design paper, but it shows the approach is practical. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) sets out the record design, and [Keep the sources; let the summary regenerate](https://lowob.com/research/keep-the-sources-let-the-summary-regenerate/) covers provenance.

## Answer change questions with a timeline

For trajectory questions, top-k retrieval is the wrong shape. Ten relevant fragments sorted by similarity hide the order of events. Return the ordered sequence of states for the entity in question, with dates and the reason for each change. The model is much better at reading a timeline than reconstructing one, and MemTrace's trajectory results show how badly reconstruction goes once memory is full.

## A note on graphs

Graphs help with some of this and cost more than teams expect. Microsoft Research's GraphRAG work found that baseline retrieval "struggles to connect the dots" and does poorly on questions that need aggregation across a whole dataset. One practitioner write-up, published in April 2026, reports vector search better for specific lookups (54% against 35%) and graph retrieval about three to four times better for aggregation and cross-document questions. The same piece states that production graphs without automated refresh drift 15 to 20% from ground truth per quarter, and that teams report spending two to three times more engineering on freshness than on the initial build. It gives no underlying study for those last two figures, so treat them as practitioner estimates. The direction is still the useful part: budget for upkeep, or do not build the graph. Our comparison of [vector databases and knowledge graphs](https://lowob.com/research/vector-database-vs-knowledge-graph/) goes further.

## In practice

Add status, validity dates, provenance and supersession links to the records your agents retrieve. Write explicit precedence rules into the instructions that consume them. Build twenty trajectory questions from your own history ("how did our view of X change in 2026?") and score your system on them, once with a fresh store and again after a few months of use.

If you run a graph, put its refresh cost in the budget before its build cost.

**What would prove this wrong:** a retrieval-only improvement, with no standing metadata, that closes most of the gap on trajectory and knowledge-update questions in an independent benchmark.

## lowob takeaways

- **The evidence is usually there.** MemTrace found it retrievable ten times more often than missing when systems failed.
- **Change questions are the weak point.** Trajectory accuracy fell from about half to about one in five as memory filled.
- **Give evidence a standing.** Status, validity dates, provenance and supersession links, with written precedence rules.
- **Return timelines, not fragments.** Ordered states with dates and reasons answer "how did this change".
- **Budget graph upkeep first.** Freshness costs more than the build.

## Common questions

### Why do AI memory systems give wrong answers when the data is there?

The failure usually comes after retrieval, in how evidence is used. MemTrace, a June 2026 benchmark of 835 facts across 13 memory configurations, found the relevant evidence retrievable about ten times more often than it was missing when systems failed.

### How do I stop an AI agent mixing up old and new information?

Give each record a status (current, superseded, disputed or unverified), validity dates, provenance and links to what it replaced, and write precedence rules: verified beats unverified, current beats superseded, primary source beats summary, and conflicting current claims are flagged.

### Does RAG stop AI hallucinations?

Not on its own. Stanford researchers found retrieval-backed legal research tools gave wrong answers in more than 17% of queries, partly because they retrieved sources that did not apply to the question's jurisdiction or time period.

### Are knowledge graphs better than vector search for RAG?

For different questions. Practitioner tests find vector search better for specific lookups and graphs better for aggregation and cross-document questions, but graphs need continuous refresh, so budget for upkeep before building one.

## Sources and notes

- [Wu et al., LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813v2), October 2024, revised March 2025. Academic preprint; synthetic chat histories.
- [Stanford HAI, AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 (or More) Benchmarking Queries](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-trial-legal-models-hallucinate-1-out-6-or-more-benchmarking-queries), 23 May 2024, updated 30 May 2024. Academic study of commercial legal tools in 2024; products have changed since.

# From Hype to Revenue: Web3's Next Competitive Advantage Is Operating Discipline

Source: https://lowob.com/research/from-hype-to-revenue/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-27 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Web3 has never struggled to generate attention; converting it into a durable business is the hard part. The evidence on incentive-led launches shows attention fading within weeks, and US regulators are now asking token projects for principles-based disclosure of token economics and, for larger raises, GAAP financial statements. The advantage goes to teams that start from a commercial objective, test it with the smallest credible campaign and keep only what persists.

Web3 has never had much trouble generating attention. Converting that attention into a durable business model has always been the challenge. The evidence on incentive-led launches shows attention fading fast: Keyrock found most of 62 airdropped tokens fell within 15 days. Meanwhile the SEC's 2026 crypto offering proposal would ask issuers for principles-based disclosure, including token economics, and for GAAP financial statements in larger raises. Hype is not the problem. Hype that goes nowhere is.

The crypto industry has historically been adept at generating excitement around launches, tokens, communities, incentives, partnerships and new narratives. That is a real strength. In emerging markets attention matters, and crypto has shown repeatedly that a strong story can move users, capital and developers very quickly.

The problem is the aftermath. A project can look successful for a few months, or even a few years, and still have no clear answer for why people should keep using it, paying for it or building around it. As the market matures, the more useful question is no longer "can this get attention?" It is "can this turn attention into adoption and revenue?"

## What fades when the campaign ends

The on-chain record now gives a fairly clear picture of what happens after incentive-led bursts of attention.

| Evidence | Finding | What it says about attention |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Keyrock, 62 airdrops across 6 chains, 2024 | Most airdrops "crash within 15 days"; only 8 showed positive 90-day results | Price-led attention is short-lived without a product underneath |
| Messias, Yaish and Livshits, nine airdrops | Up to 66% of claimed tokens went to exchanges in the first transfer; engagement did not last | Many recipients were there for the reward |
| Nansen via The Block, ZKsync, 2024 | 41.1% of the top 10,000 recipients sold everything within 24 hours | Distribution and retention are different events |
| Keyrock, launch valuations | Higher launch FDV correlated with a greater chance of a significant price drop | A headline valuation is not a market |

None of this says narrative is useless. Keyrock's best case combined an established user base, a tiered release, a conservative valuation and seeded liquidity. The attention worked because there was a business for it to land on.

## Funnel inputs, not outcomes

Web3 growth has traditionally been judged on metrics that too often amount to noise: social followers, Discord members, momentary spikes in TVL, impressions inflated by bot activity, wallet connections, fully incentivised campaign participation, token volume and launch traction that fades when the incentives do.

Those numbers can all be informative. The problem comes when they are treated as the final outcome rather than as the top of a funnel. Our piece [stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) makes the general case; in crypto the reach number is often bought with the project's own token, which makes it more expensive and less informative at the same time.

The questions that separate a business from a moment are plain:

- Do users come back without being paid to do so?
- Does the product solve a problem that still matters when sentiment shifts?
- Is there a clear buyer?
- Are there distribution or partner channels that can be repeated?
- Is revenue coming from something the team understands well enough to reproduce?

None of this is complicated in theory. The hard part is building the discipline to measure it and let the outcomes decide what the team does next.

## Start from the commercial objective and work backwards

A more useful approach starts with the commercial objective. If the goal is adoption, define which users matter and what meaningful adoption looks like. If the goal is revenue, identify which products, customer segments and partner channels produce it. If the goal is ecosystem growth, decide what a partner should contribute beyond a logo and a vague partnership announcement.

| Objective | The audience that matters | The behaviour that proves it | The number to report |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adoption | A named user segment | A first meaningful action, then a return | 30-day and 90-day retained users, with and without incentives |
| Revenue | Paying segments and channels | Fees paid and retained by the protocol | Protocol revenue by source, monthly |
| Ecosystem growth | Partners and integrators | Live integrations carrying users or capital | Retained users or capital per partner |
| Liquidity | Capital providers | Capital that stays at useful depth | Retained capital at 90 days, and its concentration |

The table is the same shape as the [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) in any business: a small set of measures tied to a stated objective, defined the same way every period. Our piece on [protocol revenue](https://lowob.com/research/protocol-revenue-fees-real-yield-and-what-to-report/) sets out the revenue line in detail.

> Hype is not the problem. Hype that goes nowhere is.

## Disclosure is moving the same way

The regulatory direction reinforces the commercial one. In the US, the SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published in August 2026, would create offering exemptions for crypto-related investment contracts: up to $5 million over four years for startups, and up to $75 million in 12 months under a two-tier fundraising exemption. The Congressional Research Service's summary describes principles-based disclosure across ten topics, including the network, development plans and token economics such as supply, lockups and release schedules. The fundraising route would require financial statements prepared under US GAAP, audited for the larger tier, with annual, semiannual and current reports until the issuer certifies its promised efforts are complete.

It is a proposal; comments closed on 20 October 2026, and Congress's market-structure bill, the CLARITY Act, failed a Senate cloture vote 49 to 50 on 15 September 2026. The rules are not settled. But the direction is clear enough to plan around: teams that can already explain their economics in a consistent format will find disclosure cheaper than teams that cannot. This is not legal advice.

## Operating discipline without losing speed

Operating discipline does not mean giving up what made Web3 effective. The sector's speed, experimentation and ability to mobilise networks are worth keeping. The useful shift is to combine that speed with clearer ownership, measurable outcomes, viable revenue models and a willingness to move from hype as an end in itself towards products with durable demand.

Campaigns become tests of a commercial hypothesis instead of isolated bursts of activity. Partnerships are judged by what they actually deliver: users, integrations, sustainable liquidity, distribution, credibility or revenue. Community supports onboarding, education, retention, product feedback and referrals that stick. Content explains the product, drives demand and supports sales or partnership conversations instead of filling a posting calendar.

In practice the loop is simple. Settle on a commercial objective. Define the audience. Decide what behaviour would prove the idea is working. Build the smallest credible campaign or distribution motion around it. Measure the result. Keep what worked, cut what did not, and carry the learning into the next round. Our playbook on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set the decision rule before the test starts.

The strongest companies will still use narrative aggressively. They will still experiment with incentives, creators, partnerships, communities and market moments. The difference is that those tactics will have somewhere to go. They will feed an operating model rather than sit side by side as unrelated growth activity.

## lowob takeaways

- **Attention is an input.** Followers, members, TVL spikes and wallet connections belong at the top of the funnel.
- **Start from the objective.** Adoption, revenue, ecosystem growth and liquidity each need their own audience, behaviour and number.
- **Run campaigns as tests.** Smallest credible motion, a decision rule, then keep or cut.
- **Disclosure rewards discipline.** The SEC's 2026 proposal asks for the economics a disciplined team already tracks.

## Common questions

### Why do so many Web3 projects fail after launch?

Often because launch attention was bought with incentives and there was no product reason to stay. Keyrock found most of 62 airdropped tokens fell within 15 days; projects that held up had existing users, staged releases and conservative valuations.

### What metrics should a Web3 company track instead of followers?

Retained users at 30 and 90 days with and without incentives, protocol revenue by source, live integrations that carry users or capital, and retained capital and its concentration, each tied to a stated commercial objective.

### What does operating discipline mean for a crypto startup?

Setting a commercial objective, defining the audience and the behaviour that proves progress, running the smallest credible campaign, measuring it and keeping only what works, with clear ownership of each number.

### What will US regulators require crypto projects to disclose?

Under the SEC's August 2026 proposal, which is not final, issuers using the new exemptions would give principles-based disclosure including token economics, and larger raises would need GAAP financial statements and periodic reports.

## In the news

- 2 October 2026 · Orrick[The CLARITY Act stalls in the Senate](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-02-the-clarity-act-stalls-in-the-senate)US market structure stays unsettled into 2027. Token decisions should work without counting on it passing.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

## Sources and notes

- [Keyrock, Airdrops in the barren desert](https://keyrock.com/airdrops-in-the-barren-desert/), 25 September 2024, updated July 2025. Research by a crypto market maker; price outcomes only.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: giving money away is harder than it seems](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), arXiv, revised 2025. Academic study of nine airdrops.
- [The Block, 41% of top ZKsync token airdrop recipients sold full allocation: Nansen](https://www.theblock.co/post/300608/zksync-token-airdrop-sales-nansen), 18 June 2024. Analytics vendor data via a news report; top addresses and first 24 hours only.

- The objective table is **lowob**'s framework.

- [The Build Order for Crypto and Digital Assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/)

## Next move

Take your last three campaigns and write, for each, the commercial objective, the behaviour that would have proved it and what remained 90 days later. Cut the next campaign that cannot fill in the first two lines before launch.

# What Is a Go-to-Market Strategy?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-27 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A go-to-market strategy sets out how a company reaches and wins customers at a cost that leaves a business. lowob treats it as four decisions that must agree: who exactly, what they must believe, how trust moves, and what evidence proves it. Buyer research shows why the third has become harder: buyers use more channels and many prefer to buy without a seller.

A go-to-market (GTM) strategy is the plan for how a company finds customers, persuades them to buy and does so at a cost that leaves a profitable business. **lowob** treats it as four decisions that must agree with each other: who exactly the buyer is, what they must believe, how trust moves from first contact to contract, and what evidence will show it is working. A list of channels and campaigns is not a GTM strategy; it is a list of tactics.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a go-to-market strategy means

The term covers the commercial choices that sit between having a product and having revenue. Gartner's framework for sales leaders defines it as "a plan that details how an organization can engage with customers" and names five components: target market identification, the first customer touchpoint, sales compensation planning, corporate investments and voice of the customer.

**lowob**'s working definition, set out in [What Go-to-Market Means](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/), groups the choices into four decisions. Each constrains the others.

| Decision | Question it answers | Evidence it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who, exactly | Which narrowly defined buyers have the costliest version of the problem, the authority and budget to fix it, and a reason to act now? | Win rates and sales cycle by segment |
| What they must believe | What change does the buyer want, in their own language? | Buyers repeat the message back; loss reasons shift |
| How trust moves | What is the path from first contact to signed contract: self-serve, sales-led, partner-led or community-led? | Conversion and cost at each step of the path |
| What proves it | Which few numbers will show the strategy is working, and by when? | Agreed targets, reviewed on a fixed rhythm |

A GTM strategy is not the same as a marketing plan, a sales target or a product launch. Those are parts of it. The strategy is the agreement between the parts.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buyers have changed the path

The third decision, how trust moves, has become harder. McKinsey's B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers, published in September 2024, found buyers used an average of ten channels in their buying journey, up from five in 2016. It also found a "rule of thirds": at each stage, roughly a third of buyers prefer in-person contact, a third remote contact and a third digital self-service.

Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, run in August and September 2024, found 61% prefer an overall rep-free buying experience. The same research found 73% avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach. A strategy that assumes every buyer wants a sales call, or that more outbound volume will compensate for a weak fit, now fails faster.

### Tactics without a strategy waste money

Without the four decisions written down, each team picks its own. Marketing targets one segment, sales chases another and partners bring a third. Spending rises while win rates stay flat. **lowob**'s piece on [strategy versus tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/) sets out the symptoms in more detail.

> A go-to-market strategy is four choices that agree. Change one and the other three must be checked.

### Agents need it written down

AI agents in sales and marketing amplify whatever strategy they are given. An outbound agent pointed at a loose ideal customer profile sends more messages to the wrong people, faster. In **lowob**'s model, the GTM choices belong in the decision record, with a reason, owner and expected outcome, so agents and people read the same version.

## How to test your go-to-market strategy

| Test | Question to ask the leadership team | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single buyer | Can three leaders describe the target buyer in the same words? | Three different answers |
| Narrowness | Could a seller name ten real accounts that fit, today? | "Mid-market companies" |
| Belief | Do win-loss interviews repeat your message? | Buyers cite price or relationships only |
| Primary motion | Is one path primary, with others in support? | Every channel funded equally |
| Economics | Do you know the cost to acquire a customer through the main path? | Nobody owns the number |
| Review | When did the strategy last change because of evidence? | Never, or every month |

Firms of between 20 and 500 people usually run more than one motion. That is workable if one is primary and the others support it. [Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/) covers how to choose.

## lowob takeaways

- **Four decisions.** Who, what they must believe, how trust moves and what proves it.
- **They must agree.** A new segment means a new message, path and set of measures.
- **The path is harder.** Buyers use more channels and many prefer to buy without a seller.
- **Write it down.** Recorded choices keep teams, and agents, working from one version.

## Common questions

### What are the components of a go-to-market strategy?

Most frameworks cover the target buyer, the value proposition or message, the channels and sales motion, pricing and the measures of success. **lowob** groups these into four decisions that must agree.

### What is the difference between a go-to-market strategy and a marketing strategy?

A marketing strategy covers how a company creates demand. A GTM strategy is wider: it also covers which buyers to pursue, how the sale happens and how success is measured across sales, marketing and partners.

### How often should a go-to-market strategy change?

When evidence contradicts it, such as win rates falling in the target segment or a new path proving cheaper. Review it quarterly; change it less often.

### Do B2B buyers still want to talk to salespeople?

Many prefer not to for much of the journey. Gartner found 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience overall, and McKinsey found preferences split roughly evenly between in-person, remote and self-service.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, Go-To-Market Strategy Framework](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/go-to-market-strategy-framework). Analyst framework page aimed at chief sales officers.
- [McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/five-fundamental-truths-how-b2b-winners-keep-growing), 12 September 2024. Consultancy survey of nearly 4,000 B2B decision makers.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 61% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Buying Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience), 25 June 2025. Analyst survey of 632 buyers, fielded in 2024.

## Related research

- [What Go-to-Market Means: A Plain Guide for Founders](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/)
- [Your Startup Needs a GTM Strategy, Not Just a List of Tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/)
- [How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)
- [Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/)
- ["We Shipped Everything and the Number Went Down"](https://lowob.com/research/we-shipped-everything-and-the-number-went-down/)

## Next move

Ask three members of your leadership team to write, separately, one sentence describing your target buyer. Compare the answers; any gap is the first decision to settle.

# What Is BANT, and Is It Still Useful?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-bant/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-27 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: BANT asks four questions about a prospect: is there budget, are we talking to someone with authority, is there a need, and is there a timeline. It is decades old and widely attributed to IBM. This explainer covers what each letter means, why buying groups and self-directed buyers have weakened it for complex sales, and where it still earns its place as a first-pass screen.

BANT is a sales qualification framework that checks four things about a prospect: Budget, Authority, Need and Timeline. It is still useful as a quick screen for inbound leads and smaller, single-buyer sales. It is weak for complex B2B deals, where authority is spread across a buying group and budget is often created after the need is proven. Most teams now use it early in the funnel and switch to a fuller framework such as MEDDICC once a deal is real.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What BANT means

BANT is the oldest widely used qualification checklist. Pipedrive's guide dates it to IBM sales leaders in the 1950s, and Backstory's describes IBM using it to sort opportunities that met its criteria and route them to the right teams. The exact origin is hard to verify from primary records, so it is safest to treat the IBM story as attribution rather than documented history.

| Letter | Question | What a good answer looks like | Where it breaks down |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Budget | Can the buyer pay? | A funded line, or a clear route to funding | New categories often have no budget line yet |
| Authority | Is this person able to decide? | The decision owner, or a clear path to them | Decisions sit with groups, not individuals |
| Need | Is there a problem we solve? | A stated problem with a cost attached | Need and want are easily confused |
| Timeline | When must they act? | A date tied to an event | Dates without a trigger are wishes |

Each question is simple, which is both the strength and the weakness. A new seller can learn BANT in an hour. A buyer can also tell when they are being run through it.

## Why it has weakened for complex sales

Three changes in buying have reduced BANT's predictive value for larger deals.

**Authority is shared.** Forrester found 13 people on average involved in a buying decision, and 89% of purchases spanned two or more departments. Asking one contact whether they are the decision-maker rarely gets a reliable answer. Backstory's guide notes that many people are not forthcoming about their place in the chain of command.

**Budget often follows need.** For a new category, or a problem the buyer has not yet costed, there is no budget to confirm. Disqualifying on budget at first contact removes deals that a stronger business case could have funded. Backstory also warns that asking about budget too soon can seem aggressive and can anchor the buyer's expectations too low.

**Buyers arrive late and informed.** Gartner's 2026 survey found 67% of B2B buyers preferred a rep-free experience. By the time a seller asks about need and timeline, the buyer may already have a shortlist and criteria. BANT says nothing about decision criteria, the decision process or competition, which is where those deals are won or lost.

Pipedrive's guide summarises the critique: BANT is seen as outdated for modern sales, partly because of multiple decision-makers and partly because, used badly, it becomes a box-ticking exercise.

## Where BANT still earns its place

BANT remains useful where the sale is small, the buyer is one person, or the question is simply whether a lead deserves a seller's time.

| Situation | Use BANT? | Better option if not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inbound lead routing by a development rep | Yes, as a light screen |  |
| Small deal, single buyer, short cycle | Yes |  |
| Mid-market deal, several stakeholders | Partly: need and timeline first | Add economic buyer and champion |
| Enterprise deal, buying group, procurement | No | MEDDICC or MEDDPICC |
| New category with no budget line | Not on budget | Qualify on need and cost of inaction |

Practical adjustments make it more useful:

1. **Reorder it.** Start with need, then timeline, then authority, then budget. Need is the natural opening question, because the other three depend on it.
2. **Tie timeline to an event.** A contract renewal, a regulatory date or a board meeting is evidence. "This quarter" is not.
3. **Record answers as fields.** If the answers live only in call notes, they cannot be checked or used by anyone else, including an AI assistant summarising the account.
4. **Hand off cleanly.** When a lead passes the screen, the record should show what was confirmed, so the account executive does not ask the same questions again.

In **lowob**'s model, BANT answers are early context in the commercial record. They are not judgments about whether to pursue an account. That decision, with its reason and owner, belongs to a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **BANT is a screen, not a forecast.** It filters leads well and predicts complex deals poorly.
- **Authority now sits with groups.** With 13 people in the average decision, one contact cannot confirm it.
- **Lead with need.** Asking about budget first can disqualify good deals and anchor price low.
- **Graduate to MEDDICC.** Once a deal involves a buying group, switch to a framework that covers criteria, process and competition.

## Common questions

### What does BANT stand for in sales?

Budget, Authority, Need and Timeline. It is a checklist for deciding whether a prospect is worth pursuing.

### Is BANT still relevant?

Yes, as a quick screen for inbound leads and small, single-buyer sales. For complex B2B deals with buying groups, frameworks such as MEDDICC are more predictive.

### Who created BANT?

It is widely attributed to IBM sales leaders in the 1950s, though primary documentation of its origin is hard to find.

### What is the difference between BANT and MEDDICC?

BANT checks four basic conditions. MEDDICC adds metrics, decision criteria, decision process, a champion and competition, which matter in larger deals.

# What Thought Leadership Actually Is

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-thought-leadership-actually-is/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-27 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Thought leadership is a defensible position, supported by evidence the audience could not assemble, with a consequence for the reader, sustained over time. Edelman and LinkedIn's research finds buyers reward evidence and challenge, and drop vendors whose thinking is weak. Most of what carries the name is agreeable content measured by impressions. The real thing comes from a founder's actual thinking, on a cadence the founder can sustain.

Thought leadership is a defensible position, supported by evidence the audience could not assemble, with a consequence for the reader, sustained over time. Buyers say it matters: in the 2026 Edelman-LinkedIn study, 73% of B2B decision makers said useful data or evidence is what makes thought leadership worth sharing, and 59% of final decision makers said poor or absent thought leadership had led to a vendor being dropped. Most of what carries the name is agreeable content measured by impressions. The real thing comes from a founder's or senior operator's actual thinking, on a cadence they can sustain.

Thought leadership is content published to establish a person or a company as an authority: someone whose view of a market is worth seeking out, quoting and acting on. The term has been used so loosely that it now mostly describes LinkedIn posts. The original idea is worth recovering, because the real thing is one of the few marketing assets that compounds.

## What it requires

| Element | What it means | Example of the difference |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A position | A specific, defensible claim, not a subject | Topic: "distribution for restricted categories". Position: "the channels the platforms leave to restricted categories are cheaper because the platforms restrict them." |
| Evidence | Observation, data, experience or examples the audience could not assemble themselves | A position without evidence is an opinion, and the internet has enough |
| Consequence | Something the reader should do differently | Authority is earned by being useful, not by being interesting |
| Consistency | A body of work returning to the same territory, developing it, being proved right or adjusting when wrong | One good piece is an article; a sustained argument is authority |

## What buyers say they value

The most useful evidence on this comes from the annual B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report by Edelman and LinkedIn. Both organisations sell services that benefit from more thought leadership spending, so read the figures as buyer opinion gathered by interested parties. The samples are large and the direction has been consistent across editions.

The 2026 edition, published in November 2026, surveyed more than 1,100 business executives in seven countries:

| Finding (2026 edition) | Share |
| --- | --- |
| Used AI to summarise thought leadership during vendor evaluation | 84% |
| Said thought leadership helped assess whether a vendor understood their needs | 76% |
| Named useful data, research or evidence as what makes it worth sharing | 73% |
| Final decision makers who said poor or absent thought leadership led to a vendor being removed | 59% |
| Said the strongest trust driver is showing clear understanding of their challenges | 56% |
| Said the strongest trust driver is the strength of the product or service | 14% |

The 2025 edition, which surveyed nearly 2,000 professionals including "hidden" buyers outside the formal decision group, found 86% favoured perspectives that challenge their assumptions, and 91% of hidden buyers wanted insights that reveal unseen risks or opportunities. It also found 79% were more likely to champion a vendor in a formal evaluation if it consistently published quality thought leadership.

Three of the four requirements above show up directly in what buyers report: evidence (73%), consequence (understanding their challenges and revealing risks), and position (challenging assumptions). The fourth, consistency, is what "consistently publishes" measures.

> Real thought leadership ends with a claim the reader could disagree with. The imitation ends with "the future is exciting and organisations must adapt."

## Why most attempts fail

They start from the desire to be seen as a leader rather than from a view. They pick topics that are safe, which means topics where the author agrees with everyone. They avoid specifics for fear of being wrong. They are written by a marketing team imitating an executive who has not supplied any thinking. And they measure themselves by impressions, which rewards being agreeable and punishes being right.

The tell is the ending. Real thought leadership ends with a claim the reader could disagree with.

AI has raised the stakes in two directions. Drafting is now cheap, so agreeable content is abundant; our piece [Judgment is the moat](https://lowob.com/research/judgment-is-the-moat/) covers what that does to differentiation. And the reader is often a model: when 84% of decision makers summarise thought leadership with AI, a piece with no specific claim summarises to nothing. A position with evidence survives compression. A tone does not.

## How it differs from content marketing

Content marketing answers questions the audience already has, so that they find the company when searching. Thought leadership raises questions the audience had not thought to ask, so that they seek the company out.

|  | Content marketing | Thought leadership |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts from | A question buyers already search for | A belief the market currently gets wrong |
| Asset type | Search and citation asset | Reputation asset |
| Who must supply it | Anyone with subject knowledge | Someone with a view and evidence for it |
| Success looks like | Found, cited, used at the right buying stage | Sought out, quoted, argued with |
| Typical volume | Many pieces | Few pieces, sustained |

Both are valuable. Most companies need more of the first than they think and less of the second than they produce. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) covers the first; [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) covers how to put the second into deals.

## How to produce it without a full-time writer

The thinking has to come from a person who has it, usually a founder or a senior operator. That person's time is scarce. The system that works:

1. **A recurring interview.** Forty-five minutes, on one question, conducted by someone who challenges abstractions and asks for examples.
2. **A transcript.** The raw material, kept.
3. **A short editorial process.** AI-assisted extraction and structure, producing a flagship piece and a small set of adaptations, with the founder approving anything in their voice.
4. **A ledger of positions.** A record of what the company has argued, so each piece builds on the last rather than starting over.

That system produces a piece every two to four weeks with about two hours of the founder's time. It does not produce daily posts, and it should not try to. Our piece on the [founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) sets out the workflow, and [from founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) covers what happens when the founder can no longer be the only source.

## The test

Before publishing, ask three questions. Could a competent competitor have written this from public information? What would a smart person in the audience disagree with? What should the reader do on Monday? If the answers are yes, nothing and nothing, it is content. It may still be worth publishing. It is not thought leadership.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write a position, not a topic.** A claim someone could dispute, with evidence they could not assemble.
- **Lead with evidence.** It is what buyers say makes thought leadership worth sharing.
- **Write for the summary.** If a model compresses your piece, the claim should survive.
- **Sustain it.** A cadence the founder can keep beats a burst of volume.

## Common questions

### What is thought leadership?

Content that establishes a person or company as an authority whose view is worth seeking out and acting on. It needs a defensible position, evidence the audience could not assemble, a consequence for the reader, and consistency over time.

### What is the difference between thought leadership and content marketing?

Content marketing answers questions the audience already has, so they find you in search. Thought leadership raises questions they had not thought to ask, so they seek you out.

### Does B2B thought leadership influence buying decisions?

Buyers say so. In the 2026 Edelman-LinkedIn study, 76% said it helped them judge whether a vendor understood their needs, and 59% of final decision makers said weak or absent thought leadership had led to a vendor being dropped.

### How can a founder produce thought leadership without a full-time writer?

Hold a recurring 45-minute interview on one question, transcribe it, and run a short AI-assisted editorial process with the founder approving anything in their voice. That yields a piece every two to four weeks.

## In the news

- 9 November 2026 · Edelman[Edelman and LinkedIn on what executives do with thought leadership](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-11-09-edelman-and-linkedin-on-what-executives-do-with-thought-lea)The measure that matters is what a reader does next, not whether they read. That is the bar for every piece we publish.

Edelman commentary on the 2026 Edelman-LinkedIn report; survey of more than 1,100 executives in seven countries; agency and platform research.

# Gateway 3: When Commercial Is Ready to Share Its Brain

Source: https://lowob.com/research/gateway-three-when-commercial-is-ready-to-share-its-brain/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-26 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The commercial record should spread only when it already works: decisions recorded, outcomes written back, value reported in money, permissions holding and a named owner in the next function asking for it. Delivery is the natural second function, finance the third, and people decisions the last, because they change the legal footing. Each extension brings a new owner, a new outcome lag and a lower ceiling on autonomy.

Gateway 3 is the point at which the commercial record is extended to delivery, finance and people. It should be passed on evidence, not ambition: one decision class recorded for at least two quarters, outcomes written back, value reported in money, permissions holding, an export tested, and a named owner in the next function asking for the record. Delivery comes first because it inherits the client from sales. Finance comes second because it already audits the dollar figures from Gateway 2. People decisions come last, because hiring, promotion and performance carry legal duties that commercial decisions do not, including EU AI Act high-risk obligations for employment systems from 2 December 2027. At each step the owner changes, the outcome lag lengthens and the ceiling on autonomy drops.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

The previous two gateways tested the commercial build from inside: Gateway 1 asked whether every outbound action has a named approver, and Gateway 2 asked whether every recorded decision carries a value and an outcome. Gateway 3 asks a different question. Is the commercial record good enough that another function should build on it, rather than start its own?

That question matters because the alternative is common. Each function buys its own assistant and its own connectors, records decisions in its own way, and the firm ends up with four partial brains that cannot read each other. IBM's 2025 CEO study found half of CEOs saying the pace of recent investment had left them with disconnected, piecemeal technology. Extending one working record is how a firm avoids building four.

## Why the brain should not spread early

There are two ways to fail at this gateway: too early and never. Too early is the more expensive.

The evidence on scaling is thin because so few firms have done it. McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey of 1,993 participants found 23% scaling an agentic system somewhere in the enterprise, but no more than 10% reporting scaling agents in any single business function. IBM found only 16% of AI initiatives scaled enterprise-wide. A firm whose commercial record is still unreliable will export the unreliability: missing reasons, unwritten outcomes, inconsistent definitions. A second function inheriting that will conclude the record does not work, and will be right.

Our scale guide, [*The scale ladder*](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/), makes the general version of this point: build the layer the next stage will break, not one two stages ahead. Gateway 3 is that rule applied to functions instead of headcount.

## The six tests

Each test has a yes or no answer. All six should be yes before the record extends.

| Test | Evidence that it passes | Why it matters for the next function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A class recorded for two quarters | Records exist for every decision in the class, not a sample | The next function needs a working template, not a pilot |
| Outcomes written back on time | At least four in five records have outcomes by the check date | Proves the habit survives after launch enthusiasm |
| Value reported in money | Finance has accepted at least one quarterly money report | The next function's sponsor will ask the same renewal question |
| Permissions holding | Permission review done, no open leakage incident, account scoping in place | Delivery, finance and HR data are more sensitive than sales data |
| Export tested | A full export of records and history reloaded elsewhere | Shared records raise the cost of a lock-in mistake |
| A pull, not a push | A named owner in the next function has asked for access | Records spread by mandate are filled in to satisfy a review |

The last test is the one we weight most. When a delivery lead starts asking for the pursue-or-pass record before a project kick-off, or a finance director asks to see discount reasons before approving terms, the record has become useful outside its home. If nobody asks, extending it is a mandate, and [Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) made the point that records filled in to satisfy a review are worse than no records, because they look like evidence and are not.

## Delivery: the record follows the client

Delivery is the natural second function because it inherits the client from sales. Every promise made in the pitch becomes a constraint on the work, and most of the costly misunderstandings in a services or project business happen at that handover.

**What changes.** The decision classes shift from winning work to running it: scope changes, staffing choices, write-offs of time, and escalations. The owner moves from the head of sales to delivery leads. The outcome lag lengthens, from a sales cycle to the length of a project or a renewal. And the context becomes more confidential, because delivery holds the client's own data and problems as well as the firm's view of the client.

**The first shared class.** The sale-to-delivery handover. A short record at the moment a deal closes: what was promised, what was priced in and what was not, the client's stated success measure, and the discount or concession granted and why. The delivery lead reads it before kick-off; the outcome (project margin, scope disputes, renewal) is written back to the original commercial decisions. That closes a loop sales has never had: whether the way a deal was won made it profitable to deliver.

**The dial.** Agents can prepare kick-off briefs and flag scope drift against the handover record. Anything that reaches the client still passes Gateway 1.

## Finance: the dollar figure gets a co-owner

Finance is already involved by Gateway 3. It signed off the value-at-stake definitions at Gateway 2 and reviews the quarterly money report. Extending the record turns finance from auditor of the commercial record into a contributor to it.

Finance teams are cautious adopters, with reason. Gartner's 2025 survey of 183 finance leaders found 59% using AI in the finance function, up only slightly from 58% in 2024, with knowledge management (49%), accounts payable automation (37%) and anomaly detection (34%) as the leading uses. Weak data quality was the largest barrier, and 91% initially reported low or moderate impact. A finance team that has watched the commercial record produce accepted money reports has evidence that most of those respondents lacked.

**What changes.** Decision classes such as credit terms for new clients, payment-term exceptions, write-offs and collections priority. These sit inside the firm's financial controls, so segregation of duties applies: the person who records a payment-term exception should not be the one who approves it. The record becomes evidence for auditors, which raises the standard for status and supersession fields ([*Supersede, never overwrite*](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)).

**The dial.** Agents prepare and reconcile; they do not approve. A collections agent can draft a prioritised list with reasons. A person decides who is chased.

## People: the step that changes the legal footing

People decisions pass every test of frequency and consequence, and they are the last function the record should reach. The reason is law, not technology.

| Regime | What it requires | Status in 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EU AI Act, Annex III (employment) | Risk management, data governance, logging and human oversight for AI used in recruitment, promotion, termination, task allocation and performance monitoring | Under the Digital Omnibus (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, in force since 27 July 2026), applies from 2 December 2027 |
| NYC Local Law 144 | Bias audit within a year before using an automated employment decision tool, a public summary, and notice to candidates | Enforced since July 2023 |
| UK GDPR, Article 22C, as amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 | For solely automated significant decisions: information, a chance to make representations, meaningful human review and a way to contest | ICO guidance in draft, updated March 2026 |

The ICO's draft guidance is direct about the human review: it "cannot be tokenistic", and the reviewer must have authority to change the outcome. That rules out the pattern of an agent ranking candidates and a person approving the list.

Enforcement has been patchy. New York State's Comptroller found in December 2025 that the city's consumer agency had received only two complaints under Local Law 144 in two years and, in compliance reviews of 32 companies, had found one instance of non-compliance where the auditors identified at least 17 potential instances. Patchy enforcement is not a reason to build carelessly. It is a reason to expect enforcement to tighten.

**What changes.** The owner is HR, with legal involved. The sensitivity is the highest in the firm. The outcome lag is longest: a hire is graded over a year or more. **The dial.** Record people decisions, with reasons, so the firm can explain them. Let agents answer questions and draft, at most. No agent ranks, screens or scores people at this stage of the build.

> Each function the record reaches brings a new owner, a longer wait for outcomes and a lower ceiling on what agents may do alone.

## What changes at each step

| Function | First shared decision class | New owner | Outcome lag | Main risk | Autonomy ceiling |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial | Discount exceptions, pursue or pass | Head of sales | A sales cycle | Review fatigue | Act with approval |
| Delivery | Sale-to-delivery handover | Delivery leads | A project or renewal | Client confidentiality | Draft |
| Finance | Payment-term exceptions, write-offs | Finance director | A quarter to a year | Segregation of duties | Draft and reconcile |
| People | Hiring and promotion reasons | HR, with legal | A year or more | Employment law and bias | Answer and draft |

The order bends where the business does. In a firm where delivery and sales are the same people, as in many small consultancies, delivery is not a separate extension; it is part of the commercial record from the start. In a regulated lender, finance controls may arrive with the first commercial record, as [Part 10](https://lowob.com/research/the-same-build-in-four-industries/) found.

Gateway 3 is also not passed once. In [*The transitions that break the brain*](https://lowob.com/research/the-transitions-that-break-the-brain/) we listed the moments when firms lose their reasoning: a reorganisation that orphans record ownership, an acquisition that brings a second set of definitions, a platform migration that drops supersession links. Any of these should send the firm back through the six tests before the record extends further.

Illustrative example: the handover record that delivery asked for

Decision
:   Extend the commercial record to delivery with one shared class, the sale-to-delivery handover, after two quarters of discount and pursue-or-pass records.

Reason and owner
:   Delivery leads had begun asking sellers for discount reasons before kick-offs, after two projects ran at a loss on concessions nobody had passed on. Owned by the head of delivery, with the head of sales as co-owner.

What changed
:   Every closed deal now carries a handover record; project margin is written back to the original pursue-or-pass and discount records. Finance and people extensions were deferred to the following year.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consultancy, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Extend on evidence, not ambition.** Six tests; all should be yes.
- **Wait for the pull.** The best signal is a named owner in another function asking for the record.
- **Delivery, then finance, then people.** Each step lengthens the outcome lag and lowers the autonomy ceiling.
- **People decisions change the law that applies.** Record them; do not automate them.
- **Re-test after every transition.** Reorganisations, acquisitions and migrations reset the gateway.

Gateway card

### Gateway 3: before the record leaves the commercial line

- One commercial decision class recorded in full for two quarters
- Outcomes written back by the check date on at least four in five records
- At least one quarterly money report accepted by finance
- Permission review complete and account scoping in place
- Export of records and history tested by reloading it elsewhere
- A named owner in the receiving function who has asked for access
- For people decisions: legal review of the applicable employment and data protection rules

## Common questions

### When should AI be extended beyond sales and marketing?

When the commercial build is working on evidence: decisions recorded with outcomes for two quarters, value reported in money, permissions holding, an export tested, and a named owner in the next function asking for access.

### Is AI used in hiring regulated?

Yes. NYC Local Law 144 requires bias audits for automated employment decision tools, UK GDPR requires safeguards for solely automated significant decisions, and EU AI Act obligations for employment systems apply from 2 December 2027 under the Digital Omnibus.

### How should finance teams use AI decision records?

To record and reconcile decisions such as payment-term exceptions and write-offs, with segregation of duties preserved. Agents prepare and reconcile; people approve.

### What is the first decision to share between sales and delivery?

The sale-to-delivery handover: what was promised, what was priced in, the client's success measure and any concession granted, with project margin written back to the original commercial decisions.
