# The Reason Nobody Types

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-reason-nobody-types/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-26 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The operative reason for many decisions is political, personal, embarrassing or legally sensitive, so a system that records only the sayable reason produces clean, coherent and quietly false records. Research on organisational silence, psychological safety and premortems explains why, and AI-drafted rationales make it worse. No design fully fixes this, but a completeness flag, scoped visibility, a cynic's question and outcome write-back make it much better.

The operative reason for many decisions is political, personal, embarrassing or legally sensitive. A system that only records the sayable reason produces clean, coherent and quietly false records, and precedent built on them misleads. Research on organisational silence and psychological safety explains why people withhold, and Gary Klein's premortem shows that changing the frame of a question changes what people will say. No design fully fixes this, but a completeness flag, scoped visibility, a cynic's question and outcome write-back make it much better.

Ask anyone who has run decision reviews: the stated reason and the operative reason often differ. The deal was approved partly because the sponsor is leaving and wanted a win. The vendor was chosen because the alternative's team burned someone two years ago. The launch slipped because nobody had the capacity, not because of the market conditions in the memo. None of that gets typed into a shared system.

This matters more for judgment systems than for any other kind of record. A [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) exists to be reused as precedent. If the stated reasons are systematically incomplete, precedent misleads. The next person sees a coherent rationale and copies a decision whose real driver no longer applies.

## Why the sayable reason wins

Organisational research has described this for a quarter of a century. Elizabeth Morrison and Frances Milliken's 2000 paper in the Academy of Management Review introduced "organisational silence": the collective withholding of concerns, information and opinions, made the default by managerial beliefs and organisational structures. A decision log does not escape those forces. It inherits them, and adds permanence.

Amy Edmondson's 1999 study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company defined team psychological safety as "a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking". Teams with more of it showed more learning behaviour: seeking feedback, discussing errors, experimenting. Writing the real reason for a decision into a system colleagues can read is interpersonal risk taking of a very direct kind.

A new problem arrives with AI. Teams increasingly ask a model to draft the rationale from meeting notes or an email thread. The model will produce the reason that reads best from the material it was given, which is the sayable one. Miles Turpin and colleagues showed in 2023 that model explanations can "systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction", producing plausible justifications that omit what actually drove the answer. A drafted rationale is fluent by construction. Fluency is not evidence that it is the reason.

> A record that contains only the sayable reason is not incomplete. It is coherent, which is worse.

## Four kinds of unsayable reason

It helps to separate them, because each needs a different response.

| Kind | Example | Why it goes unrecorded | Response |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Political | Sponsorship, internal alliances, timing around people | Naming it exposes colleagues | Scoped visibility; cynic's question |
| Relational | History with a counterparty; personal trust or distrust | Feels unprofessional to write | Completeness flag |
| Embarrassing | Lack of time or skill; a mistake being quietly corrected | Exposes the writer | Builders go first; cynic's question |
| Legally sensitive | Reasons that should not be written casually at all | Records are discoverable | Counsel's design, not more capture |

The last category deserves a direct statement. Some reasons genuinely should not be in a broadly accessible record. Under Rule 26(b)(1) of the US Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, parties "may obtain discovery regarding any nonprivileged matter that is relevant to any party's claim or defense", subject to proportionality. Other jurisdictions differ in detail, not in principle. The right answer is counsel's design, not more capture. A judgment system in a regulated firm should be designed with legal and compliance from the start, including what is written, where, and who can see it. Our piece on [the permission problem](https://lowob.com/research/the-permission-problem-when-commercial-context-leaks/) covers access design.

## What helps with the rest

**A completeness flag.** Let people mark "stated reason, not the whole story" without requiring the whole story. It is honest and cheap, and it tells later readers to weight the precedent accordingly. A system that retrieves precedent should show the flag beside the rationale, not bury it in metadata.

**Scoped visibility.** Some reasoning can be visible only to the decision owner and the review gate. Narrower audiences produce franker records. The scope should be set at the field level, so the decision and outcome stay broadly visible while the frank rationale does not. Our explainer on [permission-aware retrieval](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/) covers how AI search respects those scopes.

**The cynic's question.** Ask, as an optional field: "What would a sceptical colleague say was the real reason?" It gives people a deniable way to record the operative driver, and it is often answered with surprising candour. The mechanism has a well-studied cousin. Gary Klein's premortem, described in Harvard Business Review in 2007, asks a team to assume a project has already failed and write down why. Klein cites research finding that this "prospective hindsight" increases the ability to correctly identify reasons for future outcomes by 30%, and argues the method works partly by "making it safe for dissenters" to speak. Both techniques change the frame from confession to analysis.

**Outcomes as a truth serum.** Over time, [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) exposes the gap. Decisions whose stated reasons repeatedly fail to predict their results are telling you that the stated reasons are not the real ones. You do not need anyone to confess; the pattern shows itself.

| Design | What it costs | What it catches | What it misses |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Completeness flag | One checkbox | Records known to be partial | Records the writer thinks are complete |
| Scoped visibility | Field-level permissions | Political and relational reasons | Reasons nobody will write anywhere |
| Cynic's question | One optional field | Embarrassing and political drivers | Writers who skip optional fields |
| Outcome write-back | A review step at a set date | Systematic gaps, after the fact | Single decisions; it needs a pattern |

## The builders go first

The first test of any judgment system is whether its own builders record their unflattering reasons. If the team running the programme writes only polished rationales, everyone else will too. Model the behaviour publicly, in your own records, before asking it of anyone else. Edmondson's finding cuts both ways: psychological safety is a property of the team, and the team learns what is safe from what its leaders do. Our piece [Dissent is the data you are throwing away](https://lowob.com/research/dissent-is-the-data-you-are-throwing-away/) covers the related problem of recording the views that lost.

## In practice

Add a completeness flag and the optional cynic's question to the record. Agree visibility scopes with legal and compliance before launch, not after the first awkward record. If a model drafts rationales, label them as drafts and require the owner to edit or confirm them. Quarterly, list decisions whose stated reasons failed to predict their outcomes, and review them privately with the owners.

Write three of your own honest, unflattering records in the first month.

## What would prove this wrong

Evidence that stated reasons in a well-designed system predict outcomes as well as private, candid accounts of the same decisions. Then the gap between stated and operative reasons is smaller than practitioners believe, and the extra fields are ceremony. We know of no study that has tested this directly. Running the comparison on your own records, once outcomes are in, is the honest way to find out.

## lowob takeaways

- **Coherent is not complete.** A record with only the sayable reason misleads every later reader.
- **Match the fix to the kind.** Flag, scope, ask the cynic's question, or hand it to counsel.
- **Treat AI-drafted rationales as drafts.** Fluent explanations can omit the real driver.
- **Let outcomes do the auditing.** Stated reasons that keep failing to predict results are not the real ones.

## Common questions

### Why are decision records often misleading?

The stated reason and the operative reason often differ, because the real driver is political, personal, embarrassing or legally sensitive. If stated reasons are systematically incomplete, precedent misleads.

### How can a decision log capture the real reasons behind decisions?

Add a completeness flag, scope visibility so frank reasoning is seen only by the owner and review gate, ask an optional cynic's question, and use outcome write-back to expose the gap over time.

### Should sensitive reasons be written into a shared decision system?

Some should not. In US litigation, any relevant nonprivileged record can be discoverable, so a judgment system in a regulated firm should be designed with legal and compliance from the start.

### Can AI write the rationale for a business decision?

It can draft one, but it will produce the reason that reads best from the material given, usually the sayable one. Research shows model explanations can misrepresent what drove an output, so the owner should confirm or edit.

Add two fields to your decision template this week: a "stated reason, not the whole story" checkbox and the optional cynic's question. Then fill both in honestly on your own next three decisions.

# Ask for the Gap, Not the Summary

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ask-for-the-gap-not-the-summary/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A good judgment system does not ask people to summarise everything. It compares each live decision record against a template of what that decision class needs, finds the most important missing item, and asks one specific question of the person most likely to know. Alert-fatigue and context research explain why one question beats five.

A good judgment system does not ask people to tell it everything. It knows what the next decision will need, notices what it is missing, and asks for exactly that, of the person most likely to know. The method is simple: write a needs template for each decision class, compare the live record against it, rank the gaps, and ask only the top one. One sharp question is answered in seconds. Five are an interrogation, and the research on alert fatigue shows what people do with too many prompts.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

The default capture prompt is "summarise the meeting". It produces long, generic text in which the one thing that mattered is buried or absent. People learn quickly that nobody reads the summary, and they stop writing good ones.

The better pattern is gap-seeking, and it is more tractable to build than it sounds.

## Why the summary fails

Summaries fail for two reasons, one about machines and one about people.

For the machine, more text is not more context. Anthropic's engineering guidance treats context as "a finite resource with diminishing marginal returns", cites research showing recall falls as context grows, and advises finding "the smallest set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of your desired outcome." A long meeting summary is the opposite: many tokens, little signal, and the critical fact somewhere in the middle. Our explainer on [context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/) covers the mechanics.

For people, a summary records what was discussed, and what was discussed is mostly what everyone already knew. Stasser and Titus's 1985 experiments found group discussion centres on shared information, while facts held by only one member are rarely raised. A summary of that discussion inherits the bias. The item that would change the next decision is often the one nobody said aloud. [Conversation intelligence](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversation-intelligence/) tools can transcribe everything; they cannot record what was never said.

## How to compute a gap

Every decision class has an implicit list of what a good decision needs. Make that list explicit as a template for each class, in the same spirit as the structured fields of a decision record: Martin Fowler's architecture decision record and the UK government's 2025 framework both specify the fields up front so that nothing important depends on someone remembering to include it.

| Decision class | What a good decision needs |
| --- | --- |
| Renewal | Budget holder, usage trend, competitive threat, relationship temperature, open support issues, contract terms |
| Credit review | Recent financials, loan-condition status, ownership changes, sector view, covenant headroom |
| Discount exception | Deal size, standard terms, precedent for similar exceptions, approver, competitive pressure |
| Partnership | Partner's incentive, exclusivity terms, owner on each side, exit terms, first milestone |

Then, after any interaction touching a live decision, compare the record's current state with the template. The difference is the gap list. The ten decision types in [The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) are a reasonable place to start writing templates.

## Rank, then ask one

Rank gaps by three things: how much the next decision depends on the item, how stale the current information is, and how cheap it is to answer. Ask only the top one.

| Gap in a renewal record | Decision depends on it | Staleness | Cost to answer | Ask now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Budget holder after the reorganisation | High | Six months old | One sentence | Yes |
| Competitor in the account | High | Three months old | One sentence, may be unknown | Next time |
| Usage trend | Medium | Available from product data | Zero, fetch it | Fetch, do not ask |
| Relationship temperature | Medium | Two weeks old | One word | No |

The discipline of one question is not politeness. It is what keeps the questions answered. In a review of 17 studies, Heleen van der Sijs and colleagues found clinicians overrode drug safety alerts in roughly 49% to 96% of cases. Among the system flaws they identified were low specificity, unclear information and unnecessary disruption to work. A capture system that sends five questions after every call is building the same habit. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently; a question queue adds to that load unless every question earns its place.

> A single, sharp question is answered in seconds. Five questions feel like an interrogation and get skipped.

## Good gap questions are specific and answerable

"Did the budget holder change after the reorganisation?" "Was the objection about price, or about timing?" "Is the March waiver of the loan condition still in force?"

Each can be answered in a few words. "I don't know" is a valid answer and itself useful: it marks an item the next person should verify, not assume.

**Route the question to whoever knows.** Gap-seeking does not have to ask the person who just finished the interaction. The system often knows who touched the account last, who owns the relationship, or who analysed the sector. Route the question to the person most likely to answer it well. Given what the group research shows about knowledge held by one person, this is often the only way that knowledge reaches the record. It turns the system from a form into something closer to a well-informed colleague who knows who to ask.

## Gaps that recur are schema problems

Track which gaps appear most often across records. A gap that recurs across many decisions is usually a field the schema lacks, or a source the system is not connected to. In the ranking table above, usage trend should never be a question: it is a data connection waiting to be made. Recurring gaps are the cheapest product research you will ever get, because the system is telling you, in aggregate, what it does not know.

**Mind the tone.** A system that only ever asks what is missing can feel like an auditor. Pair every gap question with a give: the precedent, the warning, the drafted brief. And never ask the same person more than one gap question per interaction. Our review of [AI notetakers for decision capture](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-notetakers-for-decision-capture/) covers which tools can be configured to work this way.

## What would prove this wrong

Records built from free-form summaries proving as complete and as useful for later decisions as records built from targeted gap questions, at similar cost in time. Then the summary is good enough. This is testable: run both on one decision class for a quarter and compare how often each record answered the questions asked of it later.

## lowob takeaways

- **Template first.** Write the six to ten things a good decision in each class needs.
- **Compare, rank, ask one.** Dependence, staleness and cost to answer decide which gap comes first.
- **Route to whoever knows.** The person who just left the meeting is not always the right one.
- **Fix recurring gaps in the schema.** A question asked every week is a missing field or connection.

## Common questions

### What is gap-seeking in a knowledge or decision system?

Instead of asking for a summary, the system compares a decision record with a template of what that decision class needs and asks for the single most important missing item.

### How many follow-up questions should a system ask after a meeting?

One. A single sharp question is answered in seconds, while several feel like an interrogation and get skipped. Never ask the same person more than one gap question per interaction.

### Who should a gap question go to?

The person most likely to answer it well, such as whoever last touched the account, owns the relationship or analysed the sector, not necessarily the person who just finished the interaction.

### Why are AI meeting summaries often useless?

They record what was discussed, which is mostly what everyone already knew, and they bury the one item that matters in long text. A targeted question about the missing item is shorter and more useful.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
- [Stasser and Titus, Pooling of unshared information in group decision making](https://www.uni-muenster.de/imperia/md/content/psyifp/aeechterhoff/vorlesungkommunikation/stasser_titus_unsharedinfogroupdisc_jpsp1985.pdf), *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology* 48(6), 1985. Laboratory experiment with student groups.
- [van der Sijs, Aarts, Vulto and Berg, Overriding of drug safety alerts in computerized physician order entry](https://repub.eur.nl/pub/60465), *JAMIA* 13(2), 2006. Peer-reviewed review of 17 clinical studies; an analogue, not a study of business capture tools.
- [Gartner, Survey finds 77% of sellers struggle to complete their assigned tasks efficiently](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-11-02-gartner-survey-finds-77-percent-of-sellers-struggle-to-complete-their-assigned-tasks-efficiently), 2 November 2023. Analyst survey of 501 sellers; self-reported.

- [GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/architectural-decision-record-framework/architectural-decision-record-framework), 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard.
- The templates and ranking table are **lowob**'s illustrations and working method.

## Related research

## Next move

Write a needs template for one decision class this week (renewals are the usual choice) and compare your five most recent renewal records against it. The gap that appears in most of them is your first new field.

# Integrators, OEMs and Channel Partners

Source: https://lowob.com/research/integrators-oems-and-channel-partners/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: In emerging tech the buyer already trusts someone else's hands, so the job is to make integrators and partners want to carry you, one partner at a time. Canalys estimated 70% of technology spending in 2025 would go through partners. Do the first deployments direct, productise the playbook, and measure only partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot.

In emerging tech the buyer already trusts someone else's hands; your job is to make those hands want to carry you, one partner at a time. Most technology spending already moves that way: Canalys estimated 70% of customer spending on technology, IT services and telecom services would go through partners in 2025. Do the first deployments yourself, productise the playbook into documents a partner can use, then work one partner's live deal to paid pilot before adding a second. Measure partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot, and nothing else.

## The buyer already has suppliers

[Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) made the case that when platforms are closed, distribution has to be built. In emerging tech the platforms are people. A utility, a port operator, a hospital group or a mine does not buy a robot, a sensor network or a verification layer from a startup. It buys from whoever already holds three things.

The relationship: an integrator or engineering firm that has been on site for years. The procurement vehicle: a framework agreement, an approved vendor list, a distributor already in the system. The liability: a managed service provider who answers the call at 3am and carries the insurance.

The scale of that structure is measurable in technology markets generally. Canalys, an analyst firm, forecast worldwide IT spending of $5.44 trillion in 2025 and estimated that 70% of it would go through partners, down from 71% in 2024 and 73% in 2023. Forrester's 2025 buyers' journey survey, cited in February 2026, found an average of nine people from outside the buying organisation involved in a purchase decision. Many of those outside voices are the integrators and advisers the buyer already pays.

You can fight that structure or use it. Fighting it means two-year sales cycles against a buyer who wants to say no. Using it means selling once to the partner and letting the partner sell many times.

## What the partner believes

[Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) asked for a belief per audience. The partner's belief is not your customer's belief. The customer wants risk retired. The partner wants three plainer things.

Margin: a deal that pays better than reselling what they already resell. Differentiation: something to say in a tender that the next integrator cannot say. No support burden: confidence that your product will not turn their engineers into your unpaid support desk.

If your pitch to a partner is the same deck you show customers, you have not done the work. Write the partner's belief as one sentence and put it in the claims register.

## What a channel partner needs from you

Partners are not evaluating your technology. They are evaluating the cost of carrying it. Five things lower that cost.

| What the partner needs | What good looks like | What fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A reference deployment | Live, with a customer who will take their call | A pilot under NDA nobody can speak about |
| A certified integration | Tested and documented with what the partner already installs | Roadmap |
| Training | A module their field and sales teams can complete, with a pass mark | A deck and a recorded webinar |
| Partner margin | Survives their cost of sale, which carries travel, site time and bid cost | Your direct discount, relabelled |
| A support path | A service level, an escalation route and a named person on your side | A shared inbox |

Miss any one and the partner will sign your agreement and sell what they already know. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) sets out how to define the partner's role in the sale and pay each type accordingly.

## Direct first, channel second

The temptation is to recruit partners before the product is stable, because partners look like a multiplier. They multiply only once there is something repeatable to multiply.

Do the first deployments yourself. [Part 33](https://lowob.com/research/first-customers-in-a-market-that-doesnt-exist-yet/)'s design partners are where the playbook comes from. You learn the site-survey questions, the installation sequence, the failure modes, the commissioning test, and what the customer calls the thing you sell. Write all of it down as you go.

Then productise the playbook. Installation guide, commissioning checklist, training module, support runbook, pricing sheet with partner margin. That document set is what you hand a partner. Without it you are asking them to learn at their own cost.

> Partners multiply only once there is something repeatable to multiply.

## OEM, embedded and platform programmes

Two other routes sit beside the channel.

OEM or embedded deals put your technology inside someone else's product. A perception module in a robotics platform, a verification layer in an identity product, a control algorithm in a battery system. In our experience these are slow to close, often eighteen months or more, sticky once live and lower margin than direct, and the reach can be larger than anything you could build. Price them as licences or per-unit royalties. Protect your right to sell direct and to serve other OEMs, and write down in advance which accounts each route owns. [Channel conflict, and how to manage it](https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/) covers the rules that stop an OEM and your direct team from bidding against each other.

Ecosystem and platform programmes are distribution with a badge. Cloud marketplaces, chip-vendor partner programmes, robotics platform ecosystems, standards-body member lists. They open procurement vehicles, co-marketing and sometimes co-selling. They rarely close deals on their own. Treat them as a channel to partners, not a channel to customers.

The procurement value is real and growing. Canalys projected in August 2024 that sales through hyperscaler cloud marketplaces would grow from $16 billion in 2023 to $85 billion by 2028, and that more than half would flow through the channel by 2027, using partner private offer programmes from AWS, Microsoft and Google Cloud. A marketplace listing lets a buyer spend committed cloud budget; a partner private offer lets the integrator keep its margin on that spend. [Marketplace listings for B2B sellers](https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/) and [co-selling with platforms](https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/) cover how each works.

## The trap, and the measure

The trap is ten signed partners who do nothing. The partner agreement costs nothing to sign and nothing to ignore. A logo slide of integrators is not a channel.

The industry is moving the other way on volume. Forrester's 2025 partner ecosystem marketing survey found most vendors expected their ecosystems to grow in number of partners across every type, and 67% expected indirect revenue to grow by more than 30%. More partners raise the risk that each one gets less attention. Depth beats count.

Pick one partner with a live deal in front of them and a named owner inside their business who is paid on that deal. Work that deal with them to paid pilot. Then do it again with the same partner before you add a second.

Measure partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot. Not partners signed, not partner-registered leads, not joint webinars. One number, reported monthly alongside the direct equivalent. Where partners register deals, [deal registration](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-deal-registration/) rules decide who is credited and protected.

| Stage | What counts | What does not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recruited | Named owner, live deal identified | Signed agreement |
| Enabled | Training passed, integration certified | Deck sent |
| Selling | Partner-sourced paid pilot | Registered lead |
| Scaling | Second paid pilot, same partner | Second partner |

## The checklist

| Item | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Partner belief | Written as one sentence and in the claims register |
| Playbook | First deployments done direct; the document set exists |
| First partner | One partner has a live deal, a named owner and a commission on it |
| Margin | Tested against the partner's real cost of sale |
| Support | Service levels and an escalation route in place |
| Measure | Partner-sourced pipeline to paid pilot is the only channel metric reported |

## lowob takeaways

- **Sell to whoever holds the relationship, the vehicle and the liability.** Most technology spend already moves through partners.
- **Write the partner's belief, not the customer's.** Margin, differentiation and no support burden.
- **Go direct first, then hand over a document set.** Partners will not learn your product at their own cost.
- **Treat marketplaces and programmes as routes to partners.** They open procurement; they rarely close deals.
- **Measure paid pilots, not signatures.** Depth with one partner beats a logo slide of ten.

## Common questions

### How do emerging tech startups sell through channel partners?

Sell once to the partner and let the partner sell many times. Give them a live reference deployment, a certified integration, training with a pass mark, a margin that survives their cost of sale, and a support path with a service level.

### When should a startup start recruiting channel partners?

Only once there is something repeatable to multiply. Do the first deployments yourself, write the playbook down, then productise it before handing it to a partner.

### What metric should I use to measure channel partner performance?

Partner-sourced pipeline that reaches paid pilot, reported monthly alongside the direct equivalent. Not partners signed, partner-registered leads or joint webinars.

### How should OEM or embedded technology deals be priced?

Price them as licences or per-unit royalties, and protect your right to sell direct and to serve other OEMs, with written rules on which accounts each route owns.

- [Canalys, IT spending forecasts 2025](https://canalys.com/insights/it-spending-forecasts-2025), November 2024 (undated page). Analyst forecast; covers technology, IT services and telecom broadly, not emerging tech specifically.
- [Canalys, Hyperscaler cloud marketplace sales to hit US$85 billion by 2028](https://canalys.com/newsroom/hyperscaler-cloud-marketplace), 15 August 2024. Analyst forecast.
- [Forrester, Continued growth in scale and complexity: the state of partner ecosystems in 2025](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-state-of-partner-ecosystems-2025/), 7 July 2025. Analyst blog on Forrester's Partner Ecosystem Marketing Survey; sample not stated in the post; respondent expectations, not outcomes.
- [Forrester, Three realities about B2B buying networks](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/three-realities-about-b2b-buying-networks/), 23 February 2026. Analyst blog citing the Buyers' Journey Survey, 2025.
- The partner needs table, the stage table and the OEM timing are **lowob**'s framework and field experience, not survey data.

# Measuring Brand in B2B

Source: https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: B2B brand work is cut first because attribution cannot see it, yet most buying groups have ranked their vendors before first contact. We set out five measures that hold up in B2B, how to adapt them to small markets with few buyers, and how to turn brand spend into a recorded decision with an expected outcome and a check date.

Measuring brand in B2B means tracking whether buyers think of you, and rank you, before they contact anyone. That ranking now happens early: 6sense's 2025 survey of more than 4,000 buyers found 94% of buying groups had ranked preferred vendors before first contact, and the favourite usually won. Attribution systems see only what happens after that moment, which is why brand budgets are cut first and defended worst. Five measures hold up in B2B: share of search, shortlist rate, mental availability against buying situations, branded demand, and win rate and price when the buyer already knew you. Each needs adapting when a market has a few hundred buyers rather than millions.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Performance spend comes with a dashboard. Brand spend comes with a belief, and when the quarter is tight, the belief loses. This piece is not an argument for spending more on brand; our explainer *Brand vs performance marketing* covers how the two work on different timescales. The question here is what a 50- to 500-person B2B firm can measure, cheaply and honestly, to know whether its brand is doing its job.

## Why brand goes unmeasured in B2B

Three structural reasons keep brand off the dashboard.

**Attribution only sees the in-market few.** The B2B Institute, LinkedIn's research unit, worked with John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute on what they call the 95:5 rule. Their illustration: if most companies switch business banks about once every five years, roughly 20% are in market in a year, about 2% in a month and about 1% in a fortnight. Dawes's own May 2021 report puts the quarterly figure at something like 5%, reasoning from corporations changing providers such as their principal bank or law firm around once every five years. Attribution tools record the clicks and form fills of that small in-market group. The memory built among everyone else does not appear until months later, and then it appears as "direct" or "organic".

**Spending skews to activation.** Les Binet and Peter Field's analysis of B2B cases in the IPA Databank, published by the B2B Institute, found B2B businesses grew best with about 46% of budget on brand building and 54% on activation, and noted that spending tends to drift toward activation because sales targets are more pressing. Our earlier piece suggests a smaller firm still finding its first channel may start nearer 75:25. Either way, the drift is real and it happens by default.

**The sample is small.** A consumer brand can run a tracker on thousands of respondents. A firm selling to 400 mid-market manufacturers cannot. Most B2B brand measurement fails not because the measures are wrong but because they were borrowed from consumer markets without adjustment.

## What the evidence says brand decides

The case for measuring brand rests on where B2B decisions are now made.

| Finding | Source | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 94% of buying groups ranked preferred vendors before first contact | 6sense, 2025 Buyer Experience Report, 4,000+ buyers | The shortlist is set before sales can influence it |
| The preferred vendor chosen before seller contact wins about 80% of deals; buyers bought from the favourite 77% of the time | 6sense, 2025 | Being the favourite matters more than being on the list |
| 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience; 45% used AI in a recent purchase | Gartner, March 2026, 646 buyers | More of the early research happens where you cannot see it |
| Brands whose share of voice exceeds their share of market tend to grow | Binet and Field, IPA Databank B2B cases | Brand spend relative to competitors is a growth input |
| Campaigns aimed at fame and mental availability outperform others | Binet and Field | Brand objectives should be measured as mental, not only behavioural |

The 6sense and Gartner figures are self-reported surveys, so read them as direction rather than precision. The direction is consistent: a buyer forms a preference from memory, peers, reviews and AI assistants, and arrives at the first sales conversation with a ranking. Brand decides your place in it.

> If the shortlist is set before first contact, the first measure of brand is whether you were on it.

## Five measures that hold up

No single brand number is enough. The five below work together, and each answers a different question.

| Measure | Question it answers | Data source | Cadence | Main failure mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Share of search | Is interest in us rising relative to rivals? | Search volume for your brand name against named competitors | Monthly, read quarterly | Breaks when volumes are tiny or the name is a common word |
| Shortlist rate | Were we on the list before first contact? | A required field at first meeting: "who else are you considering, and had you heard of us?" | Monthly | Sellers skip the field unless it is short and reviewed |
| Mental availability | Do buyers think of us in the situations that trigger a purchase? | Survey of category buyers against a list of buying situations | Twice a year | Too few respondents, or situations written in your language rather than the buyer's |
| Branded demand | Are buyers seeking us by name? | Branded search clicks, direct inbound, "heard of us from" answers | Monthly | Paid branded search inflating the number |
| Known-buyer win rate and price | Does familiarity pay at close? | Win rate and discount for deals where the buyer knew you first, against those where they did not | Quarterly | Too few deals per quarter to separate noise |

**Share of search.** Les Binet presented this at the IPA's EffWorks Global in October 2020. Across automotive, energy and mobile handsets, a brand's share of category search tracked its market share, rises tended to precede share gains, and the lead could be as long as a year in cars. Binet called it "by no means a silver bullet": price and other factors affect conversion. In B2B it works best in categories with real search volume, such as software, payments or logistics, and poorly in niches where monthly searches are in the dozens.

**Shortlist rate.** This is the cheapest measure most firms are not collecting. Add two fields to the first-meeting record in the CRM: which competitors the buyer is considering, and whether they knew of you before outreach. Over a year, the share of first meetings where you were already known and already shortlisted is a brand measure your sales team generates for free. It also improves the closed-lost record, which our explainer *What is a closed-lost reason?* covers.

**Mental availability against buying situations.** Jenni Romaniuk's work with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, adapted for B2B by the B2B Institute, frames brand as a network of category entry points: the situations in which a buyer starts to need the category. A logistics platform's entry points might be "a carrier fails peak season" or "we are expanding into a new country". The method is to list the situations, prune those with low credibility, high competition or low frequency, and survey buyers on which brands come to mind for each. The measure is how many situations you are linked to, and by how many buyers.

**Branded demand.** Report paid branded search separately, or the brand team is measuring its own media budget.

**Known-buyer win rate and price.** The commercial test of brand is whether familiarity changes the close. If buyers who knew you before first contact win more often, or need less discount, the brand is earning money a finance team can see. Our piece *Attribution vs incrementality* explains why this comparison is suggestive rather than causal.

## Measuring brand when the market is small

The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's November 2025 report *Easy to Find* surveyed more than 500 B2B marketers in the US and UK and found they used an average of 3.7 sales channels, and that about 30% could not estimate how much of their revenue came from their core product. If a firm cannot see its own portfolio, it is unlikely to see its brand clearly. The fix is to scale the measures to the market.

| Market shape | Example | Measures that work | Measures to skip |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thousands of buyers, real search volume | Mid-market software, payments | All five; share of search as the lead indicator | None |
| Hundreds of named accounts | Industrial components, specialist data | Shortlist rate, known-buyer win rate, a short survey of named accounts | Share of search; large trackers |
| Dozens of buyers | Infrastructure, enterprise platforms | Shortlist rate, structured win-loss interviews, analyst and partner mentions | Any survey-based tracker |
| New category, little search | Emerging technology, early AI tooling | Mental availability for the problem, not the category; branded demand from zero | Share of search until volume exists |

For a market of a few hundred accounts, a survey of 80 to 150 buyers twice a year can be enough to see movement in mental availability, provided the same situations are tested each time. For a market of dozens, the honest answer is that brand is measured one account at a time, through win-loss interviews and what partners and analysts say about you. Our explainer *What is win-loss analysis?* covers the interview method.

With 45% of buyers using AI in a recent purchase, how assistants describe you is now part of your brand; *How LLMs choose sources* covers how to check.

## Brand spend as a recorded decision

Brand budgets are lost because they are defended once a year, from memory, against a dashboard. The alternative is to treat brand spend the way The Build Order treats any commercial decision: written down with a reason, an owner, an expected outcome and a date to check it (*The commercial decisions worth recording*).

A brand decision record has five fields:

| Field | Example entry |
| --- | --- |
| Decision | Hold brand spend at 35% of programme budget for four quarters |
| Reason | Shortlist rate fell from roughly half to roughly a third of first meetings over the past year |
| Owner | Head of marketing; reviewed with the revenue leader |
| Expected outcome | Shortlist rate recovers; share of search stops falling against the two nearest rivals |
| Check date | Quarterly, with a full review at four quarters |

The argument with finance is no longer "brand matters" but "we expected these two numbers to move by this date; here is what happened". If they did not move, the record shows that too. *Stop reporting reach* covers why impressions belong outside this record.

The quarterly commercial review in Part 6 of this series is the natural home for the check. The KPI set in Part 7 should carry at least one brand measure, usually shortlist rate, so that it sits beside pipeline rather than in a separate marketing report.

Illustrative example: a software firm finds its brand problem in the CRM

Decision
:   Add two required fields to the first-meeting record (competitors considered; known before outreach) and report shortlist rate monthly.

Reason and owner
:   Paid search costs were rising and win rates falling, with no brand measure to explain either. Owned by the head of revenue operations.

What changed
:   After two quarters the firm saw it was known before outreach in under a third of first meetings, and that those deals closed with less discount. Brand spend was moved into the quarterly review with an expected shortlist rate and a check date.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Measure the moment before first contact.** Most buyers have ranked vendors by then; shortlist rate tells you where you stood.
- **Use several measures, scaled to the market.** Share of search needs volume; small markets need named-account surveys and win-loss interviews.
- **Separate paid from earned branded demand.** Otherwise the brand number is a media budget in disguise.
- **Record brand spend as a decision.** An expected outcome and a check date turn an annual argument into a quarterly review.

Gateway card

### Before your next brand budget review

- Shortlist and "known before outreach" fields added to the first-meeting record
- Share of search tracked against two or three named rivals, if volume allows
- Five to ten buying situations listed in the buyer's language
- Win rate and discount compared for known and unknown buyers
- Brand spend recorded with an expected outcome and a check date

## Common questions

### How do you measure brand awareness in B2B?

Combine share of search, a shortlist field captured at first sales contact, a survey of category buyers against buying situations, branded demand reported separately from paid search, and win rate for buyers who knew you before outreach.

### What is share of search?

Your brand's share of search volume among named competitors in a category. Les Binet's 2020 IPA work found it tracked market share in three categories and often moved first, though it needs meaningful search volume to work.

### What is the 95:5 rule in B2B marketing?

A rule of thumb from the B2B Institute and the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute that only a small share of business buyers are in market at any time, so most marketing should build memory among the larger group who will buy later.

### How much should a B2B company spend on brand versus performance?

Binet and Field's B2B analysis points to about 46% brand and 54% activation for established firms. Smaller firms still finding a channel often start with more performance spend and shift toward brand as the channel proves itself.

# Web3 Does Not Have One Customer. That Is Why Most Launch Plans Break.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/web3-multi-audience-launch-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-25 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A protocol may need users, developers, capital providers, distribution partners, institutions and governance participants before it works, and each is waiting for evidence from another. Map the groups, launch in the order the dependencies require, keep one product truth explained differently for each, and measure participation rather than attention. In the EU and US, consistency across audiences is now also a regulatory expectation.

A Web3 product can attract thousands of people to a launch announcement and still have almost nobody using it a month later, because it reached an audience but not the people needed to make it work. A protocol may need users, developers, capital providers, distribution partners, institutions and governance participants, each waiting for evidence from someone else. Map those groups, launch in the order the dependencies require, keep one product truth explained differently for each, and measure participation rather than attention.

Unlike a simple consumer app, a protocol may need several groups to participate before it works as intended. Users, developers, liquidity providers, ecosystem partners and institutions may each be waiting for evidence from someone else. A launch plan should solve those dependencies, not simply announce to everyone at once.

The evidence that announcements alone do not create usage is now well documented. Academic analysis of nine major airdrops found activity rose temporarily but lasting engagement did not follow, and after Arbitrum's airdrop, transactions per address fell even as total fees rose. Attention arrived. Most of the participants the network needed did not stay.

## Start with the people who make the product work

Six groups recur across Web3 launches. Not every project needs all six. A wallet app and a regulated asset platform have very different needs.

| Group | Role in the system | What it needs before it acts | Typical first measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Users | Use the product | A clear reason to try it, what it costs, how to exit | First meaningful action; return within 30 days |
| Developers and integrators | Build on or connect to it | Current documentation, a reliable integration path, support | Successful integrations in production |
| Capital and liquidity providers | Make it usable at size | Risk disclosure, audits, economic terms | Committed versus actively used capital, and how long it stays |
| Distribution partners | Bring their customers | What they gain, support obligations, demand evidence | Qualified introductions and downstream use |
| Institutions | Allocate, custody or list | Operating, compliance and accountability information | Diligence completed; first allocation |
| Community and governance | Sustain and steer it | A reason to take part, real decisions to make | Contributors and proposals with participation |

Write down the role each group plays. That is more useful than treating everyone as a single group called "the community". The same announcement is unlikely to answer all of those questions. The same logic applies in B2B selling, where the several members of a [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) each need different evidence before a deal moves.

## Launch in the order your product actually needs

Consider a hypothetical tokenised-asset platform. A broad marketing campaign might create awareness, but it would not replace custody arrangements, onboarding requirements or a way for investors to access the product.

A sensible sequence might be: confirm the legal and custody model; secure an anchor distribution or liquidity partner; test onboarding with a limited group; document the issues; and only then expand public promotion. The exact order depends on the business. The principle is to identify what must be true before the next audience can act.

- **First, readiness:** what needs to work for the first users or partners to take part.
- **Next, proof:** which successful integration, product action or operating result would make another group comfortable.
- **Then, distribution:** who can bring more of the right participants once that proof exists.

Regulation has made the readiness step more concrete in 2026. In the EU, MiCA's transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, and ESMA told unauthorised service providers to stop onboarding EU clients and stop marketing to them immediately. For a platform that depends on an exchange, custodian or broker to reach EU users, the partner's authorisation status is now a launch dependency, not a detail. In the US, the SEC's March 2026 interpretation clarified which tokens fall outside securities law, while its proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published in August 2026, is still a proposal. Institutions will ask where a product sits under both. Get counsel; this is not legal advice.

> A launch is not coordinated because every account posted on the same day. It is coordinated when one group's participation makes the next group's more likely.

## Keep one product truth, but change the explanation

Suppose the product makes it easier to access a particular financial instrument. A user wants to know what they can do and what it costs. A wallet integration team wants implementation details. A partner wants to understand demand and support obligations. An institution wants documentation, risk controls and accountability.

The product should not tell four contradictory stories. It should explain one real capability in four useful ways. For each audience, write down the claim, the evidence, the next action and the main reason they might hesitate. If the evidence does not exist yet, say that internally rather than filling the gap with marketing language. Our piece [one truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) sets out the method, and [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the truth in the first place.

Consistency is also a legal expectation. MiCA Article 7 requires crypto-asset marketing communications to be fair, clear and not misleading and consistent with the white paper, and bars marketing before a required white paper is published. The SEC's 2026 interpretation turns on what an issuer promised, when and through which medium, and Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous". A deck that tells investors one thing and a community post that implies another is a positioning problem and a disclosure problem at once.

## Use a 90-day plan as a sequence, not a countdown

| Phase | Work | Exit test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Days 1 to 30 | Interview the participants who matter most; identify blockers; test approved claims; make the first integration or onboarding reliable; define success | Named first users and partners; one working path end to end |
| Days 31 to 60 | Work with a small group of real users and partners; run developer sessions or walkthroughs; turn objections into documentation and product fixes | Repeat use from the first group; recurring objections answered in docs |
| Days 61 to 90 | Expand the channels and groups showing genuine activity; announce partnerships that create access or utility; use creators and community programming to explain what people already need help with | Activity growing in groups the next one depends on |

This is an illustrative sequence, not a promise that any Web3 project can reach launch readiness in exactly 90 days. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) covers the commercial record the team should keep through it.

## Measure useful participation, not just attention

Different participants need different measures: for users, a first meaningful action and whether they return; for developers, successful integrations; for capital providers, committed versus actively used capital and its persistence; for partners, qualified introductions and downstream product use. Link those outcomes to the cost of acquiring them where possible.

Capital providers will also judge risk, and the record gives them reason to. Chainalysis estimated over $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025. A launch plan that reaches liquidity providers before audits are named and dated asks them to take a risk the team has not yet reduced. Our piece on [the user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/) covers what each audience needs to see.

## lowob takeaways

- **Map the actual participants.** Do not treat users, builders, capital and partners as one audience.
- **Find the dependency chain.** Make the thing the next group needs to trust or use before inviting them.
- **Tailor the proof, not the truth.** Each group needs different evidence for the same consistent claim.
- **Measure continuing use.** A successful announcement is not the same as a working market.

## Common questions

### How do you plan a Web3 product launch?

List the groups the product needs, such as users, developers, liquidity providers, partners and institutions, and what each needs before acting. Sequence the launch by dependency: readiness first, then proof, then wider distribution.

### Who are the audiences for a crypto protocol launch?

Usually some of six groups: users, developers and integrators, capital and liquidity providers, distribution partners, institutional stakeholders, and community or governance participants. Not every project needs all six.

### Can a crypto project tell investors and users different stories?

It should explain one product truth differently for each, but never contradict itself. MiCA requires marketing to be consistent with the white paper, and US analysis of tokens turns on what issuers promised in public.

### How do you measure a Web3 launch?

By participation for each group: first meaningful actions and returns for users, live integrations for developers, actively used capital for liquidity providers, and qualified introductions for partners, linked to acquisition cost where possible.

- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 7, marketing communications](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-7-marketing-communications). EU regulation text.

Start with the commercial problem that needs solving. List the groups your product needs, write one line on what each must see before it acts, and put them in the order the dependencies require before any launch date goes on the calendar.

# What Are Embeddings?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-are-embeddings/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a piece of text, an image or another item, placed so that similar items sit close together. Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations, deduplication and retrieval for AI assistants. They measure similarity, not truth, and no single embedding model is best at every task.

An embedding is a list of numbers that represents a piece of text, an image or another item, arranged so that items with similar meaning sit close together. Comparing those numbers lets software find related content without matching exact words. Embeddings power semantic search, recommendations and retrieval for AI assistants. They measure similarity, not truth, and the right model depends on the task.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What embeddings mean

Computers compare numbers easily and meaning poorly. An embedding model bridges the gap. It reads an input, such as a sentence, an email or a product description, and outputs a fixed-length list of numbers. Each list is a point in a space with hundreds or thousands of dimensions.

The model is trained so that position carries meaning. Google's machine learning crash course uses food as its example. In a simple illustrative space, hot dog and shawarma sit near each other, while apple strudel sits further away. Real embeddings have far more dimensions; Google notes that word embeddings often use 256, 512 or 1,024, and that the individual dimensions are rarely as readable as "sandwich-ness".

The same course makes a point that matters for buyers: embeddings reflect the task they were trained for. Cereal and breakfast sausage might sit close together in a model organised by time of day and far apart in one organised by vegetarian or not.

| Embeddings are | Embeddings are not |
| --- | --- |
| Numeric representations of meaning | A summary a person can read |
| A way to measure similarity between items | A check on whether content is true |
| Produced by a separate, usually cheap, model | The language model that writes answers |
| Comparable only within the same embedding model | Portable between providers without re-embedding |

## How embeddings work, and why they matter for a commercial team

The workflow has three steps. Each document, record or passage is converted to an embedding and stored, usually in a vector database. A query is converted with the same model. The system then finds the stored items whose vectors sit closest to the query. OpenAI recommends cosine similarity, a measure of the angle between two vectors, as the distance function.

OpenAI lists the main uses as search, clustering, recommendations, anomaly detection, diversity measurement and classification. For a commercial team these translate into concrete jobs:

- Finding past proposals that answered a similar question, even when the wording differs.
- Matching inbound leads to the closest existing accounts to catch duplicates.
- Grouping win-loss notes by theme without a fixed tag list.
- Retrieving the relevant policy or case study before an assistant drafts a reply, the retrieval step in RAG.

Embedding is also cheap compared with generation. OpenAI estimates about 62,500 pages per dollar with text-embedding-3-small and about 9,615 with the large model, assuming roughly 800 tokens a page. A library of 10,000 documents can be embedded for a small one-off cost, though it must be redone when content changes or the model is replaced.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, embeddings sit in the wiring stage. They help the context layer choose what reaches the model. They do not record what was decided or why; that belongs in the record.

## How to evaluate embeddings, and common mistakes

| Check | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Test on your own queries | Public rankings average many tasks that may not match yours |
| Check language coverage | Performance varies by language and domain vocabulary |
| Decide chunk size | Whole documents blur meaning; very short passages lose context |
| Plan for re-embedding | Vectors from different models cannot be compared |
| Restrict access in the store | Embeddings derived from sensitive text remain sensitive |

The MTEB benchmark, published in October 2022 by Muennighoff and colleagues, tested 33 models and concluded that no particular method dominated across all tasks. A model that ranks first for retrieval may rank lower for clustering. Build a test set of 30 to 50 real queries with the documents a person would expect to see, and measure how often the right one appears in the top five.

The most common mistake is treating similarity as relevance. Two contracts can be close in embedding space and differ on the one clause that matters. A second is ignoring security. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications lists vector and embedding weaknesses as a risk category of their own. An assistant that retrieves from a shared store can surface content a user should not see. Apply the same permissions to the vector store as to the source documents.

## lowob takeaways

- **Embeddings measure closeness of meaning.** They let software find related content without exact words.
- **They are task-specific.** Test on your own queries before choosing a model.
- **Similar is not correct.** Retrieval narrows the field; a person or a check still decides.
- **Permissions travel with the data.** Secure the vector store like the source system.

## Common questions

### What are embeddings in simple terms?

They are lists of numbers that represent the meaning of text or other data. Items with similar meaning get similar numbers, so software can find related content by comparing them.

### What is the difference between embeddings and a vector database?

Embeddings are the numeric representations. A vector database stores them and finds the closest matches to a query quickly, often across millions of items.

### Are embeddings the same as a large language model?

No. Embedding models convert input into vectors for comparison. Language models generate text. Many AI systems use both: embeddings to retrieve, a language model to write.

### Can embeddings leak sensitive data?

They can. OWASP lists vector and embedding weaknesses among its 2025 LLM risks. Treat vector stores as sensitive and apply the same access rules as the source documents.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Vector embeddings guide](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/embeddings.md), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; page-per-dollar figures are vendor estimates.
- [Google for Developers, Machine Learning Crash Course: Embedding space](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/embeddings/embedding-space), accessed November 2026. Educational material; food examples are illustrative.
- [Muennighoff et al., MTEB: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.07316v3), October 2022, revised March 2023. Academic benchmark; model rankings have since changed.
- [OWASP, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/), November 2024. Community security project.

# From Founder-Led to Team-Led Marketing

Source: https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Founder-led marketing usually ends in one of two failures: a first hire dropped into a positioning vacuum, or a founder who never lets go. The fix is to transfer decision rights in sequence and hand over the reasoning in writing. McKinsey's research found delegated decisions were the least likely to be rated high quality, which is an argument for structure, not for keeping everything. This piece sets out a decision-rights table, a six-document handover pack, how to choose the first hire, and the role the founder should keep.

Marketing moves from founder-led to team-led when decision rights transfer in a deliberate order and the founder's reasoning is handed over in writing, not when a marketing hire starts. The usual failures are a first hire asked to generate demand before the position is settled, and a founder who approves every post for two years. The evidence argues for structure: McKinsey found only 46% of respondents rated delegated decisions high quality, against 65% for big bets, and Gartner found 69% of buyers see inconsistencies between a supplier's website and its sellers. Transfer execution first, then channels and budget, then messaging. The founder keeps the position and a voice, not the approvals.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 11 described a loop in which sales evidence shapes the firm's positions and positions become tools for sales. In a young firm, the founder runs that loop alone, often without noticing. They hear the objections, write the posts, choose the events and decide what the company believes. That works until the firm needs more marketing than one person can produce, and it fails quietly when the founder's time runs out.

Our piece [Founder-led GTM has an expiration date](https://lowob.com/research/founder-led-gtm-expiration-date/) sets out the wider test for when a founder should step back from go-to-market, and the three stages from explorer to architect to executive sponsor. This part applies that idea to marketing specifically: which decisions move, in what order, and what has to be written down so that the reasoning moves with them.

## Why the transition usually fails

Two failure modes account for most of it.

**The hire into a vacuum.** The founder hires a demand generation manager to "scale what is working". But what is working is the founder: their network, their judgment about which conversations matter, and a position that exists only in their head. The new hire, measured on pipeline, does what the role is designed to do and buys reach for a message nobody has written down. Within two quarters the founder concludes the hire was wrong.

**The founder who never lets go.** The opposite failure is a marketing team that cannot publish a post, change a page or book an event without the founder's approval. Work queues behind one calendar. Good people leave, because a role with no decisions is not a role.

Both failures have the same cause: decision rights were never made explicit, so they were either dropped all at once or kept entirely. Bain's founder's mentality research found 85% of executives surveyed said internal obstacles, not external ones, kept their companies from growing profitably. A marketing handover that stalls is one of those internal obstacles.

## What the evidence says about delegation

The case for a structured handover rests on three findings.

**Delegated decisions are where quality drops.** McKinsey's survey of 1,228 executives found 65% rated their organisation's big-bet decisions as high quality, but only 46% said the same of delegated decisions. Delegation without context, criteria and a record of past choices produces worse decisions. The answer is not to stop delegating. It is to hand over the reasoning with the right.

**Inconsistency costs trust.** Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers said. A founder speaking, a marketing team writing and sellers selling from three different mental models produce exactly that.

**Reputation has to move from the person to the firm.** 6sense's 2024 research found 81% of buyers already had a preferred vendor at first contact. In a founder-led firm much of that preference attaches to the founder. Forrester's 2024 research found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, which is more people than any founder can reach. The firm's marketing has to carry the founder's thinking to the rest of the buying group.

> Hand over the reasoning with the right. A decision right without the reasoning behind it is a guess with a job title.

## Which decisions move, and in what order

The order matters more than the timing. Execution can move early because it is easy to check. Positioning should move last because it is hard to check and expensive to get wrong.

| Decision | Founder-led | Transition | Team-led | Founder's remaining role |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Production and publishing | Founder writes and posts | Team drafts; founder approves | Team owns | None, beyond their own posts |
| Events and sponsorships | Founder chooses | Team proposes against agreed criteria | Team decides within budget | Attends the ones that matter |
| Channel mix and budget | Founder's intuition | Team proposes; founder signs | Team decides within a payback target | Agrees the target with finance |
| Campaign tests | Rarely run | Team runs with a decision card | Team owns the test log | Reads the log quarterly |
| Messaging | Founder's phrasing | Team writes from the voice sheet | Team owns, checked against the ledger | Flags drift |
| Positions and point of view | Founder holds them | Team extracts from founder interviews | Team proposes; founder signs | Signs off new positions |
| Core positioning | Founder decides | Founder decides, written down | Leadership decides, recorded | One voice among several |

Each move from one column to the next is a decision worth recording: what is transferring, to whom, against what criteria, and when it will be reviewed. The record matters because, six months later, nobody will remember whether the founder delegated event selection or just stopped having time for it.

Part 8's payback target and Part 10's decision card are what make the middle rows transferable. A team can own budget once there is a ceiling to spend against, and own tests once there is a written rule for what each result means.

## The handover pack

The founder's reasoning has to exist in documents before it can move. Six cover most of it.

| Document | What it holds | Who writes it first | Further reading |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Positioning record | The category, the alternative the firm replaces, and why it wins | Founder, with an editor | [Positioning vs messaging vs branding](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-vs-messaging-vs-branding/) |
| Ideal customer profile | Who the firm is for, who it is not for, and the evidence | Founder and sales | [How to write an ICP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) |
| Voice sheet | The founder's phrases, what they never say, examples of good and bad | Editor, from interviews | [The founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) |
| Position ledger | Each point of view with claim, evidence, tools and review date | Editor, signed by founder | Part 11 of this series |
| Metric dictionary | The definitions marketing will be measured on | Marketing and finance | Part 7 of this series |
| Test and decision log | What has been tried, what was decided, what was ruled out | Whoever runs marketing | Part 10 of this series |

Most founders resist writing these, because the knowledge feels obvious and the time feels better spent selling. The practical route is interview, not authorship: an editor or the first marketing hire interviews the founder for an hour a week and writes the documents for the founder to correct. Correcting is faster than writing, and the corrections are often the most useful part, because they expose the reasoning the founder did not know they used.

Our piece [Handovers are where reasoning pours out](https://lowob.com/research/handovers-are-where-reasoning-pours-out/) describes what is lost when this step is skipped. In marketing, the loss shows up as a team that can copy what the founder did but cannot say why, and so cannot adapt it.

## Choosing the first hire

Hire for the bottleneck the firm has now, not the function it will need later. If the position is settled and written down, and the constraint is volume of qualified opportunities, a demand generation specialist fits. If the position is still moving, the first hire should be someone who can hold and articulate it: a senior generalist or product marketer who can run founder interviews, write the handover pack and say no to channels that do not fit.

Three questions help:

1. **Can someone other than the founder explain why customers choose the firm?** If not, the first hire is a positioning hire.
2. **Is there a channel that already produces qualified opportunities below its cost ceiling?** If yes, a specialist can scale it. If no, a specialist will be asked to find one, which is a strategy job.
3. **Will the founder accept the hire's judgment on the decisions in the transition column?** If not, delay the hire and fix that first.

Not every firm needs a full-time hire first. Our piece on [the modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/) covers when a small senior core with specialists added for limited periods fits better than an early permanent team.

## What the founder keeps

The founder should not disappear from marketing. Two things argue against it.

The first is distribution. Search sends fewer clicks than it did: Pew found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% without one, and the Reuters Institute's 2026 report cites Chartbeat data showing publisher search traffic down 33% globally in a year. When owned and search channels lose reach, a founder's personal audience and network become relatively more valuable, not less.

The second is cost. Bessemer's analysis of its cloud portfolio found sales and marketing to be the largest cost centre, averaging about half of revenue even at $100m of recurring revenue. Outside software the line is still large: Gartner's 2025 CMO Spend Survey of 402 marketing leaders put marketing budgets at 7.7% of company revenue. A function of that size cannot be run on one person's intuition, but it also benefits from one person's judgment at the points where judgment matters most.

So the founder keeps three things: a public voice, fed by the same interview process and checked against the same ledger as everything else; sign-off on new positions; and a small number of relationships, such as key analysts, partners and design customers, where the founder's presence is the asset. Everything else moves.

Illustrative example: transferring channel and budget rights

Decision
:   Transfer channel and event decisions to the head of marketing within a 12-month payback target, with the founder retaining sign-off on new positions only.

Reason and owner
:   Events and sponsorships were queuing for the founder's approval, and two strong proposals had lapsed. Owned by the chief executive; criteria and target agreed with the finance director and recorded with a six-month review date.

What changed
:   The founder's weekly marketing time fell to a one-hour interview, the team booked events against written criteria, and the first review moved one sponsorship out of the budget for missing its cost ceiling.

Illustrative: a composite of a B2B technology firm of around 40 people, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Transfer rights, not just work.** Make each decision right explicit and record when it moves.
- **Move execution first and positioning last.** The harder a decision is to check, the later it transfers.
- **Write the reasoning down by interview.** The founder corrects; someone else writes.
- **Hire for the bottleneck.** Positioning hire if the position is unsettled; specialist if a channel already works.
- **Keep the founder's voice.** Public voice, position sign-off and a few key relationships stay; approvals go.

Gateway card

### Before marketing moves off the founder's desk

- A written positioning record someone other than the founder can explain
- An ICP with who the firm is not for
- A voice sheet built from founder interviews
- A position ledger with owners and review dates
- A decision-rights table showing what has transferred and what has not
- A payback target and decision card so the team can own budget and tests

## Common questions

### When should a founder stop leading marketing?

When marketing demand exceeds the founder's time and the firm's reasoning can be written down. The transfer should be staged: execution first, channels and budget next, messaging after, core positioning last.

### What should a startup's first marketing hire be?

Hire for the current bottleneck. If the positioning is unsettled, hire a senior generalist or product marketer; if a channel already produces qualified opportunities profitably, hire a specialist to scale it.

### How do you transfer a founder's voice to a marketing team?

Interview the founder regularly, build a voice sheet of their phrases and the things they never say, and check all content against a ledger of the firm's positions that the founder signs off.

### Should founders keep posting on LinkedIn after hiring a marketing team?

Usually yes. A founder's personal audience becomes more valuable as search sends fewer clicks, so a public founder voice, fed by the same interview process as company content, is worth keeping.
