# How to Measure AI ROI in a Commercial Team

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-measure-ai-roi/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Most firms cannot show a return on AI: 56% of CEOs in PwC's 2026 survey report no significant financial benefit. The usual reason is that they measure activity rather than money. In a commercial team, return is measured at the level of decisions: value at stake, realised value against a comparison, and the cost of the people who review the output.

AI return on investment in a commercial team is the money gained from decisions and work the AI informed, minus what it cost to run, including the time people spend reviewing its output. It cannot be read from seats activated or hours saved. It is measured by attaching a value at stake to each decision when it is made, writing back the realised value later against a comparison, and netting off tool cost and review time. That is Gateway 2 in **lowob**'s Build Order.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What AI ROI means in a commercial team

The arithmetic of return on investment is simple: gain minus cost, divided by cost. The difficulty is the gain. A drafting agent produces emails. A research agent produces account briefs. Neither is money until it changes a decision that moves money: a deal pursued or dropped, a discount given or refused, a renewal saved.

So measurement stalls. Teams report what is easy to count, and finance discounts it, because a draft is not revenue.

| Level of measure | Example | What it tells you | Will finance accept it? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Adoption | Seats active, prompts sent | People are using the tool | No |
| Time saved | Self-reported hours saved per week | Possible capacity released | Rarely; it is an estimate and the time is not banked |
| Output | Drafts produced, briefs written | Volume of work | No, unless tied to an outcome |
| Decision value | Margin retained, deals won, renewals saved, against a comparison | Money changed by decisions | Yes, if the comparison is credible |

## Why most firms cannot show a return

The surveys agree on the outcome, if not the cause. PwC's survey, published in January 2026, found 56% of CEOs had seen no significant financial benefit from AI. IBM's Institute for Business Value, surveying 2,000 CEOs between February and April 2025, found a quarter of AI initiatives had delivered expected ROI. The MIT NANDA report *The GenAI Divide*, covered by The Register in August 2025, claimed 95% of organisations had seen zero return; it drew on 52 interviews, a survey of 153 people and a review of over 300 public initiatives, so treat it as directional.

One reading is that the tools do not work. Another, which fits what **lowob** sees in client briefs, is that most firms never set up the arithmetic. Success measures are written as adoption or time saved, with no link to a decision that moved money.

If about half of generative AI spending sits in sales and marketing, as the MIT report found, that is where the measurement gap costs most.

> A build that cannot state its value will be cancelled by someone who can state its cost.

## How to measure it

The method is set out in full in [Gateway 2: Put a Dollar Figure on Every Commercial Decision](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-two-a-dollar-figure-on-every-commercial-decision/). In brief, it needs four things.

| Step | What it involves | Who owns it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Record the decision | The commercial decisions the AI informs, with reason, owner and expected outcome | Deal or account owner |
| 2. Set value at stake | One number when the decision is made, using a definition agreed with finance per decision class | Finance defines, owner fills in |
| 3. Write back against a comparison | Realised value at the check date, compared with a matched group of similar decisions | Revenue operations |
| 4. Net the cost | Subtract tool cost and the loaded cost of review and write-back time | Finance |

Three points make the difference between a number finance accepts and one it ignores.

**The comparison.** A discounted deal that closes looks like a win. If standard-price deals in the same segment closed at the same rate, the discount bought nothing. Without a comparison group, AI gets credit for outcomes that would have happened anyway.

**Review time.** For a system where people approve drafts and check records, human minutes are usually a larger cost than tokens. **lowob**'s measure is reviewer minutes per useful decision, tracked against a baseline set before launch.

**Leading and lagging.** In long sales cycles, report value at stake and the share of records with outcomes written back each quarter, and realised value when outcomes land. Do not present a quarter's figure as final.

## Common mistakes

1. **Counting hours saved as money.** Hours saved are only money if they are redeployed to something measured, or if headcount changes.
2. **Crediting the agent.** The record shows a decision was informed by the AI's preparation, not that the AI caused the outcome. Credit the decision.
3. **Changing the definition every quarter.** Keep each value-at-stake definition stable for at least two quarters, or comparisons reset.
4. **Tying pay to it too early.** If individual pay depends on recorded value in the first year, people choose which decisions to record.

## lowob takeaways

- **Measure decisions, not activity.** Seats and prompts describe adoption, not return.
- **Value at stake first.** Set one number when the decision is made, defined with finance.
- **Always compare.** Realised value means little without a matched group.
- **Net off the people.** Review time is part of the cost and often the largest part.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate the ROI of AI in sales?

Attach a value at stake to each decision the AI informs, record the realised value at a check date against a comparison group, then subtract tool cost and human review time and divide by total cost.

### Why do most companies see no return on AI?

Surveys from PwC and IBM show most firms cannot point to a financial return. A common reason is measuring adoption or time saved instead of linking AI to decisions that move money.

### Is time saved a good measure of AI ROI?

On its own, no. Time saved is an estimate, and it becomes money only if the time is redeployed to measured work or reduces cost.

### How long before AI shows a return in a commercial team?

Expect two quarters of recorded decisions and outcomes before a credible figure. In long sales cycles, realised value may take a year.

## Sources and notes

- [PwC, PwC 2026 Global CEO Survey](https://www.pwc.com/gx/en/news-room/press-releases/2026/pwc-2026-global-ceo-survey.html), 19 January 2026. Self-reported survey of 4,454 CEOs in 95 countries and territories.
- [IBM, IBM Study: CEOs Double Down on AI While Navigating Enterprise Hurdles](https://newsroom.ibm.com/2025-05-06-ibm-study-ceos-double-down-on-ai-while-navigating-enterprise-hurdles), 6 May 2025. Vendor-run survey with Oxford Economics; IBM sells AI services.
- MIT NANDA, The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025, as reported by [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/08/18/generative_ai_zero_return_95_percent), 18 August 2025. Small sample; secondary report of the study.

## Related research

- [Gateway 2: Put a Dollar Figure on Every Commercial Decision](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-two-a-dollar-figure-on-every-commercial-decision/)
- [Reviewer Minutes per Useful Decision](https://lowob.com/research/reviewer-minutes-per-useful-decision/)
- [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)
- [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)

## Next move

Pick one commercial decision class that your AI tools touch, such as discount exceptions. Agree with finance this week how its value at stake is defined, and start recording it on every new decision.

# AI Agents in Sales: What They Can Do Now, Task by Task

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A task-by-task guide to AI agents in sales, built on the seventeen sales rows of the lowob Agent Task Directory. Each task carries an autonomy level, a reliability rating, its main risk and the control it needs. The guide maps every task to the layer of the brain it reads and writes, sets a starting autonomy level, and names the first three tasks to hand over.

Of the seventeen sales tasks in the **lowob** Agent Task Directory, three can run and report today, three can act with a seller's approval, ten should stay as drafts and one, approving a discount, should never leave a person. Agents are reliable on internal work a seller can check in a minute: call summaries, stale-deal flags, source tags and meeting briefs. They are weak wherever a task reaches a prospect, commits money or shapes the forecast. Start with the first group and move one task up the dial at a time, on evidence.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

The common brief for a first sales agent researches prospects, writes sequences and sends them. It pairs the task agents do best (research) with the one they do worst (unsupervised contact with buyers). This guide walks all seventeen sales rows of the [Agent Task Directory](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/). The ratings are **lowob**'s working framework for 20- to 500-person teams, reviewed quarterly, and assume the control in the last column is in place. If it is not, drop the task one level.

## The seventeen sales tasks, rated

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research an account before a meeting | 1 Draft | High | Stale or wrong facts in the brief | Sources attached; current-or-superseded marking |
| Summarise a sales call and extract next steps | 3 Act and report | High | Missed commitment or misheard figure | Recording consent; owner reviews within 48 hours |
| Draft a follow-up email after a meeting | 1 Draft | High | Wrong figure or tone sent to a client | Queue to account owner; nothing sends |
| Update deal stage from email and calendar evidence | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Forecast distorted by wrong stage | Suggested change accepted by owner |
| Flag stale opportunities | 3 Act and report | High | Noise if definitions are loose | Agreed stale rule (for example 30 days) |
| Tag lead source from a fixed list | 3 Act and report | High | Misattributed channel spend | Fixed list; weekly spot-check |
| Qualify an inbound lead | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Good leads dropped | Owner approves drops; record the reason |
| Prioritise accounts for the quarter | 1 Draft | Medium | Bias toward accounts with more data | Leadership decides; record the reasoning |
| Draft a proposal from approved templates | 1 Draft | Medium | Unapproved claims or terms | Template library; proposal approver |
| Price a proposal | 1 Draft | Low | Margin loss; inconsistent pricing | Pricing rules; finance approval for exceptions |
| Approve a discount | 0 Answer | Low | Commits money without accountability | Human decision with recorded reason |
| Write outbound sequences | 1 Draft | Medium | Spam, brand damage, compliance breach | Approval per sequence; volume caps |
| Send outbound sequences autonomously | 2 Act with approval | Low | Reputational and deliverability damage | Not a first agent; gate and caps required |
| Prepare a win-loss summary | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong reason recorded as fact | Interview evidence; owner sign-off |
| Draft a mutual action plan | 1 Draft | Medium | Commitments the client never agreed | Shared with the client only after review |
| Answer a security questionnaire | 1 Draft | Medium | Inaccurate security claims | Approved answer library; security owner review |
| Forecast the quarter | 1 Draft | Medium | False confidence | Human forecast call; agent shows evidence |

METR's study of long tasks found model success falls as the human time a task needs rises. A call summary is short and bounded, with the answer in the transcript; a forecast is a long chain of judgments. The reliability column tracks that difference. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sellers put selling time at 40% of the week, and Australian respondents expected agents to cut research time by 36% and email drafting by 37%. Those savings sit in the level 1 and 3 rows, not the client-facing ones.

## Where each task plugs into the brain

**lowob** treats the brain as a loop: the **store** (CRM, email, calendar, recordings), the **context** layer that wires them with definitions and permissions, the **record** of decisions with reason, owner, status and expected outcome, **reasoning** by models and agents, and **learning** when outcomes are written back. Each task leans on one layer, and fails there if the build is weak.

| Task | Main layer | Start at | Move up when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account research | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Call summary and next steps | Store | 2, then 3 | Four clean weekly spot-checks |
| Follow-up email | Reasoning | 1 | Stays at 1; nothing sends |
| Deal stage update | Record | 1, then 2 | Most suggestions accepted unedited |
| Stale-opportunity flags | Context | 3 | Stale rule agreed first |
| Lead-source tags | Store | 3 | Fixed list agreed first |
| Inbound qualification | Record | 1, then 2 | Every drop has a recorded reason |
| Account prioritisation | Reasoning | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Proposal from templates | Context | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Proposal pricing | Record | 0, then 1 | Pricing rules written and current |
| Discount approval | Record | 0 | Never |
| Outbound copy | Reasoning | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Autonomous outbound send | Reasoning | Not started | A quarter of gate logs on drafts |
| Win-loss summary | Learning | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Mutual action plan | Record | 1 | Stays at 1 |
| Security questionnaire | Context | 1 | Answer library approved and dated |
| Quarterly forecast | Learning | 0, then 1 | Stage definitions stable two quarters |

Tasks on the store or context layers (tags, flags, summaries, research) are reliable once the data is clean and the definitions are written. Tasks on the record or learning layers (stage, qualification, pricing, win-loss, forecast) depend on reasons people have rarely written down, and an agent cannot reconstruct a reason that was never recorded. That is why [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) comes before most of these tasks can move up.

## The five tasks that decide the programme

Five rows carry the weight: the best early win, and the common ways a programme ends badly.

### Call summaries and next steps

The strongest level 3 task in sales: the transcript is the source and the output is checkable against it. The control has two parts. The first is consent. California Penal Code section 632 makes it an offence to record a confidential communication without the consent of all parties, with fines of up to $2,500 per violation, and several other jurisdictions have similar all-party rules. Recording consent belongs in the meeting invite and the opening of the call. The second is review within 48 hours, because a misheard figure in a summary becomes a wrong figure in a follow-up.

### Deal stage updates

An agent can read an email that says "we signed" or a cancelled steering meeting and suggest a stage change. It should not make it. Stage drives the forecast, so the control is a suggestion the owner accepts, with the evidence attached. Read acceptance rates with care: our piece on [approval rate and fatigue](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/) shows how approval climbs as reviewers tire, so pair it with a weekly random sample.

### Inbound qualification

A wrongly dropped lead is invisible unless the drop is recorded. The agent scores and routes at level 2; every drop needs an owner's approval and a reason from a fixed list. Those reasons calibrate next quarter's qualification rules, which is the learning layer doing its job.

### Pricing and discounts

Pricing is level 1, Low; discount approval is level 0. A price stated to a client can bind the firm. In *Moffatt v. Air Canada* (2024), the British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal held the airline responsible for a fare policy its website chatbot misstated, rejecting the argument that the chatbot was a separate entity. The company owns what its software tells a customer. An agent can show the pricing rules, past precedent and the margin effect; a person sets the price, and a named approver signs any exception with a recorded reason. [Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out the approval gate.

### Autonomous outbound

The most requested sales agent is rated lowest. Writing sequences is level 1, Medium; sending them without review is rated Low. The constraints are external. Gmail's sender guidelines require anyone sending more than 5,000 messages a day to Gmail to authenticate with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, offer one-click unsubscribe on marketing mail and keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.30%, with 0.10% recommended. The FTC states that CAN-SPAM "makes no exception for business-to-business email", that opt-outs must be honoured within 10 business days, that a firm cannot contract its liability away to a vendor, and that each violating email can draw a penalty of up to $53,088. An agent sending at volume can breach all of these in an afternoon. The controls are approval per sequence, hard volume caps and a quarter of gated drafts before any send is automated.

> An agent that drafts a bad email costs a seller a minute. An agent that sends one costs the domain.

## The security and tool-access rule

Sales agents read the most untrusted content in the firm. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications traces excessive agency to excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy. Its mitigations translate directly: only the tools the task needs, the seller's own permissions rather than an administrator's, human approval for high-impact actions, and logged, rate-limited tool calls. In practice a research agent cannot write to the CRM, a follow-up agent has no send permission, and no agent both reads inbound mail and sends outbound mail. Read more in [What Is Excessive Agency?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/).

## Start here: the first three tasks

Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs and unclear business value. The defence is a measurable first-quarter gain on low-risk work.

1. **Summarise sales calls and extract next steps.** Level 2 for four weeks (seller confirms), then level 3. Baseline: meetings with no logged next step. Control: consent wording in every invite.
2. **Flag stale opportunities and tag lead source.** Level 3 from the start, once the stale rule (for example, 30 days without activity) and source list are agreed. Baseline: open deals with no recent activity. Control: nightly report, weekly spot-check.
3. **Research the account before each meeting.** Level 1. The brief lands in the calendar with sources attached and old facts marked superseded. Baseline: seller-reported preparation time.

This is the pipeline clerk from [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/), plus one brief. Follow-up drafts come fourth; proposals and outbound copy after a quarter of evidence.

Illustrative example: scoping a sales agent pilot

Decision
:   Approve call summaries, stale-deal flags and meeting briefs for a twelve-seller team; decline a vendor's autonomous outbound proposal.

Reason and owner
:   The approved tasks are internal and checkable in a minute; the outbound proposal had no volume caps, no per-sequence approval and send rights on the main domain. Owned by the head of sales; revenue operations runs spot-checks.

What changed
:   After four weeks, meetings without a logged next step fall and every stale deal is flagged; outbound copy drafting follows at level 1.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## Moving a task up the dial

**lowob** uses three tests before any move up. The directory control has run for at least four weeks. A weekly random sample shows errors that are few, internal and caught before reaching a client. The decision the task touches is recorded with a reason, so a later review can see why the agent acted.

Zapier's 2026 survey of 513 US managers at firms of 1,000 or more staff found only 30% of leaders say their agents handle a majority of tasks without human help. For most sales teams the realistic target this year is a few level 3 tasks on the store and context layers, and a larger set of level 1 drafts that make sellers faster without speaking for them.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start where the seller can check in a minute.** Summaries, flags, tags and briefs earn trust first.
- **Keep money and prospects behind a person.** Pricing, discounts and sends stay at level 2 or below.
- **Record the reason with the change.** Stage, drop and discount decisions need it.
- **Treat outbound as compliance work.** Sender rules and CAN-SPAM apply first.

Gateway card

### Before a sales agent goes live

- Task found in the directory and set at or below its level
- Recording consent wording in every meeting invite
- Agent permissions limited to the task; no send rights on any drafting agent
- Stale rule and lead-source list written and agreed
- Baseline counts taken for missed next steps and stale deals
- Named owner, nightly report and weekly random spot-check

## Common questions

### What can AI agents do in sales today?

Reliably: call summaries, stale-opportunity flags, lead-source tags, account research and follow-up drafts. With a seller approving: stage changes and inbound qualification. Pricing, discounts and unsupervised outbound stay with a person.

### Can an AI agent send sales emails on its own?

It can, but it should not be a first agent. Autonomous sending is rated Low, and the sender is bound by Gmail's bulk sender rules and by CAN-SPAM, which covers business email.

### Is it legal to have an AI notetaker record sales calls?

It depends on the jurisdiction. California, among others, requires the consent of all parties to record a confidential conversation. Put consent wording in the invite and the call opening, and take legal advice.

### Should an AI agent forecast the sales quarter?

It should assemble the evidence: stage history, activity and slippage. The call stays with a person, because the main risk is false confidence in a number the board relies on.

# Intent, Not a Destination

Source: https://lowob.com/research/intent-not-a-destination/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Every interaction a judgment system records should serve an explicit outcome, but naming the conclusion in advance bends the reasoning to reach it. Research on sycophancy and unfaithful explanations shows models follow the framing they are given and justify it fluently. The craft is keeping the purpose fixed and the answer open: name the decision, ask in a fixed schema, and make advocacy a separate, paired step.

Every interaction a judgment system records should serve an explicit outcome. But naming the conclusion in advance bends the reasoning to reach it. Anthropic's research found five leading assistants consistently tailored answers to the user's stated view, and a 2023 study found biased prompts cut model accuracy by up to 36% while the explanations never mentioned the bias. The craft is keeping the purpose fixed and the answer open: name the decision, ask in a fixed schema, and run any case for something beside the case against.

There is a tension at the heart of purposeful AI design, and most teams resolve it in the wrong direction.

On one side, interactions without a stated business outcome drift into busywork. Summaries pile up that serve no decision, and the record fills with noise. Intent is what makes a record worth keeping.

On the other side, a prompt that asks for an opportunity, a recommendation or a win points the model at a conclusion. Language models are very good at constructing a plausible path to wherever they are pointed. The reasoning quietly reshapes itself to arrive, and the evidence that would have argued otherwise is underweighted or left out.

## Separate the outcome you serve from the answer you expect

The resolution is a distinction that is easy to state and surprisingly easy to lose in practice.

| Intent (names the decision) | Destination (names the answer) | What the destination presumes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decide whether to renew this account | Find reasons to expand this account | That expansion is right |
| Assess this counterparty's exposure to the sector downturn | Identify the risks in this counterparty | That material risks exist |
| Should we enter this market this year? | Build the case for entering this market | That entry is the answer |
| Which of these three segments should we prioritise? | Why is segment A our best opportunity? | The ranking |
| What explains the drop in win rate this quarter? | Show that pricing caused the drop | The cause |

The second version in each pair produces a more confident, more coherent and less trustworthy answer. Anthropic's own prompting guidance says that explaining why an instruction matters "can give Claude more information about your goals and help it deliver more targeted responses". That is the case for intent. Giving the goal helps. Giving the answer is a different act.

## Why framing bends the answer

Two lines of research explain the mechanism.

**Models tend to agree with the user.** Anthropic's alignment team published "Towards Understanding Sycophancy in Language Models" in October 2023. It found five state-of-the-art assistants "consistently exhibit sycophancy behavior across four varied free-form text-generation tasks". It traced part of the cause to training on human preferences: "when a response matches a user's views, it is more likely to be preferred", and both people and preference models "prefer convincingly-written sycophantic responses over correct ones a non-negligible fraction of the time". A prompt that names a conclusion is a stated view. The model has been trained, in part, to agree with stated views.

**Models rationalise without saying so.** Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez and Samuel Bowman tested what happens when a prompt contains a biasing feature, such as reordering multiple-choice options so the answer is always (A), or a suggested answer from the user. Across 13 BIG-Bench Hard tasks with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0, accuracy fell by as much as 36%. The models' step-by-step explanations did not mention the bias. When pushed toward a wrong answer, they wrote reasoning that justified it. The authors warn that such explanations "systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction".

Both studies used older models, and current models are better trained against sycophancy. The direction has not been shown to reverse. For a judgment system, the second finding is the more serious one, because the explanation is what gets recorded. A destination-framed prompt does not only risk a biased answer. It produces a well-argued record of one.

> A destination-framed prompt does not only risk a biased answer. It produces a well-argued record of one.

## Ask as a schema, not as a request

The practical tool is to ask every commercial or analytical question in a fixed shape rather than as an open request:

> signal · evidence (linked) · confidence · implication · what would change this

| Field | What goes in it | Why it resists bias |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Signal | The observation, stated neutrally | Separates what happened from what it means |
| Evidence (linked) | Sources, each with a link or quote | Lets a reviewer check, not trust |
| Confidence | Low, medium or high, with one line of reason | Forces a view on the strength of the case |
| Implication | What this means for the named decision | Keeps the purpose in view |
| What would change this | The evidence that would reverse the implication | Makes a one-sided case visible |

The schema keeps the purpose in view because every field relates to the decision. It leaves the conclusion open because no field asks for one. The last field does the most work. Being required to say what would change the conclusion makes it much harder to produce a one-sided case without noticing.

The schema also fits how models are best instructed. Anthropic's guidance recommends structured formats such as JSON "to make schema requirements explicit", and for long documents advises asking the model to "quote relevant parts of the documents first". Our explainer on [structured output](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-structured-output/) covers how to enforce a schema in production, and [Prompt engineering vs context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/prompt-engineering-vs-context-engineering/) covers where it sits in the wider prompt.

## When you genuinely want the case for something

Sometimes you do want advocacy: a pitch, a board paper, a response to a sceptic. Fine. Make it an explicit, separate step, and run the case against in the same schema at the same time. Record both. The decision record then shows that advocacy happened, which is very different from advocacy dressed as analysis.

The paired case against has a human precedent. Gary Klein's premortem asks a team to assume a project has already failed and list why; he cites research finding this kind of "prospective hindsight" improves the identification of reasons for future outcomes by 30%. Asking a model for the strongest case against a proposal applies the same reframing, and costs one more call.

## Not every interaction needs to be recorded

Intent also tells you what to leave out. An interaction that serves no current decision does not belong in the judgment record. It may belong in a general knowledge store, but mixing the two dilutes [decision precedent](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) with noise. A lean record that maps cleanly to decisions is more useful than a complete one that maps to nothing. Our piece [Buy context, own judgment](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/) sets out where the two stores sit.

## In practice

Audit your ten most-used prompts. Rewrite any that name a conclusion as ones that name a decision. Adopt the five-field schema for analytical questions, with "what would change this" required. Make advocacy an explicit step, always paired with the case against.

Tag every recorded interaction with the decision it serves. Untagged interactions go elsewhere.

## What would prove this wrong

A blind comparison in which destination-framed prompts produce outputs no more one-sided, and no less accurate, than schema-framed ones on the same cases. If framing does not bend the reasoning, the discipline is ceremony. The published research points the other way for the models it tested; newer models may narrow the gap. The test is cheap to run on your own cases: take ten past decisions with known outcomes, ask each both ways, and have someone who does not know which is which score the answers.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the decision, not the answer.** Intent improves output; a stated conclusion bends it.
- **Expect fluent rationalisation.** Models justify the framing they are given and do not flag it.
- **Use the five-field schema.** "What would change this" is the field that catches one-sided cases.
- **Pair every case for with a case against.** Record both, labelled as advocacy.

## Common questions

### Why do AI prompts that ask for a recommendation give biased answers?

A prompt that names a conclusion acts as a stated view, and models trained on human preferences tend to agree with stated views. Research found biased prompts cut accuracy by up to 36% without the explanation mentioning the bias.

### How should I frame analytical questions for an AI model?

Name the decision rather than the answer, and ask in a fixed schema: signal, linked evidence, confidence, implication, and what would change this. The last field makes a one-sided case visible.

### What is AI sycophancy?

The tendency of AI assistants to tailor answers to what the user appears to believe. Anthropic's 2023 research found it across five leading assistants and traced it partly to training on human preference ratings.

### What if I actually want the AI to argue for something?

Make advocacy an explicit, separate step and run the case against in the same schema at the same time. Record both, so the record shows advocacy happened.

- [Turpin, Michael, Perez and Bowman, Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04388v2), December 2023. Academic preprint; GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0 on BIG-Bench Hard tasks.
- [Anthropic, Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/be-clear-and-direct), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Klein, Performing a Project Premortem](https://wiki.duraspace.org/download/attachments/104563925/ProjectPremortem.pdf?api=v2), Harvard Business Review, September 2007. Practitioner article; the 30% figure comes from 1989 research it cites.

# What Makes a Case Study Believable

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A case study is evidence, not advertising. A believable one keeps the specific situation, the real sequence including setbacks, dated numbers with a baseline and the customer's own voice, even when the name has to go. Research on reviews and two-sided messages suggests some acknowledged weakness raises credibility, and US rules treat testimonials as claims that need substantiation.

A prospective customer reads your case study to learn one thing: have you solved a problem like mine, and can you show me what happened? A logo, a polished testimonial and a large percentage will not answer that on their own. A believable case study reads like an account of a project: the starting situation, the decisions made, what changed with a baseline and a date, and what the evidence cannot support. Research on reviews suggests a little visible imperfection raises trust, and in the US, the FTC treats claims made through testimonials as claims the advertiser must substantiate.

## Start with a situation the reader recognises

"We helped a fintech company grow" tells a potential client almost nothing. What kind of fintech company? Was it struggling to acquire users, get partners to respond or explain a complex product? What could the team afford to try? Which constraints made the job difficult?

For example, an anonymous payments start-up with a two-person sales team and a limited marketing budget is already more useful context than "a leading fintech innovator." The reader can judge whether the example resembles their own business.

Then explain what the provider actually did. Do not say it "optimised the growth engine." Say that it rewrote an unclear landing page, interviewed five customers, launched a partner referral campaign or stopped spending on ads that brought the wrong people. The specific work is the useful part of the story.

| Element | Weak version | Believable version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situation | "A leading fintech innovator" | An anonymous payments start-up, two sellers, limited budget, partners not responding |
| Work | "Optimised the growth engine" | Rewrote the landing page, interviewed five customers, launched partner referrals |
| Result | "Leads up 40%" | Qualified demo requests from 10 to 14 a month over eight weeks |
| Limits | None stated | The sales process changed too, so the result cannot be attributed to one activity |
| Cost | Omitted | The time, people and budget the work required |
| Voice | "They were amazing to work with" | The customer describing what was hard or surprising |

## A percentage needs a starting point and a date

Imagine a case study that says "qualified leads increased 40%." Did the company go from five to seven leads a month, or 500 to 700? Was this measured over a week or a year? Did the sales team also hire more people or change the definition of a qualified lead?

**Hard to evaluate:** "We boosted qualified leads by 40% through our proprietary approach."

**Much more useful:** "In this illustrative eight-week project, monthly qualified demo requests rose from 10 to 14 after changes to the website and partner outreach. The team also changed its sales process, so the result cannot be attributed to one activity alone."

Both statements are illustrative, not real campaign results. The second tells a reader what the number means and what remains uncertain. That is more valuable than an enormous percentage with no baseline.

Be just as clear about the cost of the work. If the result required six months of engineering, a new salesperson and a large advertising budget, that matters to a buyer deciding whether the approach is realistic for them.

## Why setbacks make the story more credible

Real projects involve delays, wrong assumptions and changes in direction. Perhaps the first set of ads attracted too many irrelevant visitors. Maybe the original message confused customers. Or a potential partner declined to participate, forcing a different approach.

The research on persuasion supports including them. Martin Eisend's 2006 meta-analysis of two-sided advertising, messages that admit a weakness alongside strengths, found the effect depends on how much negative information is included, and that the relationship with brand attitude is curvilinear: some acknowledged weakness helps, too much hurts. Consumer review data point the same way. Northwestern University's Spiegel Research Center, analysing PowerReviews data across more than 40 product categories, found purchase likelihood peaks when average ratings sit between 4.2 and 4.5 stars and falls as they approach a perfect 5. It also cited PowerReviews research that 82% of shoppers seek out negative reviews.

Retail ratings are not B2B case studies, but the mechanism is general. Include one or two meaningful decisions the team changed because of what it learned. That lets the reader see judgment in action rather than a flawless sequence written after the fact.

> A case study with no setbacks reads as edited. One honest correction does more for credibility than five adjectives.

## Testimonials are claims, too

A direct customer comment can help, especially when it describes what was difficult or surprising. But a quote is not proof of every claimed outcome.

The US Federal Trade Commission's revised Guides Concerning the Use of Endorsements and Testimonials in Advertising, effective 26 July 2023, are specific. Advertisers must have adequate substantiation for claims made through endorsements, just as for claims they make directly; "consumer endorsements themselves are not competent and reliable scientific evidence." And when a testimonial describes a result on a key attribute, the ad is likely to be read as saying that result is typical. If the advertiser cannot substantiate that, it must clearly disclose what people can generally expect.

The FTC went further in August 2024 with a final rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, effective 21 October 2024. It prohibits creating or disseminating testimonials that misrepresent whether the person exists, whether they used the product or service, or what their experience was. Morgan Lewis's summary notes penalties of up to $51,744 per violation, adjusted annually for inflation.

The practical rule: a happy customer can describe their experience; factual performance claims still need evidence you can produce.

## When the client cannot be named

For regulated financial products, enterprise infrastructure and competitive projects, naming the client or sharing exact figures may not be allowed. That does not mean the case study must become useless. It does mean the provider needs explicit permission for whatever it publishes.

Describe the business problem, type of customer, work and outcome at a level the client approves. Use ranges or percentages only when the underlying figures are real and the client agrees to that presentation. Be careful: revealing the geography, company size, product category and timeline together may identify a customer even without its name.

Ask for approval of the project description, individual quotes, performance claims and any screenshots. A composite story based on several engagements may be useful as an industry observation, but it must be labelled as a composite and never passed off as a single verified customer result.

## When you do not have a case study yet

Do not manufacture one. Instead, show how you would approach a problem: the questions you would ask, what you would inspect, the work you would try first, and what evidence you would need before recommending more spending.

Then make case-study permission part of the next engagement. Agree early which measurements can be retained and whether the customer might approve a public or anonymous summary. You cannot force an endorsement, but you can make it easier to document real work without scrambling for data months later. A [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) of recent deals will show which proof buyers actually asked for, and our piece on [proposal standards](https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/) covers where that proof belongs in a bid.

One believable story about a modest result is more useful than five vaguely impressive success stories. In the terms of [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/), a case study serves the supplier-selection stage, and its reader is usually the evaluator who has to defend the choice to everyone else.

## lowob takeaways

- **Show the starting situation.** The buyer needs to recognise the problem, the customer and the constraints.
- **Make results checkable.** Baseline, time period, method and what else changed.
- **Keep the setbacks.** Some acknowledged weakness raises credibility; a flawless story does not.
- **Treat testimonials as claims.** Substantiate what they imply, get approval, and label composites.

## Common questions

### What makes a good B2B case study?

A recognisable starting situation, the specific work done, results with a baseline and a time period, the cost of the work, at least one setback or change of course, and the customer's own description of what was hard. All of it should be approved by the customer.

### Can you publish a case study without naming the client?

Yes, with the client's explicit permission for every element you publish. Describe the type of company and problem, use ranges only if the client agrees, and check that the combination of details does not identify them anyway.

### Do testimonials need to be substantiated?

In the US, yes. The FTC's Endorsement Guides require advertisers to substantiate claims made through testimonials, and a testimonial about a key result is read as typical unless the advertiser can support that or discloses otherwise.

### Should a case study include what went wrong?

Yes, within reason. Research on two-sided messages finds that some acknowledged weakness increases credibility, while too much hurts. One or two real corrections show judgment and make the result easier to believe.

Primary US regulatory guidance (16 CFR Part 255); US only.
- [Morgan Lewis, FTC issues final rule on consumer reviews and testimonials](https://www.morganlewis.com/pubs/2024/08/ftc-issues-final-rule-on-consumer-reviews-and-testimonials), August 2024. Law firm summary of the rule; penalty figure adjusts annually.

# Clipping Is Not a Fad. It Is Paid Distribution With a Human Face.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/clipping-paid-distribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A clipping programme pays many small accounts, usually $1 to $5 per thousand views, to cut long-form content into short clips and post them. Treated as paid media, it has a price, a yield and a set of controls: verified views, written edit rules, disclosure on every clip and a cost per outcome compared with every other channel.

A clipping programme pays people, usually per thousand views, to cut long-form content into short-form video and post it on their own accounts. Digiday reported typical rates of $1 to $5 per thousand views, capped per campaign. Treat it as a fad and it will look like one. Treat it as paid distribution bought at a rate per view and executed by hundreds of small publishers, and it becomes a channel with a price, a yield and a set of controls. Disclosure rules apply to every paid clip, whoever posts it.

Somewhere on your phone is a clip of a founder saying something sharp, posted by an account you have never heard of, with several hundred thousand views.

The account is not a fan. It is a participant in a clipping programme: a structure that pays people, usually per thousand views, to cut long-form content into short-form video and post it on their own accounts. The brand supplies the raw material and the terms. The clippers supply the editing, the accounts, and the volume.

The market has formalised quickly. Clipping historically ran through private Discord servers; Digiday reported that the creator platform Whop launched a public clipping marketplace in March 2025, taking 10% of commission fees, and that users ranged from large creators and music and film rights holders to apps and investment services.

## Why it exists

Short-form platforms reward volume, novelty, and native-looking content, and they distribute from small accounts as readily as from large ones. That makes a swarm of small accounts posting many variations of the same source material a more efficient way to reach a platform's audience than a single official account posting once.

For companies in reviewed categories, the channel has a second attraction: it does not require an ad account. The content is organic on the clipper's account. The company is paying for distribution, not for placement. One agency executive told Digiday: "You get around a lot of the paid-sponsor ad type rules."

That is also the channel's central risk, and it needs to be said plainly. A clipping programme that hides the commercial relationship, or that uses the channel to say things the company could not say in an ad, is not a distribution strategy. It is a compliance problem waiting for a screenshot. Disclosure rules apply to paid posts whoever posts them. The FTC's guidance treats any financial relationship as a material connection that must be disclosed in the video itself, in audio and on-screen text, not only in a description. The UK's October 2026 influencer guide from the ASA, CAP and CMA says payment includes commission and that everyone in the chain, brand included, is responsible for the label. Digiday found many clippers do not disclose, and that Whop's terms require compliance without a way to enforce it. The brand carries that exposure. Our piece [Meta said no. That is not the end of your distribution plan.](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) sets clipping in the wider set of options for reviewed categories.

## What the money buys

A programme pays per thousand views, with a rate that varies by platform and by the quality of the source material, and usually a cap per clip and per clipper. The source material is the constraint: a founder who talks well on camera, a product demo that surprises, a recorded event, a podcast appearance. Our piece on the [founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) covers how to produce source material worth cutting.

The economics are simple to model. Views multiplied by rate, divided by the outcomes the company's tracking can confirm, gives a cost per outcome that can be compared with every other channel. If the company cannot connect views to outcomes, it is buying awareness and should price it as such.

| Input | Illustrative figure | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rate | $2 per 1,000 verified views | Inside the $1 to $5 range Digiday reported |
| Verified views in the month | 5,000,000 | After removing bot and reposted views |
| Spend | $10,000 | Rate multiplied by verified views |
| Tracked sign-ups | 200 | From clip links, codes and a direct-traffic baseline |
| Cost per sign-up | $50 | Compare with paid social, creators and affiliate |

The figures are illustrative. The method is the point: the comparison is to what the same outcome costs elsewhere, and our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) sets out how to run that comparison across channels.

> The question is not whether the clips are good. It is what a thousand verified views cost and what they produced.

## Where programmes go wrong

**No source material worth clipping.** The channel amplifies; it does not create. A brand with nothing interesting to say gets many views of nothing.

**Paying for views the platforms discount.** Bot views, view farms, and reposted clips inflate the count. The programme needs a verification step and a payment delay long enough to remove them. The platforms themselves now discount unoriginal clips, which changes what a view is worth:

| Platform | Programme rule | What it means for clipping |
| --- | --- | --- |
| YouTube | Reused content without significant original commentary or modification is not monetisable; "repetitious" was renamed "inauthentic content" in July 2025 | Clips need added commentary or substantive editing to be treated as original |
| X | Original Content Rewards excludes copied, minimally modified, aggregated and cross-platform reposted content; payouts count only qualified impressions from Premium users | Lightly edited clips earn nothing from X and may be ranked as unoriginal |
| TikTok | Creator Rewards favours original videos over one minute, with originality one of four core metrics | Short reposts are outside the rewards programme |

Clippers paid by a brand do not need platform payouts, but the rules signal how each platform values reposted material. Views counted on clips the platform treats as unoriginal are worth less than the same views on original work. In the US, paying for fake views also carries legal risk: the FTC's 2024 rule bans buying bot-generated "indicators of social media influence" to misrepresent influence commercially.

**No brand control.** Clippers optimise for views. Without written rules on what may be cut, captioned, or implied, the best-performing clip is often the most misleading one.

**Measuring as content.** A clipping programme is media. The question is not whether the clips are good. It is what a thousand verified views cost and what they produced.

## Run it as a channel

Write the terms: rate, caps, platforms, verification, payment schedule, disclosure language, and prohibited edits. Produce a source library and refresh it monthly. Recruit clippers through a public programme and pay reliably; the good ones have choices. Track with a link or code where possible, and with a brand-search or direct-traffic baseline where not. Review weekly, remove the accounts producing views without outcomes, and reallocate.

On YouTube, a paid clip should also be declared through the platform's paid promotion setting; YouTube's branded content policy covers Shorts and says creators remain "ultimately responsible" for clear disclosure. Write that step into the terms.

Run each change as a test with a decision attached. Our playbook on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers sizing the test so a weekly review can act on it.

Clipping sits alongside creator programmes and affiliate as one of the channels that carry a category when the platforms will not. It is never the whole plan, and it is never sold as one. Attached to a programme that is already working, it is one of the cheapest sources of verified attention available.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price it as media.** Rate per thousand verified views, divided by confirmed outcomes.
- **Disclose every clip.** Paid clips are endorsements in the US and ads in the UK, whoever posts them.
- **Verify before paying.** Delay payment long enough to remove bot and reposted views.
- **Write the edit rules.** The best-performing clip is often the most misleading one without them.

Gateway card

### Before launching a clipping programme

- Source library of material worth cutting, refreshed monthly
- Written terms: rate, caps, platforms, verification, payment schedule
- Disclosure language for each platform, plus prohibited edits and claims
- Tracking by link or code, with a direct-traffic baseline
- A weekly review that removes accounts producing views without outcomes

## Common questions

### What is a clipping campaign?

A programme that pays many small accounts, usually per thousand views, to cut a brand's or creator's long-form content into short clips and post them on their own accounts. It is paid distribution, not organic reach.

### How much do clipping programmes pay?

Digiday reported typical rates of $1 to $5 per thousand views, with payouts capped per campaign. Rates vary by platform and by the quality of the source material.

### Do clippers have to disclose that they are paid?

Yes. Under FTC guidance a paid clip is an endorsement that needs a clear disclosure in the video itself, and UK guidance treats commission as payment that requires an upfront "#Ad" label.

### Can clipped videos earn platform payouts?

Mostly not without real changes. YouTube, X and TikTok all limit monetisation of reused or minimally edited content, so lightly edited clips are treated as unoriginal.

# The Trade Must Clear on the Spot

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-trade-must-clear-on-the-spot/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: People share what they know when they get something back in the same moment. A promise of future collective value is a public-goods problem, and two decades of research on knowledge sharing show it gets under-supplied. Knowledge capture should give a private, immediate, visible return: precedent, a warning, work done for them, or credit when their record is reused.

People share what they know when they get something back in the same moment. A promise of future collective value is a public-goods problem, and public goods are under-supplied: organisational researchers have described knowledge sharing as a social dilemma since at least 2002. The smartest capture designs are two-way. The system gives the person something useful at the moment of work and takes their knowledge in return, and both halves land in the same interaction. Make the return private, immediate and visible.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

## The economics of a capture prompt

Every capture prompt in a decision system is a small trade. The person spends time writing down a reason, a context or an outcome. Someone else, usually later, gets the benefit. When the return to the contributor is "it will help the team", the trade does not clear.

This is not a new observation. Cabrera and Cabrera, writing in Organization Studies in 2002, framed knowledge sharing in organisations as a social dilemma of the public-goods kind. Sharing costs the contributor time and sometimes advantage, while the group benefits whether or not each person contributed. Non-contribution is individually tempting, and a few free riders can pull a group into a low-cooperation equilibrium. Their remedies were to restructure the payoffs, to show contributors their efficacy, and to strengthen group identity.

The empirical work since has refined the picture rather than overturned it. Kankanhalli, Tan and Wei's 2005 study of electronic knowledge repositories in public-sector organisations found that knowledge self-efficacy and enjoyment in helping others significantly predicted contribution, while the effect of codification effort depended on context. People contribute when they believe what they know is useful and when the act itself is rewarding. Both are in the designer's hands.

So the economics are simple. The contributor pays now, the organisation collects later, and rational people stop paying. Price the trade so it clears in the session.

## Four returns that clear on the spot

**Precedent.** The next screen shows the three most comparable prior decisions and how they turned out. This is the strongest return because it helps with the decision the person is making right now. Our explainer on [decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) covers how the precedent slot is assembled.

**A gap they had not seen.** "The last two decisions in this segment were reversed after the regulatory change in March." A warning delivered at the right moment is worth more than any summary. [Ask for the gap, not the summary](https://lowob.com/research/ask-for-the-gap-not-the-summary/) makes the wider case.

**Work done for them.** If the record is drafted from the memo, call or email they were going to produce anyway, and the record in turn drafts the next memo, capture costs almost nothing. The best capture is a by-product of work the person had to do regardless. This is Cabrera and Cabrera's first remedy, lowering the cost of contribution, built into the workflow.

**Credit.** Tell people when their record is reused. "Your note on the loan waiver was surfaced in four decisions this quarter, and two of them changed course." Few things motivate experts more than evidence that their judgment travels, and it is cheap to build. The research supports it directly. Wasko and Faraj's 2005 study of 173 members of a professional network, using recorded contributions rather than self-reports, found people contributed more when they saw it as enhancing their professional reputation. Expectations of reciprocity were not a significant driver.

| Return | What the person receives in the session | Why it clears | Research it draws on |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Precedent | The three closest prior decisions and their outcomes | Helps the decision in hand | Payoff restructuring (Cabrera and Cabrera) |
| A gap | A warning about a reversal, rule change or missing fact | Prevents a mistake now | Perceived efficacy (Cabrera and Cabrera) |
| Work done | A drafted record and a drafted next memo | Capture costs almost nothing | Lower contribution cost (Cabrera and Cabrera; Kankanhalli et al.) |
| Credit | Notice of reuse and what it changed | Builds reputation | Reputation drives contribution (Wasko and Faraj) |

> If the honest answer to "what does the person get back?" is "it will help the team", expect the prompt to be ignored within a month.

## Why AI raises the stakes

AI assistants make the trade harder to clear, not easier. A person who can get a private answer from a model has even less reason to contribute to a shared record.

The clearest evidence comes from public Q&A. Del Rio-Chanona, Laurentsyeva and Wachs, writing in PNAS Nexus in 2024, found user activity on Stack Overflow fell 25% within six months of ChatGPT's release, relative to similar platforms where access was restricted. The decline affected users at all experience levels. The authors describe "a significant shift of knowledge from public to private domains". Inside a firm the same thing happens when staff ask an assistant instead of writing down what they decided.

The fix is the same: make contribution return something the private answer cannot. A model can draft. It cannot tell a person what their own firm decided last quarter, why, and how it turned out, unless someone recorded it. That is what the decision record is for, and why [The commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) starts with the decisions that recur often enough to produce precedent quickly.

## Give first, then ask

The sequence matters. If you launch by asking for reasons and promise precedent later, people experience the system as a tax. Launch with the give side working, even if thin, and ask for contribution only once people are already coming back for it.

The cold-start problem is real, because precedent needs records. Solve it deliberately. Before launch, backfill ten to twenty past decisions in the target class through short structured interviews with the people who made them. It takes a few days, and it means the system has something to give on day one. Cabrera and Cabrera make the same point in their terms: a shared pool is only worth the individual cost once it reaches critical mass.

## A check for every prompt

For each capture prompt in your design, write down what the person receives in the same session. If the honest answer is "it will help the team", expect the prompt to be ignored within a month. If it is "the next screen shows the three closest prior cases and their outcomes", it has a chance. If there is no same-session return, remove the prompt or move it to a moment where there is one.

| Capture prompt | Same-session return | Keep, move or cut |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reason for a discount above band | Three closest past discounts and whether the deal renewed | Keep |
| Closed-lost reason | Pattern across the last ten losses in the segment | Keep |
| Free-text "lessons learned" at quarter end | None | Cut, or move to the next comparable decision |
| Outcome of a past decision | Notice of where the record has been reused | Keep, and send the notice |

Measure return visits per user per week. If they are not rising, the give side is not good enough yet. Our explainer on [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers closing the loop so outcomes are captured as well as reasons.

**What would prove this wrong.** Sustained, high-quality contribution to a system that offers contributors nothing in the moment, driven by mandate alone. Some regulated settings achieve this; if they do so without quality decay, the trade is less essential than this piece claims. The research also suggests one refinement: intrinsic motives such as enjoyment in helping others do drive some contribution. They are real, but they are not something a system can rely on at scale.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat capture as a price, not a culture.** The contributor pays now; make the return arrive in the same session.
- **Lead with precedent.** The three closest prior decisions and their outcomes is the strongest same-moment return.
- **Build the reuse notification early.** Reputation drives contribution, and the notice is cheap to build.
- **Backfill before launch.** Ten to twenty interviewed decisions give the system something to offer on day one.
- **Cut prompts with no return.** A prompt without a same-session return will be ignored.

## Common questions

### Why don't employees contribute to knowledge management systems?

Contributors pay now while the organisation collects later, so rational people stop paying. Researchers have described this as a public-goods social dilemma since 2002. It is a pricing problem, not a culture problem.

### How do I get people to share knowledge in a decision system?

Give a return in the same interaction: comparable precedents, a warning they had not seen, drafting done for them, or credit when their record is reused.

### Does recognition actually make people share knowledge?

The evidence says reputation matters. A 2005 MIS Quarterly study found members of a professional network contributed more when it enhanced their professional reputation, while expected reciprocity was not a significant driver.

### How do I solve the cold-start problem for a decision database?

Before launch, backfill ten to twenty past decisions in the target class through short structured interviews with the people who made them, so precedent exists on day one.

## Sources and notes

- [Cabrera and Cabrera, Knowledge-sharing dilemmas](https://dea.uib.cat/digitalAssets/123/123492_knowsharingdilemmas.pdf), Organization Studies 23(5), 2002. Theory paper; proposes interventions without testing them.
- [Kankanhalli, Tan and Wei, Contributing knowledge to electronic knowledge repositories: an empirical investigation](https://misq.org/contributing-knowledge-to-electronic-knowledge-repositories-an-empirical-investigation.html), MIS Quarterly 29(1), 2005. Survey of public sector organisations; pre-dates generative AI.
- [Wasko and Faraj, Why should I share? Examining social capital and knowledge contribution in electronic networks of practice](https://verdi.cs.ucl.ac.uk/constructDB/publications/wasko-why-2005.html), MIS Quarterly 29(1), 2005. Study of 173 members of one professional network, as summarised on the linked page.

## Next move

List every capture prompt in your decision system and write its same-session return beside it. Cut or move any prompt with no return this week, and schedule five backfill interviews before the next launch.

# What Is AI Hallucination?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: AI hallucination is a plausible but false statement produced by a language model. OpenAI's 2025 research argues models hallucinate partly because training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty. Retrieval reduces the problem but does not remove it, and a 2024 tribunal ruling confirmed that firms remain liable for what their chatbots say.

AI hallucination is when a language model produces a statement that sounds plausible but is false, such as an invented figure, policy or citation. NIST calls it confabulation. It happens because models generate likely text rather than checking facts, and because standard training and testing reward a confident guess over "I don't know". It can be reduced but not eliminated, so outputs that reach clients need a person to check them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What AI hallucination means

A language model writes by predicting the next token from patterns in its training data and its input. Nothing in that process checks the output against a source. When the model lacks the information, it can still produce fluent text that fills the gap.

OpenAI's research paper "Why language models hallucinate", published in September 2025, gives a second reason. Standard training and evaluation reward guessing over acknowledging uncertainty. Under accuracy-only scoring, a lucky guess scores better than an honest abstention, so models learn to guess.

Its SimpleQA example makes the trade visible. One model abstained on 52% of questions, answered 22% correctly and was wrong on 26%. An older model abstained on 1%, was correct on 24% and wrong on 75%. The second looks slightly more accurate on a leaderboard and is far more likely to tell you something false.

| Type | What it looks like at work |
| --- | --- |
| Fabricated fact | A revenue figure, date or product feature that does not exist |
| Fabricated source | A citation, case or link that was never published |
| Misgrounded answer | A real source cited for a claim it does not support |
| Wrong policy | A confident statement of terms, pricing or eligibility that is out of date or invented |
| Unfaithful summary | A call summary that adds a commitment nobody made |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The risk is not that a model is wrong sometimes. People are wrong sometimes. The risk is that a model is wrong in the same confident tone it uses when it is right, and at volume.

Retrieval helps but does not solve it. Stanford's RegLab and Human-Centered AI researchers tested legal research tools that ground answers in case law databases. In their May 2024 preprint, the tools hallucinated on more than 17% of benchmark queries, less often than a general model but far from zero. Thomson Reuters said the study tested the wrong product, and LexisNexis said its own analysis found a lower rate. The study also counted misgrounded citations as hallucinations. Even with those caveats, the finding holds: a retrieval system can still invent or misattribute.

Liability stays with the business. In Moffatt v. Air Canada, decided on 14 February 2024, the airline's website chatbot told a customer he could claim a bereavement fare after travel. The policy said otherwise. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal rejected Air Canada's argument that the chatbot was a separate legal entity and awarded about CA$650 in damages, plus interest and fees. The amount was small. The principle is that what an AI tool tells a customer is what the company told the customer.

For a revenue team the exposure sits in client-facing text: proposals, questionnaire answers, renewal emails and support replies. That is where **lowob**'s rule applies: nothing sends without a person.

## How to reduce hallucination in practice

| Control | What it does | Limit |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ground in supplied sources | Retrieval or attached documents give the model facts to use | Retrieval can miss or misrank; the model can still misread |
| Require citations | Each claim points to a source a reviewer can open | Citations can themselves be wrong; check a sample |
| Allow "I don't know" | Instructions and scoring that accept abstention | Fewer answers, more escalations |
| Automated grounding checks | Guardrail tools flag responses not supported by the source | Catch some errors, not all |
| Evaluation sets | A test set of real questions with known answers | Only measures what you thought to test |
| Human review before send | A named person approves client-facing output | Costs time; reviewers fatigue |

Two design choices do most of the work. First, keep facts that change, such as prices, terms and product details, in a maintained record and supply them at run time. Second, set the autonomy dial by consequence. Internal research notes can run at level 1, draft only. Anything a client or regulator reads should stay at level 2, act with approval, until evaluation data shows the error rate is acceptable for that task.

## lowob takeaways

- **Hallucination is built in.** Models generate likely text; they do not check it.
- **Accuracy scores can hide it.** A model that guesses more can look better and be wrong more.
- **Retrieval reduces, not removes.** Grounded legal tools still erred on more than one query in six.
- **The firm is liable.** A tribunal has ruled that a chatbot's answer is the company's answer.

## Common questions

### What is an AI hallucination?

It is a false statement produced by an AI model and presented as fact, such as an invented statistic, policy or citation. NIST's term for it is confabulation.

### Why do AI models hallucinate?

They predict likely text rather than verifying facts. OpenAI's 2025 research adds that training and evaluation reward guessing over admitting uncertainty, so models learn to answer anyway.

### Does RAG stop hallucinations?

No. Retrieval reduces them by supplying sources, but a 2024 Stanford study found retrieval-based legal tools still hallucinated on more than 17% of test queries.

### Is a company liable for what its AI chatbot says?

In Moffatt v. Air Canada in 2024, a Canadian tribunal held the airline responsible for its chatbot's incorrect advice. Firms should assume the same applies to their own tools.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, Why language models hallucinate](https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/), 5 September 2025. Vendor research; examples use OpenAI's own models.
- [NIST, AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. US standards body guidance.
- [LawSites, Stanford will augment its study finding AI legal research tools hallucinate in 17% of queries](https://www.lawnext.com/2024/05/stanford-will-augment-its-study-finding-that-ai-legal-research-tools-hallucinate-in-17-of-queries-as-some-raise-questions-about-the-results.html), May 2024.
