# First Customers in a Market That Doesn't Exist Yet

Source: https://lowob.com/research/first-customers-in-a-market-that-doesnt-exist-yet/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: In a market that does not exist yet, first customers are chosen as design partners and references at once, bought through institutional procurement, reached through practitioner networks and standards bodies, and measured by risk retired rather than pipeline value. This playbook adds the facts that shape those pilots: procurement thresholds in England, how selective regulator sandboxes are, and where AI standards are being written.

In a market that does not exist yet, first customers are chosen as design partners and references at once, bought through institutional procurement, reached through practitioner networks, and measured by risk retired. The institutions that buy first are slow for reasons that can be mapped in advance: procurement thresholds, security review, liability terms and planning calendars. Sandboxes and standards bodies are distribution as well as compliance, but they are selective: the UK Financial Conduct Authority accepted 14 of 142 sandbox applications in its 2025/26 financial year.

## Design partners who are also references

[Part 7](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/) said the first ten customers are design partners. In long cycles that rule tightens. Each design partner costs a year or more of attention. You cannot afford one who shapes the product and then will not say so.

Choose design partners on three tests. They own the cost from [Part 31](https://lowob.com/research/selling-what-nobody-has-a-budget-line-for/). They can deploy in a setting that looks like the wider market. And they agree up front, in the pilot terms, to act as a reference if the agreed success criteria are met.

Write the success criteria into the pilot agreement. Vague pilots never end. Specific pilots convert or close, and both are useful. A [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/) is the working document: dated steps, an owner for each, and the reference commitment written in as a step rather than a hope.

Expect fewer partners than a software company would run. Three good ones, each in a different buyer type, teach more than ten shallow ones.

## Pilots with governments, regulators, utilities and large corporates

These are the natural first buyers for robotics, infrastructure, energy, identity and verification. They are also the slowest. Four things differ from selling to a startup.

| Area | What differs | What to prepare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procurement | Formal process, frameworks, thresholds, often tender rules | Map the route before first contact; find the threshold that allows a direct pilot |
| Security | Review before any data or site access | Security pack, data handling, access controls, ready on day one |
| Liability | Risk sits with the vendor; insurance and indemnity are negotiated | Insurance in place; a lawyer who has seen the buyer's standard terms |
| Timelines | Budget cycles, annual plans, committee calendars | Know their planning calendar and work back from it |

Thresholds are the first thing to check, because they decide whether a pilot can be bought quickly or must be tendered. In England, procurements starting on or after 1 January 2026 under the Procurement Act 2023 use a threshold of £135,018 including VAT for central government supplies and services, £207,720 for sub-central authorities, and £415,440 for utilities. Value is calculated including VAT, so a contract that looks under the line net of VAT can be over it. Other jurisdictions have their own figures. The point is the same everywhere: a pilot priced below the relevant threshold, with a clear scope, is a decision a budget holder can make; one above it is a process.

Security is the second. Institutions will expect the same questionnaires a large company sends, and often more. Our playbook on [the pilot that survives security review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) sets out the pack, and our explainer on [SOC 2 for AI vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/) covers what a report does and does not prove.

The lesson is to sell the pilot as a project the institution can approve, not as a trial it can tolerate. That means a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date. Pilots without those are favours, and favours do not convert.

[Part 4](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) said run the round like a sales process. Run institutional pilots the same way: stages, owners, exit criteria.

> Pilots without a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date are favours, and favours do not convert.

## Consortia and standards bodies as distribution

[Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) said find channels that are open when platforms are closed. In emerging tech the open channel is often an industry consortium, a standards working group or a regulator's sandbox.

They are slow and unglamorous. They are also where the buyers sit when they are deciding what the category means. A company in the working group that writes the standard is a company every member has met.

AI is a live example. The European Commission asked CEN and CENELEC to develop harmonised standards for the AI Act in ten areas, from risk management and data governance to human oversight and quality management, and the work sits in their Joint Technical Committee 21. The first, EN 18286 on quality management systems for AI Act purposes, was published on 14 October 2026 and referenced in the Official Journal by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2026/2274. Applying harmonised standards is voluntary, but it gives a presumption of conformity, which is why buyers' compliance teams follow the committee's work closely. Our guide to [the EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) covers what applies and when.

Treat these bodies as distribution, not PR. Pick the one where your buyers are, not the one with the best logo. Send the person who can speak to the technical detail. Show up for the whole cycle, not the launch.

The same applies to regulator sandboxes. A sandbox place is a pilot with a clearance attached, which [Part 32](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-long-cycles/) said is a milestone. It is also competitive. The FCA's freedom of information response in May 2026 showed 142 applications and 14 acceptances in its 2025/26 financial year, and 52 applications with 16 acceptances the year before. Under the EU's amendments to the AI Act, member states' deadline to set up AI regulatory sandboxes moved to 2 August 2027, according to Gibson Dunn's summary of the agreement, so EU sandbox capacity is still being built.

| Channel | What it gives you | What it costs | Selectivity |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Industry consortium | Access to members deciding what the category means | Membership fee and a senior person's time | Usually open to paying members |
| Standards working group | Influence on requirements buyers will audit against | A technical expert for a multi-year cycle | Open through national standards bodies |
| Regulator sandbox | A supervised pilot and a clearance signal | Application effort, reporting, constraints on scope | Selective: about one in ten at the FCA in 2025/26 |

## The first hundred are practitioners, not a public community

[Part 6](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) said the first hundred people are the ones who will tell others. [Part 5](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) said community is a job. In emerging tech the hundred are not a public community at all.

They are the field engineers, grid operators, compliance leads, security researchers and procurement specialists who decide whether a new thing is credible. They do not gather on social platforms. They gather in working groups, technical forums, conferences with small audiences and private channels.

Build the list by name. Know what each person needs to see before they will vouch for you. Give it to them before you ask for anything.

[Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) said stop reporting reach. Here that means a hundred practitioners who will return a call matters more than ten thousand followers who will not.

## Measure progress by risk retired

Pipeline value is the wrong measure when deals take two years. A large pipeline of unconverted pilots is a cost, not an asset.

Measure what reduces risk. Technical milestones met in the field. Paid pilots signed and paid. Security reviews passed. Regulatory clearances won. References agreed in writing. Each one makes the next sale faster and the next raise cheaper.

Report those monthly, to the team and the board. [Part 10](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/)'s ten-question self-score works here with one change: replace revenue questions with risk-retired questions until revenue arrives.

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Design partners | Each owns the cost, resembles the wider market and has agreed in writing to be a reference |
| Pilot terms | Success criteria, a sponsor, a budget and an end date |
| Institutional readiness | Procurement route and threshold, security pack, insurance and timeline per buyer type |
| Open channel | One consortium, standards body or sandbox chosen where the buyers sit |
| Practitioners | The first hundred listed by name with what each needs to see |
| Reporting | Monthly risk retired and paid pilots, not pipeline size |

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose design partners who will say so.** They own the cost, resemble the market and agree in writing to be a reference.
- **Sell a project, not a trial.** Budget, sponsor, procurement route and end date, priced with the threshold in mind.
- **Join where the category is defined.** Standards bodies and sandboxes are distribution, and they are selective.
- **Report risk retired.** Field milestones, paid pilots, security reviews, clearances and written references.

## Common questions

### How do I find first customers for a product in a brand-new market?

Choose a few design partners who own the cost, can deploy in a setting like the wider market, and agree up front to be references if agreed success criteria are met. Three good partners in different buyer types teach more than ten shallow ones.

### How should a startup run a pilot with a government or large corporate?

Sell it as a project the institution can approve, with a budget, a sponsor, a procurement route and an end date. Check the procurement threshold first; in England the central government services threshold is £135,018 including VAT from January 2026.

### Is it worth applying to a regulatory sandbox?

Often, if your buyers are regulated, because a sandbox place is a supervised pilot with a clearance signal. Expect competition: the FCA accepted 14 of 142 applications in 2025/26.

### Are standards bodies worth a startup's time?

Yes, as distribution. They are slow, but buyers sit there while deciding what the category means. Pick the one where your buyers are and attend the whole cycle.

## Sources and notes

- [Financial Conduct Authority, Information on number of sandbox applications received from 2021 to 2025](https://www.fca.org.uk/freedom-information/information-number-sandbox-applications-received-2021-2025-may-2026), May 2026. Freedom of information response; some cases may have been pending at the cut-off.
- [Bevan Brittan, Procurement: updated thresholds for January 2026 published](https://www.bevanbrittan.com/insights/articles/2025/procurement-updated-thresholds-for-january-2026-published/), 2025. Law firm summary of the regulations; England only; check the regulations before relying on a figure.
- [European Commission, Standardisation of the AI Act](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/ai-act-standardisation), as listed in November 2026. Official policy page; other harmonised standards are still in development.
- [Gibson Dunn, EU AI Act Omnibus Agreement: Postponed High-Risk Deadlines and Other Key Changes](https://www.gibsondunn.com/eu-ai-act-omnibus-agreement-postponed-high-risk-deadlines-and-other-key-changes/), 2026. Law firm analysis of the agreement later adopted as Regulation (EU) 2026/1744.
- The tables and checklist are **lowob**'s framework.

For your top three target institutions, write down the procurement threshold that applies, the date their next budget is set and the name of the person who owns the cost. If any of the three is blank, that is this week's work.

# What Is Permission-Aware Retrieval?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Permission-aware retrieval filters what an AI assistant or agent can retrieve to what the requesting person is allowed to open in the source system. It is the standard design for enterprise assistants. It inherits every overshared file and lags behind permission changes, so commercial content should be audited and tested with restricted users before it is connected.

Permission-aware retrieval is search for AI systems that returns only the documents and records the requesting person could already open in the source system. It is the standard design for enterprise assistants and the right one. It also inherits every bad permission a company has: a pricing file shared with the whole firm was harmless while nobody could find it, and becomes visible once an assistant can. Audit permissions on commercial content before connecting it, and test with a restricted user.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What permission-aware retrieval means

An assistant answering from company content first retrieves relevant material, then writes from it. That is [retrieval-augmented generation](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/). Permission-aware retrieval adds one rule to the first step: nothing comes back that the person asking could not open themselves.

To do that, the system needs three things for every item: the content, a list of who may see it, and a reliable map of who each person is and which groups they belong to. Microsoft's synced connectors ingest each item with "an access control list (ACL) that enforces permissions". Glean's indexing SDK takes per-document lists of allowed users and groups, and warns against flattening groups into user lists because flattened lists go stale as memberships change.

There are four common approaches, often combined.

| Approach | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stored ACL filter | Permissions copied into the index; results filtered at query time | Fast at scale | Only as current as the last sync |
| Live source check | Each candidate result is checked with the source system before use | Reflects current access | Slower; costly across large result sets |
| Two-stage | Filter on stored ACLs, then verify the shortlist with the source | Speed with a current check | More moving parts |
| Partitioning | Separate stores or indexes per team, client or region | Hard boundary, simple to explain | Duplication; cross-team search is harder |

AWS's October 2026 post describes the two-stage design. The first stage applies ACLs stored in the index, because "real-time API calls for every document in the index would be too costly at scale". The second checks candidates against the source using the user's own token and drops any the user cannot open.

## Why it inherits bad permissions

Permission-aware retrieval does exactly what it promises, and that is the problem. Microsoft's own guidance says it is "important that you're using the permission models available in Microsoft 365 services, such as SharePoint, to help ensure the right users or groups have the right access". Before assistants, an overshared folder was protected by obscurity: finding it required knowing it existed. Retrieval removes that protection. Our glossary puts it plainly: it inherits every bad permission in the underlying systems.

Timing is a second gap. AWS notes that pull-based syncs leave permissions out of date between runs, that some sources do not announce group changes, and that changes to a source's sharing model can expose content until connectors are updated. A person removed from a deal team may still retrieve its files until the next sync.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial content is exposed in a particular way. Rate cards, discount reasons and client renewal threads are created quickly, in shared folders, by people optimising for speed. Each is mild alone and sensitive in combination.

There is also a gap that user permissions cannot close. A senior seller may legitimately open files for two competing clients. An agent drafting for one of them should still not retrieve the other's terms. Permission-aware retrieval answers "may this person see this?" It does not answer "should this task use this?" For agents, scope retrieval to the account in hand as well as to the user. OWASP's guidance on cross-context leaks in shared stores points the same way.

Agents also need their own identity. If an agent retrieves on a shared service account, it sees what that account sees, not what the person asking may see. See [What Is Agent Identity?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/).

## How to start

1. **Find the broad shares.** List commercial sites and folders shared with everyone in the company, or with anyone holding the link.
2. **Fix before connecting.** Narrow those shares, then connect.
3. **Test negatively.** Pick three documents a junior seller should not see and search for them as that seller. Glean's documentation is right that the search result is the test.
4. **Measure lag.** Remove someone's access to a test file and time how long the assistant keeps returning it.
5. **Log retrievals.** Keep a record of what was retrieved for whom, as OWASP recommends.

## lowob takeaways

- **It returns only what the person could open.** That is the right design.
- **It inherits every overshare.** Retrieval removes the obscurity that used to protect them.
- **Permissions lag.** Indexes hold a snapshot from the last sync.
- **Scope agents by task too.** User permission does not stop cross-client mixing.

## Common questions

### What does permission-aware mean in AI search?

That results are filtered so each user only receives content they already have permission to open in the original system, such as SharePoint, Google Drive or a CRM.

### Can Microsoft Copilot see files I don't have access to?

Microsoft states Copilot only surfaces organisational data the user has at least view permission for. The risk is files you have access to but were never meant to see, because of broad sharing.

### How do you test permission-aware retrieval?

Search as a restricted user for documents that user should not see, and confirm they never appear. Then revoke access to a test file and measure how long it stays retrievable.

## In the news

- 7 October 2026 · AWS Machine Learning Blog[AWS on access control for retrieval with Amazon Quick and Bedrock](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-07-aws-on-access-control-for-retrieval-with-amazon-quick-and-b)Vendor-written, but a useful pattern: the retriever should only see what the person asking is allowed to see.

Ask a junior member of the commercial team to search your assistant for "discount", "rate card" and "renewal". Anything they should not have seen marks the first folder to fix.

# A Loop With Good Context

Source: https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An agent is a loop, so the engineering that matters is what the loop knows when it asks. Research on long inputs shows that more context makes models less reliable, so teams must choose what enters. The most valuable context almost nobody supplies is prior judgment on comparable cases, delivered through a precedent slot filled before each task runs and tested blind.

An agent is a loop. The engineering that matters has moved from what you ask to what the loop knows when it asks. Research on long inputs shows that adding more context makes models less reliable, so every serious team ends up choosing what enters. The most valuable context almost nobody supplies is prior judgment on comparable cases: a precedent slot of three to five past decisions, each with its reason, outcome and any dissent, filled before the task runs and tested blind against the current version.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

An agent has been described, memorably, as a for-loop with better PR. The joke carries a design rule. If the loop is a commodity, the work is in what enters it. Our explainer on [the agent loop](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/) covers the mechanics; this piece is about the inputs.

## The loop is cheap; the context is the work

Anthropic's engineering guidance describes context engineering as "the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens" during a model's work, and treats it as the successor to prompt engineering. Its goal is the "smallest possible set of high-signal tokens" that makes the desired outcome likely. The reason is empirical. Chroma's July 2025 technical report tested 18 models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Alibaba and found reliability fell as input length grew, even on simple retrieval tasks. Liu and colleagues had earlier found that models do best when relevant information sits at the start or end of a long input and worse when it sits in the middle.

Public accounts from teams building on financial data describe the same pressure from the practitioner side. Nicolas Bustamante, who builds a financial-research agent at Fintool, wrote in February 2026 that "past 32K tokens, most models show sharp performance degradation" in his experience, and that crossing 200,000 input tokens triggers premium pricing on some models. In a January 2026 account he wrote that normalising financial data was "80% of the work", with off-the-shelf parsers failing on multi-column proxy statements and scanned exhibits. These are one builder's observations, not a controlled study, but they match the research.

The lesson every serious team reaches is the same: you cannot pour everything in. You have to choose. Our comparison of [long context windows and RAG](https://lowob.com/research/long-context-vs-rag/) covers the trade-offs in more depth. That shift, from prompt engineering to context engineering, has a corollary few teams act on.

## Documents tell the loop what is true. Decisions tell it what we do.

Most context pipelines carefully index the material that describes the world. They index the company's own past decisions not at all. The loop is then asked to reason like a senior analyst while seeing only what a capable new hire would see on day one: the facts, without the house view of what the facts usually mean.

| Context source | What it tells the loop | Usually indexed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Policies and rules | What is allowed | Yes |
| Research, filings, reference data | What is true about the world | Yes |
| Product documentation | What the company sells and how it works | Yes |
| Prior decisions with reasons and outcomes | What this company does in cases like this, and what happened | Rarely |
| Recorded dissent | Where the people who knew the case disagreed | Almost never |

A senior analyst's edge is rarely that they know more facts. It is that they remember the three similar cases, what was decided, what went wrong in one of them, and which signal turned out to matter. That is retrievable, if anyone wrote it down. Our explainer on [decision precedent in AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/) sets out how precedent differs from rules, memory and format examples.

> A senior analyst's edge is rarely that they know more facts. It is that they remember the three similar cases and what went wrong in one of them.

## Designing a precedent slot

The practical design is a reserved section of every agent's context, a precedent slot, filled before the task runs.

**What goes in.** The three to five most comparable prior decisions in the same class. Each carries the decision, the one-sentence reason, the outcome if known, and any recorded dissent. Superseded decisions are excluded or clearly marked as replaced, for the reasons set out in [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

**How comparability is judged.** Selection matters. Liu and colleagues showed in 2021 that GPT-3's results varied widely with the choice of in-context examples, and that retrieving examples close to each new input beat random choice, with reported gains of 41.9% on a table-to-text task and 45.5% on open-domain question answering. Their closeness was measured in sentence-embedding space, which works when similar wording means a similar task. For business decisions it often does not. Text similarity matches cases that are described alike. Applicability fields match cases that are alike.

| Applicability field | Example values | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision class | Renewal discount, credit exception, partner terms | Precedent from another class misleads |
| Segment | Mid-market, enterprise, public sector | Same request, different economics |
| Size band | Contract value or headcount range | Thresholds change by size |
| Stage | New business, renewal, expansion | Different risks at each stage |
| Jurisdiction | Country or regulatory regime | Rules and norms differ |
| Trigger | Competing quote, budget cut, late payment | The cause often decides the answer |

Records need those fields at capture time, or similarity search degrades into keyword matching. Our piece on [the commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) lists where to start.

**How much budget.** Small. A few hundred tokens per precedent, summarised from the source record, with a link back. Anthropic's guidance favours "diverse, canonical examples" over long lists of edge cases, and the same applies here. Precedent should be dense, not long.

## The failure mode to design against

Precedent creates anchoring. In our experience, a model given three prior approvals will find reasons to approve. Two guards help.

First, always include outcomes, and deliberately include at least one comparable case that went badly, when one exists. A precedent set made only of successes is a pitch.

Second, instruct the loop to state how the current case differs from each precedent before it uses them. The differences are often where the judgment lies. If the loop cannot name a difference, that is itself worth a reviewer's attention.

Illustrative example: a renewal-preparation agent

Decision
:   Add a precedent slot to the agent that prepares renewal briefs, holding the four closest prior renewal decisions by segment, size band and trigger.

Reason and owner
:   Reviewers said briefs were accurate but generic, and kept adding "last time we did X" by hand. Owned by the head of account management.

What changed
:   The slot included one renewal where a discount was granted and the account churned anyway. The agent began flagging when a new request matched that pattern, and stated how the current case differed.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## Test it blind before you trust it

Pick one agent workflow and add a precedent slot. Add four or five applicability fields to the decision records it draws from, so comparability is about situation, not wording. Then run the precedent version side by side with the current version on twenty cases. Give both preparations to the usual reviewer without saying which is which, and record which was more useful and why.

Twenty cases is small. Read the result as direction, not proof, and look at the reasons as much as the tally. Useful signals are whether the reviewer cited a precedent in the final decision, whether the stated differences were correct, and whether review took less time.

**What would prove this wrong:** a blind comparison in which adding precedent makes no difference to reviewer-judged quality, or makes it worse through anchoring that the guards do not fix.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose what enters the loop.** Longer context is less reliable, so selection is the engineering.
- **Index decisions, not just documents.** Policies say what is allowed; precedent says what the company does.
- **Match on situation.** Applicability fields such as segment, stage and jurisdiction beat text similarity.
- **Guard against anchoring.** Include a case that went badly and make the loop state how the current case differs.
- **Test blind.** Twenty cases, the usual reviewer, no labels.

## Common questions

### What is a precedent slot in an AI agent?

A reserved section of an agent's context, filled before the task runs, holding the three to five most comparable prior decisions with the decision, the one-sentence reason, the outcome if known and any recorded dissent.

### Does a bigger context window remove the need to choose what an agent sees?

No. Chroma's tests of 18 models found reliability falls as input length grows, and earlier research found models miss information placed mid-context. Selecting a small, high-signal set still matters.

### How do you pick comparable past cases for an AI agent?

Use applicability fields that describe the situation, such as decision class, segment, size band, stage, jurisdiction and the trigger for the decision. Text similarity matches cases described alike, which degrades into keyword matching.

### Does giving an AI agent past decisions cause anchoring?

It can. Include outcomes and at least one comparable case that went badly, and have the loop state how the current case differs from each precedent before it uses them.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
- [Chroma, Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot), 14 July 2025. Vendor technical report; 18 models on synthetic tasks.
- [Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172v3), July 2023. Academic preprint; models tested are older than current ones.
- [Liu et al., What Makes Good In-Context Examples for GPT-3?](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2101.06804), January 2021. Academic preprint; benchmark tasks, not business decisions.
- [Nicolas Bustamante, The LLM Context Tax](https://www.nicolasbustamante.com/p/the-llm-context-tax-best-tips-for), 10 February 2026. Practitioner essay by a vendor founder; observations, not a controlled study.
- [Nicolas Bustamante, Lessons from Building AI Agents for Financial Services](https://nicolasbustamante.com/blog/lessons-from-building-ai-agents-for-financial-services), 23 January 2026. Practitioner account from one product team.
- The precedent slot, applicability fields and anchoring guards are **lowob**'s working method.

Pick one agent workflow and add a precedent slot with three comparable prior decisions, outcomes and dissent. Run it side by side with the current version on twenty cases and have the usual reviewer judge, blind, which preparation was more useful.

# Community Management vs Social Media Management

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Social media management is editorial: the company's voice on its own accounts. Community management is hosting: members' voices in spaces the company runs. The two jobs have different daily work, measures and temperaments, and combining them by default sets one of them up to be neglected. This guide sets out what each requires and how to staff them at different sizes.

Social media management is editorial work: the company's voice on its own accounts, measured by reach, response and traffic. Community management is hosting work: members' voices in spaces the company runs, measured by returning members and how much they help each other. Job descriptions routinely merge the two, and the evidence suggests the merged role is already stretched: CMX's 2025 survey found around 30% of community teams are one person. When one person holds both, the job that gets done depends on their temperament, not the company's needs.

Job descriptions routinely ask for a "community and social media manager", as though the two were one skill with two channels. They are different jobs, with different daily work, different measures and different temperaments. A person good at one is frequently poor at the other. This guide sits alongside our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/), which covers what a community needs once you have decided to run one.

## Social media management: a publication

The job is to represent the company on its own social accounts. Plan and publish content, adapt the company's messages to each platform's format, respond to public comments and mentions, monitor conversation about the brand, coordinate with founders and executives on their accounts, and report on reach and engagement.

The response part of the job is now an expectation with a clock on it. Sprout Social's 2025 Index found about three-quarters of consumers expect a brand to respond within 24 hours or sooner, and its Q4 2025 Pulse survey found 51% of people who reach out publicly expect a public acknowledgement before being moved to a private message. Those are vendor surveys, but the direction is clear: the public feed generates a queue, and the queue has a deadline.

The temperament is editorial. Good social managers are writers and editors who understand format, timing and platform behaviour. They are producing a publication. Our playbook on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) applies to their output: every post should have a reader, a purpose and a next action.

## Community management: an institution

The job is to build and maintain a group of people who participate with one another, in spaces the company hosts or convenes: a Discord, a forum, a customer group, an ambassador programme, working sessions, events. Welcome new members, design the ways people can contribute, moderate, resolve conflicts, surface what members are saying to the company and recognise contribution.

The measures are about members, not the company: returning active members, member-to-member interaction against staff-to-member, unique contributors, time to first useful response, movement up the participation ladder, and knowledge or value created by members.

These measures are harder to tie to money, and the profession knows it. CMX's 2025 Community Industry Report, a survey of 589 community professionals, found only 24% could confidently quantify the value of their community, and "difficulty proving ROI to justify budget" was the top budget challenge at 37%. Where community and customer data were connected in the CRM, teams were twice as likely to rate their impact extremely successful (24% against 11.5%).

The temperament is hosting. Good community managers are facilitators who are comfortable letting others speak, who notice individuals and who can hold a room. They are running an institution, not a publication.

|  | Social media management | Community management |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Whose voice | The company's | The members' |
| Where | The company's own accounts on public platforms | Spaces the company hosts or convenes |
| Daily work | Plan, write, publish, reply, monitor | Welcome, moderate, connect, recognise, escalate |
| Core measures | Reach, engagement, relevant follower growth, traffic, response time | Returning members, member-to-member help, contributors, time to first useful response |
| Time horizon | Days and weeks | Quarters |
| Temperament | Editor | Host |
| Typical failure | Generic content on every platform | An announcement channel with a member count |

## Why combining them fails

The daily work competes. A publishing schedule and community presence both demand attention at the same hours, and the public queue is louder. When a mention needs a reply within the day and a quiet member's first question can wait, the quiet member waits.

The measures pull in different directions. A social manager is rewarded for the company's voice being heard. A community manager is rewarded for members' voices being heard, including when the company is not in the conversation at all. One report cannot serve both without one half becoming a footnote.

The skills rarely coincide. The editor who writes a sharp thread is not automatically the host who makes a quiet member feel welcome, and the host who can calm an argument is not automatically the writer who can make a product launch land on five platforms.

The staffing data makes the risk concrete. CMX found around 30% of community teams are a single person, and 17% of respondents said no one in their organisation works full time on community, the highest share the survey has recorded. Marketing was the most common reporting line at 31%, ahead of customer success and support at 19%. A one-person community function reporting into marketing is the role most likely to be asked to "also run social", and the least able to absorb it.

> When one person holds both jobs, which one gets done depends on their temperament, not on what the company needs.

## What each requires from the company

Social media management requires a point of view, a voice guide, access to the people whose thinking the content represents, and a decision about which platforms matter. Without those, the manager produces generic content on every platform. Our piece on [founder, brand and community accounts](https://lowob.com/research/founder-brand-community-social-strategy/) covers how to divide the voice between people and the company.

Community management requires a reason for people to participate with one another, a decision about what the community is for, consequential roles for members and patience measured in quarters. It also requires operating support the company often forgets. Discord's own moderation guidance recommends letting automation handle routine issues around the clock while keeping judgment calls with people, turning recurring questions into a read-only FAQ channel, and keeping enforcement "as fair and consistent as possible". That is a process, not a posting rota. Without it, the manager runs an announcement channel with a member count, the failure our piece on [community as a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) describes.

## How to staff by company type

For most small companies: one editorial person for social, part-time or shared with content, and a decision about whether a community is warranted at all. Many companies need excellent social presence and customer support and do not need a member-led community, and forcing one wastes a hire.

Where a community is warranted, hire for hosting, not for writing, and give the role a measurable purpose. CMX's data on objectives is a useful starting list: teams focused on support most often measured active users (41%) and case deflection (38%), teams focused on retention measured customer retention (72%), and teams focused on product feedback measured product ideas (71%). Pick one objective and its measure before the hire starts.

| Company situation | Usually primary | Usually secondary | Staffing pattern |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder with a following | Social, partly the founder's own | Community | Editorial support for the founder; community only if members ask for it |
| Web3 project | Community | Social | A host first, with social shared with content or the founder |
| Enterprise fintech | Social and executive presence | Community, often customer advisory groups | An editor first; a small customer group run by customer success |
| B2B SaaS with an active user base | Depends on the support model | The other | Two roles once both have a measurable purpose |

Where both are needed, they are two roles, or one role with a clear primary and an honest acknowledgement of what will be secondary. The [shift from founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) is often the moment this decision has to be made explicitly, because the founder stops covering one of the jobs by default.

## lowob takeaways

- **Different jobs.** Social is editorial and publishes the company's voice; community is hosting and builds members' voices.
- **Different clocks.** Social replies are expected within a day; community value shows up over quarters, so the community half is neglected first.
- **Different measures.** Report reach and response time for social, and returning members and member-to-member help for community.
- **Decide the primary.** For a Web3 project community is usually primary; for an enterprise fintech, social usually is.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a community manager and a social media manager?

A social media manager represents the company on its own accounts and is measured by reach, engagement and response time. A community manager builds a group whose members participate with one another in company-hosted spaces and is measured by returning members and member-to-member help.

### Should one person handle both community and social media?

Usually not. The work competes for the same hours, the public feed carries a same-day response expectation, and the skills rarely coincide, so one job tends to be neglected. If one person must do both, name the primary job in writing.

### Does every startup need a community manager?

No. Many companies need excellent social presence and customer support and do not need a member-led community. Hire a community manager only when there is a reason for members to help each other and a measure for whether they do.

### How do you measure a community manager's performance?

Against one stated objective: active users and case deflection for a support community, retention for a customer community, product ideas for a feedback community. Add returning members and time to first useful response as health measures.

## Sources and notes

- [CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report](https://start.bevy.com/hubfs/2025%20CMX%20Community%20Industry%20Report-1.pdf?hsLang=en), 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals, May to June 2025; distributed by Bevy, a community platform vendor; self-reported.
- [CMX, Community Industry Report 2026](https://cmxhub.com/community-industry-report). Landing page for the 2026 edition; only headline findings are public, so this piece uses the 2025 figures.
- [Sprout Social, Social media customer service statistics](https://sproutsocial.com/insights/social-media-customer-service-statistics/), updated October 2026. Vendor research drawing on the 2025 Sprout Social Index and a Q4 2025 Pulse survey; sample sizes not stated on the page.
- [Discord, Tools for automating server management](https://discord.com/community/automating-moderation-community-support). Platform guidance on combining automation with human moderators.
- The comparison and staffing tables are **lowob**'s framework.

## Related research

- [Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/)
- [From Founder-Led to Team-Led Marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/)
- [Content With a Job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/)

## Next move

Before you post the next "community and social" job description, write one sentence naming which job is primary and the single measure it will be judged on. If you cannot name a community measure, hire for social and leave community for later.

# The Permission Problem: When Commercial Context Leaks

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-permission-problem-when-commercial-context-leaks/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Permission-aware retrieval does what it promises: it shows each user what they already have access to. In most firms that is far more than it should be, and commercial context such as pricing, discount reasons and client confidences is among the most sensitive material an assistant can surface. This piece sets out four leak paths (oversharing, cross-client leakage, prompt injection and excessive agency) and seven controls a 20- to 500-person firm can run without a security team.

The assistants and context layers sold to mid-size firms are permission-aware: they only retrieve what the user could already open. That is the right design, and it is also the problem, because most firms' permissions were never meant to be searched. A pricing sheet shared "with anyone in the company" three years ago was safe while nobody could find it. Once an assistant can, it is not. Commercial context leaks by four paths: oversharing through inherited permissions, cross-client leakage when an agent mixes one account's context with another's, prompt injection through content an outsider controls, and excessive agency when an agent holds more access than its job needs. Each has a control a firm without a security team can run. Most of them belong in the context step of the build, before any agent drafts for a client.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

[Part 5](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/) followed one account through the context layer and showed what good wiring makes possible: the emails, call notes, proposals and invoices for a client, connected and searchable in the order a person would want them. This piece is about the other side of the same wiring. Everything that makes the context layer useful to a seller makes it useful to anyone else who can query it, including people inside the firm who should not see a given client's terms, and people outside it who can get text in front of the model.

## Permission-aware retrieval inherits your permission debt

Microsoft is clear about the design. Its guidance states that Copilot grounds its responses in the data users already have permission to access. That sentence is reassuring to a security reviewer and alarming to anyone who has audited a shared drive. Permissions accumulate. Sites are shared broadly to save time, leavers' accounts stay enabled, and folders inherit access from parents nobody remembers configuring.

Before assistants, this permission debt was mostly harmless, because finding an overshared file required knowing it existed. Retrieval removes that protection. A Gartner analyst put it plainly in 2024: "The better the information retrieval tool, the better your information governance has to be." In the same Gartner survey of 132 IT leaders, 40% said oversharing concerns had delayed their Copilot rollouts by three months or more.

Vendor data suggests the debt is near universal. Varonis's 2025 State of Data Security report, based on 1,000 IT environments and nearly 10 billion files, found 99% of organisations had sensitive data that AI could easily surface, 88% had stale but enabled "ghost" users, and only 1 in 10 had labelled their files. Varonis sells data security tools, so treat the figures as an upper bound from a motivated source. The direction matches what we see.

Commercial context is unusually exposed for two reasons. It is created fast, in shared folders and threads, by people optimising for speed. And it is unusually sensitive in combination: a rate card is mild; a rate card plus the discount reasons in the decision record plus one client's renewal thread is a negotiating brief for that client's competitor.

## Four ways commercial context leaks

| Leak path | How it happens | Commercial example | First control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Oversharing | Assistant retrieves files the user can open but was never meant to see | A junior seller asks about "standard discounts" and gets the board's pricing review | Clean up permissions on commercial sites before connecting them |
| Cross-client leakage | Context from one account enters work for another | A proposal draft for one client cites another client's terms or case | Scope agent context to one account per task |
| Prompt injection | Text an outsider controls instructs the model | A prospect's email or a supplier's PDF carries hidden instructions to summarise and send internal data | Remove the outbound channel from any agent that reads untrusted content |
| Excessive agency | An agent holds more tools or permissions than its job needs | A meeting-prep agent can also send email and edit CRM records | Grant per-task permissions, logged against a named agent identity |

The OWASP Top 10 for Large Language Model Applications, a widely used security reference for this class of system, covers each row. LLM02 (sensitive information disclosure) calls for least-privilege access and warns that instructions in a system prompt about what not to reveal "may not always be honored" and can be bypassed. LLM08 (vector and embedding weaknesses) names cross-context leaks in shared stores and recommends "permission-aware vector and embedding stores" with data partitioned by access rights. Our explainers on [*prompt injection*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/) and [*excessive agency*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/) cover the other two.

## Cross-client leakage is the commercial line's own risk

Oversharing is a general governance problem. Cross-client leakage belongs to the commercial line, and it is the one most build plans miss.

A firm with competing clients has always relied on people to keep them apart. In professional services that is a formal conflicts wall; in agencies and publishers it is often an informal understanding about who works on which account. [Part 10](https://lowob.com/research/the-same-build-in-four-industries/)'s publisher split its wiring into two context layers so that sales context never reached the newsroom. The same logic applies between clients. An assistant asked to "draft a renewal proposal using our best recent examples" will retrieve the best recent examples it can see. If the seller has access to two competing accounts, the draft may carry one client's pricing, logo or results into the other's proposal.

Permissions do not solve this, because the seller is entitled to see both accounts. What is needed is task scope: the agent preparing work for account A is given account A's context and the firm's general material, and nothing else. In practice that means three things. Account is a required field on every document and record the context layer indexes. Agent tasks are launched from an account, not from a blank prompt. And anything client-identifying in a draft is checked against the target account before the draft reaches the approver.

The decision record raises the stakes. Part 9's records hold the reason a discount was granted, often naming a competitor's quote or a client's budget pressure. That is exactly the material a seller should consult as precedent and exactly the material that must not travel into another client's document. Precedent can be retrieved as a pattern ("discounts above 10% in this segment have not improved win rates") without the client detail attached.

> Permissions decide who can see a file. They do not decide which client's work it belongs in. For an agent drafting commercial documents, the second question matters more.

## Prompt injection: the path that needs no insider

Oversharing and cross-client leakage are failures of internal boundaries. Prompt injection comes from outside, and commercial teams are its natural target, because their job is to read content from strangers: inbound emails, RFP documents, prospect websites, supplier PDFs.

The clearest public example is EchoLeak, disclosed by Aim Security and fixed by Microsoft in June 2025 as CVE-2025-32711, rated 9.3 on the CVSS scale. An attacker sent an ordinary-looking email containing hidden instructions. When the recipient later asked Copilot a routine question, the retrieval step pulled the email into the model's context alongside internal data, and the instructions caused that data to be sent out through crafted Teams and SharePoint URLs. No click was required. No exploitation in the wild was reported and the fix required no customer action, but the pattern is general.

Simon Willison's description of the "lethal trifecta" is the most useful frame for a non-specialist. An agent becomes exploitable when it has all three: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. His recommendation is to avoid the combination entirely. He is sceptical of guardrail products that claim to catch 95% of attacks, noting that in web security 95% "is very much a failing grade".

For a commercial build the implication is concrete. An agent that reads inbound email and has access to the CRM must not also be able to send, post or fetch external URLs. That is Gateway 1 doing security work: if [nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/), the third leg of the trifecta is removed for outbound messages. It does not remove links and images rendered in a draft, which is how EchoLeak exfiltrated data, so drafts produced from untrusted content should render as plain text until approved.

## Seven controls a mid-size firm can run

None of these require a dedicated security team. Most use controls already in the firm's suite.

| Control | What it does | Owner | When in the build |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Permission review of commercial sites | Finds overshared folders before they are indexed | Build owner with IT | Before the context layer is connected |
| Exclude high-risk sites from AI search | Keeps board, HR and pricing-review material out of retrieval | IT | Before the context layer is connected |
| Remove ghost users and stale shares | Closes access nobody is using | IT | Before, then quarterly |
| Account as a required field | Makes task scoping possible | Revenue operations | With the CRM clean-up |
| One account per agent task | Prevents cross-client leakage | Build owner | With the first agent |
| Break the trifecta | No agent combines untrusted input, private data and an outbound channel | Build owner | With the first agent |
| Log retrieval and actions | Lets the firm reconstruct what an agent saw and did | IT | With the first agent |

On Microsoft 365, SharePoint Advanced Management, which Microsoft includes with Copilot licences, provides data access governance reports to find overshared sites, restricted content discovery to keep named sites out of Copilot, restricted access control, and site access reviews delegated to owners. Google Workspace has its own sharing and data-protection controls; the principle is the same whichever suite was chosen at Gateway 0.

Two questions come up at this point in most builds. The first is whether a dedicated governance platform is needed. For most firms under a few hundred people it is not yet; our ranking of [*AI governance and audit trail tools*](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/) was written for banks and insurers with model-risk obligations. The second is how to answer a client's or partner's security questionnaire. [*The pilot that survives security review*](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) sets out the written pack reviewers expect: where data goes, who can see it, whether it trains models, how long it is kept.

Illustrative example: the proposal that nearly carried another client's numbers

Decision
:   Scope the proposal-drafting agent to one account per task and exclude the pricing-review site from AI search.

Reason and owner
:   In testing, a draft renewal proposal for one client quoted results from a competing client's case study, which the seller was entitled to see. Owned by the head of operations, with IT running the permission review.

What changed
:   Agent tasks now launch from the account record; general case studies are tagged as cleared for reuse; the permission review closed broad sharing on most commercial folders before connection.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size agency, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Permission-aware means permission debt is searchable.** Clean up commercial sites before they are connected, not after the first incident.
- **Scope by account as well as by user.** Cross-client leakage happens inside legitimate access.
- **Break the trifecta.** No agent should read untrusted content, hold private data and have an outbound channel at once.
- **Use the suite's controls first.** Dedicated governance platforms are for firms with model-risk obligations.

Gateway card

### Before commercial context is connected to an agent

- Permission review completed on every commercial site and shared drive in scope
- High-risk sites excluded from AI search
- Ghost users and stale broad shares removed
- Account recorded on every document and record to be indexed
- Every agent task scoped to one account
- No agent holds untrusted input, private data and an outbound channel together
- Retrieval and actions logged against a named agent identity

## Common questions

### What is AI oversharing?

Oversharing is when an AI assistant surfaces files a user technically has permission to open but was never meant to see, because the underlying sharing settings were broader than intended. Permission-aware tools make this existing problem searchable.

### Does Microsoft 365 Copilot respect permissions?

Yes. Microsoft states that Copilot grounds responses in data the user already has permission to access. The risk is that many organisations' permissions are broader than they realise, which is why Microsoft offers oversharing controls through SharePoint Advanced Management.

### How can prompt injection leak company data?

An attacker places hidden instructions in content the AI will read, such as an email or document. If the AI also has access to private data and a way to send information out, the instructions can make it leak that data, as the EchoLeak flaw in Microsoft 365 Copilot demonstrated in 2025.

### How do you stop an AI agent leaking one client's data into another client's work?

Scope each agent task to a single account, require an account field on every indexed document and record, and check client-identifying content in drafts against the target account before approval.

## Sources and notes

- [Varonis, 2025 State of Data Security Report](https://www.varonis.com/blog/state-of-data-security-report), June 2025. Vendor research by a data security seller; 1,000 environments.
- [OWASP, LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm02/). Community standard; guidance, not regulation.

# Thought Leadership That Sales Can Use

Source: https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Thought leadership earns its cost when it changes what happens in a sales conversation, and most of it never gets there. Gartner finds confident buyers are twice as likely to report a high-quality deal, and Challenger's research attributes around half of lost deals to no decision. Both point to the same use: a firm's point of view should help a buyer decide. This piece shows how to convert one published position into five sales tools, how to feed sales evidence back into the positions, and how to measure the result by position rather than by piece.

Thought leadership pays when a seller can use it in a conversation to help a buyer decide, and most of it is never used that way. The evidence on buying points to why that use matters: Gartner's 2026 survey found confident buyers were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal, and Challenger's analysis of 2.5 million sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision. A published position becomes usable when it is converted into five things a seller can carry: a discovery question, a diagnostic, a business case line, an objection answer and a first step. The loop closes when what sellers hear flows back into the positions.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 9 gave each piece of content a job. Thought leadership has the hardest job of all: to change how a buyer thinks about a problem before they have decided to buy anything. That makes it the most difficult content to connect to revenue, and the easiest to cut when budgets tighten.

Our explainer [What thought leadership actually is](https://lowob.com/research/what-thought-leadership-actually-is/) sets out the standard a piece has to meet: a specific claim, evidence the audience could not gather alone, a practical consequence and consistency over time. This part assumes that standard is met. Its subject is what happens next: how a position that passes the test reaches the conversations where deals are won and lost.

## The gap between the byline and the call

In most firms, thought leadership and selling are run by different people on different calendars. Marketing publishes a position; sales may read it, may share it on social media, and rarely uses it in a meeting. Buyers notice the disconnect. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 B2B buyers found 69% reported inconsistencies between what a supplier's website said and what its sellers told them.

The sales side has its own overload. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently, and 82% of sales leaders said enablement content or delivery needed to change significantly to meet revenue goals. Forrester found reps choosing from an average of 1,400 sales assets. Adding a thought leadership article to that pile does not help. Converting it into something a seller can say in a meeting does.

## What buyers need from a point of view

The case for thought leadership in sales rests on how buyers decide, and the recent evidence is consistent.

**Buyers say it opens the door.** In Edelman and LinkedIn's 2025 thought leadership study, 95% of hidden buyers said strong thought leadership makes them more receptive to sales and marketing outreach. The study is run by a communications agency and a platform that sells B2B advertising, so read it as direction rather than measurement.

**Buyers form preferences early.** 6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers nearly 70% of the way through their process before contacting a seller, with 81% already holding a preferred vendor at first contact. Whatever shapes the buyer's view of the problem in that period shapes the shortlist.

**Buyers need confidence more than information.** Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 buyers found confident buyers were twice as likely to report a high-quality deal as buyers with low decision confidence. Gartner frames the seller's task as "value clarity": a clear understanding of how a solution improves outcomes in the buyer's specific role and context. A position that explains the problem in the buyer's own terms is the raw material for that.

**The main competitor is indecision.** Challenger's research on 2.5 million recorded sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision. Its analysis found win rates of 6% where buyer indecision was high, against 30% where it was medium. Buyers stall when they are unsure the problem is real, unsure which approach is right, or afraid of getting it wrong. Each of those is a question a good point of view answers.

> Thought leadership that only shapes opinion stops at the shortlist. Thought leadership that sales can use carries on into the decision.

## Five tools from one position

A single published position, if it meets the standard above, contains everything a seller needs. The work is to extract it into forms that fit a conversation.

| Part of the position | Sales tool | Where it is used | Test of whether it works |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The claim | A discovery question that tests whether the claim applies to this buyer | First and second meetings | The buyer answers with specifics, not a polite yes |
| The evidence | A diagnostic the buyer can run on their own numbers | Between meetings, often shared internally | The buyer comes back with a result |
| The consequence | One line for the business case, with the cost of inaction | Proposal and sponsor's internal pitch | The line appears in the buyer's own documents |
| The disagreement | An answer to the most likely objection | Whenever a sceptic joins the buying group | The objection stops recurring |
| The Monday action | A first step for the mutual plan | Commit stage | The step is agreed and dated |

Take an illustrative position from a firm that sells commercial advisory work: "most mid-size firms report pipeline coverage without the win rate behind it, so their boards cannot tell whether the pipeline is enough." Converted:

- **Question:** "When your board sees pipeline coverage, does it also see the win rate and cycle length that make it meaningful?"
- **Diagnostic:** a one-page calculation the buyer runs to find the coverage they actually need, given their own win rate and cycle.
- **Business case line:** the gap between reported and required coverage, expressed as bookings at risk.
- **Objection answer:** for "our coverage rule has always worked", a short explanation of the one case where three times coverage holds, and how often it does not.
- **First step:** restate last quarter's coverage with its win rate before the next board meeting.

None of those needs a new piece of content. All of them need someone to do the extraction, test it with two or three sellers, and keep it current. The diagnostic is usually the most valuable, because it gives the buyer something to take to colleagues the seller will never meet. Forrester's 2024 research found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, so a tool that travels without the seller does much of the work. Edelman and LinkedIn's 2025 study of nearly 2,000 professionals points the same way: among the buying group members it calls hidden buyers, 71% said they had little or no interaction with sales teams, and 52% of hidden decision-influencers said high-quality thought leadership helps them persuade other members of the buying group.

## Sales feeding the positions

The loop has to run both ways. Positions written from the marketing team's view of the market drift away from what buyers actually say. Positions written from sales evidence stay close to it.

Win-loss evidence is the best source, and it routinely surprises firms. In a 2026 interview published by Showpad, the co-chief executive of win-loss provider Clozd cited its research finding that 85% of CRM loss reasons did not match what buyers said drove their decision, and that 77% of the factors that influenced decisions never came up in sales conversations. Those are vendor figures and should be read as such, but the direction matches the experience of most firms that interview buyers. Our explainer on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers how to run the interviews.

| Input | Who supplies it | How often | What it changes |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Questions buyers ask that the firm cannot yet answer well | Sellers | Weekly, in pipeline review | Candidate topics for new positions |
| Objections that recur | Sellers and sales leadership | Monthly | The objection answer, or the position itself |
| Win-loss interview themes | Whoever runs win-loss | Quarterly | Which positions to strengthen, retire or start |
| Language buyers use for the problem | Call notes and recordings | Ongoing | The words the position and its tools use |

The [founder interview method](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) we have described elsewhere is one way to turn this evidence into publishable positions. The point here is the direction of flow: sales evidence in, positions out, tools back to sales.

Each position should sit in a single ledger with its claim, its evidence, its five tools, its owner and its review date. When a position changes, the tools change with it, and the change is recorded like any other commercial decision. That is the practical answer to Gartner's 69% inconsistency figure: one source for what the firm believes, read by marketing and sales alike.

## Measuring by position, not by piece

Measuring thought leadership by the piece leads back to impressions. Measuring by the position, across every piece and tool that carries it, connects it to deals.

Four signals do most of the work. **Use:** the share of open opportunities where a seller used one of the position's tools, taken from the CRM. **Echo:** whether buyers repeat the position's language in their own emails, briefs or requests for proposal, which is the clearest evidence that it shaped their thinking. **Progression:** whether opportunities where the diagnostic was run moved through the next stage faster. **No-decision rate:** whether deals where the position was used stall less often than those where it was not.

Volumes will be small and the comparison is not a controlled test, so read these over two or three quarters as direction. Part 10 sets out what it would take to test them properly. The aim is modest: to know which positions sellers use and which buyers repeat, so that the next position is chosen on evidence. Our piece [Dissent is the data you are throwing away](https://lowob.com/research/dissent-is-the-data-you-are-throwing-away/) makes the related case for recording the objections, not just the agreements.

Illustrative example: one position, five tools

Decision
:   Convert the firm's best-performing published position into a discovery question, a buyer-run diagnostic, a business case line, an objection answer and a mutual plan step, and track use in the CRM for two quarters.

Reason and owner
:   Sellers shared the article but never used it in meetings, and win-loss interviews showed deals stalling at the sponsor's internal pitch. Owned by the head of marketing, with two senior sellers testing each tool before release.

What changed
:   The diagnostic became the most attached asset in mid-stage deals, buyers began quoting its result in their own business cases, and two objection answers were rewritten after the first quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B advisory and services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Aim at the decision.** A point of view should help the buyer decide, not just admire the firm.
- **Extract five tools.** Question, diagnostic, business case line, objection answer and first step.
- **Build tools that travel.** The diagnostic reaches the buying group members the seller never meets.
- **Run the loop both ways.** Sales evidence and win-loss themes should choose the next position.
- **Measure the position.** Use, echo, progression and no-decision rate, read over quarters.

Gateway card

### Before you publish the next position

- A claim that a seller can test with one discovery question
- A diagnostic a buyer can run on their own numbers
- One business case line with the cost of inaction
- An answer to the most likely objection
- A first step that fits a mutual plan
- An owner, a review date and a place in the position ledger

## Common questions

### How do you use thought leadership in sales?

Convert each published position into tools a seller can carry: a discovery question, a diagnostic the buyer runs, a business case line, an answer to the main objection and an agreed first step.

### How do you measure the ROI of B2B thought leadership?

Measure by position rather than by piece: how often sellers use its tools in open deals, whether buyers repeat its language, whether those deals progress faster, and whether they stall less often.

### Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers stall when they are unsure the problem is real, which approach fits or whether they will get it wrong. Challenger's research on 2.5 million sales calls found around half of lost deals ended in no decision.

### How should sales and marketing work together on thought leadership?

Sales supplies the questions, objections and buyer language that choose and shape each position; marketing turns positions into tools; both work from a single ledger of what the firm believes.
