# The First Two-Fifths

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-first-two-fifths/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: What has shipped as an "enterprise brain" is the context layer: knowledge and governance, the easy two-fifths of the idea, with meaning built in a few places. Memory is arriving as a feature but does not yet track change, and judgment is skipped, because nothing in the stack writes an outcome back to a decision.

What has shipped as an "enterprise brain" is the context layer. It is the easy two-fifths of the idea, and it is the part being paid for. Data owners sell knowledge into other firms' agents, software incumbents sell governance, and meaning is being built in a few places. Memory is arriving as a feature but, on the benchmarks, does not yet track how facts change. Judgment is skipped. The missing pieces share one root cause: nothing in the stack writes an outcome back to a decision.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## Five components, and how they map to the build

Take the full promise apart and it has five components. **Knowledge**: the documents, data and definitions the organisation holds. **Memory**: what happened, across sessions and people. **Meaning**: a semantic layer that makes terms consistent across agents. **Governance**: permissions, identities and audit. **Judgment**: how the organisation decides, and whether it decided well.

In 2026 the market built the first and the fourth with real money behind them, built the third in a few places, and largely skipped the second and fifth. The second needs a qualification: memory is sold as a feature, but not yet as memory that spans time.

The Build Order describes the same system as layers in build order. The vocabularies reconcile as follows.

| Component (this piece) | Build Order layer | Who sells it in 2026 | Own or rent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge | Store, reached through the wiring | Data owners, suite vendors | Rent |
| Memory | Store, read over time; agent memory in the reasoning layer | Context platforms, memory start-ups | Rent the tool, check it tracks change |
| Meaning | Wiring: shared definitions | Data platforms, a few consultancies | Rent the layer, own the definitions |
| Governance | Wiring, plus the approval gate | Software incumbents | Rent |
| Judgment | Record, plus learning | Nobody | Own |
| Not listed | Reasoning | Model and agent vendors | Rent |

Reasoning is missing from the component list because it is the model, which every firm already rents. The [enterprise brain explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/) covers the five layers.

## What the market built in 2026

The figures below are the vendors' own, from earnings calls and launches, as dated.

| Component | Who | Date | What was reported |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Knowledge | FactSet | 1 Jul 2026 | Over 10% of ASV growth from AI products; over 450 clients on its MCP server under contract or trial; API call volume 13 times the prior quarter |
| Knowledge | S&P Global (Kensho) | Q2 2026 results, July 2026 | Over 500 customers on LLM-ready APIs and MCP-connected solutions, up more than 70% in a quarter |
| Governance | Microsoft Agent 365 | 29 Jul 2026 | "Nearly 40 million agents registered across tens of thousands of companies" two months in |
| Governance | ServiceNow AI Control Tower | 6 May 2025 | One place to govern "any ServiceNow and third-party AI agent, model, and workflow" |
| Governance | Workday Agent System of Record | 11 Feb 2025 | One hub for agents managed by Workday or third parties, with access, cost and on/off controls |
| Meaning | Open Semantic Interchange | 23 Sep 2025 | Snowflake, Salesforce, dbt Labs, BlackRock and others on a vendor-neutral standard for semantic metadata |
| Meaning | McKinsey Lilli | Aug 2023 onwards | 40+ curated sources, hundreds of human data stewards, an expert finder; 72% of the firm active |
| Memory | Google Gemini agent | 8 Oct 2026 | Four memory types, including execution history |

**Data owners built knowledge.** The major financial-data incumbents adopted the same agent connection protocol, MCP, in quick succession, and the ones that disclose numbers are monetising distribution of trusted data into other people's AI. FactSet's chief executive said "over 10% of the ASV growth came directly from AI SKUs". S&P Global said customers using Kensho's LLM-ready APIs and MCP-connected solutions exceeded 500, up more than 70% on the prior quarter. [The financial data providers your agents can call today](https://lowob.com/research/the-financial-data-providers-your-agents-can-call-today/) compares them.

**Software incumbents built governance.** Microsoft's chief executive described Agent 365 as "a control plane that extends companies' existing governance, identity, security, and management frameworks to agents". ServiceNow, Workday and Google each want to be the registry other vendors' agents must check in with; Google's October launch gives each agent its own Workspace account and routes traffic through an Agent Gateway. The fight is about who holds agent identity, which the new library explains in [What is agent identity](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/).

**Meaning arrived in a few places.** Consultancies built a narrow form: curated retrieval maintained by human stewards. McKinsey's own account of Lilli describes "more than 40 carefully curated knowledge sources", hundreds of data stewards checking content and removing client-confidential material, and a tool that can "identify experts in the appropriate fields". Data platforms are building the other form, shared metric definitions, through efforts such as the Open Semantic Interchange; the explainer [What is a semantic layer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) covers it.

**Memory shipped as a feature.** WRITER launched a team-level Agent Memory alongside its Enterprise Brain in September 2026, and Google's Gemini agent describes four memory types. The benchmarks are less encouraging. Patronus AI's MEMTRACK, built from simulated work across Slack, Linear and Git, found adding the Mem0 or Zep memory layers produced no significant improvement. The MemTrace benchmark (June 2026) found systems that recalled a fact's current and earlier state could still fail to track how it changed. Memory that stores what happened is being built; memory that knows which version is current, across months, is not.

None of this is a criticism. Context is genuinely hard. Entity resolution across hundreds of millions of companies, entitlements that follow every query, decades of history, definitions that actually agree: that is a moat, and it took decades to dig.

But it is a moat around the inputs to a decision, not around the decision.

> The market has built a moat around the inputs to a decision. Nobody has built one around the decision.

## Why the last two pieces keep getting skipped

Memory and judgment share a property the other three lack. They depend on **time running forward after the system has acted**. Knowledge can be loaded today. Governance can be configured today. Judgment can only be evidenced later, when the outcome arrives, and only if something connects that outcome back to the call that preceded it.

Three things make that connection rare.

**Outcomes live in other systems.** The credit decision is in one platform; the default shows up in another, eighteen months later, owned by a different team.

**Outcomes are slow.** A pricing call is graded in two quarters, a partnership in two years. Most programme roadmaps are planned in sprints.

**Outcomes are awkward.** A record that links a decision to a bad result names the person who made it. Systems that would surface that link meet quiet resistance.

The adoption research describes the consequence. MIT Project NANDA's 2025 report, based on more than 300 public initiatives, 52 interviews and 153 survey responses, put its central finding plainly: "Most GenAI systems do not retain feedback, adapt to context, or improve over time." The sample is small; the diagnosis matches.

So the industry ships what a pilot can demonstrate, and labels the whole thing a brain. The companion piece, [The enterprise brain is a record, not a mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/), sets out what the missing record holds; [What is outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/) covers the step that closes the loop.

## A quick test for your own programme

Open your AI roadmap and classify every item into one of the five components. Be strict.

| Roadmap item | Counts as | Only counts as more if |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A connector or MCP server | Knowledge | Never; it is access |
| A permissions model or agent registry | Governance | Never; it is control |
| Shared metric or term definitions | Meaning | It is enforced across agents and reports |
| A vector index or agent memory | Knowledge | It spans time and marks which version is current, then it is memory |
| A decision log | Memory | It records a prediction and later compares it with a result, then it is judgment |

Run honestly, a typical roadmap comes out heavy on knowledge and governance, light on meaning, empty on judgment. That is a fine portfolio for a context layer. It is the wrong portfolio for a programme whose sponsor was promised compounding.

The cheapest correction is not a new platform. It is one decision class with outcome write-back: a single field on each record that names what should happen if the decision was right, a date to check, and someone accountable for checking. Start there and the other components acquire a purpose.

Illustrative example: reclassifying a roadmap

Decision
:   Rename the programme from "enterprise brain" to "context layer" and add one judgment item: discount approvals recorded with expected outcome, check date and owner.

Reason and owner
:   Classified strictly, eleven of the twelve roadmap items were knowledge or governance and none was judgment. Owned by the head of revenue operations.

What changed
:   The sponsor's success measure moved from documents indexed to discount outcomes checked at close, reviewed quarterly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## What would prove this wrong

A horizontal product that, without per-client outcome plumbing, measurably improves decisions across unrelated decision classes. If one ships with independent evidence, the judgment layer is a product problem, not an organisational one. We had seen no such evidence by November 2026.

## lowob takeaways

- **The full promise has five parts.** Knowledge, memory, meaning, governance and judgment.
- **The market is paying for two.** Knowledge and governance have the disclosed money.
- **Judgment can only be evidenced later.** It needs an outcome connected back to the decision.
- **Start with one decision class.** Expected outcome, check date and owner on every record.

## Common questions

### What do enterprise brain products actually include?

Mostly the context layer: connectors to company knowledge, permissions and agent governance, and in some cases shared definitions and agent memory. None of the products launched in 2026 records decisions against their outcomes.

### What is the difference between a context layer and an enterprise brain?

A context layer gives agents governed access to what a company knows. A brain also records what the company decided, why, and what happened next, so later decisions can learn from earlier ones.

### Why don't enterprise AI systems learn from their decisions?

Nothing in the stack writes outcomes back to decisions. Outcomes live in other systems, arrive slowly, and are awkward because they name the person who decided.

### How can I tell if my AI roadmap is building judgment or just context?

Classify every item into the five components. Nothing counts as judgment unless it records a prediction and later compares it with a result.

# What Is a Token in AI, and Why Does It Drive Cost?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-token-in-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A token is a chunk of text, often part of a word, that a language model processes. Providers price every request per million input and output tokens, and output typically costs about five times as much as input. Agents multiply token use because each step re-reads its context, so cost control is mostly a design question.

A token is the unit of text a language model reads and writes, usually a word or part of a word. In English, one token is roughly four characters, or about three-quarters of a word. Providers charge per million tokens, with separate prices for input and output, so token count is what turns an AI task into a bill. Agents use far more tokens than chat because every step re-reads its context.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a token means

A model does not read letters or whole words. A component called a tokeniser splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary. Common words are often one token. Rare words, names and numbers are split into several. Spaces and punctuation count too.

OpenAI's help documentation gives the working ratios for English: one token is about four characters, one to two sentences is about 30 tokens, and a paragraph is about 100. It also notes that tokenisation varies by language. Its example is the Spanish phrase "Cómo estás", which is 5 tokens for 10 characters. Each model family has its own tokeniser, so the same text can produce different counts on different providers.

Tokens also cover more than the visible prompt and reply. Anthropic's documentation states that the system prompt, every message, tool results, documents and tool definitions all count. When a model "thinks" before answering, those thinking tokens are billed as output.

| Counts as tokens | Often overlooked |
| --- | --- |
| Your question or instruction | The system prompt sent with every request |
| The model's reply | Hidden reasoning ("thinking") tokens, billed as output |
| Documents and records you attach | Tool definitions an agent carries on every call |
| Earlier turns in the conversation | Tool results, such as a full CRM record returned by a search |

## Why tokens drive cost for a commercial team

Every API provider prices per million tokens, input and output separately. Anthropic's published prices in November 2026 illustrate the shape. Claude Sonnet 5.5 is $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output. Claude Opus 5.5 is $4 and $20. Claude Haiku 5.5 is $0.10 and $0.50 for prompts up to 100,000 tokens. The ratio matters more than the level: writing costs several times more than reading.

A worked example, illustrative. A meeting-brief assistant reads 20,000 tokens of CRM notes and email, then writes a 1,000-token brief on Sonnet 5.5. Input costs $0.04 and output $0.01, so about $0.05 per brief. Fifty briefs a working day for 22 days is 1,100 briefs, or about $55 a month.

Agents change the arithmetic. An agent that takes ten steps, each re-reading the same 20,000 tokens of context, consumes 200,000 input tokens for one task. On the same prices that is $0.40 before it writes anything. Token use grows with the number of steps, not just the size of the answer. This is why per-seat chat plans and usage-based API bills can differ by an order of magnitude for similar work.

Prices are also falling fast. Stanford's 2025 AI Index found that querying a model at GPT-3.5's level dropped from $20 to $0.07 per million tokens in about 18 months. A budget built on today's per-token price will be wrong within a year, usually in the buyer's favour, while volume tends to rise.

## How to estimate and control token cost

| Lever | What it does | Typical effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batch processing | Runs non-urgent jobs asynchronously | Anthropic lists a 50% discount on input and output |
| Prompt caching | Reuses a fixed prefix, such as instructions or a policy document | Cache hits billed at 0.025x to 0.1x the input price, depending on the Anthropic model |
| Smaller model for simple steps | Routes classification or extraction to a cheaper model | Haiku 5.5 input is one-twentieth of Sonnet 5.5's |
| Trimmed context | Sends the relevant records, not the whole account history | Cuts input tokens on every step |
| Shorter outputs | Asks for structured fields rather than prose | Cuts the most expensive token type |

Start by measuring. Log input and output tokens per task for two weeks, not per user. Then set a cost-per-task figure next to the value of the task: a qualified meeting, a completed renewal brief, an answered questionnaire. A $0.05 brief that saves a seller 20 minutes needs no optimisation. An agent loop that costs $2 per attempt and succeeds half the time does.

## lowob takeaways

- **Tokens are the billing unit.** Roughly three-quarters of an English word, more for other languages.
- **Output costs more than input.** Five times more on Anthropic's main models; ask for less prose.
- **Agents multiply tokens.** Each step re-reads context, so cost scales with steps.
- **Measure cost per task.** Compare it with the value of the task, not with the seat price.

## Common questions

### How many words is 1,000 tokens?

In English, about 750 words, using OpenAI's rule of thumb that 100 tokens is roughly 75 words. Other languages and technical text usually produce more tokens per word.

### Why are output tokens more expensive than input tokens?

Providers set output prices higher and rarely publish the full reasoning. The ratio is what matters for budgeting: on Anthropic's main models in November 2026, output was five times the input price.

### Do AI chat subscriptions charge by token?

Seat-based plans usually charge a flat fee with usage limits. API access and many agent products charge per token, so heavy or automated use is billed by volume.

### How can I reduce AI token costs?

Send only the relevant context, cache fixed instructions, batch non-urgent jobs, use a smaller model for simple steps and ask for short, structured outputs.

## Sources and notes

- [OpenAI, What are tokens and how to count them](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/4936856-what-are-tokens-and-how-to-count-them), accessed November 2026. Vendor help article; ratios are approximate.
- [Anthropic, Pricing (Claude API documentation)](https://platform.claude.com/en/docs/about-claude/pricing), accessed November 2026. Vendor list prices; subject to change.
- [Anthropic, Understanding the context window](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/context-windows), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation on what counts toward token use.
- [Stanford HAI, AI Index 2025: State of AI in 10 Charts](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-index-2025-state-of-ai-in-10-charts), April 2025. Independent academic index; based on list prices.
- The worked example and cost-per-task method are **lowob**'s illustration, using the list prices above.

## Related research

- [Seats, Usage or Outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)
- [What Is Usage-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/)
- [Which AI Assistant, Which Seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/)
- [The Enterprise AI and Commercial System Glossary](https://lowob.com/research/enterprise-ai-glossary/)
- [The Trade Must Clear on the Spot](https://lowob.com/research/the-trade-must-clear-on-the-spot/)

## Next move

Pick one AI task your team runs daily and log its input and output tokens for a week. Divide the cost by the number of useful results to get a cost per task.

# KOL Campaigns Need More Than Impression Screenshots

Source: https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Impression screenshots show that content was delivered, not that anyone understood or used the product. Define the behaviour you are buying, instrument the path from click to wallet action before paying, judge creators on distribution, activation, durability and economics, and make the second payment conditional on evidence. Disclosure is part of the brief: US, UK and EU rules all treat a paid crypto post as advertising.

An impression screenshot proves a post was delivered. It does not prove anyone understood the product, connected a wallet or came back. Buy a defined behaviour, not a follower count; instrument the path from click to on-chain action before the campaign starts; judge each creator on distribution, activation, durability and economics; and make the second payment conditional on evidence. Disclosure belongs in the same brief: the FTC, the SEC, the UK FCA and MiCA all treat a paid crypto post as advertising.

Reach is visible. Commercial impact is usually harder to prove. That asymmetry is why so many creator reports in crypto are folders of impression screenshots and launch-day charts. The useful question is narrower: did this creator bring a relevant audience to a specific action, and did that behaviour persist after the campaign ended? This is as much a buying problem as a tracking problem. A team can commission a campaign before defining whom it needs to reach, what the audience should do, or how the result will be measured. This piece is part of our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/), because a KOL campaign that brings the wrong people in makes the community's job harder.

## KOL is the default. That does not make it effective

Paid creator promotion is one of the most common acquisition formats in crypto, and spend tends to cluster around launches and major events rather than recurring budgets. That concentrates the whole explanation of a product into one window, and judges it on one spike. A widely adopted channel can still be poorly measured.

This is not an argument against KOL partnerships. Focused technical creators, educators and researchers can explain a product better than the team can, to an audience that trusts them. Our piece on the difference between [influencers, creators, KOLs and ambassadors](https://lowob.com/research/influencer-creator-kol-ambassador/) sets out the formats. The argument is against judging success by a screenshot.

## Define the job before choosing the voice

Set the intended outcome first. A staking product might need users to connect a wallet and delegate. An infrastructure team might need credible developers to try an integration. A tokenised-asset provider might need informed conversations with a small set of decision makers. Those are different jobs. Each needs a different audience, a different landing page and a different measure.

Creator selection follows the job. Check who actually engages with the creator, the questions their audience asks, whether the creator understands the product well enough to explain it, and any sponsorship conflicts with competing projects. A focused technical creator may deliver fewer views and more valuable actions than a larger generalist account.

## Connect the click to the action

The main measurement gap is between a click and later wallet behaviour. Standard web analytics record visits but do not automatically link them to on-chain actions. Consider a user who clicks a creator's link, leaves, returns two days later on another device, connects a wallet and deposits. Linking that deposit to the creator requires campaign context to survive the gap, and it often does not: device changes, cleared browser data and privacy settings all break the chain.

So plan measurement before launch. Give each creator a unique link, preserve campaign context through wallet connection where users consent to it, and track the first meaningful action and later behaviour. Our explainer on [lead source attribution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) covers the general mechanics; the crypto-specific step is carrying the source across the wallet connection.

Then evaluate in four stages.

| Check | What it measures | The question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Distribution | Qualified views, referral visits, audience relevance | Did the message reach people who might use the product? |
| Activation | Attributed wallet connections, first deposits, swaps or other product actions | Did a referral become meaningful product use? |
| Durability | 7-day and 30-day cohorts, repeat actions, retained value | Did activity continue after the campaign ended? |
| Economics | Full channel spend divided by verified activated users, compared with alternatives | Is there evidence to invest in this creator again? |

Be honest about what the numbers are. A wallet is not necessarily a person: academic analysis of airdrops documents a single farmer operating over 20,000 accounts on one network. A connection is not necessarily a customer. Attribution is often partial, so state which outcomes are observed, which are inferred and which are unknown. A useful KOL report should make it possible to cut, renew or redesign the next campaign. If it only proves content was delivered, it is a fulfilment report.

Illustrative example: two creators, one budget

Decision
:   Renew Creator B for a second, smaller test and pause Creator A, despite A's larger reach.

Reason and owner
:   Creator A drove 400 wallet connections, of which 12% completed a first transaction and 18% were active at 30 days. Creator B drove 150 connections, of which 31% completed a first transaction and 34% were active at 30 days. First transactions were roughly equal, around 48 and 46, but B's users stayed. Owned by the growth lead.

What changed
:   Before the renewal, the team checked deposit size, repeat use and the full cost of each creator, not only the fee.

Illustrative: adapted from an illustrative comparison published by an on-chain analytics vendor; not a client case study or a reported campaign result.

## Price the full cost of acquisition

Creator fees are only part of the cost. Include briefing, strategy, editing, management, event support, incentives, data tooling and moderation of the traffic that arrives. Compare KOLs with other channels on the same basis: partnerships, founder-led education, organic research content, affiliates and paid media.

Cost per activated wallet is more useful than cost per click, but only when paired with retention, wallet quality and downstream value. Otherwise a campaign optimised for activation can simply purchase the cheapest one-time action. The discipline is the same as any [campaign test that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/): decide in advance what result would justify more spend, and what would end it. Our piece on [attribution vs incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the harder question of whether the creator caused the action or only touched it.

> Buy a defined behaviour, not a creator's follower count, and make the second payment conditional on evidence.

## Disclosure is part of the brief

A paid creator post about a token is advertising in every major jurisdiction, and the brief should say so before the post is written.

| Jurisdiction | Rule | What it means for a KOL brief |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US, FTC | Endorsement Guides, 16 CFR 255.5 | A material connection the audience would not expect must be disclosed "clearly and conspicuously": difficult to miss and easily understood |
| US, SEC | Anti-touting provision | Where the token is a security, promoters must disclose the nature, source and amount of compensation; the SEC's 2022 case over an undisclosed $250,000 post ended in a $1.26 million settlement |
| UK, FCA | FG24/1 and the cryptoasset promotions regime | Influencers can be caught without direct payment if they have a commercial interest; firms remain responsible for promotions they cause to be made; breach can be a criminal offence |
| EU, MiCA | Article 7 | Marketing communications must be clearly identifiable as such, fair, clear and not misleading, and consistent with the white paper |

The US position on which tokens are securities shifted in 2026, with the SEC's March interpretation placing many native network tokens outside securities law. The FTC's endorsement duty does not depend on that question. It applies to any paid endorsement. This is not legal advice; route each brief through counsel for the markets the creator reaches.

Compare KOL deals with accountable alternatives too. Referral, affiliate or partner arrangements can tie payment to verified value, provided they guard against gaming and do not treat attributed wallets as unique customers. Our piece on [creator partnerships outside crypto](https://lowob.com/research/creator-partnerships-fintech-ai/) shows how fintech and AI firms structure them.

## lowob takeaways

- **Buy a defined behaviour.** Different goals need different creators, landing pages and measures.
- **Instrument before paying.** Without attribution through the wallet connection, you get a traffic report.
- **Judge on four stages.** Distribution, activation, durability and economics, with observed and inferred outcomes labelled.
- **Disclose by default.** Treat every paid post as an advertisement under FTC, FCA and MiCA rules.

## Common questions

### How do you measure a KOL campaign in crypto?

Track each creator through four stages: qualified distribution, attributed wallet activation, 7-day and 30-day retention, and full cost per verified activated user compared with other channels. Use unique links and carry campaign context through the wallet connection.

### What is a good cost per wallet for a crypto KOL campaign?

There is no reliable universal benchmark. Cost per activated wallet only means something alongside retention, wallet quality and deposit or usage value, and wallets are not unique people, so compare creators and channels on the same full-cost basis.

### Do crypto influencers have to disclose paid posts?

Yes in practice. The FTC requires clear and conspicuous disclosure of material connections, the SEC requires disclosure of compensation for promoting crypto asset securities, the UK FCA regulates crypto promotions, and MiCA requires marketing to be identifiable as such.

### Should KOL deals be paid upfront?

Test with a small first payment tied to delivery, and make renewals or larger payments conditional on activation and retention evidence. Where conversions can be verified, referral or affiliate terms can align payment with value.

## Sources and notes

- [eCFR, 16 CFR Part 255, Guides concerning the use of endorsements and testimonials in advertising](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255). Current US regulation text; guides, not a statute.
- [US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC charges Kim Kardashian for unlawfully touting crypto security](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2022-183), 3 October 2022. Settled without admitting or denying findings.
- [Financial Conduct Authority, FG24/1 Financial promotions on social media](https://www.fca.org.uk/publication/finalised-guidance/fg24-1.pdf), March 2024. UK regulator guidance.
- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 7, marketing communications](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-7-marketing-communications). EU regulation text.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: giving money away is harder than it seems](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), arXiv, revised 2025. Academic study; cited for evidence on multi-account farming.
- [Sullivan & Cromwell, SEC clarifies application of securities laws to crypto assets](https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/March/SEC-Clarifies-Application-Securities-Laws-Crypto-Assets), 19 March 2026. Law-firm reading of the SEC and CFTC interpretation; not legal advice.
- The four-stage table and the creator example are **lowob**'s methodology and illustration, not reported campaign results.

- [Campaign Testing That Reaches a Decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/)

Before approving another creator package, write down the behaviour it should produce, the link and wallet attribution that will record it, and the 30-day result that would justify a second payment. Add the disclosure wording to the brief.

# What AI Agents Can Do: A Task Directory for Commercial Teams

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A reference directory of sixty commercial tasks across sales, marketing, partners, customer success and commercial operations. Each task is rated on lowob's autonomy scale, with today's reliability, the main risk and the guardrail required, and linked to the research behind it.

This directory rates sixty commercial tasks by how far an AI agent can take them today. Each row gives the highest sensible autonomy level on **lowob**'s five-step scale, a plain reliability rating, the main risk, and the control that has to be in place. Use it to choose first agents, to challenge vendor claims, and to decide where a person must stay in the loop. Ratings reflect our working view for mid-size commercial teams in late 2026 and will move as capability improves.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

## How to read the directory

The directory is the reference table. The [Agents at Work](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/) series walks it one function at a time, with a start-here sequence for each: [sales](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/), [marketing](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-marketing-what-they-can-do-now/), [commercial operations](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-commercial-operations/), [partners and distribution](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-partners-and-distribution/) and [customer success](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-customer-success-and-account-management/). [What AI Agents Still Cannot Do](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-still-cannot-do/) covers the limits across all sixty tasks.

**Autonomy level** is the highest level we would set for a mid-size firm today: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. See [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/) for the full scale.

**Reliability today** is our rating of how often current tools complete the task to a standard a reviewer would accept without major edits: High, Medium or Low. It reflects the evidence that agents handle checkable, internal work far better than open-ended or client-facing work. METR's measurements show success rates falling sharply as tasks lengthen, and Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey found the time sellers expect agents to save sits in research and drafting.

**Main risk** is what goes wrong when the task fails. **Control** is the minimum guardrail. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications is the reference for the security controls: limit tool scope and permissions, require approval for high-risk actions, and log every tool call.

## Sales

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research an account before a meeting | 1 Draft | High | Stale or wrong facts in the brief | Sources attached; current-or-superseded marking |
| Summarise a sales call and extract next steps | 3 Act and report | High | Missed commitment or misheard figure | Recording consent; owner reviews within 48 hours |
| Draft a follow-up email after a meeting | 1 Draft | High | Wrong figure or tone sent to a client | Queue to account owner; nothing sends |
| Update deal stage from email and calendar evidence | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Forecast distorted by wrong stage | Suggested change accepted by owner |
| Flag stale opportunities | 3 Act and report | High | Noise if definitions are loose | Agreed stale rule (for example 30 days) |
| Tag lead source from a fixed list | 3 Act and report | High | Misattributed channel spend | Fixed list; weekly spot-check |
| Qualify an inbound lead | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Good leads dropped | Owner approves drops; record the reason |
| Prioritise accounts for the quarter | 1 Draft | Medium | Bias toward accounts with more data | Leadership decides; record the reasoning |
| Draft a proposal from approved templates | 1 Draft | Medium | Unapproved claims or terms | Template library; proposal approver |
| Price a proposal | 1 Draft | Low | Margin loss; inconsistent pricing | Pricing rules; finance approval for exceptions |
| Approve a discount | 0 Answer | Low | Commits money without accountability | Human decision with recorded reason |
| Write outbound sequences | 1 Draft | Medium | Spam, brand damage, compliance breach | Approval per sequence; volume caps |
| Send outbound sequences autonomously | 2 Act with approval | Low | Reputational and deliverability damage | Not a first agent; gate and caps required |
| Prepare a win-loss summary | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong reason recorded as fact | Interview evidence; owner sign-off |
| Draft a mutual action plan | 1 Draft | Medium | Commitments the client never agreed | Shared with the client only after review |
| Answer a security questionnaire | 1 Draft | Medium | Inaccurate security claims | Approved answer library; security owner review |
| Forecast the quarter | 1 Draft | Medium | False confidence | Human forecast call; agent shows evidence |

## Marketing

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monitor competitors and market news | 3 Act and report | High | Missing a material change | Named sources; weekly human read |
| Turn an interview into draft posts | 1 Draft | High | Claims the company cannot support | Claims checked by a subject owner |
| Publish social posts | 1 Draft | Medium | Public error; regulatory breach in finance or crypto | Nothing publishes without a person |
| Draft campaign variants for testing | 1 Draft | High | Off-brand or unapproved claims | Brand and claims rules in context |
| Reallocate campaign budget | 1 Draft | Low | Spend moved on weak evidence | Budget holder approves; record expected outcome |
| Build audience segments from CRM data | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Consent or privacy breach | Consent fields respected; privacy review |
| Write SEO and answer-engine content briefs | 1 Draft | High | Thin or duplicative content | Editorial owner; check existing pages first |
| Draft long-form research | 1 Draft | Medium | Invented sources or statistics | Every figure opened and cited by a person |
| Score leads | 3 Act and report | Medium | Scores that encode old bias | Quarterly calibration against outcomes |
| Produce a monthly marketing report | 3 Act and report | High | Activity reported as impact | Report against agreed outcome measures |
| Personalise website content | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Wrong message to the wrong audience | Approved variants only |
| Reply to community questions | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong or market-moving statements | Named communications owner approves |
| Translate and localise approved content | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Mistranslated claims in regulated markets | Native reviewer for regulated content |

## Partners and distribution

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research and rank potential partners | 1 Draft | Medium | Partners chosen on surface signals | Human selection; record the reasoning |
| Draft partner outreach | 1 Draft | High | Overpromising terms | Approved terms only |
| Track referrals and attribute partner-sourced deals | 3 Act and report | Medium | Disputes over credit | Agreed attribution rules |
| Prepare partner quarterly reviews | 1 Draft | High | Missing context from the relationship | Partner manager edits |
| Monitor marketplace listings and reviews | 3 Act and report | High | Missed negative signal | Weekly human read |
| Respond to marketplace leads | 1 Draft | Medium | Slow or wrong first response | Queue with response-time alert |
| Draft co-marketing content | 1 Draft | High | Partner brand or claims breach | Both parties approve |
| Detect channel conflict on a deal | 3 Act and report | Medium | Two partners claim the same deal | Rules of engagement written down |
| Prepare partner onboarding and enablement packs | 1 Draft | High | Inconsistent messaging across partners | Approved enablement kit as the only source |

## Customer success and account management

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Prepare a renewal brief from usage and delivery data | 1 Draft | High | Missing a known issue | Account owner review |
| Flag at-risk accounts | 3 Act and report | Medium | False alarms or missed churn | Health score calibrated against outcomes |
| Draft a renewal or expansion proposal | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong pricing or terms | Proposal approver |
| Summarise support tickets for an account | 3 Act and report | High | Misread sentiment | Linked to source tickets |
| Answer routine customer questions | 2 Act with approval | Medium | Wrong answer stated as fact | Approved knowledge base; escalation path |
| Resolve support cases end to end | 3 Act and report | Medium | Incorrect resolution | Outcome-priced tools allow measurement; sampling |
| Remind advisers of client moments (clienteling) | 3 Act and report | High | Relationship feels automated | Adviser writes every client message |
| Schedule quarterly business reviews | 3 Act and report | High | Clashes and missed stakeholders | Calendar rules |
| Draft a quarterly business review deck | 1 Draft | High | Stale or cherry-picked metrics | Figures pulled from live sources and checked |

## Commercial operations

| Task | Autonomy | Reliability today | Main risk | Control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| De-duplicate and clean CRM records | 3 Act and report | High | Wrong merge of distinct accounts | Merge rules; reversible changes; nightly report |
| Enrich records with third-party data | 3 Act and report | Medium | Inaccurate or non-consented data | Approved sources; privacy rules |
| Draft quotes from a price book | 1 Draft | Medium | Wrong price becomes a binding offer | Quote reviewer; price book marked current |
| Check contract terms against standard | 1 Draft | Medium | Missed non-standard clause | Legal owner reviews flagged items |
| Prepare the weekly pipeline review pack | 3 Act and report | High | Misleading summary | Links to underlying records |
| Reconcile delivery against what was sold | 3 Act and report | High | Under-delivery missed | Exceptions routed to account owner |
| Record decisions with reasons | 1 Draft | Medium | Reasons invented after the fact | Captured at the moment of approval |
| Write outcomes back to decisions | 3 Act and report | Medium | Wrong outcome linked | Owner confirms at check date |
| Maintain shared definitions | 0 Answer | Low | Definitions drift silently | Named owner per definition |
| Grant or change system access | 0 Answer | Low | Excessive agency; data exposure | Never delegated to an agent |
| Run the commission calculation | 3 Act and report | Medium | Disputes and trust loss | Finance review before payout |
| Monitor agent activity and cost | 3 Act and report | High | Runaway spend or loops | Spend caps; kill switch |

> If the control in the last column is not in place, drop the task one autonomy level.

## What the pattern shows

Three things make a task safe to delegate further: it is internal, it is checkable within minutes, and it is reversible. Research, summaries, tagging and record hygiene meet all three, which is why they cluster at level 3 and at High reliability. Three things hold a task back: it reaches a client or the public, it commits money or terms, or it reads untrusted content while holding permissions. Outbound, pricing, discounts, public posts and access changes all fall here.

The evidence on adoption supports this pattern. Zapier's 2026 survey of enterprise leaders found most production agents still need a person to finish the job, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic projects to be cancelled by 2027, citing costs, unclear value and weak risk controls. Our earlier piece [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/) sets out how to choose from the left-hand side of this directory first.

Illustrative example: using the directory to scope a pilot

Decision
:   Pilot three tasks rated High reliability (account research, call summaries, stale-deal flags) and decline an autonomous outbound pilot rated Low.

Reason and owner
:   The three tasks are internal, checkable and reversible; outbound reaches prospects directly. Owned by the head of revenue operations.

What changed
:   The pilot reports weekly against preparation time and stale-deal counts; outbound is revisited after the approval gate has three months of logs.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start on the left of the table.** Internal, checkable, reversible tasks earn trust first.
- **Read the control column first.** No control, one level lower.
- **Client-facing and money-committing tasks stay at level 2 or below.** Until there is sustained evidence.
- **Re-rate quarterly.** Capability is moving faster than any static rating.

Gateway card

### Before you assign a task to an agent

- Task found in this directory, or rated the same way
- Autonomy level set at or below the directory level
- The control in the last column in place
- A named owner and a weekly spot-check

## Common questions

### What can AI agents do for a sales team today?

Reliably: account research, call summaries, follow-up drafts, CRM hygiene, stale-deal flags and lead-source tagging. With a person approving: stage updates, qualification and proposal drafts. Not yet wisely: autonomous outbound, pricing and discount approval.

### Which marketing tasks can AI agents automate?

Monitoring, drafting campaign variants and content briefs, monthly reporting and lead scoring with calibration. Publishing and budget moves should stay with a person.

### What should an AI agent never do without approval?

Send anything to a client or the public, commit money or terms, change system access, or act on untrusted inbound content with broad permissions.

### How often should these ratings change?

Review them quarterly. Agent capability on long tasks has been improving rapidly, but reliability on client-facing work improves more slowly than headline benchmarks suggest.

# What Is a Deal Desk?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A deal desk reviews deals that fall outside standard pricing or terms, and decides quickly who must approve them. Its value rests on a simple fact: small price leaks have a large effect on profit. This explainer covers what a deal desk does, how it has evolved from a compliance checkpoint, and how a 20-to-500-person firm can set one up with an approval matrix and a written record of each exception.

A deal desk is a cross-functional team, or in a smaller firm a named role, that reviews deals falling outside standard pricing, discount or contract terms. It decides what can be approved, by whom and how fast. A good deal desk protects margin without becoming a queue: most deals pass straight through, and exceptions get a fast, recorded decision.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a deal desk means

Most deals should not need one. Standard price, standard terms and a standard contract can go straight from seller to signature. The deal desk handles the rest: discounts above a threshold, multi-year ramps, unusual payment terms, custom legal clauses, bundles that are not on the price list, and responses to procurement forms.

Salesforce's description lists the typical work: checking custom quotes against pricing guidelines, assessing discount thresholds and the revenue impact of multi-year ramp deals, reviewing contract terms with legal input, and handling RFPs and vendor forms. Its members usually come from sales operations, finance and legal, and sometimes marketing.

| A deal desk is | A deal desk is not |
| --- | --- |
| A fast route for exceptions | A review step for every deal |
| The owner of the approval matrix | The owner of pricing strategy |
| A record of why exceptions were granted | A place where deals wait without a deadline |
| A source of pattern data for pricing | A substitute for seller judgement on standard deals |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The case for a deal desk is about the size of small leaks. Marn and Rosiello's Harvard Business Review article, based on the average economics of 2,463 companies, found that a 1% improvement in price raised operating profit by 11.1%. A 1% improvement in volume raised it by only 3.3%. The same article reported average declines from invoice price to pocket price of 16.7% to 28.9% across the companies it profiled, driven by transaction-specific items such as prompt-payment discounts and volume bonuses.

Forrester's Steve Silver described how deal desks have changed. They "were originally intended to provide a process for ensuring pricing compliance", which often missed strategic value. They have since moved towards "helping sales improve strategic deal positioning, win rates and deal velocity". The third level, deal pursuit, brings the desk into structuring large deals before the proposal goes out.

Speed is the other half. Everstage's 2026 survey of 195 VP-level revenue leaders found 47% of teams took three or more days to clear a pricing exception, and 40% still built quotes and set pricing by hand. The survey is vendor-run and self-reported, but the pattern is familiar: if approval is slow, sellers either wait or work around it.

In **lowob**'s model, an approved exception is a commercial decision. It should carry its reason, the approver, and the expected outcome, such as the renewal price after a first-year discount. That record is what lets the firm see, a year later, whether its exceptions paid back.

## How to set one up at 20 to 500 people

A firm this size rarely needs a dedicated team. It needs an owner, a matrix and a deadline.

1. **Name the owner.** Often a revenue operations lead or a finance partner. One person runs the process and keeps the record.
2. **Write the approval matrix.** Set discount bands and term changes, with an approver and a response time for each.
3. **Set a default.** If the approver does not respond within the time limit, the request escalates, rather than sitting in a queue.
4. **Record every exception.** Capture discount, term, reason, approver and expected outcome in the CRM or quoting tool.
5. **Review quarterly.** Look at which exceptions recur. A discount granted to most deals is a pricing problem, not an exception.

An illustrative approval matrix:

| Request | Approver | Response time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Discount up to 10% | Seller, within policy | Immediate |
| Discount 10% to 20% | Sales manager | Same day |
| Discount above 20%, or multi-year ramp | Deal desk owner and finance | 1 business day |
| Non-standard legal terms | Legal | 2 business days |
| Payment terms beyond standard | Finance | 1 business day |

AI assistants are starting to draft quotes and check them against policy. On **lowob**'s autonomy dial, that is level 1 (draft) or level 2 (act with approval). The assistant can flag which band a quote falls into and route it. The approval itself stays with a person, and nothing goes to the customer until that person has signed off.

## lowob takeaways

- **Most deals should pass straight through.** A deal desk exists for exceptions, not for every quote.
- **Price leaks are expensive.** A 1% price change moved operating profit by about 11% in the HBR analysis.
- **Speed is part of the job.** An approval matrix with response times keeps exceptions from stalling deals.
- **Record the reason.** Each exception is a decision whose outcome can be checked at renewal.

## Common questions

### What does a deal desk do?

It reviews and approves deals outside standard pricing, discount or contract terms, routes them to the right approver, and keeps a record of each exception.

### Who sits on a deal desk?

Usually people from sales operations, finance and legal. In a smaller firm, one revenue operations or finance lead often runs it with named approvers.

### When does a company need a deal desk?

When non-standard deals are common enough that approvals are slow, inconsistent or untracked. A rising average discount is an early sign.

### What is a deal desk approval matrix?

A table that sets which discount levels and term changes need which approver, and how quickly each approver must respond.

## Sources and notes

- [Salesforce, What Is a Deal Desk?](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/sales/deal-desk/), undated. Vendor guide; source of the definition and typical scope.
- [Forrester, Defining Deal Management And Review Levels](https://www.forrester.com/report/defining-deal-management-and-review-levels-/RES172218), September 2018, by Steve Silver. Analyst report; summary only is public.
- [Michael V. Marn and Robert L. Rosiello, Managing Price, Gaining Profit, Harvard Business Review](https://pages.charlotte.edu/wp-content/uploads/sites/868/2014/12/ManagingPrice.pdf), September to October 1992. Course copy of the article; figures are from Compustat averages of the time.
- [Everstage, Approval Queue Report: Pricing Exception Data](https://www.everstage.com/approval-queue-report), 2026. Vendor-run survey of 195 VP-level revenue leaders; self-reported.

Export last quarter's closed-won deals with list price and final price. Group the discounts into bands, and you have the first draft of your approval matrix and a measure of how much margin went out without a recorded reason.

# What Is Outcome Write-Back?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Outcome write-back is the step that records what happened after a decision against the decision itself, in the system the next decision will read. It is the learning stage of the enterprise brain. The plumbing to move data back into a CRM already exists; what is usually missing is a decision to attach the outcome to.

Outcome write-back is the step where what actually happened after a decision is recorded against that decision, in the system the next decision will read from. It is the learning stage of the enterprise brain. Without it, agents and people see what was decided but never whether it worked, so the same mistakes repeat with more confidence each time.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What outcome write-back means

Most AI deployments run in one direction. Context goes in, an answer or a draft comes out, and the system forgets. Outcome write-back adds the return path. When a decision reaches its check date, the result is recorded on the decision record, with the evidence and a short note on whether the expected outcome was met.

The mechanics are not new. Data teams have used "reverse ETL" for years. Hightouch defines it as syncing data directly from a data warehouse into operational tools, and gives the example of pushing a lead score into Salesforce. That moves numbers back into the CRM. It does not say which decision the number grades. Write-back, in our sense, needs three things the sync does not provide: a decision with an expected outcome, a check date, and an owner who confirms the result.

|  | Data sync (reverse ETL) | Outcome write-back |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What moves | Fields and scores | A result plus a verdict on the expectation |
| Attached to | A record, such as a contact or account | A specific decision and its reason |
| Triggered by | A schedule | The decision's check date |
| Who confirms | Nobody; it is automatic | The decision owner or a named observer |
| What it enables | Current data in the CRM | Precedent an agent can learn from |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Agents now act on records automatically, which makes stale or ungraded records costly. In Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketing professionals, nearly 78% of C-suite respondents said they had acted on an AI recommendation they later suspected was wrong because of bad underlying data. Two in three organisations had increased the marketing decisions delegated to autonomous agents in the past year. Validity sells data-quality software, so this is vendor research, but the direction is clear: more decisions are being made by systems that never learn whether the last one worked.

Regulators and standards bodies point the same way. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework asks that post-deployment monitoring plans are implemented, including mechanisms for capturing and evaluating input from users, and that measurable activities for continual improvement are built into system updates. For a regulated firm, a written-back outcome is part of the evidence chain: what was decided, by whom, on what basis, and what followed.

Write-back also protects against a quieter failure. Approval rates on agent drafts look healthy when reviewers are tired as well as when the drafts are good. Only the outcome, such as a reply received or a deal advanced, tells the two apart.

## Where to start

Pick decisions whose outcomes arrive within a quarter and already land in a system you own.

| Decision | Outcome to write back | Where it comes from | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discount approved | Won or lost; margin realised | CRM and invoice | At close |
| Account prioritised for the quarter | Pipeline created | CRM | Quarter end |
| Agent follow-up draft approved | Reply received; edits made | Email and approval log | After 14 days |
| Deal marked lost | Confirmed loss reason; any return | CRM and call notes | 90 days later |
| Pricing exception granted | Renewal at or above prior value | Billing | At renewal |

Three rules keep it working. Put the check date in the owner's calendar, not only in the record. Record the outcome as a new entry or a status change, so the original reason stays visible; changing the record in place destroys the comparison that makes it useful. Report the share of decisions reviewed on time, because a loop that is never closed looks identical to one that is.

## lowob takeaways

- **No record, no write-back.** An outcome needs a decision and an expectation to grade.
- **Timing is the failure point.** Calendar the check date when the decision is made.
- **Add, do not overwrite.** The original reason and the result belong side by side.
- **Measure the loop itself.** Track the share of decisions reviewed on time.

## Common questions

### What does write-back mean in AI?

Recording the result of an AI-assisted decision or action back into the system that future decisions read from, so the next answer reflects what actually happened.

### Is outcome write-back the same as reverse ETL?

No. Reverse ETL syncs data from a warehouse into tools such as a CRM. Outcome write-back attaches a result to a specific decision and records whether the expected outcome was met.

### How do AI agents learn from outcomes without retraining?

By reading past decisions and their recorded outcomes as context. An agent shown three comparable cases, including one that went badly, can reason from precedent without any change to the model.

### What should a commercial team write back first?

Outcomes that arrive within a quarter: discount approvals graded at close, account priorities graded at quarter end, and agent drafts graded by replies.

## Sources and notes

- [Ankura, Implementing the NIST AI Risk Management Framework: Manage](https://ankura.com/insights/implementing-the-nist-artificial-intelligence-risk-management-framework-manage), quoting NIST AI 100-1 subcategories MANAGE 4.1 and 4.2. Secondary summary of a primary standard.
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2026](https://www.validity.com/press-releases/validity-releases-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2026-report-revealing-marketers-trust-in-their-data-hasnt-caught-up-with-their-ai-goals/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey.
- [Hightouch, What is reverse ETL?](https://hightouch.com/blog/reverse-etl). Vendor explainer.
- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), March 2026, on superseding rather than editing records.

## Related research

- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/)
- [A Loop With Good Context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/)

## Next move

Find the five largest discounts approved last quarter and record, against each, whether the deal closed and at what margin. That table is your first written-back outcome set.

# Campaign Testing That Reaches a Decision

Source: https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A campaign test is only worth running if its result changes what the firm does next. At B2B volumes most tests are too small to detect the effects teams hope for: detecting a lift from 3% to 3.6% conversion needs roughly 14,000 visitors per arm. This piece sets out the arithmetic, how to choose a metric close enough to revenue to matter and far enough upstream to measure, which test designs survive low volume, and a pre-written decision card that stops tests ending in "promising".

A campaign test reaches a decision when three things are fixed before it starts: the metric, the smallest effect worth acting on, and what the firm will do for each possible result. Most B2B tests skip all three and are too small to detect anything. Detecting a lift in landing page conversion from 3% to 3.6% needs about 14,000 visitors in each arm; Forrester finds fewer than 1% of leads become closed deals, so testing on revenue directly is rarely possible. The workable approach is to test bigger changes on upstream metrics, use concurrent holdouts rather than before-and-after comparisons, and record every result, including the null ones.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 8 set a cost ceiling for every demand channel, and Part 9 gave every piece of content a job. Both create questions a test could answer: does this channel beat its ceiling, does this piece move its stage. This part covers how to run those tests so they end in a decision.

Our earlier piece [Tests that close questions](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/) made the core argument for early-stage firms choosing between channels: write a threshold, run two or three options in parallel, fund the winner. This part assumes that discipline and adds what it leaves out: the arithmetic of sample size, the choice of metric, and what to do when the numbers are too small for any test at all.

## Why most tests end in "promising"

The usual campaign test runs for a few weeks, compares two versions, shows one ahead, and is reported as promising. Nothing is decided because nothing was set in advance. There was no agreed metric, no agreed size of effect that would justify a change, and no agreed action for a win, a loss or a tie.

This is a decision problem before it is a statistics problem. McKinsey's survey of 1,228 executives found only 20% said their organisations excel at decision making, and 61% said most of the time they spent on decisions was used ineffectively. A test without a pre-written decision adds to that time. It produces a number, a meeting about the number and, usually, a second test.

## The arithmetic of B2B volumes

The second reason tests fail is that they are too small. The number of observations needed to detect a difference depends on the baseline rate and the size of the difference. Using the standard approximation for comparing two rates, at a 5% significance level and 80% power, the requirements look like this.

| What is being tested | Baseline | Rate worth detecting | Needed in each arm |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Landing page conversion, modest lift | 3% | 3.6% (20% relative) | about 13,900 |
| Landing page conversion, large lift | 3% | 4.5% (50% relative) | about 2,500 |
| Outbound reply rate | 2% | 3% | about 3,800 |
| Outbound reply rate, higher base | 5% | 7.5% | about 1,500 |
| Meeting to qualified opportunity | 20% | 25% | about 1,100 |
| Meeting to qualified opportunity, large lift | 20% | 30% | about 290 |

The figures are **lowob**'s calculation and assume a simple random split. They show two things. Small improvements on low base rates need traffic most B2B firms do not have. And tests further down the funnel, where rates are higher, need fewer observations but each observation is much more expensive to produce: 290 meetings per arm is a quarter's work for many teams.

Revenue is out of reach for most tests. Forrester's research finds fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals. A test that waits for closed revenue would need thousands of leads per arm and a full sales cycle, by which time the market has moved.

> If the test is too small to detect the effect you hope for, the result will be noise, and you will act on it anyway.

## Choosing the metric

The metric should be the closest step to revenue that the test can measure in its time window, and sales should agree that a movement in it matters. In practice that is usually qualified opportunities, accepted meetings, or progression from one defined stage to the next, using the [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) the firm already has.

Three traps are common.

**The platform's own number.** Ad platforms report conversions using their own models. Google, for example, retired first-click, linear, time-decay and position-based attribution in 2023 and made data-driven attribution the default in Google Ads and Analytics. A data-driven attribution figure is a model's allocation of credit, not the result of a controlled comparison. Our piece on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the difference.

**Winning against the wrong alternative.** Challenger's research on 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found around half of lost deals ended in no decision rather than a loss to a competitor. A test that measures share of wins against competitors can miss the effect that matters most, which is whether the buyer decided at all.

**The cheap upstream proxy.** Click-through rate is easy to move and weakly connected to revenue. A subject line that doubles opens and halves replies has lost.

## Designs that survive low volume

The design matters as much as the size. Before-and-after comparisons are the most common and the least reliable, because the baseline moves on its own. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies, recorded win rates 18% lower than in 2022 and found 44% of deals delayed or pushed back. A campaign launched into that environment will look worse than last year whatever it does. A concurrent comparison, where the test and control run at the same time, removes most of that drift.

Non-randomised methods can mislead even at very large volumes. Gordon, Zettelmeyer and colleagues compared common observational measurement methods against 15 randomised advertising experiments at Facebook, published in *Marketing Science* in 2019, and found the observational methods generally overestimated ad effectiveness, and in some cases underestimated it.

| Design | How it works | When it is valid | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Random split | Visitors or contacts randomly assigned to version A or B | High volume, short feedback loop | Needs the sample sizes above |
| Account holdout | A random set of target accounts receives nothing for a period | Account-based programmes, outbound, events | Fewer units; needs accounts of similar size and fit |
| Geographic or time holdout | A region or period without the campaign | Paid media with clear geographic targeting | Regions and periods differ in other ways |
| Before and after | Compare the period after a change with the period before | Rarely; only for very large, abrupt effects | Baselines move; seasonality and market shifts dominate |
| Platform lift study | The ad platform runs its own holdout | Paid social and search, with enough spend | The seller of the media designs and reports the test |

Account holdouts suit B2B best. Randomly withholding a campaign from a fifth of the target list for a quarter, then comparing qualified opportunities per account between the two groups, measures what Forrester calls marketing lift: the gain above a baseline. It uses accounts as the unit, which matches how buying groups actually buy, and it can run at the volumes most firms have.

## Write the decision before the test

Every test should start with a decision card, completed and agreed before launch. It is short.

1. **The question.** One sentence: does version B produce more qualified opportunities per account than version A?
2. **The metric and its source.** Named field, named system, named definition.
3. **The smallest effect worth acting on.** Set from the economics in Part 8: the improvement that would move a channel inside its cost ceiling.
4. **The sample and the stop date.** From the arithmetic above. If the sample is not reachable, change the test or do not run it.
5. **The decision for each result.** If B wins by at least the minimum effect: switch and scale. If B loses: stop B. If neither: keep A, record the null and do not extend more than once.
6. **The owner.** The person who will make the call on the stop date.

Two rules make the card work. Do not stop early when the result looks good: checking repeatedly and stopping at the first favourable reading makes false positives far more likely than the significance level suggests. Johari, Pekelis and Walsh showed that with continuous monitoring, even at 10,000 samples, the false positive rate can easily rise fivefold above the nominal level. And treat a null result as a result. "We could not detect a difference of 20% or more" is useful; it means the cheaper option is fine.

Tests on real buyers also have a cost beyond budget. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 73% actively avoid suppliers who send irrelevant outreach. A badly targeted outbound variant does not just lose the test. It can lose the account.

## When the volume is too low to test

Many questions a 50-person firm faces cannot be tested at all: whether to attend a particular conference, whether to reposition for a new segment, whether to hire a partner manager. The honest answer is to decide by judgment and record the decision properly: the choice, the reason, the owner, the expected outcome and a check date, as Part 9 of The Build Order sets out. That is not a weaker form of testing. It is the right tool when the sample is one.

Between full tests and pure judgment there are useful middle options. Test bigger differences, because large effects need far smaller samples. Pool similar tests across quarters. And run qualitative tests: five buyer interviews on two versions of a message will not produce statistics, but they will often show which one is misunderstood. Our piece on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers how to run those conversations without leading the buyer.

Whatever the method, every test and every judgment call goes in one log: the card, the result, the decision taken and a ruled-out list of what was tried and failed. After a year that log is the firm's real evidence about what works in its market, and the most useful document a new head of marketing can inherit.

Illustrative example: replacing a split test with a holdout

Decision
:   Abandon a planned A/B test of two outbound sequences and run a one-quarter account holdout instead, withholding the new sequence from a random fifth of 400 target accounts.

Reason and owner
:   The decision card showed the A/B test would need about 3,800 contacts per arm to detect a reply-rate lift from 2% to 3%, more than the quarter's list. Owned by the head of growth; minimum effect set from the channel's cost ceiling.

What changed
:   The holdout measured qualified opportunities per account, which sales already trusted; the null result on the first sequence was recorded and the second sequence was tested with a larger change.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements; figures are illustrative.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the decision first.** Metric, minimum effect, sample, stop date and the action for each result.
- **Do the arithmetic before launch.** If the sample cannot detect the effect, change the test.
- **Measure close to revenue.** Qualified opportunities or stage progression, agreed with sales.
- **Run concurrent comparisons.** Holdouts beat before-and-after because baselines move.
- **Record nulls and judgment calls.** The test log is the firm's evidence about its market.

Gateway card

### Before you launch a campaign test

- A one-sentence question and a named metric with its source
- A minimum effect worth acting on, taken from the channel economics
- A sample size calculation showing the test can detect that effect
- A concurrent control or holdout, not a before-and-after comparison
- A written action for a win, a loss and a null
- A named owner and a stop date that will not move

## Common questions

### How big a sample do you need for a B2B A/B test?

It depends on the baseline and the lift. At a 3% conversion rate, detecting a rise to 3.6% needs about 14,000 visitors per version; detecting a rise to 4.5% needs about 2,500.

### What should you measure in a B2B marketing test?

The step closest to revenue that the test can measure in time, usually qualified opportunities, accepted meetings or stage progression, defined in the CRM and agreed by sales.

### What is a holdout test in B2B marketing?

A random set of target accounts is excluded from a campaign for a period, and outcomes per account are compared between the two groups. It measures lift above a baseline at volumes most firms have.

### What do you do with an inconclusive test result?

Treat it as a result. If no difference of the size you cared about was detected, keep the cheaper option, record the null, and extend the test at most once.
