# Gateway 2: Put a Dollar Figure on Every Commercial Decision

Source: https://lowob.com/research/gateway-two-a-dollar-figure-on-every-commercial-decision/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Most firms cannot say what their AI spending returned: 56% of CEOs in PwC's 2026 survey report no significant financial benefit yet. Gateway 2 fixes the measurement rather than the model. Each recorded commercial decision carries a value at stake, the realised value is written back when the outcome lands, and review time is netted off, so the build reports in money rather than activity.

Gateway 2 asks one thing of the commercial record: that every recorded decision carries the money it puts at stake, and that the realised value is written back when the outcome arrives. Without that, a build can only report activity: drafts produced, hours saved, seats active. Finance does not fund activity twice. The evidence says most firms are stuck there. In PwC's 2026 Global CEO Survey, 56% of 4,454 CEOs reported no significant financial benefit from AI to date. The fix is not a better model. It is two fields on the record, a quarterly reconciliation and an honest line for the human time the system consumes.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

[Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/) set out the ten commercial decisions worth recording and the six fields each record needs: decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back. Its closing checklist ended with one line that this piece expands: a value at stake recorded, so the build can report in money.

That line is the second gateway in The Build Order. The first, [*nothing sends without a person*](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/), protects the firm from what the system does. The second protects the build from the question every sponsor eventually faces at renewal: what did this return?

## The build reports activity, and finance hears nothing

The market's difficulty with that question is well documented. IBM's Institute for Business Value surveyed 2,000 CEOs between February and April 2025 and found that only 25% of AI initiatives had delivered their expected return, and only 16% had been scaled across the enterprise. McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey of 1,993 participants found 39% attributing any EBIT impact to AI at the enterprise level, and most of those said the share was under 5%. PwC's January 2026 survey found 12% of CEOs reporting both cost and revenue benefits, and 56% reporting no significant financial benefit. Finance teams are no more convinced: in Gartner's 2025 survey of 183 finance leaders, 91% initially reported low or moderate impact from AI.

Two readings of those numbers are possible. One is that the tools do not work. The other is that most firms never set up the arithmetic that would show whether they work. The second reading fits what we see in briefs: success measures written as adoption (seats active, prompts sent) or as time saved, with no link to a decision that moved money.

Gartner forecast in June 2025 that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing rising costs and unclear business value. Unclear value is a measurement failure before it is a technology failure. A build that cannot state its value will be cancelled by someone who can state its cost.

## Value at stake: one number, set at the moment of decision

Value at stake is the money a decision commits or risks, estimated when the decision is made. It is not a forecast of the return. It is the size of the bet. Recording it does two things: it lets the firm rank decisions by consequence, and it gives the written-back outcome something to be measured against.

The rule that makes it workable is one definition per decision class, agreed with finance once, then applied mechanically.

| Decision class | Value at stake, defined as | Estimated from | Outcome lands within |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Discount or price exception | Margin conceded against the standard tier | Quote and price book | One sales cycle |
| Pursue or pass on a pitch | Expected contract value times historical win rate for the segment | CRM history | One sales cycle |
| Qualify or drop an inbound lead | Average first-year value for the source, times stage conversion | CRM history | Weeks |
| Campaign spend and reallocation | Budget committed | Media plan | A quarter |
| Account prioritisation | Pipeline value of the accounts moved up or down | CRM | A quarter |
| Closed-lost reason | Value of the lost deal | CRM | Already known |

Three cautions apply. First, use a range where the estimate is soft, and record the midpoint; false precision invites argument about the number rather than the decision. Second, keep the definition stable for at least two quarters, because changing it resets every comparison. Third, the person who sets the value should not be the person graded on the outcome, or estimates drift upwards. Finance or revenue operations usually owns the definitions; the deal owner fills them in.

## Writing the outcome back without fooling yourself

The outcome field turns a record into evidence ([*What is outcome write-back?*](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)). For Gateway 2 it needs two additions: realised value in money, and a comparison.

| Field | Example (discount exception) | Set by | When |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Value at stake | $6,000 margin conceded on a $60,000 deal | Deal owner, using finance's definition | At approval |
| Expected outcome | Win within 30 days | Deal owner | At approval |
| Check date | 30 days after approval | System | At approval |
| Outcome | Won, at the discounted price | Deal owner | At check date |
| Comparison | Win rate of standard-tier quotes in the same segment that quarter | Revenue operations | Quarterly |
| Realised value | Deal value won, less margin conceded, adjusted for the comparison | Finance | Quarterly |

The comparison is the field most firms skip and the one that matters most. A discounted deal that closes looks like a success. If standard-price deals in the same segment closed at the same rate, the discount bought nothing and cost $6,000. Part 10's distributor reached exactly this finding: once outcomes were recorded, discounts in some product lines won no more often than standard quotes.

The comparison need not be an experiment. A matched group from the same quarter, segment and deal size is enough for a commercial decision. Where volume is too low for a group, record a probability alongside the expected outcome and track calibration over quarters, as we argued in [*Calibration is the honest learning signal*](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/).

> A decision that cost money and changed nothing is the most valuable record the brain will hold, because it is the one nobody would have found without it.

## Netting the cost: review time is the larger bill

A gross figure flatters the build. The net figure subtracts what the system costs to run, and for a judgment system the largest cost is usually human.

In [*Reviewer minutes per useful decision*](https://lowob.com/research/reviewer-minutes-per-useful-decision/) we argued that token costs attract the attention while review, adjudication and outcome checks are the bigger expense, and that the honest unit is human minutes divided by the decisions the decision-maker judged were helped. In [*The humans carrying context are the price signal*](https://lowob.com/research/the-humans-carrying-context-are-the-price-signal/) we made the related point that context held in one person's head is a cost the firm pays in labour until it is written down.

Gateway 2 puts both into the same sum:

- **Realised value** from the decisions the system prepared or informed, adjusted for the comparison.
- **Less tool cost:** seats, usage charges and connectors, which [*Seats, usage or outcomes*](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) explains how to forecast.
- **Less review time:** minutes spent approving drafts, checking records and writing back outcomes, at a loaded hourly rate.
- **Less build-owner time:** the protected hours agreed at Gateway 0.

An illustrative quarter: forty discount exceptions recorded, $240,000 of margin conceded in total. After write-back, exceptions in one service line show no higher win rate than standard pricing; tightening that line would have retained around $70,000 of margin. Review and write-back take roughly fifteen minutes per record, ten hours across the quarter. The numbers are invented for illustration. The structure is the point: the saving is a pricing decision the record made visible, and the cost includes the time it took to see it.

Expect the review line to rise before it falls. Early on there are few precedents and reviewers are learning the tool. Set a baseline before launch and a date by which review minutes per useful decision must fall below it.

## Reporting the build in money

Once two quarters of records carry values and outcomes, the build can report on one page. We suggest five lines, all in money or derived from it.

| Report this | Drop this |
| --- | --- |
| Value at stake recorded this quarter, by decision class | Seats activated |
| Share of records with outcomes written back on time | Prompts or queries run |
| Realised value against expected, with the comparison stated | "Hours saved" estimated by users |
| Net value after tool cost and review time | Number of agents deployed |
| The one decision rule changed because of the record | Satisfaction scores for the assistant |

The fifth line is the most persuasive. A finance director can disagree with an estimate of realised value. It is harder to dismiss a rule the head of sales changed because the record showed the old one was costing margin.

Where the money goes matters here too. The MIT NANDA report *The GenAI Divide*, as reported by The Register in August 2025, found about half of generative AI budgets going to sales and marketing, and its authors pointed buyers towards uses with measurable results such as lead qualification and customer retention. Those are decision classes with a value at stake and an outcome inside a quarter. They are exactly what Gateway 2 is built to count.

## Where the dollar figure misleads

The method has limits, and a sponsor should hear them before finance finds them.

**Long cycles.** Where outcomes take a year, report value at stake and leading indicators each quarter and realised value annually. Do not pretend a quarter's figure is final.

**Attribution creep.** The record shows that a decision was informed by the system's preparation, not that the system caused the result. Credit the decision, not the agent.

**Uncomfortable numbers.** The first finding is often that a practice the team believed in does not pay. That is the record working. It is also the moment the build becomes a pricing or sales-management conversation, and the sponsor needs to be ready to have it.

**Incentive damage.** Do not tie individual pay to realised value from the record in the first year. People will start choosing which decisions to record, and the record will stop being honest.

**Small volumes.** Below about ten decisions a month in a class, comparison groups are too thin. Record the values anyway and compare against expectations until volume allows more.

Illustrative example: the first money report

Decision
:   Replace the quarterly AI adoption report with a five-line money report built from discount and pursue-or-pass records.

Reason and owner
:   The sponsor could not answer the renewal question from adoption figures. Owned by the head of revenue operations, with value definitions agreed by the finance director.

What changed
:   After two quarters the report showed net value positive in one decision class and negative in another; review effort moved to the class that paid, and one discount rule was tightened.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size services firm, built from patterns across engagements; all figures in this piece are illustrative.

## lowob takeaways

- **Set the value when the decision is made.** One definition per class, agreed with finance, applied mechanically.
- **Write back against a comparison.** A win that would have happened anyway is not value.
- **Net off the people.** Review and write-back time belong in the sum, and usually dominate it.
- **Report five lines in money.** Retire adoption metrics from the sponsor's report.
- **Expect the first number to be uncomfortable.** That is the record doing its job.

Gateway card

### Gateway 2: before the build reports in money

- A value-at-stake definition for each recorded decision class, signed off by finance
- Value at stake filled in at the moment of decision, not afterwards
- Outcomes written back by the check date on at least four in five records
- A comparison group or calibration method named for each class
- Review and write-back time logged and costed
- One quarterly report in money, with adoption metrics removed

## Common questions

### How do you measure the ROI of AI in sales?

Record the commercial decisions the system informs, attach a value at stake to each when it is made, write back the realised value at a check date against a comparison group, and subtract tool cost and human review time.

### What is value at stake in a decision record?

The money a decision commits or risks, estimated at the time: the margin conceded on a discount, the expected value of a pitch, or the budget committed to a campaign. It is the size of the bet, not a forecast of the return.

### Why do most companies see no financial return from AI?

Surveys such as PwC's 2026 Global CEO Survey show most firms report no significant financial benefit yet. A common cause is that success is measured as adoption or time saved, with no link to decisions that moved money.

### Should AI ROI include employee review time?

Yes. For systems that prepare or draft decisions, the time people spend reviewing, approving and recording outcomes is often the largest cost, and it should be netted off before value is reported.

# The Channels Nobody Can Take Away From You Are the Ones You Keep Neglecting.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/owned-channels-email-content/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Owned channels are the ones where a company holds the relationship directly: email, content on its own site, the search presence that content earns, and the product's own messages. They are slow and thinly bid, which is why they compound. With search clicks falling and platform rules shifting, build email first, give every piece of content a job, and route every rented channel to an address the company keeps.

Owned channels are the ones where a company holds the relationship directly and no third party can revoke it: email, content on property it controls, the search presence that content earns, and the product's own messages. They are slow and do not look like marketing, so most companies neglect them, which is exactly why they are thinly bid. Rented channels keep changing: Chartbeat data show Google search referrals to news sites down 33% in a year and Facebook referrals down 43% over a longer period. Build email first, give every piece of content a job, and connect every rented channel to an address the company keeps.

Ask a company what would survive if every rented channel disappeared tomorrow (the ad accounts, the marketplace listing, the creator relationships, the app-store placement), and the honest answer is usually a mailing list nobody has written to since spring and a blog with four posts.

Those are the owned channels. For a company the ad platforms restrict, they are not a nice-to-have. They are the only band where no platform reviews what you say before it reaches the reader.

## Owned, rented and the difference in control

| Channel | Who holds the relationship | Who can change the terms | What happens when you stop paying |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Email list | You | Mailbox providers set technical standards; you control content and cadence | Nothing; the list stays |
| Content on your site | You | Search engines and answer engines decide how often it is surfaced | It keeps working until it goes stale |
| Product messages | You | App stores for push; you for in-product | Nothing |
| Paid search and social | The platform | The platform, at any time | Reach stops |
| Social accounts | The platform | The platform's ranking and policy teams | Reach decays |
| Marketplaces and creators | The partner | The partner | Access stops |

The first three rows are not free of rules. Gmail and Yahoo require authentication and low complaint rates, and search engines decide what ranks. But those are standards you can meet, not a reviewer who can refuse your category. Our guide to [email deliverability](https://lowob.com/research/email-deliverability-explained/) covers what the mailbox providers require.

The rented rows change without notice. Google's advertising policy for cryptocurrency products, for example, requires advertisers to be certified by Google and to meet country-specific licensing rules, and it was amended again in July 2025 to allow exchanges and wallets in Canada if registered with FINTRAC. Each amendment changes who can buy reach, where. A company whose whole plan sits in those rows is renting its distribution from someone else's policy team.

## Why they are neglected

Owned channels are slow, and they do not look like marketing. An email list grows one address at a time. Content earns search presence over months. Neither produces a dashboard that moves this week. Compared with a channel that can be turned on with a credit card, they feel like a project rather than a purchase, and the person who champions them is asking the company to spend now for a return that arrives after the next planning cycle.

That timing is real. It is also the reason owned channels are thinly bid. Most companies will not wait, so the companies that do are building something their competitors have declined to build.

## The honest economics

In **lowob**'s experience, content and search often take six to twelve months before organic acquisition covers the cost of producing them. For a company with a short runway, that payback can be longer than the runway, and it is fair to say so and put the budget in faster channels.

The calculation has also shifted under content's feet. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025 and found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when one did not; links inside the summary were clicked on about 1% of visits. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to 2,576 publisher sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and that referrals from Facebook fell 43% and from X 46% over a longer period. Publishers are not B2B suppliers, but the direction is the same for anyone who relied on search and social to deliver readers.

Two conclusions follow. Content whose only job was "rank and get the click" is worth less than it was, and needs to be the source the answer cites. Our pieces on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) and [what SEO is now](https://lowob.com/research/what-seo-is-now/) cover that. And the address the reader leaves is worth more, because it is the one route to them that does not depend on a ranking.

The calculation also changes in two situations. When the company already has a distribution asset (a founder's following, an existing list, a community that reads what it publishes), owned channels are cheap to activate because the audience is already there. And when the rented channels are closed to the category, the comparison is not owned versus paid. It is owned versus nothing.

> When the rented channels are closed to the category, the comparison is not owned versus paid. It is owned versus nothing.

## Email is the one to build first

Of the owned channels, email has the fastest payback and the most direct commercial use.

Every channel the company does use (affiliate, creator, programmatic, events) should end at a place where the customer can leave an address. The list becomes the layer that keeps working when any single acquisition channel stops. A partner-driven customer who joins the list can be reached next year without paying the partner again. A creator's audience that subscribes is now the company's audience too.

Run it with restraint:

- A regular, useful message the reader would miss if it stopped.
- Segmentation by what the reader actually did, not by what the company hopes.
- Unsubscribes and complaints watched as closely as opens; Google asks bulk senders to keep complaints below 0.3% and recommends below 0.1%.
- In regulated categories, the same compliance review the ads would have received.

## Content that does a job

The failure mode of content is the calendar: a schedule of posts with no thesis, produced because the schedule exists.

Content that earns its cost does one of three jobs. It answers the question the buyer is already searching for, in enough depth to be the answer. It explains something the company believes that the market currently gets wrong. Or it gives the reader a tool (a checklist, a worksheet, a comparison) they will return to.

Each piece should have a purpose, a reader and a next step. Each should be the canonical version, published on property the company owns, and adapted for social rather than pasted there. Most companies need far fewer pieces than they produce, and far more that anyone remembers. Our piece [Content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) turns this into a brief, a measure and a retirement rule.

## The compounding argument

Rented channels are priced fresh every month. Owned channels are paid for once and produce for years, provided they are maintained. A company that builds them while the rented channels are working arrives at the next platform policy change with an audience, a search presence and a list. A company that did not arrives with a screenshot.

## lowob takeaways

- **Build email first.** It has the fastest payback and survives any single channel's failure.
- **Route every rented channel to an address.** Creators, partners and ads should all end in a sign-up you keep.
- **Give content a job.** An answer, a position or a tool; never a calendar slot.
- **Plan for fewer clicks.** Write to be the source an answer cites, and value the address over the visit.

## Common questions

### What are owned media channels?

Channels where the company holds the relationship directly: its email list, its website and the content on it, the search presence that content earns, and the messages its own product sends. No platform can switch them off.

### Why is email marketing still important?

Because it is the one route to a customer that does not depend on a platform's ranking or ad policy. As search clicks fall and social referrals shrink, an address the reader chose to give is worth more, not less.

### How long does content marketing take to pay back?

Often six to twelve months before organic acquisition covers production cost, in **lowob**'s experience, and longer if pieces have no clear job. Firms with an existing audience or closed paid channels see the case change sooner.

### How do you build an email list from other channels?

Make every channel end at a page that offers something worth an address: a guide, a tool, a briefing. Creator posts, partner referrals, events and ads should all lead there rather than to a homepage.

## Sources and notes

- [Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/), 22 July 2025. 900 US adults, searches in March 2025; consumer, not B2B-specific.
- [Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026), 12 January 2026. Chartbeat publisher traffic data plus a survey of 280 media leaders; publishers, not B2B suppliers; referral time frames differ between chapters.
- [Google Ads, Updates to cryptocurrencies and related products policy (July 2025)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16345928?hl=en), 1 July 2025. Platform policy notice.
- [Google, Email sender guidelines](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/81126?hl=en), consulted November 2026. Platform requirements for sending to Gmail.
- The six-to-twelve-month payback is **lowob**'s experience, not a measured benchmark. The control table is **lowob**'s framework.

## Next move

List every rented channel you spend on and where each sends people. Any that ends on a homepage or a social profile should end on a page that asks for an address by the end of this month.

# What Is Lead Source Attribution?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Lead source attribution assigns each lead, and the revenue that follows, to the channel that produced it. It is one of the most-used fields in a CRM and one of the least reliable, because most B2B buying happens before a buyer is visible. This explainer covers how the field works in common CRMs, the main attribution approaches, and a setup a mid-size firm can trust.

Lead source attribution is the practice of recording where each lead came from and carrying that source through to the opportunity and the revenue it produces. In most CRMs it starts as a single field holding one value, which means it captures first touch only. It answers "which channels bring us business" well enough to steer spend, provided the source list is fixed, the field is protected, and nobody mistakes it for proof of cause.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What lead source attribution means

Every commercial team wants to know which activity produced its revenue. Lead source attribution is the simplest answer: tag each lead with its origin, then follow that tag through to the deal and its value.

In Salesforce, Lead Source is a standard picklist with defaults such as Web, Phone Inquiry, Partner Referral, Trade Show, Word of mouth, Employee Referral and Other. Each lead holds one value. On conversion, the value can be inherited by the contact, the account and the opportunity. A Salesforce Ben guide notes a common trap: the opportunity inherits the lead source only when created during conversion or from the contact, not when created from the account page.

HubSpot works differently. A deal's Original Traffic Source comes from the associated contact with the earliest activity, and a separate Record Source property records how the deal was created.

| Approach | What it credits | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lead source field (first touch) | The first recorded origin | Simple, complete, cheap | Ignores everything after first touch |
| Last touch | The final interaction before conversion | Easy to track online | Overcredits search and direct traffic |
| Multi-touch (rules-based) | Several touches by fixed weights | Shows the journey | Weights are arbitrary |
| Data-driven (algorithmic) | Touches by modelled contribution | Adapts to data | Opaque, needs volume |
| Self-reported | What the buyer says | Captures untracked channels | Memory is imperfect |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Budget follows the field

Whatever the source field says gets funded. If referrals are recorded as "Web" because the buyer filled in a form after a colleague recommended the firm, the referral programme looks worthless and the website looks brilliant. The field is a decision input, so its definitions need the same care as stage definitions.

### Most of the journey is invisible

6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers were nearly 70% through their purchasing process before engaging sellers, and that buyers initiated first contact more than 80% of the time. Gartner reported in 2020 that buyers spend only 17% of their purchase time meeting potential suppliers. Tracking sees the form fill. It rarely sees the conversation that caused it. 6sense is a vendor, and its figures are survey-based, but the direction is consistent with Gartner's.

### The tools have narrowed the choice

In April 2023 Google announced that first-click, linear, time-decay and position-based models would be removed from Google Ads and GA4, with remaining conversion actions switched to data-driven attribution from September 2023. Last click remains available. For a mid-size B2B firm, that means web analytics will not resolve the attribution question on its own. The CRM record has to.

## How to set it up so it can be trusted

1. **Fix the list.** Eight to twelve source values, each defined in one sentence. Add a dependent "source detail" field for the campaign or event name.
2. **Protect the field.** Make the source field read-only for users who do not need to edit it, as Salesforce Ben recommends. Corrections go through the RevOps owner.
3. **Ask the buyer.** Add an open "How did you hear about us?" question to enquiry forms and first calls. Record the answer alongside the tracked source.
4. **Fill account source.** Set a value on existing accounts, even "unknown", so later conversions do not overwrite history.
5. **Compare quarterly.** Put tracked source and self-reported source side by side. Large gaps show which channels tracking undercounts.
6. **Treat it as correlation.** Attribution shows where deals entered, not what caused them. Testing cause needs holdouts, covered in *Attribution vs incrementality*.

In **lowob**'s model, source is one of the eight store fields the brain reads. A fixed list and a protected value are what let an AI system group deals by source without inventing categories.

## lowob takeaways

- **One field, first touch.** The standard lead source field records origin, not the full journey.
- **Ask as well as track.** Self-reported source captures referrals and conversations that tracking cannot see.
- **Protect the original value.** Overwritten sources destroy the history the field exists to keep.
- **Do not read it as cause.** Attribution allocates credit; incrementality tests whether a channel made a difference.

## Common questions

### What is lead source attribution?

It is recording where each lead came from and carrying that source through to the opportunity and revenue, so channels can be compared by the business they produce.

### What is the difference between lead source and attribution?

Lead source is usually a single first-touch field. Attribution is the broader practice of assigning credit, which may spread it across several touches.

### What attribution models are left in GA4?

After Google's 2023 changes, data-driven and last-click attribution remain. First-click, linear, time-decay and position-based were removed.

### Is self-reported attribution reliable?

It is imperfect but useful. Buyers' answers capture channels like referrals and peer conversations that tracking misses, so it works best alongside tracked source.

## Sources and notes

- [Salesforce Ben, Let's Talk About Salesforce Lead Source](https://www.salesforceben.com/lets-talk-about-salesforce-lead-source), updated February 2024. Practitioner guide to the standard field and conversion mapping.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, HubSpot's default deal properties](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/properties/hubspots-default-deal-properties). Vendor documentation for Original Traffic Source and Record Source.
- [Google Ads Help, First click, linear, time decay, and position-based attribution models are going away](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13427716), April 2023.
- [6sense via Business Wire, 6sense Launches 2024 Buyer Experience Report](https://www.businesswire.com/news/home/20241009142556/en/6sense-Launches-2024-Buyer-Experience-Report-Unveiling-Global-B2B-Buyer-Trends), October 2024. Vendor-run buyer survey.
- [Gartner, Gartner Says 80% of B2B Sales Interactions Between Suppliers and Buyers Will Occur in Digital Channels by 2025](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-09-15-gartner-says-80--of-b2b-sales-interactions-between-su), September 2020.

## Next move

Pull the last 20 won deals and ask each owner how the client first heard of the firm. Compare the answers with the recorded lead source and count how many differ.

# Founder, Brand and Community Accounts Need Different Jobs

Source: https://lowob.com/research/founder-brand-community-social-strategy/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When a founder, company and community account all repeat the same announcement, people have fewer reasons to follow each one. Give the founder judgment, the company clarity and proof, and the community participation. Cascade one fact through three voices, decide who speaks in a crisis before it happens, and run the system from an operating matrix.

When a founder, company and community account all repeat the same announcement, people have fewer reasons to follow each one. Give every account a distinct purpose. A founder, a company and a community have different sources of authority: the founder's is judgment, the company's is proof, the community's is participation. Trust data supports separating them. The 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer found 66% of employees trust their own CEO, and the Reuters Institute found 27% of people get news from creators and personalities, so a person and an institution are trusted for different things.

Many startups operate several social accounts but only one voice.

The founder posts corporate announcements. The company account tries to sound personal. Community channels repeat the same copy with more emojis. Every surface distributes the same message without adding context, credibility or participation.

This wastes the reason those channels exist separately.

## The founder account: judgment and conviction

People follow founders to understand how they see the world, why they are building and how they make decisions.

That can mean explaining a difficult tradeoff, sharing a lesson from building, recognising a customer or partner, or expressing a view on where the market is heading. The founder has credibility because they are close to these decisions, not because they repeat the latest press release.

The audience for that view is commercial as well as social. In the 2024 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report, 73% of decision-makers said a firm's thought leadership was a more trustworthy basis for judging its capabilities than its marketing materials. Our piece on [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) covers how a founder's position turns into discovery questions and objection answers, and the [founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) covers how to produce it without making the founder a full-time creator.

It should not become a copy-and-paste distribution endpoint for every press release. A founder's credibility comes from proximity to the decisions and willingness to express a real view.

## The company account: clarity and proof

The company account is the canonical source for what the organisation knows, offers, ships and can substantiate.

Use it for reliable product explanations, launches, customer and partner evidence, helpful educational resources, event information, recruiting updates and corrections. Readers should know where to find the authoritative version of a claim.

Its tone can be recognisable without pretending to be a person. The standard is clarity, consistency and reliability. Cadence helps here in a way it does not for founders: LinkedIn's own guidance, vendor advice from the platform, says companies that post weekly see twice the engagement on their Page content, and recommends notifying employees of important posts no more than once a week.

## Community channels: participation and interpretation

Community surfaces should help members understand, discuss, question and extend what the company is doing.

Member questions, feedback, working sessions and resources created by the community belong here. Members should be able to contribute knowledge and interpret product news for one another, rather than waiting for staff to supply every conversation.

The company may facilitate the environment, but community value should increasingly move between members. Our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/) sets out how to test whether members are creating value for each other, and [Community management vs social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) covers why the two need different people.

| Account | Source of authority | Belongs here | Does not belong here | Measured by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Founder | Judgment and proximity to decisions | Tradeoffs, lessons, market views, recognition | Copied press releases, unverified product claims | Qualified discussion, inbound from priority buyers |
| Company | Substantiation | Product facts, launches, evidence, corrections, events | Personal opinion presented as company position | Comprehension and action |
| Community | Participation | Member questions, working sessions, member-made resources | Announcements with nothing to discuss | Participation and member output |

## Use a message cascade

One important announcement can appear across all three surfaces without becoming identical.

Suppose a company launches a new institutional product.

**Founder:** Explains why the product had to exist, what the team learned from early buyers, and what belief drove the decision.

**Company:** Publishes the authoritative explanation, functionality, eligibility, proof and next steps.

**Community:** Hosts a question session, gathers implementation feedback, surfaces member use cases and preserves answers.

The underlying fact is consistent. The value added by each voice is different.

> The underlying fact is consistent. The value added by each voice is different.

## Define boundaries before a difficult moment

Account roles become especially important during incidents, rumours, market volatility or criticism.

Decide which account publishes confirmed facts, when a founder speaks personally, what moderators can answer and when legal, security or executive review is required. Keep updates in one durable place so speculation cannot replace the company's official account.

For listed companies, regulators have already drawn this line. In 2013 the US SEC investigated after Netflix's chief executive announced a viewing milestone on his personal Facebook page without a press release or filing. It concluded that companies may use social media for material announcements "so long as investors have been alerted about which social media will be used." Most startups are not subject to that rule, but the principle transfers: tell people in advance which account carries confirmed facts, and keep to it.

Disclosure applies on personal accounts too. The FTC's staff guidance says that when an employee promotes their employer's product, "listing your employer on your profile page isn't enough"; the connection should be clear in the post. A founder's connection to their own company is usually obvious, but staff and advisers posting about a launch should say who they work for.

Without these rules, urgency produces contradictory messages and unauthorised interpretation.

## Create a practical operating matrix

Give each recurring content type a primary account, a responsible owner, any required approval and a way to measure success. Supporting accounts should add context or participation, not copy the original announcement.

| Content type | Primary account | Owner | Approval | Supporting accounts add |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Market opinion | Founder | Founder | Founder only | Company links to a fuller article |
| Product launch | Company | Product marketing | Product and legal for claims | Founder explains why; community hosts questions |
| Incident update | Company | Communications lead | Legal, security, executive | Founder speaks only after the company post |
| Contributor programme | Community | Community operations | Community lead | Company recognises output |
| Hiring | Company | People lead | People lead | Founder explains the team's next problem |

Do not force equal activity. A founder may post only when they have something worth saying. The company may maintain a predictable editorial cadence. Community channels may be active every day because members are interacting. Consistency means fulfilling the account's promise, not hitting the same quota everywhere.

Resource-constrained teams should begin with the surfaces that match their actual objectives. A founder selling enterprise software may benefit more from a strong personal LinkedIn presence and company knowledge base than from maintaining six weak channels. A consumer crypto network may require much stronger real-time community operations, and [Discord is not a community strategy](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/) covers that case. As the company grows, [from founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) covers which of the founder's channels transfer to the team and which stay personal.

Social strategy becomes simpler when each account answers one question: why should someone follow this source in addition to the others? If the answer is unclear, the account does not yet have a job.

## lowob takeaways

- **Give each account a job.** Founder judgment, company proof, community participation.
- **Keep the fact, vary the value.** One announcement, three different contributions.
- **Name the official channel in advance.** Decide who publishes confirmed facts before an incident.
- **Run it from a matrix.** Primary account, owner, approval and measure for each content type.

## Common questions

### Should a founder post company announcements on their personal account?

Not as a copy. The company account should carry the authoritative announcement, and the founder should add what only they can: why the decision was made and what the team learned.

### What should a startup's company social account post?

Product explanations, launches, customer and partner evidence, educational resources, events, hiring and corrections: the authoritative version of anything the company can substantiate.

### How should founder, company and community accounts work together in a crisis?

Decide in advance which account publishes confirmed facts, when the founder speaks personally, what moderators may answer and what needs legal or security review, and keep updates in one durable place.

### Do employees need to disclose when they post about their company?

Under FTC staff guidance, listing an employer on a profile is not enough when an employee promotes the company's products. The relationship should be clear in the post itself.

# How to Read a Creator Media Kit

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-read-a-creator-media-kit/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A creator media kit is a sales document prepared by the seller. Read past the follower count to median engagement, real demographics and repeat sponsors, ask for the numbers it leaves out, check for paid relationships and fake metrics, and test on cost-per-outcome terms before buying a package.

A creator media kit is a sales document prepared by the seller. Read past the follower count to median engagement, real demographics and repeat sponsors, ask for the numbers it leaves out, and test on cost-per-outcome terms before buying a package. Buyers have reason to be careful: a third of US creator ad buyers told the IAB in 2025 that finding the right creators was their biggest hurdle, and the US Federal Trade Commission now bans buying or selling fake follower and view counts used to misrepresent influence.

A media kit is the document a creator or publisher sends to a company considering paying them: audience size, demographics, engagement, past partners, formats offered, and rates. It is a sales document, prepared by the seller, and it should be read as one.

The money involved is no longer small. The IAB estimated US advertisers spent $37 billion with creators in 2025, and Goldman Sachs Research estimated in 2023 that brand deals make up about 70% of creator income. When most of a creator's revenue comes from sponsors, the media kit is the creator's most important sales tool, and it is written accordingly.

## What is usually in it

| Section | What it shows | What it hides | What to ask for instead |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audience size | Followers, subscribers, listeners, recipients by platform | Inactive accounts, bots, followers from years ago | Views or reach per post over ninety days |
| Engagement | Average likes, comments, shares, views, opens, clicks | Selection of best posts; bought engagement | Median over the last thirty posts |
| Demographics | Age, gender, location, sometimes interests | Whether the audience buys your category | Share of audience in your markets and roles |
| Past partners | Logos of companies that paid before | Who paid twice | Repeat sponsors and a reference |
| Formats and rates | Prices per post, mention, story, integration, placement | Flexibility, performance terms | A first piece on cost-per-outcome terms |
| Case studies | One past campaign with results | How the result was measured | The tracking method and the sponsor's own view |

## What each number means, and what it hides

**Follower count** is the least informative figure and the one most prominently displayed. It includes inactive accounts, bots, and people who followed years ago for a different reason. On platforms where reach is algorithmic, followers barely predict how many people see a post. Rival IQ's 2025 benchmark of brand accounts, vendor data that divides interactions by follower count, found median engagement fell 16% on Instagram, 34% on TikTok and 48% on X year on year. A follower count says less each year about who interacts with a post.

**Average engagement** is more useful, and is routinely calculated on the creator's best-performing recent posts. Ask for the median over the last thirty posts, not the average over the best ten. One viral post can double an average; it barely moves a median. Expect smaller accounts to post higher rates. HypeAuditor's 2025 report, vendor analysis of 76 million Instagram accounts, put nano-influencers (1,000 to 10,000 followers) at a 2.19% engagement rate, the highest of any tier. A large account with a rate well above its tier deserves a second look.

**Bought numbers** are now a legal question as well as a commercial one. The FTC's August 2024 rule on reviews and testimonials prohibits buying or selling bot-generated or hijacked-account metrics, "fake indicators of social media influence", where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them for a commercial purpose. Ask the creator to confirm in writing that no followers, views or engagement were bought.

**Demographics** come from platform analytics and are reasonably reliable for age, gender, and country. They say nothing about whether the audience buys the category. A finance creator's audience may be mostly other finance creators.

**Past partners** tell you who paid once. They do not tell you who paid twice, which is the figure that matters.

**Rates** are a starting position. They vary by month, by how full the creator's calendar is, and by whether the deal is flat or performance-based.

> A creator who returns to the follower count has told you what the media kit was for.

## The numbers that are not on it

Audience overlap with other creators the company is considering. Share of audience in the geographies the product serves. Evidence that the audience has adopted products the creator recommended before. Retention: how many people who came through this creator last time are still customers. Whether the creator will accept cost-per-outcome terms, which reveals more about their confidence in their audience than any slide.

And the creator's other commercial relationships, including competitors and, in crypto, tokens they hold. The cost of missing this is documented. In October 2022 the US Securities and Exchange Commission settled with a celebrity who had been paid $250,000 to post about a crypto token without disclosing the payment; the settlement totalled $1.26 million. The SEC chair's statement was direct: promoters must disclose "when and how much they are paid to promote investing in securities." A brand that pays a creator who is also paid by, or invested in, a competing token inherits a disclosure problem.

## The questions to ask

1. May we see platform analytics directly, screen-shared, for the last ninety days?
2. What did the last three sponsors in our category see, and may we speak to one?
3. What share of your audience is in our markets?
4. Would you do a first piece on a cost-per-outcome basis, with a tracked link, before we discuss a package?
5. What are your current paid relationships, and are any in our category? Do you hold tokens or equity in anything you cover?
6. What disclosure language do you use, and where does it appear?

The last question has a right answer. FTC guidance asks for disclosures that are hard to miss, placed with the endorsement, and, in video, given both in audio and in on-screen text. A creator who discloses only in a profile bio or behind a "more" link is a compliance risk for the brand as well as the creator.

A creator who answers those readily is a professional with a real audience. A creator who returns to the follower count has told you what the media kit was for.

## Read it against the job

The kit describes the creator. The decision depends on the job: awareness, explanation, conversion, or authority in a specialist audience. A large, lightly engaged audience may suit the first and fail at the rest. A small, deeply trusting audience may do the opposite. Our guide to [influencers, creators, KOLs and ambassadors](https://lowob.com/research/influencer-creator-kol-ambassador/) sets out which kind of person sells which job.

| Job | What the kit must show | Test before a package |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Awareness | Verified reach in your markets | Branded search and direct traffic against a baseline |
| Explanation | Watch time or read depth on similar topics | Questions and replies from the right roles |
| Conversion | Past tracked sales in the category | One piece on a tracked link, paid per outcome |
| Specialist authority | Audience of practitioners, repeat sponsors | A reference call with a peer sponsor |

Match the kit's numbers to the job, test small before committing, and pay for the outcome the job requires. Our playbook on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to size the test so the answer is usable.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read it as a sales document.** The seller chose which numbers to show.
- **Ask for medians and the missing numbers.** Thirty-post median, audience in your markets, repeat sponsors, other paid relationships.
- **Get the no-fake-metrics promise in writing.** Bought followers and views are a US federal rule issue.
- **Pay for the job.** Test one piece on outcome terms before buying a package.

## Common questions

### How do I evaluate an influencer's media kit?

Treat it as a sales document. Look past follower count to median engagement, platform-sourced demographics and repeat sponsors, and ask to see platform analytics directly for the last ninety days.

### What questions should I ask a creator before sponsoring them?

Ask to see analytics screen-shared, what the last three sponsors in your category saw, what share of the audience is in your markets, whether they will do a first piece on cost-per-outcome terms, and what paid relationships or holdings they have.

### How can you tell if an influencer has fake followers?

Compare engagement to the norm for the account's size, look at the median rather than the average, and ask for screen-shared analytics. In the US, buying fake influence metrics for commercial use breaches an FTC rule, so ask for a written confirmation.

### What is missing from most media kits?

Audience overlap with other creators, share of audience in your geographies, evidence of past product adoption, retention of customers they sent, and their other commercial relationships, including token holdings in crypto.

## Sources and notes

- [Goldman Sachs, The creator economy could approach half-a-trillion dollars by 2027](https://www.goldmansachs.com/insights/articles/the-creator-economy-could-approach-half-a-trillion-dollars-by-2027), 19 April 2023. Investment bank research; creator income mix from survey data; older than other sources.
- [Federal Trade Commission, Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/08/federal-trade-commission-announces-final-rule-banning-fake-reviews-testimonials), 14 August 2024. US regulator; applies to US commerce.
- [Federal Trade Commission, Disclosures 101 for social media influencers](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers), November 2019, page updated December 2024. US regulator staff guidance.

Take the media kit on your desk and ask for three things this week: the thirty-post median, screen-shared analytics for ninety days, and a list of current paid relationships. Offer a first piece on a tracked link before discussing a package.

# Selling What Nobody Has a Budget Line For

Source: https://lowob.com/research/selling-what-nobody-has-a-budget-line-for/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: When no budget line exists, sell against the cost of what the buyer does today, through a category they already recognise, to the person who owns the pain. The real competitor is the status quo: research on 2.5 million sales calls found 40% to 60% of lost deals end in no decision. The category story is for investors; customers buy a specific problem solved this quarter.

When no budget line exists, you sell against the cost of what the buyer does today, through a category they already recognise, to the person who owns the pain. The category story is for investors. The evidence on lost deals supports this: Matthew Dixon and Ted McKenna's analysis of 2.5 million recorded sales conversations found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision. In emerging technology, the status quo is the competitor you lose to most.

## The buyer has no budget, no title and no comparison set

In an established market, the buyer knows what they are shopping for. They have a budget line, a job title that owns it, and three vendors to compare. Emerging technology has none of that.

That changes the job. You are not winning a comparison. You are creating a purchase that did not exist in the plan. Every step of the sale has to answer a different question: not "why you" but "why spend at all".

Each audience needs one belief (see [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/)). In emerging tech the customer's belief is narrow and concrete. It is "this costs me money now and that can stop". Anything wider belongs in the investor deck.

The money for new technology does exist, but it moves quickly out of experimental pots. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 enterprise CIOs found innovation budgets had fallen from about a quarter of AI model spend to 7%, as spend moved into centralised IT and business-unit budgets. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey found new budgets funded 55% of incremental enterprise AI spend, with existing software budgets funding 22%. Both are investor surveys about AI, not every emerging category, but the pattern is the one that matters: once a technology proves a saving, an owner creates a permanent line for it. Until then, you are competing for money that is already allocated to the current way of doing things.

## Position against the status quo, not against competitors

You do not have competitors in the usual sense. You have the current way of doing things. That is your real rival, and it is cheaper to describe than a category.

The research on indecision makes the point in numbers. Dixon and McKenna's work, published as *The JOLT Effect*, found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision rather than a loss to a rival, and that prospects showed some indecision in about nine in ten calls. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in May 2025, found 74% of buyer teams showed "unhealthy conflict" during the decision, and that groups reaching consensus were 2.5 times as likely to report a high-quality deal. A new category adds to both problems: nobody has a reference point, so every member of the group can hold a different one.

Write down what the status quo costs. Manual inspections and the people who do them. Downtime between failures. Compliance fines and the audit hours that precede them. Energy bought at the wrong time. Fraud losses and the checks that fail to catch them.

Then price your product against that number, not against a budget that does not exist. A buyer can approve a saving. They cannot approve a category. Our explainer on [value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/) sets out how to price against the buyer's next best option.

Be specific about where the cost sits. "Inefficiency" is not a line item. "Four field engineers spending a day a week on site visits that a sensor could replace" is.

| Status quo cost | Where it sits | Who owns it | Evidence to ask for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Labour on manual checks | Operations headcount | Head of operations | Hours per week, loaded cost per hour |
| Unplanned downtime | Maintenance and lost output | Plant or service lead | Incidents per year, cost per incident |
| Compliance effort and fines | Risk and audit budget | Compliance or risk lead | Audit hours, findings, penalties paid |
| Losses the current checks miss | Fraud or write-off line | Risk or finance lead | Loss rate and the sample it comes from |

> A buyer can approve a saving. They cannot approve a category.

## Borrow a category to get the meeting, then expand

Buyers file new things under old names. Use that. If your agent infrastructure looks like workflow automation to a procurement team, let it get in the door as workflow automation. Our comparison of [workflow automation and AI agents](https://lowob.com/research/workflow-automation-vs-ai-agents/) shows how close the two can look from the outside.

The borrowed category is a door, not a home. Once you are inside and the first use case is proven, you widen the frame. The sequence is: familiar name, narrow pilot, visible result, then the real story.

Founders resist this because the borrowed category undersells the product. That is fine. The first meeting does not need to understand you. It needs to happen.

| Stage | What you call it | Who hears it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| First meeting | The nearest existing category | Procurement, the budget holder |
| Pilot | A narrow problem with a cost attached | The operational owner |
| Expansion | What it really is | The sponsor and the board |

## Sell to the person who feels the pain today

The visionary in the organisation will love your product. They will take every meeting. They rarely sign.

Find the person with a hard cost on their own budget: the head of operations with a maintenance bill, the risk lead with a loss number, the compliance manager with an audit deadline. They have a reason to act this quarter. The visionary has a reason to talk.

Use the visionary as a sponsor. Ask them to open the door to the owner of the cost. Then build the case for that owner, in their numbers, on their timeline. Gartner's consensus finding is the reason to do it in that order: the cost owner is the person who can turn a group of different opinions into one decision. Our explainer on the [buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) covers the other roles to map.

First customers are design partners (see [Your first ten customers are design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/)). Here the design partner must also be a cost owner, or the pilot never converts. The next part of this series, [First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet](https://lowob.com/research/first-customers-in-a-market-that-doesnt-exist-yet/), sets out how to choose them.

## Product truth and the claims register for something new

The product truth still applies: one sentence about what the product does that is true today. For a new technology, the temptation is to write what it will do. Resist it.

The claims register is harder when references are few. Keep three columns: what we claim, what evidence supports it, who can verify it. Where the evidence is a lab result rather than a deployment, say so. Where the only reference is a pilot under NDA, record what you can share and what you cannot.

Buyers in new categories expect thin proof. They do not expect exaggeration. One overstated claim costs more than ten honest gaps.

## Investor story versus customer story

The investor buys the category: why it will exist, how big it gets, why you win it. The customer buys a problem solved: this process, this quarter, this saving.

Keep them in separate documents with separate owners. When the customer story leaks into the investor deck, the raise looks small. When the investor story leaks into the sales deck, the buyer cannot find the number and the deal stalls.

This is one system, not three problems (see [You don't have three problems](https://lowob.com/research/you-dont-have-three-problems/)). In emerging tech that means the two stories share a product truth and a claims register, and nothing else.

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Status quo cost | Written down in the buyer's own numbers |
| Category | A borrowed category gets the first meeting; the expansion story is ready for after the pilot |
| Buyer | A named cost owner, not the visionary |
| Product truth | Describes what works today, not the roadmap |
| Claims register | Each claim marked as deployed, piloted or tested in lab |
| Two stories | Investor story and customer story in separate documents |

## lowob takeaways

- **Position against the status quo.** Price against what it costs, not against a budget that does not exist.
- **Expect to lose to no decision.** Make the cost of waiting visible to every member of the buying group.
- **Sell to the cost owner.** Use the visionary as a sponsor.
- **Keep two stories apart.** Investor and customer stories in separate documents with separate owners.

## Common questions

### How do you sell a new technology when the customer has no budget for it?

Write down what the current way of doing things costs in the buyer's own numbers, then price the product against that. A buyer can approve a saving, not a category. Once the saving is proven, the owner can create a permanent budget line.

### Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers stall when they fear making the wrong choice and when the buying group disagrees. Dixon and McKenna's analysis of 2.5 million sales calls found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, and Gartner found 74% of buyer teams showed unhealthy conflict.

### Who should I sell emerging tech to inside a large organisation?

The person with a hard cost on their own budget, such as a head of operations or risk lead. The visionary rarely signs, so use them to open the door.

### Should a startup describe itself as a new category in sales meetings?

Not at first. Use the nearest existing category to get the meeting, prove a narrow pilot, then widen the frame to what the product really is.

Menlo invests in AI companies, so weigh it against buyer-side data.

# The Same Build in Four Industries

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-same-build-in-four-industries/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Four composite cases test The Build Order across sectors. A mid-market lender moves the record ahead of the first agent because supervisors may ask it to reconstruct decisions. A regional publisher needs a firewall between sales and editorial context. A parts distributor learns fastest because quotes are graded in days. A luxury jeweller connects less, by design. Three patterns hold across all four.

We ran The Build Order through four composite firms in different sectors: a mid-market lender, a regional publisher, an industrial parts distributor and a luxury jeweller. The commercial line was the right place to start in all four, the wiring was necessary but not sufficient, and the best first agent was always unglamorous. The wider evidence points the same way. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for AI, a reminder that every one of these firms started with a store that needed work before any agent could rely on it. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, which is why the first agents in all four firms targeted preparation and administration rather than the conversation itself. And Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, on cost, unclear value or weak risk controls, describes exactly what a boring first agent and a logged gate are designed to avoid.

Two things changed with the sector. Regulation moved the decision record ahead of the first agent at the lender, and the time it takes for an outcome to arrive decided how fast each firm learned.

*Figure: Orange marks the gateway where each firm got stuck. Green marks where the lender changed the order: the record came before the first agent.*

The first nine parts of this series set out a sequence for building a company's brain: three decisions before any tool, the commercial line as the starting point, the wiring, the record, a first agent and an approval gate. The obvious question is whether the sequence travels. Advisory and services firms have unusually clean commercial decisions: pitches are discrete, the people who win work also deliver it, and the CRM maps reasonably well to how the business runs.

This piece tests the sequence in four other sectors. Each firm is a composite, built from patterns across briefs and engagements rather than from any single company, and each section follows the same structure: where the commercial line really sits, what the wiring connects, the first record and first agent, the gateway that bit, and whether the order held.

## A mid-market lender

**Where the commercial line is.** A lender of around 300 people grows through relationship managers and a network of brokers who refer business. Its commercial decisions are which referrals to prioritise, which pricing exceptions to approve and which brokers deserve more attention. All are frequent and similar, and their outcomes show within months: a loan funds or it does not.

**The wiring.** Email, calendar and the CRM connect as they would anywhere. The difference is what stays out. Identity checks, credit files and account data sit in systems the commercial build must not touch, and the data-access approver named at Gateway 0 does real work. A compliance officer, not the build owner, decides what crosses the wall.

**The record and the first agent.** Here the order bends. Before any agent drafts anything, the lender builds a record of pricing exceptions: the request, the reason, the approver, the expected outcome and the check date. In *Regulators want the chain, not the model* we argued that supervisors inspect the chain of evidence, approval and outcome rather than the model's internals, and supervisory commentary on autonomous AI in US broker-dealers points the same way. The first agent, when it arrives, prepares relationship managers for broker meetings from the CRM and that record. It writes nothing outbound.

**The gateway that bit.** Gateway 1. Every client-facing word already passes compliance review, so "nothing sends without a person" is an existing rule the system must respect. The friction is volume: once drafting is cheap, review queues fill. Our earlier piece *Approval rate measures fatigue too* is the warning: a reviewer approving almost every draft may simply be tired.

**Did the order hold?** No. The record moved ahead of the first agent, and the audit trail became part of the context layer rather than an addition to it.

## A regional publisher

**Where the commercial line is.** A publisher of around 150 people across several titles earns most of its revenue from advertising and sponsorship. Its commercial decisions are which advertisers to pursue, when to grant a rate exception, and how to handle under-delivery through make-goods, credits and renewals.

**The wiring.** Rate cards, the inventory system and campaign delivery reports join the usual email, calendar and CRM. One wall matters more than any other: sales context must not reach the newsroom. An assistant that can see an advertiser's renewal thread and an editor's draft side by side breaches the publication's independence, whatever the permissions technically allow. The wiring is split by design into two context layers that never meet.

**The record and the first agent.** Rate exceptions become the first record, because they are frequent, similar and graded at renewal. The first agent chases insertion orders, compares delivery with what was sold, and drafts renewal briefs from the numbers. In builds like this the renewal brief is often the first AI output sales staff trust, because it is built from delivery data they can check.

**The gateway that bit.** Gateway 1, for a different reason: brand safety. A drafted message that misstates audience figures is a commercial problem; one that implies editorial influence is a reputational one. Approval rules are stricter for anything touching sponsored content.

**Did the order hold?** Yes: commercial first, then wiring, record and agent. It needed a firewall in the middle.

## A parts distributor

**Where the commercial line is.** A distributor of around 220 people sells industrial components to manufacturers and contractors. Its commercial line is not a pipeline in the CRM sense; it is quoting. Inside sales staff answer requests for quotes all day, deciding which to quote, what discount to offer against the price book and what lead time to promise.

**The wiring.** The "CRM" turns out to be the ERP's customer table, plus the price book and a library of specification sheets. That changes the build more than the order. The context layer is mostly the ERP, and the definitions that matter are product codes, customer tiers and what counts as "in stock".

**The record and the first agent.** Quoting is close to the ideal case in *Where judgment arrives first*: thousands of similar decisions a year, outcomes known within days, and a sales director who defends margin every month. The record is the quote itself with two added fields: the reason for any discount beyond the standard tier, and the outcome. The first agent drafts quotes from the request, the price book and the customer's history, and places them in a queue for a person to check.

**The gateway that bit.** Gateway 2, the dollar figure. Because quotes are so measurable, the distributor reaches outcome write-back faster than the others, and the numbers are uncomfortable. Discounts the team believed were winning business turn out, once recorded, to win no more often than standard quotes in some product lines. That is the brain doing its job. It is also the moment the build stops being an IT project and becomes a pricing conversation.

**Did the order hold?** Yes, and it moved fastest. The lesson for other sectors is that the shorter the outcome lag, the sooner the record pays.

## A luxury jeweller

**Where the commercial line is.** A jeweller of around 60 people, with showrooms and a wholesale arm, sells through client advisers and a network of dealers. Its commercial decisions are which clients to invite to private previews, which pieces to place with which dealers, and how to price bespoke commissions.

**The wiring.** The relationship lives in places most build plans ignore: advisers' client books, messaging apps and the order history in the commerce platform. Connecting them raises the sharpest consent question of the four. Clients shared anniversaries, preferences and sizes with an adviser, not with a system. The wiring follows what clients agreed to, and some of the most valuable context is deliberately never connected.

**The record and the first agent.** The first record is preview invitations: who was invited, why, and whether they bought within ninety days. Volume is lower than quoting but the decisions are similar enough to learn from across a season. The first agent prompts advisers rather than clients: an anniversary approaching, a piece matching a past request arriving, a dealer who has not reordered. The adviser decides whether to reach out.

**The gateway that bit.** Gateway 1, in reverse. The risk is not that a bad message is sent; it is that a good relationship starts to feel automated. The firm adopts a stricter rule than "nothing sends without a person": nothing reaches a client that the adviser did not write.

**Did the order hold?** Yes. The commercial line came first and the record paid back within a season, but the wiring step was smaller than anywhere else, by choice.

## What held, and what bent

|  | Lender | Publisher | Distributor | Jeweller |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial line | Broker referrals and pricing exceptions | Advertising and sponsorship sales | Quoting | Clienteling and dealer placement |
| Main context | CRM; credit data walled off | Rate cards, inventory, delivery reports | ERP, price book, specifications | Client books, messaging, order history |
| First record | Pricing exceptions | Rate exceptions | Discount reasons on quotes | Preview invitations |
| First agent | Meeting preparation for relationship managers | Insertion orders and renewal briefs | Draft quotes in a review queue | Prompts for advisers |
| Outcome lag | Months | A renewal cycle | Days | A season |
| Gateway that bit | 1: review fatigue | 1: brand safety | 2: uncomfortable numbers | 1: the human relationship |
| Order held? | Bent: record first | Held, with a firewall | Held, fastest | Held, lighter wiring |

Three findings held in all four firms.

**The commercial line was the right place to start.** In every case it had the most frequent, most gradable decisions and someone who had to defend them.

**The wiring was necessary and insufficient.** Every firm got faster preparation from connecting its sources. None got a reason it had not recorded.

**The best first agent was unglamorous.** Meeting preparation, renewal briefs, draft quotes and reminders. Nothing autonomous reached a customer.

The wider evidence points the same way. Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for AI, a reminder that every one of these firms started with a store that needed work before any agent could rely on it. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, which is why the first agents in all four firms targeted preparation and administration rather than the conversation itself. And Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by 2027, on cost, unclear value or weak risk controls, describes exactly what a boring first agent and a logged gate are designed to avoid.

Two things changed with the sector. Regulation moved the record ahead of the first agent at the lender. And the outcome lag set the pace of learning: days at the distributor, a season at the jeweller, months at the lender.

> The shorter the time between a decision and its outcome, the sooner the record pays for itself.

Illustrative example: the distributor's discount rule

Decision
:   Stop discretionary discounts beyond the standard tier on two product lines for one quarter.

Reason and owner
:   Six months of recorded outcomes showed no higher win rate for discounted quotes in those lines. Owned by the sales director.

What changed
:   Quotes in those lines carry a flag so outcomes can be compared; the rule is reviewed after a quarter.

Illustrative: all four firms in this piece are composites built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The commercial line travels.** It looks different in every sector, but it is always where decisions are most frequent and most gradable.
- **Find the sector's wall.** Credit files, the newsroom, client confidences: every industry has context that must never be connected.
- **Outcome lag sets the pace.** The shorter it is, the sooner the record pays back.
- **Regulation moves the record forward.** Where a supervisor will ask why, record before you automate.

Gateway card

### Before moving to Gateway 2 in your sector

- One commercial decision class recorded with reasons and outcomes
- The sector's wall named and enforced in the wiring
- A first agent that drafts but never sends
- The outcome lag for your main decision measured

## Common questions

### Does the same AI build order work in every industry?

It held in three of the four sectors we tested. In regulated sectors such as lending, the decision record and audit trail should come before the first agent, because supervisors may ask the firm to reconstruct automated decisions.

### What is the best first AI agent for a distributor?

A quoting assistant that drafts quotes from the price book and customer history into a review queue. Quotes are graded within days, so the record of discount reasons pays back quickly.

### How should publishers use AI agents in ad sales?

For insertion orders, delivery reconciliation and renewal briefs, with a strict separation between sales and editorial context.

### Can luxury retailers use AI without losing the personal touch?

Yes, if agents prompt client advisers rather than clients, and nothing reaches a client that the adviser did not write.
