# What Is Agentic AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agentic-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agentic AI describes systems where a language model decides its own steps and uses tools to reach a goal, rather than answering a single prompt. Gartner expects a third of enterprise applications to include it by 2028, and also expects over 40% of current projects to be cancelled. The safe path is to treat autonomy as a dial and start with low-risk internal work.

Agentic AI is software that pursues a goal by planning its own steps, calling tools and acting on the results, with limited human supervision. It differs from a chatbot, which answers one prompt, and from a fixed workflow, which follows steps written in advance. The category is growing fast and failing often. Teams that succeed set the level of autonomy per task and start with work that is cheap to get wrong.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What agentic AI means

IBM's definition is a useful starting point: agentic AI is a system that can accomplish a specific goal with limited supervision. Where generative AI produces content in response to a prompt, agentic AI applies those outputs towards a goal, one step after another.

Anthropic, in its December 2024 guidance on building agents, draws a sharper line. Workflows are systems where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are systems where the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use. Both are "agentic systems", and both are built from the same unit: a model with access to retrieval, tools and memory.

Anthropic's advice is to find the simplest solution possible and add complexity only when needed. Many business problems need a workflow, not an agent.

| It is | It is not |
| --- | --- |
| A model that plans steps and chooses tools to reach a goal | A chatbot that answers one question and stops |
| Software that reads from and writes to other systems | A rules engine or RPA script with fixed branches |
| Something whose autonomy you set per task | A product that is either "on" or "off" |
| A component inside a larger system of data, records and review | The whole system on its own |

## How it works, and why it matters on the commercial line

An agent runs a loop: it receives a goal, reads from connected systems, calls a tool such as a CRM search, checks the result and decides again. Standards such as the Model Context Protocol make those connections cheaper to build.

The loop makes agents both useful and risky. A model that can update a CRM record can update the wrong one. So the question for a commercial team is what the agent may do without a person.

**lowob** treats this as a dial with five settings:

| Level | What the agent does | Example on the commercial line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0 Answer | Responds to questions only | "Which deals have had no activity in 30 days?" |
| 1 Draft | Prepares work for a person to send or apply | Follow-up email drafts in a review queue |
| 2 Act with approval | Takes an action once a person approves it | Updates a deal stage after a click to confirm |
| 3 Act and report | Takes reversible actions and reports them | Fixes missing fields, then lists the changes nightly |
| 4 Act alone | Acts without review | Rarely appropriate for anything client-facing |

Nothing client-facing should sit above level 1 at the start. Nothing sends without a person.

Gartner predicts that by 2028 at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agentic AI, up from 0% in 2024. Yet in its January 2025 poll of 3,412 webinar attendees, only 19% reported significant investment.

## Where to start, and the common mistakes

The failure pattern is consistent. Gartner's Anushree Verma said most agentic AI projects are "early stage experiments or proofs of concept". McKinsey's 2025 survey of 1,993 respondents found that while 62% were experimenting with agents, only 23% were scaling them anywhere in the enterprise.

Three mistakes account for most of the waste:

- **Starting with the most visible job.** Autonomous outbound or a prospect-facing chatbot reaches clients directly, so a bad day becomes a client apology.
- **Buying a label.** Many products marketed as agents are assistants or scripts renamed. See our explainer on agent washing.
- **Skipping the record.** An agent that acts without writing down what it did, and why, leaves nothing to audit and nothing to learn from.

A better first job is frequent, checkable, low in blast radius and disliked. On the commercial line, a pipeline clerk that keeps the CRM current and drafts follow-ups passes all four tests.

Agents are also only the reasoning stage of what **lowob** calls the enterprise brain. Without clean data and a decision record around them, they reason over noise.

## lowob takeaways

- **Define it by behaviour.** An agent chooses its own steps and tools; a workflow follows steps you wrote.
- **Prefer the simpler option.** Use a workflow unless the task really needs the model to decide the path.
- **Set autonomy per task.** Reversible internal changes can run and report; client-facing work stays a draft.
- **Start boring.** Pick a first job whose worst day is an internal annoyance.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between agentic AI and generative AI?

Generative AI produces content in response to a prompt. Agentic AI uses those outputs to pursue a goal across several steps, calling tools and acting on results with limited supervision.

### Is an AI agent the same as a workflow automation?

No. In a workflow, a developer fixes the steps in code. In an agent, the model decides which steps and tools to use. Many business tasks are better served by a workflow.

### Why do agentic AI projects fail?

Gartner cites escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Ambitious, client-facing first projects make all three more likely.

### How much autonomy should an AI agent have?

Set it per task. Answering and drafting are safe starting points; acting alone should be reserved for reversible, internal work with a track record.

## Sources and notes

- [IBM, What is agentic AI?](https://ibm.com/think/topics/agentic-ai), undated explainer. Vendor definition.
- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), 19 December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance.
- Gartner forecast and January 2025 poll, 25 June 2025, as reported by [RCR Wireless](https://www.rcrwireless.com/20250627/business/agentic-ai) and [Reuters via The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says). Analyst predictions; poll of webinar attendees, not a random sample.
- McKinsey, The state of AI in 2025, as reported by [IDM](https://idm.net.au/node/15415). Self-reported survey of 1,993 respondents, June to July 2025.
- The autonomy dial and four tests for a first job are **lowob**'s working method.

- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [What Is Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in the Age of Agents?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-robotic-process-automation/)

## Next move

List three agent ideas your team has discussed and assign each an autonomy level from 0 to 4. Any idea that only works at level 4 should not be your first project.

# Demand Generation Economics

Source: https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Lead counts are the wrong unit for B2B demand: Forrester finds fewer than 1% of leads become closed deals. The useful chain runs from spend to qualified opportunities, wins, gross margin and payback. Worked back from a payback target, that chain gives every channel a maximum cost per opportunity. This piece sets out the arithmetic, the benchmarks and their limits, and why demand capture always looks cheaper than demand creation.

Demand generation should be managed on the cost of a qualified opportunity and the time it takes a won customer to pay that cost back, not on lead volume. Forrester's research finds fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, so a programme optimised for leads is optimised for the wrong thing. Work backwards from a payback target and every channel gets a ceiling: the most it can spend to produce one qualified opportunity. The harder part is that buyers are, by 6sense's estimate, nearly 70% through their process before they speak to a seller, so the spend that creates demand is the spend that is hardest to measure.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 7 set out the commercial measures a board will trust. CAC payback was one of them. This part opens it up, because the number a board sees at the end of a quarter is the product of dozens of smaller spending decisions made by the marketing team during it. If those decisions are made on lead volume or cost per click, the payback figure arrives as a surprise. If they are made on the same chain the board uses, it does not.

## Lead volume is the wrong unit

Most marketing teams still report leads, and many are paid on them. The problem is that the lead is a poor proxy for what the business buys. Forrester's analysis, published in November 2023, found fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, and that multiple leads typically feed a single opportunity. The same work found 28% of B2B buyers purchase in groups of four to nine people and another 46% in groups of two to three.

That has two consequences. A team rewarded for leads will generate several per opportunity and count each one. And a team that sees three people from one company each download one asset will score them as three weak leads, when Forrester's point is that this is a stronger signal than one person downloading three. McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found buyers use about ten interaction channels during a purchase, double the 2016 figure, which makes any single-touch lead count even less representative.

The fix is to move the unit of account up one level, to the qualified opportunity: a buying group with a confirmed need, a budget holder in contact and a dated next step. Our explainer on [the marketing funnel](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-marketing-funnel/) covers how stages are usually drawn; the point here is that the economics should be calculated at the opportunity stage, because that is the first point at which sales and marketing agree something real exists.

## The chain from spend to cash

The chain that matters has five links: spend, qualified opportunities, win rate, contract value after gross margin, and payback. ChartMogul's definition of the last link is standard: CAC payback in months equals customer acquisition cost divided by monthly revenue per account multiplied by gross margin. Gross margin belongs in the denominator because only the margin left after delivery costs can repay what was spent to win the customer.

A worked quarter shows how the links combine.

| Link | Illustrative figure | How it is calculated |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Programme spend | £60,000 | Media, events, content and tools for the quarter |
| Qualified opportunities | 40 | Opportunities meeting the written definition |
| Cost per qualified opportunity | £1,500 | £60,000 ÷ 40 |
| Win rate | 25% | Won ÷ qualified, for this cohort |
| New customers | 10 | 40 × 25% |
| Sales cost for the quarter | £90,000 | Salaries, commission and tools, allocated |
| Customer acquisition cost | £15,000 | (£60,000 + £90,000) ÷ 10 |
| Annual contract value | £30,000 | Average for won deals |
| Monthly gross margin per customer | £1,750 | £30,000 ÷ 12 × 70% margin |
| CAC payback | 8.6 months | £15,000 ÷ £1,750 |

All figures are illustrative. The structure is what matters: a change in any one link moves payback, and the marketing team controls two of them directly (spend and the number of qualified opportunities) and influences a third (win rate, through the quality of what it sends).

## Working backwards to a ceiling

The same chain run in reverse gives each channel a spending limit. Suppose the board has agreed a payback target of 12 months. Then:

1. **Maximum acquisition cost** is 12 × £1,750 = £21,000 per customer.
2. **Subtract sales cost per win.** At £90,000 a quarter and ten wins, that is £9,000, leaving £12,000 for marketing.
3. **Multiply by win rate.** At 25%, the maximum marketing cost per qualified opportunity is £12,000 × 25% = £3,000.

Any channel producing qualified opportunities below £3,000 is inside the target; any channel above it is either subsidised by cheaper channels or losing money. The ceiling moves with win rate, which is why a segment where the firm wins one deal in eight can afford far less marketing per opportunity than one where it wins one in three. That is the economic case for the segment choices in Part 3.

> A payback target is a budget rule in disguise. Work it backwards and every channel gets a price it must beat.

Two cautions. The ceiling uses average sales cost, and the marginal cost of the next opportunity is usually higher than the average, because the cheapest sources are used first. And win rate must be measured on the cohort of opportunities a channel produced, not on the firm's overall rate, or a channel that sends weak opportunities will borrow the credibility of the strong ones.

## What the benchmarks say, and what they hide

Benchmarks are useful for orientation and dangerous as targets. Bessemer's analysis of its cloud portfolio found average CAC payback of about 15 months for companies with $1m to $10m of annual recurring revenue, and suggested targets of under 12 months for small-business customers, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. ChartMogul gives similar ranges, noting that sales cycle length and churn both affect whether a given payback is healthy.

Payback on its own hides retention. The 2025 SaaS Benchmarks report from Growth Unhinged and High Alpha, drawn from more than 800 companies, grouped respondents by payback and net revenue retention. Companies with low payback and high retention averaged 71% growth; those with high payback and low retention averaged 10%. A firm can hit its payback target by acquiring customers cheaply who leave quickly, and the payback figure will not show it. Report payback beside gross retention, as Part 7 recommends.

Benchmarks also come from recurring-revenue software firms. A services firm with project revenue has no monthly recurring margin to divide by. The equivalent is gross margin from the first year of work per client, and the same arithmetic applies.

## Capture and creation

The hardest problem in demand economics is that the two kinds of spend behave differently and are measured as if they were the same.

6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers are nearly 70% of the way through their purchasing process before they contact a seller, and 81% already have a preferred vendor at first contact. Most of the decision is made before any lead form is filled in. Spend that reaches buyers in that period creates demand. Spend that catches them when they finally search for a vendor captures it.

The pool being captured is also small at any one time. John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, in a May 2021 report for LinkedIn's B2B Institute, estimated that something like 5% of B2B buyers are in the market in a given quarter, reasoning from corporations changing providers such as their principal bank or law firm around once every five years. Capture spend competes for that 5%; creation spend reaches the other 95% before they need to buy.

|  | Demand capture | Demand creation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Examples | Brand search, retargeting, review sites, inbound follow-up | Research, events, partner programmes, thought leadership, outbound to new segments |
| Time to effect | Days to weeks | Months to quarters |
| How it looks in attribution | Cheap, because it sits next to the conversion | Expensive, because credit is diluted or lost |
| What it actually tells you | How efficiently existing demand is harvested | Whether the pool of future buyers is growing |
| The usual error | Over-funding it because the cost per opportunity looks low | Cutting it because the cost per opportunity looks high |

Capture channels always look efficient because they sit closest to the conversion. Our piece on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers how to estimate what they actually cause, including converting an incrementality share into a cost per caused outcome. The economic consequence is simple: apply the cost-per-opportunity ceiling to capture channels on an incremental basis, and judge creation channels on a longer window with a leading indicator agreed in advance, such as qualified opportunities from target accounts that had no prior contact.

Our explainer on [brand versus performance marketing](https://lowob.com/research/brand-vs-performance-marketing/) covers the wider argument. Binet and Field's 2019 analysis of IPA effectiveness data for the B2B Institute found B2B businesses grew best with about 46% of budget on brand building and 54% on activation. Treat that as a reference point drawn from award-entry cases, not a target. For budget purposes, the practical rule is to set the split deliberately, record it, and review it annually rather than letting the quarterly cost-per-opportunity report shift money towards capture one quarter at a time.

## Velocity is part of the cost

The economics also depend on how fast opportunities turn into cash. Pipedrive's version of the standard sales velocity formula multiplies the number of opportunities by average deal size and win rate, and divides by sales cycle length. Shortening the cycle raises velocity without any change in spend.

That matters for demand budgets because cycle length sets how much pipeline is needed. As Part 7 noted, coverage requirements fall as cycles shorten. A firm that cuts its average cycle from 90 to 60 days needs roughly a third less pipeline in flight to land the same bookings in a year, which means a third less demand spend at the same cost per opportunity. Work that removes friction from the sales process is, in economic terms, demand generation.

## Making the budget a recorded decision

The budget itself should be recorded as a decision, in the format The Build Order uses for any commercial decision worth recording: the allocation by channel, the reason, the owner, the expected cost per qualified opportunity for each channel, and a check date. At the check date, the actual cost per opportunity and the cohort win rate are written back.

After two or three quarters the record answers questions that a dashboard cannot: which channel forecasts were consistently optimistic, which channels improved with more spend and which degraded, and whether the creation budget produced the leading indicator it was meant to. Our piece on [single-channel dependency](https://lowob.com/research/single-channel-dependency/) covers the related risk of a budget that has drifted into one source.

**Where the method strains.** Long enterprise cycles mean a quarter's cohort may not close for a year; use stage progression as a leading indicator and say so. Small volumes mean a channel producing six opportunities a quarter will show noisy win rates; pool two or three quarters before acting. And opportunity definitions must be stable, or the cost per opportunity improves simply because the bar was lowered.

Illustrative example: the ceiling meets the events budget

Decision
:   Set a maximum cost per qualified opportunity of £3,000 for all capture channels, measured on incremental opportunities, and fund events on a two-quarter window against target-account opportunities.

Reason and owner
:   Events had been cut twice because their cost per lead looked high, while brand search absorbed the savings. Owned by the head of marketing; ceiling agreed with the finance director from the 12-month payback target.

What changed
:   Two paid search campaigns fell above the ceiling once measured incrementally and were cut; the events budget was restored for two quarters with a written check date.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B technology firm, built from patterns across engagements; figures are illustrative.

## lowob takeaways

- **Count opportunities, not leads.** The qualified opportunity is the first unit sales and marketing both believe in.
- **Run the chain both ways.** Forward it gives payback; backward it gives every channel a cost ceiling.
- **Read payback with retention.** Cheap customers who leave are not efficient acquisition.
- **Measure capture incrementally.** Channels next to the conversion always look cheaper than they are.
- **Record the budget.** Expected cost per opportunity by channel, written back at a check date.

Gateway card

### Before you set next quarter's demand budget

- A written definition of a qualified opportunity, agreed by sales and marketing
- Cost per qualified opportunity by channel for the last two quarters
- Win rate by channel cohort, not the firm-wide average
- A payback target agreed with finance, and the ceiling it implies
- The split between capture and creation stated and recorded
- A check date for each channel's expected cost per opportunity

## Common questions

### How do you calculate CAC payback?

Divide customer acquisition cost by the monthly revenue per account multiplied by gross margin. A £15,000 acquisition cost against £1,750 of monthly gross margin pays back in about 8.6 months.

### What is a good CAC payback period for B2B?

Bessemer suggests under 12 months for small-business customers, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. Read it alongside retention, because cheap customers who churn can produce a good payback figure.

### Why should marketing stop reporting leads?

Forrester finds fewer than 1% of leads become closed deals and several leads often feed one opportunity, so lead volume rewards activity rather than revenue. Qualified opportunities are a better unit.

### How much should we spend per opportunity?

Work backwards from a payback target: maximum acquisition cost, minus sales cost per win, multiplied by win rate, gives the most marketing can spend per qualified opportunity.

# What Is Pipeline Coverage?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-pipeline-coverage/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pipeline coverage compares the value of open opportunities with the revenue still to be won in a period. The familiar 3x rule only holds at a one-in-three win rate, so firms that copy it often plan with too little or too much pipeline. This explainer sets out the formula, how to derive your own ratio from win rate and cycle length, and how to stop coverage being inflated by deals that will never close.

Pipeline coverage is the value of open opportunities expected to close in a period, divided by the revenue target still to be met in that period. A ratio of 3x means there is three times as much pipeline as target. The right ratio is not a constant: it is roughly the inverse of your win rate by value, adjusted for how much of the pipeline can close in time. Coverage is only as reliable as the stage definitions and close dates behind it.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What pipeline coverage means

The basic formula is simple:

**Pipeline coverage = open pipeline value for the period ÷ remaining target for the period**

HubSpot's example is $500,000 of pipeline against a $100,000 quarterly target, a 5x ratio. The numerator should include only opportunities with a close date inside the period and a stage beyond initial qualification. The denominator should be the target still to win, not the full quota, once part of the quarter has closed.

This explainer is about the ratio and how to set it. The rules that decide what counts as a real opportunity in each stage are covered separately in [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/). The two depend on each other: coverage built on loose stages measures optimism.

## Why 3x is a rule of thumb, not a target

The 3x convention comes from an implicit one-in-three win rate. Jordan's article for Salesforce makes the point directly: the ratio holds only at a 33% win rate and a one-year cycle. A seller who wins 10% of pipeline value needs about ten times their target; one who wins 50% needs about twice. Short cycles change the picture too, because pipeline created during the period can still close within it.

| Win rate by value | Coverage needed (no new pipeline closing in period) |
| --- | --- |
| 50% | 2.0x |
| 33% | 3.0x |
| 25% | 4.0x |
| 20% | 5.0x |
| 10% | 10.0x |

Win rates are not stable. Ebsta and Pavilion's analysis of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies found win rates in 2023 down 18% on 2022 and 27% on 2021. A team that set its coverage target in 2021 and kept it would have been under-covered without knowing it. The same data showed 73% of reps missed quota in the second half of 2023.

There is also a ceiling. HubSpot's warning about ratios above 8x reflects a common pattern: the more pipeline sits in the CRM, the less of it has been tested. Very high coverage usually means old opportunities with rolling close dates.

## How to set and use your own ratio

A defensible coverage target takes an afternoon with CRM data:

1. **Calculate win rate by value.** Use opportunities that reached your first qualified stage in the last four quarters. Divide closed-won value by the total value that reached a decision, including closed-lost and no-decision.
2. **Split by segment.** New business and expansion usually win at very different rates. So do enterprise and mid-market. One company-wide ratio hides both.
3. **Invert it.** Required coverage is roughly one divided by win rate. Add a margin if close dates regularly slip out of the quarter.
4. **Measure at fixed points.** Record coverage on day one of the quarter and again at week six. Coverage that drops sharply mid-quarter shows deals with false close dates.
5. **Clean before counting.** Exclude opportunities with no activity in 30 days, no next step, or a close date already moved twice.

Gartner's finding that fewer than half of sales leaders trust their forecast points to the same root cause. Its 2020 survey also found only 47% of respondents believed their organisation had high-quality data. Coverage inherits that quality.

For **lowob**, coverage is a reading of the record, not a target to hit. When an agent or assistant summarises pipeline health, it reads the same stages and close dates a person would. If those fields are stale, the agent reports false coverage with confidence. The fix is in the record, not the model.

## lowob takeaways

- **Derive the ratio.** Required coverage is roughly the inverse of your own win rate by value.
- **Segment it.** New business, expansion and deal size each need their own figure.
- **Distrust high coverage.** Above about 8x, the pipeline usually needs cleaning, not celebrating.
- **Fix the inputs first.** Stage definitions and close dates decide whether coverage means anything.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate pipeline coverage?

Divide the value of open opportunities with a close date in the period by the revenue target still to be met in that period.

### What is a good pipeline coverage ratio?

It depends on win rate. At a 33% win rate, 3x is about right. At 20%, you need about 5x. Calculate yours from the last four quarters.

### Why is 3x pipeline coverage the standard?

It assumes a one-in-three win rate. Teams with lower win rates or longer cycles need more coverage, and teams with higher win rates need less.

### What is the difference between pipeline coverage and sales velocity?

Coverage is a snapshot of how much pipeline exists against target. Sales velocity measures how fast pipeline turns into revenue, combining volume, deal size, win rate and cycle length.

## Sources and notes

- [HubSpot, Sales Pipeline Coverage](https://www.hubspot.com/glossary/sales-pipeline-coverage), undated. Vendor glossary; source of the formula, common ratios and the 8:1 warning.
- [Salesforce, Pipeline Coverage](https://www.salesforce.com/blog/pipeline-coverage/), undated, by Jason Jordan. Vendor-hosted article; source of the win-rate logic behind 3x.
- [Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks](https://www.ebsta.com/ebsta-pavilion-b2b-sales-benchmarks-2024/), 2024. Vendor dataset of 4.2 million opportunities across 530 companies.
- [Gartner, Less Than 50% of Sales Leaders Have High Confidence in Forecasting Accuracy](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-02-12-gartner-says-less-than-50--of-sales-leaders-and-selle), February 2020. Survey; sample size not stated in the release.

## Related research

- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)
- [What Is Sales Velocity?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-velocity/)
- [What Is CRM Data Hygiene?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [Qualification Frameworks Compared](https://lowob.com/research/qualification-frameworks-compared/)

## Next move

Calculate your win rate by value for the last four quarters, split into new business and expansion. Invert each figure, and compare the result with the coverage ratio your team currently aims for.

# What Is UGC, and Why Brands Now Pay for It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ugc/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: UGC now means two things: genuine customer content, credible because it was not commissioned, and paid creator content styled to look organic, which performs in paid social. Use both, keep them distinct, and disclose and review the paid kind as the advertising it is, including the FTC's rules on actual consumers, typical results and fake reviews.

UGC now means two things: genuine customer content, credible because it was not commissioned, and paid creator content styled to look organic, which performs in paid social. Use both, keep them distinct, and disclose and review the paid kind as the advertising it is. The rules are specific. The FTC's Endorsement Guides say ads that present people as actual consumers should use actual consumers or say otherwise, and its 2024 rule bans testimonials from people who never used the product.

User-generated content, UGC, originally meant exactly what it says: content made by users, customers posting photos, reviews, and videos about products on their own initiative. Brands loved it because it was credible and free. Nielsen's 2021 Trust in Advertising study found recommendations from people consumers know were the most trusted channel, at 89% of respondents.

The term has since been adopted by the advertising industry to describe something different: content produced by paid creators, deliberately styled to look like an ordinary person's post, for use in the brand's own advertising. The two meanings now coexist, and the distinction matters for both effectiveness and law.

## The two kinds

**Organic UGC** is made by real customers, unpaid, on their own accounts. Brands can request permission to reuse it, feature it, and reward it, and it remains the most credible form of social proof available because it was not commissioned.

**Commissioned UGC-style content** is made by creators paid to produce it, usually not posted on the creator's own account at all but delivered to the brand for use in paid ads. The creator's following is irrelevant; what the brand is buying is the format, a person on a phone talking about the product the way a friend would, because that format performs in paid social far better than polished production does.

|  | Organic UGC | Commissioned UGC-style content | Creator post on own account |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who makes it | A real customer, unpaid | A paid creator, often acting | A paid creator, as themselves |
| Where it runs | Customer's account; brand reposts with permission | Brand's ad account | Creator's account, sometimes boosted |
| What the brand buys | Permission to reuse | The format and usage rights | Reach, voice and the format |
| Legal status | Brand becomes responsible once it reuses or rewards it | The brand's own advertising | An endorsement with a material connection |
| Disclosure | Disclose any reward or incentive given | Platform ad label; if presented as a real customer, use one or say otherwise | Clear label such as "ad" in the post itself |

## Why brands pay for it

Paid social platforms reward content that looks native to the feed. Studio-produced ads are identified and skipped; a person holding a phone is watched. Commissioned UGC-style content is cheap to produce in volume, fast to iterate, and allows dozens of variations to be tested against one another. For a performance programme that needs new creative every few weeks, it has become the default.

The platforms have built products around it. TikTok's Spark Ads let an advertiser promote an organic post from its own account or from a creator's account that has authorised it, with the creator choosing an authorisation period of 7, 30, 60 or 365 days when generating the code. That choice is a usage-rights decision made in an app, and it should match the contract.

The spend behind creator content is growing. The IAB put US creator ad spend at $37 billion in 2025 and projected $44 billion in 2026.

## What it costs

Commissioned content is priced per piece, from a modest fee for a short video from a newer creator to considerably more from experienced UGC creators with a track record of producing ads that convert. Platforms and marketplaces exist to source and manage creators at scale. Usage rights, how long and where the brand may run the content, are priced separately and are often the larger cost.

A usage-rights clause should name four things: the channels (organic, paid social, website, connected TV), the territories, the term, and whether the brand may edit or cut the footage. A thirty-day paid social licence and a perpetual all-media licence for the same video are different purchases.

> The "it looks organic" quality that makes the format effective is precisely what the disclosure rules exist to address.

## The disclosure question

When commissioned content runs as the brand's own ad, in the brand's ad account, it is an advertisement and is treated as one; the person in it is effectively an actor, and the platform labels it as sponsored. Claims made in it are the brand's claims and must meet the same standards as any ad, including, in reviewed categories, the same compliance review.

The actor point has a specific rule. The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in 2023, say advertisements presenting endorsements by people represented as "actual consumers" should use actual consumers "in both the audio and video," or clearly and conspicuously disclose that they are not. A UGC-style ad scripted for a paid performer and framed as a customer's story needs that disclosure.

When a paid creator posts UGC-style content on their own account presenting it as their own opinion, it is an endorsement, and the material connection must be disclosed clearly and conspicuously under the endorsement rules that apply in most jurisdictions. The "it looks organic" quality that makes the format effective is precisely what the disclosure rules exist to address. In the UK the ASA, CAP and CMA's October 2026 guide asks for "#Ad" at the very beginning of the content and notes that AI-generated content must comply too.

Testimonial content also carries its own rules: claims about results must reflect what a typical customer can expect, or say otherwise, and fabricated or scripted testimonials presented as genuine are prohibited. The Endorsement Guides treat a result as implying typicality unless the advertiser discloses what people generally achieve, and found generic disclaimers such as "results not typical" insufficient in the Commission's testing. The FTC's 2024 rule on reviews and testimonials goes further: it bans testimonials attributed to people who do not exist, including AI-generated ones, or who had no real experience with the product, and lets the FTC seek civil penalties from knowing violators. The brand can be liable even when the creator is not.

## Using it well

Brief creators on the product truth and the audience's actual doubts, and let them speak naturally; scripted UGC reads as scripted. Produce in volume and test; the format's advantage is iteration. Our playbook on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set up variant tests that end in a choice.

Keep organic UGC separate and honest: feature real customers, with permission, and never edit their words into claims they did not make. The same standard runs through [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/). Give each piece a job as well: our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) covers naming the reader, decision and next action before commissioning.

Apply the compliance library to every piece, because a creator saying "I earned twelve percent" is a yield claim whoever says it. In UK financial services, the FCA's guidance on social media promotions expects promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading and to give a balanced view of benefits and risks, in any format. And in restricted categories, remember that the content still has to run somewhere; UGC-style creative does not open a platform that has closed the category. Our explainer on [landing pages and ad review](https://lowob.com/research/landing-pages-and-ad-review/) covers what happens at the review stage.

## lowob takeaways

- **Keep the two kinds apart.** Organic UGC is earned proof; commissioned UGC-style content is advertising.
- **Buy the rights explicitly.** Channels, territories, term and edit rights, matched to any platform authorisation.
- **Do not present actors as customers.** Use real customers or disclose that they are not.
- **Review every claim.** Results must be typical or qualified, and yield claims are yield claims whoever says them.

## Common questions

### What does UGC mean in advertising?

Originally content made by customers on their own initiative. It now also means content produced by paid creators, styled to look like an ordinary person's post, for use in the brand's own advertising.

### Why do brands pay for UGC-style content?

Paid social platforms reward content that looks native to the feed. UGC-style content is cheap to produce in volume, fast to iterate, and lets dozens of variations be tested against one another.

### Do paid UGC creators have to disclose that they were paid?

When a paid creator posts on their own account as their own opinion, it is an endorsement and the connection must be disclosed clearly. When it runs as the brand's ad and presents the person as a customer, the FTC expects real customers or a disclosure that they are not.

### Are fake or AI-generated testimonials illegal?

In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule bans testimonials attributed to people who do not exist, including AI-generated ones, or who never used the product, with civil penalties for knowing violations. UK rules also prohibit fake reviews.

## Sources and notes

- [eCFR, 16 CFR Part 255, Guides concerning the use of endorsements and testimonials in advertising](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255), revised July 2023. US federal guides; interpretive, not a rule.
- [Federal Trade Commission, Final rule banning fake reviews and testimonials](https://www.ftc.gov/news-events/news/press-releases/2024/08/federal-trade-commission-announces-final-rule-banning-fake-reviews-testimonials), 14 August 2024. US regulator; applies to US commerce.
- [ASA, CAP and CMA, Influencers' guide to making clear that ads are ads](https://www.asa.org.uk/static/17cf70a4-f904-4684-a68c8310ba7700e1/Influencers-guide-to-making-clear-that-ads-are-ads.pdf), October 2026. UK regulator guidance under the CAP Code and the DMCC Act 2024.

- [FCA, FG24/1: Finalised guidance on financial promotions on social media](https://fca.org.uk/publications/finalised-guidance/fg24-1-finalised-guidance-financial-promotions-social-media), 26 March 2024. UK regulator guidance; financial promotions only.

# In Emerging Tech, the Only Strategy Question Is Which Bets You Can Take Back.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/emerging-tech-reversible-bets/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Companies in emerging categories are told to move fast and to be careful. Both are true, and the way to hold them together is a sorting rule: make reversible decisions quickly, cheaply and in parallel, and irreversible ones slowly, one at a time, after the reversible ones have produced evidence. This playbook applies the rule to AI and Web3, with the regulatory and market evidence that shows which decisions cannot be taken back.

Companies in emerging categories are told two contradictory things: move fast, because the window is closing, and be careful, because the rules are still being written. Both are true. The way to hold them together is not a balance between speed and caution. It is a sorting rule: which decisions can be taken back, and which cannot. Reversible decisions should be made quickly, cheaply and in parallel. Irreversible ones should be made slowly, one at a time, after the reversible ones have produced evidence.

## Two kinds of decision

A reversible decision is one where being wrong costs a bounded amount and the company can return to roughly where it started. A channel test. A pricing experiment. A partnership with a short term. A market segment tried for a quarter. A feature built behind a flag.

An irreversible decision is one where being wrong changes what the company is. A regulatory posture chosen before the rules are clear. A token launched. A category claimed publicly. A large client accepted at a share of revenue that makes the company dependent on it. A platform relied on as the only channel. A name filed as a trademark. Capital raised on a thesis the company will be held to.

The distinction is old and well tested. Jeff Bezos's 2016 letter to Amazon shareholders described many decisions as "reversible, two-way doors" that can use a lightweight process, and argued that most decisions "should probably be made with somewhere around 70% of the information you wish you had."

Emerging-tech companies fail in a characteristic way: they treat irreversible decisions as if they were reversible, because everyone around them is moving fast, and they treat reversible decisions with a slowness that belongs to the irreversible ones, because the uncertainty makes everything feel weighty.

## The rule

Reversible decisions should be made quickly, cheaply and in parallel. Irreversible ones should be made slowly, expensively and one at a time, after the reversible ones have produced evidence.

That is the same discipline we apply to distribution: observe cheaply in several places, commit completely to one. It generalises to company strategy because the underlying problem is the same. Uncertainty is high, information is expensive, and the cost of a wrong commitment is asymmetric. Our piece on [GTM strategy versus tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/) makes the distribution version of the argument.

> Speed belongs to decisions you can take back, and care belongs to the ones you cannot.

Record the irreversible ones as you make them. A [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with the reason, the owner, the evidence relied on and the expected outcome is what lets a company learn from a one-way door it has already walked through.

## Applying it in AI

In AI, the reversible decisions are which buyer to serve first, which channels to test, which integrations to build, what to charge. The irreversible ones are which model providers to depend on, which data the product accumulates and under what terms, which claims about accuracy and safety the company makes in public, and which regulated use cases it enters.

The evidence shows why those four belong on the slow list.

**Model dependency hardens over time.** Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 CIOs found agentic workflows were making it harder to switch between models, because the surrounding prompts, tools and checks are tuned to each. A model choice that was reversible at prototype stage becomes much less so once customers depend on the workflow. Menlo Ventures' 2026 data shows the supply side is not stable enough to bet on a single provider: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. Our guide to [build versus buy for AI agents](https://lowob.com/research/build-vs-buy-ai-agents/) covers how to keep that door open.

**Public claims do not come back.** In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers for saying they used AI in ways they did not, with $400,000 in combined penalties. In September 2024 the FTC's Operation AI Comply targeted companies whose AI claims could not be substantiated. An enforcement record stays public long after the copy is corrected.

**The rules move under you.** The EU AI Act's stand-alone high-risk obligations under Annex III were deferred to 2 December 2027 by the amendments in Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. A company that rebuilt its product around the original timeline made a reasonable choice that turned out to be early. A company that entered a high-risk use case without a compliance plan made one that will be expensive to reverse. Our guide to [the EU AI Act for commercial teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/) covers the current dates.

A company that spends its first year testing buyers and channels cheaply, while being deliberately slow about its data terms and public claims, will look less decisive than one that announced a category on day one. It will also still exist when the category's rules are written.

## Applying it in Web3

In Web3, the reversibility line is unusually sharp, because so much is literally irreversible. A token, once distributed, cannot be un-distributed. A treasury decision made on-chain is public forever. A regulatory posture, once a product is live in a jurisdiction, is a fact the regulator has already observed.

The EU shows what that last point means in practice. ESMA's June 2026 statement on the end of MiCA's transitional period on 1 July 2026 told unauthorised crypto-asset service providers to stop onboarding new EU clients, stop marketing, restrict services to an orderly exit and tell clients repeatedly about wind-down timelines. A firm that treated its EU posture as something it could settle later found the decision had been made for it. Our piece on [token or no token](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) applies the same logic to the launch decision.

The reversible decisions (which audience to serve first, which distribution partners to try, which incentives to test at small scale) deserve speed. The irreversible ones deserve the slowest, most expensive process the company can afford, including advice the founders would rather not pay for.

| Decision | Reversible? | Fast path | Slow path: evidence needed first |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| First buyer segment | Yes | Test two segments for a quarter each | Not needed |
| Channel mix | Yes | Small budgets in several channels, one owner | Not needed |
| Price point | Mostly | Price experiment with a review date | Not needed |
| Primary model provider | Becomes less so | Run the core workflow on a second model | Cost, quality and switching time on both |
| Public accuracy or safety claim | No | None | A dated eval a buyer or regulator could check |
| Regulated use case or jurisdiction | No | None | Legal opinion, compliance plan, licence route |
| Token launch | No | None | User demand without the token, legal review, distribution plan |

## Timing windows are real, and they are narrower than they look

Emerging categories have moments when decisions get made: budget cycles, regulatory clarity, a platform opening or closing a category, a competitor's failure, the weeks after a major model release. A company should know which windows matter to its buyers and prepare reversible experiments to run inside them.

But a window is a reason to be ready, not a reason to make an irreversible commitment in a hurry. The company that has already run its cheap tests enters the window with evidence. The company that has not enters it with conviction, which is what a bet feels like from the inside.

## A one-page strategy discipline

List the ten decisions in front of the company this quarter. Mark each reversible or irreversible. For the reversible ones, write the test, the budget and the date. For the irreversible ones, write what evidence would have to exist before the decision is made, and which reversible decisions produce that evidence.

| Column | For a reversible decision | For an irreversible decision |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owner | One named person | One named person, plus who must agree |
| Test or evidence | The test and what result would change the plan | The evidence that must exist before deciding |
| Budget | The most it can cost if wrong | The cost of being wrong, written down |
| Date | When the test reports | The earliest date the evidence can exist |
| Feeds | Which irreversible decision this informs | Which reversible tests produce the evidence |

Most companies discover that they have been arguing about the irreversible decisions and neglecting the reversible ones that would settle the argument.

In an emerging category, speed belongs to decisions you can take back and care belongs to the ones you cannot. Run the reversible tests first, and let them earn the irreversible commitment.

## lowob takeaways

- **Sort before you debate.** Mark every decision reversible or irreversible before arguing about it.
- **Move fast on the reversible.** Audience, channels, small incentive tests and prices deserve speed and parallel tests.
- **Slow down on the irreversible.** Model dependency, public claims, regulated entry and tokens deserve the slowest process the company can afford.
- **Let tests settle arguments.** Most arguments about one-way doors are settled by two-way tests nobody has run.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a reversible and an irreversible business decision?

A reversible decision costs a bounded amount if wrong and lets the company return to roughly where it started, such as a channel test or a price experiment. An irreversible one changes what the company is, such as a public claim, a token launch or a regulated market entry.

### How should startups make decisions under uncertainty?

Make reversible decisions quickly, cheaply and in parallel, and irreversible ones slowly and one at a time, after the reversible tests have produced evidence. Write down, for each irreversible decision, what evidence must exist first.

### Which AI startup decisions are hard to reverse?

Dependence on one model provider, the data the product accumulates and its terms, public accuracy and safety claims, and entry into regulated use cases. Switching models gets harder as agentic workflows are built around them.

### Why is timing so important in emerging technology markets?

Categories have windows, such as budget cycles, regulatory clarity or a major model release. A window is a reason to have tests ready, not a reason to make an irreversible commitment in a hurry.

# What Is Model Risk Management for AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Model risk management covers the inventory, development, validation, monitoring and governance of models whose errors could cause loss. In April 2026 US banking agencies rescinded SR 11-7 and issued principles-based guidance, SR 26-2, which explicitly excludes generative and agentic AI. The UK PRA's SS1/23 still covers AI used in modelling. For firms outside banking, the discipline is a useful template for AI tools that drive decisions.

Model risk management (MRM) is the discipline of identifying, validating, monitoring and governing the models an organisation relies on, so that a wrong or misused model does not cause financial loss or poor decisions. It grew up in banking. In April 2026 US banking agencies rescinded the long-standing SR 11-7 guidance and replaced it with shorter, risk-based guidance, SR 26-2, which leaves generative and agentic AI out of scope. Firms using AI to drive decisions still need the same core habits: an inventory, a materiality judgment, independent challenge and ongoing monitoring.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What model risk management means

Model risk is the risk of loss from a model that is wrong, or from a correct model used for the wrong purpose. MRM manages it through a lifecycle. SR 26-2 keeps the familiar components while cutting the detail.

| Component | What SR 26-2 says | What it looks like in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory | Should hold "sufficient information to understand model risks", individually and in aggregate | A register of each model, owner, purpose and risk rating |
| Development | Aligned with "model purpose, business use, and banking organization policy" | Documented design choices and data sources |
| Validation | Evaluates "whether models perform as expected", including reliability and limits | Conceptual review, outcomes analysis, ongoing monitoring |
| Monitoring | Whether a model "is performing as expected" over time | Drift checks, overrides tracked, periodic review |
| Governance | Policies and controls across the lifecycle | Approval rights, escalation, internal audit |

## What changed in April 2026

SR 11-7 had been the reference text for MRM, inside and outside banking, since 2011. The agencies' view was that it had come to be applied more prescriptively than intended, especially at smaller banks. SR 26-2 is shorter and principles-based, and states that it does not set enforceable standards.

| Topic | SR 11-7 (2011) | SR 26-2 (2026) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Status | Supervisory guidance, widely treated as a rulebook | Principles; non-compliance alone does not trigger criticism |
| Scope threshold | Commonly applied from $1 billion in assets | Most relevant above $30 billion |
| Model definition | Included mathematical theories | Statistical, economic or financial theories only; spreadsheets and rule engines excluded |
| Risk tiering | General expectation of proportionality | Inherent risk combined with materiality; light oversight for immaterial models |
| Effective challenge | Incentives, competence and influence | Expertise, independence sufficient for objectivity, standing to drive change |
| Generative and agentic AI | Not addressed | Explicitly out of scope |
| Vendor models | Within the MRM framework | Principles still apply where banks cannot validate vendor models; customisations documented |

The AI exclusion is the most discussed change. It does not mean generative AI in banks is unsupervised. The agencies direct banks to their broader risk management and governance for those tools, and have said they will issue a request for information on AI use, including generative and agentic AI.

Outside the US, the UK PRA's supervisory statement SS1/23 applies to UK banks and building societies with internal model approval. Its five principles cover all models used to inform business decisions, built or bought, and one sub-principle addresses the risks of using AI in modelling techniques.

> The new US guidance took generative AI out of model risk scope. It did not take it out of risk management.

## Why it matters outside banking

A 20- to 500-person firm will rarely be supervised for model risk. The discipline is still useful wherever an AI tool influences a decision with money attached: pricing, credit terms for customers, lead prioritisation that sets where sellers spend time, or forecasts presented to a board.

A proportionate version borrows four habits:

| Habit | Question | **lowob** equivalent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory with materiality | Which AI tools drive decisions, and how much money rides on each? | AI inventory with an exposure column |
| Effective challenge | Who outside the owning team reviews the tool's output? | A named reviewer with standing to stop it |
| Outcomes analysis | Did the predictions or recommendations turn out right? | Outcomes written back to the decision record |
| Vendor accountability | What can we check when we cannot see inside the model? | Output sampling, vendor documentation, contract terms |

The third habit is where most firms are weakest. Validation in MRM compares what a model said with what happened. That is the learning step of the enterprise brain: a decision recorded with its expected outcome, and the actual outcome written back later. Without it, nobody can say whether an AI-assisted forecast or score is improving or drifting.

## lowob takeaways

- **SR 11-7 is gone.** SR 26-2 replaced it on 17 April 2026 with principles-based, risk-tiered guidance.
- **Generative and agentic AI sit outside SR 26-2.** Banks govern them through broader risk management, pending further agency work.
- **Materiality decides effort.** Immaterial models get light oversight; decision-driving ones get challenge and validation.
- **Outcomes are the test.** Recording expected and actual outcomes is validation in its simplest form.

## Common questions

### What is model risk management?

The practice of inventorying, validating, monitoring and governing models so that errors or misuse do not cause losses or poor decisions.

### Was SR 11-7 replaced?

Yes. On 17 April 2026 the Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC rescinded SR 11-7 and issued SR 26-2, Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management.

### Does SR 26-2 apply to generative AI?

No. Its footnote 3 places generative and agentic AI models outside its scope. Banks are directed to broader risk management and governance for those tools.

### Do non-banks need model risk management for AI?

Not by regulation in most cases, but the habits of an inventory, independent review and outcome tracking suit any AI tool that drives material decisions.

## Sources and notes

- [Federal Reserve, SR 26-2: Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/sr2602.htm), 17 April 2026, and [attached guidance](https://www.federalreserve.gov/supervisionreg/srletters/SR2602a1.pdf). Primary source; model definition and AI footnote.
- [Orrick, Agencies overhaul model risk management guidance for banks: here's what changed](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/04/Agencies-Overhaul-Model-Risk-Management-Guidance-for-Banks-Heres-What-Changed), April 2026. Law firm analysis comparing SR 11-7 and SR 26-2.
- [Bank of England PRA, SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss), updated 23 April 2026. Primary UK supervisory statement.

## Related research

- [Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/)
- [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [What Is AI Governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/)

## Next move

List the AI tools whose output changes a price, a credit term, a forecast or where sellers spend their time. For each, name one reviewer outside the owning team and start recording expected against actual outcomes.

# Commercial KPIs a Board Will Trust

Source: https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Boards discount commercial numbers because definitions drift, sources disagree and forecasts miss. Gartner found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers have high confidence in their forecast accuracy. A trusted KPI passes four tests: one written definition, a reconciliation to the financials, a stable history with restatements recorded, and a named owner. This piece sets out the tests, an eight-measure pack and how to change a definition without losing the board.

A board trusts a commercial KPI when it has one written definition, reconciles to a number finance already reports, keeps the same meaning from quarter to quarter, and has a named owner who can explain a movement. Most commercial packs fail at least one of those tests. Gartner found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers have high confidence in their organisation's forecasting accuracy, and only 47% believe their organisation has high-quality data. The fix is not more metrics. It is fewer, defined once, with every change of definition recorded like any other commercial decision.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 6 set out the commercial operating rhythm: what gets reviewed weekly, monthly and quarterly. This part covers the numbers that rhythm produces once they leave the building. A sales team can live with rough figures in its own pipeline review, because the people in the room know the caveats. A board cannot. It sees the number without the caveats, compares it with last quarter's, and draws conclusions about strategy, hiring and cash.

## Why boards discount commercial numbers

Finance numbers arrive with a reconciliation and an audit trail. Commercial numbers usually arrive with neither. Three failures account for most of the distrust.

**Definitions drift.** "Qualified pipeline" means one thing in January and another in June, because a new sales leader tightened the stage criteria or marketing started counting webinar sign-ups. Nobody restates the history, so the trend line is two different measures joined together. Our explainer on [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/) covers why stage exit criteria have to be written down for this reason alone.

**Sources disagree.** Marketing reports sourced pipeline from the automation platform, sales reports it from the CRM, and finance reports bookings from the billing system. The three rarely add up, and the board learns to trust none of them. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete, and 37% reported revenue lost as a direct result of poor data.

**Forecasts miss without explanation.** A missed forecast is survivable. A missed forecast with no account of why is not. Gartner's survey of 303 sales leaders, reported in February 2024, found 84% said sales analytics had influenced sales performance less than they expected, with poor data quality cited by 44% as a top barrier.

The common thread is that commercial numbers are produced by the people being measured, from systems that were configured for selling rather than reporting. That is not a reason to distrust the people. It is a reason to put the same controls around commercial numbers that finance already puts around its own.

## Four tests a trusted KPI passes

Finance teams already know how to make an adjusted measure credible: define it, reconcile it to the audited figure, and explain any change in how it is calculated. The standard setters say so. The SEC's 2020 guidance on metrics in MD&A expects a clear definition, how the metric is calculated, why it is useful and how management uses it, and notes that effective controls matter when such metrics are material. IFRS 18, effective from 1 January 2027, requires a note for management-defined performance measures that reconciles each one to an IFRS subtotal and explains how it is calculated and any changes to it. Commercial KPIs need the same treatment, expressed as four tests.

| Test | What it means | The failure it prevents | How to check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Defined once | One written definition, including inclusions, exclusions and the system of record | Two teams reporting the same name for different numbers | Ask two people to calculate it independently |
| Reconciled | The figure ties to something finance reports, or the gap is explained | Pipeline and bookings that never meet revenue | A reconciliation line in the appendix each quarter |
| Stable | The definition has not changed, or history has been restated | A trend that is really two measures stitched together | A change log with dates and the restated series |
| Owned | A named person explains movements and answers for the data | Numbers nobody can defend under questioning | The owner's name printed next to the measure |

The tests are deliberately boring. None requires new software. Each requires someone to write something down and keep it current, which is why they are skipped.

The a16z guide to startup metrics shows how often the first test fails in practice. It warns that bookings and revenue are not interchangeable, that annual recurring revenue should exclude one-time and professional service fees, and that blended customer acquisition cost can hide whether paid campaigns are profitable. Each is a definitional choice a board needs to see stated, because each can move the headline number without anything changing in the business.

## The eight measures that hold up

Most 20- to 500-person B2B firms can run a board pack on eight commercial measures. Services firms will substitute backlog and utilisation for some of the recurring-revenue measures; the tests stay the same.

| Measure | Question it answers | Reconciles to | Typical owner | Leading or lagging |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| New bookings | How much new committed value did we sign? | Contract values; revenue as delivered | Head of sales | Lagging |
| Net revenue retention | Did existing customers grow, net of losses? | Recurring revenue by cohort | Head of account management | Lagging |
| Gross revenue retention | How much did we keep before expansion? | Recurring revenue by cohort | Head of account management | Lagging |
| Pipeline coverage | Is there enough qualified pipeline for the target? | Win rate and cycle length | Head of revenue operations | Leading |
| Win rate by segment | Are we winning where we chose to compete? | Closed-won and closed-lost records | Head of sales | Lagging |
| Sales cycle length | How long does a qualified deal take? | Stage dates in the CRM | Head of revenue operations | Leading |
| CAC payback | How long to recover the cost of winning a customer? | Sales and marketing spend; gross margin | Finance director | Lagging |
| Forecast accuracy | How close was the forecast to what landed? | Bookings | Head of sales | Both |

Three of these need particular care.

**Net revenue retention** blends expansion with churn. The a16z guide notes that net revenue churn "understates the losses" because upsells offset them, which is why gross retention sits beside it. For reference, SaaS Capital's 2025 survey of private B2B SaaS companies put median net revenue retention at 102% for firms with annual contract values of $25,000 to $50,000. A board seeing 102% should know whether that is healthy expansion over heavy churn or flat accounts with little of either.

**Pipeline coverage** is the most quoted and least understood. Salesforce's own guidance points out that the common "three times quota" rule holds only when the win rate is 33% and the sales cycle is one year; a seller winning 10% of pipeline revenue needs about ten times coverage. Report coverage alongside the win rate and cycle length that make it meaningful, or the board will apply the rule of thumb to a business it does not fit.

**Forecast accuracy** is the measure that most directly earns or loses trust. Report the forecast made at the start of the quarter, the forecast at mid-quarter and the outcome, every quarter, for eight quarters. A forecast that is consistently 10% optimistic is more useful to a board than one that is right on average and wildly wrong in either direction. Our piece on [calibration](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/) sets out why the pattern of misses matters more than any single miss.

> A board will forgive a missed number. It will not forgive a number that changed meaning without anyone saying so.

## Define once, in one place

The practical form of the first test is a metric dictionary: one document or table listing each measure, its formula, its inclusions and exclusions, its system of record, its owner and the date it was last changed. It does not need special tooling. A shared document with version history is enough for a firm of 50.

Larger firms, or those already running a data warehouse, can put the definitions into code. The dbt documentation describes MetricFlow as a way to define each metric once, centrally, so that analysts do not each write their own version, noting that ad hoc queries "can lead to confusion, inconsistencies, and a headache for data management." Our explainer on [semantic layers](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/) covers this pattern. The principle is the same at any size: the definition lives in one place, and every report reads from it.

The harder work is agreement. McKinsey's 2021 survey of more than 2,500 B2B respondents found that companies using commercial analytics effectively were 1.5 times more likely to achieve above-average growth, and that the first behaviour separating them was building cross-functional consensus on where analytics would create value. For KPIs, consensus means sales, marketing and finance signing the dictionary before it reaches the board. Gartner's 2024 finding points the same way: analytics led by the chief sales officer were 2.3 times more likely to achieve higher forecast accuracy, which suggests ownership matters as much as method.

None of this works on a CRM that cannot be trusted. Stage dates, close dates and amounts have to be maintained as a discipline, not cleaned up the week before the board meeting. Our explainer on [CRM data hygiene](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/) covers the routine.

## Changing a definition without losing the board

Definitions should change when the business changes. A firm that moves upmarket will tighten qualification; a firm that adds a partner channel will need to decide how partner-sourced pipeline is counted. The problem is never the change. It is the change made quietly.

The SEC's guidance sets a useful standard for any audience: when a metric's calculation changes, disclose how it differs from prior periods, why it changed and the effect on the reported figures, and consider whether to recast prior periods.

Treat a definition change as a commercial decision and record it the way Part 9 of The Build Order recommends for any decision worth recording: the decision, the reason, the owner, the status, the expected effect on the reported number, and a check date. Then do three things.

1. **Restate history.** Recalculate at least four prior quarters on the new definition, so the trend line compares like with like. If the old data cannot support the new definition, say so and show both series for a transition period.
2. **Tell the board first.** Flag the change in the pack before the number moves, with the size of the effect. A two-line note in the appendix is enough.
3. **Keep the old version.** The superseded definition stays in the dictionary, marked as replaced, with the date. Our piece [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/) explains why the history of a definition is evidence in its own right.

The same discipline applies to targets. A target revised mid-year is a decision with a reason, and the board should see the original target, the revision and why.

## What the board pack looks like

The pack itself should be short. One page of commercial measures, with eight quarters of trend for each, the owner's name beside each line, and two or three sentences of commentary that name decisions rather than describe movements. "Win rate in the mid-market segment fell from 24% to 19% after we raised list prices; we are holding price and will review at the end of next quarter" is commentary. "Win rate decreased this quarter" is not.

Behind the page sits an appendix: the metric dictionary, the change log, and a reconciliation of bookings to recognised revenue. Most board members will never read it. The ones who do are the ones whose trust matters most.

Leave out what the board cannot act on. Our piece [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) argues the same point for early-stage firms: impressions, follower counts and raw lead volumes belong in the marketing team's own review, not in the pack.

Illustrative example: the pipeline restatement

Decision
:   Redefine qualified pipeline to require a confirmed budget holder and a dated next step, and restate the previous four quarters on the new basis.

Reason and owner
:   Marketing-sourced and sales-reported pipeline differed by more than a third, and the board had stopped referring to either. Owned by the head of revenue operations; definition signed by the heads of sales and marketing and the finance director.

What changed
:   Reported pipeline fell by roughly a quarter on restatement, coverage was reported with its win rate for the first time, and the board's questions moved from whether the number was real to whether it was enough.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size B2B services firm, built from patterns across engagements; figures are illustrative.

## lowob takeaways

- **Fewer measures, defined once.** Eight well-defined KPIs beat thirty that nobody can calculate twice.
- **Reconcile to finance.** Every commercial number should tie to something finance reports, or the gap should be explained.
- **Quote coverage with its assumptions.** Pipeline coverage means nothing without the win rate and cycle length behind it.
- **Record definition changes as decisions.** Restate history, tell the board first, keep the old version.
- **Name an owner on the page.** A number with a name beside it gets defended and maintained.

Gateway card

### Before the next board pack

- A metric dictionary covering every commercial measure in the pack
- Each measure signed off by sales, marketing and finance
- Bookings reconciled to recognised revenue in an appendix
- Pipeline coverage shown with its win rate and cycle length
- Forecast accuracy shown for at least four quarters
- A change log listing every definition change in the last year, with restated history

## Common questions

### What sales and marketing KPIs should a board see?

Most B2B boards need about eight: new bookings, net and gross revenue retention, pipeline coverage, win rate by segment, sales cycle length, CAC payback and forecast accuracy. Each should have one written definition and a named owner.

### How do you make sales metrics trustworthy for a board?

Define each metric once, reconcile it to a figure finance reports, keep the definition stable or restate history when it changes, and print the owner's name beside it.

### Is 3x pipeline coverage a good rule?

Only in a narrow case. Salesforce notes the three times rule holds at a 33% win rate and a one-year sales cycle. Lower win rates need more coverage and shorter cycles need less.

### How should a company report a change in KPI definition to the board?

Flag it before the number moves, state the size of the effect, restate at least four prior quarters on the new basis, and keep the old definition on file marked as superseded.

Analyst survey; sample size not stated in the release; older than the other sources here.
