# The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-08-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A decision record pays back fastest where decisions are frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended. On the commercial line ten decision classes meet that test, from discount exceptions to closed-lost reasons. Each record needs a reason, an owner, a status, an expected outcome and a check date, and the outcome must be written back.

The record is the part of the brain a company must own, and it pays back fastest where decisions are frequent, similar, quickly graded and later defended. On the commercial line, ten decision classes meet that test, from discount exceptions and lead qualification to campaign spend and closed-lost reasons. Each record needs five fields (the decision, its reason, owner, status, and an expected outcome with a date to check), plus a sixth, the outcome, written back when it arrives. Start with one class, not ten.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every firm loses deals for reasons it has seen before. A pitch is lost on price; six months later a similar pitch is lost the same way. Nobody connects the two, because neither decision was recorded anywhere a person or an agent could find it. The context layer can now retrieve the proposal, the emails and the invoice. It cannot retrieve a reason nobody wrote down.

This is the record layer, the half of the brain we argue a company must own (*Buy context, own judgment*). The question is which decisions deserve a record. Recording everything creates a filing burden nobody maintains. Recording nothing leaves the reasoning layer guessing.

## Which decisions deserve a record

We published the test in *Where judgment arrives first*: a decision layer earns its keep first where decisions are frequent, similar to past cases, graded quickly by an outcome, and later defended by someone accountable. Gartner has forecast that at least 15% of day-to-day work decisions will be made autonomously through agentic AI by 2028; the decisions that get there first will be the ones with a record behind them.

## The ten commercial decisions

| # | Decision class | Typical frequency | Outcome known within | Who defends it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Discount or price exception | Weekly | One sales cycle | Finance and head of sales |
| 2 | Qualify or drop an inbound lead | Daily | Weeks | Head of sales |
| 3 | Pursue or pass on a pitch or RFP | Weekly | One sales cycle | Leadership |
| 4 | Pricing a proposal | Weekly | One sales cycle | Account owner and finance |
| 5 | Campaign spend and reallocation | Monthly | A quarter | Budget holder |
| 6 | Partner or channel selection | Quarterly | Two quarters | Revenue leader |
| 7 | Account prioritisation for the quarter | Quarterly | A quarter | Revenue leader |
| 8 | Approving a public or marketing claim | Weekly | Weeks, or at audit | Marketing and compliance |
| 9 | Follow-up timing and next step on key deals | Daily | Weeks | Account owner |
| 10 | Why a deal was won or lost | Weekly | Already known | Head of sales |

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

The list is deliberately commercial and deliberately ordinary. These are the calls a mid-size firm makes every week and rarely writes down. Three of them (discount exceptions, pursue or pass, and win-loss reasons) recur so often and grade so quickly that they will show patterns within a single quarter.

## What each record must hold

In *The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind* we set out the core of a useful record: the decision, the reason and owner, and what changed. In *The field that makes a record a judgment* and *Supersede, never overwrite* we added the fields that let a system learn. For the commercial line, five fields are the minimum, and the sixth arrives later.

| Field | Example (discount exception) | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision | Approve 12% off list for a two-year term | What was decided, in one line |
| Reason | Competing quote at a lower price; strategic logo in a new sector | What the reasoning layer will retrieve as precedent |
| Owner | Head of sales | One accountable person |
| Status | Current, superseded or reversed | Stops old guidance being treated as current |
| Expected outcome and check date | Win within 30 days; renewal at full price in two years | Makes the decision gradable |
| Outcome (written back) | Won; renewal pending | Turns the record into evidence |

The last two rows are what make a log into a judgment record. Without an expected outcome there is nothing to compare the result with. Without the written-back outcome there is nothing to learn from.

> A decision without an expected outcome cannot be graded, and a decision that cannot be graded cannot be learned from.

## Where the record should live

Choose the place already open when the decision is made.

| Option | Good for | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A custom object or fields in the CRM | Discounts, pursue or pass, win-loss | Keep it to the six fields; avoid free text only |
| A shared table (Airtable, a sheet, a database) | Campaign spend, partner selection, prioritisation | Needs a clear owner and an export path |
| A document workspace (Notion or similar) | Claims approvals with attached evidence | Structure must stay consistent enough to query |

Whichever you choose, apply the three tests from *Buy context, own judgment*: can every record and its history be exported in a documented format, will it survive a change of vendor, and does the company control retention and deletion?

## The capture habit

Records fail when they depend on memory. Attach capture to moments that already exist:

- **At approval.** A discount or price exception cannot be approved without its reason and expected outcome.
- **At stage change.** Moving a deal to won or lost requires the reason.
- **At the weekly review.** Pursue-or-pass and prioritisation calls are recorded in the meeting, not after it.
- **At the check date.** The owner gets a reminder to record the outcome.

The data shows why capture must be designed rather than requested. Validity's 2025 survey found 37% of CRM users reporting revenue lost to poor data quality, and 37% reporting colleagues fabricating data to satisfy decision-makers. Records filled in to satisfy a review are worse than no records.

## Start with one class

Pick one decision class whose outcome shows within a quarter and record it properly for 90 days. Discount exceptions and closed-lost reasons are the usual choices because both are frequent, already partly captured in the CRM, and defended by someone who cares about the answer. After 90 days, look at the outcomes against the expectations. The first uncomfortable finding is usually the moment the build stops being an IT project.

Illustrative example: recording discount exceptions

Decision
:   Record every discount beyond the standard tier with its reason, owner, expected outcome and a 30-day check.

Reason and owner
:   Discounts were rising with no evidence they improved win rates. Owned by the head of sales.

What changed
:   After a quarter, discounts in two service lines show no higher win rate than standard pricing; the rule for those lines is tightened and reviewed again in a quarter.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size services business, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Record decisions, not everything.** Ten commercial classes pass the test; most of what a team does does not need a record.
- **Six fields.** Decision, reason, owner, status, expected outcome with a check date, and the outcome written back.
- **Capture at moments that already exist.** Approvals, stage changes, weekly reviews and check dates.
- **Start with one class for 90 days.** Usually discount exceptions or closed-lost reasons.

Gateway card

### Gateway 2 begins here

- One decision class chosen
- Six fields defined and required at the moment of decision
- Expected outcome and check date on every record
- Outcomes written back on schedule
- A value at stake recorded, so the build can report in money

## Common questions

### What is a decision record?

A structured entry for an important decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, whether it is current, what outcome was expected and when to check, and later what actually happened.

### Which sales decisions should be recorded?

Those that are frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended: discount and price exceptions, lead qualification, pursue-or-pass on pitches, proposal pricing, campaign spend, partner selection, account prioritisation, claims approvals, follow-up timing on key deals, and win-loss reasons.

### Where should decision records live?

Where the decision is made: CRM fields for deal decisions, a shared table for budget and partner decisions, or a document workspace for claims with evidence. Records must be exportable.

### How does a decision record help AI agents?

Agents can read comparable past decisions as precedent before acting, and outcomes written back to records let the system learn which reasoning worked.

## Sources and notes

- Gartner forecast on autonomous work decisions, June 2025, as reported by [W.Media](https://w.media/over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-could-face-the-axe-by-end-of-2027-gartner/).
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2025](https://validity.com/resource-center/the-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2025), and [MediaPost coverage](https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/407342/crm-data-drag-systems-are-not-delivering-and-bra.html). Survey of 602 CRM users.
- The ten decision classes and frequencies are **lowob**'s illustration; they vary by firm.

## Related research

- [Where Judgment Arrives First](https://lowob.com/research/where-judgment-arrives-first/)
- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [What We Would Cut From the Build Order](https://lowob.com/research/what-we-would-cut-from-the-build-order/)

## Next move

Pick one of the ten decisions and look at the last ten times your team made it. How many have a written reason, and how many have a known outcome? That gap is the first thing to close.

# From Reach to Recurring

Source: https://lowob.com/research/from-reach-to-recurring/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Reach is rented and recurring is owned. Google search traffic to publishers fell by a third in a year, and AI summaries cut clicks further. Media businesses should move to products people pay for repeatedly, measured by paid conversion, churn, revenue per subscriber, sponsor renewal and the share of revenue not dependent on platforms.

Reach is rented; recurring is owned. The move is from traffic-dependent revenue to products people pay for repeatedly, measured by conversion, churn, revenue per subscriber and platform independence. The pressure is measurable: Chartbeat data cited by the Reuters Institute shows Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% globally between November 2024 and November 2025, and Pew found people clicked a search result on 8% of visits that showed an AI summary, against 15% without one.

## The answer-engine problem

For twenty years the deal was simple. You published, search engines sent people, and you sold the attention. That deal is being rewritten without you.

AI summaries and assistants now answer directly. A reader asks a question, gets a synthesised answer, and often never visits the page that supplied the facts. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025: when an AI summary appeared, users clicked a link inside it on just 1% of visits. Publishers expect worse. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends survey of 280 media leaders found they expect search traffic to fall by more than 40% over three years, while noting it is unclear how much of the recent fall is due to AI summaries.

Chatbots themselves are still a small route to news. Weekly use for news rose from 7% to 10% in the 2026 Digital News Report, and 42% of chatbot news users said they always or often click through to sources. The exposure today sits mainly in search, where summaries now sit above the links.

Any media business whose revenue depends on search referrals is exposed. Programmatic advertising, affiliate links on evergreen pages, and traffic-based sponsor pricing all sit in the path.

Three responses hold up.

**Owned channels.** Email, membership, apps and communities are relationships no intermediary can intercept. [An audience is not a business](https://lowob.com/research/an-audience-is-not-a-business/) covers why owned beats rented. This is the practical reason.

**Be the source.** Assistants cite original reporting, proprietary data, and clear expert positions. They do not cite the fourth rewrite of a press release. Being cited builds brand and sends some traffic, but the real value is authority that converts to paid. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers the mechanics.

**Products that do not need traffic.** Everything in the rest of this piece.

## Subscriptions and memberships

The paid relationship is the core of a recurring media business. It is also where most founders under-invest, because free growth feels better than paid conversion.

The ceiling is real. Across 20 markets where paywalls are common, 17% of people paid for online news in the past year, roughly flat, according to the Reuters Institute. Its 2026 report also found reader revenue gains coming increasingly from price and product mix rather than more subscribers: the share of New York Times subscribers paying only for news access fell from 17% to 12%, as most pay for bundles, and USA Today Co. reported total subscribers down 30% in 2025 while revenue per user rose 27%.

Three decisions drive it: what is behind the wall, how you ask, and what happens after someone pays.

Behind the wall should sit the thing your point of view produces: analysis, access, data, or community. Not the news everyone has. The ask should be specific and tied to a moment of value, not a generic banner. After payment, onboarding and the first renewal matter more than acquisition.

The research on retention supports that order. Northwestern University's Medill researchers analysed about 13 terabytes of subscriber data from three US metro newspapers and found that how often people read was the single biggest predictor of whether they kept paying, ahead of the number of stories or time spent. Habit, not volume, keeps a subscriber.

Membership adds a second layer: belonging, access to people, and influence over what gets made. [Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) covers community as a job, and our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/) covers how members are recruited and kept. Membership is where that job gets paid for.

## B2B data, research and sponsorship on quality

Business audiences pay for things that reduce their risk or save them time. A publisher covering a sector sits on exactly that material.

Data products: benchmarks, pricing, deal flow, rankings, directories. Research products: reports, briefings, surveys, advisory calls. Both sell on annual contracts with renewal, and both are priced on usefulness, not on audience size.

Sponsorship changes with the same logic. Stop selling CPM. Sell access to a defined audience with a defined behaviour, and price on that. Buyers are asking for it: the IAB's 2025 creator economy study, a trade-body survey of US ad buyers, found 40% ranked overall return on investment as their top measure for creator campaigns, and listed tools that link activity to business outcomes among their main gaps.

| Old sponsorship | Quality sponsorship |
| --- | --- |
| Priced per thousand impressions | Priced per campaign against a named audience |
| Proof is delivery numbers | Proof is response, leads or renewal |
| Sold to media buyers | Sold to marketing and sales leaders |
| Renewal depends on traffic | Renewal depends on results |

A sponsor who renews is worth more than three who try once. Build the sales process around renewal from the first conversation. [Your first ten sponsors are design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-sponsors-are-design-partners/) sets out how.

> A sponsor who renews is worth more than three who try once.

## Affiliate, commerce and events

Affiliate and commerce work when they match the point of view and are disclosed clearly. Recommending what you would recommend anyway, with a visible note that you earn on it, keeps trust intact. In the US the FTC's guidance is specific: disclose the commission next to the link, and "affiliate link" alone is not adequate. Hiding it loses the trust and the revenue together.

Keep affiliate revenue out of the core forecast if it depends on search traffic. It belongs in the exposed column until it is driven by owned channels.

Events can be the highest-margin line or the most expensive mistake. The difference is the model. Small, repeated, sponsor-backed gatherings with ticketed access tend to work. One large annual event with a cost base set before sponsors sign tends not to. Publishers are leaning in: 54% of the media leaders in the Reuters Institute's trends survey named online and physical events a key revenue focus, behind subscriptions at 76%.

[Distribution when the platforms are closed](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) covers distribution when platforms will not carry you. Events are distribution and revenue in one, which is why they deserve a proper plan rather than an experiment. Our piece on [events that pay back](https://lowob.com/research/events-that-pay-back/) sets out the business case to write before booking.

## Metrics for the move

[Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) argues for measures that show something happened. Media needs a short set of numbers that show the move from traffic to recurring.

| Metric | Definition | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Share of revenue not dependent on platforms | Revenue from owned channels and direct contracts, divided by total revenue | Whether the business is yours or the platform's |
| Paid conversion | Share of free audience that becomes paying over a defined period | Whether the paid product is worth the ask |
| Churn | Share of paying relationships lost per period, by cohort | Whether the habit holds after the first renewal |
| Revenue per subscriber | Total recurring revenue divided by paying relationships | Whether bundles and price are doing their job |
| Sponsor renewal rate | Share of sponsors who buy again | Whether sponsorship is a product or a one-off |

Report these monthly. Put the first one at the top. I treat it as the single figure that tells a media founder whether the business is theirs or the platform's. Our explainer on [customer churn](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/) covers the cohort calculation.

[Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) covers the operating side. In media that means systems for renewal, sponsor reporting and product delivery that do not route through the founder's inbox.

## lowob takeaways

- **Label the exposed revenue.** Programmatic, evergreen affiliate and traffic-priced sponsorship sit in the path of AI summaries.
- **Build the habit.** Reading frequency predicts retention better than reading volume.
- **Sell sponsorship on results.** Per campaign, against a named audience, proved by response.
- **Lead with platform independence.** Report the share of revenue not dependent on platforms first, every month.

Gateway card

### Before the next quarterly plan

- Traffic-dependent revenue identified and labelled as exposed
- Owned channel growth tracked separately from platform growth
- Paid product defined around the point of view, not around general news
- Sponsorship priced on audience definition and results, not CPM
- Affiliate and commerce disclosed, and excluded from the core forecast if traffic-driven
- Five recurring metrics reported monthly, platform independence first

## Common questions

### How do AI answer engines affect publisher revenue?

AI summaries reduce clicks: Pew found users clicked a search result on 8% of visits with a summary, against 15% without. Revenue tied to search referrals, such as programmatic ads, evergreen affiliate pages and traffic-priced sponsorship, is exposed.

### What metrics should a media business track instead of reach?

The share of revenue not dependent on platforms, paid conversion, churn by cohort, revenue per subscriber and sponsor renewal rate, reported monthly with platform independence first.

### How should a niche publisher price sponsorships?

Per campaign against a named audience, proven by response, leads or renewal rather than impressions, and sold to marketing and sales leaders rather than media buyers.

### What predicts whether a digital subscriber renews?

Habit. Northwestern's Medill research across three US newspapers found reading frequency was the strongest predictor of retention, ahead of stories read or time spent.

## Sources and notes

- [Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2026/dnr-executive-summary), June 2026. Online survey across 48 markets; payment figures cover 20 paywall-heavy markets; company figures as reported by the Institute.
- [Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026), 12 January 2026. Survey of 280 digital leaders plus Chartbeat traffic data; a strategic sample, not representative.
- [Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/), 22 July 2025. Browsing data from 900 US adults in March 2025; consumer searches.
- [Nieman Lab, Researchers crunched 13 TB of local newspaper subscriber data](https://www.niemanlab.org/2019/02/researchers-crunched-13-tb-of-local-newspaper-subscriber-data-heres-what-they-found-about-who-sticks-around/), 5 February 2019. Report on Medill Local News Initiative research at Northwestern University; three US metro titles; older than the other sources.

Split last quarter's revenue into two columns: dependent on platforms and search, and not. Put the second column's share at the top of next month's report.

# What Is AI Governance?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-30 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI governance is how an organisation decides which AI uses are allowed, who owns them and how risk is checked. Three reference points dominate: the voluntary NIST AI RMF, the certifiable ISO/IEC 42001 management system standard, and the EU AI Act, whose high-risk obligations now apply from December 2027.

AI governance is the set of roles, policies, records and controls through which an organisation decides how it uses AI, who is accountable for each use and how risks are found and managed. Three frameworks shape most programmes: NIST's voluntary AI Risk Management Framework, the ISO/IEC 42001 management system standard, and the EU AI Act. For a company of 20 to 500 people, governance starts with an inventory, named owners and a record of decisions, not a committee.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What AI governance means

Governance answers four questions for every AI use: is it allowed, who owns it, how is it checked, and what is recorded. Policy documents are the visible part. The working parts are an inventory of AI systems, an owner for each, a risk classification, approval rules and evidence that the rules were followed.

| AI governance is | AI governance is not |
| --- | --- |
| Named owners and decisions for each AI use | A single ethics statement on the website |
| A risk-based inventory updated as tools change | A one-off procurement checklist |
| Evidence: approvals, logs, incidents, reviews | A tool that can be bought and switched on |
| Proportionate to the firm's size and exposure | A copy of a large bank's framework |

## The three reference frameworks

**NIST AI RMF.** NIST describes the framework as guidance for voluntary use by organisations designing, developing, deploying or using AI. Its core has four functions: govern (culture, roles and policy), map (context and risks of each use), measure (assessment and tracking) and manage (prioritising and acting on risks). A companion Playbook suggests actions for each. The Generative AI Profile, NIST AI 600-1, applies the framework to generative systems.

**ISO/IEC 42001.** The standard "specifies the requirements and provides guidance for establishing, implementing, maintaining and continually improving" an AI management system. It is intended for any organisation providing or using AI-based products or services. Like ISO 27001 for information security, it can be certified by an accredited body: BSI announced Dutch accreditation in December 2024, and UKAS granted its first UK accreditation for 42001 certification in January 2026.

**EU AI Act.** The Act is law, not guidance, and classifies AI uses by risk. Prohibited practices and AI literacy duties applied from 2 February 2025, and general-purpose AI model rules from 2 August 2025. Article 50 transparency duties generally apply from 2 August 2026. The Digital Omnibus, in force since 27 July 2026, moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027 and product-embedded high-risk systems to 2 August 2028.

| Framework | Type | Best used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NIST AI RMF and AI 600-1 | Voluntary US guidance | Structuring risk thinking for each use |
| ISO/IEC 42001 | Certifiable international standard | Showing customers a management system exists |
| EU AI Act | Binding EU regulation | Legal obligations by risk category |

> Governance is a record of decisions with owners, not a document that says decisions will be made.

## How a mid-size company starts

Large-enterprise programmes do not scale down well. **lowob**'s Gateway 0 asks for three decisions before any AI tool is bought, and the same logic gives a proportionate starting set.

| Step | What it produces | Framework link |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inventory every AI use, including features inside existing software | A list with owner, purpose and data touched | NIST map; ISO 42001 scope |
| Classify by exposure | Client-facing, regulated or internal; check EU high-risk categories | EU AI Act risk tiers |
| Set the autonomy level per use | Answer, draft, act with approval, act and report, act alone | NIST manage |
| Name approvers and a kill switch owner | A matrix of who approves what | EU AI Act Article 14 oversight |
| Record decisions and outcomes | Reason, owner, status and expected outcome for each change | ISO 42001 documented information |
| Review quarterly | Updated inventory and incident list | NIST govern; ISO continual improvement |

For many mid-size firms, customer due diligence will ask for this list before any regulator does. A buyer's security questionnaire asking how AI is governed is answered by the inventory and the decision record, which is why **lowob** argues governance should start on the commercial line.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with the inventory.** Governance cannot cover AI uses nobody has listed.
- **Pick frameworks by purpose.** NIST for structure, ISO 42001 for certification, the AI Act for legal duties.
- **Check the dates.** EU high-risk obligations moved to December 2027 and August 2028.
- **Keep the evidence.** Owners, approvals and outcomes recorded are what governance looks like to an auditor.

## Common questions

### What is AI governance?

The roles, policies, records and controls an organisation uses to decide how it uses AI, who is accountable for each use, and how risks are managed.

### What is the difference between NIST AI RMF and ISO 42001?

The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance for managing AI risk. ISO/IEC 42001 is an international standard for an AI management system that an accredited body can certify.

### When does the EU AI Act apply to high-risk AI?

After the Digital Omnibus, obligations for Annex III high-risk systems apply from 2 December 2027, and for AI embedded in regulated products from 2 August 2028.

### Does a small company need AI governance?

Yes, in proportion. An inventory, a named owner per use, approval rules for client-facing output and a decision record cover most of what customers and regulators ask.

- [NIST, AI RMF Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile (NIST AI 600-1)](https://www.nist.gov/node/1855536), 26 July 2024. Primary publication.

Accreditation announcements; BSI is a certification vendor.

# Your Customers Already Wrote Your Messaging. Claude Can Help You Find It.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/claude-voice-of-customer-research/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The strongest messaging is recovered from the market, not invented in a workshop, and the evidence sits scattered across calls, tickets, reviews and lost-deal notes. Claude can read that material at scale if the method is disciplined: structured extraction with quoted excerpts first, clustering by buying situation, a disagreement report against internal copy, and a monthly refresh. Research on AI coding shows why quotes matter: models match humans on explicit themes and fall short on interpretive ones.

Most companies write messaging from the inside out, and sales then discovers that buyers use different language for the problem. The strongest messaging is recovered from the market. Claude is useful as a qualitative research layer across calls, tickets, reviews and lost-deal notes, provided the team uses a disciplined method: extract fields with quoted excerpts before summarising, cluster by buying situation, and compare customer language with the company's own. A 2024 study found GPT-4 matched human coders on explicit themes but fell short on interpretive ones, which is why every finding needs its quote.

Most companies write messaging from the inside out. The product team describes what was built. The founder explains the vision. Marketing turns those descriptions into benefits. Sales then discovers that buyers use completely different language for the problem.

The strongest messaging is rarely invented in a workshop. It is recovered from the market. Customers explain what was happening before they searched for a solution, what triggered urgency, what alternatives they tried, what made them sceptical and what outcome finally mattered. The difficulty is that this evidence is scattered across call transcripts, emails, support tickets, community channels, reviews, CRM notes and private conversations.

Claude is particularly useful as a qualitative research layer across that material, provided the team uses a disciplined method rather than asking for a generic summary. Our piece on [positioning vs messaging vs branding](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-vs-messaging-vs-branding/) covers which of the three this work fixes.

## Build the evidence set

Start with material that records actual customer language:

- discovery and sales-call transcripts
- onboarding and implementation notes
- churn interviews and lost-deal explanations
- support requests and community questions
- product reviews, your own and competitors'
- successful customer emails and public forum discussions.

Remove information the model should not receive, follow the company's data policies, and separate current customers, prospects, churned users and non-buyers. Those groups may describe the same product very differently. If the material comes through connectors, note that Anthropic's documentation says Claude "inherits each person's permissions from the connected service", and that connected services process data under their own terms. The researcher's access sets the boundary of the evidence set, so check it covers what the study needs and nothing it should not.

A Claude Project is a practical container: its knowledge base holds the evidence set and its instructions hold the extraction schema, so every analyst works from the same material and rules. Our explainer on [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) covers how to collect the lost-deal row properly.

## Do not ask for "key themes" yet

A general theme summary compresses the evidence too early. Begin with structured extraction. For every conversation, ask Claude to record ten fields.

| Field | What to capture |
| --- | --- |
| Situation before | What was happening before they looked for a solution |
| Trigger | The event that created urgency |
| Job | What they were trying to get done |
| Cost of inaction | What leaving the problem unresolved would cost |
| Alternatives | What they considered or tried |
| Objections and risks | Fears, doubts, perceived risks |
| Problem in their words | The exact phrases used |
| Desired outcome | What success looks like to them |
| Proof required | What they needed to believe it would work |
| Stakeholders | Who else was involved in the decision |

Require short supporting excerpts and source labels for every field. This allows a human reviewer to distinguish a repeated pattern from a polished inference.

The evidence explains why. Elisabeth Kirsten and colleagues compared GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 with human coders on 47 interview transcripts in 2024. On a descriptive coding task, GPT-4 matched the humans' agreement, with a Cohen's kappa of 0.97. On the most interpretive task, the two human coders agreed at 0.63 and GPT-4 reached 0.55 to 0.58. On one task, GPT-3.5 invented 47 codes that were not in the codebook. The study was small and the models are now older, but the shape matches practice: explicit statements extract well, and inferred meaning needs a person.

Anthropic's own prompting guidance points the same way. For long documents it advises asking Claude "to quote relevant parts of the documents first before carrying out its task". Teams building on the API can go further with its Citations feature, which returns the exact passages behind each claim; the documentation says citations "are guaranteed to contain valid pointers to the provided documents". A pointer that resolves still has to be read: it shows where a claim came from, not that the claim is a fair reading.

> A quote lets a reviewer tell a repeated pattern from a polished inference. Without one, every theme is a guess written well.

## Cluster by buying situation, not demographics

Teams often segment evidence by company size or industry because those fields are already in the CRM. Those attributes can matter, but they do not necessarily explain behaviour. More useful clusters often emerge around the buying situation:

| Buying situation | What it usually changes |
| --- | --- |
| A new executive has been hired | Appetite for change; a short window to act |
| A product is approaching launch | A fixed deadline and low tolerance for risk |
| An incumbent vendor failed | Scepticism; proof matters more than vision |
| New regulation changed the risk calculation | Compliance and legal join the buying group |
| A partnership created unexpected demand | Capacity, not budget, is the constraint |
| A team is overwhelmed by manual work | Time saved is the outcome that sells |
| Revenue pressure created a deadline | Speed to value outranks features |

These triggers help explain why two otherwise similar companies move at different speeds. Ask Claude to assign each conversation to a situation, quote the evidence, and flag conversations that fit none. The unassigned pile is where new situations appear first.

## Convert the findings into a message architecture

Once the evidence has been reviewed, translate it into five layers.

**Problem.** Use the customer's clearest description of what is not working.

**Consequence.** State the operational, financial, reputational or long-term cost.

**Change.** Explain what becomes possible after the problem is resolved.

**Mechanism.** Describe how the product creates that change without drowning the buyer in features.

**Proof.** Match evidence to the buyer's perceived risk.

For example, "AI-powered community intelligence" describes a capability. "See emerging customer complaints across Discord, Reddit and Telegram before they become a launch problem" describes a situation, consequence and outcome a buyer can recognise. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how the architecture sits under a positioning statement.

## Create a disagreement report

One of the most valuable Claude workflows is comparing internal messaging with external language. Give it the website, the main deck and the extraction output, and ask it to identify:

1. phrases the company uses that customers never use
2. problems customers repeat that the website barely mentions
3. benefits marketing emphasises that do not influence decisions
4. objections sales encounters that content never addresses
5. segments whose language differs enough to need separate messaging.

Each item should cite both sides: the company's sentence and the customers' quotes. This is not an instruction to copy every customer phrase literally. Customers understand their pain better than they understand the architecture of the solution. The company still needs judgment. But messaging should begin from recognisable market reality.

## Make voice-of-customer research continuous

Do not conduct this exercise once and declare the positioning complete. Create a monthly workflow in which new calls and community conversations are classified with the same schema, compared with the previous period and reviewed for emerging language. Track which phrases appear in successful deals, which objections are growing and which promised outcomes correlate with retention. Packaging the schema and steps as a Claude Skill keeps the method identical month to month, which is what makes the comparison valid. Our piece [Claude is not your intern](https://lowob.com/research/claude-gtm-operating-system/) shows where this fits in a weekly GTM system.

The value compounds when the findings update sales enablement, landing pages, product education, content priorities and the questions asked in future calls. Your customers have already written much of your messaging. The job is to listen carefully enough to find it, and exercise enough judgment to know what deserves to become the company's story. Use Claude to increase the surface area of listening, not to replace contact with the market.

## lowob takeaways

- **Extract before summarising.** Ten fields per conversation, each with a quote and a source.
- **Trust explicit, check interpretive.** Models match humans on what was said, not on what it meant.
- **Cluster by situation.** Triggers explain buying speed better than firmographics.
- **Run the disagreement report monthly.** Your copy against their words, with both sides quoted.

## Common questions

### How do you use AI for voice-of-customer research?

Gather transcripts, tickets, reviews and lost-deal notes, then have the model extract fixed fields per conversation with quoted excerpts and source labels. Only then cluster and summarise, with a person reviewing each theme against its quotes.

### Can Claude analyse customer interview transcripts accurately?

For explicit, descriptive content, models now match human coders closely. For interpretive judgments, a 2024 study found clear gaps, so require quotes and have a person review any inferred theme.

### What should a voice-of-customer analysis extract?

The situation before, the trigger, the job, the cost of inaction, alternatives, objections, the problem in the customer's words, the desired outcome, the proof required and the stakeholders.

### How often should voice-of-customer research be updated?

Monthly works for most B2B teams: classify new conversations with the same schema, compare with the previous period, and update messaging, enablement and content where language has shifted.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Prompting best practices](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/be-clear-and-direct), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation.
- [Anthropic, Citations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/citations), accessed November 2026. Vendor API documentation; the guarantee covers pointers to source text, not the accuracy of the claim.

## Next move

Pull ten recent discovery-call transcripts. Run the ten-field extraction on each with quotes required, then put the "problem in their words" column next to your homepage headline and count how many customers used any of its words.

# What Is App Store Optimization? Fintech and Crypto Apps

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-app-store-optimization/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: App store optimization is improving how an app ranks in store search, converts from listing to install, and passes store review. Apple says nearly 65% of App Store downloads happen directly after a search, and both stores now offer native listing tests and keyword-targeted pages. For fintech and crypto apps that cannot buy installs freely, the store is open-band distribution every other channel depends on, so the listing is the channel.

App store optimisation (ASO) is the practice of improving how an app is found and chosen in the app stores: its ranking in store search, its conversion from store page to install, and its eligibility for featuring. Apple says nearly 65% of App Store downloads happen directly after a search. For fintech and crypto apps that cannot buy installs freely, the store is open-band distribution every other channel depends on, and store review is a constraint to plan around, so the listing is the channel.

For any company whose product is an app, the store is a distribution channel with its own rules, and for reviewed categories it is often the largest channel that cannot be bought. That framing matters more as of November 2026 than it did a year ago, because the stores have added keyword-targeted pages, native experiments and stricter licensing declarations, and Apple has said it will add more paid placements to search results during 2026.

## How the stores decide what to show

Apple states its search factors plainly: results are based on "text relevance (matches for your app's title, subtitle, keywords, and primary category), as well as user behavior (downloads, ratings and reviews, and more)." App names are limited to 30 characters and the keyword field to 100 characters. Google Play also caps titles at 30 characters. Neither store publishes the full list or the weights. Install volume and velocity, retention and engagement signals the stores measure themselves, and conversion from the listing are the behavioural inputs most ASO work targets.

Featuring (editorial placement on store pages) is decided by store teams based on quality, design, use of platform features, and, to a degree nobody outside the stores fully understands, relationships and timing.

Both stores also review apps against content and category policies before listing and at every update. Financial, crypto, health and gambling apps face specific requirements: licensing evidence, geographic restrictions, disclosure of risks and limits on what the listing may claim.

## What ASO involves

**Metadata.** Title, subtitle, keywords and description written for how people actually search, not for how the company describes itself. People search "savings account" and "budget app", not the brand's category invention.

**Conversion assets.** Screenshots, preview video and icon that explain the product in the two seconds a browser gives them. The first screenshot does most of the work; Apple notes that an app's rating and up to three screenshots or previews may display in search results themselves.

**Ratings and reviews.** Prompting satisfied users at the right moment, responding to reviews, and fixing what the negative ones repeat. Apple confirms ratings and reviews "can influence how your app ranks." On conversion, the best-known public evidence is a 2015 survey of 350 US smartphone owners by Apptentive, a feedback-software vendor: 96% said they would consider an app with a four-star rating, about half at three stars and 15% at two. That is stated intent from an old vendor sample, not measured conversion, so treat four stars as a working threshold rather than a proven cliff.

**Localisation.** Listings adapted to each market's language and search behaviour, not machine-translated.

**Ongoing testing.** The stores offer native tools to test listing variations, set out below. In our work, few fintech teams run them continuously.

| Tool (as documented, November 2026) | Store | What it does |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Custom product pages | Apple | Up to 70 extra versions of the product page, varying screenshots, promotional text and previews; each can be assigned keywords to appear in search, and can deep link into the app |
| Product page optimization | Apple | Tests up to three alternative icons, screenshot sets or previews against the default, shown to random user groups |
| In-app events | Apple | Timely events shown on the product page, in search results and in editorial and personalised recommendations |
| Custom store listings | Google Play | Up to 50 listings targeted by country, pre-registration, inactive users, Google Ads campaign or unique URL |
| Store listing experiments | Google Play | Up to two variants against the current listing; one default graphics experiment or up to five localised experiments at a time, with a set minimum detectable effect and confidence level |

Apple doubled the custom product page limit to 70 and added keywords for those pages on 29 October 2025. It reports that custom product pages lifted conversion by an average of 2.5 percentage points against the default page. AppTweak, an ASO vendor, notes that only five in-app events can be published at once, and that the event name and short description are indexed for search while the long description is not. Treat listing tests as experiments with a written threshold, as in [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/); Google's minimum detectable effect setting exists for exactly that reason.

## Why it matters more for reviewed categories

A fintech or crypto app that cannot buy installs through the large ad platforms depends on the store for a larger share of its acquisition than a game or a productivity app does. Our pieces on [restricted categories](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) and [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) cover why. The store is open-band distribution: nobody has to approve a search result. That makes the listing's quality, its ranking and its conversion worth more, and it makes the store review process a constraint the company has to plan around rather than discover.

> Every other channel ends at the store. For reviewed categories, the listing is the channel.

The review rules are specific and have tightened.

| Rule | Apple App Store | Google Play |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who may submit | Apps in highly regulated fields, including banking, financial services and crypto exchanges, should be submitted by the legal entity providing the service (guideline 5.1.1(ix)) | Crypto exchanges and software wallets must complete the Financial Features Declaration |
| Crypto exchanges | Only in countries or regions where the app holds appropriate licensing (3.1.5(iii)) | Country-specific licences; for example FinCEN money services business registration plus state money transmitter status, or a bank charter, in the US; MiCA CASP authorisation in the EU; FCA registration in the UK |
| Wallets | Must be offered by developers enrolled as an organisation (3.1.5(i)) | Non-custodial software wallets can declare themselves as such where no local licence applies |
| Metadata | No packing with trademarked terms, popular app names, pricing or irrelevant phrases; Apple may modify keywords (2.3.7) | No repetitive or unrelated keywords; no "#1", "best" or price promotions in title, icon or developer name |

Google's policy page carried a change log dated October 2026 and adds EEA provisions from July 2026, so check it before each submission. The sector build orders for [financial services and fintech](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-financial-services-and-fintech/) and [crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) cover where store review sits among a firm's other approval gates.

## The mistakes

Treating the listing as an afterthought written by whoever was free. Keyword stuffing the title, which both stores' metadata policies now prohibit. Screenshots that show interface rather than outcome. Ignoring reviews. Claims in the listing that the compliance team would never approve in an ad, which the store reviewers catch and which delay every subsequent update. And, for restricted categories, submitting without the licensing and disclosure documentation the store requires, then losing weeks in review.

## The relationship to everything else

Every other channel ends at the store. A creator's link, an affiliate placement, a programmatic ad and a search result all deliver a person to the listing, where the conversion rate determines how many of them become users. An improvement in store conversion improves the cost per install on every channel at once. For companies that fought to open each of those channels, that is the cheapest gain available. Custom product pages make the link explicit: each campaign can land on a page written for the audience that campaign reached. The discipline is the same as [conversion rate optimization](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversion-rate-optimization/) on a website, with the store's reviewers in the loop.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write metadata for search.** Use the words people type, inside 30-character titles and a 100-character keyword field.
- **Use the native tools.** Custom pages with their own keywords, and listing experiments with a threshold set in advance.
- **Protect the rating.** Apple says ratings influence ranking, and a vendor survey found willingness to install falls sharply below four stars.
- **Plan for review.** Have licences, entity enrolment and disclosures ready before submission, and check policy change logs.

## Common questions

### What is app store optimisation?

The practice of improving how an app is found and chosen in the app stores: its search ranking, its conversion from store page to install, and its eligibility for featuring.

### What factors affect App Store search ranking?

Apple names text relevance across title, subtitle, keywords and primary category, plus user behaviour such as downloads, ratings and reviews. Install velocity, retention and listing conversion also matter; exact weights are not published.

### Why does ASO matter more for fintech and crypto apps?

Apps that cannot buy installs freely through large ad platforms rely more on the store, where nobody has to approve a search result, and they face licensing checks that can delay every update.

### Can you A/B test an app store listing?

Yes. Apple's product page optimization tests up to three treatments of icon, screenshots and previews; Google Play's store listing experiments test up to two variants against the current listing.

## Next move

Write metadata for how people search, such as "budget app", not for the brand's own category name. This week, set up one custom product page for your largest paid or partner channel and one listing experiment with its threshold written down.

# What Is Robotic Process Automation (RPA) in the Age of Agents?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-robotic-process-automation/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Robotic process automation uses software robots to repeat a person's actions on screen, which makes it useful for legacy systems with no API. Vendors now position RPA robots as the deterministic executors inside agentic automation, with agents handling judgment and people approving. The practical order is API first, RPA for legacy screens, and an agent only where a decision is needed.

Robotic process automation (RPA) is software that repeats a person's actions on a screen, such as clicking, typing and copying data between applications, to run rule-based tasks. It is most useful where a system has no API or connector. In the age of agents, RPA has become the dependable executor that agents and workflows call, while models handle the judgment that RPA scripts never could.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What RPA means

An RPA robot is a script that drives a user interface. It opens an application, reads a value from a field, pastes it into another system and clicks submit, exactly as a person would. Microsoft's training material describes Power Automate for desktop recording "mouse clicks, keyboard inputs, and data entry" and extracting information from the screen.

The appeal is that no integration project is needed. Many older finance, logistics and insurance systems expose no API, so the screen is the only way in. Microsoft says desktop flows are a valid route "when no other alternative is available, or when developing an integration would be expensive and time-consuming."

The weaknesses follow from the same design. A robot that depends on a screen layout breaks when the layout changes. It handles structured inputs well and unstructured ones poorly. It follows its script even when the situation calls for a different action.

| RPA is | RPA is not |
| --- | --- |
| A script that repeats on-screen actions | A model that interprets or decides |
| Strong on stable, rule-based, high-volume tasks | Suited to emails, contracts or call transcripts on its own |
| A way into systems with no API | A replacement for a proper integration where one exists |
| Predictable and easy to audit step by step | Tolerant of screens or fields that change without notice |

## How RPA and agents fit together

The vendors that built the RPA market now sell it as one layer of a larger system. UiPath describes agentic automation as "the orchestration of agents, robots, and humans in a unified automation ecosystem." In that design an agent reads an unstructured input and decides what should happen, a robot carries out the fixed steps in the systems that have no API, and a person approves anything with consequences.

Gartner's evaluation of the market has moved the same way. Its business orchestration and automation technologies category covers platforms that automate processes "with varying levels of autonomy", and requires support for agent orchestration and governance. Listings in the category show the incumbents positioning around it: one RPA vendor describes its platform as extending "existing RPA and BPM investments rather than replacing them."

| Layer | Role | Commercial example (illustrative) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model or agent | Reads unstructured input, proposes a decision | Reads a customer email asking to change an order |
| Workflow or orchestrator | Routes the case and enforces approval rules | Sends the proposed change to the account owner |
| RPA robot | Executes fixed steps in a legacy screen | Updates the order in an older ERP with no API |
| Person | Approves or rejects | Account owner confirms before anything changes |

This is the **lowob** autonomy dial applied to automation. The agent sits at level 1 or 2, drafting or acting with approval. The robot executes only what has been approved.

## When to use RPA, an API or an agent

The order of preference is straightforward. Use an API or a native connector first, because it is faster and does not break when a screen changes. Use RPA second, for legacy systems where the screen is the only interface. Add a model or an agent only where a step needs interpretation or judgment.

| Situation | Better choice |
| --- | --- |
| The system has an API and the rules are fixed | Workflow automation over the API |
| No API, stable screens, fixed rules | RPA |
| Unstructured input, fixed destination | Workflow with a model step, RPA if the destination has no API |
| Steps vary case by case and need judgment | Agent proposing, robot executing, person approving |

Three mistakes recur. The first is automating a broken process: a robot that copies bad data between systems copies it faster. The second is leaving robots without owners. Unattended robots log in with credentials, so each one needs a named owner, scoped access and an entry in the AI and automation inventory, the same as an agent identity. The third is treating an agent as a cheaper robot. Where the steps are fixed, a deterministic robot is more predictable and easier to audit than a model choosing its own path.

## lowob takeaways

- **RPA drives screens, not decisions.** It repeats fixed actions where no API exists.
- **APIs come first.** Use RPA for legacy systems, not where a connector already works.
- **Agents decide, robots execute.** Vendor platforms now combine the two, with people approving.
- **Every robot needs an owner.** Unattended bots hold credentials and belong in the inventory.

## Common questions

### What is robotic process automation in simple terms?

Software that repeats the clicks, keystrokes and copy-paste steps a person would make on screen, so that rule-based tasks run without someone doing them by hand.

### Is RPA the same as AI?

No. A classic RPA robot follows a script and makes no judgments. It is often combined with AI models that read documents or decide what the robot should do.

### Will AI agents replace RPA?

In some tasks, but RPA remains useful where steps are fixed and systems lack APIs. Vendors now sell robots and agents together, with agents deciding and robots executing.

### What is the difference between attended and unattended RPA?

Attended robots are started by a user at their own machine. Unattended robots run on their own, typically on virtual machines, without a person present.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft Learn, Power Automate for desktop](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/training/modules/robotic-process-automation/2-pad), accessed November 2026. Vendor training material on RPA, legacy apps, attended and unattended runs.
- [UiPath, About agents](https://docs.uipath.com/agents/automation-cloud/latest/user-guide/about-agents), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation on robots, agents and agentic automation.
- [Gartner Peer Insights, Business orchestration and automation technologies](https://www.gartner.com/reviews/market/business-orchestration-and-automation-technologies), accessed November 2026. Market definition and vendor listings; listing text is vendor-supplied.
- [Reuters via The Star, Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027, Gartner says](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says), 25 June 2025. Analyst predictions, including the 2028 decision forecast.

# What Is ISO/IEC 42001?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-iso-42001/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-27 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: ISO/IEC 42001, published in December 2023, sets requirements for an AI management system and can be certified by an accredited body. It follows the familiar ISO clause structure and adds 38 reference controls in Annex A. A companion standard for certification bodies, ISO/IEC 42006, followed in July 2025, and UKAS accredited its first certifier in January 2026.

ISO/IEC 42001 is the international standard that specifies requirements for an AI management system: the policies, roles, risk processes and records through which an organisation governs the AI it builds or uses. Unlike the NIST AI RMF, it can be certified by an accredited third party. For a mid-size company it matters most when enterprise buyers start asking for proof that AI is governed, in the way they already ask for ISO 27001 or SOC 2.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What ISO/IEC 42001 means

A management system standard does not tell an organisation which AI to use or how to build it. It requires a working system for deciding, checking and improving: a defined scope, an AI policy, assigned responsibilities, a risk and impact assessment process, controls chosen in response, internal audit and management review. The certificate says that system exists and operates, not that any individual AI output is correct.

| ISO/IEC 42001 is | ISO/IEC 42001 is not |
| --- | --- |
| Requirements for an AI management system | A technical test of model accuracy or safety |
| Certifiable by an accredited body | A legal licence to operate AI |
| Applicable to AI users as well as builders | Only for companies that train models |
| Compatible with ISO 27001 and ISO 9001 | A substitute for EU AI Act compliance |

## How the standard is structured

The body follows the high-level structure shared by ISO management system standards, which makes it easier to run alongside ISO 27001 for information security.

| Clause | Topic | What an auditor looks for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 4 | Context of the organisation | Scope of the AI management system, interested parties |
| 5 | Leadership | AI policy, roles and authorities |
| 6 | Planning | AI risk assessment, risk treatment, AI system impact assessment, objectives |
| 7 | Support | Resources, competence, awareness, documented information |
| 8 | Operation | Risk and impact assessments carried out in practice |
| 9 | Performance evaluation | Monitoring, internal audit, management review |
| 10 | Improvement | Nonconformities, corrective action, continual improvement |

Annex A lists 38 reference controls in nine sections, and Annex B gives implementation guidance for each. Annex C lists AI-related objectives and risk sources, and Annex D covers use across sectors and integration with other management system standards. As with ISO 27001, an organisation documents which controls apply and why in a statement of applicability.

The AI system impact assessment is the clause that most distinguishes 42001 from a security standard. It asks the organisation to consider consequences for individuals and groups affected by an AI system, not only risks to the organisation itself.

## How certification works

Certification is carried out by a certification body accredited by a national accreditation body, such as UKAS in the UK. The infrastructure is still young: ISO/IEC 42006, which sets the extra competence and audit requirements for those bodies, was published in July 2025, and UKAS granted its first 42001 accreditation, to BSI, in January 2026. Buyers should check that a certificate comes from an accredited body, not only from a firm that offers audits.

ISO/IEC 42001 is also the base for the EU's first harmonised AI standard. EN 18286, a quality management system standard for providers of high-risk AI, was published by the Commission on 14 October 2026 and uses the same management system structure, designed to be layered on top of 42001. Orrick notes that conforming to ISO/IEC 42001 alone does not give the presumption of conformity under the EU AI Act; EN 18286 does, for the requirements it covers.

| Stage | What happens | Typical duration (CSA guidance) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stage 1 | Documentation and design review: scope, policies, risk and impact methods, statement of applicability | 1 to 2 days |
| Gap | Fix findings before the main audit | Typically 4 to 12 weeks, no more than six months |
| Stage 2 | Evidence that the system operates: risk management, governance, controls | 3 to 9 or more days |
| Surveillance | Annual sampling audits to confirm continued conformity | About a third of initial audit time |

Durations depend on scope and size. A firm that uses a handful of vendor AI tools in one function can draw a narrow scope; a firm that sells an AI product will usually need a broader one.

## Who should pursue it

Certification is worth the cost when customers ask for it. That usually means selling AI-enabled services to enterprises or regulated buyers whose procurement teams have added AI questions to security reviews. For most 20- to 500-person firms the better first step is to build the parts of the system that any buyer will ask about: the inventory, the owner of each AI use, the risk and impact notes, and a record of decisions. These map to clauses 6 to 9 and become the evidence base if certification follows.

This is the **lowob** position on governance generally. The standard describes a loop of deciding, checking and improving. The decision record is where that loop leaves evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **It certifies the system, not the model.** A 42001 certificate shows AI governance operates, not that outputs are right.
- **The structure is familiar.** Clauses 4 to 10 mirror ISO 27001, so firms with security certification can extend existing processes.
- **Check accreditation.** Certification bodies for 42001 are newly accredited; ask which accreditation body stands behind a certificate.
- **Build the record first.** Inventory, owners, impact notes and decisions are the evidence an auditor will sample.

## Common questions

### What is ISO 42001 in simple terms?

An international standard for running an AI management system: policies, roles, risk and impact assessments and reviews that govern how an organisation builds or uses AI.

### Is ISO 42001 certification mandatory?

No. It is voluntary, but enterprise customers increasingly ask for it, and its processes support evidence for laws such as the EU AI Act.

### What is the difference between ISO 42001 and ISO 27001?

ISO 27001 covers information security management. ISO 42001 covers AI management, adding AI risk and impact assessments and AI-specific controls. Both share the same clause structure.

### How long does ISO 42001 certification take?

The audit itself runs in two stages over several weeks to months, after preparation. Certificates last three years with annual surveillance audits.

## In the news

- 27 October 2026 · Orrick[First harmonised standard published under the EU AI Act](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-27-first-harmonised-standard-published-under-the-eu-ai-act)EN 18286 turns parts of the Act into something an auditor can check. Firms working towards ISO 42001 should map the overlap.
