# The Commercial Operating Rhythm: Weekly, Monthly, Quarterly

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-operating-rhythm/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-26 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A commercial system without a rhythm drifts: definitions erode, forecasts are argued rather than built, and strategic choices are never reviewed against outcomes. A working rhythm has three cadences. The weekly meeting decides deals and coverage, the monthly meeting sets the forecast and reallocates channel and campaign effort, and the quarterly review grades the strategic decisions on segment, position, price and the market map. Each meeting should leave decisions on the record, which is how the commercial system feeds the brain.

A commercial operating rhythm is the fixed sequence of meetings in which a firm reviews its commercial numbers and makes its recurring commercial decisions. It has three cadences. Weekly, the team decides on deals and account coverage. Monthly, it sets the forecast and moves channel and campaign effort. Quarterly, it grades the strategic choices on segment, position, price and the market map against outcomes. The rhythm matters because commercial decisions are frequent and decision time is poorly used: McKinsey's 2019 survey found managers spend 37% of their time making decisions and that most of that time is used ineffectively. A good rhythm uses one set of numbers, ends each meeting with recorded decisions, and is the point where the commercial system writes its outcomes back.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Parts 2 to 5 of this series covered the strategic choices: the position, the segment, the price architecture and the market map. Each is a decision that should be reviewed against what happened. Without a rhythm, none of them is. The position stays on the website long after win-loss interviews have contradicted it. The segment choice is revisited only when a quarter is missed. The pricing rules erode one exception at a time.

The rhythm is what turns a set of choices into a system. It is also the part of the commercial system that matters most to The Build Order, because it is where outcomes come back and meet the decisions that caused them.

## A system without a rhythm drifts

Decision time is the scarce resource. McKinsey's 2019 survey of 1,228 managers found respondents spent 37% of their working time making decisions, and 61% said most of that time was used ineffectively. The same survey found organisations that make decisions quickly are twice as likely to make high-quality decisions as slow ones. Speed and quality move together.

Commercial meetings are where much of that time goes, and where drift shows. Typical symptoms are recognisable.

| Symptom | What it indicates |
| --- | --- |
| The pipeline meeting reviews every deal in order | No rule for which deals need a decision |
| Marketing and sales bring different pipeline numbers | No shared definitions or source of truth |
| The forecast changes most in the last two weeks of a quarter | Forecast categories are not applied consistently |
| Strategic choices are discussed only after a miss | No quarterly review with grading |
| Meetings end without a list of decisions | Nothing to grade later |

## The three cadences

Each cadence has a different job. Mixing them is the commonest design fault: strategy debated in a weekly deal review, or deal detail consuming a quarterly session.

| Cadence | Purpose | Inputs | Decisions made | Attendees | Length |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Weekly | Move deals and cover priority accounts | Pipeline changes, slipped deals, Tier 1 coverage | Deal actions, resourcing, exceptions within limits | Sales lead, sellers, revenue operations | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Monthly | Set the forecast and reallocate effort | Forecast by category, coverage, channel and campaign results | Forecast call, budget shifts, partner priorities | Commercial lead, sales, marketing, partners, finance | 90 minutes |
| Quarterly | Grade strategy against outcomes | Decision record outcomes, win-loss themes, segment metrics, pocket price | Keep, change or supersede position, segment, price rules and tiers | Leadership | Half a day |

The cadences should share one data source and one set of definitions, the condition set out in Part 1 ([The Commercial System: what it is](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/)). If the weekly meeting uses a CRM report and the monthly meeting uses a spreadsheet, the rhythm will spend its time reconciling.

## Weekly: deals and coverage

The weekly meeting should review changes, not the whole pipeline. Three questions organise it.

**What slipped?** Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies, found win rates fell 67% when deals slipped, especially for deals delayed by more than eight weeks. A slipped deal is the clearest sign that something has changed, and it needs a decision: re-qualify, escalate or close.

**What has gone quiet?** The same benchmarks found more than seven days of inactivity with no future activity scheduled cut win rates by 65%. A simple report of open deals with no next step dated is the most useful page in the meeting.

**Is Tier 1 covered?** The market map from Part 5 gives each Tier 1 account an owner and a status ([Market maps that sales actually uses](https://lowob.com/research/market-maps-that-sales-actually-uses/)). The weekly question is which Tier 1 accounts had no meaningful contact.

Exceptions within the pricing rules from Part 4 can be approved here. Exceptions above them go to the named approver, on the record.

## Monthly: forecast and allocation

The monthly meeting has two jobs: a forecast the firm can plan against, and decisions about where effort goes next.

Forecasting is the weaker of the two in most firms. Gartner's 2020 research found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers had high confidence in their organisation's forecasting accuracy, and only 47% believed their organisation had high-quality data. A 2021 Forrester Consulting study of 327 revenue operations decision makers, commissioned by Clari, found only 18% said their quarterly forecasts were within 5% of actual revenue, and 55% said they missed by more than 10% on average.

A forecast improves most from consistent categories. Microsoft's Dynamics 365 documentation uses a typical set: pipeline for early or stalled deals, best case where the deal is progressing without commitment, and committed where the customer has committed and the firm is waiting on paperwork. The value lies less in the labels than in applying the same entry rule every month.

| Forecast input | What to check | A common fault |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Committed | Customer commitment recorded, not inferred | Deals marked committed on seller confidence |
| Best case | A dated next step with the buyer | Best case used as a holding category |
| Pipeline coverage | Pipeline value against target for the period | A single ratio applied regardless of win rate |
| Slipped from last month | Count and value, with reasons | Slips moved silently to the next period |

Pipeline coverage needs care. HubSpot's guidance puts typical coverage at three to five times target and treats ratios above eight as a possible sign of poor qualification. The right ratio is the inverse of the firm's own win rate for the period: a team that wins 25% of qualified pipeline needs about four times coverage. The general rule is a starting point; the firm's win rate is the evidence.

The allocation half of the meeting reviews channel, partner and campaign results against what each was expected to produce, and moves budget or effort accordingly. Each move is a decision with an expected effect.

> A meeting that ends without a list of decisions has nothing to grade next quarter.

## Quarterly: grading the strategy

The quarterly review is where the strategic choices from Parts 2 to 5 are graded. It should be short on presentation and long on judgment.

| Strategic decision | Evidence to bring | The question to answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Position (Part 2) | Win-loss themes, share of losses to no decision | Is the stated alternative the one buyers weigh? |
| Segment (Part 3) | Win rate, cycle, retention by segment; recorded exceptions | Does the chosen segment still score best? |
| Price architecture (Part 4) | Pocket price waterfall, discount outcomes | Did exceptions buy anything? |
| Market map (Part 5) | Tier 1 coverage, trigger conversion, re-tiering outcomes | Is tiering predicting where deals come from? |
| Last quarter's recorded decisions | Expected against actual outcomes | Which judgments held, and whose? |

The last row is the one most firms skip. It turns the review from a discussion of the quarter into a test of the firm's judgment. Our piece on calibration argues that comparing what people expected with what happened is the most honest learning signal a firm has ([Calibration is the honest learning signal](https://lowob.com/research/calibration-is-the-honest-learning-signal/)).

When a strategic decision changes, it should be superseded on the record rather than overwritten, so the next review can compare results before and after.

## Where the rhythm meets the brain

The Build Order describes a brain as a loop: store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning. The commercial operating rhythm is where the last step happens in practice. A weekly meeting that records its deal decisions, a monthly meeting that records its forecast call and allocation moves, and a quarterly review that grades them, together produce exactly the record the brain needs ([The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

The rhythm is also a natural place for a first agent. Preparing the weekly slip report, the monthly forecast pack and the quarterly evidence table is research and assembly work, the kind The Build Order recommends automating first ([The first AI agent should be boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)). The decisions stay with people. An agent can draft the pack; nothing it drafts changes a forecast or a price rule without a named person's approval ([Gateway 1: Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)).

Illustrative example: changing the weekly agenda

Decision
:   Replace the full pipeline walk-through with three standing items: slipped deals, deals with no dated next step, and uncovered Tier 1 accounts.

Reason and owner
:   The meeting ran over 90 minutes, reviewed every deal at equal length and rarely ended with recorded actions. Owned by the head of sales; revenue operations prepares the reports.

What changed
:   The meeting fell to 50 minutes; each item ends with a recorded decision and owner; the monthly forecast now starts from the slip log rather than seller estimates.

Illustrative: a composite of a 90-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Give each cadence one job.** Deals weekly, forecast and allocation monthly, strategy quarterly.
- **Review changes, not the whole pipeline.** Slipped and quiet deals are where decisions are needed.
- **Set coverage from your own win rate.** General ratios are a starting point, not a target.
- **Grade last quarter's decisions.** Expected against actual is how the system and the brain learn.

Gateway card

### Before you run the new rhythm

- One data source and one set of definitions for all three cadences
- A weekly report of slipped deals, deals with no dated next step and uncovered Tier 1 accounts
- Forecast categories with written entry rules
- A coverage target derived from your own win rate
- A quarterly evidence table for position, segment, price and map
- A decision log kept at every meeting, with owners and expected outcomes

## Common questions

### What is a commercial operating rhythm?

The fixed sequence of weekly, monthly and quarterly meetings in which a firm reviews its commercial numbers and makes its recurring commercial decisions, with each decision recorded.

### What should a weekly sales pipeline meeting cover?

Changes rather than the whole pipeline: deals that slipped, deals with no dated next step, and priority accounts with no recent contact. Each item should end with a decision and an owner.

### How accurate are B2B sales forecasts?

Often not very. A 2021 Forrester Consulting study for Clari found only 18% of revenue teams forecast within 5% of actual quarterly revenue, and Gartner found only 45% of sales leaders had high confidence in forecast accuracy.

### How much pipeline coverage do you need?

Roughly the inverse of your win rate for the period. A team that converts 25% of qualified pipeline needs about four times its target. HubSpot cites three to five times as typical.

## Sources and notes

- [McKinsey, Decision making in the age of urgency](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/decision-making-in-the-age-of-urgency), April 2019. Survey of 1,228 respondents fielded in 2018; self-reported.
- [Gartner, less than 50% of sales leaders have high confidence in forecasting accuracy](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-02-12-gartner-says-less-than-50--of-sales-leaders-and-selle), February 2020. Sample not stated in the release.
- [Forrester Consulting for Clari, revenue operations study](https://pages.clari.com/rs/866-BBG-005/images/forrester-clari-revops-study-2021.pdf), August 2021. Commissioned by a forecasting vendor; 327 US software revenue operations decision makers.
- [Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks](https://www.ebsta.com/ebsta-pavilion-b2b-sales-benchmarks-2024/). Vendor analysis of 4.2 million opportunities, 2023 data; associations, not causes.
- [Microsoft Learn, forecast categories in Dynamics 365 Sales](https://learn.microsoft.com/nb-no/dynamics365/sales/capture-forecast-category-opportunity). Vendor product documentation.

## Next move

At your next pipeline meeting, write down every decision made and who owns it. If the list has fewer than five items after an hour, change the agenda before changing the tools.

# Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person

Source: https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Gateway 1 requires that anything an agent sends outside the company passes a named approver, with the approval logged. It addresses the leading security risks in OWASP's 2025 list, satisfies supervisors who must reconstruct automated decisions, and works only if reviewers actually verify; approval rates alone measure fatigue as well as quality.

Gateway 1 is a single rule: nothing an agent produces leaves the company until a named person approves it, and every approval is logged with who, when and what they saw. It is the most common control in serious agent deployments because it addresses the leading security risks for AI systems, gives regulated firms the evidence supervisors ask for, and keeps the first mistakes internal. It only works if reviewers actually check, so the gate needs its own measures.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every commercial agent eventually produces something meant for someone outside the company: a follow-up email, a proposal, a quote, a reply to a community question. The first time one goes out with the wrong figure, the wrong name or a claim the company cannot support, the programme loses the trust it needs to continue.

The control that prevents this is not new or sophisticated. It is a person who approves outbound work before it leaves, and a log that records the approval. It is also the one design choice that every credible agent architecture we reviewed for this series shares.

## Why the gate is the industry's answer

**Security.** OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications ranks prompt injection as the leading risk and lists excessive agency (a model with too many tools and too much permission) sixth. The two combine dangerously in a commercial agent that reads inbound email, holds a user's access and can send messages. OWASP's recommended mitigations are architectural: minimise tool scope and permissions, require explicit approval for high-risk actions such as sending or deleting, and log every tool call with its parameters. A human gate before anything outbound implements the middle control directly.

**Supervision.** In financial services, supervisors increasingly expect firms to reconstruct the full chain of automated activity behind a client outcome. In *Regulators want the chain, not the model* we argued that what gets inspected is the sequence of evidence, approval and outcome, not the model's internals. A logged approval is the anchor of that chain.

**Trust.** Gartner's forecast that over 40% of agentic projects will be cancelled by 2027 cites inadequate risk controls among the causes. A visible gate is how a sponsor shows the board that the first mistakes will be caught internally.

> The gate is not a lack of nerve. It is how autonomy is earned.

## Designing the gate

*Figure: Five plug points: identity and limits, context in, precedent in, the gate, and the outcome written back.*

### A queue, not an inbox

Drafts land in a queue owned by the person accountable for the client relationship. Each item carries the draft, the sources the agent used and a one-line reason. The reviewer has three actions:

| Action | When | What gets logged |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approve | The draft is correct as written | Approver, time, version sent |
| Edit and approve | The draft is close; the reviewer changes it | Approver, time, the edits made |
| Return | The draft is wrong or should not be sent | Approver, time, a short reason |

The edits and the return reasons are the most valuable data the gate produces. They show where the agent is weak and become precedent for the next run.

### Who approves what

| Output | Approver | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Routine follow-up to an existing client | Account owner | Fast path; spot-checked weekly |
| First contact with a new prospect | Account owner | Check claims and personalisation |
| Proposal or pricing | Account owner plus a second approver for non-standard terms | Discounts beyond standard need finance |
| Public post or community reply | Named communications owner | Strictest in crypto and fintech |
| Anything regulated (financial promotion, health claim) | Compliance reviewer | Existing review rules apply unchanged |

### The guardrails around the gate

- **Kill switch.** One named person can stop every agent immediately, and everyone knows who it is.
- **Spend caps.** Each agent has a usage budget with an alert well before the limit.
- **Test before change.** Any change to an agent's instructions runs against a small set of past cases before it goes live.
- **Logs with cost.** Every action is recorded with what the agent saw, what it did and what it cost.

## When the gate becomes a rubber stamp

A gate works only if reviewers verify. The risk is well documented. In *Approval rate measures fatigue too* we set out how approval rates rise when reviewers tire, trust fluent text, see only easy cases, or when agents learn to produce safer, blander drafts. In *A reviewer who does not verify is not a control* we argued that an approval without verification is a signature, not a check.

Measure the gate itself:

| Measure | How | What it tells you |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Independent spot-check | A second person reviews a random few percent of approved items blind | The real error rate behind the approval rate |
| Seeded errors | Occasionally insert a draft with a known flaw | Whether reviewers catch what they should |
| Time on item | Distribution of review times | Approvals in seconds on complex items are not reviews |
| Edit and return rates | Share of items edited or returned, by agent and task | Where the agent is weak, and whether reviewers are engaged |

## Raising autonomy at the gate

The gate is also where trust is earned. When a task shows a low error rate on spot-checks for a sustained period, its autonomy can rise one level for that task only: from draft to act-with-approval, or from act-with-approval to act-and-report for reversible internal changes. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is strong evidence, and in regulated firms it may stay there permanently.

## Where the order bends

| Industry | What the gate must catch |
| --- | --- |
| Financial services and fintech | Financial promotions, suitability, anything a supervisor may reconstruct |
| Crypto and digital assets | Public statements that can move markets or create disclosure issues |
| Media and publishing | Brand safety and any blurring of editorial and commercial content |
| Healthcare and life sciences | Promotional claims and anything near patient data |
| Industrial distribution | Price, lead time and specification accuracy on quotes |
| Professional services | Confidential information from one client reaching another |

Illustrative example: catching a wrong figure

Decision
:   Route every agent-drafted client email through the account owner's queue, with sources attached, and spot-check 5% of approvals weekly.

Reason and owner
:   A draft follow-up quoted last quarter's pricing; it was caught by chance rather than by design. Owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   Return reasons show stale pricing as the most common error, which leads to marking price documents current or superseded in the context layer.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **One rule, logged.** Nothing leaves the company without a named approver and a record of what they saw.
- **Design for three outcomes.** Approve, edit or return; the edits and returns are the most useful data.
- **Measure the gate.** Spot-checks and seeded errors, not approval rates alone.
- **Earn autonomy task by task.** Raise one level at a time, on evidence.

Gateway card

### Gateway 1

- Every outbound action has a named approver
- Approvals, edits and returns are logged with sources and time
- A kill switch with a named owner
- Spend caps and alerts per agent
- Weekly spot-checks of approved items

## Common questions

### What is human-in-the-loop for AI agents?

A design in which a named person approves an agent's output before it takes effect outside the company, with the approval logged. It limits the damage from errors and prompt injection and creates evidence for audits.

### Do AI agents need human approval?

For anything that reaches clients or the public, yes, at least until a task has a sustained record of low errors. Reversible internal changes can often run and report instead.

### How do you stop human review becoming a rubber stamp?

Measure it: blind spot-checks of approved items, occasional seeded errors, time spent per item, and edit and return rates by task.

### What is excessive agency in AI?

An OWASP risk category describing AI systems given more tools, permissions or autonomy than their task requires, so that a small error or manipulation can cause a damaging action.

- Gartner forecast, June 2025, as reported by [Reuters via The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says).
- Supervisory expectations in financial services summarised from [Snell & Wilmer on FINRA's 2026 oversight report](https://www.swlaw.com/publication/finras-2026-oversight-report-signals-a-supervisory-reckoning-for-autonomous-ai/).
- The approval matrix and gate measures are **lowob**'s working method.

Ask who would notice, today, if an agent sent a client the wrong figure. If the answer is "the client", the gate comes before the next agent.

# What Is Marketing Mix Modeling? A Small-Company Guide

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-marketing-mix-modeling/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Marketing mix modelling estimates each channel's total contribution to an outcome from aggregate weekly data, without tracking individuals. Google's Meridian and Meta's Robyn have made the method free, but both are clear that it needs history, variation and calibration. Combined with attribution and incrementality tests, it gives the most honest picture a company can assemble.

Marketing mix modelling (MMM) is a statistical method that estimates how much each marketing channel, and other factors such as price and seasonality, contributed to an outcome. It works from aggregate weekly data and does not track any individual, which is why it has returned as individual tracking has declined. Google's Meridian and Meta's Robyn have made the software free. Both are clear about what it needs: history, real variation in spend, and experiments to calibrate it. The results are rough, and combined with attribution and incrementality tests they are the most honest picture a company can assemble.

MMM was built for large consumer companies with years of data and television budgets. A version of it now works for companies much smaller than that, provided they accept what the method can and cannot tell them.

## What it does

Given a history of spend by channel and outcomes over the same periods, the model estimates the relationship between each channel's spend and the outcome. It allows for two things a simple regression misses. Google researchers set them out in the 2017 paper behind much of the current tooling: advertising "usually has lag effects and diminishing returns." The lag is called carryover or adstock, the decaying effect of an ad after it runs. The diminishing return is called saturation or shape: each extra dollar buys less than the last.

The model also includes factors the company does not control, so they are not mistaken for channel effects. The output is an estimate of each channel's contribution, its return at the current spend, and, with care, what would happen if spend were shifted between channels.

| Method | Question it answers | Data it needs | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Attribution | Which touches preceded each conversion? | User-level tracking | Counts presence, not cause |
| Incrementality test | What did this channel cause, in this window? | A holdout group or region | One channel, one period at a time |
| Marketing mix model | What did each channel contribute, in total, over time? | Two-plus years of weekly aggregate data | Rough, and sensitive to assumptions |

Unlike attribution, which assigns credit to touches on converting customers, MMM attempts to measure the total effect of a channel, including the customers it influenced without a trackable touch. Unlike incrementality tests, it does not require holding anything out; it infers from natural variation in spend and outcomes. Our piece on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the other two.

## The tools: Meridian and Robyn

Two open-source packages from the largest ad platforms have changed who can run MMM.

**Meridian** is Google's. It opened to all marketers in January 2025, after testing with hundreds of brands. It is Bayesian: it combines prior knowledge with the data, and lets results from incrementality experiments be added as priors. It can use reach and frequency, not only impressions, and works at national or regional (geo) level.

**Robyn** is Meta's. It uses ridge regression, which handles channels whose spend moves together better than ordinary regression, and tunes adstock and saturation settings within ranges the analyst sets. Its documentation includes an analyst's guide that is one of the clearest public statements of what an MMM needs.

Both are built by companies that sell advertising. The code is open and inspectable, which is the main safeguard. The assumptions, priors and channel definitions are still the analyst's, and they decide the answer.

## What it needs

**Enough history.** Robyn's guide is direct: "an MMM will need a minimum of two years of historical weekly data." With only monthly data, it suggests four to five years.

**Enough data per thing being estimated.** Robyn recommends about ten observations per independent variable. Meridian frames the same point as data points per model parameter, and is more cautious. Its own worked example: two years of weekly national data, 104 points, for a model with 26 parameters gives about four points per parameter, and "this sample size is too low to estimate the model reliably." Three years for ten parameters might "glean some directional information." The fix is fewer channels, more history, or regional data.

**Real variation in spend.** If a channel was always on at the same level, the model cannot tell what it did. Meridian notes that insufficient variation in spend "adversely impacts national models."

**Clean, consistent data.** Spend, impressions where available, and outcomes, all by week, all defined the same way throughout.

**Knowledge of the external factors.** Pricing changes, launches, seasonality, competitor events, platform policy changes, so they can be included rather than mistaken for channel effects.

**Experiments to calibrate it.** Robyn's guide says "we strongly recommend using experimental and causal results that are considered to be the ground truth to calibrate MMM", and warns against using low-confidence ones. Meridian accepts experiment results as priors. And someone who understands both the statistics and the business, because a model will produce a confident answer to a badly posed question.

> A mix model will produce a confident answer to a badly posed question. The variation in the data, not the software, decides what it can know.

## Where it goes wrong

Too little variation, so the model attributes outcomes to whatever happened to move. Channels that were turned on and off together, so their effects cannot be separated; Robyn's guide calls this multicollinearity and recommends checking correlations before modelling. Outcomes with long lags, where this quarter's result reflects last quarter's spend. Over-trust in point estimates that have wide uncertainty: the 2017 Google paper found that with small samples the priors strongly shape the results and may bias them, and that the recommended optimal mix has high variance. And the temptation to use the model to justify a plan already decided, by adjusting assumptions until it agrees.

## A lightweight version for a small company

A company with a year or two of weekly data across four to eight channels can run a simple model with Meridian or Robyn. At that size, the documentation's own arithmetic says to keep the model small: group minor channels, keep only the controls that matter, and treat the output as directional. The results will be rough. They will also be more informative than a platform's attribution report, because they attempt to answer the right question.

The practical approach is to combine three things: attribution for running the week, one or two incrementality tests per quarter on the biggest channels, and a simple mix model refreshed quarterly to check that the whole picture is consistent. The tests also calibrate the model. Where the three disagree, the disagreement is the finding. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers test design at low volumes, and [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers effects too slow for weekly data to show.

A company can also create the variation a model needs. Deliberately flexing a channel's spend up and down in planned weeks, or in chosen regions, turns a flat history into one the model can read.

## For companies whose tracking is fragile

Companies in restricted categories lose pixel history every time an account is suspended and cannot rely on platform reporting. Aggregate methods do not care. A model built on the company's own weekly spend and outcome data survives every account reset, which makes it unusually valuable for exactly the companies least likely to have heard of it. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) covers the channel side.

## lowob takeaways

- **History and variation come first.** Two years of weekly data with real movement in spend, or the model guesses.
- **Keep the model small.** Data points per parameter, not the number of channels, decides what it can estimate.
- **Calibrate with experiments.** Both Meridian and Robyn are built to accept incrementality results.
- **Use all three methods.** Attribution for the week, tests for allocation, MMM for the whole picture; disagreement is the finding.

## Common questions

### What is marketing mix modelling?

A statistical method that estimates how much each marketing channel, and factors such as price and seasonality, contributed to an outcome such as sales. It works from aggregate data over time and does not track individuals.

### How much data do you need for marketing mix modelling?

Meta's Robyn guide asks for at least two years of weekly data and about ten observations per variable. Google's Meridian documentation warns that two years of national data supports only a small model.

### Can a small company use marketing mix modelling?

Yes, with limits. A company with a year or two of weekly data across four to eight channels can run a small model in Meridian or Robyn. Treat the result as directional and calibrate it with holdout tests.

### What is the difference between Meridian and Robyn?

Meridian is Google's Bayesian MMM, which accepts experiment results as priors and supports geo-level and reach and frequency data. Robyn is Meta's, using ridge regression and tuning adstock and saturation within set ranges. Both are free and open source.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, announcement opening Meridian to all marketers](https://blog.google/products/ads-commerce/meridian-marketing-mix-model-open-to-everyone/), 29 January 2025. Vendor announcement; Google sells advertising.
- [Google for Developers, Meridian: amount of data needed](https://developers.google.cn/meridian/docs/pre-modeling/amount-data-needed?hl=en). Vendor documentation; Google calls its guidance "rough and directional."
- [Meta, Robyn: An Analyst's Guide to MMM](https://facebookexperimental.github.io/Robyn/docs/analysts-guide-to-MMM). Vendor documentation; Meta sells advertising.
- [Jin, Wang, Sun, Chan and Koehler, Bayesian Methods for Media Mix Modeling with Carryover and Shape Effects](https://research.google/pubs/bayesian-methods-for-media-mix-modeling-with-carryover-and-shape-effects/), Google, 2017. Research paper by Google authors; applied to one advertiser's data.
- The method comparison table is **lowob**'s synthesis.

## Next move

Pull two years of weekly spend by channel and weekly outcomes into one sheet. Count the channels whose spend never moved; those are the ones no model can measure until you flex them on purpose.

# Your First Ten Sponsors Are Design Partners

Source: https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-sponsors-are-design-partners/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Sponsorship, data and research are B2B sales. Treat the first ten sponsors as design partners: agree a named audience segment, a success test and a two-way reporting format before any money moves, price the first campaign for evidence, and measure renewal from the first conversation.

Sponsorship, data and research are B2B sales; treat the first ten buyers as design partners, agree the test and the report before the money moves, and measure renewal from day one. Buyers are ready for that framing. In the IAB's 2025 study of US creator ad buyers, 40% ranked overall return on investment as their top measure, and the most requested improvements were attribution, consistent reporting and tools that connect activity to business outcomes.

## A B2B sale with a media name

[An audience is not a business](https://lowob.com/research/an-audience-is-not-a-business/) identified the buyers for a media business, plus an investor. Sponsors, data buyers and research buyers are all business buyers. They have a budget, a boss and a number to hit. The sale works like any other B2B sale, which is what [Your first ten customers are design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/) described.

That sale is rarely made by one person. Forrester's 2024 State of Business Buying found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments. A sponsorship that has to be justified to finance and sales leadership needs a result someone can show them.

The mistake is to sell it like inventory. A rate card, a slot, a count of people who might see it. That is how large publishers sell to agencies. It does not work for a niche business with a precise audience, because it hides the only thing you have that they cannot buy elsewhere.

## Pick the first ten for fit and renewal

The first ten sponsors set the pattern for the next fifty. Choose them for two things.

**Fit:** their customer is your member. Not adjacent, not "also interested". The same job titles you recruited by name in [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/). The IAB found audience alignment was among buyers' top two creator selection criteria, at 56%, so fit is also what the sponsor will check first.

**Renewal potential:** they have a recurring need and a budget that resets. A company launching one product has one campaign in them. A company with a quarterly pipeline target has four.

Logo is a trap. A well-known name that does not fit will not renew, and you will have built your reporting around a buyer you cannot repeat.

| Signal | Strong design partner | Weak design partner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Customer match | Sells to the exact roles in your membership | Sells to an adjacent or general audience |
| Budget | Quarterly pipeline target, recurring programme budget | One launch, one-off fund |
| Buyer | Marketing or sales leader who owns a number | Media buyer or agency with a cost-per-unit brief |
| Success test | Can name a result they would act on | Wants impressions or "awareness" |
| Reporting | Will share what happened to the leads | Will not report back |

## What a design-partner sponsorship contains

Four parts, agreed in writing before any money moves.

**A named audience segment.** Not "our readers". The segment by role, company type and size, verified from your membership data. The sponsor is buying access to that segment, and the segment is what the claims register in [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) has to support.

**A shared success test.** Agree what counts: replies, qualified leads, meetings booked, survey responses. Not impressions, not opens. If the sponsor cannot name a result they would act on, they are not ready to be a design partner.

**A reporting format.** One page, agreed before the campaign. What you will report, how often, and what the sponsor will report back about what happened to the leads. The second half is where most publishers lose the renewal.

**A price after the first campaign.** Run the first at a modest fixed fee or a reduced rate. Then set the real price from what it produced. You are buying evidence; they are buying a lower-risk test. Both sides get a case to use. Our explainer on [value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/) covers how to set a price from the value a buyer receives.

The one-page agreement works like a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/) in an enterprise sale: both sides sign up to the steps, dates and evidence before the work begins.

> You are buying evidence; they are buying a lower-risk test. Both sides get a case to use.

## The sponsor's belief and the proof they accept

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) said every audience has one belief that has to be true before they buy. A sponsor's belief is that your members are the people they are trying to reach and that those people respond.

Three forms of proof work. Verified audience composition, from your own data, with a method you can describe. Past response rates from earlier campaigns, with the test defined. A case from a peer sponsor, in the sponsor's own words.

The first sponsor gets none of these. That is why the first sponsorship is priced for evidence and why the reporting format matters so much.

Set expectations on timing as well. LinkedIn's B2B Institute, drawing on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, estimates that about 95% of potential business buyers are not in the market at any given time; for example, about 80% of companies change banking services once every five years. A single campaign will reach mostly people who are not buying this quarter. A success test built only on immediate sales sets the sponsor up to cancel. Pair a near-term response measure, such as replies or meetings, with a longer one the sponsor tracks, such as pipeline from the segment over two quarters.

## Who to sell to

Sell to marketing and sales leaders, not media buyers. A media buyer's job is to compare channels on cost per unit. You will lose that comparison every time, and the buyer will not care about the result.

A marketing leader with a pipeline number cares about response. A sales leader cares about meetings. Both can judge a design-partner test and both can renew without an agency approving it.

| Package | What it is for | Renewal cycle |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Campaign | A single test with a defined result | One-off, converts to season |
| Season | A quarter of placements against one segment | Quarterly |
| Annual partnership | Category presence across content, events and data | Yearly, your core line |
| Research sponsorship | A named report with the sponsor's question inside it | Per report |
| Event sponsorship | Access to members in a room, through the membership's rituals | Per event |

Lead with campaign and season. Move the ones that work to annual. Publishers broadly are moving in this direction: in the Reuters Institute's 2026 survey of 280 media leaders, 64% named native advertising and 54% named events as key revenue priorities. Our piece on [events that pay back](https://lowob.com/research/events-that-pay-back/) covers the event line from the buyer's side.

## Renewal is the metric, and the pipeline tracker

Renewal is the measure from the first conversation, not the second year. Ask it on the first call: "What would need to be true for you to do this again next quarter?" Write the answer down. That is your success test.

Run sponsors in the pipeline tracker from [Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/). Stage, next step, owner, date, and the success test agreed. Add two columns: the reporting date and the renewal conversation date, booked before the campaign starts. Our [renewals and expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) playbook covers how to run the renewal conversation once the evidence is in.

Stop selling CPM, one-off posts and "reach". Each of these invites comparison on the one axis where you cannot win. [From reach to recurring](https://lowob.com/research/from-reach-to-recurring/) covers what the recurring lines look like once the first ten are in.

Illustrative example: one sponsor, two quarters

Decision
:   Run a first campaign for a software vendor selling to finance leads at a modest fixed fee, against a segment of members verified by job title, with meetings booked as the success test.

Reason and owner
:   The vendor's marketing lead owned a quarterly pipeline target and agreed to report back which leads became meetings. Owned by the publisher's commercial lead.

What changed
:   The one-page report showed which content formats produced replies. The vendor renewed for a season at a price set from the first campaign's result, and the case became the proof for the next two sponsors in the same category.

Illustrative: a composite of a niche B2B publisher, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose for fit and renewal.** The customer is your member, and the budget resets.
- **Agree four things first.** Segment, success test, two-way report, price after the first campaign.
- **Sell to an owner of a number.** Marketing and sales leaders, not media buyers.
- **Book the renewal before the launch.** Ask on the first call what would make them buy again.

Gateway card

### Before the first sponsor signs

- First ten sponsors selected for member fit and recurring budget, not logo
- Each sponsorship names a verified segment and a shared success test
- Reporting format agreed in writing, both directions, before the campaign
- First campaign priced for evidence; real price set from the result
- Buyer is a marketing or sales leader with a pipeline number
- Sponsors tracked in the pipeline with reporting and renewal dates booked up front

## Common questions

### How should a niche media company sell sponsorships?

As a B2B sale, not as inventory. Sell access to a verified audience segment against a shared success test, to marketing or sales leaders rather than media buyers.

### How do I choose my first sponsors?

Pick for fit, meaning their customer is your member, and for renewal potential, meaning a recurring need and a budget that resets. A well-known logo that does not fit will not renew.

### How should I price a first sponsorship?

Run the first campaign at a modest fixed fee or reduced rate, then set the real price from what it produced.

### What should a newsletter or media sponsorship agreement include?

A named audience segment, a shared success test such as replies or meetings booked, a one-page reporting format in both directions, and a price after the first campaign.

## Sources and notes

- [IAB, Creator economy ad spend to reach $37 billion in 2025](https://www.iab.com/news/creator-economy-ad-spend-to-reach-37-billion-in-2025-growing-4x-faster-than-total-media-industry-according-to-iab/), 20 November 2025. Trade body study of US ad buyers; creator-specific, sample size not stated in the release.
- [Forrester, The State of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated.
- [LinkedIn B2B Institute, The 95-5 rule](https://business.linkedin.com/it/it/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/b2b-research/trends/95-5-rule), undated. Platform-owned research unit, which sells advertising; category purchase-cycle examples, not a universal rate.
- [Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026), 12 January 2026. Survey of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries; a strategic sample, not representative.

# Creator Partnerships Outside Crypto Make the Same Mistakes With Fewer Excuses.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/creator-partnerships-fintech-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Web3 paid publicly to learn what creator partnerships do and do not do. Fintech and AI companies moving budget into the channel can read those lessons, and regulators have since made several of them law: the FTC's 2024 rule bans buying fake followers and views, and the FCA holds firms responsible for what their influencers promote. Run creators as a programme with terms, briefs, tracking, disclosure and pay per outcome.

Web3 spent several years and a great deal of money learning what creator partnerships do and do not do: reach that produced nothing, screenshots instead of evidence, undisclosed payments, and audiences that turned out to be other creators. Fintech and AI companies now moving budget into the same channel can read those lessons, and regulators have turned several of them into rules. The FTC's 2024 rule bans buying fake followers and views, its Endorsement Guides make advertisers liable for deceptive endorsements, and the FCA holds firms responsible for financial promotions their influencers make. Creators are worth doing well, as a programme rather than a set of posts.

## Why the channel is worth doing well

For a category the ad platforms restrict, creators are one of the few channels where the product can be explained, at length, by someone the audience already trusts. A personal-finance creator can walk through a new account product in eight minutes. An AI tooling creator can show a workflow from start to finish. No paid placement offers that.

The money is moving. The Performance Marketing Association's 2025 industry study, conducted with London Research, put US affiliate and performance partnership investment at about $13.6 billion in 2024. Financial services rose from 12% to 15% of that spend, and content creators and bloggers took a larger share of investment. This is trade-body research, but the direction is consistent with what fintech teams report.

The channel is also thinly bid relative to its value, for the unglamorous reason that it takes work. Recruiting, briefing, tracking and paying two hundred creators is a programme, not a media buy. Most companies will not build it, which is why the price is still reasonable.

## The five mistakes, translated

**Buying reach instead of audience.** A creator with a million followers who are mostly other creators, or mostly outside the geography the product serves, produces impressions and nothing else. Ask for audience composition, geography and evidence of past products the audience adopted, then run one small test before believing any of it. Our guide to [reading a creator media kit](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-read-a-creator-media-kit/) covers what to request. Fake reach is now also a legal problem: the FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, in force since 21 October 2024, prohibits buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as followers, views and likes generated by bots, where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake.

**Briefing a script instead of a job.** A creator handed approved claims and asked for enthusiasm produces an ad, and the audience knows. A creator briefed on the real problem, the product truth, what may not be said and the question the audience will ask produces an explanation in their own words. The second converts. The first gets skipped.

**Paying flat when the product converts.** A creator paid a flat fee is paid for publishing. A creator paid per activated account, approved application or retained subscriber is paid for the outcome, and will tell you quickly whether the product converts with their audience. For products that do convert, cost-per-outcome terms are cheaper and self-correcting. For products that do not convert yet, creators are the wrong channel, and the flat fee only hides that.

**Treating disclosure as a formality.** The FTC's Endorsement Guides, revised in June 2023, require material connections such as payment, free product and affiliate commissions to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously. The revision says a disclosure must be "unavoidable", so one hidden behind a "more" link does not count, and that advertisers are liable for deceptive endorsements and must run "reasonable programs" to train and monitor endorsers. The FTC's influencer guidance adds that video disclosures belong in the video, not only the description, and that a creator cannot describe experience with a product they have not tried. AI companies should note that the 2023 revision says virtual, AI-generated influencers can count as endorsers.

**Measuring at the post.** Views and engagement describe the post. Accounts, applications, activations and retention describe the business. Give every creator a link, code or landing page the company controls, and report on outcomes the company's own tracking confirmed. [KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) covers the reporting standard.

| Mistake | Fix | Rule or evidence behind it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Buying reach | Audience data plus one paid test | FTC rule bans buying fake followers and views |
| Scripted brief | Brief the job, the limits and the likely question | Audience trust depends on the creator's own words |
| Flat fee | Pay per verified outcome once the product converts | Outcome pay exposes poor fit within weeks |
| Disclosure as formality | Specify wording in the brief; check every post | FTC guides: disclosure must be unavoidable; advertisers liable |
| Post-level reporting | Company-controlled links and codes, outcome reports | Only confirmed outcomes connect to revenue |

## Financial products carry an extra layer

For financial products, disclosure is the floor, not the ceiling. What the creator may claim is regulated too.

The UK is the clearest case. The FCA's FG24/1 guidance says firms working with affiliate marketers such as influencers "should take proactive responsibility" for them, and should consider how to monitor their partners' marketing. An influencer who promotes a regulated product without approval from an authorised person may be committing a criminal offence under section 21 of FSMA, punishable by up to two years' imprisonment. Each promotion must be standalone compliant, and firms should not rely on the social platform to keep their records.

The FCA enforces this. In a week of action starting 20 April 2026, as one of 17 regulators taking part, it made 120 account takedown requests, issued 34 warning alerts and identified 1,267 illegal financial adverts on Meta platforms reaching at least 2.3 million UK accounts.

> A regulator does not distinguish between the creator's mistake and the company's. Neither should your programme.

In the US, the FTC's endorsement rules apply across consumer categories, and other regulators add their own for specific products. The SEC's marketing rule, for example, requires an investment adviser's advertisements to disclose clearly and prominently whether a promoter is a client and whether they are paid. The brief should carry the approved claims and disclosure language, and the programme should check compliance before and after posting, because the FTC's guidance notes it is easier to review posts before they go live than to search for them afterwards.

## Choosing the tier

Creators are not one channel. They are three, with different jobs.

| Tier | Job | How to pay | How to measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A handful of authorities | Change what an audience believes; launches and products that need explaining | Negotiated fee, sometimes with an outcome element | Comprehension and qualified action, not volume |
| A middle tier of subject-matter creators | The core of a performance programme | Cost per outcome, structured briefs, monthly creative refresh | Verified outcomes and cost per outcome |
| A long tail of small creators | Volume at the best unit cost | Public terms, paid per outcome, run as a channel | Cost per outcome; accept unpredictable volume |

The long tail often produces the best cost per outcome and the least predictable volume. A programme needs all three tiers, in proportions that match the product's stage. A company that buys only the first tier has a launch. A company that builds only the third has a channel with no story.

## The structure that makes it a channel

Written terms. A standard brief. Product access and an FAQ. Creative the creator can adapt. Tracking per creator. A named person who answers within a day. A monthly review of who is producing outcomes and who is producing posts. Clear disclosure language and a compliance check.

That is a programme. It is the same programme Web3 needed and mostly did not build. Our [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set roles and pay across partner types, and [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers registering and paying for introductions so the economics hold. The companies entering the channel from fintech and AI have no excuse for skipping it, and every reason to build it before their competitors clear the review queue.

## lowob takeaways

- **Buy audience, not reach.** Ask for composition and past adoption, test small, and treat bought followers as a legal risk as well as a waste.
- **Brief the job, not the script.** The creator's own explanation converts; approved claims and limits keep it safe.
- **Pay per outcome once the product converts.** A flat fee pays for publishing and hides poor fit.
- **Own disclosure and compliance.** The advertiser is liable in the US and responsible in the UK; specify the wording and check every post.
- **Run the long tail as a channel.** Public terms, pay per outcome and a monthly review turn small creators into the best unit cost.

## Common questions

### Do fintech companies need to disclose paid influencer partnerships?

Yes. In the US, the FTC requires material connections such as payment, free product or affiliate commissions to be disclosed clearly and unavoidably, and holds advertisers liable for deceptive endorsements. In the UK, firms are responsible for financial promotions their influencers make.

### Can an influencer promote a financial product in the UK?

Only if the promotion is made or approved by an FCA-authorised person and meets the financial promotion rules. The FCA says unauthorised influencers promoting regulated products without approval may be committing a criminal offence.

### Should you pay creators a flat fee or per result?

Pay per verified outcome, such as an activated account or approved application, once the product converts. Flat fees pay for publishing and hide whether the audience adopts the product.

### Is it illegal to buy followers for an influencer campaign?

In the US, the FTC's rule in force since October 2024 prohibits buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as bot followers and views, for commercial purposes where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake.

# What Is Agent Memory?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agent memory is the mechanism that carries information across an agent's steps and sessions. Research frameworks split it into working, episodic, semantic and procedural memory. Benchmarks show accuracy falls on long interactions and changed facts, so memory should be tested on a company's own history and kept separate from the decision record.

Agent memory is the mechanism that lets an AI agent carry information from one step, task or session to the next: facts about customers, what happened in earlier conversations, and the rules for doing a job. Short-term memory lasts for one conversation and is now built into most platforms. Long-term memory persists across sessions and is where products differ. It is useful, but it is not the same as a company's record of decisions, and it struggles most with facts that have changed.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What agent memory means

A language model has no memory between calls. Everything it knows about the current task has to be placed in front of it each time. Agent memory is the software that decides what to keep, where to store it and what to bring back.

The most cited framework is CoALA (Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents), from Princeton researchers Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan and Griffiths, published in *Transactions on Machine Learning Research* in 2024. It borrows four categories from cognitive science.

| Type | What it holds | Commercial example | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Working | The active task: inputs, retrieved material, goals | The account brief being drafted now | Overloaded context, slow and costly |
| Episodic | Past interactions and actions | Last quarter's emails with this buyer | Old episodes treated as current |
| Semantic | Facts about the world and the company | "This client renews in March" | Facts that changed but were not updated |
| Procedural | Rules and instructions for a task | "Discounts above 10% need finance approval" | Rules edited silently, with no history |

LangChain's documentation for its LangGraph framework uses a simpler split. Short-term memory is thread-scoped and remembers interactions within a single conversation. Long-term memory is stored in namespaces and recalled across any thread. It also distinguishes two ways of writing memories: in the "hot path", during the response, which adds latency; or in the background, as a separate task, which raises the question of when to run it.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Memory is now a product category. WRITER made team-level Agent Memory, which retains decisions and preferences across sessions, generally available in September 2026. Specialist memory layers sell the same capability to teams building their own agents.

The evidence on long-term recall is weaker than the marketing. LongMemEval, a 500-question benchmark published in 2024 and presented at ICLR 2025, tests five abilities: information extraction, multi-session reasoning, temporal reasoning, knowledge updates and abstention. Its authors found an accuracy drop of about 30% for commercial chat assistants and long-context models across sustained interactions. Knowledge updates matter most for a sales team, because prices, contacts, owners and terms change constantly.

That is why memory and the decision record should stay separate. Memory helps an agent pick up where it left off. The record says what the company decided, why, and what has since superseded it. If an agent's memory says one discount ceiling and the record says another, the record should win, and the conflict should be flagged to a person.

## How to evaluate a memory layer

We have not found independent testing that shows any memory layer improving agents on long tasks, so treat vendor benchmark scores as claims. A short test on your own data is more informative.

1. Write 50 questions from your own commercial history: 20 lookups, 20 "how did this change?" questions, and 10 that assume something you have since reversed.
2. Run the same agent and model with no memory layer, then with each candidate.
3. Score correctness, and separately score how often the agent corrects the false premise.
4. Ask each vendor for its benchmark harness, not just its score.

Check two properties alongside the score. Can every memory be traced to a source and exported? Are old facts marked as superseded, with a date, rather than overwritten? A plain database with status fields, validity dates and supersession links is often enough for a mid-size team.

## lowob takeaways

- **Short-term memory is solved.** Most platforms provide it within a conversation.
- **Long-term memory is the open question.** Benchmarks show sharp drops on long interactions and changed facts.
- **Memory is not the record.** When they disagree, the decision record wins and a person is told.
- **Test before buying.** Fifty questions from your own history, against a no-memory baseline.

## Common questions

### What is memory in AI agents?

The mechanism that stores information from earlier steps or sessions and brings the relevant parts back into the model's context, so an agent can continue work without being told everything again.

### What is the difference between short-term and long-term agent memory?

Short-term memory lasts for one conversation or thread. Long-term memory persists across sessions and has to be deliberately written, stored and retrieved.

### What are episodic, semantic and procedural memory in AI agents?

Episodic memory holds past interactions, semantic memory holds facts, and procedural memory holds the rules and instructions for doing a task. The split comes from the CoALA framework.

### Do we need a separate memory layer for our AI agents?

Not always. Platform-native memory covers single conversations. For long-term facts, test a candidate against a no-memory baseline on your own data first; a well-structured database is often enough.

## Sources and notes

- [Sumers, Yao, Narasimhan and Griffiths, Cognitive Architectures for Language Agents](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2309.02427), TMLR, 2024. Academic framework.
- [Wu et al., LongMemEval: Benchmarking Chat Assistants on Long-Term Interactive Memory](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.10813v2), October 2024, revised March 2025. Academic benchmark; not an enterprise product test.
- [LangChain documentation, Memory overview](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/concepts/memory). Vendor documentation.
- [CMSWire, WRITER launches Enterprise Brain to unify AI agent context](https://www.cmswire.com/customer-experience/writer-launches-enterprise-brain-to-unify-ai-agent-context/), September 2026. Vendor announcement, reported.

## Related research

- [The 5 Agent Memory Layers Worth Testing, and How to Test Them](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-agent-memory-layers-worth-testing-and-how-to-test-them/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)
- [The Financial Data Providers Your Agents Can Call Today](https://lowob.com/research/the-financial-data-providers-your-agents-can-call-today/)

## Next move

Write ten "how did this change?" questions about your largest accounts, such as who owns the relationship now and what the current price is, and ask your assistant. The wrong answers show where memory needs a record behind it.

# Market Maps That Sales Actually Uses

Source: https://lowob.com/research/market-maps-that-sales-actually-uses/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most market maps are slides of logos in boxes that sellers never open. A usable map is a list of named accounts held in the CRM, tiered by fit and potential, with the trigger that makes each one timely, an owner and a status. This piece sets out the layers of a working map, how to tier it, how triggers and the installed base make it actionable, and the monthly rhythm that keeps it from going stale.

A market map that sales uses is not a slide. It is a list of named accounts held in the CRM, each with a segment, a tier, the trigger that makes it timely, an owner and a status, refreshed on a fixed rhythm. Most maps fail because they describe the market rather than direct the work. Gartner found 84% of sales leaders said analytics had less influence on sales performance than expected, and Forrester found sellers choosing from an average of 1,400 sales assets. Another document will not help. A working map turns the segment choice from Part 3 into a weekly list of who to call and why.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Every commercial team has a market map somewhere. Usually it was built for a board meeting or a fundraise: a grid of categories, logos in boxes, perhaps a total addressable market figure in the corner. It describes the market accurately. Nobody in sales opens it again.

That is not a failure of effort. It is a failure of form. Sellers work from lists, not landscapes. A map that cannot be filtered, assigned and updated in the system they already use competes with everything else on their screen, and loses. Gartner's 2023 survey of 501 sellers found 77% struggled to complete their assigned tasks efficiently. A map that adds work will be ignored.

## Why most market maps die in a slide deck

Five properties separate a map that is used from one that is admired.

| Property | Slide map | Working map |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit | Categories and logos | Named accounts with a record each |
| Location | A deck or a design file | The CRM, as fields and views |
| Ownership | Whoever built it | An owner per account and an owner for the map |
| Timing | A snapshot | A trigger and status per account, refreshed monthly |
| Action | None implied | A next step per tier |

The analytics evidence explains why form matters. A Gartner survey of 303 sales leaders, reported in February 2024, found 84% said analytics had less influence on sales performance than expected, and recommended a decision-driven approach: start from the decision a seller has to make, not from the data available. Forrester's 2022 research found reps had an average of 1,400 sales assets to choose from. A market map built as one more asset joins that pile.

## The layers of a working map

A working map has four layers. Each lives in the CRM or in a tool connected to it.

| Layer | Contains | Where it lives | Who updates it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Universe | Every account that meets the segment filters from Part 3 | Account records, tagged by segment | Revenue operations, quarterly |
| Fit and tier | Fit score, potential and tier for each account | Account fields | Revenue operations, with sales input, quarterly |
| Timing | Current trigger, its date and source | Account field or activity | Sellers and data feeds, continuously |
| Coverage | Owner, status, last meaningful contact, next step | Account and activity records | Account owner, weekly |

The universe should be finite and countable. If it holds 1,200 accounts, everyone should be able to see the same 1,200. That number also anchors the bottom-up sizing check in Part 3 ([Segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/)).

## Tiering the map

Tiers decide where effort goes. They should combine fit (how closely the account resembles customers who won, stayed and grew) with potential (the realistic value if it buys). Current spend is a weak proxy for either.

Gartner research reported in 2021 found that customers elevated to key-account status mainly for their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time, and that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed key-account quota. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found top performers prioritised accounts and personas they had successfully closed before. Fit, in other words, predicts better than size.

| Tier | Typical share of the universe | Criteria | Coverage | Motion |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tier 1 | 5% to 10% | High fit, high potential | Named owner, account plan, multi-threaded | Account-based, with partner and executive involvement |
| Tier 2 | 20% to 30% | High fit, moderate potential, or the reverse | Named owner, triggered outreach | Signal-led sequences and events |
| Tier 3 | The rest | Meets segment filters | Pooled or marketing-led | Content, partners and inbound |
| Excluded | Recorded separately | Fails a disqualifier | None | Taken only as a recorded exception |

The shares are illustrative starting points, not benchmarks. What matters is that Tier 1 is small enough for each account to have a plan. The account-based approach for Tier 1 is covered in our explainer ([What is account-based marketing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/)).

## Triggers make the map timely

A tier says who matters. A trigger says why now. Without triggers, sellers work the map alphabetically or by habit.

A trigger is evidence that an account's commercial conditions have changed in a way that alters the likelihood, timing or value of a purchase: a regulatory deadline, a new executive, an expansion, a failed implementation, a contract renewal date. Our piece on signal-based outbound sets out how to score signals by recency, relevance, magnitude, access and proof ([Signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/)).

The evidence for timing is consistent. Ebsta found high-intent accounts closed at 3.4 times the velocity of others. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 73% actively avoided suppliers who sent irrelevant outreach. A trigger is what makes outreach relevant.

| Trigger type | Example | Source | Decay |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Regulatory | A rule with a compliance date that affects the account | Regulator publications | Slow: months to the deadline |
| People | New head of the buying function | Public profiles, announcements | Medium: first 90 days matter most |
| Corporate | Expansion, acquisition, new market entry | Filings, press | Medium |
| Technology | Retiring a system the offer replaces | Job posts, partner intelligence | Medium |
| Relationship | Contract renewal with a competitor | Partners, past conversations | Fast once the date passes |

Record the trigger on the account with its date. A trigger older than its decay period should drop the account's priority automatically.

> A tier says who matters. A trigger says why now. A map needs both to direct a week of work.

## Whitespace and the installed base

Most market maps show only prospects. The installed base often holds faster revenue. A whitespace view lists each current customer against the offers the firm sells, and marks what each has bought, what it could buy and what it has declined.

McKinsey's 2021 analysis of B2B commercial analytics described a distributor that was losing customers representing up to 30% of its yearly sales and, by focusing analytics on churn first, added $5 million to $10 million in run-rate revenue within eight months. Gartner's account-growth research found organisations that frequently update account plans are three times more likely to build customer decision confidence.

| Customer (illustrative) | Core offer | Offer B | Offer C | Renewal date | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Account 1 | Bought | Declined, 2025: budget | Fit, not discussed | Q2 | Introduce C with a reference |
| Account 2 | Bought | Bought | Not a fit | Q4 | Renewal review |
| Account 3 | Bought | Fit, in discussion | Fit, not discussed | Q1 | Resolve B before renewal |

Recording why an offer was declined, and when, is what lets the firm return at the right moment.

## Keeping the map alive

Maps decay. People change jobs, companies are acquired and triggers expire. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete. A map built on that data will mislead unless it is maintained ([What is CRM data hygiene?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/)).

The maintenance rhythm is modest and fits the operating rhythm in Part 6.

| Cadence | Task | Owner |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Weekly | Update status and next step on owned accounts | Account owners |
| Monthly | Refresh triggers; expire stale ones; review Tier 1 coverage | Revenue operations and sales lead |
| Quarterly | Re-score fit and potential; re-tier; review exclusions | Commercial lead |
| Annually | Re-run segment selection against a year of outcomes | Leadership |

Every re-tiering is a decision. Recording who moved an account, why and with what expectation lets the firm test its tiering logic against outcomes later. This is also where the map meets The Build Order. A context layer can assemble an account brief from the CRM, email and filings in minutes ([The context layer, followed through one account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)). It cannot tell a seller why the account is Tier 1 unless someone recorded the reason.

Illustrative example: from slide to CRM

Decision
:   Retire the market map slide and rebuild it as CRM fields: segment, tier, trigger with date, owner and status, with a saved view per seller.

Reason and owner
:   Sellers reported working from personal lists; only a minority of Tier 1 accounts had any logged contact in the previous quarter. Owned by the revenue operations lead; agreed with the head of sales.

What changed
:   The weekly pipeline meeting opens with Tier 1 coverage; triggers older than 90 days expire automatically; re-tiering requires a recorded reason.

Illustrative: a composite of a 150-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Build lists, not landscapes.** A map sellers use is a set of named accounts in the CRM.
- **Tier on fit, not spend.** Accounts that resemble customers who won and grew deserve the effort.
- **Add the trigger and its date.** Timing is what turns a list into a week of work.
- **Map the installed base.** Whitespace and declined offers, with reasons, are often the fastest revenue.

Gateway card

### Before you hand the map to sales

- A finite, countable account universe tagged by segment
- Tier criteria written down, based on fit and potential
- A trigger field with a date and a decay rule
- An owner, status and next step on every Tier 1 and Tier 2 account
- A whitespace view of current customers with declined offers recorded
- A monthly refresh with a named owner

## Common questions

### What is a market map in sales?

A list of named accounts in a target market, organised by segment and tier, with the trigger, owner and status for each, held in the CRM so sellers can work from it.

### How do you tier accounts for sales?

Combine fit (how closely an account resembles customers who won and stayed) with potential value. Keep Tier 1 small enough for each account to have a plan.

### What is whitespace analysis?

A view of current customers against every offer the firm sells, showing what each has bought, what it could buy and what it has declined, with reasons and dates.

### How often should a market map be updated?

Status weekly, triggers monthly, tiers quarterly and the segment choice annually.
