# The First AI Agent Should Be Boring

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by 2027, and the riskiest first agents are the most visible ones. A good first job is frequent, checkable, low in blast radius and disliked by people. On the commercial line that is a pipeline clerk that keeps the CRM current and drafts follow-ups into a queue, measured for four weeks before it is given anything else.

The first agent on the commercial line should be boring: a job that happens often, can be checked quickly, does little damage if it goes wrong, and that people dislike doing. Autonomous outbound, the most requested first agent, fails three of the four tests. A pipeline clerk passes them: it keeps the CRM current, flags stale deals and drafts follow-ups into a queue, and it never sends anything itself. Measure it for four weeks before giving it anything else.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

When a commercial team decides to deploy its first agent, the request is usually ambitious: an AI sales development rep that researches prospects, writes sequences and sends them, or an agent that runs campaigns end to end. These are the most visible jobs and the most likely to fail first.

Gartner's mid-2025 forecast was blunt: more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls. Its analysts also observed that many use cases positioned as agentic do not need agents at all. The first agent should be chosen to avoid all three failure modes, which means choosing something unglamorous.

## Four tests for a first job

| Test | Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Frequent | Does it happen daily or weekly? | Enough runs to measure within a month |
| Checkable | Can a person verify the output in under a minute? | Errors are caught before they compound |
| Low blast radius | If it is wrong, who notices and what does it cost? | A bad first incident ends the programme |
| Disliked | Do people avoid doing it today? | Adoption follows relief, not mandate |

### How the common candidates score

| Candidate first agent | Frequent | Checkable | Low blast radius | Disliked | Verdict |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Autonomous outbound ("AI SDR") | Yes | No: quality shows weeks later | No: reaches prospects directly | Partly | Not first |
| Auto-published social content | Yes | Partly | No: public | Partly | Not first |
| Website chatbot for prospects | Yes | No | No: client-facing | No | Not first |
| Meeting preparation briefs | Yes | Yes | Yes: internal | Yes | Good first |
| Pipeline clerk (CRM hygiene and follow-up drafts) | Yes | Yes | Yes: drafts only | Yes | Best first |

The pattern is consistent. Anything that reaches a client directly fails the blast-radius test, and anything whose quality shows weeks later fails the checkable test. Internal, reviewable work passes.

## Why the pipeline clerk

The clerk works exactly where commercial time is lost. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, with junior sellers losing about two hours a week to manual data entry. Sellers using agents expected them to cut prospect research time by about a third and email drafting by a similar share. Validity's 2026 survey found 62% of marketers believed poor CRM data had cost revenue. A clerk addresses the data, the drafting and the follow-up gap at once, without touching a client.

## Specifying the pipeline clerk

A clerk's specification fits on one page. That is part of the point.

| Element | Specification |
| --- | --- |
| Goal | Keep every open opportunity current, and make sure no follow-up is forgotten |
| Runs | Overnight for hygiene; on demand for follow-up drafts |
| Reads | CRM, email and calendar for the commercial cohort; the definitions from Part 5 |
| Writes (level 3: act and report) | Source tags from a fixed list; activity dates; "stale" flags on deals with no activity in 30 days |
| Writes (level 1: draft only) | Stage changes suggested, not made; follow-up emails placed in each owner's queue |
| Never | Sends email; changes values or close dates; deletes records |
| Reports | A nightly summary to the build owner: changes made, drafts queued, exceptions |
| Owner | The head of operations, with each seller approving their own drafts |

The split between level 3 and level 1 matters. Low-risk, reversible changes (tags, dates, flags) can run and be reported. Anything that changes the commercial picture or reaches a client stays as a draft.

### A day in the clerk's life

1. Overnight, it reads the day's email and calendar activity for the cohort and matches it to accounts and opportunities.
2. It updates last-activity dates, tags new opportunities with their source, and flags deals with no activity in 30 days.
3. For each meeting held with no follow-up sent within 48 hours, it drafts a follow-up email and places it in the owner's queue with the meeting notes attached.
4. It suggests stage changes where the evidence is clear (a signed proposal, a lost-deal email) and leaves them for the owner to accept.
5. It sends the build owner a summary: what changed, what is waiting, and anything it could not resolve.

## Measuring it for four weeks

Measure before giving the clerk anything else. Four weeks is long enough to see a pattern and short enough to keep attention.

| Measure | Baseline from Part 4 | What good looks like after four weeks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open deals with no activity in 30 days | Counted at clean-up | Down, and every remaining one flagged |
| Meetings without follow-up in 48 hours | Counted from calendar and email | Close to zero |
| Draft acceptance rate | n/a | High, with edits; read alongside the checks below |
| Seller time on CRM updates | Self-reported estimate | Down |
| Errors found on spot-check | n/a | Few, and none reaching a client |

Draft acceptance on its own is a weak measure. In *Approval rate measures fatigue too* we showed how approval rates rise when reviewers tire, so pair it with a weekly spot-check of a random sample of the clerk's changes.

> Choose a first agent whose worst day is an internal annoyance, not a client apology.

## What comes after the clerk

Once the clerk has four good weeks, the next steps are natural extensions of the same pattern: meeting preparation briefs, then draft proposals from approved templates, then prioritised account lists for the quarter. Each one moves only one notch up the autonomy dial, on evidence. Autonomous outbound may come eventually; it should not come first.

Illustrative example: replacing an "AI SDR" pilot

Decision
:   Decline an autonomous outbound pilot and deploy a pipeline clerk for the commercial cohort instead.

Reason and owner
:   The outbound pilot would reach prospects directly with no way to check quality for weeks; the clerk addresses stale deals and missed follow-ups, which the CRM baseline showed were common. Owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   After four weeks, missed follow-ups fall sharply and stale deals are all flagged; meeting briefs become the second agent.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pick for the worst day, not the best demo.** A first agent's mistakes should be internal and cheap.
- **Use the four tests.** Frequent, checkable, low blast radius, disliked.
- **Split autonomy by task.** Reversible changes can run and report; anything client-facing stays a draft.
- **Measure for four weeks.** Then move one notch up the dial, on evidence.

Gateway card

### Before the first agent goes live

- Goal, runs, reads, writes and "never" list on one page
- Autonomy level set per task
- Baseline counts from the CRM clean-up
- A weekly random spot-check scheduled
- A named owner and a nightly report

## Common questions

### What should be my first AI agent in sales?

A pipeline clerk: an agent that keeps CRM records current, flags stale deals and drafts follow-up emails into a queue for sellers to approve. It is frequent, checkable, low-risk and addresses work sellers dislike.

### Should we start with an AI SDR for outbound?

Usually not. Autonomous outbound reaches prospects directly and its quality shows only weeks later, so errors are costly and hard to catch. It is better as a later step once simpler agents have a track record.

### How do you measure an AI agent's performance?

Against a baseline taken before launch: stale deals, missed follow-ups, time spent on CRM updates, and errors found in a weekly random spot-check. Approval rates alone can be misleading.

### Why do agentic AI projects fail?

Gartner cites escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. Choosing an ambitious, client-facing first agent makes all three more likely.

## Sources and notes

- Gartner forecast, June 2025, as reported by [Reuters via The Star](https://www.thestar.com.my/tech/tech-news/2025/06/25/over-40-of-agentic-ai-projects-will-be-scrapped-by-2027-gartner-says) and [Martechvibe](https://martechvibe.com/?p=49029).
- [Salesforce, State of Sales 2026](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/state-of-sales-report-announcement-2026/), with detail via [Dynamic Business](https://dynamicbusiness.com/topics/news/high-performing-sales-teams-are-1-7x-more-likely-to-use-ai-agents). Vendor-run survey; expected savings.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/).
- The four tests, scoring and clerk specification are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [Claude Is Not Your Intern. Build a Repeatable GTM Workflow](https://lowob.com/research/claude-gtm-operating-system/)
- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)

## Next move

Write your first agent's specification on one page, including the list of things it must never do. If it does not fit on a page, the job is too big for a first agent.

# What Is Ad Fraud? Bots, MFA Sites, and Controls

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ad-fraud/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ad fraud is any scheme that generates fake advertising activity so someone is paid for attention that never happened, and it hides inside good-looking reports. Estimates range from under 1% invalid traffic in TAG Certified channels to 22% of all online spend. Buy through inclusion lists with pre-bid verification, validate outcomes in your own systems and use partners not paid more when volume rises.

Ad fraud is any scheme that generates fake advertising activity (impressions, clicks, installs, views, leads) so that someone is paid for attention that never happened. It hides inside good-looking reports, because most of it is recorded as performance. How much a buyer loses depends on how it buys: TAG found invalid traffic under 1% in its certified US channels in 2024, while Juniper Research estimated 22% of all online ad spend was lost to fraud in 2023. Buy through inclusion lists with pre-bid verification, validate outcomes in your own systems, watch for numbers that are too clean, and use partners who are not paid more when volume rises.

## The main forms

| Form | How it works | Where it shows up | First control |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Invalid traffic | Bots and scripts load pages, view ads and click; ranges from crude data-centre traffic to hijacked residential devices | Impressions, clicks, video views | Pre-bid verification from an MRC-accredited vendor |
| Made-for-advertising sites | Pages built only to host ads, filled with cheap or scraped content and fed with bought traffic | Low CPMs, high viewability, no outcomes | Inclusion lists |
| Domain and app spoofing | Low-quality inventory misrepresented in the auction as a premium publisher or app | Premium prices for junk | Buy only from sellers authorised in ads.txt and sellers.json |
| Ad stacking and pixel stuffing | Many ads layered in one slot, or an ad rendered in a one-pixel frame | Impressions nobody could have seen | Viewability measurement |
| Click and install fraud | Fake clicks, click injection that claims credit for organic installs, device farms | Cost-per-click and cost-per-install campaigns | Attribution windows and install validation |
| Lead and affiliate fraud | Fabricated form submissions, stolen identities, cookie stuffing, coupon-code abuse | Lead and affiliate programmes | Validation periods and checks in your own systems |

The Media Rating Council's invalid traffic guidelines, first issued in 2015, give the industry its working vocabulary. General invalid traffic (GIVT) is what routine, list-based filtering catches: known bots, spiders, crawlers and non-browser traffic. Sophisticated invalid traffic (SIVT) needs "advanced analytics, multipoint corroboration, human intervention" to find, and includes hijacked devices, adware, malware and misappropriated content. The distinction matters to a buyer because a vendor that filters only GIVT will report a clean campaign that is not clean.

Made-for-advertising inventory sits in an awkward place. The visitors may be human, so it is not always classed as invalid traffic, and the ANA counted it as a loss of media productivity alongside non-viewable and non-human impressions rather than as fraud. To the buyer the effect is the same: money spent on pages with no audience anyone wanted to reach. The ANA's 2023 study found such sites took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend among the 21 advertisers it examined.

## How large the problem is

Estimates vary by method and vary widely, which is itself informative.

| Estimate | Figure | What it measures | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| TAG, US Fraud Benchmark 2024 | Invalid traffic under 1% | Impressions in TAG Certified channels, January to June 2024 | Covers only channels that meet TAG's standards |
| TAG, October 2024 analysis | $10.8 billion saved in 2023 | Losses avoided by industry anti-fraud programmes | Industry body estimate |
| Juniper Research | $84 billion, 22% of online ad spend, in 2023 | Global losses across 45 countries | Analyst model; far above certified-channel rates |

The range is the point. A buyer that works only through certified, verified channels with inclusion lists is close to the bottom of it. A buyer on the open exchange with no verification is nearer the top. The number that matters is not the global one. It is the share of your own buy that verification rejected, and if you do not have that figure, assume it is not small.

> Fraud scales instantly, and real audiences do not. When a cheap channel suddenly grows, look before you celebrate.

Newer channels are not immune. Industry reporting on the IAB's 2026 video study cited DoubleVerify data showing CTV fraud schemes up 140% in the first quarter of 2026 against a year earlier, and the IAB found 56% of buyers who mistrust the open exchange for CTV cite fraud as a reason.

## How it is detected

Third-party verification vendors accredited by the MRC measure invalid traffic, viewability and placement quality, pre-bid where possible and post-bid otherwise. TAG's benchmark, run by The 614 Group, analysed all impressions from agency holding companies and their MRC-accredited vendors across display, video, mobile, in-app and CTV.

Platforms filter the crude forms themselves and report the invalid activity they caught; they are less forthcoming about what they missed. IAB Tech Lab's ads.txt, sellers.json and SupplyChain object make spoofing harder by letting buyers see whether the seller of an impression was authorised. Affiliate networks apply validation periods and fraud scoring to conversions.

The company's own analytics, compared with partner reports, is the final check. Outcomes a partner claims that the company's systems cannot see are the signal. Our piece on [lead source attribution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) covers how to record where each lead came from in a way that can be reconciled against partner claims.

## The practical controls

Buy through inclusion lists, not blocklists. Require pre-bid verification on every programmatic buy and read the rejection report. Optimise towards outcomes further down the funnel than clicks or installs; fraud is cheapest at the top. Validate every paid outcome in your own systems before paying for it, with a delay long enough to catch reversals.

Watch for the tells: conversion rates too good, traffic from unexpected geographies, activity at unusual hours, a partner whose numbers never fluctuate. Cap any single partner or placement so that one bad source cannot swamp the rest. And pay attention when a cheap channel suddenly scales.

For affiliate and referral programmes the controls are contractual as well as technical: a validation window before commission is paid, the right to claw back reversed conversions, and a ban on brand-term bidding and coupon sites unless agreed. Our piece on [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) sets out where those programmes lose value and how to close each gap.

## Why the fee structure matters here too

Every intermediary paid on volume has a reduced incentive to reject volume. A desk paid a flat fee, with rejection rate as a reported metric, is structurally aligned with catching fraud. A partner paid a percentage of spend is not. The controls above work best when the person applying them is not paid less for applying them. Our piece on [programmatic numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) shows how to put the rejection rate on the monthly report.

## lowob takeaways

- **Know the forms.** Invalid traffic, MFA sites, spoofing, stacking, click and install fraud, and lead fraud need different controls.
- **Ask for SIVT, not just GIVT.** Routine filters miss the sophisticated forms.
- **Your rate depends on how you buy.** Certified, verified channels sit near 1%; unverified open buys can be far higher.
- **Validate outcomes yourself.** If your systems cannot see it, do not pay for it.
- **Align the fee.** A partner paid on volume is paid to accept fraud.

## Common questions

### What is ad fraud?

Any scheme that generates fake advertising activity, such as impressions, clicks, installs, views or leads, so that someone is paid for attention that never happened. Most of it is paid for by advertisers whose reports show it as performance.

### What is the difference between GIVT and SIVT?

General invalid traffic is caught by routine filters, such as known bots and crawlers. Sophisticated invalid traffic needs advanced analytics and human review to detect, and includes hijacked devices, adware and malware.

### How much money is lost to ad fraud?

Estimates vary widely. TAG found invalid traffic under 1% in its certified US channels in 2024, while Juniper Research estimated $84 billion, or 22% of online ad spend, was lost globally in 2023.

### How can I protect my ad budget from fraud?

Buy through inclusion lists, require pre-bid verification and read the rejection report, validate every paid outcome in your own systems before paying, cap any single partner or placement, and watch for numbers that are too clean.

- [PR Newswire, Media Rating Council issues final version of invalid traffic detection and filtration guidelines addendum](https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/media-rating-council-mrc-issues-final-version-of-invalid-traffic-detection-and-filtration-guidelines-addendum-300166843.html), 27 October 2015. Ask your verification vendor for last month's rejection report split into general and sophisticated invalid traffic, by partner. Then pick the channel with the cleanest-looking numbers and check its claimed conversions against your own systems.

# Airdrops Can Buy Attention. They Cannot Buy Belief.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Airdrops, points, ambassador programmes and referral rewards are mechanism-design choices that redefine what participation means. The on-chain evidence shows most airdrops lose recipients and value quickly: Keyrock found most of 62 airdrops fell within 15 days, and academic work found up to 66% of claimed tokens went straight to exchanges. Reward contribution quality and persistence, count incentives as acquisition cost, and model what remains when the reward stops.

Airdrops, points, ambassador programmes and referral rewards can overcome a cold start, but they also teach a community what the project values. The on-chain evidence on airdrops is consistent: Keyrock's review of 62 airdrops found most tokens fell within 15 days, and an academic study of nine major airdrops found up to 66% of claimed tokens moved to exchanges in the first transfer. Reward contribution quality and persistence, delay the largest rewards until value is observable, and count every incentive as acquisition cost.

Web3 gives companies an unusually effective growth tool: the ability to reward participation with assets, access, status or future economic value. It also creates an unusually efficient way to attract people who care only about extracting the reward.

An airdrop can overcome a cold start, distribute ownership, reward early users and create awareness. Points can make progress visible. Ambassador programmes can extend education and distribution. Referral rewards can accelerate acquisition. But incentives do not simply increase desired behaviour. They redefine what participation means. This analysis sits within our hub on [building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## What the airdrop evidence shows

Three independent lines of on-chain analysis point the same way.

| Study | Sample | Finding | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keyrock, September 2024 | 62 airdrops across 6 chains | Most airdrops "crash within 15 days"; 8 of 62 showed positive 90-day results | Market-maker research; price-based, not user-based |
| Messias, Yaish and Livshits, arXiv | Nine airdrops including Arbitrum, Optimism, Uniswap, ENS | Up to 66% of claimed tokens went to exchanges in the first transfer; activity rose temporarily but engagement did not last | Academic; measures transfers, not intent |
| Nansen via The Block, June 2024 | Top 10,000 ZKsync recipients | 41.1% sold their full allocation within 24 hours; 28.8% held everything | Analytics vendor; top addresses only, first day only |

The academic paper adds detail that matters for design. On day one, 87% of eligible Arkham accounts, 77% of Lido accounts and 73% of Arbitrum accounts claimed, which the authors read as "strong anticipation or automation". After Arbitrum's airdrop, transactions per address fell even as total fees rose. Keyrock's work found the allocation size mattered: airdrops of under 5% of supply often held up at 15 days but dumped within three months, while larger allocations did better over longer horizons. Keyrock's winner case, Drift, combined an established user base, tiered release, a conservative valuation and seeded liquidity. Its failure case attracted reward hunters to a product with "no significant product or brand recognition".

The pattern is not that airdrops fail. It is that an airdrop amplifies whatever was already there. Where there was a product people used, some of them stay. Where there was only the reward, the reward leaves with them.

## Every incentive teaches the community what matters

If a project rewards transaction count, participants will maximise transactions. If it rewards raw referrals, they will maximise signups. If it rewards posting, they will maximise content volume. The measured behaviour may grow while the underlying network becomes noisier, more expensive or easier to game.

The farming is industrial. The same paper documents a single farmer on ZKsync Era using over 20,000 accounts and deploying a fake, closed-source exchange to qualify, and notes that LayerZero offered self-reporting sybils 15% of their allocation. A design that pays per wallet is paying per account a farmer can create.

Before launching an incentive, write down the behaviour being rewarded, the durable value it creates, how it can be faked or farmed, what happens when the reward ends, which participant type it will attract, and whether it creates regulatory, disclosure or reputational risk. On the last point, the regulatory position has moved in 2026. In the US, the SEC's March 2026 interpretation said airdrops of non-security crypto assets to recipients who give no money, goods, services or other consideration are generally not securities offers. In the EU, MiCA exempts free offers from white-paper requirements, but an offer is not treated as free if recipients must provide personal data in exchange. An airdrop gated on an email address or KYC can fall outside the exemption. Get counsel on both; this is not legal advice.

If the team cannot explain the bridge between the rewarded action and durable network value, it is subsidising activity rather than growth.

## Choose the mechanism for the job

| Mechanism | Useful for | Risky when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Points | Making progress and eligibility visible | Ambiguity about future value becomes the main product |
| Airdrops | Distributing ownership; rewarding meaningful past participation | Criteria invite sybil behaviour, or retention has no independent foundation |
| Ambassador programmes | Education, localisation, events, member support | Ambassadors are cheap promotional labour paid for noise |
| Referrals | An existing member identifying someone who will benefit | The reward overwhelms the social judgment that makes a referral credible |
| Access and status | Recognising expertise without financialising every action | Titles become political, opaque or detached from responsibility |

Ambassadors who post about a token for rewards are also endorsers. Our piece on [KOL campaign measurement](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) covers the disclosure duties that follow.

## Reward contribution quality and persistence

The strongest programmes attach rewards to outcomes a human or a well-tested system can evaluate: a bug identified and reproduced, a developer integration used by others, a high-quality educational resource, a customer introduced who becomes active, peer support that resolves real issues, research that changes a decision, governance work that improves a proposal. This is harder than counting clicks, but it aligns recognition with network value. The academic authors reach a similar conclusion, recommending rewards for value-creating users such as liquidity providers and contract creators, fee discounts for ongoing use, and multi-phase drops that refine eligibility each round.

One-time actions are easy to buy and easy to fake. Durable participation is more informative. Reward repeated useful behaviour rather than one burst, require activity across different periods, distinguish acquisition from activation and retention, create increasing responsibility rather than only increasing rewards, and delay the largest rewards until value is observable.

> A person who returns after the speculative moment passes is a stronger signal than a wallet that completed fifty tasks in one afternoon.

## Model the post-incentive community and the full cost

Ask what remains when the programme stops. Is the product useful? Are member relationships valuable? Has contribution created reputation? Do developers have reasons to keep building? Is there governance worth taking part in? If the answer is no, the campaign has rented behaviour. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) sets out what to build before the drop.

Crypto growth measurement should treat token incentives, quests, selective airdrops, sponsorships and programme operations as acquisition costs, not free community growth. Track cost per qualified participant, activation after receiving the reward, retention at 30, 60 and 90 days, concentration among likely farmers, contribution or revenue created, support and moderation cost, behaviour after rewards decline, and reputational effects. That is the same discipline as [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) in any other market: cost per retained customer, not cost per arrival, and a [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) calculation that counts the tokens at what they cost the treasury.

The most important comparison is not participants before and after the campaign. It is the value created relative to the full cost, and what persists afterwards.

Illustrative example: a two-phase drop

Decision
:   Replace a single airdrop to all past wallets with a smaller first phase for wallets active across three separate months, and a second phase six months later weighted to liquidity provided and integrations shipped.

Reason and owner
:   Eligibility analysis showed a large share of candidate wallets had acted in a single week before the snapshot. Owned by the growth lead, with criteria reviewed by the engineering lead.

What changed
:   The first phase went to far fewer wallets, and the team could report 90-day retention by phase before committing the larger allocation.

Illustrative: a composite of a DeFi protocol, built from patterns across engagements, not a reported result.

## lowob takeaways

- **Incentives define participation.** Whatever you reward is what the network will produce.
- **Airdrops amplify what exists.** The evidence shows quick selling where the product was not the reason to stay.
- **Pay for quality and persistence.** Reward verified contribution across time and delay the largest rewards.
- **Count the full cost.** Tokens, quests and operations are acquisition costs, judged against what remains at 90 days.

## Common questions

### Do crypto airdrops retain users?

Usually not on their own. Keyrock found most of 62 airdrops fell in price within 15 days, and academic analysis of nine airdrops found activity rose briefly while lasting engagement did not follow. Airdrops retain users where a useful product already existed.

### How do you prevent sybil farming in an airdrop?

Reward behaviour that is costly to fake: activity across separate periods, liquidity that stays, integrations others use, verified contribution. Run multi-phase drops that refine eligibility, and avoid paying per wallet for one-off actions.

### Are airdrops securities in the US?

Under the SEC's March 2026 interpretation, airdrops of non-security crypto assets to recipients who provide no consideration are generally not securities offers. The analysis is fact-specific and changes if the token is tied to an investment contract; get counsel.

### Does MiCA apply to airdrops?

MiCA exempts crypto-assets offered for free from white-paper requirements, but an offer is not free if recipients must provide personal data or the offeror receives fees or other benefits in exchange. Gated airdrops may need legal review.

## Sources and notes

- [Keyrock, Airdrops in the barren desert](https://keyrock.com/airdrops-in-the-barren-desert/), 25 September 2024, updated July 2025. Research by a crypto market maker; price outcomes only; the headline 11% success rate does not exactly match its own 8 of 62 count.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: giving money away is harder than it seems](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), arXiv, revised 2025. Academic study of nine airdrops; some work done while two authors were at Matter Labs.
- [The Block, 41% of top ZKsync token airdrop recipients sold full allocation: Nansen](https://www.theblock.co/post/300608/zksync-token-airdrop-sales-nansen), 18 June 2024. Analytics vendor data via a news report; top 10,000 addresses and first 24 hours only.
- [Sullivan & Cromwell, SEC clarifies application of securities laws to crypto assets](https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/March/SEC-Clarifies-Application-Securities-Laws-Crypto-Assets), 19 March 2026. Law-firm reading of the SEC and CFTC interpretation of 17 March 2026; not legal advice.

# What Is Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-19 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Retrieval-augmented generation is a technique where an AI system searches a knowledge base for relevant passages and adds them to the model's input before it answers. It grounds responses in your own documents, but it does not eliminate errors: a Stanford study found RAG-based legal tools still hallucinated on more than 17% of queries. Retrieval quality, source freshness and citations decide whether it works.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a technique in which an AI system first searches a store of documents for passages relevant to a question, then gives those passages to a language model to write its answer. It lets a general model answer from your proposals, contracts and policies without retraining it. It reduces made-up answers but does not remove them. Most RAG failures are retrieval failures, so the quality of what goes in decides the quality of what comes out.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What RAG means

Language models know what was in their training data, up to a cut-off date. They do not know your price list, last quarter's proposals or the terms in a client's contract. Retraining a model on that material is slow and costly, and it goes stale.

RAG solves this by looking things up at the moment of the question. The term was introduced in a May 2020 paper by Lewis and colleagues, who combined a model's built-in knowledge with a retrievable index of documents. They found the combined system produced "more specific, diverse and factual language" than a model alone.

| RAG is | RAG is not |
| --- | --- |
| Looking up relevant passages before answering | Training or fine-tuning a model on your data |
| A way to ground answers in current documents | A guarantee that answers are correct |
| Only as good as the documents and search behind it | A substitute for keeping source documents current |
| Usually paired with citations to the passages used | A record of decisions or their reasons |

## How it works

A RAG system has two phases. In preparation, documents are split into chunks, usually no more than a few hundred tokens each, and indexed. The index is commonly a vector database that stores each chunk as an embedding, a list of numbers capturing its meaning, often alongside a keyword index. At question time, the system finds the chunks most similar to the question and adds them to the model's input with an instruction to answer from them.

Each step can fail. Chunking can cut a sentence from the context that gives it meaning, so a passage saying "revenue grew 3%" loses which company and which quarter. Search can return near-matches rather than the right passage. The model can ignore what it was given.

Anthropic's September 2024 work on "contextual retrieval" measured some of the fixes. Adding a short explanation of each chunk's context before indexing cut failed retrievals by 35%. Adding keyword search on top took the reduction to 49%. Reranking the results brought it to 67%. These are vendor figures from Anthropic's own test sets, but the direction is consistent with wider practice: hybrid search beats meaning-based search alone.

## Why it matters for a commercial team, and how to evaluate it

RAG is the technology behind most "chat with your documents" features in sales tools, proposal software and AI assistants. It is how an assistant answers "what did we propose to this client last year" or "what are our standard payment terms".

The main risk is trust. Vendors have described RAG as a cure for hallucination. Stanford's 2024 study tested that claim on legal research tools from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters. Lexis+ AI and Ask Practical Law AI produced incorrect information more than 17% of the time; Westlaw AI-Assisted Research did so more than 34% of the time. These were specialist tools built on curated sources.

| Question to ask of a RAG system | What good looks like |
| --- | --- |
| Does every answer cite the passages it used? | Yes, with links to the source document |
| How fresh are the indexed documents? | Re-indexed on change, with a visible date |
| Does it combine keyword and meaning-based search? | Yes, hybrid search with reranking |
| What happens when nothing relevant is found? | It says so instead of guessing |
| Can you test it on 20 questions with known answers? | Yes, before rollout and after changes |

**lowob**'s view is that retrieval is rarely the real bottleneck. Most failures trace back to what is in the store: duplicate proposals, outdated price sheets, no record of which version was approved. RAG retrieves documents; it does not know which decision superseded which. Keeping a decision record, with status and owner, alongside the documents is what lets retrieval return the current answer rather than a plausible old one.

## lowob takeaways

- **RAG looks up before it answers.** It grounds a general model in your documents without retraining.
- **It reduces errors, not to zero.** Specialist legal RAG tools still erred on more than one query in six.
- **Retrieval quality decides results.** Context-aware chunks, hybrid search and reranking measurably help.
- **Fix the store first.** Duplicate and outdated documents produce confident wrong answers.

## Common questions

### What is RAG in simple terms?

RAG is a way for an AI model to look up relevant passages in your documents before answering, so its response draws on your own information rather than only its training data.

### Does RAG stop AI hallucinations?

No. It reduces them, but Stanford researchers found RAG-based legal tools still produced incorrect information on more than 17% of test queries.

### What is the difference between RAG and fine-tuning?

Fine-tuning changes the model itself by training it on new data. RAG leaves the model unchanged and supplies relevant documents at the moment of each question.

### Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Usually, but not always. Many systems combine a vector index with keyword search, and a small knowledge base can sometimes be placed directly in the prompt.

## Sources and notes

- [Lewis et al., Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401), arXiv, May 2020. Academic paper that named the technique.
- [Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval), 19 September 2024. Vendor research on its own test sets.
- [Stanford HAI, AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 (or More) Benchmarking Queries](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/ai-trial-legal-models-hallucinate-1-out-6-or-more-benchmarking-queries), May 2024. Academic benchmark; tools have been updated since.
- The evaluation questions are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)

## Next move

Write 20 questions your team asks often, with the correct answer and source document for each. Run them through your current AI assistant and count how many it answers correctly with a citation.

# What Is Excessive Agency in AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Excessive agency is OWASP's name for AI systems that can do more than their job requires. It has three root causes: too many functions, too many permissions and too little verification. The fix is scoping each agent to its task and putting a person in front of high-impact actions.

Excessive agency is the risk that an AI system holds more tools, permissions or freedom to act than its task needs, so that a hallucination or a manipulated input turns into a damaging action. OWASP lists it as LLM06 in its 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications. It is the reason prompt injection becomes a breach rather than a bad answer, and it is fixed by scoping, not by smarter models.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What excessive agency means

OWASP describes excessive agency as "the vulnerability that enables damaging actions to be performed" in response to unexpected, ambiguous or manipulated model output. The trigger can be anything: a hallucination, a direct or indirect prompt injection, or a compromised plug-in or peer agent. The point is that the model will sometimes be wrong, and agency decides what being wrong costs.

OWASP breaks it into three root causes.

| Root cause | What it looks like | OWASP example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Excessive functionality | The agent has tools it does not need | A document reader whose extension can also modify and delete |
| Excessive permissions | A tool has broader access than its task | A read-only lookup connected with an account that can update and delete |
| Excessive autonomy | High-impact actions run without verification | A deletion feature that runs without asking the user |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

OWASP's own attack scenario is a commercial one. An assistant reads a user's email in order to summarise it, but the mail plug-in it uses can also send. An attacker emails hidden instructions; the model searches the inbox for sensitive information and forwards it. OWASP's three fixes are a read-only extension, a read-only OAuth scope, and requiring the user to review and send every draft.

The same pattern is easy to reproduce in sales and account work. A CRM connector installed by an admin can inherit that admin's rights. An email integration approved for reading may also be able to send. A shared service account can let one agent see every user's files, which is OWASP's own example of excessive permissions. None of this is visible from the agent's interface, which is why OWASP treats it as a design flaw rather than a model flaw.

The agentic list published in December 2025 extends the concern. It includes ASI02, tool misuse and exploitation, and ASI03, identity and privilege abuse, where agents reuse or escalate inherited credentials. Its guiding principle is "least agency": granting agents only the minimum autonomy required to perform safe, bounded tasks. The NCSC adds a related rule: an LLM's privileges should drop to those of the party whose information it is processing.

> Agency is set by what the agent can touch, not by what it is asked to do.

## How to scope an agent

**lowob** treats autonomy as a dial with five settings: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. Excessive agency is any gap between where the dial sits on paper and what the agent's tools and credentials actually allow. OWASP's mitigations map onto a short seven-point review.

| Check | Pass condition |
| --- | --- |
| Tool inventory | Every tool is needed for the current task; unused or abandoned ones are removed |
| Narrow tools | Purpose-built functions rather than open shell, URL-fetch or "do anything" tools |
| Permissions | Downstream systems grant the least access, enforced by those systems |
| User context | The agent acts as a specific user with narrow scopes, not a shared admin account |
| Approval | A person approves high-impact actions such as sending, paying or deleting |
| Complete mediation | Authorisation is checked in the downstream system, not left to the model |
| Monitoring | Tool calls are logged and rate-limited, to contain damage if the rest fails |

A practical test is to read the agent's job description aloud and then list what its credentials allow. If the job is "summarise inbound requests" and the credentials allow sending, editing contacts and exporting the CRM, the difference is the exposure. Close it before raising the dial.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume the model will err.** Agency decides whether an error is a bad answer or a bad action.
- **Check three things.** Functions, permissions and autonomy, each against the task as written.
- **Enforce outside the model.** Permissions belong in the systems the agent calls, not in its prompt.
- **Raise the dial on evidence.** Grant more agency task by task, after a record of low errors.

## Common questions

### What is excessive agency in OWASP's Top 10 for LLMs?

It is risk LLM06 in the 2025 list: an AI system given more functionality, permissions or autonomy than it needs, so faulty or manipulated output leads to harmful actions.

### What is the difference between excessive agency and prompt injection?

Prompt injection is one way a model is manipulated. Excessive agency is what lets that manipulation do damage. An injected agent with read-only tools can do far less harm.

### What is the principle of least agency?

A principle in OWASP's Top 10 for Agentic Applications: give agents only the minimum autonomy needed to perform safe, bounded tasks.

### How do you prevent excessive agency in AI agents?

Remove unneeded tools, narrow each tool's functions, grant least-privilege access in downstream systems, act in the user's context and require human approval for high-impact actions.

## Sources and notes

- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/), 2025. Community standard; the source of the root causes, mitigations and email scenario above.
- [TechRepublic, OWASP drops first AI agent risk list](https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-owasp-ai-agent-risk-list/), 19 December 2025. Press summary of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, including the least-agency principle.
- [UK National Cyber Security Centre, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse)](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection), 8 December 2025. Government guidance on reducing LLM privileges and relying on deterministic safeguards.
- The autonomy dial and scoping review are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)
- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production, by State Model and Cloud](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/)

## Next move

Pick your most-used AI integration and compare the scopes it was granted with the job it does. Remove any write, send or delete permission it has not needed in the last month.

# Membership Is the Job

Source: https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A media audience is a list until it becomes a membership: people who pay, show up, contribute and refer. With only 17% paying for online news across 20 markets in 2026, membership has to offer more than access. Build it on sourcing, peer amplification and peer value, keep it on channels you control, and measure it monthly like a business line.

A media audience is a list until it is a membership. Build the membership on sourcing, amplification and peer value, then measure it like a business line. The market makes the case: the Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found 17% of people across 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news, flat on the year, and reach of publishers' own sites and apps down 12 percentage points since 2021.

This is the media chapter of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## The number that is not a community

Media founders report audience numbers because they are easy to count. Subscribers, followers, opens, downloads. None of these are a community. A community is a set of people with a relationship to you and to each other.

Our piece [An audience is not a business](https://lowob.com/research/an-audience-is-not-a-business/) made the point that an audience does not pay the bills on its own. The same logic applies here. An audience is not a community either. It is the pool you recruit a community from.

[Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) defined community as a job with an owner, a budget and a measure. In media the job is membership. The output is people who pay, show up, contribute and refer. If a person does none of those four things, they are a reader, not a member.

The pool is harder to convert than it was. The Reuters Institute surveyed 97,520 people in 48 markets for its 2026 report. Across the 20 markets where paywalls are common, 17% paid for online news, with falls of four points in the US and six in Austria. Most payers (81%) cited direct benefits, but 46% also gave values-based reasons, such as supporting journalism. The Membership Puzzle Project, a research collaboration between NYU's Jay Rosen and De Correspondent that ran from 2017 to 2021, defined membership as "a social contract between a news organization and the community it serves", in which members give time, money and ideas. Its review of nearly 100 membership models concluded that "no one has ever become an enthusiastic member of a commodity news site."

## The three contributions that matter

Members do a lot of things. Three of them change the business.

**Sourcing.** Members send tips, data, documents and questions. The best stories in niche media come from the people closest to the subject. A member who sends one good lead a quarter is worth more than a thousand passive subscribers. Make it easy: a standing inbox, a members' thread, an editor who replies within a day. The Membership Puzzle Project documented members contributing tips, expertise, moderation and co-reporting across the sites it studied.

**Amplification, but the right kind.** You do not need members who post your work to the public. You need members who forward it to the three peers who matter. Niche media grows through private channels: a message to a colleague, a mention in a team meeting. Ask for that explicitly. "Who on your team should see this?" beats "please share."

**Peer value.** This is the one that holds. Members who want access to each other will stay through a bad month of content. A platform can copy your format and outbid you for writers. It cannot copy a room of people who already trust each other. Everything in the design below serves this.

Expect the contributions to come from a few. Participation research consistently finds a small core doing most of the work: in one study of four online networks, the top 1% of members wrote about 75% of posts. A contribution rate of a few percent is normal. The aim is to know who those people are and keep them.

> A platform can copy your format and outbid you for writers. It cannot copy a room of people who already trust each other.

## Designing the membership

Four decisions, made deliberately.

| Decision | What to decide | What goes wrong without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is behind the wall | Things that depend on trust: data, source documents, the editor's working notes, members' questions to each other | The wall becomes a paywall on content readers can get elsewhere |
| Rituals | A fixed time when members expect each other: a weekly call with an agenda, a Monday thread, an annual gathering | No peer value; members meet the content, not each other |
| Recognition | Contributors named in the work; access to the editor that readers do not get | The people doing the sourcing stop doing it |
| A members' council | Six to ten members, rotating, meeting quarterly | Drift goes unnoticed and recruitment has no advocates |

Keep the public layer strong enough to recruit from. Rituals are the mechanism for peer value: without them, the wall is just a paywall. An annual gathering can be twenty people in a borrowed room. Recognition costs attention, not money, and it is the cheapest retention tool you have. The council tells you what the membership wants and when you have drifted, and its members become your first recruiters, because the role gives them something to say about you.

## The first hundred for media

[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) argued that the first hundred people set the shape of everything after. For media, the test is simple. The first hundred members are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in the sponsor deck.

That means recruiting by name, not by funnel. List the hundred. Write to each one. Tell them what the membership is for and why they specifically are on the list. Expect to do this yourself, because nobody else can. The composition of the first hundred becomes your pitch to sponsors later. It also becomes the peer value for the next hundred. Get the roles right before you get the number up.

## Owned channels only

Members live on channels you control: email, and a members' space on a platform where you hold the export and the relationship. For membership the rule is stricter than for audience: if the platform can change the terms, it cannot hold the membership.

The Reuters Institute data shows why. Social and video networks, at 54%, are now the most used route to online news, ahead of news sites and apps at 51%, and owned-site reach has fallen since 2021. A social platform group is fine for recruiting. It is not where the membership lives. The moment you depend on a feed to reach your own members, you have handed the job to someone who does not have it.

## What to measure

Four numbers, reported monthly, replacing the audience numbers you report now.

| Measure | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Member retention | Whether the wall and the rituals are worth paying for |
| Contribution rate | Share of members who sourced, posted or asked in the period |
| Member referrals | New members who were introduced by an existing one |
| Paid revenue from referring members | Whether peer value is funding the business |

The last one matters most. If a growing share of paid revenue comes from members who brought someone, the membership is working. If it stays flat while the list grows, you have a newsletter with a paywall. [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) covers why reach reporting hides this, and our explainer on [customer churn](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/) sets out how to calculate the retention figure consistently.

## lowob takeaways

- **Recruit from the list.** Subscribers, followers, opens and downloads are the pool a community is recruited from, not the community.
- **Ask for the three contributions.** Sourcing, peer amplification and peer value, explicitly.
- **Run rituals.** A weekly call or a Monday members' thread is the mechanism for peer value.
- **Report like a business line.** Retention, contribution rate, referrals and revenue from referring members, monthly.

## Common questions

### How do you turn a newsletter audience into a paid community?

Decide what goes behind the wall, set fixed rituals where members meet each other, recognise contributors, and run a rotating members' council. Recruit the first hundred personally, by name and job title.

### What is the difference between a subscription and a membership?

A subscription sells access to content. A membership is a relationship in which people pay, show up, contribute and refer, and get value from each other as well as from you.

### What metrics should a media membership track?

Member retention, contribution rate, member referrals and paid revenue from referring members, reported monthly. If revenue from referring members stays flat while the list grows, you have a newsletter with a paywall.

### Should a media membership live in a social media group?

No. A social platform group is fine for recruiting, but members should live on email and a space where you hold the export and the relationship.

## Sources and notes

- [Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2026/dnr-executive-summary), 16 June 2026. Online survey of 97,520 people in 48 markets; payment figures are for 20 markets with common paywalls.
- [Membership Puzzle Project, The Membership Guide](https://membershippuzzle.org/), project ran 2017 to 2021. Research collaboration of NYU and De Correspondent; practitioner guidance and case studies.
- [Jay Rosen and Gonzalo del Peon, What your site can learn from our database of nearly 100 membership models](https://membershippuzzle.org/what-your-site-can-learn/), 5 October 2017. Qualitative review; not a survey.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; health networks, not media memberships.
- The design and measurement tables are **lowob**'s framework.

# What Is a Commercial Operating System?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-commercial-operating-system/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A commercial operating system is how a firm runs its revenue line: the definitions it agrees, the records it keeps, the routines it follows and the tools that support them. It is broader than a CRM and broader than RevOps. This explainer sets out its components, how it relates to AI, and how a mid-size firm can assemble one without buying a platform.

A commercial operating system is the combined set of definitions, data, decision records, routines and tools a firm uses to find, win and keep clients. It is not a product. It is the agreed way the commercial line runs, written down and wired into the systems people use. Its test is whether a new hire, a board member or an AI agent would reach the same answer from the same records.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What a commercial operating system means

Most firms have the parts of a commercial operating system without the system. There is a CRM, a marketing tool, a proposal folder, a weekly pipeline meeting and a set of habits that live in senior people's heads. Each works. Together they do not reconcile.

A commercial operating system names the parts and connects them. It has six components, which map directly onto **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain as a loop rather than a product.

| Component | What it contains | Enterprise brain layer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definitions | ICP, qualified lead, stage criteria, source list, loss reasons | Rules the store follows |
| Store | CRM, marketing automation, billing, kept clean | Store |
| Wiring | Integrations and connectors that give tools shared context | Context layer |
| Decision record | Commercial decisions with reason, owner, status and expected outcome | Record |
| Rhythms and reasoning | Pipeline reviews, forecasts, assistants and agents | Reasoning |
| Learning | Outcomes written back against decisions | Learning |

The decision record is the component most firms lack. A CRM records that a deal was lost. It rarely records the decision to pursue it, who made it, why, and what they expected. Without that, outcomes cannot be traced to judgment.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buying has become harder to follow

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey, covering nearly 4,000 decision makers in 13 countries, found buyers use ten interaction channels on average, up from five in 2016, and 42% used more than 11 touchpoints. Each channel creates records in a different tool. Without shared definitions and wiring, the firm sees fragments of each buyer.

### Analytics pays only on a working system

McKinsey's 2021 research on commercial analytics, based on a survey of more than 2,500 respondents, found companies that use analytics effectively in marketing and sales are 1.5 times more likely to achieve above-average growth. Its recommendations are operational: agree where value lies first, start with the data already held, and build tools into the frontline's weekly routines. Those are operating system decisions, not software purchases.

### AI agents need it more than people do

People compensate for gaps. They know that one seller's "proposal" is another's "early chat". An agent does not. McKinsey's 2024 survey found 19% of B2B sales forces were already implementing gen AI use cases, with another 23% in development or experimentation. Validity's 2026 survey found only 21% of marketers rated their CRM data very well prepared for AI. Gartner predicted in 2021 that 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a RevOps model by 2025. The common thread is that AI rewards firms whose commercial line already runs on shared rules.

**lowob**'s position is to rent the wiring and own the record. Connectors, models and agents change quickly and are best bought. Definitions and the decision record are the firm's own judgment and should stay portable.

## How to assemble one at 20 to 500 people

| Step | Output | Typical effort |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Name an owner | One accountable person for commercial definitions | A decision |
| 2. Write the rulebook | Two pages: ICP, stages, sources, loss reasons, active client | One week |
| 3. Clean the store | Duplicates merged, stale deals closed, required fields set | One week |
| 4. Start the decision record | Pursue, price and pass decisions logged with reason and owner | Ongoing, minutes per decision |
| 5. Fix the rhythm | Weekly pipeline review reads from the record, not from slides | One meeting redesign |
| 6. Add reasoning carefully | One assistant or agent at draft level; nothing sends without a person | After steps 1 to 5 |
| 7. Write outcomes back | Each closed deal linked to the decision that started it | Monthly |

The order matters. Adding an agent before the rulebook exists automates whatever inconsistency is already there.

## lowob takeaways

- **It is a system, not a product.** Definitions, store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning together.
- **The decision record is the missing piece.** Most firms record outcomes; few record the judgments behind them.
- **Rent the wiring; own the record.** Buy connectors and models; keep definitions and decisions portable.
- **Rules before agents.** An agent added to an undefined process automates the inconsistency.

## Common questions

### What is a commercial operating system?

It is the agreed set of definitions, data, decision records, routines and tools a firm uses to find, win and keep clients, written down and built into the systems people use.

### How is a commercial operating system different from a CRM?

The CRM is one component, the store. The operating system also includes the definitions the CRM follows, the integrations around it, the record of decisions and the routines that use it.

### How is it different from revenue operations?

RevOps is usually the function that owns much of it. The operating system is the thing it owns, extended to include decision records and learning from outcomes.

### Do you need a commercial operating system before using AI agents?

You need its core: shared definitions, clean records and a human approval step. Without them, an agent acts on inconsistent data.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Why Revenue Operations (RevOps) Should Be On Your Radar](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/why-revenue-operations-revops-should-be-on-your-radar), August 2024. Analyst definition of RevOps.
- [McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/five-fundamental-truths-how-b2b-winners-keep-growing), September 2024. B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers.
- [McKinsey, B2B commercial analytics: What outperformers do](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/b2b-commercial-analytics-what-outperformers-do), December 2021. Survey of more than 2,500 respondents.
- [Gartner, Gartner Predicts 75% of the Highest Growth Companies Will Deploy a RevOps Model](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2021-05-17-gartner-predicts-75--of-the-highest-growth-companies-), May 2021. A prediction, not a measured outcome.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey.

- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)

## Next move

Write one page listing your firm's definitions of qualified lead, each pipeline stage, source values and loss reasons. Wherever you cannot fill a line, you have found a gap in your commercial operating system.

# What Is an Enterprise Brain?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-16 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An enterprise brain is a loop, not a product: a store of records, wiring that connects them, a record of decisions with reasons, models and agents that reason over them, and outcomes written back. Vendors sell parts of it, mostly the store and the wiring. The decision record is the part a company should own, and the commercial line is the place to start.

An enterprise brain is the system that lets a company's people and AI agents act on what the company knows, has decided and has learned. It is a loop, not a product: a store of records, wiring that connects them, a record of decisions with reasons, models and agents that reason over all three, and outcomes written back. Vendors now sell parts of it under the name, but no single tool is the whole thing.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What an enterprise brain means

The word "brain" suggests a mind that thinks for the company. We use it for something plainer: an accountable record that people and agents can read before they act, and write to after. A model can reason. It cannot know which price was approved last quarter, who approved it, or why an earlier offer was withdrawn, unless someone recorded it.

The term has entered the market. WRITER describes its Enterprise Brain as a governed, universal context layer that captures brand knowledge, decision logic and live business data across teams and agents. It is one part of the loop described below, as is every other product sold under the name.

| Part | What it holds | Typical tool | Own or rent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Store | What happened: email, deals, invoices, files | CRM, office suite, shared drives | Rent |
| Wiring | Connectors, permission-aware retrieval, shared definitions | Context platforms, MCP connectors | Rent |
| Record | Decisions with reason, owner, status and expected outcome | A structured table or database | Own |
| Reasoning | Models and agents that answer, draft and act | Assistants, agent frameworks | Rent |
| Learning | Outcomes written back against each decision | The record, plus a review routine | Own |

The rule that follows is short. Rent the wiring, own the record. No platform can supply a reason that was never written down, and a company's record of its own judgement should stay portable when it changes vendor.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Decision quality was a problem before AI arrived. In a McKinsey survey of 1,228 managers, fielded in 2018 and published in 2019, only 20% said their organisation excelled at decision making, and 61% said most of their decision-making time was used ineffectively.

AI agents raise the stakes because they act on records automatically. In Validity's 2026 survey of 500 marketing professionals, 21% said their CRM data was very well prepared to support AI. Nearly 78% of C-suite respondents said they had acted on an AI recommendation they later suspected was wrong because of bad underlying data. Validity sells data-quality software, so treat the survey as vendor research.

The commercial line is where the build should start. Decisions about discounts, account priorities and follow-ups happen every week. Their outcomes, won or lost, renewed or churned, show up within a quarter. The data already sits in email, calendar and CRM.

## What it is and what it is not

| An enterprise brain is | An enterprise brain is not |
| --- | --- |
| A loop that runs from record to action to outcome and back | A single platform, assistant or vendor |
| A record of decisions, reasons and owners | A search index over every document |
| Built on rented wiring and models | A custom model trained on company data |
| Governed: nothing sends without a person | An autonomous system acting alone from day one |
| Measured by fewer repeated mistakes | Measured by documents indexed or prompts sent |

Autonomy inside the brain is a dial, not a switch: level 0 answers, level 1 drafts, level 2 acts with approval, level 3 acts and reports, level 4 acts alone. Most commercial work should start at levels 0 and 1, and move up one notch at a time on evidence. Gartner's forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 is a reason to move slowly.

## lowob takeaways

- **It is a loop.** Store, wiring, record, reasoning and learning; remove one and the system stops improving.
- **Rent the wiring, own the record.** Retrieval is a commodity; your reasons and outcomes are not.
- **Start commercial.** Frequent decisions and fast outcomes make the loop measurable within a quarter.
- **Move the dial slowly.** Begin with answers and drafts, and keep a person before anything leaves the company.

## Common questions

### What is an enterprise brain in AI?

It is the system that lets people and AI agents act on what a company knows, has decided and has learned. It combines a store of records, a context layer, a decision record, models and agents, and outcomes written back.

### Is an enterprise brain a product I can buy?

Parts of it are. Vendors sell context layers and agent memory under the name. The decision record and the outcomes written back against it have to come from the company's own judgement.

### How is an enterprise brain different from enterprise search?

Search finds documents. A brain also records which decision is current, who made it, why, and what happened next, so an agent can tell a live answer from a superseded one.

### Where should a mid-size company start building one?

On the commercial line: one recurring decision, such as discount approvals, recorded with a reason and owner, and checked against the outcome at close.

## Sources and notes

- [CMSWire, WRITER launches Enterprise Brain to unify AI agent context](https://www.cmswire.com/customer-experience/writer-launches-enterprise-brain-to-unify-ai-agent-context/), September 2026. Product description is the vendor's own.
- [w.media, Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects could face the axe by end of 2027: Gartner](https://w.media/over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-could-face-the-axe-by-end-of-2027-gartner/), June 2025. Analyst forecast, reported secondhand.
- [McKinsey, Decision making in the age of urgency](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/decision-making-in-the-age-of-urgency), April 2019. Self-reported survey of managers.
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2026](https://www.validity.com/press-releases/validity-releases-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2026-report-revealing-marketers-trust-in-their-data-hasnt-caught-up-with-their-ai-goals/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey.

## Related research

- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [Why the Brain Starts at the Commercial Line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/)
- [The First Two-Fifths](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-two-fifths/)
- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)

## Next move

List the three commercial decisions your team makes most often, and check whether the reason for the last one is written anywhere a new hire could find it. If not, that decision is where the brain starts.
