# What Is CAC Payback?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: CAC payback measures how many months of gross profit a new customer must generate before the cost of acquiring them is recovered. It is one of the clearest tests of whether growth spending is affordable. This explainer sets out the formula, the benchmarks investors use, and the choices that make the number honest or flattering.

CAC payback is the number of months it takes for the gross profit from a new customer to repay the cost of acquiring that customer. The common formula is customer acquisition cost divided by monthly revenue per customer multiplied by gross margin. A shorter payback means growth ties up less cash and survives more churn. The number is only useful if the cost side includes everything spent to win the customer.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What CAC payback means

Customer acquisition cost (CAC) is the sales and marketing spend in a period divided by the number of new customers won. Payback converts that cost into time. Bessemer describes it as "the rate at which the costs spent to acquire a customer are repaid by that customer", and measures it against gross margin-adjusted revenue rather than top-line revenue.

Gross margin matters because a customer's revenue does not all come back to the business. Hosting, support, model inference and delivery staff take their share first. Two firms with the same price and the same CAC can have very different paybacks if one keeps 80% of each pound of revenue and the other keeps 50%.

An illustrative calculation for a mid-size software firm:

| Input | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Sales and marketing spend in the quarter | £300,000 |
| New customers won | 20 |
| CAC | £15,000 |
| Monthly revenue per new customer | £1,500 |
| Gross margin | 75% |
| Monthly gross profit per customer | £1,125 |
| CAC payback | 15,000 ÷ 1,125 = 13.3 months |

On Bessemer's targets, 13.3 months is acceptable for a mid-market seller and slow for an SMB one.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Acquisition is paid for up front and recovered slowly. Payback is the period during which cash is tied up in a customer who might still leave. A customer who churns in month 10 of a 13-month payback never repays their cost. ChartMogul describes under about 12 months as strong for SMB-focused SaaS and 12 to 24 months as typical for larger-contract enterprise software.

Payback is also the most useful way to compare channels. Blended CAC averages paid campaigns with referrals and inbound demand, which can hide a channel that loses money. Andreessen Horowitz notes that blended CAC "doesn't inform how well your paid campaigns are working and whether they're profitable", and that investors treat paid CAC as more important when judging viability.

For **lowob**, each decision to fund or cut a channel belongs in the commercial record: the payback assumed, the owner, and the payback observed two quarters later. Without that record, the same channel debate repeats every budget cycle with fresh numbers and no memory.

## How to calculate it honestly

Most disagreement about CAC payback comes from a handful of choices. Making them explicit, and holding them constant, matters more than the exact convention chosen.

| Choice | Flattering version | Honest version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Costs included | Media spend only | Sales and marketing salaries, commissions, tools, agencies, events, and discounts or credits given to win the deal |
| Revenue basis | Total revenue | Gross margin-adjusted revenue |
| Customers counted | All new logos, including referrals | Paid CAC by channel, alongside blended CAC |
| Timing | Spend and customers in the same month | Spend lagged by your typical sales cycle |
| Segment | One company-wide figure | Separate figures for SMB, mid-market and enterprise |

Bessemer notes that CAC typically includes sales, marketing and sometimes customer success costs. If customer success time goes into onboarding new accounts, include that share. If it goes into renewals, leave it out and track it against retention instead.

Three common mistakes are worth checking for:

1. **Counting first-month revenue only.** Ramped contracts and usage pricing start low. Use the expected run-rate after onboarding, and say so.
2. **Ignoring expansion and churn.** Payback on a single customer's starting revenue misses later upsell and early loss. Read it alongside net revenue retention.
3. **Mixing services and software margin.** If implementation fees carry a different margin from the subscription, calculate gross profit for each.

For a firm without subscription revenue, such as an advisory practice, the same logic works per client: the cost to win the engagement divided by monthly gross profit from it. If most clients do one project and leave, payback must happen inside that project.

## lowob takeaways

- **Payback is time, not a ratio.** It tells you how long cash is at risk in each new customer.
- **Margin belongs in the formula.** Revenue that goes straight to delivery costs does not repay acquisition.
- **Compare by channel.** Blended figures can hide a channel that never pays back.
- **Read it with retention.** A customer who leaves before payback is a net loss, whatever the average says.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate CAC payback period?

Divide customer acquisition cost by the monthly gross profit from a new customer, which is monthly revenue multiplied by gross margin. The result is in months.

### What is a good CAC payback period?

Bessemer's targets are under 12 months for SMB-focused companies, under 18 for mid-market and under 24 for enterprise. Shorter is safer when churn is high.

### Should CAC payback use revenue or gross margin?

Gross margin. Revenue-based payback overstates how quickly a customer repays their cost, especially where delivery or inference costs are high.

### What is the difference between CAC payback and LTV to CAC?

Payback measures how long recovery takes. LTV to CAC compares lifetime profit with acquisition cost. Bessemer suggests investing in acquisition when the lifetime value ratio is 3x or higher.

## Sources and notes

- [ChartMogul, CAC Payback](https://chartmogul.com/saas-metrics/cac-payback/), undated. Vendor metrics library; source of the formula and ranges quoted.
- [Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million](https://www.bvp.com/assets/uploads/2021/09/scaling-to-100-million-by-mary-d-onofrio.pdf), 2021. Venture firm analysis of cloud companies; benchmarks reflect a high-growth sample.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), August 2015, updated 2024. Investor guidance on CAC definitions.

## Related research

- [What Is Net Revenue Retention (NRR)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/)
- [What Is Lead Source Attribution?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/)
- [CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL, ROAS Explained: Which to Run On](https://lowob.com/research/cpm-cpc-cpa-cpl-roas-explained/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)

## Next move

Calculate last quarter's CAC payback twice: once with media spend only, once with every sales and marketing cost included. The gap between the two numbers is the size of the conversation your leadership team needs to have.

# Brand Safety vs Brand Suitability: What They Cost You

Source: https://lowob.com/research/brand-safety-and-suitability/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Brand safety keeps ads away from harmful content; brand suitability keeps them near content that fits the brand. Both are enforced by blunt tools that over-block by default: an IAS and Reuters analysis found a typical keyword blocklist would flag 54% of brand-suitable news URLs. GARM, the industry's shared framework, was discontinued in 2024, so each buyer now has to set its own standard.

Brand safety keeps a company's ads away from content that would harm it by association. Brand suitability keeps them near content that fits the brand and away from content that is legal and harmless but wrong for it. Both matter, and both are enforced by blunt tools that over-block by default: an analysis by Integral Ad Science and Reuters found a typical keyword blocklist would flag 54% of brand-suitable URLs in Reuters' news section. The industry's shared framework, GARM, was discontinued in August 2024. Set standards from actual risk, prefer category controls to keyword lists, allow reputable news and review what was blocked.

Brand safety is the practice of keeping a company's ads away from content that would harm it by association: violence, hate, illegal activity, adult material, misinformation. Brand suitability is the narrower practice of keeping ads near content that fits the brand and away from content that is legal and harmless but wrong for it: a children's product beside crime reporting, a wealth product beside a story about layoffs.

Both matter. Both are also enforced by blunt tools that cost advertisers more reach than they realise.

## How enforcement works

| Tool | How it works | Strength | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Keyword blocklists | The ad does not serve if listed words appear on the page | Simple and widespread | Crude: "shooting" blocks a photography site, "crash" blocks a market recovery story |
| Category classification | Verification vendors classify pages by content category and risk level; buyers choose which to allow | More precise than keywords | Depends on the vendor's classifier, and vendors disagree |
| Inclusion lists | The buyer names the sites and apps where ads may appear | The most protective approach | Limits reach the most |
| Pre-bid verification | Filters an impression before the buyer bids | Protects | Only as good as the rules set |
| Post-bid verification | Measures what happened after the ad served and, at best, refunds it | Reports | Money is already spent |

Pre-bid protects; post-bid reports. A buyer relying on post-bid reports is paying to learn what went wrong.

Classifiers disagree more than buyers assume. An independent analysis by Adalytics found that on WSJ.com two verification vendors' labels agreed on only 58.7% of a sample of 25,730 articles. IAS disputed parts of that analysis, and it was observational rather than a test of live campaigns. But it is a reason to treat a vendor's "unsafe" label as an opinion to be checked, not a fact.

## What over-blocking costs

Blunt safety settings have defunded quality journalism, particularly news, by blocking ads on any page that mentions difficult subjects, which is most of the news. The evidence comes from verification vendors and independent researchers rather than from neutral industry bodies, so read it with that in mind, but it points one way.

| Study | Finding | Caveat |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Integral Ad Science and Reuters, reported April 2026 | 54% of brand-suitable URLs in Reuters' news section would be flagged by a typical keyword blocklist; 4.27% in lifestyle | Vendor analysis; URLs, not impressions; no live campaigns |
| Adalytics, updated February 2021 | 21.4% of sampled Economist articles and 30.3% of sampled New York Times articles carried "unsafe" labels; an Economist obituary of Diego Maradona was among them | Independent, observational; IAS disputed the findings |

The advertiser loses reach among engaged, affluent readers; the publisher loses revenue; and the budget flows instead toward content designed to trip no filter, which is often the made-for-advertising inventory that adds nothing. The ANA's 2023 programmatic study found such sites took about 21% of impressions in its sample. Over-blocking and MFA growth are two halves of the same mistake.

> The cost of over-blocking is invisible on the report, because the report shows what was blocked, not what was lost.

## After GARM

For five years the industry had a shared reference point. The World Federation of Advertisers launched the Global Alliance for Responsible Media (GARM) in 2019, after footage of the Christchurch mosque shootings was live-streamed on Facebook. GARM published a Brand Safety Floor, content no advertiser should fund, and an adjacency standards framework setting out how close an ad could sit to sensitive content. It gave buyers, platforms and vendors a common vocabulary.

GARM was discontinued in August 2024, days after X filed an antitrust lawsuit against it, the WFA and several members, alleging an organised advertiser boycott. GARM said the case had drained its resources. Its documents can still be read, but they are no longer maintained, so buyers cannot treat them as a current industry standard.

The practical consequence is that there is no longer an industry default to defer to. Each buyer has to set and document its own standard. That is more work, and it is also an opportunity: suitability was always a judgment about fit that should be made by the brand, and our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) is a better starting point for that judgment than any vendor's default list.

## Setting standards that work

Start from what would actually harm the brand, not from a vendor's default list. Then work through five settings.

1. **Prefer category and risk-level controls over raw keyword lists.** Review any keyword list for words that are only dangerous in context.
2. **Split the buy.** Use inclusion lists for the core buy and controlled category rules for the reach buy.
3. **Allow reputable news with sensible exclusions** rather than excluding news wholesale. The IAS and Reuters gap between 54% in news and 4.27% in lifestyle shows where blunt rules do the most damage.
4. **Review the blocked-inventory report monthly** for false positives, and ask the vendor which rule blocked each high-value domain.
5. **Write the standard down,** with an owner and a review date, so that it survives staff changes and vendor changes.

Treat verification as a setting to be managed, not a box to be ticked.

## The other direction: suitability for restricted categories

For companies in reviewed categories the question runs the other way as well. Publishers and platforms apply their own suitability rules to advertisers, and a financial or crypto product can be excluded from inventory by the publisher's standards regardless of the buyer's. Roku's self-serve ad policies, for example, require prior approval for any crypto ad and limit approvals to the US. Google Ads requires certification for crypto exchanges and wallets and runs them only in approved countries.

That is another reason the band map matters: some of the inventory that appears open on a DSP is closed by the publisher when the ad arrives, and the rejection appears as low delivery rather than as a message. Our piece on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) explains the band map, and [the build order for media and publishing](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-media-and-publishing/) covers how publishers themselves record and apply those advertiser decisions.

## The honest summary

Brand safety protects against a real, if rare, harm. Brand suitability is a judgment about fit that should be made by the brand, not by a default. Both are enforced by tools that block far more than they should when left alone. The buyer who manages them gains reach that competitors have blocked themselves out of, and the buyer who ignores them is paying for both the harm and the waste.

## lowob takeaways

- **Separate safety from suitability.** One is harm, the other is fit, and only the brand can judge fit.
- **Distrust keyword lists.** They block more than half of brand-suitable news in at least one vendor's analysis.
- **There is no industry default now.** GARM ended in 2024; write your own standard.
- **Review what was blocked.** The report shows blocks, not lost reach.
- **Expect publishers to judge you too.** In restricted categories, low delivery can be a silent rejection.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between brand safety and brand suitability?

Brand safety keeps ads away from content that would harm the brand, such as violence, hate or misinformation. Brand suitability keeps ads away from content that is harmless but wrong for that particular brand.

### Why is my brand safety setup reducing my reach?

Blunt keyword lists and default settings block far more than they should, including safe news pages. IAS and Reuters found a typical keyword blocklist would flag 54% of brand-suitable Reuters news URLs.

### What happened to GARM?

The Global Alliance for Responsible Media, run by the World Federation of Advertisers, was discontinued in August 2024, days after X filed an antitrust lawsuit against it. Its framework is no longer maintained.

### Why is my crypto or fintech campaign under-delivering on a DSP?

Publishers and platforms apply their own suitability rules to advertisers, so some inventory that looks open on a DSP is closed when the ad arrives, and the rejection appears as low delivery.

# What Is a Closed-Lost Reason, and Why Does It Matter for AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A closed-lost reason is the field that records why a deal was lost. It is usually optional, often blank, and frequently wrong, yet it is the main link between a commercial outcome and its cause. This explainer covers what the field is, why AI systems depend on it, and how to design a reason list people will fill in honestly.

A closed-lost reason is the value recorded in the CRM to explain why an opportunity was lost, usually chosen from a fixed list with a short note. It is the field that connects an outcome to a cause. For AI systems that score, forecast or recommend, it is the difference between knowing that deals are lost and knowing why, and without it they can only learn correlation.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a closed-lost reason is

When an opportunity closes without a sale, the CRM marks it lost. HubSpot's default sales pipeline, for example, ends in a "Closed lost" stage with 0% probability, and its default deal properties include a separate "Closed lost reason" field. Salesforce, Microsoft Dynamics 365 and most other CRMs offer an equivalent, standard or custom.

The field is simple. Its value is not. It is the only structured place where a firm says what it believes caused a loss. In *The field that makes a record a judgment* we argued that one field, recorded at the moment of decision, is what turns a log into something a system can learn from. On the commercial line, this is that field.

| Good closed-lost reason | Poor closed-lost reason |
| --- | --- |
| Chosen from 6 to 10 fixed values | Free text, different every time |
| Plus a one-line note in the buyer's terms | "Price" with no context |
| Includes "no decision" as an option | Every loss blamed on a competitor |
| Recorded at close, by the owner | Back-filled months later |
| Checked against buyer interviews for a sample | Never verified |

## Why it matters for AI

### Outcomes without causes teach the wrong lesson

An AI system that scores leads or recommends next steps learns from the history in the CRM. If lost deals carry no reason, the model can only find correlations: industry, deal size, source, rep. It cannot tell a deal lost on price from one lost because the buyer's budget was frozen. Those call for opposite responses.

If reasons are present but systematically wrong, the problem is worse. Clozd reports that buyer and seller loss reasons align only 15% of the time. That is a vendor figure, but the mechanism is well understood: sellers must log a reason at close even when they do not know it, and "price" or "lost to competitor" is the easiest answer. A model trained on those values will conclude the firm loses on price, and an agent may then recommend discounting.

### No decision is a category of its own

Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's research, covering about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations, found that 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision. Many CRM reason lists have no value for this. Losses to inaction get recorded as competitive losses or "other", and the largest category of loss disappears from the data.

### Agents act before anyone reviews

Validity's 2026 State of CRM Data survey found 45% of marketers already used agentic AI that can act without human review. In the same survey, 19% said they had frequently acted on an AI recommendation they later suspected was wrong because of poor underlying data. A blank or false loss reason is exactly that kind of data. Under **lowob**'s autonomy dial, any agent that reads loss reasons to act should stay at level 2, acting with approval, until the reasons are verified.

## How to design a reason list people will use

1. **Keep it to six to ten values.** Long lists produce "other". A workable starting set is shown below.
2. **Separate the reason from the competitor.** Record "lost to competitor" as the reason and the competitor's name in its own field.
3. **Require a one-line note.** A short sentence in the buyer's own terms carries most of the value.
4. **Make it required at close, not before.** Asking earlier invites guessing.
5. **Verify a sample.** Interview a handful of lost buyers each quarter and compare their answer with the recorded reason. Report the match rate.

| Reason value | Use when |
| --- | --- |
| No decision / status quo | Buyer did not proceed with anyone |
| Lost to competitor | Buyer chose another provider (name in separate field) |
| Price or commercial terms | Terms, not value, were the stated blocker |
| Fit or capability gap | Requirements we could not meet |
| Timing or budget | Need is real but deferred |
| Champion or sponsor left | Internal change on the buyer's side |
| Disqualified by us | We chose not to pursue |
| Duplicate or admin | Not a real loss; exclude from analysis |

The last value matters. Excluding admin closures keeps the analysis honest.

## lowob takeaways

- **It is the cause field.** Without it, a lost deal is an outcome with nothing to attach it to.
- **Seller reasons need checking.** Verify a sample against buyer interviews each quarter.
- **Add no decision.** It is often the largest category, and many lists omit it.
- **Gate the agents.** Keep any agent that acts on loss reasons at act-with-approval until the reasons are trusted.

## Common questions

### What is a closed-lost reason in a CRM?

It is the field recording why an opportunity was lost, usually a value from a fixed list plus a short note, entered when the deal is closed.

### What are good closed-lost reasons?

A short list of six to ten values, such as no decision, lost to competitor, price or terms, capability gap, timing or budget, sponsor left, and disqualified by us.

### Should the closed-lost reason be a required field?

Yes, at the moment of closing. Requiring it earlier encourages guessing, and leaving it optional leaves most losses unexplained.

### Why do closed-lost reasons matter for AI?

AI systems learn from outcomes. Without accurate reasons, they can only find correlations and may recommend the wrong response, such as discounting when the real cause was inaction.

## Sources and notes

- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, HubSpot's default deal properties](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/properties/hubspots-default-deal-properties). Vendor documentation for the Closed lost reason and Closed won reason properties.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Set up and customize pipelines](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/object-settings/set-up-and-customize-pipelines). Default stages and probabilities.
- [Clozd, Win-loss analysis guide](https://clozd.com/guides/win-loss-analysis). Vendor-reported figure on buyer and seller reason alignment; methodology not published.
- [Challenger, How to Overcome Customer Indecision Using the JOLT Effect Approach](https://challengerinc.com/losing-to-customer-indecision/), February 2024. Summary of Dixon and McKenna's research.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey of 500 marketers.

## Related research

- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is Revenue Intelligence?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-intelligence/)

## Next move

Export last quarter's lost deals and count how many have no reason, and how many say "other". If the two together exceed a third, replace the list this week and make it required at close.

# In Fintech, Trust Is the Product and the Channel Is Whoever Already Has It.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/fintech-gtm-trust-distribution/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-14 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A fintech can beat an incumbent on price and experience and still struggle to acquire customers, because people are being asked to trust an unfamiliar company with their money. Ad platforms now verify financial advertisers before they run, and regulators hold firms responsible for what partners and influencers say. The channels that work are the people and platforms customers already trust, supplied with approved facts and measured on funded, retained use.

A fintech product can offer a better price and a cleaner experience than an established competitor and still struggle to acquire customers, because people are being asked to trust an unfamiliar company with their money, identity or financial information. Paid channels add their own gate: Google now requires financial services advertisers to prove regulatory authorisation in a growing list of countries, with the US and Canada due in early 2027. The channels that work best are the people and platforms customers already trust, given approved facts to repeat and measured on funded, retained use rather than traffic.

*This is strategic guidance from go-to-market work, not legal or regulatory advice.*

## Trust comes before traffic

People are asked to hand an unfamiliar company their savings, their payroll or their identity documents. A good website alone does not settle that concern. So the distribution question for a fintech is not only where to buy attention. It is how to help the right customer understand what the product does, who is responsible for it and why its claims should be believed.

Paid channels make the point formally. Google's financial products and services policy requires that disclosures be "clearly and immediately visible without needing to click or hover over anything", and that financial ads provide the business's physical address, all associated fees and links to any accreditation they claim. Some locations add a verification step covering licences and registration numbers. Google's financial services verification page lists 42 countries in its location menu, and in Australia, for example, advertisers must prove they are licensed by ASIC before ads run.

The gate is widening. Google launched verification in the UK in September 2021 and reported "a pronounced decline in reports of ads promoting financial scams" afterwards. In October 2026 it announced that the programme will reach the US and Canada in early 2027, working with the American Bankers Association to verify authorised banks. A fintech that relies on paid search should treat proof of authorisation as a launch dependency, not a later task.

An advertising approval is only one obstacle. A prospective customer still asks who holds the money, what happens if something fails, which fees apply and whether a person can be reached. Marketing that promises safety without explaining the protections, or highlights a return while hiding the conditions, may win attention but erodes the trust the business needs. Our piece [Trust is the product](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/) sets out the order in which buyers run those checks.

## Work through people and platforms customers already use

The shortest route to trust is through someone the customer already trusts. The Edelman Trust Barometer 2026, a survey of nearly 34,000 people in 28 countries, found that net trust in "my neighbours, family and friends" and "my coworkers" each rose 11 points over recent years, while trust in national government leaders fell 16. Seven in ten respondents said they were unwilling or hesitant to trust someone with different values. Trust is concentrating in people and institutions close to the customer.

There is evidence that customers who arrive through a trusted route are worth more. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank by Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte found referred customers had a roughly 18% lower hazard of leaving than comparable customers acquired otherwise, and were at least 16% more valuable over six years.

| Route | Who it is | What it needs from you | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product and distribution partners | Payroll, accounting, wallet or marketplace platforms whose users fit | Integration work, support ownership, a reason to believe the product suits their users | Slow negotiation; the partner's users may not fit |
| Practitioners and educators | Accountants, advisers, specialist educators and creators | Accurate explanations, approved claims, clear disclosure of any payment | Paid relationships that are not disclosed; unapproved promotions |
| Owned resources | Product guide, pricing page, help centre, customer emails | Plain answers kept current | They are only believed once something else has earned trust |

**Product and distribution partners.** A payroll or accounting platform might introduce a financial service to customers who already rely on its software. A wallet or marketplace can do the same. The partner still has to believe the product is suitable for its users, and its reputation is now attached to yours. Our [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the partner's role and pay before recruiting.

**Practitioners and educators.** Accountants, advisers and specialists can explain a product's purpose and limits. A walkthrough or a carefully written comparison answers questions a short ad cannot. Any paid relationship and the relevant disclosures should be clear.

**Owned resources.** A plain product guide, pricing page, help centre and customer emails answer questions after the first encounter. These channels are under the company's control, though customers still need a reason to trust what they say.

None of these routes is guaranteed to be cheap or simple. Partner distribution takes negotiation and integration work, and a creator's audience may be poorly matched. The right channel is the one that reaches suitable customers and produces meaningful product use. [Distribute through whoever already holds the customer](https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/) covers the channel economics.

## Make the proof visible before asking for commitment

Consider a **hypothetical small-business payments platform**. A promising introduction comes from an accounting software company. Before referring its customers, the partner wants to understand reconciliation, failed payments, support ownership and fees. Its customers care less about the technology than about whether payments arrive on time and errors are put right.

The useful marketing response is a clear guide to how payments work, realistic examples of the settlement process, approved descriptions of risk and accessible support details. Those assets help the partner decide whether to refer and help the customer decide whether to sign up.

> When the customer needs trust before acting, distribution should help establish that trust, not just buy more impressions.

Use the same approved facts in outreach, presentations and product pages. When the operating details change, update the material promptly. A partner that finds your deck contradicting your fee page will stop referring before it tells you why.

## Make compliant marketing easier to repeat

Do not treat legal and compliance review as the last obstacle before publishing. Work with the appropriate advisers to build an approved set of claims, disclosures and examples that the team and its partners can use.

The rules reach partners as well as the firm. The FCA's FG24/1 guidance on financial promotions on social media says firms working with affiliate marketers such as influencers "should take proactive responsibility", and that firms "remain responsible for the compliance of every promotion they make or cause to be made". It expects each promotion to be standalone compliant, judged on its own rather than as part of a wider journey, and notes that a breach of section 21 of FSMA is a criminal offence punishable by up to two years' imprisonment. In the US, the FTC tells advertisers they "need to have reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network", and that delegating to an outside company does not relieve them of responsibility.

An approved set may record which products can be advertised in each market, what evidence supports each claim, how fees must be described and what disclosures a creator or affiliate needs. The requirements depend on the product and jurisdiction, and an internal template is not a substitute for legal review. The benefit is practical: sales, partnerships and marketing can move faster without improvising on sensitive claims.

## Judge channels by customers, not just leads

Start with a small number of suitable channels and decide how each will be measured before it launches. A newsletter might produce visits, a partner may introduce qualified businesses and a creator may generate sign-ups. Those actions sit at different distances from revenue.

| Channel output | What it proves | Distance from revenue | Measure that matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Visits | Someone looked | Far | Share who start an application |
| Sign-ups | Someone started | Middle | Share who pass verification and fund |
| Qualified referrals | A trusted party vouched | Middle | Share who complete onboarding |
| First funded transaction | The customer acted | Near | Time from verification to funding |
| Retained use at 90 and 365 days | The trust held | Revenue | Revenue per active funded account, by channel |

For an account-based product, follow the path from qualified referral to completed onboarding, first meaningful financial action and retained use. Include referral fees, incentives and integration work in the cost. A channel producing fewer but better-qualified customers may be worth more than one producing the most traffic. [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) sets out the full chain, and [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers paying partners only for what they actually produce.

## lowob takeaways

- **Lead with what customers need to verify.** Explain custody, fees, risk and support clearly, before asking for registration or funds.
- **Treat ad verification as a launch dependency.** Google already verifies financial advertisers by country and plans the US and Canada for early 2027.
- **Choose trusted channels deliberately.** Partners and practitioners help when their audience and the product actually fit.
- **Make claims review reusable.** Approved language and clear disclosures make partnerships easier to operate, and the firm stays responsible for what partners say.
- **Measure meaningful use.** Track qualified onboarding and retention, not just visits or sign-ups.

## Common questions

### How do fintech startups acquire customers when ad platforms restrict financial ads?

By working through people and platforms customers already trust, such as payroll and accounting software, practitioners and educators, and by making sure paid ads meet verification and disclosure rules before launch. Measure each channel on funded, retained accounts.

### Does Google require verification for financial services ads?

In many countries, yes. Google's financial services verification asks advertisers to prove they are authorised by the relevant regulator, and Google announced in October 2026 that the programme will reach the US and Canada in early 2027.

### Is a fintech responsible for what influencers and affiliates say about it?

In the UK, the FCA says firms remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made and should monitor affiliates. In the US, the FTC expects advertisers to train and monitor their endorsers.

### What is the best distribution channel for a fintech?

Usually the one whose audience already trusts the source and fits the product, often a platform or practitioner already serving your customer. Judge it on funded accounts and retention rather than traffic.

Fintechs that rely on paid search should start gathering licence evidence now.

# Pricing Architecture for Services Firms

Source: https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Price is the largest profit lever most services firms have and the one they manage least. A pricing architecture is the set of rules that turns a rate card into the fee a firm actually keeps: the fee model, the packages, the discount and exception rules, scope change terms and payment terms. This piece sets out each element, shows where a typical engagement leaks value between list and pocket, and explains why every price exception should be recorded with a reason and an outcome.

A pricing architecture is the set of rules that turns a firm's rate card into the fee it actually keeps: the fee model, the packages, the discount and exception rules, the scope change terms and the payment terms. Most services firms have a rate card and no architecture, so the realised price is set deal by deal. That matters because price is the strongest profit lever available. Marn and Rosiello's classic *Harvard Business Review* analysis found a 1% price improvement, with volume unchanged, lifted operating profit by 11.1%, against 3.3% for a 1% volume gain. Design the architecture once, measure the gap between list and pocket price, and record every exception so the rules can learn.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 3 of this series covered which segments to pursue. Pricing is the next Strategy decision, and in services firms it is usually the least designed. A rate card exists. Proposals are priced by the partner or founder who writes them. Discounts are agreed in the last week of a deal. Nobody can say, at year end, what the firm realised against what it quoted.

A pricing architecture fixes that without making every proposal identical. It sets the rules that most deals follow, the limits within which people can use judgment, and the route for exceptions.

## Price is the largest lever, and the least managed

The case for designing price rests on how far price moves profit. Marn and Rosiello's 1992 analysis in *Harvard Business Review*, using average economics across 2,463 companies, found a 1% improvement in price, with no loss of volume, increased operating profit by 11.1%. The same 1% improvement in volume added about 3.3%, a 1% cut in variable cost about 7.8%, and a 1% cut in fixed cost about 2.3%. The figures are old and the mix of companies was industrial, but the arithmetic holds wherever margins are thin relative to revenue.

More recent work points the same way. McKinsey's 2026 analysis of 140 public distributors found a 1% price increase could lift EBITDA margin by more than 22%, and described a building materials distributor where sales staff were overriding system prices in more than half of all transactions until a pricing architecture cut manual overrides by 80%. Distributors are not services firms. The pattern, discretion without rules leaking margin, is the same.

## What a pricing architecture contains

| Element | The question it answers | What it looks like in a services firm |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Value metric | What the client pays for | Days, deliverables, outcomes, a retained capacity, or a mix |
| Fee model | How the fee is structured | Project, retainer, time and materials, success fee or hybrid |
| Packages | Which standard offers exist | Two to four defined scopes with a price each |
| Rate card | What a unit of time or work costs | Rates by role, used for estimating and change requests |
| Discount rules | Who may lower the price, by how much, and why | Approval levels and allowed reasons |
| Scope change terms | What happens when work grows | Change request threshold and pricing method |
| Payment terms | When the money arrives | Deposit, milestones, days to pay, late-payment terms |
| Review rhythm | When the rules are checked against results | Quarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected |

Most firms have the rate card and some packages. The elements that protect realised price (discount rules, scope change terms and the review rhythm) are the ones usually missing.

## Choosing the fee model

The fee model decides who carries risk and what behaviour the fee rewards. Our piece on how marketing services are priced makes the point that the clearest guide to a provider's incentive is what makes its fee go up ([How marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/)). The same test applies to a firm pricing its own work.

| Fee model | What it rewards | Who carries estimation risk | Suits |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Time and materials | Hours worked | The client | Unclear scope, short or exploratory work |
| Fixed project fee | Finishing efficiently | The firm | Defined deliverables with a clear end |
| Retainer | Keeping the relationship | Shared; drifts to the firm if scope grows | Ongoing work with a stable shape |
| Success or outcome fee | The agreed outcome | The firm | Measurable outcomes the firm can influence |
| Hybrid: fixed base plus variable | Both delivery and outcome | Shared | Engagements with a defined core and uncertain upside |

Time-based pricing deserves particular scrutiny. It ties revenue directly to utilisation, and utilisation is under pressure. SPI Research's 2026 Professional Services Maturity Benchmark, published with Deltek, put billable utilisation at 66.4%, its lowest in nearly two decades, against 75% for high-performing firms. Thomson Reuters' 2026 survey of more than 1,500 professionals recorded growing concern that AI may threaten billing models. If AI shortens the hours a task takes, a firm billing by the hour passes the whole gain to the client. A fixed fee or a value metric lets the firm keep part of it. Our piece on seats, usage and outcomes covers the same choice for software ([Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/)).

## The pocket price: where services firms leak

Marn and Rosiello defined the pocket price as the revenue truly left in a company's pocket from a transaction, after every deduction between list and payment. They called the chart of those deductions the pocket price waterfall. Services firms have their own version.

| Step (illustrative engagement) | Amount | Remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Work delivered at rate card: 500 hours at $200 |  | $100,000 |
| Negotiated discount at contract, 10% | −$10,000 | $90,000 |
| Overrun absorbed without a change request: 40 hours | −$8,000 | $82,000 |
| Invoice written off after a dispute | −$2,000 | $80,000 |
| Cost of payment received 90 days late, at 8% a year | −$1,600 | $78,400 |
| Pocket price |  | $78,400, or 78.4% of standard value |

The discount is the line everyone sees. In this example it is less than half the leak. The overrun, the write-off and the slow payment are rarely reported together, because they sit with delivery, finance and the account lead respectively. A pricing architecture puts them on one page.

> The discount is the leak everyone sees. In most services engagements it is less than half of the loss.

## Discount and exception rules

Discounts are not wrong. Undesigned discounts are. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities, found discounts offered early in a deal were associated with a 39% drop in win rates. Early discounting tends to signal that the price was never firm.

A simple rule set covers most firms.

| Discount or exception | Who approves | Required on the record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Up to 5%, standard terms | The deal owner | Reason from an agreed list |
| 5% to 15%, or a non-standard payment term | Commercial lead | Reason, what the client gives in return, expected outcome |
| Above 15%, a cap on change requests, or a success-only fee | Founder or finance lead | Full rationale, risk to margin, review date |
| Any price for a segment the firm has declined | Commercial lead | Why the exception is worth taking |

Two principles make the rules work. First, every discount should trade for something: a longer term, a faster decision, a case study, a larger scope or prepayment. A discount that buys nothing is a price cut. Second, the allowed reasons should come from a short, fixed list, so exceptions can be compared over a year.

## Recording price decisions so the rules learn

A pricing architecture improves only if its exceptions are graded. That requires the record The Build Order describes: each exception with its reason, approver, status and expected outcome, written back when the outcome is known ([The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

After two or three quarters the record answers questions that otherwise run on anecdote. Did discounted proposals win more often than standard ones in each segment? Which reasons predicted renewals? Which clients generated the most absorbed overrun? In Part 10 of The Build Order, a composite distributor found its discounts won no more often than standard quotes in some product lines once the outcomes were recorded ([The same build in four industries](https://lowob.com/research/the-same-build-in-four-industries/)). Services firms usually find something similar.

Pricing for AI-assisted work adds a new question. Software vendors are moving to hybrid structures: Metronome's 2026 review of more than 50 AI pricing models, a vendor catalogue, found most combine subscriptions with usage or credits. Services firms delivering AI-assisted work face the same choice between charging for effort and charging for the result ([What is outcome-based pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/)). Whatever they choose, the record makes the effect visible.

Illustrative example: closing the overrun leak

Decision
:   Require a change request for any overrun above 10% of estimated hours, priced at the rate card, before the work is done.

Reason and owner
:   A quarterly comparison of quoted, invoiced and collected fees showed absorbed overruns cost more than negotiated discounts across the year. Owned by the head of delivery; agreed with the commercial lead.

What changed
:   Proposals state the change threshold; project leads log overruns weekly; the pricing review now reports discounts, overruns, write-offs and days to pay on one page.

Illustrative: a composite of a 120-person technical services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Design the rules, not every price.** An architecture sets defaults, limits and an exception route.
- **Measure pocket price.** Discounts, overruns, write-offs and slow payment belong on one page.
- **Choose the fee model by risk and reward.** Hourly billing passes efficiency gains, including AI gains, to the client.
- **Make every discount trade for something.** Record the reason and grade the outcome.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a pricing architecture

- A chosen fee model and value metric for each offer
- Two to four packages with stated scope and price
- Discount approval levels with a fixed list of allowed reasons
- A change request threshold written into every proposal
- A quarterly report of quoted, invoiced and collected fees
- Every exception recorded with an approver and an expected outcome

## Common questions

### What is a pricing architecture?

The set of rules that turns a rate card into the fee a firm keeps: fee model, packages, discount and exception rules, scope change terms, payment terms and a review rhythm.

### How should a professional services firm price its work?

Choose a fee model by who should carry estimation risk and what it rewards, define packages for common scopes, and set discount and change request rules so the realised price stays close to the quoted one.

### What is a pocket price?

The revenue left after every deduction between the list price and payment. For services firms that includes discounts, unbilled overruns, write-offs and the cost of late payment.

### Should services firms stop billing by the hour?

Not always. Hourly billing suits unclear or exploratory work, but it ties revenue to utilisation and passes efficiency gains to the client, so defined work is usually better priced as a fixed fee or by value.

- [McKinsey, Pricing in distribution: A strategic growth engine](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/industrials/our-insights/pricing-in-distribution-a-strategic-growth-engine), July 2026. Distribution sector, not services; case figures are McKinsey's.

# What Investors Fund in Media Now

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-investors-fund-in-media-now/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Investors fund media businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary products those audiences need, and revenue that does not depend on a platform. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. With search traffic to publishers down a third and only 17% of people paying for online news, the evidence that counts is repeat behaviour: paid conversion, renewal, sponsor renewal and signed licensing.

Investors fund media businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary products those audiences need, and revenue that does not depend on a platform. Reach is the raw material, not the asset. The 2026 data explains why: Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 publisher sites fell 33% in a year, the share of people paying for online news held at about 17% across 20 countries, and media leaders expect AI licensing to be a minor contribution at best.

*This is commercial advisory, not investment advice.*

## What stopped getting funded

Ad-supported reach was fundable when traffic was cheap and advertisers paid by volume. Neither holds now. Platforms changed their terms, programmatic rates fell, and the cost of acquiring attention rose.

The traffic data is stark. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing Google organic search traffic to more than 2,500 news sites fell by a third globally, and by 38% in the US, between November 2024 and November 2025. Referrals from Facebook fell 43% and from X 46% over roughly three years. Publishers surveyed expect search traffic to fall by more than 40% over the next three years. The Reuters Institute's Digital News Report 2026 found social and video networks are now the most used way to reach online news, at 54% of respondents, ahead of news organisations' own sites and apps at 51%.

Venture money has followed. Carta's first-half 2026 data shows capital raised by advertising technology companies on its platform falling from $335 million to $65 million year on year.

Investors who backed that model carry the scars. When a media founder leads with page views and impressions, the first reaction is not interest. It is pattern recognition.

That does not mean media is unfundable. It means the thing being funded has changed. [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) says raise on what users have done. In media, the narrative is almost always growth in attention. The evidence is growth in money from people who chose to pay.

## What gets funded

Five models attract capital in media today. Most funded companies combine two or three.

| Model | What proves it | The main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Owned audience that pays | Free-to-paid conversion and renewal after the first term | A low ceiling on willingness to pay |
| Proprietary data or research for B2B buyers | Annual contracts, daily use, low churn | Buyers build or buy it elsewhere |
| Licensing | Signed agreements with terms | Uneven demand; many publishers get no offer |
| Events and community with margins | Sponsor renewal, ticket revenue, a visible cost base | Break-even events that look like growth |
| Tooling or software on the audience | Software margins attached to distribution | Becoming a software company without the team |

**Owned audience with demonstrated willingness to pay.** Paid subscriptions, memberships, premium tiers. The proof is not the list size; it is the conversion from free to paid and the renewal after the first term. The ceiling is real: the Digital News Report 2026 found the share paying for online news across its 20-country basket was 17%, against 18% in 2025, with Norway at 40% and the UK at 10%. Even large publishers are not immune. The same report notes USA Today Co. reported a 30% drop in total subscribers during 2025. [Membership is the job](https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/) covers how to give paying members a reason to stay.

**Proprietary data or research that B2B buyers pay for.** Market maps, benchmarks, deal data, rankings, surveys. Buyers put these in budgets, sign annual contracts, and rarely churn if the data is used daily.

**Licensing.** Syndication, republication, archive access, and now content licensing to AI developers. The AI licensing market is real, but uneven: terms vary widely, demand favours depth and originality, and many publishers get no offer at all. The Reuters Institute's survey of 280 media leaders found 20% expect AI-related revenue to be substantial, 49% expect a minor contribution, and another 20%, mostly local publishers, public broadcasters and those in smaller countries, expect none. Treat it as upside, not a plan.

**Events and community with margins.** Not a conference that breaks even. A programme with sponsor renewal, ticket revenue, and a cost base you can show. Events are rising as a priority: 54% of media leaders in the Reuters Institute survey named them as increasingly important, behind subscription and membership at 76%.

**Tooling or software layered on the audience.** Directories, calculators, job boards, deal-flow tools, databases. Software margins attached to a distribution advantage.

## The evidence that counts

Most media decks lead with audience growth charts. Investors look past them to a short set of figures that describe whether the business works.

| Evidence | What it proves |
| --- | --- |
| Paid conversion rate | The audience values the product enough to pay |
| Renewal rate | They still value it after they have had it |
| Revenue per subscriber | The economics of one relationship |
| Sponsor renewal rate | Advertisers got results, not just impressions |
| Signed licensing agreements | A third party has valued the content in writing |
| Share of revenue not platform-dependent | What survives a policy change |

Notice that every line is about repeat behaviour. One-off revenue tells an investor you can sell. Repeat revenue tells them you have built something. Report retention the way a subscription business does: our explainers on [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/) and [NRR vs GRR](https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/) cover which number to show.

If you cannot populate this table yet, that is your pre-raise work. [Your first ten sponsors are design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-sponsors-are-design-partners/) covers the media version of design partners: your first paying cohort and your first renewing sponsors.

> A sponsor buys next quarter. An investor buys the next five years.

## Alternatives to venture capital

Venture suits a small share of media businesses: those with a software layer, a large addressable B2B market, or a data product that compounds. For many others, venture terms are a poor fit for the growth rate media can deliver.

| Route | Suits | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Venture | Software layer, large B2B market, compounding data | A path to venture-scale growth |
| Revenue-based finance | Predictable subscription or sponsorship income | Steady monthly revenue to repay from |
| Strategic investors | Audience or data a larger company wants | Clarity on what they get and the exit path |
| Partnerships | A product line a sponsor or platform will fund | Terms on exclusivity or first access |
| Bootstrapping | Profitable niches | Patience; the business stays sellable at any point |

Each route needs the same evidence as venture. The buyer changes, the proof does not.

## Running the raise

[Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) covers the method. Media founders often skip this because they are used to pitching sponsors, which is a different sale.

A sponsor buys next quarter. An investor buys the next five years. The materials need to show the model, not the audience. The data room needs the claims register from [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/), the evidence table above, and the cohort behaviour behind it. Our [Build Order for media and publishing](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-media-and-publishing/) covers how to keep those records as routine.

The most common gap I see is a strong audience and no revenue story. Fix the revenue story first. It changes who you can talk to and what they will offer.

## lowob takeaways

- **Reach is raw material, not the asset.** Platform traffic is falling and investors know it.
- **Lead with repeat behaviour.** Conversion, renewal, sponsor renewal and signed licences.
- **Treat AI licensing as upside.** Most media leaders expect a minor contribution or none.
- **Compare routes before choosing venture.** Each needs the same evidence; the terms differ.

## Common questions

### What kind of media companies do investors fund today?

Businesses with owned audiences that pay, proprietary data or research B2B buyers pay for, licensing, events and community with margins, and software layered on the audience. Most funded companies combine two or three.

### What metrics do investors look for in a media startup?

Paid conversion rate, renewal rate, revenue per subscriber, sponsor renewal rate, signed licensing agreements, and the share of revenue not dependent on platforms. Every line is about repeat behaviour.

### Is AI content licensing a reliable revenue stream for publishers?

Not yet. In the Reuters Institute's 2026 survey of 280 media leaders, 20% expected substantial AI revenue, 49% a minor contribution and 20% none. Treat it as upside, not a plan.

### How many people pay for online news?

About 17% across the Reuters Institute's 20-country basket in 2026, against 18% in 2025, with wide variation: 40% in Norway and 10% in the UK.

## Sources and notes

- [Reuters Institute, Journalism, media and technology trends and predictions 2026](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/journalism-media-and-technology-trends-and-predictions-2026), 12 January 2026. Strategic sample of 280 digital leaders in 51 countries, plus Chartbeat traffic data; not representative of all publishers.
- [Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: executive summary](https://reutersinstitute.politics.ox.ac.uk/digital-news-report/2026/dnr-executive-summary), 16 June 2026. Online survey of 97,520 people across markets, about 2,000 per market; online samples under-represent offline users.
- [Carta, The venture market shifted in the first half of the year](https://carta.com/data/newsletter-venture-market-shifted-first-half/), 8 July 2026. Carta platform data; advertising technology category is Carta's.

Fill in the six-line evidence table with your own verified numbers this week. Any line you cannot fill is your pre-raise work; any line that depends on one platform is your first risk to price.

# What Is a Sales Playbook?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-playbook/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A sales playbook sets out how a team handles specific selling situations, from first contact to close. Forrester research found playbooks among the least used and least influential sales assets, largely because they live outside the seller's workflow. This explainer covers what a playbook contains, why most go unused, and how to build one that sits where sellers work and improves from evidence.

A sales playbook is a written guide to how a team sells in defined situations: which buyers to pursue, what to ask, what to say, what evidence to share and what to do next at each stage. Its purpose is to make good practice repeatable across sellers. Most playbooks fail because they are long documents kept outside the CRM; the ones that work are short, situation-specific and built into the tools sellers already use.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What a sales playbook means

A playbook answers the question a seller has at a specific moment: what do I do now, with this kind of buyer, at this stage? It is not a sales methodology, which sets out a general philosophy of selling, and not a training course, which builds skills over time. It is the practical layer between the two.

A useful playbook usually covers a small number of named situations, each with the same structure:

| Section | What it contains | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Situation | When this play applies | Inbound lead from a regulated firm with 50 to 200 staff |
| Buyer | Who is involved and what they care about | Operations lead, compliance officer, finance approver |
| Questions | What to ask to qualify and diagnose | Current process, trigger for change, decision deadline |
| Evidence | What to share and when | One relevant case study, security summary, pricing range |
| Objections | Common pushbacks and tested responses | "We tried this before", "Not this year" |
| Next step | What must happen to move the deal | Second meeting with the approver, booked before the call ends |
| Exit criteria | What must be true to advance the stage | Named sponsor, confirmed problem, agreed timeline |

## Why most playbooks go unused

### They compete with too much content

Forrester analysts reported in 2022 that the average rep has about 1,400 sales assets to choose from, and that buyer interactions per buying cycle had risen 54% over the previous two years. In that environment, sales playbooks showed low influence and low utilisation across every stage of the buyer's journey. By contrast, conversation intelligence tools, which analyse recorded calls, were influential at all stages. The difference is that one sits in the seller's daily workflow and the other sits in a shared drive.

### They describe behaviour rather than change it

Gartner's 2023 research found 77% of sellers struggle to complete their assigned tasks efficiently, and 82% of 213 sales leaders said enablement content or delivery must change significantly to meet revenue goals. Gartner's recommendation is to move enablement from learning towards behaviour change, tie specific behaviours to sales goals, and use just-in-time prompts rather than one-off training. A 40-page playbook delivered at onboarding is the opposite of that.

### Buyers need less of the seller's script

Gartner's 2026 buyer survey found 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience, and 45% used AI in a recent purchase. Buyers arrive having done more of the research themselves. A playbook that scripts a generic product pitch adds little. One that helps a seller diagnose the buyer's situation and answer the specific questions research has not resolved adds more.

## How to build one that gets used

1. **Start from wins and losses.** Pick the two or three situations that account for most of your revenue, then use win-loss interviews and call recordings to find what the best sellers actually do in them.
2. **Keep each play to one screen.** Situation, questions, evidence, objections, next step. If it does not fit, it is two plays.
3. **Put it where sellers work.** HubSpot, for example, shows playbooks as interactive cards on contact, company and deal records; answers can update record properties and are logged to the timeline. Other CRMs and sales engagement tools offer similar features.
4. **Tie plays to stage exit criteria.** The play for each stage should end with the evidence needed to move the deal forward, so the playbook and the pipeline definitions agree.
5. **Review quarterly with evidence.** Compare deals where the play was followed with those where it was not. Keep what works; cut what does not.

AI changes delivery more than content. An assistant can surface the right play on a deal record or draft follow-up from it. In **lowob**'s terms, that is autonomy level 1, draft: the seller decides what is sent, and nothing sends without a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write plays for situations, not for the whole sale.** A seller needs the next move, not the full manual.
- **Keep it in the workflow.** A playbook in a shared drive competes with hundreds of other assets.
- **Build from evidence.** Win-loss interviews and call reviews show what actually works.
- **Revise it on a cadence.** A playbook that never changes is describing last year's buyers.

## Common questions

### What is a sales playbook?

It is a written guide to how a team handles specific selling situations, covering target buyers, questions, evidence, objections, next steps and stage exit criteria.

### What should be included in a sales playbook?

For each situation: when it applies, who the buyers are, what to ask, what to share, common objections and responses, the next step and what must be true to advance.

### What is the difference between a sales playbook and a sales methodology?

A methodology is a general approach to selling. A playbook applies it to specific situations, with concrete questions, evidence and next steps for each.

### Why don't sales reps use playbooks?

Common reasons are length, location outside the CRM and content that does not match real situations. Forrester found playbooks among the least used sales assets.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, The Great Sales Content Disconnect](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-great-sales-content-disconnect), April 2022. Analyst blog summarising Forrester survey research; sample not stated in the post.
- [Gartner, Gartner Survey Finds 77% of Sellers Struggle to Complete Their Assigned Tasks Efficiently](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2023-11-02-gartner-survey-finds-77-percent-of-sellers-struggle-to-complete-their-assigned-tasks-efficiently), November 2023. Surveys of 501 sellers and 213 sales leaders.
- [Gartner, Gartner Sales Survey Finds 67% of B2B Buyers Prefer a Rep-Free Experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025.
- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Use playbooks](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/playbooks/use-playbooks). Vendor product documentation; some question types require Enterprise plans.

## Related research

- [What Is Win-Loss Analysis?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/)
- [What Is Selling Time, and Why Do Sellers Spend So Little of It Selling?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/)
- [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)

## Next move

Ask your two best sellers what they do in the first ten minutes of a discovery call with your most common buyer. Write it on one screen and attach it to that deal stage in the CRM.

# What Is a Knowledge Graph (for AI)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A knowledge graph represents information as entities, such as accounts, people and contracts, joined by named relationships. It lets an AI system answer questions that need connections across many documents, which plain vector search handles poorly. Microsoft's GraphRAG showed language models can build such graphs from text, but a graph is only as current as the facts written into it.

A knowledge graph stores information as entities, such as companies, people, products and contracts, connected by named relationships, such as "works at", "signed" or "replaced". For AI, it gives a model a map of how facts connect, so it can answer questions that need several hops across sources. Text search finds similar passages; a graph follows links. Graphs help most where relationships matter and least where nobody maintains them.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a knowledge graph means

A knowledge graph is a way of storing facts as a network. Each node is an entity, a thing with an identity. Each edge is a relationship with a name. For example, the sentence "a mid-size logistics client renewed its contract on 1 March" becomes a set of linked facts: the client, the contract, the renewal, the date, and the person who signed it.

The idea is older than the current AI wave. The W3C's Resource Description Framework (RDF) standardises the basic unit; its 1.1 version, a 2014 W3C Recommendation, states that an RDF triple consists of a subject, a predicate and an object, and that a graph is a set of triples. Google's Knowledge Graph, launched in May 2012, made the idea familiar to search users. Its launch post described a graph of more than 500 million objects and over 3.5 billion facts and relationships, designed to understand "real-world entities and their relationships to one another: things, not strings."

| Knowledge graph | Vector index | Relational database |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stores entities and named relationships | Stores embeddings of text chunks | Stores rows in fixed tables |
| Answers "how is A connected to B" | Answers "what text is similar to this" | Answers "which rows match these values" |
| Good for multi-step, relational questions | Good for finding relevant passages | Good for transactions and reporting |
| Needs a schema or extraction step | Needs an embedding model | Needs a fixed schema |

## How it works for AI

A language model can either query an existing graph, often fed by pipelines from systems such as a CRM, or build the graph itself from documents.

Microsoft Research's GraphRAG, announced in February 2024, is a widely cited example of the second approach. A language model reads a document collection, extracts entities and relationships into a graph, groups closely related entities into clusters and writes a summary of each cluster in advance. At question time, those summaries and graph links feed the model's context.

Microsoft's post set out the weakness of standard RAG it was designed to address. Its researchers found that vector-based retrieval "struggles to connect the dots" when an answer requires linking separate pieces of information, and performs poorly on questions about a whole dataset, such as "What are the top 5 themes in the data?" The accompanying paper by Edge and colleagues reported substantial improvements in the comprehensiveness and diversity of answers on such global questions, tested on datasets of around one million tokens.

## Why it matters for a commercial team, and when to use one

Commercial questions are often relational: which open deals depend on a partner whose contract ends this quarter, or which proposal superseded which. Text search struggles because the answer is not written in any single document.

| Use a knowledge graph when | Avoid one when |
| --- | --- |
| Questions follow relationships across records | Questions are answered by finding one passage |
| Entities are stable and well defined, such as accounts and contracts | Entities are vague or change meaning often |
| Someone owns keeping relationships current | Nobody will maintain it after the build |
| You need to explain why an answer was reached | A ranked list of documents is enough |

The common mistake is to treat a graph built once by a language model as a source of truth. Extraction makes errors, and a graph does not update itself when a contract is renewed or a contact changes role. A stale edge is worse than a missing one, because the model will follow it with confidence.

In **lowob**'s model, the most valuable graph on the commercial line is a small one: decisions linked to the accounts, owners and outcomes they concern, with each decision able to supersede an earlier one rather than overwrite it. That is the record stage of the enterprise brain. Rent the extraction tools if useful; own the record of what was decided.

## lowob takeaways

- **Graphs store connections.** Entities and named relationships let AI follow links that text search misses.
- **They complement vectors.** Use similarity search to find passages and a graph to answer how things relate.
- **Language models can build them.** GraphRAG shows the method, but extracted graphs need checking.
- **Maintenance decides value.** A graph without an owner goes stale and misleads.

## Common questions

### What is a knowledge graph in AI?

A structured store of facts in which entities are connected by named relationships. AI systems use it to answer questions that require following connections across many sources.

### What is the difference between a knowledge graph and a vector database?

A vector database finds text similar in meaning to a query. A knowledge graph stores explicit relationships between entities, so it can answer how things are connected.

### What is GraphRAG?

A Microsoft Research method in which a language model builds a knowledge graph from documents and uses it, with pre-written cluster summaries, to answer questions that standard RAG handles poorly.

### Do small companies need a knowledge graph?

Usually not a large one. A small graph linking decisions to accounts, owners and outcomes is often more useful than a broad graph of everything.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, Introducing the Knowledge Graph: things, not strings](https://blog.google/products/search/introducing-knowledge-graph-things-not/), 16 May 2012. Vendor announcement; figures are from launch.
- [W3C, RDF 1.1 Concepts and Abstract Syntax](https://w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/), 25 February 2014. Standards body Recommendation.
- [Microsoft Research blog, GraphRAG announcement](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/blog/graphrag-unlocking-llm-discovery-on-narrative-private-data/), 13 February 2024. Vendor research.
- [Edge et al., From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130v1), arXiv, April 2024. Microsoft-authored paper; results on the authors' own test sets.
- The decision graph and usage guidance are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)

## Next move

Write down five questions your team asks that need more than one record to answer, such as which deals depend on a single contact. If most of them involve relationships, sketch the entities and links a small graph would need.
