# Which AI Assistant, Which Seats

Source: https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The model is the fastest-changing and least sticky layer of the stack. Choose an assistant by suite fit, connector depth and open-standard support, administrative and data controls, and whether outputs and approvals can be logged. Buy seats for the people in the first workflow, not the whole company.

Most firms choose an AI assistant by comparing model benchmarks, then buy seats for everyone. Both choices are usually wrong. The model is the fastest-changing layer of the stack and the least sticky; what lasts is how well the assistant fits your suite, reaches your systems, respects your controls and records what it did. And seats bought ahead of a workflow go unused. Buy for the people in the first commercial workflow, and expand on evidence.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Choosing a business AI assistant has become a ritual of comparison tables and benchmark scores. A team reads which model leads this month's leaderboard, runs a few prompts, and signs for enough seats to cover the company. Three months later, weekly use has settled at a fraction of seats, and the leaderboard has changed.

The problem is not the choice of model. It is treating the model as the decision.

## The model is the least sticky layer

Every layer of the brain changes at a different speed. The suite (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) changes over years. The CRM changes over years. The record of decisions should outlive them both. The model underneath an assistant changes every few months.

The market already reflects this. Microsoft added Anthropic's Claude models to Microsoft 365 Copilot in 2026, and reporting on the paid Copilot tier described model choice as its standout addition. When the largest assistant vendor lets customers pick the model inside its product, the model has become a setting rather than a platform.

Spending data points the same way. Menlo Ventures' December 2025 survey of enterprise decision-makers put Anthropic at about 40% of enterprise large-language-model spend, OpenAI at 27% and Google at 21%; Menlo is an investor in Anthropic, and we note that. Card-spend data from Ramp, reported in mid-2026, showed Anthropic and OpenAI each paid for by roughly two-fifths of US businesses with AI subscriptions. Different methods, similar conclusion: buyers use more than one provider, and leadership shifts.

## What to compare instead

| Criterion | Question to ask | Why it lasts |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suite fit | How deeply does it read our email, files and meetings? | The suite changes slowly; native access beats bolt-ons |
| Connectors | Does it connect to our CRM and documents natively or through MCP servers? | Open-standard connectors survive a change of assistant |
| Admin and data controls | Can we set who sees what, control retention and exclude data from training? | Controls are what security review will test |
| Logging | Can we export what it was asked, what it saw and what it produced? | The gate in Part 8 depends on it |
| Agent support | Can it run multi-step tasks with tools and approval pauses? | Determines how far up the autonomy dial it can go |
| Model choice | Can we change the underlying model without changing the product? | Protects against leaderboard churn |

Vendor capabilities change quickly, so any comparison table is a snapshot. We would rather give buyers the questions than a ranking that will be wrong next quarter. Our guide *The pilot that survives security review* covers the controls in more depth.

### How the main options line up, in general terms

| Option | Natural fit | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot | Firms running on Microsoft 365, with data in SharePoint, Outlook and Teams | Paid add-on pricing per user; weekly use after rollout |
| Gemini for Google Workspace | Firms running on Google Workspace | Coverage of non-Google systems through connectors |
| ChatGPT (business tiers) | Teams wanting a general assistant across tools | Depth of connection into the suite of record |
| Claude (business tiers) | Teams doing long-form analysis, writing and agentic work with MCP connectors | Depth of connection into the suite of record |

None of these is the right answer for every firm, and several firms will reasonably run two: a suite-native assistant for everyday work and a second for heavier analysis or agent building. The test is whether each seat has a job.

## Fewer seats, more wiring

The adoption record argues for starting small. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of payers use it weekly, according to figures reported by Windows Latest in July 2026. Microsoft separately reported around 30 million paid seats. A large absolute number and a small share of the base: both are true, and both suggest that seats without a workflow drift.

The alternative is to buy for the commercial cohort only: the people in the first workflow chosen at Gateway 0. Wire the assistant into their email, calendar and CRM first (Part 5). Measure weekly active use and the workflow's own measure, such as hours of meeting preparation. Expand seat by seat where both move.

> Buy seats for a workflow, not for a headcount.

## The cost question

Seat prices are visible; the larger costs are not. Microsoft's pricing page listed Microsoft 365 Copilot Business at $21 per user per month on annual billing in November 2026, on top of an existing Microsoft 365 licence, and the other assistants publish similar business tiers. For a cohort of twenty people that is a modest line. The cost that matters is unused seats across a whole company, and the time spent rolling out an assistant nobody was asked to use for anything in particular. Our analysis *Seats, usage or outcomes* covers how AI vendors price, and why usage-based billing is spreading.

Illustrative example: right-sizing the seats

Decision
:   Cut assistant seats from company-wide to the 18 people in the commercial workflow, and wire those seats into email, calendar and CRM first.

Reason and owner
:   Weekly use across company-wide seats was low and flat; nobody had a defined task. Owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   Weekly use in the cohort is tracked alongside meeting preparation time; seats are added team by team where both improve.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Do not choose by leaderboard.** The model is the layer most likely to change next quarter.
- **Choose by fit, connectors, controls and logs.** These outlast any single model.
- **Expect to run more than one.** Many firms reasonably use a suite-native assistant plus one for heavier work.
- **Buy for a workflow.** Seats follow evidence, not headcount.

Gateway card

### Before you buy seats

- The first workflow and its cohort named
- Suite fit and connectors to CRM and documents confirmed
- Admin, retention and training-data controls checked
- Logging of prompts, sources and outputs available
- Weekly use and the workflow measure set up before rollout

## Common questions

### Which AI assistant is best for business?

It depends less on the model than on fit: the assistant that reads your suite natively, connects to your CRM and documents, meets your controls and logs its work is usually the right first choice. Many firms reasonably run two.

### Should we buy Microsoft 365 Copilot for everyone?

Usually not at first. Buy for the people in the first workflow, wire the assistant into their systems, and expand where weekly use and the workflow measure both improve.

### Can Microsoft Copilot use Claude models?

Yes. Microsoft added Anthropic's Claude models to Microsoft 365 Copilot in 2026, making the model a choice within the product.

### How should we compare ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot?

Compare suite fit, connector depth and MCP support, administrative and data controls, logging, agent support and model choice. Benchmark rankings change too often to anchor a purchase.

## Sources and notes

- [Microsoft, Microsoft 365 Copilot plans and pricing](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/microsoft-365-copilot/pricing), accessed November 2026. Vendor pricing page; US prices, promotional terms time-limited.
- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/), December 2025, as summarised by [AIgazine](https://aigazine.com/markets/anthropic-captures-40-of-enterprise-llm-market-as-ai-spending-hits-37-billion-in-2025--ms). Menlo invests in Anthropic.
- Ramp AI Index, June 2026, as reported by [FourWeekMBA](https://fourweekmba.com/anthropic-overtakes-openai-enterprise-adoption-ramp-ai-index/). Card-spend data from US businesses.
- [Windows Latest, 7 July 2026](https://www.windowslatest.com/2026/07/07/microsoft-365-copilot-adoption-is-under-4-5-after-3-years-only-1-use-it-weekly-yet-prices-went-up/), including Copilot pricing and model choice. Industry figures, not Microsoft filings.
- [UC Today on Microsoft's Q4 FY26 results](https://www.uctoday.com/unified-communications/microsoft-365-copilot-passes-30-million-paid-seats-as-cloud-and-ai-growth-power-record-quarter/), July 2026.
- The comparison criteria are **lowob**'s; vendor capabilities change frequently and should be checked at purchase.

- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)

- [The Model Is Not the Product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/)
- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)

## Next move

Count your assistant seats and your weekly active users. If the ratio is poor, the fix is rarely a different model; it is a defined workflow and a smaller cohort.

# What Is AI Orchestration?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-orchestration/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI orchestration is the coordination of models, tools, data and human steps so they run as one process. It ranges from fixed workflows, where code sets the path, to agents that choose their own steps. Vendor guidance is to start with the simplest pattern that works, because each added step trades cost and latency for capability.

AI orchestration is the coordination of AI models, tools, data sources and human steps so they work together as one process. It decides which model handles which step, what data each step sees, which tools can be called, and where a person approves. It ranges from fixed workflows, where code sets the path, to agents that decide their own next step. Most commercial processes are best served by the simpler end.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What AI orchestration means

A single model call answers a single prompt. Real business processes need more: fetch the account, check the contract, draft a reply, check the draft, route it for approval, log the outcome. Orchestration is the layer that strings those steps together and manages state between them.

IBM describes three parts. Integration links models to tools, databases and other systems through pipelines and APIs. Automation runs the steps with minimal manual input, such as a model calling a tool. Management oversees the lifecycle, including governance, security and compliance.

Anthropic's "Building effective agents", published in December 2024, gives the most useful distinction for buyers. In a workflow, models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. In an agent, the model directs its own process and tool use. Both are orchestration. The difference is who decides the next step: your code or the model.

| Orchestration is | Orchestration is not |
| --- | --- |
| The control flow across models, tools and people | A model or an agent in itself |
| Where approval steps and limits are enforced | A connector standard such as MCP |
| A choice between fixed paths and model-chosen paths | Automatically multi-agent |
| Where state, retries and logs are managed | The record of what was decided and why |

## How it works, and why it matters for a commercial team

Anthropic's five workflow patterns cover most commercial uses.

| Pattern | How it works | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Prompt chaining | Steps run in sequence, with checks between them | Extract call notes, then draft a follow-up, then check tone |
| Routing | Classify the input, then send it to a specialised step | Sort inbound email into sales, support or billing |
| Parallelisation | Run subtasks at once, or the same task several times and compare | Score a lead against five criteria in parallel |
| Orchestrator-workers | A central model splits a task and delegates parts | Assemble an RFP response from several source libraries |
| Evaluator-optimiser | One model drafts, another critiques, in a loop | Draft a proposal section, then check it against the brief |

The patterns sit beside two other layers that are often confused with orchestration. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardises how a model reaches tools and data. The Agent2Agent protocol standardises how agents from different vendors talk to each other. Orchestration decides when each of those is used and in what order.

The tooling ranges widely. IBM lists LangChain for building modular AI applications and Kubernetes for running them at scale. LangGraph, from the LangChain team, describes itself as a low-level orchestration framework and runtime for long-running, stateful agents. Its documented features include durable execution, so a process can resume after a failure, and human-in-the-loop controls. Its documentation names Klarna, Uber and J.P. Morgan as users, a vendor claim.

Anthropic adds a caution about frameworks: they speed up setup but can hide the underlying prompts and responses, which makes debugging harder. It suggests starting with direct API calls, since many patterns need only a few lines of code.

In **lowob**'s model, orchestration is where the operating rules become real. "Nothing sends without a person" is not a policy document; it is an approval step in the flow that the agent cannot route around. The orchestration layer should also write each decision, with its reason, owner and outcome, to a record the business owns.

## Where to start, and common mistakes

| Decision | Start here | Move on when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Workflow or agent | Fixed workflow with set steps | The path genuinely varies case by case |
| Number of models | One model, one or two calls | Evals show a step needs a specialist |
| Approval | A person approves every external action | Eval data supports a higher autonomy level |
| Framework | Direct API calls or the vendor's built-in tools | State, retries and resumption become hard to manage by hand |
| Logging | Every step, input and output | Never stop |

The common mistakes follow from skipping that order. Teams build a multi-agent system for a task a three-step chain would handle. They adopt a framework before they understand the prompts it sends. They put the approval step at the end of a long chain, so a reviewer sees only the final draft and none of the reasoning. Anthropic notes that agents' autonomy brings higher costs and the potential for compounding errors. Each extra step should earn its place on an eval, not on a diagram.

## lowob takeaways

- **Orchestration is control flow.** It decides which model, tool and person acts at each step.
- **Workflows before agents.** Fixed paths cost less and are easier to audit.
- **Approvals live in the flow.** A rule the agent can route around is not a control.
- **Log and record every step.** The orchestration layer is where the decision record is written.

## Common questions

### What is AI orchestration?

It is the coordination of AI models, tools, data and human steps into one process, managing the order of steps, the data each sees and where approvals happen.

### What is the difference between AI orchestration and an AI agent?

An agent is a model that chooses its own next steps. Orchestration is the wider control layer, which may run fixed workflows, agents or a mix of both.

### What is multi-agent orchestration?

It is a setup where a coordinating model or program splits work across several specialised agents and combines their results. Anthropic calls one version the orchestrator-workers pattern.

### Do I need a framework like LangGraph for AI orchestration?

Not to start. Anthropic suggests beginning with direct API calls. Frameworks help when processes run for a long time, need to resume after failures or need structured human review.

## Sources and notes

- [IBM, What is AI orchestration?](https://www.ibm.com/think/topics/ai-orchestration), accessed November 2026. Vendor explainer.
- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), 19 December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance; some tooling has since changed.
- [LangChain, LangGraph overview](https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/overview), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; customer names are vendor-reported.
- The approval-in-the-flow principle and the starting order are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production, by State Model and Cloud](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/)
- [What Is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/)
- [What Is the Agent2Agent (A2A) Protocol?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-agent2agent-protocol/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)

## Next move

Map one commercial process your team wants to automate as a list of steps. Mark which steps need a model, which need a tool and where a person must approve, before choosing any software.

# The Enterprise AI and Commercial System Glossary

Source: https://lowob.com/research/enterprise-ai-glossary/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A reference glossary of more than 110 terms across AI agents, the context layer, the decision record, governance and risk, pricing and the commercial system, written for business readers and linked to lowob research and explainers.

This glossary defines the terms used across The Build Order and the wider enterprise AI market in plain English. Each entry gives a working definition, notes where vendors use the word differently, and links to the research or explainer that goes deeper. Terms are grouped by layer of the brain: agents and reasoning, the wiring, the record, governance and risk, pricing, and the commercial system.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

## Agents and reasoning

### AI agent

A model working in a loop toward a goal: it chooses its next step, acts through tools, checks the result and repeats until it finishes or a limit stops it. See [What Is an AI Agent?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/).

### Agentic AI

AI systems that plan and take multi-step actions with tools rather than only answering questions. Used loosely in marketing. See [What Is Agentic AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agentic-ai/).

### Agent washing

Rebranding assistants, chatbots or automation as "agents" without real agentic capability. Gartner estimated in 2025 that only about 130 of thousands of vendors making agentic claims offered genuine capability. See [What Is Agent Washing?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/).

### AI copilot

An assistant embedded in a work tool that helps a person do a task; the person stays in control of each step. Compare with an agent, which chooses its own steps. See [AI Copilot vs AI Agent](https://lowob.com/research/ai-copilot-vs-ai-agent/).

### Autonomy level

How much an agent may do without a person, on **lowob**'s five-step scale: 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone. Most commercial value today sits at levels 1 to 3. See [What Is an AI Autonomy Level?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/).

### Agent loop

The repeated cycle of reason, act and observe that defines an agent. The loop is becoming a commodity; what differs is the context and limits around it. See [A loop with good context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/). See [What Is an Agent Loop?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-loop/).

### Reasoning layer

The layer of the brain where models and agents read across the wiring and the record and connect the dots. Rent the models; own the instructions and precedents. See [What Is a Reasoning Model?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-reasoning-model/).

### Time horizon

METR's measure of agent capability: the length of task, in human-expert time, an agent completes at a given success rate. Reported at 50% and 80% success; the gap between them matters. See [What Is an AI Agent's Time Horizon?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-time-horizon/).

### Agent framework

Software that runs agent loops, manages state and pauses for approval. See [Top 5 agent frameworks for production](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/). See [What Is an Agent Framework?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-agent-framework/).

### Pipeline clerk

**lowob**'s recommended first commercial agent: it keeps CRM records current, flags stale deals and drafts follow-ups into a queue, and never sends. See [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/).

### Large language model (LLM)

A model trained on large amounts of text to predict and generate language; the engine inside assistants and agents. See [What Is a Large Language Model?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-large-language-model/).

### Token

The unit of text a model reads and writes, roughly three-quarters of an English word. Most AI usage pricing is per token. See [What Is a Token in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-token-in-ai/).

### Context window

The amount of text a model can consider at once. Larger windows do not guarantee the model uses all of it well. See [What Is a Context Window?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-context-window/).

### Embeddings

Numerical representations of text that place similar meanings close together; the basis of vector search. See [What Are Embeddings?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-embeddings/).

### Fine-tuning

Further training a model on specific examples to change its behaviour. Usually less useful for business knowledge than better context. See [What Is Fine-Tuning?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-fine-tuning/).

### Hallucination

A confident output that is not supported by the model's sources or by fact. See [What Is AI Hallucination?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-hallucination/).

### Guardrails

Controls that constrain what an AI system may receive, produce or do. See [What Are AI Guardrails?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-guardrails/).

### Evals

Structured tests that measure an AI system's output quality against defined cases before and after changes. See [What Are AI Evals?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/).

### Orchestration

Coordinating models, tools, agents and steps into a working process. See [What Is AI Orchestration?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-orchestration/).

### Workflow automation

Software that runs a fixed sequence of steps. Better than an agent when the steps are stable. See [Workflow Automation vs AI Agents](https://lowob.com/research/workflow-automation-vs-ai-agents/).

### Robotic process automation (RPA)

Software that mimics a person clicking through applications to complete repetitive tasks. See [What Is RPA?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-robotic-process-automation/).

## The wiring (context layer)

### Context layer

The wiring that lets AI read a company's systems: connectors, permission-aware retrieval and shared definitions. Rent it rather than build it. See [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/).

### Context engineering

The practice of deciding what an agent sees before and during a task: which documents, data, definitions and precedents, in what form and order. See [What Is Context Engineering?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/).

### Model Context Protocol (MCP)

An open standard for connecting AI assistants and agents to tools and data, donated by Anthropic to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. See [What Is the Model Context Protocol?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/).

### Agent2Agent protocol (A2A)

An open protocol, originated by Google and hosted by the Linux Foundation, for agents built by different vendors to communicate. See [What Is the Agent2Agent Protocol?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-agent2agent-protocol/).

### Connector

An integration that makes one system (email, CRM, drive) readable or writable by an assistant or agent. See [What Is an AI Connector?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-connector/).

### Permission-aware retrieval

Search that returns only what the requesting person could already open. It inherits every bad permission in the underlying systems, so audit before connecting. See [What Is Permission-Aware Retrieval?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-permission-aware-retrieval/).

### Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

Retrieving relevant documents and supplying them to a model so its answer draws on company material. See [What Is RAG?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/).

### Vector database

A database that stores numerical representations of text so that similar content can be found by meaning. See [What Is a Vector Database?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-vector-database/).

### Knowledge graph

A structure that stores entities and their relationships explicitly. Stronger than vector search on aggregation and cross-document questions; costly to keep fresh. See [What Is a Knowledge Graph?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-knowledge-graph/).

### Semantic layer

Shared, written definitions of business terms so people and agents mean the same thing by "active client" or "qualified". See [What Is a Semantic Layer?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/).

## The record

### Enterprise brain

In **lowob**'s usage, the loop that connects what a company stores, records what it decided and why, reasons across both, and learns when outcomes come back. No single product is the brain. See [What Is an Enterprise Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-enterprise-brain/).

### Store

The systems where data sits: CRM, drive, inbox, ERP. Necessary for the brain, never sufficient. See [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/).

### Decision record

A structured entry for an important decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its status, the expected outcome and check date, and later the actual outcome. See [What Is a Decision Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/).

### Precedent slot

A reserved part of an agent's context holding three to five comparable past decisions, including at least one that went badly. See [A loop with good context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/). See [What Is Decision Precedent in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-decision-precedent-in-ai/).

### Outcome write-back

Recording an outcome against the decision that caused it, so the system can learn which reasoning worked. See [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/).

### Supersession

Marking an older decision or fact as replaced rather than deleting it, so history is preserved and current guidance is clear. See [Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/).

### Agent memory

Mechanisms that let an agent retain information across sessions. Independent tests often reproduce vendor memory scores much lower than claimed. See [What Is Agent Memory?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-memory/).

### System of record

The authoritative source for a type of data, such as the CRM for accounts and opportunities. See [What Is a System of Record?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/).

## Governance and risk

### Human-in-the-loop

A design in which a named person approves an agent's output before it takes effect, with the approval logged. See [What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/) and [Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/).

### Approval gate

The checkpoint where outbound work is approved, edited or returned. Gateway 1 in The Build Order. See [What Is an Approval Gate for AI Agents?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/).

### Prompt injection

Manipulating an AI system through crafted input, often hidden in content it reads. Ranked first in OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications. See [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/).

### Excessive agency

Giving an AI system more tools, permissions or autonomy than its task needs. Sixth in OWASP's 2025 list. See [What Is Excessive Agency?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/).

### Agent identity and registry

Treating each agent as its own account with its own permissions, listed in a register with its goal, tools, autonomy level and owner. See [What Is Agent Identity?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/).

### LLM observability

Tracing what models and agents saw and did, and evaluating output quality over time. See [What Is LLM Observability?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/).

### AI audit trail

A record that lets a firm reconstruct the chain of evidence, action, approval and outcome behind an automated decision. See [What Is an AI Audit Trail?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/).

### AI governance

The policies, roles and controls for using AI responsibly, often mapped to frameworks such as NIST's AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001. See [What Is AI Governance?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-governance/).

### Kill switch

A control that lets a named person stop every agent immediately. See [What Is an AI Kill Switch?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-kill-switch/).

### EU AI Act

The EU's risk-based AI law. Several high-risk obligations were deferred in 2026; check current dates before relying on any timeline. See [The EU AI Act for Commercial Teams](https://lowob.com/research/the-eu-ai-act-for-commercial-teams/).

### NIST AI Risk Management Framework

A voluntary US framework for managing AI risk, organised around govern, map, measure and manage. See [What Is the NIST AI RMF?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-nist-ai-risk-management-framework/).

### ISO/IEC 42001

An international standard for an AI management system that organisations can be certified against. See [What Is ISO/IEC 42001?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-iso-42001/).

### Model risk management

The discipline of validating, monitoring and governing models whose errors can cause loss, long established in banking. See [What Is Model Risk Management for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-model-risk-management/).

### Data residency

Where data is stored and processed geographically, often set by contract or regulation. See [What Is Data Residency for AI Tools?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-residency-for-ai/).

### Zero data retention

A vendor commitment not to store prompts and outputs beyond processing them. See [What Is Zero Data Retention?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/).

### SOC 2

An audit report on a service provider's security and related controls. Useful for AI vendors, and limited in what it says about model behaviour. See [SOC 2 for AI Vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/).

## Pricing

### Seat-based pricing

Charging per user per month, as most AI assistants do. See [Seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/). See [What Is Seat-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/).

### Usage-based pricing

Charging by consumption: tokens, tasks or credits. See [What Is Usage-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/).

### Outcome-based pricing

Charging for a measured result, such as a resolved support case. Works where outcomes can be counted. See [What Is Outcome-Based Pricing for AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/).

## The commercial system

### Commercial line

The sales, marketing and account-management work where a company wins and keeps revenue. The Build Order's starting point. See [Why the Brain Starts at the Commercial Line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/).

### Commercial operating system

The connected set of definitions, stages, tools, rituals and records a company uses to run its commercial line. See [What Is a Commercial Operating System?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-commercial-operating-system/).

### Revenue operations (RevOps)

The function that aligns sales, marketing and customer success processes, data and tools. See [What Is Revenue Operations?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/).

### CRM data hygiene

Keeping CRM records accurate, complete and de-duplicated. See [What Is CRM Data Hygiene?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/).

### Pipeline stage definitions

Written criteria for each stage of an opportunity, so stages mean the same thing to every seller and agent. See [What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/).

### Closed-lost reason

The recorded reason a deal was lost, chosen from a fixed list. The field most often left blank and the most useful for learning. See [What Is a Closed-Lost Reason?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/).

### Win-loss analysis

Systematic review of why deals are won or lost. See [What Is Win-Loss Analysis?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/).

### Lead source attribution

Recording where each opportunity came from, from a fixed list, so channels can be compared. See [What Is Lead Source Attribution?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/).

### Selling time

The share of a seller's time spent actually selling. Salesforce's 2026 survey put it at about 40%. See [What Is Selling Time?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/).

### Commercial system

The connected strategy, growth, distribution and revenue practices a company uses to win and keep business. See [The Commercial System](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/).

### Positioning

The choice of who a company is for, what it is compared with, and why it wins. In complex markets, positioning has to survive a buying committee. See [Positioning for Complex Markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/).

### Segment selection

Choosing which customer segments to pursue, using evidence on fit, value and ability to win. See [Segment Selection With Evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/).

### Pricing architecture

The structure of offers, price points, packaging and discount rules, separate from the price of any single deal. See [Pricing Architecture for Services Firms](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/).

### Market map

A structured view of segments, buyers, competitors and channels that sellers can act on. See [Market Maps That Sales Actually Uses](https://lowob.com/research/market-maps-that-sales-actually-uses/).

### Commercial operating rhythm

The fixed weekly, monthly and quarterly meetings and reviews where commercial decisions are made and recorded. See [The Commercial Operating Rhythm](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-operating-rhythm/).

### Commercial KPIs

The small set of measures leadership and the board use to judge commercial performance. See [Commercial KPIs a Board Will Trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/).

### Demand generation

Marketing that creates and captures buying interest, measured against pipeline and revenue rather than activity. See [Demand Generation Economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/).

### Campaign test

A campaign designed to answer one question with enough volume and time to reach a decision. See [Campaign Testing That Reaches a Decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/).

### Thought leadership

Published expertise that changes how buyers frame a problem, ideally in a form sellers can use in conversations. See [Thought Leadership That Sales Can Use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/).

### Brand measurement (B2B)

Ways of tracking whether more of the market knows and prefers a company, such as share of search and aided awareness. See [Measuring Brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/).

### Partner channel

Selling or delivering through other companies such as resellers, referral partners, platforms or integrators. See [Partner Channel Design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/).

### Referral partner

A company or person that introduces business in return for a fee or reciprocal benefit, without selling it. See [Referral Partners Without Leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/).

### Marketplace listing

A product or service listed in a platform marketplace, such as a cloud provider's, where customers can buy through existing contracts. See [Marketplace Listings for B2B Sellers](https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/).

### Co-selling

Selling jointly with a platform or partner's sales team on shared opportunities. See [Co-Selling With Platforms](https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/).

### Channel conflict

Competition between a company's own sellers and its partners, or between partners, for the same customer. See [Channel Conflict](https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/).

### Deal registration

A partner programme rule that gives the partner who registers an opportunity first protection or better terms. See [Channel Conflict](https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/). See [What Is Deal Registration?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-deal-registration/).

### Qualification framework

A shared checklist for deciding whether an opportunity is worth pursuing, such as BANT or MEDDICC. See [Qualification Frameworks Compared](https://lowob.com/research/qualification-frameworks-compared/).

### Discount governance

Rules for who may approve which discounts, with recorded reasons, so price exceptions do not erode margin. See [Discount Governance](https://lowob.com/research/discount-governance/).

### Proposal standard

A consistent structure and approval process for proposals, so they win more and teach the firm what works. See [Proposal Standards](https://lowob.com/research/proposal-standards/).

### Forecast category

A seller's judgment of a deal's likelihood (for example commit, best case, pipeline), separate from its stage. See [Forecasting That Holds](https://lowob.com/research/forecasting-that-holds/). See [What Is a Forecast Category?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-forecast-category/).

### Renewal and expansion

Keeping existing customers and growing what they buy; often the largest source of revenue growth. See [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/).

### Win-loss programme

A recurring process of interviewing buyers about won and lost deals and acting on the findings. See [Running a Win-Loss Programme](https://lowob.com/research/win-loss-programmes/).

### Sales capacity

How much revenue a sales team can realistically produce, given headcount, ramp time and productivity. See [Sales Capacity and Quota Setting](https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/).

### Quota

The revenue or bookings target assigned to a seller or team for a period. See [Sales Capacity and Quota Setting](https://lowob.com/research/sales-capacity-and-quota-setting/).

### Sales-to-delivery handover

The transfer of commitments, context and expectations from the people who sold the work to the people who deliver it. See [The Handover From Sales to Delivery](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/).

### Pricing experiment

A controlled change to price or packaging, run long enough to learn whether it changes win rates or margin. See [Pricing Experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/).

### Agent task directory

A reference rating sixty commercial tasks by the autonomy level an agent can safely be given today. See [What AI Agents Can Do](https://lowob.com/research/what-ai-agents-can-do-task-directory/). Walked function by function in [the Agents at Work series](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-sales-what-they-can-do-now/).

### Gateway

In The Build Order, a test that must be passed before the next layer is built. Gateway 0: owner, suite and CRM decided. Gateway 1: nothing sends without a person. Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision. Gateway 3: commercial ready to share its brain. See [The RFP Nobody Can Answer Yet](https://lowob.com/research/the-rfp-nobody-can-answer-yet/).

### TAM, SAM and SOM

Total, serviceable and obtainable market: three nested estimates of the revenue opportunity. See [What Are TAM, SAM and SOM?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-tam-sam-som/).

### CAC payback

The months it takes to recover the cost of acquiring a customer from that customer's gross margin. See [What Is CAC Payback?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/).

### Net revenue retention (NRR)

Revenue retained from existing customers over a period, including expansion and net of churn and contraction. See [What Is Net Revenue Retention?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/).

### Pipeline coverage

Open pipeline value divided by the target it must deliver. See [What Is Pipeline Coverage?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-pipeline-coverage/).

### Sales velocity

How quickly the pipeline turns into revenue, from deal count, value, win rate and cycle length. See [What Is Sales Velocity?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-velocity/).

### Deal desk

A function that reviews and approves non-standard deals, pricing and terms. See [What Is a Deal Desk?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-deal-desk/).

### MEDDICC

A qualification framework for complex sales: metrics, economic buyer, decision criteria, decision process, identify pain, champion and competition. See [What Is MEDDICC?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-meddicc/).

### BANT

An older qualification shorthand: budget, authority, need, timing. See [What Is BANT?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-bant/).

### Account planning

A structured plan for growing and protecting a priority account. See [What Is Account Planning?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-planning/).

### Intent data

Signals suggesting an organisation is researching a topic or category, of varying reliability. See [What Is Intent Data?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-intent-data/).

### Data enrichment

Adding third-party information to CRM records. See [What Is Data Enrichment?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-data-enrichment/).

### Sales forecasting

Predicting revenue for a period from pipeline and history. See [What Is Sales Forecasting?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-forecasting/).

### Customer health score

A composite measure of how likely a customer is to renew or expand. See [What Is Customer Health Scoring?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/).

### Partner programme

A structured way of recruiting, enabling and rewarding companies that sell or refer your services. See [What Is a Partner Program?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-partner-program/).

### Lead scoring

Ranking leads by likelihood to buy using fit and behaviour. See [What Is Lead Scoring?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-scoring/).

### Sales playbook

The documented plays a team runs in specific selling situations. See [What Is a Sales Playbook?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-playbook/).

## Common questions

### What is the difference between a context layer and an enterprise brain?

A context layer is the wiring that lets AI read a company's systems. An enterprise brain, in **lowob**'s usage, also includes a record of decisions and reasons, a reasoning layer and outcomes written back.

### What is the difference between an AI copilot and an AI agent?

A copilot helps a person with each step and leaves control with them. An agent chooses its own steps toward a goal within limits.

### What does MCP stand for in AI?

Model Context Protocol, an open standard for connecting AI assistants and agents to tools and data, now hosted by the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation.

### What is human-in-the-loop?

A design where a named person approves an AI system's output before it takes effect, with the approval recorded.

# Segment Selection With Evidence

Source: https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most firms choose segments by the size of the market and the size of the logos. The evidence for where to compete is usually already in the CRM: win rates, deal sizes, cycle lengths and retention by segment. This piece sets out a scoring method that combines them, a bottom-up check on whether the chosen segment is large enough, what to do with too little data, and how to record the choice and its disqualifiers so it can be graded.

Segment selection is the decision about which groups of buyers the firm pursues first, which it serves when they arrive, and which it declines. Most firms make it on market size and logo appeal. The better evidence is usually in the CRM already: win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention by segment, combined into a value per opportunity. Gartner's research on key accounts found that customers elevated mainly for their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time, a reminder that size is not the same as potential. Choose on evidence, check the chosen segment is large enough from the bottom up, and record the choice with its disqualifiers and a review date.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

Part 2 of this series argued that a position starts with a named buyer. This piece is about choosing that buyer from evidence. It is the most consequential decision in the Strategy part of the commercial system, because every later part inherits it: Growth targets the segment, Distribution chooses partners who reach it and Revenue qualifies against it.

A segment, here, is a group of potential buyers who share the characteristics that change how they buy: sector, size, situation, the problem they have and the route by which they purchase. A segment is narrower than a market and broader than an ideal customer profile. The profile describes the best accounts inside the chosen segment ([How to write an ICP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)).

## Why most segment choices are made on size

The usual process starts with a market report, a total addressable market figure and a slide showing the firm's share of it. That process answers a real question, whether the segment is big enough to matter, but it is the second question, not the first.

Wing VC's guide to market sizing describes top-down sizing as starting from public industry data and narrowing with filters, and notes that industry sources are not always available or current in fast-moving markets. For emerging technology firms that caveat is often decisive. The category may not exist in any report yet.

The bias toward size also distorts account choice. Gartner research reported in 2021 found that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of their large spend were 51% less likely to increase that spend over time, and that 58% of B2B sales organisations missed key-account quota. Large is attractive. It is not evidence of fit.

| Question | Top-down sizing answers it | Win-loss and CRM evidence answers it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Does the segment exist and is it large? | Yes | Partly |
| Can we win there? | No | Yes |
| How fast do deals close? | No | Yes |
| Do customers stay and expand? | No | Yes |
| Can we reach buyers through channels we have? | No | Partly |

## The evidence the firm already holds

Most firms with 20 or more customers can rank segments from their own records. Four numbers do most of the work.

**Win rate by segment.** Closed-won divided by closed-won plus closed-lost, including no-decision losses, over the last four to eight quarters.

**Deal size.** First-year contract value, using realised price after discounts.

**Cycle length.** Days from qualified opportunity to close. Ebsta's 2024 benchmarks, drawn from 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies, found that win rates fell 67% when deals slipped, especially beyond eight weeks. Long cycles carry a hidden cost beyond time.

**Retention.** Gross and net revenue retention for the segment's customers. SaaS Capital's 2025 benchmarks found net retention rises with contract value, with a median of 102% for contracts of $25,000 to $50,000. Growth Unhinged's 2025 survey of more than 800 software firms found companies with high net retention and short CAC payback grew at 71% on average, against 10% for those weak on both.

Ebsta's analysis adds one behavioural finding: top performers prioritise the accounts and personas they have closed before. The best sellers already select segments from evidence. The firm's job is to make that selection explicit.

## Scoring segments: a worked method

Combine the four numbers into a single figure: expected value per opportunity-month. It rewards segments that win often, pay well, close quickly and stay.

Expected value per opportunity-month = win rate × first-year value × gross retention ÷ cycle length in months.

| Segment (illustrative) | Win rate | First-year value | Gross retention | Cycle (months) | Value per opportunity-month |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A: mid-size operators with a regulatory trigger | 30% | $40,000 | 90% | 4 | $2,700 |
| B: large enterprises, central IT buyer | 18% | $90,000 | 85% | 9 | $1,530 |
| C: small firms, founder buyer | 40% | $15,000 | 70% | 2 | $2,100 |

Segment B has the largest deals and would lead most board slides. On evidence, A is the better first choice: each month a seller spends on an A opportunity is worth almost twice a month on a B opportunity. Segment C wins most often but churns.

Two adjustments keep the score honest. First, add cost to serve where it differs materially: onboarding effort, support load or required customisation. Second, add a reach factor. A segment the firm cannot reach through channels it already has will need investment in Distribution before the score is realised. Ebsta found partnership channels returned 3.8 times the velocity, yet only 8% of businesses had one.

> The largest deals are rarely the best segment. The best segment is where a seller's month is worth most.

## Sizing what you chose, from the bottom up

Once a segment ranks well, check it is large enough. Bottom-up sizing starts from the firm's own numbers rather than an industry total. Wing VC's guide describes it as average price multiplied by the number of buyers, and notes it needs some sales history to work.

A worked check for segment A:

| Step | Figure (illustrative) | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts meeting the segment filters | 1,200 | Company registry or data provider, filtered |
| Share showing the trigger in a year | 25%, or 300 accounts | Trigger tracking, past deal history |
| Accounts the team can engage in a year | 100 | Seller capacity and channel reach |
| Win rate | 30% | CRM |
| New customers per year | 30 | 100 × 30% |
| New first-year value | $1.2m | 30 × $40,000 |

If $1.2m of new business a year meets the plan, the segment is sufficient. If not, the constraint is visible: more capacity, a channel that widens reach, or a second segment. The calculation also names the assumption most worth testing, here the 25% trigger rate.

## When there is not enough data

Firms with fewer than ten customers cannot rank segments statistically. That is normal for early emerging technology firms, and the answer is not to choose on size by default. It is to treat the choice as a hypothesis with a test that could disprove it ([First customers in a market that doesn't exist yet](https://lowob.com/research/first-customers-in-a-market-that-doesnt-exist-yet/)).

A useful test has a fixed budget, a fixed period and a pre-agreed result that would change the decision. Our piece on testing sets out how to design one ([Tests that close questions](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/)).

| Evidence available | What to do |
| --- | --- |
| Fewer than 10 customers | Choose one segment as a hypothesis; run 20 to 30 qualified conversations; record why each did or did not progress |
| 10 to 30 customers | Rank segments on win rate and cycle length; treat retention as provisional |
| More than 30 customers with a year of history | Use the full score, with cost to serve and reach |
| Any size, entering a new segment | Score it on comparable segments and set an earlier review date |

Forrester's 2023 analysis found that clients who brought three or more buying-group members into the sales process saw a 50% increase in meeting-to-close conversion. For a segment test, that suggests a practical rule: count a conversation as evidence only if it reached more than one role.

## Record the choice and the disqualifiers

A segment choice is a strategic decision and belongs in the decision record: the segments chosen, the segments declined, the score and the assumptions behind it, the owner, the expected win rate and cycle length, and a review date ([The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

The declined segments matter as much as the chosen one. Disqualifiers stop sellers spending months on deals that will not close or will churn. When a declined-segment deal does arrive, the record makes the exception visible: someone can still take it, but on the record, with a reason. Over a year, those exceptions become evidence for the next review.

This is where segment selection meets The Build Order. Agents that score inbound leads, draft outreach or prepare account briefs need the segment definition and disqualifiers as rules they can read. A brain that has them qualifies consistently. One that does not reproduces each seller's private judgment.

Illustrative example: choosing the smaller deals

Decision
:   Make mid-size operators with a regulatory trigger the primary segment for the next two quarters, and stop outbound to large enterprises with a central IT buyer.

Reason and owner
:   Segment scoring on six quarters of CRM data showed almost twice the value per opportunity-month, driven by a shorter cycle and higher win rate. Owned by the commercial lead; agreed by the founders.

What changed
:   Outbound lists, partner briefs and qualification criteria were rewritten; enterprise deals that arrive inbound are taken as recorded exceptions; the review is set for two quarters out.

Illustrative: a composite of an 80-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Size tells you a segment exists, not that you can win it.** Rank on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention.
- **Score value per seller-month.** It exposes segments with large deals that consume the team.
- **Size from the bottom up.** Accounts, triggers, capacity and win rate show whether the segment is big enough and which assumption to test.
- **Record what you decline.** Disqualifiers and recorded exceptions are the evidence for the next review.

Gateway card

### Before you commit to a segment

- Win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention calculated per segment
- Cost to serve and reach noted where they differ materially
- A bottom-up check showing the segment meets the plan
- The weakest assumption named, with a way to test it
- Declined segments and disqualifiers written down
- The choice recorded with an owner and a review date

## Common questions

### How do you choose a target market segment in B2B?

Rank candidate segments on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention from your own CRM, then check the best-ranked segment is large enough using bottom-up sizing.

### What is the difference between a segment and an ideal customer profile?

A segment is a group of buyers who share characteristics that change how they buy. An ideal customer profile describes the best accounts within the chosen segment, including disqualifiers.

### Is top-down or bottom-up market sizing better?

They answer different questions. Top-down shows whether a market is large; bottom-up, built from your own prices and win rates, shows what you can realistically capture.

### How do you choose a segment with very few customers?

Treat it as a hypothesis. Pick one segment, run a fixed number of qualified conversations within a set period, and agree in advance what result would change the decision.

# Ad Network vs Ad Exchange vs DSP: The Middlemen

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ad-network-vs-exchange-vs-dsp/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ad networks bundle and resell publisher inventory with little visibility, ad exchanges run real-time auctions, and DSPs are the software buyers use to bid. The DSP is where control lives. Audits by ISBA, PwC and the ANA show how much of a dollar each layer absorbs, and IAB Tech Lab standards show how to check who is selling.

Ad networks bundle and resell publisher inventory with little visibility, ad exchanges run real-time auctions, and demand-side platforms (DSPs) are the software buyers use to bid. The DSP is where control lives. Audits show what is at stake: ISBA and PwC found UK publishers received 51% of advertiser spend in 2020, and the ANA found 29% of each US programmatic dollar went to transaction costs in 2023. Buyers should know which intermediary they are paying, what it charges and what it lets them see.

Between a company's media budget and the page where its ad appears sit several intermediaries with overlapping names. Three of them account for most of the confusion: ad networks, ad exchanges and demand-side platforms. Knowing which one you are dealing with tells you what you are paying for and what you can control. Our [plain-English guide to programmatic](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-programmatic-advertising/) covers the auction itself; this piece is about the companies in it.

## Ad networks

An ad network aggregates inventory from many publishers, packages it and sells it to advertisers. The network buys or represents the publishers' ad space, often at a negotiated rate, and resells it, usually as bundles by category, audience or format. The advertiser deals with the network's sales team or interface; the network decides where the ads run within the bundle.

Networks are the oldest model and the simplest to buy from. Their weakness is opacity: the advertiser rarely sees exactly which sites ran the ads, at what cost to the network, or how much of the budget reached the publisher. The network's margin is the difference between what it charges and what it pays, and the advertiser does not see it. The ANA's 2023 study told advertisers to establish whether their agency was buying media as their agent or selling them inventory as a principal, because the incentives differ. A network is usually the second kind: it sells inventory it controls, at a price it sets.

Networks still matter, particularly in specialised verticals and in regions and categories the large platforms do not serve well, including some restricted categories that vertical networks were built to carry.

## Ad exchanges

An ad exchange is a marketplace where ad impressions are auctioned in real time. Publishers, usually through a supply-side platform (SSP), offer impressions to the exchange; buyers, through DSPs, bid on them. The exchange runs the auction and takes a fee, typically a percentage of the winning bid.

Advertisers do not usually deal with an exchange directly. They reach it through a DSP. The exchange is infrastructure, and the practical questions about it are which exchanges a DSP is connected to, what fees each charges, and how well each polices fraud and low-quality inventory. The same impression is often offered through several exchanges at once, so a buyer can end up bidding against itself for one person's attention through different routes. Reducing those duplicate routes is what the industry calls supply path optimisation.

## Demand-side platforms

A DSP is the software an advertiser or its agency uses to buy programmatically: to define audiences, set budgets and bid rules, upload creative, connect to exchanges, apply verification and report. The DSP charges a platform fee, typically a percentage of media spent through it, plus fees for data and verification features.

The DSP is where control lives. Inclusion lists, verification standards, frequency caps and optimisation goals are set here. A buyer who does not set them accepts the DSP's defaults, and the defaults favour volume. The ANA found the average campaign in its study ran across more than 40,000 websites, and recommended that advertisers negotiate access to log-level data so they could see where the money went.

|  | Ad network | Ad exchange | DSP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it does | Packages and resells publisher inventory | Runs real-time auctions between sellers and buyers | Lets a buyer bid, target, verify and report across exchanges |
| Who uses it | Advertiser buys from it | Reached through SSPs and DSPs | Advertiser or agency operates it |
| How it is paid | Margin between buy and sell price | Fee on the winning bid | Percentage of media, plus data and feature fees |
| What the buyer sees | Usually a bundle, often without site-level detail | Little, directly | Placements, bids and costs, if the contract allows log-level data |
| Where control sits | With the network | With the auction rules | With whoever sets the DSP's settings |

## The money, end to end

An advertiser's dollar spent programmatically passes through the DSP fee, data fees, verification fees, the exchange fee, the SSP fee and, if there is one, an agency fee, before reaching the publisher. ISBA and PwC's 2020 UK study matched impressions end to end for 15 advertisers and 12 publishers and found publishers received 51% of advertiser spend on average. A further 15%, roughly a third of all supply chain costs, could not be attributed to any party. ISBA called it the "unknown delta".

The picture has improved where buyers have pushed. The second ISBA and PwC study, on data from late 2022, found the publisher share had risen to 65% and the unknown delta had fallen to 3%, with 58% of impressions matched. The ANA's 2023 US study, of 21 advertisers, put transaction costs at about 29% of each dollar entering a DSP. Each intermediary is providing a service. The question for a buyer is whether it knows what each one charged.

> If a partner cannot show you the placements, the fees and the rejection rate, you do not yet know which kind of middleman you are paying.

## How to check who is selling

IAB Tech Lab has published three standards that make the chain visible. Publishers post an ads.txt file listing who is authorised to sell their inventory. In April 2019 the Tech Lab released sellers.json, published by ad systems to identify the sellers they represent, and the SupplyChain object, which travels inside the OpenRTB bid request and lists every party that touched the sale. A buyer can use the three together to see whether the seller of an impression was authorised and how many resellers stood between the buyer and the publisher.

Most DSPs can filter on these signals. Asking for it is cheap. A buy restricted to impressions sold directly by the publisher, or through one authorised reseller, removes much of the inventory where fees stack up and nobody can say who took what.

## Which one you are dealing with

| What you see | What you are dealing with | The question to ask |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A salesperson sells a bundle of sites and you never see the auction | A network | Which sites ran the ads, and what did the network pay for them? |
| You or your desk operate software that bids on impressions across many sources | A DSP, with exchanges behind it | What are the fees per layer, and do we get log-level data? |
| A partner "has access to premium inventory" but cannot show placements, fees or rejections | Unknown | Find out before the next invoice |

Networks bundle and resell inventory opaquely; exchanges run the auctions; DSPs are the software buyers use to bid, and where control lives. Know which one you are paying, what it charges, and what it lets you see. The same logic applies to how the desk itself is paid: our piece on [percentage-of-spend media fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) explains why a fee tied to volume works against rejection. For a wider view of how intermediary costs sit inside acquisition economics, see [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) and the board-level discipline in [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the middleman.** Network, exchange and DSP are paid differently and show you different things.
- **Control lives in the DSP.** Set inclusion lists, verification, caps and goals, or accept defaults that favour volume.
- **Ask for the fee per layer.** Audits have traced between 3% and 15% of spend to nobody, depending on how hard buyers pushed.
- **Use the supply chain standards.** ads.txt, sellers.json and the SupplyChain object show who sold each impression.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an ad network, an ad exchange and a DSP?

An ad network packages and resells inventory from many publishers. An ad exchange is a marketplace that auctions impressions in real time. A DSP is the software an advertiser uses to bid, set budgets, apply verification and report.

### How much of programmatic ad spend reaches the publisher?

ISBA and PwC found UK publishers received 51% of advertiser spend in 2020 and 65% in their 2023 follow-up. The ANA found about 29% of each US programmatic dollar went to transaction costs.

### How do I tell if my ad partner is a network or a DSP?

If someone sells you a bundle of sites and you never see the auction, it is a network. If you operate software that bids on impressions across many sources, it is a DSP with exchanges behind it.

### What is sellers.json?

A file published by ad systems listing the sellers they represent. Used with publishers' ads.txt files and the SupplyChain object, it lets a buyer see whether each seller of an impression was authorised.

## Sources and notes

- [News Media Association, ISBA programmatic study: publishers receive half of advertiser spend](https://newsmediauk.org/blog/2020/05/07/isba-programmatic-study-publishers-receive-half-of-advertiser-spend/), 7 May 2020. Trade body summary; 15 advertisers, 12 publishers, UK only.
- [ISBA and PwC, Programmatic supply chain study II (summary)](https://www.isba.org.uk/system/files/media/documents/2023-01/ISBA%20%20PwC%20programmatic%20supply%20chain%20study%20II%20%28summary%29-%2018%20January%202023.pdf), January 2023. UK; two months of 2022 data; 58% of impressions matched.

Take last month's programmatic invoice and list every layer between your budget and the publisher: DSP, data, verification, exchange, SSP, agency. Ask your partner to fill in the fee for each. Any blank is the next conversation.

# What Are AI Guardrails?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-guardrails/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI guardrails are controls placed around a language model to check what goes in, what comes out and what actions it takes. Products from AWS, NVIDIA and others offer content filters, topic blocks, data masking and grounding checks. Filters catch some failures; the controls that matter most for a commercial team are narrow permissions and human approval before anything sends.

AI guardrails are controls placed around a language model that check its inputs, its outputs and the actions it takes against a set of rules. They can block harmful content, keep an assistant on topic, mask personal data, flag answers not supported by sources and limit which tools an agent may call. Guardrails reduce risk but do not remove it. The strongest ones are design choices: narrow permissions and a person approving anything that leaves the company.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What AI guardrails mean

A model's own training includes some refusals and safety behaviour. Guardrails are separate. They are software checks that sit in front of, behind or alongside the model and apply rules the business sets.

NVIDIA's NeMo Guardrails documentation gives a useful map of where checks can sit. Input rails check and clean user messages before they reach the model. Retrieval rails screen retrieved material so only trusted context is passed in. Dialog rails keep multi-turn conversations on track. Execution rails govern tool and function calls, including their inputs and outputs. Output rails review replies and can filter, rewrite or block them.

Amazon Bedrock Guardrails describes the checks by type rather than position. Content filters cover categories such as hate, violence, misconduct and prompt attacks. Denied topics block subjects you define. Word filters block specific terms. Sensitive information filters block or mask personal data. Contextual grounding checks flag responses not supported by the source material. Automated reasoning checks validate responses against logical rules.

| Guardrails are | Guardrails are not |
| --- | --- |
| Rules applied to inputs, outputs and actions | A guarantee of safe or correct output |
| Configurable by the business, per use case | The same as the model's built-in safety training |
| A layer you can test and log | A substitute for narrow permissions |
| Useful against known failure types | Reliable against every new attack |

## Why guardrails matter for a commercial team

The risks are now catalogued. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications lists, in order: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation and unbounded consumption. Most map to a guardrail type. Input rails address injection. Sensitive information filters address disclosure. Grounding checks address misinformation.

For a revenue team the practical failures are specific. A support assistant quotes a discount it was never authorised to offer. A proposal assistant pastes one client's details into another's draft. An inbound email contains hidden instructions that tell an agent to forward the pipeline report. A content filter does little about the first two. An execution rail and a permission model do.

NIST's July 2024 generative AI profile treats guardrails as something to maintain, not install once. Its suggested actions include regularly reviewing security and safety guardrails, especially when a system is used in new circumstances, and regularly evaluating vulnerabilities to circumvention of safety measures. It also recommends AI red-teaming.

In **lowob**'s view, filters are the outer layer. The inner layer is the autonomy dial: answer, draft, act with approval, act and report, act alone. A guardrail that blocks bad output after the fact is useful. An agent that can only draft, never send, does not need the guardrail to be perfect.

## Where to start with guardrails

| Layer | What it checks | Commercial example | Typical product category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Permissions | What the agent can reach and do | Read-only CRM access; draft-only email | Identity and access management |
| Input | Messages and documents before the model | Strip hidden instructions from inbound email | Prompt attack filters |
| Retrieval | Which sources may be used | Only approved case studies and current price list | Retrieval rails, access-controlled stores |
| Execution | Tool calls and their arguments | Block any "send" or "delete" call | Execution rails, tool allow-lists |
| Output | The reply before a person sees it | Mask personal data; flag ungrounded claims | Content filters, grounding checks |
| Human approval | The final decision to send | Named reviewer for every client-facing message | Workflow approval step |

Start from the inside. Scope permissions first, because they limit damage whatever the model does. Add an approval step for anything client-facing. Then add filters for the failures you have actually seen in testing, not every category a product offers.

The common mistakes are relying on the model's own refusals, switching on a vendor's default filters without testing them on real traffic, and running guardrails without logging what they blocked. AWS's documentation recommends benchmarking configurations with its built-in test tools. A guardrail with no record of what it caught cannot be tuned or audited.

## lowob takeaways

- **Guardrails are checks around the model.** They screen inputs, outputs and actions against your rules.
- **Permissions come first.** An agent that cannot send does not rely on a perfect filter.
- **Test on real traffic.** Default settings rarely match your failure cases.
- **Log what they catch.** Unlogged guardrails cannot be tuned or audited.

## Common questions

### What are guardrails in AI?

They are controls around a language model that check inputs, outputs and tool actions against rules, for example blocking a topic, masking personal data or stopping an unapproved action.

### What is the difference between AI guardrails and AI governance?

Governance sets policy, ownership and accountability for AI use. Guardrails are the technical controls that enforce parts of that policy in a running system.

### Can guardrails stop prompt injection?

They can catch some attempts, but not all. OWASP ranks prompt injection as the top LLM risk. Narrow permissions and human approval limit the damage when a filter misses.

### What tools provide AI guardrails?

Options include cloud services such as Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, open-source libraries such as NVIDIA NeMo Guardrails, and checks built into AI platforms and agent frameworks.

## Sources and notes

- [NVIDIA, NeMo Guardrails: rail types](https://docs.nvidia.com/nemo/guardrails/about-nemo-guardrails-library/rail-types.md), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation for an open-source library.
- [AWS, Detect and filter harmful content by using Amazon Bedrock Guardrails](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails.html), accessed November 2026. Vendor documentation; no published catch rates.
- [OWASP, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025](https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/), November 2024. Community security project.
- [NIST, AI 600-1: Generative Artificial Intelligence Profile](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ai/NIST.AI.600-1.pdf), July 2024. US standards body guidance.
- The autonomy dial and inside-out ordering are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is Prompt Injection?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/)
- [What Is Excessive Agency in AI?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-excessive-agency/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [Top 5 AI Governance and Audit-Trail Tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/)
- [SR 26-2 vs SR 11-7: What Changed in US Model Risk Guidance](https://lowob.com/research/sr-26-2-vs-sr-11-7/)

## Next move

List the tools each AI assistant or agent in your team can call. Remove any send, delete or bulk-update action that does not have a named person approving it.
