# Founder-Led GTM Is Not a Vibe. It Is a Job With an Expiration Date.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/founder-led-gtm-expiration-date/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Founder-led go-to-market is a phase, not an identity. Its purpose is to discover and encode a commercial motion that other people can operate. This playbook sets out what the founder should keep and hand off, a dependency test, a debrief that captures the founder's invisible decisions, and three stages from explorer to executive sponsor.

"Founder-led GTM" is often used as flattering shorthand for an early-stage company with a charismatic founder and no repeatable sales process. At the beginning, that can work. But founder-led GTM is a phase, not an identity. Its purpose is to discover and encode a commercial motion that other people can eventually operate. The research on startup sales and founder succession points the same way: the skills that find the first customers are not the skills that scale the sale, and the transfer fails when the founder's judgment was never written down.

"Founder-led GTM" is often used as flattering shorthand for an early-stage company with a charismatic founder and no repeatable sales process.

At the beginning, that can work.

The founder carries context nobody else has. They can change the product during a customer conversation, explain an emerging category, recruit early believers and make commitments across product, partnerships and capital. Buyers may take the meeting because the founder's conviction transfers trust.

But founder-led GTM is a phase, not an identity. Its purpose is to discover and encode a commercial motion that other people can eventually operate. Our guide [What go-to-market means](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/) describes the four answers that phase is meant to find.

## What the founder keeps and what they hand off

Early in a market, the founder should personally own a short list of things. Delegating those activities too early separates the company from its most important source of learning. Other work should leave the founder's desk as soon as it can be done to a standard.

| The founder keeps | The founder hands off |
| --- | --- |
| Category and company narrative | Scheduling and meeting preparation |
| Conversations with the most important early customers | Routine research |
| Discovery of the real buying trigger | CRM hygiene |
| High-consequence partnerships | Standard follow-up |
| Product trade-offs exposed by the market | Repeated product explanations |
| Recruitment of initial champions | Qualification that can be expressed as criteria |
| Definition of what the company will not become | Every social post; every relationship after it becomes operational |

The dividing line is not importance. It is whether the task depends on founder-specific judgment or can be performed through a standard with appropriate oversight.

The research on early sales supports keeping the learning with the founder until it is understood. Mark Leslie and Charles Holloway of Stanford Graduate School of Business, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2006, argued that startups often hire and launch a sales force before they understand their market, overstaff sales and set unrealistic targets. They proposed a "sales learning curve": a period after product development in which the company learns how customers will buy and use the product. Leslie's summary of the trade-off was that "the time to break even will be a little further out, but the cash to break even will be much less." They recommended a small group of salespeople working directly with customers and product developers, people "comfortable with ambiguity", before scaling.

## The founder-dependency test

Five questions show how much of the motion still lives in one person. Score each yes or no.

| Question | A "no" means |
| --- | --- |
| Can another person explain the company clearly without the founder present? | The narrative has not left the founder's voice |
| Can the team identify a qualified opportunity using shared criteria? | Qualification is intuition, not a rule |
| Do customer insights enter a common system, or remain in the founder's memory? | The company forgets what the founder learns |
| Can a deal advance one stage without founder intervention? | The sales path has no stages anyone else can run |
| Do important relationships belong to the company or only to the founder? | Key accounts and partners leave if the founder steps back |

If the answer to most is no, the company has not yet converted founder activity into organisational capability.

The first question has a measurable symptom outside the company. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. When the narrative lives only in the founder, every other surface drifts from it.

> The goal is not to remove the founder from the market. It is to stop requiring the founder for every instance of the motion.

## Write down the invisible decisions

The hardest part of replacing founder involvement is not documenting the obvious steps. It is surfacing the decisions the founder makes intuitively.

Why did one introduction receive an immediate response while another waited? Why was a promising prospect disqualified? Why did the founder change the pitch halfway through a call? Which objection signals interest, and which signals fundamental misalignment?

This is what Ikujiro Nonaka, in "The Knowledge-Creating Company" (*Harvard Business Review*, 1991), called tacit knowledge: "highly personal," "hard to formalize and, therefore, difficult to communicate to others." He quoted Michael Polanyi: "We can know more than we can tell." Nonaka's term for the critical step is articulation, "converting tacit knowledge into explicit knowledge." His best-known example is a product team that learned to make bread by training with a hotel's head baker, then turned the baker's kneading technique into machine specifications. A founder's sales judgment needs the same treatment: someone has to watch it, ask about it and write it down.

After important conversations, record a short decision debrief:

1. What did we believe before the call?
2. What changed?
3. Which signal mattered most?
4. What did the buyer not believe?
5. Why is the next step appropriate?
6. What should another team member learn from this?

Over time, these debriefs become qualification rules, messaging guidance, call preparation standards and escalation criteria. Each one is a small [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/): dated, with a reason and an owner, so the pattern can be checked later. Our piece [Two people: the founders' ledger](https://lowob.com/research/two-people-the-founders-ledger/) covers how to keep them at the earliest stage.

## Move through three stages

Companies move out of founder-led GTM in three stages, and the middle one is the one most often skipped.

| Stage | Founder's role | Evidence it is time to move on | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Founder as explorer | High-frequency market conversations; changes the thesis quickly | The same profile and triggers keep appearing | Staying here because it feels productive |
| 2. Founder as architect | Works with a commercial operator to turn patterns into a defined process, shared materials and measurable stages | A deal can advance a stage without the founder | Skipped entirely |
| 3. Founder as executive sponsor | Enters selectively: category-defining conversations, major accounts, partnerships, moments where authority changes the outcome | The team owns the motion and the number | Founder becomes absent, not selective |

Companies often try to jump from explorer to absent executive. That produces a premature hire expected to reproduce intuition that was never transferred. The missing stage is architecture. For the marketing side of the same transition, [From founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) sets out which decisions transfer in which order, and [What is a sales playbook?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-playbook/) covers the document stage two should produce.

The stakes are personal as well as commercial. Noam Wasserman of Harvard Business School studied more than 200 US startups for "The Founder's Dilemma" (*HBR*, 2008) and found that by about year three, half of founders were no longer CEO. His earlier research explained the timing: once the product is built, the company must sell it, which means building a sales organisation and managing more functions, and many founders lack those skills. Outside investors often make a new CEO a condition of new capital. The architect stage is how a founder builds the capability without being replaced by it.

## Know when the phase is ending

Founder-led GTM is ready to evolve when several conditions are present:

- The same customer profile repeatedly advances.
- The same buying triggers appear.
- The narrative survives outside the founder's voice.
- The sales path contains recognisable stages.
- Objections can be anticipated.
- Proof can be packaged.
- Enough qualified volume exists for specialisation.

The goal is not to remove the founder from the market. It is to stop requiring the founder for every instance of the motion.

Founder-led GTM succeeds when it converts proximity, judgment and relationships into a commercial system the company can own.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat it as a phase.** Founder-led GTM exists to discover and encode a motion others can run.
- **Split by judgment, not importance.** Keep what needs founder-specific judgment; hand off what can be done to a standard.
- **Debrief the important calls.** Six questions turn tacit decisions into qualification rules and messaging guidance.
- **Do not skip the architect stage.** Jumping from explorer to absent executive leaves a hire to reproduce intuition nobody transferred.

## Common questions

### What is founder-led sales?

Founder-led sales is the early phase in which the founder runs the main customer conversations personally. Its purpose is to discover who buys, why and how, well enough that other people can operate the motion.

### When should a founder hire their first salesperson?

When the same customer profile and triggers keep appearing, the narrative works without the founder, the sales path has recognisable stages and there is enough qualified volume to specialise. Hiring before that asks the hire to reproduce intuition nobody wrote down.

### Why do first sales hires fail at startups?

Often because the company skipped the stage of turning the founder's patterns into a defined process. Stanford research on the sales learning curve found startups typically overstaff sales before they understand how customers buy.

### How does a founder transfer sales knowledge to the team?

Record a short debrief after important calls: what you believed, what changed, which signal mattered, what the buyer did not believe, why the next step fits and what others should learn. Over time these become rules.

# What Are Pipeline Stage Definitions?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pipeline stage definitions set out, in writing, what must be true for a deal to sit in each stage of the sales pipeline. Without them, stage names mean different things to different sellers, and forecasts built on stage probabilities drift. This explainer covers what good definitions contain, how CRMs support them, and how to write a set in a week.

Pipeline stage definitions are the written rules for what must be true before an opportunity enters each stage of the sales pipeline. Good definitions are based on verifiable buyer actions, not seller feelings, and each stage has exit criteria that can be checked in the CRM. They are what make a stage-weighted forecast mean something, and what let an AI system read "stage" as a fact.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What pipeline stage definitions mean

Every CRM lets a firm name its sales stages. Naming them is easy. Agreeing what they mean is the work.

A stage definition has four parts: the stage name, the entry criteria (what must be true to enter), the exit criteria (what must be true to move on), and the evidence (where in the CRM that can be checked). A probability is often attached, used to weight the forecast.

HubSpot's documentation shows how CRMs build this in. Its default pipeline runs "Appointment scheduled" (20%), "Qualified to buy" (40%), "Presentation scheduled" (60%), "Decision maker bought-in" (80%), "Contract sent" (90%), then "Closed won" (100%) and "Closed lost" (0%). The board view multiplies each deal's amount by its stage probability to produce a weighted amount. HubSpot also supports conditional stage properties: fields that must be completed before a deal can be moved into a stage.

| Element | Example for a "Qualified" stage | Where it is checked |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry criteria | Buyer has confirmed a problem we solve | Discovery notes field |
| Exit criteria | Budget range and decision date confirmed by buyer | Budget and decision date fields filled |
| Owner action | Next meeting booked with a second stakeholder | Next step and date |
| Probability | Set from the firm's own historical conversion | Stage settings |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### The forecast is built on them

A weighted forecast is the sum of deal values times stage probabilities. If one seller moves deals to "Proposal" after a friendly call and another waits for a written request, the same stage carries two different realities and the same probability. Gartner's 2020 research found only 45% of sales leaders and sellers had high confidence in their forecasting accuracy, and only 47% believed their organisation had high-quality data. The 2021 Forrester Consulting study for Clari, a survey of 327 US revenue operations decision-makers, found 55% missed their quarterly forecast by more than 10%, and only 18% landed within 5%.

### Stage and forecast category are different things

Some CRMs separate the stage from a forecast category. Microsoft Dynamics 365 Sales, for example, uses Pipeline, Best Case, Committed and Omitted, with Won and Lost set automatically at close. Stage describes where the buying process is. Category describes the seller's confidence for this period. Keeping them separate stops sellers advancing a stage to signal optimism.

### AI reads stage as fact

AI forecasting tools and pipeline agents treat the stage field as data. In **lowob**'s model, stage is one of the eight store fields the brain needs. If the definition is loose, the model learns the habits of individual sellers, not the behaviour of buyers. Tight definitions are the precondition for any agent that flags at-risk deals or drafts next steps.

## How to write a set in a week

1. **Map the buyer's process first.** List the steps a typical client goes through, from first conversation to signature. Stages should follow buyer milestones, not internal tasks.
2. **Keep the count small.** Five to seven open stages is typical. Each must be distinguishable by evidence.
3. **Write exit criteria as buyer actions.** "Buyer confirmed budget range" is checkable. "Strong interest" is not.
4. **Attach a field to every criterion.** If a criterion cannot be checked in the CRM, either add the field or drop the criterion.
5. **Set probabilities from history.** Use the firm's own stage-to-win conversion over the last four to six quarters, not the CRM defaults.
6. **Add an age limit.** Flag any deal that has sat in one stage for more than twice the median time.

| Common mistake | Effect | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stages named after seller tasks ("Demo done") | Progress without buyer commitment | Rename to buyer milestones |
| Default probabilities never changed | Forecast weighted by a vendor's guess | Recalculate from own history |
| No stage for "on hold" | Stalled deals inflate pipeline | Use a forecast category or close them |
| Criteria in a slide, not the CRM | Nobody checks them | Required fields at stage entry |

## lowob takeaways

- **Define by buyer action.** Each stage should be entered because the buyer did something verifiable.
- **Put the criteria in the CRM.** Required fields at stage entry enforce what a slide cannot.
- **Use your own probabilities.** Defaults are a starting point, not a forecast.
- **Separate stage from confidence.** A forecast category stops stage inflation.

## Common questions

### What are pipeline stages in sales?

They are the named steps an opportunity moves through from first qualification to close, each with criteria for entry and exit.

### How many stages should a sales pipeline have?

Most B2B firms work with five to seven open stages, plus closed won and closed lost. Fewer, well-defined stages beat many vague ones.

### What are exit criteria in a sales pipeline?

They are the conditions that must be met before a deal moves to the next stage, ideally a buyer action that can be checked in a CRM field.

### How do you set stage probabilities?

Calculate the share of deals that reached each stage and went on to win, using the last four to six quarters of your own data.

## Sources and notes

- [HubSpot Knowledge Base, Set up and customize pipelines](https://knowledge.hubspot.com/object-settings/set-up-and-customize-pipelines). Vendor documentation; default stages, probabilities and conditional stage properties.
- [Microsoft Learn, Capture forecast category for an opportunity in Dynamics 365 Sales](https://learn.microsoft.com/nb-no/dynamics365/sales/capture-forecast-category-opportunity). Vendor documentation.
- [Gartner, Less Than 50% of Sales Leaders Have High Confidence in Forecasting Accuracy](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-02-12-gartner-says-less-than-50--of-sales-leaders-and-selle), February 2020.
- [Forrester Consulting for Clari, Revenue Operations And Intelligence Delivers Predictable Growth](https://pages.clari.com/rs/866-BBG-005/images/forrester-clari-revops-study-2021.pdf), August 2021. Vendor-commissioned survey of 327 US decision-makers.

## Related research

- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)
- [Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool](https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/)

## Next move

Ask three sellers to write, independently, what must be true for a deal to be in your "Proposal" stage. Where their answers differ, you have found the first definition to write down.

# Positioning for Complex Markets

Source: https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: In complex markets most buying happens without a seller present, buying groups are large and the most common outcome of a lost deal is no decision at all. A position that works there has to name the buyer, the problem, the real alternative, the difference and the proof, and it has to give each member of the buying group a reason to agree. It should be tested against win-loss evidence and recorded as a decision with an owner and a review date.

Positioning is the choice of which buyer you serve, which problem you solve and which alternative you replace. In complex markets that choice has to work without a seller in the room, across a buying group of a dozen people, against a competitor that is usually inaction. Forrester's 2024 study found 13 people involved in the average purchase and 91% of purchases stalling at some point. Research by Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna found 40% to 60% of lost deals end in no decision. A position built for those conditions names the status quo as the alternative, gives each role in the buying group a reason to agree, and carries proof a buyer can check alone.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

A complex market, for this piece, is one where the purchase is large relative to the buyer's budget, several functions must agree, the cycle runs for months and the category may still be forming. Most emerging technology sales meet all four conditions. So do many services, infrastructure and regulated products.

Positioning is the first decision in the Strategy part of the commercial system described in Part 1. It shapes what Growth says, which channels Distribution chooses and how Revenue qualifies a deal. We have covered the general distinction between positioning, messaging and branding elsewhere ([Positioning vs messaging vs branding](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-vs-messaging-vs-branding/)). This piece covers what changes when the market is complex.

## The position has to work without you in the room

Buyers in complex markets do most of their work alone. Gartner's 2018 survey of 750 B2B buyers in complex purchases found they spent 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier under consideration. Gartner's 2025 survey of 632 buyers found 61% preferred a rep-free buying experience overall.

Vendor research points the same way. 6sense's 2024 Buyer Experience Report found buyers were nearly 70% through their purchasing process before engaging sellers, and 81% already had a preferred vendor at first contact. These are vendor figures, consistent with Gartner's.

The position is formed before the first meeting, from material the seller did not present: the website, analyst notes, peer conversations, partner recommendations and, increasingly, AI-assisted research. If that material is vague, the buyer fills the gap with the nearest familiar category. Gartner's 2025 survey also found 69% of buyers reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. That is a positioning failure that shows up as a sales problem.

## The real competitor is usually no decision

Most positioning work defines the competition as other vendors. In complex markets the more common rival is the buyer's current way of working.

Dixon and McKenna's research for *The JOLT Effect*, which analysed about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations, found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, and that some level of buyer indecision was present in roughly nine of ten sales calls. Forrester's 2024 finding that 91% of purchases stall at some point is the same pattern seen from the buyer's side.

| Alternative the buyer weighs | What the position must answer | Typical weak answer | Stronger answer |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Do nothing | Why act this quarter rather than next year | "Market-leading capability" | A cost of delay the buyer can calculate |
| Build in-house | Why buy rather than assign the team | "Faster time to value" | What the internal build would need, in named roles and months |
| Use an adjacent tool already owned | Why a new line item | "Purpose-built" | The specific job the owned tool cannot do, shown |
| Hire a firm or agency | Why this model rather than people | "Scalable" | What the buyer keeps when the engagement ends |
| A direct competitor | Why us over them | Feature comparison | The buyer type for whom the difference matters most |

A position that names a direct competitor as its alternative wins comparisons it is invited to. A position that names the status quo also gets invited. When the category itself is new, the work starts earlier still: our piece on selling into markets without a budget line covers that case ([Selling what nobody has a budget line for](https://lowob.com/research/selling-what-nobody-has-a-budget-line-for/)).

## A buying group needs a reason for each role

Forrester's 2024 study, drawing on more than 16,000 global business buyers, found 13 people involved in the average purchase and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. A position written for the economic buyer alone tends to persuade one person and leave the rest to object.

The fix is not a different message for every role. It is one position that each role can restate in its own terms.

| Role in the buying group | What they need to believe | Evidence that persuades them |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Budget holder | The problem costs more than the solution, soon | Cost of delay, comparable payback |
| Day-to-day user | Work gets easier, not just different | A trial or demonstration on their real task |
| Technical or security reviewer | It will pass review and not create new risk | Documentation, certifications, architecture |
| Finance or procurement | Terms are standard and the price is defensible | Pricing logic, reference contracts |
| Executive sponsor | It supports a priority they already own | A link to a stated objective |

Forrester's 2023 analysis of lead management found that clients who brought three or more buying-group members into the sales process saw a 50% increase in conversion from meeting to closed-won. A position each role can repeat is what makes that possible.

## The five components of a position

A position can be written as one sentence: we help a named buyer solve a named problem, instead of their current alternative, because of a difference, and here is the proof. Each component can be tested.

| Component | Question it answers | Weak version | Strong version |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buyer | Who, specifically, and when | "Mid-market companies" | A segment from the ideal customer profile, with a trigger |
| Problem | What hurts, in the buyer's words | A capability gap | A cost, risk or delay the buyer already measures |
| Alternative | What they would do otherwise | The nearest vendor | The status quo, named |
| Difference | What changes if they choose you | A feature list | One outcome the alternative cannot produce |
| Proof | Why they should believe it | Logos | A checkable result from a buyer like them |

The buyer component should come from the ideal customer profile, not from a separate workshop ([How to write an ICP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)). Proof is the component most often missing in emerging technology firms, because there are few customers yet. In that case the honest proof is a design partner's measured result, or a clearly labelled pilot. Our piece on believable case studies sets out what buyers accept ([What makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/)).

> In a complex market the competitor you most often lose to is the buyer's current way of working.

## Testing a position with evidence

A position is a hypothesis about buyers. It can be tested before and after it ships.

**Before.** Ask five people inside the firm to complete the sentence "we help [who] do [what] instead of [alternative]". If the answers differ, the firm does not yet have a position to test. Then run the same sentence past five recent buyers and five recent losses.

**After.** Win-loss interviews are the most direct test ([What is win-loss analysis?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/)). Three questions do most of the work: what alternative the buyer seriously considered, which role in the buying group raised the hardest objection, and what proof decided it.

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey found buyers used ten interaction channels on average and more than half would likely switch after a poor cross-channel experience. A useful operational test follows: pick five touchpoints a buyer meets before the first call and check whether each states the same buyer, problem and alternative.

| Signal | What it suggests |
| --- | --- |
| Losses mostly to no decision | The alternative or cost of delay is weak |
| Losses mostly to one competitor | The difference is unclear for a specific buyer type |
| Deals stall at security or procurement review | The position does not reach those roles |
| Long first calls spent explaining the category | The position is not carrying itself before contact |
| Wins concentrated in one segment | The buyer component is too broad |

## Recording the position as a decision

Positioning is usually treated as a document. In a commercial system it is a decision, and it should be recorded as one: the chosen buyer, problem and alternative, the reason, the owner, the expected effect on win rate or cycle length, and a review date.

That matters for two reasons. First, a recorded position can be graded. If the expected effect does not appear within two or three quarters, the review date forces the question. Second, positions change, and the history matters. When a firm repositions, the old position should be superseded on the record, not deleted, so later analysis can compare deals won under each ([Supersede, never overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)).

This is also where positioning meets The Build Order. A brain that drafts outreach, prepares meeting briefs or answers buyer questions needs the current position as a definition it can read. Without one, each draft improvises its own.

Illustrative example: repositioning against the status quo

Decision
:   Change the stated alternative from two named competitors to "managing it in spreadsheets and email", and add a cost-of-delay calculation to the first meeting.

Reason and owner
:   Win-loss interviews showed more than half of recent losses ended with no purchase at all, and buyers rarely mentioned the named competitors. Owned by the commercial lead; reviewed by the founders.

What changed
:   Website, partner materials and first-call deck were rewritten to the same sentence; the review date was set two quarters out, with no-decision rate as the measure.

Illustrative: a composite of a 45-person emerging technology vendor, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the status quo.** In complex markets the most common loss is no decision, so the position must explain why to act now.
- **Write for the buying group.** One position that each role can restate beats separate messages for each.
- **Ship proof, not adjectives.** A checkable result from a similar buyer persuades more than any claim.
- **Record the position.** Treat it as a decision with an owner, an expected effect and a review date.

Gateway card

### Before you ship a new position

- The buyer drawn from the ideal customer profile, with a trigger
- The status quo named as an alternative, with a cost of delay
- A reason to agree written for each buying-group role
- One checkable proof point from a buyer like the target
- Five pre-contact touchpoints checked for the same sentence
- The position recorded with an owner, expected effect and review date

## Common questions

### What is positioning in B2B marketing?

Positioning is the decision about which buyer you serve, which problem you solve and which alternative you replace. Messaging and branding follow from it.

### How do you position a product in a complex B2B market?

Name the buyer and trigger, treat the status quo as the main alternative, give each role in the buying group a reason to agree, and attach proof a buyer can check without a seller.

### Why do so many B2B deals end in no decision?

Buyers face large groups, long cycles and uncertainty about outcomes. Dixon and McKenna's research found 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision, often because buyers feared making the wrong choice.

### How often should a company revisit its positioning?

Set a review date when the position is adopted, usually two to four quarters out, and revisit earlier if win-loss evidence shows a consistent new pattern.

## Sources and notes

- [Challenger, Losing to customer indecision](https://challengerinc.com/losing-to-customer-indecision/), summarising Dixon and McKenna's research for *The JOLT Effect*. Commercial training firm's summary of the authors' analysis.
- [Gartner, B2B buyers spend 17% of their time meeting suppliers](https://gcom.pdo.aws.gartner.com/smarterwithgartner/b2b-sales-reps-maximize-customer-interactions), August 2018. Survey of 750 buyers; older data.
- [Gartner, 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience), June 2025. Survey of 632 buyers, fielded August to September 2024.

Pull your last ten lost deals and mark each as lost to a competitor or lost to no decision. If no decision is the larger group, rewrite the alternative in your position before changing anything else.

# An Audience Is Not a Business

Source: https://lowob.com/research/an-audience-is-not-a-business/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An audience is an asset, not a business. A media business starts when you can say who the audience is, what it does, who pays for access to it and which part you own. With platforms now the main route to news and only 17% paying for online news in 2026, the owned audience and a claims register for every number are what buyers and investors check.

An audience is an asset, not a business. A media business starts when you can say who the audience is, what it does, who pays for access to it, and which part of it you actually own. The market has made that test harder to dodge. The Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found that social and video platforms are now the most used route to online news, ahead of publishers' own sites and apps, and only 17% of people in 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news in the past year.

## Three buyers and an investor

Most media founders pitch one thing to everyone: size. That fails because a media company sells to at least three different buyers.

Readers and subscribers buy time saved, judgment they trust, or access they cannot get elsewhere. The Reuters Institute found the most common reason people give for paying for news is "to get useful content I can't access any other way", with 81% citing a direct benefit of some kind. Advertisers and sponsors buy attention from a specific kind of person at a specific moment. Licensees and data buyers buy content or signals they can use inside their own products. Then there is the investor, who buys the future cash flows of all of the above.

Our piece on [one truth and three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) covers one product truth and a belief per audience. In media that discipline matters more, because the buyers are so unlike each other. The reader does not care about your CPM. The sponsor does not care about your editorial mission unless it explains who reads you.

| Buyer | What they buy | The belief that must be true | Proof they accept |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Reader or subscriber | Time saved, trusted judgment, access | "I get something here I cannot get free elsewhere" | Sampling, renewal, word of mouth |
| Sponsor or advertiser | Attention from a defined person at a defined moment | "These are the people I sell to, and they respond" | Verified composition, past response |
| Licensee or data buyer | Content or signals for their own product | "This is original, usable and legally clean" | Rights, format, update frequency |
| Investor | Future cash flows of all three | "This revenue repeats and does not depend on one platform" | Owned audience, retention, revenue mix |

Write the four beliefs down. If two of them are the same sentence, you have not done the work.

## Reach is the weakest claim

Reach is easy to state and easy to discount. Everyone has a number, most of them are platform-reported, and buyers have learned to divide them by something.

Buyers have reason to be sceptical. The IAB's 2025 creator economy study, a trade body survey of US ad buyers, listed standards for audience authentication and fraud prevention among the main gaps buyers want closed. In August 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission finalised a rule that bans buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence, such as bot-generated followers or views, where the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them to misrepresent influence for a commercial purpose. An inflated follower count is no longer only a credibility problem.

The stronger claim is about composition and behaviour. Who are these people, and what do they do? Three verbs matter most to the people who pay you:

| Verb | What it means for the audience | Who pays for it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decides | Signs off budgets, policy, hiring, vendors | Sponsors, B2B data buyers |
| Buys | Purchases in a category you cover | Affiliates, commerce partners, sponsors |
| Builds | Ships products or code in your field | Tooling sponsors, recruiters, licensees |

A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls. Your positioning should state the verb, the category, and the proof.

"Read by people who run treasury at mid-sized funds" is a position. "Two hundred thousand followers" is a number.

> A small audience that decides outperforms a large audience that scrolls.

## Owned versus rented

Every media business has two audiences and only one of them is yours.

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill, the subscribers whose details sit in your systems. You set the rules, you can move platforms, and nobody can throttle you.

The rented audience is everyone who follows you on a platform. The platform owns the relationship, the algorithm, the data, and the right to change the terms tomorrow. That last right is exercised often. X closed new enrolments to its Creator Revenue Sharing programme on 7 August 2026 and ended its earnings on 7 September 2026, moving creators to a new Original Content Rewards programme with its own eligibility tests.

The rented side is growing. The Reuters Institute found 54% of people now use social and video networks to get news online, against 51% for news websites and apps, and that publishers' own sites and apps have lost 12 percentage points of reach since 2021. Its 2026 trends survey of 280 media leaders found 70% concerned about competition from creators and influencers.

Rented reach has a job: it feeds the owned list. That is its whole purpose in a commercial model. If your rented numbers are growing and your owned numbers are flat, you are building someone else's asset.

State the owned number first, clearly and separately, and treat the rest as a funnel. Our [build order for media and publishing](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-media-and-publishing/) applies the same logic to which revenue decisions a publisher should record first.

## Editorial point of view is the product truth

In most verticals the product truth is a feature or an outcome. In media it is the point of view.

A point of view is what makes someone read you instead of the free summary. It is why a sponsor wants to appear next to you and not next to a competitor with the same audience size. It is why a licensee pays for your version of a story that exists elsewhere.

The free summary is now a real competitor. Weekly use of AI chatbots for news rose from 7% to 10% in a year, according to the Reuters Institute, and 16% among under-35s. A publication with no distinct view is easy for a summary to replace.

Write it in one sentence. It should be something a reasonable person in your field could disagree with. If nobody could disagree, it is not a point of view, it is a category description.

Everything downstream, from the subscription pitch to the sponsor deck, should be able to trace back to that sentence.

## A claims register for audience numbers

Our piece on [one truth and three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) introduced the claims register. Media needs its own version because audience figures are the claims buyers check hardest.

Keep one sheet with every number you use externally. For each, record the source and the status:

| Status | Examples | Where it can appear |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Verified | Email list size, paid subscribers, renewal counts; from your own systems, exportable, auditable | Investor and sponsor materials without a label |
| Platform-reported | Followers, impressions, listens; from a dashboard you do not control | Anywhere, with a label every time |
| Estimated | Household reach, pass-along, total audience; derived or modelled | Out of the deck unless you can show the method |

The register also protects the founder. Goldman Sachs Research estimated in 2023 that about 4% of the world's roughly 50 million creators earn more than $100,000 a year, and that brand deals make up about 70% of creator revenue. When most income comes from selling access to an audience, buyers check the numbers. A register answers before they ask. The same discipline runs through our piece on [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/).

This register is usually the first document we build with a media client, because it tends to change the pitch before anyone writes a slide.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write four beliefs.** One each for the reader, the sponsor, the licensee and the investor, and no two the same.
- **Position on behaviour.** State what the audience decides, buys or builds, not how many there are.
- **Owned first, rented second.** Report the owned audience separately; give rented reach the job of feeding it.
- **Register every number.** Verified, platform-reported or estimated, with estimates kept out of the deck without a method.

Gateway card

### Before the next sponsor or investor deck

- One belief written for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee, investor
- Positioning that states what the audience does, not how many there are
- Owned audience reported separately from rented audience, owned first
- Editorial point of view in one sentence someone could disagree with
- Claims register with every external number tagged verified, platform-reported or estimated
- Each rented channel given an explicit job: feeding the owned list

## Common questions

### How should a media startup pitch its audience to investors and sponsors?

Write a separate belief for each buyer: reader, sponsor, licensee and investor. Position on what the audience does, such as deciding, buying or building, and lead with the owned audience you can export.

### What is the difference between an owned and a rented audience?

The owned audience is the list you can email, the members you can bill and the subscribers in your own systems. The rented audience is your platform followers, where the platform owns the relationship, the algorithm, the data and the terms.

### Which audience numbers can go in an investor deck?

Only verified numbers from your own systems go in without a label. Platform-reported numbers get a label every time, and estimates stay out unless you can show the method.

### Is it illegal to buy followers for a media business?

In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule bans buying or selling fake indicators of social media influence when the buyer knew or should have known they were fake and used them to misrepresent influence commercially.

# Native Advertising and Sponsored Content Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/native-advertising-and-sponsored-content/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Native advertising is paid placement that matches the form of the content around it; sponsored content is the subset where the advertiser supplies or commissions an actual piece. Both suit products that need explaining, but disclosure is not optional: the FTC, the EU's Unfair Commercial Practices Directive and the UK's ASA all require paid content to be clearly identifiable, and the advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher.

Native advertising is paid placement designed to match the form and function of the content around it. Sponsored content is the subset where the advertiser supplies or commissions an actual piece, published by a third party with a paid label. Both exist because conventional ad formats are ignored, and both carry a risk conventional ads do not: being mistaken for editorial. In one University of Georgia study only 7% of readers identified a sponsored article as advertising. Disclosure is not optional, the advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher, and the format works best for products that need explaining.

Native advertising takes many forms: a promoted article in a publication's feed, a recommended story at the end of a news piece, a sponsored post in a social feed, a paid segment in a newsletter. What they share is that the reader meets them in a mode of attention rather than avoidance.

## The main forms

| Form | How it is bought | Strength | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| In-feed native units | Programmatically or directly, on social platforms and publisher sites; look like posts or articles and lead to the advertiser's page | Scale, targeting | Low-quality placements if bought on defaults |
| Content-recommendation placements | Through networks that place "you may also like" modules across many publishers | Cheap, broad | Variable quality; headings that look editorial |
| Sponsored articles and videos | From a publication, newsletter or creator, produced by the publisher's studio or supplied by the advertiser | Room to explain | Being mistaken for editorial |
| Newsletter and podcast sponsorships | The host reads or writes about the sponsor in their own voice | The host's trust transfers | Claims the host cannot substantiate |

Newsletter and podcast sponsorships are among the most effective forms for considered products, because the trust of the host transfers. Our piece on [sponsorships, events, newsletters and podcasts](https://lowob.com/research/sponsorships-events-newsletters-podcasts/) covers how to price and evaluate them.

## Why they work when they work

They meet the reader in a mode of attention rather than avoidance. A reader of a personal-finance newsletter who encounters a sponsored explanation of a product, in the newsletter's voice, with the publisher's implicit endorsement, is more receptive than the same reader seeing a banner. For products that need explaining, which describes most fintech, AI and Web3 products, the format allows explanation.

The same quality is the risk. Wojdynski and Evans's experiments at the University of Georgia, published in the Journal of Advertising in 2015, found that in one study only 17 of 242 readers (7%) identified a sponsored article as advertising, and in an eye-tracking study 17% did. Readers were about seven times more likely to recognise the ad when it was labelled "advertising" or "sponsored content" than when it was labelled "brand voice" or "presented by". A format that persuades because it resembles editorial will mislead unless the label does real work.

## Where the line is

Disclosure is not optional. Regulators in the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom and elsewhere require that paid content be clearly identified as such, in a way the reader will notice before or as they engage with it.

| Jurisdiction | Rule | What it means in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| United States | FTC Enforcement Policy Statement and business guide on native advertising, December 2015 | Ads must be identifiable before the reader reaches the main advertising page; labels go immediately in front of or above the headline |
| European Union | Unfair Commercial Practices Directive, Annex I, point 11 | Using paid editorial content to promote a product without making that clear is banned in all circumstances |
| United Kingdom | CAP Code section 2, applied by the ASA | Marketing must be obviously identifiable; the ASA suggests labels such as "ad", "paid-for ad" or "ad link" near recommendation headings |

The FTC's guidance is the most specific. It names "Ad", "Advertisement", "Paid Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" as labels likely to be understood. It warns that "Promoted" and "Promoted Stories" are ambiguous, because they may suggest the publisher endorses the content. It says "Sponsored by [X]", "Presented by [X]" and "Brought to you by [X]" may be read as meaning the sponsor paid for the content but did not create or influence it, which is misleading when the sponsor wrote it. And it says a disclosure placed below or to the right of the headline is less likely to be seen. A small grey "Promoted" on the far side of the page fails on both counts.

The ASA has applied the same logic. It found a "Recommended by" footer and the heading "You may also like these" insufficient on a content-recommendation widget, and in October 2026 ruled that a footer disclaimer labelling a page as advertorial did not make the ads obviously identifiable.

The advertiser is responsible alongside the publisher. The FTC's guide addresses advertisers directly and says everyone involved in creating or presenting native ads, including agencies and affiliate networks, should make sure they do not mislead about their commercial nature.

> A format that persuades because it resembles editorial will mislead unless the label does real work.

Beyond the legal line is a reputational one. Sponsored content that pretends to be independent, or that makes claims the publisher would never make editorially, damages both parties when discovered, and it is discovered.

## How to buy it well

1. **Choose publishers whose readers are the buyer,** not whose traffic is large.
2. **Brief for a job, not a talking point:** the reader's question, the product truth, what may not be said. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out a one-page brief that works for sponsored pieces as well as owned ones.
3. **Let the publisher write in their voice.** Content that reads like the advertiser's brochure fails.
4. **Insist on the disclosure the law requires and make it visible:** a clear word such as "Advertisement", above the headline, on every device and in shared links.
5. **Track with a dedicated link or code.**
6. **Measure comprehension and action, not impressions.**
7. **In reviewed categories, apply the same claims library that governs the ads,** because the publisher's lawyers will ask for it and the regulator will not distinguish.

The best sponsored pieces carry an argument the advertiser could also use in a sales conversation. Our piece on [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) shows how one position can become a diagnostic, a business case and an objection answer, which is the raw material a publisher's studio needs.

## For companies the platforms restrict

Native and sponsored placements are often available to categories the large ad platforms refuse, because the decision is the publisher's rather than a classifier's. A publication that covers personal finance will run a compliant sponsored explanation of a savings product; a platform's automated review may not. That makes the format part of the open band for many restricted businesses, and one of the few that allows the full explanation the product needs. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) places native alongside the other open-band channels.

## lowob takeaways

- **Native fits its surroundings.** That is why it works and why it can mislead.
- **Use a plain label.** "Ad" or "Advertisement", above the headline; avoid "Promoted".
- **The advertiser is responsible too.** FTC, EU and UK rules do not leave it to the publisher.
- **Brief for the reader's question.** Let the publisher's voice carry the explanation.
- **Measure action.** Dedicated links or codes, not impressions.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between native advertising and sponsored content?

Native advertising is any paid placement designed to match the surrounding content. Sponsored content is the subset where the advertiser supplies or commissions an actual article, video or guide, published by a third party with a paid label.

### What disclosure labels does the FTC accept for native ads?

The FTC's guidance names "Ad", "Advertisement", "Paid Advertisement" and "Sponsored Advertising Content" as likely to be understood. It calls "Promoted" and "Promoted Stories" ambiguous, and warns that "Sponsored by" may suggest the sponsor did not create the content.

### Is advertorial content legal in the EU and UK?

Yes, if it is clearly identified. EU law bans paid editorial that is not made clear to the reader, and the UK's ASA requires marketing to be obviously identifiable, ruling footer-only labels insufficient.

### Can restricted-category companies use native advertising?

Often yes. Publishers decide what they run, so a personal-finance publication may run a compliant sponsored explanation that a platform's automated review would reject.

## Sources and notes

- [FTC, Native Advertising: A Guide for Businesses](https://ftc.gov/tips-advice/business-center/guidance/native-advertising-guide-businesses), December 2015. US regulator guidance; companion to the Enforcement Policy Statement on deceptively formatted advertisements.
- [legislation.gov.uk, Directive 2005/29/EC (Unfair Commercial Practices Directive), Annex I](https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eudr/2005/29/annex/I/adopted), as adopted. EU law; check member state implementation and later amendments.
- [ASA, Recognising ads: native advertising](https://www.asa.org.uk/advice-online/recognising-ads-native-advertising.html), updated 23 October 2026. UK self-regulatory advice; not a statute.
- [University of Georgia, Despite growth, native advertising is still difficult for consumers to recognize](https://news.uga.edu/native-advertising-research-2015/), 16 December 2015. University summary of a peer-reviewed study; small samples, older formats.

## Related research

- [Content With a Job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/)
- [Thought Leadership That Sales Can Use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/)
- [Event, Newsletter, and Podcast Sponsorships Explained](https://lowob.com/research/sponsorships-events-newsletters-podcasts/)
- [Meta Said No. That Is Not the End of Your Distribution Plan.](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/)

## Next move

Look at your last three sponsored placements as a reader would. If the label is anything other than a plain "Ad" or "Advertisement" above the headline, ask the publisher to change it, and brief the next piece around one question your buyer actually asks.

# The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A context layer combines connectors, permission-aware retrieval and shared definitions so that agents can read a company's systems. It should be rented rather than built, connected in the order that improves real client work, audited for permissions before launch, and paired with a decision record, because no connector can retrieve a reason nobody wrote down.

A context layer is the wiring that lets AI read a company's own systems: connectors into email, CRM, documents and calls; retrieval that respects existing permissions; and shared definitions so that every agent means the same thing by "active client". It should be rented, not built. The decisions that matter are what to connect first, what to wall off, and how to mark which information is current. Even done well, it cannot retrieve a decision nobody recorded, which is why the record comes next.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

The easiest way to understand a context layer is to follow one account through it.

Consider a mid-size advisory firm pitching a mid-market lender for the second time. The first pitch, eighteen months earlier, went well until it did not. Before the second meeting, someone has to rebuild the history, and it is scattered across nine places: two senior people's inboxes, a call recording in a meeting tool, three versions of the proposal in a shared drive, a chat thread about price, a CRM record marked "lost" with no reason, an invoice for a small diagnostic engagement in between, two calendars, and one person's memory that the lender's new chief operating officer was a client at a previous firm.

Rebuilding that history takes most of a morning. The brief is good, out of date within a week, and seen by nobody else. That request (know everything we know about a client before every meeting) is the context layer. It is also where many builds stop and call themselves a brain.

*Figure: The wiring turns nine places into one brief. It cannot retrieve a decision nobody wrote down; that is the record's job.*

## What a context layer is

In *The first two-fifths* we described the full brain as five parts: knowledge, memory, meaning, governance and judgment. The context layer covers knowledge, governance and part of meaning. In practice it is three pieces of wiring.

| Component | What it does | What good looks like |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Connectors | Make company systems readable by an assistant or agent | Native or open-standard connectors; no copies of data in spreadsheets |
| Permission-aware retrieval | Finds relevant material and shows each person only what they can already see | The assistant never surfaces a file the user could not open directly |
| Shared definitions | Fix the meaning of key terms across people and agents | Written definitions, each with an owner, read by every agent |

### Connectors and the open standard

Connectors increasingly follow an open standard. The Model Context Protocol (MCP), created by Anthropic, was donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, when more than 10,000 MCP servers had been published. Google's Agent2Agent protocol, for communication between agents, also sits under the Linux Foundation. The practical effect for a buyer is less lock-in at this layer: a connector built to an open standard works with more than one assistant, so changing assistants does not mean rebuilding the wiring.

### Rent it, then decide the order

The large platforms now sell the context layer directly. Microsoft's Work IQ, generally available since June 2026, is a permission-aware context layer billed on usage. Google's October 2026 Gemini Enterprise launch described a shared knowledge catalogue and connection to MCP servers inside and outside the company. Specialist platforms compete on the same ground, and our list *The 5 enterprise context platforms, ranked for regulated firms* compares them. This is the half of the brain we recommend renting (*Buy context, own judgment*). For a mid-size firm the real decision is not which platform to build. It is what to connect, in what order, and what to keep out.

## Connect in this order

Connect sources in the order they improve the next client meeting, not the order in which they are easiest to switch on.

| Order | Source | Why at this point | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Email and calendar | Every relationship leaves a trail here, and the suite connects them natively | Personal mail, partner-only threads, excluded mailboxes |
| 2 | CRM | The spine: accounts, stages, owners and outcomes | Stale records feeding confident answers (Part 4) |
| 3 | Call notes and recordings | What was actually said, including objections | Consent to record; summaries replacing the source |
| 4 | Proposals and deliverables | What was offered, at what price and on what terms | Old versions treated as current |
| 5 | Chat channels | The informal reasoning behind decisions | Noise; private channels; jokes read as facts |
| Later | Finance, HR, delivery files | Useful, but outside the commercial line | Confidentiality and scope creep |

Test each step on real meetings before adding the next. If the assistant's brief for an upcoming pitch is not better than one a person would prepare, adding another source will not fix it.

## Permissions are inherited, including the bad ones

Permission-aware retrieval shows each person only what they could already open. That protects the firm only if the underlying permissions are right, and in most firms they are not. Shared drives accumulate "anyone in the organisation" links for years. Old project folders remain open after the project ends. A search tool makes all of this findable at once.

So the first connection is also an audit. Before the drive is connected, someone should check what "everyone" can see: compensation files, board papers, other clients' pricing, conflict notes. The fix is mundane and it is usually the most valuable afternoon in the build. Security guidance points the same way: as one analysis of the OWASP list put it, the right control point is the data access decision at retrieval time, so the model never sees data the requester is not allowed to see.

## Five definitions to agree first

A brain that returns three answers to the same question is worse than none. That happens when words drift, which we described in *Fifty people: when words start to mean different things*. For the commercial line, agree five definitions before automating anything:

1. **Active client.** Billed in the last twelve months, under contract now, or engaged in the last ninety days. Pick one.
2. **Qualified opportunity.** What must be true before an opportunity enters the pipeline.
3. **Won, lost and no decision.** Including what counts as "no decision" and when a stalled deal is closed.
4. **Account owner.** One person, not a team.
5. **Source.** Where an opportunity came from, chosen from a fixed list.

Write each definition down, name its owner, and put the definitions where every agent reads them.

## Give evidence a standing

Connecting nine sources solves the search problem and creates a new one. The assistant now finds both prices: the one in the March proposal and the one in the June email. Which is current?

In *Retrieval is not the bottleneck* we cited benchmark evidence that relevant material is usually retrievable and that failures come when systems weigh it, especially for questions about change over time. The fix is to give important items a standing: whether they are current, superseded, disputed or unverified; when they became true; who asserted them; and what they replaced. On the commercial line that means, at minimum, marking proposals and prices as current or superseded and preferring the CRM's recorded outcome to anyone's recollection.

> No connector can retrieve a decision nobody recorded.

## What the wiring cannot do

Connect all nine places and the assistant can now produce the meeting brief in minutes. It can say what was proposed, what was said and what was invoiced. It still cannot say why the first pitch was lost, because that reason was never written down. No connector retrieves what was never recorded.

That is the boundary between the wiring and the record, and it is why the context layer sits in the middle of the build order rather than at the end. The record (the commercial decisions worth keeping, with their reasons and outcomes) is what turns a well-informed assistant into one that knows what the firm does. In *A loop with good context* we described how the record then flows back in, as a precedent slot of three to five comparable past decisions placed in front of an agent before it acts.

## The risk nobody budgets for

Once the wiring is live, the assistant reads content the firm did not write: inbound email, web pages, attachments. If it can also act (send a message, update a record), untrusted content now sits beside a user's permissions and an outbound channel. OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications ranks prompt injection first and excessive agency sixth for this reason. The practical answer for a mid-size firm is not a security programme. It is the gateway in Part 8: nothing sends without a person, and every tool call is logged.

## Where the order bends

| Industry | What is different at the context layer |
| --- | --- |
| Professional services | Conflict and confidentiality walls between clients |
| Financial services and fintech | Identity checks, credit files and account data stay outside the commercial build |
| Media and publishing | Sales context must never reach editorial systems |
| Crypto and digital assets | The richest context is public (on-chain, community), so connection is easy and permissions are loose |
| B2B SaaS | Product usage data joins early and is often the strongest signal |
| Retail, DTC and luxury | Client books and messaging apps hold the relationship; consent governs both |
| Industrial distribution | The ERP, price book and specification sheets are the context |
| Healthcare and life sciences | Patient data never enters the commercial layer |

Illustrative example: wiring the priority accounts

Decision
:   Connect email, calendar, CRM and call notes for the top 40 accounts first; proposals next; chat later.

Reason and owner
:   These four sources cover most meeting preparation. Owned by the head of operations; shared-drive permissions audited first.

What changed
:   Meeting preparation drops from a morning to under an hour. The reason the earlier pitch was lost is still missing, which becomes the case for the decision record.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size advisory firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Rent the wiring; decide the order.** What you connect first matters more than which platform you choose.
- **Audit before you connect.** The assistant inherits every bad permission in the drive.
- **Agree five definitions.** Active client, qualified, won and lost, owner, source.
- **Know the limit.** The wiring retrieves what was recorded. It cannot retrieve a reason nobody wrote down.

Gateway card

### Context layer ready

- Email, calendar, CRM and call notes connected for priority accounts
- Shared-drive permissions audited
- Five definitions written, each with an owner
- Proposals and prices marked current or superseded
- Briefs tested against real meetings before adding sources

## Common questions

### What is a context layer in AI?

It is the wiring that lets AI read a company's own systems: connectors into email, CRM, documents and calls, retrieval that respects existing permissions, and shared definitions so every agent uses terms the same way.

### What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

An open standard for connecting AI assistants and agents to tools and data. It was donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, when more than 10,000 MCP servers had been published.

### What data should we connect to AI first?

For commercial teams: email and calendar, then the CRM, then call notes and recordings, then proposals, then chat. Finance, HR and delivery files come later.

### Is a context layer the same as an enterprise brain?

No. It is one part. A brain also needs a record of decisions and reasons, a reasoning layer, and outcomes written back. The context layer cannot retrieve a decision nobody recorded.

## Sources and notes

- [IT Brief, Anthropic donates MCP to new Agentic AI Foundation](https://itbrief.com.au/story/anthropic-donates-mcp-to-new-agentic-ai-foundation), January 2026; [IT Brief UK on the Agentic AI Foundation](https://itbrief.co.uk/story/linux-foundation-launches-agentic-ai-open-standards-hub).
- [Microsoft Learn, Work IQ](https://learn.microsoft.com/microsoft-365/copilot/extensibility/work-iq/). Vendor documentation.
- [Google Cloud, Gemini at work, 8 October 2026](https://cloud.google.com/blog/products/ai-machine-learning/welcome-to-gemini-at-work-2026). Vendor announcement.
- [OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025](https://www.hackerone.com/blog/owasp-top-10-llms-2025-how-genai-risks-are-evolving), via HackerOne; retrieval-time access control per [NHI Mgmt Group's summary](https://nhimg.org/articles/owasp-llm-top-10-shows-where-app-security-breaks-down/).
- The connection order and definitions are **lowob**'s recommendations for mid-size commercial teams; regulated firms will need more.

# What Is Human-in-the-Loop AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-human-in-the-loop-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Human-in-the-loop AI places a named person at the point where an AI output becomes an action. The EU AI Act, UK data protection guidance and OWASP all describe versions of it. It only counts as a control if the reviewer can understand, override and stop the system, and actually does check.

Human-in-the-loop AI is a design in which a person reviews, approves or can override an AI system's output before it takes effect. It appears in the EU AI Act's human oversight article, in UK data protection guidance and in OWASP's security mitigations. It is a real control only when the reviewer understands the output, can reject or stop it, and is measured on whether they actually check.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What human-in-the-loop means

The term covers a range of designs that differ in when the person acts. The useful distinction for a business is whether the person stands before the action or after it.

| Pattern | When the person acts | Typical use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the loop | Before the output takes effect; nothing proceeds without approval | Client emails, proposals, payments, public posts |
| On the loop | After or during; the system acts and a person monitors and can intervene | Reversible internal updates such as CRM hygiene |
| Out of the loop | No routine human role | Low-stakes, fully reversible tasks with a long clean record |

**lowob**'s autonomy dial maps onto this: level 1 (draft) and level 2 (act with approval) are in the loop, level 3 (act and report) is on the loop, and level 4 (act alone) is out of it.

## Why regulators and security teams ask for it

**The EU AI Act.** Article 14 says high-risk AI systems must be designed so they "can be effectively overseen by natural persons" while in use. Overseers must be able to understand the system's limits, remain aware of automation bias, interpret the output, decide not to use it or "override or reverse" it, and interrupt the system through a "stop" button. For certain biometric identification, two competent people must verify a result before anyone acts on it. Under the Digital Omnibus, which entered into force on 27 July 2026, the Annex III high-risk obligations now apply from 2 December 2027.

**UK data protection.** Article 22 of the UK GDPR restricts solely automated decisions with legal or similarly significant effects, such as mortgage decisions or job offers. The ICO's guidance says a person who only supplies data to the system is not meaningfully involved. Review counts when it comes after the automated decision and relates to its actual outcome.

**Security.** OWASP lists "require human approval for high-risk actions" among its mitigations for prompt injection, and "require user approval" for excessive agency. Its example is an email assistant that drafts replies but leaves the user to review and send each one.

**Financial supervision.** FINRA's 2026 report, released in December 2025, lists for firms exploring agents: monitoring system access, "determining where human-in-the-loop oversight is required", tracking agent actions and decisions, and setting guardrails.

> A reviewer who cannot say no, or never does, is not oversight.

## How to stop it becoming a rubber stamp

The EU AI Act names the core failure: the tendency to over-rely on automated output. A queue that receives hundreds of items a day will be approved on reflex unless the design prevents it. These checks keep review real.

| Check | What it shows |
| --- | --- |
| Sources attached to each item | Whether the reviewer can verify without redoing the work |
| Three outcomes: approve, edit, return | Whether rejection is as easy as approval |
| Edit and return rates by task | Where the agent is weak and whether reviewers engage |
| Time spent per item | Approvals in seconds on complex items are not reviews |
| Blind spot-checks and seeded errors | Whether reviewers catch problems placed on purpose |
| A named kill switch owner | Whether anyone can halt the system, as Article 14 expects |

Approval rate alone is a weak measure, because it rises with reviewer fatigue as well as with agent quality. The logs from the queue also become the audit trail: who approved what, when, and on which evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **Put the person before the action.** For anything client-facing, approval comes before sending, not after.
- **Give reviewers real power.** They must be able to edit, return and stop, and doing so must be easy.
- **Measure the reviewer.** Spot-checks and seeded errors, not approval rates.
- **Move tasks along the dial on evidence.** From in the loop to on the loop, one task at a time.

## Common questions

### What does human-in-the-loop mean in AI?

A design in which a person reviews or approves an AI system's output before it takes effect, and can reject, change or stop it.

### What is the difference between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop?

In the loop, nothing proceeds without a person's approval. On the loop, the system acts and a person monitors and can intervene afterwards.

### Does the EU AI Act require human-in-the-loop?

Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to allow effective human oversight, including the ability to override outputs and stop the system. It does not mandate approval of every output.

### What is automation bias?

The tendency to over-rely on an automated system's output. The EU AI Act names it explicitly as something human overseers must be able to recognise.

## Sources and notes

- [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 14: Human oversight](https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/ai-act/ai-act-regulation/article-14/), Official Journal text via SpringLex, 12 July 2024. Applies to high-risk systems only.
- [National Law Review, EU Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), 31 July 2026. Law firm summary of the revised high-risk timeline.
- [UK Information Commissioner's Office, What is the impact of Article 22 of the UK GDPR on fairness?](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/artificial-intelligence/guidance-on-ai-and-data-protection/how-do-we-ensure-fairness-in-ai/what-is-the-impact-of-article-22-of-the-uk-gdpr-on-fairness), regulator guidance.
- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm062025-excessive-agency/), 2025. Community security standard.
- [Debevoise & Plimpton, FINRA's 2026 Regulatory Oversight Report](https://www.debevoise.com/insights/publications/2025/12/finras-2026-regulatory-oversight-report-continued), December 2025. Law firm summary of the FINRA report.

## Related research

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [Regulators Want the Chain, Not the Model](https://lowob.com/research/regulators-want-the-chain-not-the-model/)
- [Agentic AI vs Generative AI: What Changes When the Model Can Act](https://lowob.com/research/agentic-ai-vs-generative-ai/)
- [Human-in-the-Loop vs Human-on-the-Loop](https://lowob.com/research/human-in-the-loop-vs-human-on-the-loop/)

## Next move

For each AI output that reaches a client today, write down who approves it and whether that approval is logged. Any output without both is the first gap to close.
