# Attribution vs Incrementality: What Did Your Marketing Actually Cause?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Every attribution model is a story about who deserves credit; none measures what would have happened without the spend. Field experiments at Facebook and eBay show how far the stories can drift from the truth. This piece sets out the holdout designs a smaller company can run, how to read the result, and a three-layer measurement stack.

Attribution assigns credit for a conversion. Incrementality asks whether it would have happened without the campaign. Only the second answers the question a budget decision depends on, and it is answered by experiment, not by model. The research is blunt: in 15 Facebook experiments, observational methods using rich individual data were often off by a factor of three, and eBay found its brand search ads bought almost no traffic it would not have had anyway.

Every attribution model is a story about who deserves credit. Last click gives it to whoever touched the customer last. First click gives it to whoever introduced them. Linear shares it out. Data-driven models let the platform that sold the ad decide how much the ad mattered; it is Google Ads' default, and in 2023 Google removed the first-click, linear, time-decay and position-based models altogether. Each story is coherent. None of them is a measurement of what would have happened without the spend.

That question, what would have happened anyway, has a name: incrementality.

## Why attribution flatters

Attribution counts touches on customers who converted. It cannot see the customers who would have converted without any touch at all, and those are precisely the ones the crowded channels are best at reaching. Brand-name search, retargeting and coupon sites all appear at the end of a journey that was already ending. They are credited with outcomes they observed.

The best-known test of this is eBay's. Blake, Nosko and Tadelis switched off brand keyword ads on MSN and found that about 99.5% of the click traffic was retained, almost all of it arriving through the organic result directly underneath. A follow-up on Google lost about 3%. On non-brand search, a geographic experiment across about 30% of US markets found no statistically significant sales effect, and frequent buyers, who generated most of the attributed sales, were largely unaffected. Naive regression on the same data implied returns above 1,400%. The experiment implied a short-term return of minus 63%. eBay is a famous brand with strong organic rankings, so the size of the effect will not transfer to every advertiser. The direction does.

For a company whose ad accounts get suspended, attribution has a second weakness. Every suspension resets the pixel, the conversion history and the platform's learning. The models are rebuilt on a fresh, thin data set, and the numbers they produce for the next quarter are guesses dressed as reports. Our piece on [how marketing tracking works](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/) covers why pixel data is thinner than it was even without suspensions.

## The evidence that models cannot fix it

The obvious response is a better model. Gordon, Zettelmeyer, Bhargava and Chapsky tested that directly. Working with 15 US advertising experiments at Facebook, covering 1.6 billion impressions, they compared the lift measured by randomised trials with the lift that standard observational methods estimated from the same data, including matching and regression on detailed demographic and behavioural variables.

| Study (checkout outcome) | Lift from the randomised test | Naive exposed vs unexposed | Best or closest observational estimate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Study 1 | 30% | 217% | Statistically indistinguishable from the test |
| Study 4 | 73% | 316% | 222% on age and gender matching; richest variables came close |
| Study 9 | 2.4% | Not reported here | 1,306% |

Across the studies, the authors found that in half of them the estimated increase in purchases was off by a factor of three, whichever method was used, and that the error went in both directions. Their conclusion, in the publisher's summary, was that even fairly comprehensive individual-level data were inadequate for reliable estimates, and that large randomised trials should be used wherever possible. These were consumer campaigns at a platform with unusually good data. A smaller company's attribution model has less to work with.

> Attribution tells you who was present at the sale. Incrementality tells you who caused it. Budgets should follow the second.

## What incrementality asks

Take a group who could have been reached. Reach some of them; do not reach the rest. Compare outcomes. The difference is what the spend caused.

That is the whole idea, and it is available to companies far smaller than the ones that usually run it.

**Geographic holdouts.** Run a channel in some regions and not in comparable others. Compare outcomes across the two sets over the same weeks. Works for programmatic, creator and affiliate programmes, and does not require the platform's cooperation.

**Time-based holdouts.** Pause a channel for a defined window and watch what happens to outcomes, brand search and direct traffic. Crude, but clarifying, particularly for retargeting and brand search, which often turn out to have been observing rather than causing.

**Partner-level holdouts.** In an affiliate or creator programme, hold a matched set of partners inactive for a period. Compare the outcomes of active and inactive partners' audiences where the tracking allows.

**Lift studies where the platform offers them.** Google's Conversion Lift splits users or geographies into treatment and control and reports incremental conversions and incremental cost per action; it is not available to every account and needs enough conversion volume. Meta and others run similar studies. Platform designs have improved: the "ghost ads" method developed by Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer logs the ads a control user would have seen without showing them, which in their retail case cut the cost of a test from about $45,000 to about $5,000 for similar precision. The caution remains that the platform is grading its own work.

None of these is perfect. All of them are closer to the truth than a model that only counts touches. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers sample sizes and decision rules at low volumes.

## Reading the result

Incrementality tests produce a single figure: the share of attributed outcomes that would not have happened without the spend. Divide the attributed cost per outcome by that share to get the cost per outcome caused.

| Channel | Attributed cost per outcome | Incrementality | Cost per outcome caused |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A: brand search and retargeting | $30 | 25% | $120 |
| B: prospecting on a new audience | $80 | 90% | about $89 |

The second channel is cheaper. The attribution report would have said the opposite. The figures are illustrative, but the pattern, where capture channels look cheapest and prove dearest, is the one the eBay experiment found.

## A measurement stack for a company the platforms restrict

The practical design has three layers.

**Own the tracking.** First-party conversion events, server-side where possible, in an analytics account in the company's name. Platform pixels are a convenience, not a record.

**Attribute for operations.** Use a simple, stable attribution rule to run the week: pay partners, pause placements, allocate creative. Do not pretend it measures cause.

**Test for allocation.** Once a quarter, run one incrementality test on the channel taking the most budget. Let that result, not the attribution report, decide the next quarter's split. A [marketing mix model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-marketing-mix-modeling/) refreshed quarterly checks that the pieces add up.

That is a small amount of discipline. It is also the difference between a media budget allocated on evidence and one allocated to whichever channel is best at taking credit.

## lowob takeaways

- **Do not confuse credit with cause.** Last-touch and data-driven credit both describe who was present, not what the spend produced.
- **Better models do not close the gap.** Facebook's own experiments found observational estimates off by a factor of three in half the studies.
- **Holdouts are cheap.** Geographic, time-based and partner-level designs need no platform cooperation.
- **Let tests decide the split.** One incrementality test a quarter on the biggest channel; the attribution report runs the week.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between attribution and incrementality?

Attribution assigns credit for a conversion among the touches that preceded it. Incrementality measures whether the conversion would have happened without the campaign, using a control group that was not reached.

### How do you measure incrementality without a platform lift study?

Run a geographic holdout, switching a channel off in comparable regions; a time-based pause; or a partner-level holdout in affiliate and creator programmes. Compare outcomes against the reached group over the same weeks.

### Is data-driven attribution accurate?

It is more nuanced than last click, but it still divides credit among touches on people who converted. It cannot see who would have converted anyway, and the platform selling the ads runs the model.

### Do brand search ads drive incremental sales?

Often far fewer than reported. eBay found about 99.5% of brand-ad traffic was retained through organic search when the ads stopped. Test it with a holdout before assuming either way.

## Sources and notes

- [Gordon, Zettelmeyer, Bhargava and Chapsky, A Comparison of Approaches to Advertising Measurement: Evidence from Big Field Experiments at Facebook](https://www.kellogg.northwestern.edu/faculty/gordon_b/files/fb_comparison.pdf), *Marketing Science*, 2019. Academic paper; 15 US consumer campaigns on one platform, using Facebook data.
- [INFORMS, How measurable is online advertising?](https://www.informs.org/News-Room/INFORMS-Releases/News-Releases/How-measurable-is-online-advertising), 20 March 2019. Publisher's summary of the paper above.
- [Blake, Nosko and Tadelis, Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness: A Large Scale Field Experiment](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20171.pdf), NBER Working Paper 20171, 2014; later published in *Econometrica*. Field experiment at eBay; a very well-known brand, so the brand-search result is an upper bound for most advertisers.
- [Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer, Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Online Ad Effectiveness](https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f84173.pdf), February 2016. Academic paper; one retailer case; the method depends on the ad platform implementing it.
- [Google Ads Help, About Conversion Lift](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/12003020?hl=en-GB). Platform documentation; availability depends on the account and conversion volume.
- [Google Ads Help, First click, linear, time decay, and position-based attribution models are going away](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13427716), April 2023. Platform announcement; data-driven became the default.
- The reading table and the three-layer stack are **lowob**'s framework; the channel figures are illustrative.

## Related research

## Next move

Pick the channel taking the most budget this quarter and design one holdout for it: matched regions or partners, a fixed window and a written rule for what result would cut or scale it. Run it before the next budget meeting.

# What Is Net Revenue Retention (NRR)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Net revenue retention measures whether a firm's existing customers are worth more or less to it than they were a year ago. Above 100% means expansion outweighs losses; below it means the firm must replace revenue before it can grow. This explainer gives the formula, recent benchmarks for private software companies, and the measurement errors that most often inflate the figure.

Net revenue retention (NRR) is the revenue a firm earns from a group of existing customers at the end of a period, divided by what the same customers paid at the start. It includes expansion, downgrades and churn, and excludes new customers. Above 100% means the existing base grows on its own. Its companion, gross revenue retention (GRR), excludes expansion and can never exceed 100%.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What net revenue retention means

NRR is a cohort measure. It fixes a group of customers at a start date and follows their revenue over a set period, usually 12 months. SaaS Capital's definition uses December to December: recurring revenue this December from customers who were also customers last December, divided by all recurring revenue last December. It includes upsells, cross-sells and price increases, so it can run well above 100%. GRR uses the same formula without upsells, cross-sells and price increases.

An illustrative cohort:

| Movement over 12 months | Revenue |
| --- | --- |
| Starting annual recurring revenue from the cohort | £1,000,000 |
| Expansion (upsell, cross-sell, price rises) | +£150,000 |
| Contraction (downgrades, fewer seats) | −£40,000 |
| Churn (customers who left) | −£80,000 |
| Ending revenue from the same customers | £1,030,000 |
| **NRR** | **103%** |
| **GRR** (excludes expansion) | **88%** |

Revenue from customers won during the year is excluded from both. Including it is the most common way NRR gets overstated.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

NRR shows how much of next year's growth the firm already has. At 110%, the existing base adds 10% before any new customer is signed. At 95%, sales must replace five points of lost revenue before growth begins. SaaS Capital found that companies with NRR of 110% or more grew faster than the 24% median for companies above $1 million of ARR, while those below 100% grew more slowly.

Benchmarks vary by sample and segment. Bessemer reported much higher averages than the private-company surveys, which partly reflects its sample of fast-growing cloud businesses. It also found smaller-contract businesses typically retain less: its examples included one company at 109% on contracts of about $2,000 and another at 123% on contracts above $50,000. SaaS Capital likewise reports that higher net retention correlates with higher contract values, and recommends benchmarking against firms of similar contract size rather than similar age or revenue.

Andreessen Horowitz makes the key caution in its startup metrics guide: gross churn "estimates the actual loss to the business, while net revenue churn understates the losses." A firm with 115% NRR and 75% GRR is losing a quarter of its starting revenue every year and buying it back through expansion. That is a different business from one with 105% NRR and 95% GRR.

In **lowob**'s model, retention is an outcome to write back. Each renewal, expansion or loss should carry its reason in the commercial record, so the firm can see which decisions produced the number and not just the number itself.

## How to measure it without flattering it

| Question | Recommended practice | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which customers are in the cohort? | Only those billing at the start date | New logos inflate NRR |
| What period? | 12 months, trailing | Monthly figures are noisy and seasonal |
| Which revenue? | Recurring revenue only | One-off services distort expansion |
| Price increases? | Include, but report separately | Price-led NRR may not repeat |
| Report alone? | Always with GRR and logo retention | NRR can mask broad churn |

For firms without subscriptions, such as agencies or advisory practices, the equivalent is repeat revenue: what last year's clients paid this year, as a share of what they paid last year. The same exclusions apply.

Three checks catch the common errors. First, rebuild the cohort from billing data, not the CRM, since CRM close dates and invoice dates often differ. Second, split NRR by segment and contract size. Third, list the ten largest expansions and the ten largest losses, with reasons. If a handful of accounts produce most of the expansion, the headline figure is fragile.

## lowob takeaways

- **NRR measures the base, not the funnel.** New customers stay out of the calculation.
- **Report GRR beside it.** Expansion can hide churn that would otherwise be obvious.
- **Benchmark by contract size.** Smaller contracts retain less, so compare like with like.
- **Record the reasons.** A renewal or loss with no reason attached cannot inform the next decision.

## Common questions

### How do you calculate net revenue retention?

Take recurring revenue now from customers who were customers a year ago, and divide it by total recurring revenue from those customers a year ago. Exclude revenue from new customers.

### What is a good NRR?

The 2024 KeyBanc and Sapphire survey put private SaaS net retention at about 101%. SaaS Capital's 2025 median for $25,000 to $50,000 contracts was 102%, with a top quartile of 111%.

### What is the difference between NRR and GRR?

NRR includes expansion such as upsells and price rises. GRR excludes expansion and counts only what was kept after downgrades and churn, so it cannot exceed 100%.

### Is NRR the same as net dollar retention?

Yes. Net dollar retention (NDR) and net revenue retention are used interchangeably, though firms define the cohort and period differently, so check the definition.

## Sources and notes

- [SaaS Capital, SaaS Retention Benchmarks for Private B2B Companies](https://www.saas-capital.com/research/saas-retention-benchmarks-for-private-b2b-companies/), September 2025. Lender's annual survey of private SaaS firms; definitions and medians used here.
- [Sapphire Ventures, KeyBanc Capital Markets and Sapphire Ventures Private SaaS Company Survey](https://sapphireventures.com/press/keybanc-capital-markets-and-sapphire-ventures-private-saas-company-survey-reveals-a-continued-focus-on-operational-efficiency-and-profitability/), October 2024. Press release on a survey of 100+ private SaaS companies.
- [Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million](https://www.bvp.com/assets/uploads/2021/09/scaling-to-100-million-by-mary-d-onofrio.pdf), 2021. Venture firm analysis; sample skews to high-growth cloud companies.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), August 2015, updated 2024. Investor guidance on gross versus net churn.

## Related research

- [What Is CAC Payback?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/)
- [What Is Outcome Write-Back?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/)
- [What Is Win-Loss Analysis?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Pull last year's customer list from billing, not the CRM, and calculate both NRR and GRR for that cohort. If the gap between them is more than 15 points, list the accounts that produced the expansion and ask whether it will repeat.

# What Is Sales Forecasting, and Why Is It Usually Wrong?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-sales-forecasting/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A sales forecast predicts what will close in a period, usually by combining pipeline data with seller and manager judgment. Gartner found fewer than half of sales leaders and sellers have high confidence in their forecast. This explainer covers the main forecasting methods, the structural reasons forecasts miss, and how a mid-size firm can measure and reduce its error.

Sales forecasting is the practice of estimating how much revenue a team will close in a given period, usually a month or quarter. Most forecasts combine pipeline data with the judgment of sellers and managers. They are usually wrong for structural reasons: stage probabilities are guesses, close dates slip, data is incomplete, and nobody measures past error, so the same bias repeats.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What sales forecasting means

A sales forecast answers one question: how much will we close in this period? Finance uses it for cash and hiring plans. Leadership uses it to decide whether to act before the quarter ends. Boards and investors use it to judge whether management understands the business.

Forecasts are built bottom-up, from individual deals, or top-down, from historical patterns. Most mid-size firms use a bottom-up call: each seller places deals into categories, managers adjust, and the totals roll up. Salesforce's standard categories show the typical structure: Pipeline, Best Case, an optional Most Likely, Commit and Closed. Each opportunity stage maps to a category by default, and managers can record a judgment on a deal or adjust the total without changing the deal record itself.

| Method | How it works | Main weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seller and manager call | Sellers commit deals, managers adjust | Optimism, sandbagging, recency bias |
| Stage-weighted pipeline | Deal value multiplied by stage probability | Probabilities are rarely calibrated |
| Historical run-rate | Prior periods projected forward | Misses changes in market or team |
| Driver-based | Pipeline coverage, conversion and cycle time | Needs clean stage and date history |
| Statistical or machine learning | Model trained on past deal outcomes | Needs volume; can hide its reasoning |

## Why forecasts are usually wrong

### The probabilities are invented

A stage-weighted forecast assumes that a deal in "proposal" closes, say, 50% of the time. In many firms that number was set when the CRM was configured and never checked. If proposal-stage deals actually close at 30%, every forecast overstates by the same margin. Written stage definitions with verifiable exit criteria are the precondition for meaningful probabilities.

### The data is incomplete

Gartner's research found fewer than half of respondents believed their data was high quality, and 13% said it was poor. Missing close dates, stale amounts and deals nobody has touched for 60 days all flow into the total. Gartner's recommendations are practical: build CRM compliance into the culture, define data quality standards based on what the CRM is for, and make data quality a regular topic in manager and seller conversations.

### The incentives distort the call

Sellers who are measured on hitting their commit have reasons to understate it. Sellers worried about headcount reviews have reasons to overstate pipeline. Neither is dishonest in intent, but both bias the number. A manager adjustment corrects for the bias only if the manager knows which way each seller leans.

### Nobody measures the error

The most common failure is the absence of feedback. Teams produce a forecast every week, but few store each call and compare it with the outcome. Without that record, a team cannot tell whether it is consistently 15% high or randomly wrong, and the two need different fixes. Gartner found that analytics led by the chief sales officer were 2.3 times more likely to achieve higher forecast accuracy than analytics led elsewhere, which suggests ownership matters as much as tooling.

## How to make a forecast more honest

1. **Freeze the call.** Record the forecast at fixed points, for example week 2, week 6 and week 10 of the quarter, by category and by seller.
2. **Measure the error.** At quarter end, compare each frozen call with the result. Note whether the miss was high or low, and by how much.
3. **Calibrate stage probabilities.** Replace configured percentages with actual historical conversion by stage, refreshed each quarter.
4. **Separate commit from upside.** A deal in Commit should meet written criteria, such as a confirmed decision date and a named signer, not just a seller's confidence.
5. **Track bias by person.** After two or three quarters, each seller and manager has a measurable tendency. Adjust for it openly.

In **lowob**'s terms, a forecast is a decision with an expected outcome. Recording it, then writing the actual result back against it, is the learning loop. Calibration, not a better model, is usually the first gain.

## lowob takeaways

- **Store every forecast.** A call that is not recorded cannot be checked.
- **Check the stage probabilities.** Configured percentages are assumptions until compared with history.
- **Write criteria for Commit.** Confidence is not evidence of a close.
- **Measure bias, then correct it.** Consistent error is fixable; unmeasured error is not.

## Common questions

### What is sales forecasting?

It is the practice of estimating how much revenue a sales team will close in a set period, usually by combining pipeline data with seller and manager judgment.

### Why are sales forecasts inaccurate?

Common causes are uncalibrated stage probabilities, incomplete CRM data, close dates that slip, seller incentives that bias the call, and no record of past forecast error.

### What are the main sales forecasting methods?

Seller and manager roll-ups, stage-weighted pipeline, historical run-rate, driver-based models and statistical or machine learning models trained on past deals.

### How do you measure forecast accuracy?

Record the forecast at fixed points in the period, compare each with the actual result, and track both the size and the direction of the error over several periods.

Analyst press release from the State of Sales Operations Survey; sample size not stated.

# The Commercial System: What It Is, and Why Most Firms Run Without One

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A commercial system is the connected set of choices, definitions, records and routines a firm uses to decide whom to serve, create demand, reach buyers and win and keep revenue. Most firms run these as four functions with four sets of definitions, and the losses sit at the seams between them. The commercial system is also what The Build Order's brain operates on: the commercial line is where the brain starts because this is where decisions are frequent and graded.

A commercial system is the connected set of choices, definitions, records and routines by which a firm decides whom to serve, creates demand, reaches buyers and wins and keeps revenue. We split it into four parts: Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue. Most firms run all four as activity rather than as a system, with separate definitions and tools, and the money is lost at the seams. The commercial system is also what The Build Order's brain runs on: the brain starts at the commercial line because decisions there are frequent and quickly graded, but it can only learn from a system that has agreed what its words mean.

*Figure: The Build Order: three decisions, four layers on the commercial line, then three gateways before the brain spreads.*

Ask the head of marketing, the head of sales and the finance director at a 100-person firm what a qualified opportunity is. In most firms the answers differ, and the board pack, the pipeline review and the campaign report end up describing different businesses.

That gap is the subject of this series. The Build Order set out how to build a company's brain. The Commercial System is its companion: it covers what the brain operates on.

## Most firms have commercial activity, not a commercial system

Activity can look like a system from inside. There is a CRM, a marketing calendar, a partner list, a pipeline meeting and a pricing sheet. Each works. None was designed with the others in mind.

The problem is old. In 2006 Philip Kotler, Neil Rackham and Suj Krishnaswamy described the tension between sales and marketing in *Harvard Business Review* as both economic, because the two share a budget, and cultural, because they attract different people with different working habits. Fifteen years later, Gartner's 2021 research on revenue operations made the same point in operational terms: functional silos that hand clients from department to department, each with separate technology, people and processes, are a barrier to revenue growth. Gartner predicted that 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a revenue operations model by 2025.

Revenue operations is part of the answer. Forrester defines it as an iterative commercial execution strategy that unifies data, processes, technology and talent across the customer lifecycle. A commercial system starts earlier, with the choices the plumbing serves: market, buyer, position, channel and price. Most companies have a list of tactics rather than a commercial thesis, and the problem is coherence, not effort ([GTM strategy vs tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/)).

## The four parts, and the decisions each owns

We divide the commercial system into four parts. The division follows decisions, not departments. A firm of 30 people may have one person making decisions in all four.

| Part | The question it answers | Main recurring decisions | What it should leave on record | How it is graded |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strategy | Where do we compete, and on what terms? | Segment, ideal customer, position, price architecture, account priorities | The chosen segment and its disqualifiers, the position, the price rules | Win rate and margin in the chosen segment over two to four quarters |
| Growth | How do the right buyers come to know and prefer us? | Campaign spend, content priorities, tests, brand investment | Each test with its hypothesis, budget and result | Qualified pipeline created, cost per qualified opportunity |
| Distribution | Through whom and where do we reach buyers? | Partner selection, channel terms, events, marketplaces | Each partner or channel with its expected and actual contribution | Partner-sourced and partner-influenced revenue, channel cost |
| Revenue | How do we win, price and keep the deal? | Qualification, discount exceptions, proposals, forecast calls, renewals | Every exception and loss with a reason and an owner | Forecast accuracy, realised price, retention |

Two features matter more than the rows. Each part produces something another consumes: Strategy produces the ideal customer profile that Growth targets and Revenue qualifies against ([How to write an ICP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)), and Revenue produces the loss reasons that should change Strategy's position. And every part has decisions that recur, which is what makes the commercial line the right place for a learning system to start.

## Why the system has become harder to run

McKinsey's 2024 B2B Pulse survey of nearly 4,000 decision makers found buyers used an average of ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016, and more than half would likely switch supplier after a poor experience across channels. Each channel creates records in a different tool.

The buying group has grown too. Forrester's 2024 State of Business Buying study, drawing on more than 16,000 global business buyers, found 13 people involved in the average purchase decision, with 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Nearly all purchases, 91%, stalled at some point.

Buyers also spend little of that time with suppliers. Gartner's 2018 survey of 750 B2B buyers in complex purchases found they spent 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier considered. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase.

A buyer who meets the firm through a partner, a webinar, a search result and a seller will notice if the four describe different offers. A commercial system is how a firm makes sure they do not.

## Where the four parts break: the seams

Marketing usually runs campaigns competently, and sales usually runs deals competently. The money leaks where one part hands to another.

| Seam | What should pass across it | What usually passes instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strategy to Growth | A named segment with disqualifiers | A broad description and a list of job titles |
| Growth to Revenue | Opportunities with a buying group attached | Individual leads, scored on activity |
| Distribution to Revenue | Partner-sourced deals, tagged at creation | Deals whose source is argued about at commission time |
| Revenue to Strategy | Loss reasons and price exceptions, with patterns | A closed-lost stage with no reason recorded |

The Growth-to-Revenue seam is the best documented. Forrester research cited in its 2023 analysis of marketing-qualified leads found fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, partly because several leads contribute to one opportunity and attributing a deal to any one of them is meaningless. Firms that pass buying groups rather than leads do better: Forrester found clients who delivered three or more buying-group members to sales saw a 50% increase in conversion from meeting to closed-won.

The Revenue-to-Strategy seam is the least visible. Without recorded loss reasons, positioning and pricing follow the loudest anecdote. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users found 37% reported revenue lost as a direct result of poor data quality, and 76% said less than half of their organisation's CRM data was accurate and complete.

> The losses rarely sit inside a function. They sit where one function hands to another.

## How the commercial system relates to The Build Order

The Build Order argued that the brain should start at the commercial line ([Why the brain starts at the commercial line](https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/)), because decisions that are frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended are where a decision system learns first. Almost every recurring decision in the four-part table passes that test. The commercial system supplies the definitions and decisions; The Build Order supplies the layers that store, connect, record and learn from them.

| Commercial system element | Build Order layer | What breaks if it is missing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Agreed definitions: segment, qualified opportunity, stage, loss reason | Rules the store follows | The CRM holds data nobody can compare |
| Systems of record for accounts, deals, partners and campaigns | Store | Context is spread across inboxes and memory |
| Shared view of each account across the four parts | Context layer | Each function sees a fragment of the buyer |
| Recorded decisions: segment choice, price exceptions, partner terms, forecast calls | Decision record | Outcomes cannot be traced to the judgment that caused them |
| Operating rhythm that reviews outcomes | Learning | The firm repeats its errors at the same cadence |

The order matters. A brain wired onto a commercial line with no shared definitions will reason fluently over inconsistent data. Our explainer sets out the components in more detail ([What is a commercial operating system?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-commercial-operating-system/)), and Part 9 of The Build Order lists the decisions worth recording first ([The ten commercial decisions worth recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)).

This series takes the four parts in order. Parts 2 to 6 cover Strategy: positioning, segment selection, pricing architecture, market maps and the operating rhythm that holds the system together.

## Building one without a reorganisation

A commercial system does not require a new department. In firms of 20 to 500 people it usually requires four things, most of which cost time rather than money.

**One accountable owner.** Someone must own the seams, not just the parts: often the founder in a small firm, a revenue operations lead in a larger one. Specialists without a single named owner of the commercial problem become a roster ([The modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/)).

**One set of definitions.** Segment, qualified opportunity, stage entry criteria, partner-sourced, loss reasons. Agreed once, changed only by a recorded decision.

**One record of decisions.** Recurring commercial decisions, written with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome.

**One rhythm.** A weekly, monthly and quarterly cadence in which the four parts read the same numbers. Part 6 covers it.

A 20-person firm can run all of this in a shared document and a weekly meeting; a 200-person firm needs it in the CRM ([The scale ladder](https://lowob.com/research/the-scale-ladder/)).

Illustrative example: one definition of a qualified opportunity

Decision
:   Replace three competing definitions of a qualified opportunity (marketing's, sales' and the partner team's) with one, tied to the ideal customer profile and a named buying-group contact.

Reason and owner
:   Board reports and pipeline reviews showed pipeline figures that differed by more than a third depending on who prepared them. Agreed by the leadership team; owned by the commercial lead.

What changed
:   Marketing reports opportunities, not leads; partner deals are tagged at creation; the definition is reviewed quarterly and any change is recorded with its reason.

Illustrative: a composite of a 70-person emerging technology firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Design the seams, not just the parts.** Most commercial losses happen where one function hands work to another.
- **Divide by decision, not department.** Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue each own recurring decisions that can be recorded and graded.
- **Agree the words before wiring the tools.** A brain built on inconsistent definitions reasons well over bad inputs.
- **Start small and on the record.** One owner, one set of definitions, one decision record and one rhythm is enough to begin.

Gateway card

### Before you call it a commercial system

- One named owner for the seams between the four parts
- Written definitions for segment, qualified opportunity, stage and loss reason
- Partner and channel source captured when a deal is created
- A required loss reason on every closed-lost deal
- A weekly, monthly and quarterly review that uses the same numbers

## Common questions

### What is a commercial system in business?

It is the connected set of choices, definitions, records and routines a firm uses to decide whom to serve, create demand, reach buyers and win and keep revenue. We divide it into Strategy, Growth, Distribution and Revenue.

### What is the difference between a commercial system and revenue operations?

Revenue operations unifies the data, processes, technology and people behind revenue. A commercial system includes that, plus the strategic choices it serves: segment, position, channel and price.

### Why do sales and marketing disagree on pipeline numbers?

Usually because each uses its own definition of a qualified opportunity. One written definition, changed only on the record, removes most of the disagreement.

### Where should a company start building its commercial system?

With definitions: agree what a qualified opportunity and a loss reason are, then record the recurring decisions that depend on them.

# Claude Is Not Your Intern. Build a Repeatable GTM Workflow

Source: https://lowob.com/research/claude-gtm-operating-system/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-01 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most teams use Claude like an intern with amnesia: a blank chat, a vague request, a fresh start tomorrow. Claude's Projects, Skills and connectors, as documented in November 2026, let a team hold commercial context, run named workflows and set approval rules for actions. The advantage is not access to the model but the context, procedures and learning loop a company builds around it.

Starting from a blank AI chat every day creates a lot of disconnected drafts. The better use is to give Claude maintained product facts, named commercial workflows and a clear human review rule. As documented in November 2026, Claude's Projects hold shared knowledge and instructions, Skills package repeatable procedures, and connectors reach company systems with per-tool approval settings. Those features make the model a context-aware operating layer. The durable advantage is the company-specific context and procedures, because competitors have the same model.

Most teams use Claude like a talented intern with amnesia. They open a blank chat, paste a vague request, receive a competent answer and start again the next day. The model never receives a durable picture of the company, the market, the customer, the sales process or the standard by which good work should be judged. The result is helpful output without organisational advantage.

Claude becomes substantially more useful when it is treated as a context-aware operating layer: a system that works from the same commercial source material, follows repeatable procedures, produces standard outputs and knows when human approval is required. This is not specific to Claude. McKinsey's 2025 State of AI survey found the organisations getting most value from AI were nearly three times as likely as others to have redesigned individual workflows, and more likely to have defined when outputs need human validation. The features below are how one assistant supports that work. Our piece [Which AI assistant, which seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/) covers the choice of tool.

## Start with a GTM context pack

The foundation is not a clever prompt. It is a maintained set of company knowledge.

**Company and product facts.** Define what the business does, who it serves, what the product can and cannot do, and which claims are approved.

**Customers and positioning.** Keep priority segments, buying triggers, objections, qualification criteria, competitor alternatives and evidence in one maintained place.

**Commercial operations.** Document pipeline stages, handoffs, content voice, source rules and required approvals. These should be short, current records that a teammate can verify.

Keep each component short enough to maintain. A stale 80-page brand book is less useful than eight precise documents that reflect the current business. Our explainer on [context engineering](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/) covers why the selection matters more than the volume.

In Claude, this pack lives in a Project. Anthropic's help centre describes Projects as "self-contained workspaces with their own chat histories and knowledge bases", each with its own instructions. On paid plans, retrieval expands project knowledge "by up to 10x" when content nears the context limit. On Team and Enterprise plans, a project can be shared with named people or the whole organisation, with "can view" or "can edit" rights. That last point matters: only the people who own the facts should be able to change them.

| Context pack component | Where it lives in Claude | Owner | Review cadence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Product facts and approved claims | Project knowledge | Product lead | On every release |
| Segments, triggers, objections, evidence | Project knowledge | Commercial lead | Monthly |
| Pipeline stages and handoffs | Project knowledge | Revenue operations | Quarterly |
| Voice, source rules, approval rules | Project instructions | Marketing lead | Quarterly |
| Named workflows | Skills | Workflow owner | When the output changes |

Feature descriptions are as documented by Anthropic in November 2026; plan availability changes, so check the current help centre before rollout.

## Turn repeated work into named workflows

Once the context is stable, identify tasks the team performs repeatedly. Give each workflow a name, a required input, a sequence, a defined output and an approval point.

Start with the work that repeats every week: a market signal brief, an account research dossier, sales-call preparation or analysis of customer conversations. Campaign reviews and competitor changes can use the same approach once the first workflows are reliable.

For a priority account dossier, Claude should not merely "research the account". The workflow should specify what matters.

| Dossier field | What it contains | Verification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Company priorities | Stated goals from filings, results or leadership statements | Source link required |
| Current initiatives | Projects, launches, hiring patterns | Source link required |
| Relevant executives | Names and roles tied to the likely problem | Checked against the company's own site |
| Likely problem and buying trigger | The hypothesis, labelled as one | Marked "inference" |
| Existing stack and partner overlap | Known tools and shared partners | Source or "unknown" |
| Risk factors | Reasons the account may not buy | Required, even if short |
| Opening thesis | One sentence the account owner could test | Approved by the account owner |
| Open questions | What needs verifying before outreach | Listed, not guessed |

That consistency makes the output comparable across accounts and useful to a team.

Claude's Skills feature is built for this. Anthropic describes skills as "folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically", loaded by progressive disclosure so only the relevant skill enters the context. On Team and Enterprise plans, owners can provision a skill for every member, so the dossier runs the same way for every seller. Skills require code execution to be enabled.

## Separate generation from decision-making

An operating system needs boundaries.

| Claude can | A person decides |
| --- | --- |
| Propose priority accounts | A commercial lead approves the prioritisation |
| Draft outbound language | The account owner verifies the premise and sends it |
| Identify patterns in calls | The team decides whether they justify repositioning |
| Produce a campaign brief | A person approves claims, budget and audience |

The principle is simple:

*Automate preparation and pattern recognition before automating consequential decisions.*

This keeps the system fast without allowing plausible but unverified output to enter the market as fact. On **lowob**'s autonomy dial, most GTM work belongs at level 1 (draft) or level 2 (act with approval). Our piece [Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out the rule.

Connectors are where the boundary is enforced. Anthropic's documentation says connectors "let Claude access your apps and services, retrieve your data, and take actions", and custom connectors can reach any service that supports the Model Context Protocol. "Claude inherits each person's permissions from the connected service", so it cannot see a CRM record the user cannot. On Team and Enterprise plans, admins can set each tool to always allow, needs approval or blocked, with read-only and write or delete tools grouped separately, and users cannot override those limits. A sensible default is read-only tools allowed and every write tool set to needs approval. Our explainer on [AI connectors](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-connector/) covers the security questions.

> The durable advantage is not access to Claude. Competitors have that too. It is the context, procedures and learning loop built around it.

## Connect the commercial loop

The highest-value design is not a collection of independent prompts. It is a loop.

Market research identifies a new buying signal. That signal changes account priority. Account conversations produce objections and language. Those conversations update the messaging system. The revised message informs content and campaigns. Campaign and pipeline performance create new evidence. The evidence updates the next market brief.

Claude can help maintain continuity across this loop because its role is not limited to drafting. It can compare new inputs with the established context, flag contradictions, identify missing evidence and prepare the next decision. The loop only works if someone writes outcomes back into the project knowledge. A context pack that is never updated becomes the stale brand book it replaced.

## The minimum viable Claude GTM system

A small company can begin with four workflows, each a Skill working from the same Project.

| When | Workflow | Output | Approved by |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Monday | Market and account signal brief | One page of changes, each with a source | Commercial lead |
| Before calls | Standard preparation dossier | The dossier fields above | Account owner |
| After calls | Notes to objections, next steps and CRM-ready fields | Structured fields plus messaging insights | Account owner, before CRM write |
| Friday | What changed in market, pipeline and customer language | Recommended experiments | Team review |

That alone can improve the quality and continuity of a small GTM team without pretending the model should operate the business autonomously. Our piece on [the commercial operating rhythm](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-operating-rhythm/) shows how the weekly cadence connects to monthly and quarterly reviews.

## lowob takeaways

- **Context before prompts.** A short, owned, current context pack in a shared Project.
- **Name the workflows.** Input, sequence, output and approval point, packaged so every seller runs the same one.
- **Set approvals in the connector.** Read tools allowed; write tools need approval.
- **Write outcomes back.** The loop is what competitors cannot copy.

## Common questions

### How do I use Claude for go-to-market work?

Put a maintained context pack of product facts, positioning and commercial rules in a Claude Project, package recurring tasks such as account dossiers as Skills, and keep claims, prioritisation, spend and outreach approvals with people.

### What is the difference between Claude Projects and Skills?

Projects are workspaces with their own knowledge and instructions; Skills are packaged procedures with instructions and scripts that Claude loads when a task needs them. A project holds what the team knows, a skill holds how a task is done.

### Is it safe to connect Claude to a CRM?

Connectors inherit each user's permissions in the source system, and on Team and Enterprise plans admins can require approval for write actions. Start with read-only access and add write tools with approval required.

### Should Claude send outbound emails automatically?

Not as a starting point. Let it draft and prepare; the account owner verifies the premise and sends. Automate preparation before consequential decisions.

## Sources and notes

# SOC 2 for AI Vendors: What It Covers and What It Does Not

Source: https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-01 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: SOC 2 is an attestation report on a service organisation's controls against the AICPA Trust Services Criteria. For AI vendors it covers security, access and change management well, and model behaviour poorly. In October 2026 the AICPA proposed revised criteria with AI points of focus, effective for engagements from 31 December 2027 if approved.

SOC 2 is an independent auditor's report on whether a service organisation's controls meet the AICPA Trust Services Criteria for security and, optionally, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. For an AI vendor it tells you a good deal about access control, change management and incident handling, and very little about whether the model is accurate, unbiased or well monitored. The current criteria date from 2017; the AICPA proposed a revision with AI-specific points of focus in October 2026.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What a SOC 2 report is

SOC 2 is an attestation, not a certification. A CPA firm examines the vendor's description of its system and tests its controls against criteria set by the AICPA's Assurance Services Executive Committee. The output is a report, generally restricted to customers and prospects under NDA, with the auditor's opinion, the system description and the tests performed with results.

| Report | What it says | Use in procurement |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SOC 2 Type 1 | Controls were suitably designed at a specified date | Acceptable for a new vendor, with a Type 2 to follow |
| SOC 2 Type 2 | Controls were suitably designed and operated effectively over a period | The standard ask for any vendor holding client data |
| SOC 3 | Same subject as SOC 2, without test detail | Public marketing document; not enough for diligence |

Security is the only mandatory category. Processing integrity is the category closest to asking whether outputs are complete and accurate.

## What it covers and what it does not

| Covered well | Covered only if scoped or chosen by the auditor | Not covered |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Logical access, including admin access to customer data | Processing integrity of model outputs | Whether the model is accurate for your use |
| Change management for code and infrastructure | Model drift detection and accuracy monitoring | Bias and fairness of outputs |
| Incident response and monitoring | Inference logging and model lineage | Training data provenance, unless chosen |
| Vendor management of subservice organisations | Controls over AI agents acting without a human request | Compliance with the EU AI Act or other AI law |
| Encryption and data retention commitments | Unsanctioned AI tools used by vendor staff | Explainability of individual decisions |

Two scoping details matter more for AI vendors than for ordinary SaaS. The first is the model provider. Most AI vendors call a third-party model, and that provider may be a subservice organisation rather than a simple supplier. Reports often carve it out of scope, which means the report covers the vendor's controls over its AI dependency, not the model provider's own controls. The second is the system description: an AI feature launched after the audit period may not appear at all.

A Cloud Security Alliance research note in August 2026 found that auditors were requesting AI evidence ad hoc and inconsistently, and that a clean SOC 2 report could include no tested controls for drift or model accuracy.

## The proposed 2027 criteria

On 28 October 2026 the AICPA published an exposure draft of revised Trust Services Criteria, the first major overhaul since 2017. A summary by the audit firm A-LIGN reports that the common criteria would consolidate from 33 to 20, and that AI appears as points of focus under 17 criteria rather than as a separate AI criterion. Proposed additions include access for AI agents and accounts, unsanctioned AI tools, model drift and data poisoning in risk assessment, and AI models, APIs and plugins as third-party components. If approved, the criteria would apply to engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027, with early adoption allowed.

Until then, treat a SOC 2 report as evidence of operational hygiene, and ask separately about AI.

## How to read an AI vendor's SOC 2

| Check | What to look for |
| --- | --- |
| Report type and period | Type 2, period ending within the last 12 months, or a bridge letter |
| Categories in scope | Security plus confidentiality; processing integrity if outputs drive decisions |
| System description | The AI features you are buying are named and described |
| Subservice organisations | Which model providers are carved out, and what the vendor monitors |
| Exceptions | Any failed tests, and management's response |
| Complementary user controls | What you must do yourself for the controls to work |

Then ask the questions SOC 2 does not answer: how outputs are evaluated, how drift is detected, what is retained, and whether the vendor holds ISO/IEC 42001 certification. **lowob**'s view is that the buyer's own record (which AI uses are approved, at what autonomy level and with what result) is what turns a vendor report into a governed decision.

## lowob takeaways

- **SOC 2 tests controls, not models.** It is strong on access and change, weak on accuracy and bias.
- **Ask for Type 2 with the right scope.** Confidentiality and processing integrity matter for AI vendors.
- **Read the carve-outs.** The model provider is often outside the report.
- **Watch the 2027 criteria.** AI points of focus are proposed but not yet final.

## Common questions

### Does SOC 2 cover AI?

Only partly. The current criteria have no AI-specific requirements, so model behaviour is tested only if the auditor includes it. Proposed 2027 criteria add AI points of focus.

### What is the difference between SOC 2 Type 1 and Type 2?

Type 1 assesses whether controls are suitably designed at a point in time. Type 2 also tests whether they operated effectively over a period, typically six months or more.

### Is SOC 2 or ISO 42001 better for AI vendors?

They answer different questions. SOC 2 attests to security and operational controls; ISO/IEC 42001 certifies an AI management system. Enterprise buyers increasingly ask for both.

### When do the new SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria take effect?

If approved, for engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027, with early adoption permitted. Comments on the exposure draft close on 15 January 2027.

## In the news

- 28 October 2026 · AICPA and CIMA[AICPA proposes updated SOC 2 trust services criteria](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-10-28-aicpa-proposes-updated-soc-2-trust-services-criteria)An exposure draft, so the criteria can still change. AI vendors in security review should know it is coming.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

## Sources and notes

- [AICPA, 2017 Trust Services Criteria with revised points of focus 2022](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/resources/article/2017-trust-services-criteria-with-revised-points-of-focus-2022), posted 30 September 2023. Primary criteria source.
- [AICPA, AICPA proposes update of SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria](https://www.aicpa-cima.com/news/article/aicpa-proposes-update-of-soc-2-r-trust-services-criteria-to-enhance-the-relevance-usability-and-value-of-cpas-reports), 28 October 2026. Primary announcement; exposure draft, not final.

Report types; AI providers as subservice organisations.

# From Funded Account to Lifetime Value

Source: https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Revenue in fintech is a chain from acquisition to lifetime value. The two leaks that break it are accounts that never fund and accounts that fund once and go dormant. Measure the chain per channel, not blended, put fraud losses and compliance cost in the same table as revenue, and report active funded accounts as the growth number.

Revenue in fintech is a chain from acquisition to lifetime value, and the two leaks that break it are accounts that never fund and accounts that fund once and go dormant. Losses are the third line most models leave out: LexisNexis Risk Solutions estimates that each dollar of fraud loss now costs US financial services firms $5.75 in total, up from $4.00 in 2021. Build the chain per channel, not blended, because channels that cost the same to acquire through can retain very differently.

*This is an operating note on how to measure a business, not financial advice.*

## Name your revenue model

Fintech revenue per funded account comes from a short list of sources. Which ones apply depends on the product, so name them and write down the rate each earns.

| Revenue line | Applies if you | What sets the rate | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Interchange | Issue cards | Network rates and, in the US, whether the issuing bank is capped | Rule changes; the issuing partner's size |
| Transaction or FX fees | Move money | Your pricing and the corridor | Competitor price cuts |
| Interest margin | Lend | Cost of funds and credit losses | Loss rate by cohort |
| Subscription | Sell software to businesses | Plan mix | Downgrades hidden by new sales |
| Interest on balances | Hold customer funds and earn on them | Rates and the share passed to customers | Rate cycle |

Interchange shows why the detail matters. In the US, Regulation II caps debit interchange for issuers with $10 billion or more in assets at 21 cents plus 5 basis points of the transaction, plus a 1 cent fraud-prevention adjustment. Issuers below $10 billion are exempt from the cap. The Federal Reserve proposed in 2023 to lower the cap to 14.4 cents plus 4.0 basis points and a 1.3 cent adjustment; we could not confirm whether a final rule had taken effect at the time of writing. A card programme's revenue per account therefore depends on which bank issues the card, and can change with a rule.

Most products have one primary line and one or two secondary lines. A deck that says "multiple revenue streams" without a per-account figure is hiding that the lines have not been measured. [Raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) made the same point to investors. This piece makes it to you.

## The unit economics chain

Every funded account travels a chain. Each link has a cost or a yield. The table is the whole model.

| Link | What you measure | Typical leak |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acquire | Cost per sign-up, by channel | Paying for sign-ups that never verify |
| Verify and onboard | Cost per verified account, pass rate | Drop-off at identity checks, manual review cost |
| Activate | Share of verified accounts with a first funded transaction | Accounts that never fund |
| Earn | Monthly revenue per funded account | Low usage, wrong product mix |
| Retain | 30, 90 and 365-day retention of funded accounts | Dormancy after first use |
| Lifetime value | Revenue per funded account over its retained life, less losses and compliance cost | Unallocated losses hiding the real number |

Run the numbers per channel, not blended. [Distribute through whoever already holds the customer](https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/) showed that a partner channel and a paid channel can have the same cost per funded account and very different retention. The academic evidence points the same way. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte tracked about 10,000 customers of a German bank over 33 months. Referred customers had a roughly 18% lower hazard of leaving, with 82.0% retained at the end against 79.2% for others, and were at least 16% more valuable over six years. A blended figure would have hidden that difference.

> If the board asks for a growth number, give them funded accounts that are still active. That is the only growth that compounds.

## The two leaks

The first leak is accounts that never fund. They passed verification, they cost money, and they sit at zero. The cause is usually friction between "approved" and "first transaction": a funding method that does not work with the customer's bank, a limit that is too low, or no reason to move money today.

The friction starts before approval. Signicat's 2022 survey of 7,600 consumers in 14 European countries found 68% had abandoned a financial application in the previous year, the highest since the study began in 2016. The most cited reason, at 38%, was lacking the right identity credentials. Average time before abandoning was just under 19 minutes. This is vendor research from an identity verification company, but it shows how much of the chain is lost before an account exists.

Fix: measure time from verification to first funding. Set a target in days. Anything beyond it gets a prompt, a person or a smaller first step.

The second leak is dormancy. An account funds once, does the thing it came for, and goes quiet. It still counts as a funded account. It earns nothing. This is the hidden churn in fintech, because nobody closes the account. They just stop.

Define dormant in your product's terms, for example no transaction in 60 days. Then report funded accounts and active funded accounts as two numbers. The gap between them is your real retention problem. Our explainer on [customer churn](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/) covers the formulas.

## Activation and habit

Activation is the first funded transaction. Habit is the tenth.

Design for both. Activation needs the smallest possible first step: a low minimum, a pre-filled funding route, a clear reason to act now. Habit needs a recurring reason: a payroll date, a monthly transfer, a card used for one specific category of spend.

Find the behaviour that predicts retention in your own data. It is usually a single action done twice within the first month. Build onboarding to get customers to that action, and measure the share who reach it.

Illustrative example: two channels, one acquisition cost

Decision
:   Shift budget from a paid social channel to an accounting-software partner, although both cost about the same per funded account.

Reason and owner
:   Cohort reporting by channel showed the partner's funded accounts were still active at 365 days at a much higher rate, with lower fraud losses per account. Owned by the head of growth, with finance confirming the loss allocation.

What changed
:   Lifetime value per funded account, net of losses and compliance cost, rose for the blended book, and payback shortened, without any change to the product.

Illustrative: a composite of a small-business payments product, built from patterns across engagements. No figures are from a real company.

## Cross-sell, losses and compliance

Once an account is funded and active, the main lever on lifetime value is the second product. A customer who trusts you with payments will consider you for savings, lending or FX, and the cost to sell that second product is a fraction of acquisition cost. Measure products per funded account, and track which first product leads to which second one. [Trust is the product](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/) argued that trust is the product. Cross-sell is where that trust pays back.

Then come the lines most founders leave out. Fraud and credit losses, allocated per funded account by channel and cohort. Compliance cost per account: monitoring, manual review, reporting. The LexisNexis True Cost of Fraud study, a 2025 survey of 507 risk and fraud executives, found each dollar of fraud cost US financial services firms $5.75, up from $4.00 in 2021, and that 30% of their fraud occurred at new account creation. That last figure ties losses directly to acquisition channels. A channel with cheap acquisition and high loss rates is not cheap. You only see it when losses sit in the same table as revenue.

## What to report monthly

[Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) made the general case. In fintech, the monthly report has eight lines.

| Line | Cut by |
| --- | --- |
| Funded accounts, new and total active | Channel, cohort |
| Activation rate from verified to funded | Channel |
| Retention of funded accounts at 30, 90 and 365 days | Cohort and channel |
| Revenue per funded account | Product |
| Loss rate | Channel, cohort |
| Cost per funded account | Channel |
| Payback period | Channel |
| Products per funded account | First product |

Stop reporting downloads, sign-ups and total accounts. They are inputs, not outcomes, and they inflate every number downstream. Our [Commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) covers how to define each measure once and reconcile it to finance, and [LTV:CAC vs CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/ltv-cac-vs-cac-payback/) covers which ratio to lead with.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name every revenue line with a rate per funded account.** Check which rules and partners set each rate.
- **Build the chain per channel.** Channels with the same acquisition cost can retain very differently.
- **Measure time from verification to first funding.** Set a target in days and intervene when it slips.
- **Report active funded accounts separately.** Dormancy is churn that nobody announces.
- **Put losses and compliance cost in the same table as revenue.** Allocate them by channel and cohort.

## Common questions

### What are the biggest revenue leaks in a fintech app?

Accounts that pass verification but never fund, and accounts that fund once and go dormant. Dormancy is hidden churn because nobody closes the account; they just stop.

### How do you calculate lifetime value for a fintech customer?

Revenue per funded account over its retained life, less fraud and credit losses and compliance cost. Run it per channel and cohort, not blended.

### What metrics should a fintech report to its board each month?

Funded accounts new and total active, activation rate from verified to funded, retention at 30, 90 and 365 days by cohort and channel, revenue per funded account, loss rate, cost per funded account by channel, payback by channel and products per funded account.

### How much does debit card interchange earn a US fintech?

It depends on the issuing bank. Regulation II caps debit interchange for issuers with $10 billion or more in assets at 21 cents plus 5 basis points and a 1 cent fraud adjustment; smaller issuers are exempt. A 2023 proposal would lower the cap.

## Sources and notes

- [Federal Reserve, Debit Card Interchange Fees and Routing, proposed rule](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/FR-2023-11-14/html/2023-24034.htm), Federal Register, 14 November 2023. Primary source for the current cap and the proposal; final status not confirmed for this article.
- [LexisNexis Risk Solutions, Every dollar lost to fraud costs North America's financial institutions $5](https://risk.lexisnexis.com/about-us/press-room/press-release/20250910-fraud-multiplier), 10 September 2025. Vendor research; survey of 507 executives by KS&R, April to May 2025.
- [The Fintech Times, 68% of European consumers abandon financial applications during onboarding, finds Signicat](https://thefintechtimes.com/68-of-european-consumers-abandon-financial-applications-during-onboarding-finds-signicat/), 1 April 2022. Vendor survey of 7,600 consumers in 14 countries; older than the other sources.
- [Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte, Referral Programs and Customer Value](https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Schmitt-Skiera-vandenBulte-2011-Referral-Programs-Customer-Value.pdf), Journal of Marketing, 2011. Academic study of one German bank, 2006 to 2008.
- The revenue table, unit economics chain, monthly report and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

Pull last quarter's verified accounts and split them by channel into never funded, funded and active, and funded and dormant. If you cannot produce that split, make it the first report you build.
