# What Is Connected TV Advertising? Should You Buy It?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-connected-tv-advertising/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-30 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Connected TV is television watched through an internet connection, with advertising bought and measured like digital media. The IAB forecast US CTV spend growing 13.8% in 2026, and CTV was about 40% of programmatic spend in the ANA's Q4 2025 benchmark. It is best entered programmatically, measured by lift rather than clicks, and worth buying once a company has a working acquisition motion, a measurable brand constraint and confirmation its category is permitted.

Connected TV (CTV) is television watched through an internet connection: streaming services, smart TV apps and devices plugged into a screen. Advertising on it is bought and measured like digital media, with audiences, frequency caps and reporting, while being seen like television, on a large screen with sound on. It is growing quickly: the IAB's 2026 Outlook forecast US CTV ad spend up 13.8%. It is best entered programmatically, measured by lift rather than clicks, and worth buying once a company has a working acquisition motion, a measurable brand constraint and confirmation that its category is permitted.

It has grown quickly because audiences moved, and because it lets companies that could never afford broadcast television buy the screen in small amounts. The IAB's January 2026 Outlook Study, based on about 200 US buyers, forecast CTV spend growing 13.8% in 2026, behind only social media. Its May 2026 digital video report put CTV growth at 11% and total US digital video spend above $80 billion, more than 60% of all TV and video ad spend for the first time.

## How it is bought

| Route | How it works | Suits | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Direct from a streaming service or broadcaster | Insertion order with the service's ad sales team | Large budgets wanting specific programmes | Minimum spends; one service only |
| Platform self-serve or managed | The streaming platform's own buying tools | Small tests on one platform | Category policies applied by the platform |
| Programmatic through a DSP | CTV inventory across many apps and services, with the same audience, verification and optimisation tools used for display and video | Most mid-sized buyers | Inventory transparency and fraud on open routes |

Programmatic is where most mid-sized buyers end up, because it allows small tests, audience definitions the buyer controls, and inventory across services rather than a commitment to one. The market has largely moved to curated deals. In the ANA's fourth-quarter 2025 programmatic benchmark, built with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia, CTV was about 40% of total programmatic spend and private marketplaces accounted for 100% of CTV transactions.

Curated does not mean transparent. The IAB's 2026 Digital Video Ad Spend and Strategy report, a survey of 360 US buyers, found that even on the routes buyers trust most (publisher-direct deals, programmatic guaranteed and publisher self-service) 43% had only some or no confidence in where their ads ran. On the open exchange only 33% had high confidence, and 56% of those who mistrusted it cited fraud. Our [guide to programmatic](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-programmatic-advertising/) covers the supply chain standards that help a buyer check who is selling.

## How it is measured

Impressions and completed views are the basic units. CTV ads are usually unskippable, so completion rates are high and say little. Viewability is harder than on the web: the ANA's benchmark noted that server-side ad insertion and limited signals led to more CTV impressions being classed as non-viewable, because the measurement could not confirm them, not necessarily because nobody watched.

More useful measures connect exposure to behaviour:

| Measure | What it shows | Weakness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Household visits and conversions | Whether households that saw the ad later visited or bought, matched through IP address or device graphs | Matching degrades as IP signals weaken; correlation, not cause |
| Branded search and direct traffic lift | Whether people looked for the company during flights | Noisy at small budgets |
| Geographic incrementality test | Whether outcomes rose in matched regions where ads ran versus where they did not | Needs enough budget and regions to read |

Attribution is weaker than on click-based channels because nobody clicks a television. The IAB found 39% of buyers named the lack of a direct click-through as a barrier to lower-funnel CTV, and 38% the need for a second device. The honest measurement question is whether outcomes rose where the ads ran compared with where they did not. Our pieces on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) and [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) set out how to design a geographic test that produces a decision rather than a debate.

> CTV amplifies a working acquisition motion. It does not create one.

## What it costs

CTV costs meaningfully more per thousand impressions than display or social video, reflecting the screen, the attention and the completion. Minimum tests that produce a readable signal are larger than for other channels, because the effect is measured at the household and geography level rather than per click. The IAB found small and mid-sized buyers were more likely than large ones to report high cost-per-acquisition concerns, 44% against 28%, which is what that minimum looks like from a smaller budget.

## When it makes sense, and when it does not

| Buy CTV when | Do not buy it yet when |
| --- | --- |
| The product can be understood in fifteen or thirty seconds | The company has not found a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost |
| The company knows its cost per outcome on other channels and wants reach beyond them | The budget cannot support a test large enough to read |
| Brand recognition is a measured constraint: visitors convert poorly because they have never heard of the company | The category is restricted on the streaming platforms in the target geographies |
| The audience can be defined and matched, so the buy is not paying for households that could never be customers | The only measure available is completed views |

The third row on the left deserves a number before it is used as a reason. Our piece on [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers share of search and shortlist rate, two ways to show that recognition, not interest, is what is holding conversion back.

## For restricted categories specifically

Streaming services apply their own category policies, often stricter than the open web, and programmatic CTV inventory varies widely in what it will carry. Roku's self-serve Ads Manager is a useful example of the pattern. It requires prior approval for any cryptocurrency ad and limits approvals to items such as licensed exchanges and mining hardware in the US; it bans ads for individual securities; it requires credit, loan and insurance advertisers to show licensing on request; and it prohibits healthcare and pharmaceutical ads through the self-serve platform. Direct and programmatic deals with the same platform can carry different rules.

Before planning any CTV spend, confirm which services and exchanges will run the category, with what disclaimers, in which geographies. Where it is open, CTV can be a thinly bid channel for reviewed categories, for the usual reason: the competitors who would crowd it are in the same review queue. Our piece on [thin bidding](https://lowob.com/research/thin-bidding/) explains why that matters.

## lowob takeaways

- **CTV is TV bought like digital.** Programmatic access makes it available to mid-sized budgets.
- **Curated is not the same as transparent.** Ask where the ads ran, even on private marketplace deals.
- **Measure lift, not clicks or completions.** Geographic tests answer the only question that matters.
- **It amplifies; it does not create.** Find a working channel first.
- **Check category rules first.** Streaming platforms often restrict finance, crypto and health.

## Common questions

### What is connected TV advertising?

Advertising on television watched through an internet connection, such as streaming services, smart TV apps and plugged-in devices. It is bought and measured like digital media but seen like television, on a large screen with sound on.

### How do you measure CTV ad performance?

Connect exposure to behaviour: visits and conversions from households that saw the ad, lift in branded search and direct traffic during flights, and incrementality tests across matched geographies. The honest question is whether outcomes rose where ads ran compared with where they did not.

### How much is spent on CTV advertising?

The IAB's January 2026 Outlook forecast US CTV ad spend growing 13.8% in 2026; its May 2026 video report put CTV growth at 11% within a US digital video market above $80 billion.

### Can fintech or crypto companies advertise on CTV?

Often only with restrictions. Roku's self-serve policy, for example, requires prior approval for crypto ads, limits them to the US and bans ads for individual securities. Confirm each service's rules by geography before planning spend.

- [IAB, US digital video ad spend to surpass $80B in 2026](https://www.iab.com/news/u-s-digital-video-ad-spend-to-surpass-80b-in-2026/), 5 May 2026. Trade body forecast with Advertiser Perceptions and Guideline; later figure than the Outlook.
- [PPC Land, IAB: 43% of CTV buyers doubt where their ads actually ran](https://ppc.land/iab-43-of-ctv-buyers-doubt-where-their-ads-actually-ran/), July 2026. Trade press summary of the IAB's full 2026 video report; survey of 360 US buyers spending at least $1 million a year.
- [ANA, Q4 2025 Programmatic Transparency Benchmark](https://www.ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2026-02-programatic), 25 February 2026. Press release; built with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia; sample size not stated.

# Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain

Source: https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: The CRM is the store layer of the brain: necessary, not sufficient. Most CRM data is not ready for AI, and agents now act on its errors automatically. The fix is a short list of fields the brain needs, a time-boxed clean-up, automatic capture of activity, and a required reason for every lost deal.

A CRM is the brain's store: it holds what happened, and it does not reason about it. That makes it necessary and insufficient. Most CRM data is not ready for AI, and the risk has changed: an agent now acts on bad records automatically, before anyone reviews the decision. Before the brain can use the CRM, it needs a short set of fields kept current, a time-boxed clean-up, activity captured without typing, and a required reason for every deal that is won or lost.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

There is a tempting shortcut in the enterprise brain conversation: treat the CRM as the brain, add an assistant, and call it done. Vendors encourage it, because every system of record now positions itself as the place agents should start. The shortcut fails for a simple reason. A CRM stores what happened. It does not connect the dots, weigh which record is current, or learn from outcomes. It is memory, and often unreliable memory.

That does not make it unimportant. On the commercial line the CRM is the most structured data most firms own, and it is where outcomes (won, lost, renewed) already sit. The brain needs it. It just needs it in better shape than it usually is.

## The state of CRM data

The evidence on CRM data quality has been consistent for years, and the arrival of AI has made it more urgent.

| Source | Sample | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Validity, State of CRM Data 2026 | 500 marketers, July 2026 | 91% say data readiness is critical for AI; only 21% say their CRM data is very well prepared |
| Validity, State of CRM Data 2026 | Same | 62% say poor CRM data probably or definitely cost revenue, through missed renewals, inaccurate forecasts and lost deals |
| Validity, State of CRM Data Management 2025 | 602 CRM users and stakeholders | 37% report revenue lost as a direct consequence of poor data quality |
| Validity, State of CRM Data Management 2025 | Same | 37% report staff fabricating data to satisfy decision-makers |
| Salesforce, State of Sales 2026 | 4,000+ sales professionals | Sellers spend about 40% of their time selling; junior sellers lose about two hours a week to manual data entry |

The last two rows explain the first three. Data entry is tedious, it is done by the people with the least time, and when it is reviewed for the sake of a meeting, people fill fields to satisfy the review rather than to describe reality.

### Why agents raise the stakes

Bad CRM data used to produce bad reports, which humans could question. An agent acts on the record directly: it scores a lead, drafts an outreach sequence, flags an account for renewal or reallocates attention. As the MarTech summary of Validity's 2026 findings put it, errors that once meant a manual clean-up can now be acted on automatically, before anyone reviews the decision. The quality bar for the store rises the moment an agent can read it.

## What the brain needs from the CRM

The brain does not need every field. It needs a small set kept current, because those are the fields the reasoning layer reads and the learning layer writes back to.

| Field | Why the brain needs it | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account | The unit everything else attaches to | Duplicates and subsidiaries recorded separately |
| Contacts and roles | Who decides, who influences, who has left | Departed contacts never removed |
| Stage | Where the opportunity actually is | Deals left "open" long after they died |
| Owner | One accountable person | Shared ownership, or the original owner after they moved on |
| Source | Where the opportunity came from, from a fixed list | Free-text sources nobody can group |
| Next step and date | What happens next, and when | Blank, or a date long passed |
| Value | What is at stake | Placeholder figures never updated |
| Reason won or lost | Why the deal moved or died | The field everyone skips |

The last row matters most. A closed-lost deal without a reason is an outcome with nothing to attach it to. In *The field that makes a record a judgment* we argued that one field, recorded at the moment of decision, is what turns a log into something a system can learn from. On the commercial line, that field is the reason.

> A closed-lost deal with no reason is an outcome with nothing to attach it to.

## A one-week clean-up

Most firms do not need a migration. They need a time-boxed clean-up with clear rules, run by the build owner from Gateway 0.

1. **Day 1: export and measure.** Export accounts, contacts and open opportunities. Count duplicates, open deals with no activity in 90 days, blank next steps and blank loss reasons. These four counts are your baseline.
2. **Day 2: merge and archive.** Merge duplicate accounts. Archive contacts who have left. Close or archive opportunities with no activity in 180 days, with the reason "stale".
3. **Day 3: fix the lists.** Replace free-text sources with a fixed list of eight to twelve values. Create a closed-lost reason list of six to ten options plus a short note.
4. **Day 4: switch on capture.** Turn on email and calendar sync so meetings and correspondence are recorded without typing. Confirm which mailboxes are excluded.
5. **Day 5: set the rules.** Make the loss reason required. Agree what counts as an active client and a qualified opportunity (Part 5 covers these definitions). Rerun the four counts.

The before-and-after counts are the first measurable return of the build, and they are worth reporting. Validity's 2025 survey found over half of organisations still rely on manual clean-up efforts; the aim here is one deliberate clean-up followed by rules and capture that keep it clean.

## Choosing or keeping a CRM

If the firm already has a CRM, the default is to keep it and clean it. Migration is expensive, and the problems above are behavioural rather than technical. If the firm has no CRM, or one nobody opens, choose by how people will use it.

| Test | What to check | Why it matters for the brain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic capture | Native email and calendar sync | Activity recorded without typing |
| Speed | A deal update in under a minute, including on a phone | Senior people keep it current |
| Required fields | Can loss reasons be mandatory without workarounds? | The outcome gets a reason |
| Connectors | Native connectors or an MCP server for your assistant | The wiring layer can reach it |
| Export | Full export of records and history in a documented format | The record stays portable at renewal |

The export test comes from *Buy context, own judgment*: if a tool holds decision history you cannot take with you, it holds part of your judgment hostage.

## What the CRM will never do

Even clean, the CRM will not tell you why the firm decided to pursue one pitch and pass on another, whether that decision was right, or what the three most similar past deals have in common. Those questions need the record and the reasoning layers. The CRM's job is to be the reliable store they read from and the place outcomes land. That is a more modest role than vendors suggest and a more important one than most firms treat it as.

Illustrative example: a CRM clean-up week

Decision
:   Run a one-week clean-up instead of migrating to a new CRM.

Reason and owner
:   A baseline showed hundreds of duplicate accounts and most lost deals with no reason recorded; the CRM was under-used rather than unsuitable. Owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   Duplicates merged, stale deals archived, loss reasons made mandatory, email and calendar sync switched on. The four baseline counts are reported monthly.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **The CRM is the store, not the brain.** Necessary for the brain and never sufficient on its own.
- **Agents raise the bar.** Errors that once skewed a report can now trigger an action.
- **Eight fields, kept current.** And the loss reason matters most.
- **Clean once, then capture automatically.** A time-boxed clean-up plus email and calendar sync beats repeated manual effort.

Gateway card

### Store ready for the brain

- Baseline counts taken: duplicates, stale deals, blank next steps, blank loss reasons
- Duplicates merged and stale deals archived
- Fixed lists for source and loss reason
- Loss reason required
- Email and calendar capture switched on

## Common questions

### Is a CRM an AI brain?

No. A CRM is the store layer: it records what happened. A brain also needs wiring to other systems, a record of decisions and reasons, a reasoning layer that connects them, and outcomes written back.

### Is my CRM data ready for AI agents?

Probably not yet. In Validity's 2026 survey only 21% of marketers said their CRM data was very well prepared for AI. Check duplicates, stale opportunities, blank next steps and missing loss reasons before connecting an agent.

### Which CRM fields matter most for AI?

Account, contacts and roles, stage, owner, source, next step and date, value, and the reason a deal was won or lost. The loss reason is the field most often blank and the one that matters most for learning.

### Should we migrate CRMs before adding AI?

Usually not. Most CRM problems are behavioural. A one-week clean-up, required loss reasons and automatic email and calendar capture recover most of the value without a migration.

## Sources and notes

- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/). Survey of 500 B2B and B2C marketers at organisations with 100+ employees, July 2026.
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2025](https://validity.com/resource-center/the-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2025), and coverage in [MediaPost](https://www.mediapost.com/publications/article/407342/crm-data-drag-systems-are-not-delivering-and-bra.html). Survey of 602 CRM users in the US, UK and Australia.
- [Salesforce, State of Sales 2026](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/state-of-sales-report-announcement-2026/), with regional detail via [Dynamic Business](https://dynamicbusiness.com/topics/news/high-performing-sales-teams-are-1-7x-more-likely-to-use-ai-agents). Vendor-run survey.
- The field list and clean-up plan are **lowob**'s working method for mid-size commercial teams.

## Next move

Export your open opportunities today and count how many have no next step and how many lost deals have no reason. Those two numbers are the honest starting point for any AI layer on top.

# What Is Retargeting, and Why It Overclaims Credit

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retargeting/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Retargeting shows ads to people who already know the company, which makes it cheap and makes its attributed results unreliable. Field experiments find real but modest lift: one retailer's retargeting raised purchases by about 11%. Exclude people who converted, cap frequency, shorten windows, test with a holdout, and remember that email is retargeting you own.

Retargeting, also called remarketing, is advertising shown to people who have already visited a website, used an app or otherwise identified themselves to a company. It is cheap, it reports extraordinary results, and it is the channel most likely to be taking credit for customers who were coming anyway. Controlled experiments find its real effect is positive but modest: in one retailer's campaign, retargeting lifted purchases by about 11%, while an attribution report would have credited it with every purchase among the people it reached. Exclude converters, cap frequency, shorten windows, test with a holdout, and remember that email is retargeting you own.

## How it works

A visitor arrives. A pixel or server-side event records the visit and adds the visitor to an audience. Ad platforms then show that audience the company's ads as they move around the web and social platforms. Audiences can be segmented: everyone who visited, people who viewed pricing, people who started an application and stopped, existing customers to be excluded or upsold.

The identity layer underneath has been shifting. Other browsers had already moved away from third-party cookies, and Google spent years planning to remove them from Chrome. In April 2025 Google announced it would keep its current approach to third-party cookies in Chrome and would not introduce a standalone prompt, and the wider Privacy Sandbox effort was later wound down. Retargeting has moved toward audiences built from first-party data anyway: email lists matched to platforms, logged-in users and platform-internal signals, and toward the walled gardens where the platform can recognise its own users without cookies. Our explainer on [intent data versus first-party data](https://lowob.com/research/intent-data-vs-first-party-data/) covers why the first-party route is more reliable regardless of what browsers do.

## What it is good for

Bringing back people who were interrupted: an application abandoned at the identity step, a cart left, a trial that stalled. Reminding people who compared options and left. Reaching existing customers with something new. Sequencing a message: a visitor who read an explainer sees proof next, then an offer.

For considered purchases, which describes most financial and business products, some of that is valuable. People do return, and a well-timed reminder with the right message does move some of them. The evidence supports timing the message to the person's stage. Lambrecht and Tucker's field experiment with an online travel firm, published in the Journal of Marketing Research in 2013, found dynamic retargeted ads showing the exact products a person had viewed were, on average, less effective than generic brand ads. The exception was people whose preferences had narrowed, for example those who had visited review sites: for them, specific ads stopped underperforming.

## Why the reported results are inflated

Retargeting reaches people who already know the company and were already likely to convert. Under any attribution model that counts a view or a click before conversion, retargeting is credited with a large share of conversions that would have happened without it. The channel looks like the best performer in the account because it stands closest to the checkout.

The experimental evidence is consistent: the true contribution is real, and a fraction of the attributed one.

| Study | Setting | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Johnson, Lewis and Nubbemeyer, Journal of Marketing Research, 2017 | Randomised test of an online retailer's display retargeting | Site visits up about 17%, purchases up about 11% |
| Lambrecht and Tucker, Journal of Marketing Research, 2013 | Field experiment at an online travel firm | Product-specific retargeting less effective on average than generic ads |
| Blake, Nosko and Tadelis, Econometrica, 2015 | Large-scale paid search experiments at eBay | Returns a fraction of non-experimental estimates; frequent buyers largely unaffected yet received most spend |

The eBay study is about search rather than retargeting, but the mechanism is the same: ads aimed at people who were already going to buy get credit for the purchase. A simple calculation shows the scale. If retargeting lifts purchases by 11% among the people it reaches, then of every 111 purchases in that group, about 11 were caused by the ads. An attribution report that credits retargeting with all 111 overstates its contribution roughly tenfold.

> This is not an argument against retargeting. It is an argument against believing its dashboard.

Our pieces on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) and [lead source attribution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) cover why click-based credit and causal effect diverge, and how to record sources so the gap can be seen.

## How to run it without paying twice

| Setting | What to do | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exclusions | Exclude people who already converted, unless the message is specifically for them | Paying to show an ad to someone who already bought is the most common and most avoidable waste |
| Frequency | Cap it, start low, and test a higher cap rather than assuming more is better | Following a person around the internet with the same ad for a month annoys them |
| Segments | Segment by intent and message accordingly | An abandoned application needs a different message from a first visit, as Lambrecht and Tucker's results suggest |
| Window | Set a short window and extend it only if a test shows the later days add anything | Audiences that stretch to ninety days mostly pay for people who have moved on or will return anyway |
| Holdout | Hold out a random share of the audience and compare conversion rates | If the held-out group converts nearly as well, the budget belongs elsewhere |

The holdout is the one that matters most, and it is cheap. Many ad platforms offer lift or holdout tools, and a company can create one itself by randomly excluding a share of its own audience list. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) sets out how large the holdout needs to be at the volumes a mid-size company sees, and how to write the decision rule before the test starts.

## For restricted categories

Retargeting depends on the platforms that carry the category. Where the large platforms will not run the ads, retargeting through them is not available, and the company relies on programmatic retargeting against its own audiences and on email, which is retargeting the company owns. That is a reasonable place to be: email reaches the same people at a fraction of the cost and does not need anyone's approval. Our pieces on [owned channels](https://lowob.com/research/owned-channels-email-content/) and [email deliverability](https://lowob.com/research/email-deliverability-explained/) cover how to make that channel carry the job.

Illustrative example: the holdout that moved the budget

Decision
:   Hold out a random 20% of the retargeting audience for six weeks and compare application completion rates.

Reason and owner
:   Retargeting was reported as the account's best channel by cost per application, and the growth lead was asked to double it. Owned by the growth lead, with finance agreeing the decision rule in advance.

What changed
:   The held-out group completed applications at a rate close to the exposed group. The retargeting window was cut from 60 days to 7, converters were excluded, and the freed budget moved to a prospecting test.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consumer lending company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Retargeting stands closest to the checkout.** That is why its dashboard looks best.
- **Its real effect is positive and modest.** One randomised study found about 11% more purchases, not all of them.
- **Match the message to the stage.** Product-specific ads work better once preferences have narrowed.
- **Exclude, cap and shorten.** Converters, frequency and windows are where the waste sits.
- **Test with a holdout.** It is the cheapest honest measure available.

## Common questions

### What is retargeting?

Advertising shown to people who have already visited a website, used an app or otherwise identified themselves to a company. It is also called remarketing.

### Why does retargeting look so effective in reports?

It reaches people already likely to convert, so attribution models credit it with conversions that would have happened anyway. A randomised study of one retailer's retargeting found purchases rose about 11%, far less than attribution would claim.

### How do I test whether retargeting actually works?

Hold out a random share of the audience and compare conversion rates. If the held-out group converts nearly as well, the channel is observing, not causing.

### Does retargeting still work without third-party cookies?

Yes, through first-party data such as email lists matched to platforms and logged-in users. Google decided in April 2025 to keep third-party cookies in Chrome, but other browsers restrict them, so first-party audiences are the more durable route.

## Sources and notes

- [London Business School, When does retargeting work? Information specificity in online advertising](https://www.london.edu/faculty-and-research/academic-research/w/when-does-retargeting-work-information-specificity-in-online-adver), Journal of Marketing Research, 2013. Peer-reviewed field experiment at one travel firm; older data.
- [NBER conference paper, Ghost Ads: Improving the Economics of Measuring Ad Effectiveness](https://conference.nber.org/conf_papers/f84173.pdf), February 2016 version; published in the Journal of Marketing Research, 2017. One retailer's campaign; working paper version opened.
- [NBER, Consumer Heterogeneity and Paid Search Effectiveness: A Large Scale Field Experiment](https://www.nber.org/papers/w20171), 2014; published in Econometrica, 2015. Paid search at eBay, not retargeting; the mechanism is analogous.
- [Google Privacy Sandbox, Next steps for Privacy Sandbox and tracking protections in Chrome](https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/privacy-sandbox-next-steps), 22 April 2025. Company announcement.
- [Center for Democracy and Technology, Google's Privacy Sandbox is dead](https://cdt.org/insights/googles-privacy-sandbox-is-dead-the-fight-for-real-online-privacy-continues/), 9 June 2025. Advocacy group commentary on the decision.

Set up a random holdout of 10 to 20% of your retargeting audience this week and agree with finance, in writing, what conversion gap would justify keeping the budget. Run it for a full purchase cycle before deciding.

# One Channel Is Carrying You, and It Isn't Yours.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/single-channel-dependency/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-24 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: The most dangerous distribution position is being visible on one channel someone else controls. Platform rules, ranking systems and click behaviour all shifted on dated announcements in 2024 to 2026. Price the dependency with three numbers, build a second channel with a different failure mode while the first still pays for it, and keep no channel above half of outcomes for more than two quarters.

The most dangerous distribution position is not being invisible. It is being visible on one channel that someone else controls. Platforms change rules, ranking systems and features on their own dates: Meta removed lookalike audiences for US financial ads in January 2025, Google cut low-quality results in search by 45% in 2024, and Pew found users clicked a result about half as often on Google searches that showed an AI summary. Price the dependency with three numbers, build a second channel with a different failure mode while the first one still pays for it, and keep no channel above half of outcomes for more than two quarters.

The company is working. Accounts are opening, subscriptions are starting, the cost per outcome is acceptable. Almost all of it comes from one place: one ad platform, one app store, one creator, one search engine, one marketplace. The dashboard is green, and the board is relaxed.

Then a policy changes on a Tuesday. A category is reclassified. An algorithm is adjusted. A creator moves on. An app-store review is reversed. The channel does not fail slowly. It stops.

## The channel owner sets the calendar

This is not a hypothetical risk. The large channels publish their changes, and the dates are theirs.

| Date | Channel | What changed | Who it hit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| March to April 2024 | Google Search | A core update and new spam policies; Google reported 45% less low-quality, unoriginal content in results once the rollout finished on 19 April 2024 | Publishers and sites relying on search traffic |
| January 2025 | Meta ads | Financial products and services ads to US audiences required to run in a special ad category; lookalike audiences unavailable; some customer-list audiences ineligible from March 2025 | Fintechs whose acquisition ran on lookalikes |
| March 2025 data, published July 2025 | Google Search | Pew found users clicked a result on 8% of visits with an AI summary, against 15% without | Any business whose content depended on the click |
| June to July 2026 | Google Ads | Financial services verification extended to 24 EEA markets; advertisers that do not complete it by their enforcement date lose the ability to show financial services ads there | Financial advertisers in those markets |
| Ongoing | Apple App Store | Apple describes its review guidelines as "a living document" where "new apps presenting new questions may result in new rules at any time" | Any app-dependent business |

None of these was a failure of the companies affected. Each was a reasonable decision by a channel owner pursuing its own goals. That is the point: a channel you do not own will always be run for someone else's reasons.

## Why it happens to good companies

Concentration is what success looks like when it is early.

A channel reads, and the sensible thing is to put everything behind it. That is correct, and we would advise it. The mistake is not the commitment; it is forgetting to start the next measurement once the commitment is made. The company that found its first channel in month three is still on it alone in month eighteen, because it worked, and nobody wanted to spend money learning something they did not need to know yet.

In categories the platforms review, the risk is sharper, because the channel carrying the company is often one that tolerates the category rather than welcomes it. Tolerance is revoked more easily than approval. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how platforms make that call.

> Tolerance is revoked more easily than approval.

## Price the risk before it is priced for you

Three numbers turn a vague worry into a decision.

**Share of outcomes from the largest channel.** Above half, the company has a dependency. Above three quarters, it has a single point of failure with a marketing department attached.

**Time to replace.** If the channel stopped today, how many weeks until an alternative could carry even half the volume? For a company with nothing else built, the honest answer is often a quarter or more.

**Cost of the gap.** Weekly outcomes from the channel, multiplied by the weeks to replace, multiplied by the value of an outcome. That figure is what the dependency is worth, and it is usually large enough to justify building the alternative now.

| Input | Illustrative figure |
| --- | --- |
| Outcomes per week from the largest channel | 400 funded accounts |
| Share of all outcomes | 80% |
| Weeks to replace half the volume with nothing else built | 13 |
| Value of an outcome (contribution over first year) | $120 |
| Cost of the gap: 400 × 13 × $120 | $624,000 |

*Illustrative arithmetic, not a client figure. Use your own contribution value, not revenue.*

Set that figure beside the cost of standing up a second channel at modest scale for two quarters; that comparison is the decision. [Demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to value an outcome so the calculation holds up with finance.

## Build the second channel while the first one is still working

The counterintuitive part is timing. The right moment to stand up the second channel is when the company can least see the need for it: when the first one is performing and the budget seems better spent there.

That is because a second channel takes time nobody has once the first one fails. An affiliate programme needs terms, partner recruitment, tracking and a few months of history before it carries real volume. A creator programme needs relationships. A programmatic buy needs inventory standards and a learning period. All of that can be built at modest cost while the main channel pays for it. None of it can be built in the two weeks after an account is suspended.

## What the alternatives look like

The point is not to abandon the channel that works. It is to add channels with different failure modes.

| Dependent on | Add | Why it fails differently |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One ad platform | An affiliate and partner programme | Partners choose to carry a product, and no reviewer can un-choose it for them |
| One creator | A second tier of smaller creators in a structured programme | No single relationship carries the category |
| Search | Owned email and content | No ranking update can remove a list you own |
| One marketplace | Direct distribution | The customer relationship sits with you, not the platform |
| One partner | A second partner of a different type | Channel rules stop one partner's terms becoming yours |

Each of these is unglamorous compared with the channel that is working. Each is also thinly bid, for the same reason; our piece on [thin bidding](https://lowob.com/research/thin-bidding/) makes the case. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set up partner types so they do not compete for the same deals, and [channel conflict and how to manage it](https://lowob.com/research/channel-conflict-and-how-to-manage-it/) covers the rules that keep a second channel from cannibalising the first. For software sellers, [marketplace listings](https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/) are a procurement route that can sit beside direct sales rather than replace it.

## The rule of thumb

No channel above half of outcomes for more than two quarters. When a channel crosses that line, the next measurement starts, funded from the channel that is working. Report the share of the largest channel to the board alongside cost per outcome, so concentration is visible before it becomes a crisis.

The goal is a small constellation of channels rather than one bright light: individually faint, together recognisable, and still visible when any single one goes out. A channel that works is a reason to start building the next one, not a reason to stop.

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume the owner will change the rules.** Google, Meta and Apple all did, on dated announcements, in the last three years.
- **Price the dependency in money.** Weekly outcomes times weeks to replace times contribution per outcome.
- **Build the second channel early.** It takes months to carry volume and can be funded by the first.
- **Choose a different failure mode.** Partners, owned lists and direct relationships fail for different reasons.
- **Cap concentration at half.** Two quarters above it starts the next measurement.

## Common questions

### What is single-channel dependency in marketing?

When most of a company's customers come from one channel it does not control, such as one ad platform, app store, search engine, creator or marketplace. A single rule or algorithm change can stop acquisition.

### How do you measure channel concentration risk?

Track the share of outcomes from the largest channel, estimate the weeks to replace half its volume, and multiply weekly outcomes by those weeks and by the contribution value of an outcome. That is the cost of the gap.

### How many marketing channels should a company have?

Enough that no single channel carries more than half of outcomes for more than two quarters. Two or three working channels with different failure modes are usually sufficient.

### When should a startup add a second acquisition channel?

While the first channel is still performing and can fund it. A second channel needs months to carry volume, so it cannot be built after the first one fails.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, New updates to address spam and low-quality results](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/search/google-search-update-march-2024/), 5 March 2024, updated 26 April 2024. Company announcement; the 45% figure is Google's own measure.
- [Meta for Developers, Out-of-cycle changes 2024](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/marketing-api/out-of-cycle-changes/occ-2024), entries dated October 2024 to January 2025. Developer changelog; US-focused.
- [Meta for Developers, Special Ad Categories](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/marketing-api/audiences/special-ad-category), checked 16 November 2026. Developer documentation.
- [Pew Research Center, Google users are less likely to click on links when an AI summary appears](https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2025/07/22/google-users-are-less-likely-to-click-on-links-when-an-ai-summary-appears-in-the-results/), 22 July 2025. 900 US adults, consumer searches in March 2025.
- [Google Ads, Introducing new verification requirements for certain financial services advertisers (June 2026)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/17127726?hl=en), posted 23 June 2026. Covers 24 EEA markets.
- [Apple, App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/), checked 16 November 2026. Platform rules.
- The three numbers, the illustrative calculation and the half-of-outcomes rule are **lowob**'s framework.

# The People Who Vouch for You

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-people-who-vouch-for-you/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-24 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: In fintech, your community is the practitioners who advise your segment and the customers willing to be named. Build a vouching system, not a chat room: give it three jobs (referrals, feedback, public trust signals), pay referrers openly where the rules allow it, and measure referred funded accounts and their retention. A bank study found referred customers stayed longer and were worth at least 16% more.

In fintech, your community is the practitioners who advise your segment and the customers willing to be named. Give them a job, pay them openly where the rules allow, and measure referred funded accounts. The evidence that referrals are worth building is good: a study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers were at least 16% more valuable over six years and less likely to leave. The rules are specific too. The FTC bans rewards conditioned on positive reviews, the FCA treats some practitioner posts as financial promotions, and in some products, such as US mortgage settlement services, paying for referrals is prohibited outright.

*This is strategic guidance from go-to-market work, not legal or regulatory advice.*

## Who the community actually is

[Trust is the product](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/) set out the order buyers check: who is behind it, who holds the money, who else like me uses it. The third question is answered by people, not copy.

In fintech those people fall into two groups. Practitioners: accountants, bookkeepers, advisers, fractional finance leads, payroll bureaus. And users: the treasury team, the small-business owner, the operations manager who lives in your product.

Neither group wants a server to hang out in. They want to look competent in front of their clients and their boards. Your product either helps with that or it does not. So drop the word community if it leads you to build a chat room. Build a vouching system instead.

## The job, applied to fintech

[Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) said give the community a job before you count it. In fintech there are three jobs, and each is measurable.

**Referrals.** A practitioner who recommends you to a client is the cheapest route to a funded account you will find. [Distribute through whoever already holds the customer](https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/) covered the channel economics. The academic evidence supports the bet. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte tracked about 10,000 customers of a German bank for almost three years. Referred customers had a higher contribution margin at first, a retention advantage that persisted, and an average value at least 16% higher than other customers. The bank paid a €25 voucher per referral, and the authors estimated a return of about 60% on it over six years.

**Product feedback from power users.** A treasury team that reconciles daily will find your edge cases before your QA does. A small-business owner will tell you what the onboarding form got wrong. Both are worth more than a survey.

**Public trust signals.** Reviews on the platforms your segment reads. References you can hand to a procurement team. Complaints answered in public, quickly.

| Job | Owner | Cadence | Number |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Referrals | Partnerships lead | Monthly review per practitioner | Referred funded accounts and their 90- and 365-day retention |
| Product feedback | Product lead | Quarterly advisory group, plus a standing channel | Issues raised that shipped |
| Trust signals | Customer or marketing lead | Weekly review response | Response time; named references available |

Each job gets an owner, a cadence and a number. That is the whole difference between a community and a mailing list.

## The first hundred, fintech version

[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) described the first hundred members as people chosen on purpose. For fintech the composition is specific.

Eighty practitioners who advise your target segment. Not followers. People who sit with your customers and are asked "what should I use for this?"

Twenty customers willing to be named. Named means a logo, a quote, a reference call, or a case study with a real number in it. Each of the twenty should map to one of the beliefs in the claims register described in [Trust is the product](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/).

Recruit the practitioners first. A practitioner who already trusts you brings the named customers with them.

## The practitioner programme

A practitioner programme has four parts. Keep it that simple.

**Education.** Short, useful sessions on the problem, not the product. How to run client treasury. What changes when a client crosses a payment threshold. Practitioners share things that make them look sharp.

**Early access.** Let them see a feature before their clients ask about it. It costs you nothing and makes them the person who knew first.

**A direct line.** One named person they can message when a client is stuck. Not a ticket queue. This single thing does more than any incentive.

**Payment.** Pay per funded account if you choose to, and disclose it to the client every time. A referral fee that is hidden becomes a trust problem the day it surfaces. One that is disclosed is how the market works. The research suggests rewards earn their keep in exactly this setting: in Ryu and Feick's experiments, offering a reward raised referral likelihood by more than 20 percentage points for a weaker brand, and mattered most between people with weak ties.

> A referral fee that is hidden becomes a trust problem the day it surfaces. One that is disclosed is how the market works.

Disclosure is the minimum, and some rules go further. Check the referrer's own rules and the product's before agreeing terms. Our [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers registering, paying and disclosing introductions so the economics and the trust both hold.

| Who refers | Rule to check | What it asks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UK chartered accountants | ICAEW Code of Ethics and guidance | Obtain client consent and notify clients of the amounts received |
| Promoters of a US SEC-registered adviser | SEC marketing rule | Clear and prominent disclosure of whether the promoter is a client and is paid; a written agreement above $1,000 a year |
| Anyone referring US mortgage settlement business | RESPA Section 8 (Regulation X, 12 CFR 1024.14) | Fees for referrals are prohibited |
| Anyone promoting a regulated UK financial product | FCA financial promotion rules (FG24/1) | Approval by an authorised person; the firm stays responsible |

For small-business and institutional products, add a user advisory group: six to ten customers, quarterly, with a roadmap in front of them. They tell you what to build. You tell them what you decided and why.

## Reviews and complaints as infrastructure

Review platforms are part of the vouching system whether you manage them or not. Someone will check. Claim the profile, respond to every review, and ask satisfied customers to post without offering anything for it.

Complaint handling is the other half. A complaint answered in public, within hours, with a clear fix, is a trust asset. A buyer reading it learns how you behave when something goes wrong, which is the fourth question in the buyer's order, answered by evidence. Build the process before you need it: who sees the complaint, who answers, how fast, and what they are allowed to say.

## The lines you don't cross

Some things turn a community asset into a liability overnight.

**No incentivised reviews.** The FTC's rule on consumer reviews and testimonials, in force since 21 October 2024, prohibits paying or rewarding reviews that express a particular sentiment. A small reward for any honest review is not inherently unlawful, but a discount for a five-star review is. The FTC's guidance puts it plainly: "You can't condition an incentive, for example a discount, on a review being positive." Penalties can reach $51,744 per violation, adjusted annually.

**No testimonial you cannot substantiate.** If a named customer says they saved a number, you need the number in a file.

**Nothing that reads as a financial promotion without approval.** A practitioner's post about your yield product may be a promotion in your regulator's eyes. The FCA's FG24/1 says firms working with affiliates should take proactive responsibility and remain responsible for every promotion they make or cause to be made. Give practitioners approved wording and a review step.

Then measure the thing that matters: referred funded accounts, by practitioner and by channel, and their 90-day and 365-day retention. Referrals that fund and stay are the only proof the community is doing its job.

## lowob takeaways

- **Recruit eighty practitioners and twenty named customers.** Practitioners first; they bring the customers.
- **Give each job an owner, a cadence and a number.** Referrals, feedback and trust signals.
- **Pay openly, and check the rules first.** Disclosure is the minimum; some referrers need client consent and some products ban referral fees.
- **Never reward sentiment.** Ask for honest reviews and offer nothing tied to the rating.
- **Measure referred funded accounts and their retention.** By practitioner, at 90 and 365 days.

## Common questions

### How should a fintech company build a community?

Build a vouching system of practitioners, such as accountants, bookkeepers and advisers, and named customers. Give it three measurable jobs: referrals, product feedback and public trust signals.

### Can fintechs pay accountants or advisers for referrals?

Often, but check the rules first and disclose the payment every time. UK chartered accountants must obtain client consent and notify amounts received; promoters of US investment advisers must disclose compensation; referral fees for US mortgage settlement services are prohibited.

### Can I offer customers a discount for a five-star review?

No. In the US, the FTC's 2024 rule prohibits rewarding reviews that express a particular sentiment. Ask satisfied customers to post honestly without tying anything to the rating.

### Are referred customers more valuable for a bank or fintech?

The best evidence says yes. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers had higher early margins, lower churn and at least 16% higher value over six years.

- [Baylor University Keller Center, Referral reward programs and referral likelihood](https://kellercenter.hankamer.baylor.edu/news/story/2008/insider-referral-reward-programs-and-referral-likelihood), 2008. # Gateway 0: Three Decisions Before Any AI Tool

Source: https://lowob.com/research/gateway-zero-three-decisions-before-any-ai-tool/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Gateway 0 is three decisions made before any AI tool is purchased: a named owner with protected time, the suite of record (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365), and a CRM chosen for how people will actually use it. Regulated firms add a fourth: who signs off on data access.

Before buying any AI tool, answer three questions. Who owns the build, with protected time each week? Which suite is the company's system of record, Google Workspace or Microsoft 365? And which CRM will people actually keep current? Regulated firms add a fourth: who decides what data the system may see. Most stalled builds we encounter skipped at least one of these, and each is cheaper to answer up front than to unwind later.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

*Figure: Gateway 0 is three decisions. Nothing gets bought until all three are answered.*

The commonest pattern in a stalled AI build is not a bad tool. It is a good tool bought before anyone decided who would make it work. Licences arrive, a launch email goes out, and usage settles at a small fraction of seats within weeks.

The pattern is visible at the largest scale. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of those who pay use it in a given week, according to figures reported by Windows Latest in July 2026. Seats are a purchase. Use is a project, and projects need an owner.

That is why the build order starts with a gateway rather than a tool. Gateway 0 is three decisions. Until all three are made, nothing gets bought.

## Decision 1: who owns the build

One named person, with protected hours every week. Not "the partners", not "IT", and not a steering group that meets monthly.

The owner's first month has four jobs:

1. Confirm the other two decisions below.
2. Choose the one commercial workflow the build will serve first, using the test in Part 2.
3. Set the single measure that will show it worked, with a review date.
4. Decide who approves anything the system drafts before it reaches a client.

The owner does not need to be technical. They need to understand the commercial line, have authority to change how people record their work, and have time. In the mid-size firms we work with, four ring-fenced hours a week is usually enough for the first quarter; less than two rarely is. That is a smaller commitment than a steering group assumes and a larger one than most firms actually make.

### What the owner is accountable for

| Area | The owner decides | The owner does not need to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scope | Which workflow comes first, and what waits | Design the architecture |
| Measure | The one number and its review date | Build dashboards |
| Data | What may be connected, with any approver in regulated firms | Configure connectors |
| Approvals | Who signs off on anything that leaves the firm | Approve every draft personally |
| Vendors | Which tools are bought, and on what terms | Run procurement alone |

## Decision 2: Google Workspace or Microsoft 365

The suite decides more than it appears to. It shapes which assistant fits most naturally, which connectors work without extra plumbing, and where the company's email, files and meetings can be searched. Microsoft's paid Copilot add-on reads email, files and meetings through Microsoft Graph; Google's assistant is built into Workspace in the same way. Each sees its own suite best, and both now sell the context layer on top of it.

The rule is simple: pick the suite your email already lives in. Migrating suites to suit an assistant is almost never worth it, because the assistant is the faster-changing layer and the suite is the slower one. Models improve every few months, and most now work across suites. The suite should anchor the build.

Where a firm genuinely runs on both (one office in Google, another in Microsoft, or a merger not yet integrated), the owner's job is to decide which suite is the system of record for client communication and to accept that the other will be connected second.

## Decision 3: the CRM people will actually update

Not the best CRM. The one your least patient senior person will open.

The brain needs a store for the commercial line to read from and write outcomes into. That store is only as good as the people who keep it, and in many firms the people closest to the client are the least willing to type. Validity's 2025 survey of CRM users found 37% reporting revenue lost as a direct consequence of poor data quality, and its 2026 survey found only 21% of marketers considered their CRM data very well prepared for AI.

So choose by behaviour rather than features:

- **Automatic capture.** Does it sync email and calendar so activity is recorded without typing?
- **Speed of update.** Can a senior person move a deal or add a next step in under a minute, from a phone?
- **Required reasons.** Will people accept a short closed-lost reason as a required field?
- **Exportable history.** Can every record and its history be exported in a documented format? (*Buy context, own judgment* sets out why this matters at renewal.)

A simpler CRM kept current beats a powerful one maintained by a junior colleague on Friday afternoons. If the firm already has a CRM, the decision is usually to keep it and clean it, which is the subject of Part 4.

## A fourth decision for regulated firms

In financial services, healthcare, and any firm with client-confidentiality or conflict duties, add one more: who signs off on what the system may see. Identity checks, credit files, patient records and conflict files should usually stay outside the commercial build entirely. Name the person who decides this before any connector is switched on, and record their decisions in the same way as any other. Our guide *The pilot that survives security review* covers what reviewers will ask.

> Seats are a purchase. Use is a project, and projects need an owner.

## What skipping the gateway costs

Builds that skip Gateway 0 tend to fail in one of three recognisable ways:

| Skipped decision | What it looks like six months later | Cost to unwind |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No owner | Seats unused, renewal questioned, no measure to defend | A relaunch, and lost credibility with staff |
| No suite decision | Two half-connected suites; an assistant that sees neither well | Re-scoping connectors and permissions |
| No CRM decision | Confident AI answers drawn from stale, duplicated records | Data clean-up under time pressure, after trust is lost |

Each is more expensive to fix than the decision would have been to make.

Illustrative example: a Gateway 0 decision

Decision
:   The head of operations owns the build; Microsoft 365 is the suite of record; the existing CRM stays and is cleaned.

Reason and owner
:   Email and files already live in Microsoft 365; the CRM is under-used rather than unsuitable. Signed off by the managing partner.

What changed
:   Unused assistant seats are cut at renewal; the remaining users become the first commercial cohort, with meeting preparation time as the measure.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size advisory firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name an owner before you name a vendor.** One person, protected time, authority over how work is logged.
- **Let the suite anchor the build.** Pick the one your email lives in; the assistant follows.
- **Choose the CRM by behaviour.** The one people keep current beats the one with more features.
- **Regulated firms add a data-access approver.** Decide what stays out before the first connector goes live.

Gateway card

### Gateway 0

- A named owner, with hours protected weekly
- The suite of record confirmed
- The CRM chosen, with email and calendar sync switched on
- One commercial measure agreed, with a review date
- Regulated firms: a named data-access approver

## Common questions

### What should a company decide before buying AI tools?

Who owns the build with protected time, which suite (Google Workspace or Microsoft 365) is the system of record, and which CRM people will actually keep current. Regulated firms should also name who approves data access.

### Should we switch from Google Workspace to Microsoft 365 to use Copilot, or the reverse?

Almost never. The suite changes slowly and the assistant changes quickly; build on the suite your email already lives in and connect the other if needed.

### Who should own an AI rollout in a mid-size firm?

One named person who understands the commercial workflow, has authority to change how work is recorded, and has protected time each week. They do not need to be technical.

### How do I choose a CRM for AI?

Choose by behaviour: automatic capture of email and calendar activity, quick updates from a phone, a required reason for lost deals, and full export of records and history.

## Sources and notes

- [Windows Latest, 7 July 2026](https://www.windowslatest.com/2026/07/07/microsoft-365-copilot-adoption-is-under-4-5-after-3-years-only-1-use-it-weekly-yet-prices-went-up/). Industry figures; also describes what the paid Copilot add-on can access.
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2025](https://validity.com/resource-center/the-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2025). Survey of 602 CRM users and stakeholders.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/).
- Owner time estimates and failure patterns are drawn from **lowob**'s engagements, described in aggregate.

## Related research

- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)
- [The Pilot That Survives Security Review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/)
- [Claude Is Not Your Intern. Build a Repeatable GTM Workflow](https://lowob.com/research/claude-gtm-operating-system/)

## Next move

Can you name your build's owner, its suite of record and its CRM in one sentence? If not, that is the first decision to make, before any vendor conversation.

# What Is Agent Washing?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agent washing is the practice of marketing existing assistants, chatbots or automation scripts as autonomous AI agents. Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic products offer genuine agentic features. Regulators already act against false AI claims, and buyers can test a vendor in one demo with five questions.

Agent washing is the practice of rebranding existing AI assistants, chatbots or robotic process automation (RPA) tools as "agentic AI" without adding real agent capabilities. Gartner, which uses the term in its agentic AI research, estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic products are genuine. For a buyer, the risk is paying agent prices for assistant behaviour. A short, structured demo usually exposes the difference.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What agent washing means

Gartner used the term in its June 2025 forecast on agentic AI. Its analysts observed that many vendors were contributing to market hype by rebranding existing products as agentic: AI assistants, chatbots and RPA tools. By its estimate, only about 130 of the thousands of vendors making agentic claims actually offer genuine agentic features.

The same forecast predicted that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027. Gartner's Anushree Verma said most agentic AI propositions "lack significant value or return on investment". Agent washing feeds that failure rate. A team that buys a relabelled chatbot expecting an agent will find the gap only after deployment.

The term borrows from "AI washing", a phrase regulators already use. In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers, Delphia and Global Predictions, for claiming AI capabilities they did not have. Then-chair Gary Gensler said: "Such AI washing hurts investors." In September 2024 the FTC announced Operation AI Comply, a set of actions against deceptive AI claims. Chair Lina Khan said there is "no AI exemption from the laws on the books."

| Genuine agent | Agent-washed product |
| --- | --- |
| Decides its own sequence of steps towards a goal | Follows a fixed script or decision tree |
| Chooses which tools to call based on the situation | Calls one integration in a predetermined order |
| Reads results and changes course when a step fails | Stops or returns an error when the script breaks |
| Can show a log of the steps it chose and why | Shows only the final output |
| Lets you set autonomy per task | Offers one mode: on |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial teams are a prime target. "AI SDR" and "autonomous agent" have become common labels on tools that schedule sequences or summarise calls. Those tools may be useful; the problem is the price and expectations the label brings.

Agent washing creates three specific costs. First, pricing: vendors often charge per agent or per outcome, which only makes sense if the product does the work of a person. Second, risk: a buyer who believes a tool will catch its own mistakes may give it more autonomy than it can handle. Third, opportunity: a team that spends a quarter discovering a product is a chatbot has lost a quarter on its first real agent.

There is a reverse problem too. Anthropic's guidance on building agents notes that many tasks are better served by a workflow, with steps fixed in code, than by a true agent. A relabelled workflow is not always a bad product. It is a mislabelled one, and should be priced and governed as what it is.

## How to test a vendor's agent claim

Five questions, asked in a live demo on your own data, separate most genuine agents from relabelled assistants.

| Question to ask | What a genuine agent shows | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Give it a goal it has not seen. What does it do?" | It plans steps and explains them | It asks for a template or a script |
| "Break one of its tools mid-task." | It notices and tries another route | It fails silently or stops |
| "Show me the log of what it chose and why." | A step-by-step trace with tool calls | A final answer only |
| "What can it never do, and where is that set?" | A configurable list of permissions | "It is safe by design" |
| "Which actions need a person to approve?" | Per-task autonomy settings | One global on/off switch |

Ask also how the vendor measures success: task completion and error rates on real work, not message counts.

Then write the answers down. In **lowob**'s view a buying decision is a record worth keeping: decision, reason, owner and expected outcome. If the product underperforms, the record shows whether the claim or the deployment was at fault.

## lowob takeaways

- **Treat "agent" as a claim to test.** Gartner thinks most vendors using the label do not meet it.
- **Test on your data, live.** A goal the product has not seen, a broken tool and a request for the log reveal most washing.
- **Price what it is.** A relabelled workflow can be useful, but should not carry agent pricing or agent autonomy.
- **Record the decision.** Write down what the vendor claimed and what you expect, so the outcome can be checked.

## Common questions

### What does agent washing mean?

It means marketing an existing chatbot, AI assistant or RPA tool as an autonomous AI agent without adding real agent capabilities. Gartner used the term in its 2025 agentic AI forecast.

### How many agentic AI vendors are real?

Gartner estimates that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors claiming agentic AI products offer genuine agentic features.

### Is agent washing illegal?

The term itself has no legal definition, but false AI claims have been penalised. The SEC fined two advisers for AI washing in 2024, and the FTC has brought actions over deceptive AI claims.

### How can I tell if an AI product is a real agent?

Give it an unseen goal on your own data, break one of its tools mid-task and ask for a log of its decisions. A genuine agent plans, adapts and shows its steps.
