# One Founder Interview Should Produce a Month of Content. Here Is the System.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-20 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Founder content fails when the founder is asked to become a full-time creator or when marketing imitates a voice it cannot access. Treat the founder's time as a source session instead: one focused interview on one thesis, AI-assisted extraction, an asset tree where each piece has a different job, a voice sheet, and an approval ladder that keeps the founder off the critical path.

Most founder-content programmes fail for one of two reasons: the founder is asked to become a full-time creator, or a marketing team imitates the founder without regular access to how the founder actually thinks. A better system treats the founder's time as a high-value source session. One focused interview records original thinking; a structured editorial workflow turns it into multiple useful assets without diluting the point of view. The payoff is credibility: in the 2024 Edelman-LinkedIn study, 73% of decision-makers said a firm's thought leadership was a more trustworthy basis for judging its capabilities than its marketing materials.

Asking the founder to become a full-time creator is unsustainable. Imitating the founder produces a polished corporate voice that sounds like nobody.

The bar is also higher than most teams assume. Only 15% of the 3,484 executives in the 2024 Edelman-LinkedIn B2B Thought Leadership Impact Report rated the thought leadership they read as very good or excellent. Volume does not fix that. The Content Marketing Institute's 2026 survey of 861 B2B marketers found 65% under more pressure to produce content faster, and the most reported effects were burnout, less original thinking (32%) and more generic content (29%). The founder's own thinking is the scarce input, and the system exists to protect it.

## Do not interview for "content"

Generic questions produce generic material. Do not ask, "What trends are you excited about?" Ask questions designed to uncover decisions, tension and evidence.

Useful prompts include:

- What does the market currently believe that you think is wrong?
- Which customer conversation changed how you describe the product?
- What did you try that failed?
- Where are teams spending money before they are ready?
- What changed in the last six months?
- What tradeoff do customers repeatedly underestimate?
- Which company appears to be executing unusually well, and why?
- What would you tell a founder six months behind you?

The interviewer should challenge abstractions. When the founder says "community is important", ask which behaviour made it valuable, what the team did and what changed as a result.

These answers are also what search systems reward. Google's guidance on helpful content asks whether a page shows "first-hand expertise and a depth of knowledge" and whether it is self-evident who wrote it. A founder describing a decision they made is first-hand by definition.

## Record one thesis, not fifteen topics

A 45-minute interview should revolve around one central question. That focus creates enough depth for a flagship article and enough supporting material for derivative posts.

Record the conversation with permission. Preserve the transcript. Mark claims that require verification, stories that require approval and statements that may reveal confidential information.

## Use Claude as an editorial analyst

Provide the transcript along with the company voice guide and ask Claude to extract:

- The strongest central argument
- Supporting claims and examples
- Counterarguments the founder addressed or ignored
- Memorable phrases worth preserving
- Claims requiring verification
- Potential audiences and their different needs
- Questions that should be asked in a follow-up

Do not immediately ask for 30 posts. First approve the thesis and supporting evidence. Otherwise the workflow multiplies fragments before deciding what the company actually wants to say.

There is a second reason to approve first. Doshi and Hauser's 2024 experiment in *Science Advances*, with 300 writers and 600 evaluators, found AI-generated ideas made individual stories more novel but made them 10.7% more similar to one another. A team that asks a model for posts before fixing the thesis gets copy that sounds like everyone else's AI-assisted copy.

## Build the asset tree

From one approved source interview, create the assets below. This is not ten copies of the same text. Each asset should do a different job.

| Asset | Count | Its job |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flagship article, 1,200 to 1,800 words | 1 | Establishes the argument |
| Founder LinkedIn post stating the core belief | 1 | Makes the position personal |
| Company LinkedIn post presenting the framework | 1 | Makes it teachable |
| X thread, six to ten posts | 1 | Creates progression |
| Short standalone observations | 3 | Test which line travels |
| Checklist or diagram | 1 | Gives the reader something to apply |
| Newsletter introduction | 1 | Sends the owned audience to the flagship |
| Sales-enablement excerpts | 3 | Help commercial conversations |
| FAQ update from questions surfaced | 1 | Converts market confusion into product education |
| Follow-up interview brief | 1 | Deepens the thesis next month |

Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out how to brief each asset with a reader, a decision and a next action, and [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) covers turning the flagship argument into discovery questions and objection answers. A recorded interview is also the source material a [clipping programme](https://lowob.com/research/clipping-paid-distribution/) needs.

> One founder interview should not be squeezed for volume. It should be developed for consequence.

## Preserve the founder's verbal fingerprints

AI-assisted editing often removes the irregularities that make a voice recognisable.

Create a voice sheet containing: sentence length and rhythm; preferred terminology; recurring metaphors; degree of directness; words the founder never uses; examples of approved posts; how disagreement is expressed; and how technical detail is introduced. The CMI survey found 52% of B2B marketers using AI named maintaining brand voice and authenticity as a challenge, close behind accuracy and quality control at 54% each. A voice sheet is the cheapest control for that problem.

Ask Claude to preserve specific phrases from the transcript, but never invent quotations. The founder should approve anything published in the first person. Google's guidance is blunt on the wider point: fabricating creator profiles is a form of deception, and readers benefit from knowing how automation was used.

## Establish an approval ladder

Not every asset needs the same review burden.

| Level | What it covers | Who approves | What they check |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| One | Factual, product, legal and customer claims | The owner of the claim, directly | Accuracy and permission |
| Two | First-person founder content | The founder | Voice and intent |
| Three | Company-channel adaptations inside established language | The content lead | Consistency with approved source |
| Four | Reposts and excerpts of approved assets | Scheduled automatically | Nothing new is said |

This prevents the founder from becoming the bottleneck while protecting the areas where their judgment matters. It is the same principle as [nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/): the gate sits where judgment is needed, and only there. Our explainer on [approval gates](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-approval-gate/) covers how to set them. As the team grows, [from founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) covers which of these approvals transfer first.

## Measure thesis resonance

Do not judge the system only by how many assets it produces. Track which ideas create:

- Substantive replies from priority buyers
- Saves and shares with commentary
- Invitations to speak or collaborate
- Prospect references in sales calls
- Direct traffic to related service or product pages
- Newsletter subscriptions from relevant organisations

The evidence that this matters to revenue is reasonably strong. In the Edelman-LinkedIn study, 86% of decision-makers said they would be moderately or very likely to invite a firm with consistently high-quality thought leadership to bid, and 54% of C-suite respondents said thought leadership had at least occasionally led them to question an existing supplier.

The winning thesis can then be deepened through a case study, research report, webinar or event rather than abandoned after one publishing cycle.

Founder content scales when the founder supplies the judgment and the system handles extraction, adaptation and distribution.

## lowob takeaways

- **Interview for decisions.** Ask what the market gets wrong, what failed and what changed.
- **Approve the thesis before the posts.** AI ideas raise individual novelty and reduce collective variety.
- **Give every asset a different job.** Argument, position, framework, progression, application.
- **Gate by judgment.** Claims and first-person content get approval; approved excerpts do not.

## Common questions

### How do you create founder-led content without taking up the founder's time?

Run one focused 45-minute interview a month on a single thesis, then use an editorial workflow to extract, adapt and distribute it, with the founder approving only claims and first-person content.

### What questions should you ask in a founder interview?

Questions that surface decisions, tension and evidence: what the market believes that is wrong, which customer conversation changed the pitch, what failed, and what tradeoff customers underestimate.

### Can AI write in a founder's voice?

It can help adapt approved material, but it tends to smooth out a recognisable voice. Use a voice sheet, preserve phrases from the transcript, never invent quotations, and have the founder approve anything in the first person.

### How do you measure founder thought leadership?

By thesis resonance rather than volume: substantive replies from priority buyers, shares with commentary, invitations, mentions in sales calls and relevant subscriptions.

## In the news

- 4 November 2026 · Content Marketing Institute[CMI and MarketingProfs publish the 2026 B2B content trends](https://lowob.com/news/#2026-11-04-cmi-and-marketingprofs-publish-the-2026-b2b-content-trends)A survey of 1,132 marketers, mostly in North America. Read it for where budgets are moving, not for what works.

Tracked on the [**lowob** News Desk](https://lowob.com/news/).

Agency and platform research; 3,484 executives surveyed via LinkedIn in seven countries, November to December 2023.
- [Content Marketing Institute, 9 takeaways from the 2026 B2B content and marketing trends report](https://contentmarketinginstitute.com/articles/b2b-content-marketing-trends-research), 4 November 2026. Survey with MarketingProfs of 861 B2B marketers, mostly North American; self-reported.

Book 45 minutes with the founder this month and send one central question in advance. Before anyone drafts a post, get the thesis and its three supporting claims approved in writing.

# What Is an AI Audit Trail?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-audit-trail/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-20 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI audit trail links inputs, model and version, outputs, tool actions, human approvals and outcomes into a chain a supervisor can follow. The EU AI Act sets log and retention rules for high-risk systems, FINRA asks firms to track agent actions, and model risk guidance in the US and UK shapes the governance around it.

An AI audit trail is the record that lets a firm reconstruct, after the fact, what an AI system was given, what it produced or did, which model and instructions it used, and who approved the result. In financial services it is the evidence a supervisor asks for when a client outcome is questioned. Logs from tools are part of it; the decisions, approvals and outcomes the firm records are the rest.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

## What an AI audit trail means

A system log records events. An audit trail records a chain: enough linked evidence that someone who was not there can follow a decision from input to outcome. For an AI system that chain has six links.

| Link | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Input | The request, the documents or data retrieved, and their versions |
| System | Model, version, prompt or instruction set, and configuration at the time |
| Output and actions | What the system produced and every tool call it made, with parameters |
| Human decision | Who approved, edited or returned it, when, and what they saw |
| Outcome | What happened afterwards: sent, executed, complained about, reversed |
| Change history | When the model, prompt or permissions changed, and who signed off |

**lowob**'s view is that the first three come mostly from tools and observability platforms, while the last three belong in a record the firm owns. Rent the wiring, own the record.

## What regulators expect

**EU AI Act.** Article 12 requires high-risk systems to "technically allow for the automatic recording of events (logs) over the lifetime of the system", to support risk identification, post-market monitoring and operational oversight. Article 26 requires deployers to keep logs under their control for at least six months. Financial institutions subject to EU financial services governance rules keep them as part of that existing documentation. The Digital Omnibus moved Annex III high-risk obligations to 2 December 2027.

**FINRA.** The 2026 Annual Regulatory Oversight Report, released on 9 December 2025, notes that generative AI can engage rules on supervision, communications and recordkeeping. For firms exploring agents it lists monitoring system access and data handling, deciding where human-in-the-loop oversight is required, and "tracking agent actions and decisions". Its broader generative AI discussion mentions keeping prompt and output logs for accountability and troubleshooting.

**US model risk guidance.** SR 11-7, the Federal Reserve's 2011 model risk guidance, was rescinded on 17 April 2026. The Federal Reserve, OCC and FDIC replaced it with Revised Guidance on Model Risk Management. According to Orrick's analysis, the new guidance is most relevant to banks above $30 billion in assets and excludes generative and agentic AI in a footnote, telling banks to rely on broader risk governance for those tools. Its ideas of inventory, validation and documentation remain useful, but it should no longer be cited as current guidance.

**UK model risk guidance.** The PRA's SS1/23 sets five principles: model identification and classification, governance, development and use, independent validation, and risk mitigants. It applies to UK banks, building societies and PRA-designated investment firms with internal model approval for regulatory capital, and the current version took effect on 23 April 2026. It covers models used to inform business decisions "regardless of technology" and refers explicitly to machine learning. Firms outside its scope can still use the five principles as a reference point.

> Supervisors inspect the chain of evidence, approval and outcome, not the model's internals.

## How to start one

Most firms already hold pieces of the trail in different places: traces in an observability tool, approvals in email, outcomes in the CRM. The work is to link them with a shared identifier.

| Step | Practical test |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory AI use | Every model, agent and AI feature has an owner and a purpose |
| Give each run an ID | The trace, approval and outcome can be joined on one key |
| Version instructions | You can say which prompt and model produced last month's output |
| Log approvals with evidence | The reviewer's name, time and the sources they saw are stored |
| Write outcomes back | Complaints, reversals and corrections are linked to the run |
| Set retention | At least six months where the AI Act applies, longer if recordkeeping rules require |

## lowob takeaways

- **A trail is a chain.** Logs become an audit trail only when input, action, approval and outcome are linked.
- **Check what you cite.** SR 11-7 was rescinded in April 2026; its replacement excludes generative AI.
- **Use existing rules.** Supervision and recordkeeping duties already apply to AI-assisted work.
- **Own the record.** Keep approvals and outcomes in a store the firm controls, not only in vendor logs.

## Common questions

### What is an AI audit trail?

A linked record of what an AI system received, which model and instructions it used, what it produced or did, who approved it and what happened next.

### How long must AI logs be kept under the EU AI Act?

Deployers of high-risk systems must keep logs under their control for a period appropriate to the purpose, of at least six months, unless other law says otherwise.

### Is SR 11-7 still in force?

No. US banking agencies rescinded it on 17 April 2026 and issued revised model risk guidance, which excludes generative and agentic AI from its scope.

### Does PRA SS1/23 apply to AI?

It applies to models used to inform business decisions regardless of technology, including machine learning, for UK banks with internal model approval.

## Sources and notes

- [Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act), Article 12: Record-keeping](https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/ai-act/ai-act-regulation/article-12/) and [Article 26: Obligations of deployers](https://www.springlex.eu/en/packages/ai-act/ai-act-regulation/article-26/), Official Journal text via SpringLex. Applies to high-risk systems.
- [Debevoise & Plimpton, FINRA's 2026 Regulatory Oversight Report](https://www.debevoise.com/insights/publications/2025/12/finras-2026-regulatory-oversight-report-continued), December 2025. Law firm summary of FINRA's report.
- [Orrick, Agencies overhaul model risk management guidance for banks](https://www.orrick.com/en/Insights/2026/04/Agencies-Overhaul-Model-Risk-Management-Guidance-for-Banks-Heres-What-Changed), April 2026. Law firm analysis of the rescission of SR 11-7.
- [Bank of England PRA, SS1/23 Model risk management principles for banks](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/prudential-regulation/publication/2023/may/model-risk-management-principles-for-banks-ss), current version effective 23 April 2026. Primary regulator text.
- [National Law Review, EU Digital Omnibus on AI enters into force](https://natlawreview.com/article/eu-digital-omnibus-ai-enters-force), 31 July 2026. Law firm summary of revised AI Act dates.

## Related research

Choose one AI-assisted client communication from last month and try to reconstruct it: input, model, prompt version, approver and outcome. Each link you cannot find is the next thing to record.

# What SEO Is Now: How Search Ranking Works Today

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-seo-is-now/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Modern SEO rewards pages that answer the query better than the alternatives, are technically sound and are trusted by other sites; it punishes volume and tricks. AI summaries now cut clicks on many informational queries by half or more, and AI assistants are a parallel channel that rewards the same things. Payback is slower than most plans assume, but every company should do the minimum.

Modern SEO rewards pages that answer the query better than the alternatives, are technically sound and are trusted by other sites; it punishes volume and tricks. Search engines now answer many queries directly, and Ahrefs found an AI Overview correlated with a 58% lower click-through rate for the top result by late 2025. AI assistants are a parallel channel, and both reward clear early answers and checkable claims. Payback is slow, often slower than plans assume, but every company should do the minimum.

Search engine optimisation is the practice of making a website more likely to appear when people search for what it offers. The name has survived twenty-five years. The practice underneath it has changed almost completely, and a great deal of advice still circulating describes a search engine that no longer exists.

## How ranking works, in outline

A search engine crawls the web, reads pages, stores what it finds and, when someone searches, picks and orders the pages most likely to satisfy the query. Google's own description lists five "key Search signals": the meaning of the query, the relevance of content, the quality of content, its usability, and the searcher's context and settings, such as location and search history.

Two further statements on the same page matter. Google says "one of the factors used to determine quality is understanding if other prominent websites link or refer to the content". And it says "we also use aggregated and anonymized interaction data to assess whether search results are relevant to queries". In other words, the ordering considers what the page says, how usable it is, what other sites say about it, and how searchers have responded to it.

The engine's interest is the searcher's satisfaction. Everything that has changed in SEO is the engine getting better at measuring that and worse at being fooled.

## What still matters

**Content that answers the query better than the alternatives.** Google defines "people-first content" as "content that's created primarily for people, and not to manipulate search engine rankings". Its self-assessment asks whether a page provides "original information, reporting, research, or analysis".

**Technical health.** Pages that load fast, render on phones, can be crawled and are not duplicated. Google says that when other signals are similar, more usable pages may rank higher.

**Clear structure.** Titles, headings and links that describe what is where.

**Authority.** Being linked to, cited and mentioned by sites the engine already trusts.

**Demonstrable expertise.** Named authors with real credentials, especially for financial and health topics. Google's guidance says "Your Money or Your Life" topics, which affect health, finances, safety or wellbeing, receive extra scrutiny, and that trust carries the most weight among its experience, expertise, authoritativeness and trust criteria.

**Satisfying the intent.** A searcher who wanted a comparison, given a sales page, leaves, and the engine notices.

## What stopped mattering, or became harmful

Keyword density and exact-match repetition. Buying links. Spinning many thin pages around variations of a phrase. Tricks that show the engine something different from what users see. And publishing large volumes of generic content, now easier than ever with AI and more heavily penalised for the same reason.

Google's helpful content guidance lists warning signs, including "Are you using extensive automation to produce content on many topics?" Its July 2026 guide on AI features states that creating pages primarily "to manipulate rankings or generative AI responses in Google Search" violates its scaled content abuse policy. Independent evidence points the same way for AI answers: in the GEO study (KDD 2024), keyword stuffing lowered a source's visibility in generated answers by about 8%, while adding statistics and quotations raised it.

| Still matters | Stopped mattering or now harmful | Changed most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Answering the query better than alternatives | Keyword density and exact-match repetition | Fewer clicks on informational queries |
| Crawlable, fast, mobile-ready pages | Bought links | Answers assembled from several sub-searches |
| Links and mentions from trusted sites | Thin pages spun around phrase variants | AI assistants as a parallel channel |
| Named, credible authors on finance and health | Mass-produced generic content | Citation rather than rank as the goal for many queries |
| Matching what the searcher wanted | Showing engines different content from users | Measurement: impressions without visits |

## What changed most recently

Two things. The engines now answer many queries directly, with a summary at the top generated from pages they retrieve, and searchers increasingly do not click through. And AI assistants have become a parallel search channel with their own retrieval and citation behaviour.

The click evidence is consistent across independent and vendor sources:

| Study | Sample | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pew Research Center, July 2025 | 900 US adults, 68,879 searches, March 2025 | Result clicked on 8% of visits with an AI summary, 15% without; session ended on 26% against 16% |
| Ahrefs, February 2026 (vendor) | 300,000 keywords, December 2023 against December 2025 | AI Overview correlated with 58% lower click-through for the top result |
| Seer Interactive, November 2025 (agency) | 3,119 informational queries across 42 clients | Organic CTR on AI Overview queries fell from 1.76% to 0.61%; cited brands had higher CTR than uncited ones |

The direction matters more than any single figure. Seer's own numbers are internally inconsistent in places, and both vendor studies show correlation, not cause. But no credible study shows clicks rising on informational queries.

Both shifts reward the same things: pages that state a clear answer early, make specific checkable claims, are structured so a machine can extract them, and are corroborated by other trusted sources. Both punish content that exists to rank rather than to answer. Google says its AI features need "no additional requirements" beyond ordinary eligibility for Search. Our pieces on [how AI answer engines choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) and the [LLM optimization checklist](https://lowob.com/research/llm-optimization-checklist/) cover the mechanics.

> Everything that has changed in SEO is the engine getting better at measuring searcher satisfaction and worse at being fooled.

## What this means for a company deciding whether to invest

SEO has a long payback. Our working assumption has been six to twelve months before organic traffic covers the cost of the content. The evidence says to treat that as the fast case. Ahrefs' 2025 study of new pages found only about 6% of English pages reached the top 10 for any keyword within a year. The average page in position one was five years old, and 72.9% of top-10 pages were more than three years old. Pages that do break through can move fast: about 41% of those reaching the top 10 did so within a month. Most never do. Fewer clicks per ranking stretch the payback further.

For a company with a short runway and no existing audience, that can be longer than it can afford, and it is fair to say so. Our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) sets out how to compare a slow channel with faster ones.

The calculation changes when the company already has authority to build on, when the category's paid channels are closed to it, or when the content would be written anyway for sales, support or partners. In those cases, writing it once, properly, for search and AI citation together, is close to free distribution. Our guide to [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) covers the closed-channel case.

## The honest minimum

Even a company that decides not to invest in SEO should do the minimum:

1. A fast, crawlable site with accurate titles and descriptions.
2. Business information that is consistent everywhere it appears.
3. Structured data for the organisation.
4. A handful of pages that answer the questions buyers actually search for, each with a named author where expertise matters.
5. No technical mistakes that hide the site, including robots.txt rules that block search crawlers by accident.

In our experience that is about a week of work, and it is the difference between being findable and not. Payback is slow, so invest deliberately, but never skip the minimum.

## lowob takeaways

- **The engine measures satisfaction.** Meaning, relevance, quality, usability and context, plus links and interaction data.
- **Volume is now a liability.** Mass-produced pages breach Google's scaled content abuse policy and do worse in AI answers.
- **Clicks are falling on informational queries.** Plan for citation and for fewer visits per ranking.
- **Payback is slower than most plans.** Treat six to twelve months as the fast case; most new pages never reach the top 10.

## Common questions

### What still matters for SEO in 2026?

Content that answers the query better than alternatives, technical health, clear structure, links and mentions from trusted sites, named authors with real expertise on finance and health topics, and matching what the searcher wanted.

### How long does SEO take to pay off?

Plan on at least six to twelve months, and longer in competitive categories. Ahrefs found only about 6% of new English pages reached the top 10 within a year, though those that did often got there within a month.

### Do AI Overviews reduce clicks to websites?

The evidence says yes for informational queries. Pew found result clicks fell from 15% to 8% of visits when a summary appeared, and Ahrefs measured a 58% lower click-through rate for the top result.

### What is the minimum SEO every company should do?

A fast, crawlable site with accurate titles and descriptions, consistent business information, organisation structured data, a few pages answering what buyers search for, and no technical mistakes that hide the site.

# What Is a Vector Database?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-vector-database/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A vector database stores numerical representations of text, images or other data, called embeddings, and retrieves the items closest in meaning to a query. It is the usual index behind retrieval-augmented generation. Vector search has become a standard feature of existing databases such as Postgres, so most mid-size firms do not need a separate product.

A vector database stores data as embeddings, lists of numbers that capture meaning, and finds the items whose meaning is closest to a query. This lets an AI system find a proposal about "customer churn" when the user asked about "clients leaving", even though the words differ. It is the usual index behind retrieval-augmented generation. Vector search is now a feature in many standard databases, so for most mid-size firms the question is which existing system to switch it on in, not which new product to buy.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a vector database means

Traditional databases find records by exact values: a customer ID, a date, a word. That fails when people describe the same thing in different words. An embedding model solves this by converting a piece of text into a vector, a long list of numbers, so that texts with similar meaning have vectors close together.

A vector database stores those vectors and answers one main question quickly: which stored items are nearest to this query vector. Common distance measures include cosine distance, Euclidean distance and inner product. The results are then passed to a language model, as in retrieval-augmented generation, or shown directly as search results.

| A vector database is | A vector database is not |
| --- | --- |
| An index for finding items by similarity of meaning | A system of record for customers or deals |
| Usually the retrieval layer behind RAG | The AI model that writes answers |
| Approximate by design, trading some recall for speed | A guarantee that the best match is returned |
| Often a feature of an existing database | Necessarily a separate product to buy |

## How it works

Comparing a query against every stored vector is exact but slow at scale. Most systems therefore use approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes. The best known is HNSW, Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs, introduced by Malkov and Yashunin in 2016. It builds layered graphs of connected points, so a search starts with long jumps across the top layer and narrows down through the lower ones.

The Postgres extension pgvector shows the trade-offs plainly. By default it performs exact search, with perfect recall. Adding an HNSW index gives better speed-recall trade-offs but takes longer to build and uses more memory. An IVFFlat index builds faster and uses less memory but queries less efficiently. Its documentation warns that results may change after an approximate index is added.

The market has two camps. Forrester's 2024 Wave distinguished native vector databases, purpose-built for vector workloads, from multi-model databases adding vector capabilities to existing engines. Native products had the head start; established vendors were catching up. By late 2025, commentary in VentureBeat described vector search as a "checkbox feature" in cloud data platforms rather than a standalone advantage.

## Do you need one: how to evaluate

For most firms with 20 to 500 people, the honest answer is that you need vector search, not necessarily a vector database. If your documents already live in Postgres or a cloud platform that offers vector search, start there.

| Situation | Sensible choice |
| --- | --- |
| Under about 200,000 tokens of reference material | Possibly no index at all; place it in the prompt |
| Documents already in Postgres or a cloud data platform | Turn on its vector feature, such as pgvector |
| Your AI assistant or CRM offers built-in document search | Use the vendor's index; rent the wiring |
| Millions of items, strict latency needs, dedicated team | Evaluate a native vector database |

Three mistakes recur. The first is relying on similarity alone. Similarity search returns near-misses: a query for one error code can return a neighbouring one. Practitioners now pair vectors with keyword search, metadata filters and reranking, an approach Anthropic's retrieval research also supports. The second is indexing everything. Duplicate and outdated documents sit close together in vector space and crowd out the current version. The third is treating the index as memory. A vector database finds similar text; it does not know which proposal was approved, who owns the account or what was decided.

In **lowob**'s model, the vector index sits in the wiring stage. It helps the right material reach the model. The record of decisions, with reason, owner and status, belongs in a system you own, and the index should point to it rather than replace it.

## lowob takeaways

- **It finds meaning, not words.** Embeddings let search match "clients leaving" to "customer churn".
- **It is approximate.** Fast indexes such as HNSW trade some recall for speed.
- **It is usually a feature now.** Check your existing database before buying a new one.
- **Pair it with keywords and filters.** Hybrid search avoids near-miss answers.

## Common questions

### What is a vector database used for?

Mainly for finding items by similarity of meaning, most often as the retrieval layer that supplies relevant documents to an AI model in retrieval-augmented generation.

### Do I need a vector database for RAG?

Not always a separate one. Many existing databases, including Postgres with pgvector, offer vector search. Small knowledge bases can sometimes skip retrieval entirely.

### What is the difference between a vector database and a traditional database?

A traditional database matches exact values. A vector database stores embeddings and returns the items nearest in meaning, usually by approximate search.

### What is HNSW?

Hierarchical Navigable Small World, a graph-based index for fast approximate nearest neighbour search, introduced in 2016 and used by many vector databases.

## Sources and notes

- [Malkov and Yashunin, HNSW paper, arXiv 1603.09320](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320v2), March 2016. Academic paper.
- [pgvector on PGXN](https://pgxn.org/dist/vector), open-source extension documentation, version 0.8.7 (October 2026).
- [Forrester, Unleashing the first Forrester Wave for vector databases](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/unleashing-the-first-forrester-wave-for-vector-databases), 1 October 2024. Analyst evaluation; full report is paywalled.
- [VentureBeat, From shiny object to sober reality: the vector database story, two years later](https://venturebeat.com/infrastructure/from-shiny-object-to-sober-reality-the-vector-database-story-two-years-later), 16 November 2025. Opinion piece by a practitioner.
- [Anthropic, Introducing Contextual Retrieval](https://anthropic.com/research/contextual-retrieval), 19 September 2024. Vendor research; source of the 200,000-token threshold.

## Related research

- [The 5 Agent Memory Layers Worth Testing, and How to Test Them](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-agent-memory-layers-worth-testing-and-how-to-test-them/)
- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)

- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Check whether the database or platform that already holds your documents offers vector search. If it does, run a pilot there on one document set before evaluating any new product.

# Distribute Through Whoever Already Holds the Customer

Source: https://lowob.com/research/distribute-through-whoever-already-holds-the-customer/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Fintech cannot buy its way to customers. Trust moves through partners who hold the relationship, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and owned channels. Paid goes last and small, because it is a reviewed category with low conversion rates, and the measures that matter are cost per funded account and retention, not sign-ups.

Fintech cannot buy its way to customers. Trust moves through partners who already hold the relationship, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and the company's own channels. Paid advertising goes last and small: it is a reviewed category, approval can take weeks and be withdrawn, and search benchmarks show finance converting below average. The only measures that matter are cost per funded account and whether the account is still funded at 30, 90 and 365 days.

## Paid is a reviewed category

Ad platforms treat financial products as a category needing review. You submit licensing, business documentation, sometimes the landing pages themselves. Approval can take weeks and can be withdrawn. Certain product types are restricted outright in certain markets.

The rules are specific and they move. Google's financial products and services policy requires verification in some locations, asks for licences and registration numbers, and requires the physical address and fees to be visible on the page. In June 2026 it extended verification to 24 more European markets, with rolling enforcement from 23 July 2026. Meta has required financial ads to US audiences to run in a special ad category since January 2025, with fixed age ranges, no gender targeting and no lookalike audiences.

When approved, you enter an auction shared with incumbent banks, large lenders and insurers. The incumbent next to you in the auction already has the trust you are trying to build.

The usual objection is cost per click, and the evidence is more nuanced than the folklore. WordStream's 2026 benchmarks, from 13,474 US search campaigns, put the average finance and insurance cost per click at $3.39, below the all-industry $5.42. The problem is what happens after the click: finance converted at 2.64%, and cost per lead was $74.44 against an all-industry $66.69. A lead is not a funded account, so the cost per funded account is higher again. Strangers clicking on a money product mostly do not convert, which is the trust problem in numbers.

So paid goes last, as in [Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/). In fintech, it goes last and small: retargeting people who already visited, and search terms that signal intent to switch. Everything else runs through the four channels below.

## Partners who hold the relationship

The customer already trusts someone with their money or their work. Employers run payroll. Accounting and payroll software holds the business's books. Marketplaces hold the seller's payouts. Community organisations hold membership and trust. Each of these can carry you to the customer inside a relationship that already exists.

This is embedded distribution, and it has a specific shape. It is slow to establish. Expect months of integration work, security review, and legal and compliance review on both sides. The partner's compliance team will read your claims register before their marketing team does.

It is also hard to revoke. Once a fintech is integrated into a payroll run or a marketplace payout, removing it costs the partner more than keeping it. Slow in, slow out. For a trust product, that is the trade you want. BCG's 2025 embedded finance research found US small-business adoption of vertical software reached 59% in 2024, described that software as a highly efficient distribution channel for embedded finance, and reported a 2.5 times lower attrition rate for embedded payments than for non-embedded.

Start with one partner who holds the segment you chose in [Part 7](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/). Build the integration properly. Reference it in the next conversation. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the partner's role and payment before the first call.

> Slow in, slow out. For a trust product, that is the trade you want.

## Practitioners who explain

Between the product and the customer there is often a person who explains money for a living. Accountants for small businesses. Personal-finance creators for consumers. Newsletter authors for a specific profession. Bookkeepers, financial coaches, small-business advisers.

These people are trusted because they are independent. Pay them as if they will stay that way. The terms that work are cost per funded account, not cost per click or per sign-up. The practitioner is paid when the customer does the thing that matters, which aligns their advice with your outcome.

Brief them from the claims register. Give them the approved answers on safety, fees, protection and what happens when something goes wrong. Their audience will ask. If the practitioner improvises, the regulator will not blame only the practitioner.

The rules are explicit in the main markets. The UK Financial Conduct Authority's 2024 guidance on social media promotions says influencers who promote a regulated product without approval from an authorised firm may be committing a criminal offence; in 2024 it interviewed 20 finfluencers under caution. The US Federal Trade Commission's 2023 Endorsement Guides set out the potential liability of advertisers as well as endorsers, and require disclosure that is clear and conspicuous. [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to register, pay and disclose.

## Comparison and affiliate publishers

Comparison sites and affiliate publishers already rank for the question your customer is typing. They already answer it, and they already list your competitors. Not being there means the buyer sees the whole category except you.

Treat them as a channel with rules. They want accurate data on rates, fees and eligibility, kept current. They want a tracking link and a commission, which again should be per funded account. They want compliance-approved wording they can quote without their own legal review.

A listing on a comparison site is also a trust signal in its own right. The buyer reads it as "this product is established enough to be compared."

| Channel | What transfers the trust | Time to establish | How to pay |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Partners who hold the relationship | The partner's existing relationship | Months | Revenue share or per funded account |
| Practitioners who explain | Independence and expertise | Weeks | Per funded account |
| Comparison and affiliate publishers | Being listed beside incumbents | Weeks | Per funded account |
| Owned channels | Your own track record | Ongoing | Your time |
| Paid | None; it points at the others | Days to weeks to approve, if approved | Per click; low conversion |

## Owned channels and findable answers

Email, content and the product itself are the channels nobody can revoke. In fintech their main job is to hold the compliance-approved answers where buyers and answer engines can find them.

Every question from [Part 21](https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/)'s table gets a page: who is behind this, who holds the money, what happens when it goes wrong, what the fees are. Written plainly, approved once, kept current. Partners link to them. Practitioners quote them. Comparison sites pull from them. Answer engines ([Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/)) cite them.

The product is also a channel. A funded account that works well is the referral source every other channel is trying to imitate. Make it easy for a satisfied customer to send a friend, with approved wording and a tracked link, and check that referral incentives are lawful for the product and market.

## Measure funded accounts, not sign-ups

[Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) said stop reporting reach. In fintech, stop reporting sign-ups too. A sign-up that never funds is a verification cost and a data liability.

Measure cost per funded account by channel. Then measure whether the account is still funded at 30, 90 and 365 days, by channel. Practitioners and comparison sites will show you different retention than partners do. That difference tells you where to put the next quarter's effort. [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) covers the next step.

| Checklist item | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Paid | Budgeted last, limited to retargeting and switch-intent search terms |
| Embedded partner | One partner who holds your chosen segment is in integration or live |
| Terms | Practitioner and affiliate terms set per funded account, not per click or sign-up |
| Briefs | Every practitioner and publisher brief carries the claims register answers on safety, fees and problems |
| Owned pages | A page exists for each trust question and is the source every channel links to |
| Reporting | Cost per funded account and retention at 30, 90 and 365 days, by channel |

## lowob takeaways

- **Put paid last and small.** It is reviewed, withdrawable and converts strangers poorly in finance.
- **Start with one partner who holds the segment.** Embedded distribution is slow to win and slow to lose.
- **Pay practitioners and publishers per funded account.** Brief them from the claims register; liability follows the firm.
- **Make owned pages the source of truth.** Partners, publishers and answer engines all draw on them.
- **Measure funded accounts and retention by channel.** Sign-ups that never fund are a cost.

## Common questions

### What is the best way for a fintech to acquire customers?

Distribute through whoever already holds the customer: partners such as payroll, accounting software and marketplaces, practitioners who explain money, comparison and affiliate publishers, and your own channels. Paid advertising goes last and small.

### Is Google Ads expensive for fintech?

Not per click: WordStream's 2026 benchmarks put finance and insurance at $3.39, below the $5.42 average. The cost shows up in conversion, at 2.64%, and in a cost per lead above average, before any account is funded.

### How should fintechs pay affiliates and finance creators?

Pay per funded account, not per click or sign-up, so the practitioner is paid when the customer does the thing that matters. Brief them from the claims register on safety, fees and what happens when something goes wrong, and require disclosure.

### What metrics should a fintech track for acquisition?

Cost per funded account by channel, and whether accounts are still funded at 30, 90 and 365 days. A sign-up that never funds is a verification cost and a data liability.

## Sources and notes

- [Google Ads, Financial products and services policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998/financial-products-and-services?hl=en-GB), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.
- [Google Ads, Introducing new verification requirements for certain financial services advertisers (June 2026)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/17127726?hl=en), posted 23 June 2026. Covers 24 EEA markets.
- [Meta for Developers, Special Ad Categories](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/marketing-api/audiences/special-ad-category), checked 16 November 2026. Developer documentation; US scope.

# Email Deliverability Explained: SPF, DKIM, DMARC

Source: https://lowob.com/research/email-deliverability-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Deliverability rests on three layers: authentication, reputation, and content and behaviour. Gmail and Yahoo now require SPF, DKIM, DMARC, one-click unsubscribe and spam rates below 0.3% from bulk senders, Outlook requires the same authentication, and all three enforce it by rejecting mail. Set up the records, warm the domain, send only to people who asked, clean the list and watch the reports.

Deliverability is whether your email reaches the inbox, and it rests on three layers: authentication, reputation, and content and behaviour. Since February 2024, Gmail and Yahoo have required bulk senders to authenticate with SPF, DKIM and DMARC, offer one-click unsubscribe and keep spam complaints below 0.3%. Outlook began rejecting non-compliant bulk mail in May 2025, and Gmail ramped up enforcement from November 2025. Set up the records once, warm the domain, send only to people who asked, clean the list and monitor the reports.

An email list is the most durable channel a company owns, and it is worth nothing if the messages do not arrive. Deliverability has become more technical in the last three years, and the largest mailbox providers now enforce it with rejections rather than warnings.

## The three layers

**Authentication** proves that an email claiming to come from your domain did. Three standards do this, and all three are entries in your domain's DNS.

| Standard | What it does | Current specification |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SPF | Publishes which servers may send mail for your domain | RFC 7208 |
| DKIM | Signs each message so the receiver can verify it came from an authorised source and was not altered | RFC 6376; Google requires keys of at least 1024 bits and recommends 2048 |
| DMARC | Tells receivers what to do with mail that fails SPF and DKIM alignment, and sends you reports on who is sending as your domain | RFC 9989 (May 2026), with reporting in RFC 9990 and 9991 |

DMARC changed this year. The IETF published RFC 9989 in May 2026 as a Proposed Standard on the Internet Standards Track, obsoleting the 2015 specification, RFC 7489. Existing records still begin `v=DMARC1` and keep working. The practical changes are small: updated receivers ignore the `pct` tag, and a new `np` tag sets policy for non-existent subdomains. There is no migration to run.

Setting up the three records is a few hours of work, once. Skipping it means the large providers will throttle or reject your mail regardless of content.

**Reputation.** Mailbox providers score sending domains and IP addresses on how recipients respond: opens, replies, deletions without reading, spam complaints, bounces from dead addresses, and whether people move messages out of spam. A new domain has no reputation and has to build one gradually. A domain that sends a large blast to a cold list on day one earns a bad reputation that takes months to repair.

**Content and behaviour.** Link shorteners, image-only emails, deceptive subject lines and mismatched sender names hurt. So does sending to people who did not ask, sending to addresses that bounce, and ignoring unsubscribe requests, which is also illegal in most places.

## What the major providers now require

Google's sender guidelines took effect on 1 February 2024 and Yahoo began enforcement the same month. Microsoft followed for Outlook.com, Hotmail and Live addresses, with rejection of non-compliant mail from 5 May 2025.

| Requirement | Gmail (over 5,000 a day) | Yahoo (bulk senders) | Outlook.com (over 5,000 a day) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SPF and DKIM | Both required | Both required | Both must pass |
| DMARC | Record required; p=none allowed; From domain must align | p=none or stricter; must pass; relaxed alignment allowed | p=none or stricter; align with SPF or DKIM |
| Spam rate | Below 0.3%; aim below 0.1% | Below 0.3% | Not specified in the announcement |
| One-click unsubscribe | Required for marketing mail, plus a visible link | Required; RFC 8058 POST method "highly recommended" | Not specified in the announcement |
| Unsubscribe processing | 48 hours recommended | Within 2 days | Not specified |
| Enforcement | Ramping up since November 2025; temporary and permanent rejections | Gradual from February 2024 | Rejection with error 550 5.7.515 since May 2025 |

All senders to Gmail, not only bulk senders, must use SPF or DKIM, valid forward and reverse DNS, TLS and a spam rate below 0.3%.

One-click unsubscribe means two headers. RFC 8058, published in January 2017, specifies a `List-Unsubscribe-Post: List-Unsubscribe=One-Click` header alongside a `List-Unsubscribe` header containing an HTTPS address. The mailbox provider sends a POST request to that address when the user clicks unsubscribe, and the message must carry a DKIM signature covering both headers. Most email platforms set this up for you; check that yours does.

> Authentication is a few hours of work, once. Reputation is earned or lost with every send.

## Why legitimate email lands in spam

Usually one of six things:

1. Authentication missing or misconfigured, often a third-party tool sending as your domain without being added to SPF or DKIM.
2. A purchased or scraped list, which produces complaints and bounces.
3. Sending volume that jumped suddenly from a new domain.
4. A list that has not been cleaned, so a large share of addresses are dead.
5. Content that looks like what spammers send.
6. A shared sending service whose other customers behaved badly.

DMARC aggregate reports find the first cause quickly: they list every source sending as your domain.

## The practical setup

| Step | What to do | When |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Authenticate | SPF, DKIM (2048-bit where supported) and DMARC at p=none with reporting | Before any volume |
| Separate | Send marketing from a subdomain so a problem there does not affect transactional or personal mail | At setup |
| Tighten | Move DMARC to quarantine once reports show only legitimate sources | After two to four weeks of clean reports |
| Warm | Start with small volumes to engaged recipients and increase over several weeks | Every new domain or IP |
| Consent | Double opt-in, or at minimum clear consent | Every sign-up |
| Clean | Remove hard bounces immediately and unengaged addresses after a defined period | Every send and quarterly |
| Unsubscribe | One-click headers and a visible link, honoured within two days | Every marketing message |
| Monitor | DMARC reports, bounce rate, complaint rate in Google Postmaster Tools, inbox placement | Weekly |

Outbound sales email is not exempt: a sequence tool sending from the company domain counts towards the same reputation. Our piece on [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) argues for lower volume on relevance grounds; the 0.3% ceiling makes the same argument on technical ones. If your sellers use a [sales engagement platform](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-sales-engagement-platform/), check which domain it sends from and whether it is authenticated.

## For regulated senders

Financial, health and crypto senders face two additional constraints: content rules that apply to the message body as they would to an ad, and heightened scrutiny from mailbox providers whose filters have learned that those categories attract fraud. Compliant, consistent, well-authenticated mail from a warmed domain gets through. Anything that looks like a shortcut does not.

## Why it matters more than it seems

Email is the layer that keeps working when every rented channel changes its rules. A company that has built a list carefully and can reliably reach it has distribution that no platform can suspend. A company that has neglected deliverability has a list of addresses and no way to use them. Our piece on [owned channels](https://lowob.com/research/owned-channels-email-content/) makes the wider case.

## lowob takeaways

- **Authenticate everything that sends as you.** SPF, DKIM and DMARC, including every third-party tool.
- **Stay well under 0.3%.** Aim for Google's 0.1% guideline, and treat complaints as an early warning.
- **Make leaving easy.** One-click unsubscribe, honoured within two days.
- **Watch the reports.** DMARC aggregates and Postmaster Tools show problems before customers do.

## Common questions

### Why are my legitimate emails going to spam?

Usually one of six things: missing or misconfigured authentication, a purchased or scraped list, a sudden volume jump from a new domain, an uncleaned list, spam-like content, or a shared sending service whose other customers behaved badly.

### What are the Gmail and Yahoo bulk sender requirements?

Senders of more than about 5,000 messages a day must use SPF and DKIM, publish a DMARC record (p=none is allowed), keep spam complaints below 0.3%, and offer one-click unsubscribe. Yahoo requires unsubscribes to be honoured within two days.

### What is RFC 8058 one-click unsubscribe?

It is the standard for unsubscribing with one click from the mail client. The message carries a List-Unsubscribe header with an HTTPS address and a List-Unsubscribe-Post header; the mailbox provider sends a POST request to unsubscribe the user.

### How do I warm up a new email sending domain?

Start with small volumes to engaged recipients and increase over several weeks while watching bounces and complaints. A large blast to a cold list on day one earns a reputation that takes months to repair.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, Email sender guidelines FAQ](https://support.google.com/mail/answer/14229414?hl=en-2), consulted November 2026. Source for the November 2025 enforcement ramp-up and the 48-hour unsubscribe recommendation.
- [Yahoo Sender Hub, Sender best practices](https://senders.yahooinc.com/best-practices), consulted November 2026. Platform requirements; enforcement from February 2024.

# AI Companies Have a Distribution Problem Disguised as a Model Problem.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-companies-distribution-problem/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Enterprise AI spend is large and growing, yet many AI products with strong demos still struggle to find paying customers. Buyers say most models are now good enough, procurement looks like ordinary software buying, and Gartner expects over 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027 for cost and unclear value. This piece separates product problems from distribution and adoption problems and sets out how to diagnose which one a company has.

A company can build an impressive AI product, show a great demo, and still struggle to find paying customers. Often the problem is not that the model needs another improvement. It is that the company has not worked out who needs the product, why they should trust it, or how they will discover it. The market evidence points the same way: enterprise AI spend reached about $177 billion in 2026 by Menlo Ventures' estimate, yet buyers increasingly say the models perform well enough, and they now judge AI products on security, cost, integration and proof.

Model quality matters. But better model performance does not automatically create a distribution system. This piece sets out the evidence that the constraint has moved, and a way to tell which problem a company actually has before deciding what to build next. Our explainer on [what a go-to-market strategy is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) covers the wider plan this sits inside.

## A better model isn't a go-to-market plan

Picture a small AI company that can summarise and search internal contracts. Its team spends weeks improving response quality. Meanwhile, the potential buyers are asking different questions. Can we connect it to the documents we already use? Who can see sensitive information? How would we check an incorrect answer? Who owns the rollout?

The demonstration proves a capability. It does not yet make the product easy to adopt. This is a hypothetical example, but it captures the gap between building something useful and persuading an organisation to depend on it.

The buyer evidence supports the distinction. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 CIOs across 15 industries found that "procurement now mirrors traditional software buying", with more rigorous evaluations and more price sensitivity. Security and cost had gained weight relative to accuracy and reliability. One leader put it plainly: "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now."

Gartner's June 2025 forecast that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027 names escalating costs and unclear business value as the causes. Neither is a model problem. Both are problems of fit, proof and adoption.

A company can still need better technology. The point is to distinguish product problems from distribution and adoption problems before deciding what to build next.

## Name the buyer and the job they need done

"Businesses that want to use AI" is too broad to guide marketing. "Legal operations teams that spend hours finding clauses across supplier contracts" is more specific. It points to a job, a person responsible for it, a current alternative and a meaningful outcome.

Start with three questions. Who has the problem often enough to pay? What do they do today instead? What would convince them to change? Interview buyers rather than answering from the product team's imagination. Our guide to [writing an ICP sales will use](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) sets out the fields worth recording.

The money is there for companies that answer those questions well. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey of nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers estimated deployment spend at $176.8 billion through September 2026, up 5.4 times on the prior year. New budgets funded 55% of the incremental spend, and AI-native vendors captured 77% of application-layer spend. Adoption grew more slowly, from 55% to 65% of enterprises, which means spend is concentrating in buyers who have already found a job worth paying for.

Not every AI product needs to own an entire workflow. Some successful products are focused components inside systems customers already use. In either case, the integration and the end result matter more to adoption than the isolated model demo.

## Show what the product does, and where it can fail

Trust grows when people can inspect the work. A short demonstration with a real workflow, realistic inputs and clearly identified limitations is more persuasive than a claim that the tool is "revolutionary". In higher-stakes uses, explain what happens when the system is uncertain and how people can review its output.

Buyers are primed to discount broad claims. Gartner estimated in 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI were offering real agentic capability, the practice our explainer on [agent washing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) describes. Gartner's survey of 645 B2B buyers, published in May 2026, found 45% had used generative AI during a purchase, 51% believed they were more likely to get misleading information from it, and 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep. A vendor that makes its proof easy to check is answering the question buyers are already asking.

For the contract product, useful proof might include sample tasks, permission controls, a documented evaluation process and feedback from a pilot customer, with the customer's permission. Avoid claiming a universal accuracy rate based on a small internal test. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to build a test a buyer can read.

> The demonstration proves a capability. It does not yet make the product easy to adopt.

The team should record objections from sales calls and use them to improve the product, the explanation and the onboarding process.

## Build channels that reach the people doing the work

Generic AI announcements compete with thousands of similar launches. An industry practitioner demonstrating a workflow, an integration into software buyers already use, or a useful comparison published where teams research solutions may do more to reach a qualified buyer.

The data on how AI products are adopted backs this. Menlo's 2025 survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision makers found 27% of AI application spend came through product-led growth, against 7% in traditional software. Adoption often started with individual users who proved value in daily work before any central contract. Menlo reported that Cursor reached $200 million in revenue before hiring an enterprise sales rep. That is one company, reported by an investor, but the pattern across the survey is consistent: in AI, the person doing the work often finds the product first.

Prioritise a few channels you can test: direct conversations with target accounts, credible practitioner partnerships, integrations and instructional content. Cloud marketplaces can shorten procurement once a buyer is interested, as our piece on [marketplace listings for B2B](https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/) explains. Add paid acquisition where the economics make sense and the claims are supportable. Keep the resulting contacts and learning in systems the company controls.

Choose a distribution approach that remains useful even if the underlying models improve or suppliers change. Menlo's 2026 data shows how fast the supply side moves: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. A channel built on the buyer and the workflow survives those swings. A pitch built on whichever model leads this quarter does not.

## Measure adoption, not demo applause

Track the path from a relevant conversation to a trial, a completed job, repeat use and, when applicable, paid retention. If the product's value is saving time, measure the quality of the result alongside the time saved. A faster answer that creates rework is not a win.

Conversion is achievable. Menlo's 2025 survey found 47% of AI deals reached production, against 25% for traditional SaaS. The companies that convert are those whose pilots end in a completed job a buyer can point to.

When prospects consistently fail at setup, improve onboarding. When nobody can explain the return, improve proof. When the right people never see the product, improve distribution. Those are different problems, and they deserve different responses.

| What you see | What kind of problem it is | The response |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strong demo reactions, few trials | Reach or targeting | Narrow the buyer; test practitioner and integration channels |
| Trials start, setup stalls | Adoption | Fix onboarding, connectors and permissions before features |
| Trials complete, no purchase | Proof or value | Publish the eval; tie the result to the buyer's own cost |
| Purchases, low repeat use | Product or fit | Revisit the job; this is where model or workflow work pays |
| Repeat use, slow expansion | Distribution inside the account | Name the next team and the owner who will carry it |

Only one row in that table is primarily a model problem. Most AI companies that believe they need a better model are sitting in one of the other four.

## lowob takeaways

- **Separate capability from adoption.** A better model alone will not fix a missing buyer or channel.
- **Sell a specific job.** State who needs the product, what they do today and what improves.
- **Make proof easy to inspect.** Real workflow examples and honest limitations build more trust than broad claims, and buyers now check.
- **Measure repeat use.** Trials and demos matter only if the product becomes useful work.

## Common questions

### Why do AI startups struggle to get customers even with a good product?

Usually because the company has not named a specific buyer and job, made its proof easy to check, or built a channel that reaches the people doing the work. Buyers increasingly say models perform well enough for most tasks, so they judge on fit, security, cost and evidence.

### How do you know if an AI company has a product problem or a distribution problem?

Look at where prospects stop. Few trials point to reach; stalled setup points to onboarding; completed trials without purchase point to proof; purchases without repeat use point to product fit. Only the last is mainly a model problem.

### Why are so many enterprise AI projects cancelled?

Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, citing escalating costs and unclear business value. Projects without a defined job, owner and success measure are the most exposed.

### What distribution channels work best for AI products?

Channels that reach practitioners: direct conversations with target accounts, integrations into tools buyers already use, practitioner partnerships and instructional content. Product-led adoption carried 27% of AI application spend in Menlo's 2025 survey, against 7% for traditional software.

## Sources and notes

Investor research; nearly 400 US enterprise decision makers surveyed by Morning Consult, 8 to 26 September 2026. Menlo invests in AI companies.
- [Menlo Ventures, 2025: The State of Generative AI in the Enterprise](https://menlovc.com/perspective/2025-the-state-of-generative-ai-in-the-enterprise/), 9 December 2025. Investor research; 495 US enterprise AI decision makers, November 2025. Private-company revenue figures are Menlo's estimates.

Pull the last twenty prospects who saw a demo and mark where each one stopped: no trial, stalled setup, no purchase or low repeat use. Fix the row with the most names before you schedule the next model improvement.

# What Is Agent Identity and an Agent Registry?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-identity/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-15 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agent identity treats each AI agent as a distinct, accountable actor with its own credentials, scoped permissions and a human sponsor. An agent registry is the inventory of those agents. NIST, the OpenID Foundation and OWASP all flag identity as a gap in current agent deployments.

Agent identity means giving each AI agent its own identity, separate from the people who use it, with its own credentials, scoped permissions and a named human owner, so that every action can be traced to the agent and to the person who authorised it. An agent registry is the inventory of those agents: what exists, who owns it, what it can reach and whether it is still in use. Together they answer the question a security team or auditor will ask first: which agents act for this company, and on whose authority.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What agent identity means

The simplest way to deploy an agent is to let it borrow an identity: it runs on the installing user's login, a shared service account or an API key in a configuration file. That works until something goes wrong, and then the logs show a person, or nobody, where the agent acted.

An agent identity separates the two. NIST's concept paper names the building blocks it wants to test with existing standards:

| Element | Question it answers | Standards named by NIST |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Identification | Is this an agent or a person, and which agent? | SPIFFE/SPIRE for workload identity |
| Authentication | Is it really that agent? | OpenID Connect |
| Authorisation | What may it do, on which data? | OAuth 2.0 and 2.1 |
| Delegation | On whose behalf is it acting? | Open question in the paper |
| Lifecycle | When was it created, changed or revoked? | SCIM |
| Audit and non-repudiation | Can its actions be proven and tied to a human approval? | Open question in the paper |

The paper also asks how agents can log their actions and intent "in a tamper-proof and verifiable manner", and calls for linking specific user identities to agents to maintain accountability.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial agents act across many systems: CRM, email, calendar, document stores, proposal tools. Each connection is a credential. Without a separate identity, three problems follow.

**Excess privilege.** OWASP's ASI03 describes agents that reuse, escalate or expose inherited credentials. An agent that runs as a sales director inherits the director's access to every account.

**Broken delegation.** The OpenID Foundation's October 2025 paper notes that today's authentication frameworks work for simple, single-organisation agents but "weren't designed for recursive delegation chains", where one agent calls another on a user's behalf. The NCCoE paper puts "on behalf of" delegation on its list of open questions.

**No accountability.** If the logs cannot separate the agent from its user, an audit trail cannot show who decided what. **lowob**'s rule that nothing sends without a person depends on knowing which agent drafted and which person approved.

> Every agent should have an owner who can be named and a permission set that can be read.

## What an agent registry holds

A registry is the inventory that makes identities manageable. Microsoft describes its Agent 365 registry as "a unified inventory of all agents operating in the organization, including both Microsoft and non-Microsoft agents", including agents without an Entra identity. A firm without that product can keep the same record in a spreadsheet or its governance tool.

| Field | Why it is needed |
| --- | --- |
| Agent name and purpose | Ties the agent to a task as written |
| Human owner or sponsor | Someone answers for it and approves changes |
| Identity and credential type | Shows whether it runs as itself or borrows a person's access |
| Systems and scopes | The real extent of its agency |
| Autonomy level | 0 answer, 1 draft, 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone |
| Model and instruction version | Links runs to the configuration that produced them |
| Status and review date | Retires agents nobody uses, before they become a risk |

The registry is also the starting point for AI governance. An inventory of models and tools misses the agents built on top of them, and those are the ones that act.

## lowob takeaways

- **Give agents their own identity.** Borrowed logins make actions untraceable and access too broad.
- **Name a human owner.** Every agent needs a sponsor who answers for its behaviour.
- **Keep a registry.** List every agent, its scopes and autonomy level, and review it on a schedule.
- **Use existing standards first.** OAuth, OpenID Connect, SPIFFE and SCIM cover much of the need today.

## Common questions

### What is an AI agent identity?

A distinct digital identity for an AI agent, with its own credentials, permissions and a named owner, so its actions are recorded separately from the people who use it.

### What is an agent registry?

An inventory of every AI agent an organisation runs, with its owner, purpose, systems accessed, permissions, autonomy level and status.

### Why should AI agents not use a person's login?

Because the agent inherits all of that person's access, and the logs cannot show whether the person or the agent acted.

### What standards apply to AI agent identity?

NIST's NCCoE is examining OAuth 2.0 and 2.1, OpenID Connect, SPIFFE/SPIRE and SCIM for agent identity and authorisation.

## Sources and notes

- [NIST NCCoE, Accelerating the Adoption of Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization (concept paper)](https://www.nccoe.nist.gov/sites/default/files/2026-02/accelerating-the-adoption-of-software-and-ai-agent-identity-and-authorization-concept-paper.pdf), February 2026, with [NIST's announcement](https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/02/new-concept-paper-identity-and-authority-software-agents). Draft for comment; not final guidance.
- [OpenID Foundation, New whitepaper tackles AI agent identity challenges](https://openid.net/new-whitepaper-tackles-ai-agent-identity-challenges/), 7 October 2025. Standards body summary of its whitepaper.
- [TechRepublic, OWASP drops first AI agent risk list](https://www.techrepublic.com/article/news-owasp-ai-agent-risk-list/), 19 December 2025. Press summary of the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications.
- [Microsoft Learn, Agent registry convergence with Microsoft Agent 365](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/agent-registry-convergence) and [What's new in Agent ID](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/entra/agent-id/whats-new-agent-id), 2026. Vendor documentation, cited as an example of the category.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [Top 5 AI Governance and Audit-Trail Tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/)
- [Top 5 Agent Frameworks for Production, by State Model and Cloud](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-agent-frameworks-for-production-by-state-model-and-cloud/)

## Next move

List every agent and automation that connects to your CRM or email, and note whose credentials each one uses. Any that run on a named person's login are the first to move to their own identity.
