# Why the Brain Starts at the Commercial Line

Source: https://lowob.com/research/why-the-brain-starts-at-the-commercial-line/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Commercial decisions are frequent, similar, graded within a quarter and defended by a budget holder, and they sit on the most structured data most firms own. Firm-wide knowledge bases are the most requested starting point and the hardest to justify a year later. Regulated sectors and long sales cycles change the order.

Start the brain where you can count what it changed within a quarter. In most mid-size firms that is the commercial line: sales, marketing and account management. Commercial decisions recur weekly, resemble each other, show their outcome within months and have a budget holder who must defend them, and they already sit on a structured system: the CRM. The firm-wide knowledge base, the most common alternative, delivers value that is real but rarely measurable, which makes it hard to fund twice.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

When a company decides to build its brain, two starting points usually compete. One is the firm-wide knowledge base: every methodology, template and past deliverable, searchable by anyone. It addresses a real complaint, because new staff spend weeks asking where things are. The other is the commercial line: the accounts, the pitches, the pipeline and the follow-ups that keep slipping.

Both address real pain. Only one lets a sponsor say, at the end of a quarter, what the build was worth. That difference decides whether the second phase gets funded.

## The knowledge-base trap

A firm-wide knowledge base is useful in the way a good filing system is useful: everyone benefits a little, and nobody can say by how much. It is also the use case that broad assistant rollouts most resemble, and the adoption record is sobering. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of those who pay open it in a typical week, according to figures Windows Latest reported in July 2026. An assistant that can see everything but has no particular job tends to become an expensive search box.

There is a second, structural problem. A knowledge base collects documents. Documents tell a system what is true; decisions tell it what the company does. In *A loop with good context* we described the precedent an experienced person carries (three similar past cases, what was decided, what went wrong) and noted that it is retrievable only if someone recorded it. A knowledge base built first almost never captures it.

## The test: where judgment arrives first

We have published a test for where a decision layer starts to earn its keep. Judgment arrives first in decisions that are frequent, similar, quickly graded, and later defended by someone with budget or regulatory accountability (*Where judgment arrives first*). Run the commercial line through it.

| Commercial decision | Frequency | Similar to past cases? | Outcome known within | Who defends it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qualify or drop an inbound lead | Daily | Yes | Weeks | Head of sales |
| Pursue or pass on a pitch | Weekly | Mostly | One sales cycle | Partners or leadership |
| Approve a discount beyond standard | Weekly | Yes | One sales cycle | Finance and sales |
| Set or shift campaign spend | Monthly | Mostly | A quarter | Budget holder |
| Record why a deal was lost | Weekly | Yes | Already known | Head of sales |
| Prioritise accounts for the quarter | Quarterly | Mostly | A quarter | Revenue leader |

Almost every row passes on all four counts. Now run a typical knowledge-base decision through the same test: "which version of the methodology document is canonical" happens rarely, varies each time, has no clear outcome and no budget holder defending it. It is a worthwhile decision, but it belongs in a disciplined record people read, not in a system expected to learn.

## Where the recoverable time actually is

The commercial line also has unusually well-documented slack. Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found that sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, with the rest consumed by administration, data entry, research and internal coordination. Sellers already using agents expect them to cut prospect research time by about a third and email drafting time by a similar share, and top-performing sellers were 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use agents for prospecting.

Those are vendor-run figures and expected rather than measured savings, so we treat them as direction rather than proof. But they point to the same tasks where agents are most reliable today: research, preparation, record hygiene and first drafts. The brain's first job on the commercial line is to return that time without adding risk.

## You already own the store

The commercial line has a structured home that most other functions lack: the CRM. It holds accounts, contacts, stages, owners and dates. That matters because the brain needs somewhere to write outcomes back, and a closed-won or closed-lost deal is exactly that link, already sitting in a field.

The store is rarely in good shape. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users and administrators found 37% reporting revenue lost as a direct result of poor data quality, and its 2026 survey of 500 marketers found only 21% considered their CRM data very well prepared for the AI tools they use or plan to use. That is an argument for starting here, not against it. Cleaning the store is part of the build, and it pays for itself in forecasting and follow-up even before any agent is switched on. Part 4 covers how.

## Where the money is going

Spending patterns point the same way. Menlo Ventures estimates that more than half of the $37bn companies spent on generative AI in 2025 went to applications rather than infrastructure, and that departmental spending reached $7.3bn, led by coding. Buyers are paying for software that does a job in a function they can measure. A brain that begins by doing a commercial job is easier to buy, easier to evaluate and easier to fund a second time than one that begins as general infrastructure.

> Start where you can say, after one quarter, what moved. If you cannot, you started in the wrong place.

## The case against starting here

The argument has limits, and we would rather name them than leave a reader to find them.

**Regulated firms.** In banking, insurance and healthcare, the first decisions that must be defended are often compliance decisions. A supervisor may ask the firm to reconstruct why a pricing exception was granted or a client communication sent. There, the decision record and audit trail come before any commercial agent. The order bends but the logic holds: start where decisions are defended.

**Long enterprise sales cycles.** If a deal takes eighteen months, the "quickly graded" test fails. The workaround is leading indicators (meetings held, stage progression, stakeholder coverage) chosen with care, because a system optimises whatever proxy it is given.

**Service-led firms.** Where the client relationship lives in delivery rather than in sales, the commercial line may run through account management and renewals. Start there; the reasoning is the same.

**Very small teams.** Below about ten people, the record may be a shared document and a weekly review rather than a system. Our scale guide, *The scale ladder*, describes what to build at each size.

Illustrative example: choosing the starting point

Decision
:   Build on the commercial line first and schedule the firm-wide knowledge base for after Gateway 3.

Reason and owner
:   Commercial decisions pass all four tests and already have a system of record; the knowledge base has no agreed success measure. Agreed by leadership; owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   The knowledge base becomes a later phase with its own measure (time to first billable work for new hires) rather than the first spend.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size advisory firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start where you can count the change.** If nothing measurable moves in a quarter, the starting point was wrong.
- **Test decisions, not departments.** Frequent, similar, quickly graded and defended decisions are where a brain learns first.
- **Clean the store as part of the build.** Poor CRM data costs revenue on its own; fixing it is the first return.
- **Know when the order bends.** Regulated firms record first; long cycles need careful leading indicators.

Gateway card

### Before you commit to a starting point

- The five most frequent commercial decisions listed
- For each: how often, how similar, how soon graded, who defends it
- One measure that will move within a quarter
- The CRM's current data quality estimated, honestly

## Common questions

### Where should a company start its enterprise AI build?

Usually on the commercial line, because its decisions are frequent, similar, graded within months and defended by a budget holder, and because the CRM already provides a structured record to write outcomes into.

### Why not start with a company-wide knowledge base?

A knowledge base delivers diffuse value that is hard to measure, and it captures documents rather than decisions. It is a better second or third phase than a first one.

### How much time do salespeople spend selling?

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found sellers spend about 40% of their time selling, with the remainder on administration, research and data entry.

### When should a company not start with sales and marketing?

In regulated sectors where compliance decisions must be reconstructed first, in businesses with very long sales cycles, and where the client relationship sits in delivery rather than sales.

- [Salesforce, State of Sales 2026](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/state-of-sales-report-announcement-2026/). Survey of 4,000+ sales professionals; vendor-run; expected savings.
- [Validity, State of CRM Data Management in 2025](https://validity.com/resource-center/the-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2025). Survey of 602 CRM users and stakeholders.

# What Is Context Engineering?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-context-engineering/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-14 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Context engineering is the practice of curating everything a language model sees when it works: instructions, retrieved documents, tool results and conversation history. Research shows model accuracy falls as context grows, so more is not better. For a commercial team, it means deciding which account facts an assistant needs for each task, and keeping them clean.

Context engineering is the practice of choosing and maintaining the information an AI model sees at each step of a task: its instructions, the documents and records retrieved for it, the results of tools it calls and the history of the conversation. It extends prompt engineering from the wording of a request to everything around it. The discipline exists because models get worse, not better, when given too much. The right few facts beat a full data dump.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What context engineering means

The term spread in mid-2025. Shopify's chief executive Tobi Lütke called it a core skill, and Andrej Karpathy, formerly of OpenAI, described it as the "delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step." In September 2025 Anthropic published engineering guidance defining it as the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens during inference.

The difference from prompt engineering is scope. Prompt engineering is about how instructions are written. Context engineering covers the whole state the model works from, including system instructions, tool definitions, retrieved data and message history. For an agent that runs many steps, that state changes at every step, so curation is continuous rather than a one-off.

| Prompt engineering | Context engineering |
| --- | --- |
| Wording one request well | Choosing everything the model sees |
| Mostly a writing task | A data and systems task |
| Done once per template | Done at every step of a task |
| Fixes tone and format | Fixes accuracy and relevance |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

The case rests on a finding that surprises many buyers: larger context windows do not solve the problem. Chroma's research team tested 18 models in 2025 and found that performance "grows increasingly unreliable as input length grows." Distracting but irrelevant material made it worse. Earlier, Liu and colleagues showed in "Lost in the Middle" that models recall information best when it sits at the beginning or end of a long input.

Anthropic's guidance calls this "context rot" and describes a model's attention as a finite budget. Every extra token draws on it.

For a commercial team, the practical meaning is clear. An assistant asked to prepare for a renewal call does not need the whole CRM history, every email and every document in the account folder. It needs the current contract terms, open issues, the last three interactions, decisions already made about this account, and the stakeholders. Giving it everything makes the brief longer and less accurate.

This is the wiring stage in **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain. The store holds the data. The context layer decides which slice of it reaches the model for a given task. Decision records with a reason, owner and status are some of the highest-value context available, because they tell the model what has already been agreed and why.

## How to start: four techniques

Anthropic's guidance describes several techniques for agents working on long tasks. Each has a direct commercial equivalent.

| Technique | What it does | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Just-in-time retrieval | Keeps references, such as record IDs or links, and loads data only when needed | An assistant fetches the contract only when asked about terms |
| Compaction | Summarises a long session and restarts with the summary | A multi-day deal review carries forward a short summary, not every message |
| Structured notes | The agent writes notes to a file outside its context and reads them later | A running account note of decisions and open questions |
| Sub-agents | Focused agents work in clean context and return condensed results | One agent reads support tickets and returns a five-line summary for the brief |

Three mistakes are common. The first is connecting every system and letting the model sort it out. The second is relying on a larger context window instead of better selection. The third is letting stale data in: a CRM field last updated a year ago is worse than an empty one, because the model will treat it as true.

A good starting exercise is to write down, for one recurring task, the fields and documents a skilled person would actually look at. That list is the first version of the task's context.

## lowob takeaways

- **Less, chosen well, beats more.** Model accuracy falls as irrelevant context grows.
- **Design per task.** A renewal brief and a pipeline review need different slices of the same data.
- **Put decisions in the context.** Records of what was agreed, and why, prevent the model from reopening settled questions.
- **Clean before you connect.** Stale fields become confident errors.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between context engineering and prompt engineering?

Prompt engineering is about wording instructions. Context engineering covers everything the model sees, including retrieved data, tool results and history, and manages it at every step.

### Does a bigger context window remove the need for context engineering?

No. Studies including Chroma's 2025 test of 18 models show accuracy degrades as input length grows, so selecting the right information still matters.

### What is context rot?

Anthropic's term for the decline in a model's ability to recall information accurately as its context fills with more tokens.

### How do I start with context engineering?

Pick one recurring task, list the records and documents a skilled person uses for it, and give the assistant only those. Measure accuracy before adding more.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Effective context engineering for AI agents](https://anthropic.com/research/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents), 29 September 2025. Vendor engineering guidance.
- [Chroma, Context rot: how increasing input tokens impacts LLM performance](https://www.trychroma.com/research/context-rot), 14 July 2025. Vendor research; Chroma sells retrieval infrastructure.
- [Liu et al., Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.03172v3), arXiv, July 2023 (revised November 2023). Academic paper; tested models of that period.
- Karpathy and Lütke remarks, June 2025, as reported by [The Decoder](https://the-decoder.com/shopify-ceo-and-ex-openai-researcher-agree-that-context-engineering-beats-prompt-engineering/). Social media posts reported by trade press.
- The commercial mappings are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)
- [Retrieval Is Not the Bottleneck](https://lowob.com/research/retrieval-is-not-the-bottleneck/)
- [A Loop With Good Context](https://lowob.com/research/a-loop-with-good-context/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Choose one recurring task, such as preparing for a renewal call, and write the list of fields and documents a senior person actually checks. Give your assistant only that list and compare the result with an unrestricted run.

# What Is a Decision Record?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A decision record captures one decision with its reason, owner, status and expected outcome. The format comes from software architecture decision records, which are never edited once accepted but superseded by new ones. On the commercial line it is the part of the enterprise brain no connector can supply.

A decision record is a short, dated entry that captures one decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its current status and what outcome is expected. The format comes from software architecture, where Michael Nygard proposed architecture decision records in 2011. For a commercial team it is the part of the enterprise brain that no connector can supply, because a reason nobody wrote down cannot be retrieved.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What a decision record means

The idea is older than AI. Martin Fowler describes an architecture decision record as a short document that captures and explains a single decision, ideally about a page long, covering the decision, its context and its significant consequences. Michael Nygard coined the term in 2011. AWS published prescriptive guidance on the practice in 2022, describing records as hand-over and reference documentation for future teams.

The UK Department for Science, Innovation and Technology published an Architectural Decision Record framework on 4 November 2025. It asks for a title, date, status, context, decision, consequences, the stakeholders consulted and links to supporting documents. It is mandated for cross-government decisions and recommended everywhere else.

Two conventions carry over to business decisions. First, a record has a status. Fowler lists proposed, accepted and superseded. Second, once a record is accepted it is not reopened. If the decision changes, a new record supersedes it and the old one links forward. The log then shows what was decided, and how long each decision governed the work.

## How it works on the commercial line

A commercial decision record needs fewer words than an architecture one, and one field architecture records often skip: the outcome expected.

| Field | What to write | Illustrative example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Decision | One sentence, stated first | Approve a 12% discount on a two-year renewal |
| Reason | Why, including the evidence that mattered | Competing quote received; account expanding into a second region |
| Owner | One named person | Head of sales |
| Date | When it was made | The approval date |
| Status | Proposed, accepted, superseded or closed | Accepted |
| Expected outcome | Measure, threshold, date | Renewal signed at or above the prior year's value by quarter end |
| Check date and links | When to review; links to the quote and thread | Quarter end; CRM opportunity and email |

The expected outcome is what makes the record a judgement rather than a press release. "If it does not work out" leaves the meaning to be decided later. A measure, a threshold and a date can be checked by someone other than the author. When the check date arrives, the outcome is written back to the same record.

For AI agents, the record does a second job. An agent preparing a renewal can read the last three comparable discount decisions, their reasons and what happened. Documents tell an agent what is true. Decisions tell it what the company does.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Why it fails | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Editing the record when the decision changes | The reason for the change disappears | Supersede with a new record and link both |
| Free-text reasons only | Records cannot be grouped or compared | Add a few fixed fields: segment, deal type, size band |
| Recording every decision | The habit collapses within weeks | Record the ten or so that recur and carry money |
| AI summaries as the only copy | Nobody can inspect the source | Keep the original record; let summaries point to it |
| No check date in a calendar | Outcomes never get written back | Put the check date in the owner's calendar |

The cost of not keeping records is measurable in time. In McKinsey's 2019 survey of 1,228 managers, respondents spent an average of 37% of their working time on decisions, and 61% said most of that time was used ineffectively. A record does not make the decision better on its own. It makes the next similar decision faster, and makes a bad pattern visible.

## lowob takeaways

- **One decision, one record.** Short, dated, owned and given a status.
- **Supersede, never overwrite.** The change and its reason are the most useful information you hold.
- **Write the expected outcome first.** A measure, threshold and date make the decision gradable.
- **Start small.** The recurring commercial decisions that carry money come first.

## Common questions

### What is a decision record?

A short, dated entry that captures one decision: what was decided, why, who owns it, its status and what outcome is expected. It is linked to the documents and conversations behind it.

### What is an architecture decision record (ADR)?

A one-page document that captures a single software architecture decision with its context and consequences. Michael Nygard proposed the format in 2011, and it is now common in engineering teams and the UK public sector.

### What should a decision log include?

At minimum: the decision, the reason, the owner, the date, the status, the expected outcome and a check date. Links to supporting evidence make it auditable.

### Why do AI agents need decision records?

Because connectors can only retrieve what was recorded. Without decisions and reasons, an agent cannot tell which price or policy is current, or why an earlier one was withdrawn.

## Sources and notes

- [Martin Fowler, Architecture Decision Record](https://www.martinfowler.com/bliki/ArchitectureDecisionRecord.html), March 2026. Practitioner reference; credits Nygard's 2011 original.
- [GOV.UK, Architectural Decision Record framework](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/architectural-decision-record-framework/architectural-decision-record-framework), DSIT, 4 November 2025. Public-sector standard.
- [AWS Prescriptive Guidance, Using architectural decision records](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/prescriptive-guidance/latest/architectural-decision-records/welcome.html), March 2022. Vendor guidance.
- [McKinsey, Decision making in the age of urgency](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organizational-performance/our-insights/decision-making-in-the-age-of-urgency), April 2019. Self-reported survey.
- The commercial fields and expected-outcome structure are **lowob**'s adaptation of the ADR format.

## Related research

- [The Ten Commercial Decisions Worth Recording](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-decisions-worth-recording/)
- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Take the last discount your team approved and write it up in the seven fields above. If the reason or the expected outcome cannot be found, start recording the next one.

# Forget 10,000 Followers. Find Your First 100 People Who Actually Care.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-12 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: The first meaningful community milestone is 100 people who understand why the project matters and repeatedly choose to participate. This piece covers running that first group: defining caring as behaviour, a narrow member thesis, one recurring ritual, consequential roles, a weekly member-health review and growth through density.

The first meaningful community milestone is not 10,000 followers, 5,000 Discord members or a trending announcement. It is 100 people who understand why the project matters and repeatedly choose to participate. Our piece [The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) covers recruiting them; this one covers running them: what counts as caring, the one ritual to start with, the roles to give, the weekly review and when to grow.

A hundred is small enough for a team to know many members directly and large enough for useful patterns, peer relationships and early culture to emerge. It forces the company to learn why people return before paying to acquire thousands who do not. This is the operating stage of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## Define "cares" as behaviour

Do not define an active member as someone who joined a server or reacted to an announcement. For the first 100, require one or more meaningful behaviours:

| Behaviour | What it shows | How to record it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Attended two sessions | Returning, not sampling | Attendance list |
| Answered another member's question | Peer value exists | Thread or channel log |
| Tested the product and gave useful feedback | Product contribution | Feedback tracker |
| Created a resource, integration or piece of content | Building on the project | Resource list |
| Introduced a relevant participant | Willingness to vouch | Referral log |
| Returned in multiple weeks | Habit | Weekly activity |
| Completed an economically or commercially valuable action | Value to the business | Product or CRM data |

The definition should reflect what makes the product or network stronger. Platform metrics can help but do not replace it. Discord's Server Insights separates "visitors", members who open a channel, from "communicators", members who post, and tracks new member retention as the share of new members who return after a week. Discord suggests about 30% communicators as a healthy goal. Those figures describe presence. The table above describes contribution.

## Recruit from a narrow shared problem

Broad communities struggle because members have little reason to recognise one another. "People interested in Web3" is not a useful initial group. "Treasury leaders at crypto companies evaluating stablecoin yield and counterparty risk" is. Narrowness increases the probability that one member's question is valuable to another.

Begin with a member thesis:

*We are assembling [specific people] who are actively trying to [specific outcome] and can help one another by [specific exchange].*

This is more compelling than asking strangers to join a company server. The founding team should recruit the first 25 to 40 members through direct relationships and high-context outreach, using the loop described in [The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/). The invitation should explain why that person specifically belongs, who else will participate and what the first experience will deliver. Exclusivity without relevance is vanity. Relevance creates the feeling of being in the right room.

## Start with one recurring ritual

Do not launch with twenty empty channels. Launch with one repeatable reason to gather: a weekly product teardown, a private market-signal briefing, a founder problem-solving session, an integration clinic for developers, a rotating member case study or a research exchange around a narrow market.

The ritual should make members useful to one another, and the first test is whether newcomers get a response. Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet groups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got none. Replies from established members and replies using inclusive "we" language were linked to longer stays. Kraut and Resnick's *Building Successful Online Communities* (MIT Press) turns findings like these into design claims about contribution and commitment. A ritual with a host who makes sure every first question gets answered is that research put into practice.

Collect the best questions, decisions and resources from each session, then return them to the group as a growing knowledge base. Our piece on [Discord and Telegram strategy](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/) covers how to stop that knowledge disappearing into chat.

> Do not ask how to make a community look large. Ask what would make 100 specific people return without being chased.

## Give members consequential roles

Early members should be able to influence something real. They might test a feature, shape documentation, help select speakers, lead a working group, nominate future members or contribute to a public guide. The role must have a visible effect. Decorative councils and meaningless badges teach people that participation is theatre.

Recognition should follow contribution. Highlight the member who solved a difficult problem, introduced two collaborators or produced a resource, not merely the person who posted most often. Nielsen's work on participation inequality makes the same warning: rewarding raw activity lets the most prolific few dominate, so promote quality contributions instead.

## Run a weekly member-health review

For every member, track:

- Source of introduction
- Reason for joining
- First meaningful action
- Relationships formed
- Contributions made
- Last meaningful participation
- Likely next role

Each week, identify five members who need a better introduction, a clearer invitation or a direct conversation. Early community operations are closer to relationship management than mass social media. Our piece on [community management versus social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) explains why the person running this review should be a host, not a publisher.

Illustrative example: one ritual, one review

Decision
:   A B2B data infrastructure company replaced a 14-channel public server with a fortnightly integration clinic for 40 invited engineers and a weekly member-health review.

Reason and owner
:   Most channels were silent and support questions were going unanswered. The developer-relations lead owned the clinic and the review.

What changed
:   Each clinic ended with notes returned to members. After two months, members were answering most clinic follow-up questions themselves, and the next cohort was invited from their introductions.

Illustrative: a composite of developer-community patterns, not a single company.

## Grow through member density

Invite the next cohort only when the first group is receiving consistent value. Ask active members whom they know with the same problem and what expertise is missing from the room.

This creates density: a higher probability that any member can find a relevant conversation, collaborator or answer. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found average engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, with smaller communities engaging at higher rates and real-time chat declining fastest as communities grew. Density matters more than raw size because it produces the experiences people describe to others. In-person sessions can raise it further; [events that pay back](https://lowob.com/research/events-that-pay-back/) covers how to judge whether they do.

The first 100 members establish norms the next 1,000 will inherit. If the initial culture rewards speculation, extraction and staff dependence, scale will amplify those behaviours. If it rewards useful contribution, informed disagreement and peer support, growth has something worth multiplying.

## lowob takeaways

- **Define caring as behaviour.** Count answers, tests, resources and returns, not joins and reactions.
- **Keep the group narrow.** A shared, specific problem makes members useful to one another.
- **Answer every first question.** Newcomers who get replies are far more likely to stay.
- **Set the norms early.** The first 100 establish what the next 1,000 will inherit.

## Common questions

### How do you build a community from zero?

Write a narrow member thesis, recruit the first 25 to 40 people personally, start one recurring ritual that makes members useful to each other and grow only when that group gets consistent value.

### What counts as an active community member?

Someone who does something that makes the network stronger: answers a question, tests the product, creates a resource, introduces a relevant person or returns over several weeks. Joining or reacting does not count.

### How do you keep new community members engaged?

Make sure their first contribution gets a response. Research on online groups found newcomers whose first post drew several replies were more than twice as likely to still be active a month later.

### When should a small community start growing?

When the first group is receiving consistent value. Ask active members who they know with the same problem and what expertise is missing, and invite the next cohort from those answers.

## Sources and notes

- [Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities](https://www.dhi.ac.uk/san/waysofbeing/data/communication-zangana-kraut-2008.pdf), manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures only.
- [Kraut and Resnick, Building Successful Online Communities: Evidence-Based Social Design, MIT Press](https://mitpressbookstore.mit.edu/book/9780262528917), paperback edition February 2016. Academic book; design claims drawn from social science research.
- [Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights](https://discord.com/community/understanding-server-insights), undated. Platform documentation; the 30% communicator goal is Discord's guidance, not a research finding.
- [Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report](https://www.commonroom.io/blog/360-community-led-growth-report/), 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room.

- [Discord Is Not a Community Strategy. Neither Is Telegram.](https://lowob.com/research/discord-telegram-community-strategy/)

## Next move

Write your member thesis in one sentence, then pick the one ritual you will run every week for the next two months. Before the first session, decide who will make sure every newcomer's question gets an answer.

# How Marketing Teams Actually Use AI Tools

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-teams-use-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-11 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: AI tools in marketing have settled into research, drafting, extraction, analysis and quality control, ideally working from shared context and named workflows with a human review rule. Surveys show near-universal use but gains mostly in speed, not quality, and few teams with rules on when not to use AI. The tools do not supply judgment, verified claims or contact with the market.

AI works best in marketing when it helps people read, organise, draft and check real work. The problem starts when teams mistake more output for more customer understanding. Surveys now show near-universal use: 88% of B2B marketers in the 2026 CMI and MarketingProfs survey said their organisation uses AI content tools. But 78% credited AI with speed and only 17% with quality, and 37% had no guidelines on when AI should not be used. The jobs that work are specific, repeatable and reviewed.

A few years into widespread use, AI tools in marketing teams have stopped being a novelty and become a set of habits. The habits are more specific and less dramatic than the early demonstrations suggested.

The surveys agree on breadth. McKinsey's State of AI survey of 1,993 respondents, fielded in mid-2025, found 88% of organisations using AI in at least one function, with marketing and sales consistently among the most common. The Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs' survey of 861 B2B marketers, fielded June to August 2026, found 88% of organisations using AI content tools and AI agent use up to 59% from 28% a year earlier. Breadth is not depth. Only 39% of McKinsey's respondents attributed any EBIT impact to AI, and most of those said less than 5%.

## The jobs AI does well

**Research and synthesis.** Reading call transcripts, support tickets, reviews and competitor pages, and pulling out patterns: the words customers use, the objections that recur, the claims competitors make. This is useful because the source material already exists but teams rarely have time to read it closely. Our piece on [voice-of-customer research with Claude](https://lowob.com/research/claude-voice-of-customer-research/) covers the method.

**First drafts and variants.** Turning a brief, a transcript or an approved article into a first draft, a set of headlines, a social adaptation, an email sequence or a version for a different audience. Fast, competent, and only as good as the source material.

**Structured extraction.** Converting unstructured notes into fields: objections, next steps, account details, campaign results. This reduces the administrative tax on people who talk to customers.

**Analysis assistance.** Explaining a data set, spotting anomalies in a report, drafting the query, comparing two periods. Not a replacement for someone who understands the numbers, but a faster path for them.

**Quality control.** Checking copy against a voice guide, a claims library, a compliance list or a banned-words list. Helpful for routine checks, provided the rules and source facts are current.

| Job | What AI does reliably | Where it fails | Review rule |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Research and synthesis | Finds recurring, explicit themes across many documents | Interpretive judgments; invents tidy patterns | Every theme carries source excerpts |
| Drafts and variants | Adapts approved material to a format or audience | Introduces claims not in the source | Claims checked against the approved library |
| Structured extraction | Fills defined fields from notes | Fields with no clear definition | Spot-check a sample each week |
| Analysis assistance | Drafts queries, flags anomalies | Explaining why a number moved | Analyst signs off on any conclusion |
| Quality control | Checks against written rules | Rules that are out of date | Owner updates the rules monthly |

The research row deserves a caution from the evidence. Elisabeth Kirsten and colleagues tested GPT-4 against human coders on interview transcripts in 2024. On descriptive codes, the model matched the human coders' agreement (Cohen's kappa 0.97). On the most interpretive task, human agreement was 0.63 and the model reached only 0.55 to 0.58. It was a small, preliminary study with an older model, but the pattern is the one practitioners report: the more a judgment depends on context, the more a person needs to check it.

## What this looks like in practice

The deployments that report clear gains are narrow. DEPT, an agency, described AI quality-control agents in April 2025 that check brand assets for logos, colours, fonts, image relevance and template alignment. It reported that for a global online marketplace, content approval times fell by 75%, and that for a retail media platform running over 100 campaigns a month, assets were reviewed in about 20 seconds with roughly 91% accuracy. These are the agency's own figures, not an independent audit.

The useful lesson is in the accuracy figure. At 91%, roughly nine assets in every hundred are judged wrongly. That is a good first pass and a poor final word. The agent removes the routine checking so a person can look at the exceptions; it does not remove the person. This is the pattern our piece [The first AI agent should be boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/) argues for: a repetitive task with clear rules, measured outputs and a human at the end.

McKinsey's data points the same way. Organisations it classed as AI high performers, about 6% of respondents, were nearly three times as likely as others to have fundamentally redesigned individual workflows. They were also more likely to have defined when model outputs need human validation. Our task-by-task guide to [AI agents in marketing](https://lowob.com/research/ai-agents-in-marketing-what-they-can-do-now/) maps which jobs are ready.

## Where AI needs human judgment

AI can produce a polished argument without knowing which position a company should actually take. Original points of view still require people who understand the market, can weigh evidence and are prepared to be accountable for their conclusions. The same goes for facts and public claims: every important number, product capability and regulatory statement needs verification before it is published.

The surveys suggest many teams have not drawn these lines. In the CMI survey, 54% cited ensuring accuracy as a challenge, 54% maintaining quality control and 52% maintaining brand voice. 37% said their organisation had no guidelines for when AI should not be used, and 52% had no policy on disclosing AI use. Of the contributions marketers credited to AI, speed led at 78%; quality came last at 17%.

Automated outreach and public replies create a different risk. A plausible but incorrect message can reach a customer or regulator before anyone notices. And a team that replaces real customer conversations with AI summaries may lose the direct observations that make its strategy useful. The best role for AI is to prepare and test material, not replace the decisions or relationships behind it. Our piece [Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out the approval rule.

> Teams that use AI to produce more output at the same quality mostly become louder.

## How a small team should set it up

Start with a shared, maintained source of truth: the company's products, approved claims, customer language, competitors and editorial standards. Then choose a few recurring tasks with clear inputs and outputs, such as turning customer calls into CRM notes or reviewing copy against an approved claims library.

Package each task so it runs the same way every time. Anthropic's Skills feature is one example of the format: it describes skills as "folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically", and on Team and Enterprise plans an organisation owner can provision them for every member. Other tools have equivalents. The tool matters less than writing the procedure down once.

Set a review rule before automating publication. Routine formatting might need a light check, while public claims or sensitive material may require an owner or legal reviewer. Store approved outputs so each new task builds on what the team already learned. Our piece on [building a repeatable GTM workflow in Claude](https://lowob.com/research/claude-gtm-operating-system/) gives a weekly version.

## Honest expectations

The potential gains are meaningful: a small team can prepare research, drafts and administration faster. The gains are also bounded. The work that creates value, deciding what the company believes, talking to customers and choosing where to look, still takes people. Teams that use AI to do more of that second kind of work, with the time saved on the first, get ahead. Teams that use it to produce more output at the same quality mostly become louder. Our analysis [AI did not fix your marketing](https://lowob.com/research/ai-made-average-marketing-cheaper/) makes that case in full.

## lowob takeaways

- **Use AI on preparation and checking first.** Research, drafts, extraction and QC have clear inputs and reviewable outputs.
- **Expect speed, not quality.** Marketers credit AI with speed far more than quality; plan review accordingly.
- **Write the "do not use" rules.** Over a third of teams have none.
- **Keep a person on public claims.** Accountability for what is published cannot be delegated to a tool.

## Common questions

### How are marketing teams using AI in 2026?

Mainly for research and synthesis, first drafts and variants, structured extraction from notes, analysis assistance and quality control. In the 2026 CMI survey, 88% of B2B marketers said their organisation uses AI content tools.

### What are the biggest risks of AI in marketing?

Inaccurate claims, loss of quality control and brand voice, and automated messages reaching customers unchecked. Accuracy and quality control were each cited by 54% of marketers as their top AI content problems.

### Can AI analyse customer interviews accurately?

For explicit, descriptive themes, often yes. A 2024 study found GPT-4 matched human coders on descriptive codes but fell well short on interpretive ones, so every theme should carry quoted evidence a person can check.

### How should a small marketing team start with AI?

Build a maintained source of approved facts and customer language, pick two or three recurring tasks with clear inputs and outputs, and set a review rule for anything that will be published.

## Sources and notes

- [McKinsey, The state of AI in 2025: Agents, innovation, and transformation](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/artificial-intelligence/the-state-of-ai-2025), 5 November 2025. 1,993 respondents in 105 countries; self-reported; consultancy research.

# Raising in a Regulated Category

Source: https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-11 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Show the licence as an asset with a dated path, build unit economics per funded account, put compliance cost and losses in the model, and have a plan for when a partner bank leaves. The 2024 Synapse failure and a wave of 2026 US charter approvals have made the partner bank question the first one experienced investors ask.

Fintech investors underwrite trust and durability, not growth alone. Show the licence as an asset, the economics per funded account, the losses and the compliance cost in the model, and the plan for when a partner leaves. Two recent events sharpen every one of those questions: the 2024 bankruptcy of the banking-as-a-service provider Synapse, which led the FDIC to propose new recordkeeping rules for fintech custodial accounts, and a run of 2026 US charter approvals that gave some fintechs a path to holding the customer relationship themselves.

*This is operating guidance from go-to-market work, not investment, legal or regulatory advice.*

## Licensing is an asset: price it like one

Most decks bury licensing in "regulatory" on the risks slide. Move it to the assets slide.

A granted licence tells an investor three things. The regulator looked at you and said yes. You can operate without borrowing someone else's permission. And the next competitor needs the same months and the same spend to catch up.

The months are real and measurable. Davis Wright Tremaine's August 2026 review of OCC approvals traced one de novo national bank from application on 18 December 2025 to conditional OCC approval on 8 May 2026 and FDIC deposit insurance approval on 4 August 2026. Circle's national trust bank received conditional approval in December 2025 and final approval on 10 July 2026. The same review notes the OCC said in June 2026 that filings must be complete at submission and that it may return materially deficient ones. In the UK, the FCA reported that 97.9% of authorisation cases were decided within their deadline from April to June 2026, but that new firm authorisations and payment services and e-money authorisations both missed their targets.

A licence in progress is still an asset if you show the path: the application date, the stage, the known gaps, the budget, the fallback if it slips. [Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) said raise on evidence. A dated application with a named responsible person is evidence.

What you cannot do is leave it vague. "We are exploring licensing options" reads as "we have not started."

| Licence status | What to show | What it signals |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Granted | Licence, scope, conditions, supervisor | Permission to operate in your own name |
| Filed | Filing date, stage, open questions, budget | A path with a timeline an investor can test |
| Planned | Target regime, adviser, filing date, cost | Intent; fundable only with a partner in place |
| Not needed yet | The partner whose licence you use, and why | Dependency, which the partner slide must answer |

## The unit is a funded account

Sign-ups are not the unit in fintech. Downloads are not the unit. A verified account with no money in it is a cost, not a customer.

Build the unit economics around the funded account: cost to acquire one, cost to verify and onboard one, revenue per funded account per month, and how long a funded account stays funded. Then the [payback period](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) on that basis.

Investors who know the category will convert your sign-up numbers to funded accounts in their heads anyway. Do it for them and show the ratio. A low ratio with a clear plan beats a hidden ratio every time. [From funded account to lifetime value](https://lowob.com/research/from-funded-account-to-lifetime-value/) covers the full calculation.

## Compliance and losses belong in the model

Two lines fintech models often leave out: the cost of compliance and the cost of losses.

Compliance cost is people, tooling, audits, legal, and the verification spend per account. It scales with accounts and with the number of markets. Put it in as its own line so an investor can see it does not eat the margin at scale.

Losses are fraud, chargebacks, credit losses if you lend, and operational errors. Show the rate, the trend, and what you changed when it moved. A loss rate that fell after a control change is a strong slide. A loss rate that is absent is a question you will get asked in a worse setting.

## The partner bank question

If you run on a partner bank or a BaaS provider, every experienced fintech investor will ask the same question. What happens if they give notice?

The question has a recent history. Synapse Financial Technologies, a banking-as-a-service intermediary, went bankrupt in April 2024. In September 2024 the FDIC proposed recordkeeping and reconciliation requirements for banks holding custodial deposit accounts with transactional features, which Sullivan & Cromwell described as a response to that bankruptcy and as requiring significant changes to the account structures many banks and fintechs use. We could not confirm whether a final rule has been issued. Separately, the 2023 interagency guidance from the OCC, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC sets out how banks must manage third-party relationships across their life cycle, scaled to how critical the activity is. Your partner bank is applying that guidance to you.

They are not asking whether you have a dependency. Almost everyone does. They are asking whether you understand it. The answers they want:

| What they ask | What a good answer contains |
| --- | --- |
| Who is the partner? | Named, with the agreement term and notice period |
| What do they control? | Account issuance, custody, card programme, compliance sign-off, or all of it |
| What do they cost? | Fees in the model, including minimums and step-ups |
| What is concentrated? | Share of revenue or accounts running through that partner |
| Who holds the ledger? | Where the record of each customer's balance lives, and how often it is reconciled with the bank |
| What is the exit plan? | Second partner in diligence, or a licence path that removes the dependency, with a timeline |

A one-slide version of this table does more for the round than another slide on market size.

> Investors find the uncomfortable items anyway. Finding them in your room says you run the company; finding them elsewhere says you hide things.

## The fintech data room

[Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) said build the data room before the first meeting. In fintech the room has a specific extra shelf.

Licences and registrations, current and in progress. The compliance programme: policies, the named compliance officer, the monitoring approach, the last audit or review and what it found. Bank partner and BaaS agreements. Ledger reconciliation reports. Any external audit or attestation. Loss data by month with the control changes marked. Complaint volumes and resolution times. Regulatory correspondence, including anything uncomfortable.

The uncomfortable items go in on purpose. Investors find them anyway. Our [Build Order for financial services and fintech](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-financial-services-and-fintech/) covers how to keep these records as a matter of routine, so the room is an export rather than a project.

## Strategic investors want distribution or data

Banks, payment networks and large payroll or accounting platforms invest in fintech for reasons that are not purely financial. Usually they want one of three things: distribution into your customers, data on a segment they cannot see, or an option to acquire you later.

None of these is bad. All of them change the deal. A strategic investor can bring a partnership that cuts your acquisition cost in half. They can also bring exclusivity terms that close off the other channels in [Distribution when the platforms are closed](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/). PitchBook's midyear 2026 outlook noted that public-market favour was going to sectors with regulatory support, naming fintech and crypto among them, which makes the "option to acquire" conversation more likely to come up.

Decide what you want from them before the meeting. Then ask directly what they want from you. The answer tells you whether the cheque is worth the terms.

## lowob takeaways

- **Move licensing to the assets slide.** Show status, dates, budget and a responsible person.
- **Build economics per funded account.** State the sign-up to funded ratio before an investor works it out.
- **Give compliance cost and losses their own lines.** Show the trends and the control changes.
- **Answer the partner bank question on one slide.** Include who holds the ledger and the exit plan.

## Common questions

### What do fintech investors look for in a pitch?

Trust and durability, not growth alone: licensing shown as an asset, economics per funded account, compliance cost and losses in the model, and a plan if a partner bank leaves.

### How should a fintech startup answer the partner bank question from investors?

Name the partner with the agreement term and notice period, what they control and cost, how concentrated you are, who holds the ledger, and the exit plan: a second partner in diligence or a licence path, with a timeline.

### How long does it take a fintech to get a US bank charter?

It varies. One 2026 de novo national bank went from application in December 2025 to conditional OCC approval in May 2026 and FDIC approval in August 2026, and conditional approval still has to be followed by final approval.

### What should be in a fintech data room?

Licences and registrations, the compliance programme, bank partner and BaaS agreements, ledger reconciliation reports, audits or attestations, monthly loss data with control changes marked, complaint data and regulatory correspondence.

## Sources and notes

- [Davis Wright Tremaine, OCC's recent charter approvals signal momentum for digital-asset bank charters](https://www.dwt.com/blogs/financial-services-law-advisor/2026/08/occ-signals-digital-asset-charter-momentum), 5 August 2026. Law firm commentary; approval dates as reported there.
- [FCA, Authorisations operating service metrics 2026/27 Q1](https://www.fca.org.uk/data/fca-authorisations-operating-service-metrics-2026-27-q1), 2 October 2026. Regulator data for April to June 2026; UK only.
- [OCC Bulletin 2023-17, Interagency Guidance on Third-Party Relationships: Risk Management](https://occ.treas.gov/news-issuances/bulletins/2023/bulletin-2023-17.html), 6 June 2023. Joint OCC, Federal Reserve and FDIC guidance; US banks.
- [Sullivan & Cromwell, FDIC proposes recordkeeping and reconciliation requirements for fintech custodial accounts](https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2024/September/FDIC-Proposes-Recordkeeping-Reconciliation-Requirements-Fintech-Custodial-Accounts), 23 September 2024. Law firm memo on a proposed rule; final status not confirmed for this article.
- [Nasdaq, FDIC sets new standard for custodial account reporting](https://www.nasdaq.com/articles/fintech/regulatory-news/fdic-sets-new-standard-custodial-account-reporting), 16 December 2024. News summary of the proposal; source for the April 2024 Synapse bankruptcy date.
- [PitchBook, 2026 US Venture Capital Outlook: Midyear Update](https://pitchbook.brightspotcdn.com/08/99/054b9fa74bf8b54581807f394575/2026-us-venture-capital-outlook-midyear-update.pdf), 22 June 2026. Analyst outlook; qualitative on fintech.

Draft the partner bank slide this week using the six questions in the table. If you cannot say who holds the ledger and how often it is reconciled, ask your partner before an investor asks you.

# The RFP Nobody Can Answer Yet

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-rfp-nobody-can-answer-yet/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-10 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Buyers are issuing RFPs for AI tooling, a context layer and an enterprise brain in a single brief, with no owner, sequence or success measure. Vendors answer differently because nobody has shipped the full brain: what exists is mostly the context layer. The Build Order sets out a sequence that starts at the commercial line and passes four gateways.

More of the requests for proposals reaching us ask for three things in one brief: AI tooling, a context layer and an "enterprise brain". Very few say who will own the work, what success looks like or what should happen first. Vendors answer these briefs in incompatible ways because nobody has shipped the full brain; what exists, at scale, is the context layer. The Build Order is our answer to the missing sequence: decide three things before buying any tool, build on the commercial line first, and pass a named gateway before each next layer.

*Figure: The Build Order, end to end. This piece maps the whole route.*

A pattern has become hard to miss in the briefs we receive. A company issues one RFP asking for an assistant for its staff, connectors into its email, drive and CRM, and something it calls a brain, knowledge base or "single source of truth" that AI agents can work from. The requirements are reasonable. The structure is not. Everything is due at once, the internal owner is rarely named, and the brief seldom says how anyone will know, six months later, whether it worked.

Vendors respond in kind. A search vendor proposes to index everything. A CRM vendor proposes an upgrade with an assistant attached. A consultancy proposes a multi-month programme ending in an operating model. Each answer is defensible on its own terms, and they cannot be compared, because each vendor has quietly defined "brain" as the thing it sells.

This piece explains why the briefs look like this, what the market can and cannot deliver today, and the order of build that the rest of this series follows.

## What these RFPs are actually asking for

With the vendor vocabulary removed, three requests remain.

| Layer | What the brief asks for | What it usually means in practice |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tooling | "AI for all staff", assistant licences, automation | Seats for a chat assistant, plus some workflow glue |
| Context layer | "Connect our systems", "one source of truth" | Connectors into suite, CRM and drive, with search that respects permissions |
| Brain | "Institutional memory", "knows our clients", "agents that act" | A system that knows what the firm decided, remembers what happened, and lets agents act on it |

The third row is where the budget really sits and where the brief is least specific. It is also the part no single product delivers.

What the briefs leave out is consistent. They rarely set a sequence, so tooling, connectors and agents are scoped in parallel. They rarely name an internal owner with time to make it work. And they rarely define a measure of success that a finance director would accept. Those three gaps, more than any vendor choice, decide whether the programme survives its first renewal.

## Why nobody can answer it yet

The honest reason vendors answer so differently is that the full brain does not exist as a product.

In *The first two-fifths* we broke the promise into five parts: knowledge, memory, meaning, governance and judgment. The market has built two of them well. Data owners and search vendors have built knowledge: trusted content, made callable by agents. Software incumbents have built governance: identity, permissions and agent registries. Meaning exists in narrow form. Memory and judgment are largely missing, because both depend on something software rarely does: link an outcome back to the decision that caused it.

The large platforms now sell the context layer explicitly. Microsoft made Work IQ generally available in June 2026 as a permission-aware context layer billed on usage. Google's October 2026 Gemini Enterprise launch described an agent with four memory types and a shared knowledge catalogue. Both are serious products. Neither claims to know why a company made a decision, or whether that decision was right.

Memory is where claims and evidence diverge most. Patronus AI's MEMTRACK benchmark, which simulates work spread across Slack, Linear and Git, found current models and memory add-ons struggling to track state over long horizons and to resolve conflicting information. Independent reproductions summarised by Mnemoverse found vendor-reported memory scores of 92% to 97% falling to 49% to 74% when third parties ran them. In *Retrieval is not the bottleneck* we reached the same conclusion from a different direction: systems usually find the right material and then weigh it badly when facts have changed.

## Spending has outrun use

Meanwhile money has arrived ahead of architecture. Menlo Ventures estimates that companies spent $37bn on generative AI in 2025, up from $11.5bn in 2024, with more than half going to applications rather than infrastructure. Buyers are paying for things that do a job.

Seats, though, are easy to buy and hard to use. Fewer than 4.5% of Microsoft 365's roughly 450 million commercial customers pay for Copilot, and only 20% to 30% of paying users open it in a given week, according to figures reported by Windows Latest in July 2026, which put weekly active use at around 1% of the commercial base. Microsoft separately reported around 30 million paid seats in July 2026. The two figures are compatible: a very large number in absolute terms, and a small share of a very large base.

Put these facts together and the RFPs make sense. Buyers have been sold a destination. Nobody has drawn them the road.

## The north star: what the brain should be

Before the road, the destination, stated precisely enough to test.

> The brain is the loop that turns a company's tools into judgment. It connects what the company stores, remembers what it decided and why, reasons across both, and learns when outcomes come back. No single tool is the brain. The loop is.

*Figure: No single layer is a brain. The brain is the loop: what is stored, wired, recorded, reasoned over and learned from.*

Each layer does one job, and none qualifies on its own:

- **Store.** The CRM, drive, inbox and ERP. Every company has one. On its own it is a filing cabinet.
- **Wiring.** Connectors, permissions and shared definitions that make the store callable. On its own it is a better search box. Rent it: vendors do this well and it changes quickly.
- **Record.** The company's decisions, each with a reason, an owner, a status (current or superseded), an expected outcome and a date to check. On its own it is memory without reasoning. Own it: it carries the company's judgment and cannot be recovered from a vendor at renewal (*Buy context, own judgment*).
- **Reasoning.** Models and agents that read across the wiring and the record and connect the dots: that a prospect's new COO was a client at a previous firm, that the last pitch was lost on price, that two current claims conflict. On its own it is a mind that makes things up. Rent the models; own the instructions and precedents.
- **Learning.** Outcomes written back to the decisions that caused them, so the next round of reasoning starts from what happened. Only possible with the other four.

### Why we still use the word "brain"

"Brain" is an imperfect word and we use it deliberately. It is the term buyers write into RFPs and vendors put on products, so it is the term this series has to meet. It invites two errors. The first is calling a single tool a brain: a CRM, an index or an assistant. None of these thinks. The second is imagining a mind that simply knows things. The useful version is neither. It is the loop above, and when we use the word, that loop is what we mean.

## The build order

This is the sequence we would build in, and the one the rest of the series follows.

*Figure: The Build Order: three decisions, four layers on the commercial line, then three gateways before the brain spreads.*

**Gateway 0: three decisions before any tool.** Who owns the build, with protected time. Whether the company runs on Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, because that decides the natural assistant, the native connectors and where search happens. And which CRM people will actually keep current. Nothing is purchased until these are answered.

**Tooling on the commercial line.** A CRM clean enough to trust, assistant seats for the people in the commercial workflow, and the automation between them. Not seats for everyone.

**Context on the commercial line.** Email, calendar, call notes and proposals connected for the accounts that matter, with permissions that mirror the underlying files and a small set of agreed definitions.

**Record and reasoning on the commercial line.** A record of the commercial decisions worth keeping, and one deliberately unglamorous first agent that works from it.

**Gateway 1: nothing sends without a person.** Every outbound action has a named approver, and every approval is logged.

**Gateway 2: a dollar figure on every decision.** Each recorded decision carries the value at stake, and its outcome is written back, so the build reports in money rather than activity.

**Gateway 3: commercial is ready to share its brain.** Only then does the record extend to delivery, finance and people.

Each gateway is a test. If the answer is no, the build stays where it is until the answer is yes.

## Why the commercial line comes first

Part 2 makes the full case. The short version comes from a test we have already published: judgment arrives first in decisions that are frequent, similar, quickly graded and later defended (*Where judgment arrives first*). Commercial decisions fit that description better than almost anything else in a mid-size company. Which leads to qualify, which pitches to pursue, what discount to allow and what to spend on a campaign recur weekly, resemble each other, show their outcome within a quarter, and have a budget holder who must defend them. They also sit on the most structured data most firms own: the CRM.

A firm-wide knowledge base, the most common alternative starting point, produces value that is real but hard to count. That is difficult to fund a second time.

## Where the order bends

The series takes this sequence through eight industries. It holds in most and bends in two.

| Industry | Does the order hold? | Where it bends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Professional services | Holds | Confidentiality and conflict walls arrive with the context layer |
| Financial services and fintech | Bends: record first | A supervisor may ask the firm to reconstruct any automated decision |
| Media and publishing | Holds | Sales context must be walled off from editorial |
| Crypto and digital assets | Holds | Public statements make Gateway 1 strict |
| B2B SaaS | Holds | Product usage data joins the context layer early |
| Retail, DTC and luxury | Holds | Client consent governs what can be connected |
| Industrial distribution | Holds | Quoting is the commercial line |
| Healthcare and life sciences | Bends: compliance first | Privacy and promotional review precede any commercial agent |

The two that bend share a feature: a regulator who will ask the company to reconstruct what happened. There, the record is a requirement before it is an advantage, as we argued in *Regulators want the chain, not the model*.

Illustrative example: rewriting the brief

Decision
:   Withdraw a single RFP for "AI, connectors and a brain" and reissue it as a sequenced brief: Gateway 0 first, then a scoped commercial build.

Reason and owner
:   Three vendor responses could not be compared because each defined the brain differently. Owned by the head of operations, with four protected hours a week.

What changed
:   The new brief names one success measure (hours of meeting preparation per pitch) and a 90-day review date.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size professional services firm, built from patterns across briefs we have seen.

## lowob takeaways

- **The wish list is right; the order is missing.** Tooling, context and brain all belong in the brief. State which comes first and what must be true before the next.
- **Rent the wiring, own the record.** The context layer is worth buying well. The decision record carries your judgment.
- **Start where outcomes can be counted.** For most firms that is the commercial line.
- **Treat each gateway as a test.** A "no" means stay, not skip.

Gateway card

### Before the next RFP goes out

- A named owner with protected time
- Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 confirmed as the suite of record
- The CRM people will actually update, chosen
- One success measure that can be counted within a quarter
- A review date

## Common questions

### What is an enterprise brain?

It is the loop that connects what a company stores, records what it decided and why, reasons across both, and learns when outcomes come back. No single product delivers all of it today; most products sold under the name deliver the context layer.

### What should an enterprise AI RFP include?

A named internal owner, the suite of record, the CRM, a sequence of build, and one success measure that can be counted within a quarter. Without these, vendor responses cannot be compared.

### Where should a company start an AI build?

On the commercial line, where decisions are frequent, similar and graded within months, and where a structured system of record already exists. Regulated firms may need to build the audit trail first.

### Is a CRM an enterprise brain?

No. A CRM is the store, one layer of five. It becomes useful to the brain when it is wired to other sources, read alongside a decision record and updated with outcomes.
