# What Is Win-Loss Analysis?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Win-loss analysis asks buyers, not just sellers, why a deal went the way it did. Research suggests seller-recorded reasons often differ from what buyers report, and that many losses are to no decision rather than a competitor. This explainer covers what win-loss analysis is, how a programme works, and how a mid-size firm can run a first round.

Win-loss analysis is the structured study of why deals are won or lost, based mainly on interviews with the buyers who made the decision. It compares what buyers say with what the CRM recorded, finds patterns across deals, and feeds them back into positioning, sales process, pricing and product. Done well, it turns closed deals from outcomes into evidence.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What win-loss analysis means

Every CRM records whether a deal was won or lost. Few record why with any reliability. Win-loss analysis fills that gap by going to the source: the buyer.

A programme has three parts. First, it collects evidence from buyers after a decision, usually in a 20- to 30-minute interview, sometimes supplemented by a short survey. Second, it codes the answers into themes and compares them with seller-recorded reasons and deal data. Third, it routes the findings to the people who can act: marketing for positioning, sales leadership for process, product for the roadmap, and finance for pricing.

| Win-loss analysis is | Win-loss analysis is not |
| --- | --- |
| Buyer interviews after a decision | A seller filling in a loss reason |
| Wins, losses and no-decisions together | A post-mortem on the biggest lost deal |
| Patterns across many deals | One anecdote repeated in a meeting |
| Findings routed to owners with actions | A slide deck read once |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Seller reasons are a weak signal

Sellers are asked for a loss reason at the moment they least want to give one, and they often do not know. Buyers hold internal debates and executive conversations that never reach the seller. Clozd, which sells win-loss services, reports that buyer and seller reasons align only 15% of the time, and that sellers are wrong about why deals are won and lost 60% to 85% of the time. The figures are vendor-reported without published methodology, so treat them as an indication of direction rather than a benchmark.

### Many losses are not to a competitor

Matt Dixon and Ted McKenna's research, published in *The JOLT Effect*, analysed about 2.5 million recorded sales conversations and found that 40% to 60% of lost deals ended in no decision. A programme that only interviews competitive losses misses the largest category. Berkowitz makes the same point: interview wins and losses, and do not ignore buyers who chose to do nothing.

### Rigour is what produces the gain

The Gartner work, as summarised by Berkowitz, sets out the conditions. Interviews should be run by an independent party with no stake in the outcome. They should cover the whole decision process, because early-stage issues often surface later as closing failures. Findings should feed segmentation, sales process and product roadmap. Gartner research cited by Clozd associates rigorous, ongoing programmes with up to a 50% improvement in win rates and a 15% to 30% increase in revenue. Those are upper bounds from organisations already committed to the practice, not a typical result.

## How to run a first round

A mid-size firm does not need a platform to start. It needs a short list of deals, a neutral interviewer and a fixed question set.

1. **Pick the deals.** Select 12 to 20 decisions from the last two quarters: roughly equal wins, competitive losses and no-decisions. Clozd suggests themes reach saturation around 25 to 30 interviews per segment, so treat a first round as directional.
2. **Choose the interviewer.** Someone who did not work the deal: an operations lead, a founder for lost deals they did not touch, or an outside firm.
3. **Ask about the decision, not the seller.** What triggered the search, who was involved, what alternatives were considered, what nearly changed the outcome, and what the deciding factor was.
4. **Code against the CRM.** Put the buyer's stated reason next to the recorded loss reason for each deal. The mismatch rate is your first finding.
5. **Route and record.** Each theme gets an owner, an action and a review date. In **lowob**'s terms, each becomes a decision in the record, with reason, owner, status and expected outcome.

| Method | Strength | Weakness | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Buyer interview | Depth, nuance, unprompted reasons | Costly, smaller sample | Strategic or high-value deals |
| Buyer survey | Scale, trend tracking | Low response, shallow answers | Validating interview themes |
| CRM loss reasons | Complete coverage, cheap | Seller bias, often wrong | Triage and trend lines |
| Call recording review | Shows what was actually said | Misses internal buyer debate | Execution and messaging gaps |

## lowob takeaways

- **Ask the buyer.** Seller-recorded reasons are a starting point, not an answer.
- **Include no-decisions.** Losses to the status quo are often the largest category.
- **Use a neutral interviewer.** Independence is what makes buyers candid.
- **Route every finding to an owner.** Analysis without a recorded decision changes nothing.

## Common questions

### What is win-loss analysis in sales?

It is the structured study of why deals are won or lost, mainly through interviews with the buyers who decided, compared against CRM records and deal data.

### How many win-loss interviews do you need?

A first round of 12 to 20 gives direction. Clozd suggests themes stabilise at around 25 to 30 interviews per segment.

### Who should conduct win-loss interviews?

Someone with no stake in the deal. Gartner's guidance is that an independent party produces more candid answers than the seller or their manager.

### Should you interview won deals as well as lost ones?

Yes. Wins show what to repeat, and Gartner's guidance treats them as among the most instructive interviews in a programme.

## Sources and notes

- Gartner, *Tech Go-to-Market: Three Ways Marketers Can Use Data From Win/Loss Analysis to Increase Win Rates and Revenues*, as summarised in [Business 2 Community via Yahoo News](https://news.yahoo.com/gartner-boost-sales-win-rates-50-via-win-133103162.html). Secondary summary of an analyst report; publication date not stated.
- [Clozd, The Gartner report on the benefits of win-loss analysis](https://clozd.com/blog/gartner-report-benefits-of-win-loss-analysis). Vendor summary of Gartner findings.
- [Clozd, Win-loss analysis guide](https://clozd.com/guides/win-loss-analysis). Vendor-reported figures on reason mismatch, participation and sample size.
- [Challenger, How to Overcome Customer Indecision Using the JOLT Effect Approach](https://challengerinc.com/losing-to-customer-indecision/), February 2024. Summary of Dixon and McKenna's research on about 2.5 million sales conversations.
- [Showpad, What buyer win-loss interviews reveal about the sales execution gap](https://www.showpad.com/blog/what-buyer-win-loss-interviews-reveal-about-the-sales-execution-gap), August 2026. Vendor blog presenting Clozd research.

- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)

## Next move

List the last ten closed deals, wins and losses, and ask someone who did not work them to call three of the buyers. Put each buyer's reason next to the CRM reason and count the mismatches.

# AI Copilot vs AI Agent: What Is the Difference?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-copilot-vs-ai-agent/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-08 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A copilot assists a person inside their work: it answers, drafts and summarises, and the person decides every step. An agent pursues a goal in a loop, chooses its next step and acts through tools within limits. The difference is a position on the autonomy dial, and most commercial teams should start with copilots and boring, supervised agents.

An AI copilot assists a person who stays in control of every step: it answers questions, drafts text and summarises, and the person decides what happens next. An AI agent is given a goal and works toward it in a loop, choosing its own next step and acting through tools within set limits. The practical difference is how far up the autonomy dial the system sits, and who is accountable when it acts.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the terms mean

"Copilot" began as a product name and became a category. It describes an assistant that sits inside a person's tools: email, documents, meetings, code. Microsoft's own description is a salesperson example in which Copilot acts as a personal assistant, drafting emails and recapping meetings. The person reads the output and decides what to do with it.

An agent has a goal and a loop. Anthropic's widely cited guide, *Building effective agents* (December 2024), draws the line clearly. Workflows are systems where models and tools are orchestrated through predefined code paths. Agents are systems where models dynamically direct their own processes and tool usage. Microsoft makes a similar distinction within its own products: declarative agents handle straightforward tasks inside Copilot's existing capabilities, while custom engine agents suit complex workflows where agents need autonomy to plan, make decisions and operate independently.

|  | AI copilot | AI agent |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starts from | A person's request | A goal |
| Who chooses the next step | The person | The agent, within limits |
| Acts through tools | Rarely, and only when asked | Yes, as part of the loop |
| Typical output | An answer or a draft | A completed task, or a task handed back |
| Autonomy dial | 0 answer, 1 draft | 2 act with approval, 3 act and report, 4 act alone |
| Main failure | A wrong answer | A wrong action, taken with real permissions |
| Who is accountable | The person who used the output | The owner who set the goal and limits |

## Why the difference matters for a commercial team

The labels are blurred in the market. Gartner calls the practice "agent washing": rebranding assistants, robotic process automation and chatbots as agentic without substantial agentic capability. It also expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be cancelled by the end of 2027, because of rising costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.

The distinction decides three things. First, the risk. A copilot can give a wrong answer, which a person may catch. An agent can take a wrong action, such as updating a CRM record or sending an email, before anyone looks. Second, the controls. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments, appropriate guardrails, human checkpoints and stopping conditions such as a maximum number of iterations. Third, the price. Copilots are usually sold per seat; agents are increasingly billed on usage or outcomes.

Anthropic's guide also gives the most useful buying advice: find the simplest solution possible, and increase complexity only when needed. Many tasks sold as agentic work well as a fixed workflow.

## Which one to start with

Most commercial teams should begin with a copilot for the people in one workflow, then add one supervised agent for a boring job. The four tests for that first job are that it is frequent, checkable in under a minute, low in blast radius, and disliked by the people who do it today.

| Job | Copilot or agent | Dial level to start |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meeting preparation brief | Copilot, or agent drafting overnight | 1: draft |
| CRM hygiene: stale flags, activity dates | Agent | 3: act and report, on internal fields only |
| Follow-up emails after meetings | Agent drafting into a queue | 1: draft; a person sends |
| Proposal from an approved template | Copilot | 1: draft |
| Autonomous outbound to new prospects | Agent | Not first: client-facing and hard to check |

Whatever the label, one rule applies: nothing an agent produces leaves the company until a named person approves it, and every approval is logged. Move up the dial one notch at a time, after a few weeks of evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **The difference is who chooses the next step.** The person with a copilot; the agent, within limits.
- **Agents carry action risk.** A wrong action with real permissions costs more than a wrong answer.
- **Check the label.** Many products sold as agents are assistants or fixed workflows.
- **Start simple.** A copilot for one cohort, then one boring, supervised agent.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an AI copilot and an AI agent?

A copilot assists a person who decides each step. An agent is given a goal and works toward it in a loop, choosing its own steps and acting through tools within set limits.

### Is Microsoft Copilot an AI agent?

Microsoft 365 Copilot is primarily an assistant. Microsoft also offers agents that run inside Copilot, from simple declarative agents to custom engine agents with autonomy to plan and act.

### What is agent washing?

Gartner's term for rebranding existing assistants, chatbots or automation as agentic AI without substantial agentic capability.

### Should a small business use an AI copilot or an AI agent first?

Usually a copilot for the people in one workflow, followed by one supervised agent on a frequent, low-risk internal task such as keeping the CRM current.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents), December 2024. Vendor engineering guidance; some tooling advice is dated.
- [Microsoft, AI agents: what they are, and how they'll change the way we work](https://news.microsoft.com/source/features/ai/ai-Agents-what-they-are-and-how-theyll-change-the-way-we-work), November 2024. Vendor article.
- [Microsoft Learn, Introduction to agents](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-au/agents/design-guidelines/intro-to-agents). Vendor documentation.
- [w.media, Over 40 percent of agentic AI projects could face the axe by end of 2027: Gartner](https://w.media/over-40-percent-of-agentic-ai-projects-could-face-the-axe-by-end-of-2027-gartner/), June 2025. Analyst forecast, reported secondhand.
- The autonomy dial and first-job tests are **lowob**'s framework.

List the AI tools your team pays for and mark each one copilot, workflow or agent, using who chooses the next step as the test. Anything marked agent should have a named owner and an approval step before it sends.

# What Is an AI Agent's Time Horizon?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-time-horizon/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-07 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: METR's task-completion time horizon measures how long a task, timed on skilled humans, an AI agent can finish with 50% reliability. It has roughly doubled every seven months since 2019, and faster recently. It is mostly measured on software tasks, and a 50% success rate is far from what client work needs.

An AI agent's time horizon is the length of task, measured by how long it takes a skilled human, that the agent can complete with a stated probability, usually 50%. The measure comes from METR, an AI evaluation non-profit, which found that the 50% horizon of frontier models has doubled roughly every seven months since 2019. It is a useful signal of how fast agents are improving, and a poor guide to how much client work an agent can be trusted with unsupervised.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What the time horizon means

METR times skilled people on a suite of tasks, mostly software, machine learning and related technical work, ranging from seconds to many hours. It then runs AI agents on the same tasks and fits a curve of success rate against human task length. The 50% time horizon is the human task length at which the agent succeeds half the time.

In the original March 2025 study, models succeeded almost always on tasks taking humans under about four minutes and less than 10% of the time on tasks over about four hours. Claude 3.7 Sonnet's 50% horizon was about one hour.

| The time horizon is | The time horizon is not |
| --- | --- |
| The human task length an agent completes 50% of the time | How long the agent itself takes to run |
| Measured mainly on software and research tasks | A measure of sales, legal or account management work |
| A trend line for comparing models over time | A guarantee for any single task |
| Sensitive to task choice and human baselines, by METR's own account | A precise number to plan staffing on |

## What the trend shows

**Doubling.** METR's original estimate was a doubling every seven months over roughly six years. When it fitted only 2024 and 2025 data, forecasts for month-long tasks came about 2.5 years sooner, which METR flagged as a real source of model uncertainty.

**Time Horizon 1.1.** In January 2026 METR increased its suite from 170 to 228 tasks, raised the number of tasks over eight hours from 14 to 31, and moved to the Inspect evaluation framework. Under TH1.1 the doubling time since 2023 was about 131 days and since 2024 about 89 days. Claude Opus 4.5 had the highest TH1.1 estimate reported in that post, 320 minutes, with a wide confidence interval of 170 to 729 minutes.

**Limits.** METR's time-horizons page, last updated in September 2026 and no longer actively maintained, says measurements above 16 hours are unreliable with the current suite. Its July 2025 cross-domain study found exponential trends across nine benchmarks, but with horizons ranging widely: software, maths and question answering clustered around 50 to 200 minutes or more, while visual computer use was 40 to 100 times shorter. METR also cautions that benchmarks are likely easier for models than real-world tasks.

> A 50% time horizon tells you how fast agents are improving. It does not tell you what to let them send.

## How a business should use it

The measure answers a research question, not an operating one. Four adjustments make it useful for planning.

| Adjustment | Why |
| --- | --- |
| Discount for reliability | Client work needs far more than 50% success; METR notes that measuring 99% would need many more, very short tasks |
| Discount for domain | Commercial work involves screens, documents and judgment, often closer to computer-use tasks than to code |
| Separate capability from speed-up | In a separate METR trial, 16 experienced developers took 19% longer with AI tools while believing they were about 20% faster |
| Keep a person at the gate | Longer horizons mean longer unsupervised chains, so errors compound before anyone looks |

The practical reading is that agents will take on longer chains of work each year, and that the share of a workflow an agent can draft will grow. It argues for building the context layer, the decision record and the approval gate now, so that when an agent can handle a two-day task, the firm has the evidence to decide whether to let it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Know what is measured.** Human task length at 50% success, mostly on software tasks.
- **Expect fast change.** Horizons have doubled every few months on METR's recent estimates.
- **Discount for your work.** Higher reliability needs and different domains shorten the useful horizon.
- **Raise autonomy on your own evidence.** Benchmarks set expectations; your error rates set the dial.

## Common questions

### What is METR's time horizon?

A measure of the length of task, timed on skilled humans, that an AI agent can complete with a given probability, usually 50%.

### How fast is the AI time horizon growing?

METR's original study found doubling about every seven months since 2019. Its January 2026 update estimated about 131 days since 2023 and about 89 days since 2024.

### Does a longer time horizon mean AI can replace human work?

Not directly. It is measured at 50% success, mostly on software tasks, and METR notes benchmarks are likely easier for models than real work.

### What is the difference between the 50% and 80% time horizon?

The 80% horizon is the task length an agent completes four times in five. It is shorter than the 50% horizon because higher reliability is harder to reach.

## Sources and notes

- [METR, Measuring AI ability to complete long tasks](https://metr.org/blog/2025-03-19-measuring-ai-ability-to-complete-long-tasks/), 19 March 2025. Original study; METR notes some figures predate TH1.1.
- [METR, Time Horizon 1.1](https://metr.org/blog/2026-01-29-time-horizon-1-1/), 29 January 2026. Updated task suite and doubling estimates.
- [METR, Task-completion time horizons of frontier AI models](https://metr.org/time-horizons/), last updated 8 September 2026. Methodology page; no longer actively updated.
- [METR, How does time horizon vary across domains?](https://metr.org/blog/2025-07-14-how-does-time-horizon-vary-across-domains), 14 July 2025. Cross-benchmark analysis; METR calls many estimates noisy.
- [The Decoder, AI coding can make developers slower even if they feel faster](https://the-decoder.com/ai-coding-can-make-developers-slower-even-if-they-feel-faster/), 11 July 2025. Press report of METR's randomised trial.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)
- [Where Judgment Arrives First](https://lowob.com/research/where-judgment-arrives-first/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)

## Next move

Time one recurring commercial task end to end, such as preparing an account review. Compare it with the horizons above, then test an agent on the first draft only, and record its error rate before giving it more.

# Performance Marketing Is Not a Channel. It Is a Way of Paying.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/performance-marketing-way-of-paying/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-06 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Performance marketing means paying when something happens rather than when something is shown. It works only when the outcome is observable in the company's own tracking, attributable with enough confidence to pay against, and worth the payment. This piece sets out the three conditions, the evidence on where last-click payment goes wrong, four weekly numbers and the honest limits.

Performance marketing is a way of paying, not a channel. The company pays when something happens (an account opened, a subscription started, a qualified lead delivered) rather than when something is shown. It only works when three conditions hold: the outcome is observable in the company's own tracking, attributable with enough confidence to pay against, and worth the payment over a realistic horizon. If any of the three fails, the company is not paying for performance. It is paying for a story about performance.

Ask three people what performance marketing is and you will get three answers. To one, it is the paid-social team. To another, it is affiliate. To the third, it is anything with a dashboard. All three are describing a channel. None of them is describing the idea.

Performance marketing is a way of paying. Everything else is a mechanism for making that payment possible. The definition matters because it travels. It applies to a creator paid per activated account, an affiliate paid per approved application, a programmatic buy optimised to cost per acquisition, and a partner paid a revenue share. It also makes clear where a programme stops being performance marketing and becomes exposure with a spreadsheet attached.

## The three conditions

A channel can be run on performance terms only if three conditions hold.

**The outcome is observable.** The company can see, with its own tracking, that the paid-for event occurred. Not the partner's report of it. Its own. This has become harder: Apple's App Tracking Transparency rules mean an app user who declines tracking shows an advertising identifier of all zeros, and browsers block much cross-site tracking. Our piece on [how marketing tracking works](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/) covers the first-party and server-side setup that keeps outcomes observable.

**The outcome is attributable.** The company can connect the event to the source that produced it with enough confidence to pay against it. This is where most programmes quietly break. Last-click attribution pays whoever touched the customer last, which rewards coupon sites and browser extensions that appeared at checkout after the actual persuasion happened elsewhere.

**The outcome is worth the payment.** A cost per acquisition is only a number until it is compared with what an acquired customer is worth over a realistic horizon, net of refunds, fraud and churn. Performance programmes with generous payouts and loose definitions are a machine for buying customers who leave. Our explainer on [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) covers the calculation.

| Condition | The test | Where it usually fails | The fix |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Observable | Does our own tracking record the event? | Partner reports only; app tracking declined | First-party events, server-side, unique codes |
| Attributable | Can we tie it to the source with confidence? | Last click credits the checkout touch | Stand-down rules, holdouts, payment on approved outcomes |
| Worth it | Does value over the horizon exceed the payout? | Loose definitions, early churn | Written definition, clawback window, payback limit |

## Where last-click payment leaks

The attribution failure is not hypothetical. In late 2024 and early 2025, content creators filed class actions alleging that PayPal's Honey browser extension replaced their affiliate cookies with its own at checkout, taking commission for sales the creators had referred. The complaint alleges Honey was built to avoid "standing down" for ordinary shoppers while complying when it suspected it was being tested. In June 2026 a federal judge denied PayPal's renewed motion to dismiss, sending the case to discovery. That is not a finding of liability; PayPal disputes the claims. It does show how a last-click payment rule can be captured by whoever sits closest to the checkout.

The same pattern appears in paid search. When eBay switched off its brand keyword ads in a field experiment, about 99.5% of the click traffic arrived anyway through organic search. A performance programme paying per click on the company's own brand name would have paid for customers it already had.

The remedy is not to abandon performance terms. It is to pay on outcomes the company has approved, to require stand-down from coupon and cashback partners when another partner referred the visit, and to test the biggest partners with holdouts. Our piece on [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers the registration and protection rules, and [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) covers the holdout designs.

> If the outcome is not observable, attributable and worth the payment, the company is not paying for performance. It is paying for a story about performance.

## Performance terms for a company the platforms restrict

For fintech, AI and other reviewed categories, the performance question is sharper, because the channels most companies default to may not be available at all.

That turns out to be a useful constraint. The open-band channels (affiliate, creator, clipping, programmatic against defined audiences) are the ones that most naturally accept performance terms. A creator will accept a cost-per-account deal when the product converts. An affiliate network runs on it. A programmatic partner can be paid on a flat fee while the buy itself is optimised to cost per outcome.

The company that cannot buy the crowded auction is pushed toward the channels where paying for outcomes is normal. That is a better place to start than most companies realise. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) covers the channel map.

## The four numbers to keep

Skip the twenty-tab report. Four figures, tracked weekly, are enough to run a performance programme without fooling anyone.

| Number | Definition | What it tells you | Warning sign |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost per qualified outcome | Total payout divided by outcomes meeting the written definition | What the programme really costs | Definition changed mid-quarter |
| Approval rate | Share of reported outcomes the company's own tracking confirms and accepts | Fraud and quality | A widening gap between reported and approved |
| Payback | Months of realistic customer value to recover the acquisition cost | Whether the price is affordable | Payback lengthening as volume grows |
| Concentration | Share of outcomes from the top three partners or placements | Dependency risk | Above half: one relationship, not a channel |

"Qualified" should be defined in writing and held fixed for the quarter. A definition that moves is the easiest way to make a programme look better than it is.

## Where performance marketing stops being true

Two honest limits.

Performance terms push risk onto the partner, and partners price that risk in. A creator paid per account will ask for more per account than the equivalent flat fee, and will drop the product if it does not convert. That is a fair trade, but it is a trade.

And some things that matter cannot be paid for per outcome. Trust in a financial product, comprehension of a new category, a founder's reputation in a market: these move the outcome numbers without ever appearing in them. The research on advertising effectiveness supports the point. Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases found brand effects decay slowly and build over years, while activation effects are large and short; in their B2B work the best-performing balance was 46% brand and 54% activation. A performance programme that starves the slow work will see its cost per outcome rise for reasons the dashboard cannot explain. Our piece on [brand versus performance marketing](https://lowob.com/research/brand-vs-performance-marketing/) covers the split.

Performance marketing is a payment standard, not a department. Apply it wherever an outcome can be observed, attributed and valued, and be honest about the places where it cannot.

## lowob takeaways

- **Observe it yourself.** The company's own tracking, not the partner's report, confirms the paid-for event.
- **Do not pay the last touch by default.** Stand-down rules and holdouts stop checkout tools collecting for others' work.
- **Define "qualified" in writing.** Hold the definition fixed for the quarter.
- **Track four numbers weekly.** Cost per qualified outcome, approval rate, payback and concentration.

## Common questions

### What is performance marketing?

A way of paying for marketing in which the company pays when a defined outcome happens, such as an account opened or a qualified lead, rather than when an ad is shown. It can apply to affiliate, creator, programmatic and partner channels.

### What is the difference between performance marketing and affiliate marketing?

Affiliate is one channel that runs on performance terms. Performance marketing is the payment standard itself, which also covers creators paid per account, programmatic buys optimised to cost per acquisition and revenue-share partners.

### What metrics should a performance marketing programme track?

Cost per qualified outcome with a written definition, approval rate against the company's own tracking, payback in months and concentration in the top three partners.

### Why is last-click attribution a problem for affiliate programmes?

It pays whoever touched the customer last, which favours coupon sites and browser extensions at checkout. Creators' lawsuits against PayPal's Honey allege an extension overwrote their affiliate cookies this way.

Write the definition of a qualified outcome for your largest performance partner on one line, and compare last month's reported outcomes with the ones your own tracking approved. If the gap is above a fifth, fix the definition before you renew the terms.

# What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-05 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An AI agent is a model working in a loop toward a goal, choosing its next step and acting through tools within set limits. Capability is rising quickly on long software tasks, enterprise adoption is broad but mostly supervised, and reliability falls sharply between 50% and 80% success. Agents create durable value only when they read from a decision record and write outcomes back to it.

An AI agent is a model working in a loop toward a goal: it chooses its next step, acts through tools, checks the result and repeats until it finishes or a limit stops it. Agents can now complete long, well-specified software tasks, and most large companies report using them, but reliability falls sharply as tasks lengthen and most production agents still hand work back to a person. They become valuable to a business when they are plugged into a company's brain: the wiring that connects its systems, the record of what it decided and why, a gate before anything leaves the building, and a path for outcomes to flow back.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

The word "agent" now covers almost everything sold with a model inside it. A chat window that answers questions, a workflow that runs the same five steps every night, and a system that decides its own next move while holding a user's email permissions are routinely marketed under the same label. Gartner has a name for the practice, "agent washing", and in mid-2025 it estimated that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors making agentic claims offered genuine agentic capability.

The confusion matters because the label decides what gets bought, what gets approved and who is accountable when something goes wrong. A chat assistant can give a wrong answer. An agent can take a wrong action, confidently, with real permissions. This piece sets out a working definition, what the evidence says agents can do today, and how they connect to the system we call the enterprise brain. It is the reference point for the rest of The Build Order.

## A working definition of an AI agent

An AI agent is a model working in a loop toward a goal. It decides what to do next, uses tools to act, observes the result, and repeats until the goal is met or a limit stops it.

We wrote in *A loop with good context* that the loop itself is becoming a commodity. The frameworks that run it are converging, and the protocols that connect it to tools are standardising. What separates a useful agent from a risky one is everything around the loop. Five components define it:

1. **Goal.** A statement of what done looks like and when to stop: "a two-page brief for Tuesday's meeting", "every deal with no activity in 30 days flagged", "a draft quote for this request using the current price book".
2. **Loop.** Reason about the next step, act, observe, decide again. This is the defining feature. A script follows a fixed path; an agent chooses its path.
3. **Tools.** The actions available to it: search the CRM, read an inbox, query a database, draft an email, update a record, call another agent.
4. **Context.** What it can see before and during the task: documents, data, shared definitions and, most often missing, the company's past decisions on similar cases.
5. **Limits.** What it may touch, what it may spend, which actions need human approval, and when it must stop and ask.

### Three things sold as agents

|  | Chat assistant | Workflow automation | AI agent |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who chooses the next step | The person | The designer, in advance | The model, within limits |
| Acts on company systems | Rarely | Yes, in fixed ways | Yes, in ways it selects |
| Typical failure | A wrong or invented answer | Breaks when inputs change | A wrong action, taken confidently |
| Best suited to | Questions, drafts, analysis | Stable, repeatable steps | Varied tasks with a clear goal |
| Main control | Reader judgment | Testing the workflow | Permissions, approval gates, logs |

Gartner's own guidance draws the same line: many use cases positioned as agentic do not need agentic implementations, and automation remains the better tool for routine, stable workflows. A useful test for any product labelled an agent is to ask what it decides for itself. If the answer is nothing, it is automation, and it should be bought, tested and priced as automation.

### Autonomy is a dial, not a switch

The more useful question is how much an agent may do without a person. We use a five-level scale.

*Figure: Autonomy is a dial, not a switch. Client-facing work stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.*

| Level | What the agent does | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0. Answer | Responds to a question | "What did we propose to this client last year?" |
| 1. Draft | Prepares work for a person to review | A meeting brief; a follow-up email waiting in a queue |
| 2. Act with approval | Takes an action once a named person approves | Updates deal stages after a manager signs off |
| 3. Act and report | Acts within fixed bounds, then reports | Tags lead sources overnight and sends a summary |
| 4. Act alone | Acts with no review inside hard limits | Rare in commercial work, and rarely wise today |

Most of the value commercial teams report today sits at levels 1 to 3. Anything that reaches a client stays at level 2 or below until there is evidence to move it.

## What AI agents can do now

The evidence in late 2026 supports two statements at once: agent capability is improving faster than almost any other measure of AI, and the share of real business work agents can complete reliably and unsupervised is still small.

### Capability: long tasks, but at uneven reliability

The most cited independent measure is METR's task-completion time horizon. METR estimates how long a task takes a human expert, then measures the length of task at which an agent succeeds a given share of the time. Its January 2026 suite (Time Horizon 1.1) expanded to 228 tasks across software engineering, machine learning and cybersecurity, including 31 tasks estimated at eight or more human hours.

| Measure | What was reported | Source status |
| --- | --- | --- |
| METR's January 2026 update | Claude Opus 4.5 at about 320 minutes (5.3 hours) of expert work at a 50% success rate | Published by METR |
| Later 2026 assessments | About 14.5 hours at 50% for Claude Opus 4.6; about 16 to 20 hours at 50% and 3 to 4 hours at 80% for the strongest agents assessed in February to March 2026 | Reported in secondary coverage of METR's work |
| Trend | Time horizon roughly doubling every four to seven months, depending on the window measured | METR's fitted trend, as reported |
| Caveat | METR treats estimates above 16 hours as unreliable; tasks are software, ML and cyber tasks | Published by METR |

Two points matter for a business reader. First, the gap between the 50% and 80% figures is large: a task an agent completes half the time is a draft, not a delegated job. Design around the reliable number. Second, these are well-specified technical tasks with checkable answers. Commercial work is messier: goals are vaguer, data is incomplete, and success is judged weeks later.

### Adoption: broad, but mostly supervised

Surveys agree that agents are now common in large companies and disagree on how deep that goes.

| Source | Sample | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zapier, 2026 | Enterprise leaders | 71% report agents in production, up from 40% in 2025; most agents still need a person to finish the job |
| Mayfield CXO Survey, 2026 | 266 IT and innovation leaders, Fortune 2000 | 42% in production; 72% in production or pilot |
| ChapsVision / Sinequa, 2026 | 740 executives at $1bn+ companies | 51% report agents in live production, but most deployments are assistive rather than agentic |
| Anthropic enterprise survey, 2026 | Enterprises building agents | Nearly 90% use AI in software development; 86% deploy agents for production code |
| Gartner forecast | Analyst projection | 40% of enterprise applications to include task-specific agents by end of 2026 |
| Gartner forecast | Analyst projection | Over 40% of agentic AI projects cancelled by end of 2027 on cost, unclear value or weak risk controls |

Read together, these describe agents arriving inside software companies already use, mostly at levels 1 and 2 of the dial, with coding far ahead of every other function. Vendor-run surveys tend to report higher adoption than independent ones, and "in production" is defined differently by each.

### In commercial work specifically

Salesforce's 2026 State of Sales survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals found that sellers spend about 40% of their time selling. Sellers using agents expect them to cut prospect research time by about a third and email drafting time by a similar share, and top-performing sellers were 1.7 times more likely than underperformers to use agents for prospecting. The survey is vendor-run, and expected savings are not measured savings, but the pattern is consistent with what we see: the time agents recover sits in research, preparation, data entry and first drafts.

For a mid-size commercial team, our working view of the current boundary:

| Reliable today | Useful with a person in the loop | Not yet, or not wisely |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research an account and write a brief | Draft outbound and follow-up emails | Send client communications unsupervised |
| Summarise calls and extract next steps | Update CRM stages and fields | Set prices or approve discounts |
| De-duplicate, tag and flag stale records | Draft quotes from a price book | Make low-volume strategic calls |
| Compare delivery against what was sold | Prepare campaign variants for testing | Track what changed over months without a record |
| Monitor news and signals for named accounts | Triage and route inbound requests | Act safely on untrusted inbound content |

### Two limits that point straight at the brain

**Memory over time.** Agents struggle to track how things changed over long periods. Patronus AI's MEMTRACK benchmark, built from realistic work spread across Slack, Linear and Git, found current models and memory add-ons struggling with long-horizon state and with conflicting information. Our own reading, in *Retrieval is not the bottleneck*, is that most failures come after search: the right material is found, then weighed badly when facts have changed. A bigger memory does not solve that. A record that marks which decision is current does.

**Untrusted content.** OWASP's 2025 Top 10 for LLM applications ranks prompt injection first and lists "excessive agency" sixth: the risk that a model with too many tools and too much permission turns a small error into a damaging action. An agent that reads inbound email, holds a user's access and can send messages combines all three conditions. OWASP's recommended controls are architectural: minimise tool scope and permissions, require approval for high-risk actions, and log every tool call.

## How agents plug into the enterprise brain

This is the centre of the series. We define the brain as a loop, not a product: it connects what a company stores, remembers what it decided and why, reasons across both, and learns when outcomes come back. A CRM, a drive or a search index is the store. Agents are the reasoning layer, the part that connects the dots. They depend on every other layer, and they plug into it at five points.

*Figure: Five plug points: identity and limits, context in, precedent in, the gate, and the outcome written back.*

**1. Identity and limits.** Every agent should act as its own registered identity with its own permissions, not borrow a person's login. That makes each action traceable and keeps access narrow. Large vendors now treat agents as accounts to be registered and governed; Microsoft reported nearly 40 million agents registered in its control plane within two months of launch. A mid-size firm needs the same idea at small scale: a register listing each agent, what it may touch, its autonomy level and its owner.

**2. Context in, through the wiring.** The agent reads company systems through connectors. The Model Context Protocol has become the common standard: Anthropic donated it to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025, when more than 10,000 MCP servers had been published, and Google's Agent2Agent protocol for agent-to-agent communication also sits under the Linux Foundation. For buyers the consequence is practical: a connector built to an open standard works with more than one assistant, which makes the wiring layer less of a lock-in than it was two years ago.

**3. Precedent in, from the record.** Before acting, the agent sees the few most comparable past decisions: what was decided, the reason, the outcome, and at least one case that went badly. We call this the precedent slot. It is the difference between an agent that knows what is true and one that knows what the company does.

**4. The gate.** Anything that leaves the building passes a named person who approves it, and the approval is logged with who approved, when, and what they saw. The gate is also where autonomy is set. An agent can be promoted from level 1 to level 2 for one task, on evidence, without being trusted everywhere.

**5. Outcome written back.** When the result arrives (the deal closes, the quote is lost, the campaign underperforms), it is written back to the decision that caused it. In *The first two-fifths* we argued that this is the step almost nobody builds. It is also the step that lets the next run start from what actually happened.

> The agent's own loop runs in minutes. The brain's loop, from decision to outcome to precedent, runs over months. A company that builds only the first gets faster. A company that builds both gets better.

## How to choose and govern your first agent

The first agent should be dull: frequent, checkable, low in risk, and doing work people dislike. On the commercial line that usually means meeting preparation, CRM hygiene, or follow-up drafts that sit in a queue. Start at level 1 and earn level 2 with evidence.

Before any agent goes live, three questions should have written answers:

- What is its goal, and what is its stop condition?
- Which tools can it use, and which systems can it read?
- For one complete run, can you show what it saw, what it did and who approved the output?

If any answer is missing, it is not ready. Our guide *Top 5 agent frameworks for production* covers the engineering side: whether a run can pause for approval, survive a crash and swap models.

### Where agents earn their keep, by industry

| Industry | Where agents are useful now | The limit that matters most |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Professional services | Meeting briefs, proposal first drafts, research | Client confidentiality and conflicts |
| Financial services and fintech | Alert triage, case preparation, memo drafting | Reconstructing the chain for a supervisor |
| Media and publishing | Insertion orders, delivery reconciliation, renewal briefs | Sales context kept out of editorial |
| Crypto and digital assets | Community triage, monitoring, research | Nothing public without a person |
| B2B SaaS | Account research, expansion signals from usage | Product data permissions |
| Retail, DTC and luxury | Prompts for client advisers, order follow-up | Client consent and the human relationship |
| Industrial distribution | Draft quotes from price books and specifications | Price and lead-time accuracy |
| Healthcare and life sciences | Commercial operations support | Patient data never enters the loop |

Illustrative example: an agent register

Decision
:   Every agent in the firm gets a one-line register entry: goal, tools, systems it can read, autonomy level and owner.

Reason and owner
:   Three tools were being called agents and nobody could say what each one could touch. Owned by the head of operations.

What changed
:   An "autonomous SDR" proposal is declined; the overnight CRM clean-up is reclassified as a level 3 agent with a nightly report.

Illustrative: a composite of an 80-person advisory firm, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **An agent is a loop with tools and limits.** If it does not choose its next step, buy it as automation.
- **Plan around the reliable number.** Agents complete far longer tasks at 50% success than at 80%.
- **Agents act; the brain remembers.** Without a record and outcome write-back, agents make a company faster but not better.
- **Govern five plug points.** Identity and limits, context in, precedent in, the gate, and outcomes written back.

Gateway card

### Before you call it an agent

- A written goal and stop condition
- Every tool and system it can reach, listed
- Its autonomy level set, and who can change it
- A named owner
- One run you can replay: what it saw, what it did, who approved it

## Common questions

### What is an AI agent?

An AI agent is a model working in a loop toward a goal. It chooses its next step, uses tools to act, checks the result and repeats until the goal is met or a limit stops it.

### How is an AI agent different from a chatbot or automation?

A chatbot answers questions and leaves actions to the person. Automation follows steps designed in advance. An agent chooses its own steps within limits, which makes it more flexible and more risky.

### What can AI agents reliably do in 2026?

They reliably research accounts, summarise calls, clean records and draft work for review. Independent measurements show multi-hour software tasks completed at 50% success, but much shorter tasks at 80%, so most business deployments keep a person in the loop.

### How do AI agents connect to an enterprise brain?

Through five points: their own identity and permissions, context read through connectors, precedent from a decision record, an approval gate before anything leaves the company, and outcomes written back to the decisions that caused them.

### Why do so many agentic AI projects fail?

Gartner cites escalating costs, unclear business value and inadequate risk controls. In our experience the common root is an agent given a vague goal, broad permissions and no record of past decisions to work from.

- [The 5 Agent Memory Layers Worth Testing, and How to Test Them](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-agent-memory-layers-worth-testing-and-how-to-test-them/)

## Next move

List every tool in your company that someone calls an agent. For each one, can you say what it can touch, what level of autonomy it has and who approves what it sends? If the list surprises you, start there.

# What Is Conversion Rate Optimization, and When to Do It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversion-rate-optimization/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: Conversion rate optimisation increases the share of visitors who sign up, apply, fund, buy or book, through diagnosis, hypothesis, testing and measurement. Baymard's checkout research shows how much loss comes from fixable friction. It needs enough traffic to test, the conversion the business actually runs on, and the right visitors; if the visitors were never going to buy, the problem is upstream.

Conversion rate optimisation (CRO) is the work of finding what stops suitable visitors from taking a useful action, changing it for a reason and checking whether the change helped. Much of the loss is friction rather than reluctance: Baymard Institute finds 70.22% of online carts are abandoned, and among the reasons shoppers give, unexpected extra costs lead at 40%. CRO needs the right success metric, enough traffic to test honestly, and visitors who were plausible buyers in the first place.

Your website is attracting visitors, but too few are signing up, booking a call or completing an application. Before spending more money bringing people in, it makes sense to ask what is stopping the people already there. That is the job of CRO.

## CRO is not changing the button colour

A typical process is simple: look at where visitors leave, talk to customers or review support questions, form a hypothesis and test a specific improvement. You might simplify an application, explain a confusing fee or make the next step clearer on a mobile screen.

A new design can help, but a prettier page is not proof of better conversion. Neither is a temporary spike in sign-ups after a small edit. The discipline is in the sequence: evidence of a problem, a stated reason for the change, and a measurement plan agreed before anyone looks at results.

## Optimise the action the business actually needs

Imagine a hypothetical fintech app whose landing page converts more visitors into sign-ups after a redesign. That looks promising until the team discovers that fewer of those users fund their accounts. If the business earns revenue from active funded customers, the measure cannot stop at registration.

| Business | Easy conversion to report | Conversion the business runs on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Consumer fintech | Registrations | Accounts that pass identity checks and fund |
| Enterprise software | Demo form fills | Qualified demos that become opportunities |
| Developer platform | Sign-ups | Successful first integrations |
| Commerce | Orders | Orders not refunded or returned |

The right conversion sits as close to revenue as you can measure in a reasonable time. A useful frame is three questions in order: are the visitors looking for a problem this product solves (attract); can they understand the offer and complete the next meaningful step (activate); and do new customers keep using the product or reach the intended outcome (retain)? Our piece on [what a marketing funnel is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-marketing-funnel/) covers how to find which of those stages is the constraint.

## Look for confusion before assuming people need persuasion

Start with analytics that show the path through the product, and pair those numbers with what users report. Do support tickets mention unclear pricing? Do people abandon a form when asked for identity documents? Is the mobile page too slow to use?

Baymard Institute's checkout research shows how much of the loss is friction. Its average documented cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, the mean of 50 studies published between 2006 and 2025. After excluding shoppers who were just browsing, US shoppers in Baymard's survey gave these reasons:

| Reason for abandoning during checkout | Share of US shoppers |
| --- | --- |
| Extra costs too high (shipping, tax, fees) | 40% |
| Delivery too slow | 20% |
| Did not trust the site with card details | 19% |
| Site required account creation | 18% |
| Checkout too long or complicated | 17% |
| Website errors or crashes | 17% |
| Could not see or calculate total cost up front | 12% |

Every row except delivery speed is a design or disclosure problem. Baymard estimates the average large ecommerce site could raise conversion by 35.26% through better checkout design, while noting such gains "won't come easy". Retail checkouts are not B2B forms, but the pattern carries: hidden costs, forced steps and unexplained requests lose people who intended to act.

For a regulated product, explain why personal information is required and what happens next. Make fees, eligibility and important conditions easy to understand. Clarity can reduce wasted applications as well as increase qualified ones.

A useful hypothesis is specific: "Applicants may leave at the identity-check step because the page does not explain why the information is needed." That is easier to investigate than "the landing page needs to convert better."

> Conversion work is powerful when qualified people meet unnecessary friction. It cannot turn irrelevant traffic into customers.

## Two kinds of evidence: observation and experiment

**Usability testing finds problems.** Jakob Nielsen's analysis for Nielsen Norman Group found the first five test users reveal about 85% of usability problems, and recommended several small rounds with fixes in between rather than one large study. It works at any traffic level, and it tells you why people struggle. It does not tell you how much a fix will lift conversion.

**A/B testing measures effects.** An A/B test compares experiences to see whether a change improves an outcome. It needs a sample size and a measurement plan chosen before the test starts. As a rough illustration from the standard two-proportion formula, a page converting at 3% needs on the order of 14,000 visitors per variation to detect a 20% relative lift (to 3.6%) at 95% confidence and 80% power. Smaller effects need far more. Use a sample-size calculator with your own assumptions rather than declaring a winner after a few dozen visits.

Do not stop a test the moment it looks significant. Evan Miller's widely cited analysis showed that checking for significance after every observation and stopping at the first 5% result produces false positives 26.1% of the time, more than five times the stated rate. Fix the sample size in advance, or use a sequential or Bayesian method designed for repeated looks. If a test is inconclusive, say so, and use what you learned to sharpen the next hypothesis. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers test design in more depth.

| Situation | Method | What it can claim |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Low traffic, clear friction | Usability test with five users, fix, repeat | Problems found and removed |
| High traffic, specific hypothesis | A/B test with planned sample size | Measured lift, with confidence |
| Either, with ambiguous results | Report as inconclusive | A refined next hypothesis |

## CRO cannot fix the wrong audience

If almost nobody visits a page, the team may not have enough data for a meaningful A/B test. It can still fix confusing forms, missing disclosures or broken mobile layouts through observation and review. Those are sensible fixes, not statistically proven lifts, and should be reported that way.

If most visitors were never likely to buy, fix the audience, offer or acquisition channel first. The economics matter here too: a conversion gain that comes from discounting or loosening qualification can raise acquisition numbers while lengthening [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Find the blocker first.** Investigate what confuses or stops suitable visitors before redesigning.
- **Use the conversion the business runs on.** Funded accounts and qualified demos, not registrations.
- **Be honest about evidence.** Observation finds problems; experiments measure effects; neither should be dressed as the other.
- **Fix acquisition when necessary.** CRO cannot rescue a page filled with the wrong audience.

## Common questions

### What is conversion rate optimisation in simple terms?

It is improving the share of visitors who take a valuable action, such as buying, booking or applying, by finding what stops them, changing it for a stated reason and measuring the result.

### How much traffic do you need for A/B testing?

It depends on your baseline rate and the lift you want to detect. As a rough guide, a 3% conversion rate needs around 14,000 visitors per variation to detect a 20% relative lift with standard settings. Low-traffic sites should rely on usability testing.

### What are the most common reasons people abandon a checkout?

In Baymard Institute's survey of US shoppers, unexpected extra costs led at 40%, followed by slow delivery, distrust of the site with card details, forced account creation and long or complicated checkouts.

### When is CRO a waste of time?

When the visitors are the wrong audience, when traffic is too low to test and the team treats small samples as proof, or when the metric being optimised is not the one the business earns from.

## Sources and notes

- [Baymard Institute, Cart abandonment rate statistics](https://baymard.com/lists/cart-abandonment-rate), updated 28 October 2026. Independent UX research firm; abandonment reasons from a survey of US shoppers; ecommerce, not B2B.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Why you only need to test with 5 users](https://nngroup.com/articles/why-you-only-need-to-test-with-5-users/), 18 March 2000. Practitioner analysis; applies to qualitative usability testing, not quantitative studies.
- [Evan Miller, How not to run an A/B test](https://www.evanmiller.org/how-not-to-run-an-ab-test.html), 18 April 2010. Statistician's essay; simulation of repeated significance testing.
- The sample-size illustration is **lowob**'s calculation using the standard two-proportion formula; the metric and method tables and the fintech example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

## Related research

- [Campaign Testing That Reaches a Decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/)
- [What Is a Marketing Funnel, and When Does It Help?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-marketing-funnel/)
- [What Is CAC Payback?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/)
- [A $10,000 Test That Closes a Question Beats a $10,000 Bet That Leaves It Open.](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/)

## Next move

Pick the one step where most suitable visitors leave. Watch five people from your target audience try to complete it this week, write down every hesitation, and fix the most common one before planning any A/B test.

# Trust Is the Product

Source: https://lowob.com/research/trust-is-the-product/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: In fintech, trust is the product and the feature list is secondary. Trust is borrowed from institutions the buyer already trusts, proved in the order buyers check, and every claim about money is compliance copy that should come from a claims register. Recent rules make the custodian question sharper: the FDIC treats a non-bank's failure to say it is not a bank as a material omission, and UK payment and e-money funds sit outside the FSCS.

In fintech, trust is the product and the feature list is secondary. Trust is borrowed from institutions the buyer already trusts, proved in a fixed order, and every claim you make about money is compliance copy. The order matters more than it used to: the FDIC now treats a non-bank's failure to disclose that it is not a bank as a material omission, and the FCA reminds UK customers that funds held by payment and e-money firms are not directly protected by the FSCS. Lead with who holds the money. Put the yield second.

*This is strategic guidance from go-to-market work, not legal or regulatory advice.*

## Trust is transferred, not created

No ad has ever made someone trust a company with their savings. What an ad can do is point at something the buyer already trusts and say "we are attached to that."

That is the whole mechanism. A licence from a regulator they recognise. A custodian bank whose name they know. A payment network logo. An auditor. An accountant who recommends you. A friend with a funded account.

The survey evidence fits. The Edelman Trust Barometer 2026 found that trust in companies headquartered in the respondent's own country "far exceeds" trust in foreign companies, with gaps of 29 to 31 points in Canada, Japan and Germany. Familiar institutions carry trust that a new name has to borrow. Agency research of this kind measures attitudes, not behaviour, but the direction matches what fintech buyers do.

Your positioning job is to decide which trusted thing you are attached to and put it where the buyer looks first. [One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) set a single product truth. In fintech that truth usually has a second half: "and here is who stands behind it."

If you have nothing trusted to attach to yet, that is your positioning problem. Fix it before you spend on reach.

## The order the buyer checks

Fintech buyers run the same checks in roughly the same order, whether they are a consumer, a finance lead at a small business or a treasury team. They stop at the first unanswered question.

| Question in the buyer's head | What answers it | Where it must live |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Who is behind this? | Named founders, backers, licence, regulator | Homepage, first screen |
| Which institution holds the money? | Custodian or partner bank, named, with the protection scheme that applies | Homepage, onboarding, FAQ |
| Who else like me uses it? | Customers in their segment, numbers you can stand behind | Case pages, onboarding |
| What happens when something goes wrong? | Dispute process, support hours, what is covered and what is not | A page you link to, not a line in the terms |
| What are the fees, actually? | A full fee table, including the ones you would rather not show | One page, one table |
| What do I earn or save? | Yield, rate or savings claim, compliance-approved | After the above |

Most fintech sites invert this table. They answer question six on the hero and question two in the footer. The buyer reads that as a signal.

Platforms enforce part of the order already. Google's financial products policy requires financial ads to show the business's physical address and all associated fees, "clearly and immediately visible without needing to click or hover." A fee table you would rather hide is one an ad reviewer will ask for anyway.

## Who holds the money is a regulated claim

The second question has become the one with the most legal weight, in both the US and the UK.

In the US, the FDIC's revised rule on signs, advertising and misrepresentation of insured status took effect on 1 April 2024, with full compliance required by 1 January 2025. Its preamble sets out that a non-bank's failure to disclose that it is not a bank is a material omission, as is failing to state that non-deposit products, now defined to include crypto-assets, are not FDIC-insured, and failing to state the conditions for pass-through insurance. A fintech that partners with a bank cannot let customers infer that the fintech itself is insured.

In the UK, the FSCS deposit protection limit rose from £85,000 to £120,000 on 1 December 2025. That protection covers deposits at banks, building societies and credit unions. The FCA states plainly that "funds held by payment and e-money firms are not directly protected by the Financial Services Compensation Scheme." Those firms safeguard customer money instead, and the FCA tightened the safeguarding rules from 7 May 2026 after finding that payment firms which became insolvent between 2018 and 2023 had average shortfalls of 65% of customer funds.

The practical consequence is that "where is my money, and what protects it" has one correct answer per product, and it must be written down exactly. Our [Build Order for financial services and fintech](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-financial-services-and-fintech/) covers keeping that answer in the decision record so it changes in one place.

## The claims register is compliance copy

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) introduced the claims register: the list of things you are allowed to say, with the evidence beside each. In most categories it is a sales tool. In fintech it is a compliance document that sales happens to use.

Yield and return claims, safety and protection language, "better than your bank" comparisons, "guaranteed", "free" and "instant" each have rules, and the rules differ by market and licence type. The FCA expects financial promotions to be "fair, clear and not misleading", to give a balanced view of benefits and risks, and to be standalone compliant: each communication is judged on its own, not as part of a wider journey.

| Claim type | Why it is risky | What the register records |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yield or rate | Regulated in most markets; easy for a rival to beat | Approved figure, conditions, date, risk wording |
| "Insured" or "protected" | Wrong scheme or wrong entity is a misrepresentation | Which institution, which scheme, what limit, pass-through conditions |
| "Free" | Fees elsewhere contradict it | The full fee table it was checked against |
| "Instant" | Settlement and review times vary | The operating condition that makes it true |
| Comparisons | Need a like-for-like basis | The comparator, the date and the method |

The register records the approved wording, the required disclaimer, the date it was approved and who approved it. Then it becomes the only source: ads, landing pages, creator briefs, partner decks, support macros and the founder's posts. Nobody writes a new claim about money. They pick one from the register.

This is slower on day one and much faster from day thirty. Nothing gets pulled, re-reviewed or quietly screenshotted by a competitor's lawyer.

> The first screen names who holds the money. The second names what you earn.

## Lead with the custodian, not the yield

The yield is the most tempting thing to lead with. It is also the claim most likely to be regulated, the easiest for a competitor to beat next week, and the one the buyer trusts least when it comes first.

Lead instead with what cannot be beaten next week: the licence, the custodian, the protection scheme, the audit. These change slowly and are hard to copy.

A practical rule: the first screen names who holds the money, and the second names what you earn. If the first screen has to be the yield, the custodian goes in the same sentence.

## A belief per audience

Fintech audiences differ more than most, because they are trusting you with different things.

Consumers need to believe the money is safe and reachable. Their trusted sources are the protection scheme, the bank name and people they know. Small businesses need to believe the product works with how they already run money. Their trusted source is the practitioner who advises them: the accountant, the payroll bureau, the bookkeeping software. Institutions need to believe you will still exist and still be compliant in three years. Their trusted sources are the licence, the audit, the controls and your reporting. Investors need to believe trust is converting into funded accounts that stay; [Raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) covers that evidence.

Four audiences, four beliefs, one product truth, one register. The copy changes. The claims do not.

## lowob takeaways

- **Borrow trust deliberately.** Trust is transferred from a recognised regulator, custodian bank, payment network, auditor or recommender, not created by ads.
- **Answer in the buyer's order.** Most fintech sites put yield on the hero and the custodian in the footer. Reverse it.
- **Write the custody sentence once.** Name the institution, the scheme and the limit, and say plainly what is not covered.
- **Run every money claim through the register.** Approved wording, disclaimer, date and approver, for every channel including partners and creators.

Gateway card

### Before the homepage ships

- The first screen names who holds the money
- A fee page exists with every fee in one table
- A "what happens when something goes wrong" page is linked from onboarding
- The custody and protection wording matches the product's legal structure in each market
- The claims register holds wording, disclaimer, approval date and approver for every money claim
- Each audience has one written belief and the trusted source that transfers it

## Common questions

### How do fintech startups build trust with customers?

By attaching to something the buyer already trusts, such as a recognised regulator's licence, a known custodian bank, a protection scheme, an auditor or a recommending accountant, and putting it where the buyer looks first.

### Should a fintech homepage lead with the yield or interest rate?

No. Lead with who holds the money: the licence, custodian, protection scheme or audit. If the first screen has to be the yield, the custodian goes in the same sentence.

### Can a fintech say customer money is FDIC-insured?

Only accurately. FDIC insurance covers deposits at insured banks, and the FDIC's 2024 rule treats a non-bank's failure to disclose that it is not a bank, or to state pass-through conditions, as a material omission. Take legal advice on the exact wording.

### Are e-money and payment accounts protected by the FSCS in the UK?

Not directly. The FCA says funds held by payment and e-money firms are not directly protected by the FSCS; they must be safeguarded instead. Bank deposits are protected up to £120,000 from 1 December 2025.

## Sources and notes

- [FDIC, Official Signs and Advertising Requirements, False Advertising, Misrepresentation of Insured Status, and Misuse of the FDIC's Name or Logo](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2024/01/18/2023-28629/fdic-official-signs-and-advertising-requirements-false-advertising-misrepresentation-of-insured), Federal Register, 18 January 2024. Final rule; US only; read with legal advice.
- [FCA, FCA sets out changes to payment safeguarding rules](https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/payment-safeguarding-rules-changes), 7 August 2025. UK regulator press release; shortfall figure covers insolvencies from Q1 2018 to Q2 2023.
- [Bank of England, PRA confirms FSCS deposit limit to be increased to £120,000 from 1 December](https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/news/2025/november/pra-confirms-fscs-deposit-limit-to-be-increased-to-120000-from-1-december), 18 November 2025. UK regulator announcement.
- [FCA, FG24/1 Finalised guidance on financial promotions on social media](https://www.fca.org.uk/publication/finalised-guidance/fg24-1.pdf), 26 March 2024. UK guidance; sets out how existing rules apply.
- [Google Ads Help, Financial products and services policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998), accessed November 2026. Platform policy; varies by location.
- [Edelman, 2026 Edelman Trust Barometer](https://www.edelman.com/news-awards/2026-edelman-trust-barometer-society-slides-into-insularity), January 2026. Agency research; online survey of nearly 34,000 people in 28 countries; not financial-services specific.
- The buyer-order table, the claims table and the checklist are **lowob**'s framework.

## Related research

- [In Fintech, Trust Is the Product and the Channel Is Whoever Already Has It.](https://lowob.com/research/fintech-gtm-trust-distribution/)

## Next move

Open your homepage and onboarding flow and write down which of the six buyer questions each screen answers. If the institution holding the money is not named in the first two screens, rewrite the hero this week.
