# Landing Pages and Ad Review: Why Yours Gets Rejected

Source: https://lowob.com/research/landing-pages-and-ad-review/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the ad platform before the visitor sees it. Google's destination, misrepresentation and financial services rules spell out most of what reviewers check. To pass and convert, match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the visitor's doubts, and never show reviewers and users different pages.

A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the ad platform before the visitor sees it. Reviewers check that the page matches the ad, works, identifies the business, carries the disclosures the category requires and makes no claims it cannot support; Google publishes most of these checks in its destination, misrepresentation and financial services policies. To pass and convert, match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the visitor's doubts, and never show reviewers and users different pages.

A landing page is the page a visitor arrives at from a particular source: an ad, a creator's link, an affiliate placement, an email. It exists to do one thing, and it is reviewed by two audiences before it does it: the platform's reviewer, and the person who arrives.

For companies in reviewed categories, the first audience is where most landing pages fail.

## What a landing page is for

One source, one message, one action. A visitor who clicked an ad about a savings account should land on a page about that account, not on the homepage. The page should confirm they are in the right place, state the offer, answer the two or three doubts that stop people, provide proof, and ask for a single action. Everything else is a distraction, and on a page with a specific job, distraction is measured in lost conversions.

The same logic sits behind [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/): a named reader, a decision, a next action. A landing page is the shortest piece of content a company writes, and the one with the most precise job.

## How ad platforms review it

Every major platform reviews the landing page as well as the ad, and rejects the pair if the page violates policy. Google's published rules are the most detailed, and they describe what other platforms check in similar terms.

| What reviewers check | Where Google says it | What the page needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The page works and can be crawled | Destination requirements: pages that "don't function properly", return errors to Google's crawler, or are not crawlable are disapproved | A live, fast page that loads for the crawler and in every targeted location |
| The ad and page match | Destination requirements on mismatched domains and redirects; misrepresentation rules on "unclear relevance" and "unavailable offers" | The offer in the ad, findable on the page, on the same domain |
| Real content, not a shell | Destination requirements on pages "designed for the primary purpose of showing ads" or with insufficient original content | A complete page with original material |
| Who is behind it | Misrepresentation rules on "obscuring, or omitting material information about your identity" | Legal name, address, contact and registration details |
| What it costs | Misrepresentation rules on failing to disclose "the payment model or full expense" | Fees and pricing stated plainly |
| Category disclosures | Financial services policy: physical address, fees and accreditation links, visible immediately | Required disclaimers, licences and registration numbers on the page itself |
| Claims | Misrepresentation rules on "unreliable claims" that promise "an improbable result", and on clickbait | Claims the company can evidence, with no manufactured urgency |
| Same page for everyone | Circumventing systems policy on cloaking | One page, shown identically to reviewers and users |

*Google policies checked on 16 November 2026.*

Pages fail review most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, and category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy. The financial services rule is stricter than many teams realise: Google says disclosures "can't be posted as roll-over text or made available through another link or tab". A fee table in a collapsed accordion can fail on that alone.

Other platforms push the same disclosures onto the page. TikTok's financial services policy requires advertisers of loans and credit cards in several European markets to disclose rates, fees and repayment terms on their landing pages.

## Why restricted-category pages get rejected

The categories the platforms review (financial products, crypto, health, supplements, gambling, dating) are reviewed against stricter claim rules, and the page is often what triggers the classification. A page that mentions yield, returns, weight or winnings is sorted into the category by its vocabulary before a human reads it. Google's healthcare policy states this directly for drugs: it restricts the use of prescription-drug terms "in ads, landing pages, and keywords".

That is worth knowing, but it is not an invitation to disguise the page. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or route reviewers differently from users are the fastest way to a permanent account ban and, in regulated categories, to a regulator's attention. Google's circumventing systems policy treats cloaking as egregious: the account is suspended upon detection, without prior warning, and the advertiser cannot advertise with Google Ads again.

A page in a restricted category should be visibly and compliantly in that category, with the licences, disclaimers and disclosures the platform requires, and the company should know from its band map whether that platform will run it at all. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers the map.

> A page in a restricted category should be visibly and compliantly in that category.

## What a page that passes and converts contains

| Element | Why it is there |
| --- | --- |
| A headline that repeats the promise the visitor clicked on, in their words | Confirms they are in the right place; satisfies the match check |
| One or two sentences on what changes for them | States the offer without inflating it |
| The action, visible without scrolling, with a label that says what happens next | One page, one action |
| The two or three most common doubts answered briefly: is my money safe, what does it cost, how long does it take | Removes the questions that stop people |
| Proof matched to those doubts: the custodian, the licence, the review, the number | Turns claims into evidence |
| Business identity in the footer: legal name, address, contact, registration | Satisfies identity and category disclosure rules |
| Required disclaimers and a privacy policy, linked, with category disclosures on the page itself | Meets the "visible immediately" standard where it applies |
| Speed on mobile | Most reviewed-category traffic is mobile |

Nothing else. Each extra element is a new place for a claim to go wrong and a new distraction from the action. Test changes one at a time against a decision written in advance; [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how.

## For channels other than ads

Affiliate, creator and email traffic lands too, and those pages are not reviewed by a platform, which tempts companies to relax. Do not. The compliance library that governs the ads should govern every page, because regulators read landing pages and creators send their audiences there.

The regulators' standard does not depend on the channel. The UK Financial Conduct Authority requires cryptoasset promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading, with specific risk warnings and a 24-hour cooling-off period for first-time investors, whatever route the visitor took. The US Federal Trade Commission's 2023 Endorsement Guides set out the potential liability of advertisers, not only endorsers, for what is said on their behalf. A partner page with a loose claim is still the company's claim. [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to brief partners so their pages stay inside the claims library.

And every page should ask for an email address before or after the main action, because the visitor arrived through a rented channel and the company should leave with something it owns.

A landing page does one job for one source and is reviewed by the platform before the visitor sees it. Match the ad, disclose the business, make compliant claims, answer the doubts, and never build a page designed to be read differently by reviewers and users.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the page for the reviewer first.** Working, crawlable, matched to the ad, with real content.
- **Put identity and fees on the page.** Google's financial rules require them visible immediately.
- **Expect vocabulary to trigger review.** Yield, returns and drug terms sort a page into its category.
- **Never cloak.** One page for reviewers and users, or a permanent ban.
- **Apply the same library to partner pages.** Regulators read them, and advertisers carry liability.

## Common questions

### Why does my landing page keep getting rejected by ad platforms?

Most often for missing business information, unsupported claims, or category signals the reviewer treats as restricted regardless of the copy. Reviewers also check that the page works, can be crawled, matches the ad, carries required disclaimers and avoids fake urgency.

### What does Google require on a financial services landing page?

The physical address of the business, associated fees and links to any claimed accreditation, visible immediately rather than in roll-over text or behind another link or tab, plus loan terms such as maximum APR for personal loans.

### Can I hide that my landing page is about crypto or finance to pass ad review?

No. Pages that hide the category, swap content after review, or show reviewers something different from users are treated as circumventing systems, which Google punishes with suspension on detection and no right to advertise again.

### What should a high-converting landing page contain?

A headline repeating the promise the visitor clicked on, a line on what changes for them, a visible action, brief answers to the two or three most common doubts with matching proof, business identity in the footer, required disclaimers, and fast mobile load.

## Sources and notes

- [Google Ads, Destination requirements policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6368661?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.
- [Google Ads, Misrepresentation policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/6020955?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy with ten sub-policies.
- [Google Ads, Financial products and services policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998/financial-products-and-services?hl=en-GB), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.
- [Google Ads, Healthcare and medicines policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/176031?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy; country rules vary.
- [Google Ads, Circumventing systems policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15938075?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.

# You Are Buying Media and You Do Not Trust the Numbers. You Are Right Not To.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-06-02 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Programmatic reports are built to be legible, not true. The ANA found only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer, so the reported CPM understates the price of impressions that could have mattered. This playbook sets out how to calculate a real CPM, why the rejection rate is the number to watch, and six questions to ask before the next invoice.

The programmatic report arrives on the first of the month, and it is beautiful: impressions in the tens of millions, a CPM lower than last quarter's, a cost per click that seems too good. If you have wondered what any of that actually bought, you are not being paranoid. The ANA found that only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer. The reporting layer of programmatic advertising was designed to be legible, not to be true. The fix is to report a different set of numbers: real CPM, verification pass rate and rejection rate.

## Impressions are the least informative number on the page

An impression is a record that an ad was served. It says nothing about whether a human was present, whether the page had any reason to exist beyond hosting ads, or whether the placement was one the company would ever have chosen on purpose.

The Association of National Advertisers' 2023 study of programmatic supply chains analysed 35.5 billion impressions from 21 advertisers. It found that made-for-advertising (MFA) sites, pages built to be filled with ads and visited by arbitraged traffic, took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend. The average campaign ran across more than 40,000 websites. Those impressions are cheap. They lower the average CPM. They also do nothing.

A low CPM, in other words, can be a symptom rather than a result.

Viewability is better than an impression count, but it is a floor rather than a measure of value. The Media Rating Council's standard counts a display ad as viewable when 50% of its pixels are on screen for one continuous second, and a video ad for two. A viewability rate in the high sixties means roughly a third of what was paid for did not meet even that bar.

## What a real CPM is

Take the media cost. Remove the impressions that failed verification: invalid traffic, out-of-geography, non-viewable, made-for-advertising placements, and any inventory outside the company's own inclusion list. Divide the money by what is left, and multiply by a thousand.

| Line | Impressions | Note |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Served and reported | 20,000,000 | Reported CPM on $50,000 spend: $2.50 |
| Less invalid traffic | 600,000 | Bots and automated traffic caught by verification |
| Less non-viewable | 6,000,000 | Failed the MRC viewability standard |
| Less MFA placements | 2,400,000 | Sites built to host ads |
| Less out-of-geo and off inclusion list | 1,000,000 | Outside the buyer's own rules |
| Impressions that could have mattered | 10,000,000 | Real CPM: $5.00 |

*Illustrative figures, assuming no overlap between categories.*

That number is the real CPM, and it is often two to three times the reported one. The ANA's figures support the range: if only 36 cents of a dollar reaches a consumer, the effective price of a useful impression is nearly three times the headline. Its quarterly benchmark, built with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia, found that in the fourth quarter of 2025 the stronger advertisers had 56.7% of programmatic spend meet its quality criteria (fraud-free, measurable, viewable and MFA-free), against 37.5% for the weaker ones. That is a multiple of about 1.8 for the first group and 2.7 for the second.

It is the only CPM worth comparing across partners, months or channels, because it is the price of impressions that could conceivably have mattered. A desk that cannot produce this figure is reporting the price of a bag of impressions without opening the bag. The ANA benchmark also reported advertiser cases in which cost per conversion fell by nearly 40% after optimising on quality-adjusted measures instead of CPM, even though nominal CPMs rose.

> Reported CPM, impressions and viewability describe a bag of inventory. Real CPM, verification and rejection rate describe what was inside it.

## Rejection rate is the number to watch

The most useful single figure in programmatic is the rejection rate: the share of bid opportunities or served impressions the buy declined or discarded because they failed the company's standards.

A high rejection rate is not a problem. It is evidence that someone is choosing. A buy with a rejection rate near zero is accepting whatever the exchanges offer, and the exchanges offer what is cheapest to fill. The ANA's advice to rely on inclusion lists rather than exclusion lists, which it called "largely ineffective" because new domains appear daily, is in practice advice to reject more.

Ask for the rejection rate by partner and by reason. Then ask what the standards were. If nobody can answer the second question, there were no standards.

## Six questions before the next invoice

| Question | What a good answer looks like |
| --- | --- |
| What share of impressions passed verification, and what did the rest fail on? | A pass rate by partner, with failures split into invalid traffic, viewability, geography, MFA and brand safety |
| Which domains and apps received the most spend, and would we have chosen them ourselves? | A top-50 placement list the marketing lead can read and defend |
| What is the real CPM, after removing everything that failed? | A single figure, calculated the same way every month |
| What is the rejection rate, and what rules produced it? | A rate by partner and reason, and the written standard behind it |
| Which fees sit between our budget and the publisher, and what share of the dollar arrives? | A fee per layer, from log-level data the contract gives you access to |
| Which outcomes, not clicks, can the buy be connected to, using tracking we control? | Leads, applications or sales matched in your own systems, ideally with a holdout |

None of these is hostile. A competent desk will have the answers before you ask. A dashboard will not. The last question deserves the most weight: our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to design a holdout at volumes a mid-size buyer can afford, and [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) sets out why a measure must reconcile to finance before anyone acts on it.

## Why the fee structure decides the answers

Media bought on a percentage of spend rewards spending. Every incentive in that arrangement points toward more impressions at a lower average price, which is exactly the recipe for made-for-advertising inventory and a rejection rate of zero. The ANA's study, which found transaction costs absorbed about 29% of each dollar, recommended that advertisers hold direct contracts with each link in the chain and secure access to log-level data. Both are easier when the desk has no reason to resist them.

A flat fee per account changes the question the desk is answering. It stops being "how much can we place?" and becomes "did it work, and can we show it?" That is also why a desk should never front the media spend: the moment the desk is a lender, its interest in the volume of spend returns through the back door. Our piece on [percentage-of-spend media fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) sets out the alternatives in detail.

The numbers can be trusted. They just have to be the right numbers, produced by someone with no reason to flatter them.

Illustrative example: changing the report before changing the buy

Decision
:   Replace the monthly programmatic report's headline CPM with a real CPM, a verification pass rate by partner and a rejection rate by reason, before changing any targeting.

Reason and owner
:   The marketing lead could not reconcile a falling CPM with flat lead volume. Owned by the head of marketing, with the desk producing the figures.

What changed
:   The first real CPM was a little over twice the reported one. Two partners with the lowest reported CPMs had the highest real CPMs and were cut; the remaining budget moved to an inclusion list of about 300 domains.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consumer finance advertiser, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Distrust the headline CPM.** It is lowered by the impressions least likely to matter.
- **Calculate the real CPM.** Media cost divided by impressions that passed verification and your own rules.
- **Read the rejection rate.** Near zero means nobody is choosing.
- **Ask the six questions.** A competent desk has the answers ready.
- **Check the fee.** A percentage of spend pays the desk to accept volume.

## Common questions

### How do I know if my programmatic advertising is working?

Look past impressions and CPM. Ask for the share of impressions that passed verification, the placements that received the most spend, the real CPM after removing failed impressions, and outcomes matched in your own systems.

### What is a real or effective CPM?

Media cost divided by the impressions that passed verification and the buyer's own standards, times a thousand. It is usually around two to three times the reported CPM, because the cheapest impressions are the ones most likely to fail.

### What are made-for-advertising sites?

Sites built to host as many ads as possible, usually visited by bought traffic. The ANA found they took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend in its 2023 programmatic study.

### What is a good rejection rate in programmatic buying?

There is no universal figure, but a rate near zero means the buy is accepting whatever exchanges offer. A meaningful rate, reported by partner and reason, shows standards are being applied.

## Sources and notes

- [ANA, Programmatic Media Supply Chain Transparency Study](https://ana.net/programmatic), December 2023. Trade body study of 21 advertisers' log-level data; full report members-only.
- [Katten, ANA Study Finds Over $20 Billion in Efficiency Gains Possible in Programmatic Advertising Spend](https://quickreads.ext.katten.com/post/102iufy/ana-study-finds-over-20-billion-in-efficiency-gains-possible-in-programmatic-a), 2023. Law firm summary; secondary source for the MFA, website-count and fee figures.
- [Marketing Brew, ANA report finds that only around a third of ad dollars reach intended audiences](https://www.marketingbrew.com/stories/2023/12/05/ana-report-finds-that-only-around-a-third-of-ad-dollars-reach-intended-audiences), 5 December 2023. Trade press; source for the 35.5 billion impressions and the study period.

# What Is LLM Observability?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-llm-observability/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-31 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: LLM observability extends application monitoring to systems whose outputs vary from run to run. It rests on traces of each request, cost and latency data, and evaluations of quality. OpenTelemetry is standardising the format, but the conventions are still in development.

LLM observability is the practice of recording what an AI application did on every run, including the prompts, model responses, tool and retrieval steps, tokens, cost, latency and quality scores, so a team can see why it behaved as it did. Ordinary monitoring tells you a service is up. Observability for LLMs tells you whether the answer was right, what it cost and which step went wrong.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What LLM observability means

Langfuse defines observability as the ability to monitor and understand the internal states of an LLM application. The difference from conventional software is that outputs vary. A test can confirm that a function returns the right number; it cannot confirm in advance that an agent's follow-up email is accurate. Observability replaces some of that certainty with evidence gathered from real runs.

It has three layers.

| Layer | What it records | Question it answers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Traces | Each run as a tree of steps: model calls, retrievals, tool calls, sub-agents | What happened, in what order? |
| Metrics | Tokens, cost, latency and error rates per model, agent or task | What did it cost and how fast was it? |
| Evaluations | Scores on outputs from automated judges, reviewers or users | Was the output any good? |

## How it works

**Traces.** Instrumentation wraps each step of a run. OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, now maintained in their own repository, name an inference span after the operation and model, for example "chat gpt-4". They require the operation name and provider, and recommend recording input and output token counts. Agent runs appear as invoke\_agent spans and tool calls as execute\_tool spans, so a multi-step agent becomes a readable tree.

**Content capture.** The conventions keep prompts and completions out of span attributes and make content capture opt-in. That matters for a commercial team: a trace of a sales agent may contain client names, pricing and email text. Decide what is retained, for how long and who can read it before turning capture on.

**Evaluations.** Langfuse lists model-based evaluations, user feedback and manual labelling as the main methods. The model-based approach, often called LLM-as-a-judge, was studied by Zheng and colleagues in 2023. Strong judges matched human preferences over 80% of the time, about the level at which humans agree with each other. The same paper documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, so automated scores need periodic checks against human review.

**Security.** The UK NCSC recommends logging LLM inputs and outputs and tool or API calls in enough detail to spot suspicious activity. The trace that helps an engineer debug is the same one that helps a security team investigate a prompt injection.

> A trace tells you what the agent did. A decision record tells you why the business let it.

## What to evaluate before choosing a tool

The category includes open-source tools such as Langfuse, vendor platforms from model and framework providers, and LLM features added to existing application monitoring suites. The differences that matter to a business buyer are rarely the dashboards.

| Question | Why it matters |
| --- | --- |
| Does it accept OpenTelemetry data? | Avoids rewriting instrumentation if you change vendor |
| Can it trace agents and tools, not only model calls? | Errors can start in retrieval or tool steps, not only the model |
| How is prompt and output content stored and redacted? | Traces may hold client and personal data |
| Can it be self-hosted or kept in-region? | Matters for regulated firms and data residency |
| Does it support human review queues and scores? | Links evaluation to the approval gate |
| Can cost be split by agent, task and team? | Spend caps need per-agent numbers |

Observability is wiring, not the record. In **lowob**'s model it sits alongside the context layer: rent it, but keep decisions, approvals and outcomes in a record the business owns, so that changing tools does not erase the history.

## lowob takeaways

- **Trace every step.** Model calls alone miss errors that start in retrieval and tool steps.
- **Treat content as sensitive.** Decide what prompts and outputs are retained before capture is switched on.
- **Check the judges.** Automated scores are useful and biased; sample them against human review.
- **Prefer open formats.** OpenTelemetry support keeps the traces portable as tools change.

## Common questions

### What is LLM observability?

Recording what an AI application did on each run, including prompts, outputs, tool calls, tokens, cost, latency and quality scores, so teams can debug and improve it.

### What is the difference between LLM monitoring and LLM observability?

Monitoring tracks known measures such as uptime, latency and cost. Observability adds traces and evaluations that let you explain why a particular output was wrong.

### What is LLM-as-a-judge?

Using a language model to score another model's outputs. It agrees with human preferences often, but it has known biases and should be checked against human review.

### Does OpenTelemetry support LLMs?

Yes. It has GenAI semantic conventions for model calls, tools and agents, though they remain at Development status and may change between releases.

## Sources and notes

- [Langfuse, LLM observability FAQ](https://langfuse.com/faq/all/llm-observability.md), vendor documentation. Open-source vendor; definitions reflect its product.
- [Dash0, OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions explained](https://www.dash0.com/knowledge/opentelemetry-genai-semantic-conventions-explained), September 2026. Vendor explainer of the OpenTelemetry specification.
- [Zheng et al., Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685), arXiv, June 2023. Academic study; agreement figures are for chat preference tasks.
- [UK National Cyber Security Centre, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse)](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection), 8 December 2025. Government guidance on logging LLM inputs, outputs and tool calls.

## Related research

- [Top 5 LLM Observability and Evaluation Platforms](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-llm-observability-and-evaluation-platforms/)
- [The Enterprise Brain Is a Record, Not a Mind](https://lowob.com/research/the-enterprise-brain-is-a-record-not-a-mind/)
- [Approval Rate Measures Fatigue Too](https://lowob.com/research/approval-rate-measures-fatigue-too/)
- [What Is Synthetic Data?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-synthetic-data/)
- [LLM Observability vs Application Monitoring](https://lowob.com/research/llm-observability-vs-apm/)

## Next move

Pick one live AI workflow and ask for the trace of its last bad output. If nobody can produce it within an hour, instrument that workflow before adding another.

# Protocol Revenue: What the Protocol Keeps and What to Report

Source: https://lowob.com/research/protocol-revenue-fees-real-yield-and-what-to-report/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-29 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Report what the protocol keeps, with and without incentives, where it came from and what it cost to get, on one page, monthly, in the same format. TVL is a balance, not revenue; protocol revenue is the fee income retained after suppliers are paid. The SEC's 2026 offering proposal points the same way, asking for token economics and, for larger raises, GAAP financial statements.

Report what the protocol keeps, with and without incentives, where it came from and what it cost to get. One page, monthly, same format every time. TVL is a balance, not revenue, and gross fees are not revenue either: protocol revenue is what is left after suppliers are paid. The evidence on incentives shows why the "without" column matters: after Arbitrum's airdrop, total fees rose while activity per address fell. And in the US, the SEC's 2026 offering proposal would ask issuers for exactly this kind of consistent economic disclosure.

## TVL is a balance, not revenue

In crypto, TVL is reach (see [stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/)). It is a snapshot of money parked, often rented with your own token, and it can leave in an afternoon.

A balance tells you what is sitting there today. It does not tell you what the protocol earns, what it costs to hold, or whether it will be there next month. Reporting TVL as a headline number tells a sophisticated reader that you do not know the difference. Or worse, that you do.

Keep TVL on the page. Just stop leading with it. The same goes for headline valuation: Keyrock's review of 62 airdropped token launches found higher launch FDV correlated with a greater chance of a significant price drop, and one launch carried an estimated $6 million of liquidity against a $13 billion FDV. Neither number is a measure of the business.

## What revenue actually is

Revenue for a protocol is the fee income the protocol or its treasury keeps. Not the fees that pass through on the way to someone else.

| Line | What it is | Who it belongs to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gross fees | Everything users paid to use the protocol | Nobody yet |
| Supplier share | Fees paid out to LPs, lenders, depositors, curators | Them |
| Protocol revenue | What is left, retained by the protocol or treasury | You |

Many decks report line one and call it revenue. Investors read line three. The gap between the two is the first thing they will ask about, so put it on the page before they do. Public analytics dashboards label these lines in different ways, so state your own definitions on the page and check which one a data provider uses before you quote its figure.

If protocol revenue is zero by design, say so and explain the plan. Zero with a reason is a strategy. Zero hidden behind gross fees is a problem waiting for a diligence call.

## Incentive-adjusted everything

Every operating metric gets two columns: with incentives, without.

TVL with and without token rewards. Volume with and without rewards. Active users with and without a campaign running. Fees with and without the subsidised rate.

The evidence shows how far the columns can diverge. Academic analysis of Arbitrum's airdrop found transactions per address fell after the drop even as total daily fees rose; the same study found up to 66% of claimed tokens across nine airdrops went to exchanges in the first transfer. A fee line inflated by a campaign is real money in the period. It is not evidence of next period.

Investors do this calculation themselves. Curators do it before listing you. The only question is whether you show your working or they show theirs. [Community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) applies the same rule to community: measure what remains when the incentive stops.

The "without" column is the business. The gap between the columns is the cost of appearing bigger than the business. Both are useful. Only one is revenue.

> The "without" column is the business. The gap is what it costs to look bigger than you are.

## Retention and concentration

Deposits that arrive are reach. Deposits that stay are the product working.

Report retained deposits at 30 and 90 days, by cohort. A cohort is a month of arrivals. Then split each cohort by source: which integration brought it, which issuer, which campaign. [Issuers, integrations and curators](https://lowob.com/research/issuers-integrations-and-curators/) covers building those channels. This is where you find out which ones delivered money that stayed. It is the protocol version of [net revenue retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-net-revenue-retention/): what a cohort is worth a year after it arrived.

Then concentration. Share of TVL from the top three depositors. If one closed fund is your biggest market, you have a ceiling and a single point of failure in the same row. Their redemption is your drawdown.

Concentration is not shameful early. Hiding it is. Show the number and show the plan for bringing it down.

## The cost side and the treasury

Everything above has a cost. Put it on the same page.

Incentive spend per dollar of TVL that was still there at 90 days. Not per dollar that arrived. Per dollar that stayed. That is your acquisition cost, and it will be higher than you want it to be. The arithmetic is the same as [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) in any other business: the cost of the retained customer against the margin they produce, with tokens counted at what they cost the treasury.

Grant money is acquisition cost too. A grant that pays for a deployment on a new chain is a marketing spend with a different name. Count it, in the same currency, in the same table.

Treasury is reported in stablecoin terms. Not in your own token at today's price. Holdings, monthly burn, months of runway. If the treasury is mostly your own token, say what it would be worth at a third of the price, because someone will ask.

## Where disclosure is heading

The one page is not only good practice. US regulators are moving towards asking for something like it. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published on 18 August 2026, would create offering exemptions for crypto-related investment contracts. The Congressional Research Service's summary describes principles-based disclosure across ten topics, including token economics: supply, pricing, lockups, release schedules and mechanisms for creating or destroying the asset. The larger fundraising route would require financial statements under US GAAP, audited for its top tier, with annual, semiannual and current reports. Comments closed on 20 October 2026 and the rule is not final. This is not legal advice, but a protocol that already publishes a consistent monthly page will find the disclosure work far smaller.

In the EU, MiCA Article 6 bars white papers from making assertions on a token's future value. An APY in marketing sits uncomfortably next to that rule, which is another reason the one page leaves it out.

## What to stop reporting, and the one page

Stop reporting headline TVL on its own. Stop reporting APYs anywhere (see [the user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/)). Stop counting markets as progress; ten markets with no retained deposits is a maintenance burden, not traction. Stop announcing partnerships that are not live with money in them.

| Section | Contents |
| --- | --- |
| Revenue | Gross fees, supplier share, protocol revenue |
| Core metrics | TVL, volume, users and fees, each with and without incentives |
| Retention | Retained deposits at 30 and 90 days, by cohort and source |
| Concentration | Top three depositors' share, and the plan to reduce it |
| Acquisition cost | Incentive and grant spend per dollar of 90-day retained TVL |
| Treasury | Holdings, burn and runway in stablecoin terms |
| Commentary | Three sentences on what changed and why |

Same format every month. A curator reads it to size a listing. An investor reads it to check the business. The community reads it to see whether the team tells the truth when the numbers are down. One page that serves all three is the test of whether the business is real. Build it so someone else can produce it when you are not there (see [build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/)), and hold it to the standard of [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Three revenue lines.** Gross fees, supplier share and protocol revenue, with your definitions stated.
- **Two columns for everything.** With and without incentives; only the second is the business.
- **Retention, concentration, cost per sticky dollar.** By cohort and source, at 30 and 90 days.
- **Stablecoin treasury, no APYs.** Report runway in stablecoins and drop yields, market counts and unlive partnerships.

## Common questions

### Is TVL the same as protocol revenue?

No. TVL is a snapshot of money parked, much of it rented with the protocol's own token. Revenue is the fee income the protocol or treasury keeps after suppliers such as LPs and lenders are paid.

### How should a DeFi protocol report revenue to investors?

As three lines: gross fees users paid, the supplier share paid to LPs, lenders and depositors, and the protocol revenue retained. Show each core metric with and without incentives, on one page, monthly.

### What does incentive-adjusted mean for crypto metrics?

Every operating metric is shown with and without token rewards or subsidised rates. The "without" column is the business; the gap is the cost of appearing bigger.

### Will crypto protocols have to publish financial statements?

Under the SEC's August 2026 proposal, which is not final, issuers using the larger fundraising exemption would file US GAAP financial statements and periodic reports, and all issuers using the exemptions would disclose token economics.

## Sources and notes

- [Congressional Research Service, SEC proposes Regulation Crypto Assets](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/LSB11480.html), 10 September 2026. Nonpartisan legal summary of a proposal, via a public mirror.
- [US Securities and Exchange Commission, Regulation Crypto Assets proposed rule](https://sec.gov/rules-regulations/2026/08/s7-2026-27), 18 August 2026. Proposal; not final.
- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: giving money away is harder than it seems](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), arXiv, revised 2025. Academic study of nine airdrops.
- [Keyrock, Airdrops in the barren desert](https://keyrock.com/airdrops-in-the-barren-desert/), 25 September 2024, updated July 2025. Market-maker research; FDV and liquidity figures are its estimates.
- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 6, content and form of the white paper](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-6-content-and-form-crypto-asset). EU regulation text.
- The revenue lines and the one-page format are **lowob**'s framework.

Measure incentive and grant spend per dollar of TVL still present at 90 days. Put that number, the three revenue lines and the top-three concentration on one page, and send it to your investors in the same format next month.

# Cold Outreach Works Better With a Real Reason to Talk

Source: https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-28 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Personalisation theatre (a line about the prospect's podcast on top of a generic pitch) is not a reason to talk. Signal-based outbound starts from an observable change in the prospect's business, scores it for recency, relevance, magnitude, access and proof, and writes from a hypothesis. With about 95% of buyers out of market at any time, the discipline is as much about who not to contact as who to contact.

Mentioning a prospect's podcast is not a reason to send a sales pitch. Better outreach starts with an observable change in the prospect's business and a problem you might solve because of it. Most buyers are not in market at any given time, and Gartner finds 67% would prefer to buy without a rep at all, so the bar for interrupting someone is high. Score each signal before you spend time on it, write from a hypothesis rather than a diagnosis, and use automation to cut research cost, not to raise send volume.

Cold outreach has developed a personalisation theatre problem. A seller mentions the prospect's university, praises a recent podcast, inserts a line about the funding round, and then sends the same irrelevant pitch that went to everyone else.

The email is personalised. The reason for the conversation is not. Buyers do not owe a response because a system proved it could scrape their biography. They respond when the message connects a real change in their business to a problem worth solving now. That is the difference between cosmetic personalisation and signal-based outbound.

## Why the reason matters more than the greeting

Two facts set the bar. First, most of any market is not buying. The B2B Institute at LinkedIn, drawing on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argues that about 95% of potential buyers are "out-market" at any given time, because companies replace most products and services only every few years. A generic message reaches mostly people with no reason to act.

Second, buyers increasingly prefer not to talk to sellers. Gartner's survey of 646 B2B buyers, published in March 2026, found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Gartner's buying-journey research found buyers spend only 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers. A seller's message has to earn a place in that small share.

A signal is how you find the minority with a live reason, and how you show them you noticed it.

## A signal is evidence of a changing commercial condition

Product launches, market expansion, new executives and hiring can signal a change in priorities. So can a relevant integration, a shift in regulation, customer complaints, a competitor's move or repeated questions from users.

A signal matters only when it changes the probability, timing or value of a buying decision. Funding alone is weak. Funding specifically allocated to enterprise expansion, paired with hiring a head of partnerships, tells a more specific story.

| Weak signal | Why it is weak | Stronger version |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Raised a round | Says money exists, not what it is for | Raised to expand into a named market, and hiring there |
| New executive | Most new hires change nothing you sell into | New head of a function you serve, with a public mandate |
| Spoke on a podcast | Personal trivia | Said publicly that a problem you solve is a priority |
| Visited your pricing page | Could be a student or a competitor | Several people from one target account visited in a week |

Third-party intent data can add signals, with caveats about accuracy. Our explainer on [intent data](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-intent-data/) covers how far to trust it.

## Build the outreach thesis before writing the email

For each account, complete four fields:

- **Observed change:** what happened, with a link to the evidence.
- **Likely implication:** what new pressure, opportunity or coordination problem it could create.
- **Relevant capability:** how your product or service might help.
- **Credible next step:** a small conversation or artefact that would be useful even if the prospect does not buy.

That produces a reason-to-talk statement: *Because the company is doing X, the team may now encounter Y. We have relevant experience with Z and can offer Q as a useful next step.*

Claude can help assemble evidence, compare it with your [ideal customer profile](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/) and draft a hypothesis. The account owner should verify the source, test the logic and decide whether the implication is credible.

## Score signals before spending time on them

Score each signal from zero to two on five dimensions:

| Dimension | 0 | 1 | 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Recency | Over six months old | One to six months | Within the last month |
| Relevance | Unconnected to your problem | Indirectly connected | Directly creates the problem you solve |
| Magnitude | Cosmetic change | Affects one team | Changes the business's direction or risk |
| Access | No route to the decision owner | Route to an influencer | Route to the owner or a warm introduction |
| Proof | Nothing relevant to show | Adjacent experience | Direct, evidenced experience |

Accounts scoring eight to ten receive high-effort research and direct outreach. Accounts scoring five to seven enter a lighter nurture motion. Lower-scoring accounts stay monitored rather than forced into a campaign. The time bands above are **lowob**'s defaults; set your own to match your sales cycle.

## Write from hypothesis, not certainty

Signal-based outreach can still fail if it pretends to know too much.

Do not write: "You must be struggling to manage your community after the launch."

Write: "The launch appears to have created a sharp increase in product questions across Discord and X. Teams at this stage often have trouble separating support issues from broader narrative risk. Is that showing up for you?"

The second version shows attention without claiming private knowledge. It opens a conversation instead of performing a diagnosis.

Keep the first message to four sentences: the signal, why it may matter, your relevant experience, and one low-friction question or offer.

*Saw that you are expanding the product from crypto-native users into financial institutions. That transition usually changes the buying committee, proof requirements and content needed to support a sale. We have been mapping that shift across several infrastructure teams. Happy to share the institutional GTM checklist if it would be useful.*

There is no fake compliment and no miniature brochure. The value of the message is the relevance of the premise.

> Automation should reduce research cost while raising the threshold for contact.

## Use AI to protect seller time, not buyer attention

A strong Claude workflow can monitor an approved account list, extract supported signals, score them against the ICP and prepare a research brief. It can flag missing evidence and generate several opening hypotheses.

It should not automatically send every message it can produce. When the marginal cost of outreach approaches zero, organisations are tempted to spend buyer attention carelessly. That is precisely when judgment matters more. Our piece [Nothing sends without a person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/) sets out the approval gate, and [what an AI SDR can and cannot do](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-sdr/) covers the tools.

There is also a hard technical limit. Google's sender guidelines require all senders to keep the spam rate reported in Postmaster Tools below 0.3%, and recommend staying below 0.1%; Yahoo applies the same 0.3% ceiling. Since November 2025 Gmail has been ramping up enforcement, including rejecting non-compliant mail. A high-volume, low-relevance sequence can damage the reputation of the domain your invoices and customer emails also use. Our guide to [email deliverability](https://lowob.com/research/email-deliverability-explained/) covers the setup.

## lowob takeaways

- **Find a commercial signal, not trivia.** A real change in the business beats a compliment about a podcast.
- **Score before you write.** Recency, relevance, magnitude, access and proof decide where effort goes.
- **Write a hypothesis.** Show what you noticed and ask whether it is true.
- **Raise the threshold as costs fall.** Cheap drafting is a reason to send less, better, with a person approving.

## Common questions

### What is signal-based outbound?

It is prospecting that starts from an observable change in a target company, such as an expansion, a relevant hire or a regulatory shift, and contacts the company only when that change makes your offer timely. The message is built around the signal.

### What are examples of buying signals in B2B?

Strong signals include a funded expansion into a market you serve, a new leader of a function you sell to, a public statement that your problem is a priority, a relevant regulatory change, or several people from one target account researching your category.

### Does personalising cold emails improve response rates?

Personalising the greeting does little if the reason for writing is generic. What helps is a specific, verified reason the message is relevant now, stated as a hypothesis the reader can confirm or reject.

### Can AI write and send cold emails automatically?

It can draft and research well, but sending without review risks spam complaints, inaccurate claims and domain damage. Google and Yahoo cap spam rates at 0.3%. Keep a person approving each send.

## Sources and notes

- [The B2B Institute at LinkedIn, The 95-5 rule](https://business.linkedin.com/it/it/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/b2b-research/trends/95-5-rule), undated. Published by an advertising platform; based on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute.
- [Gartner, Sales survey finds 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), 9 March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025.

## Next move

Take this week's outbound list and score every account on the five dimensions. Send only to those scoring eight or more, each with a four-sentence message built on its signal, and compare replies with last week's.

# What Is Account-Based Marketing? A Small-Team Version

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-27 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Account-based marketing concentrates marketing and sales effort on a named list of accounts worth winning. It fits complex, high-value sales to identifiable buyers, where purchases involve around 13 people. A small team can run it with a short list, research, one owner per account and measures that track account movement rather than email volume.

Account-based marketing (ABM) is a way of concentrating sales and marketing effort on a named set of companies that fit the product, rather than trying to reach everyone and hoping the right buyers respond. It fits sales of meaningful value that take time and involve several people; Forrester finds an average of 13 people involved in a B2B purchase. A small team can run it without a large platform: a short list, research on each account, one owner per account and measures that track account progress, not email volume.

A small B2B company does not always need thousands of leads. If ten customers could meaningfully change its revenue, it may make more sense to identify those customers and work deliberately to earn their business. That is account-based marketing.

## What account-based marketing actually means

Start with a shortlist of companies whose problems the product can solve. Learn who is involved in the buying decision, why the timing may be right and what would make the company willing to talk. Use that knowledge to make outreach, content and follow-up relevant.

LinkedIn's marketing glossary defines ABM as "a strategic approach that focuses on targeting and engaging specific high-value accounts or companies" and describes three stages: account research, content creation for each account, and execution and measurement. A small team can do those jobs with ordinary research tools and a CRM rather than an enterprise software package.

This is not a mass-email sequence with someone's first name inserted. It is a coordinated way of deciding where limited sales and marketing effort should go. The unit of attention changes from the lead (one person who filled in a form) to the account (the company and the group of people inside it who will decide). Our comparison of [lead scoring and account scoring](https://lowob.com/research/lead-scoring-vs-account-scoring/) covers what that change does to qualification.

## When ABM is the right motion

ABM is a natural fit when a sale has meaningful value, takes time and involves several stakeholders. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. When that many people decide, reaching one of them through a form fill is not enough. Our explainer on [the buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) sets out the roles.

| Signal | ABM likely fits | Broad inbound or product-led likely fits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deal value | High enough that one win changes the quarter | Low; volume carries the economics |
| Buyer identity | You can name target companies in advance | Buyers are anonymous until they arrive |
| Buying group | Several departments, technical and commercial diligence | One person can buy alone |
| Sales cycle | Months, with stages that can stall | Days, often self-serve |
| Example contexts | Fintech infrastructure sold to banks; AI for a regulated workflow; services for funds and custodians | Low-cost software, consumer apps |

It is less suitable when the product is cheap, self-serve and bought spontaneously. The key question is whether knowing and contacting a particular company is worth the work involved.

## What the evidence says, and what it does not

Most ABM research comes from people who practise it, so read it as direction rather than proof. Momentum ITSMA's benchmark study, run with the ABM Leadership Alliance and published in March 2023, surveyed 279 ABM heads and practitioners. It found 72% said ABM delivers higher ROI than other types of marketing, and ABM accounted for 28% of their 2022 marketing budgets. It also found only 17% of programmes were fully embedded in go-to-market strategy. Most programmes, in other words, are still bolted on.

Forrester's 2022 State of ABM survey found the most common reason for adopting account-based strategies was sourcing new pipeline, and Forrester advised against over-relying on sourcing metrics. It also found average ABM budgets of $590,000 excluding headcount, a figure far above what a small team will spend, and that 39% of programmes were still pilots.

The fair reading: ABM works for the people who choose it and run it well, which is a self-selected group. It is not automatically cheaper than other channels. It works when the value of winning a fitting account justifies the research and follow-up time.

> A hundred opens are not a substitute for one serious buyer conversation.

## Build a short list you can actually work

For a hypothetical fintech infrastructure company, a sensible starting list might be 20 to 50 accounts, not an arbitrarily large database. The right size depends on deal value and team capacity: a list is the right length when every account on it gets real research and a named owner.

For each account, record four things:

| Field | What goes in it | Test |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fit | Why the product demonstrably solves this company's problem | Would it pass your [ideal customer profile](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)? |
| Reason to talk | A relevant, verified change: a launch, a hire, an expansion, a public statement, an introduction | Can you link to the evidence? |
| Buying roles | Likely sponsor, evaluator, finance, security, legal | Do you know at least two names? |
| Next step | One person, one credible message, one follow-up owner | Is the owner written down? |

Verify the signal rather than inventing a problem from a job title. A company launching a new payment product, hiring for treasury operations or expanding internationally may have a specific need. Our piece on [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) covers how to score those signals.

## Run a small programme before buying a platform

Prepare a short research note for each account. Write a message based on the business problem, not biographical trivia. Support it with material that does a job for that reader: a relevant product explanation, technical documentation or a properly evidenced case study.

Use partner introductions, thoughtful email and professional communities where relevant. A small roundtable can help with conversations that need several stakeholders in the room. Coordinate follow-ups in a shared CRM, and give each account one owner so marketing and sales are not contacting the same people with conflicting messages.

Review the list every two weeks. Ask which accounts have progressed, what objections came up and whether the list still makes sense. Accounts that have shown no movement in two review cycles should be replaced, not chased harder. For the largest accounts, [account planning for the top twenty](https://lowob.com/research/account-planning-for-the-top-twenty/) describes the next level of depth.

## Measure progress by account

Track what moves an account towards a decision:

1. **Relevant meetings.** Conversations with people who hold part of the decision.
2. **Stakeholders engaged.** How many of the buying roles you now know and have spoken to.
3. **Diligence completed.** Technical, security or commercial review started or passed.
4. **Qualified opportunities and wins.** The outcome, with the time from first contact recorded.

Include the team's research and follow-up hours in the economics. ABM is often more expensive per account than broad channels, and that is fine when the accounts are worth it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Start with identifiable, high-fit buyers.** A short, worked list beats a large, unworked one.
- **Research the business need.** Personalise the reason to talk, not the greeting.
- **One owner per account.** Coordinated sales and marketing, one coherent approach.
- **Read the ROI surveys carefully.** They are self-reported by practitioners; measure your own account movement.

## Common questions

### What is account-based marketing in simple terms?

It is focusing sales and marketing effort on a named list of companies that fit the product, researching each one and coordinating outreach to the people who will make the decision, instead of generating as many leads as possible.

### Is account-based marketing worth it for a small company?

It can be, when deals are valuable, buyers can be identified in advance and purchases involve several people. A small team can run it with 20 to 50 accounts, a CRM and disciplined research. It rarely pays for cheap, self-serve products.

### How many accounts should an ABM programme target?

As many as the team can research properly and assign an owner to. For a small team that is often 20 to 50. The constraint is research and follow-up time, not the size of the database.

### How do you measure account-based marketing?

By account progress: meetings with decision makers, buying roles engaged, diligence completed, qualified opportunities and wins. Email opens and clicks say little about whether an account is moving.

## Sources and notes

- [LinkedIn Marketing Solutions, Account-based marketing (ABM)](https://business.linkedin.com/advertise/resources/marketing-terms/abm), undated. Glossary from an advertising platform that sells ABM targeting.
- [Forrester, The State of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated in the release.
- [Momentum ITSMA, annual ABM benchmarking study](https://prnewswire.com/news-releases/momentum-itsmas-annual-abm-benchmarking-study-shows-no-signs-of-slow-down-for-account-based-marketing-301760194.html), 2 March 2023. Survey of 279 ABM practitioners by an ABM consultancy; self-reported.
- [Forrester, New State of Account-Based Marketing survey](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/new-forrester-state-of-account-based-marketing-survey-reveals-how-abm-budgets-are-shifting/), 6 July 2022. Analyst blog; respondent count not stated; sample skewed to smaller firms.
- The fit table, account record and fintech list size are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

Write down the 20 companies that would most change your revenue if they bought this year. For each, fill in the four fields above, assign an owner, and book the first two-weekly review.

# Build an Affiliate Program Without Paying for Coupon Leaks

Source: https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-program-asset-or-coupon-leak/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: An affiliate programme is a set of terms under which other people are paid to bring you customers. Badly designed terms pay coupon sites and browser extensions for sales that would have happened anyway. Design the terms before choosing a network, recruit the first partners by hand, and judge the programme on approved outcomes, partner mix and concentration.

Affiliate programmes can introduce new customers, but weak commission rules also reward partners for sales that would have happened anyway. The most common leak is a coupon site or browser extension that appears at checkout, after the customer has decided, and collects the commission under last-click attribution. Google judged the practice serious enough to change its Chrome Web Store rules in 2025. The fix is in the terms: what is paid for, who qualifies, what is prohibited and how outcomes are validated, set before the programme goes on a network.

An affiliate programme is a set of terms under which other people are paid to bring you customers.

That is all it is, and it is why the channel is so often misjudged. Companies picture coupon sites and conclude the channel is low quality. Or they picture a network dashboard and assume the programme runs itself. Both are true of badly built programmes. Neither is true of a programme that was designed.

For a company in a category the ad platforms restrict, the affiliate channel has a property few others have: no platform has to approve each placement. Partners choose to carry the product because the terms make it worth their while. That does not remove the rules on what partners say, which the last section covers.

## The coupon leak

Start with the failure, because most companies are living in it.

A customer decides to buy. At checkout, they search for a discount code. A coupon site appears, offers a code and drops a cookie. Under last-click attribution, that site is paid a commission for a customer who had already decided.

Multiply by every checkout and the programme is paying a tax on its own conversions. The reported numbers look excellent, because the programme appears to drive sales that were happening anyway. The finance team sees a rising affiliate bill and a flat top line and concludes, correctly, that something is wrong. Our piece on [attribution vs incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) explains why the reported number and the caused number diverge.

Browser extensions are the automated version of the same leak. In March 2025 Google tightened its Chrome Web Store policy so that an extension may add or replace affiliate links only when the programme is disclosed, the user takes an action first, and the link "is tied to a direct benefit for the user at that moment." A coupon extension "must not insert an affiliate link if no coupon or discount is found." Enforcement began on 10 June 2025, with removal from the store for violations. A platform rule is not a fix for your programme, but it confirms the leak is real.

The industry is aware of it. At a September 2025 Performance Marketing Association session on coupons, practitioners said "most programs are still last click", that public vanity codes "can be scraped", and recommended single-use or capped codes and commissioning "for contribution rather than proximity to checkout."

The fix is in the terms, not the platform. Exclude or tier coupon and loyalty partners. Pay on first click, or on a weighted model, for content partners who introduced the customer. Require that a discount code be one the partner was issued, not one scraped from the checkout page. Approve partners individually rather than accepting every application.

## Design the terms before choosing the network

A programme's terms determine who joins it. Set them first.

| Term | Decision | Default to avoid |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is paid for | A funded account, an approved application, a first transaction above a threshold, a subscriber retained at 30 days | Paying on the event that is easiest to count |
| How much, for how long | Flat bounty, percentage or revenue share, with a cookie window that matches the buying cycle | One window for every product |
| Who qualifies | Content publishers, comparison sites, creators, communities, coupon and loyalty sites, sub-networks, each on stated terms | Accepting every application |
| What is prohibited | Brand-name bidding, misleading claims, unissued codes, incentivised traffic, unapproved regulated claims | Relying on the network's standard list |
| How outcomes are validated | Which events your own tracking confirms, validation period, treatment of refunds, chargebacks and fraud | Paying on the network's report alone |

**Cookie windows** should reflect the real decision: seven days for a decision people make in an afternoon, sixty for one they research. **Prohibitions** for regulated products should include any language the company could not say itself.

Only then choose where the programme lives. The large networks bring existing partners and handle payments; some carry restricted categories and some do not, which is the first thing to check. A direct platform gives more control and less reach. A company can run both.

Whoever runs it, keep judgment in-house. Edelman and Brandi's study in the Journal of Marketing Research, of merchants overseeing thousands of affiliates they had never met, found outside specialists were better at excluding affiliates that clearly broke the rules, while in-house staff were better at catching "borderline" affiliates whose practices still worked against the merchant. Coupon leakage is usually borderline, not fraud.

> The fix for the coupon leak is in the terms, not the platform.

## Recruit like a partner programme, not a listing

A programme on a network with no recruitment is a listing. Partners do not find it; they are found.

Choose the first thirty partners by hand: the comparison sites that already rank for the category, the newsletters whose readers already ask about it, the creators whose audience already buys similar products, and the communities where the question already comes up. Each gets a specific offer, product access, creative that does not need to be rebuilt, and a named person to talk to.

That is a few weeks of work. It is also why the channel keeps producing when the platforms change their minds about the category. The market is large enough to reward it: the Performance Marketing Association's 2025 study put US affiliate investment at about $13.6 billion in 2024, with financial services rising from 12% to 15% of spend. Our [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set roles and tiers once the base grows.

## What a programme that works looks like

| Signal | **lowob**'s working threshold | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Approved outcomes | Rising month over month | The only volume that counts |
| Coupon partners' share of paid outcomes | Below a fifth | Above it, much of the bill is likely the leak |
| Largest single partner | Below a third of paid outcomes | Concentration is a dependency |
| Approval rate | Above 90% | Low rates mean poor traffic or poor terms |
| Cost per approved outcome | Stable or falling as the mix improves | Shows the partner base is getting better |
| Partner behaviour | Asking for creative before you send it | Partners invested in the product |

The thresholds are **lowob**'s working rules, not industry standards. For context, the PMA reported that coupon sites' share of US affiliate investment fell from 16% to 10%, while loyalty and cashback held at 35%. If loyalty partners also sit at checkout in your programme, count them with the coupon share.

That is an asset. It has terms, a partner base, a reporting history and a reason to keep working when any single channel goes dark. Unlike a rented ad account, it is something the company owns.

## Disclosure and responsibility

Where affiliates endorse products or receive commissions, disclosure matters too. The US FTC's endorsement guidance says affiliates should disclose the relationship clearly, close to the recommendation, and that "affiliate link" on its own is not enough. It also says advertisers "need to have reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network", and that delegating to an outside company "doesn't relieve you of responsibility." For regulated financial products in the UK, the FCA's FG24/1 guidance says firms working with affiliates should take proactive responsibility for their promotions. Other jurisdictions impose different rules, so write the disclosure language into the terms and check it.

## lowob takeaways

- **Define the action worth paying for before recruiting affiliates.** Pay for the event that matters, validated by your own tracking.
- **Close the coupon leak in the terms.** Tier coupon and loyalty partners, issue single-use codes and pay content partners for introductions.
- **Check whether partners introduce customers you would not otherwise reach.** Recruit the first thirty by hand.
- **Choose partners whose audiences have a genuine need for the product.** Approve individually and keep borderline calls in-house.
- **Own the disclosure.** The advertiser stays responsible for what affiliates say.

## Common questions

### How do coupon sites affect affiliate programmes?

Under last-click attribution, a coupon site that appears at checkout can be paid a commission for a customer who had already decided to buy. Tier or exclude coupon partners, issue single-use codes and pay content partners who introduced the customer.

### What is a good affiliate commission structure?

Pay for a validated event that matters, such as an approved application or a retained subscriber, with a cookie window that matches the buying cycle and clear rules for refunds, chargebacks and fraud.

### Are browser coupon extensions allowed to replace affiliate links?

Under Chrome Web Store policy enforced from June 2025, extensions may apply affiliate links only after a user action, with disclosure, and when the user gets a direct benefit such as a coupon actually found.

### Do affiliates have to disclose commissions?

In the US, the FTC says affiliates should clearly disclose that they are paid, close to the recommendation, and that advertisers must train and monitor their affiliates.

## Sources and notes

- [Google, Chrome Web Store policy updates: strengthening our policies on affiliate programs in Chrome extensions](https://developer.chrome.com/blog/cws-policy-update-affiliate-ads-2025), 11 March 2025. Platform policy announcement; enforcement from 10 June 2025.
- [Performance Marketing Association, Beyond the Affiliate Coupon Code](https://thepma.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Beyond-the-Affiliate-Coupon-Code-Whitepaper.pdf), webinar held 23 September 2025. Trade body summary of a practitioner panel; qualitative, with figures from the PMA study.
- [Performance Marketing Association, Industry Study 2025](https://thepma.org/pma-study-affiliate-marketing-industry-grows-49-8-to-13-63-b-outpacing-e-commerce-growth-by-2x/), 18 June 2025. Trade association research with London Research; methodology not stated in the release.
- [Edelman and Brandi, Risk, Information, and Incentives in Online Affiliate Marketing](https://www.benedelman.org/risk-information-and-incentives-in-online-affiliate-marketing/), Journal of Marketing Research 52(1), 2015. Academic study; data predates current extension rules.

- [FCA, FG24/1 Finalised guidance on financial promotions on social media](https://www.fca.org.uk/publication/finalised-guidance/fg24-1.pdf), 26 March 2024. UK guidance for regulated financial promotions.
- The terms table and the health thresholds are **lowob**'s framework.
