# What Is CRM Data Hygiene?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-crm-data-hygiene/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: CRM data hygiene is the ongoing discipline that keeps commercial records accurate and current. Surveys show most firms fall short, and the cost has risen now that agents act on records directly. This explainer defines the term, sets out the dimensions that matter, and gives a monthly routine a mid-size firm can keep.

CRM data hygiene is the routine practice of keeping CRM records accurate, complete, unique and current. It covers preventing bad data at entry, finding and fixing errors already in the system, and measuring quality over time. It is a habit rather than a project: a single clean-up decays within months unless rules and automatic capture keep it clean.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What CRM data hygiene means

Every CRM degrades. Contacts change jobs, companies merge, deals stall without being closed, and people type the same account twice with different spellings. Data hygiene is the set of rules and routines that counter this decay.

The term is often used loosely to mean "a clean-up". That is the least useful part. A one-off clean-up fixes a snapshot. Hygiene is what keeps the next snapshot from looking the same. Gartner's 2020 guidance for sales operations leaders made the same point: define data quality standards aligned with what the CRM is for, then measure quality and make it a regular topic in manager and seller conversations.

| Dimension | Question it answers | Typical failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | Is the value true? | Wrong deal value or close date |
| Completeness | Is the required value present? | Blank next step, blank loss reason |
| Uniqueness | Is there exactly one record? | The same account under three names |
| Timeliness | Is the value current? | Contacts who left a year ago |
| Consistency | Is the value in the agreed format? | Free-text sources nobody can group |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### The numbers people present depend on it

The evidence is consistent. Validity's 2025 survey of 602 CRM users and stakeholders found 37% reported lost revenue as a direct result of poor data quality, and 76% said less than half their CRM data was accurate and complete. Its 2026 survey of 500 marketers found 62% said poor CRM data had probably or definitely cost revenue. Nearly 69% said a revenue, pipeline or performance number had been challenged or walked back because the data was wrong, rising to nearly 75% among directors and above. Both are vendor-run surveys from a data quality company, so read them as directional.

### Agents act on what they read

The second reason is the shift from reporting to action. In the 2026 survey, 45% of marketers said they already used agentic AI that can act without human review, and 19% said they had frequently presented or acted on an AI recommendation they later suspected was wrong because of poor underlying data. A duplicate account in a report is an annoyance. A duplicate account read by an agent can mean two outreach sequences to the same buyer.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, the CRM is the store. Hygiene is what makes the store safe for the wiring and reasoning layers to read, and it is the precondition for any agent above autonomy level 1.

## How to keep it: prevention first

Most hygiene effort goes into cleaning. Most of the return comes from prevention.

### Prevent at entry

- **Matching and duplicate rules.** Salesforce's standard matching rules compare names, titles and addresses using fuzzy methods such as Jaro-Winkler distance, and duplicate rules decide whether to warn or block. Most CRMs offer an equivalent.
- **Fixed picklists.** Replace free-text source, industry and loss reason fields with a short controlled list.
- **Required fields at the right moment.** Require next step and date on open deals, and a loss reason at close. Do not require everything at creation, or people will fabricate values.
- **Automatic capture.** Email and calendar sync record activity without typing, which removes the most tedious source of gaps.

### Detect and fix on a rhythm

A monthly routine of under an hour is enough for most mid-size firms:

| Check | How to count it | Typical action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Duplicate accounts | Duplicate report or matching rule output | Merge, keep the record with the most history |
| Stale open deals | Open, no activity in 90 days | Ask the owner to update or close |
| Missing next steps | Open deals with blank or past next-step date | Return to owner |
| Missing loss reasons | Closed-lost in the month with blank reason | Return to owner before month end |
| Departed contacts | Bounced emails or known leavers | Mark inactive, keep history |

Report the counts, not just the fixes. A falling trend is the evidence that the rules are working.

### Common mistakes

1. **Treating hygiene as a project.** A clean-up without entry rules decays back within a quarter.
2. **Requiring too many fields.** A field that must be filled before a record can be saved will be filled, whether or not the person knows the answer. Over-required fields invite invented values.
3. **No owner.** Only 41% of respondents in Validity's 2026 survey had a dedicated data governance team or owner.
4. **Deleting history.** Mark records inactive or superseded rather than deleting them, so outcomes stay attached to the decisions that produced them.

## lowob takeaways

- **Hygiene is a habit.** Entry rules and a monthly count keep data clean; a one-off clean-up does not.
- **Prevent before you clean.** Matching rules, fixed picklists and automatic capture remove most errors at source.
- **Measure five counts.** Duplicates, stale deals, missing next steps, missing loss reasons and departed contacts.
- **Agents raise the bar.** Records that an agent can read need a higher standard than records only people read.

## Common questions

### What is CRM data hygiene?

It is the ongoing practice of keeping CRM records accurate, complete, unique and current, through entry rules, regular checks and fixes, and measurement over time.

### How often should you clean CRM data?

Run a short check monthly and a deeper review once or twice a year. The monthly counts matter more than the size of any single clean-up.

### What causes bad CRM data?

Manual entry, duplicate creation, contacts changing jobs, deals left open after they die, and free-text fields with no agreed values.

### Why does CRM data quality matter for AI?

AI agents act on CRM records directly. Errors that once skewed a report can now trigger outreach, scoring or prioritisation before anyone reviews them.

## Sources and notes

- [Validity, The State of CRM Data Management in 2025](https://validity.com/resource-center/the-state-of-crm-data-management-in-2025). Vendor-run survey of 602 CRM users and stakeholders.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey of 500 marketers at firms with 100+ employees.
- [Gartner, Less Than 50% of Sales Leaders Have High Confidence in Forecasting Accuracy](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-02-12-gartner-says-less-than-50--of-sales-leaders-and-selle), February 2020. Includes Gartner's data quality recommendations.
- [Salesforce Trailhead, Duplicate Management: matching and duplicate rules](https://trailhead.salesforce.com/content/learn/modules/sales_admin_duplicate_management/sales_admin_duplicate_management_unit_2). Vendor documentation; other CRMs offer comparable features.

## Related research

- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)
- [Supersede, Never Overwrite](https://lowob.com/research/supersede-never-overwrite/)
- [The Field That Makes a Record a Judgment](https://lowob.com/research/the-field-that-makes-a-record-a-judgment/)
- [What Is a Quarterly Business Review (QBR)?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-quarterly-business-review/)

## Next move

Run the five counts in the table above this week and write the numbers down. Repeat them in 30 days; the difference tells you whether your rules are working.

# Issuers, Integrations and Curators

Source: https://lowob.com/research/issuers-integrations-and-curators/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: When paid channels are closed, crypto distribution comes from people who already want you to succeed: issuers, integrations, curators and ecosystems. Google bans ads for DeFi protocols everywhere and the UK bans refer-a-friend bonuses for crypto, so work that list before spending on reach, and keep every piece of copy free of APYs and yield promises.

When paid channels are closed, distribution in crypto comes from the people who already have a reason to want you to succeed: issuers, integrations, curators and ecosystems. The closure is specific: Google bans ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools and initial coin offerings in every market, and the UK bans refer-a-friend bonuses for crypto promotions. Work the list of people who gain when you grow before you spend a dollar on reach, and keep every piece of copy free of APYs and yield promises.

## The three bands for crypto

[Part 8](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) laid out distribution when platforms are closed. Crypto needs its own version because the closure is tighter and the exceptions change often.

| Band | What sits in it (policies checked 16 November 2026) | How to treat it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Owned media, integrations, partner co-marketing, ecosystem programmes, answer engines | Build here first; this is most of your distribution |
| Restricted | Google ads for exchanges and software wallets, with certification and local registration such as FCA registration in the UK or MiCA authorisation in the EU; TikTok crypto ads in markets that permit them, through a sales representative; paid placements and sponsorships with disclosure and legal review | Use sparingly, with every piece of copy reviewed before it runs |
| Closed | Google ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools, crypto loans, unregulated dApps and ICOs, in every market; crypto ads in markets where TikTok lists them as not allowed; anything that promises returns | Do not plan around it; policy can shift, but not on your timeline |

Put every channel you are considering into a band before you budget for it. Most teams discover that their plan was mostly in the closed band and their time was mostly in the restricted one.

The restricted band does move. Google opened exchange and wallet advertising in Canada in July 2025, Argentina in September 2025 and Indonesia in February 2026, each subject to local registration and Google certification. For a DeFi protocol, none of those changes applied. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how the sorting works across platforms.

## The free BD list

Here is the list you already have. Every asset you support, list, lend against or route through has an issuer. That issuer wants more venues, more liquidity and more use for their asset.

You are a new place for their asset to be used. That is a reason to promote you, and most will if asked.

Work the list properly. Name a contact at each issuer. Offer something specific: a launch announcement, a joint piece of content, a shared integration guide, a slot in their community call. Ask for the same in return, in writing, with dates.

| Issuer BD list field | What it holds |
| --- | --- |
| Asset and issuer | The token, and the team behind it |
| Named contact | One person, not a general channel |
| What you offer | Launch announcement, joint content, integration guide or community call slot |
| What you ask | The same, in their channels |
| Dates | Agreed in writing |
| Result | What it produced, recorded after launch |

This is BD, not marketing. It takes one person with a spreadsheet and a calendar. It is the cheapest distribution you will ever buy, and almost nobody does it systematically. The wider pattern, using partners' customer overlap to win and keep users, is covered in [What is ecosystem-led growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/).

## Integrations: go where the users already are

A user in crypto rarely goes to a new site to find a new product. They find it inside the tools they already use.

That means wallets, front-ends, aggregators and lending markets are distribution, not just engineering. Each integration puts you in front of an active user at the moment they are deciding what to do with capital.

Treat the integration roadmap as a channel plan. Rank by where your target users already spend time, not by which team replied to your email first. Ship the integration, then do the co-marketing that goes with it. An integration nobody announces is a channel nobody uses. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to agree roles and obligations with each integration partner before launch.

> An integration nobody announces is a channel nobody uses.

## Curators and allocators: sell the inventory, not the TVL

In DeFi there is a layer of people whose job is to decide where capital goes. Curators, vault managers, allocators, risk teams at treasuries. They are a distribution channel, and most teams pitch them wrong.

The role is formal on some protocols. Morpho's documentation describes a curator as the party that sets a vault's risk parameters and liquidity rules, decides which adapters can route vault capital, and defines exposure limits, or caps, on risk factors such as collateral, oracle and protocol exposure. Curators appoint allocators, who make day-to-day allocation decisions within those limits, and most significant curator actions sit behind a timelock so depositors can exit.

The wrong pitch is a TVL number and a growth chart. They have seen it, and they know how it was built.

The right pitch is inventory. What can they deploy into, at what size, with what risk parameters, and what happens when they need to exit. Give them the documentation a risk committee would ask for, before they ask.

| Allocator pack section | What it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | What capital can be deployed into, and in which markets |
| Size | Depth at which the position still behaves as described |
| Risk parameters | Collateral, oracle and protocol exposure, and the caps that apply |
| Exit path | How and how fast capital comes out under stress |
| Documentation | Audits, governance powers, timelocks and incident history |

One serious allocator who understands the position is worth more than a thousand wallets that arrived for a point multiplier. Build the materials for that allocator and the rest follows.

## Foundations, grants and KOLs

Ecosystem foundations fund teams because they want activity on their chain. That makes them a distribution partner, not only a funding source. [Part 17](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) made the point that chain choice is a distribution decision. Here is where you collect on it.

Ask every grant for what comes with it: announcement slots, event placement, introductions to the wallets and front-ends in their ecosystem, co-marketing from their own channels. If a grant offers money with no distribution, weigh it against one that offers both.

KOLs are a legitimate channel when done in the open. Paid partnership disclosed as such, every time. The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance says the disclosure belongs in the endorsement itself, in plain words such as "ad" or "sponsored", and in the video for video content. In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority's 2024 guidance says influencers who promote a regulated product without approval from an authorised firm may be committing a criminal offence. The claims rules below apply to their copy as much as to yours. A KOL who will not disclose is a liability with a follower count.

## Claims rules and answer engines

Every piece of copy, from a landing page to a reply in a community channel, follows the claims register from [Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/). In crypto, that register has two hard lines.

No APYs. No yield promises. Not projected, not historical, not "up to". If a number about returns appears in your copy, it appears with context, a date and a reviewer's sign-off, or it does not appear. That is **lowob**'s rule and it is stricter than most regulation, which is the point.

The regulation is moving the same way. The FCA's cryptoasset promotions regime, in force since 8 October 2023, requires promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading, carry specific risk warnings, include a 24-hour cooling-off period for first-time investors, and it bans refer-a-friend bonuses. Under the EU's Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation, Article 7 requires marketing communications to be clearly identifiable, fair, clear and not misleading, and consistent with the crypto-asset white paper, and none may be disseminated before the white paper is published.

Never screenshot a thin dashboard. A chart with three days of data and one large depositor is not proof of traction. It is evidence you were in a hurry. Wait until the picture is real.

Answer engines now shape a large share of how people first hear about a product. They read your documentation, your integration guides and your public records, and they repeat what is there. Write those pages plainly, keep them current, and make sure the claims in them are the ones you are willing to defend. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers the mechanics.

## lowob takeaways

- **Band every channel per market first.** Some crypto closures, such as Google's ban on DeFi protocol ads, are global.
- **Work the issuer list systematically.** A named contact, a specific offer and dates in writing.
- **Rank integrations by where users already are, and announce each one.** Unannounced integrations carry no one.
- **Pitch curators inventory and risk parameters.** Caps, exposures and exit paths, not TVL.
- **Hold the claims line everywhere.** No APYs, no yield promises, no thin dashboards, disclosed KOLs.

## Common questions

### How do crypto projects market when ad platforms are closed to them?

Build mostly in open channels: owned media, issuer co-marketing, integrations, ecosystem programmes and answer engines. Use restricted paid placements sparingly with review, and do not plan around closed channels such as Google ads for DeFi protocols.

### Can DeFi protocols advertise on Google?

No. Google's cryptocurrency policy prohibits ads for DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools, crypto loans and initial coin offerings regardless of location. Exchanges and software wallets can advertise in approved markets once certified.

### How should I pitch a DeFi protocol to curators and allocators?

Pitch inventory, not TVL: what they can deploy into, at what size, with what risk parameters, and what happens when they exit, with the documentation a risk committee would ask for.

### Can crypto projects use KOLs for marketing?

Yes, when done in the open: paid partnerships disclosed in the content every time, with the same claims rules applied to their copy as to yours, and with local promotion rules such as the UK's checked first.

## Sources and notes

- [Google Ads, Cryptocurrencies and related products policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/14009787?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.
- [Google Ads, Updates to Cryptocurrencies and related products policy (July 2025)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16345928?hl=en), posted 1 July 2025. Canada only; Argentina (September 2025) and Indonesia (February 2026) updates follow the same pattern.
- [TikTok for Business, Financial services ad policy](https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/tiktok-ads-policy-financial-services), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy; crypto treatment varies by market.
- [UK Financial Conduct Authority, FCA introduces tough new rules for marketing cryptoassets](https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/fca-introduces-tough-new-rules-marketing-cryptoassets), 8 June 2023, last updated 6 February 2026. UK rules in force from 8 October 2023.
- [UK Financial Conduct Authority, Cryptoasset firms marketing to UK consumers](https://www.fca.org.uk/firms/cryptoassets/marketing-uk-consumers), last updated 6 February 2026. Source for the 24-hour cooling-off period.

Build the issuer BD list this week: every asset you support, a named contact at each issuer, one specific co-marketing offer and one specific ask, with dates. Ask every grant you hold or apply for what distribution comes with it.

# Product-Led vs Sales-Led vs Partner-Led Growth

Source: https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-22 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Product-led, sales-led and partner-led growth are different organisations, not just different tactics. Choose the primary motion from the product and the buyer, build the organisation for it, and add the others in support. Restricted categories tilt the choice towards partners and relationships.

Every company acquires customers through some combination of three motions: the product sells itself, people sell it, or other companies sell it. These are product-led, sales-led and partner-led growth. Most companies use more than one, but each needs a primary motion, because the three require different organisations. Choose the primary motion from how the buyer discovers, tries and buys the product, not from which one is cheapest, and add the others where they support it.

Every company acquires customers through some combination of three motions: the product sells itself, people sell it, or other companies sell it. The words for these are product-led, sales-led, and partner-led, and while most companies use more than one, each needs a primary motion, because the three require different organisations.

## Product-led

The product is the main acquisition channel. People find it, try it free or cheaply, get value quickly, and pay to get more. Marketing drives sign-ups; the product does the convincing; sales, if it exists, arrives late to expand accounts.

It requires a product that delivers value without a conversation, a short time to that value, a price low enough to decide alone, and a buyer who can decide alone. It breaks when the product needs setup, integration, or trust before it is useful, when the buyer needs approval from others, or when the price is high enough to need a business case.

The economics are attractive: low cost per customer, high volume. The volume part is not optional. Kyle Poyar's summary of the investor OpenView's 2023 Product Benchmarks report, built with Pendo from more than 1,000 products, is a useful reference. Its illustrative funnel for an average freemium product has roughly 5% of new free sign-ups converting to paying customers. That is investor research from a self-selected sample, but it sets the scale: a product-led company needs about twenty sign-ups for each paying customer, and more if activation is weak.

The buyer side is pulling in two directions. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience, which favours self-serve. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments, which works against a buyer who can decide alone. The constraint is that it only works for products and buyers that fit, and many founders decide they are product-led because it is cheaper rather than because it is true. Our explainer [What is product-led growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-product-led-growth/) covers the metrics in more detail.

## Sales-led

People sell the product. Marketing generates and qualifies leads; sales runs a process from discovery to close; customer success keeps and expands the account. The product may be complex, expensive, or dependent on trust and configuration.

It requires a price high enough to pay for the sales cost, a buyer who expects a conversation, a repeatable process, and enough qualified demand to keep the team busy. It breaks when the price cannot carry the cost of selling, when the founder is the only person who can sell it, or when the pipeline depends on channels that have been closed to the category.

The economics are heavier and more predictable. The constraint is that it scales with headcount, and headcount is slow and expensive. The founder dependency is a separate failure, covered in [Founder-led GTM is a job with an expiration date](https://lowob.com/research/founder-led-gtm-expiration-date/).

## Partner-led

Other companies distribute the product: platforms that embed it, resellers, agencies, integration partners, affiliates, marketplaces. The company's own marketing and sales are aimed at partners as much as at end customers.

It requires a product that fits inside another company's offer, terms that make the partner money, and the patience to build relationships that take months to produce. It breaks when the partner's incentive is misaligned, when the company depends on one partner, or when the product needs more support than the partner can give.

The economics can be the best of the three once running: low marginal cost per customer, and distribution that no ad platform can revoke. Partners already hold much of the market. Canalys forecast in late 2024 that 70% of worldwide spending on technology, IT services and telecoms in 2025 would be delivered through partners, down from 73% in 2023. That is a forecast for the IT market as a whole, not for startups. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 benchmarks, vendor research across 530 companies, found partnership channels returned 3.8 times the deal velocity of outbound, inbound and paid channels, yet only 8% of the businesses studied had one. The constraint is time to first revenue, and the risk of concentration in a single partner. Our piece on [partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers roles, payment and tiers.

|  | Product-led | Sales-led | Partner-led |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who convinces the buyer | The product | A salesperson | The partner |
| Requires | Fast time to value; a buyer who decides alone | A price that pays for selling; a repeatable process | A product that fits a partner's offer; terms that pay the partner |
| Breaks when | Setup, approvals or a business case are needed | The price cannot carry the sales cost; only the founder can sell | Incentives misalign; one partner dominates |
| Cost per customer | Low, at high volume | High, predictable | Low at the margin, once running |
| Main constraint | Only fits some products and buyers | Scales with headcount | Time to first revenue; concentration |
| Core team | Product, data, growth engineering | Sales, enablement, pipeline marketing | Partner managers, programme terms, partner marketing |

> Many founders decide they are product-led because it is cheaper rather than because it is true.

## Why a primary motion matters

Each motion needs a different organisation. Product-led needs product, data, and growth engineering. Sales-led needs a sales team, enablement, and pipeline marketing. Partner-led needs partnership managers, programme terms, and partner marketing. A small company that tries to build all three builds none properly.

Choose the primary motion from the product and buyer, not from preference. Then add the others where they support it: sales to expand product-led accounts, partners to extend a sales-led company's reach, product-led onboarding to reduce a partner-led company's support burden.

Three questions about the buyer usually settle it. Can one person get value without help in the first session? Can that person pay without anyone else's approval? Does the buyer already buy adjacent products through someone else? Yes to the first two points to product-led; no to either points to sales-led; yes to the third makes partner-led worth testing early. Partners that bring customer overlap and introductions rather than resale are a variant covered in [What is ecosystem-led growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/)

## For a company the platforms restrict

Restricted categories tilt the choice. Product-led motions that depend on cheap paid acquisition through the large platforms lose their main engine. Partner-led and sales-led motions, which run on relationships, affiliates, and channels that choose to carry the product, are less exposed. That is one reason affiliate and partner programmes are often the first thing worth building in these categories.

The restrictions are specific and change often. Google Ads, for example, requires advertisers of cryptocurrency exchanges and software wallets to be certified by Google and to meet local legal requirements country by country; its July 2025 update allowed certified advertisers targeting Canada if they were registered with the national money services regulator. A product-led plan built on search ads in that category depends on a certification process the company does not control. Our pieces on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) and [affiliate programs without coupon leaks](https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-program-asset-or-coupon-leak/) cover the alternatives.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose one primary motion based on how buyers make decisions.** Who gets value, who pays and who approves decide it.
- **Build the product and team to make that motion work.** Each motion is a different organisation.
- **Check the economics against the benchmark.** Product-led needs volume; sales-led needs price; partner-led needs patience.
- **Add other channels only where they reinforce the main path.** Sales expands product-led accounts; partners extend a sales-led reach.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between product-led and sales-led growth?

In product-led growth the product does the convincing: people sign up, get value and pay without talking to anyone. In sales-led growth a salesperson runs the process from discovery to close, which suits complex, expensive or trust-dependent products.

### What is partner-led growth?

A motion in which other companies distribute the product: platforms that embed it, resellers, agencies, integration partners, affiliates and marketplaces. It can have low marginal cost once running but takes months to produce revenue.

### Can a company be both product-led and sales-led?

Yes, but one motion should be primary. A common pattern is product-led acquisition with sales arriving later to expand larger accounts.

### What is a good free-to-paid conversion rate for product-led growth?

Benchmarks vary by model. An illustrative funnel from OpenView's 2023 study put roughly 5% of free sign-ups converting to paid for an average freemium product. Free-trial products are benchmarked separately.

## Sources and notes

- [Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged: Your guide to SaaS product metrics](https://www.growthunhinged.com/p/your-guide-to-saas-product-metrics), 19 July 2023. Investor commentary on OpenView and Pendo's 2023 Product Benchmarks (1,000+ products); self-selected sample; the funnel is an illustrative average.
- [Gartner, 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), 9 March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025; stated preference.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated in the release.
- [Canalys, IT spending forecasts 2025](https://canalys.com/insights/it-spending-forecasts-2025). Analyst forecast, not actuals; covers the whole IT, services and telecoms market.
- [Ebsta and Pavilion, 2024 B2B Sales Benchmarks](https://www.ebsta.com/ebsta-pavilion-b2b-sales-benchmarks-2024/). Vendor analysis of 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies; Ebsta sells sales software.

- The comparison table and the three buyer questions are **lowob**'s framework.

Answer the three buyer questions for your last ten customers this week: did one person get value alone, could they pay without approval, and did they already buy adjacent products through someone else. Let the pattern, not preference, pick the primary motion.

# What Is a Semantic Layer (Shared Definitions for AI)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-semantic-layer/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-21 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A semantic layer fixes the meaning of business terms and metrics once, so that dashboards, people and AI agents calculate them the same way. In data teams it is a tool category with an emerging open standard. For a mid-size commercial team it starts as five written definitions, each with an owner, read by every agent.

A semantic layer is a shared set of business definitions, such as revenue, active client or qualified lead, that every report, person and AI agent reads the same way. In data teams it is software that maps business terms to the tables and calculations underneath. For a commercial team it starts more simply: a handful of written definitions, each with an owner. Without one, two agents asked the same question can give two confident and different answers.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What a semantic layer means

Every company has terms that mean different things to different teams. Finance counts revenue when it is invoiced; sales counts it when the contract is signed. One team calls an account "active" if it bought this year, another if anyone has spoken to it this quarter. People resolve this in conversation; an agent does not. It picks whichever definition it finds first and presents the answer with the same confidence either way.

A semantic layer removes the choice. It is the part of the context layer that fixes meaning. dbt Labs' MetricFlow, which powers the dbt Semantic Layer, defines semantic models, entities, dimensions and metrics in YAML. Metric logic is written once, committed to version control, reviewed by data and business teams as the single source of truth, and queried by every connected tool.

| Element | What it fixes | Commercial example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entity | What a thing is, and how records join | An account is the parent company, not each subsidiary |
| Dimension | How results are sliced | Region, segment, source, quarter |
| Metric | How a number is calculated | Net revenue retention, on a stated formula |
| Definition | What a term means in words | "Qualified" means budget, owner and timeline confirmed |
| Owner | Who can change it | Head of revenue operations |

## Why it matters for AI

Agents answer questions by turning words into queries. Shared definitions make a measurable difference to how often they get it right. Juan Sequeda, Dean Allemang and Bryon Jacob tested GPT-4 on enterprise questions over an insurance company's SQL schema in 2023. Asked directly against the tables, it answered 16% correctly. When the same data was described through a knowledge graph that carried business meaning, accuracy rose to 54%. The authors work at data.world, a data-catalogue vendor, so treat the result as vendor research on a single domain. The model had the same data in both tests; what changed was whether the business meaning was explicit.

The industry is moving towards a common format. In September 2025, Snowflake, Salesforce, dbt Labs and others launched the Open Semantic Interchange to standardise how semantic models are defined and shared between tools. In 2026 it entered the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie, a YAML-based specification. IT Brief reported in July 2026 that the coalition had grown from 17 founding partners to more than 50 organisations. For a buyer, the point is portability: definitions in an open format survive a change of tool.

## How to start without a data team

A 20-to-500-person firm rarely needs semantic-layer software on day one. It needs the definitions written down, agreed and read by every agent. Start with five.

| Term | Typical disagreement | Write down |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Active client | Bought this year, or engaged this quarter? | One test, with a date window |
| Qualified | Any meeting, or budget and owner confirmed? | The criteria, in order |
| Won and lost | Signed, invoiced or paid? Lost, or stalled? | The event that changes the stage |
| Owner | Who sourced it, or who manages it now? | One named person per account |
| Source | Free text, or a fixed list? | The list, and who can add to it |

Give each definition an owner and a date. When a definition changes, record the change as a new version with its reason, rather than editing the old text, so past reports can still be read on the terms they used. Then put them where every agent will read them, such as a pinned document or the CRM's field descriptions.

## lowob takeaways

- **Meaning is part of the context layer.** Connectors find the data; definitions decide what it means.
- **Shared definitions change answers.** Benchmarks show large accuracy gains when business meaning is explicit.
- **Start with five terms.** Active client, qualified, won and lost, owner and source.
- **Version the definitions.** A changed term gets a new version and a reason, not a silent edit.

## Common questions

### What is a semantic layer in simple terms?

A single agreed set of business definitions and metric calculations that every report, dashboard and AI agent uses, so the same question gets the same answer.

### Why do AI agents need a semantic layer?

Because they turn words into queries. Without fixed definitions they choose one silently, and two agents can return different numbers for "revenue" or "active clients" with equal confidence.

### What is the Open Semantic Interchange (OSI)?

An industry initiative launched in September 2025 by Snowflake, Salesforce, dbt Labs and others to standardise semantic model definitions. It entered the Apache Incubator as Apache Ossie in 2026.

### Do small companies need semantic layer software?

Usually not at first. Five written definitions, each with an owner and read by every agent, cover most commercial questions.

## Sources and notes

- [Sequeda, Allemang and Jacob, A Benchmark to Understand the Role of Knowledge Graphs on LLM Accuracy for Question Answering on Enterprise SQL Databases](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07509v1), November 2023. Authors are from a data-catalogue vendor.
- [dbt Labs documentation, About MetricFlow](https://docs.getdbt.com/docs/build/about-metricflow). Vendor documentation.
- [TechTarget, New consortium to aid AI by standardizing semantic modeling](https://www.techtarget.com/searchdatamanagement/news/366631576/New-consortium-to-aid-AI-by-standardizing-semantic-modeling), September 2025.
- [IT Brief UK, Apache Ossie joins incubator to standardise metrics](https://itbrief.co.uk/story/apache-ossie-joins-incubator-to-standardise-metrics), July 2026. Membership figures as reported.
- The five starting definitions are **lowob**'s recommendation for mid-size commercial teams.

## Related research

- [The Context Layer, Followed Through One Account](https://lowob.com/research/the-context-layer-followed-through-one-account/)
- [The 5 Enterprise Context Platforms, Ranked for Regulated Firms](https://lowob.com/research/the-5-enterprise-context-platforms-ranked-for-regulated-firms/)
- [How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

## Next move

Ask two people on your team, separately, how many active clients you have. If the numbers differ, write the definition this week, name its owner and give it to every assistant you use.

# What Is Prompt Injection?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-injection/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Prompt injection is the leading risk in OWASP's 2025 list for LLM applications. The UK's National Cyber Security Centre warns it may never be fully mitigated, because language models do not separate instructions from data. The practical answer is design: limit what an agent can reach and require a person before anything leaves the company.

Prompt injection is an attack in which instructions hidden in text an AI model reads cause it to do what the attacker wants instead of what its owner intended. It ranks first in OWASP's 2025 list of risks for LLM applications. Because language models do not reliably separate instructions from data, it cannot be patched away; it has to be contained by limiting what an agent can reach and do.

*Figure: Agents are the reasoning layer, and they touch every stage of the build.*

## What prompt injection means

OWASP defines a prompt injection vulnerability as one where input alters a model's behaviour or output in unintended ways. The input does not need to be visible to a person, only parseable by the model. OWASP separates it from jailbreaking, which aims to make the model abandon its safety rules altogether.

There are two forms. **Direct injection** is typed by the user, deliberately or by accident. **Indirect injection** reaches the model through content it ingests: a web page it summarises, a PDF in a shared drive, an inbound email. Kai Greshake and colleagues described the indirect form in a February 2023 paper, arguing that LLM-integrated applications "blur the line between data and instructions".

| Prompt injection is | Prompt injection is not |
| --- | --- |
| Untrusted text steering what a model does | A bug in one vendor's model that a patch will close |
| A problem for any system that reads outside content | Limited to chatbots typed into by attackers |
| Contained by limiting tools, permissions and outbound actions | Solved by a filter or a stronger system prompt alone |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Commercial agents are exposed by design. A sales or account agent reads prospect websites, inbound email, call transcripts and shared documents, all written by people outside the company. OWASP's examples include a web page carrying hidden instructions that leak a conversation, and a CV with split instructions that push an AI screener towards a positive recommendation.

Simon Willison's "lethal trifecta", published in June 2025, is the clearest test for when the risk becomes serious. An agent is exposed when it combines three things: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content, and the ability to communicate externally. A pipeline agent that reads CRM notes, opens inbound email and can send replies has all three. Willison notes that guardrail products claiming to stop 95% of attacks would earn "a failing grade" in ordinary web security.

The NCSC makes the same point from the government side. Its December 2025 post argues that prompt injection is not like SQL injection, which parameterised queries fixed. A language model is an "inherently confusable deputy", so the aim is to reduce the likelihood and the impact of attacks rather than to eliminate them.

> The question is not whether an agent can be tricked. It is what a tricked agent is able to do.

## How to contain it

OWASP is candid that "it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention". Its mitigations, and the NCSC's, converge on a short list that a business owner can check without reading code.

| Control | What to ask the team | Source |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Least privilege | Does the agent hold only the access its task needs, through its own credentials? | OWASP LLM01, NCSC |
| Deterministic checks | Are high-risk decisions enforced in code or downstream systems, not by the model? | NCSC |
| Separate untrusted content | Is outside text marked as data before the model sees it? | OWASP LLM01 |
| Human approval | Does a named person approve anything sent, paid or deleted? | OWASP LLM01 |
| Logging | Are inputs, outputs and tool calls recorded so an incident can be traced? | NCSC |
| Adversarial testing | Has anyone tried to break it with hostile documents and emails? | OWASP LLM01 |

The most effective single move for a commercial team is to break the trifecta at the outbound step. If an agent drafts but cannot send, a successful injection produces a bad draft in a queue, not a leaked file in a stranger's inbox. That is the logic behind **lowob**'s rule that nothing sends without a person, and behind keeping first agents at autonomy level 1 (draft) or 2 (act with approval).

## lowob takeaways

- **Assume it will happen.** Prompt injection is a property of how language models read, not a defect a vendor will patch.
- **Watch for the trifecta.** Private data, untrusted content and external communication in one agent is the danger signal.
- **Contain by design.** Least privilege and checks outside the model do more than better prompts.
- **Gate the outbound step.** A person approving sends turns a breach into a returned draft.

## Common questions

### What is a prompt injection attack in simple terms?

It is when someone hides instructions in text an AI system reads, such as an email or web page, and the AI follows those instructions instead of its owner's.

### What is the difference between direct and indirect prompt injection?

Direct injection comes from what a user types into the model. Indirect injection arrives inside outside content the model processes, such as a document, website or inbound message.

### Can prompt injection be prevented completely?

Not with current models, according to both OWASP and the UK NCSC. The realistic goal is to limit what a manipulated model can reach and do.

### How do you protect an AI agent from prompt injection?

Give it the minimum permissions its task needs, enforce important rules outside the model, log its tool calls and require human approval before anything is sent, paid or deleted.

## Sources and notes

- [OWASP Gen AI Security Project, LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection](https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/), 2025. Community standard; mitigations are recommendations, not guarantees.
- [UK National Cyber Security Centre, Prompt injection is not SQL injection (it may be worse)](https://www.ncsc.gov.uk/blog-post/prompt-injection-is-not-sql-injection), 8 December 2025. Government guidance blog, aligned to ETSI TS 104 223.
- [Greshake et al., Not what you've signed up for: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.12173v2), arXiv, February 2023. Academic preprint; examples predate current agent tools.
- [Simon Willison, The lethal trifecta for AI agents](https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/), 16 June 2025. Practitioner analysis by an independent developer.

## Related research

- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)
- [Top 5 AI Governance and Audit-Trail Tools](https://lowob.com/research/top-5-ai-governance-and-audit-trail-tools/)
- [What Is the NIST AI Risk Management Framework?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-nist-ai-risk-management-framework/)

## Next move

List every agent or AI feature you run that reads outside content. For each, mark whether it also touches private data and can send externally; any with all three needs an approval step this week.

# Community That Survives the Airdrop

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Incentives buy activity, not community. On-chain studies of major airdrops show most recipients sell quickly and few stay active. Plan the airdrop as an acquisition cost, allocate for repeated use, give holders a real job and measure who keeps using the product after the payments stop.

Incentives buy activity, not community. Build for the people who stay when the payments stop, give them a job, and keep the record of who they are on channels you own. The on-chain record is consistent: two years after the Uniswap airdrop, Dune data showed 93% of recipients had sold all their UNI, and an academic study of nine airdrops found up to 66% of tokens were sold soon after claiming.

This is the crypto chapter of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/). It applies the argument that [community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) to the one sector where the number is easiest to inflate.

## Farmers sell, and that is fine

An airdrop farmer is a rational actor doing exactly what the programme paid for. They completed the task, claimed the reward and sold it. Nothing in that sequence was a relationship.

Messias, Yaish and Livshits studied nine airdrops, including Uniswap, Arbitrum and Optimism, using on-chain data to October 2024. For several, a large share of tokens went straight to exchanges as the recipient's first action: 65.75% for Lido, 58.67% for 1inch and 48.21% for Optimism. Within 24 hours, 66.09% of 1inch recipients had sent tokens to an exchange. The authors conclude that airdrops "may be necessary to attract users initially, but insufficient on their own".

The Uniswap airdrop of September 2020 is the clearest long view. A Dune analysis two years later found more than 75% of recipients sold within seven days, 93% had sold everything, and about 98% had never taken part in governance.

The mistake is not that farmers exist. The mistake is counting them as users. The claim rate goes in the launch deck, the sell-through is never mentioned, and the team wonders where everyone went. In crypto, the number is unusually easy to inflate. So the job matters more, not less.

## Plan it as an acquisition cost

Plan the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate. Then design for the fraction who stay.

Price outcomes vary with design. Keyrock, a crypto market maker, reviewed 62 airdrops across six chains in 2024 and found only eight were trading above their launch price after 90 days. Larger distributions, above 10% of supply, held up better over time than small ones. Price is not community, but it shapes who has a reason to stay.

| Line in the plan | What to write down before launch |
| --- | --- |
| Expected sell-through | Share of claimants likely to sell within 30 days |
| Cost per retained user | Value distributed divided by users active after incentives stop |
| Sybil exclusion | Rules, tests and appeal route, fixed before the snapshot |
| Holder job | The work holders will be invited to do |
| Owned record | Where the member list and contribution log live |

A token distribution deserves the cost-per-outcome treatment our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) applies to any acquisition budget.

## Quests, points and the platform you do not own

Quest platforms produce completion. A wallet connects, follows an account, retweets a post, joins a server. Every box is ticked and nobody has used the product.

Pay-to-post programmes were the same pattern with more money attached. On 15 January 2026, X's product lead announced that X had revoked API access for apps that paid users to post. The Block reported the KAITO token fell 14.5% that day, and Kaito said it would wind down its incentivised leaderboards. Teams that had built their whole engagement layer on that machinery lost it in one policy change they had no vote on.

The lesson is platform dependency, not any one platform. Any channel you rent can be repriced or removed. Our piece on [distribution when the platforms are closed](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/) covers this across sectors. In crypto, the dependency is usually deeper and the switch-off is usually faster. Keep using the platforms. Just never let them hold the only copy of your community.

## Earned allocation with filters that bite

If you are going to distribute tokens to users, distribute them for behaviour you want repeated. Not for showing up. For using the product in the way a long-term user would.

That means allocation weighted to usage over time, not usage in a single window. Position size matters less than consistency. Sybil filtering is a product feature, built before the snapshot, not a clean-up after. Messias and colleagues document a farmer on ZKsync Era who used more than 20,000 accounts and deployed a fake exchange to qualify for one distribution. Their recommendations include scaling rewards with the costs users incur, and running several smaller distributions over time rather than one.

Expect the filters to be contested. Publish the rules in advance, apply them without exception, and keep an appeals channel that a human reads. The people who argue in good faith are often the users you most want to keep. Our companion piece on [airdrops, points and community incentives](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) sets out how each mechanism shapes behaviour.

> A holder with nothing to do is a seller waiting for a price. A holder with a job has a reason to stay that is not the chart.

## Give holders a job

The jobs that work are real work, not engagement theatre:

- **Test** new markets or features before they go live, with feedback visible and acted on.
- **Curate** listings, parameters or content where judgment matters and you cannot automate it.
- **Govern** decisions that have consequences, not polls about logo colours.
- **Refer** people they are willing to vouch for, with their name on the referral.

Governance needs particular care, because token voting concentrates fast. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap found only about 5% of tokens were cast on a typical proposal and the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote.

Our piece on [first customers as design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/) described the first ten customers as design partners. Holders with a job are the same idea at a hundred people. Treat their output as product input, and say so publicly when it ships.

## The first hundred in crypto, and the only metric

[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) argued that the first hundred people are the whole company for a while. In crypto, the trap is picking them by wallet balance. The first hundred you want are daily DeFi users: people who already move capital across protocols most days, understand the risks without being told, and will say plainly when something is wrong. Find them in governance forums, support channels and among people who read audit reports. Recruit them by hand and give them direct access to the team.

The only community metric worth trusting is retention measured after the money stops. Define it before you start. Pick the action that means someone is using the product, not visiting it. Run incentives for a set period. Then stop, and count how many people keep doing that action in the following weeks. That number is your community. Everything else is a cost of acquiring it.

Keep that record on systems you own: a member list, a contribution log, an email address or a wallet you can reach without a third party. [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) made the general case. In crypto, start reporting who is still here.

## lowob takeaways

- **Cost the airdrop.** Plan it as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate, not as a conversion.
- **Reward persistence.** Weight allocation to repeated usage over time, and build sybil filters before the snapshot.
- **Assign a job.** Holders who test, curate, govern or refer have a reason to stay that is not the price.
- **Count after the money stops.** Retained usage after incentives end is the community; the rest is acquisition cost.

## Common questions

### How do you keep crypto users after an airdrop?

Design for the fraction who stay. Allocate for repeated usage over time, give holders a real job, keep their record on channels you own and measure who keeps using the product after incentives stop.

### What percentage of airdrop recipients sell their tokens?

It varies by programme, but it is usually high. Dune data showed 93% of Uniswap airdrop recipients had sold all their UNI after two years, and one academic study found up to 66% of tokens in some airdrops were sold quickly.

### Are airdrop farmers a problem?

Farmers are rational actors doing what the programme paid for. The mistake is counting them as users rather than planning the airdrop as an acquisition cost with an expected loss rate.

### How should sybil filtering work for a token distribution?

Build it as a product feature before the snapshot, publish the rules in advance, apply them without exception, and keep an appeals channel that a human reads.

## Sources and notes

- [Messias, Yaish and Livshits, Airdrops: Giving Money Away Is Harder Than It Seems, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2312.02752v4), revised July 2025. Academic preprint; nine airdrops, on-chain data to October 2024; exchange flows are a proxy for selling.
- [Dune, The Uniswap Airdrop: Lessons for the Industry](https://community.dune.com/blog/uni-airdrop-analysis), late 2022. Community analysis on Dune's analytics platform; data to September 2022; one airdrop.
- [Keyrock, Airdrops in the Barren Desert](https://keyrock.com/airdrops-in-the-barren-desert/), 25 September 2024. Research by a crypto market maker; 62 airdrops in 2024; price performance, not user retention.
- [The Block, Kaito token plummets after X revises API policies to ban InfoFi crypto projects](https://www.theblock.co/post/385805/kaito-token-plummets-x-revises-api-policies-ban-infofi-crypto-projects), 15 January 2026. News report; intraday price data.
- [Falk, Pathan, Rigas and Tsoukalas, Blockchain Governance: An Empirical Analysis of User Engagement on DAOs, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.10945v1), 15 July 2024. Preprint; four DeFi protocols to December 2022.
- The planning table and recommendations are **lowob**'s framework.

## Next move

Before your next distribution, write down the action that means someone is really using the product and the date incentives will stop. Thirty days after that date, count who is still doing it and report that number alongside the claim rate.

# Audience vs Community: What Actually Makes the Difference?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-audience/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A large follower count or Discord server is not automatically a community. The difference is whether people help, learn from and create value for one another. This piece separates audiences, users, network participants and communities, sets out the peer-value test, and lists the measures that show which one a company actually has.

A large follower count or Discord server is not automatically a community. The difference is whether people help, learn from and create value for one another. An audience receives. A customer transacts. A user engages with a product. A community member participates in a group whose value is partly created by other members. Each needs a different strategy, and the most common mistake is designing for one while measuring another.

This piece is the definitional starting point of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

Many companies say they have a community because they have opened a Discord server, accumulated followers or issued a token. Those things can assemble people in the same digital space. They do not automatically create relationships, shared identity or participation.

## Four groups companies routinely confuse

| Group | Who they are | Where value flows | What to measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Audience | People who pay attention to the company or its ideas | Company to individual | Qualified reach, return readership |
| Customers or users | People who exchange money, data or behaviour for a product outcome; they may never meet | Product to individual | Activation, retention, revenue |
| Network participants | People whose activity increases the utility of a shared system: developers, liquidity providers, creators, node operators | Participant to system | Integrations, liquidity, uptime, usage of what they built |
| Community | People who develop repeated relationships, shared norms, identity and mutual value around an interest or purpose | Member to member | Peer help, distinct contributors, returning members |

One person can occupy several roles. A developer may use the product, contribute code, answer peer questions and publicly advocate for the network. But the roles should not be treated as identical.

Research on online communities draws a related line. Kraut and Resnick's *Building Successful Online Communities* (MIT Press) treats building members' commitment through the theory of interpersonal bond formation as a separate design problem from encouraging contribution. Bonds between people are what distinguish the last row of the table from the first three.

## The peer-value test

Remove the company from the room for one week. Would members still help one another, exchange knowledge, build things, organise activities or maintain relationships?

If all activity stops, the company may have an audience or support channel rather than a community. That is not necessarily a failure. A useful customer-support environment can be more valuable than a forced community. The mistake is designing for one group while measuring another.

The test can be run on data as well as by absence. Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities, a vendor study of its own customers, found that outside GitHub, community members replied to each other 28% of the time against 13% for company staff. Where members answer more questions than staff do, there is peer value. Where staff answer everything, the company is running a support desk with a chat interface.

> If the only reason members return is to receive your announcements, you have a distribution channel, not a community.

## Community requires a reason to return

People do not repeatedly participate because a brand wants engagement. They return because the group provides a recurring form of value.

Some communities bring together experts who exchange information and help one another solve problems. Others give members a professional identity, a chance to collaborate, influence over a product or access to economic opportunities. People may also return because they are learning, gaining recognition or developing a sense of belonging.

The company should be able to complete this sentence:

*Members return because they can \_\_\_\_\_\_ with people they could not easily \_\_\_\_\_\_ elsewhere.*

If the answer is "receive our announcements", the company has a distribution channel. Our piece on [community management versus social media management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/) sets out why those are different jobs needing different people.

## Design participation, not just programming

Events, AMAs, office hours and announcements are programming. They can create occasions for participation, but only if members have a role beyond attendance.

Participation often starts with observing and asking questions. As people become more comfortable, they share useful resources, join working sessions and contribute to projects. Eventually some members lead discussions or shape a product or governance decision. Each stage needs a clear invitation, not just a request to "engage".

Expect the ladder to narrow. Jakob Nielsen's analysis of participation inequality found that in most online communities about 90% of people only read, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. Nielsen argued the pattern cannot be removed, only improved: lower the barrier to a first contribution, let people edit rather than create from scratch, and promote quality rather than volume. Each of those is an invitation to the next rung.

| Rung | Typical behaviour | The invitation that moves people up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Observe | Reads, attends | A starter resource and a clear first step |
| Ask | Posts a question | A fast, useful reply from a member or host |
| Share | Posts a resource or answer | Public credit for the contribution |
| Contribute | Joins a working session or project | A specific brief with an end date |
| Lead | Runs a discussion or shapes a decision | A real decision, and evidence it was shaped |

## Measure relationships and contribution

Member count is the easiest number to inflate and one of the weakest indicators of community health.

Look at how many newcomers make a meaningful first contribution, how often people return and whether members help each other without relying on staff. Track distinct contributors, the time to a useful response, and work that generates product, support, knowledge or distribution value. These measures tell a more useful story than server size or message volume alone.

Discord's own Server Insights guidance treats engagement and retention as the main signs of health. It separates visitors, who open a channel, from communicators, who post, and tracks new member retention as the share of new members who return after a week. It also notes that engagement and retention are among the factors it reviews for its Partner programme.

The field still leans on headcount. CMX's 2025 survey of community professionals found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%, and only 24% could confidently put a financial value on their community. Our piece [Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) sets out the contribution measures that fit each kind of community.

## Be willing to say you do not need a community

Some products need excellent onboarding, support, education and customer communication, not a member-led social system.

Community becomes commercially useful when peer relationships, contribution, identity or network participation improve the product or purpose. If none of those conditions exists, forcing customers into a chat room creates operational cost without durable value. That cost is real: CMX found 17% of organisations had no one working full time on community, the highest share it had recorded. An under-resourced community that nobody needs is worse than none.

Where the honest answer is an audience, build an audience well; our piece on [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers how to judge one. Where the answer is users, invest in onboarding and retention. The strongest community strategy sometimes begins with intellectual honesty: deciding which group the company actually has and what that group needs.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the group you have.** Distinguish audiences, customers, users, network participants and active contributors.
- **Run the peer-value test.** If activity stops when the company steps away, it is an audience or support channel.
- **Create reasons for members to help one another.** Complete the "members return because" sentence before building anything.
- **Measure participation and relationships.** Peer help, distinct contributors and returning members, not member count.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an audience and a community?

An audience receives from the company; value flows one way. A community is a group whose value is partly created by its members, through repeated relationships, shared norms and mutual help.

### How do you know if you have a real community?

Run the peer-value test: remove the company for a week and see whether members still help each other, share knowledge and organise. Also compare how many questions members answer against how many staff answer.

### What metrics show community health?

Newcomers' first meaningful contributions, return frequency, peer help without staff, distinct contributors, time to a useful response and work that creates product, support, knowledge or distribution value.

### Does every company need a community?

No. Some products are better served by strong onboarding, support and education. A community is worth building when peer relationships or contribution improve the product or its purpose.

## Sources and notes

- [Discord, Getting to Know Your Server With Server Insights](https://discord.com/community/understanding-server-insights), undated. Platform documentation; definitions apply to Discord servers.
- [Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report](https://www.commonroom.io/blog/360-community-led-growth-report/), 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room; 2022 data.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
- [Kraut and Resnick, Building Successful Online Communities: Evidence-Based Social Design, MIT Press](https://mitpressbookstore.mit.edu/book/9780262528917), paperback edition February 2016. Academic book; publisher description consulted.
- [CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report](https://start.bevy.com/hubfs/2025%20CMX%20Community%20Industry%20Report-1.pdf?hsLang=en), 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals; CMX is owned by Bevy, a community software vendor; self-reported.
- The four-group and participation-ladder tables are **lowob**'s framework.

## Related research

- [Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/)
- [Community Is a Job, Not a Number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/)
- [Community Management vs Social Media Management](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-social-media-management/)
- [Measuring Brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/)
- [What Is Product-Led Growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-product-led-growth/)

## Next move

Complete the sentence "members return because they can \_\_\_ with people they could not easily \_\_\_ elsewhere." Then count last month's answered questions and how many were answered by members rather than staff.
