# What Is a Marketing Funnel, and When Does It Help?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-marketing-funnel/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-18 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: The marketing funnel is a useful model of stages that need different things and a poor model of how individuals actually buy. Google and Gartner research both find buyers loop rather than descend. Find the stage that limits revenue now, concentrate there, and treat "full-funnel" as a warning sign rather than a plan.

A marketing funnel is a model of the stages a stranger passes through before becoming a customer: awareness, consideration, evaluation, purchase and retention. It helps teams find where potential customers stop making progress. It is less useful as a map of how any individual buys, because research from Google and Gartner shows buyers loop back and skip stages. Use it to find the one stage that limits revenue now, and be wary of any plan described as "full-funnel".

The funnel is the oldest model in marketing: a wide opening of people who have never heard of you, narrowing through stages of awareness, interest and evaluation, to a small number who buy. Everyone uses it, and it is worth understanding both for what it explains and for what it hides.

## Where the funnel comes from

The earliest version is AIDA: attention, interest, desire, action. EBSCO's reference entry credits Elias St. Elmo Lewis, an American advertising adviser, with coining it around 1898, and Edward Strong with refining it in the 1920s. Later versions added stages after the sale, such as retention and satisfaction, because the model's original endpoint, a purchase, stopped being where most of the value sat.

The stages, plainly:

| Stage | What is true of the person | Weak measure | Better measure |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Awareness | Knows the company or category exists | Impressions, reach | Unprompted recall, branded search volume |
| Consideration | Sees the problem as theirs; includes you as an option | Page views | Return visits, sign-ups, questions asked |
| Evaluation | Actively comparing options and looking for proof | Content downloads | Demo requests, trials, pricing views, sales conversations |
| Purchase | Buys | Bookings alone | Revenue, and the cost of all stages above divided by buyers |
| Retention and advocacy | Stays, expands, tells others | Satisfaction scores | Retention, expansion, referrals |

The right-hand column is where the funnel earns its keep. Every stage has a cheap measure that moves easily and a harder one closer to the decision.

## What the model gets right

People do move through states of knowledge, and those states need different things. Someone who has never heard of a category will not respond to a comparison chart, and someone comparing three vendors does not need to be told the problem exists. Matching content and channel to stage is the funnel's lasting lesson. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) turns that lesson into a commissioning brief.

The model also makes conversion between stages visible. If a thousand people reach evaluation and ten buy, the problem is in evaluation, not in awareness. Spending more at the top makes it worse, because it pushes more people into the stage that is already failing them.

## What the model gets wrong

Real buying is not linear. Google's consumer insights team, in research published in July 2020 that simulated 310,000 purchase scenarios, described a "messy middle" between trigger and purchase, where shoppers "loop through these twin modes of exploration and evaluation" until they decide. Gartner's model of B2B buying says the same about business purchases: buyers complete six buying jobs, from problem identification to consensus creation, and loop back to revisit each at least once. Gartner also found buyers spend only 17% of their buying time meeting potential suppliers.

So people enter at any stage, skip stages and return to earlier ones. They are influenced by things no funnel records: a colleague's recommendation, a podcast heard six months ago, a competitor's failure. In B2B the "person" in the funnel is often a group; Gartner puts a typical buying group for a complex purchase at six to ten decision makers. The funnel describes an average path that almost nobody takes individually. Our explainer on [the buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) covers what that means for who you are actually moving.

The model also encourages the belief that more at the top produces more at the bottom. It does not, if the middle is broken or the top is filled with the wrong people. A funnel full of unqualified awareness is expensive at every stage below.

> The funnel describes an average path that almost nobody takes individually. Use it to find the leak, not to script the buyer.

## Why "full-funnel" usually means nothing

"Full-funnel marketing" is the claim that a company or agency addresses every stage. In practice it usually means spending in every channel without deciding which stage is the constraint. It sounds thorough. It is often the absence of a decision dressed as completeness.

There is a real argument for investing above the funnel. The B2B Institute at LinkedIn, drawing on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, argues that about 95% of potential buyers are not in market at any given time, which is why brand-building reaches people long before they buy. That argument is about awareness as a long-term asset. It is not a licence to spread one quarter's budget evenly across five stages.

A useful plan identifies which stage is limiting revenue right now and concentrates there. Each constraint calls for different spending, and spending on the others is waste until the constraint moves:

| Symptom | Likely constraint | Where the next quarter's effort goes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nobody has heard of you; branded search is flat | Awareness | Reach in channels your buyers use, earned media, partners |
| Traffic but few sign-ups or questions | Consideration | Positioning, the offer, landing pages ([conversion rate optimization](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-conversion-rate-optimization/)) |
| Trials or demos that do not convert | Evaluation or product | Proof, onboarding, the product itself, sales process |
| Customers who leave in year one | Retention | Fit at the point of sale, delivery, customer success |

## How to use it well

Draw the funnel with real numbers for the last quarter: how many at each stage, and the conversion between each. Find the stage where the drop is largest relative to what a healthy business in your category would show. Put the next quarter's effort there. Redraw it each quarter, because the constraint moves once it is fixed.

Illustrative example: the leak was not at the top

Decision
:   Hold paid acquisition flat for a quarter and move the budget to the evaluation stage.

Reason and owner
:   The quarter's funnel showed 4,000 site visitors, 400 sign-ups, 120 demos and 6 customers. Visitor-to-demo rates were in line with the firm's history; demo-to-customer had halved. The head of growth owned the change.

What changed
:   The team rebuilt the demo around the buyer's own data and added a security answers document. Demo-to-customer recovered over the next two quarters with no increase in spend.

Illustrative: a composite of a B2B software firm, built from patterns across engagements.

The numbers in the example are illustrative, but the method is general: a funnel is a diagnostic, and a diagnostic is only useful if it changes where the next pound or dollar goes. Our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) sets out how to put a cost on each stage.

Finally, for a company the ad platforms restrict, the top of the funnel is partly closed in the crowded channels and open in the thinly bid ones. The funnel does not change. Where it can be filled does.

## lowob takeaways

- **Diagnose, do not dictate.** Funnel stages show where people stall; they do not describe any one buyer's path.
- **Measure close to the decision.** Each stage has a cheap metric and a better one; use the better one.
- **Find the constraint.** The largest abnormal drop between stages is where the next quarter goes.
- **Treat "full-funnel" as a question.** Ask which stage is the constraint before approving spend across all of them.

## Common questions

### What are the stages of a marketing funnel?

The common stages are awareness, consideration (or interest), evaluation (or intent), purchase, and retention and advocacy. Each needs different content and is measured differently, from branded search at the top to retention and referral at the bottom.

### Is the marketing funnel still relevant?

As a diagnostic, yes: conversion between stages shows where people stall. As a description of how people buy, it is weak. Google's messy-middle research and Gartner's B2B buying jobs both show buyers looping back rather than moving in order.

### What does full-funnel marketing mean?

It is the claim that a plan or agency covers every stage. In practice it often means spending across all channels without deciding which stage is limiting revenue. A better plan names the constraint and concentrates there.

### How do I find the bottleneck in my funnel?

Count the people at each stage for the last quarter, calculate conversion between stages, and compare each rate with your own history or a credible benchmark. The stage with the largest abnormal drop is the constraint.

## Sources and notes

- [EBSCO Research Starters, AIDA model](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/marketing/aida-model), undated. Reference summary; used for the model's origin and attribution to E. St. Elmo Lewis.
- [Google (Think with Google), Navigating purchase behavior and decision-making](https://business.google.com/in/think/consumer-insights/navigating-purchase-behavior-and-decision-making/?hl=en-US), 14 July 2020. Research by Google's own insights team; consumer categories, not B2B.
- [Gartner, The B2B buying journey](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/insights/b2b-buying-journey), undated insight page. Analyst research summary; survey sample sizes not stated on the page.
- [The B2B Institute at LinkedIn, The 95-5 rule](https://business.linkedin.com/it/it/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/b2b-research/trends/95-5-rule), undated. Published by an advertising platform with an interest in brand spend; based on joint research with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute.
- The stage, constraint and example tables are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

## Related research

## Next move

Pull last quarter's numbers for each funnel stage into one row and calculate the conversion between them. Circle the largest drop, and decide this week whether next quarter's budget follows it.

# What Is Outcome-Based Pricing for AI?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-18 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Outcome-based pricing charges for a measured result rather than for access or volume. Customer-service AI vendors have led, charging per resolution. It aligns cost with value only when both sides can measure and trust the result, so the buyer's main task is to read, test and audit the vendor's definition of an outcome.

Outcome-based pricing for AI charges only when the AI delivers a defined result, such as a support ticket resolved without a human. It is the most attractive pricing model for buyers and the hardest to run, because everything depends on how the outcome is defined and who measures it. Customer service is where it works today. Elsewhere, it is still rare.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: Gateway 0.*

## What outcome-based pricing means

Seats charge for access. Usage charges for volume. Outcome-based pricing charges for a result. Bret Taylor, co-founder of Sierra, described it in 2025 as paying for "a job well done". At Sierra, customers pay when the AI agent resolves an issue, and pay nothing when it escalates to a human.

Customer service leads because the outcome is countable. A conversation either ended with the customer's problem solved or it did not, and the vendor's own software sees both. Zendesk's August 2024 announcement said customers would incur costs only for issues resolved autonomously by AI, with a starter allowance included in its plans.

Intercom publishes its definition in detail, and it shows how a unit can move. Until March 2026 Fin was charged at $0.99 per resolution, counted when the customer confirmed the answer helped or left without asking for more help. On 12 March 2026 Intercom switched the billable unit to the "outcome", priced from $0.99, which covers resolutions, procedure handoffs to a person or workflow, and qualification results, while a customer simply asking for a human is not billed. A buyer who signed for resolutions now pays for a wider set of events, which is why the definition belongs in the contract. Our guide to [AI pricing models](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) covers the contract terms. Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

|  | Seat | Usage | Outcome |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Charges for | Named users | Volume: actions, credits, tokens | A defined result |
| Fits when | A person uses it daily | Value scales with volume | The result is countable and attributable |
| Who carries delivery risk | Buyer | Buyer | Vendor |
| Main buyer risk | Unused seats | Bill shock | A loose outcome definition |
| Where it is common | Assistants and suites | Agent platforms, APIs | Customer-service AI |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

Outcome pricing moves the risk of the AI failing from buyer to vendor. That is real value. A support team paying per resolution does not pay for an agent that loops or hands everything back.

It also moves the argument to the definition. Intercom's "assumed resolution" is a reasonable design choice, and it shows the issue: a customer who gives up and phones instead may count as resolved. The buyer has to check a sample of charged outcomes against what happened next. If either side can dispute the number, the model breaks.

Outside customer service, outcomes are harder to define. A qualified lead, a won deal or a renewed account has many causes, arrives weeks later and is measured in systems the vendor does not control. Gartner noted in July 2026 that current outcome-oriented agentic solutions typically require heavy services engagement. Deloitte's 2026 predictions say widespread outcome-based pricing is still a long way off, and expect hybrids combining licences with usage or outcome fees to become standard.

## What to check before you sign

| Check | What to ask | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Definition | What exactly counts as an outcome, in writing? | Everything else follows from it |
| Measurement | Whose system records it, and can we export the raw events? | You need to audit the count |
| Exclusions | What is not charged: escalations, repeats, spam? | Exclusions drive the effective price |
| Reversal | Is a charge reversed if the problem returns? | Protects against shallow resolutions |
| Audit right | Can we sample charged outcomes each month? | Catches drift in the definition |
| Floor and cap | Is there a minimum fee, and a maximum? | Hybrids often hide a platform fee |

Then run your own check for a month. Sample 50 charged outcomes and follow each one forward: did the customer come back, call in or churn? Compare the effective cost per real outcome with your current cost per ticket handled by a person, including review time. Outside the support queue, the default for anything client-facing remains that nothing sends without a person.

## lowob takeaways

- **You pay for results.** The vendor carries the risk of the AI failing.
- **The definition is the contract.** Read it, test it and audit a sample monthly.
- **Customer service is the proven case.** Resolutions are countable; most commercial outcomes are not yet.
- **Expect hybrids.** A platform fee plus an outcome charge is the common shape.

## Common questions

### What is outcome-based pricing in AI?

A pricing model where the buyer pays only when the AI delivers a defined result, such as a resolved support conversation, rather than per user or per unit of usage.

### How much does Intercom Fin cost per resolution?

Intercom now bills Fin per outcome, from $0.99, rather than per resolution. Since 12 March 2026 an outcome includes resolutions and some procedure handoffs; a customer asking for a human is not billed. Check the current definition before you sign.

### Which companies use outcome-based pricing for AI agents?

Customer-service vendors have led, including Intercom, Zendesk and Sierra. Each charges for conversations or issues resolved by AI.

### What are the risks of outcome-based pricing?

A loose definition of the outcome, measurement held only in the vendor's system, and hidden platform fees. Buyers should secure audit rights and sample charged outcomes.

## Sources and notes

- [Salesforce, Salesforce signs definitive agreement to acquire Fin](https://www.salesforce.com/news/press-releases/2026/06/15/salesforce-signs-definitive-agreement-to-acquire-fin/), 15 June 2026. Vendor press release; Fin is the former Intercom.
- [Intercom Help Center, Understanding Fin outcomes](https://www.intercom.com/help/en/articles/13513868-understanding-fin-outcomes), accessed 16 November 2026. Vendor documentation; the outcome definition and the March 2026 change.
- [Intercom Help Center, Fin pricing and resolutions](https://www.intercom.com/help/en/articles/8205718). Vendor documentation; definitions may change.
- [Zendesk, Outcome-based pricing announcement](https://zendesk.co.uk/newsroom/articles/zendesk-outcome-based-pricing), 28 August 2024. Vendor announcement; no prices stated.
- [Inference by Sequoia, How AI is reinventing software business models, with Bret Taylor](https://inferencebysequoia.substack.com/p/how-ai-is-reinventing-software-business), May 2025. Founder interview.

# What Is Selling Time, and Why Do Sellers Spend So Little of It Selling?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seller-time-to-sell/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Selling time is the share of a seller's working week spent engaging prospects and clients. Salesforce's surveys have put it between roughly 30% and 40% for years, with the rest lost to administration, internal meetings and data entry. This explainer defines the measure, explains where time goes, and sets out how to recover it without simply adding tools.

Selling time is the share of a seller's working week spent directly engaging prospects and clients: prospecting, meetings, calls and correspondence with buyers. Large surveys put it at roughly 30% to 40% of the week. The rest goes to administration, internal coordination, data entry and searching for information, most of which can be reduced by better process before any AI tool is added.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What selling time means

Selling time is a simple ratio: hours spent engaging buyers divided by total working hours. "Engaging buyers" usually includes prospecting, discovery calls, meetings, demonstrations, proposals discussed with the client and follow-up correspondence. It excludes internal meetings, CRM updates, approvals, research done alone and travel, though some surveys count travel within in-person meetings.

The measure matters because it is the capacity of the sales team. A firm with ten sellers at 30% selling time has the equivalent of three full-time sellers in front of clients.

| Counts as selling time | Does not count |
| --- | --- |
| Prospecting calls and emails | Updating CRM fields |
| Discovery and needs meetings | Internal pipeline reviews |
| Proposal walk-throughs with the buyer | Writing proposals alone |
| Negotiation and closing calls | Deal desk and approval chasing |
| Client check-ins and renewals | Searching for content or past work |

## Why sellers spend so little of it selling

### The numbers have been stable for years

Salesforce's sixth State of Sales report surveyed 5,500 sales professionals across 27 countries. As reported by diginomica in August 2024, it found 70% of working time went to non-sales tasks. Customer-facing time split into roughly 8% prospecting, 9% virtual customer contact and 12% in-person meetings including travel.

Salesforce's 2026 report, a survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals, put the global average at 40% of time spent selling. Gen Z sellers spent 35%, and lost about two hours a week to manual data entry. The two surveys use different samples, so the change between them should not be read as a precise trend. Both are vendor-run, by a company that sells CRM and AI tools.

### Where the rest goes

The causes are mostly structural, not individual:

1. **Data entry.** Logging calls, emails and meetings by hand, often twice.
2. **Information search.** Finding the latest proposal, pricing, case study or the history of an account.
3. **Internal coordination.** Approvals, handoffs, pipeline meetings and forecast calls.
4. **Tool switching.** Moving between CRM, email, document storage and messaging.
5. **Unqualified pipeline.** Time spent on deals that should have been disqualified earlier.

### Buyers give sellers little time anyway

Gartner reported in 2020 that buyers considering a purchase spend only 17% of that time meeting potential suppliers, shared across every supplier they consider. Seller time is scarce on both sides. Recovering hours only helps if they go to the right accounts, which is why the ICP and stage definitions matter as much as admin reduction.

## How to recover selling time

The first gains come from process, not tools. AI then helps with the remainder, provided it works from clean records.

| Lever | What it removes | Example action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Automatic capture | Manual activity logging | Turn on email and calendar sync in the CRM |
| Fewer required fields | Form-filling at every stage | Require fields only at stage entry and close |
| Content in one place | Searching for past work | One indexed library of proposals and cases |
| Earlier disqualification | Time on deals that will not close | Written exit criteria for the qualification stage |
| Shorter internal reviews | Status meetings | Review exceptions only, from CRM data |
| Drafting assistance | Writing first drafts of emails and summaries | An assistant at autonomy level 1, drafts only |

Salesforce's 2026 research found 54% of sellers had used AI agents, with nearly nine in ten planning to by 2027. The useful early applications are the boring ones: summarising calls into the CRM, drafting follow-ups and assembling account briefings. In **lowob**'s model, these sit at autonomy level 1, drafting only, and nothing sends without a person. That keeps the time saving without handing judgment to a tool reading imperfect data.

Measure before and after. A two-week time diary for three or four sellers, split into the categories above, gives a baseline that any change can be judged against.

## lowob takeaways

- **Selling time is capacity.** At 30% to 40%, most of a sales team's paid hours are not spent with buyers.
- **The causes are structural.** Data entry, search, coordination and weak qualification account for most lost time.
- **Fix process first.** Automatic capture and fewer required fields recover hours before AI is involved.
- **Use AI to draft, not decide.** The safest early gains come from summaries and drafts a person approves.

## Common questions

### How much time do salespeople actually spend selling?

Salesforce's surveys put it between about 30% and 40% of the working week, with the 2026 global average at 40%.

### What do sales reps spend most of their time on?

Administration, data entry, internal meetings, searching for information and coordinating approvals, according to repeated State of Sales surveys.

### How do you increase selling time?

Automate activity capture, require fewer fields, centralise content, disqualify weak deals earlier and use AI assistants for drafts and summaries.

### Can AI agents give sellers more time to sell?

They can remove drafting and logging work. The gain depends on clean CRM data and a person approving anything sent to a client.

## Sources and notes

- Salesforce, State of Sales (sixth edition), as reported by [diginomica](https://diginomica.com/state-sales-ai-incoming-there-are-caveats-according-salesforce-data), August 2024. Vendor-run survey of 5,500 sales professionals in 27 countries.
- Salesforce, State of Sales 2026, as reported by [Dynamic Business](https://dynamicbusiness.com/topics/news/high-performing-sales-teams-are-1-7x-more-likely-to-use-ai-agents), February 2026. Vendor-run survey of more than 4,000 sales professionals.
- Salesforce, State of Sales 2026, as reported by [Rework](https://resources.rework.com/news/sales-tech/salesforce-state-of-sales-2026-ai-agents-sales-ops). Source of the AI agent adoption figures.
- [Gartner, Gartner Says 80% of B2B Sales Interactions Between Suppliers and Buyers Will Occur in Digital Channels by 2025](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-09-15-gartner-says-80--of-b2b-sales-interactions-between-su), September 2020.

## Related research

- [The First AI Agent Should Be Boring](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-ai-agent-should-be-boring/)
- [Gateway 1: Nothing Sends Without a Person](https://lowob.com/research/nothing-sends-without-a-person/)
- [Your CRM Is Memory, Not a Brain](https://lowob.com/research/your-crm-is-memory-not-a-brain/)

Ask three sellers to keep a simple time diary for one week, split into the categories in the first table. The share spent with buyers is your baseline, and the largest non-selling category is your first fix.

# What Is Revenue Operations (RevOps)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-revenue-operations/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Revenue operations joins the operational work behind marketing, sales and customer success into one function with one set of definitions and one data model. Analysts have tracked it for years, and it matters more now that AI agents read the same records. This explainer covers what RevOps is, what it owns, and how a 20 to 500 person firm can start.

Revenue operations (RevOps) is a single function that owns the data, processes, tools and definitions behind marketing, sales and customer success. It replaces three separate operations teams with one view of how revenue is generated and kept. Its main output is not a report but agreement: one pipeline, one set of stage definitions, one source of truth that people and AI agents can both rely on.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## What revenue operations means

Most firms grow their operations in pieces. Marketing operations runs the automation platform and lead scoring. Sales operations runs the CRM, territories and the forecast. Customer success runs renewals in a third tool. Each team defines its own terms, and the numbers rarely reconcile at the board meeting.

Revenue operations puts that work under one owner. Forrester's definition is deliberately broad: "a highly configured, iterative commercial execution strategy designed to maximize customer value and company performance," which unifies data, processes, technology and talent across the customer lifecycle. Gartner framed the same shift in 2021, predicting that 75% of the highest-growth companies would deploy a RevOps model by 2025 and arguing that functional silos are a barrier to revenue growth.

The practical test is simple. If marketing, sales and customer success would give different answers to "how much pipeline did we create last quarter", the firm does not yet have revenue operations, whatever its org chart says.

| RevOps is | RevOps is not |
| --- | --- |
| One owner for commercial data, process and tooling | A new name for the CRM administrator |
| A shared rulebook of definitions | A dashboard project |
| Accountable for forecast inputs | Accountable for hitting the number |
| The steward of the commercial record | The owner of every commercial decision |

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### The forecast depends on it

Forecasts are built from stage, value and close date, the fields RevOps governs. A 2021 Forrester Consulting study commissioned by Clari surveyed 327 US software and technology revenue operations decision-makers. It found 55% missed their quarterly forecast by more than 10% on average, and only 18% said quarterly forecasts landed within 5% of actual revenue. The study is vendor-commissioned, but the pattern matches Gartner's 2020 finding that only 45% of sales leaders and sellers had high confidence in their forecasting accuracy.

### Agents read what RevOps maintains

The second reason is newer. AI assistants and agents now read the CRM directly to score leads, draft outreach and flag renewals. In Validity's 2026 State of CRM Data survey, 39% of senior respondents said marketing and IT or RevOps collaborate very well to keep data usable, and only 41% said their organisation had a dedicated data governance team or owner. Where nobody owns the definitions, an agent inherits the confusion and acts on it.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, RevOps is the natural owner of the store and the steward of the record on the commercial line. It does not need to own the reasoning layer. It does need to make sure the fields that reasoning reads are defined, current and trusted.

### What RevOps typically owns

| Area | Typical responsibilities | Failure when unowned |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data | Field definitions, deduplication, required fields | Three versions of the customer list |
| Process | Lead routing, stage exit criteria, handoffs | Deals that skip stages or stall unseen |
| Tooling | CRM, automation, integrations, licences | Overlapping tools nobody fully uses |
| Reporting | Pipeline, forecast inputs, conversion rates | Numbers challenged in every meeting |
| Enablement links | Playbooks tied to stages | Training disconnected from the system |

## How to start at 20 to 500 people

A firm of this size rarely needs a RevOps department. It needs one accountable person, often an operations lead or a senior sales operations hire, and a short written rulebook. A sensible sequence:

1. **Name the owner.** One person signs off any change to a commercial field, stage or picklist.
2. **Write the definitions.** Qualified lead, opportunity, each pipeline stage, source, active client and loss reason, each in one or two sentences.
3. **Reconcile one number.** Pick last quarter's new pipeline and get marketing, sales and finance to agree on it. The disagreements show where definitions are missing.
4. **Audit the tools.** List every system that holds customer data and who updates it. Retire or integrate the ones that duplicate the CRM.
5. **Set a review rhythm.** A monthly 30-minute review of data quality counts: duplicates, stale deals, blank next steps, blank loss reasons.

Forrester's 2021 Revenue Operations and Buying Groups survey found the most cited impacts of an operations function were improved revenue growth (41%), improved customer satisfaction (36%) and increased profitability (35%). Those are self-reported, but they point to the same place: the value comes from alignment, not from the software.

## lowob takeaways

- **One owner, one rulebook.** RevOps is defined by accountability for commercial data and definitions, not by headcount.
- **The forecast is the first test.** If the pipeline number is challenged every month, the definitions are not yet shared.
- **Agents raise the stakes.** Whatever RevOps leaves undefined, an AI agent will act on anyway.
- **Start with a reconciliation.** Agreeing one historical number exposes the gaps faster than any audit.

## Common questions

### What does a revenue operations team do?

It owns the data, processes, tools and reporting behind marketing, sales and customer success. That includes field definitions, lead routing, stage criteria, CRM administration and forecast inputs.

### What is the difference between sales operations and RevOps?

Sales operations supports the sales team alone. RevOps covers the full customer lifecycle, from first marketing touch to renewal, under one owner and one set of definitions.

### Does a small company need revenue operations?

It needs the function, not necessarily a team. At 20 to 500 people, one accountable person with a written rulebook and a monthly data review usually covers it.

### How does RevOps relate to AI in sales?

AI assistants and agents read the CRM fields RevOps maintains. Clear definitions and clean records are what make their outputs trustworthy.

## Sources and notes

- [Forrester, Why Revenue Operations (RevOps) Should Be On Your Radar](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/why-revenue-operations-revops-should-be-on-your-radar), August 2024. Analyst blog; source of the definition used here.
- [Forrester, The WIIFM Of Revenue Operations](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-wifm-whats-in-it-for-me-of-revenue-operations), June 2023. Reports the 2021 Revenue Operations and Buying Groups survey; self-reported impacts.
- [Gartner, Gartner Predicts 75% of the Highest Growth Companies Will Deploy a RevOps Model](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2021-05-17-gartner-predicts-75--of-the-highest-growth-companies-), May 2021. A prediction, not a measured outcome.
- [Forrester Consulting for Clari, Revenue Operations And Intelligence Delivers Predictable Growth](https://pages.clari.com/rs/866-BBG-005/images/forrester-clari-revops-study-2021.pdf), August 2021. Vendor-commissioned survey of 327 US decision-makers.
- [Gartner, Less Than 50% of Sales Leaders Have High Confidence in Forecasting Accuracy](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2020-02-12-gartner-says-less-than-50--of-sales-leaders-and-selle), February 2020.
- Validity, State of CRM Data 2026, as reported by [MarTech](https://martech.org/marketers-know-ai-is-using-bad-data-to-make-decisions/), August 2026. Vendor-run survey of 500 marketers.

## Next move

Ask marketing, sales and finance separately for last quarter's new pipeline figure. If the three numbers differ, write down why, and you have the first page of your RevOps rulebook.

# What Is the Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-the-model-context-protocol/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-15 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: The Model Context Protocol is an open standard, released by Anthropic in November 2024, that lets AI applications connect to tools and data through one common interface instead of custom integrations. By December 2025 it had more than 10,000 active public servers and was donated to a Linux Foundation fund. It is wiring: useful to rent, but it needs permissions and logging around it.

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is an open standard for connecting AI applications to the systems where data and tools live, such as a CRM, a document store or a database. Instead of building a custom integration for every pairing of AI tool and business system, each system exposes one MCP server and any MCP-compatible assistant can use it. It is now supported by most major AI products. It is wiring, not judgment, so it needs permissions and logs around it.

*Figure: Where this piece sits in The Build Order: the context layer.*

## What MCP means

Before MCP, every connection between an AI assistant and a business system was a one-off build. Anthropic's launch post described models as "trapped behind information silos and legacy systems", with each new data source needing its own integration. Five assistants and ten systems meant up to fifty integrations.

MCP replaces that with one protocol. A system exposes its data and actions through an MCP server. An AI application acts as an MCP client and connects to any server it is allowed to use. Anthropic's launch named early adopters including Block and Apollo, and development tool makers including Zed, Replit, Codeium and Sourcegraph.

Adoption since then has been broad. Anthropic's December 2025 announcement listed support in ChatGPT, Cursor, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Visual Studio Code, alongside Claude. The same month, MCP became a founding project of the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, with support from Google, Microsoft, AWS, Cloudflare and Bloomberg. MCP's maintainers keep control of the technical direction; the foundation provides neutral governance.

| MCP is | MCP is not |
| --- | --- |
| A standard way for AI applications to reach tools and data | A model, an agent or an AI product |
| A connector layer each system implements once | A data store or a CRM |
| A way to expose actions such as "search deals" or "create task" | A permission system on its own |
| Vendor-neutral, governed under the Linux Foundation | A guarantee that a given server is safe |

## How it works, and why it matters for a commercial team

An MCP server describes what it offers: tools the model can call, data it can read and prompts it can use. The AI application reads those descriptions, decides which tool fits the task and calls it. A CRM's MCP server might offer "find account", "list open deals" and "add note". A calendar server might offer "list meetings this week".

For a commercial team, the practical effect is that an assistant can assemble account context from several systems at once. A meeting brief can draw on the CRM, the last email thread and the shared drive without anyone building three integrations.

In **lowob**'s model of the enterprise brain, MCP sits in the wiring stage, between the store (where data lives) and reasoning (where models and agents work). The principle is to rent the wiring and own the record. MCP is a good thing to rent: it is a standard, many vendors maintain servers for their own products, and switching assistants does not mean rebuilding connections. What MCP does not provide is the record of what was decided, by whom and why. That remains yours to keep.

## Common mistakes and how to start safely

The same openness that makes MCP useful makes it a security surface. The Cloud Security Alliance's May 2026 paper on MCP security describes two main risks. Tool poisoning is a form of indirect prompt injection, where hostile instructions are hidden in a server's tool descriptions. The confused deputy problem arises when a server holding powerful credentials is manipulated into using them for an action its owner never intended.

| Risk | What it looks like | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tool poisoning | A third-party server's description tells the model to send data elsewhere | Approve servers like software suppliers; pin and review versions |
| Over-broad credentials | One token gives an assistant full CRM admin rights | Scope each connection to read-only or narrow write access |
| Silent actions | The assistant updates records with no trace | Keep append-only logs of every tool call |
| Client-facing sends | An email tool is exposed with "send" as well as "draft" | Expose draft actions only; nothing sends without a person |

A safe start has three steps. Connect read-only servers first, so the assistant can answer questions but not change anything. Add draft-only write tools next, such as creating a note or a task for review. Only after several weeks of logs should any server be allowed to make changes without approval.

## lowob takeaways

- **MCP is a plug, not a brain.** It connects assistants to systems; it does not decide or remember.
- **Rent it.** It is an open, widely supported standard governed under the Linux Foundation.
- **Scope every connection.** Start read-only, then draft-only, and log every call.
- **Vet servers as suppliers.** A tool description is code the model will follow.

## Common questions

### What is MCP in AI?

MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is an open standard that lets AI applications connect to external tools and data through one common interface. Anthropic released it in November 2024.

### Who owns the Model Context Protocol?

Since December 2025 MCP has been a project of the Agentic AI Foundation, a directed fund under the Linux Foundation. Its maintainers still set technical direction.

### Is MCP secure?

The protocol can be used securely, but servers can carry risks such as tool poisoning and over-broad credentials. Scope permissions narrowly, vet third-party servers and log every tool call.

### What is the difference between MCP and an API?

An API is specific to one system. MCP is a common layer on top, so any compatible AI application can discover and use a system's tools without a custom integration.

## Sources and notes

- [Anthropic, Introducing the Model Context Protocol](https://www.anthropic.com/news/model-context-protocol), 25 November 2024. Vendor announcement.
- [Anthropic, Donating the Model Context Protocol and establishing the Agentic AI Foundation](https://anthropic.com/news/donating-the-model-context-protocol-and-establishing-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation), 9 December 2025. Vendor-reported usage figures.
- [MCP blog, MCP joins the Agentic AI Foundation](https://blog.modelcontextprotocol.io/posts/2025-12-09-mcp-joins-agentic-ai-foundation/), 9 December 2025. Project's own account of governance.
- [Cloud Security Alliance, MCP security: tool poisoning and the confused deputy problem](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research-rb/csa-whitepaper-mcp-security-agentic-attack-surface-20260516/), 16 May 2026. Industry body research note.
- The wiring stage and staged rollout are **lowob**'s working method.

## Related research

- [What Is an AI Agent, and Where Does It Fit in the Brain?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-agent/)
- [Buy Context. Own Judgment. What Enterprise AI Teams Should Build](https://lowob.com/research/buy-context-own-judgment-what-to-build-at-each-size/)

## Next move

List the systems your commercial team uses daily and check which already offer an official MCP server. Connect one, read-only, to the assistant your team already uses.

# How to Write an Ideal Customer Profile Sales Will Use

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-write-an-icp/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An ideal customer profile is a narrow, evidence-based description of the customer a company should pursue first: most likely to buy, succeed and stay. It includes firmographics, situational triggers, the buying committee, disqualifiers and evidence. If every prospect qualifies, it is not an ICP.

An ideal customer profile (ICP) is a written description of the customer a company should pursue first: the one most likely to buy, most likely to succeed with the product, and most likely to stay. It should tell sales whom to pursue, why a company fits, and when to move on. A working ICP has five parts: firmographic facts, situational triggers, the buying committee, disqualifiers and the evidence it was built from. If every prospect qualifies, it is not an ICP.

An ideal customer profile (ICP) is a written description of the customer a company should pursue first: the one most likely to buy, most likely to succeed with the product, and most likely to stay. It is the practical output of positioning, and it is the document that keeps marketing and sales pointed at the same people.

Most ICPs are written once, put in a slide, and ignored, because they describe a customer so broadly that every prospect qualifies.

## What an ICP contains

**Firmographic or demographic facts.** For business buyers: industry, size, geography, stage, structure. For consumers: age, situation, income band, location. These are the filters, and they are the least interesting part.

**Situational triggers.** What is happening to the customer that makes the problem urgent now: a new regulation, a product launch, a failed vendor, a new leader, a funding event, a growth spurt, a deadline. Triggers explain why two identical companies buy at different times, and they are what makes an ICP useful for outbound.

**The buying committee.** Who feels the problem, who approves the spend, who can block it, and who has to implement. For consumer products, who influences the decision.

**Disqualifiers.** The characteristics that predict a bad customer: too small to pay, a technical stack the product does not fit, a use case it does not serve, a regulatory position the company cannot support. The disqualifier list is usually more valuable than the qualifier list, because it stops the pipeline filling with deals that will not close or will churn.

**Evidence.** The customers this description was built from, and what happened to them.

| Component | What to write | Illustrative entry | Where the evidence comes from |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Firmographics | Industry, size, geography, stage | Regulated lenders, 200 to 2,000 staff, US | CRM fields on won deals |
| Triggers | The event that makes it urgent now | New disclosure rule due within two quarters | Discovery notes on the last ten wins |
| Buying committee | Who feels, approves, blocks, implements | Compliance lead feels it; CFO approves; IT security can block | Contacts engaged on won and lost deals |
| Disqualifiers | What predicts a bad customer | No in-house compliance owner; legacy core system the product cannot connect to | Churned accounts and lost deals |
| Evidence | The customers it was built from | Named internally, with outcome for each | Retention and expansion data |

The buying committee row is longer than most teams write it. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. Our explainer [What is a buying committee?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) covers the roles to record.

## ICP versus persona

An ICP describes the account or the customer: the company or person worth pursuing. A persona describes an individual within the buying process: their role, goals, fears, and how they evaluate. A company sells to an ICP and communicates with personas. Confusing the two produces marketing aimed at "the CFO" with no view on which CFOs, at which companies, in which situation.

|  | Ideal customer profile | Persona |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Describes | The account worth pursuing | A person inside the buying process |
| Answers | Should we pursue this company, now? | What does this person need to believe, and how do they evaluate? |
| Built from | Won, lost and churned accounts | Interviews and call recordings |
| Used by | Sales for qualification, marketing for targeting, outbound for lists | Marketing for messaging, sales for call preparation |
| Fails when | Every prospect qualifies | It is written without an ICP behind it |

The distinction matters for measurement. Forrester's analyst Simon Daniels wrote in 2023 that fewer than 1% of leads convert to closed deals, partly because several leads contribute to one opportunity. Forrester clients reported a 50% increase in meeting-to-closed-won conversion when marketing delivered three or more members of the buying group to sales. An ICP tells you which accounts; personas tell you which people in them to reach.

## How to build one from evidence

Start with the customers who bought fastest, paid the most, expanded, and stayed. Pull their characteristics, the trigger that made them buy, who was involved, and what they said the problem was. Do the same for customers who churned or deals that were lost, and record what distinguished them. The pattern across both sets is the ICP. The differences are the disqualifiers.

This is also the raw material of positioning. April Dunford's method counts best-fit customers as one of the five components of a position, and starts from competitive alternatives: what those customers would do if the product did not exist. An ICP and a position built from the same customer set will agree with each other.

Size and logo appeal are poor substitutes for that evidence. Gartner research reported by *CRM Magazine* in December 2021 found 58% of B2B sales organisations missed quota on key accounts, and that customers elevated to key-account status mainly because of their large spend were 51% less likely to increase it over time. The largest account is not always the best fit.

Sales benchmarks point the same way. Ebsta and Pavilion's 2024 analysis of 4.2 million opportunities at 530 companies, which is vendor research, found top performers prioritised the kinds of accounts and personas they had closed before and disqualified poor-fit opportunities early. Successful deals engaged about nine contacts by the solution-presented stage, against about two for lost deals.

If the company has fewer than ten customers, the ICP is a hypothesis, and it should say so. Write it narrowly anyway; a narrow hypothesis can be tested, and a broad one cannot. Our piece on [segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/) shows how to score segments on win rate, deal size, cycle length and retention once the data exists.

> A narrow hypothesis can be tested, and a broad one cannot.

## The mistakes that make it useless

Five mistakes account for most ICPs that nobody uses.

1. Writing it broadly so nobody is excluded.
2. Building it from who the company wishes it sold to rather than who actually bought.
3. Leaving out triggers, so it cannot inform timing.
4. Leaving out disqualifiers, so it cannot inform saying no.
5. Writing it once and never revising it as the customer base changes.

The fifth is the slowest to show. A profile built from the first ten customers often describes early adopters, who tolerate gaps that the next fifty will not. Revisit it each quarter against the accounts won, lost and churned since the last version.

## How to tell whether it is working

An ICP is working when four things are true. Sales can disqualify a lead in one call using shared criteria. Marketing can describe the audience for a channel test in the ICP's terms. Outbound lists are built from the triggers, not from a title search. And the customers acquired this quarter look more like the profile than the ones acquired last quarter.

An ICP that does those four things is a working document. One that does not is a slide. The next step is to turn it into a list of named accounts with owners, which [Market maps that sales actually uses](https://lowob.com/research/market-maps-that-sales-actually-uses/) covers, and into outbound built on triggers, covered in [Cold outreach works better with a real reason to talk](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Use real customer outcomes and buying signals to define fit.** Build from who bought, paid, expanded and stayed, not who you wish you sold to.
- **Include reasons to disqualify an account.** The disqualifier list stops the pipeline filling with deals that will not close or will churn.
- **Write the triggers.** They make the ICP useful for timing and for outbound.
- **Check that marketing and sales use the same criteria.** One profile, used to qualify, target and build lists.

## Common questions

### What should an ideal customer profile include?

Firmographic or demographic facts, the situational triggers that make the problem urgent, the buying committee, disqualifiers, and the evidence: the customers it was built from and what happened to them.

### What is the difference between an ICP and a buyer persona?

An ICP describes the account worth pursuing. A persona describes a person inside the buying process, their role, goals and how they evaluate. A company sells to an ICP and communicates with personas.

### How do you build an ICP with few customers?

Treat it as a hypothesis and say so. Write it narrowly from the customers you have, including why they bought and who was involved, and test it against the next deals.

### How often should an ICP be updated?

Review it each quarter against the accounts won, lost and churned since the last version, and revise it when the customers being acquired stop matching it.

- [Forrester, Saying Goodbye to MQLs](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/saying-goodbye-to-mqls-sweet-and-no-sorrow), Simon Daniels, 21 November 2023. Analyst blog citing Forrester client data.

# A $10,000 Test That Closes a Question Beats a $10,000 Bet That Leaves It Open.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-13 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Most growth tests are small versions of what the company already wanted to do, and they end in "promising". A test closes a question when the threshold and the decision on each side are written before any money is spent. Measure two or three channels cheaply and in parallel, read the results against the thresholds, then commit budget to one channel at a time.

A test is defined by the decision it forces, not by its size. Write the question and the threshold first, measure several channels cheaply at once, then commit to one properly. The discipline matters because most ideas do not work: Kohavi and Thomke reported that only about a third of Microsoft's experiments improved the metric they targeted, and 10% to 20% at Google and Bing. A company that cannot say in advance what result would stop it will read most of its failures as "promising".

Every company says it tests before it scales. Very few can show you the question a test was designed to answer, or the decision that followed.

The reason is that most tests are not tests. They are small versions of the thing the company already wanted to do, run for long enough to produce a number that can be described either way. Ten thousand dollars goes into a channel. A report comes back. The channel is "promising". Another ten thousand follows.

That is a bet. A test is different in one respect: it is designed so that when it ends, a question is closed.

## Write the question before spending a dollar

A test worth running can be stated as a question with a threshold and a decision on each side.

Not: "Let's try personal-finance creators."

But: "Can personal-finance creators on cost-per-account terms produce funded accounts below eighty dollars each, at a volume of at least fifty in two weeks, using tracking we control? If yes, we build the program. If no, we do not revisit creators for two quarters."

The second version is uncomfortable to write, because it commits the company to a decision before it knows the answer. That discomfort is the point. A test without a pre-committed decision becomes an argument after the results arrive, and arguments are won by whoever wanted the channel in the first place.

Researchers have a name for this. Nosek and colleagues, in the paper published in *PNAS* in 2018 as "The preregistration revolution", define preregistration as committing to analytic steps without advance knowledge of the research outcomes. They separate prediction, which tests an idea about what will happen, from postdiction, which uses the data to explain what already did. The risk they name is hindsight bias: outcomes look more predictable after the fact. A growth report written after the money is spent is postdiction. Stefan Thomke makes the business version of the point in Harvard Business School's Working Knowledge: a sound experiment needs a testable hypothesis, a control and an organisation that agrees in advance to abide by the result.

| Field | Example |
| --- | --- |
| Question | Can personal-finance creators produce funded accounts on cost-per-account terms? |
| Threshold | Below $80 per funded account |
| Minimum volume | At least 50 funded accounts |
| Window | Two weeks |
| Tracking | Links and codes the company controls, reconciled to its own account data |
| If yes | Build the creator program and give it an owner |
| If no | Do not revisit creators for two quarters; record why |

## Why most ideas fail the threshold

The pre-written threshold matters more than intuition suggests, because most ideas do not clear it. In "The surprising power of online experiments", published in *Harvard Business Review* in 2017, Ron Kohavi and Stefan Thomke reported that across Microsoft about a third of experiments proved effective, a third were neutral and a third were negative. At Google and Bing only about 10% to 20% generated positive results. Thomke has since put the general rate at roughly one experiment in ten improving the bottom line.

These are organisations with large engineering teams, careful idea selection and millions of users. A growth team picking channels on a hunch will not beat their hit rate. If most ideas fail, a process that lets each failure be described as "promising" will fund mostly failures.

> A test without a pre-committed decision becomes an argument after the results arrive, and arguments are won by whoever wanted the channel in the first place.

## Measure cheaply, in several places at once

The instinct is to test one channel at a time, thoroughly. It is the wrong instinct, for two reasons.

Sequential tests are slow, and distribution questions have a season. A company that tests one channel per month spends a year learning what it could have learned in a month.

And sequential tests are biased. The first channel gets the most attention and the best creative. By the fourth, everyone is tired. Running channels in the same weeks also means they face the same market, the same news and the same seasonality, which a month-by-month sequence cannot hold constant.

Run the two or three most plausible channels in parallel, each with a small budget, its own tracking, and its own written question. A week is enough to learn whether there is water under the hull. It is not enough to learn what the voyage will earn, and a test that claims otherwise is overselling itself.

Own the tracking. Gordon, Zettelmeyer, Bhargava and Chapsky compared observational measurement with randomised experiments across 15 advertising studies at Facebook, published in *Marketing Science* in 2019. The observational methods often failed to measure the true effect and generally overstated it. A platform's own attribution report is an observational method. For the difference between what a channel was credited with and what it caused, see [attribution vs incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/).

## Commit expensively, one at a time

Here is where most companies drift. Having run three small tests, they scale all three a little, on the theory that diversification is prudent.

It is not prudent. It is three half-run experiments with none of them funded well enough to prove anything. Parallel measurement exists to choose. Once something reads, the budget, the creative attention, and the operating effort go there, until that channel is either built properly or shown to have a ceiling.

The sequence is the discipline: observe cheaply and in parallel, commit expensively and one at a time. Companies that hold those two ideas loosely end up doing neither. The commitment phase is also where the arithmetic of proper testing applies; [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers sample sizes and holdouts at B2B volumes. Kohavi and Thomke note that any company with at least a few thousand daily active users can run controlled tests. Below that, the parallel read and a written decision are the honest alternative.

## The one-week diagnostic

This is the shape of the [diagnostic week](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-distribution-diagnostic/) **lowob** runs, and it is the shape a company can run for itself.

**Day one:** Map which channels are open to the category, which require paperwork, and which are closed. Write the question for each channel worth testing.

**Days two through five:** Stand up tracking the company owns. Place the small budgets. Recruit the handful of partners or creators the test requires. Watch the early numbers for tracking failures, not for results.

**Day six:** Read the results against the thresholds written on day one. No re-interpretation.

**Day seven:** Write down the decision, what it cost, and what was ruled out. The ruled-out list is the most valuable page, because it is the one the company will otherwise re-argue every quarter. Our piece on [the graveyard](https://lowob.com/research/the-graveyard/) sets out how to keep that list so it can be consulted later.

## What a small test cannot tell you

Honesty about limits keeps the method credible.

| A one-week, small-budget test can show | It cannot show |
| --- | --- |
| Whether a channel is open to the category | Long-run customer value |
| Whether it converts at all | Seasonal effects |
| Roughly what an outcome costs at small scale | How the channel behaves at ten times the volume |
| Whether the tracking works | Whether the first cohort retains |

That is enough to decide where the next serious money goes, and it is far more than most companies know when they make that decision. For pricing questions, where the same logic applies but legal and volume limits are tighter, see [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/).

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the decision first.** A question, a threshold, a minimum volume and what happens on each side, before the first dollar.
- **Expect most ideas to fail.** Even the best testing programmes see a minority of positive results, so "promising" is not a result.
- **Test in parallel, on tracking you own.** Two or three channels in the same weeks, each with its own question.
- **Commit to one.** Fund the channel that read until it is built or shows its ceiling.
- **Keep the ruled-out list.** It stops the same channel being re-argued every quarter.

## Common questions

### How do you design a marketing test that leads to a decision?

Write the question, the threshold, the minimum volume, the time window and the decision for each outcome before spending anything. Read the result against those terms only, and record what was ruled out.

### Should you test marketing channels one at a time or in parallel?

In parallel, with a small budget, separate tracking and a written question for each. Sequential tests are slow and biased, because the first channel gets the most attention and later ones face a different market.

### What percentage of A/B tests succeed?

A minority. Kohavi and Thomke reported about one third of Microsoft experiments improved their target metric, and 10% to 20% at Google and Bing.

### What can a small, one-week marketing test tell you?

Whether a channel is open, whether it converts, roughly what an outcome costs at small scale and whether tracking works. It cannot tell you long-run customer value, seasonal effects or behaviour at much larger volume.

## Sources and notes

- [Kohavi and Thomke, The surprising power of online experiments](https://web-docs.stern.nyu.edu/executive/The%20Surprising%20Power%20of%20Online%20Experiments.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, September to October 2017. Practitioner article from large technology firms; hit rates reflect their idea pipelines, hosted copy.
- [Nosek, Ebersole, DeHaven and Mellor, The preregistration revolution](https://errorstatistics.com/wp-content/uploads/2017/07/nosek-et-al-preregistration-revolution.pdf), preprint of the paper published in *PNAS*, March 2018. Written for scientific research, not marketing; the principle is borrowed.
- [Harvard Business School Working Knowledge, Creating the experimentation organization](https://www.library.hbs.edu/working-knowledge/creating-the-experimentation-organization), 4 December 2019. Interview with Stefan Thomke on his book; the one-in-ten figure is his general estimate.
- [INFORMS, How measurable is online advertising?](https://www.informs.org/News-Room/INFORMS-Releases/News-Releases/How-measurable-is-online-advertising), 20 March 2019. Press release on Gordon et al., *Marketing Science*; 15 Facebook experiments, consumer advertising.

## Next move

Take the next channel your team wants to try and write its question card: threshold, minimum volume, window, tracking and the decision on each side. If nobody will sign the "if no" line, the test is a bet.

# Token or No Token

Source: https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-12 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A token should reduce coordination cost or create ownership; if it does neither, do not issue one. If you do, the money you raise decides your go-to-market, and float, release schedules, stablecoin runway and liquidity depth matter more than headline FDV. The 2026 US and EU position makes what you promise in public part of the legal analysis, so legal belongs inside GTM.

A token should reduce coordination cost or create ownership. If it does neither, do not issue one, and if you do, the type of money you raise decides your go-to-market before you write a line of it. Circulating float, the release schedule, stablecoin runway and liquidity depth say more than headline FDV. And in 2026 the US and EU both tie the legal treatment of a token to what the team says about it, so legal review is part of GTM, not a box ticked before it.

*This is not investment or legal advice. Token structures are fact-specific; get your own counsel.*

## What a token is actually for

Strip away the narrative and a token does one of two jobs. It coordinates people who do not trust each other, or it gives them ownership they cannot get another way.

Everything else is a worse version of something cheaper. Settlement can run on stablecoins. Loyalty can run on points. Access control can run on a database with a login page.

So the first question is not "what will our token do". It is "what breaks if we do not have one". If nothing breaks, you have your answer for now. You are not closing the door. You are refusing to open it before the room is built.

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) argued for raising on proof. In crypto, the token is where narrative hides best. Treat it with the same discipline, and write the answer down as a [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) with a reason and an owner, reviewed by someone outside the founding team.

## Three kinds of money and what each wants

The money you take is a GTM commitment. Each source wants something different from how you go to market.

| Source | What they are buying | What it pulls your GTM towards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity only | A business that compounds | Revenue, retention, a product that sells without a token |
| Equity plus token warrant | A business and a launch event | A credible launch date, exchange relationships, a liquid market |
| Ecosystem or foundation money | Activity on their chain | Building where they live: their users, their events, their co-marketing |

None of these is wrong. All of them are binding. Ecosystem money in particular is often read as cheap grant capital. It is not. It is a distribution deal, and chain choice is the term that matters most. If you build on a chain because the grant was there, you have chosen your first hundred users without meeting them. Make sure they are the users you want.

## Float, release schedules and runway beat FDV

Headline FDV is the number people quote at dinner. It tells you almost nothing about the next eighteen months, and the evidence suggests a high one is a liability. Keyrock's review of 62 airdrop launches found higher launch FDV correlated with a greater likelihood of a significant price drop. One token in its sample launched at a $13 billion FDV with an estimated $6 million of liquidity, and fell 83%.

Three numbers tell you more. Circulating float at launch, because thin float means price is a story, not a market. The release schedule, because every cliff is a sell event you have to plan communications around. Treasury runway in stablecoins, because a treasury denominated in your own token is runway you cannot spend in a drawdown.

US regulators now ask for the same numbers. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets, published in August 2026, would require principles-based disclosure that, in the Congressional Research Service's summary, covers token economics: supply, pricing, lockups, release schedules and mechanisms for creating or destroying the asset. A team that already runs its GTM calendar off the release calendar has most of that section written.

Build the GTM calendar around the release calendar, not the other way round. If a large release lands the same month as your biggest product launch, one of them moves.

## Legal does not end at launch

The specifics belong with counsel. The general point is that legal clarity is a fact pattern, not a one-time stamp, and the 2026 position makes that more literal, not less.

| Jurisdiction | Current position, November 2026 | What it means for GTM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| US, SEC and CFTC | Joint interpretation of 17 March 2026 sets five categories: digital commodities, collectibles, tools and payment stablecoins outside securities law; tokenised securities inside it. A non-security token can still be sold as part of an investment contract, which can end when promised efforts are completed or abandoned | What the team promises, when, and through which medium feeds the analysis. Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous" |
| US, SEC proposal | Regulation Crypto Assets, proposed 18 August 2026: a $5 million four-year startup exemption, a fundraising exemption of up to $75 million in 12 months, and a safe harbor once promised efforts are complete. Comments closed 20 October 2026; not final | Plan for principles-based disclosure and antifraud liability whatever exemption you use |
| US, Congress | The CLARITY Act passed the House 294 to 134 in July 2025 but failed Senate cloture 49 to 50 on 15 September 2026; passage this Congress is widely seen as unlikely. The GENIUS Act of 2025 covers payment stablecoins | Agency rules can be reversed; build for uncertainty |
| EU, MiCA | White papers "shall not contain any assertions as regards the future value" of the token, must state it may lose value in part or in full, and marketing must be consistent with the white paper. The transitional period for service providers ended 1 July 2026 | Every public claim has to match a filed document; exchange and custody partners must be authorised |

The common thread is that a marketing claim your team makes in month nine can matter as much as the structure you set in month one. That makes legal part of GTM. Your claims register from [one truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) needs a legal reviewer with sign-off, not a courtesy copy. Our piece on [raising in a regulated category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/) covers how that changes the fundraising conversation.

> Legal clarity is a fact pattern, not a stamp. What you say in public in month nine is part of it.

## Liquidity depth is a product requirement

Founders treat liquidity as a market-maker problem. It is a product problem. If a user cannot enter or exit at reasonable size without moving the price, the token does not work as a coordination tool. It works as a trap. Users notice, and your most active users notice first.

Set a minimum liquidity depth as a product requirement, in writing, before launch. Fund it, or do not launch. This is the same logic as not shipping a checkout page that fails above a certain basket size.

## The readiness gate

Before any token launch, we ask teams to score themselves against a gate. Not a pass-fail test: a practice that forces the honest conversation before the calendar does.

| Dimension | Evidence that earns a high score |
| --- | --- |
| Retention without incentives | Cohorts returning with rewards switched off |
| Token necessity | A written answer to "what breaks without it", reviewed externally |
| Legal clarity | Counsel's analysis in each launch market, and a claims register with sign-off |
| Security review | Named, scoped and dated audits; unaudited components listed |
| Treasury runway | Months of runway in stablecoins |
| Distribution in place | Channels that deliver users without the token |
| Liquidity depth | A funded minimum depth |
| Comms readiness | Release calendar and launch calendar reconciled |
| Incident response | A named owner and a rehearsed plan |

Incident response is on the list because something will go wrong in the first week. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with one exchange compromise accounting for $1.5 billion. Score each dimension, write one sentence of evidence beside each score, and where the evidence is thin, the score is low, whatever the team feels. The thresholds are yours to set. The point is to make the decision visible, so a weak dimension gets fixed or gets owned. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) shows where that record lives.

Gateway card

### Before you issue a token

- Written answer to "what breaks without a token", reviewed by someone outside the founding team
- Funding source chosen with its GTM pull named, including chain choice as distribution
- Release calendar laid over the GTM calendar, with conflicts resolved
- Treasury runway stated in stablecoins, not in your own token
- Minimum liquidity depth written down as a product requirement and funded
- Counsel's view for each launch market, and a claims register with legal sign-off
- Readiness gate scored with evidence per dimension, and an incident response owner named

## lowob takeaways

- **Ask what breaks.** If nothing breaks without a token, do not issue one for now.
- **Money is a GTM choice.** Ecosystem money is a distribution deal, and chain choice is its main term.
- **Float, releases and runway.** They say more than FDV, and US disclosure proposals ask for them too.
- **Legal is part of GTM.** In the US and EU, what you say in public shapes how the token is treated.

## Common questions

### Does my crypto startup need a token?

Only if it reduces coordination cost between people who do not trust each other or creates ownership they cannot get another way. If nothing breaks without one, you have your answer for now.

### Is FDV a good metric for a token launch?

No. Keyrock found higher launch FDVs correlated with steeper price falls. Circulating float at launch, the release schedule and treasury runway in stablecoins tell you more about the next eighteen months.

### Are tokens securities in the US in 2026?

Under the SEC and CFTC interpretation of March 2026, many native network tokens, collectibles, tools and payment stablecoins are outside securities law, but a token sold with promises of managerial effort can be part of an investment contract. It is fact-specific; get counsel.

### What does MiCA require before a token launch in the EU?

For offers needing one, a white paper with no assertions on future value and a statement that the token may lose value, marketing consistent with it and not issued before it, and authorised service providers since the transitional period ended on 1 July 2026.

- [Raising in a Regulated Category](https://lowob.com/research/raising-in-a-regulated-category/)

## Next move

Set a minimum liquidity depth as a product requirement, in writing, before launch. Fund it, or do not launch. Then lay the release calendar over the launch calendar and move whichever event collides.
