# Percent of Spend Is a Conflict of Interest With a Logo on It.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Media agencies paid a percentage of spend earn more when clients spend more, not when the spending works. ANA research has documented rebates, principal-based markups and commissions that persist for media long after other services moved to fees. lowob runs media on three rules: a flat fee per account, no fronted spend, and fixed fees against written scope.

Most media agencies are still paid, in whole or part, as a percentage of what their clients spend. The agency's revenue goes up when spending goes up, not when spending works, so every recommendation about budget, channel or pace is made by a party paid more if the answer is "more." That is not an accusation of bad faith. It is a conflict of interest with a logo on it. The ANA's own research shows how the incentive plays out, and three rules remove it.

The arrangement is so common that it rarely gets examined. It is easy to administer, it scales with the account, and it sounds fair: the agency does more work when the budget is larger, so it earns more.

Look at it for one minute from the client's side and the problem is obvious. The agency's revenue goes up when the client's spending goes up. It does not go up when the spending works. Most people in the industry are trying to do good work inside a structure that rewards something else.

## How agencies are paid now

The industry has moved, but less for media than for anything else. The ANA's 18th Trends in Agency Compensation study, published in December 2022 from 101 client-side marketers covering 336 agency relationships, found 82% used fee-based compensation, up from 68% in 2016. Performance incentives were falling: 41% used them, down from 61% in 2013. Media was the exception. Only about half of ANA members paid media agencies by fee, the lowest of any service, and 19% still used commissions for media planning or buying, against 7% for agency services overall.

| Model | How the partner earns more | What it rewards | Who holds the risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Percentage of spend | The client spends more | Volume | The client |
| Hourly or labour-based fee | More hours are billed | Time | The client |
| Fronted spend with a margin | More media passes through the partner | Credit and control | Split, with the partner controlling the account |
| Principal-based (resold) media | The markup on inventory | Inventory the partner owns | The client, often without seeing the markup |
| Flat fee per account against written scope | The client hires them for the next account | Finishing the defined work | Shared, and visible |

## What the incentive produces

Percentage fees shape behaviour in ways that are easy to see once named.

Budgets rarely come down. When a channel is underperforming, the recommendation is to test more creative, not to pause. Cheap inventory is attractive because it inflates volume at the same fee rate. "Always-on" spending is defended on principle. Reports emphasise scale over outcomes. And the agency has little reason to tell a client that a channel is closed to their category, because a closed channel is budget that cannot be placed.

The evidence shows the incentive extends beyond the headline fee. In 2016 the ANA commissioned K2 Intelligence to investigate media buying in the US. From 150 sources, the report found cash rebates paid to agencies by media sellers based on spend, often without the advertiser knowing; rebates disguised as research or consulting fees; and principal-based buying, where the agency buys inventory for itself and resells it to the client, at markups ranging from about 30% to 90%. Some media buyers reported pressure to steer client spend toward that inventory. The study was not an audit, named no companies, and five of six major holding companies declined to make executives available. It is still the most detailed public account of how volume incentives travel through the system.

Cheap volume has a measurable cost too. In the ANA's 2023 programmatic study, made-for-advertising sites took 21% of impressions and 15% of spend, and the average campaign ran on about 44,000 domains. A fee calculated on spend is indifferent to which of those domains the money reached.

The alternative is to set the budget from the company's own unit economics (cost per qualified opportunity and payback), as our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) describes, so that the size of the spend is never the partner's call alone.

None of that requires anyone to be dishonest. It only requires people to respond to how they are paid.

> A fee structure is not a detail of the contract. It is the strongest predictor of the advice you will receive.

## Three rules that remove the conflict

We run media on three rules, and we publish them because they are the answer to the question every media buyer should be asking.

**A flat fee per account, never a percentage of spend.** The fee is for the work of running the account: setup, inventory standards, verification, optimisation, reporting. It is the same whether the client spends thirty thousand or three hundred thousand. The only way to earn more is to earn the next account, which happens when this one works.

**We never front media spend.** The client pays the platforms and partners directly, or funds a media account in their own name. The moment an agency lends money to buy media, it becomes a creditor with an interest in volume, and it gains control of the account history, pixel data and platform relationships that should belong to the client. On Google Ads, for example, if a manager account holds ownership of a client's account, its admins can change who has access to it.

**Fixed fee against written scope, never hourly.** The scope says what will be done, what will be delivered, how long it takes, and what it does not include. Hourly billing rewards slowness. A percentage rewards volume. A fixed fee against a written scope rewards finishing. The ANA's data shows the largest advertisers moving the same way: among those spending $500 million or more a year, 53% used fixed or output-based fees in 2022, up from 5% in 2016.

## How to ask for it

A client does not have to hire us to use this. Ask any media partner three questions.

1. **If I halve my budget next month, what happens to your fee?**
2. **Whose name is on the ad accounts, and who holds the pixel and conversion history if we part ways?**
3. **What is in scope, in writing, and what is excluded?**

Add a fourth if the plan includes programmatic: **do you, or any company you own, sell us inventory as principal, and do you receive rebates or volume incentives from sellers?** The K2 findings are why.

The answers tell you what the partner is actually selling. A partner paid a percentage is selling placement. A partner who fronts spend is selling credit. A partner paid hourly is selling time. A partner on a flat fee against written scope is selling the outcome of a defined piece of work, and can be judged on it. Our guides to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) and [pricing architecture for services firms](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/) cover the wider fee landscape.

## The honest limit

Flat fees have a floor. Below a certain account size the work does not cover the fee, and a good partner will say so rather than take the account and under-serve it. That is why we publish a minimum and the next step in the same proposal: the client should always know what the engagement costs, what it includes, and what it would cost to go further, before anyone starts.

Flat fees also move a risk to the client: a partner paid the same regardless of spend has less reason to find more scale when scale is the right answer. Written scope and a quarterly review of what the account produced handle that. Our piece on [self-serve, managed desk or agency](https://lowob.com/research/self-serve-vs-managed-media/) covers when each model fits.

## lowob takeaways

- **Percentage fees pay for volume.** Every budget recommendation comes from a party paid more if the answer is "more."
- **The incentive travels.** Rebates and principal-based markups were documented by the ANA's own investigation.
- **Three rules remove it.** A flat fee per account, no fronted spend, fixed fees against written scope.
- **Ask before you sign.** What happens to the fee at half the budget, whose name is on the accounts, and what is in scope.

## Common questions

### How are media agencies paid?

By a percentage of media spend, labour-based or fixed fees, performance incentives, or a mix. ANA data from 2022 shows fees dominate overall, but media is the service where commissions persist most, at 19% of marketers.

### What is wrong with paying an agency a percentage of ad spend?

The agency earns more when you spend more, not when the spending works. That shapes advice on budget, channel and pace, and makes cheap volume attractive.

### What is principal-based media buying?

An agency buys media inventory for itself and resells it to the client at a markup. The ANA's 2016 K2 report found markups of about 30% to 90%, often without full disclosure.

### What questions should I ask a media agency about fees?

Ask what happens to the fee if the budget halves, whose name is on the ad accounts and conversion history, what is in written scope, and whether they sell inventory as principal or take rebates.

Send your current media partner the three questions in writing this week. If the answer to the first is that the fee falls with the budget, you are paying for placement; ask for a flat-fee alternative against written scope.

# Positioning vs Messaging vs Branding: Which Is Broken?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/positioning-vs-messaging-vs-branding/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-07 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Positioning is the decision about where the company sits, messaging is the words that carry it, and branding is how the company is recognised. Diagnose and fix them in that order, because a brand refresh cannot fix a positioning problem. A five-person sentence test shows which layer is broken.

When marketing isn't connecting with buyers, a rebrand may be the wrong first fix. Positioning is the decision about what the company is, for whom and against what alternative. Messaging is the words that carry that decision. Branding is the system that makes the company recognisable and remembered between contacts. They are done in that order, and the cheapest test of which one is broken is to ask five people in the company to finish one sentence.

When a company says its marketing "isn't landing," the diagnosis is usually one of three problems wearing the same symptoms. Positioning, messaging, and branding are different jobs, done in a particular order, and fixing the wrong one is expensive.

|  | Positioning | Messaging | Branding |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| What it is | A decision about where the company sits | The words that carry the decision | The system that makes the company recognisable |
| Main output | Buyer, problem, alternative, category, reason to choose | Problem statement, promise, proof, objection answers | Name, mark, visual identity, tone, consistent behaviour |
| Who owns it | The CEO or business owner, with a small team | Marketing, from customer evidence | Marketing and design |
| Broken when | People describe different customers | The site is accurate and still unclear | The company looks different on every surface |
| Typical fix | A workshop and a decision | A week of writing | A design project |

## Positioning: the decision about where you sit

Positioning is the choice of what the company is, for whom, and against what alternative. It is a decision, not a document. It answers: which buyer, which problem, which category the buyer will put us in, and why we are the better choice inside that category.

April Dunford's method breaks the decision into five components, worked in a set order: competitive alternatives (what customers would do if you did not exist), distinct capabilities, differentiated value, best-fit customers, and market category. She argues the category should come last, and that starting with it is "the tail wagging the dog." A category's job, in her words, is to take a prospect who knows little about the product and "point them in the direction of your differentiated value." A poor category forces sales and marketing to spend their time undoing wrong assumptions.

A fintech product can be positioned as a bank alternative, a savings tool, a treasury product for small businesses, or an embedded feature for other platforms. Each is a different buyer, a different competitor set, and a different price. The product may be identical. The company is not.

Positioning is broken when different people in the company describe a different customer, when prospects compare the product with things it was never meant to compete with, or when sales conversations begin with a long explanation of what category the product belongs to. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers how to choose the alternative when the main rival is inaction and a dozen people decide.

## Messaging: the words that carry the position

Messaging is the set of things the company says to make the position land: the problem statement, the promise, the proof, the objections answered, the phrases used consistently across every surface. It depends entirely on positioning; messaging written before the position is decided is copy in search of a strategy.

Dunford makes the same dependency explicit: "Everything we do downstream from positioning - creating messaging, building a sales pitch deck, creating other marketing and sales materials - is all oriented around helping our best-fit customers understand our value."

Good messaging uses the buyer's language for the problem, states the change the product makes rather than the features that make it, and matches proof to the buyer's actual doubts.

Messaging is broken when the website describes the product accurately and prospects still do not understand what it is for, when sales uses different words from marketing, or when the most common objection in calls appears nowhere on the site. The second symptom is common. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them.

## Branding: how the company is recognised

Branding is the system of recognition: name, mark, visual identity, tone of voice, and the consistent behaviour that makes the company feel like one thing across time. It is what remains in a buyer's memory between contacts.

That memory is most of the job in B2B, because most buyers are not buying. John Dawes of the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, in a 2021 report for LinkedIn's B2B Institute, estimated that about 20% of business buyers are in market over a year and roughly 5% in any quarter; he calls the "95-5 rule" a heuristic, not a law. Brands are chosen when a buyer enters the market and recalls them. The same report found well-established brands linked to only 20% to 30% of buyers' category entry points, with market leaders around 50%. Category entry points, a concept developed by Jenni Romaniuk at Ehrenberg-Bass, are the buying situations a brand should be linked to in memory. Our piece [Measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers how to track them.

Branding is broken when the company looks different on every surface, when the visual identity contradicts the position (a compliance-grade product that looks like a consumer game), or when nobody can describe the company's tone.

> Six months later the marketing still is not landing, now in a nicer font.

## The order

Positioning first, because everything else depends on the decision. Messaging second, because it carries the decision into words. Branding third, or in parallel with messaging, because the identity should express the position rather than precede it.

Companies routinely do this backward. They commission a brand refresh because the site "feels dated," write new copy to fit the new design, and never revisit the positioning that was the actual problem. Six months later the marketing still is not landing, now in a nicer font.

The order also explains why brand work is not wasted when it comes last. Memory structures take years to build, so a brand that encodes the wrong position is expensive to unwind. Building it on a settled position means the recognition it earns points at the right buyer and the right buying situations.

## A quick diagnostic

Ask five people in the company to write one sentence: we help [who] do [what] instead of [alternative]. If the sentences differ, the problem is positioning. If they agree and the website does not say it plainly, the problem is messaging. If the website says it plainly and the company is still forgettable or inconsistent, the problem is branding.

| Result of the five-sentence test | Broken layer | First fix | Relative cost |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The sentences name different buyers or alternatives | Positioning | A positioning workshop, ending in a written decision | Low: time from senior people |
| The sentences agree, the site does not say it | Messaging | Rewrite from customer calls and objection logs | Low: about a week of writing |
| The site says it, buyers still forget or confuse you | Branding | A design and identity project built on the position | Higher: external design spend |

Fix in that order. Positioning is a workshop and a decision. Messaging is a week of writing from customer evidence. Branding is a design project. Only the last one costs much money, and it is the one least likely to be the problem. If the problem turns out to be in a pitch deck rather than the website, [The story isn't landing](https://lowob.com/research/the-story-isnt-landing/) applies the same logic to investors.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the buyer and competitive alternative before polishing copy.** Positioning is the decision everything else carries.
- **Make the message explain the position clearly.** Use the buyer's words, state the change, match proof to doubts.
- **Let the visual identity reinforce a decision already made.** In B2B, brand mostly works through memory when buyers enter the market.
- **Diagnose before spending.** The five-sentence test costs an afternoon; a rebrand costs months.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between positioning and messaging?

Positioning is the decision about which buyer you serve, which problem you solve and which alternative you replace. Messaging is the set of words that makes that decision land on the website, in sales calls and in content.

### What is the difference between branding and positioning?

Positioning decides where the company sits in the buyer's mind. Branding is the system of name, identity, tone and behaviour that makes the company recognisable and remembered. The brand should express the position, not precede it.

### Should a startup rebrand if marketing is not working?

Usually not first. Test positioning and messaging before commissioning design. If five people in the company describe different customers, a rebrand will not fix it.

### In what order should you fix positioning, messaging and branding?

Positioning first, messaging second, branding third or in parallel with messaging. Each depends on the one before it.

## Sources and notes

- [April Dunford, Understanding the Job of a Market Category](https://aprildunford.substack.com/p/understanding-the-job-of-a-market), 11 January 2024. Practitioner's newsletter; method and opinion, not data.
- [Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Advertising effectiveness and the 95-5 rule: most B2B buyers are not in the market right now](https://marketingscience.info/news-and-insights/advertising-effectiveness-and-the-95-5-rule-most-b2b-buyers-are-not-in-the-market-right-now), John Dawes, May 2021. Produced for LinkedIn's B2B Institute; in-market share is an estimate from replacement cycles.
- [LinkedIn B2B Institute, Category Entry Points in B2B](https://business.linkedin.com/advertise/resources/b2b-institute/cep-in-b2b). Written by Jenni Romaniuk with the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute; method guide; LinkedIn sells B2B advertising.
- [Gartner, 61% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free buying experience](https://gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-06-25-gartner-sales-survey-finds-61-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-buying-experience), 25 June 2025. Survey of 632 B2B buyers, August to September 2024.

Ask five people in the company, separately, to finish the sentence "we help [who] do [what] instead of [alternative]" this week. Compare the answers before you approve any copy or design work.

# The User Story Before the Token Story

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Write what the protocol does for a user in one sentence with no token in it; if you cannot, you have an instrument, not a product. Then give each audience one belief and one piece of evidence, and keep a claims register with no yield numbers, no 'safe' and every audit named and dated. MiCA and the SEC's 2026 interpretation both make public claims part of the legal record.

Write what the protocol does for a user in one sentence with no token in it. If you cannot, you have an instrument, not a product. Then give each audience one belief and one piece of evidence, and keep a claims register that survives both an audit and a narrative rotation: no yield numbers, no "safe", every audit named and dated. Regulators now read the same claims: MiCA requires marketing to be fair, clear, not misleading and consistent with the white paper, and the SEC's 2026 interpretation turns on what a team promised in public.

*This is not legal advice. Claims rules are jurisdiction-specific; get your own counsel.*

## The token collapses your audiences

[One truth, three audiences](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/) set the rule: one product truth, a belief per audience. Crypto makes that harder because the token merges the audiences into a single word.

A holder may be an investor, a community member and a customer at the same time. Each wants something different. The investor wants a business. The customer wants a thing that works. The community member wants a reason to stay.

When the deck leads with the token, each reader filters it through their own need, and none of them is satisfied. The token story drowns the product story because it is louder and easier to write. So the order matters. Product truth first. Token second. Always. Our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers the general method; this is the crypto edition.

## One sentence, no token

Write what the protocol does for a user. One sentence. The token is not allowed in it.

The shape is simple: this lets a certain kind of user do a certain thing, without a certain cost or dependency. If you cannot write it, you do not have a product yet. You have an instrument. Some projects are instruments, and that is fine, but say so and position accordingly.

Test the sentence on someone who has never read your docs. If their first question is "and what is the token for", good. That is the second sentence, not the first.

The sentence also does legal work. The SEC and CFTC interpretation of March 2026 treats a token whose value depends on a network's programmatic functioning differently from one sold with promises of an issuer's managerial efforts, and Chairman Atkins said promises that create reliance "must be explicit and unambiguous". A team whose first sentence is about price is making a promise about price. A team whose first sentence is about a user is describing a product.

## A belief per audience

Each audience needs one belief and one piece of evidence.

| Audience | What they need to believe | What proves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Users | It works and I can exit | Live app, withdrawals working in normal and stressed weeks, a status page that tells the truth |
| Integrators and allocators | Safe to build on or deploy into | Current docs, named and dated audits, incident history, a plain risk page |
| Holders | The token has a job | A written description of what the token does in the system, and what it does not |
| Investors | There is a business under the token | Fees retained, costs, who pays and why |

Notice the holder row. "The token has a job" is a product claim, not a price claim. If the only job is "goes up", you do not have a belief. You have a hope. Our piece on [token or no token](https://lowob.com/research/token-or-no-token/) covers what to do about that, and [protocol revenue](https://lowob.com/research/protocol-revenue-fees-real-yield-and-what-to-report/) covers the investor row's numbers.

The integrator row carries the heaviest evidence burden, because the downside is concrete. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025. An allocator reading "audited by leading firms" with no names, scopes or dates has learned nothing, and will assume the worst.

## The claims register, crypto edition

One truth, three audiences introduced the claims register: every public claim, its evidence, its owner, its date. Crypto adds hard lines.

| Rule | Why | Where regulators already draw the line |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No yield numbers in marketing: not "up to", not "historical", not a screenshot | Yields change daily and read as a promise | MiCA Article 6 bars white-paper assertions on future value and requires a statement that the token may lose value in part or in full |
| No "safe", "secure", "risk-free" or "guaranteed" | If legal would not sign the word, it is a liability | MiCA Article 7 and the UK FCA both require promotions to be fair, clear and not misleading |
| Audits named: firm, scope, date, link; unaudited components listed | "Audited by leading firms" is a claim with no evidence | Allocators' diligence asks for exactly this |
| Deprecated docs removed, not banner-archived | Stale docs are how an integrator deploys against a contract you retired | MiCA Article 7 requires marketing consistent with the white paper; old docs are public claims too |
| Every number has an owner and a date | If nobody owns it, nobody corrects it | The SEC's 2026 interpretation weighs who said what, when and in which medium |

If nobody owns a claim, it comes down. In the UK, crypto promotions to consumers have been regulated since 8 October 2023 and must carry specific risk warnings; a promotion made outside the permitted routes can be a criminal offence. In the EU, MiCA Article 7 also requires marketing to be clearly identifiable as such and bars it before a required white paper is published.

> If legal would not sign the word, do not post it.

## Vocabulary and chain choice

Docs, app and deck must use the same names for the same things. "Vault" in the docs, "pool" in the app and "strategy" in the deck reads as three products. An allocator will assume you have three teams who do not talk.

Keep a glossary. One owner. When a name changes, it changes everywhere in the same week.

Chain choice is also a positioning statement, whether you intended it or not. Where you deploy picks your users, your integrators, your liquidity sources and your grant counterparties. Say why in one line. "We are here because our users are here" is positioning. "We are multi-chain" with no primary home is the absence of positioning. In the EU, the choice of venue and custody partner now also carries a regulatory test: since MiCA's transitional period ended on 1 July 2026, ESMA expects unauthorised service providers to stop onboarding and marketing to EU clients.

## The narrative trap

Labels rotate: RWA, AI, restaking and whatever is next. A label gets you attention this quarter and makes you a casualty of the rotation the quarter after.

The product truth must not contain the label. Use the label as a door people walk through, not as the foundation they stand on. If the only reason someone would use the protocol is the category it sits in, the protocol is the category's hostage.

Test it the same way as the token. Remove the label from the homepage. Check whether the first sentence still describes something a user wants. Our piece on [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/) covers the evidence that survives a rotation: named users, dated outcomes, numbers with owners.

Gateway card

### Before the next deck, page or post goes out

- One sentence describing what the protocol does for a user, with no token in it
- One belief and one piece of evidence each for users, integrators and allocators, holders and investors
- Claims register live: no yields, no "safe", every audit named, scoped and dated
- Deprecated docs removed, not banner-archived
- One glossary; docs, app and deck use identical names
- One line explaining the chain choice, and a homepage that still makes sense without this quarter's label

## lowob takeaways

- **Product first, token second.** The token merges your audiences; the user sentence separates them again.
- **One belief per audience.** Each with one piece of evidence that a sceptic can check.
- **Hard lines in the register.** No yields, no "safe", audits named and dated, every number owned.
- **Claims are legal facts.** In the EU and US, what you say in public shapes how the token is treated.

## Common questions

### How should a crypto project explain itself without leading with the token?

Write one sentence describing what the protocol lets a certain user do, without a certain cost or dependency, with no token in it. The token's purpose is the second sentence.

### What should a crypto protocol avoid saying in marketing?

Yield numbers, including "up to" or historical figures, and words like "safe", "secure", "risk-free" or "guaranteed". MiCA and the UK FCA require crypto marketing to be fair, clear and not misleading, and vague claims such as "audited by leading firms" are a liability.

### What do integrators and allocators need to see before using a protocol?

Current docs, named and dated audits with their scope, a list of unaudited components, incident history and a plain risk page.

### Does MiCA regulate crypto marketing?

Yes. Article 7 requires marketing communications to be clearly identifiable, fair, clear and not misleading, consistent with the white paper, and not issued before a required white paper is published.

## Sources and notes

- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 7, marketing communications](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-7-marketing-communications). EU regulation text.
- [ESMA, Interactive single rulebook: MiCA Article 6, content and form of the white paper](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-and-data/interactive-single-rulebook/mica/article-6-content-and-form-crypto-asset). EU regulation text.

- [US Securities and Exchange Commission, Chairman Atkins, Regulation Crypto Assets: a token safe harbor](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/speeches-statements/atkins-remarks-regulation-crypto-assets-031726), 17 March 2026. Speech; the Chairman's views, not a rule.
- [Sullivan & Cromwell, SEC clarifies application of securities laws to crypto assets](https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/March/SEC-Clarifies-Application-Securities-Laws-Crypto-Assets), 19 March 2026. Law-firm reading of the interpretation; not legal advice.

# What Is a Distribution Diagnostic? One Week, Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-distribution-diagnostic/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A distribution diagnostic is a short, paid, scoped piece of work that answers which channels can carry a product to its buyer, what each costs, and where the next serious money should go. It has a fixed duration, price and written output, runs small real tests, and carries no obligation to continue. A week can show whether a channel is open and converts at all; it cannot replace the four to six weeks platforms recommend for a controlled experiment.

A distribution diagnostic is a short, paid, scoped piece of work that answers which channels can carry a product to its buyer, what each costs, and where the next serious money should go. It has a fixed duration, price and written output, runs small real tests, and carries no obligation to continue. It differs from the free alternatives because someone pays for it: the European agency association found an average new-business pitch costs an agency about €43,800, and that cost is recovered in the engagement that follows. A week can show whether a channel is open and converts at all. It cannot replace the four to six weeks Google recommends for a controlled experiment.

Companies are offered "audits", "assessments", "discovery" and "free strategy sessions" constantly. Most are sales conversations with a document attached. A diagnostic is a different thing, and the difference is worth understanding before paying for one, or accepting a free one.

## The definition

A distribution diagnostic is a short, paid, scoped piece of work that answers a specific question: which channels can carry this product to its buyer, what does each one cost, and where should the next serious money go. It has a fixed duration, a fixed price, a written output, and no obligation to continue.

We sell one as the Sounding, a one-week paid distribution diagnostic. The mechanics below are the ones we use, and they are the ones a company can use to evaluate anyone else's.

## What it includes

**A band map.** For each channel and geography that matters, whether the platform carries the category openly, with conditions, or not at all, and what any conditions require. Written down, so it can be argued with.

**A read of what exists.** The current tracking, the accounts, the data, the content, the partner relationships, and the claims the company can substantiate. Not an audit of everything, but enough to know what a channel test can be built on.

**Two or three small tests, run in parallel.** Each in an open-band channel, each with a written question and a threshold, each with tracking the company controls, each funded modestly. A week is long enough to learn whether a channel is open, whether it converts at all, and roughly what an outcome costs at small scale.

**A written answer.** Which channel read, which did not, what each cost, what was ruled out and why, and what the next step should be, priced. The ruled-out list is the most durable page, because it stops the same arguments recurring every quarter.

| Band | What it means | Example of what the map records | What the diagnostic does with it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Open | The platform carries the category under its standard rules | Normal ad review, no certification | Candidate for a test this week |
| Conditional | Allowed with certification, licensing or country limits | Google certification plus a local licence for crypto exchange ads in a named country | Records the conditions and lead time; tests only if already met |
| Closed | The platform does not carry the category, or not in this market | No permitted route for the product in that country | Ruled out in writing, with the reason |

The band map is not a one-off. Platform rules move. Google's cryptocurrency policy, for example, permitted exchange and software wallet ads in Argentina from September 2025 for advertisers on the national securities regulator's registry and certified by Google, and in Indonesia from February 2026 for advertisers licensed by the Financial Services Authority. A map dated six months ago can be wrong in both directions, which is why it is written down with a date. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how the conditional band works.

## What one week cannot tell you

Long-run customer value. Seasonal effects. How a channel behaves at ten times the volume. Whether a restricted-band approval will arrive. Whether a partner programme will produce in month six what it produced in week one.

A diagnostic that claims to answer those questions is overselling. What it can do is close the question of where the next dollar goes, which is more than most companies know when they spend it.

The platforms say the same about their own tests. Google's guidance for Google Ads experiments recommends running them for at least four to six weeks, longer where there is a long conversion delay, and waiting one to two conversion cycles before reading the result. A one-week test is therefore a read, not a controlled experiment. It answers "is this channel open, and does it convert at all at a cost worth pursuing", and it hands the controlled comparison to the next step. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers sample sizes and holdouts for that next step, and [A $10,000 test that closes a question beats a $10,000 bet that leaves it open](https://lowob.com/research/tests-that-close-questions/) makes the case for writing the question before the test starts.

> A provider who offers all of that is selling you an answer. A provider who offers it free is selling you the engagement that follows.

## How it differs from the alternatives

**A free proposal** is a sales document. Its cost is recovered in the engagement that follows, and its recommendations are shaped by what the provider wants to sell. It has no defined end and no obligation on the provider to be right. The cost is real: the European Association of Communications Agencies surveyed 412 agencies in 2025 and found the average new-business pitch cost about €43,800, with teams of five to eight people contributing more than 44 hours each.

**An audit** reviews what exists and lists what is wrong. Useful, but it does not test anything, so it produces opinions about channels rather than evidence from them.

**A strategy engagement** produces a plan, usually over several weeks, at consultancy rates, and leaves execution to someone else. Valuable for large, complex questions; oversized for "which channel should we try first".

|  | Free proposal | Audit | Strategy engagement | Distribution diagnostic |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Paid | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Defined end | No | Usually | Yes, after several weeks | Yes, fixed |
| Tests channels | No | No | Rarely | Yes, two or three small tests |
| Output | Pitch for the next engagement | List of problems | A plan | A written answer, ruled-out list and priced next step |
| Obligation on the provider to be right | None | Limited | On the analysis | On the answer it writes down |

A diagnostic is smaller than a strategy engagement, more evidence-based than an audit, and, because it is paid and scoped, more honest than a free proposal.

## What to insist on

A fixed price and a fixed end date. A written question the work will answer. Tracking in your own name. Small real tests rather than desk research alone. A written output you can act on without hiring the provider. And the next step priced in the same document, so you know what continuing would cost before you decide whether to.

Tracking in your own name matters more than it sounds. If the test runs in the provider's ad account or analytics property, the evidence leaves when they do. Our piece [Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) lists the accounts to own, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to turn a test's cost per outcome into a budget ceiling for the next quarter.

A provider who offers all of that is selling you an answer. A provider who offers it free is selling you the engagement that follows.

A distribution diagnostic is a paid, scoped week that maps which channels can carry your product, tests the likely ones cheaply, and tells you in writing where the next dollar should go. It cannot tell you the voyage's earnings. It can tell you whether there is water under the hull.

## lowob takeaways

- **Ask for the four parts.** A band map, a read of existing assets, two or three small parallel tests, and a written answer.
- **Date the band map.** Platform rules change by country and by quarter.
- **Treat a week as a read.** It closes "where does the next dollar go", not long-run value or scale.
- **Own the evidence.** Fixed price and end date, tracking in your name, and the next step priced in the same document.

## Common questions

### What is a distribution diagnostic?

A short, paid, scoped assessment of which channels can carry a product to its buyer, what each costs, and where the next serious money should go, with a fixed duration, fixed price, written output and no obligation to continue.

### How is a distribution diagnostic different from a marketing audit?

An audit reviews what exists and lists what is wrong but tests nothing, so it gives opinions about channels. A diagnostic runs small real tests and gives evidence.

### How long should a marketing channel test run?

Long enough to answer its question. A week can show whether a channel is open and converts at all. For a controlled comparison, Google recommends at least four to six weeks, and longer with a long conversion delay.

### Should I accept a free strategy proposal from an agency?

A free proposal is a sales document shaped by what the provider wants to sell, with no defined end and no obligation to be right. A provider who offers it free is selling the engagement that follows.

- [Google Ads Help, Experiments FAQs](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/13826584?hl=en). Platform guidance on experiment duration and conversion cycles; written for Google Ads experiments, not every channel.
- [Google Ads, Updates to Cryptocurrencies and related products policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16560115?hl=en), September 2025. Platform policy notice for Argentina.
- [Google Ads, Updates to Financial products and services policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16885619?hl=en), February 2026. Platform policy notice covering crypto exchange and wallet ads in Indonesia.
- [EACA, Europe's billion euro pitching problem](https://eaca.eu/eaca-cost-of-pitching-2025/), 11 June 2025. Trade-association survey of 412 member agencies; self-reported costs.

Write the one question you would want a diagnostic to answer, then list your channels and mark each open, conditional or closed for your category and countries. Any channel you cannot mark is the first thing to find out.

# AI Did Not Fix Your Marketing. It Made Your Mediocrity Cheaper.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/ai-made-average-marketing-cheaper/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-05-03 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: When every company has the same models, production speed stops being an advantage and the scarce inputs become judgment, access, evidence and a point of view. Research shows AI help makes individual work better but collective work more alike, and marketers credit AI with speed far more than quality. The fix is a proprietary-input test before publishing and a point-of-view ledger that feeds the calendar.

The easiest thing to do with AI is produce more, and it is the least interesting. When every company has capable models, production speed stops being an advantage; the scarce inputs become judgment, access, evidence and a point of view. A 2024 Science Advances study found AI ideas made individual stories better but made the stories more similar to one another, and B2B marketers credit AI with speed (78%) far more than quality (17%). If the input is public consensus, the output will be polished consensus.

More posts. More emails. More landing pages. More summaries. More variations of the same announcement with slightly different verbs.

When every company has access to capable models, production speed stops being a meaningful advantage. The scarce inputs become judgment, access, taste, evidence and a point of view worth remembering. AI can lower the cost of expression. It cannot manufacture a reason for an audience to care.

This is why many AI-enabled content programmes feel strangely lifeless. The sentences are clean. The structure is competent. The output is technically correct. Yet nothing in the piece could only have come from that company.

## Why AI content converges

There is now direct evidence for what readers sense. Anil Doshi and Oliver Hauser ran an experiment, published in Science Advances in 2024, in which 300 writers produced short stories, some with access to AI-generated ideas, and 600 people rated them. Writers with the most AI access produced stories rated 8.1% higher for novelty. Less creative writers gained most: with five AI ideas, their stories improved by 10.7% on novelty and 11.5% on usefulness. But stories written with one AI idea were 10.7% more similar to each other than those written without.

That is the whole problem in one result. Each piece gets better. The set gets more alike. A company that adopts AI drafting improves its own average and moves closer to everyone else's.

The market pressure runs in the same direction. In the 2026 Content Marketing Institute and MarketingProfs survey of 861 B2B marketers, 65% said they had faced more pressure to produce content faster in the previous 12 months. Asked what AI contributed, 78% said speed, 59% efficiency and 44% volume; 22% said innovation and 17% quality. Among those under pressure, 35% reported burnout or creative fatigue.

| What AI changes | What it does not change |
| --- | --- |
| Cost of a draft | Cost of a reader's attention |
| Time to publish | Whether there is anything new to say |
| Quality of an individual piece | Distinctiveness of the set |
| Volume a team can ship | Evidence the team holds |

## The five symptoms of AI-mediated sameness

You can usually recognise average AI content before finishing the first paragraph.

It begins with an inflated statement about a changing landscape. It explains obvious background to an audience that already understands it. It presents five interchangeable best practices. It avoids a defensible opinion. It concludes that the future is exciting and organisations should adapt.

The problem is not that a model wrote the sentences. The problem is that the company supplied no proprietary material.

Search engines have reached the same conclusion. Google's helpful content guidance asks whether a page provides "original information, reporting, research, or analysis", and lists as a warning sign "using extensive automation to produce content on many topics". Its July 2026 guide to AI search asks for "unique expert or experienced takes that go beyond common knowledge". Content that any company could have produced is the content both readers and engines can do without.

> If the input is public consensus, the output will be polished consensus.

## The new content advantage

The strongest content systems begin with assets that cannot be generated from the public internet alone:

- direct customer conversations
- original data or structured market observations
- an operator's experience of what actually failed
- access to founders, buyers, creators and partners
- a repeatable analytical framework
- a clear belief about where the market is wrong.

AI can then help organise, compare, challenge, adapt and distribute those assets. That is a meaningful division of labour. It preserves the part that creates value and accelerates the work surrounding it.

| Humans should own | AI can accelerate |
| --- | --- |
| The thesis | Transcript analysis and theme extraction |
| Source relationships and interviews | Counterarguments to the thesis |
| Judgment and risk decisions | Outline variants and headline exploration |
| Examples and their accuracy | Channel adaptation |
| Voice and final approval | Editorial QA and archive retrieval |

Consider a founder interview. The valuable asset is not a model-generated article about "five trends in fintech". It is the founder explaining why three enterprise pilots stalled, what buyers misunderstood and what finally changed the sales process. AI can identify themes across the transcript, compare the account stories, propose a structure and produce channel variants. The substance still comes from lived commercial evidence. Our piece on the [founder interview content engine](https://lowob.com/research/founder-interview-content-engine/) sets out the method.

## The proprietary-input test

Before publishing, ask one question:

*What is present in this piece that another competent company could not produce by entering the same topic into the same model?*

If the answer is nothing, the draft is not finished. Add one or more of the following:

1. A specific observation from the market.
2. A decision framework with named variables.
3. A real example with enough detail to be useful.
4. A counterintuitive position the company can defend.
5. A tool the reader can apply immediately.

The test is cheap to run. Give the draft's title to a general-purpose model with no other context and compare the two. Whatever survives in yours and is missing from the model's is the proprietary content. If very little survives, that is the finding. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) adds the other half of the brief: who reads it and what they decide.

## Build a point-of-view ledger

Most companies maintain a content calendar. Fewer maintain a record of what they actually believe.

Create a point-of-view ledger with five fields:

| Field | Question it answers |
| --- | --- |
| Market belief | What do we think is changing? |
| Consensus view | What does the market normally say? |
| Our disagreement | Where do we see it differently? |
| Evidence | What have we observed that supports the position? |
| Implication | What should a founder or buyer do differently? |

This ledger should feed the content calendar. Without it, the team is scheduling formats before identifying ideas. Each entry is a small [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/): it has an owner, a date and evidence, and it can be revised when the evidence changes. Over a year, the ledger shows which positions held and which did not, which is itself content no competitor can copy.

## Measure recognition, not production

AI makes word count and post frequency easier to inflate, which makes them even less useful as measures of quality. Look instead for signals of recognition and consequence.

| Signal | How to record it |
| --- | --- |
| The right people share the piece with their own commentary | Log shares by named target accounts and partners |
| Prospects repeat the framing in sales conversations | Tag call notes where a buyer uses the firm's language |
| Partners ask the team to brief them on the topic | Count inbound briefing requests per quarter |
| Readers save templates or return to related pieces | Downloads and return visits on tool pages |
| The content creates qualified conversations | First meetings where the buyer cites a piece |

The goal is not to prove that the company can publish every day. The goal is to become associated with a valuable way of seeing the market. Our piece [Thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) covers how to turn that association into pipeline.

AI is an extraordinary production and analysis layer. But when it is used to avoid the harder work of developing judgment, it allows a company to become forgettable at higher speed. The AI content advantage is not more content. It is extracting more value from insight that only your company can provide.

## lowob takeaways

- **Better pieces, more alike.** AI raises individual quality and lowers collective distinctiveness.
- **Supply proprietary material.** Conversations, data, failures and a stated disagreement with consensus.
- **Run the proprietary-input test.** Compare the draft with what a bare model produces from the title.
- **Keep a point-of-view ledger.** Beliefs, evidence and implications feed the calendar, not the reverse.

## Common questions

### Why does AI-generated marketing content all sound the same?

Models produce the most likely text from the input they are given. If the input is public consensus, the output converges. A 2024 study found AI ideas made stories 10.7% more similar to each other.

### Does Google penalise AI-generated content?

Google targets content made primarily to manipulate rankings, including mass-produced pages, whoever or whatever wrote it. Its guidance rewards original information, research or analysis and flags extensive automation across many topics.

### How do you make AI content stand out?

Feed it material competitors do not have: customer conversations, original data, operator experience and a defensible position. Then test whether the draft contains anything a bare model would not produce from the same title.

### What is a point-of-view ledger?

A record of what the company believes is changing, the consensus view, where it disagrees, the evidence, and what a buyer should do differently. It feeds the content calendar.

## Sources and notes

- [Doshi and Hauser, Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content, via ScienceDaily](https://sciencedaily.com/releases/2024/07/240712222127.htm), July 2024. Summary of a Science Advances paper (DOI 10.1126/sciadv.adn5290); 300 writers and 600 raters; short fiction, not marketing.
- [Content Marketing Institute, B2B content and marketing trends research](https://contentmarketinginstitute.com/articles/b2b-content-marketing-trends-research), November 2026. CMI and MarketingProfs survey of 861 B2B marketers, June to August 2026; self-reported.
- [Google Search Central, Creating helpful, reliable, people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content), last updated 5 October 2026. Google's own guidance.
- [Google Search Central, Optimizing your website for generative AI features on Google Search](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/ai-optimization-guide), last updated 10 July 2026. Google's own guidance.
- The division-of-labour table, the proprietary-input test and the point-of-view ledger are **lowob**'s framework.

Take the last three pieces your team published. Give each title to a general-purpose model with no other context, compare the outputs with what you shipped, and write one line per piece naming what only you could have said.

# Thin Bidding: The Cheapest Attention Is Wherever Nobody Else Is Buying.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/thin-bidding/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-30 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: The first cause of what a click costs is crowding: how many companies bid for the same person at the same moment. Alphabet, Amazon and Meta take about 56% of global ad spend, and the crowd follows them. Bidding thins where channels are unglamorous, inconvenient or closed to a category, and thin channels reward buyers who measure before they commit.

Ask a media buyer why a click costs what it costs and you will hear about audiences, creative and relevance scores. All of that is true, and none of it is the first cause. The first cause is the number of companies bidding for the same person's attention at the same moment. Where the crowd is thick, attention is expensive; where it is thin, attention is cheap, whether or not anyone has noticed. WARC estimates Alphabet, Amazon and Meta took 56.1% of global ad spend outside China in 2025. Look where few look, and measure before you commit.

That is the whole idea behind how we choose channels, and it is simple enough to put in one sentence: look where few look.

## Why the crowd gathers in the same place

Companies buy where the buying is easy. The large platforms made a specific bet: give any company with a credit card a self-serve interface, an audience of billions and instant reporting, and the bidding will take care of itself. It did. The convenience is real, and so is the price it produces.

The concentration is measurable. WARC's December 2025 forecast put Alphabet, Amazon and Meta at 56.1% of global advertising spend outside China in 2025, about $556.6 billion, rising to 58.0% in 2026 and 58.8% in 2027. WARC expected the three to absorb the vast majority of incremental ad spend over that period. When most new money goes to the same few auctions, the same few auctions get more crowded.

The price follows. Meta reported that in the third quarter of 2026 its ad impressions rose 10% year on year while the average price per ad rose 14%. Price per ad also reflects ad performance, format and geographic mix, so the figure is not a pure measure of crowding. But price rising faster than supply is also what a crowded auction looks like from the outside.

The result is a market in which most marketing budgets compete in the same three or four auctions, against the same well-funded companies, for the same scroll. In that market, the buyer with the largest budget or the most patient investors wins, and everyone else pays a premium to be visible for a moment.

## Where the bidding thins out

Bidding thins for three reasons, and only one of them is that a channel is bad.

| Why bidding thins | Typical channels | What it asks of the buyer | How to read it |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The channel is unglamorous | Affiliate programmes, comparison sites, maintained email lists, niche newsletters, mid-sized creators with buying audiences | Patience with small volumes and plain reporting | Cost per outcome in your own systems |
| The channel is inconvenient | Anything that requires recruiting people rather than uploading a file, or six weeks to stand up rather than six minutes | Operational work most competitors will not do | Outcome per hour of setup, as well as per dollar |
| The platforms said no to the category | Affiliate and creator networks, programmatic inventory and publishers that carry restricted categories | Compliance work and a claims library | Delivery and outcome by source, against the platform you cannot use |

**The channel is unglamorous.** None of the first row makes a good slide. All of it is priced accordingly.

**The channel is inconvenient.** It reports in spreadsheets rather than dashboards. Inconvenience is a form of thin bidding, because most companies will not do the work.

**The platforms said no to the category.** This is the one that matters most to the companies we work with. Google Ads, for example, requires certification for crypto exchanges and software wallets, approves them only in listed countries, and prohibits initial coin offerings and DeFi trading protocols outright. Roku's Ads Manager requires prior approval for any crypto ad, limits approvals to the US, and bans ads for individual securities. When a platform restricts a category, the well-funded competitors who would otherwise crowd the open channels are stuck in the same review queue. The affiliate networks, creator networks and programmatic inventory that carry those categories are thinly bid, not because they do not work, but because the platforms that would have made them unnecessary said no. Our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) maps that open band in more detail.

> The channels your category can actually use are usually the ones your competitors have written off, which is precisely why they are worth measuring first.

## Thin is not the same as cheap

There is a trap in the idea, and it is worth naming. The cheapest inventory in advertising is the open programmatic exchange, and much of it is cheap for a reason. The ANA's 2023 study found made-for-advertising sites, pages built to host ads and filled with bought traffic, took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend in its sample. That inventory is not thinly bid attention. It is barely attention at all.

Thin bidding means a real audience that few competitors are paying to reach. A personal-finance newsletter with, say, 40,000 engaged readers and three sponsors is thinly bid. A page of scraped content with twelve ad slots is cheap. The test that separates them is the same in both cases: did anything happen that your own systems can see? Our pieces on [programmatic numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) and [ad fraud](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ad-fraud/) cover how to tell a low price from a low-value impression.

## The discipline that makes it work

Cheap attention is only valuable if you can tell whether it did anything. Thin bidding without measurement is just a smaller invoice.

So the method has two halves that have to be held together. Measure cheaply, in several places at once, before committing anything. Then, when a channel reads, put everything behind it. Companies that only do the first half end up with a portfolio of half-run experiments. Companies that only do the second half are back in the crowded auction, having skipped the part where they found out.

| Half | What it means | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Measure cheaply, in several places | Small, simultaneous tests with tracking the company controls and a decision written in advance | Tests too small to read, or measured on clicks |
| Commit when a channel reads | Move budget decisively to the channel with the best cost per outcome | Spreading budget evenly to avoid choosing |

Thin channels make the first half harder, because volumes are small. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) sets out the sample sizes a test needs at B2B volumes, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) shows how to set a cost-per-outcome ceiling before the first dollar goes out, so a channel that reads can be scaled without a second debate.

## What this looks like in practice

The answer is not always the obscure channel. Sometimes the crowded auction is worth its price. The point is that the decision is made on a measurement rather than on convenience.

Illustrative example: letting the measurement choose

Decision
:   Before consolidating spend onto the largest platform, run a one-week measurement across the three channels competitors were ignoring, with tracking the company controlled.

Reason and owner
:   A noisy fintech company was spending across six channels and could not say which one produced a customer. The instinct was to consolidate onto the platform with the best reporting. Owned by the growth lead.

What changed
:   Two of the three ignored channels produced nothing readable. One niche publisher produced funded accounts at a lower cost than the main platform and was scaled. The main platform stayed in the mix, now judged on the same outcome.

Illustrative: a composite of a mid-size consumer fintech, built from patterns across engagements.

The price of attention is a crowding effect. The channels your category can actually use are usually the ones your competitors have written off, which is precisely why they are worth measuring first.

## lowob takeaways

- **Price is crowding.** The number of bidders sets the cost of attention before creative or targeting do.
- **The crowd is concentrated.** Three platforms take most global ad spend and most of its growth.
- **Thin channels are unglamorous, inconvenient or closed to rivals.** All three can be opportunities.
- **Thin is not cheap.** Low-priced inventory with no real audience is waste, not opportunity.
- **Measure, then commit.** Small tests in several places, then decisive budget behind the one that reads.

## Common questions

### Why are online ads getting more expensive?

Mostly because more advertisers bid for the same audiences in the same few auctions. WARC estimates Alphabet, Amazon and Meta took 56.1% of global ad spend outside China in 2025, and Meta's average price per ad rose 14% year on year in Q3 2026.

### What are underpriced marketing channels?

Channels where few competitors bid: affiliate programmes, comparison sites, niche newsletters, mid-sized creators and, for restricted categories, publishers and networks the large platforms do not replace. Each has to be measured on outcomes before it is scaled.

### Where can crypto and fintech companies advertise if platforms restrict them?

Often through affiliate and creator networks, programmatic inventory and publishers that accept the category, subject to their own policies. Google and Roku, for example, allow some crypto advertising only with certification or prior approval, and only in listed markets.

### Is cheap inventory the same as an underpriced channel?

No. Much cheap programmatic inventory sits on made-for-advertising sites with no real audience. An underpriced channel has a real audience that few competitors are paying to reach.

# Brand vs Performance Marketing: Different Time Horizons

Source: https://lowob.com/research/brand-vs-performance-marketing/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-29 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Brand and performance marketing are not rivals; they work on different clocks. Performance buys measurable outcomes now, while brand makes future outcomes more likely and cheaper. The IPA evidence puts the long-run optimum near 60:40 brand to activation for consumer brands and 46:54 in B2B. Most small companies should fund performance first, then shift a growing share toward brand, measuring each on its own timescale.

Brand and performance marketing are not rivals; they work on different clocks. Performance buys measurable outcomes now. Brand makes future outcomes more likely and cheaper. The best-known evidence, Binet and Field's analysis of IPA effectiveness cases, puts the long-run optimum near 60% brand and 40% activation for consumer brands, and 46:54 in B2B. Most small companies cannot start there. They should fund performance first, then shift a growing share toward brand as revenue allows, measuring each on its own timescale.

Marketing teams have argued about brand versus performance for as long as both words have existed. The argument is real, but it is mostly about time.

## The two, defined

**Performance marketing** is spending aimed at a measurable outcome in a short window: a click, a lead, an account, a purchase, attributed to the spend that produced it. It is judged in days or weeks, on cost per outcome. Its tools are the auction platforms, affiliate, creator programmes on cost-per-outcome terms, programmatic optimised to conversions. Our piece on [performance marketing as a way of paying](https://lowob.com/research/performance-marketing-way-of-paying/) sets out when those terms hold.

**Brand marketing** is spending aimed at changing what people know, believe or feel about the company, so that future outcomes become more likely and cheaper. It is judged over months or years, on recall, consideration, preference and, eventually, on the falling cost of performance marketing. Its tools are content, earned media, events, sponsorship, design, consistent presence and advertising that explains rather than asks.

|  | Performance | Brand |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aim | An outcome now | More likely and cheaper outcomes later |
| Audience | People in the market | Future buyers, most of whom are not in the market |
| Clock | Days to weeks | Months to years |
| Primary measure | Cost per outcome against customer value | Branded search, share of search, recall, the trend in cost per outcome |
| Typical tools | Search, paid social, affiliate, creator CPA deals | Content, earned media, events, sponsorship, explanatory advertising |
| Failure mode | Rising cost per outcome as easy customers run out | Spend nobody can connect to revenue |

## Why they look like rivals

They compete for the same budget and report on different clocks. In any given quarter, performance marketing can show what it produced and brand marketing cannot. The finance team, reasonably, funds what it can see.

Binet and Field's work on the IPA Databank, the UK's archive of effectiveness award entries, shows why the clocks differ. In their analysis, rational, activation-style messaging produced a large direct sales effect that "decays quickly"; emotional brand priming produced a smaller effect that decayed slowly and built over time. The share of emotional campaigns reporting very large profit effects rose from 13% at one year to 30% at two years and 43% at three or more. For rational campaigns the figures were 10%, 20% and 23%. A quarterly report will always favour activation.

Over several quarters, the reverse problem appears. Performance marketing on its own gets more expensive: the easiest customers are found first, the auctions get more crowded, and the company is buying every customer from scratch because nobody has heard of it. The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work that was not done.

> The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work that was not done.

## How they interact

Brand lowers the cost of performance. People who recognise a company click more, convert more and cost less to acquire. Binet and Field's B2B summary makes the same point: brand memories make later activation more effective, which is why brand results need a longer measurement window. Their consumer analysis also found brands with more very large brand effects saw larger reductions in price sensitivity.

The mechanism is reach into future demand. The Ehrenberg-Bass Institute's John Dawes estimates that only about 5% of business buyers are in the market for a typical category in a given quarter, derived from companies changing key suppliers roughly once every five years. Performance marketing competes for the 5%. Brand work reaches the 95% who will be in the market later, so the company is familiar when they arrive.

Performance funds brand. Without a working acquisition engine, there is no revenue to invest in the slow work.

And performance generates the evidence brand needs. The language customers respond to, the objections that stop them, the segments that convert: these come from the performance side and should inform what the brand side says.

## The honest constraints for a small company

A company with limited cash cannot fund work with an eighteen-month payback, however sound. The sequence for most small companies is performance first, to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost, then a growing share of budget toward owned and earned brand work as revenue allows.

Two exceptions. A company with an existing distribution asset (a founder with a following, a list, a community) can do brand work cheaply from day one, because the audience already exists. And a company in a category the ad platforms restrict is pushed toward earned and owned channels early, because the performance auctions are partly closed to it. In both cases, the usual sequence compresses.

## A working division

The IPA benchmarks are long-run optima for established brands: about 60:40 brand to activation in Binet and Field's consumer work, and 46:54 in their B2B study. They are where a company should be heading, not where a company with six months of cash should start.

For a company past its first channel, a workable starting point is roughly three quarters of spend on performance, measured on cost per outcome against customer value, and roughly a quarter on brand. Then move the split toward the benchmarks as cash and payback allow.

Measure the brand quarter on its own clock. Branded search and direct traffic are free and weekly. Share of search, a brand's share of organic searches in its category from Google Trends, was shown by Les Binet in an IPA presentation to correlate with and lead market share in three consumer categories, by up to a year in cars. Recall can be surveyed where budgets allow. Above all, watch the trend in performance cost per outcome over time. Our piece on [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers share of search, shortlist rate and category entry points in detail, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers the capture and creation split.

Illustrative example: moving the split

Decision
:   Move from 90:10 performance to brand toward 70:30 over three quarters.

Reason and owner
:   Cost per acquisition on the main paid channel had risen for four consecutive quarters while volume stayed flat, and branded search was flat. Owned by the head of growth, with the finance lead agreeing a payback limit for the performance share.

What changed
:   Branded search and direct sign-ups rose over the following two quarters, and the rise in cost per acquisition slowed. The split was held at 75:25 while the trend was confirmed.

Illustrative: a composite of a B2B software company with around 60 staff, built from patterns across engagements.

The point is not the ratio. It is that both sides are funded, both are measured on their own clock, and the company understands that the second one is what makes the first one affordable.

## lowob takeaways

- **Different clocks, not different teams.** Performance is judged in weeks on cost per outcome; brand over months or years.
- **Brand lowers the cost of performance.** The rising cost per outcome is the bill for the brand work not done.
- **Start where cash allows, head for the benchmark.** Roughly 75:25 for a small company past its first channel, moving toward 46:54 in B2B or 60:40 in consumer markets.
- **Measure brand on its own clock.** Branded search, share of search, recall and the trend in cost per outcome.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between brand marketing and performance marketing?

Performance marketing aims at a measurable outcome in a short window, judged on cost per outcome. Brand marketing aims at changing what people know, believe or feel about a company, judged over months or years on recall, consideration and the falling cost of performance.

### What is the 60:40 rule in marketing?

Binet and Field's finding, from IPA effectiveness cases, that consumer brands grow best with about 60% of spend on brand building and 40% on activation. Their B2B study put the balance at 46:54.

### How should a small company split its budget between brand and performance?

Start with performance to find a channel that produces customers at a survivable cost. Once past the first channel, roughly three quarters performance and a quarter brand is a workable start, moved toward the benchmarks as cash allows.

### How do you measure brand marketing?

On branded search, direct traffic, share of search, recall where it can be surveyed, and above all the trend in performance cost per outcome over time.

## Sources and notes

- [IPA, The Long and the Short of It, presentation by Les Binet and Peter Field](https://ipa.co.uk/media/14463/long_and_short_of_it_presentation_final_030424.pdf). Analysis of IPA Databank effectiveness award entries, largely UK consumer brands; award entries skew to successful campaigns.
- [LinkedIn, How B2B marketing really drives growth](https://business.linkedin.com/en-uk/marketing-solutions/blog/posts/B2B-Marketing/2019/How-B2B-marketing-really-drives-growth), 16 October 2019. Platform summary of Binet and Field's B2B Institute study; LinkedIn sells B2B advertising.
- [Ehrenberg-Bass Institute, Advertising effectiveness and the 95-5 rule](https://marketingscience.info/news-and-insights/advertising-effectiveness-and-the-95-5-rule-most-b2b-buyers-are-not-in-the-market-right-now), John Dawes, May 2021. Produced for LinkedIn's B2B Institute; the 5% is a heuristic estimate from replacement cycles.
- [IPA, Binet presents fast, cheap, predictive Share of Search metric](https://ipa.co.uk/news/binet-presents-fast-cheap-predictive-share-of-search-metric/), 14 October 2020. Three consumer categories; B2B use is by extension.
- The comparison table, the 75:25 starting point and the example are **lowob**'s guidance and illustration, not findings from these sources.

## Next move

Chart your cost per outcome on the main paid channel by quarter for the last two years next to branded search volume. If cost is rising while branded search is flat, move a fixed slice of next quarter's budget to brand and agree in advance how you will judge it.
