# Seats, Usage or Outcomes

Source: https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-29 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: There are three ways to charge for an AI product, seats, usage and outcomes, and most companies now combine them. This guide sets out the fit test, real published price points from Microsoft, Salesforce, Intercom and Zendesk, a worked cost-per-task and gross-margin example, the contract terms that protect both sides and the eight monthly numbers that show whether the business works.

Pick the pricing model that matches how value shows up, know your cost per task, and report the eight numbers that show whether the business works. Seats fit when a named person uses the product daily; usage fits when value scales with volume; outcomes fit when both sides trust the measurement. Most AI companies now land on a hybrid: Kyle Poyar's 2026 survey of 230 software companies found 37% use one, up from 25% a year earlier. Whatever the model, a price set without a known cost per task is a guess.

This page is the hub of **lowob**'s pricing library. Each model has its own explainer: [seat-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-seat-based-pricing-for-ai/), [usage-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/) and [outcome-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/). The cost side is covered in [what AI inference cost is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/), and the logic behind charging for results in [value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/). This piece is where they meet: which model to choose, what it costs to serve, and how to write the contract.

## Three models and the fit test

There are three ways to charge for an AI product. Each fits a specific situation, and forcing the wrong one creates friction with buyers and finance teams.

| Model | Fits when | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seats | A named human uses it daily and the value is their time | Usage spread across few heavy users |
| Usage | Value scales with volume and the buyer accepts variable bills | Bill shock, procurement blocking variable spend |
| Outcomes | You can measure the result and the buyer trusts the measurement | Disputes over attribution |

Seats work when the product sits in a person's daily workflow. The buyer understands the model and can budget for it. The weakness is that AI products often do the work of several people. Seat pricing then undercharges.

Usage pricing matches value to volume. It fits products that process documents, tickets, calls or records. Buyers accept it only with caps, estimates and alerts. Without them, finance will not sign.

Outcome pricing is the most attractive and the hardest to run. You need a result you can measure, and a buyer who accepts your measurement. Resolved tickets, qualified leads, completed filings. If either side can argue about the number, the model breaks.

### What the market charges

Prices below were checked on the vendors' own pages on 16 November 2026, in US dollars.

| Vendor and product | Model | Published price | Detail that matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Microsoft 365 Copilot Business | Seat, with metered extras | $21 per user per month on annual billing; $25.20 monthly | Promotional $18 for the first year, 1 July to 31 December 2026. Some advanced features bill through Copilot Credits |
| Salesforce Agentforce add-ons | Seat (unmetered) | $125 per user per month | Sales, Service, Field Service and Operations; Industries add-ons $150 |
| Salesforce Flex Credits | Usage (prepaid credits) | $500 per 100,000 credits | Salesforce prices each action at $0.10 |
| Salesforce Conversations | Usage (per conversation) | $2 per conversation | The original Agentforce unit, regardless of task complexity |
| Intercom Fin | Outcome | From $0.99 per Fin outcome | Charged at most once per conversation; no seats needed for Fin alone |
| Zendesk AI agents | Outcome, with an allowance | Not published; through sales | 5 to 15 automated resolutions per agent per month included, by plan |

Salesforce is the clearest case: the same agent can be bought per user, per conversation or per action. Its own example puts a three-to-six action sales interaction at $0.30 to $0.60 under Flex Credits, against $2 per conversation.

The table also shows why seat pricing undercharges for agents. One $125 seat covers a person supervising an agent. If that agent handles 2,000 conversations a month, the vendor collects $125 for work that would bill at $4,000 on Salesforce's own $2 per-conversation meter. Our piece on [which AI assistant to buy and for which seats](https://lowob.com/research/which-ai-assistant-which-seats/) covers the buyer's side of the same arithmetic.

## How pricing is shifting: the evidence

Four recent surveys point the same way, with a caveat on outcomes. All are run by investors, analysts or newsletter authors, not audited market data, and their samples differ.

| Publisher | Sample and date | Finding |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kyle Poyar, Growth Unhinged | 230 B2B software and AI companies, April to May 2026 | 37% use a hybrid model, up from 25%; 29% offer AI credits and 33% plan to within 6 to 12 months; three in four changed pricing or packaging in the past year |
| ICONIQ (investor), January 2026 snapshot | About 300 executives at AI software companies | Outcome-based pricing at 18%, up from 2% in Q2 2025; 37% plan to change their AI pricing model within a year |
| ICONIQ (investor), State of AI, July 2026 | About 300 executives, Q2 2026 survey | Consumption-based pricing rose from 35% to 42% and outcome-based from 18% to 23% in six months; companies blend an average of 1.7 models |
| The Futurum Group (analyst) | 830 IT decision makers, 1H 2026 | For GenAI features, 42.9% of buyers prefer consumption pricing; preference for outcome-based GenAI pricing fell from 30.9% to 26.8% |

Sellers' and buyers' data diverge on outcomes: more vendors offer outcome pricing while fewer buyers say they prefer it for AI features. Futurum's analyst read this as a case for hybrids, with stable subscriptions for the platform and transparent metering for AI. That matches **lowob**'s view. Outcome pricing is easier in a pitch than in a contract, because the buyer has to accept the seller's count.

> If either side can argue about the number, the model breaks.

## Hybrids are normal

Most AI companies land on a hybrid. A platform fee plus usage. Seats with a usage allowance and overage. A base fee with an outcome bonus.

Hybrids are fine as long as they are simple to explain in one sentence. If your pricing page needs a calculator, buyers will assume the worst case.

The platform fee covers your fixed cost of serving a customer. The variable part tracks inference. That split keeps gross margin predictable even when usage swings.

| Hybrid structure | Published example | What the variable part tracks | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Seat plus metered extras | Microsoft 365 Copilot Business | Advanced features and custom agents, in Copilot Credits | Metered spend nobody budgeted for |
| Seat plus included allowance plus overage | Zendesk Suite, with 5 to 15 automated resolutions per agent included | Resolutions above the allowance, billed monthly | Allowance expiring unused at year end |
| Seats plus per-outcome fee | Intercom seats from $19 to $132 per seat, plus Fin from $0.99 per outcome | Fin outcomes | Disputes over what counts as an outcome |
| Prepaid credits with drawdown | Salesforce Flex Credits | Actions drawn down from the prepaid credits | Credit burn rate faster than forecast |
| Platform fee plus graduated usage | Langfuse Pro: $199 a month, then $8 per 100,000 units falling to $6 at volume | Volume above an included tier, at falling unit rates | Tier boundaries that create cliff edges |

The one-sentence test applies to every row. "Each seat includes ten AI resolutions a month, and extras are billed monthly at the rate on your order form" passes.

## The gross-margin trap

Every AI pricing model fails in the same way: the company does not know what a task costs to run.

Cost per task is model cost plus compute plus any human review, divided by tasks completed. If you cannot produce that number for last month, you do not know your gross margin. Pricing decisions made without it are guesses.

The trap is real at the industry level. ICONIQ's July 2026 report puts average AI product gross margins at 45% in 2025, projected at 53% for 2026, and notes that inference takes a growing share of cost as products scale. A margin that low leaves little room for a pricing model that misreads cost.

### A worked example

The example below is illustrative. It prices an AI support agent sold at $0.99 per resolution, the entry rate Intercom lists for Fin, and runs it on a mid-tier model at Anthropic's published Claude Sonnet 5.5 rates of $2 per million input tokens, $10 per million output tokens and $0.10 per million cached input tokens (checked 16 November 2026). Intercom renamed itself Fin in May 2026, and on 15 June 2026 Salesforce signed a definitive agreement to acquire it for about $3.6 billion.

| Line | Healthy month | Drifted month |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Model calls per conversation | 4 | 4 |
| Tokens per call | 6,000 input (5,000 cached), 400 output | 6,000 input (none cached), 400 output |
| Model cost per call | $0.0065 | $0.016 |
| Model cost per conversation | $0.026 | $0.064 |
| Retrieval, tools and compute per conversation (assumed) | $0.010 | $0.010 |
| Human review: share of conversations checked, at 2 minutes and $40 an hour | 10%, so $0.133 | 20%, so $0.267 |
| Total cost per conversation | $0.169 | $0.341 |
| Resolution rate (only resolutions bill) | 60% | 40% |
| Cost per resolution | $0.28 | $0.85 |
| Gross margin at $0.99 | 71.5% | 14.0% |

Human review costs about five times the model in the healthy month, so a cost per task that leaves out people misses most of the cost. Caching alone more than halves model cost. And the resolution rate is the denominator: when fewer conversations resolve, every cost is spread over fewer billable outcomes. Under outcome pricing the drift shows up in the margin within the month.

The number must be falling. Caching repeated context, routing simple tasks to smaller models, shortening prompts, batching requests. Each one is an operating project with an owner and a target. Anthropic's published rates show the scale: its smallest current model lists at $0.10 per million input tokens against $2 for the mid-tier model, and the Batch API halves both input and output prices. Our piece on [raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) covered why investors ask for this. Here it is the difference between a business and a hobby. The [token explainer](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-token-in-ai/) shows how to estimate the inputs.

Set a margin floor per task and price above it. If a customer's usage pattern drops below the floor, you need to know within the month, not at renewal.

### Free tiers are acquisition cost

A free tier is a marketing expense that happens to look like a product. Treat it that way.

Every free task has an inference cost. Add those up by month and you have a number to put next to paid channels. If free-tier conversion to paid is weak, the free tier is an expensive campaign with no stop date.

Do not count free users as users in any report that goes to the board or to investors. Count them as a channel with a cost per acquired team, and compare that cost to the others.

## Contract terms that protect both sides

Variable pricing moves risk into the contract. The large vendors' published terms show which clauses matter.

| Term | What it settles | Published precedent | Buyer asks for | Seller needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Outcome definition | What counts as a billable result | Intercom bills resolutions, procedure handoffs, qualifications and disqualifications; a customer asking for a human is not billed | A written definition and a list of exclusions | A definition it can count automatically |
| Verification method | How a result is confirmed | Zendesk uses an LLM to check each conversation; those that fail do not consume a resolution | Access to the evidence behind each charge | Agreement that its method is the count |
| Counting window | When a result is final | Zendesk evaluates email conversations 72 hours after the first email, messaging after 2 hours by default | A window long enough for reopened cases to surface | A window short enough to bill monthly |
| Charge limit per interaction | Stops double counting | Intercom charges at most once per conversation | The same, in the order form | Clarity on what a conversation is |
| Allowance and expiry | Whether unused volume carries over | Zendesk allocations expire annually or at term end, capped at 10,000 a year | Rollover, or a lower commitment | Commitment it can plan capacity around |
| Overage rate and billing | Price beyond the commitment | Zendesk bills overage monthly, at a higher rate than committed usage | A capped overage rate and alerts at set thresholds | The right to bill monthly |
| Spend cap or pause | Protection from bill shock | Zendesk lets accounts pause AI features at the limit or pay overage as they go | A hard cap option | Notice before a cap stops service |
| True-up | Reconciling commitment with actual use | Practice varies; not on the public pages checked | Credit for under-use against renewal | Payment for over-use at an agreed rate |
| Metric change notice | Protection when the unit changes | Intercom moved from resolutions to outcomes on 12 March 2026 after emailing customers in February; Zendesk gives 30 days' notice of plan moves | Notice, and the old unit until renewal | The ability to evolve the product |

The Intercom change is the one to study. Its billable unit now includes some procedure handoffs to a human or a workflow, which a buyer might not call an outcome. That is why the definition belongs in the contract, not on a help page that can change. For the buyer's side of outcome deals, see [what outcome-based pricing for AI is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/); for credit deals, [usage-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-usage-based-pricing-for-ai/).

## What to report, and what to stop

Our piece [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) made the case for activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source over reach. For an AI product those become eight monthly numbers.

| Number | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Activation | Share of new teams that complete a first real task within a week |
| Weekly active teams | Teams, not individuals |
| Tasks completed | The unit of value delivered, defined once and not changed |
| Retention at 30 and 90 days | Measured on teams that activated |
| Net revenue retention | What last year's customers are paying now |
| Gross margin | Net of inference, with the trend |
| Cost per task | Model, compute and human review over tasks completed |
| Cost per acquired team by source | With the free tier shown as a source |

Stop reporting sign-ups, which measure a landing page. Stop reporting prompts sent, which measure curiosity. Stop reporting anything counted as "AI-generated". None of them tells you whether the product works or whether the business does.

### Pricing changes as experiments

Pricing is not set once. It is changed in small steps, each run as an experiment.

Write down the hypothesis, the segment it applies to, the number you expect to move and the stop rule. A stop rule is the condition under which you revert. Activation falls by a set amount, or churn rises, or support tickets about billing double.

Run it on new customers first. Existing customers get grandfathered until the result is in. Then decide, record the decision, and move on to the next one. Our guide to [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to read results at low volume.

## lowob takeaways

- **Run the fit test first.** Seat pricing often undercharges because AI products can do the work of several people.
- **Know the cost per task.** Model cost plus compute plus human review, divided by tasks completed, and it must fall.
- **Write the outcome into the contract.** Definition, verification, counting window and change notice, not a help-centre link.
- **Keep hybrids to one sentence.** If the pricing page needs a calculator, buyers will assume the worst case.
- **Report eight numbers.** Stop reporting sign-ups, prompts sent and anything counted as AI-generated.

Gateway card

### Before you publish a price

- Pricing model chosen against the fit test, explained in one sentence
- Cost per task known for last month, including human review, with a reduction target and an owner
- Margin floor per task set, with alerts when a customer drops below it
- Outcome or usage unit defined in the contract, with exclusions and a counting window
- Overage rate, cap option and true-up terms written down
- Free tier costed and reported as an acquisition channel
- The eight monthly numbers on one page, sign-ups and prompt counts removed
- Next pricing experiment written down with a stop rule

## Common questions

### Should I price my AI product per seat or by usage?

Seats fit when a named person uses it daily and the value is their time. Usage fits when value scales with volume and the buyer accepts variable bills, provided you offer caps, estimates and alerts. Many vendors now combine both.

### How do you calculate cost per task for an AI product?

Add model cost, compute and any human review for the month, then divide by tasks completed. Include review: in our illustrative support example it cost about five times more than the model.

### What is outcome-based pricing for AI, and how much does it cost?

The buyer pays per defined result, such as a resolved ticket. Intercom lists Fin from $0.99 per outcome, charged at most once per conversation, as checked in November 2026. The contract must define what counts.

### What is hybrid pricing for AI products?

A fixed part, such as a platform fee or seats, plus a variable part tied to usage or outcomes. Kyle Poyar's 2026 survey found 37% of software companies use one, up from 25% a year earlier.

# Your Startup Needs a GTM Strategy, Not Just a List of Tactics

Source: https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A list of channels and campaigns is not a go-to-market strategy. A strategy makes four connected decisions (market, message, motion and measurement) and every tactic then has a specific job inside them. This playbook sets out the decisions, a coherence test and seven questions to answer before approving another campaign.

A go-to-market plan connects the right buyer, a useful promise, a credible channel and measurable customer behaviour. Most startup plans are lists of tactics instead: launch the site, hire a seller, post, sponsor, build a Discord. A tactic answers what the team will do. A strategy answers why these actions should create an advantage for this company, with this customer, at this moment. The test is coherence: four decisions on market, message, motion and measurement that reinforce one another.

Most startup go-to-market plans look reassuring in a slide deck.

Launch the website. Hire a salesperson. Post on LinkedIn. Start a newsletter. Sponsor a conference. Build a Discord. Run paid media. Recruit creators. Announce partnerships.

None of those decisions is necessarily wrong. Together, however, they still do not constitute a strategy.

A tactic answers: **What are we going to do?**

A strategy answers: **Why should these actions create an advantage for this particular company, with this particular customer, at this particular moment?**

That distinction matters because activity is easy to manufacture. A small team can fill a calendar for months without learning whether anyone has a painful problem, whether the product solves it, or whether the company can reach the buyer economically. A busy launch can disguise a missing commercial thesis.

## Why a list is not a strategy

The strategy literature has made this point for decades. Michael Porter's "What Is Strategy?" in *Harvard Business Review* (1996) separated operational effectiveness from strategy: "Improving operational effectiveness is a necessary part of management, but it is not strategy." He defined strategy as "creating fit among a company's activities" and wrote that "the essence of strategy is choosing what not to do." A tactic list fails both tests. It does not choose, and its items are not designed to fit.

Richard Rumelt made a similar argument in a 2007 *McKinsey Quarterly* interview: "Most corporate strategic plans have little to do with strategy." He described much of what executives called strategy as resource budgets and market-share projections, and coined "doorknob polishing" for initiatives with no clear position behind them. A startup's launch calendar is the small-company version of the same thing.

The commercial cost shows up in the buyer. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, with 89% of purchases spanning two or more departments. Gartner's survey of 632 buyers, published in May 2025, found 74% of buyer teams showed unhealthy conflict during the decision, and groups that reached consensus were 2.5 times more likely to report a high-quality deal. Tactics aimed at one person in that group, with no view on the others, create meetings that do not become decisions.

## The four decisions hiding underneath GTM

A credible GTM strategy makes four connected decisions. They are the same four decisions set out in [What go-to-market means](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/), stated here as strategic choices.

**Market:** Which narrowly defined group has the strongest combination of pain, urgency, authority, and ability to pay?

"Fintech companies" is not a market. "U.S. consumer fintech companies preparing to launch an embedded stablecoin product in the next two quarters" might be. The second definition gives the team observable signals, relevant decision-makers, and a reason the conversation matters now.

**Message:** What must the buyer believe before taking the next step?

Early-stage teams tend to describe the product. Buyers evaluate a change. They want to know what improves, what risk disappears, why the timing matters, and why this team is credible. Good messaging translates technical capability into a change the buyer can recognise.

**Motion:** How will trust move from zero to a commercial decision?

A self-serve product, an enterprise sale, an ecosystem partnership, and a developer platform do not share the same buying journey. The motion determines whether the primary engine should be product-led onboarding, founder-led sales, channel partnerships, community adoption, or a carefully sequenced combination. [Product-led vs sales-led vs partner-led growth](https://lowob.com/research/product-led-vs-sales-led-vs-partner-led/) compares them.

**Measurement:** What evidence will tell the team that the thesis is working?

Impressions and followers can be useful leading indicators, but they are not automatically commercial evidence. A good measurement system connects attention to qualified conversations, product behaviour, pipeline progression, retention, and revenue.

## The GTM coherence test

Write one sentence for each of the four decisions. Then ask whether they reinforce one another.

| If the market is... | ...and the motion or measure is... | The incoherence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Risk-conscious institutional buyers | Viral social content and an anonymous Discord | The channel cannot carry the trust the buyer needs |
| A developer community | Executive sales meetings as the only measure | The evidence is being looked for in the wrong place |
| Not urgent | Ever more refined messaging | No message creates a buying event that does not exist |
| A 13-person buying group | Outreach to one champion only | The deal stalls at the people nobody wrote for |

A coherent example sounds more like this, illustrative and unnamed:

*We help regional financial institutions preparing stablecoin products reduce the time and operational uncertainty involved in evaluating infrastructure partners. We reach the executive sponsor through research-led account outreach and industry relationships, then support technical validation with a structured diligence process. We measure qualified evaluations, stakeholder expansion, technical milestones, and time to commercial decision.*

That is not a slogan. It is a theory of how a market turns into revenue.

> A busy launch can disguise a missing commercial thesis.

## Build the strategy before filling the calendar

Before approving another campaign, force the team to answer seven questions. Each maps to one of the four decisions and has a place to find the answer.

| Question | Decision | Where the evidence usually is |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Which customer has the most expensive version of the problem? | Market | Won deals, deal size and retention by segment |
| 2. What event makes solving it urgent now? | Market | Discovery notes; the trigger behind the last five wins |
| 3. Who feels the problem, who approves the change, and who can block it? | Motion | Contacts on won and lost deals |
| 4. What alternative is the buyer using today? | Message | Win-loss interviews; "what would you do without us" |
| 5. What must the buyer believe to move forward? | Message | Objections recorded in calls |
| 6. Which channel can transfer enough trust to earn the next step? | Motion | Source of each customer, and what it cost |
| 7. What observable behaviour would prove the thesis is working? | Measurement | The one weekly number the team agrees on |

Only after those answers are clear should the team select channels, content, events, partners, and campaign tactics. Each tactic then gets a job written against one of the four decisions. Our piece [The commercial system: what it is](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) describes how those decisions are recorded so the team keeps them, and [Positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/) covers questions 4 and 5 in depth.

## The uncomfortable conclusion

Many companies do not have a marketing problem or a sales problem. They have a coherence problem. The priority customer, narrative, distribution model, and evidence system were designed separately, or never designed at all.

**The solution is not another tactic. It is a commercial system in which every tactic has a specific job.**

Illustrative example: cutting the calendar to fit the thesis

Decision
:   Stop three planned tactics (a general conference sponsorship, a community launch and paid social) and fund research-led outreach to 40 named institutions plus a structured technical diligence pack.

Reason and owner
:   The coherence test showed the market was risk-conscious institutions, while two-thirds of the planned spend went to channels those buyers did not use to evaluate suppliers. Owned by the CEO, with the head of growth.

What changed
:   The team measured qualified evaluations and stakeholders engaged per account instead of impressions, and could say which activity produced each evaluation.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage infrastructure company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose the buyer and problem before picking channels.** Market is the first decision, and it constrains the other three.
- **Test for coherence.** Write one sentence per decision and check the motion can carry the trust this buyer needs.
- **Give every campaign a job.** Each tactic should trace to one of the four decisions and to a commercial outcome.
- **Stop funding activity that cannot show why it matters.** Choosing what not to do is the strategy.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between GTM strategy and tactics?

A tactic answers what the team will do, such as launching a newsletter or sponsoring an event. A strategy answers why those actions should create an advantage with a particular customer at a particular moment, through four connected decisions.

### What are the four parts of a go-to-market strategy?

Market (which narrowly defined group has the pain, urgency, authority and budget), message (what the buyer must believe), motion (how trust moves to a decision) and measurement (what evidence shows the thesis is working).

### How do I know if my GTM strategy is coherent?

Write one sentence for each of the four decisions and check they reinforce one another. A risk-conscious buyer reached through viral social content, or a developer audience measured only by executive meetings, fails the test.

### What should a startup decide before choosing marketing channels?

Which customer has the most expensive problem, what makes it urgent now, who approves and who blocks, what alternative they use today, what they must believe, which channel can carry enough trust, and what behaviour proves it works.

## Sources and notes

- [Michael E. Porter, What Is Strategy?](https://rogerswannell.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/11/whatisstrategy_porter_96.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, November to December 1996. Third-party hosted copy of the original article; written for established firms.
- [McKinsey Quarterly, Strategy's strategist: An interview with Richard Rumelt](https://www.mckinsey.com/~/media/McKinsey/Business%20Functions/Strategy%20and%20Corporate%20Finance/Our%20Insights/Strategys%20strategist%20An%20interview%20with%20Richard%20Rumelt/Strategys%20strategist%20An%20interview%20with%20Richard%20Rumelt.pdf), August 2007. Interview; opinion of a leading strategy scholar, about large corporations.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated in the release.
- [Gartner, Sales Survey Finds 74% of B2B Buyer Teams Demonstrate "Unhealthy Conflict"](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2025-05-07-gartner-sales-survey-finds-74-percent-of-b2b-buyer-teams-demonstrate-unhealthy-conflict-during-the-decision-process), 7 May 2025. Survey of 632 B2B buyers, August to September 2024.
- The coherence table, the seven-question table and the example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

- [The Commercial System: What It Is, and Why Most Firms Run Without One](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/)

## Next move

Take your current GTM plan and label every tactic with the one decision it serves: market, message, motion or measurement. Pause any tactic that cannot be labelled, and write the seven answers before funding it again.

# How to Read a Media Plan Before You Approve It

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-to-read-a-media-plan/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A media plan says where a marketing budget will be spent, over what period, in what proportions, and what each part should produce. Before approving one, read the objective, the expected outcomes and the cost basis, check the programmatic supply path, and ask what the plan assumes, what happens when a channel fails, and who owns the data afterwards.

A media plan is the document that says where a marketing budget will be spent, over what period, in what proportions, and what each part is expected to produce. It is the point at which strategy turns into money, and it is usually approved by people who have not been told how to read one. Read three things first: the objective, the expected outcomes and the cost basis. Then check where programmatic money actually goes, since the ANA found the average campaign in its 2023 study ran on about 44,000 websites.

## What a good plan contains

**The objective, in one sentence,** stated as an outcome the company can observe: funded accounts, qualified leads, activated users, at a cost per outcome and a volume. A plan whose objective is "awareness" or "reach" should say what awareness is expected to lead to and how anyone will know. Our piece on [measuring brand in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/measuring-brand-in-b2b/) covers what a brand objective can be measured against.

**The audience,** defined precisely enough that a channel can be chosen for it. Who, where, what they are doing when they might be reached, and what they need to believe.

**The channel mix,** listed with the share of budget for each and the reason each is there. The reason should connect to the audience and the objective, not to the channel's availability.

**The flighting:** when each channel runs, at what weight, over the plan period. A plan that spends evenly across every channel for every week has not made any decisions. It has also made the plan impossible to measure later: a [marketing mix model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-marketing-mix-modeling/) cannot separate channels whose spend never moved.

**The expected results,** by channel: the volume of outcomes, the cost per outcome, and the assumptions behind each. Where the assumption is a guess, it should say so.

**The measurement approach:** how each channel's outcomes will be tracked, in whose systems, and how the plan will be adjusted when the numbers arrive. A plan with no holdout or test on its largest line has no way to learn whether that line worked.

**The band map,** for companies in reviewed categories: which channels are open, which require approvals the plan is not counting on, and which are closed.

## The columns and what they mean

Most plans are a table.

| Column | What it says | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Channel and placement or partner | Where the money goes | Named sellers, not "run of network" |
| Format and audience | What runs, to whom | Whether the audience can actually be targeted in this category |
| Dates and weight | Flighting | Variation that later analysis can read |
| Impressions or reach | Volume of exposure | Viewable and verified, or gross |
| Cost and cost basis (CPM, CPC, CPA) | What the channel is bought on | The conversion assumption from that unit to customers |
| Expected outcomes | The plan's promise | Where each number came from |
| Share of budget | Priorities | Whether it matches the stated reasons |
| Fees | What the partner earns | In dollars, and what makes them rise |

The two columns to interrogate are expected outcomes and the cost basis. Expected outcomes are the plan's promise; ask where each number came from. The cost basis tells you what the channel is being bought on. A channel bought on CPM with an expected number of customers attached has done a conversion calculation somewhere, and the assumptions in that calculation are the plan's real content. Our explainer on [CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL and ROAS](https://lowob.com/research/cpm-cpc-cpa-cpl-roas-explained/) covers what each basis hides.

Check what "impressions" means. The Media Rating Council's viewability standard counts a display impression as viewable when half its pixels are on screen for one second. A plan's gross impressions may be well above the viewable, human ones.

## Where programmatic money goes

Programmatic lines deserve a separate look, because the supply chain between the advertiser's money and the publisher is long. ISBA and PwC's 2020 UK study traced spend through matched supply chains and found publishers received about 51% of advertiser spend, with about 15% unattributable. The ANA's 2023 US study, covering $123 million of spend, found the average campaign ran on about 44,000 top-level domains, and made-for-advertising sites took 21% of impressions and 15% of spend. The top 500 domains had a 50% lower fraud rate than the long tail.

The ANA's recommendations translate directly into plan questions: favour inclusion lists over exclusion lists, buy the fewest properties through the most direct path, and work only with sites where viewability, fraud and brand safety can be measured.

IAB Tech Lab's supply-chain standards give a way to investigate the seller path. ads.txt lets a publisher list who is authorised to sell its inventory. sellers.json, published by each ad system, discloses the legal entity paid under each seller ID and whether it is a publisher or an intermediary. The SupplyChain object lists every node that touched a bid request. Together they let a buyer ask who is in the path and why. They do not replace independent outcome measurement. Our piece on [programmatic media numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) covers the verification side.

> A channel bought on CPM with an expected number of customers attached has done a conversion calculation somewhere. The assumptions in that calculation are the plan's real content.

## The questions to ask before approving

1. **Which of these channels has this company, or this partner, run for this category before, and what happened?**
2. **If one channel fails in the first two weeks, where does its budget go, and who decides?**
3. **Which lines assume an approval that has not arrived?**
4. **What does the plan look like at half the budget?** The answer reveals which channels the planner actually believes in.
5. **For programmatic lines: how many domains, on an inclusion list or not, and through which sellers?**
6. **Who owns the accounts, the tracking and the data when the plan ends?**
7. **What is the fee, in dollars, and what makes it go up?** Our piece on [percent-of-spend fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) explains why this question matters.

## The plan for a company that cannot buy the usual channels

For a company the ad platforms restrict, a conventional media plan is mostly lines that will not run. The plan that works starts from the band map, allocates the first weeks to cheap measurement across the open-band channels, commits the bulk of the budget only after something reads, and files the restricted-band approvals with nothing forecast against them.

That plan looks less complete than a spreadsheet with every channel filled in. It is also the only one with numbers anyone should believe. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to size the measurement weeks so they produce a result.

Gateway card

### Before you approve the plan

- An objective stated as an observable outcome, with a cost per outcome and a volume
- Expected outcomes by channel, each with its assumption written down
- Flighting with real variation, and a holdout or test on the largest line
- Programmatic lines on inclusion lists, with named sellers
- A reallocation rule for any channel that fails in the first two weeks
- Accounts, tracking and data in the company's name
- Fees stated in dollars

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the promise and the cost basis together.** The conversion assumptions between them are what you are approving.
- **Check where programmatic money goes.** Domain counts, inclusion lists and the seller path, using ads.txt and sellers.json.
- **Ask for the half-budget version.** It shows which channels the planner believes in.
- **Keep measurement and account access verifiable by your company.** The plan ends; the data should stay.

## Common questions

### What should a media plan include?

An objective stated as an observable outcome, the audience, the channel mix with reasons, the flighting, expected results by channel with their assumptions, the measurement approach and, for restricted categories, which channels are open.

### How do you evaluate a media plan?

Interrogate the expected outcomes and the cost basis, ask what the plan looks like at half the budget, check where programmatic money goes, and confirm who owns the accounts and data afterwards.

### What is flighting in a media plan?

The schedule of when each channel runs and at what weight across the plan period. Varying weight deliberately is what lets later analysis tell which channels worked.

### What are ads.txt and sellers.json?

IAB Tech Lab standards. ads.txt lists who a publisher authorises to sell its inventory; sellers.json discloses who each ad system pays under each seller ID. They show the supply path, not whether the ads worked.

## Sources and notes

- [ANA, "First Look" at in-depth programmatic media transparency study](https://ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2023-06-programmaticstudy), 19 June 2023. Trade association study; 21 advertisers, $123 million of spend.
- [ANA Programmatic Media Supply Chain Transparency Study, First Look](https://info.adtheorent.com/hubfs/Gated-Downloads/ANA%20Programmatic%20Media%20Supply%20Chain%20Transparency%20Study%202023.pdf), June 2023. Study document hosted by a vendor; source of the recommendations and domain comparison.
- [Marketing Dive, 15% of programmatic ad spend disappears in the supply chain, study says](https://www.marketingdive.com/news/15-of-programmatic-ad-spend-disappears-in-the-supply-chain-study-says/577525/), 7 May 2020. Trade press report of ISBA and PwC's UK study; only 15 advertisers shared data and 290 supply chains were matched.
- [IAB Tech Lab, sellers.json specification](https://github.blesdmm.dns-dynamic.net/InteractiveAdvertisingBureau/Supply-Chain-Validation/blob/main/sellers-json.md). Standards body specification; adoption and accuracy depend on each ad system.
- [ANA, Media Rating Council updates viewable ad impression measurement guidelines](https://ana.net/content/show/id/36327), August 2015. Industry standard summary.

## Related research

- [Campaign Testing That Reaches a Decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/)

# Raising for an AI Company

Source: https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-22 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: AI took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026, but most of it went to model companies and very large rounds. Application companies are priced like software companies, on retention, margin and replaceability, with two extra costs: inference and platform risk. Raise on gross margin net of inference, falling cost per task and retained production usage, and put the model in the appendix.

Investors now price AI application companies on workflow ownership, margin and retention, so raise on that evidence and put the model in the appendix. The money is there: AI companies took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026. But a large share went to a handful of model companies, and the application companies that raise well show what any software company shows, plus two numbers only AI companies carry: gross margin after inference, and what happens when the model provider ships their feature.

*This is operating guidance, not investment advice.*

## The market has split

Two years ago "AI" in the deck earned a premium on its own. That has ended for application companies. Investors now sort the market into model companies and the companies that build on them. The two get priced on different logic.

The funding data shows the split. Crunchbase found OpenAI and Anthropic together raised $217 billion, or 43% of all global startup funding, in the first half of 2026. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor put AI at 82.7% of US deal value through September. Carta's first-quarter data is more useful for most founders: 60.7% of capital raised on its platform went to AI companies, 14.2% to foundation model companies, and 83% of capital raised by SaaS companies went to those building with AI. In software, almost everyone is now an AI company, which means the label no longer differentiates.

Model companies are priced on capability, compute access and research talent. Most founders reading this are not building one. Application companies are priced on what any software company is priced on: retention, margin, distribution and how hard the product is to replace.

The difference is that an AI application carries two extra costs. Inference, which hits gross margin. And platform risk, because the model provider can ship your feature. [The model is not the product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/) covered how to answer the "wrapper" objection. This piece is about how that answer shows up in a raise.

## The five questions you will get

Expect these in the first meeting, not the last.

1. **Gross margin after inference.** Investors want the number net of model and compute costs, and they want the trend. A flat or rising cost per task is a problem. A falling one is a story. Our explainer on [AI inference cost](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ai-inference-cost/) sets out what drives the number.
2. **What happens when the provider ships your feature.** The honest answer is that some of your product will be absorbed. The question is what remains. Data, distribution or workflow depth are the three defensible answers.
3. **Model dependency and switching cost.** Can you move to another model in a week, a month, or never? Have you done it? A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could.
4. **Data rights.** Do your contracts let you use customer data to improve the product? Many early contracts do not, because nobody asked. Fix that before the raise, not during it. A clear [data processing agreement](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-data-processing-agreement-for-ai/) is where the answer lives.
5. **Paid or free usage.** Free-tier activity is not evidence of demand. It is acquisition cost. Investors will strip it out, so strip it out first.

The switching question has become sharper in 2026. Menlo Ventures' enterprise survey, published in November 2026, found Anthropic's share of enterprise API spend rose from 40% to 55% in a year, OpenAI's from 27% to 31%, and Google's fell from 21% to 9%. Shares that move that fast mean a company locked to one provider is exposed to that provider's pricing, quality and roadmap. Menlo also found buyers prioritise capability over cost when choosing models, so the cheapest model is rarely the end state.

## The evidence that counts

[Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/) argued for raising on what customers have done rather than on the story. For an AI company the evidence has four parts.

| Evidence | What it proves | How to show it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Production usage with retention | The product does a job every week | Teams active weekly and still there at 90 days, paid only |
| Gross margin trend | The business survives its inference bill | Three or more months net of inference, moving the right way |
| Falling cost per task | The margin story is operational, not hoped for | Caching, routing to cheaper models, prompt reduction, with dates |
| Security pack that passed review | Enterprise buyers can actually sign | A real buyer's security process, completed |

Cost per task is where the work shows. [Prompt caching](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-prompt-caching/) and routing simpler requests to smaller models are the usual first moves. Record what each change did to the number.

A security pack that has been through a real buyer's process is worth more than any claim about enterprise readiness. [The pilot that survives security review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) covered the pack, and our explainer on [SOC 2 for AI vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/) covers what an attestation does and does not prove.

> A company that has swapped models once is more fundable than one that says it could.

## The capital stack

An AI raise usually has more than one source of capital, and they do not behave the same way.

| Source | What it is for | What it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equity | Runway, hiring, go-to-market | Cheap, or quick |
| Cloud and model credits | Reducing inference cost for a period | Revenue, or margin |
| Startup programmes | Credits, introductions, sometimes distribution | Validation of the business |
| Strategic investors | Distribution or data access | Neutral capital |

Credits are runway, not revenue. Show them in the plan as a cost reduction with an end date. Do not let them flatter the margin line in the pitch. Investors will find the expiry date and ask what margin looks like after it.

Strategic investors from cloud or model providers want something: distribution of their platform, or data from your use case. That can be a good trade. Know what you are giving before you take the cheque, and keep model switching possible in the terms. Corporate investors are now everywhere in large rounds: PitchBook data reported in August 2026 found corporate venture arms involved in 82.6% of US deal value in 2026.

## Narrative discipline

The deck should read like a software company that happens to use AI, not an AI company looking for a use case.

Lead with the customer and the workflow. Which job, for which team, replacing what. Then the evidence from the section above. Then the market and the plan. Menlo's survey found new budgets funded 55% of incremental enterprise AI spend in 2026, against 22% from existing software budgets. If your buyer is funding you from a new budget line, say whose line it is and who signs it.

The model, the architecture and the eval results go in the appendix. They matter in diligence. They do not carry the first meeting, and leading with them signals that you have not found the customer yet.

Run the round the way [Run the round like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) describes: a pipeline, a timeline, a named owner. PitchBook's second-quarter report noted that time between rounds has compressed, especially for AI companies. AI investors are busy and have seen a lot of similar decks. A tight process is itself evidence.

## lowob takeaways

- **The AI label no longer differentiates.** Investors price applications like software companies, plus inference and platform risk.
- **Show margin net of inference, with a trend.** Falling cost per task is the operating proof.
- **Test model switching before the raise.** Provider shares moved by double digits in a year.
- **Credits are a cost reduction with an expiry date.** Never let them flatter the margin line.

## Common questions

### How do investors value AI application startups?

On what any software company is priced on: retention, margin, distribution and how hard the product is to replace. AI applications also carry inference cost and platform risk, so investors ask for gross margin net of inference and evidence of model switching.

### What questions will investors ask an AI startup?

Gross margin after inference, what happens when the model provider ships your feature, model dependency and switching cost, data rights in customer contracts, and how much usage is paid versus free.

### Should cloud credits count as revenue in an AI startup pitch?

No. Credits are runway, not revenue. Show them as a cost reduction with an end date, because investors will find the expiry date and ask what margin looks like after it.

### How much venture funding goes to AI startups in 2026?

AI companies took 82.7% of US venture deal value through September 2026, per PitchBook-NVCA. Much of it went to a few model companies: OpenAI and Anthropic took 43% of global startup funding in the first half, per Crunchbase.

## Sources and notes

- [Carta, State of Private Markets Q1 2026](https://carta.com/data/state-of-private-markets-q1-2026-full-report/), 29 May 2026. Companies on Carta's platform; AI classification is Carta's.

Calculate gross margin net of inference for each of the last three months, and cost per task for your highest-volume workflow. If you have never run that workflow on a second model, run it this week and record the time, cost and quality difference.

# Meta Said No. That Is Not the End of Your Distribution Plan.

Source: https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-21 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: A rejected ad account is a decision about your category, made by a reviewer who never sees the product. Sort every channel into open, restricted and closed bands for each geography, build first where the answer is already yes, and file restricted-band paperwork with nothing forecast against it. Google, Meta and TikTok all tightened or re-scoped financial and crypto rules in 2025 and 2026, so the map needs a date on it.

A rejected ad account is the first distribution decision made on your behalf, and it is made by a reviewer who never sees the product. Treat the ad platforms as one band of channels among three, not as the plan. Sort every channel into open, restricted or closed for each geography, build first in the open band, and file the restricted-band paperwork with nothing forecast against it. The rules move often: Google added verification for financial advertisers in 24 European markets in June 2026, and Meta made a special ad category mandatory for US financial ads in January 2025.

Somewhere in your company there is a screenshot of a rejected ad account.

It may say the product falls under a restricted financial category. It may ask for a licence number you do not have because your product does not need one. It may say nothing beyond a policy code and a link to an appeal form that leads to another appeal form.

For a large group of legitimate companies, this is the first distribution decision anyone makes on their behalf, and it is made by a reviewer who will never see the product.

The instinct is to treat the rejection as an obstacle to be cleared. Resubmit. Reword. Try a new account. Hire someone who claims to know the trick. That instinct is expensive, and it puts the whole plan at the mercy of a decision the company does not control. The better response is to stop treating the ad platforms as the plan and start treating them as one band of channels among three.

## The rejection is about your category

Platforms publish the rules that produce most rejections, and those rules are written around categories, documents and geographies rather than products. Google's financial products and services policy says advertisers must complete a verification process to advertise financial services in some locations, typically supplying licences and registration numbers. On 23 June 2026 Google announced a new wave covering 24 European Economic Area markets, from Austria to Sweden, with rolling enforcement from 23 July 2026. Advertisers that are not directly authorised by a regulator cannot apply in their own right; an authorised firm must apply for them.

Meta works through targeting rather than only approval. Its developer documentation shows that from January 2025, financial products and services campaigns aimed at US audiences must run in a special ad category, with fixed age ranges, no gender targeting, minimum location radii and no lookalike audiences. A fintech whose plan depended on lookalikes lost that tool on a date it did not choose.

TikTok's financial services policy requires local licensing, disclosures and 18+ targeting for most permitted financial ads, and in many markets crypto advertisers must work with a TikTok sales representative to obtain permission through an application process. None of these steps involve anyone using the product. That is why a rejection says little about whether the product is good, and why rewording rarely changes it. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how the sorting works.

## Three bands, one honest map

Every channel a company could use sits in one of three bands. The assignment changes by category and geography, so the map is per market, and it carries the date it was checked.

| Band | What it means | Examples (policies checked 16 November 2026) | How to plan |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Open | Carries the category without pre-approval | Affiliate and partner programmes, creator distribution with disclosure, clipping networks, owned email and content, much of programmatic display and video | Build here first and forecast against it |
| Restricted | Carries the category with documentation, licensing or approval | Google financial services verification and crypto certification; Meta's special ad category for US financial ads; TikTok's licensing and permission process for financial and crypto ads | File the paperwork; forecast nothing until it clears |
| Closed | Will not run the category in this geography today, however the copy is worded | Google's global ban on ads for DeFi trading protocols and initial coin offerings; Google's disapproval of binary options; crypto ads in markets where TikTok lists them as not allowed | Write it down as closed and stop proposing it |

Most distribution plans fail because they are written entirely in the restricted band and hope. The company spends its first quarter of budget and attention on getting one platform to say yes, and has nothing built in the band where the answer was already yes.

## Write the closed band down first

This sounds backward. It is the most useful hour in the plan.

List every channel the company would like to use. For each one, record what the platform's published policy says about the category, what documentation it demands, and whether the company can supply it. Where the answer is no, write "closed" and move on. Where the answer is "with paperwork", write down what the paperwork costs in weeks.

| Field | What to record |
| --- | --- |
| Channel and geography | One row per platform per market |
| Policy page and date checked | The platform's own page, with the date you read it |
| Band | Open, restricted or closed |
| Documentation required | Licence, registration number, certification, third-party verifier |
| Can we supply it | Yes, no, or only through a partner's authorisation |
| Weeks to clear | Your honest estimate, with no forecast attached |

Two things happen. The plan stops carrying channels that were never going to work, so forecasts stop being fiction. And the company gains something rare in a sales conversation: the ability to tell a buyer, a board or an investor exactly where it cannot be seen, before anyone else does.

> Ad platforms make one decision about your company. Your distribution plan should never depend on it.

## Build in the open band before asking permission

The open band is not a consolation prize. In categories the platforms review, it is the band where the bidding is thinnest, because the companies that would normally crowd it are still refreshing their appeal status. Our piece on [thin bidding](https://lowob.com/research/thin-bidding/) sets out why the unglamorous channels are often the cheap ones.

A consumer fintech app that cannot get a Meta account approved can still recruit two hundred personal-finance creators on a cost-per-account basis, stand up an affiliate programme on a network that already carries its category, and buy programmatic inventory against audiences it defines itself. None of those channels asked for a licence. All of them report numbers the company can check.

Open does not mean unregulated. The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance for influencers says any financial, employment, personal or family relationship with a brand must be disclosed, placed with the endorsement itself, and in video stated in the video rather than only in the description. Financial regulators apply their own promotion rules on top. The open band is open to the category, not to loose claims. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) and [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) cover how to structure the terms so the channel holds.

Then, and only then, submit the restricted-band paperwork. If the approval arrives, the company adds a channel to a working system. If it does not, the company has lost a form, not a quarter.

## The plan in four moves

1. **Map the bands truthfully,** in writing, for every geography that matters, using the platforms' own policy pages and dating each entry.
2. **Measure for one week** the two or three open-band channels most likely to carry the product. Small budgets, real tracking, a written question each test must answer. [Campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to write the decision before the test.
3. **Build the channel that read,** properly: terms, tracking, partner recruitment, creative, reporting.
4. **File restricted-band applications in parallel,** with no forecast attached until they clear.

Re-check the map each quarter. Google posted crypto policy updates in July 2025, September 2025 and February 2026, each opening exchange and wallet advertising in another country under conditions. A channel that was closed last year can become restricted, and a restricted one can tighten.

## What this is not

This is not a method for getting past a platform's review. If a category is closed, it is closed, and a company that pretends otherwise spends money teaching the platform to distrust it.

The platforms say so plainly. Google's circumventing systems policy covers cloaking, creating new accounts after a suspension and supplying false information to verification programmes. It treats violations as egregious: accounts are suspended "upon detection and without prior warning", and the advertiser "will not be allowed to advertise with Google Ads again". Reinstatement happens only in compelling circumstances. A vendor who promises an approval is selling a route to that outcome.

The point is the opposite: know where you cannot be seen, say so, and put the budget where the answer was already yes. Map the three bands, build in the open one, and treat every approval as a bonus rather than a foundation.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the rejection as a category decision.** It is made from documents and signals, not from the product in use.
- **Map three bands per geography, with dates.** Open, restricted and closed, checked on the platforms' own pages.
- **Build where the answer is already yes.** Affiliate, creators, owned channels and programmatic first.
- **Forecast nothing in the restricted band.** An approval adds a channel; a refusal costs a form.
- **Never circumvent review.** Google bans accounts for it on detection, permanently.

## Common questions

### What should I do if Meta rejects my fintech ad account?

Do not rebuild the plan around the appeal. Record the policy and documents involved, file what you can supply, and build distribution in channels that carry the category without approval: affiliates, creators with disclosure, owned email and programmatic.

### Which ad platforms allow financial services ads?

Google, Meta and TikTok all allow many financial products with conditions. Google requires verification in a growing list of countries, Meta requires a special ad category with targeting limits for US audiences, and TikTok requires local licensing and 18+ targeting.

### Can I open a new ad account after a suspension?

Not on Google. Its circumventing systems policy bans new accounts after a suspension and suspends them on detection without warning, with no right to advertise again.

### How long does financial services verification on Google take?

Google does not publish a fixed timeline. Its June 2026 European wave gave in-scope advertisers notifications and individual enforcement dates from 23 July 2026, so plan in weeks and forecast nothing until it clears.

## Sources and notes

- [Google Ads, Financial products and services policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/2464998/financial-products-and-services?hl=en-GB), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy; country lists sit on linked pages and change often.
- [Google Ads, Introducing new verification requirements for certain financial services advertisers (June 2026)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/17127726?hl=en), posted 23 June 2026. Platform announcement; covers 24 EEA markets only.
- [Google Ads, Cryptocurrencies and related products policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/14009787?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy; approved markets change through dated updates.
- [Google Ads, Updates to Cryptocurrencies and related products policy (September 2025)](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/16560115?hl=en), posted 10 September 2025. One of several country-by-country updates; Argentina only.
- [Meta for Developers, Special Ad Categories](https://developers.facebook.com/documentation/ads-commerce/marketing-api/audiences/special-ad-category), checked 16 November 2026. Developer documentation rather than Meta's advertising standards page, which did not render for review; describes US scope.
- [TikTok for Business, Financial services ad policy](https://ads.tiktok.com/help/article/tiktok-ads-policy-financial-services), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy; rules vary market by market.
- [Google Ads, Circumventing systems policy](https://support.google.com/adspolicy/answer/15938075?hl=en), checked 16 November 2026. Platform policy.
- [US Federal Trade Commission, Disclosures 101 for social media influencers](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers), current guidance. US only; other jurisdictions apply their own rules.
- The three-band map and the four moves are **lowob**'s framework.

## Next move

Build the band map this week: one row per platform per market, the policy page and the date you read it, the documents required, and whether you can supply them. Then pick the open-band channel most likely to carry the product and write the question its first test must answer.

# How Marketing Services Are Priced: Five Fee Models

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-20 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Marketing services are priced five ways: retainer, project fee, hourly or daily, percent of spend, and performance. Each rewards the provider for something different. Large advertisers are moving away from paying for time, and AI is speeding the shift, but most still lack visibility into what agencies earn. Find what makes the fee go up and you have found the advice you will get.

Marketing services are priced five ways: retainer, project fee, hourly or daily, percent of spend, and performance. Each rewards the provider for something different, so find what makes the fee go up and you have found the advice you will get. The market is moving: a 2026 study of 69 multinational advertisers found fewer than a fifth now pay agencies mainly for time, and 61% plan to change their commercial models because of AI. Yet only 45% said they had enough visibility into how agencies cost and profit from the work.

The fee structure in a marketing proposal is the most reliable predictor of the advice you will receive. Five models cover almost every arrangement, and each one pays the provider for a different thing.

## The five models

**Retainer.** A fixed monthly fee for an ongoing scope of work. Rewards the provider for keeping the relationship. Good for continuous work, running programmes, managing channels, producing a regular cadence of content, and for predictability on both sides. The risk is scope drift: the work quietly shrinks while the fee does not, or expands while the fee does not, depending on who is paying less attention.

**Project fee.** A fixed price for a defined deliverable with a defined end. Rewards the provider for finishing. Good for work with a clear scope: a diagnostic, a positioning exercise, a programme built and handed over, a launch. The risk is the scope document: a vague one produces disputes about what "done" meant.

**Hourly or daily.** Payment for time. Rewards the provider for spending time. Good for truly unpredictable work where neither side can scope in advance, and for very short engagements. The risk is obvious: the model pays for slowness, and the client carries all the estimation risk.

**Percent of spend.** A fee calculated as a share of the media budget the provider manages. Rewards the provider for spending more. The historical standard for media agencies and the model with the sharpest conflict of interest: every recommendation about budget, channel, and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more."

**Performance.** Payment tied to outcomes: leads, customers, revenue, or a bonus above a threshold. Rewards the provider for results, in principle. In practice it depends entirely on how the outcome is defined, measured, and attributed, and on who controls the measurement. Pure performance deals also push the provider toward the easiest outcomes and away from anything slow, such as brand, content, or a channel that takes a quarter to work.

| Model | What you pay for | Fee goes up when | Fits | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retainer | Ongoing capacity | The relationship lasts | Continuous programmes and channels | Scope drift in either direction |
| Project fee | A defined deliverable | It does not, unless scope changes | Work with a clear end | A vague definition of "done" |
| Hourly or daily | Time | More time is spent | Genuinely unscoped or very short work | Pays for slowness; client carries estimation risk |
| Percent of spend | A share of media managed | The budget grows | Large media budgets, with audit rights | Advice biased toward "more" |
| Performance | Outcomes as defined | Contracted outcomes rise | Outcomes measurable in the client's systems | Gaming the definition; avoiding slow work |

## What the market data shows

The ANA's 18th Trends in Agency Compensation survey, published in December 2022, covered 101 US marketers and 336 agency relationships. It found 82% used fee-based compensation, up from 68% in 2016, and that labour-based fees, essentially paying for agency time, remained dominant, at 76% among smaller advertisers. Fixed or output-based fees had risen sharply among the largest spenders.

Outside the US the move away from time is further along. The World Federation of Advertisers and Agency Mania Solutions surveyed 69 multinationals with a combined $147 billion in marketing spend; trade press reported the results in September and October 2026. Labour-based pay as the main model had fallen from 54% of companies in 2011 to under a fifth. Fixed-fee and output models had grown to about a third. AI is a stated reason: agencies can now produce more in less time, which makes paying by the hour harder to defend. Only 20% of respondents had already changed their commercial model in response to AI, and 61% intended to.

Performance pay is talked about more than it is used. In the ANA data, 41% of advertisers used performance incentives in 2022, down from 48% in 2016 and 61% in 2013, and most said they did not know whether incentives improved agency performance. In the WFA study, performance pay made up less than 20% of total agency compensation for most respondents, and financial incentives scored 3.9 out of 6 as a driver of agency performance, against 5.6 for a good brief. Our piece [Performance marketing is not a channel, it is a way of paying](https://lowob.com/research/performance-marketing-way-of-paying/) makes the same point from the buyer's side.

> Find the fee. Ask what makes it go up. That is what the provider is being paid to do.

## What to read in a proposal

Find the fee. Ask what makes it go up. That is what the provider is being paid to do.

A retainer goes up when the relationship lasts. A project fee does not go up at all, which is why providers who quote them care about scope. Hourly goes up with time. Percent of spend goes up with budget. Performance goes up with outcomes as defined in the contract, so read the definition.

Then ask what is not included. Every model has edges, and the profitable part of many engagements is the work that falls outside the original description.

Percent of spend deserves a second read, because what the provider earns may not all appear on the invoice. The ANA's 2016 investigation by K2 Intelligence found US media agencies receiving cash rebates and free inventory based on client spend, and buying media as principals for resale to clients at mark-ups of roughly 30% to 90%. Advertisers interviewed were often unaware of the rebates. The WFA's 2026 finding that only 45% of multinationals have enough visibility into agency costing suggests the gap has not closed. Our piece [Percent of spend is a conflict of interest with a logo on it](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/) makes the wider case.

## The combination that tends to work

For most companies buying distribution work, the least conflicted structure is a project fee against a written scope for anything with an end, a flat retainer for anything ongoing, media fees stated in dollars per account rather than as a percentage, no provider fronting the media spend, and a performance component only where the outcome is defined in writing and measured in the client's own systems.

That is the structure we publish, and we publish it because the alternative, a menu of fee models chosen to suit each deal, leaves the client guessing what the advice is for.

The same logic runs through services pricing generally. A price should be anchored to the value of the outcome and stated before the work starts, which is the argument of our pieces on [pricing architecture for services firms](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/) and [value-based pricing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-value-based-pricing/). Where AI products now charge per outcome, the same definitional discipline applies; see [outcome-based pricing for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-based-pricing-for-ai/).

## Two rules for the buyer

Never accept a free proposal for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document, and the provider's cost of producing it is recovered somewhere in the engagement. The European Association of Communications Agencies put the average agency cost of a new-business pitch at about €43,800 in 2025. That money comes back in later fees. A paid, scoped first step, priced low enough to be an easy decision, produces advice with a defined end and no obligation.

And insist that the next step be priced in the same proposal as the current one. A provider who will not say what the next engagement costs until the current one is finished is pricing on dependency.

Retainers pay for relationships, project fees for finishing, hourly for time, percent of spend for spending, and performance for outcomes as defined. Find what makes the fee go up, and you have found the advice you will get.

## lowob takeaways

- **Read the fee for the incentive.** Each model pays for a different behaviour, and the advice follows the pay.
- **Treat percent of spend with care.** State media fees in dollars and secure audit rights.
- **Define performance in writing.** Measure it in your own systems, or do not pay on it.
- **Price the next step now.** A provider who will not is pricing on dependency.

## Common questions

### What are the main ways marketing agencies charge?

Five models cover almost every arrangement: a monthly retainer, a fixed project fee, hourly or daily rates, a percent of media spend, and performance-based fees tied to outcomes.

### Is percent-of-spend agency pricing a conflict of interest?

It is the model with the sharpest conflict: every recommendation about budget, channel and pace is made by a party paid more when the answer is "more." The ANA's 2016 investigation also found rebates and mark-ups clients often could not see.

### Are agencies moving away from hourly billing?

Among large advertisers, yes. A 2026 WFA study found fewer than a fifth of multinationals now pay agencies mainly for time, with fixed-fee and output models at about a third, and most expect AI to speed the shift.

### Should I accept a free marketing proposal?

Not for anything past a short conversation. A free proposal is a sales document whose cost is recovered somewhere in the engagement; a paid, scoped first step gives advice with a defined end.
