# Developers, Marketplaces and the Answer Engines

Source: https://lowob.com/research/developers-marketplaces-and-the-answer-engines/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-16 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: AI distribution runs through the platforms you plug into, the assistants buyers ask, and the people who build on you. This piece sets out how to pick one lead motion, what cloud marketplaces and model-provider directories actually require and charge, how to show up correctly when buyers ask an assistant, and why paid acquisition comes last.

AI distribution runs through the platforms you plug into, the assistants buyers ask, and the people who build on you. Pick one lead motion, layer the compounding channels, and spend on paid last. The evidence for each channel is now concrete: 45% of B2B buyers in Gartner's 2026 survey had used generative AI during a purchase, cloud marketplaces let buyers spend committed cloud budgets on your product, and product-led adoption carried 27% of AI application spend in Menlo Ventures' 2025 survey.

## Pick a lead motion

Developer-led, sales-led, partner-led. Each needs a different company. Pick one to lead and let the others support.

| Motion | When it fits | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Developer-led | Developers choose the tool and it lives inside their code | An API, docs that work on the first try, a free tier, fast answers in public |
| Sales-led | The buyer is a department, the data is sensitive and the contract is large | The pilot design from [Part 12](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) and a security pack before the first call |
| Partner-led | The product only makes sense inside another platform | Integration depth and a partner manager who answers the phone |

Trying all three at once with one small team is how a seed-stage company spends a year reaching nobody.

The developer-led case is stronger in AI than in older software. Menlo Ventures' 2025 survey of 495 US enterprise AI decision makers found 27% of AI application spend came through product-led growth, against 7% for traditional software, with adoption often starting among developers and technical teams before any enterprise contract. Our explainer on [product-led growth](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-product-led-growth/) covers when that motion fits and when it stalls.

Developers are also sceptical readers. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey of over 49,000 developers found 84% used or planned to use AI tools, but 46% did not trust the accuracy of their output, and technical documentation was the top learning resource at 68%. Docs that work on the first try are not a nicety. They are the sales process.

## Marketplaces of the platforms you plug into

Most AI products live inside something else. A help desk, a CRM, a document store, a chat tool, a cloud provider, a model provider's app directory. Each has a marketplace, and the marketplace is a channel with trust already built in.

The cloud marketplaces matter most for enterprise deals because they double as procurement routes. AWS Marketplace charges SaaS sellers 3% on public offers and on private offers under $1 million in total contract value, falling to 2% from $1 million and 1.5% from $10 million and on all renewals. On Microsoft's marketplace, when a customer buys an "Azure benefit eligible" offer, 100% of the pre-tax amount counts toward their Microsoft Azure Consumption Commitment. A buyer with unspent committed cloud budget may find it easier to buy you there than through a new vendor contract. Our pieces on [marketplace listings for B2B sellers](https://lowob.com/research/marketplace-listings-for-b2b/) and [co-selling with platforms](https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/) cover private offers and partner programmes in detail.

Model-provider directories are newer and stricter than most founders expect. OpenAI's submission guidelines for apps in ChatGPT require a clear purpose and reliable function, a published privacy policy, collection of "only the minimum data required", and a fully featured demo account for review. They state that "trial or demo plugins will not be accepted" and reject apps that serve advertisements or use misleading tool descriptions to steer the model toward them.

The listing is a sales page. Treat it like one. Clear job, screenshots of the workflow, a demo video under two minutes, pricing in the open, reviews from real users.

Integration depth decides ranking and conversion. A shallow "connects to" integration gets listed. A deep one, that reads and writes the objects the buyer cares about, gets recommended by the platform's own team.

| Platform type | What the listing must prove |
| --- | --- |
| Help desk or support | Draft quality or deflection, with a before and after |
| CRM | Data written back cleanly, no duplicate records |
| Cloud marketplace | Private offer ready, commitment-eligible where possible, security pack attached |
| Model-provider directory | Clear use case, minimal data collection, works on first run in review |
| Developer platform | Install in minutes, docs that match the current version |

## Answer-engine presence

Buyers now ask assistants before they search. "What tools help a finance team reconcile invoices?" If the assistant does not describe your product correctly, you are not in the consideration set.

The evidence is building. Gartner's survey of 645 B2B buyers, published in May 2026, found 45% had used generative AI during a purchase, mainly to research vendors and products, and 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a sales rep. Pew Research Center's tracking of 900 US adults found Google users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% without one, and clicked a link inside the summary on 1%. Pew's data is consumer search, not B2B, but the direction is clear: the summary is increasingly the whole answer.

Answer engines read what is public, plain and consistent. So put a one-paragraph product description on your site. What it does, who it is for, what it connects to. Repeat it, word for word, on marketplaces, directories and docs. Keep your pricing page readable as plain text. Publish comparison pages that are fair, because assistants quote them and buyers check. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers the mechanics.

Then test it. Ask several assistants what your product does and who it is for. Fix the gaps at the source. A press release does not fix a wrong answer. A clearer docs page does.

> A press release does not fix a wrong answer. A clearer docs page does.

## Content that demonstrates

AI buyers have seen enough claims pages. Show the product running on realistic data, end to end, with the mistakes left in. A twelve-minute recording of a real workflow converts better than a polished sixty-second montage, in our experience, because it answers the questions a sceptical buyer would otherwise ask the rep.

Publish the eval. If you claim accuracy, show the test set description, the method and the result, with a date. Those pages get cited by assistants and shared by engineers. They also feed the claims register from [Part 11](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/). Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers what a readable eval contains.

Write for the person doing the job, not the person reading the deck.

## Power users as distribution

Every AI product has a handful of users who build on it. Templates, prompts, workflows, integrations. They are your best channel, and they are cheap to serve.

Give them a place ([Part 5](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/)), credit by name, early access and a way to publish what they built. A gallery of user-built workflows is both proof and a search surface. It also shows answer engines what the product is for, in the users' own words.

## Paid last

Paid works when you know your activation rate and payback period ([Part 9](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/)). Until then, paid in an AI category buys expensive clicks from people comparing twelve tabs. Put the budget into integration depth, the security pack and one good demonstration first.

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Lead motion | One chosen and written down, with the other two as support |
| Marketplaces | Listed on every platform you integrate with, with a demo video and a private offer route |
| Product paragraph | Identical across site, docs and listings |
| Answer engines | Three assistants asked what the product does; gaps fixed at the source |
| Demonstration | One end-to-end recording and one published eval |
| Power users | Gallery live, with credit by name |

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose one lead motion.** Developer-led, sales-led or partner-led, with the others in support.
- **Treat marketplaces as procurement, not just discovery.** Private offers and commitment eligibility move enterprise deals.
- **Write one plain product paragraph.** Repeat it word for word across site, docs, marketplaces and directories, then test what assistants say.
- **Turn on paid last.** Only once you know your activation rate and payback period.

## Common questions

### How do I get ChatGPT or other AI assistants to describe my product correctly?

Answer engines read what is public, plain and consistent. Put a one-paragraph product description on your site, repeat it word for word on marketplaces, directories and docs, keep pricing readable as plain text, then ask several assistants and fix gaps at the source.

### Should an AI startup list on AWS or Azure Marketplace?

Yes, if enterprise buyers are the target. AWS charges SaaS sellers 3% on public offers and on private offers under $1 million, and eligible Azure Marketplace purchases count fully toward a customer's Azure consumption commitment, which can shorten procurement.

### Should an early AI startup run developer-led, sales-led and partner-led at once?

No. Each needs a different company. Pick one to lead and let the others support; trying all three with one small team is how a seed-stage company spends a year reaching nobody.

### When should an AI company start paid advertising?

Last, once you know your activation rate and payback period. Until then, paid in an AI category buys expensive clicks from people comparing twelve tabs.

# What Is a Restricted Category in Advertising?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-14 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Ad platforms sort products into prohibited, restricted and open groups, using a process built to refuse a legitimate business rather than approve a harmful one. Google, Meta, TikTok and Apple each publish the conditions, and they change them often. A restricted classification is a map of where to build distribution, not a review to argue with or evade.

A restricted category is a group of products an ad platform will advertise only with conditions, such as prior approval, proof of licensing, certification, geographic limits, age limits or required disclaimers. Platforms sort every product into prohibited, restricted or open, using a process built to prefer refusing a legitimate business over approving a harmful one. Financial services, crypto, health, gambling and alcohol are restricted on most platforms, with rules that differ by country and change several times a year. Treat the classification as a map of where to build, not as a review to argue with.

Every major advertising platform maintains a policy that sorts products into three groups: those it will run without question, those it will run with conditions, and those it will not run at all. The middle group is what the industry calls restricted categories, and it is larger than most founders expect until they are in it.

## The three groups

**Prohibited.** Products the platform will not advertise under any conditions. The list varies but typically includes weapons, illegal products, counterfeit goods, certain adult content and, on some platforms and in some geographies, entire financial or health sub-categories. No documentation changes the answer. Google disapproves ads for binary options and credit repair services, and bans ads for initial coin offerings and DeFi trading protocols regardless of location.

**Restricted.** Products the platform will advertise only with conditions: prior written approval, proof of licensing or registration, certification, geographic limits, age restrictions, specific disclaimers or limits on claims. Financial services, cryptocurrency, gambling, alcohol, pharmaceuticals, health and supplements, dating, political content and several others sit here on most platforms, with the exact rules differing by platform and country.

**Open.** Everything else, subject to the general policies on claims, creative and landing pages that apply to all advertisers.

## What the conditions look like on four platforms

The conditions are not secret. They are published, and they are more mechanical than most rejection emails suggest.

| Platform | Financial services | Crypto | Health |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Google Ads | Verification required in some locations, with licences and registration numbers; physical address and fees must be disclosed | Exchanges and software wallets need approval and local registration, such as FCA registration in the UK or MiCA authorisation in the EU; DeFi protocols and ICOs banned | Online pharmacies, prescription drug services and addiction services need certification; prescription opioid ads banned with limited exceptions |
| Meta | US financial ads must run in a special ad category: fixed age range, no gender targeting, no lookalike audiences | Permission, or one of Meta's accepted regulatory licences, which Meta expanded from three to 27 in December 2021 | Not reviewed here |
| TikTok | Local licensing, disclosures and 18+ targeting in most markets | Prohibited in some markets; permitted with licensing and an application through a sales representative in others | Not reviewed here |
| Apple App Store | Apps in banking and financial services must be submitted by the legal entity providing the service | Exchanges only in countries where the app holds the licences; ICO and crypto futures apps only from approved financial institutions | Healthcare apps must be submitted by the legal entity providing the service |

*Policies checked on each platform's own pages on 16 November 2026, except where noted.*

Two patterns stand out. First, most conditions are about documents and geography, not about the product's quality. Second, the rules move. Google posted crypto policy updates in July 2025 for Canada, September 2025 for Argentina and February 2026 for Indonesia, each opening exchange and wallet advertising under local licensing. In June 2026 it announced financial services verification for 24 more European markets, with rolling enforcement from 23 July 2026. A restricted classification is a fact with a date on it.

## How the decision is made

The platform's policy is written by its legal, trust-and-safety and policy teams, and it is applied by a combination of automated classifiers and human reviewers who see the ad, the landing page, the account history and sometimes the business documents, but never the product in use.

That last point explains most of the frustration. A reviewer is asked to decide quickly whether an account looks like a category that has caused the platform legal or reputational problems before. A legitimate consumer fintech app looks, to a classifier, much like a predatory one. An AI product that mentions medical or financial use cases can be sorted into those categories by a keyword. Google's healthcare policy, for example, restricts the use of prescription drug terms in ads, landing pages and keywords, so the vocabulary alone can trigger the review. A Web3 wallet is a crypto product regardless of what it holds.

Appeals exist, and sometimes succeed. They are slow, opaque and decided by the same process.

## Why legitimate companies get caught

The platform's cost of a wrong approval is high: regulatory action, press coverage, advertiser boycotts. The platform's cost of a wrong refusal is one lost small advertiser. The policy is written accordingly. Companies in reviewed categories are not being judged; they are being sorted, by a system designed to prefer refusing a legitimate business over approving a harmful one.

Regulators reinforce the asymmetry. The UK Financial Conduct Authority reported that in 2024 it had 19,766 promotions by authorised firms amended or withdrawn, interviewed 20 finfluencers under caution and issued 38 alerts against finfluencer social media accounts. A platform that carries an illegal promotion is part of that story. One that refuses a lawful one rarely is.

Recognising that is useful. It means the rejection is not personal, is not evidence the product is wrong, and is not likely to be overturned by better copy.

> Companies in reviewed categories are not being judged. They are being sorted.

## What the classification means for a distribution plan

A company that learns it is in a restricted category has learned something valuable early: which channels it cannot plan around.

The practical response is a map. For each platform and geography that matters, record whether the category is prohibited, restricted or open, what documentation a restricted approval requires, and whether the company can supply it. Then plan in three bands:

1. **Build first** in the channels that carry the category without approval: affiliate and partner programmes, creator distribution with disclosure, clipping, owned email and content, and much of programmatic.
2. **File the restricted-band paperwork** with nothing forecast against it.
3. **Write the prohibited channels down as closed,** so nobody proposes them in the next planning cycle.

The open band is usually built on partners. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers how to set the roles and payment for each partner type, and [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to register, pay and disclose referrals. Our playbook [Meta said no](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) and the [ninety-day worked example](https://lowob.com/research/restricted-category-distribution-worked-example/) show the map in use.

## What it does not mean

It does not mean finding a way around the review. Accounts created to disguise a category, landing pages that show reviewers one thing and users another, and vendors who promise approvals are all routes to permanent bans, lost account history and, in regulated categories, worse.

Google's circumventing systems policy names cloaking, new accounts after a suspension and false information in verification programmes. It treats them as egregious: the account is suspended upon detection and without prior warning, and the advertiser cannot advertise with Google Ads again. A restricted classification is a fact about where to look for distribution. It is not a puzzle to be solved.

## lowob takeaways

- **Restricted means conditions, not refusal.** Licences, certification, geography, age and disclaimers decide it.
- **The conditions are published and dated.** Read them on the platform's own page and record the date.
- **A wrong approval costs the platform far more than a wrong refusal.** Policy is written to refuse.
- **Map, then build in the open band.** File restricted paperwork with nothing forecast against it.
- **Never disguise the category.** Cloaking and new accounts after suspension end in permanent bans.

## Common questions

### What is a restricted category in advertising?

A group of products a platform will advertise only with conditions, such as prior approval, licensing proof, certification, geographic or age limits, disclaimers or claim limits. Financial services, crypto, gambling, alcohol and health sit here on most platforms.

### Why was my legitimate fintech or crypto ad account rejected?

Platforms sort accounts by how the ad, landing page and documents look, without seeing the product in use, and a wrong approval costs them far more than a wrong refusal. The rejection is not personal and is unlikely to be overturned by better copy.

### What is the difference between a restricted and a prohibited ad category?

A restricted category can run once conditions are met, such as Google certification for a crypto exchange. A prohibited one cannot run at all, such as Google's ban on ads for DeFi trading protocols or binary options.

### Should I try to get around ad platform category restrictions?

No. Disguised accounts, landing pages that show reviewers something different, and vendors who promise approvals lead to permanent bans and, in regulated categories, worse.

# The Pilot That Survives Security Review

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-09 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Revenue

> Summary: AI pilots die from security review, missing owners, demo-grade accuracy and pricing confusion, rarely from the product. Gartner expected at least 30% of generative AI projects to be abandoned after proof of concept. This playbook sets out the pilot design that passes: one narrow use case, real data in week one, a written success test, a security pack mapped to the questionnaires buyers actually send (SIG, CAIQ and SOC 2), a named owner and a paid fee.

AI pilots die from security review, missing owners, demo-grade accuracy and pricing confusion. Design the pilot to pass all four before you sign it. Gartner predicted that at least 30% of generative AI projects would be abandoned after proof of concept by the end of 2025, citing poor data quality, inadequate risk controls, escalating costs and unclear business value. Those are pilot design failures, and most of them can be closed before the first call.

## Why AI pilots die

Pilots rarely die from the product. They die from everything around it.

**Security and data review.** Where does the data go, who sees it, is it used for training, how long is it kept? If you cannot answer in writing, the pilot waits for you to write it.

**No owner.** A sponsor who likes the demo is not an owner. An owner has budget, a deadline and something to lose if it fails.

**Demo accuracy versus production accuracy.** The demo ran on clean examples. Production has typos, edge cases and missing fields. The gap surprises the buyer and confidence drops.

**Procurement.** Vendor onboarding, data processing agreement, insurance. A parallel track that nobody started until month three.

**Pricing confusion.** Seats, usage or outcomes? If finance cannot forecast the bill, finance will not approve it.

The external evidence lines up with that list. Gartner's 2024 prediction on abandoned generative AI projects named data quality, risk controls, cost and unclear value; its analyst noted that costs "aren't as predictable as other technologies". Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 CIO survey found that "procurement now mirrors traditional software buying", with security and cost gaining weight relative to accuracy. The good news is that pilots designed well do convert: Menlo Ventures' 2025 survey found 47% of AI deals reached production, against 25% for traditional SaaS.

## Scope one use case and get real data early

"Explore AI for the support team" is not a pilot. "Draft first replies for tier-one billing tickets in English" is.

Narrow scope makes the security review smaller, the success test clearer and the owner easier to find. It also makes the result believable. A win on one ticket type is a reference. A vague win on "support" is a slide.

Ask for real data in week one. A sanitised sample proves the demo, not the product. If real data access takes eight weeks, that is the pilot's real timeline. Better to know now than to discover it in week six.

## Write the success test before you start

Agree, in writing, what passing looks like. Three parts: metric, threshold, method.

Example shape: over a fixed volume and a fixed period, what share of outputs are used with minor or no edits, as judged by whom. Pick the number with the buyer, not for them. Then neither side can move it later.

Add a failure clause. If the test fails, the pilot ends and both sides say so. A pilot with no way to fail has no way to win either.

The test is also how the demo-to-production gap gets measured honestly. Run it on the buyer's real data, report the production number, and keep the demo number out of the result. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to set up a test both sides can read, and a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/) is the right place to record who signs it off and when.

> A pilot with no way to fail has no way to win either.

## The security pack

Build it before the first enterprise call. Most enterprise security questionnaires ask the same things, because most are built on a handful of standards. Answer them once, in plain language, and keep it dated.

| Questionnaire or report | Who publishes it | What it is | What to have ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SIG (Standardized Information Gathering) | Shared Assessments | The common third-party risk questionnaire, issued in Lite, Core and Detail scopes; the 2026 edition added an ISO/IEC 42001 mapping for AI governance | Answers to the Core scope, kept current each year |
| CAIQ and AI-CAIQ | Cloud Security Alliance | Self-assessment questionnaires; the AI Controls Matrix v1.1 (July 2026) has 247 control objectives across 18 domains, and its AI-CAIQ has 320 questions | A completed AI-CAIQ, optionally filed on the STAR Registry |
| SOC 2 report | Issued by a CPA firm against AICPA criteria | An attestation on security and operational controls, not on model accuracy | A Type 1 or Type 2 report, or a dated timeline |
| Data processing agreement | Required of processors under GDPR Article 28 | Contract terms for personal data, including sub-processors | Template DPA and sub-processor list |

SOC 2 is changing. In October 2026 the AICPA proposed revised trust services criteria that add points of focus on AI governance, model monitoring, prompt manipulation and data poisoning, with comments due by 15 January 2027 and a proposed effective date for engagements beginning on or after 31 December 2027. Our explainer on [SOC 2 for AI vendors](https://lowob.com/research/soc-2-for-ai-vendors/) covers what a report does and does not prove.

Under the questionnaires, the content of the pack is the same six sections.

| Section | What to include |
| --- | --- |
| Compliance status | SOC 2 or ISO status, or a plain timeline if not yet |
| Data flow | One diagram: what enters, where it is stored, where it leaves |
| Model and vendor disclosure | Which models, which providers, whether data is used for training |
| Retention and deletion | How long, where, and how a customer gets it deleted |
| Access control | Who at your company can see customer data, and when |
| Incident process | Who gets called, how fast, what they get told |

If you are not SOC 2 yet, say so and say when. Buyers forgive gaps. They do not forgive surprises in week five.

The model and vendor section matters most for AI. Buyers want to know whose servers see their data and under what terms. Have the sub-processor list ready, and say whether your model providers offer [zero data retention](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-zero-data-retention/) on the endpoints you use. Our explainer on [data processing agreements for AI](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-data-processing-agreement-for-ai/) lists the clauses buyers' lawyers check first.

## Owner, money and price

**Named owner.** Get a name, a title and a budget line before you start. If nobody will own it, nobody will buy it.

**Paid pilot.** Charge something. The amount matters less than the invoice. A paid pilot gets a deadline, a purchase order and an owner, because someone had to approve the spend. Free pilots drift.

**Price after, structure before.** Fix the pilot fee now. Agree the full-contract price after the success test, but settle the structure up front. Seats, usage or outcomes. Pick one and explain it in one paragraph. Usage-based pricing on an AI product needs a cap or an estimate, or finance will block it on principle. The a16z survey found CIOs mostly preferred usage-based pricing because outcome-based terms were hard to set and measure; our piece on [seats, usage or outcomes](https://lowob.com/research/seats-usage-or-outcomes/) covers the trade-offs.

## The checklist

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Scope | One use case, one team, one language, written in a sentence |
| Data | Real data access agreed for week one |
| Success test | Metric, threshold and method, signed by both sides, with a failure clause |
| Security pack | Complete and dated, mapped to SIG and CAIQ, including model and vendor disclosure |
| Owner and fee | Named owner with budget, and a pilot fee on an invoice |
| Pricing | Structure chosen and explained before the pilot starts |

## lowob takeaways

- **Scope one use case.** Drafting first replies for tier-one billing tickets in English is a pilot; "AI for support" is not.
- **Write the success test first.** Metric, threshold and method, plus a failure clause.
- **Answer the standard questionnaires once.** SIG, CAIQ and a SOC 2 status cover most of what buyers send.
- **Charge for the pilot.** Free pilots drift.

## Common questions

### Why do enterprise AI pilots fail?

They rarely die from the product. They die from security and data review, no real owner, the gap between demo and production accuracy, procurement started late, and pricing finance cannot forecast. Gartner cited data quality, risk controls, cost and unclear value.

### What should an AI vendor security pack include?

Compliance status, a data flow diagram, model and vendor disclosure including whether data is used for training, retention and deletion, access control and the incident process, mapped to the SIG and CAIQ questionnaires. Keep it dated and have the sub-processor list ready.

### What security questionnaires will an enterprise send an AI vendor?

Most are based on Shared Assessments' SIG, the Cloud Security Alliance's CAIQ or its AI-CAIQ, or a request for a SOC 2 report. A completed AI-CAIQ and SIG Core answer most custom questionnaires too.

### What if my startup is not SOC 2 compliant yet?

Say so and say when. Buyers forgive gaps, but they do not forgive surprises in week five. A completed CAIQ and a dated audit timeline carry most early deals.

# What Go-to-Market Means: A Plain Guide for Founders

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-gtm-for-founders/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-09 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Go-to-market is the plan for how a company finds customers, convinces them to buy, and does so at a cost that leaves a business. It is four decisions that must agree: who exactly, what they must believe, how trust moves, and what evidence proves it is working. A company has a GTM when it can write one sentence for each and the four sentences agree.

Go-to-market, GTM, is the plan for how a company will find its customers, convince them to buy, and do so at a cost that leaves a business. It is bigger than a launch calendar. It is four decisions: who exactly, what they must believe, how trust moves, and what evidence proves it is working. A company has a GTM when it can write one sentence for each of the four and the four sentences agree with each other.

"Go-to-market" is one of those phrases that everybody uses and nobody defines. Investors ask about it. Advisors recommend fixing it. Job titles contain it. Founders who came from engineering or product nod along and privately wonder what, precisely, is being asked.

Here is the plain version.

## The definition

Go-to-market, GTM, is the plan for how a company will find its customers, convince them to buy, and do so at a cost that leaves a business. It sits between the product, what was built, and revenue, what comes back, and it answers the question: how does this thing get from us to the people who will pay for it, repeatedly?

It is not marketing, though it includes marketing. It is not sales, though it includes sales. It is the whole route from a stranger to a paying customer, including the parts nobody owns.

Analyst definitions point the same way. Gartner describes a GTM strategy as "a plan that details how an organization can engage with customers," and its framework for sales leaders starts with identifying the target market, then mapping how customers enter and move through their buying process. That framework is written for large sales organisations and adds compensation and investment planning. For a founder, the four decisions below are the part that has to be right first. Our explainer [What is a go-to-market strategy?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) covers the strategy level in more detail.

## The four decisions inside it

**Who, exactly.** Which narrowly defined group of buyers has the most expensive version of the problem, the authority to fix it, the budget to pay, and a reason to act now. "Fintech companies" is not an answer. "Compliance leads at U.S. consumer lenders preparing for a new disclosure rule in the next two quarters" is.

**What they must believe.** Buyers do not buy features. They buy a change they can recognise: less risk, less time, more revenue, a problem gone. The message is the translation from what the product does to the change the buyer wants, in language the buyer already uses.

**How trust moves.** The path from first contact to a signed contract or a funded account. A self-serve product, an enterprise sale, a partner-led distribution, and a community-driven adoption are different paths with different economics. The path determines which channels can carry the product: which of them the buyer trusts, and, for reviewed categories, which of them will carry the product at all.

**What evidence proves it is working.** Not followers or impressions. Qualified conversations, activation, retention, revenue, and cost per customer against what a customer is worth.

A company has a GTM when it can write one sentence for each of the four and the four sentences agree with each other.

| Decision | The sentence it produces | Evidence that it is right | What it looks like when it is missing |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who, exactly | "We sell to [role] at [type of company] when [trigger]." | Win rate and cycle length are better in this group than outside it | Every prospect qualifies; pipeline is large and slow |
| What they must believe | "They buy because [change], and they doubt [objection]." | Prospects repeat the change in their own words | Calls start with a long explanation of what the product is |
| How trust moves | "They find us through [path] and decide via [process]." | Most customers arrived by the path the team planned | Customers arrive by accident and nobody knows why |
| What evidence proves it | "We track [measure] weekly, against [cost per customer]." | One number moves when the route works and stalls when it does not | Reports show activity, not customers |

The first decision is where most young companies fail. CB Insights analysed 101 startup post-mortems and found 42% cited no market need as a reason for failure, ahead of running out of cash at 29%. The analysis is old and based on founders' own accounts, but the pattern is consistent: a product can work and still have no buyer with enough reason to act now. Choosing the buyer from evidence is covered in [segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/).

The third decision has changed most in recent years. Gartner's March 2026 survey of 646 B2B buyers found 67% preferred a rep-free buying experience and 45% had used AI during a recent purchase. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision. Trust now has to move through a website, a forwarded document and a buying group the founder never meets, as well as through the founder's own calls.

> A company has a GTM when it can write one sentence for each of the four decisions and the four sentences agree with each other.

## What GTM is not

A list of channels. A launch plan. A hire. A slide. A brand. Companies routinely confuse each of these with GTM, and the confusion shows up as busy teams and flat revenue. Activity is easy; a coherent route to a customer is not.

| Often mistaken for GTM | What it actually is | Which decision it depends on |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A list of channels | Tactics for one part of the route | How trust moves |
| A launch plan | A single event on the calendar | All four |
| A sales or marketing hire | Capacity to run a route | All four, already written down |
| A positioning slide | One input to the message | Who, exactly, and what they must believe |
| A brand | How the company is recognised | What they must believe |

McKinsey's 2024 survey of nearly 4,000 B2B decision makers found buyers used an average of ten interaction channels, up from five in 2016. With that many channels available, a list of them is not a plan. The plan is the choice of which ones carry trust to this buyer. Our piece [Your startup needs a GTM strategy, not just a list of tactics](https://lowob.com/research/gtm-strategy-vs-tactics/) applies the same four decisions as a coherence test.

## The founder's role

Early on, the founder is the GTM. They hold the context, they take the calls, they change the pitch mid-meeting, and they learn faster than any hire could. That phase has an end, and its purpose is to discover the four answers well enough that other people can operate them. A founder who never writes the answers down never gets out of the phase.

[Founder-led GTM is a job with an expiration date](https://lowob.com/research/founder-led-gtm-expiration-date/) sets out when the phase ends and what the founder should keep. For marketing specifically, [From founder-led to team-led marketing](https://lowob.com/research/from-founder-led-to-team-led-marketing/) covers which decisions transfer first.

## How to tell whether you have one

Four tests separate a company with a go-to-market from one with traction and effort. Each can be answered in an afternoon.

1. **The absence test.** A new employee can explain who the customer is without you in the room.
2. **The reasons test.** The team can say why the last five customers bought and the last five prospects did not.
3. **The route test.** You know which channel produced each customer, at what cost.
4. **The single-number test.** One number, tracked weekly, tells you whether the route is working.

If most of those fail, the company has traction, product, and effort, but not yet a go-to-market. That is normal, and it is fixable. The fix begins with the four sentences.

## lowob takeaways

- **Choose a specific customer and problem.** "Who, exactly" is the decision most failed startups got wrong.
- **Write one sentence per decision.** Who, what they must believe, how trust moves, and what evidence proves it, and check they agree.
- **Connect the functions to one route.** Product, marketing, sales and partnerships serve the same path to the same buyer.
- **Use founder-led conversations to learn.** The founder phase exists to discover what should become repeatable, and to write it down.

## Common questions

### What does go-to-market mean?

Go-to-market is the plan for how a company finds its customers, convinces them to buy and does so at a cost that leaves a business. It covers the whole route from a stranger to a paying customer.

### What are the parts of a go-to-market strategy?

**lowob** treats it as four decisions that must agree: who exactly the buyer is, what they must believe, how trust moves from first contact to contract, and what evidence proves it is working.

### Is go-to-market the same as marketing or sales?

No. GTM includes marketing and sales but also covers the choice of buyer, the buying path and the measures, including the parts of the route nobody owns.

### How do I know if my startup has a go-to-market strategy?

A new employee can explain the customer without you, the team knows why recent deals were won and lost, you know which channel produced each customer at what cost, and one weekly number shows whether the route works.

## Sources and notes

- [Gartner, Go-To-Market Strategy Framework](https://www.gartner.com/en/sales/trends/go-to-market-strategy-framework). Analyst framework page aimed at chief sales officers of larger organizations.
- [CMO Council, Define the need before you bleed](https://www.cmocouncil.org/expert-views/cmo-blog/define-the-need-before-you-bleed-marketing-rigor-can-reduce-start-up-failure), 6 July 2021. Secondary report of CB Insights' analysis of 101 startup post-mortems; founders' own accounts, older data.
- [Gartner, 67% of B2B buyers prefer a rep-free experience](https://www.gartner.com/en/newsroom/press-releases/2026-03-09-gartner-sales-survey-finds-67-percent-of-b2b-buyers-prefer-a-rep-free-experience), 9 March 2026. Survey of 646 B2B buyers, August to September 2025; stated preference.
- [Forrester, The State Of Business Buying, 2024](https://www.forrester.com/press-newsroom/forrester-the-state-of-business-buying-2024), 4 December 2024. Analyst press release; sample size not stated in the release.
- [McKinsey, Five fundamental truths: How B2B winners keep growing](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/growth-marketing-and-sales/our-insights/five-fundamental-truths-how-b2b-winners-keep-growing), 12 September 2024. Survey of nearly 4,000 B2B decision makers in 13 countries; self-reported.
- The four-decision table, the "not GTM" table and the four tests are **lowob**'s framework.

# How Marketing Tracking Works: Pixels to Server-Side

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-03 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Pixels see less every year and platforms fill the gaps with modelled estimates. Safari blocks third-party cookies by default, Apple requires permission to track across apps, and Chrome kept third-party cookies but behind user choice. First-party data, server-side tracking, tagged links and consent are the measurement layer that survives, and the company should own it, not whoever runs its media.

Every marketing number depends on tracking: connecting a person who saw or clicked something with a person who later did something. Pixels see less every year, because Safari blocks third-party cookies by default, Apple requires permission before apps track users, and consent rules cover much of the rest. Platforms fill the gaps with modelled estimates. First-party data, server-side tracking, tagged links and consent are the measurement layer that survives, and the company should own it, not whoever runs its media.

The mechanics of tracking have changed a great deal in six years, and the changes explain why numbers that used to agree no longer do. A finance lead looking at three platform dashboards that each claim the same customers is not looking at an error. They are looking at how the system was built.

## The old model: pixels and third-party cookies

A pixel is a small piece of code on a website that reports back to a platform when a page loads or an event happens. Each ad platform issues its own. The pixel sets or reads a cookie, a small file in the visitor's browser that lets the platform recognise the same browser later.

For a decade this worked well enough. A person clicked an ad, the platform's cookie followed them to the purchase, and the platform reported a conversion. Every platform did this independently, which is why the sum of all platforms' reported conversions has always exceeded the number of actual customers. A buyer who saw a social ad, clicked a search ad and opened an affiliate email can be claimed three times.

## What changed

Four changes, in roughly this order.

| Change | Date | What it did | Effect on measurement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Safari full third-party cookie blocking | March 2020 (iOS 13.4, macOS 10.15.4) | Blocked cross-site cookies by default | Cross-site pixels lost Safari users |
| Apple App Tracking Transparency | iOS 14.5 and later | Apps need permission to track or read the advertising identifier | Declined users show an identifier of all zeros |
| Consent regimes and consent mode | Ongoing; EU, UK, several US states | Consent needed for non-essential tracking | Unconsented conversions are modelled, not measured |
| Chrome keeps third-party cookies | April 2025 decision; October 2025 Sandbox retirement | Users keep a choice; most Sandbox ad APIs retired | No industry replacement; fragmentation persists |

Apple's developer guidance is explicit. Tracking means linking data from your app with data from other companies' apps, websites or offline properties for advertising or measurement. Without permission, "the device's advertising identifier value will be all zeros", and developers may not use a hashed email or phone number to track a user who declined.

Chrome went the other way. Google spent years planning to phase out third-party cookies, then announced in 2025 that Chrome would keep its current approach, which leaves the choice with users. In October 2025 its Privacy Sandbox lead announced the retirement of most of the replacement advertising technologies, including the Attribution Reporting API, Topics and Protected Audience, citing low adoption. CHIPS, FedCM and Private State Tokens remain.

The result is not a cookieless world. It is a fragmented one. Pixels see a shrinking and uneven fraction of what happens, and platforms fill the gaps with modelled estimates. Google's guide to conversion modelling describes estimating conversions for users who decline consent, and says the modelling recovers, on average, more than half of the click-to-conversion journeys that would otherwise be lost. Reported conversions became partly measured and partly inferred, and the inference is done by the party being measured.

## First-party data

First-party data is information a company collects directly from its own customers and visitors, on its own properties, with their consent: email addresses, account activity, purchases, product usage. It is not affected by third-party cookie blocking because there is no third party.

It has become the foundation of measurement because it is the one source that does not depend on a platform's cooperation. A company that knows which of its own customers came from which source, by asking, by tagging links, by matching emails, can measure channels the pixels cannot see. Our comparison of [intent data and first-party data](https://lowob.com/research/intent-data-vs-first-party-data/) covers the B2B side, and our explainer on [lead source attribution](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-lead-source-attribution/) covers how to record the source on each record.

## Server-side tracking

Instead of the visitor's browser reporting events to each platform, the company's own server records the event and forwards what is appropriate to each platform through their conversion APIs. The company controls what is sent, the data is not blocked by browser tools, and the record exists in the company's own systems first.

Meta's documentation describes the intended setup as "redundant": the Conversions API runs alongside the Pixel, and the two are deduplicated by sending the same event ID and event name from browser and server. Duplicates arriving within 48 hours are discarded. That detail matters for anyone reading the numbers. A server-side setup without deduplication double-counts; one with it recovers events the browser lost.

Server-side tracking is more work to set up and requires care about consent and what is shared. Sending data through a server does not make consent optional, and Apple's rules on tracking apply whatever the transport. It is also the only way to keep platform reporting meaningful as browser-based tracking degrades, and it is the natural home for first-party data.

> The measurement layer underneath the media should be in the company's name, because it is the record of what the money did.

## Tagged links, codes and consent

The oldest tools still work. Parameters appended to URLs identify the source, medium and campaign of a visit in the company's own analytics. Unique codes and landing pages per partner or creator attribute outcomes without any cookie at all. For affiliate, creator and clipping programmes, these are the primary tracking method, and they should be in the company's analytics, not only in the partner's.

Consent is not a formality. In most jurisdictions where a company sells, some form of it is required before tracking beyond what is strictly necessary. A consent management platform, a clear policy and tracking that respects the visitor's choice are the minimum. Google's conversion modelling, for example, requires consent mode or the IAB Transparency and Consent Framework to be implemented correctly. Numbers gathered without consent are a liability, not an asset.

Where individual tracking fails entirely, aggregate methods take over. A [marketing mix model](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-marketing-mix-modeling/) works from weekly spend and outcomes, and a geographic holdout needs no cookie at all.

## What a company should own, regardless of who runs the media

| Asset | Why it must be in the company's name | What breaks if it is not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Analytics account | It holds the outcome history | Switching partner resets the baseline |
| Tag manager | It controls what fires, where | Changes happen without the company's knowledge |
| Server-side configuration and conversion API keys | It decides what data leaves the company | Data sharing outside the company's control |
| Consent platform | It records the legal basis for tracking | Liability without visibility |
| First-party data | It survives every platform change | The one durable asset is held elsewhere |
| Link-tagging convention | It makes sources comparable over time | Every partner names things differently |
| Tracking plan document | It says which events are tracked, where, and how each channel's outcomes are confirmed | Nobody can audit the numbers |

A media partner can and should run the accounts on the company's behalf. The measurement layer underneath them should be in the company's name.

## lowob takeaways

- **Platform totals always exceed customers.** Each platform counts independently, and modelled conversions now fill the gaps.
- **Cookies were not abolished; they fragmented.** Safari blocks them, Apple gates app tracking, Chrome leaves the choice to users.
- **Server-side tracking needs deduplication.** Same event ID from browser and server, or the numbers double.
- **Own the measurement layer.** Analytics, tag manager, server-side setup, consent platform, first-party data and the tracking plan.

## Common questions

### Why don't my ad platform conversion numbers match my actual sales?

Each platform counts conversions independently and credits itself, and as browser tracking degrades, platforms fill gaps with modelled estimates. Reported conversions are partly measured and partly inferred by the party being measured.

### Is Google still getting rid of third-party cookies?

No. In 2025 Google said Chrome would keep its current approach, leaving users a choice, and in October 2025 it retired most Privacy Sandbox advertising APIs. Safari still blocks them by default.

### What is server-side tracking?

The company's own server records events and forwards what is appropriate to each platform through their conversion APIs, instead of the visitor's browser reporting to each platform. It must be deduplicated against the pixel.

### What parts of marketing measurement should a company own if an agency runs its ads?

The analytics account, tag manager, server-side tracking configuration, consent platform, first-party data, link-tagging convention, and a document describing what is tracked and how outcomes are confirmed.

- [MacRumors, Safari in new versions of iOS and macOS includes full third-party cookie blocking](https://www.macrumors.com/2020/03/24/safari-full-third-party-cookie-blocking), 24 March 2020. Trade press report of the WebKit announcement.
- [Google Privacy Sandbox, Update on plans for Privacy Sandbox technologies](https://privacysandbox.google.com/blog/update-on-plans-for-privacy-sandbox-technologies), Anthony Chavez, 17 October 2025. Google's own announcement; retirement timelines are on Google's status page and may change.
- [PPC Land, Chrome kills most Privacy Sandbox technologies after adoption fails](https://ppc.land/chrome-kills-most-privacy-sandbox-technologies-after-adoption-fails/), October 2025. Trade press; source for the April 2025 decision to keep third-party cookies.

# The Model Is Not the Product

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-04-03 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Buyers do not pay for a model; they pay for a finished job. Enterprise buyers now run several models at once and say most perform well enough, so positioning on the model makes every pitch sound the same. This piece sets out how to position on the job and workflow, answer the wrapper objection by showing what you own, put every AI claim through a register regulators would recognise, and keep the investor and customer stories apart.

Buyers do not pay for a model. They pay for a finished job. Position on the job, prove every AI claim, and tell investors a different story from customers. The market has made this sharper: 37% of enterprises in a16z's 2025 CIO survey used five or more models, and model market share swings by double digits in a year, so a pitch built on the model is a pitch any competitor can copy.

## Why every pitch sounds the same

The model is shared infrastructure. Whatever it can do today, your competitor's version can do by Tuesday. So pitches that lead with the model converge. "AI-powered." "Built on frontier models." "Intelligent assistant for X." The buyer cannot tell you apart and stops trying.

The buyer data shows why. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 survey of 100 enterprise CIOs found 37% used five or more models, up from 29% a year earlier, choosing by use case rather than loyalty. One leader told the researchers that "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now". Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey shows how quickly the supply side moves: Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year, while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. If your advantage is the model you picked, it is an advantage you rent, and the lease is short.

Positioning starts where the model ends. What does the buyer have at the end that they did not have before? A closed ticket. A reconciled ledger. A contract redlined to their playbook. Name that, in the buyer's words, and the model becomes a detail.

## Workflow and outcome over model

Write your one product truth ([Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/)) without naming a model, a vendor or the word AI. If you cannot, you have described a feature, not a product.

Then map the workflow. Where does the work start? Who touches it? What breaks today? Where does your product sit, and what does it hand back?

Most of the value in AI products lives in the unglamorous parts. Intake. Retrieval. Permissions. Review. Exceptions. The hand-off to the system of record. That is also where it gets hard to copy. A competitor can match your prompt in an afternoon. Matching your exception handling takes a year of customer calls.

The same a16z survey adds a commercial reason to invest there. It found that agentic workflows were making it harder for enterprises to switch between models, because the prompts, tools and checks around each model become tuned to it. The switching cost sits in the workflow. A vendor that owns the workflow owns the switching cost; a vendor that only resells the model does not.

## The wrapper objection

You will hear "isn't this just a wrapper?" from investors, buyers and engineers. Do not argue. Agree that the model is rented, then show which of three things you own.

| What you own | What it looks like | How to prove it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data | Proprietary, labelled or permissioned data the model cannot see | Show results with and without it |
| Distribution | A channel, install base or integration the model provider does not have | Show where the users come from |
| Workflow depth | The steps around the prompt that make it fit a real job | Show a user doing the job end to end |

One is enough to start. Two is a business. If you own none, the objection stands, and polishing the deck will not fix it.

Distribution deserves more weight than most founders give it. Our analysis of [why AI companies have a distribution problem disguised as a model problem](https://lowob.com/research/ai-companies-distribution-problem/) sets out the evidence that buyers now choose on fit, proof and integration. If your answer to the wrapper question is "distribution", the proof is a chart of where users came from and what it cost to reach them.

> A competitor can match your prompt in an afternoon. Matching your exception handling takes a year of customer calls.

## AI claims in the claims register

AI products attract claims that cannot survive a demo. Put every one in the register from [Part 2](https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/), with evidence, owner and date.

This is no longer only a matter of buyer trust. In September 2024 the US Federal Trade Commission announced Operation AI Comply, including action against a company that marketed itself as "the world's first robot lawyer" without testing its output against lawyers' work; the chair said there was "no AI exemption from the laws on the books". In March 2024 the SEC settled charges against two investment advisers for claiming AI capabilities they did not have, which the SEC chair called "AI washing". Gartner estimated in 2025 that only about 130 of the thousands of vendors marketing agentic AI were real, the practice our explainer on [agent washing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) covers.

| Claim | The question it must answer | Evidence that holds |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accuracy | On what dataset, measured how, by whom, when? | A dated eval on a described test set, demo and production numbers labelled separately |
| "Agent" | Does it act without a human in the loop, for which steps, and what happens when it is wrong? | A list of actions it takes alone and those that need approval |
| "Learns from your data" | Does the model update, or does retrieval? | A plain statement of which, and where customer data goes |
| Time or cost saved | Against what baseline, for which task? | A before and after on one named workflow |

Accuracy: production accuracy is lower than demo accuracy. Say which one you are quoting. If you only have the demo number, say that too. Our explainer on [AI evals](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-ai-evals/) covers how to build a test a buyer can read.

"Agent": if a human approves every action, call it an assistant. Buyers trust you more for it, and the security review goes faster. Our explainer on [AI autonomy levels](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-an-ai-autonomy-level/) gives a vocabulary for saying exactly how much the product does alone.

"Learns from your data": they are different products with different risks. Say which.

Anything without a test behind it comes out of the copy. Not softened. Out.

## Investor story and customer story

Investors buy the category. Why this workflow, why now, why you will own the data or the distribution in three years.

Customers buy Tuesday. This task, this team, this cost, this risk, this quarter.

Mixing them hurts both. Customers hear "platform" and wait for the roadmap. Investors hear a feature list and see a tool. Write both stories, keep them in separate documents, and make sure the same claims register underwrites each one. If a claim is only in the investor deck, ask why. The SEC case above involved claims made to clients in filings and marketing; a claim that would embarrass you in a customer's procurement file should not be in an investor deck either. Our piece on [raising for an AI company](https://lowob.com/research/raising-for-an-ai-company/) covers what investors now test.

## The checklist

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Product truth | Written without "AI", a model name or a vendor name |
| Workflow map | End to end, with your product's entry and exit points marked |
| Wrapper answer | Data, distribution or workflow depth, with proof |
| Claims register | Every accuracy and "agent" claim has a test behind it |
| Two stories | Investor story and customer story in separate documents |
| Homepage test | Still makes sense with "AI" deleted |

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the product truth without the model.** No model name, no vendor name, no "AI".
- **Own something the model provider does not.** Data, distribution or workflow depth, with proof.
- **Treat AI claims as testable statements.** Regulators already do.
- **Keep two stories on one register.** Investors buy the category; customers buy this task, team, cost and risk this quarter.

## Common questions

### How should an AI startup position its product?

Position on the finished job, in the buyer's words, not on the model. Map the workflow end to end and show where your product sits and what it hands back. Enterprises use several models and switch by use case, so the model is not a durable point of difference.

### How do I answer the "it's just a wrapper" objection?

Agree the model is rented, then show which of three things you own: proprietary data, distribution, or workflow depth, with proof. One is enough to start; two is a business.

### When should an AI product be called an agent?

Only if it acts without a human in the loop, and you should say for which steps and what happens when it is wrong. If a human approves every action, call it an assistant. Gartner estimated only about 130 vendors marketing agentic AI were genuine.

### Can an AI company get in trouble for exaggerating what its AI does?

Yes. The FTC's Operation AI Comply and the SEC's 2024 "AI washing" settlements both targeted companies whose AI claims were not supported. Every claim should have a test, an owner and a date behind it.

Menlo invests in AI companies, so weigh it against buyer-side data.

# CPM, CPC, CPA, CPL, ROAS Explained: Which to Run On

Source: https://lowob.com/research/cpm-cpc-cpa-cpl-roas-explained/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-31 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: CPM, CPC, CPL and CPA describe what a company pays for, and each hides what the next reveals. ROAS flatters, because it counts attributed revenue against media cost alone. The number to manage the business on is customer acquisition cost against value over a realistic horizon, with payback period as the constraint.

CPM, CPC, CPL and CPA describe what a company pays for, and each one hides what the next reveals. ROAS flatters: Google's own definition divides conversion value by ad spend and nothing else, so margin, fees and the attribution model all sit outside it. The number to manage the business on is customer acquisition cost (CAC) against value over a realistic horizon, with payback period as the constraint.

Every media report is built on a small set of acronyms. They describe what was paid for and what came back, and each one hides something the others reveal. The choice of which to manage to is not a reporting preference. It decides what the media buyer, the platform's bidding system and the finance team are all optimising.

## The pricing acronyms: what you pay for

**CPM, cost per mille (thousand impressions).** The price of a thousand ad views. The oldest measure and the standard for programmatic and display. It tells you what attention costs, not whether the attention was real or did anything. Even "viewable" is a low bar: the Media Rating Council's guideline counts a display impression as viewable when 50% of its pixels are on screen for one continuous second, and a video when they are on screen for two.

A low CPM is often a symptom of poor inventory. The ANA's 2023 programmatic transparency study, covering $123 million of spend and 35.5 billion impressions from 21 advertisers, found made-for-advertising sites took 21% of impressions and 15% of spend. Cheap inventory buys a lot of volume. The same study found the top 500 domains had a 50% lower fraud rate than the long tail and were 13% more viewable. Our piece on [programmatic numbers you can trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) covers how to price CPM after verification.

**CPC, cost per click.** What you pay each time someone clicks. The standard for search and much of social. Better than CPM because a click is an action, but clicks are cheap to generate and easy to fake, and a click is not a customer.

**CPL, cost per lead.** What you pay for a contact: a form, a sign-up, a download. The standard for business-to-business and any considered purchase. Useful only if "lead" is defined tightly; a loose definition produces cheap leads nobody can sell to. Our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) argues for managing to cost per qualified opportunity instead, for exactly this reason.

**CPA, cost per acquisition (or action).** What you pay for a defined outcome: an account opened, a purchase made, a subscription started. The standard for performance marketing and affiliate programmes. The closest of the pricing acronyms to something the finance team recognises.

**CPV, cost per view,** for video and clipping programmes, and **CPI, cost per install,** for apps, follow the same logic: a price for a defined event that may or may not lead to a customer.

## The return acronyms: what you get back

**ROAS, return on ad spend.** Revenue attributed to advertising divided by the cost of the advertising. Google's help page for Target ROAS gives the formula plainly: $5 in sales divided by $1 in ad spend is a 500% target. Conversion value is whatever the advertiser reports to the platform, usually revenue. Nothing in the calculation refers to cost of goods or margin.

That makes ROAS misleading in two ways. It depends entirely on how revenue was attributed, and it ignores every cost except media. The break-even ROAS on media alone is one divided by gross margin. At 30% gross margin that is 3.33. A campaign with a ROAS of four on that product earns $1.20 of gross profit per $1 of media, leaving 20 cents to pay for the agency fee, the creative, the tools and the people. Count those, and count the share of attributed revenue that would have arrived anyway, and it is usually losing money.

**CAC, customer acquisition cost.** All acquisition spending (media, fees, creative, tools, people) divided by the number of new customers. The honest cousin of CPA. Harder to compute, harder to game. Andreessen Horowitz's widely used metrics guide makes one refinement worth keeping: blended CAC, which divides by all new customers including organic ones, is not wrong but cannot show whether paid acquisition is profitable. Report paid CAC alongside it.

**LTV, lifetime value,** or more usefully, value over a defined horizon. What a customer is worth over twelve or twenty-four months, net of refunds, churn and cost to serve. The number CAC has to be compared with for any of this to mean anything.

**Payback period.** How many months of a customer's contribution it takes to recover the cost of acquiring them. The measure a company with limited cash should watch most closely, because a channel with excellent LTV and an eighteen-month payback can still bankrupt it. Our explainers on [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) and [LTV:CAC versus payback](https://lowob.com/research/ltv-cac-vs-cac-payback/) set out the formulas.

## What each one hides

| Metric | What it measures | What it hides | Where it is standard |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CPM | Price of 1,000 impressions | Whether the impression was seen, human or useful | Display, programmatic, video |
| CPC | Price of a click | Whether the click was interested, or real | Search, much of social |
| CPL | Price of a contact | Whether the lead was qualified | B2B, considered purchases |
| CPA | Price of a defined outcome | Whether the customer stayed, and whether they would have come anyway | Performance, affiliate |
| ROAS | Attributed revenue per $1 of media | Margin, non-media costs, the attribution model | Ecommerce, platform bidding |
| CAC | All acquisition cost per new customer | Little, if paid and blended are split | Finance, board reporting |
| Payback | Months to recover CAC | Value after the payback window | Cash planning |

CAC hides nothing much, which is why fewer reports feature it.

> A media partner who reports in CPM and ROAS but cannot produce CAC and payback is reporting what they were paid to deliver, not what the company received.

## Why the platform's number is not the company's number

Every figure in the CPA and ROAS rows is calculated from conversions the platform recorded. Each platform counts independently, so the totals across platforms routinely exceed the number of real customers. Since browsers and Apple's App Tracking Transparency cut what pixels can see, platforms also fill gaps with modelled conversions: Google's guide to conversion modelling describes estimating conversions for users who decline consent. Our piece on [how marketing tracking works](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/) covers the mechanics.

The fix is a reconciliation step. Every CPA, CPL and ROAS figure in a report should say which events the company's own tracking confirmed, rather than which events a partner or platform claimed. Where the two differ, the company's number is the one to pay against.

## Which one to run on

Run the week on the pricing acronym closest to the outcome you can observe: CPA where an outcome is trackable, CPL where the sale happens offline, CPC or CPM only where nothing further down the funnel can be measured yet.

Run the quarter on CAC against value over a realistic horizon, with payback as the constraint. Use incrementality tests to correct for the conversions that would have happened anyway; our piece on [attribution versus incrementality](https://lowob.com/research/attribution-vs-incrementality/) explains how.

Illustrative example: one channel, three readings

Decision
:   Keep, cut or scale a paid social channel reporting a ROAS of 4.2 on a product with 35% gross margin.

Illustrative: a composite of a direct-to-consumer subscription business, built from patterns across engagements. Figures are invented to show the structure.

## lowob takeaways

- **CPM prices attention, not whether it was real.** A low CPM often signals poor inventory.
- **ROAS counts media cost alone.** Compare it with one divided by gross margin before reading it as profit.
- **CAC divides all acquisition spending by new customers.** Fees, creative, tools and people included, paid and blended split.
- **Run the week and the quarter on different numbers.** The pricing metric closest to an observable outcome weekly; CAC against horizon value, with payback as the constraint, quarterly.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between CPA and CPL?

CPL is what you pay for a contact such as a form or sign-up, and is useful only if "lead" is tightly defined. CPA is what you pay for a defined outcome such as an account opened or a purchase made.

### Why is ROAS misleading?

ROAS divides attributed revenue by media cost only. It ignores margin, fees, creative and people, and depends on the attribution model. At 30% gross margin a ROAS of 3.3 only covers the media.

### What is a good ROAS?

It depends on margin. Break-even ROAS on media alone is one divided by gross margin, so 2.5 at 40% margin and 5 at 20%. A good ROAS clears that line after non-media costs and incrementality.

### Which marketing metric should a company manage to?

Run the week on the pricing metric closest to an observable outcome, and the quarter on customer acquisition cost against value over a realistic horizon, with payback period as the constraint.

## Sources and notes

- [Google Ads Help, About Target ROAS bidding](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/6268637?hl=en). Platform documentation; the formula and example are Google's, and value is whatever the advertiser reports.
- [ANA, "First Look" at in-depth programmatic media transparency study](https://ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2023-06-programmaticstudy), 19 June 2023. Trade association study of 21 advertisers, $123 million of spend, September 2022 to January 2023.
- [ANA Programmatic Media Supply Chain Transparency Study, First Look](https://info.adtheorent.com/hubfs/Gated-Downloads/ANA%20Programmatic%20Media%20Supply%20Chain%20Transparency%20Study%202023.pdf), June 2023. The study document, hosted by a vendor; source of the top-500 domain fraud and viewability comparison.
- [ANA, Media Rating Council updates viewable ad impression measurement guidelines](https://ana.net/content/show/id/36327), August 2015. Industry standard summary; viewability is a minimum exposure threshold, not proof of attention.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), 21 August 2015. Investor guidance; older, but the blended versus paid CAC distinction is unchanged.
