# Build It to Run Without You

Source: https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-27 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A GTM system is only an asset if the company owns it: the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons. Knowledge walks out with people, platforms decide ownership by whose business holds the account, and EU law now backs the right to export from software providers. Build for handover from day one, write handover into any outside scope, and score yourself on ten questions to find and fix the weakest link first.

A GTM system is only an asset if the company owns it: the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons. Most firms lose the last two first. A Panopto survey estimated 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role, so it leaves when they do. Build for handover from day one, write handover into any outside scope, then score yourself across all ten parts of this series and fix the weakest link first.

This is Part 10 of [Raise, Rally, Revenue](https://lowob.com/research/raise-rally-revenue/), the series that treats fundraising, community and customers as one commercial system. The first nine parts build the system. This one makes sure the company keeps it.

## What "owning it" means

| Asset | What to own | Common failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accounts | Ad, social, email, analytics, domain, community admin rights, all in the company's name | Agency or ex-employee holds the logins |
| Records | Evidence log, investor pipeline, partner list, customer source data | Spread across personal inboxes and DMs |
| Routines | Runbooks for recurring work: investor update, partner launch, community ritual, monthly report | Only one person knows how it's done |
| Reasons | Why each major decision was made and what was rejected | The next hire repeats an experiment that already failed |

The last row is the one almost nobody keeps, and the one that saves the most money. A decision record of three lines is enough: what we chose, what we rejected, what would change our minds.

## Why the reasons row matters most

Software teams formalised this problem fifteen years ago. In 2011 Michael Nygard proposed the architecture decision record: a short, numbered note per significant decision, with its context, the decision, its status and its consequences. His argument was that a newcomer who does not know why a decision was made has two bad options: to accept it blindly or to reverse it blindly. Superseded records are kept, not deleted, so the history stays readable.

Commercial teams face the same choice every time someone leaves. Panopto's 2018 survey of 1,000 workers estimated that 42% of institutional knowledge is unique to the individual in the role, and that knowledge workers spent 5.3 hours a week waiting for information from colleagues or recreating it. In a small GTM team, the person who knows why the paid channel was cut, or why a partner was dropped, is often the founder or the agency. Our explainer on [what a decision record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) sets out the fields and how to write one well.

> A good partner should be trying to make themselves unnecessary for the work they've finished.

## Accounts: ownership is decided by whose name is on them

Ownership of an ad or analytics account is not a matter of goodwill. It is how the platforms are built. Meta's business tools treat the business that owns an asset as the one that controls it: the owner grants a partner agency access to named tasks, such as advertising or analysis, and can remove the agency from the asset. An agency cannot pass on access to assets it only holds as an agency. If the agency opened the account in its own business, the company is the guest.

Large advertisers have noticed. In the ANA's 2023 survey of 162 members, owning, controlling and protecting first-party data was one of the stated reasons for moving work in-house. A small company can get the same protection without an in-house agency: open every account in its own name and grant access outward.

Regulation is moving the same way for the tools that hold the records. The EU Data Act's switching rules have applied since 12 September 2025 to cloud and SaaS providers serving EU customers. Contracts must allow a customer to start switching on no more than two months' notice, the switch must normally complete within 30 days, the data that can be exported must be specified, and from 12 January 2027 switching charges are prohibited. That helps with the CRM and the analytics stack. It does nothing for a spreadsheet in an ex-employee's personal drive, which is why the records row says shared, owned tools.

## If you bring in outside help

Write handover into the scope at the start, not the end. Accounts opened in your name. Reports in a format your team can produce without the agency. A final session that walks your team through every runbook. A good partner should be trying to make themselves unnecessary for the work they've finished.

| Clause | What it says | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Account ownership | All accounts opened in the company's name; agency granted access | Nobody can hold the company hostage with logins |
| Data and files | Raw data, creative source files and reports delivered and stored in company tools | The history stays when the agency goes |
| Reporting format | Reports the company's team can reproduce without the agency | Continuity after handover |
| Runbooks | Written procedures for each recurring task the agency performs | The work can continue or move |
| Handover session | A final walkthrough with the team that will take over | Tacit knowledge gets transferred |
| Decision record | The agency's reasons, including what it tried and dropped | The next team does not repeat failures |

The same discipline applies inside the company. Our piece on [the handover from sales to delivery](https://lowob.com/research/the-handover-from-sales-to-delivery/) shows where promises and reasons get lost between teams, and [what a system of record is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-system-of-record/) covers how to decide which tool is authoritative for each kind of data.

## The ten-question self-score

Score each question 0 to 5. Zero means "not at all"; five means "done, with evidence I could show an investor today."

| # | Question | Part |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Do fundraising, community and customer work run off one calendar with one owner? | 1 |
| 2 | Is there a one-sentence product truth, and a belief statement per audience? | 2 |
| 3 | Is there a dated evidence log with incentivised and organic activity separated? | 3 |
| 4 | Is the raise run from a researched list, tracked like a pipeline? | 4 |
| 5 | Does the community have a named job, measured by contribution? | 5 |
| 6 | Can you name the first hundred people who'd notice if you disappeared? | 6 |
| 7 | Do you have design partners with written success tests and agreed post-pilot prices? | 7 |
| 8 | Is every channel sorted open, restricted or closed, with partners ahead of paid media? | 8 |
| 9 | Do you report activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source, instead of reach? | 9 |
| 10 | Would the system keep running if your most important person left tomorrow? | 10 |

**Reading your score (a rule of thumb, not a verdict):**

**40 to 50:** the system is in place. Spend on scale.

**30 to 39:** it works, with gaps. Fix the two lowest scores before the next big spend.

**Under 30:** you're likely spending on step eight with steps two and three unanswered. Go back to the lowest-numbered question you scored below 3 and start there.

**A zero on question 2, 3 or 7** is a stop sign regardless of total: no clear truth, no evidence or no real customer means the next dollar of fundraising or marketing is guesswork.

For teams launching a token, this sits alongside a stricter launch-readiness check covering legal, security, treasury and liquidity, which deserves its own piece.

## Closing the spine

The order matters more than any single tactic in these ten parts. Name the buyer. Write one truth. Collect evidence. Raise against it. Give your community a job. Make your first customers partners. Distribute through people who already have your buyer's trust. Measure what comes back. Then make sure you own all of it.

That's the whole system. Most teams have pieces of it. Very few have it in order.

*If you'd like a second pair of eyes on your score, bring us the commercial problem.*

## lowob takeaways

- **Own the accounts.** Every ad, social, email, analytics, domain and community admin account should be in the company's name.
- **Keep the reasons.** Three lines per major decision: what was chosen, what was rejected, what would change your mind.
- **Write handover in at the start.** Put it in an outside partner's scope on day one, not at the end.
- **Respect the stop signs.** A zero on product truth, evidence or real customers outranks the total score.

Gateway card

### The checklist

- Every account in the company's name, with an access list
- Evidence log, pipeline and monthly report in shared, owned tools
- Runbooks for the five most repeated GTM tasks
- A decision record for every major choice
- Handover written into every outside scope
- The ten-question self-score, done and dated

## Common questions

### What does it mean for a startup to own its go-to-market system?

The company owns the accounts, the records, the routines and the reasons behind decisions, so the system keeps running if a key person or agency leaves.

### Should my agency or my company own the ad accounts?

Your company. Open ad, analytics and social accounts in the company's own business account and grant the agency access. On platforms such as Meta, the owning business controls the asset and can remove an agency's access.

### What should a decision record include?

Three lines are enough to start: what we chose, what we rejected, and what would change our minds. Fuller formats add context, status and consequences.

### How do I make sure an agency hands over its work properly?

Put handover in the scope from the start: accounts opened in your name, reports your team can produce without the agency, and a final session walking your team through every runbook.

# Influencer vs Creator vs KOL vs Ambassador: Definitions

Source: https://lowob.com/research/influencer-creator-kol-ambassador/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Influencers sell reach, creators sell content and conversion, KOLs sell authority in a specific domain, and ambassadors sell an ongoing, disclosed relationship. The people may overlap, but the deals should not. Pay each for what they sell, disclose every material connection under FTC and UK ASA rules, and run the whole as a programme.

Influencers sell reach, creators sell content and conversion, KOLs sell authority in a specific domain, and ambassadors sell an ongoing, disclosed relationship. The people may overlap, but the deals should not. Pay each for what they sell, disclose every material connection, and run the whole as a programme. The spend is large enough to deserve the discipline: the IAB put US creator ad spend at $37 billion in 2025, growing about four times faster than the media industry as a whole.

The creator economy uses four words for people who are paid to talk about products, and most companies use them interchangeably. The people behind the words are often the same. The deals should not be.

## The four, defined by relationship

**An influencer** is a person with an audience who accepts payment to feature a product. The word carries the legacy of consumer brands: reach, aesthetics, a sponsored post. The relationship is transactional and usually short.

**A creator** is a person who makes content as a profession and whose audience follows them for the content itself. The word emphasises the craft. Creators may accept sponsorships, run affiliate links, sell their own products, or all three. The relationship can be transactional or long-term. Few make a living at it: Goldman Sachs Research estimated in 2023 that about 4% of roughly 50 million creators worldwide earn more than $100,000 a year.

**A KOL (key opinion leader)** is a person whose audience trusts their judgment in a specific domain: a doctor in pharmaceuticals, an analyst in finance, a researcher or trader in crypto. The idea comes from mid-century Western research: Paul Lazarsfeld's studies of the 1940 US election identified "opinion leaders" who passed media messages on to others, and Elihu Katz and Lazarsfeld developed the model in *Personal Influence* in 1955. Pharmaceutical marketing later made the paid KOL a profession; a 2008 BMJ analysis described drug companies paying leading specialists advisory and speaking fees to influence other doctors. In much of Asia the term is now the standard word for any paid creator, and in Web3 it came to mean anyone with a large following, which emptied it of meaning. Used properly, it describes authority rather than reach.

**An ambassador** is a person with an ongoing, disclosed relationship with the company, usually paid a retainer, product, or equity, who represents the brand over time, at events, in content, and in community. The relationship is the point; individual posts are incidental.

| Term | What they sell | Typical relationship | Typical payment | Wrong job to give them |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Influencer | Reach | Transactional, short | Flat fee per post or package, plus product | Conversion |
| Creator | Content and conversion | Transactional or long-term | Flat fee, affiliate, cost per outcome, licensing | Anything on a flat fee you expect to sell |
| KOL | Authority in a domain | Scoped to a job | Higher fee for an explainer, research, event | Volume |
| Ambassador | Ongoing presence | Long-term, disclosed | Retainer, product or equity, with scope and term | Cheap promotional labour |

## How each is paid

Influencers: a flat fee per post or package, sometimes plus product.

Creators: flat fees, affiliate commissions, cost-per-outcome deals, or licensing fees for content the brand reuses in its own ads. The best creator deals for a converting product are cost-per-outcome, because the creator is paid for the result and stays if it works. Buyers are moving that way: 40% of the creator ad buyers in the IAB's 2025 study ranked overall return on investment as their top measure.

KOLs: higher fees, reflecting authority; often structured around a specific job (an explainer, a research collaboration, an event) rather than a post count. In regulated categories, what a KOL may say is constrained by the same rules that apply to the company. In the UK, the FCA's 2024 guidance on social media financial promotions warns that influencers who promote a regulated product without approval from an authorised firm may be committing a criminal offence. In the US, the SEC's 2022 settlement with a celebrity paid $250,000 to promote a crypto token, without disclosing it, totalled $1.26 million.

Ambassadors: retainers or equity, with a defined scope, a term, and disclosure in every appearance.

> The people may overlap, but the deals should not.

## What each is for

Awareness at scale: influencers and large creators. Explaining a product and converting a buying audience: mid-tier creators on performance terms. Changing what a specialist audience believes: KOLs, in the proper sense. Sustained presence in a community or at events: ambassadors.

Companies go wrong when they buy one and expect another: paying an influencer for conversion, asking a KOL for volume, treating ambassadors as cheap promotional labour, or expecting a creator on a flat fee to care whether anything sold. Our guide to [reading a creator media kit](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-read-a-creator-media-kit/) shows how to check whether the person in front of you can do the job you are buying.

## The rules that apply to all four

**Disclosure of the material connection**, clearly and conspicuously, in every piece of content, in the form the relevant regulator specifies. The labels differ, so the brief should state them:

|  | United States (FTC) | United Kingdom (ASA, CAP and CMA) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What triggers disclosure | Any financial, employment, personal or family relationship, including free or discounted products | Payment of any kind, including gifts and commission, plus brand control over the content |
| Acceptable wording | "Ad", "sponsored", or a sentence naming the relationship | "#Ad", "#Advert", "#Advertising", "#Advertisement", "#AdvertisementFeature" |
| Wording to avoid | Vague terms such as "sp", "collab", or standalone "thanks" or "ambassador" | "Gift", "Affiliate", "PR", "Sponsored", "Collab" |
| Placement | Hard to miss, with the endorsement; in video, in audio and on screen | At the very beginning of the advertising content |
| Who is responsible | Advertiser and endorser; the advertiser can be liable even when the endorser is not | Influencer, brand and any agent in the chain |

Note that "ambassador" on its own is a word the FTC lists as too vague to count as disclosure. An ambassador programme still needs an explicit label in each post. The UK guide adds that disclosure is expected throughout a relationship and for 12 months after it ends, which matters for ambassadors on rolling terms.

**A brief** that explains the job, the product truth, what may not be said, and the tracking. The FTC's staff guidance expects advertisers to have reasonable programmes to train and monitor the people in their network, and recommends approving paid posts before they go live.

**A link, code, or landing page per person** so results can be attributed.

**A written agreement**, however short, covering usage rights, term, exclusivity, and what happens if the content is wrong.

## The structure that makes it a channel

One-off deals produce one-off results. A programme, with public terms for the long tail, negotiated terms for the middle tier, and a small number of authorities or ambassadors at the top, produces a channel with a cost per outcome that can be compared with everything else the company buys. That is the difference between creator marketing as an expense and creator distribution as an asset.

The structure is the same one a company uses for any partner channel. Our explainer on [partner programmes](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-partner-program/) covers tiers, benefits and obligations, and [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers registration, payment and disclosure for the performance tier. In crypto launches, [KOL campaigns need more than impression screenshots](https://lowob.com/research/web3-kol-campaign-measurement/) sets out how to measure KOLs against outcomes rather than impressions.

## lowob takeaways

- **Name the relationship before the person.** Reach, content, authority or presence.
- **Pay for what is sold.** Performance terms for conversion; scoped fees for authority; retainers for presence.
- **Write the label into the brief.** "Ambassador" alone is not disclosure under FTC guidance.
- **Run it as a programme.** Tiers, public terms and a cost per outcome you can compare.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an influencer and a KOL?

An influencer is someone with an audience who is paid to feature a product, usually for reach. A KOL, or key opinion leader, is someone whose audience trusts their judgment in a specific domain, so they sell authority rather than reach.

### How should creators be paid?

Through flat fees, affiliate commissions, cost-per-outcome deals or licensing fees. For a product that converts, cost-per-outcome is best because the creator is paid for the result.

### What is a brand ambassador?

A person with an ongoing, disclosed relationship with a company, usually paid a retainer, product or equity, who represents the brand over time at events, in content and in community.

### Do brand ambassadors have to disclose the relationship?

Yes. Under FTC guidance "ambassador" on its own is too vague, so each post needs a clear label such as "ad". UK guidance expects "#Ad" upfront, during the relationship and for 12 months after it ends.

# Stop Reporting Reach

Source: https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-23 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pick the few numbers that show attention turning into money that comes back: activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source. Report incentivised and organic activity separately, instrument every channel before spending on it, send every audience the same core numbers, and drop vanity metrics from the top of the page.

Pick the few numbers that show attention turning into money that comes back: activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source. Instrument them before you spend on growth, report them to everyone who matters, and drop the vanity metrics from the top of the page. Reach is the easiest number to grow and the weakest evidence: a display impression counts as viewable when half the ad is on screen for one second, and in Keyrock's study of 62 airdrops in 2024, 88% of tokens lost value, most within 15 days.

## The question every number has to answer

Did someone do something that makes the business more likely to exist next year? If a metric can rise while the answer is no, it belongs in an appendix.

Reach and impressions fail the test by construction. The industry standard for a viewable display impression, set by the Media Rating Council, is 50% of the ad's pixels on screen for one continuous second; for video, two seconds. That is a floor for counting exposure, not evidence anyone noticed. Follower counts and cumulative totals fail it too. Andreessen Horowitz's guide to startup metrics makes the point about cumulative charts: they always rise for any active business, so they can look healthy while the business shrinks. The same guide calls downloads "really just a vanity metric" and asks for cohort retention instead.

## What to measure

| Stage | Web3 | AI | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Activation | First deposit, first trade, first onchain action | First task completed, first integration live | Interest became use |
| Retention | Deposits and wallets still active at 30 / 90 days | Weekly active users or teams at 30 / 90 days | Use became habit |
| Revenue | Protocol revenue, net of incentives | Paid accounts, net revenue retention | Habit became money |
| Efficiency | Cost per retained depositor, incentive spend per $ of sticky TVL | Customer acquisition cost, payback period | Money exceeds what it cost |
| Source | Which partner, campaign or referral brought them | Same | Where to spend next |

Two definitions need care. "Active" means whatever the company decides it means, and the a16z guide warns that some definitions count accidental one-time users; write the definition down and keep it. And revenue is not the same as fees or bookings. DefiLlama, a widely used public DeFi dashboard, separates fees (everything users pay) from revenue (the subset the protocol keeps after paying liquidity providers) and lists incentives (tokens handed to users) as a separate line. Report revenue net of incentives. For AI and SaaS, our comparison of [NRR and GRR](https://lowob.com/research/nrr-vs-grr/) covers which retention number to put first, and [CAC payback](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-cac-payback/) covers efficiency.

## The incentive adjustment

In web3, separate what you paid for from what you earned. Report TVL, volume and users both with and without incentivised activity. If 80% disappears when incentives end, the honest number is the 20%, and investors will compute it whether you do or not.

The evidence on airdrops shows why. Keyrock's analysis of 62 airdrops across several chains in 2024 found 88% of tokens declined in value, most within 15 days of distribution, and only 8 of the 62 showed positive returns after 90 days. Its successful cases had an existing user base, rewarded actual usage and released tokens in stages; one failure attracted reward hunters because it had little prior product traction. Activity bought with incentives behaves like rented activity. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) covers how to design for the people who stay.

The same principle applies to AI products running free tiers or heavy discounts. Report the paid and the free separately. Andreessen Horowitz makes the parallel point about acquisition cost: blended CAC, which counts organic customers, cannot show whether paid acquisition is profitable, so report paid CAC beside it.

> If a metric can rise while the business is no more likely to exist next year, it belongs in an appendix.

## Instrument before you spend

The most expensive mistake in early go-to-market is a year of activity with no way to tell what worked. Before spending meaningfully on any channel:

1. Tag every link and referral by source.
2. Track activation and 30-day retention by source, not just in aggregate.
3. For web3, map wallet addresses to campaigns where you can do so properly and lawfully.
4. Write down what result would make you double the channel and what would make you stop it.

The fourth step is the one most often skipped, and the one that turns reporting into decisions. Our piece on [campaign testing that reaches a decision](https://lowob.com/research/campaign-testing-that-reaches-a-decision/) covers how to set those thresholds at low volumes.

## One report, three audiences

The monthly report you send investors should contain the same core numbers your team runs the business on, and a version of it should be what you share with your community. Different detail, same truth. If the investor update and the internal dashboard disagree, one of them is wrong. Our piece on [commercial KPIs a board will trust](https://lowob.com/research/commercial-kpis-a-board-will-trust/) covers how to define each number once and reconcile it to finance.

| Audience | Detail | Same core numbers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Team | Weekly, by channel and cohort | Activation, retention, revenue, efficiency, source |
| Investors | Monthly, with trend and commentary | The same five, incentivised and organic split |
| Community | Monthly or quarterly, summarised | The same five, without commercially sensitive detail |

## What to stop reporting

- Impressions and reach, at the top of anything.
- Follower counts as progress.
- Waitlist size without a conversion rate.
- Cumulative totals in place of monthly figures.
- Incentivised volume without the unincentivised number next to it.
- "Partnerships announced" without what each one produced.

Gateway card

### The checklist

- Five numbers: activation, retention, revenue, efficiency, source
- A written definition of "active" and of revenue net of incentives
- Incentivised and organic reported separately
- Every channel tagged before money goes in
- A double-or-stop rule for each channel
- One monthly report, the same core numbers for every audience

## lowob takeaways

- **Use one test for every number.** If it can rise while the business is no more likely to exist next year, it belongs in an appendix.
- **Separate bought activity from earned.** Most airdropped tokens lose value within weeks; report the unincentivised number.
- **Instrument before you spend.** Tag every link and referral, and track activation and 30-day retention by source.
- **Send one truth to three audiences.** Investors, the team and the community see the same core numbers at different levels of detail.

## Common questions

### What metrics should a startup report instead of reach and impressions?

Five numbers: activation, retention, revenue, efficiency and source. For web3 that means first deposit, active wallets at 30 and 90 days, protocol revenue net of incentives and cost per retained depositor; for AI, first task completed, weekly active teams, net revenue retention and payback.

### How should a crypto project report TVL that includes incentives?

Report TVL, volume and users both with and without incentivised activity. If 80% disappears when incentives end, the honest number is the 20%, and investors will compute it whether you do or not.

### Which vanity metrics should founders stop reporting?

Impressions and reach at the top of anything, follower counts as progress, waitlist size without a conversion rate, cumulative totals, incentivised volume without the unincentivised number, and partnerships announced without what each produced.

### What is the difference between protocol fees and protocol revenue?

Fees are everything users pay to use a protocol. Revenue is the part the protocol keeps after paying liquidity providers and others. Incentives paid out in tokens should be netted against revenue.

## Sources and notes

- [ANA, Media Rating Council updates viewable ad impression measurement guidelines](https://ana.net/content/show/id/36327), August 2015. Industry standard; a minimum exposure threshold, not a measure of attention.
- [Andreessen Horowitz, 16 Startup Metrics](https://a16z.com/16-startup-metrics/), 21 August 2015. Investor guidance; older, but the definitions are unchanged.
- [Keyrock, Airdrops in the Barren Desert](https://keyrock.com/airdrops-in-the-barren-desert/), 25 September 2024. Research by a crypto market maker; 62 airdrops, price outcomes rather than user retention; the article gives both 88% and 85% for the decline share.
- [DefiLlama, Data definitions](https://defillama.com/data-definitions). Public analytics dashboard's own definitions; other dashboards define revenue differently.
- The stage table, the audience table and the checklist are **lowob**'s framework.

Write a rule for each channel saying what result would make you double it and what would make you stop. Then move impressions, reach and follower counts off the first page of this month's report.

# Affiliate vs Partner vs Referral Programs: What's the Difference?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-vs-partner-vs-referral/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-20 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Affiliate programmes pay professional publishers a commission per defined event, at scale. Partner programmes are fewer, larger deals negotiated company to company. Referral schemes give existing customers small rewards for bringing people they know. Which one a company needs depends on who could plausibly send it a customer, and each needs different terms, tools and measures.

Affiliate, partner and referral programmes all pay other people to bring a company customers, but each needs different incentives and different measures. Affiliate programmes pay professional publishers a commission per defined event, at scale; US affiliate investment was about $13.6 billion in 2024. Partner programmes are fewer, larger deals negotiated between companies. Referral schemes give existing customers small rewards for bringing people they know, and the best study of them, at a bank, found referred customers were worth at least 16% more. Which one a company needs depends on who could plausibly send it a customer.

Three arrangements pay other people to bring a company customers. They share vocabulary, they are often run from the same software, and confusing them costs companies real money in the wrong terms offered to the wrong partners.

| Dimension | Affiliate programme | Partner programme | Referral scheme |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Who refers | Professional publishers: comparison and review sites, creators, newsletters, deal and coupon sites, sub-networks | Other companies: integration partners, resellers, agencies, platforms, complementary products | Existing customers, sometimes employees |
| Scale | Many partners, each running many programmes | Few partners, each significant | Many referrers, low volume each |
| How they are paid | Commission per defined event | Revenue share, referral fees, co-marketing or reciprocal distribution, negotiated | Small reward: account credit, discount or bonus |
| Where it runs | An affiliate network or a direct platform | Contracts and a partner manager | Inside the product |
| What decides success | Terms, recruitment and validation | The relationship and the fit between customer bases | Whether people talk about the product anyway |
| Main failure | Paying for sales that would have happened anyway | Slow deals that never produce customers | Rewards that are ignored, or large enough to corrupt |

## Affiliate programmes

An affiliate programme pays independent publishers a commission for customers they send. The publishers are professionals: comparison sites, review sites, content creators, newsletters, deal and coupon sites, and sub-networks that aggregate smaller publishers. They choose products to promote on the commission, the conversion rate and the fit with their audience, and they do it at scale, across many programmes at once.

The channel is large and diversifying. The Performance Marketing Association's 2025 industry study put US affiliate investment at about $13.6 billion in 2024, up 49.8% from 2021, supporting an estimated $113 billion in e-commerce sales. Retail's share of spend fell from 76% to 63% as financial services, travel and telecoms grew. This is trade-body research, and the release does not state its method.

The company sets the terms: what event is paid for, how much, for how long after the click, and what is prohibited. The programme lives on an affiliate network, which recruits publishers, tracks clicks and conversions and handles payments for a fee, or on a direct platform the company runs itself.

Affiliate is a performance channel in the strict sense. The company pays only when the defined event occurs. It scales with the number and quality of publishers recruited. It is available to many categories the ad platforms restrict, because publishers decide what to carry, though the publishers' own platforms and the category's rules still apply. The main risk is paying for customers who had already decided, which [Build an affiliate programme without paying for coupon leaks](https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-program-asset-or-coupon-leak/) covers in detail. The research is clear that the merchant should keep control: Edelman and Brandi found in-house staff were better than outside specialists at spotting "borderline" affiliates whose practices worked against the merchant.

## Partner programmes

A partner programme is a relationship between companies rather than with individual publishers. Integration partners, resellers, agencies, platforms and complementary products agree to distribute, recommend or embed the company's product in exchange for revenue share, referral fees, co-marketing or reciprocal distribution.

Partner deals are fewer, larger and slower, and each is negotiated individually. A single partnership with a platform that already has the customer relationship can outweigh an entire affiliate programme. Partner programmes are run by people, not software; the tracking and payment tools matter less than the relationship and the terms.

The design questions are different from affiliate ones: what role the partner plays in the sale, how each partner type is paid, what tiers reward, and who owns an account both sides touch. Our [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) works through those questions, [What is a partner programme?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-partner-program/) defines the parts, and [Integrators, OEMs and channel partners](https://lowob.com/research/integrators-oems-and-channel-partners/) covers the main partner types.

## Referral schemes

A referral scheme pays existing customers, or sometimes employees, for bringing in people they know. The reward is usually small, such as account credit, a discount or a bonus, and the volume per referrer is low, because each person knows a limited number of relevant others.

The evidence that referred customers are worth having is strong. Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte tracked about 10,000 customers at a German bank that paid referrers a €25 voucher. Referred customers had a higher margin at first, a lasting retention advantage and at least 16% higher value over six years. The authors estimated a return of about 60% on the reward.

Reward size and context matter. Ryu and Feick's experiments found rewards raised referral likelihood most where ties were weak, and that a reward lifted referral likelihood by more than 20 percentage points for a weaker brand. Close friends refer without being paid. Referral works when the product is something people talk about anyway and the reward is enough to prompt the conversation without being enough to corrupt it. It is a product feature more than a marketing channel, and it is usually run from inside the product.

> Ask who could plausibly send you a customer. The answer tells you which programme to build.

## Which one a company needs

Ask who could plausibly send you a customer.

If the answer is professional publishers who already reach your buyer, such as comparison sites, creators and newsletters, you need an affiliate programme, with terms designed to exclude the coupon leak.

If the answer is other companies whose customers are your customers, such as platforms, integrations and service providers, you need a partner programme, and probably a person to run it.

If the answer is your own customers, you need a referral scheme, built into the product.

Most companies past a certain size need all three, run differently. Do not try to run a partner programme on affiliate software, or an affiliate programme with referral-sized rewards. Business-to-business introductions sit between the partner and referral models, and [Referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) covers how to register, protect and pay them.

## Disclosure applies to all three

Each arrangement pays someone to recommend you, so each carries disclosure duties. The FTC's guidance says an affiliate should disclose the relationship clearly and close to the recommendation, that "affiliate link" alone is not adequate, and that advertisers need "reasonable programs in place to train and monitor members of their network." It also says a business cannot condition an incentive, such as a discount, on a review being positive. Regulated products add their own rules. Match customer referral rewards to the product and the applicable rules before launch.

## Why they should be built and owned

Affiliate and partner programmes are among the few distribution channels a company can own outright. The terms, the partner base, the reporting history and the relationships are assets that keep working when any single ad platform changes its mind. For a company in a restricted category, they are usually the first thing worth building properly, and the last thing worth outsourcing to a network's default settings.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pay affiliates for a clearly defined and verifiable outcome.** Validate it with your own tracking.
- **Treat strategic partners as ongoing company-to-company relationships.** Staff them with a person, not a dashboard.
- **Match customer referral rewards to the product and the applicable rules.** Small, disclosed and built into the product.
- **Do not mix the tools.** Partner programmes on affiliate software and affiliate programmes with referral-sized rewards both fail.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an affiliate programme and a referral programme?

An affiliate programme pays professional publishers, such as comparison sites and creators, a commission per defined event at scale. A referral programme gives existing customers a small reward for bringing people they know, and usually runs inside the product.

### What is the difference between a partner programme and an affiliate programme?

A partner programme is a negotiated relationship between companies, such as integrations, resellers and platforms, run by people. An affiliate programme is a set of public terms many publishers join, run on a network or platform.

### Are referred customers more valuable?

The best evidence says yes. A study of about 10,000 customers at a German bank found referred customers were at least 16% more valuable over six years, with lower churn.

### Do affiliate and referral programmes need disclosures?

Yes. In the US, the FTC expects paid relationships to be disclosed clearly and close to the recommendation, and advertisers to train and monitor their network. Regulated products may have extra rules.

## Sources and notes

- [Performance Marketing Association, Industry Study 2025](https://thepma.org/pma-study-affiliate-marketing-industry-grows-49-8-to-13-63-b-outpacing-e-commerce-growth-by-2x/), 18 June 2025. Trade association research with London Research; methodology not stated in the release.
- [Schmitt, Skiera and Van den Bulte, Referral Programs and Customer Value](https://faculty.wharton.upenn.edu/wp-content/uploads/2012/04/Schmitt-Skiera-vandenBulte-2011-Referral-Programs-Customer-Value.pdf), Journal of Marketing, 2011. Academic study of one German bank, 2006 to 2008.
- [Baylor University Keller Center, Referral reward programs and referral likelihood](https://kellercenter.hankamer.baylor.edu/news/story/2008/insider-referral-reward-programs-and-referral-likelihood), 2008. Secondary summary of Ryu and Feick's Journal of Marketing experiments.
- [Edelman and Brandi, Risk, Information, and Incentives in Online Affiliate Marketing](https://www.benedelman.org/risk-information-and-incentives-in-online-affiliate-marketing/), Journal of Marketing Research 52(1), 2015. Academic study of affiliate program management.
- [FTC, Endorsement Guides: What People Are Asking](https://consumer.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/ftcs-endorsement-guides-what-people-are-asking), last updated July 2025. US staff guidance, not a rule.
- The comparison table and the selection question are **lowob**'s framework.

List the last twenty customers who arrived through someone else and tag each as publisher, company partner or customer referral. The largest group tells you which programme to build properly first.

# Distribution When the Platforms Are Closed

Source: https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-the-platforms-are-closed/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Rank channels by the cost of earning a buyer's attention and start where trust is borrowed: partners, referrals, creators and owned media. Sort every channel into open, restricted or closed for your category first, using the platforms' own dated policies. Paid media comes last, once you know what converts.

Rank channels by the cost of earning a buyer's attention, and start where the attention is cheapest and the trust is borrowed: partners, referrals, creators and owned media. Paid media comes last, once you know what converts. Before any of that, sort every channel into open, restricted or closed for your category and geography, using the platforms' own published policies with the date you checked them.

## Three bands, before any plan

Before planning distribution, sort every channel into one of three bands for your category and geography.

**Open:** you can use it without pre-approval. Partners, affiliates, creators, email, content, events, much of programmatic.

**Restricted:** usable with documentation, licensing or approval. Plan for it only once the paperwork clears; never put it in a forecast before then.

**Closed:** will not carry you in this market today. Name it early and plan without it.

The bands are real and published. Google's cryptocurrency policy lets exchanges and software wallets advertise in approved markets once certified, which is restricted. It bans ads for initial coin offerings, DeFi trading protocols, token liquidity pools and crypto loans regardless of location, which is closed. TikTok's financial services policy lists crypto as not allowed in some markets and as permitted with licensing and 18+ targeting in others. The same product can sit in three bands across three countries.

Web3 teams often discover their closed band after a campaign is built. AI teams rarely face closed bands, but face crowded ones where costs climb fast. Either way, the sort comes first. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) sets out how platforms make the assignment.

## The channel ladder

| Order | Channel | Why it works early | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Partners and integrations | Borrowed trust; your customer is already there | Partnerships with no named owner or shared goal |
| 2 | Affiliates and referrals | Paid on results; scales with proof | Disclosure rules; quality of referred users |
| 3 | Creators and KOLs | Trusted voice to a specific audience | Paying for reach, not fit; disclosure; one-off posts |
| 4 | Owned media | Compounds; you keep the audience and the data | Slow to start; needs a point of view |
| 5 | Answer engines | Buyers increasingly ask AI assistants who to use | Thin or inconsistent public information about you |
| 6 | Paid media | Scale, once conversion is known | Spending before you know what converts |

The order is a ranking by the cost of earning attention, not by size. Paid can be the largest channel eventually. It is last because it is the most expensive place to learn what converts.

## Partners first

The best early partner is someone who has your customer and gains something when you succeed. For a DeFi protocol, every asset issuer whose token you support has a reason to promote a new use for it. For an AI tool, the platform you integrate with often runs a marketplace, a partner directory or co-marketing for apps that make it stickier.

The weight of evidence in technology markets points the same way. Canalys, an analyst firm, forecast that 70% of customer spending on technology, IT services and telecom services would go through partners in 2025. Forrester's 2025 buyers' journey survey, cited in a February 2026 post, found an average of nine people from outside the buying organisation involved in a purchase decision. Much of a buyer's trust is formed by people who are not you. [What is ecosystem-led growth?](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/) covers how firms use partner overlap to reach those buyers.

Write the shared goal down before the first call: what each side gets, what each side does, and the single first use case you will launch together. A partnership without a first use case is a logo swap. [Partner channel design](https://lowob.com/research/partner-channel-design/) covers roles and payment by partner type, and [co-selling with platforms](https://lowob.com/research/co-selling-with-platforms/) covers the case where the partner is a cloud or software platform.

> A partnership without a first use case is a logo swap.

## Affiliates and creators, done properly

Affiliates and referral partners are paid on results, which makes them the natural second rung: the company pays when something it can verify has happened. The terms decide whether the programme builds an asset or leaks margin to coupon sites. Our piece on [building an affiliate programme without paying for coupon leaks](https://lowob.com/research/affiliate-program-asset-or-coupon-leak/) covers the terms.

Pay creators for a job, not a post: a tutorial, a walkthrough, an honest review, a live session. Match on audience fit, not follower count. Require clear disclosure every time, both because the rules require it and because undisclosed promotion is exactly what erodes trust in crypto and AI alike.

The disclosure rule is specific. The US Federal Trade Commission's guidance says a disclosure belongs with the endorsement, not on a profile page or behind a "more" link; in video it goes in the video; on a livestream it is repeated. Plain words such as "ad" or "sponsored" work; "sp" and "collab" do not, and a platform's built-in tool may not be enough. Financial and crypto promotions carry further rules in most markets, which belong in the creator brief.

| Creator brief field | What it contains |
| --- | --- |
| The job | Tutorial, walkthrough, review or live session, with the outcome it should produce |
| Audience fit | Who watches, and why they match the customer you chose |
| Approved claims | The claims the creator may make, and the ones they may not |
| Disclosure | The exact words and where they appear |
| Payment | Per verified outcome where possible, not per post |

## Owned media and answer engines

These two are linked. When a buyer asks an AI assistant "what is the best tool for X?", the answer is assembled from what is published about you and your category. Clear, specific, consistent public material, such as docs, comparisons, research and case studies, is now distribution, not just marketing.

The shift is measurable. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025 and found users clicked a traditional result on 8% of visits when an AI summary appeared, against 15% when one did not. If fewer buyers click through, the summary is often the first impression, and it is built from whatever sources the engine trusts. Our pieces on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) and [owned channels](https://lowob.com/research/owned-channels-email-content/) cover the mechanics.

Check what the major assistants say about you today. If it is wrong or missing, that is a content gap, and it is cheaper to fix than any paid channel.

## Paid comes last, and how to know when

Paid media becomes the right next channel when three things are true. The company knows which offer converts, from the open-band channels. It knows its cost per verified outcome in those channels, so a paid result has a benchmark. And any restricted-band approval has actually cleared. Until then, paid spend buys expensive lessons the cheaper channels would have taught.

## The checklist

| Item | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| Band map | Every channel sorted into open, restricted or closed, per market, with the policy page and date checked |
| Partners | Three named partners with a first use case each |
| Referral or affiliate offer | Terms set, with clear disclosure |
| Creator brief | Pays for a job, not a post |
| Answer engines | What AI assistants say about you, checked and logged |
| Paid | Budget held until conversion is known |

## lowob takeaways

- **Sort before you plan.** Open, restricted or closed, per market, from the platforms' own dated policies.
- **Start where the customer already is.** Partners and integrations borrow trust you have not yet earned.
- **Pay creators for a job and disclose every time.** Placement of the disclosure matters as much as its presence.
- **Treat answer engines as a channel.** Fewer clicks reach the page; the summary is the first impression.
- **Hold paid until conversion is known.** It is the most expensive place to learn.

## Common questions

### How do I market a product when ad platforms won't carry it?

Sort channels into open, restricted and closed, then start with open channels where trust is borrowed: partners and integrations, affiliates and referrals, creators, owned media and answer engines. Hold paid media until you know what converts.

### What makes a good early distribution partner?

Someone who already has your customer and gains something when you succeed. Agree the shared goal, each side's role and one first use case before the first call.

### How should I pay crypto or AI creators?

Pay for a job, such as a tutorial, walkthrough, honest review or live session, not a post. Match on audience fit rather than follower count and require disclosure in the content itself, in plain words.

### Can crypto companies advertise on Google?

Some can. Exchanges and software wallets may advertise in approved markets once certified, but Google bans ads for DeFi trading protocols, initial coin offerings, token liquidity pools and crypto loans everywhere.

# How AI Answer Engines Choose Which Sources to Cite

Source: https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-17 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: AI assistants answer from what the model learned in training and from pages they retrieve at the time of the question. Citation studies show the retrieved sources change from day to day and often differ from the pages that rank in search. Content that answers a real question with checkable, sourced facts gives an engine something to use; content written only to persuade rarely does.

AI answer engines draw on two things: what the model learned in training, and pages a search system retrieves when the question is asked. The retrieved sources vary by engine, by question and by day. Ahrefs found half or more of the citations in five AI tools had gone by the next day's answer, and only about 12% of URLs cited by ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot ranked in Google's top 10 for the same prompt. No single trick guarantees a citation. The best starting point is useful, specific, verifiable information that a crawler can reach.

A growing share of the questions people once typed into a search engine is now asked of an AI assistant and answered in a paragraph rather than a list of links. For anyone whose business depends on being found, that changes what "being found" means. Pew Research Center tracked 900 US adults' Google searches in March 2025 and found an AI summary on 18% of them. Users clicked a link inside the summary on 1% of those visits.

This article explains, as plainly as the subject allows, how these systems choose what to say and what to cite. A companion piece, the [LLM optimization checklist](https://lowob.com/research/llm-optimization-checklist/), covers what to do about it.

## Two ways a model knows something

**Training.** A model generates responses from patterns learned before its knowledge cutoff. That does not mean it can show which websites supplied a particular claim, or that any one brand mention will make it recommend a company. Our explainer on [large language models](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-large-language-model/) covers how training works.

**Retrieval.** Many assistants also search a live index at the time of the question and ground the answer in what they find. This is the route that produces citations. Google's documentation says AI Overviews and AI Mode "may use a 'query fan-out' technique, issuing multiple related searches across subtopics and data sources" to build a response. Other products use their own indexes and crawlers; our explainer on [retrieval-augmented generation](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-retrieval-augmented-generation/) covers the mechanism.

| Route | Where the information comes from | Can it be cited? | What a company controls |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Training | Text gathered before the model's cutoff | No direct link to a page | Little, and only over years |
| Retrieval | A search index queried at answer time | Yes, as a linked source | Crawl access, page content, accuracy |
| Both | Model knowledge shaped by retrieved pages | Partly | The retrieved pages |

Most marketing effort is aimed at neither route. It is aimed at persuading a human who has already arrived.

## What the citation studies show

Measurement of AI citations is young and mostly comes from SEO tool vendors. Read the figures as direction. Three findings are consistent enough to plan around.

**Citations are unstable.** Ahrefs tracked about 37,500 citations daily for 20 days across Google AI Mode, AI Overviews, ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot, publishing in October 2026. By day two, 50% of AI Overview citations had gone, 58% for AI Mode, 59% for ChatGPT, 81% for Gemini and 83% for Copilot. Only 0.2% to 6.8% were still cited after 20 days. About 75% of dropped citations came back at some point, and citations that lasted eight days or more returned 96% to 99% of the time.

**Ranking in search helps, but is not the same thing.** Ahrefs' study of 15,000 long-tail queries in July 2025 found only about 12% of links cited by ChatGPT, Gemini and Copilot appeared in Google's top 10 for the same prompt. Perplexity was the outlier, at about 29%. For Google's own AI Overviews, a separate Ahrefs study of 863,000 results in March 2026 found about 38% of cited URLs ranked in the top 10, down from about 76% in its July 2025 study, though Ahrefs notes its method changed between the two. Its explanation is fan-out: the engine cites pages that rank for related sub-questions. Ranking still correlates with durability. In the stability study, pages ranking in Google for the question were cited for seven days or more about 28% to 29% of the time in Google's tools, against 4% for pages that did not rank.

**Being cited and being named are different.** In the same stability study, the cited site's brand was not named in the answer 54% to 84% of the time, depending on the tool. A company can supply the facts and receive no mention.

> An answer engine cites pages that help it answer the question it has broken yours into. A page written to persuade answers none of them.

## What makes a page easier to discover and use

Start with the basics: make the page accessible to the relevant crawlers, answer a real question clearly, publish specific and accurate information, and link to supporting evidence. Clear headings and a helpful structure improve readability for people too.

The only controlled study of what changes visibility in generated answers points the same way. Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues built GEO-bench, a benchmark of queries paired with web sources, and tested nine rewriting methods on a simulated engine (published at KDD 2024). Adding quotations improved a source's visibility measure by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31%, and citing sources by about 27%. Keyword stuffing, the oldest SEO habit, lowered it by about 8%. On Perplexity, a live engine, they reported gains of up to 37%. The authors found effects "vary across domains". This is one research setup with a 2023-era model, so treat it as evidence that substance helps, not as a formula.

Do not promise that placing an answer in the opening paragraph or adding schema will secure an AI citation. [Google's official guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) says there are "no additional requirements to appear in AI Overviews or AI Mode, nor other special optimizations necessary". A page must be "indexed and eligible to be shown in Google Search with a snippet".

Credible third-party reporting and partner documentation can help customers verify important claims. We do not know a universal formula by which every assistant weighs mentions, links or corroboration.

## Why your content might not appear

Most absences have ordinary causes.

| Cause | How to check | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Not indexed, or blocked to the engine's crawler | Search Console indexing report; robots.txt rules by user agent | Fix crawl access deliberately, engine by engine |
| Content rendered only by script | View the raw HTML | Serve the main text in HTML |
| Does not answer the question asked | Ask the assistant the question and read what it cites | Write the answer, with evidence, on one page |
| Outdated or contradicted elsewhere | Compare your page with the sources it is cited beside | Update, date and source the claim |
| Outcompeted by stronger resources | Note which sources win, and why | Add what they lack: data, first-hand detail, a usable tool |
| Cited one day, gone the next | Ask the same question across several days | Measure over weeks, not single checks |

That last row is why monitoring has to be repeated. Record the questions customers ask, note which sources appear across several runs, check what they get right or wrong, and improve the underlying page when there is a real information gap. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out how to give each page a reader, a decision and a measure.

## What this means for a regulated or restricted-category business

AI answers can become another discovery channel, but they are not a guaranteed replacement for search, partnerships or advertising. Crawl permissions are set per engine and per purpose. [OpenAI documents OAI-SearchBot separately from GPTBot](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/bots): OAI-SearchBot "is used to surface websites in search results in ChatGPT's search features", while disallowing GPTBot "indicates a site's content should not be used in training", and "each setting is independent of the others". Anthropic's help centre describes the same split: ClaudeBot for training, Claude-SearchBot for search indexing and Claude-User for retrieval when a user asks a question. A site can allow search access without permitting training.

Keep product claims, availability, risk disclosures and contact details current. An assistant citing an out-of-date page can repeat a withdrawn product to a customer. Make information clear enough for customers to verify independently, and do not treat AI visibility as a channel that cannot change or be disrupted. Our guide to [restricted categories](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers the wider distribution problem.

## lowob takeaways

- **There is no single formula.** Engines retrieve and cite differently, and the same engine changes its sources daily.
- **Substance is what gets used.** Quotations, figures and cited evidence raised visibility in the only controlled study; keyword stuffing lowered it.
- **Crawl access is a decision.** Search, training and user retrieval are separate permissions on the main engines.
- **Measure over time.** Repeat the same questions across days and record citations, mentions and accuracy.

## Common questions

### How do AI answer engines decide which sources to cite?

Most retrieve pages from a search index when the question is asked, often by running several related sub-searches, and cite the pages that best support parts of the answer. The selection varies by engine, by question and from day to day.

### Do AI Overviews only cite pages that rank in Google's top 10?

No. Ahrefs found about 38% of AI Overview citations ranked in the top 10 for the query in early 2026, with many of the rest ranking for related sub-queries. Ranking still helps a citation last longer.

### Why does my website not appear in ChatGPT or Perplexity answers?

Common causes are blocked crawlers, content rendered only by script, pages that do not answer the question directly, outdated facts, and stronger competing sources. Citations also change daily, so check across several days.

### Can I block AI training but still appear in AI search?

On the main engines, yes. OpenAI and Anthropic use separate crawlers for search and for training, and each can be allowed or blocked in robots.txt independently.

# LLM Optimization Checklist for Content and Marketing

Source: https://lowob.com/research/llm-optimization-checklist/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-11 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: To be cited by AI assistants, answer one real question per page, make claims a reader can check, keep pages crawlable, earn genuine references on sites you do not own, and measure the same questions across several days each month. Google says no special AI markup or llms.txt file is needed; the controlled evidence that exists rewards quotations, figures and cited sources.

If customers ask AI assistants about your category, your site should be easy to find, accurate, accessible and worth citing. That means one real question answered per page, claims a reader can check, crawlable HTML, genuine references on sites you do not own, and a monthly measurement routine. Google's July 2026 guidance says no llms.txt file, special schema or content chunking is needed for its AI features. The one controlled study of generated answers found quotations, statistics and cited sources raised a page's visibility, and keyword stuffing lowered it.

The previous article, [How AI answer engines choose which sources to cite](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/), explained how assistants retrieve and cite. This one is the list of things to do about it. None of it is exotic. Most of it is the discipline good content always required, applied with a machine reader in mind.

## Write pages that answer one question

Each important page should exist to answer a question a buyer actually asks, and should answer it near the top. Put the question, or a close paraphrase, in the page title and the first heading. State the answer plainly, then explain. A reader should find the central answer quickly, without wading through paragraphs of marketing language.

This is good practice for people, and it fits how retrieval works. Google says AI Overviews and AI Mode may issue "multiple related searches across subtopics" to build one response, so a page that answers one sub-question cleanly can be cited for a question nobody typed. Google's own optimisation guide, updated in July 2026, asks for "a unique viewpoint that stands out" and "unique expert or experienced takes that go beyond common knowledge".

Audit the current site for pages that do this. Most companies find that their highest-traffic pages describe the company and their most useful pages are buried three clicks down. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) gives a one-page brief for each page: reader, stage, decision and next action.

## Make claims that can be checked

Replace "leading", "innovative" and "trusted" with facts: what the product does, for whom, at what cost, since when, with what result. Give definitions where the category is new. Give numbers where they can be substantiated, and date them. Comparisons with named criteria can be useful because they answer practical buyer questions.

The evidence supports this. In the GEO study by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues (KDD 2024), rewriting sources to add quotations raised their visibility in generated answers by about 41%, adding statistics by about 31% and citing sources by about 27%, against an unedited baseline. Keyword stuffing lowered visibility by about 8%. The tests used a simulated engine built on GPT-3.5, plus a check on Perplexity, so the numbers will not transfer exactly. The direction is the point: substance is what an engine can use.

| Instead of | Write | Why it travels |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Industry-leading onboarding" | "Median time to first live account: 9 days, across 2025 customers" (with the source) | A figure, a scope and a date an engine can quote |
| "Trusted by top firms" | The number of clients in a named segment, with permission to state it | Checkable, and stays true until updated |
| "Flexible pricing" | The pricing model, the unit and what is included | Answers the question a buyer asks the assistant |
| "Innovative approach" | One sentence naming the method and when it is the wrong choice | Gives the engine a definition and a boundary |

The figures in the second column are illustrative formats, not claims about any firm.

## Structure for machines without writing for them

Use a clear heading hierarchy, short sections, and lists and tables where the content is naturally a list or a table. Use descriptive link text. Put a summary or definition block near the top of long pages. Render the main content in HTML rather than assembling it with scripts after the page loads, so crawlers that do not execute JavaScript can read it.

Use accurate structured data where it supports standard search features. Google's guide says "structured data isn't required for generative AI search, and there's no special schema.org markup you need to add", and "there's no requirement to break your content into tiny pieces for AI to better understand it". It also says "you don't need to write in a specific way just for generative AI search".

## Earn independent references without manufacturing consensus

Accurate directory entries, partner documentation and legitimate reporting can help customers discover or verify a company. Aim to be covered because there is something worth saying, not to repeat identical claims in places you control.

Google explicitly cautions that "seeking inauthentic 'mentions' across the web isn't as helpful as it might seem", and that creating pages primarily "to manipulate rankings or generative AI responses" violates its scaled content abuse policy. A citation from an assistant is not guaranteed by the number of brand mentions or backlinks. Our piece on [thought leadership that sales can use](https://lowob.com/research/thought-leadership-that-sales-can-use/) covers what makes a firm worth quoting in the first place.

> The third-party step matters most and is the one most companies skip. It is also the one that cannot be faked without breaking the rules.

## Answer the questions people ask assistants

Ask the assistants directly: what do they say about your category, your competitors and you? Which sources do they cite? What questions do they think a buyer would ask next? Those questions, and the sources currently winning them, are the content plan.

Then write the definitive answer to each, publish it on a page a machine can extract cleanly, and check that independent sources, where they exist, say something consistent. Where they say something different, find out which is right and fix your page or ask for theirs to be corrected.

## Keep the technical basics honest

Use stable canonical URLs, crawlable text, clear navigation, a clean sitemap and accurate structured data where it serves normal search needs. Google says Search does not use llms.txt files and that creating one "won't help or hurt" visibility there. Other engines may treat it differently; none of the engines whose documentation we reviewed requires it.

Review crawler rules deliberately, engine by engine.

| Engine | Search or answer crawler | Training crawler | Note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| OpenAI | OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search); ChatGPT-User for user-triggered visits | GPTBot | OpenAI says "each setting is independent of the others" |
| Anthropic | Claude-SearchBot (indexing); Claude-User (retrieval for a user's question) | ClaudeBot | Blocking Claude-User stops retrieval in response to user queries |
| Google | Googlebot, with nosnippet, max-snippet and noindex controls | Not covered here | AI features need a page "indexed and eligible to be shown ... with a snippet" |

Blocking one crawler does not automatically block another. Crawler permission alone does not guarantee inclusion.

## Measure it

Traditional analytics will show referrals from AI assistants where they pass a referrer, and branded search volume as a proxy for recall. Google's July 2026 guide points site owners to a Generative AI performance report in Search Console. Beyond that, the practical measure is manual: a monthly set of the twenty questions that matter most to the business, asked of the major assistants, with the answers and citations recorded. Watch whether the company appears, whether it is described accurately, and which sources are cited instead.

One change follows from the evidence. Ahrefs tracked about 37,500 citations for 20 days in 2026 and found 50% to 83% had disappeared by the second day, depending on the tool, though most returned later. A single monthly check is a coin toss. Ask each question on three or more days in the measurement week and record how often you are cited, not whether you were cited once. Ahrefs also found the cited site was often not named in the answer, so record citations and mentions separately.

**That is not sophisticated. It is enough to know whether the work is landing, which is more than most companies know today.**

## lowob takeaways

- **One question, one page.** Answer it early, with evidence, in HTML a crawler can read.
- **Facts over adjectives.** Quotations, figures and sources are what the controlled evidence rewards.
- **Earn references; do not manufacture them.** Google treats inauthentic mentions and mass-produced pages as manipulation.
- **Measure frequency, not presence.** Repeat each question across several days and log citations and mentions apart.

## Common questions

### How do I get my company cited by ChatGPT and other AI assistants?

Publish pages that answer specific buyer questions with checkable, sourced facts, make sure the engine's search crawler can reach them, and earn genuine references on other sites. No method guarantees a citation.

### Do I need an llms.txt file or special schema for AI search?

Not for Google. Its July 2026 guidance says Search does not use llms.txt and AI features need no special schema or chunking. Accurate structured data still helps ordinary rich results.

### Should I block GPTBot or ClaudeBot?

That is a training decision, separate from search. Blocking GPTBot or ClaudeBot opts content out of training; OAI-SearchBot, Claude-SearchBot and Claude-User govern search and retrieval and can be allowed independently.

### How do I measure visibility in AI answers?

Track a fixed set of about twenty buyer questions, ask each on several days in the same week across the main assistants, and record how often you are cited, named and described accurately.
