# Your First Ten Customers Are Design Partners

Source: https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-10 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: Pick early customers for fit and learning, not logo value. Agree a written success test up front, work closely for six to twelve weeks on the partner's real data, and convert the ones that succeed into paying customers, case studies and references. The research on lead users and on failed AI projects points the same way: the partner with the problem badly and now, and a clear measure of success, is the one that teaches you something.

Pick early customers for fit and learning, not logo value. Agree a written success test up front, work closely for six to twelve weeks, and convert the ones that succeed into paying customers, case studies and references. The evidence favours this: CB Insights found 42% of 101 startup post-mortems cited no market need, and RAND's 2024 study of AI projects found that unclear problems, unclear success metrics and missing data were among the main reasons more than 80% of them fail.

The first ten customers do two jobs: they pay, and they teach you what the product is for. A famous logo that never uses the product does neither. A design partner is chosen for the second job, and the first follows.

## Who makes a good design partner

**Has the problem badly and now.** The urgency is visible: a deadline, a cost, a regulator, a competitor.

**Has someone who owns it.** A named person with authority to try something new and time to give feedback.

**Looks like your next fifty customers.** A partner too unusual teaches you to build for one.

**Will let you talk about it** if it works, even anonymously.

The first test has a research basis. Eric von Hippel's work on lead users describes customers who face a need before the rest of the market and gain a lot from solving it. Lilien, Morrison, Searls, Sonnack and von Hippel studied the method inside 3M and published the results in *Management Science* in 2002. Ideas from the average lead-user project were projected to reach $146 million in sales after five years, more than eight times the forecast for the average conventional project run at the same time. Those are projections at one company, but the direction is clear: the customer under the most pressure teaches the most.

The third test guards against the opposite error. Amy Edmondson, writing in *Harvard Business Review* in 2011, warned that pilots are too often run under optimal conditions rather than representative ones. A design partner that is unusually sophisticated, unusually patient or unusually well resourced is an optimal condition. It will say the product works; the next forty-nine may not.

Avoid the famous logo with no owner, the friend who'll say yes to anything, and the enterprise that needs nine months of procurement before you can learn anything.

| Candidate | What it offers | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead user with the problem now | Specific needs, fast feedback, a real test | Few, if any, at the fringe of the segment |
| Famous logo, no owner | A slide | No usage, so no evidence and no reference |
| Friendly founder or investor contact | Easy yes | Feedback shaped by the relationship |
| Large enterprise, long procurement | Eventual scale | Months before any learning; security review first |
| Unusual customer with unusual needs | Strong enthusiasm | You build for one buyer |

## Finding them

Start with a named list, not a market. For a small team selling to institutions, that's account-based selling at its most basic: 30 to 50 named organisations, researched one by one, each with a specific reason to talk now. Our pieces on [account-based marketing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-account-based-marketing/) and [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) cover the mechanics, and [segment selection with evidence](https://lowob.com/research/segment-selection-with-evidence/) shows how to check that the list reflects a segment you can win.

The warmest routes are usually the ones built earlier in the series: your investors' portfolio companies, your [first hundred community members](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/), and their introductions. The [round run like a sales process](https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/) leaves behind a list of investors who know your buyer.

**Web3:** your design partners might be curators, market makers, issuers whose asset you integrate, or wallets and front-ends that distribute you. An asset issuer has a reason to want a new use for their token. That's a partnership with a built-in incentive to promote you.

**AI:** your design partners are teams with a workflow you're replacing. Get access to real data early; a model that works on your test set and fails on their tickets is the most common way AI pilots die. RAND's 2024 report, based on interviews with 65 AI practitioners, named data-driven failures as one of five root causes: organisations often lack enough good data to train an effective model. The MIT NANDA study of 2025, reported by *Fortune*, found that only about 5% of enterprise generative AI pilots achieved rapid revenue acceleration, and attributed most of the gap to tools that did not learn from or adapt to the customer's workflow.

> A model that works on your test set and fails on their tickets is the most common way AI pilots die.

## The one-page agreement

| Section | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| Problem | Their words, one paragraph |
| Success test | A measurable outcome and the date it's checked |
| Their commitment | A named owner, weekly time, access to data or systems |
| Your commitment | Roadmap priority, a direct line to the team, support level |
| Terms | Free, discounted or paid during the pilot; price after |
| If it works | Conversion to paid, a case study or reference, logo use |
| If it doesn't | What both sides learn, and a clean exit |

The success test is the line most agreements leave vague, and it is the one RAND's interviewees blamed first. The report's leading root cause was leadership-driven failure: the people commissioning the project did not convey the problem and the measure of success clearly. Writing the test in the partner's own numbers, with a date, removes that failure before it starts. A shared, dated plan with owners on both sides is also the core of a [mutual action plan](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-mutual-action-plan/), and the same format works here.

Paid pilots, even at a small fee, filter for seriousness. An AI pilot that costs nothing often gets nothing in attention. Agree the price after the pilot before the pilot starts, so the success-test review is also a purchase conversation. Our piece on [pricing experiments in B2B](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-experiments-in-b2b/) covers how to set that first price when you have few data points.

## Running it

Weekly check-ins with the owner. Ship something visible every one or two weeks. Log every piece of feedback in the evidence log from [Part 3](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/). At the success-test date, review honestly together: did it work, and what would make it a no-brainer to pay for?

Six to twelve weeks is long enough for the partner to change how it works, and short enough to keep a decision point. If the AI product touches the partner's systems, start the security questions in week one; our piece on [the pilot that survives security review](https://lowob.com/research/the-pilot-that-survives-security-review/) sets out what to prepare.

Illustrative example: two partners, one decision

Decision
:   Convert one of two design partners to a paid annual contract and close the other pilot with a written learning note.

Reason and owner
:   Both had agreed a success test of halving manual review time on their own tickets by week ten. One hit it with its real data; the other never connected its ticket system, so the test was never run. Owned by the founder.

What changed
:   The converted partner became the first case study. The closed pilot's note showed that a named owner without system access was not enough, so data access moved into the agreement as a precondition.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage B2B AI company, built from patterns across engagements.

## What you get out

A product shaped by real use. Your first case studies, which are only believable if the success test and the result are both specific; see [what makes a case study believable](https://lowob.com/research/what-makes-a-case-study-believable/). References for investors. And a clear picture of who your ideal customer actually is, which is usually narrower than the one in the deck.

That narrowing is the result. CB Insights' analysis of 101 failed startups found no market need was the most cited reason, at 42%. Ten design partners chosen for fit are the cheapest way to find out whether the need exists, and for whom, before the company spends a round finding out the hard way.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pick for the problem, not the logo.** A partner with the problem badly and now, a named owner, resemblance to your next fifty customers and permission to talk about it.
- **Avoid optimal conditions.** A partner too unusual or too well resourced tells you the product works when it may not.
- **Write the success test in their numbers.** A measurable outcome with a date, agreed before work starts.
- **Get real data early.** For AI products, the customer's own tickets are the test that matters.
- **Charge something.** A small fee and a price agreed for after the pilot filter for seriousness.

## Common questions

### How do I choose design partners for my startup?

Pick for fit and learning, not logo value: a partner with the problem badly and now, a named owner with authority and time, that looks like your next fifty customers, and that will let you talk about it if it works.

### What should a design partner agreement include?

The problem in their words, a measurable success test with a date, both sides' commitments, pilot terms and the price after, what happens if it works, such as conversion and a case study, and a clean exit if it doesn't.

### Should design partner pilots be free or paid?

Paid, even at a small fee. A fee filters for seriousness, and agreeing the post-pilot price in advance turns the final review into a purchase decision. An AI pilot that costs nothing often gets nothing in attention.

### Why do AI pilots with early customers fail?

Usually because the problem and success measure were never clear, or the model was tested on data that does not match the customer's own. RAND names both among the main root causes of AI project failure.

Natural experiment at one company, 3M; sales figures are projections, not realised results.
- [RAND, The root causes of failure for artificial intelligence projects and how they can succeed](https://www.rand.org/pubs/research_reports/RRA2680-1.html), 13 August 2024. - [Fortune, MIT report: 95% of generative AI pilots at companies are failing](https://fortune.com/2025/08/18/mit-report-95-percent-generative-ai-pilots-at-companies-failing-cfo/), 18 August 2025. Press report of the MIT NANDA study (150 interviews, 350-person survey, 300 public deployments); definitions of success are the study's own.
- [Edmondson, Strategies for learning from failure](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/53761774e4b0e8c9b2acd2a4/t/629fcc85185ef04c9d2549bc/1654639749195/Strategies+for+Learning+from+Failure.pdf), *Harvard Business Review*, April 2011. Practitioner essay drawing on the author's research; hosted copy.
- [CB Insights, The top 20 reasons startups fail](https://www.mobiliseglobal.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/02/The-20-Reasons-Startups-Fail.pdf), 2019. Vendor analysis of 101 founder-written post-mortems; self-selected sample, hosted third-party copy.
- The candidate table, agreement and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

# Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned Media Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/paid-earned-shared-owned-media/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: Every channel falls into paid, earned, shared or owned media. Paid is bought, earned is given, shared is borrowed, owned is kept. Research on trust and on publicity versus advertising explains why each does a different job. A working system routes attention from the first three toward owned media, so companies should build the owned layer before rented channels become the whole plan.

Every channel a company can use to reach people falls into one of four kinds of media. Paid is bought, earned is given, shared is borrowed, owned is kept. The model, popularised as PESO by Gini Dietrich of Spin Sucks, is useful because it shows where control and cost sit. Research explains why each does a different job: Nielsen found recommendations from people we know are the most trusted source, and a meta-analysis found publicity outperforms advertising for unfamiliar products. A working system routes attention from the first three toward the owned layer.

The categories are old, but they remain the clearest way to see where control and cost sit. Spin Sucks credits its founder Gini Dietrich with the PESO model, launched formally in 2014; the paid, earned and owned distinction it builds on was in wide use before that, and Nielsen was publishing trust research on it by 2012.

## The four

**Paid media** is attention you buy. Search and social ads, programmatic display and video, sponsored content, paid creator posts, affiliate commissions, clipping programmes. You control the message and the timing; the platform or partner controls the access and the price.

**Earned media** is attention other people give you without payment. Press coverage, reviews, organic mentions, word of mouth, unpaid creator content, podcast invitations. You control none of it directly, which is exactly why it carries trust. It is unpredictable, slow to build, and the cheapest form of credibility available once it arrives.

**Shared media** is attention that happens on social platforms and in communities, where you participate but do not own the space. Spin Sucks' definition is blunt: "Shared media is also known as social media." You control what you post; the platform controls who sees it and can change the rules on a Tuesday.

**Owned media** is attention on property you control. Your website, your email list, your content, your product's own messaging, your events. You control everything except whether anyone shows up, which is the whole challenge of it.

|  | Paid | Earned | Shared | Owned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Short definition | Bought | Given | Borrowed | Kept |
| You control | Message, timing | Nothing directly | What you post | Almost everything |
| They control | Access, price | Whether and what they say | Reach, ranking, rules | Whether anyone arrives |
| Main cost | Money on a meter | Time, relationships, news | Continuous staff time | Up-front build and upkeep |
| Trust carried | Lowest | Highest | Varies with who shares | Middle |
| When you stop | Stops at once | Persists, decays slowly | Decays | Keeps working if maintained |

## What the evidence says about trust

Nielsen's 2012 analysis of its global trust survey described a continuum running from earned media, the most trusted, through owned to paid, the least. Recommendations from people respondents knew were trusted completely or somewhat by 92%, online consumer opinions by 70% and branded websites by 58%; a majority said they did not trust TV, print, digital or radio ads much or at all. Nielsen's 2021 edition again found recommendations from people they know the most trusted channel, at 89%.

The same analysis showed the categories working together. Paid digital campaigns that drove people to the brand's site, and owned experiences on that site, produced larger effects than paid ads alone. That is the routing argument below, measured.

Academic research adds a condition. Martin Eisend and Franziska Küster's 2011 meta-analysis in the Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science found publicity more effective than advertising on average, driven mainly by its credibility advantage. But the advantage "only holds for products about which recipients lack prior knowledge"; for well-known products, advertising did better. They also found that running publicity and advertising together weakened publicity's effect.

The practical reading: earned media matters most for companies and categories the buyer does not yet know, which describes most emerging-technology firms. Once you are known, paid reach does more of the work.

> Paid is bought, earned is given, shared is borrowed, owned is kept.

## What each actually costs

Paid media costs money on a meter. Its price is set by how many other companies are bidding for the same attention, which is why it is expensive where the crowd is and cheap where it is not.

Earned media costs time, relationships and having something worth saying. It also costs the discipline to accept that it cannot be scheduled. Our guide to [what a press release is for](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-press-release/) covers one of its supporting tools.

Shared media costs staff time continuously and delivers reach that the platform can reduce at will. The Reuters Institute's 2026 trends report cites Chartbeat data showing referrals to news sites from Facebook down 43% and from X down 46% over recent years. News publishers are not typical companies, but they are among the most motivated users of social distribution, and the platforms have been sending them less. It is the category most companies overinvest in relative to what they control.

Owned media costs the most up front (building a list, producing content, maintaining a site) and the least over time, because nothing is rented.

## How they fit together

A working system routes attention from the rented categories toward the owned one. Paid and shared media create the first contact. Earned media supplies the trust. Owned media is where the relationship is kept.

| Starting point | Route | Where it ends |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A creator post (paid or earned) | Links to a page you own that asks for an email address | You can reach that person next year without paying the creator again |
| A press mention (earned) | Republished on your newsroom page (owned), shared on your accounts (shared) | The canonical record sits on your site |
| A programmatic buy (paid) | Drives to a guide (owned) | The guide ranks and is cited for years |
| A community discussion (shared) | Points to a resource on your site | The resource becomes the reference |

Companies that skip the owned layer spend on paid and shared media forever, because they have nowhere to keep what they reach. Our piece on [owned channels](https://lowob.com/research/owned-channels-email-content/) covers how to build that layer, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to put a cost on each route.

## Why the categories matter more for restricted businesses

For a company in a category the ad platforms review, the paid and shared categories are partly closed: the largest ad platforms may refuse the account, and the social platforms may limit the reach of the content. That leaves the open band of paid media (affiliate, creator, clipping and programmatic), plus earned and owned.

That is not a weak position. It is a position that forces a company to build the two categories most businesses neglect, earned and owned, earlier than its competitors will. Given the Eisend and Küster finding, it is also the right order for a firm buyers do not yet know.

## lowob takeaways

- **Know who controls each channel.** The answer predicts what happens when you stop paying.
- **Use earned media while you are unknown.** Its credibility advantage is largest before buyers know you.
- **Do not over-rely on shared reach.** Platforms change ranking and referral volumes without notice.
- **Route everything to owned.** Every paid, earned or shared contact should have a way to stay in touch.

## Common questions

### What is the PESO model in marketing?

It sorts channels into paid (attention you buy), earned (attention given without payment), shared (attention on social platforms you do not own) and owned (attention on property you control). Spin Sucks founder Gini Dietrich created the model, formally launched in 2014.

### What is the difference between shared and owned media?

Shared media happens on social platforms and communities where you post but the platform controls who sees it. Owned media is your website, email list, content and events, which you control.

### Is earned media more effective than paid advertising?

On average it is more credible, and a 2011 meta-analysis found publicity more effective than advertising, but mainly for products buyers know little about. For familiar products, advertising performed better.

### Which media channels are open to restricted categories like crypto?

Usually affiliate, creator, clipping and programmatic paid media, plus earned and owned media, since large ad and social platforms may refuse or limit them. Policies vary by platform and country.

## Sources and notes

- [Spin Sucks, What is the PESO model?](https://spinsucks.com/communication/what-is-the-peso-model/), 1 January 2020. Published by the model's creator, a communications agency.
- [Nielsen, Trust in advertising: paid, owned and earned](https://www.nielsen.com/insights/2012/trust-in-advertising-paid-owned-and-earned/), September 2012. Measurement company analysis of its global online survey; older data.
- [Nielsen, 2021 Trust in Advertising sell sheet](https://develop.nielsen.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2022/02/2021-Nielsen-Trust-In-Advertising-U.S.-sell-sheet.pdf), 2021. Sales document; online survey of about 2,000 respondents; limited methodology detail.

- The comparison and routing tables are **lowob**'s framework.

# The First Hundred

Source: https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-04 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. This piece covers the recruitment loop: list 30 names, ask for judgment on a real decision, give the yeses a job, close the loop in public and ask for the next name. Research on online groups shows why each step matters.

The first hundred community members are recruited, not attracted. Hand-pick them, give them real influence and close the loop on every contribution. They become your testers, your references and your first distribution channel. This piece is about getting them: who to list, what to ask and how 30 names become 100. Its companion, [Find your first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/), covers what to do once they are in the room.

The first hundred is the foundation stage in our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/). It follows from the argument that [community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/): before anyone can do the job, someone has to be asked.

## Why a hundred

A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to generate a steady flow of feedback, referrals and public advocacy. It is also roughly the size at which a community can begin to sustain itself: members start answering each other's questions and bringing in people you would never have reached.

Below that, it is the founder's personal network. Above it, without the first hundred in place, it is usually an audience.

The composition matters more than the count because participation is unequal from the start. In a 2014 study of four digital health networks with 63,990 members, the most active 1% wrote 74.7% of posts and the next 9% wrote 24.0%. Jakob Nielsen's 90-9-1 analysis describes the same pattern across blogs, Wikipedia and product reviews. If one person in a hundred will do most of the work, the founder's job is to make sure that person is in the first hundred.

## The recruitment loop

| Step | What you do | Why it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| List 30 names | Write down potential customers, respected builders, operators in your category and sharp critics | Forces specificity; you cannot recruit a category |
| Ask for judgment | "We're deciding between two approaches to X. Would you look at both and tell me which is wrong?" | Specific, flattering in the right way and easy to answer |
| Give the yeses a job | Early access, a test, a draft to tear apart, with an end date | Turns interest into a first contribution |
| Close the loop in public | "We changed this because Priya pointed out Y." | Shows input leads somewhere |
| Ask for the next name | "Who else should see this?" at the end of every exchange | How 30 becomes 100 without a campaign |

**List 30 names.** Pick people whose use of the product would teach you the most or whose endorsement would mean the most. Paul Graham's 2013 essay "Do Things That Don't Scale" put it bluntly: "The most common unscalable thing founders have to do at the start is to recruit users manually."

**Ask for judgment, not attention.** A request for an opinion on a live decision is easier to say yes to than a request to join something. It also tells you who thinks carefully, which is the trait you are recruiting for.

**Give the yeses a job.** Early access, a test, a draft to tear apart. Something with an end date, so saying yes is a small commitment.

**Close the loop in public where you can.** This is the step most teams skip and the one that turns a respondent into a member. The evidence for it is strong. Kraut and colleagues' study of Usenet newsgroups found 69% of newcomers left after their first day. By day 30, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still participating, against 12% of those who got no reply. A related CHI 2006 paper found 27% of posts received no response at all, and newcomers were less likely to get one than established members.

**Ask for the next name.** Each person who engages is asked who else should see it. This is the same mechanic as a good investor introduction or customer referral: give the person homework, do something visible with their answer, then ask for the next name. Run it once and it works for all three audiences.

> Give the person homework, do something visible with their answer, then ask for the next name.

## What to give them

**Access:** builds, roadmaps, the founder's time.

**Influence:** a real decision they shaped, and evidence they shaped it.

**Recognition:** named in changelogs, release notes, docs credits or onchain roles.

**Each other:** introduce members to one another. A community whose members know each other survives the founder getting busy.

What not to give them: vague promises of future token allocations, or anything you would regret seeing in a screenshot.

Rejection is the hidden cost to avoid. Halfaker and colleagues' 2013 study of English Wikipedia found the number of active editors stopped growing in early 2007 and then declined, driven by falling retention of good-faith newcomers rather than veterans leaving. Those newcomers were more likely than earlier cohorts to have their first contributions reverted, often by automated tools. In a first hundred, every early contribution deserves a human response.

## Where to keep them

Somewhere small and owned. A private group, an email list, a feedback channel. The public server can come later. The first hundred need a room where they can be candid, and you need records you keep even if a platform changes its rules.

Record each person's source, first contribution and what changed because of it. That record is what makes the loop closable, and it is the start of the member-health review described in the companion piece on the [first 100 people who actually care](https://lowob.com/research/first-100-community-members/).

## Web3 and AI notes

For a web3 protocol, the first hundred should include people who actually use DeFi daily, not only holders. They will find the confusing parts of your app in minutes. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) covers why wallet balance is the wrong recruiting filter.

For an AI product, include at least ten people who would pay for it. Enthusiasts give great feedback on features; buyers give great feedback on whether it is worth money. If the first hundred later become a source of introductions, the rules in [referral partners without leakage](https://lowob.com/research/referral-partners-without-leakage/) apply on a smaller scale: register the introduction and credit the person who made it.

Illustrative example: 30 names to 100

Decision
:   A two-founder AI analytics startup listed 30 people (eight prospective buyers, twelve practitioners, six builders of adjacent tools and four known critics) and asked each to judge two competing onboarding designs.

Reason and owner
:   The founders needed a decision within a month and had no community. One founder owned the list and every reply.

What changed
:   Nineteen replied. The team shipped the design most of them preferred, credited them by name in the release note and asked each for one more name. The group passed 100 people in about ten weeks.

Illustrative: a composite of early-stage patterns, not a single company; the figures show the shape of the loop, not a benchmark.

## The checklist

- 30 named people, written down.
- A real decision to ask them about.
- A small, owned space for the ones who say yes.
- Every contribution acknowledged in public or in the product.
- A "who else should see this?" at the end of every exchange.

## lowob takeaways

- **Recruit, do not attract.** A hundred is small enough to know by name and large enough to start sustaining itself.
- **Ask for judgment.** A real decision draws better people than a request to join.
- **Close the loop in public.** It is the step most teams skip and the one that turns a respondent into a member.
- **Include buyers.** For an AI product, include at least ten people who would pay for it.

## Common questions

### How do I get the first 100 members of a startup community?

List 30 names, ask them for judgment on a real decision, give those who say yes a job with an end date, close the loop in public, and ask each for the next name.

### Why do new community members stop participating?

Often because nobody responds. In one study of newsgroups, 31% of newcomers whose first post drew three or more replies were still active after 30 days, against 12% of those who got none.

### What should I give early community members?

Access to builds, roadmaps and founder time; real influence with evidence of it; public recognition; and introductions to each other.

### Who should be in the first hundred users of a web3 protocol?

People who actually use DeFi daily, not only holders, because they will find the confusing parts of your app in minutes.

## Sources and notes

- [Paul Graham, Do Things That Don't Scale](https://www.paulgraham.com/ds.htm), July 2013. Founder essay; examples drawn from Y Combinator companies.
- [Kraut, Wang, Butler, Joyce and Burke, Beyond Information: Developing the Relationship between the Individual and the Group in Online Communities](https://www.dhi.ac.uk/san/waysofbeing/data/communication-zangana-kraut-2008.pdf), manuscript dated 18 April 2008. Working paper; Usenet groups; behavioural measures only.
- [Arguello and colleagues, Talk to me: foundations for successful individual-group interactions in online communities, CHI 2006](https://dx.doi.org/10.1145%2F1124772.1124916), April 2006. Peer-reviewed; 6,172 messages from eight Usenet groups.
- [Halfaker, Geiger, Morgan and Riedl, The Rise and Decline of an Open Collaboration System, summary on Wikimedia Meta](https://meta.wikimedia.org/wiki/Research:The_Rise_and_Decline), 2013. Published in American Behavioral Scientist; English Wikipedia only.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed; health networks, not commercial communities.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; ratios are a rule of thumb.
- The recruitment table, checklist and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

Write down 30 names today and one real decision you have not yet made. Send each person a two-line note asking them which option is wrong, and reply to every answer within a day.

# What Is a Press Release, and When Is It Worth It?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-press-release/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-03-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Growth

> Summary: A press release is a canonical record of an announcement, not a marketing channel and not coverage. Journalists still use PR material, but Cision's 2026 survey found 82% reject pitches as irrelevant and only 22% want more press releases. Issue one when the news is material and citable, write it plainly, and do the pitching separately.

A press release is a short, formal announcement a company issues to the media, and increasingly to the public directly, about something it wants known. It is a canonical record of the facts, not a marketing channel and not coverage. Journalists still rely on PR material, but Cision's 2026 survey of 1,899 journalists found only 22% wanted more press releases, against 47% wanting data or research, and 82% rejected pitches for being irrelevant. Issue a release when the news is material and citable, write it plainly, and do the pitching separately.

The press release has existed for over a century, and it survives because it does one job well: it puts the facts of an announcement in one canonical, quotable place, with a named person to call. Everything else people expect from it is usually misplaced.

## What a press release is for

**It records the facts.** A journalist, partner, investor or customer who wants to know exactly what was announced, by whom, on what date and with what quotations, can find it in one place. That is why releases are structured the way they are.

| Part | What it contains | Common mistake |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Headline | The news, in plain words | A slogan or an adjective |
| Dateline | City and date of issue | Missing, so the release cannot be placed in time |
| Lead paragraph | Who, what, when, where and why, in one or two sentences | Background before the news |
| Supporting detail | Numbers, terms, availability, context | Unsubstantiated superlatives |
| Quotation | One named executive saying something a person would say | Three quotes of corporate boilerplate |
| Boilerplate | A short, factual paragraph about the company | A mission statement |
| Contact | A named person with an email and phone number | A general inbox |

**It signals seriousness.** Some announcements (a funding round, a regulated product launch, a senior hire, a partnership with a public company) are expected to have a release, and their absence looks odd.

**It can meet a legal disclosure standard.** For US public companies, Regulation FD, adopted by the SEC in August 2000, bars selective disclosure of material information to analysts and investors. Law firm Goodwin's guide notes that filing a Form 8-K is generally the most reliable way to make information public, but that "a press release issued through a widely circulated news or wire service" is a recognised alternative. An executive's personal social post, on its own, does not count. Private companies are not bound by Regulation FD, but investors and partners often hold them to similar expectations.

**It creates a durable, indexed record.** Releases distributed through wire services are picked up by financial data terminals, news aggregators and search engines, and increasingly by the systems that feed AI answer engines. A release is one of the few pieces of company-authored text that third parties will republish verbatim. Our piece on [how LLMs choose sources](https://lowob.com/research/how-llms-choose-sources/) covers why plain, factual, dated text tends to be cited.

## What a press release is not

**It is not coverage.** Issuing a release does not make anyone write about you. Cision's 2026 State of the Media report found most journalists sort through more than 50 pitches a week, and 72% said fewer than a quarter of the pitches they receive are relevant. Coverage comes from a story a journalist wants, a relationship and a pitch, of which the release is the supporting document.

**It is not a marketing channel.** Nobody's customer acquisition plan should contain "issue press releases". The readers of wire services are journalists, analysts and bots.

**It is not a place for adjectives.** The release that describes the company as a leading, innovative, next-generation platform is signalling to every journalist that it contains no news. In Cision's survey, 53% of journalists said they reject pitches for being too promotional or sales-focused.

## What journalists say they want

Cision's survey asks journalists what they want from PR and why they reject pitches. It is vendor research from a company that sells PR software and wire distribution, so read it as a well-sampled view of journalist preferences rather than neutral measurement.

| What journalists want PR to send more of | Share |
| --- | --- |
| Data or original research | 47% |
| Embargoed or early access information | 45% |
| Access to experts or interviews | 42% |
| Press releases | 22% |

| Why journalists reject a pitch | Share |
| --- | --- |
| Not relevant to their audience or coverage | 82% |
| Too promotional or sales-focused | 53% |
| No clear news angle or point of view | 34% |
| Too generic or mass-email feel | 27% |

Two lessons follow. The release is necessary but not sufficient: it records the news, and the pitch, the data and the expert make the story. And relevance dominates everything else, which is a targeting problem rather than a writing problem. Cision's report puts the pitch sweet spot at around 100 to 200 words, sent by email, which 97% of journalists prefer.

> A release guarantees distribution, not attention.

## How distribution works

**Wire services** charge a fee to push the release to newsrooms, terminals and aggregators. Prices vary widely with geographic reach, length and multimedia, so get quotes for the specific circuit you need. They guarantee distribution, not attention.

**Direct pitching** sends a short personal note, with the release attached or linked, to specific journalists who cover the beat. This is where coverage actually comes from, and it is the part PR agencies are paid for.

**Owned publication** posts the release on the company's own newsroom page, which is the canonical version everything else should link to. Our guide to [paid, earned, shared and owned media](https://lowob.com/research/paid-earned-shared-owned-media/) explains why that owned copy matters.

## When to issue one, and when not to bother

| Issue a release | Do not bother |
| --- | --- |
| Money raised, with amount and lead investor | Feature updates |
| A product a regulated audience needs the facts on | Blog-post-sized opinions |
| A senior appointment | "Momentum" announcements with no number |
| A partnership with a party whose name carries weight | Anything you would be embarrassed to see quoted in full |
| A milestone with a verifiable number | Filling a quiet month |
| A partner, investor or exchange expects one | Announcements nobody outside the company would act on |

Each item in the right-hand column costs money, trains journalists to ignore the company and produces a search result the company will later wish were something else.

## The **lowob** rule for releases

Write them in the plainest language available, with the news in the first sentence, one quotation a human would actually say, and a number wherever one can be substantiated. Put the canonical version on your own site. Use a wire only when the announcement is material. Bring something journalists ask for (data, early access or an expert) to the pitch. And never confuse the release with the work of getting someone to care. For the positioning the release should express, see [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/).

## lowob takeaways

- **The release is the record.** Facts, date, quote and contact in one place.
- **The pitch is the work.** Coverage comes from relevance to a specific journalist's beat.
- **Bring what journalists want.** Data, early access and experts beat a longer release.
- **Use the wire for material news.** Everything else goes on your own newsroom page or nowhere.

## Common questions

### Does a press release get you media coverage?

Not by itself. Journalists receive far more pitches than they can use; in Cision's 2026 survey, 72% said fewer than a quarter of pitches were relevant. Coverage comes from a relevant pitch, a relationship and a story, with the release as the supporting document.

### When should a company issue a press release?

When the announcement is material, such as money raised, a regulated product launch, a senior appointment, a weighty partnership or a verifiable milestone, or when a partner, investor or exchange expects one.

### What should a press release contain?

A headline, dateline, a lead paragraph with who, what, when, where and why, supporting detail, one quotation from a named executive, a short boilerplate paragraph about the company, and a named contact.

### Is a press release still relevant in 2026?

Yes, as a canonical, citable record that wires, terminals, search engines and AI answer engines republish, and as a recognised disclosure route for US listed companies. It is not relevant as an acquisition channel.

## Sources and notes

- [Cision, 2026 State of the Media report](https://www.prnewswire.com/content/dam/prnewswire/resources/white-papers/Cision_2026_State_of_the_Media_Report.pdf), May 2026. Vendor research by a PR software and wire distribution company; survey of 1,899 journalists in 19 markets.
- [Cision, PR emerges as the primary source for journalists in high-pressure newsrooms](https://www.cision.com/about/press-releases/2026-press-releases/pr-emerges-as-the-primary-source-for-journalists-in-high-pressure-newsrooms-302770936/), 13 May 2026. Vendor press release summarising the survey; fielded January and February 2026.
- [Goodwin, Regulation FD: off-the-shelf guide](https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/resource/off-the-shelf/regulation-fd), undated. Law firm guidance, not legal advice; US public companies only.
- [US Securities and Exchange Commission, Final rule: Selective disclosure and insider trading](https://www.sec.gov/rules/regulations/33-7881.htm), 15 August 2000. Primary regulatory source for Regulation FD.
- The structure, preference and decision tables are **lowob**'s framework, with figures from the Cision report.

## Next move

Before your next announcement, write the first sentence of the release and ask whether a journalist on your beat would act on it. If not, put it on your newsroom page, skip the wire, and spend the budget on one piece of data worth pitching.

# Community Is a Job, Not a Number

Source: https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-25 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for: testing, teaching, referring, building or governing. Decide the job first, design the channel, rituals and recognition around it, and measure contribution to that job instead of member count, which most community teams still lead with.

A community earns its keep by doing work the company would otherwise pay for. Decide the job first, design the community around it, and measure contribution instead of size. Member count is the most common health measure in the field, used by 84% of community teams in CMX's 2025 survey, and it is also the easiest number to inflate and the hardest for anyone outside to verify.

This piece sits at the start of our [complete guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/). The argument is simple. A community is a group of people doing a job together, and the job is what makes it worth the cost.

## Why member count misleads

Member counts are easy to buy, easy to inflate with incentives and nearly impossible for an outsider to verify. Investors know this. Customers do not care. The only person a big number reliably impresses is the founder.

The field still leads with it. CMX's 2025 Community Industry Report, a survey of 589 community professionals, found the number of active members was the most used health metric, at 84%. Only 24% said they could confidently put a financial value on their community, up from 16% the year before. Difficulty proving return on investment was the most cited budget problem, at 37%. A team that reports headcount and cannot show value is reporting the one number that does not answer the budget question.

Counts also hide how participation actually works. Jakob Nielsen's 2006 analysis of participation inequality described the 90-9-1 pattern: in most online communities about 90% of people read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. A 2014 observational study in the Journal of Medical Internet Research tested this across four digital health networks with 63,990 members. The top 1% wrote 74.7% of all posts, the next 9% wrote 24.0% and the remaining 90% wrote 1.3%. Doubling membership mostly doubles the readers.

Incentive-driven growth adds platform risk. On 15 January 2026, X's product lead announced that X had revoked API access for apps that paid users to post, citing "AI slop & reply spam". The Block reported that the KAITO token, tied to the best known of these programmes, fell more than 10% within minutes and was down 14.5% at publication. Kaito said it would wind down its incentivised leaderboards. Any community strategy that depends on one platform's API can be switched off by that platform.

## The five jobs

| Job | What the community does | What you measure | Fits best |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test | Uses early builds, reports bugs, gives feedback | Bugs found, feedback sessions, release sign-offs | Pre-launch products, AI tools |
| Teach | Answers questions, writes guides, onboards newcomers | Share of questions answered by members, guides written | Developer tools, complex DeFi |
| Refer | Brings customers, partners or hires | Referred sign-ups and their conversion | B2B AI, infrastructure |
| Build | Integrates, extends, ships on top of you | Integrations, plugins, forks used | Protocols, platforms, APIs |
| Govern | Makes real decisions with real consequences | Participation by people who are not whales or the team | DAOs, protocols with live treasuries |

Pick one or two. A community asked to do all five does none of them well.

The evidence for the measures varies by job. For teaching, Common Room's 2022 analysis of 141 communities (vendor research) found that, outside GitHub, members replied to each other 28% of the time against 13% for company staff. When the job is teaching, the share of questions members answer is the number to move, and it is measurable on most platforms.

For governing, the measure has to exclude the people who would decide anyway. A 2024 study of Aave, Compound, Lido and Uniswap governance found that on a typical proposal only about 5% of tokens were cast, and that the top three or four holders could decide almost every vote. Governance participation that counts only the largest wallets measures concentration, not community.

> Silence is the correct response to no job. A community with nothing to do will do nothing, however many people are in it.

## Web3 and AI, differently

**Web3 communities** are often holders first and users second. That is fine if you give holders a reason to become users: early access, a role in testing new markets, recognition in the product. It goes wrong when the only shared interest is price, because price is the one thing the team cannot promise. Our piece on [community that survives the airdrop](https://lowob.com/research/community-that-survives-the-airdrop/) covers how to design for the holders who stay.

**AI communities** are usually users or developers. The job is often *test* and *teach*: power users find failure cases faster than your QA, and their prompt tricks become your best onboarding content. Treat them as an extension of the product team.

## Designing for the job

**Channel:** pick the place where the job gets done. Testing happens in a structured feedback channel or a private group, not a 10,000-person server. Common Room found engagement rates of 2% to 12% across surfaces, highest in smaller communities.

**Rituals:** a weekly office hour, a monthly build review, a release preview. Rhythm beats announcements.

**Recognition:** name contributors publicly and specifically. In web3, onchain credentials or roles can make this portable; in AI, changelog credits and early feature access work well. Nielsen's advice from 2006 still holds: reward contributors, but not so heavily that the most active few crowd out everyone else.

**Ownership:** the community lives in channels where you control the records, so it survives a platform policy change.

Treat the community's output the way you treat any other content: with a named reader and a job. Our piece on [content with a job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/) sets out the same discipline for marketing content.

Illustrative example: changing the job and the measure

Decision
:   A developer-tools company stopped reporting Discord member count to its board and started reporting the share of support questions answered by members within 24 hours.

Reason and owner
:   The server had grown fourfold in a year while support tickets also rose. The head of community owned the change, with the support lead.

What changed
:   The team created one help channel, credited answerers in the changelog and moved repeated answers into documentation. Member-answered questions became the number reviewed each month.

Illustrative: a composite of patterns across early-stage technical products, not a single company.

## The checklist

| Check | Done when |
| --- | --- |
| One or two named jobs | Written down and agreed by the founder |
| A contribution metric for each job | Reported monthly in place of member count |
| No paid-for posting | No growth tactic depends on paying for posts |
| A weekly ritual | On the calendar and moving the job forward |
| Named recognition | Contributors credited by name in the product or changelog |
| Owned records | Member list and contribution log held outside any single platform |

## lowob takeaways

- **Count contribution, not people.** Member counts are easy to buy, easy to inflate with incentives and nearly impossible for outsiders to verify.
- **Pick one or two jobs.** The five community jobs are test, teach, refer, build and govern.
- **Expect inequality.** A small minority will do most of the work, so design for them and measure them.
- **Own the record.** Keep the community in channels whose records you control so it survives a platform policy change.

## Common questions

### How should a startup measure community success?

Measure contribution to a defined job, not size. Depending on the job, that means bugs found, questions answered by members, referred sign-ups, integrations shipped, or governance participation by people who are not whales or the team.

### Why is community member count a bad metric?

Member counts are easy to inflate and impossible to verify, and they hide participation inequality: in one study of four networks, the top 1% of members wrote about 75% of posts. Growth in members is mostly growth in readers.

### What are the risks of incentive-driven community growth?

It selects for people who want the reward and depends on platforms you do not control. When X revoked API access for pay-to-post apps in January 2026, those programmes shut down and the KAITO token fell sharply.

### What is the 90-9-1 rule in online communities?

It is Jakob Nielsen's observation that about 90% of members read without contributing, 9% contribute occasionally and 1% produce most of the content. Studies since have found similar patterns, so plan for a small core.

## Sources and notes

- [CMX, 2025 Community Industry Report](https://start.bevy.com/hubfs/2025%20CMX%20Community%20Industry%20Report-1.pdf?hsLang=en), 2025. Survey of 589 community professionals, May to June 2025; CMX is owned by Bevy, a community software vendor; self-reported.
- [Nielsen Norman Group, Participation Inequality: The 90-9-1 Rule](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/participation-inequality/), 8 October 2006. Practitioner analysis; the ratios are a rule of thumb, not a measured constant.
- [van Mierlo, The 1% Rule in Four Digital Health Social Networks, Journal of Medical Internet Research](https://www.jmir.org/2014/2/e33/), 4 February 2014. Peer-reviewed observational study of 63,990 members; health networks, not commercial communities.
- [The Block, Kaito token plummets after X revises API policies to ban InfoFi crypto projects](https://www.theblock.co/post/385805/kaito-token-plummets-x-revises-api-policies-ban-infofi-crypto-projects), 15 January 2026. News report; price moves are intraday.
- [Falk, Pathan, Rigas and Tsoukalas, Blockchain Governance: An Empirical Analysis of User Engagement on DAOs, arXiv](https://arxiv.org/html/2407.10945v1), 15 July 2024. Preprint; four Ethereum DeFi protocols to December 2022.
- [Common Room, 360: Community-Led Growth Report](https://www.commonroom.io/blog/360-community-led-growth-report/), 17 November 2022. Vendor research on 141 communities using Common Room; 2022 data.
- The five-jobs table, checklist and example are **lowob**'s framework and illustration.

## Related research

- [Building a Community That Lasts: The Complete Guide](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/)
- [Audience vs Community: What Actually Makes the Difference?](https://lowob.com/research/community-vs-audience/)
- [The First Hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/)
- [Content With a Job](https://lowob.com/research/content-with-a-job/)
- [Demand Generation Economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/)
- [Web3 Does Not Have One Customer. That Is Why Most Launch Plans Break.](https://lowob.com/research/web3-multi-audience-launch-plan/)

## Next move

Write down the one or two jobs your community does for the business, and the contribution measure for each. Next month, report those numbers to whoever approves the community budget instead of member count.

# What an Advisor Does for a Web3 Company

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-advisors-do-web3-companies/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-25 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: A useful Web3 advisor helps founders make a few consequential, often irreversible decisions well: sequencing audiences, restraining incentive programmes, judging regulatory posture, finding distribution beyond the crypto timeline, translating for institutions and saying no to an unready launch. In 2026 the rules on disclosure and promotion make the structure matter more: put it in writing, lock the tokens and disclose everything.

A useful Web3 advisor helps founders make a small number of consequential, often irreversible decisions well: which audience moves first, how much to spend on incentives, which decisions need counsel, where distribution exists beyond the crypto timeline, what institutions need, and when to say "you are not ready". The structure matters as much as the advice. US and EU rules treat undisclosed paid promotion and public promises as legal facts, so put the scope in writing, lock the tokens and disclose every connection.

*This is not legal advice. Advisor arrangements and token allocations are fact-specific; get your own counsel.*

For a few years, "advisor" in Web3 meant a wallet address on a token allocation and a headshot on a website. The advisor posted on launch day and was never heard from again. The category earned its reputation.

That model is gone, and what replaces it looks more like advisory in any other industry: experienced people helping founders make a small number of consequential decisions well. Our guide to [agency vs consultancy vs advisor](https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/) sets out where advisory sits among the alternatives. The decisions in Web3 are unusual enough that the help is worth having.

## What is different about Web3 decisions

Many of them are irreversible in a literal sense. A token, once distributed, cannot be recalled. A contract, once live on-chain, is public and permanent. A treasury action is on-chain for good. A regulatory posture, once a product is live in a jurisdiction, has been observed.

The record of what happens when those decisions go wrong is public. Chainalysis estimated more than $3.4 billion was stolen in crypto hacks in 2025, with one exchange compromise accounting for $1.5 billion. Academic analysis of nine major airdrops found up to 66% of claimed tokens went to exchanges in the first transfer, a distribution decision that cannot be reversed once made.

And the company usually faces several audiences at once: users, developers, liquidity providers, partners, institutions and community, each of which has to believe something different before the system works. Sequencing those audiences is the central go-to-market problem, and most founders are solving it for the first time. Our playbook on the [multi-audience launch plan](https://lowob.com/research/web3-multi-audience-launch-plan/) covers the sequence itself.

## What a useful advisor contributes

| Contribution | What it looks like in practice | The question the advisor keeps asking |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sequencing | Naming which audience must move first and what evidence it needs; holding announcements that are early | Which of the markets around this product is the real constraint? |
| Restraint on incentives | Reviewing points, airdrops and ambassador programmes before they are announced | What behaviour is rewarded, how is it farmed, and what remains when it stops? |
| Regulatory posture | Judgment about which decisions need counsel first, which jurisdictions to launch in and what not to say | Has a lawyer seen this before we commit to it in public? |
| Distribution beyond the timeline | Pointing to affiliate, partner, disclosed creator programmes, owned email and programmatic | Who already holds the customer we want? |
| Institutional translation | Explaining what diligence requires, who needs to be in the room and how long it takes | What will the allocator's risk team ask in week three? |
| A credible no | Saying "you are not ready to launch this" when the community wants the announcement | What happens to the company if this goes wrong next week? |

**Sequencing.** An advisor who has watched several launches can see the dependency chain the team is too close to notice, and can say which audience is actually the constraint.

**Restraint on incentives.** Points, airdrops and ambassador programmes are the most effective and most misused tools in the category. Our analysis of [airdrops and points](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) sets out the evidence: Nansen found 41.1% of the top 10,000 ZKsync recipients sold their entire allocation within a day. The useful advisor asks the hard questions before the programme is announced rather than after.

**Regulatory posture.** Not legal advice, but judgment. The 2026 position makes that judgment more specific. In the US, the SEC and CFTC interpretation of 17 March 2026 sorts tokens into categories and says a token can be tied to an investment contract through the issuer's promises, weighing who made them, when and through which medium. The SEC's proposed Regulation Crypto Assets of August 2026 is still a proposal, and the CLARITY Act failed Senate cloture 49 to 50 in September 2026. In the EU, MiCA requires marketing to be consistent with the white paper, and its transitional period for service providers ended on 1 July 2026. The cheapest advice in Web3 is "ask a lawyer first", and it is rarely taken without someone in the room insisting on it.

**Distribution beyond the timeline.** Crypto-native distribution runs through a small set of channels: the timeline, a handful of communities, KOLs and exchange listings. Those channels are crowded and expensive. An advisor with experience outside the category can point to the open channels the crypto-native playbook ignores, which our piece on [distribution when ad platforms restrict you](https://lowob.com/research/distribution-when-ad-platforms-restrict-you/) describes, and to [ecosystem-led growth](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-ecosystem-led-growth/) through partners who already hold the customer.

**Institutional translation.** For projects selling to funds, custodians, banks or enterprises, an advisor who has sat on the buying side can explain what diligence requires, who needs to be in the room and how long it takes. That is the difference between a pipeline and a list of logos.

**A credible no.** The most valuable sentence an advisor says is "you are not ready to launch this." Founders surrounded by a community and a timeline that want the announcement need one person whose incentive is the company's survival rather than the week's excitement.

> The most valuable sentence an advisor says is "you are not ready to launch this."

## How to structure it

The same rules as anywhere else, applied more strictly, because the regulators have already shown what goes wrong.

| Term | What good looks like | Why it matters in 2026 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Written scope | Named decisions the advisor helps with, and a named founder who prepares each session | Makes the advice auditable and the relationship easy to end |
| Vesting | A cliff on tokens as well as equity, with a lock that survives the token launch | The SEC's 2026 proposal treats lockups and release schedules as part of token-economics disclosure |
| Conflicts | Disclosure of every other project the advisor touches, checked for conflicts | Competing allocations distort the advice on sequencing and incentives |
| Public promotion | None, unless disclosed and agreed in writing | The FTC requires material connections to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously; the SEC's 2022 case over an undisclosed $250,000 post ended in a $1.26 million settlement |
| Public statements | Advisors do not make promises about the token, price or roadmap | Under the 2026 interpretation, public promises of managerial effort feed the securities analysis |

The decisions themselves deserve a record: what was decided, why, who owned it and what was expected. A short [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/) per session makes an advisor's contribution visible, and makes it obvious when there was none. Our [build order for crypto and digital assets](https://lowob.com/research/the-build-order-for-crypto-and-digital-assets/) shows where that record belongs in the commercial system.

## The signal of a good one

They ask about the customer before the token. They ask what the product does for someone who does not care about crypto. They ask what happens when the incentives stop. They ask who has reviewed the claims on the website. And they are willing to be the least popular person in the launch channel for a week.

The same tests apply to advisors for AI companies, which our piece on [what advisors do for AI companies](https://lowob.com/research/what-advisors-do-ai-companies/) covers. The Web3 version simply has less room for error.

## lowob takeaways

- **Few decisions, high stakes.** Distributed tokens, live contracts and on-chain treasury actions cannot be undone.
- **Six contributions.** Sequencing, restraint, regulatory judgment, distribution beyond the timeline, institutional translation and a credible no.
- **Regulatory posture is judgment, not legal advice.** The advisor's job is to get counsel into the room before the commitment.
- **Structure it in writing.** Scope, vesting with a lock past launch, disclosed conflicts and no undisclosed promotion.

## Common questions

### What does a Web3 advisor actually do?

Helps founders sequence which audience moves first, restrains incentive programmes, judges which decisions need counsel, finds distribution beyond crypto-native channels, translates for institutions and says when the team is not ready to launch.

### How should a Web3 advisor agreement be structured?

A written scope, vesting with a cliff on tokens and equity, a lock that survives the token launch, disclosure of other projects checked for conflicts, and no public promotion unless disclosed and agreed in writing.

### Can a crypto advisor promote the token they are paid in?

Only with clear disclosure, and ideally not at all. The FTC requires material connections in endorsements to be disclosed clearly and conspicuously, and the SEC has fined promoters who did not disclose compensation for touting a crypto asset security.

### How do I spot a good crypto advisor?

They ask about the customer before the token, what the product does for someone who does not care about crypto, what happens when incentives stop, and who reviewed the public claims.

## Sources and notes

- [US Securities and Exchange Commission, SEC charges Kim Kardashian for unlawfully touting crypto security](https://www.sec.gov/newsroom/press-releases/2022-183), 3 October 2022. Settled without admitting or denying findings.
- [eCFR, 16 CFR Part 255, Guides concerning the use of endorsements and testimonials in advertising](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-16/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-255). Current US regulation text.
- [Sullivan & Cromwell, SEC clarifies application of securities laws to crypto assets](https://www.sullcrom.com/insights/memo/2026/March/SEC-Clarifies-Application-Securities-Laws-Crypto-Assets), 19 March 2026. Law-firm reading of the SEC and CFTC interpretation; not legal advice.
- [Congressional Research Service, SEC proposes Regulation Crypto Assets](https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/LSB11480.html), 10 September 2026. Nonpartisan legal summary of a proposal, via a public mirror.
- [Troutman Pepper Locke, In the wake of the CLARITY Act's failure, agencies move forward](https://www.troutman.com/insights/in-the-wake-of-clarity-acts-failure-agencies-move-forward-without-congressional-action-or-certainty/), September 2026, updated October 2026. Before announcing the next incentive programme, ask what behaviour it rewards, how it can be farmed and what remains when it stops. If you have advisors, check that each agreement has a written scope, a token lock that survives launch and a disclosure clause.

# Run the Round Like a Sales Process

Source: https://lowob.com/research/run-the-round-like-a-sales-process/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Treat investors as accounts. Pick them for fit, including whether the fund still has capital to deploy, research the partner, get in warm, run first meetings inside a two-to-three-week window, and track every firm through pipeline stages with pass reasons logged. In 2026, with capital concentrated in large, established funds, a fit-first list matters more than a long one.

Treat investors as accounts. Pick them for fit, research each one, get in warm, run the process in a tight window, and track every firm through stages the way a sales team tracks a pipeline. Fit now includes a question many founders skip: whether the fund still has money to invest. In 2026, managers on their fourth fund or later captured 88.2% of US venture fundraising dollars through September, and first-time funds closed at a decade-low pace.

*Not investment or legal advice. **lowob** doesn't act as a placement agent or finder and takes no percentage of anything raised.*

## 1. Build the account list

Start with fit, not fame. A fund is a fit if it has made investments at your stage, in your category, recently, and has room in its current fund. Check their last 12 months of announced deals, not their homepage.

The "room in the fund" test matters more this year. The Q3 2026 PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor found US venture funds raised $108.5 billion through September, with funds of $500 million or more taking 78.1% of it while making up 6.0% of funds closed. Only 81 first-time funds closed, on pace for a decade low. PitchBook's midyear outlook noted that emerging managers who raised in 2021 or 2022 had likely used most of their dry powder. A fund that last raised four years ago may still take meetings while reserving what it has left for its existing portfolio.

| Investor type | What it wants | What to check first |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crypto-native fund | Protocol and token fit, ecosystem fluency | Recent deals at your stage, token allocation terms |
| Generalist with a crypto practice | A business that would work without the token cycle | Which partner leads crypto, and how often they lead |
| Ecosystem fund or foundation | Deployment on their chain | Whether the chain is the right GTM choice, not just the right cheque |
| AI infrastructure fund | Compute, tooling, model-layer economics | Whether it has backed applications at all |
| AI application fund | Workflow ownership, retention, margin | Recent application deals in your buyer's category |

For web3: separate crypto-native funds, generalist funds with a crypto practice, and ecosystem funds or foundations attached to a chain. Each wants a different story. Ecosystem money often wants deployment on their chain; that's a GTM decision, not just a funding one.

For AI: separate funds that back infrastructure from those that back applications. An application company pitching an infrastructure fund will hear "interesting, but not for us" for three weeks.

Tier the list. Tier 1 is 10 to 15 firms you'd be thrilled to have lead. Tier 2 is the next 20 to 30. Don't pitch Tier 1 first; practise on early Tier 2 meetings for a week.

## 2. Research the partner, not the firm

Find the person at the firm who invests in your area. Read what they've written and what they've backed. Your first email should name one specific reason you're relevant to *them*.

Concentration applies inside firms too. PitchBook's midyear outlook counted 74 seed, Series A and Series B deals by one large multi-stage firm in 2026 by mid-June. At that pace a partner sees many decks a week. The specific reason in your first line is what separates yours from the rest.

## 3. Get in warm

The best introduction is from a founder in their portfolio who knows your product. Next best: an operator or angel they trust. A cold email with sharp evidence ([Raise against evidence, not narrative](https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/)) still works better than a lukewarm intro from someone who barely knows you.

Make intros easy. Send the introducer a forwardable three-line email: who you are, what you've proven, why this investor. The same logic drives [signal-based outbound](https://lowob.com/research/signal-based-outbound/) in sales: a real reason to talk beats volume.

## 4. Compress the window

Run first meetings within two to three weeks. Overlapping interest is what creates urgency; a raise that drips out over four months signals that nobody wants it.

The cost of a slow round has grown. Carta's first-quarter 2026 data puts the median gap between seed and Series A at two years, and between Series A and Series B at 2.1 years. A round that takes six months to close eats a quarter of the runway it was raised to fund.

> If three firms pass for the same reason, that's not investor taste. It's a gap in your evidence or story.

## 5. Track it like a pipeline

| Stage | Meaning | Next action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Researched | Fit confirmed, partner identified | Find the warm route |
| Intro requested | Forwardable email sent to introducer | Follow up in 5 days |
| First meeting | Taken | Send follow-up and homework within 48 hours |
| Partner / deep dive | Second meeting or diligence | Data room access, customer references |
| Term sheet | Offer in hand | Legal review |
| Passed | Declined | Log the reason in their words |

Write the stage definitions down before the first meeting, the way a sales team writes [pipeline stage definitions](https://lowob.com/research/what-are-pipeline-stage-definitions/), so "first meeting" means the same thing every time you count it.

The "passed" reasons are gold. If three firms pass for the same reason, that's not investor taste; it's a gap in your evidence or story. Treat each one as a [closed-lost reason](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-closed-lost-reason/): recorded at the time, in the investor's words, with a category you can count later. When the round goes quiet, those reasons are the first thing to read, as [The round has stalled](https://lowob.com/research/the-round-has-stalled/) sets out.

## 6. Have the data room ready before the first meeting

Deck, a one-page memo, the model, the cap table (and token allocation for web3), the evidence log, audits or security reviews, and two or three customers willing to take a reference call. Diligence that waits on you kills momentum.

| Data room item | Why it is there before meeting one |
| --- | --- |
| Deck and one-page memo | Partners forward the memo internally, not the deck |
| Model | The first homework request is usually the model |
| Cap table and token allocation | Ownership questions stop rounds late if they arrive late |
| Evidence log | Shows the dated record behind every traction claim |
| Audits or security reviews | Removes a diligence step that otherwise takes weeks |
| Two or three reference customers | Lets an investor hear the evidence from someone else |

## lowob takeaways

- **Fit includes capital.** Check recent deals at your stage and whether the current fund has room to invest.
- **Research the partner.** One specific reason in the first line beats a generic email to a famous firm.
- **Compress the window.** First meetings inside two to three weeks create the overlap that produces decisions.
- **Log every pass in the investor's words.** Matching reasons are the clearest signal the round will give you.

## Common questions

### How do I build an investor list for a startup fundraise?

Start with fit: funds that have invested at your stage and category in the last 12 months and still have capital in their current fund. Aim for 30 to 45 named funds with a written reason for each, split into two tiers.

### How long should a fundraising process take?

First meetings should happen inside two to three weeks so interest overlaps. A raise that drips over four months signals low demand, and with a median two years between seed and Series A, a slow round eats runway.

### What is the best way to get a warm intro to a VC?

From a founder in their portfolio who knows your product, then an operator or angel they trust. Send the introducer a forwardable three-line email. A cold email with sharp evidence beats a lukewarm intro.

### What should be in a startup data room before the first investor meeting?

The deck, a one-page memo, the model, the cap table (and token allocation for web3), the evidence log, audits or security reviews, and two or three customers willing to take reference calls.

Take your current investor list and add two columns: the date of each fund's last deal at your stage, and the year its current fund closed. Cut every fund that fails either test before you send a single email.
