# What an Advisor Does for an AI Company

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-advisors-do-ai-companies/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-19 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. This guide sets out the five contributions worth equity, the market benchmarks for structuring the grant (Carta puts median pre-seed advisor equity well under 0.25%), and the requests that turn an advisor into an underpaid, unaccountable employee.

An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job. The market benchmarks are modest: Carta's data puts median pre-seed advisor equity well under 0.25%, typically vesting over two years with a short cliff, and the Founder Institute's standard template ranges from 0.15% to 1% depending on stage and commitment.

AI companies accumulate advisors faster than almost any other kind of startup. The category is new, the founders are often technical, investors ask who is around the table, and a well-known name on the deck is cheap to add.

Most of those relationships produce a logo and a quarterly call. A few produce decisions the company would not otherwise have made. The difference is in what the advisor is asked to do.

## What an advisor is

An advisor is a person with relevant experience who helps the founders make better decisions, in exchange for a small amount of equity, a modest fee, or both. The advisor does not run a function, does not do the work, and is not accountable for results. What they offer is pattern recognition: they have seen this decision before, in a company like this, and they know how it tends to go.

That is valuable in AI precisely because so few people have seen the current decisions before. But it also defines the limits. Our comparison of [agencies, consultancies and advisors](https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/) sets out where advice ends and delivery begins.

| Role | What it provides | Accountable for results | Typical payment |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Advisor | Pattern recognition, introductions, judgment on specific decisions | No | Small vested equity, a modest fee, or both |
| Fractional leader | Runs a function part-time | Yes, for that function | Retainer or day rate, sometimes equity |
| Agency or consultancy | Delivers defined work | Yes, for the deliverable | Fee per project or retainer |
| Employee | Does the job full time | Yes | Salary and option grant |

## What a good advisor contributes to an AI company

**Customer and buyer access.** The most valuable advisors introduce the company to the buyers, partners and practitioners who will decide whether it exists in two years. In AI, where trust is the product, one credible introduction can be worth more than a year of outbound. Gartner's May 2026 survey of 645 B2B buyers found 69% preferred to check AI-generated insights with a person; a trusted introduction is the same instinct applied to choosing a vendor.

**A view on what is durable.** Founders close to the technology overestimate how long a capability advantage lasts. An advisor who has watched several model cycles can say which parts of the plan survive the next release and which do not, and push the company towards the workflow, the data and the distribution that persist. The market shows why. Menlo Ventures' 2026 survey found Google's share of enterprise model API spend fell from 21% to 9% in a year while Anthropic's rose from 40% to 55%. Andreessen Horowitz's 2025 CIO survey quoted one buyer saying "for most tasks, all the models perform well enough now." If the models are converging and shares swing that fast, the durable advantage sits elsewhere, as our piece [The model is not the product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/) argues.

**Commercial translation.** Technical founders describe what the model does. Buyers want to know what changes for them. An advisor who has sold into the relevant industry can turn the first into the second, and can tell the company which claims will get it thrown out of a procurement process.

**Regulatory and reputational judgment.** What may be claimed about accuracy and safety, which use cases attract scrutiny, how a data-handling decision will read in eighteen months. This is where an advisor's caution earns its equity. The risk is not theoretical: the US FTC's Operation AI Comply in 2024 targeted companies whose AI claims could not be substantiated, and the SEC fined two investment advisers that year for claiming AI capabilities they did not have. Our explainer on [agent washing](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-agent-washing/) covers the most common overstatement.

**Distribution realism.** Which channels will carry an AI product to its buyer, what that costs, and why the crowded AI advertising auction is the wrong place to start. This is the advice we most often find missing. Our analysis of [why AI companies have a distribution problem disguised as a model problem](https://lowob.com/research/ai-companies-distribution-problem/) sets out the evidence, and our explainer on [go-to-market strategy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) covers the plan an advisor should be pressure-testing.

> The strongest advisor relationships are narrow, structured and used for decisions. The weakest are broad, casual and used for reassurance.

## How the relationship should be structured

A written scope: the topics the advisor covers, the cadence, and the introductions they will attempt. A vesting schedule on any equity, with a cliff, so an advisor who disappears does not keep the grant. A named founder who owns the relationship and prepares for each session with specific decisions rather than an update. A review at six months.

The market norms support a modest grant. Carta's data, published in February 2025, put median pre-seed advisor equity "well under 0.25%", with grants typically vesting over two years with a short cliff, or tied to performance milestones. Companies at that stage typically had one or two advisors. The Founder Institute's Founder Advisor Standard Template (FAST) sets out a widely used grid:

| FAST engagement level | Idea stage | Startup stage | Growth stage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standard (monthly meetings) | 0.25% | 0.20% | 0.15% |
| Expert (adds contacts and projects) | 1.00% | 0.80% | 0.60% |

The FAST example vests over two years, with a three-month cliff that lets an unproductive relationship end without any equity changing hands. The Founder Institute also recommends working together for at least a month before discussing terms. An advisor asking for well above these ranges at an early stage is asking to be paid like an executive without the accountability of one.

## What an advisor should not be asked to do

Run marketing. Manage vendors. Write the deck. Close the deal. Be on call. Each of these is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee, which is bad for both sides. When the company needs those things, it should hire them, from a fractional leader, an agency, or a full-time person. Our piece on [the modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/) covers how to assemble that mix.

| Request | Why it is a job | Who should do it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Run marketing | Needs weekly ownership and a budget | Fractional marketing lead or hire |
| Manage vendors | Needs contracts, follow-up and accountability | Operations lead |
| Write the deck | Needs drafting time and iterations | Founder, with advisor review |
| Close the deal | Needs pipeline ownership and negotiation authority | Founder or sales lead |
| Be on call | Needs availability the equity does not pay for | Nobody, unless contracted |

The strongest advisor relationships are narrow, structured and used for decisions. The weakest are broad, casual and used for reassurance.

An advisor helps an AI company decide, introduces it to the people who matter, and tells it which advantages will not last. Scope the relationship in writing, vest the equity, and hire separately for anything that is a job.

## lowob takeaways

- **Pay for pattern recognition.** An advisor offers judgment for a small amount of vested equity, a modest fee, or both, and does not run a function.
- **Ask for the five contributions.** Buyer access, durability, commercial translation, regulatory judgment and distribution realism.
- **Structure it like a contract.** Written scope, vesting with a cliff, a founder owner and a six-month review.
- **Hire for jobs.** Marketing, vendor management, decks, closing and on-call support are jobs.

## Common questions

### What does an advisor do for an AI startup?

Helps the founders make better decisions through pattern recognition: buyer and partner introductions, a view on which advantages are durable, commercial translation, regulatory and reputational judgment, and distribution realism.

### How much equity should a startup advisor get?

Usually less than founders expect. Carta's data puts median pre-seed advisor equity well under 0.25%, and the Founder Institute's FAST template ranges from 0.15% to 1% depending on stage and commitment, typically vesting over two years with a short cliff.

### How should an advisor relationship be structured?

With a written scope covering topics, cadence and introductions, a vesting schedule with a cliff on any equity, a named founder who owns the relationship and brings specific decisions, and a review at six months.

### What should you not ask a startup advisor to do?

Run marketing, manage vendors, write the deck, close the deal or be on call. Each is a job, and an advisor who takes it on becomes an underpaid, unaccountable employee.

## Sources and notes

- [Founder Institute, Founder Advisor Standard Template (FAST)](https://fi.co/contents/fast), version 2, as listed in November 2026. Template from an accelerator; a convention, not market data.

# Self-Serve vs Managed Desk vs Agency: Who Runs Your Media?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/self-serve-vs-managed-media/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-16 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Self-serve suits small budgets in welcome categories, if the buyer refuses the platform's defaults. A flat-fee managed desk suits budgets past the fee floor, restricted categories and channels beyond the platforms, and an agency suits large multi-channel spend. Whatever you choose, the accounts, tracking and data stay in your name.

Self-serve suits small budgets in categories the platforms welcome, provided someone refuses the defaults, which are designed around the platform's revenue. A flat-fee managed desk suits budgets past the fee floor, restricted categories and channels beyond the self-serve platforms. An agency suits large, multi-channel spend where buying power and planning matter more than fee structure. Whatever you choose, the ad accounts, conversion tracking, pixel history and analytics stay in your company's name.

Every media platform now offers a self-serve interface. Anyone with a card can open an account, upload creative, choose an audience and spend money within an hour. That raises a fair question: why pay anyone to do it for you?

The answer depends on three things: how much you spend, how much time you have, and whether the platforms will take your money at all.

## Option one: run it yourself

Self-serve works when the budget is small, the product is in a category the platforms welcome, and someone on the team has the time to learn the interface and check the numbers daily.

The advantages are obvious. No fee. Full control. Direct access to the data. The disadvantages are less visible. The interface is designed by the platform to maximise the platform's revenue, and its defaults (broad audiences, automated placements and optimisation toward cheap events) serve that purpose. A self-serve buyer who accepts the defaults is spending efficiently for the platform.

The defaults are documented. Google's auto-apply recommendations, once switched on, can add broad match keywords, add audiences, turn on Display Expansion and change CPA and ROAS targets without a person approving each change. Google's own page says auto-apply does not raise budgets. Until October 2026, Search campaigns with Display Expansion used unspent search budget on the Display Network with a backend 50% allocation that advertisers could neither see nor change; Google has since added a visible priority setting and will move these campaigns to channel prioritisation automatically from February 2027. A self-serve buyer has to know these settings exist to refuse them.

Self-serve also stops at the platform's edge. Programmatic buying at any scale, creator programmes, affiliate networks and cross-channel measurement are not self-serve products. And if the category is restricted, the self-serve interface is where you will find that out, usually after building an account you cannot use. Our explainer on [restricted categories](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers how platforms review them.

## Option two: a managed desk at a flat fee

A desk is a small team that runs the accounts on your behalf, in your name, for a fixed monthly fee per account. It sets inventory standards, manages verification, refreshes creative, optimises toward the outcome you care about, and reports the numbers that matter: real cost per impression after verification, rejection rate, cost per outcome your own tracking confirms.

The fee does not change with spend, which means the desk earns nothing extra by spending more. That is the point. It also means there is a floor: below a certain monthly budget, the fee is a large share of the total and the arrangement stops making sense.

Where the floor sits is a unit-economics question: our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to set a budget from cost per qualified opportunity and payback. A desk is right when the budget is past the floor, the channels include programmatic or anything beyond the self-serve platforms, and you want the accounts, the data and the history to stay yours. Our guide to [pricing architecture for services firms](https://lowob.com/research/pricing-architecture-for-services-firms/) covers how fixed-fee models are structured more generally.

## Option three: an agency on a percentage

A traditional agency arrangement bundles planning, buying, creative and reporting for a percentage of media spend, sometimes with the agency fronting the spend and billing you afterwards.

It scales well for large budgets and complex, multi-channel plans. It also creates the incentive problem discussed in our piece on [percent-of-spend fees](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/): the agency earns more when you spend more, and an agency that fronts spend controls the account history and platform relationships that should belong to you. The ANA's 2022 compensation study found 19% of marketers still paid commissions for media planning and buying, nearly three times the rate for agency services overall.

The largest advertisers have been moving the other way. The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey found 82% of members had in-house agencies, up from 42% in 2008, and 54% of those handled some media planning or buying. Owning and protecting first-party data was a key driver. Those who had not brought media in-house most often called it "too complex", which is the gap a desk or a specialist partner fills.

|  | Self-serve | Managed desk, flat fee | Agency, percentage |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cost structure | No fee; your time | Fixed monthly fee per account | Share of media spend |
| Incentive | Platform defaults favour platform revenue | Fee unchanged by spend | Fee rises with spend |
| Channels | Platform's own inventory | Platforms, programmatic, creators, affiliates | Full multi-channel |
| Restricted categories | Found out after setup | Plans around the band map | Varies |
| Account ownership | Yours | Yours, by contract | Often agency-held unless contracted |
| Right when | Small budget, welcome category, time to learn | Past the fee floor, restricted, beyond self-serve | Scale where buying power matters most |

> A partner who insists on holding your ad accounts is asking to own the part of your business that is hardest to rebuild.

## How to decide

**Spending under a few thousand a month, in a welcome category, with time to learn:** run it yourself, and refuse the defaults. Review auto-apply settings, network settings and audience expansion before launch, and check them monthly.

**Spending past the floor, or in a category the platforms review, or needing programmatic and other channels beyond self-serve:** a managed desk on a flat fee, with the accounts in your name.

**Spending at a scale where buying power and multi-channel planning matter more than fee structure:** an agency, with a contract that keeps the accounts yours and states the fee in dollars rather than as a percentage. Our guide to [running a marketing RFP](https://lowob.com/research/how-to-run-a-marketing-rfp/) covers how to compare proposals.

## The one thing to keep in every case

Whoever runs the media, the ad accounts, the conversion tracking, the pixel history and the analytics should be in your company's name.

This is a matter of platform mechanics, not only principle. Google Ads' access documentation says that if a manager account has ownership of your account, its admins can edit user access, managers and product links within your account. It also recommends having more than one admin, because access to tags can be lost if the only admin becomes unavailable. The company should hold admin rights itself and grant partners standard access. Our piece on [how marketing tracking works](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-tracking-works/) lists the rest of the measurement layer to keep.

## lowob takeaways

- **Refuse the defaults.** Self-serve settings are designed around the platform's revenue; know which ones apply changes without approval.
- **A flat fee removes the spend incentive.** Below a certain budget, though, the fee is too large a share.
- **Agencies suit scale, with contracts that keep accounts yours.** State the fee in dollars.
- **Hold admin rights yourself.** Ad accounts, conversion tracking, pixel history and analytics in the company's name.

## Common questions

### Should I run my own ads or hire an agency?

Run it yourself if you spend under a few thousand a month in a welcome category and have time to learn. Use a flat-fee managed desk past that floor or in restricted categories, and an agency when buying power and multi-channel planning matter most.

### What is a managed media desk?

A small team that runs ad accounts in your name for a fixed monthly fee per account, setting inventory standards, managing verification, refreshing creative and reporting costs confirmed by your own tracking.

### Should I turn on Google Ads auto-apply recommendations?

Only for recommendation types you have reviewed. Once on, auto-apply can add broad match keywords, audiences and Display Expansion and change bid targets without anyone approving each change.

### Who should own the ad accounts when working with an agency?

Your company. Hold admin rights and give the partner standard access. If a partner's manager account owns your account, its admins can change who has access to it.

- [Google Ads Help, About Display Expansion on Search campaigns](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/7193800). Platform documentation; source of the October 2026 and February 2027 changes.
- [PPC Land, Google Ads search campaigns lose 50% Display budget split in February 2027](https://ppc.land/google-ads-search-campaigns-lose-50-display-budget-split-in-february-2027/). Trade press; source of the backend 50% allocation before October 2026.

Open each ad account's access settings this week. Confirm a company employee holds admin rights, that no partner's manager account holds ownership, and that auto-apply is on only for changes you have chosen.

# Raise Against Evidence, Not Narrative

Source: https://lowob.com/research/raise-against-evidence-not-narrative/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-12 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Investors price risk. Narrative asks them to imagine the risk away, while evidence removes some of it, and in a 2026 market where capital is concentrating in fewer companies, even a small amount of real evidence changes which investors take the call. Keep a dated evidence log, strip out paid-for activity, and put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3.

Investors price risk. Narrative asks them to imagine the risk away; evidence removes some of it. Even a small amount of real evidence changes which investors take the call, how fast they move and what they ask for. That matters more in 2026 than it did two years ago, because venture money is concentrating: rounds of $100 million or more took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of the year, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by almost half.

*Not investment or legal advice. **lowob** advises on narrative and readiness; it doesn't arrange, value or negotiate rounds.*

## Why evidence carries more weight in 2026

The headline numbers say venture is booming. The PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor recorded $515.8 billion of US deal value through the third quarter of 2026, with AI companies taking 82.7% of it. Crunchbase counted a record $510 billion invested globally in the first half alone.

Underneath, the market is narrow. PitchBook's second-quarter report found megadeals took 87.5% of the $412.7 billion deployed in the first half, and deals under $100 million fell to 12.5% of value, from 43.8% in 2024. One investor quoted in the report said he had never seen a more "haves and have-nots" market. Carta, which sees rounds raised on its own platform, found seed capital fell from $6.5 billion to $3.8 billion between the first halves of 2025 and 2026, and seed round counts fell from 481 to 381 between the first quarters.

Datasets differ. PitchBook expects a record number of US first financings this year, while Carta sees fewer seed rounds. Both show the same thing for a founder outside the top tier: investors have more choice than founders do, and they choose the company that has already removed some risk.

## What counts as evidence at each stage

| Stage | Evidence investors weight most | Usually not enough on its own |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pre-seed | Founder-market fit, a sharp problem, 5 to 10 named people who'd use it | Follower counts, a waitlist nobody has been asked to act on |
| Seed | Design partners or pilots with usage, early retention, a few paying users | Testnet activity driven by points or airdrops |
| Series A | Repeatable acquisition, revenue or fees that recur, a channel that scales | One big logo with no expansion |

In web3, the trap is activity that was paid for. Points programmes and incentive campaigns produce numbers that look like adoption until the incentive stops. Sophisticated investors now strip them out, so you should strip them out first and show what's left. Our piece on [airdrops, points and community incentives](https://lowob.com/research/airdrops-points-community-incentives/) covers how to separate the two.

In AI, the trap is the demo. A good demo proves the model can do something once. Investors want to see that a customer let it do the job every day.

The bar also rises with the price. Carta's median post-money valuation was $21.6 million at seed and $63 million at Series A in the first quarter of 2026. A Series A investor paying three times the seed price is buying proof that the seed-stage evidence repeated.

## Building the evidence log

Keep one running document. Every entry is dated and specific.

- **Usage:** who used it, how often, for what.
- **Quotes:** what a user said, in their words, with permission to reuse.
- **Commitments:** pilots, LOIs, integrations, partnerships with a named counterpart.
- **Community work:** contributions, referrals, content made by people you didn't pay.
- **Losses:** deals you lost and why. Investors trust a founder who knows why they lose.

Each entry works best as a small [decision record](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-decision-record/): what happened, who was involved, the date and what it showed. The losses line follows the same discipline as [win-loss analysis](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-win-loss-analysis/) in a sales team, and it is the line founders most often leave blank.

The log has to last. Carta's first-quarter data puts the median gap between seed and Series A at two years. The log you start before the seed round is the one a Series A investor will read, so entries need dates, sources and enough context to be understood by someone who was not there.

This log is also your customer case-study source and your community recognition list. It's the first shared asset between the three workstreams from [You don't have three problems](https://lowob.com/research/you-dont-have-three-problems/).

> One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

## Rewriting the deck around it

Move your best evidence to slide 2 or 3, before the market slide. Then let the market slide answer the question the evidence raised: *if this one buyer wants it, how many more are there?*

Attention is short. DocSend's pitch deck index recorded investors spending an average of between 2 minutes 18 seconds and 2 minutes 30 seconds per deck in the weeks it reported across late 2023 and 2024. Evidence placed on slide 11 may never be read. Evidence on slide 2 sets the frame for everything after it.

The vision slide gets shorter. Evidence does the work vision was doing.

| Deck position | Narrative-led deck | Evidence-led deck |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slide 2 | The vision | What a named user did with the product, with dates |
| Slide 3 | Market size | The pattern across users: retention, payment, referral |
| Market slide | Top-down total | How many more buyers look like the ones in slide 2 |
| Vision slide | Three slides of future | One slide: what this round proves next |

## When you don't have any yet

Then the honest move is to raise less, from people who back founders at the idea stage, or to spend four to six weeks getting the first evidence before you go out. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions. Our piece on [making your first ten customers design partners](https://lowob.com/research/your-first-ten-customers-are-design-partners/) sets out how to recruit them.

Market conditions reinforce the point. PitchBook found AI companies posted a median valuation step-up of 2.2x in 2026 against 1.6x for non-AI companies. The gap rewards companies whose evidence is already strong and penalises those still selling a story, in either category.

## lowob takeaways

- **Evidence removes risk; narrative asks investors to ignore it.** In a concentrated market, investors choose the company that has already removed some.
- **Strip out paid-for activity before an investor does.** Points, airdrops and free tiers are acquisition cost, not demand.
- **Build the log to last two years.** The median seed-to-Series A gap is two years, so date and source every entry.
- **Put the best evidence on slide 2 or 3.** Investors spend minutes, not hours, on a deck.

## Common questions

### What evidence do investors want at seed stage?

Design partners or pilots with real usage, early retention and a few paying users. Testnet activity driven by points or airdrops, follower counts and untested waitlists are usually not enough on their own.

### Where should traction go in a pitch deck?

On slide 2 or 3, before the market slide. Then let the market slide answer how many more buyers look like the ones you have. Investors spent an average of under two and a half minutes per deck in DocSend's 2023 to 2024 data.

### What should I do if I have no traction before fundraising?

Raise less, from investors who back founders at the idea stage, or spend four to six weeks getting first evidence before going out. One design partner using the product weekly is worth more than another month of deck revisions.

### Is it harder to raise a seed round in 2026?

For most companies, yes. Venture totals are at records, but megadeals took 87.5% of US venture dollars in the first half of 2026, and seed capital on Carta's platform fell by almost half year on year.

# What Is Programmatic Advertising? A Plain-English Guide

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-programmatic-advertising/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-10 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Distribution

> Summary: Programmatic advertising is the buying and selling of ad space by software through real-time auctions. The ANA's 2023 study found only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer. It is cheap, fast and open to restricted categories, but it rewards buyers who set standards and punishes those who do not.

Programmatic advertising is the buying and selling of ad space by software, through auctions that take place in the time it takes a page to load. That sentence covers most of what a buyer needs to know. The rest is vocabulary, and the vocabulary is where the money hides: the Association of National Advertisers (ANA) found in 2023 that only 36 cents of each dollar entering a buying platform reached a consumer. Programmatic is useful, but only to buyers who set standards before they spend.

## What happens in the auction

A person opens a page or an app. The publisher has ad space to fill. Before the page finishes loading, the publisher's software announces the space to an exchange, along with what it knows: the page, the device, the location, an anonymous identifier, sometimes an audience segment. The format for that announcement is a bid request, and most of the industry writes it to IAB Tech Lab's OpenRTB protocol.

Buyers' software, watching the exchange, decides in a few milliseconds whether that impression matches what the buyer wants and what it is worth. Bids are placed. The highest wins. The ad is served. The person sees it, or does not, depending on whether it was on screen at all. The Media Rating Council (MRC) counts a display ad as viewable only when at least 50% of its pixels are in view for one continuous second, and a video ad for two.

This happens billions of times a day. No human looks at any individual impression. The ANA's study analysed 35.5 billion impressions from 21 advertisers over five months, which gives a sense of the scale a single buyer's log can reach.

## The parts, named

| Term | What it is | What to ask about it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DSP, demand-side platform | The software buyers use to bid. It holds the budget, audience rules, creative and bidding logic. | What is the platform fee, and can we see log-level data? |
| SSP, supply-side platform | The software publishers use to offer space to buyers. | Which SSPs does our spend pass through, and what do they take? |
| Exchange | The marketplace where the two meet. In practice SSPs and exchanges are often the same companies. | Which exchanges are switched on by default? |
| Inventory | Ad space: display, video, native, connected television, audio, in-app. | Which formats are in the plan, and why? |
| Open exchange | Anyone can bid on anything. The cheapest inventory and the least accountable. | What share of spend is here? |
| Private marketplace, PMP | A publisher offers inventory to selected buyers, often at a fixed floor price. More expensive, more predictable. | Which publishers, and at what floor? |
| Programmatic guaranteed | A direct deal executed programmatically: a fixed volume at a fixed price. | Are the volume and price written down? |
| Verification | Third-party checks on whether an impression was viewable, served to a human, in the right country, and on a page that is safe and real. | Pre-bid or post-bid, and who is accredited by the MRC? |

The market has been moving away from the open exchange. The ANA's quarterly benchmark, run with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia, found private marketplaces made up more than 92% of median spend in the fourth quarter of 2025. That is a sign that larger buyers have learned what the open exchange costs them, not that the open exchange has improved.

## Who takes a cut

Between a buyer's dollar and the publisher's revenue sit the DSP, the exchange, the SSP, verification vendors, data providers and, if there is one, the agency. The two largest audits agree on the shape of the problem. ISBA and PwC's 2020 UK study found publishers received 51% of advertiser spend on average, and 15% could not be attributed to anyone, which ISBA called the "unknown delta". Their 2023 follow-up found the publisher share had risen to 65% and the unknown delta had fallen to 3%, on a better-matched sample.

The ANA's 2023 US study measured something stricter: not what reached the publisher, but what reached a consumer. Of each dollar entering a DSP, about 29 cents went to transaction costs and about 35 cents was lost to impressions that were non-viewable, unmeasurable, on made-for-advertising sites or served to non-human traffic. That left 36 cents. The ANA put the loss at roughly $22 billion a year across US open-web programmatic.

> The question for a buyer is not whether intermediaries take a cut. It is whether the buyer knows what each one charged and what the rest of the money bought.

That is not an argument against programmatic. It is an argument for buying it with standards.

## What it is good for, and what it is bad for

| Good for | Bad for |
| --- | --- |
| Reaching audiences the buyer defines, across many sites and apps, at a price set by competition rather than by rate card | Explaining anything: banner and short video are attention formats, not comprehension formats |
| Reaching categories the large social platforms restrict, because many exchanges carry what the walled gardens will not | Building trust from nothing |
| Testing cheaply, because budgets can be small and results arrive quickly | Producing honest numbers without effort |
| Retargeting people who have already visited | Any buy left on default settings |

The last row matters most. Left alone, a programmatic buy drifts toward the cheapest inventory the exchange can find, which is the inventory least likely to matter. The ANA found made-for-advertising sites took about 21% of impressions and 15% of spend in its sample, and that the average campaign ran across more than 40,000 websites. Nobody chooses 40,000 websites. A default chooses them.

For restricted categories the breadth is a genuine advantage. Our piece on [restricted categories](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) explains why the platforms that refuse a fintech or crypto advertiser are not the whole market, and programmatic inventory is often where the rest of the market is reached. The same breadth means the buyer has to do the filtering the platform would otherwise have done.

## The three settings that matter most

**An inclusion list.** The sites and apps the buy may appear on, rather than a list of ones to avoid. The ANA called exclusion lists "largely ineffective" because new domains appear daily, and recommended inclusion lists instead.

**A verification standard.** What an impression must pass to be paid for: viewable to the MRC definition, free of invalid traffic, in the right geography, on a page the buyer would have chosen. Pre-bid filtering is better than post-bid reporting, because it stops the spend rather than describing it.

**An outcome further down the funnel than a click.** Clicks and views are cheap to fake and cheap to buy on poor inventory. A qualified lead, an application or a sale is not. Our piece on [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) sets out how to price acquisition against an outcome the finance team will accept.

A buy with those three settings is media. A buy without them is a bag of impressions.

## What the transparency standards do and do not prove

IAB Tech Lab publishes three standards that help a buyer investigate a supply path. Publishers post an ads.txt file (or app-ads.txt for apps) listing the companies authorised to sell their inventory. Ad systems publish a sellers.json file identifying the sellers they represent. The SupplyChain object, carried in the OpenRTB bid request, lists every party that touched the sale. Together they let a buyer see whether the seller of an impression was authorised and how many intermediaries stood in between.

These standards are necessary and not sufficient. They show that a seller was authorised. They do not show that a genuine person was on the page, that the page was worth reaching, or that the impression produced a sale. That is why they sit alongside verification and outcome measurement rather than replacing them. Our companion pieces on [the middlemen](https://lowob.com/research/ad-network-vs-exchange-vs-dsp/) and on [which numbers to trust](https://lowob.com/research/programmatic-media-numbers-you-can-trust/) take each of those steps further.

## lowob takeaways

- **Know the parts.** DSP, SSP, exchange and verification each take a fee and each control a different part of the outcome.
- **Expect leakage.** Audits have found between a third and two-thirds of a dollar reaching something useful, depending on what is measured.
- **Set the three settings.** Inclusion list, verification standard and an outcome your business can validate.
- **Use the standards, then go further.** ads.txt and sellers.json check the seller; only verification and outcomes check the result.

## Common questions

### What is programmatic advertising in simple terms?

It is the automated buying and selling of digital ad space by software, usually through real-time auctions that run while a page or app loads. Buyers bid through a demand-side platform and publishers sell through a supply-side platform or exchange.

### How much of a programmatic ad budget reaches the publisher?

It depends on the study and the measure. ISBA and PwC found publishers received 51% in 2020 and 65% in their 2023 follow-up. The ANA's 2023 study found only 36 cents of each dollar reached a consumer once fees and unproductive impressions were removed.

### What is the difference between open exchange and private marketplace buying?

In the open exchange anyone can bid on any impression, which is cheapest and least accountable. A private marketplace is a publisher offering inventory to selected buyers, often at a floor price, which costs more and is more predictable.

### Does ads.txt stop ad fraud?

No. ads.txt lets a publisher list who is authorised to sell its inventory, which makes domain spoofing harder. It does not show whether a human saw the ad or whether the page was worth reaching.

## Sources and notes

- [ANA, Programmatic Media Supply Chain Transparency Study](https://ana.net/programmatic), December 2023, with later benchmark updates. Trade body study of log-level data from 21 advertisers; full report is members-only.
- [Katten, ANA Study Finds Over $20 Billion in Efficiency Gains Possible in Programmatic Advertising Spend](https://quickreads.ext.katten.com/post/102iufy/ana-study-finds-over-20-billion-in-efficiency-gains-possible-in-programmatic-a), 2023. Law firm summary of the ANA study; secondary source for the 40,000-site and MFA figures.
- [ANA, Q4 2025 Programmatic Transparency Benchmark](https://www.ana.net/content/show/id/pr-2026-02-programatic), 25 February 2026. Press release; benchmark built with TAG TrustNet and Fiducia; sample size not stated.
- [News Media Association, ISBA programmatic study: publishers receive half of advertiser spend](https://newsmediauk.org/blog/2020/05/07/isba-programmatic-study-publishers-receive-half-of-advertiser-spend/), 7 May 2020. Trade body summary of the ISBA and PwC study; 15 advertisers, UK only.

## Next move

Ask whoever runs your programmatic buy for three things this week: the inclusion list, the verification standard each impression must pass, and the outcome the buy optimises toward. If any of the three is missing, set it before the next invoice.

# One Truth, Three Audiences

Source: https://lowob.com/research/one-truth-three-audiences/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-06 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Write one product truth, then one belief statement per audience, then a claims register that says what you can prove. The deck, the homepage and community announcements are all derived from those three. The register is also where regulated and AI claims are checked before they ship.

Write one product truth, then one belief statement per audience, then a claims register that says what you can prove. Everything else (the deck, the homepage, the community announcements) is derived from those three. The product truth is one sentence: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now. The claims register is a short table of every public claim with its evidence and approver; regulators in the US and UK already expect that evidence to exist before the claim is made.

## The product truth

One sentence with three parts: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now.

Bad: *"The intelligence layer for the future of work."* No buyer, no reason, no thing.

Better: *"An AI agent that answers support tickets inside the help desk your team already uses, for B2B software companies whose ticket volume grew faster than their headcount."*

The second one is less exciting and much more useful. An investor can size it. A customer can recognise themselves in it. A community member can explain it to a friend.

Each of the three parts does a specific job. "What it is" places the product in a frame the reader already understands. April Dunford, whose positioning method is widely used in B2B software, describes the job of a market category as taking a prospect who knows little about the product and pointing them towards its differentiated value. She adds that a category "doesn't replace your messaging or your sales pitch", and that choosing the category first is "the tail wagging the dog". "Who buys it" stops the sentence from serving everyone. "Why now" is the trend that makes the problem urgent; Dunford treats relevant trends as a layer on top of a clear category, not a substitute for one. The full method sits in our piece on [positioning for complex markets](https://lowob.com/research/positioning-for-complex-markets/).

## One belief per audience

Each audience needs to hold a different belief before it acts. Write them down.

| Audience | Must believe | Proof that works | Proof that doesn't |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Investors | This can be large, this team will win it, and now is the moment | Named customers, usage curves, a credible path to the next milestone | TAM slides, "the future of…" |
| Community | Being here early is worth something real | Access, a role, recognition, a visible say in what ships | Vague token hints, giveaways |
| Customers | It solves my problem, it's safe, and someone like me already uses it | A case study from a peer, an audit, a pilot with clear terms | Your raise, your investors' logos |

The right-hand column matters. Founders reuse proof across audiences because it's what they have. Investor logos impress investors and mean almost nothing to a treasury manager deciding where to deposit.

The investor row reflects how VCs say they decide. In a survey of almost 900 venture capitalists, Gompers and colleagues found 95% of firms named the team as important and 47% named it the single most important factor, with the business model named by 83%. Named customers and usage curves are how a team shows the business model works.

The customer row is often several audiences in one. Forrester's State of Business Buying 2024 found an average of 13 people involved in a purchase decision, and 89% of purchases involving two or more departments. The treasury manager, the finance director and the security reviewer each need a version of the customer belief. They should all trace back to the same truth, which is why the truth is written first. Our explainer on [the buying committee](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-buying-committee/) covers the roles.

When the truth is not written down, it drifts. Gartner's survey of 632 B2B buyers, published in June 2025, found 69% reported inconsistencies between a supplier's website and what its sellers told them. That figure is about sellers and websites, but the same drift happens between a deck, a community channel and a homepage.

> Investor logos impress investors and mean almost nothing to a treasury manager deciding where to deposit.

## The claims register

A short table of every claim you make publicly, with the evidence for each and who approved it. It sounds like compliance. It's actually the fastest way to stop a team saying five different things.

| Claim | Where it appears | Evidence | Evidence date | Approved by | Review date |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The exact wording, as published | Deck, homepage, community post, ad | The test, audit, contract or dataset behind it | When the evidence was produced | One named person | When it must be rechecked |

The register is not a new idea dressed up. The US Federal Trade Commission's Policy Statement Regarding Advertising Substantiation, issued in 1984, requires advertisers to have a "reasonable basis" for objective claims before they are disseminated. Where an advert states a level of support, such as "tests prove", the FTC expects the firm to have at least that level of substantiation. A claims register is simply where that basis is written down.

In Web3 it does double duty: claims about yield, safety and returns carry real regulatory and reputational risk, and the register is where you catch "guaranteed" before it ships. The UK Financial Conduct Authority's regime for cryptoasset promotions has applied since 8 October 2023 to every firm marketing cryptoassets to UK consumers, including firms based overseas. Promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading, carry prescribed risk warnings, and sit inside consumer journeys with positive frictions such as a 24-hour cooling-off period.

In AI it catches the accuracy number that was true on one benchmark in March. In September 2024 the FTC announced Operation AI Comply, five enforcement actions against companies making deceptive AI claims. One concerned a service marketed as "the world's first robot lawyer"; the FTC said the company had not tested its chatbot against human lawyers. The FTC chair at the time said there was "no AI exemption from the laws on the books."

## Where Web3 and AI differ

**Web3:** the token collapses audiences. Your holder is an investor, a community member and sometimes a customer. That makes the product truth more important, not less, because the token story will drown it unless it's written down first. Lead with what the protocol does for a user, and let the token be the mechanism, not the headline. [The user story before the token story](https://lowob.com/research/the-user-story-before-the-token-story/) takes this further.

**AI:** the model is not the product. Investors may care about the model; customers care about the workflow. Position on the job done and the result, and keep the model story for the deck appendix. Our piece [The model is not the product](https://lowob.com/research/the-model-is-not-the-product/) sets out why.

|  | Web3 | AI |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What collapses or splits | Audiences collapse into the token holder | The investor story and the customer story split |
| Lead the truth with | What the protocol does for a user | The workflow and the result |
| Riskiest claims | Yield, safety, returns | Accuracy, autonomy, replacement of a professional |
| Register catches | "Guaranteed" before it ships | The benchmark number that was true once |

Illustrative example: a register catching a claim

Decision
:   Remove an accuracy percentage from the homepage hero and replace it with a named customer's measured result.

Reason and owner
:   The claims register showed the percentage came from a single internal benchmark run six months earlier, with no customer data behind it. Owned by the head of product, approved by the CEO.

What changed
:   The homepage led with a peer result a buyer could check, and the accuracy figure moved to a dated technical note with its method stated.

Illustrative: a composite of an early-stage AI software company, built from patterns across engagements.

## lowob takeaways

- **Write the truth first.** One sentence: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now.
- **Map proof to belief.** Each audience accepts different proof; investor logos do not persuade a treasury manager.
- **Keep a claims register.** Every public claim, its evidence, its date and its approver, in one table.
- **Let the mechanism follow the use.** In Web3, lead with what the protocol does for a user; in AI, position on the workflow, not the model.

Gateway card

### Before the next deck, homepage or announcement

- A one-sentence product truth: what, who, why now
- A written belief statement for each audience
- The proof each audience will actually accept, mapped
- A claims register with evidence, a date and an owner
- The homepage hero tested on a customer, not an investor

## Common questions

### How do I write a product positioning statement for a startup?

Write one sentence with three parts: what it is, who buys it, and what changed that makes it necessary now. It should be specific enough for an investor to size and a customer to recognise themselves in.

### What is a claims register?

A short table of every claim you make publicly, with the evidence for each, the date of that evidence and who approved it. It stops a team saying different things and catches risky claims about yield, safety or accuracy.

### Do marketing claims legally need evidence?

In the US, the FTC has required a reasonable basis for objective advertising claims since 1984, and applies it to AI claims. In the UK, cryptoasset promotions must be fair, clear and not misleading. Take legal advice for your market.

### What proof do customers want compared with investors?

Investors want named customers, usage curves and a path to the next milestone. Customers want a peer case study, an audit or a pilot with clear terms, not your raise or your investors' logos.

## Sources and notes

- [April Dunford, Understanding the Job of a Market Category](https://aprildunford.substack.com/p/understanding-the-job-of-a-market), 11 January 2024. Practitioner's newsletter; method, not data.

# Agency Types Explained: Full-Service to Specialist

Source: https://lowob.com/research/agency-types-field-guide/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-05 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agencies specialise, and the specialisation determines what you get. The main types are full-service, performance, media, creative, PR and specialist agencies, each paid differently and good at different things. Even large advertisers now do most routine work in-house and buy agencies for capacity and specialist skill. Most small and mid-sized companies need one partner who owns distribution and brings in specialists, not a full-service agency.

Agencies specialise, and the specialisation determines what you get. The main types are full-service, performance, media, creative, PR and specialist agencies, each paid differently and good at different things. The buying pattern of large advertisers points the same way: in the ANA's 2023 survey, 82% of members had an in-house agency and 92% still used outside agencies, mainly for capacity or skills they lacked. Most small and mid-sized companies need one partner who owns distribution and brings in specialists, not a full-service agency.

"We should hire an agency" is the start of a decision, not the end of one. Agencies specialise, and the specialisation determines what you will get. The US Census Bureau's Service Annual Survey shows the scale of the market: in 2022, employer advertising agencies earned about $64 billion, public relations agencies about $20 billion, and other advertising services about $18 billion. Within those totals sit businesses with very different economics.

## The main types

**Full-service agencies** offer strategy, creative, media, digital, and often PR under one roof. The appeal is one relationship and one invoice. The trade-off is that every function is staffed to an average, and the agency's economics favour the services with the best margin, which is rarely the one you most need. Best for companies with broad needs and a budget large enough to be a priority client.

**Performance agencies** run paid acquisition, typically on the large self-serve platforms, and are judged on cost per outcome. They are fast, numerate, and dependent on the platforms working for your category. If the platforms will not carry your product, a performance agency has little to sell you. Paid by retainer, percentage of spend, or a fee plus a performance bonus.

**Media agencies** plan and buy media across channels, including programmatic, television, out-of-home, and audio. Their value is in access, negotiation, and measurement at scale. Historically paid a percentage of spend, which is the incentive problem covered in [Percent of spend is a conflict of interest with a logo on it](https://lowob.com/research/percent-of-spend-media-fees/). Best for large budgets where buying power matters.

**Creative agencies** make the work: brand identity, campaigns, film, design. They are paid by project or retainer, and their output is judged on craft and effect. They do not usually distribute what they make, and a creative agency with no distribution partner produces beautiful things nobody sees.

**PR agencies** earn coverage and manage reputation. They are paid on monthly retainers and are judged, imperfectly, on placements. Good for companies with news, a credible spokesperson, and a story a journalist would want regardless of the pitch. Poor value for companies with none of those.

**Specialist agencies** do one thing: affiliate management, influencer programmes, app-store optimisation, search, community, a single vertical. They are usually better at that thing than a full-service shop and worse at everything adjacent. Paid by retainer or project, sometimes by performance.

| Type | Sells | Usually paid by | Good fit | Poor fit |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Full-service | Breadth under one contract | Retainer, often blended with media fees | Broad needs, budget large enough to be a priority client | A company that mainly needs one function done well |
| Performance | Paid acquisition at a target cost | Retainer, % of spend, or fee plus bonus | Categories the self-serve platforms carry openly | Restricted categories; slow, considered purchases |
| Media | Planning, buying power, measurement | % of spend, increasingly fees | Large multi-channel budgets | Small budgets where buying power is irrelevant |
| Creative | Brand and campaign work | Project or retainer | A brand problem with distribution already in place | No plan for who will see the work |
| PR | Earned coverage and reputation | Monthly retainer | Real news and a credible spokesperson | No news and no story |
| Specialist | Depth in one channel or vertical | Retainer, project, sometimes performance | A defined gap with a clear owner | Expecting them to cover adjacent channels |

## What the evidence says about incentives

Two of the types carry incentive problems that are documented rather than anecdotal.

**Media.** In 2016 the ANA commissioned K2 Intelligence to investigate US media buying. The report found cash rebates paid to agencies on the basis of client spend, often unknown to the advertiser, and principal-based buying in which agencies bought inventory and resold it to clients at mark-ups of roughly 30% to 90%. Some advertiser contracts had not been reviewed in up to ten years. The ANA's recommendation was to re-examine contracts and extend audit rights to the holding company, so advertisers can follow the money. None of this means a given media agency behaves badly. It means the contract, not trust, decides what you get.

**Performance.** Performance pay is most common in media disciplines. A 2026 study of 69 multinational advertisers by the World Federation of Advertisers and Agency Mania Solutions, reported by VideoWeek, found labour-plus-performance models had grown from 9% to 21% over 15 years. Yet for most respondents performance pay was still under 20% of total agency compensation. Performance agencies talk about outcomes; the bulk of the fee usually still pays for time or spend.

## How to tell them apart in a pitch

Ask three questions and listen for where the energy goes.

**Where does most of your revenue come from?** The answer tells you what the agency is actually built to sell.

**Show me a client whose category the platforms restricted.** If the answer is a blank look, the agency is built for the crowded auction. Restrictions are specific and change often. Google, for example, permits crypto exchange and wallet ads only in listed countries, only for advertisers it has certified, and only where they meet local registration rules; it added Argentina in September 2025. An agency that has worked under rules like these will describe them without being prompted. Our explainer on [what a restricted category is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-restricted-category/) covers the wider picture.

**What would you not do for us, and who would you bring in instead?** A confident answer signals a specialist who knows their edges. A "we do everything" answer signals a generalist who will subcontract quietly.

> A "we do everything" answer signals a generalist who will subcontract quietly.

## The mix most companies actually need

Small and mid-sized companies rarely need a full-service agency. They need one partner who owns distribution and can bring in specialists for the parts that do not scale in-house: PR when there is news, creative when the brand needs work, a clipping or creator specialist when the programme calls for it.

Large advertisers have arrived at a similar shape by a different route. The ANA's 2023 in-house agency survey of 162 members found in-house teams handled an average of 61% of company work, and 65% had moved established work from outside agencies to in-house in the previous three years. Work still went outside for two reasons: the in-house team was too busy, or the company lacked a specialised capability. Gartner's 2025 CMO survey points the same way, with 39% of marketing leaders planning to cut agency budgets. The pattern is a close core with specialists at the edge, which is the model our piece on [the modular GTM team](https://lowob.com/research/the-modular-gtm-team/) sets out.

That is the model we run: distribution built and run directly, with PR, creative production, and specialist networks packaged from partners rather than staffed permanently. It keeps the core work close and the peripheral work with people who do it every day.

The same logic applies to the partners themselves. When specialists are brought in, someone needs to own the brief, the handoffs and the measure, or the company ends up integrating the work itself. Our piece on [the commercial system](https://lowob.com/research/the-commercial-system-what-it-is/) covers the shared definitions and records that make that ownership possible, and [demand generation economics](https://lowob.com/research/demand-generation-economics/) covers how to judge what each channel returns.

Agencies are specialists wearing general names. Find out where an agency's revenue comes from, whether it has worked in a restricted category, and what it would not do, before you find out the expensive way.

## lowob takeaways

- **Hire the type, not the label.** Each agency type is built to sell different work and is paid differently.
- **Read media and performance contracts closely.** The incentive problems in both are documented, and the contract decides what you get.
- **Test for category experience.** Ask to see a client the platforms restricted.
- **Keep the core close.** One partner owning distribution, with specialists at the edge, fits most mid-sized firms better than full-service.

## Common questions

### What are the main types of marketing agency?

Full-service, performance, media, creative, PR and specialist agencies. Each is built to sell different work and is paid differently, by retainer, percentage of spend, project or performance.

### Does a small company need a full-service agency?

Rarely. Small and mid-sized companies usually need one partner who owns distribution and can bring in specialists, such as PR when there is news or creative when the brand needs work.

### What is the difference between a media agency and a creative agency?

A creative agency makes the work: identity, campaigns, film and design. A media agency decides where the work runs and buys the space, and is historically paid a share of the spend it manages.

### When is a PR agency poor value?

When a company has no news, no credible spokesperson and no story a journalist would want regardless of the pitch.

# Agency vs Consultancy vs Advisor vs Fractional: Explained

Source: https://lowob.com/research/agency-vs-consultancy-vs-advisor/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-02-02 · Updated: 2026-11-16
Function: Strategy

> Summary: Agencies sell execution, consultancies sell answers, advisors sell judgment over time, and fractional executives sell part-time ownership of a function. The names overlap and the markets behind them are moving: fractional titles have more than tripled since 2019 and a fifth of CMOs say AI has cut their reliance on agencies. Match the purchase to what you are missing, and insist on a paid, scoped first step from anyone offering more than one.

Agencies sell execution, consultancies sell answers, advisors sell judgment over time, and fractional executives sell part-time ownership of a function. Each is paid differently, and the payment tells you what you are really buying. The four markets are shifting at once: Lightcast counts at least 34,000 US workers with "fractional" in their title, up 265% since 2019, and Gartner found 22% of CMOs say generative AI has reduced their reliance on agencies for creativity and strategy. Match the purchase to what you are missing, and insist on a paid, scoped first step from anyone offering more than one.

Companies looking for marketing help are usually offered four different things under overlapping names. Knowing which one you are buying saves months.

## The four, defined by what you receive

**An agency sells execution.** You receive work product: campaigns run, media bought, content produced, programmes operated. The agency staffs the work with its own people and tools, and you review outputs rather than doing them. Agencies are paid on retainers, project fees, a percentage of media spend, or, less often, on performance. It is a large, established market: US Census Bureau data show advertising agencies with employer payrolls earned about $64 billion in 2022, and public relations agencies about $20 billion.

**A consultancy sells answers.** You receive analysis and recommendations: what the market looks like, what the plan should be, how the organisation should be structured. Consultancies are paid by project or by the day, and the deliverable is usually a document and a presentation. Whether anyone acts on it is your problem. Source Global Research, which tracks firms with more than 50 consultants, expects technology consulting alone to pass $400 billion in global revenue in 2026, and found two-thirds of buyers it surveyed expect consulting prices to rise.

**An advisor sells judgment over time.** You receive access to a person with relevant experience who helps you make decisions as they come up. Advisors are paid a modest monthly fee, equity, or both, and the deliverable is the quality of the decisions you make with them in the room. They rarely do the work. The equity norms are well documented: the Founder Institute's FAST agreement, a standard one-page advisor template, suggests 0.25% of a seed-stage company for an advisor who meets monthly, vesting over two years.

**A fractional executive sells a part-time leader.** You receive someone who takes ownership of a function for a fixed number of days per week, manages people and vendors, and is accountable for results. Fractional leaders are paid a monthly fee scaled to their time, and the deliverable is a function that runs. Go Fractional, a marketplace, reports that fractional CMOs on its platform averaged 27 hours a week over the 90 days to mid-2026.

|  | Agency | Consultancy | Advisor | Fractional executive |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| You receive | Work product | A recommendation | Better decisions | A function that runs |
| Who does the work | Their team | Their analysts, then yours | You | They lead; your team and vendors deliver |
| Typical payment | Retainer, project, % of spend, performance | Project or day rate | Small monthly fee, equity or both | Monthly fee scaled to days per week |
| Accountable for | Delivering the scope | The quality of the analysis | The advice | Results of the function |
| Usual failure | Busy without effect | Report nobody implements | Asked to execute | Spread too thin to lead |

## Where the confusion comes from

The names have drifted. Agencies call themselves consultancies because it sounds senior. Consultancies offer "implementation support" to keep the engagement going. Advisors get pulled into doing work because they are close and capable. Fractional executives are asked to be advisors when the budget shrinks, and advisors are asked to be fractional when the company needs hands.

Each drift produces a mismatch between what is being paid for and what is being received. The most common failure is hiring an advisor, paying advisor rates, and expecting execution.

Two market shifts are widening the overlap. The first is AI. Gartner's 2025 survey of 402 marketing leaders found 39% planned to cut agency budgets and 22% said generative AI had already reduced their reliance on external agencies for creativity and strategy. When drafts get cheaper, every provider starts describing itself as strategic. Our piece on [why judgment is becoming the marketing moat](https://lowob.com/research/judgment-is-the-moat/) covers the effect in detail.

The second is the growth of fractional work. Lightcast, a labour-market analytics firm, found US fractional job postings more than doubled in 2025, and that 97% of fractional postings in 2026 came from small and medium-sized companies. Marketing and PR made up 10% of postings, behind finance at 46%. A growing supply of part-time leaders means more people offering a mix of advice and ownership, often without saying which.

> The most common failure is hiring an advisor, paying advisor rates, and expecting execution.

## How to choose

Ask what you are missing.

If you know what to do and lack the hands to do it, you need execution: an agency, or a fractional leader with a team.

If you do not know what to do and the question is large enough to justify a study, you need a consultancy, and you should budget for the execution that follows separately.

If you know roughly what to do but face decisions weekly that would benefit from someone who has made them before, you need an advisor.

If the function has no leader and you cannot yet justify a full-time one, you need a fractional executive.

| What you are missing | Buy | Watch for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hands, with a clear plan | Agency, or fractional leader with a team | Scope that drifts toward what the provider sells best |
| The plan itself, on a large question | Consultancy | No budget set aside for execution |
| A second view on recurring decisions | Advisor | Being asked to do work at advisor rates |
| A leader for a function | Fractional executive | Too few days to manage people properly |

The table works only if you can state the gap in a sentence. A [go-to-market strategy](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-go-to-market-strategy/) is the usual place that sentence comes from: if you cannot name the buyer, the offer and the route to market, you are missing the plan, and buying hands first will be expensive.

## The hybrid, and its condition

Some firms combine advice with execution: a short diagnostic that leads into building and running the thing that was recommended. That is what we do. The advantage is that the recommendation is made by the people who will have to deliver it, which tends to produce recommendations that are achievable.

The condition that makes a hybrid honest is a paid, scoped first step with a defined end, so that the advice is not a free sales pitch for the execution. A one-week diagnostic that costs money and produces a written answer is advice. A free proposal is marketing.

The wider market supports the caution. The European Association of Communications Agencies surveyed 412 agencies in 2025 and found the average new-business pitch cost an agency about €43,800 in people and expenses. That cost does not disappear. It is recovered in the fees of the engagement that follows, which is why free strategy tends to recommend whatever the provider sells. Our explainer on [what a distribution diagnostic is](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-distribution-diagnostic/) sets out what a paid first step should contain.

## Questions to ask any of them

Five questions sort the four quickly:

1. **What exactly will I receive, and when?** Work product, a document, access or a running function.
2. **Who does the work, and how senior are they?** The person who sold it, or someone you have not met.
3. **How are you paid, and what does that reward?** Time, spend, outcomes or the relationship continuing.
4. **What happens to my accounts, data and relationships if we stop?** The answer shows who owns the asset.
5. **What is not included?** The profitable part of many engagements sits just outside the original description.

Clear answers to those five questions tell you which of the four you are actually talking to, whatever the website says. Our guide to [how marketing services are priced](https://lowob.com/research/how-marketing-services-are-priced/) goes further on question three, and [Build it to run without you](https://lowob.com/research/build-it-to-run-without-you/) on question four.

Agencies sell execution, consultancies sell answers, advisors sell judgment, and fractional leaders sell part-time ownership. Match the purchase to the gap, and insist on a paid, scoped first step from anyone offering more than one.

## lowob takeaways

- **Buy by what you receive.** Work product, a recommendation, better decisions or a running function are four different purchases.
- **Read the fee for the product.** How someone is paid shows what they are really selling.
- **Do not expect execution at advisor rates.** It is the most common mismatch and the easiest to prevent.
- **Ask for a paid first step from hybrids.** A free proposal is marketing; a paid one-week diagnostic with a written answer is advice.

## Common questions

### What is the difference between an agency and a consultancy?

An agency sells execution: campaigns run, media bought, content produced. A consultancy sells answers: analysis and recommendations, usually delivered as a document, and whether anyone acts on it is your problem.

### What is a fractional executive?

A senior leader who owns a function, such as marketing or finance, for a fixed number of days a week, manages people and vendors, and is accountable for results. They are usually paid a monthly fee scaled to their time.

### When should a company hire a fractional executive instead of an advisor?

Hire a fractional executive when a function has no leader and you cannot yet justify a full-time one. Hire an advisor when you know roughly what to do but face weekly decisions that benefit from someone who has made them before.

### How much equity does a startup advisor usually get?

The Founder Institute's FAST template suggests 0.25% at seed for an advisor who meets monthly and up to 1% at pre-seed for a more involved expert, typically vesting over two years. Terms vary, so treat these as reference points.
